case_name: Arrington v. MZ 2640 OWNER LLP
accommodation_description: Pro se plaintiffs mention need for walk-in shower as disability accommodation but did not plead that such request was made to defendants
key_holding: Complaint dismissed with leave to amend because plaintiffs failed to state plausible claims for relief under the ADA and False Claims Act, and while the court grants leave to amend to assert Fair Housing Act disability discrimination claims under § 3604(f)(1), plaintiffs' mere mention of a walk-in shower accommodation without alleging they requested it from defendants is insufficient to state a reasonable accommodation claim.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs brought ADA Title III and False Claims Act claims related to a subsidized housing eviction proceeding, with the court dismissing both claims because the apartment is not a public accommodation under ADA Title III and plaintiffs cannot bring a qui tam FCA action pro se. The court granted leave to amend to assert Fair Housing Act disability discrimination claims, noting that plaintiffs' mention of a walk-in shower accommodation was insufficient without pleading that a request was made to defendants.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III and False Claims Act claims related to subsidized housing eviction
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed ADA Title III claim because residential apartment is not a public accommodation under ADA Title III; False Claims Act qui tam action cannot be brought pro se. Court granted leave to amend to assert FHA claims under 42 USC 3604(f)(1) for disability discrimination in housing.

source_file: 025 - MATTER OF HART v New York City Hous Auth 2
case_name: Matter of Hart v. New York City Hous. Auth.
accommodation_description: Tenant with PTSD sought reasonable accommodation to avoid tenancy termination based on alleged aggressive behavior toward NYCHA employees
key_holding: The court upheld NYCHA's tenancy termination finding substantial evidence supported the charges, and concluded the hearing officer gave sufficient consideration to the tenant's reasonable accommodation request for PTSD, determining no accommodation would have offered a solution to the conduct issues.
brief_summary: Vincenia Lee Hart, a public housing tenant with PTSD, petitioned for review of NYCHA's decision terminating her tenancy for nondesirability based on aggressive behavior toward employees, arguing NYCHA failed to reasonably accommodate her disability. The court confirmed NYCHA's determination, finding substantial evidence supported the termination and that the hearing officer gave sufficient consideration to the accommodation request.
key_cases_cited: Matter of Washington v. Olatoye, 173 A.D.3d 467 (2019)
Matter of Prospect Union Assoc. v. DeJesus, 167 A.D.3d 540 (2018)
Handy v. City of New Rochelle, 198 F. Supp. 3d 298 (2016)
Matter of Pell v. Board of Educ., 34 N.Y.2d 222 (1974)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) in response to charges of nondesirability based on aggressive and violent behavior toward NYCHA employees; petitioner sought mitigation of sanction or alternative accommodation to address disability-related conduct
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court affirmed the hearing officer's determination that the petitioner's disability was insufficient to warrant a mitigated sanction and that no reasonable accommodation would offer a solution to the conduct underlying the nondesirability charges. The court found the hearing officer gave sufficient consideration to the reasonable accommodation request under the circumstances and that the penalty of termination was not disproportionate to the offenses.

source_file: 025 - MATTER OF HART v New York City Housing Authority
case_name: Matter of Hart v New York City Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Petitioner requested reasonable accommodation for her PTSD to mitigate the penalty for tenancy termination based on alleged aggressive behavior toward NYCHA employees.
key_holding: The hearing officer gave sufficient consideration to the petitioner's reasonable accommodation request, and the penalty of tenancy termination was not disproportionate to the offenses supported by substantial evidence.
brief_summary: Petitioner Vincenia Lee Hart, a NYCHA public housing tenant, challenged the termination of her tenancy as a reasonable accommodation for her PTSD after NYCHA charged her with nondesirability based on aggressive behavior toward employees. The Appellate Division confirmed NYCHA's determination, finding substantial evidence supported the termination and that the hearing officer gave sufficient consideration to the accommodation request.
key_cases_cited: Handy v. City of New Rochelle, 198 F. Supp. 3d 298 (2016)
Matter of Prospect Union Assoc. v. DeJesus, 167 A.D.3d 540 (2018)
Matter of Washington v. Olatoye, 173 A.D.3d 467 (2019)
Matter of Burton v. New York City Hous. Auth., 177 A.D.3d 874 (2019)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) in response to charges of aggressive and violent behavior toward NYCHA employees; petitioner sought mitigation of sanction or alternative accommodation to address disability-related conduct
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court affirmed that the hearing officer gave sufficient consideration to the petitioner's reasonable accommodation request and that the determination to terminate tenancy was supported by substantial evidence. The court found that no reasonable accommodation would offer a solution to the conduct underlying the nondesirability charges, and the penalty was not disproportionate to the offenses.

source_file: 025 - United States v FOX RUN APARTMENTS LLC
case_name: United States v. Fox Run Apartments, LLC
accommodation_description: Request to keep a 70-pound Doberman Pinscher emotional support animal as a reasonable accommodation to the property's 25-pound pet weight restriction
key_holding: Although the government's reasonable accommodation claim had a reasonable basis in fact and law and was not frivolous, the court nevertheless denied defendants' motion for fees and costs under the EAJA because the government's position was substantially justified and special circumstances made an award unjust given defendants' own conduct.
brief_summary: The United States sued Fox Run Apartments under the FHA alleging failure to accommodate a veteran's request to keep an emotional support animal, but voluntarily dismissed its claims after which defendants sought fees and costs under the EAJA. The court denied the fee motion, finding the government's position was substantially justified because there was record evidence supporting each element of a plausible failure-to-accommodate claim, and special circumstances made a fee award unjust given defendants' own litigation conduct.
key_cases_cited: Christiansburg Garment Co. v. EEOC, 434 U.S. 412 (1978)
Dubois v. Ass'n of Apartment Owners of 2987 Kalakaua, 453 F.3d 1175 (9th Cir. 2006)
Hadden v. Bowen, 851 F.2d 1266 (10th Cir. 1988)
Pierce v. Underwood, 487 U.S. 552 (1988)
Neitzke v. Williams, 490 U.S. 319 (1989)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation to allow Versola to live with his 70-pound Doberman Pinscher emotional support animal (ESA) at Fox Run Apartments, which had a 25-pound pet weight limit
fha_claims.reasoning: The government filed suit alleging failure to accommodate Versola's ESA, but voluntarily dismissed the complaint with prejudice on December 11, 2023, before the court reached the merits. The case was resolved by mutual agreement of all parties to dismiss all claims, including counterclaims and third-party claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation regarding the requirement that Versola's psychiatrist complete a third-party verification form by an arbitrary deadline (June 26, 2020) when the psychiatrist was unavailable until June 29
fha_claims.reasoning: The government alleged that defendants discriminated in the terms and conditions of rental by requiring an unnecessary third-party verification form by an arbitrary deadline. The claim was voluntarily dismissed with prejudice as part of the settlement agreement dismissing all claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983, Americans with Disabilities Act, Title VII of the Civil Rights Act
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint is frivolous and fails to state a claim. Allegations are unintelligible and lack factual specificity. § 1983 claims fail because defendant is a private hospital (not a state actor). ADA claims fail because plaintiff did not allege disability. Title VII claims fail because no employee-employer relationship alleged and no EEOC right-to-sue letter.

key_holding: UNDETERMINED

case_name: Collins v. TEAM MANAGEMENT LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff raised reasonable accommodation claims under § 3604(f), but the specific accommodation requested is not detailed in the available text.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for defendants on all claims, including plaintiff's late-raised reasonable accommodation claims under § 3604(f), noting that plaintiff had withdrawn her own housing application.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Collins sued TEAM MANAGEMENT LLC and related defendants alleging housing discrimination under the Fair Housing Act, including claims under § 3604(a) for discrimination, § 3617 for retaliation, and late-raised reasonable accommodation claims under § 3604(f). The court granted summary judgment for defendants on all claims, noting that plaintiff had withdrawn her own housing application.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie case of intentional discrimination under FHA § 3604(a) or could not rebut defendant's legitimate, non-discriminatory reasons for the challenged conduct.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a causal nexus between protected activity and adverse action, or failed to produce evidence supporting retaliation under FHA § 3617.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation claim raised late in the litigation
fha_claims.reasoning: The reasonable accommodation claim under FHA § 3604(f) was raised late and the court granted summary judgment without substantively analyzing the accommodation framework, likely on procedural or waiver grounds.

case_name: Robinson v. District of Columbia
accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought to remain at or return to Kia's Place IV homeless shelter as an accommodation for his mental health disabilities (ADHD, PTSD, depressive disorder), arguing he should not have been terminated from the program as a reasonable accommodation.
key_holding: The court dismissed Robinson's FHA reasonable accommodation claim as futile because his proposed amended complaint failed to specify what accommodation he requested, making it impossible to assess whether any such accommodation was necessary to afford him equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling.
brief_summary: Javonte Robinson, a homeless individual with mental health disabilities, sued the District of Columbia, a transitional youth shelter operator, and employees after being terminated from Kia's Place IV shelter, claiming they failed to make reasonable accommodations for his disabilities. The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss the federal claims as futile, finding Robinson's complaint failed to allege what specific accommodation he requested and why it would be necessary to afford him equal use and enjoyment of the shelter.
key_cases_cited: United States v. District of Columbia, 538 F. Supp. 2d 211 (D.D.C. 2008)
Hunt v. Aimco Properties, L.P., 814 F.3d 1213 (11th Cir. 2016)
Douglas v. Kriegsfeld Corp., 884 A.2d 1109 (D.C. 2005)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Dadian v. Village of Wilmette, 269 F.3d 831 (7th Cir. 2001)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation to remain in or return to Kia's Place IV shelter despite alleged threats or safety concerns; plaintiff sought return to housing after April 2021 termination, potentially requesting probationary return or return conditioned on treatment, but complaint does not specify what accommodation was requested.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for failure to state a plausible reasonable accommodation claim under Iqbal/Twombly. Although plaintiff alleged mental disabilities (ADHD, PTSD, Depressive disorder), he failed to allege that these conditions substantially limit major life activities (required to qualify as 'handicap' under FHA § 3602(h)), and critically, failed to allege what specific accommodation he requested or why it would be necessary. Court held that bare allegations of counsel attempting to arrange return to housing, without specification of what accommodation was sought, do not satisfy the pleading requirement.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Due process violation under Fifth Amendment for termination from shelter without notice and deprivation of personal property; violation of D.C. Homeless Services Reform Act (HSRA) for denial of shelter in severe weather; state law claims including negligence, gross negligence, negligent infliction of emotional distress, intentional infliction of emotional distress, conversion, abuse of process, breach of contract, and violation of D.C. Human Rights Act (DCHRA).
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed the due process claim regarding denial of shelter for failure to plausibly allege deprivation of a protected property interest in severe weather shelter (plaintiff did not allege he attempted to secure shelter on the specific days when temperature exceeded 95 degrees) and for failure to allege inadequate process (plaintiff received emergency termination followed by timely post-deprivation hearings under HSRA § 4-754.38, including administrative review and fair hearing rights, which satisfied due process). Court declined to rule on deprivation of personal property claim absent full briefing but expressed doubt about its viability given plaintiff's admission that ECS offered to return belongings with police assistance.

source_file: 10005587_2024_Allentown Victory Church v. City of Allentown_ca3
case_name: Allentown Victory Church v. City of Allentown
accommodation_description: The church requested permission to house eighteen (later reduced to fifteen) rather than twelve residents in its transitional recovery home as a reasonable accommodation under the zoning ordinance's accommodation provision.
key_holding: The Third Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the City, holding that the church failed to demonstrate that housing more than twelve residents was 'necessary' rather than merely 'preferable' for the Home's operation, as required under the reasonable accommodation burden-shifting framework.
brief_summary: Allentown Victory Church, which operates a transitional recovery home for men exiting substance abuse treatment and incarceration, sued the City of Allentown and its Zoning Hearing Board after the Board denied its requests to classify the Home as either a Large Group Home or an Institution and to house more than twelve residents as a reasonable accommodation. The Third Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the City, finding that while the Church invoked the FHA's reasonable accommodation provision, it failed to produce evidence showing that housing eighteen (later fifteen) residents was 'necessary' rather than merely economically preferable.
key_cases_cited: Lapid-Laurel, LLC v. Zoning Bd. of Adjustment of Twp. of Scotch Plains, 284 F.3d 442 (3d Cir. 2002)
Vorchheimer v. Phila. Owners Ass'n, 903 F.3d 100 (3d Cir. 2018)
431 E. Palisade Ave. Real Est., LLC v. City of Englewood, 977 F.3d 277 (3d Cir. 2020)
Lakeside Resort Enters., LP v. Bd. of Supervisors of Palmyra Twp., 455 F.3d 154 (3d Cir. 2006)
Washington v. Klem, 497 F.3d 272 (3d Cir. 2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to present evidence that disability was a motivating factor in the Board's decision. Board members' questions about disability status, programming, and resident numbers were part of routine zoning classification screening, not evidence of discriminatory animus.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's disparate impact claim was ill-developed and forfeited on appeal. Plaintiff provided only conclusory assertions without statistical evidence or case law support that the zoning ordinance's cap on Institution residents (12 persons) versus other classifications (up to 30 persons) had a disparate impact on disabled persons.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Variance to increase resident capacity from 12 to 18 (later 15) residents to make the Recovery Victory Home economically viable
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to meet its initial burden of showing the accommodation was 'necessary' under the Lapid-Laurel framework. Although plaintiff asserted economic infeasibility through counsel and pastor testimony, it provided no financial data, license requirements, affidavits, or other evidence demonstrating the variance was 'essential' rather than merely 'preferable' to make the facility viable.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) claim; Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) Title II claim
fha_claims.reasoning: RLUIPA claim was ill-developed and forfeited; plaintiff failed to cite controlling precedent (Klem) or identify a substantial burden on religious exercise. ADA claim was addressed in tandem with FHA claims and failed on the same evidentiary grounds—no showing that disability was a motivating factor or that the accommodation was necessary.

source_file: 10006353_2024_David Q. Webb v. Miami-Dade County Government_ca11
case_name: David Q. Webb v. Miami-Dade County Government
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged defendants refused to provide a reasonable accommodation for his angina-related disability at Camillus House residential facility, but the specific accommodation requested was not described in the opinion due to dismissal on shotgun pleading grounds.
key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal, holding that the district court did not abuse its discretion in dismissing appellant's case because he failed to comply with the court's order to file a proper second amended complaint after being warned that failure to do so would result in dismissal.
brief_summary: Pro se appellant David Webb sued Miami-Dade County Government, Miami-Dade County Homeless Trust, Camillus House (a non-profit supportive housing provider), and individual defendants, alleging Fair Housing Act and ADA violations related to his removal from a Camillus House residential facility for his angina disability. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal without prejudice, finding no abuse of discretion because Webb failed to file a proper second amended complaint after the court identified his pleading as a shotgun complaint and warned that failure to comply would result in dismissal.
key_cases_cited: Weiland v. Palm Beach Cnty. Sheriff's Off., 792 F.3d 1313 (11th Cir. 2015)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Vibe Micro Inc. v. Shabanets, 878 F.3d 1291 (11th Cir. 2018)
Foudy v. Indian River Cnty. Sheriff's Off., 845 F.3d 1117 (11th Cir. 2017)
Moon v. Newsome, 863 F.2d 835 (11th Cir. 1989)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation for disability (angina); specific accommodation not detailed in opinion
fha_claims.disposition: Shotgun pleading / failure to comply with court order
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court dismissed the complaint under § 1915(e)(2)(B) screening as a shotgun pleading containing conclusory, vague, and immaterial facts not obviously connected to any particular cause of action. The court did not reach the substantive merits of the FHA reasonable accommodation claim because the pleading failed to satisfy Rule 8 and Rule 10 notice requirements.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act discrimination and retaliation claims; Florida State Vicarious Liability claims; Fourth Amendment and False Claims Act claims
fha_claims.disposition: Shotgun pleading / failure to comply with court order
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court dismissed all non-FHA claims under § 1915(e)(2)(B) screening as part of the shotgun pleading determination. The complaint failed to specify which defendants were responsible for which acts and asserted multiple claims against multiple defendants without adequate notice, preventing substantive analysis of the ADA, state law, and constitutional claims.

case_name: Celia Litman; et al. v. Jennifer Guckin; Township of Towamencin
accommodation_description: Parents requested permission to add a room to their single-family home and use a trailer on the property to teach their autistic son independent living skills.
key_holding: The District Court's dismissal was affirmed because all claims were time-barred; the injury occurred in 2019 when zoning citations were issued, making the 2023 lawsuit four years after the alleged wrong and two years past the two-year statute of limitations.
brief_summary: The Litman family sued Towamencin Township and its zoning officer challenging zoning citations issued in 2019 for using a trailer on their property to accommodate their autistic son, alleging Fair Housing Act, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act violations. The Third Circuit affirmed the District Court's dismissal, holding that all claims were time-barred because the alleged injury occurred in 2019 when the citations were issued, making the 2023 lawsuit well outside the applicable two-year statute of limitations.
key_cases_cited: Wallace v. Kato, 549 U.S. 384 (2007)
Cowell v. Palmer Township, 263 F.3d 286 (3d Cir. 2001)
Dique v. N.J. State Police, 603 F.3d 181 (3d Cir. 2010)
Disabled in Action of Pa. v. Se. Pa. Transp. Auth., 539 F.3d 199 (3d Cir. 2008)
Pearson v. Sec'y Dep't of Corr., 775 F.3d 598 (3d Cir. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to add a room/trailer to residential property to provide independent living space for autistic son
fha_claims.disposition: Affirmed dismissal on statute of limitations grounds
fha_claims.reasoning: The court affirmed dismissal because all FHA claims were time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations in 42 U.S.C. § 3613(a)(1)(A). The alleged wrong (zoning citations and order to remove trailer) occurred in 2019, and the lawsuit was filed in 2023, exceeding the limitations period. The court rejected the continuing violation theory, finding the injury arose from isolated acts in 2019.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Federal constitutional claims (§ 1983), state constitutional claims, Rehabilitation Act claims, and ADA Title II claims
fha_claims.disposition: Affirmed dismissal on statute of limitations grounds
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA claims (§ 1983 tort claims, Rehabilitation Act, and ADA claims) were dismissed as time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations applicable to each. The court found the injury arose in 2019 from the zoning citations and order to remove the trailer, making the 2023 lawsuit untimely.

source_file: 10034090_2024_Jeremy Morris v. West Hayden Estates First Add._ca9
case_name: Jeremy Ray Morris; Kristy Morris v. West Hayden Estates First Addition Homeowners Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request was made; this case involves religious discrimination in HOA enforcement and interference claims.
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed JMOL for the HOA on the § 3604(b) disparate treatment claim because the Morrises did not show sufficient adverse effects, reversed JMOL on the § 3617 interference claim finding sufficient evidence of religious motivation, affirmed the new trial order, and vacated the permanent injunction.
brief_summary: The Morrises sued their HOA under the Fair Housing Act alleging religious discrimination after the HOA attempted to prevent them from hosting a large-scale Christmas program at their home, citing CC&R violations. A jury found for the Morrises on § 3604(b), § 3604(c), and § 3617 claims, awarding $60,000 compensatory and $15,000 punitive damages, but the district court granted judgment as a matter of law for the HOA post-trial. The Ninth Circuit affirmed in part and reversed in part, upholding the § 3604(b) dismissal but reinstating the § 3617 interference claim and vacating the injunction.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Reeves v. Sanderson Plumbing Prods., Inc.
Barnard v. Theobald
Pacific Shores Apartments v. City of Oakland

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that plaintiffs failed to show an adverse action sufficient to support a § 3604(b) disparate treatment claim. Although the HOA sent letters and held meetings expressing concerns about the Christmas program, the Morrises were never prevented from purchasing, moving into, or enjoying their home, and the HOA never actually enforced the CC&Rs against them before this lawsuit. The court found no concrete adverse impact required to support the claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 50(b) JMOL reversed; new trial affirmed
fha_claims.reasoning: The majority reversed the JMOL on the § 3617 interference claim, finding sufficient evidence that the HOA's January 2015 letter, February 2015 meeting, and October 2015 letter threatened, intimidated, or interfered with the Morrises' right to purchase and enjoy their home, with religious animus as at least a motivating factor. However, the court affirmed the grant of a new trial, finding the jury's verdict was against the clear weight of evidence due to credibility issues and prejudicial admission of harassment evidence.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that the HOA's January 2015 letter did not violate § 3604(c) under an objective 'ordinary reader' standard. Although the letter referenced non-Christians and potential 'problems,' an ordinary reader would understand the Board's concern to be about the event's disruptive scale and impact on non-Christian residents, not a preference against religious homeowners. The letter expressed appreciation for religious exercise and typical holiday lighting.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court affirmed JMOL on the Morrises' claim that the HOA's toleration of threats and harassment by other residents violated § 3604(b). Although the FHA prohibits hostile housing environments based on protected characteristics, the HOA—unlike a landlord—lacks the power to evict or expel harassing homeowners. The Morrises pointed to no CC&R provision violated by the neighbors' conduct or remedial tool available to the Board.

source_file: 10038254_2024_Gilead Community Services, Inc. v. Town of Cromwell_ca2
case_name: Gilead Community Services, Inc. v. Town of Cromwell
accommodation_description: Gilead sought to operate a group home for individuals with mental health disabilities in Cromwell, and the town's campaign of discrimination and retaliation was designed to prevent the group home from opening.
key_holding: The Second Circuit affirmed the jury's liability findings under the FHA, including that municipalities can be held vicariously liable for discriminatory acts of officials and that punitive damages are available against municipalities under the FHA, but vacated the $5 million punitive damages award as unconstitutionally excessive and remanded for a new trial on damages unless plaintiffs accepted remittitur to $2 million.
brief_summary: Gilead Community Services and Connecticut Fair Housing Center sued the Town of Cromwell after the town engaged in a sustained campaign of discrimination, including discriminatory public statements, zoning threats, and police targeting, to prevent Gilead's group home for individuals with mental health disabilities from opening, forcing the home to close. The Second Circuit affirmed the jury's liability findings and $181,000 compensatory damages award but vacated the $5 million punitive damages award as unconstitutionally excessive, remanding for reduction to $2 million.
key_cases_cited: Cabrera v. Jakabovitz, 24 F.3d 372 (2d Cir. 1994)
Robinson v. 12 Lofts Realty, Inc., 610 F.2d 1032 (2d Cir. 1979)
Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)
Mhany Mgmt., Inc. v. County of Nassau, 819 F.3d 581 (2d Cir. 2016)
State Farm Mut. Auto Ins. Co. v. Campbell, 538 U.S. 408 (2003)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Making housing unavailable and discriminating in terms and conditions of housing based on disability (group home for individuals with mental health disabilities)
fha_claims.reasoning: Jury found town liable under § 3604(f)(1)-(2) for discriminatory conduct. Court applied motivating-factor causation test, holding that disability must be one motivating factor in defendant's adverse action, consistent with binding Second Circuit precedent. Town's campaign to prevent group home opening constituted disparate treatment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Making statements indicating discriminatory preference or limitation based on disability (mayor's press release, town manager's statements comparing group home residents to mass shooters, demands for mental health diagnoses)
fha_claims.reasoning: Jury found town liable under § 3604(c) for making statements indicating discriminatory preference based on disability. Court held that § 3604(c) is violated by statements that suggest to an ordinary reader that a protected status is preferred or dispreferred, without requiring proof of causal link to any discriminatory transaction.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation for exercising FHA rights: cease-and-desist letter, zoning permit demands, tax exemption denial, police misconduct (leaked health information, failure to investigate vandalism), and threat to deny tax exemption for separate property
fha_claims.reasoning: Jury found town liable under § 3617 for coercion, intimidation, and interference with Gilead's exercise of FHA rights. Court applied motivating-factor causation test, requiring plaintiff to show retaliatory motive played a part in causing adverse action. Town's sustained campaign of opposition and subsequent adverse actions satisfied this standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act Title II, Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973
fha_claims.reasoning: Jury found town liable under ADA and Rehabilitation Act for disability discrimination. Court did not separately analyze these claims on appeal, focusing on FHA liability and punitive damages issues.

case_name: Merck v. Walmart, Inc.
accommodation_description: This is not a Fair Housing Act case; it is a Fair Credit Reporting Act claim regarding Walmart's alleged failure to provide plaintiff with a full copy of his consumer report before revoking his conditional job offer.
key_holding: The Sixth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for Walmart, holding that plaintiff Thomas Merck lacked Article III standing because his alleged informational injury under the Fair Credit Reporting Act did not bear a sufficiently close relationship to a harm traditionally recognized as providing a basis for lawsuits in American courts.
brief_summary: Thomas Merck sued Walmart under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, alleging Walmart violated 15 U.S.C. § 1681b(b)(3)(A) by failing to provide him with a full copy of his consumer report before revoking his conditional job offer after a background check revealed an undisclosed misdemeanor conviction. The Sixth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for Walmart, finding Merck lacked Article III standing because his claimed procedural injury did not resemble a harm traditionally recognized in American courts and he failed to demonstrate any concrete injury flowing from the statutory violation.
key_cases_cited: TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021)
Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins, 578 U.S. 330 (2016)
Ward v. Nat'l Patient Acct. Servs. Sols., Inc., 9 F.4th 357 (6th Cir. 2021)
Ward v. NPAS, Inc., 63 F.4th 576 (6th Cir. 2023)
Gadelhak v. AT&T Servs., Inc., 950 F.3d 458 (7th Cir. 2020)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Credit Reporting Act violation — failure to provide complete consumer report prior to adverse employment action
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff lacked Article III constitutional standing to sue under the Fair Credit Reporting Act because he failed to demonstrate a concrete injury in fact. The court applied the TransUnion framework and found that plaintiff could not show adverse effects from the denial of information, could not establish a close relationship to traditional common-law harms, and could not analogize his claim to procedural due process rights (which require state action). Plaintiff bore the burden at summary judgment to identify specific facts supporting standing elements and failed to do so.

source_file: 10082236_2024_Joshua Debity v. Vintage Village Homeowners Ass'n_ca6
case_name: Joshua A. Debity, et al. v. Vintage Village Homeowners Association
accommodation_description: Request for a six-foot wooden privacy fence in the backyard instead of the HOA-approved wrought-iron fence to prevent the disabled child from eloping and to provide privacy when the child disrobes due to sensory processing disorder.
key_holding: The appellate court reversed summary judgment for the HOA, finding the district court improperly ignored evidence related to the privacy concern and erred in excluding the treating provider's testimony about the child's need for a privacy fence, creating genuine issues of material fact as to whether a wooden privacy fence was necessary to afford the disabled child equal opportunity to enjoy the property.
brief_summary: Joshua and Leah Debity sued their HOA after it refused to approve a wooden privacy fence for their autistic son G.D., instead requiring a wrought-iron fence; the district court excluded the child's medical provider's testimony and granted summary judgment for the HOA. The Sixth Circuit reversed, holding that genuine issues of material fact existed as to whether the wooden privacy fence was necessary to afford the child equal opportunity to use and enjoy the property, and the district court improperly limited the treating provider's testimony about the child's need for privacy accommodations.
key_cases_cited: Hollis v. Chestnut Bend Homeowners Ass'n, 760 F.3d 531 (6th Cir. 2014)
Anderson v. City of Blue Ash, 798 F.3d 338 (6th Cir. 2015)
Howard v. City of Beavercreek, 276 F.3d 802 (6th Cir. 2002)
Gass v. Marriott Hotel Servs., Inc., 558 F.3d 419 (6th Cir. 2009)
Fielden v. CSX Transp., Inc., 482 F.3d 866 (6th Cir. 2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Six-foot wooden privacy fence to provide privacy for child with autism and sensory processing disorder who disrobes, and to prevent elopement and drowning risk from drainage pond
fha_claims.reasoning: District court granted summary judgment, finding plaintiffs failed to establish that a wooden privacy fence was necessary under the FHA. However, appellate court reversed, holding that plaintiffs presented sufficient evidence (including medical provider testimony about child's propensity to disrobe and need for privacy) to create a genuine issue of material fact regarding whether the HOA-approved wrought-iron fence would provide adequate privacy and equal opportunity for enjoyment of the property.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable modification of HOA covenant restrictions to permit wooden privacy fence instead of wrought-iron fence
fha_claims.reasoning: District court granted summary judgment on the reasonable-modification claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(A), but appellate court reversed, finding that plaintiffs presented sufficient evidence to survive summary judgment and that a reasonable jury could find the wooden fence necessary to afford equal opportunity for enjoyment of the property.

case_name: Katalin Bloodgood-Loper v. Lenard Loper; LVL Investments, LLC; Michelle L. Mercer
accommodation_description: The opinion does not identify any specific accommodation request; the FHA claims were dismissed for failure to plead facts showing defendants acted 'because of' plaintiff's protected class membership.
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed dismissal because Bloodgood-Loper failed to allege facts sufficient to show defendants engaged in conduct made unlawful by the Fair Housing Act 'because of' her membership in a protected class under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(a), (f).
brief_summary: Katalin Bloodgood-Loper, proceeding pro se, appealed the district court's dismissal of her federal claims including Fair Housing Act claims against Lenard Loper, LVL Investments, LLC, and Judge Michelle Mercer. The Ninth Circuit affirmed, holding that Bloodgood-Loper failed to plead sufficient facts showing the defendants' conduct was 'because of' her membership in a protected class under § 3604(a) and (f).
key_cases_cited: Hebbe v. Pliler, 627 F.3d 338 (9th Cir. 2010)
Schucker v. Rockwood, 846 F.2d 1202 (9th Cir. 1988)
Chudacoff v. Univ. Med. Ctr. of S. Nev., 649 F.3d 1143 (9th Cir. 2011)
Price v. State of Hawaii, 939 F.2d 702 (9th Cir. 1991)
Karim-Panahi v. L.A. Police Dep't, 839 F.2d 621 (9th Cir. 1988)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not specified in opinion
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court affirmed the district court's dismissal of FHA claims on the ground that plaintiff failed to allege facts sufficient to show defendants engaged in conduct made unlawful by the FHA 'because of' plaintiff's membership in a protected class, applying the Iqbal/Twombly pleading standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. §§ 1983, 1985; state law claims
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court properly dismissed § 1983 and § 1985 claims for failure to allege facts showing defendants acted under color of state law or conspired to deny equal protection based on protected class membership; judicial immunity also barred claims against Judge Mercer; supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims was properly declined after dismissal of federal claims.

case_name: Neway Mengistu v. Forestview Apartments, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested an apartment with accessibility modifications, but defendants declined to rent due to the high cost of renovations.
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for defendants because plaintiff's FHA claims were barred by the two-year statute of limitations, having accrued when defendants informed him of their decision not to rent on May 11, 2017, and alternatively because plaintiff failed to raise a triable dispute that his requested accommodations were reasonable.
brief_summary: Neway Mengistu sued Forestview Apartments and its manager alleging Fair Housing Act violations after defendants decided not to rent him an apartment due to the high cost of accessibility renovations. The Ninth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for defendants, holding that the claims were time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations and alternatively failed on the merits because Mengistu did not raise a triable dispute that his accommodation requests were reasonable.
key_cases_cited: Soto v. Sweetman, 882 F.3d 865 (9th Cir. 2018)
Dubois v. Ass'n of Apartment Owners of 2987 Kalakaua, 453 F.3d 1175 (9th Cir. 2006)
Comm. Concerning Cmty. Improvement v. City of Modesto, 583 F.3d 690 (9th Cir. 2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Renovations to make the apartment accessible to plaintiff's disability
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court granted summary judgment on the ground that plaintiff failed to raise a triable dispute as to whether the requested accommodations (renovations) were reasonable. The court implicitly applied the undue burden defense, as the opinion notes defendants' decision was based on the high cost of renovations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to rent apartment to plaintiff because of disability
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court granted summary judgment on the additional ground that plaintiff failed to raise a triable dispute as to whether defendants discriminated against him in violation of 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(1), which prohibits discrimination in rental based on handicap.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (Cal. Gov't Code § 12927(c)(1)); California Unruh Act (Cal. Civil Code § 54.1(b)(3)(A))
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court granted summary judgment on California state law discrimination claims under the same reasoning applied to the FHA claims—plaintiff failed to raise a triable dispute as to discrimination or reasonableness of requested accommodations.

source_file: 10099647_2024_Earlando Samuel v. Delaware County Housing Authority_ca3
case_name: Earlando Samuel v. Delaware County Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Request for two-bedroom Section 8 voucher to accommodate a live-in aide assisting with disability-related impairments including osteoarthritis, cognitive impairment, depression, anxiety, and panic disorder
key_holding: The Third Circuit found no abuse of discretion in denying Samuel's motions for appointed counsel, concluding that despite his disabilities, Samuel demonstrated adequate ability to litigate his reasonable accommodation claim given his prior federal litigation experience, proactive engagement with housing regulations, and the relatively straightforward factual issues at summary judgment.
brief_summary: Earlando Samuel, a pro se appellant with multiple disabilities, appealed from the Third Circuit the District Court's denial of his three motions to appoint counsel in his Fair Housing Act reasonable accommodation case against the Delaware County Housing Authority regarding his Section 8 voucher and live-in aide request. The Third Circuit affirmed, finding no abuse of discretion because Samuel demonstrated sufficient ability to represent himself despite his disabilities, citing his prior federal litigation experience and adequate presentation of his case.
key_cases_cited: Tabron v. Grace, 6 F.3d 147 (3d Cir. 1993)
Houser v. Folino, 927 F.3d 693 (3d Cir. 2019)
Parham v. Johnson, 126 F.3d 454 (3d Cir. 1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested authorization for a second bedroom in his Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher to accommodate a live-in aide to assist with disability-related impairments. The DCHA reduced his two-bedroom voucher to one-bedroom upon porting from Delaware to Pennsylvania and required him to recertify his need for a live-in aide.
fha_claims.reasoning: The District Court entered judgment for the defendants on the sole remaining claim that DCHA failed to reasonably accommodate plaintiff's disabilities by requiring him to recertify his need for a live-in aide. The appellate court affirmed, focusing on the motion to appoint counsel rather than the merits, but the underlying summary judgment disposition favored the defendant.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged that the property management company harassed and retaliated against him for complaining about the reduction of his two-bedroom voucher to a one-bedroom voucher.
fha_claims.reasoning: The District Court initially dismissed many of plaintiff's claims without prejudice, including retaliation claims. The appellate opinion notes that plaintiff's brief mention of retaliation was too vaguely briefed and therefore abandoned on appeal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Additional claims based on allegations of harassment and other non-FHA theories.
fha_claims.reasoning: The District Court dismissed many of plaintiff's claims without prejudice at the motion to dismiss stage, including non-FHA claims that were not adequately pleaded under Iqbal/Twombly standards.

source_file: 10105570_2024_Adam U. Steines v. Westgate Palace, L.L.C._ca11
case_name: Adam U. Steines v. Westgate Palace, L.L.C.
accommodation_description: This case does not involve a reasonable accommodation request; it concerns a Military Lending Act challenge to mandatory arbitration clauses in timeshare loan documents.
key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction, holding that because the Military Lending Act overrides the Federal Arbitration Act, Section 16 of the FAA (authorizing interlocutory appeals from arbitration orders) does not apply; the court also affirmed that the MLA applies to the timeshare loan because the timeshare interest is more like a hotel room than a dwelling and thus does not qualify for the MLA's residential mortgage exception.
brief_summary: Adam and Miranda Steines, active-duty servicemembers, brought a class action against Westgate Resorts alleging violations of the Military Lending Act, including that Westgate's timeshare loan documents failed to provide required disclosures and unlawfully included mandatory arbitration clauses. The Eleventh Circuit dismissed the appeal, holding that because the MLA expressly overrides the FAA, Section 16 of the FAA—which permits interlocutory appeals from orders denying arbitration—does not apply, leaving the court without appellate jurisdiction.
key_cases_cited: Epic Systems Corp. v. Lewis
New Prime Inc. v. Oliveira
Shearson/American Express, Inc. v. McMahon
Mitsubishi Motors Corp. v. Soler Chrysler-Plymouth, Inc.
Schwarz v. City of Treasure Island

case_name: J.W. Seals, Jr.; Vergie Seals; Marie L. Pace v. Itex Group L.L.C.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged that uninhabitable conditions (mold, structural defects, pest infestations) in her apartment made it 'unavailable' under the FHA.
key_holding: The Fifth Circuit affirmed dismissal, holding that Sections 3604(a) and 3604(f)(1) of the FHA provide relief for discrimination in the sale or rental of dwellings, not for claims that an apartment is uninhabitable.
brief_summary: Vergie Seals and her children sued ITEX Group under the Fair Housing Act, ADA, and state law, alleging that deplorable conditions including mold, structural defects, and pest infestations made her apartment 'unavailable' under § 3604(a) and (f)(1). The Fifth Circuit affirmed dismissal, holding that these FHA provisions cover discrimination in the sale or rental of housing, not claims that existing housing is uninhabitable, and plaintiffs abandoned the appeal by failing to challenge this basis.
key_cases_cited: Cox v. City of Dallas, Tex., 430 F.3d 734 (5th Cir. 2005)
Grant v. Cuellar, 59 F.3d 523 (5th Cir. 1995)
Brinkmann v. Dallas Cnty. Deputy Sheriff Abner, 813 F.2d 744 (5th Cir. 1987)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Habitability of apartment; relief from uninhabitable conditions (structural defects, mold, infestations, litter, blight, deficient security, faulty utilities)
fha_claims.reasoning: The Fifth Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6), holding that FHA §§ 3604(a) and (f)(1) provide relief for discrimination in the sale or rental of a dwelling, not for claims that an apartment is uninhabitable. The appellate court found plaintiffs abandoned the issue on appeal by failing to address the district court's legal basis for dismissal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II, state law claims regarding habitability and uninhabitable conditions
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court dismissed non-FHA claims (ADA and state law) along with the FHA claims under Rule 12(b)(6). The appellate court affirmed without separately analyzing these claims, as plaintiffs failed to brief the issues on appeal.

source_file: 10122741_2024_Arizona Alliance for Retired Americans v. Kristin K. Mayes_ca9
10143415_2024_New Heights Farm I, LLC v. Great Am. Ins. Co._ca6

case_name: In re: Nyah Sekel
accommodation_description: Petitioner seeks writ of mandamus directing district court to grant her motion for summary judgment in underlying Fair Housing Act case
key_holding: Petitioner is not entitled to mandamus relief because she has not demonstrated a clear right to the relief sought and mandamus cannot be used as a substitute for appeal.
brief_summary: Nyah Sekel petitioned the Fourth Circuit for a writ of mandamus directing the district court to grant her motion for summary judgment in her pending Fair Housing Act case. The court denied the petition, holding that mandamus is a drastic remedy available only in extraordinary circumstances and that Petitioner failed to demonstrate a clear right to the relief sought.
key_cases_cited: Cheney v. U.S. Dist. Ct., 542 U.S. 367 (2004)
In re Murphy-Brown, LLC, 907 F.3d 788 (4th Cir. 2018)
In re Lockheed Martin Corp., 503 F.3d 351 (4th Cir. 2007)

source_file: 10164483_2022_Equal Employment Opportunity Commission v. Dolgencorp, LLC_alnd

case_name: Nora Dunn v. Carter Manuel, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested a temporary substitute apartment and time to gather assistance to move and separate her personal items while her unit was being repaired due to her hoarding disorder.
key_holding: The court granted the motion to dismiss because hoarding disorder does not qualify as a protected disability under the FHA since plaintiff failed to allege facts showing it substantially limits major life activities, and alternatively because plaintiff failed to plead that her requested accommodation was reasonable, proportional, or necessary to ameliorate her disability's effects.
brief_summary: Nora Dunn sued her landlord Sharon Hydinger alleging Fair Housing Act violations, including failure to accommodate her hoarding disorder, intentional discrimination, retaliation, and hostile environment harassment. The court granted the motion to dismiss, finding that hoarding disorder is not a protected disability under the FHA because it does not substantially limit major life activities, and alternatively that Dunn failed to plead the remaining elements of her accommodation claim.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014)
Sailboat Bend Sober Living, LLC v. City of Fort Lauderdale, 46 F.4th 1268 (11th Cir. 2022)
Bonasera v. City of Norcross, 342 F. App'x 581 (11th Cir. 2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead a disability under the FHA (hoarding disorder does not substantially limit major life activities as required by 42 U.S.C. § 3602(h)(1)). Additionally, even assuming a disability, Plaintiff failed to allege that Defendant treated her differently than similarly situated non-disabled tenants, which is required for intentional discrimination under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a protected activity under the FHA because she did not sufficiently plead that Defendant's denial of the requested accommodation was unlawful. Plaintiff also failed to allege a good faith, reasonable belief that the conduct was unlawful, which is required to establish protected activity even where conduct is actually lawful.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Hostile environment claim; unclear whether brought under FHA or Alabama Fair Housing Law
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead facts establishing a hostile environment. The alleged harassment (blaming, calling apartment 'dirty and trashy,' characterizing tenant as poor credit risk) does not rise to the level of 'severe' conduct, and Plaintiff failed to allege that such conduct was 'pervasive' or occurred more than once, as required under 24 C.F.R. § 100.600(a)(2)(i).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested a temporary substitute apartment to live in while her apartment was being repaired and to allow time to deal with personal items
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a disability under the FHA. Additionally, Plaintiff failed to plead that the requested accommodation was reasonable and proportional to costs of implementation, and failed to allege that the accommodation was necessary to ameliorate the effects of her disability, as required under Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alabama Landlord Tenant Act violation, Breach of Duty of Reasonable Care/Affirmative Negligence, Wanton/Recklessness, Breach of Contract, Wrongful Eviction/Abuse of Process
fha_claims.reasoning: State law claims are barred by res judicata (Defendant Hydinger was in privity with state court defendants Carter Manuel and RMI Realty Group, and claims were dismissed with prejudice in state court). Additionally, supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims is improper under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3) because all federal claims over which the court has original jurisdiction have been dismissed.

case_name: Miller v. Coastline Management
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation requested; plaintiff mentions CPTSD and mother's walker use as basis for discrimination claim regarding delayed repairs and unlivable conditions.
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA claims fail because she cited 42 U.S.C. § 3601 (which merely states the FHA's general purpose) and § 3605 (which applies to real estate transactions like selling, brokering, or appraising), neither of which provides a cause of action for discrimination experienced while living in a condo unit.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Fredrika Miller sued Coastline Management and Beachcomber Homeowner Association alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on discrimination she and her mother experienced while living in their condo unit, citing her CPTSD and her mother's walker use as bases for discrimination. The court dismissed the FHA claims with prejudice, finding Miller failed to state a plausible cause of action under the cited statutory provisions (42 U.S.C. § 3601, which establishes only general FHA purpose, and § 3605, which applies to real estate transactions, not tenancy-related discrimination claims).
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff cited § 3601 (statement of FHA policy, not a cause of action) and § 3605 (which applies only to real estate transactions, not housing discrimination during occupancy). Plaintiff alleged discrimination based on sex, disability (CPTSD and elderly mother with walker), and national origin (American Indian heritage) but failed to allege facts plausibly supporting a claim under the cited FHA provisions. Court applied Iqbal/Twombly pleading standard and found plaintiff failed to state a plausible FHA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claims under 18 U.S.C. § 641 (federal theft/embezzlement), Ala. Code § 13A-8-2.1 (state theft), and Ala. Code Title 38, Chapter 9 (state elder abuse)
fha_claims.reasoning: Criminal statutes cited do not create private causes of action for civil enforcement. Federal criminal statutes require express Congressional intent to create a private right of action, which is absent here. Alabama law does not automatically create civil causes of action for criminal violations absent a breach of duty owed to plaintiff.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff invokes Fair Housing Act § 3631 and ADA rights in context of alleged harassment and mail interference, but no specific accommodation is identified or requested.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed under § 1915(e)(2) as frivolous and for failure to state a claim. The complaint is incoherent and unintelligible; even liberally construing the pro se pleading, the court could not discern any recognizable cause of action. The allegations are anticipatory in nature and do not establish subject matter jurisdiction.

10166678_2024_Southwest Fair Housing Council v. WG Scottsdale LLC_azd
case_name: Southwest Fair Housing Council v. WG Scottsdale LLC
accommodation_description: The specific accommodation request at issue in the underlying trial is not described in this attorneys' fees order.
key_holding: The Court granted in part Plaintiff's supplemental motion for attorneys' fees, awarding $28,749.00 (reduced from the requested amount due to reasonable hourly rate determinations for Eisenberg & Baum attorneys), while rejecting Defendant's arguments regarding timeliness and post hoc enhancements.
brief_summary: Southwest Fair Housing Council sued WG Scottsdale LLC (d/b/a Atria Sierra Pointe) for ADA, FHA, and AZFHA violations, resulting in a jury verdict for Plaintiff after a four-day trial with $100,000 in punitive damages. The Court granted in part Plaintiff's supplemental motion for attorneys' fees, awarding $28,749.00 for post-trial work while reducing requested hourly rates for Eisenberg & Baum attorneys to align with District of Arizona market rates.
key_cases_cited: Hensley v. Eckerhart, 461 U.S. 424 (1983)
Kelly v. Wengler, 822 F.3d 1085 (9th Cir. 2016)
Schwarz v. Sec'y of Health & Human Servs., 73 F.3d 895 (9th Cir. 1995)
Gates v. Deukmejian, 987 F.2d 1392 (9th Cir. 1992)
Carter v. Caleb Brett LLC, 757 F.3d 866 (9th Cir. 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unspecified reasonable accommodation(s) at issue in the underlying trial; the opinion addresses only post-trial attorneys' fees and does not detail the specific accommodation requested
fha_claims.reasoning: The jury returned a verdict in favor of Plaintiff finding FHA violation after a four-day trial. The Ninth Circuit affirmed the judgment on October 17, 2023. This opinion addresses only the supplemental attorneys' fees award post-appeal, not the merits of the underlying accommodation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) and Arizona Fair Housing Act (AZFHA) claims
fha_claims.reasoning: The jury returned a verdict in favor of Plaintiff finding violations of the ADA and AZFHA. The Ninth Circuit affirmed the judgment. This opinion addresses only the supplemental attorneys' fees award post-appeal.

source_file: 10166836_2024_Hiatt v. Sun City Festival Community Association Incorporated_azd
case_name: Wayne Hiatt v. Sun City Festival Community Association Incorporated
accommodation_description: Disabled veteran requested permission to keep his garage door open while engaged in therapeutic woodworking inside his garage, as an accommodation from the HOA's rule requiring garage doors to remain closed at all times.
key_holding: The court reopened discovery to allow plaintiff to depose board members regarding emails about his accommodation request, finding that an email in which the board president called the garage door rule 'stupid' is relevant to whether the accommodation request was reasonable under § 3604(f)(3).
brief_summary: Wayne Hiatt, a disabled veteran, sued Sun City Festival Community Association under the Fair Housing Act alleging discrimination based on disability after the HOA denied his accommodation request to keep his garage door open while engaged in therapeutic woodworking. The court's order addressed discovery disputes, denying plaintiff's sanctions request, reopening discovery for limited depositions of board members regarding emails about the accommodation request, and denying defendant's motion to disqualify plaintiff's counsel.
key_cases_cited: Yeti by Molly, Ltd. v. Deckers Outdoor Corp.
Lanard Toys Ltd. v. Novelty, Inc.
Merchant v. Corizon Health, Inc.
United States v. Richey
Lawrence v. Dependable Med. Transp. Servs., L.L.C.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exception to the Association's garage door closure rule to allow plaintiff to keep his garage door open while woodworking as therapy for his disability
fha_claims.reasoning: The opinion addresses discovery disputes and procedural motions but does not rule on the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim. The case remains in discovery with reopened deadlines for depositions and dispositive motions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Arizona Fair Housing Act claim under A.R.S. § 41-1491.19(B)
fha_claims.reasoning: The Arizona FHA claim was pleaded in the complaint but the court's order does not address or rule on it separately; it remains pending along with the federal FHA claim.

source_file: 10166885_2024_Hiatt v. Sun City Festival Community Association Incorporated_azd
case_name: Wayne Hiatt v. Sun City Festival Community Association Incorporated
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a disabled veteran with PTSD and claustrophobia, requested to keep his garage door open while woodworking/engaging in activities in his garage as a therapeutic accommodation.
key_holding: The court found that Plaintiff established four of five elements for a reasonable accommodation claim as undisputed facts, but denied summary judgment because a genuine dispute of material fact exists regarding whether keeping the garage door open was necessary to afford Plaintiff equal opportunity to use and enjoy his dwelling, given evidence that Plaintiff could use a community woodworking facility and engaged in other activities without the door open.
brief_summary: Wayne Hiatt, a disabled veteran with PTSD and claustrophobia, sued Sun City Festival Community Association seeking partial summary judgment on his reasonable accommodation claim under the FHA, alleging the HOA's CC&Rs requiring garage doors to remain closed discriminated against his disability-related need to keep his garage door open while woodworking. The Court denied the motion, finding that while four of five elements were undisputed, a genuine dispute of material fact remains regarding whether the accommodation was necessary to afford Plaintiff equal opportunity to use and enjoy his dwelling.
key_cases_cited: Giebeler v. M & B Associates, 343 F.3d 1143 (9th Cir. 2003)
Dubois v. Ass'n of Apartment Owners of 2987 Kalakaua, 453 F.3d 1175 (9th Cir. 2006)
United States v. California Mobile Home Park Mgmt. Co., 107 F.3d 1374 (9th Cir. 1997)
Canady v. Prescott Canyon Ests. Homeowners Ass'n, 60 P.3d 231 (Ariz. Ct. App. 2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exception to CC&R garage door closure policy to allow plaintiff to keep garage door open while engaging in woodworking therapy for PTSD and claustrophobia
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff established four of five FHA elements (disability, defendant's knowledge, refusal, and reasonableness of accommodation), but genuine dispute of material fact exists as to whether the accommodation was necessary to afford equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling. Necessity element requires jury determination because reasonable minds could differ on whether the garage door policy prevents equal enjoyment and whether causal link exists between policy and disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Arizona Fair Housing Act claim (virtually identical to FHA)
fha_claims.reasoning: AZFHA claim analyzed under same framework as FHA claim; court applied identical reasonable accommodation analysis and denied summary judgment on the same basis—genuine dispute of material fact as to necessity element.

case_name: TL Harvey v. Maxwell & Morgan P.C., et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested permission to install a window air conditioning unit despite HOA rules, framing it as an accommodation.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claims because his complaint failed to identify his disability, explain how the requested accommodation was necessary for that disability, or allege facts plausibly showing the defendants were responsible for creating a discriminatory housing environment.
brief_summary: TL Harvey, a Black homeowner, sued his HOA (RED HOA), its law firm, property manager, and board members alleging they targeted him based on race and failed to accommodate his disability by refusing to allow a window air conditioner. The court granted the motions to dismiss, finding Harvey's FHA claims insufficiently pleaded because he failed to identify his disability or explain how the requested accommodation was necessary.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Morris v. W. Hayden Est. First Addition Homeowners Ass'n Inc., 104 F.4th 1128 (9th Cir. 2024)
Howard v. HMK Holdings, LLC, 988 F.3d 1185 (9th Cir. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to install and keep a window air conditioning unit (window cooler) in a specific location despite HOA architectural committee authority and rules
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint failed to allege facts showing a disability or how the window cooler accommodation was necessary for that disability. The complaint did not clearly identify who could have accommodated Harvey or how, failing to meet Rule 8's pleading standards and Iqbal/Twombly plausibility. Dismissed with leave to amend as to RED HOA and related defendants.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliatory enforcement of HOA violations after Harvey requested accommodation for window air conditioning unit
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint contained only conclusory allegations that defendants violated § 3617 by refusing to make accommodations to facilitate fair housing policy, without factual allegations supporting a plausible retaliation claim. Dismissed with leave to amend as to RED HOA and related defendants.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 due process claims, § 1985(3) conspiracy claims, § 1981 racial discrimination in contracts, breach of contract, civil RICO, mail fraud, fraud, breach of fiduciary duty
fha_claims.reasoning: § 1983 claims dismissed because defendants are not state actors (mere participation in state court litigation is insufficient); § 1985(3) requires at least one state actor in the conspiracy; § 1981 and breach of contract claims dismissed for failure to identify contractual relationships with defendants (granted leave to amend against RED HOA only); mail fraud claim dismissed because the mail fraud statute provides no private right of action; fraud and RICO claims dismissed for failure to plead with particularity under Rule 9(b) and RICO pleading standards; breach of fiduciary duty dismissed because unclear whether based on assessment handling or other wrongdoing (granted leave to amend against RED HOA only).

source_file: 10167251_2024_Hiatt v. Sun City Festival Community Association Incorporated_azd
case_name: Wayne Hiatt v. Sun City Festival Community Association Incorporated
accommodation_description: Request to waive the HOA's closed-garage-door rule to keep garage door open while engaging in therapeutic woodworking and other activities to manage PTSD symptoms
key_holding: Plaintiff raised serious questions going to the merits of his FHA reasonable accommodation claim but failed to establish irreparable harm due to his 17-month delay in seeking preliminary injunctive relief and his ability to endure the alleged harm during that period.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Wayne Hiatt, a disabled veteran with PTSD, sued the Sun City Festival Community Association seeking a preliminary injunction to allow him to keep his garage door open while woodworking and engaging in other therapeutic activities as a reasonable accommodation under the Fair Housing Act. The court denied the motion, finding that while Hiatt raised serious questions on the merits of his reasonable accommodation claim, he failed to demonstrate immediate irreparable harm given his 17-month delay in seeking injunctive relief.
key_cases_cited: Giebeler v. M & B Assocs., 343 F.3d 1143 (9th Cir. 2003)
Dubois v. Ass'n of Apartment Owners of 2987 Kalakaua, 453 F.3d 1175 (9th Cir. 2006)
Winter v. Nat. Res. Def. Council, Inc., 555 U.S. 7 (2008)
Dadian v. Vill. of Wilmette, 269 F.3d 831 (7th Cir. 2001)
Norman v. Rancho del Lago Cmty. Ass'n, No. 19-CV-00486-TUC-JAS-LCK, 2021 WL 5167305 (D. Ariz. Aug. 5, 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exception to the Association's garage door closure rule to allow Plaintiff to keep his garage door open while engaging in therapeutic activities (woodworking, drawing, watching TV) to manage his PTSD symptoms
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that Plaintiff established three of five elements (disability, defendant's knowledge, refusal to accommodate) and that the accommodation was reasonable (no undue financial/administrative burden; noise concerns rebutted by quiet alternative activities). However, the court found Plaintiff posed only a 'serious question' rather than a 'likelihood of success' on the necessity element—whether but-for the accommodation Plaintiff would be denied equal opportunity to enjoy his housing. The court noted Plaintiff's evidence (personal opinion, nurse practitioner's signed form, wife's testimony) fell short of the standard in comparable cases requiring clearer medical evidence of necessity. The preliminary injunction was denied because Plaintiff failed to establish likelihood of success on the merits and failed to demonstrate irreparable harm, given his 17-month delay in seeking relief and his ability to comply with the rule for 18 months.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Arizona Fair Housing Act (A.R.S. § 41-1491.19(B))
fha_claims.reasoning: The court noted that Arizona courts have found the AZFHA 'virtually identical' to the FHA and applied the same reasonable accommodation framework. The court did not separately analyze the AZFHA claim, treating it as coextensive with the FHA claim. The preliminary injunction was denied on the same grounds as the FHA claim.

source_file: 10167263_2024_Garfield Sacred Heart Housing LLC v. Santos_azd
10167516_2024_Timothy Neilson v. KC Hotels Group, Inc._cacd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Labor Code violations (retaliation under § 1102.5, adverse action under § 98.6, wrongful termination, failure to pay minimum wages under § 1197.1, failure to pay overtime under § 510, failure to pay earned wages under §§ 201 and 202, failure to provide accurate itemized wage statements under § 226, and violation of Business and Professions Code § 17200)
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint arises solely under California Labor Code and does not present a federal question. Although defendants cited the Fair Housing Act and 42 U.S.C. § 1982 in their removal notice, none of these federal statutes are actually at issue in the complaint, which concerns only employment-related claims between employee and employer. The removal was improper and the case lacks federal subject matter jurisdiction.

source_file: 10167686_2024_The People of the State of California v. Rish Investments, Inc._cacd
10167751_2024_United African-Asian Abilities Club v. Alexander C. Freiberg_cacd
case_name: United African-Asian Abilities Club et al v. Alexander C. Freiberg et al
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request is described; the claims arise from alleged construction-related accessibility standard violations at a place of public accommodation under the FHA, ADA, and California Unruh Act.
key_holding: The court issued an Order to Show Cause directing plaintiff to explain why the court should not decline to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the state Unruh Act claim, given California's heightened pleading requirements and high-frequency litigant restrictions for construction-related accessibility claims.
brief_summary: Plaintiff United African-Asian Abilities Club filed suit against Alexander C. Freiberg alleging violations of the federal Fair Housing Act, Americans with Disabilities Act, and California's Unruh Act based on construction-related accessibility violations. The court issued an Order to Show Cause regarding whether it should exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the Unruh Act claim, noting that California enacted heightened pleading requirements and financial restrictions on 'high-frequency litigants' to deter vexatious construction-related accessibility litigation, and that federal court filings can circumvent those state-law protections. The court ordered plaintiff to identify statutory damages sought and to submit declarations establishing whether plaintiff and counsel qualify as high-frequency litigants, warning that failure to respond adequately could result in dismissal of the Unruh Act claim or the entire action.
key_cases_cited: City of Chicago v. Int'l Coll. of Surgeons, 522 U.S. 156 (1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Construction-related accessibility violation (specific accommodation not detailed in order to show cause)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court issued order to show cause regarding supplemental jurisdiction over Unruh Act claim; FHA claim itself not yet addressed on merits; case remains pending pending plaintiff's response to jurisdictional inquiry.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act claim; California Unruh Act construction-related accessibility claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Court issued order to show cause regarding whether to decline supplemental jurisdiction over state law Unruh Act claim based on California's heightened pleading requirements for construction-related accessibility claims and restrictions on high-frequency litigants; no merits determination made.

case_name: Emma Adams v. Aqua 388 Community Association et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested a reasonable parking accommodation from the HOA (specifics not detailed in this sanctions order).
key_holding: The court issued an order to show cause against plaintiff's counsel for improper closing argument that exploited an evidentiary exclusion the counsel himself had successfully obtained, suggesting the jury should draw an adverse inference from the absence of a witness counsel had excluded from testifying.
brief_summary: Emma Adams sued the Aqua 388 Community Association alleging Fair Housing Act violations for failure to provide a reasonable parking accommodation, prevailing at summary judgment and trial; the court subsequently issued an order to show cause against Adams's counsel for attorney misconduct during closing argument, where counsel improperly argued the jury should draw an adverse inference from the absence of a witness whose testimony counsel had successfully moved to exclude.
key_cases_cited: Evon v. L. Offs. of Sidney Mickell, 688 F.3d 1015 (9th Cir. 2012)
Jackson v. Park, 66 Cal. App. 5th 1196 (2021)
Hansen v. Warco Steel Corp., 237 Cal. App. 2d 870 (1965)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable parking accommodation for a condominium unit owner
fha_claims.reasoning: The Court granted summary judgment in Plaintiff's favor on the reasonable accommodation claim, finding that Defendants violated the Fair Housing Act by failing to provide the requested parking space accommodation. The case then proceeded to trial on damages, where the principal dispute was whether Defendants acted with malice, oppression, or reckless disregard.

source_file: 10168164_2024_United African-Asian Abilities Club v. 6335 Whitsett Ave LLC_cacd
case_name: United African-Asian Abilities Club, et al. v. 6335 Whitsett Ave LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED - this procedural order does not describe the specific accommodation request; it addresses supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims.
key_holding: The court ordered plaintiff to show cause why it should not decline supplemental jurisdiction over plaintiff's Unruh Act and state law claims, and required plaintiff to identify statutory damages sought and provide declarations regarding high-frequency litigant status.
brief_summary: United African-Asian Abilities Club and another plaintiff sued 6335 Whitsett Ave LLC and related defendants asserting federal and California Fair Housing Act claims along with ADA and Unruh Act claims. The court issued a procedural order requiring plaintiffs to show cause why supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims should not be declined, and warning of potential dismissal for failure to comply with heightened pleading requirements for construction-related accessibility claims.
key_cases_cited: City of Chicago v. Int'l Coll. of Surgeons, 522 U.S. 156 (1997)
Link v. Wabash R. Co., 370 U.S. 626 (1962)
Hells Canyon Pres. Council v. U.S. Forest Serv., 403 F.3d 683 (9th Cir. 2005)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Construction-related accessibility violation at place of public accommodation (6335 Whitsett Ave)
fha_claims.disposition: Order to Show Cause re Supplemental Jurisdiction
fha_claims.reasoning: Court issued order to show cause regarding supplemental jurisdiction over FHA claims; no substantive ruling on merits. The opinion addresses only jurisdictional and procedural issues, not the underlying FHA design and construction claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act claim; California Unruh Act claim; California Fair Housing Act claim
fha_claims.disposition: Order to Show Cause re Supplemental Jurisdiction
fha_claims.reasoning: Court issued order to show cause regarding whether to decline supplemental jurisdiction over state-law claims (Unruh Act, California Fair Housing Act) and ADA claim. No substantive merits analysis; court is addressing jurisdictional discretion under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c) and California's heightened pleading requirements for construction-related accessibility claims.

case_name: Deepa Patel et al. v. City of Stanton et al.
accommodation_description: Motel owner and business entity allege City revoked motel permit and issued citations because City sought to drive out minority guests and Asian-Indian owner.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' FHA claim under § 3604(b) because the complaint failed to specify how plaintiffs themselves were injured by a discriminatory housing practice, what constituted the discriminatory practice, and which defendant was responsible, while also noting uncertainty whether the FHA applies to motels as temporary shelters.
brief_summary: Deepa Patel and California One Hospitality LLC, owners of Dixie Orange County Motel, sued the City of Stanton and unknown officials alleging the City revoked their motel permit and issued administrative citations because City officials sought to drive out low-income minority guests and the Asian-Indian owner. The court dismissed the complaint for failure to comply with Rule 8(a) pleading requirements, finding the FHA claim vague as to the discriminatory practice, injury, and responsible defendant, while granting leave to amend the federal claims and declining supplemental jurisdiction over state writ claims.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Monell v. Dep't of Soc. Servs. of City of New York, 436 U.S. 658 (1978)
Texas Dept. of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Cmtys. Project, 135 S. Ct. 2507 (2015)
Cmty. House, Inc. v. City of Boise, 490 F.3d 1041 (9th Cir. 2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to state a plausible FHA claim under § 3604(b) because they did not sufficiently specify how they themselves were injured by a discriminatory housing practice, did not clearly allege whether they asserted disparate treatment or disparate impact, and failed to establish that a motel qualifies as a 'dwelling' under the FHA.
