The court granted summary judgment for defendants, finding the County failed to present admissible expert evidence of an integrated discriminatory scheme or robust statistical causality, and failed to demonstrate actual compensable out-of-pocket damages from the alleged discriminatory foreclosures.
key_cases_cited: Bank of Am. Corp. v. City of Miami, Fla., 137 S. Ct. 1296 (2017)
Texas Dept. of Housing & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 135 S. Ct. 2507 (2015)
Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharms., 509 U.S. 579 (1993)
City of Miami v. Bank of Am. Corp., 171 F. Supp. 3d 1314 (S.D. Fla. 2016)
Cty. of Cook v. Wells Fargo & Co., 314 F. Supp. 3d 975 (N.D. Ill. 2018)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges disparate impact from equity stripping scheme affecting lending, servicing, and foreclosure practices
fha_claims.reasoning: County failed to present evidence of an integrated equity stripping scheme and lacked sufficient evidence of robust causal connection between defendants' practices and disparate impact on minority borrowers. Expert testimony was excluded as unreliable under Daubert.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges intentional discrimination targeting minority borrowers for higher-cost, higher-risk loans
fha_claims.reasoning: County failed to present evidence of intentional discrimination. Statistical disparities alone are insufficient to raise inference of discriminatory purpose without evidence that defendants selected their practices because of adverse effects on minorities. Evidence of data mining, financial incentives, and underwriting departures did not establish race-based targeting.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges disparate impact from defendants' servicing and foreclosure practices
fha_claims.reasoning: County's expert testimony regarding disparate impact in servicing and foreclosure practices was excluded as unreliable because the expert analyzed aggregated data across multiple lenders and products without tailoring analysis to specific defendant policies, contrary to federal regulatory standards. County failed to establish robust causal connection between specific policies and disparate impact.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Damages claim for out-of-pocket costs incurred in processing foreclosures; County also asserted resource-shifting/opportunity cost theory
fha_claims.reasoning: County failed to prove proximate causation of damages under City of Miami standard. Budget documents showed County's appropriations and expenditures remained stable despite spike in foreclosures, contradicting claim of increased out-of-pocket costs. Resource-shifting theory lacked evidentiary support and included overhead costs too remote from defendants' conduct to satisfy directness requirement.

source_file: 10178987_2024_Connectors Realty Group Corporation, The v. State Farm Fire _ Casualty Company_ilnd
case_name: Connectors Realty Group Corporation v. State Farm Fire & Casualty Company
accommodation_description: Not applicable - this case involves alleged racial discrimination in insurance claim denials based on zip code demographics, not a disability accommodation request
key_holding: The court denied summary judgment on the race discrimination claims (Counts I-II) because genuine issues of material fact exist regarding whether State Farm's investigation and denial of insurance claims was motivated by race, but denied class certification because individual issues predominate and plaintiff Williams presented serious credibility problems making him inadequate as a class representative.
brief_summary: The Connectors Realty Group Corporation and Darryl Williams sued State Farm Fire & Casualty Company alleging the insurer violated the Fair Housing Act and 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981-1982 by discriminatorily investigating and denying insurance claims for properties located in majority African-American zip codes. The court denied State Farm's motion for summary judgment on the discrimination claims, finding genuine disputes of material fact exist based on evidence including a former manager's testimony about a discriminatory policy and statistical analysis showing correlation between zip code demographics and claim denials, but denied the plaintiffs' motion for class certification because individual causation questions predominate and Williams' credibility issues made him an inadequate class representative.
key_cases_cited: N.A.A.C.P. v. American Family Mutual Insurance Co., 978 F.2d 287 (7th Cir. 1992)
United Farm Bureau Mutual Insurance Co. v. Metropolitan Human Relations Commission, 24 F.3d 1008 (7th Cir. 1994)
Thompson v. North American Stainless, LP, 562 U.S. 170 (2011)
Shaikh v. City of Chicago, 2001 WL 123784 (N.D. Ill. 2001)
CE Design Ltd. v. King Architectural Metals, Inc., 637 F.3d 721 (7th Cir. 2011)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied summary judgment on the FHA disparate treatment claim (Count I), finding that genuine issues of material fact exist regarding whether defendant's policy of investigating and denying insurance claims in zip codes with majority Black residents was racially motivated. Plaintiff's deposition testimony about racially charged language, expert declaration regarding the 'fill the cups' policy, and statistical analysis created sufficient evidence for jury consideration.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 and 1982 (racial discrimination in contract); 215 ILCS 5/155 (Illinois insurance law); breach of contract; breach of duty to indemnify
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied summary judgment on the §§ 1981 and 1982 discrimination claims (Count II) and state law claims (Counts III-IX, XIV) because they depend on the success of the FHA discrimination claim, which survived summary judgment. The same evidence of racial motivation and policy targeting applies to these claims.

source_file: 10179253_2024_Legal Aid Chicago v. Hunter Properties, Inc._ilnd
case_name: Legal Aid Chicago v. Hunter Properties, Inc.
accommodation_description: Fair housing organization challenges landlord's blanket no-evictions screening policy as having disparate impact on Black renters
key_holding: The court granted dismissal for lack of standing, finding Legal Aid Chicago failed to allege a concrete injury beyond ordinary program costs because the alleged injuries (sealing eviction records, litigating eviction cases, education) were precisely the organization's core mission activities rather than new burdens imposed by the defendant.
brief_summary: Legal Aid Chicago sued Hunter Properties, a Chicago property management company, alleging that its blanket no-evictions screening policy violated the Fair Housing Act by having a disparate impact on Black renters. The district court granted the motion to dismiss, finding that Legal Aid Chicago lacked organizational standing because it failed to allege a concrete injury beyond ordinary program costs—the activities it claimed as injuries (litigating eviction cases, sealing records, providing education) were precisely the organization's core mission, not new burdens imposed by the defendant's policy.
key_cases_cited: Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine, 602 U.S. 367 (2024)
Common Cause Indiana v. Lawson, 937 F.3d 944 (7th Cir. 2019)
Democratic Party of Wisconsin v. Vos, 966 F.3d 581 (7th Cir. 2020)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Legal Aid Chicago lacked Article III standing to bring the disparate impact claim because it failed to allege a concrete injury in fact to the organization itself. The alleged injury—diversion of resources to combat evictions and eviction-related housing denials—constitutes ordinary program costs within the organization's core mission, not a perceptible impairment of its ability to provide services. The court found no real-world interaction between Legal Aid Chicago and Hunter Properties, and the injury was merely a setback to the organization's abstract social interests in housing justice.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Legal Aid Chicago lacked Article III standing to bring the disparate impact claim based on race and sex discrimination against black women renters for the same reasons as Claim 1. The alleged injury to the organization itself was insufficient to establish standing, as it consisted of ordinary program costs and abstract social interests rather than a concrete, perceptible impairment of the organization's ability to provide services.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Illinois Consumer Fraud and Deceptive Business Practices Act, 815 Ill. Comp. Stat. 505/2
fha_claims.reasoning: Legal Aid Chicago lacked Article III standing to bring the state-law unfair residential leasing claim for the same reasons as the FHA claims. The court did not reach the merits of the state-law claim because subject matter jurisdiction was lacking due to the plaintiff's failure to establish standing.

source_file: 10179261_2024_Access Living of Metropolitan Chicago v. City Of Chicago_ilnd
case_name: Access Living of Metropolitan Chicago, Inc. v. City of Chicago
accommodation_description: Access Living alleges the City of Chicago's affordable housing funding and oversight program fails to ensure compliance with federal accessibility requirements, effectively excluding people with disabilities from affordable housing.
key_holding: The court denied summary judgment for the City, finding genuine issues of fact on whether Chicago's affordable housing scheme is a 'program or activity' subject to ADA, Section 504, and FHA liability, and whether the City's role in funding, approving construction, and contracting for compliance makes it responsible for design-and-construction accessibility failures.
brief_summary: Access Living of Metropolitan Chicago sued the City of Chicago alleging that the City's affordable housing funding program discriminates against people with disabilities by failing to ensure housing developments comply with federal accessibility laws under the ADA, Section 504, and Fair Housing Act. The court denied the City's motion for summary judgment, finding triable issues of fact on whether Chicago's substantial involvement in funding, approving, and contracting for accessibility compliance renders the City liable for design-and-construction accessibility failures under the FHA and for program accessibility under the ADA and Section 504.
key_cases_cited: Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Oconomowoc Res. Programs, Inc. v. City of Milwaukee, 300 F.3d 775 (7th Cir. 2002)
Ashby v. Warrick Cnty. Sch. Corp., 908 F.3d 225 (7th Cir. 2018)
Alexander v. Choate, 469 U.S. 287 (1985)
N.A.A.C.P. v. Am. Fam. Mut. Ins. Co., 978 F.2d 287 (7th Cir. 1992)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to design and construct affordable housing dwellings in a manner that is readily accessible to and usable by persons with disabilities, including those with mobility, visual, and hearing disabilities
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found a genuine issue of material fact regarding whether the City's extensive role in funding, approving, and overseeing the design and construction of affordable housing developments renders it liable under FHA § 3604(f)(3)(C) for failure to ensure accessible design. The FHA's prohibitions are outcome-focused and not actor-specific, and the City's contractual obligations and permit-review role create a jury question on liability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination in the terms, conditions, or privileges of rental of dwellings and provision of services or facilities in connection with dwellings based on disability
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied summary judgment on the FHA disparate treatment claim, finding that Access Living adequately alleged that the City's failure to ensure compliance with federal accessibility laws in its affordable housing program effectively excludes persons with disabilities from equal opportunity to obtain affordable housing, creating a jury question on whether the City discriminated based on disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (42 U.S.C. § 12131 et seq.), Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act (29 U.S.C. § 794 et seq.)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied summary judgment on ADA Title II and Section 504 claims, finding that a reasonable jury could determine that the City's affordable housing scheme constitutes a 'program or activity' of the City under both statutes, and that Access Living's clients were denied the benefits of that program based on disability. The City cannot avoid statutory obligations by delegating operations to private developers, and the City has regulatory obligations to monitor subcontractors for compliance with federal accessibility laws.

case_name: Gary Copeny v. Diana England, Matt Evans, Diana Wright
accommodation_description: No accommodation request was made; plaintiff alleges racial discrimination in the purchase of his home and return of earnest money.
key_holding: The court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim, finding no plausible federal claims against the named defendants including insufficient factual allegations connecting any defendant to racial discrimination in housing.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Gary Copeny filed suit against Diana England, Matt Evans, and Diana Wright alleging racial discrimination in the purchase of his home in Hancock County, Indiana, including claims that he was defrauded in the sale and subjected to ongoing mistreatment. The court screened the complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B) and dismissed it for failure to state a plausible claim, finding the complaint lacked factual allegations connecting any named defendant to discriminatory conduct.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Patel v. Heidelberger, 6 Fed. App'x 436 (7th Cir. 2001)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint fails to allege sufficient factual content to state a plausible claim for racial discrimination in the sale or terms of the home. Plaintiff's allegations that defendants failed to return earnest money and that 'vagrants' committed crimes do not connect these incidents to plaintiff's race, and plaintiff does not allege that named defendants knew about or could have prevented the alleged conduct.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Constitutional claims (Fourth, Eighth, Thirteenth, Fourteenth Amendments), Section 1584 (involuntary servitude), Civil Rights Act of 1964, state tort law
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacks subject matter jurisdiction over the action. Constitutional claims against private citizens (not state actors) are not cognizable; Section 1584 is a criminal statute with no private civil right of action; the Civil Rights Act of 1964 does not apply to housing discrimination; and state law claims are barred by lack of diversity jurisdiction (all parties are Indiana citizens).

source_file: 10180547_2024_FAIR HOUSING CENTER OF CENTRAL INDIANA, INC. v. M_J MANAGEMENT COMPANY, LLC, d_b_a THE SEXTON COMPANIES_insd
case_name: Fair Housing Center of Central Indiana, Inc. v. M&J Management Company, LLC, d/b/a The Sexton Companies
accommodation_description: Two-person-per-bedroom occupancy policy that excludes families with three or more minor children from renting two-bedroom units
key_holding: The court found that plaintiff established a prima facie case of disparate impact based on familial status, but denied both parties' summary judgment motions because genuine disputes exist regarding whether defendants' occupancy policy is necessary to achieve substantial, legitimate, nondiscriminatory interests.
brief_summary: Fair Housing Center of Central Indiana sued M&J Management (Sexton Companies) alleging that defendants' two-person-per-bedroom occupancy policy has a disparate impact on families with minor children in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The court denied both parties' cross-motions for summary judgment, finding that while plaintiff established a prima facie case, genuine disputes remain about whether defendants' occupancy standard is necessary to achieve substantial, legitimate, nondiscriminatory interests.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dept. of Housing and Comm. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 560 (1992)
City of Joliet v. New W., L.P., 825 F.3d 827 (7th Cir. 2016)
Louisiana Fair Hous. Action Cntr., Inc. v. Azalea Garden Properties, LLC, 82 F.4th 345 (5th Cir. 2023)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff established prima facie case of disparate impact under FHA § 3604(a) based on occupancy restriction of two persons per bedroom disproportionately excluding families with minor children (59 times greater exclusion rate for 5+ person households with children; 8-16 times greater for 3+ person households with children). However, genuine dispute of material fact remains whether defendants satisfied their burden to prove occupancy restriction is necessary to achieve substantial, legitimate, nondiscriminatory interests; defendants' evidence contained speculative and hypothetical claims without sufficient evidentiary support, requiring trial-level credibility determinations and weighing of evidence.

source_file: 10180644_2024_FAIR HOUSING CENTER OF CENTRAL INDIANA, INC. v. M_J MANAGEMENT COMPANY, LLC, d_b_a THE SEXTON COMPANIES_insd
case_name: Fair Housing Center of Central Indiana, Inc. v. M&J Management Company, LLC, d/b/a The Sexton Companies
accommodation_description: Defendants' occupancy standard limiting units to two occupants per bedroom allegedly discriminates against families with minor children.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion to preclude plaintiff's expert James Colbert from testifying at bench trial, finding his statistical methodology and qualifications sufficient for admissibility under Daubert, despite acknowledging valid concerns about his failure to consider extraneous variables.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Fair Housing Center of Central Indiana sued M&J Management Company and affiliated entities alleging that their two-occupants-per-bedroom occupancy standard discriminates against families with minor children in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The court denied defendants' motion to preclude expert testimony by plaintiff's statistician James Colbert, finding his data analysis methodology sufficiently reliable for admissibility at the upcoming bench trial despite concerns about his failure to account for alternative explanatory variables.
key_cases_cited: Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals, Inc., 509 U.S. 579 (1993)
Gopalratnam v. Hewlett-Packard Co., 877 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2017)
Kopplin v. Wisconsin Cent. Ltd., 914 F.3d 1099 (7th Cir. 2019)
Kawasaki Kisen Kaisha, Ltd. v. Plano Molding Co., 782 F.3d 353 (7th Cir. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Challenge to occupancy standard of two occupants per bedroom applied uniformly across all floor plans and ages of occupants
fha_claims.disposition: Daubert Motion to Preclude Expert Testimony
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied defendants' motion to preclude expert testimony regarding disparate impact analysis. The claim itself has not been decided on the merits; the court ruled only on the admissibility of plaintiff's expert's statistical analysis at the upcoming bench trial. The underlying disparate impact claim remains pending for trial.

source_file: 10180688_2024_FAIR HOUSING CENTER OF CENTRAL INDIANA, INC. v. M_J MANAGEMENT COMPANY, LLC, d_b_a THE SEXTON COMPANIES_insd
case_name: Fair Housing Center of Central Indiana, Inc. v. M&J Management Company, LLC, d/b/a The Sexton Companies
accommodation_description: No accommodation request at issue; this is a disparate impact challenge to occupancy restrictions affecting families with children.
key_holding: The court denied Defendants' motion to exclude evidence of rules governing children's use of common facilities, finding such evidence relevant to assessing whether occupancy restrictions constitute disparate impact; the court also denied Plaintiff's motion to preclude Defendants' Rule 30(b)(6) designee testimony but granted Plaintiff's motion to prevent Defendants from adding unidentified witnesses.
brief_summary: Fair Housing Center of Central Indiana sued M&J Management Company (d/b/a The Sexton Companies) alleging that Defendants' occupancy restrictions and rules governing children's use of common facilities violate the Fair Housing Act by having a disparate impact on families with children. The court ruled on pre-trial evidentiary motions, denying Defendants' request to exclude evidence of their common facility rules and denying Plaintiff's motion to preclude supplemental Rule 30(b)(6) testimony, while granting Plaintiff's request to prevent Defendants from adding unidentified witnesses to their trial witness list.
key_cases_cited: Tex. Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Cmtys. Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Pack v. Fort Washington II, 689 F. Supp. 2d 1237 (E.D. Cal. 2009)
Jenkins v. Chrysler Motors Corp., 316 F.3d 663 (7th Cir. 2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied defendants' motion to exclude testimony and evidence regarding rules governing use of common facilities by children, finding such evidence relevant to plaintiff's disparate impact claims under the Fair Housing Act. The court determined that whether rules could be reasonably interpreted as safety precautions versus simple prohibitions on children's use of facilities was material to the disparate impact analysis and to defendants' occupancy restriction defense.

source_file: 10180724_2024_United States v. Fox Run Apartments, LLC_ksd
case_name: United States of America v. Fox Run Apartments, LLC
accommodation_description: Veteran with PTSD/ADHD/depression requested to keep his 70-pound Doberman Pinscher emotional support animal despite a 25-pound pet weight limit.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion for attorney's fees and costs under the EAJA, finding the government's FHA reasonable accommodation claim was neither frivolous nor lacking substantial justification, as there was a reasonable basis for the factual allegations and legal theories supporting the failure-to-accommodate claim.
brief_summary: The United States sued Fox Run Apartments and related defendants under the FHA alleging failure to accommodate a veteran's ESA request for a 70-pound Doberman Pinscher, but voluntarily dismissed the claims; the court then denied defendants' motion for attorney's fees and costs under the EAJA, finding the government's position was substantially justified because the record supported that the veteran had a disability, requested a reasonable accommodation, and defendants failed to offer alternatives before he withdrew his application.
key_cases_cited: Dubois v. Ass'n of Apartment Owners of 2987 Kalakaua, 453 F.3d 1175 (9th Cir. 2006)
Christiansburg Garment Co. v. EEOC, 434 U.S. 412 (1978)
Hadden v. Bowen, 851 F.2d 1266 (10th Cir. 1988)
Pierce v. Underwood, 487 U.S. 552 (1988)
Gutierrez v. Sullivan, 953 F.2d 579 (10th Cir. 1992)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to accommodate Versola's request to live with his 70-pound Doberman Pinscher emotional support animal (ESA) by refusing to grant reasonable accommodation in rules, policies, practices, or services necessary to afford him equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found the government's claim plausible under Iqbal/Twombly, satisfying all five elements of a failure-to-accommodate claim: Versola had a disability (PTSD, ADHD, depression), defendants knew of it, accommodation was necessary for equal enjoyment, the ESA request was reasonable, and defendants refused accommodation. The claim survived the motion to dismiss but was subsequently voluntarily dismissed by the government before merits resolution.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination in terms and conditions of rental by refusing to grant reasonable accommodation to allow Versola to move in with his assistance animal and by requiring his psychiatrist to complete an unnecessary third-party verification form by an arbitrary deadline.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found this claim plausible, supported by factual allegations that defendants imposed an arbitrary June 26 deadline for third-party verification despite knowing Versola's psychiatrist was unavailable until June 29, and failed to offer alternative accommodations before Versola withdrew his application. The claim survived the motion to dismiss but was subsequently voluntarily dismissed by the government.

case_name: Edwards v. Klinedinst
accommodation_description: The court does not analyze any specific accommodation request; this opinion addresses only whether the prior state-court eviction judgment has preclusive effect on the federal FHA claims, denying defendant's summary judgment motion on res judicata grounds.
key_holding: Kansas Stat. Ann. § 61-3802 limits the preclusive effect of prior eviction judgments under the Kansas Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, allowing plaintiffs' Fair Housing Act and Section 1981 claims to proceed despite the prior state-court action.
brief_summary: Kenneth and Taaliba Edwards sued their landlord Betty Klinedinst alleging Fair Housing Act claims and Section 1981 claims for race discrimination arising from a residential tenancy in Lansing, Kansas. The court denied Klinedinst's motion for summary judgment on res judicata grounds, holding that Kansas's special eviction judgment statute (§ 61-3802) limits preclusion so that claims not included in the prior state-court eviction judgment—including federal FHA claims—may proceed.
key_cases_cited: Herington v. City of Wichita, 500 P.3d 1168 (Kan. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Three FHA claims asserted in federal complaint; specific theories not detailed in opinion
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied defendant's motion for summary judgment on res judicata grounds under Kansas law K.S.A. § 61-3802, which provides that a judgment in an eviction proceeding shall not bar subsequent lawsuits for claims not included in the prior judgment. The FHA claims were not addressed in the state court eviction proceeding and thus are not precluded.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1981 race discrimination and retaliation claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied defendant's motion for summary judgment on res judicata grounds; § 1981 claims were not included in the prior state court judgment and thus are not precluded under K.S.A. § 61-3802.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VII employment discrimination claim (hostile work environment and retaliation)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff filed suit 98 days after receiving EEOC right-to-sue letter on June 7, 2023, exceeding the 90-day filing deadline under 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-5(f)(1). Even applying a five-day presumption of receipt, the suit was untimely filed on September 13, 2023.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VII hostile work environment claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege membership in a protected class under Title VII (race, color, religion, sex, or national origin), provided only conclusory statements of harassment without specific facts, and did not adequately connect alleged harassment to any protected class membership or demonstrate severity and pervasiveness required for hostile work environment claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VII retaliation claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged retaliation for reporting 'illegal acts revolving around money,' but these allegations sound in criminal law and corporate policy violations, not Title VII protected activity. Reporting non-Title VII violations does not constitute protected opposition to discrimination under 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-3(a).

source_file: 10181821_2024_Military Road Revitalization Company, LLC v. St. Tammany Parish Government_laed
case_name: Military Road Revitalization Company, LLC et al. v. St. Tammany Parish Government et al.
accommodation_description: Developer sued municipality over moratorium ordinance allegedly blocking affordable housing development serving protected classes including persons with disabilities
key_holding: The court granted Safety National's motion to dismiss the intentional discrimination FHA claims as excluded from insurance coverage but denied the motion as to the disparate-impact FHA claim because it does not require a showing of intent and therefore does not fall within the policy's exclusion for intentional violations of law.
brief_summary: Military Road Revitalization Company sued St. Tammany Parish Government and its insurer Safety National, alleging that a municipal moratorium ordinance blocking an affordable housing development violated the Fair Housing Act by having a disparate impact on protected classes including African Americans, Hispanics, and persons with disabilities. The court granted Safety National's motion to dismiss the intentional discrimination claims as excluded from insurance coverage but denied the motion as to the disparate-impact claim, finding it does not require a showing of intent and therefore may be covered.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Tex. Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Cmtys. Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that Military Road's FHA disparate-treatment claim requires a showing of intentional discrimination, which constitutes an intentional violation of law excluded from the insurance policy. The claim was dismissed as excluded from coverage under the policy's exclusionary provision for intentional violations of law.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court declined to dismiss Military Road's FHA disparate-impact claim because disparate-impact claims do not require a showing of intent under the burden-shifting framework adopted by the Fifth Circuit. The court found that it is possible a jury could accept allegations of discriminatory impact while rejecting allegations of intent, creating a possibility of liability not unambiguously excluded from the insurance policy.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Louisiana Equal Housing Opportunity Act, ADA Title II, Rehabilitation Act § 504, Title VI Civil Rights Act of 1964, Louisiana Direct Action Statute
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA claims (state housing law, ADA, Rehabilitation Act, Title VI, and direct action against insurer) were dismissed as excluded from the insurance policy because they require a showing of intentional discrimination, which constitutes an intentional violation of law excluded from coverage.

source_file: 10181920_2024_Stennis v. The Moorings of Oak Harbor Property Owners' Association LLC_laed
case_name: Shalmon J. Stennis et al. v. The Moorings of Oak Harbor Property Owners' Association Inc. et al.
accommodation_description: Black homeowners allege HOA defendants selectively enforced community restrictions, issued fines, deactivated entry decal, and engaged in coordinated harassment against plaintiffs because of their race.
key_holding: The court denied dismissal of plaintiffs' Fair Housing Act claims under §§ 3604(a) and (b), finding plaintiffs adequately alleged discriminatory enforcement of HOA restrictions based on race and a hostile environment claim, but granted dismissal of plaintiffs' intentional infliction of emotional distress claims as insufficiently pleaded.
brief_summary: Black homeowners sued their homeowners association, property management company, and board president alleging race-based discrimination and harassment including selective enforcement of community restrictions, excessive fines, and deactivation of entry access. The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss plaintiffs' Fair Housing Act claims under §§ 3604(a) and (b), finding sufficient factual allegations of discriminatory treatment and hostile environment, but dismissed plaintiffs' state law intentional infliction of emotional distress claims as insufficiently pleaded.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Cox v. City of Dallas, 430 F.3d 734 (5th Cir. 2005)
City of Edmonds v. Oxford House, Inc., 514 U.S. 725 (1995)
Maldonado v. FirstService Residential, Inc., No. CV H-20-1484 (S.D. Tex. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss FHA § 3604(a)-(b) disparate treatment claim alleging racial discrimination in terms, conditions, and privileges of housing through unequal enforcement of community restrictions, excessive fining, and denial of access. Plaintiffs adequately pleaded facts showing race-based discrimination under Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court did not address FHA § 3617 harassment/interference claim in motion to dismiss because defendants did not seek dismissal of this claim. Claim survives and remains pending.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1981, 42 U.S.C. § 1982 (Civil Rights Act race discrimination in contracting and property rights); 42 U.S.C. § 1985(3) (conspiracy to deprive equal protection); Louisiana state law negligence and intentional infliction of emotional distress
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss § 1981 and § 1982 claims for race discrimination in contracting and property rights, finding plaintiffs adequately pleaded unequal enforcement of HOA restrictions against them compared to similarly situated white residents. Court also denied dismissal of § 1985(3) conspiracy claim, finding sufficient factual allegations of racial animus and coordinated discriminatory conduct. State law negligence claims survived; IIED claims were dismissed for failure to allege extreme and outrageous conduct.

source_file: 10182119_2024_Believe TGH LLC v. Pointe Coupee Parish_lamd
case_name: Believe TGH, LLC, et al. v. Pointe Coupee Parish
accommodation_description: Therapeutic group home operator seeks zoning variance to expand the definition of 'family' to allow more than four unrelated minors with disabilities to reside together in a Rural Agricultural zoning district.
key_holding: The court denied reconsideration of its prior ruling denying partial summary judgment because genuine disputes of material fact remain regarding whether the requested zoning accommodation is reasonable and necessary for the therapeutic group home to operate.
brief_summary: Believe TGH, LLC and related entities, which operate therapeutic group homes for minors with disabilities, sued Pointe Coupee Parish after the Parish denied their variance request to expand the zoning definition of 'family' to allow group homes with more than four unrelated residents. The court denied reconsideration of its prior ruling denying partial summary judgment, finding genuine disputes of material fact remain on whether the accommodation is reasonable and necessary under the Fair Housing Act.
key_cases_cited: Oxford House, Inc. v. Browning, 266 F. Supp. 3d 896 (M.D. La. 2017)
Oxford House, Inc. v. City of Baton Rouge, 932 F. Supp. 2d 683 (M.D. La. 2013)
Groome Resources, Ltd. v. Parish of Jefferson, 52 F. Supp. 2d 721 (E.D. La. 1999)
Allen v. Envirogreen Landscape Prof'ls, Inc., 721 F. App'x 322 (5th Cir. 2017)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Variance to expand the zoning ordinance's definition of 'family' to permit more than four unrelated individuals to live together in a single-family dwelling, to allow operation of a therapeutic group home for minors with disabilities (Lettsworth Home) in a Rural Agricultural zoning district
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether the requested accommodation was reasonable and whether it was necessary to afford equal opportunity to use and enjoy housing. On the reasonableness prong, the court found disputed facts regarding community opposition, the group home's fit with permitted uses in the agricultural district, and whether undue financial or administrative burdens would be imposed on the Parish. On the necessity prong, the court found a genuine dispute regarding whether a second group home was 'essential' given that the existing Bayou Run Home had been operating under capacity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: American Disabilities Act (Title II), Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, Louisiana Equal Housing Opportunity Act, Louisiana public accommodations law
fha_claims.reasoning: The court addressed non-FHA claims brought under the ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and state law in the same summary judgment ruling. The court denied summary judgment on these claims as well, finding genuine disputes of material fact regarding the reasonableness and necessity of the requested accommodation under the applicable legal standards.

source_file: 10182408_2024_Wood v. Kansas City Southern Railway Co_lawd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VII retaliation, ADA discrimination, ADA retaliation, ADA failure to accommodate, ADA interference, FMLA retaliation, FMLA interference
fha_claims.reasoning: All claims dismissed on summary judgment. For ADA discrimination and retaliation claims, plaintiff failed to establish prima facie case or show pretext for legitimate nondiscriminatory reasons. For failure to accommodate claim, plaintiff failed to exhaust administrative remedies by not including the claim in the EEOC charge. For ADA interference claim, plaintiff failed to show KCSR interfered on account of protected activity with intent to discriminate. For FMLA retaliation and interference claims, plaintiff failed to establish eligibility and could not overcome employer's legitimate reasons for denial of leave.

source_file: 10182858_2022_Estate of DaMon R. Fisher v. City of Annapolis_mdd
case_name: Estate of DaMon R. Fisher v. City of Annapolis
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation request at issue; this case concerns HACA's policy of not inspecting and licensing public housing, which allegedly disproportionately harmed African American residents and contributed to tenant DaMon Fisher's death from mold-related respiratory illness.
key_holding: The court denied dismissal of Fisher's FHA disparate impact claim, finding that the non-inspection policy bore more heavily on African Americans, historical background supported an inference of discriminatory intent, and Fisher adequately alleged injury from discriminatory housing conditions; however, the § 1986 claim was dismissed as untimely.
brief_summary: DaMon Fisher's estate sued the City of Annapolis and the Housing Authority of the City of Annapolis (HACA) alleging that the City's longstanding policy of exempting HACA public housing from inspection and licensing requirements violated the Fair Housing Act and civil rights laws, and that resulting mold conditions in Fisher's apartment caused his death. The court denied dismissal of Fisher's FHA disparate impact claim, finding sufficient allegations that the non-inspection policy disproportionately harmed African American public housing residents and supported an inference of discriminatory intent, while dismissing the § 1986 claim as untimely.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Reyes v. Waples Mobile Home Park Ltd. P'ship, 903 F.3d 415 (4th Cir. 2018)
Vill. of Arlington Heights v. Metro. Hous. Develop. Corp., 429 U.S. 252 (1977)
White v. City of Annapolis, 439 F. Supp. 3d 527 (D. Md. 2020)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Fisher sufficiently pleaded disparate impact under the FHA by alleging that HACA's non-inspection policy had a racially disproportionate effect on African Americans and contributed to housing segregation. The court rejected HACA's arguments regarding the appropriate comparison group and HACA's agency in the policy, finding the claim plausibly stated at the pleading stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1982 (Civil Rights Act of 1866), 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (Equal Protection Clause), 42 U.S.C. § 1985 (conspiracy to deprive rights), Maryland Declaration of Rights Article 24, Maryland Consumer Protection Act, Annapolis Municipal Code § 18.08.010, negligence
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied dismissal of the § 1982, § 1983, § 1985, and state constitutional claims without deciding the merits, finding that Fisher had pleaded sufficient facts to survive the motion to dismiss under the Iqbal/Twombly standard. The court also found the Maryland Consumer Protection Act claim timely and plausibly stated, as Fisher alleged HACA misrepresented that the unit was licensed when it was not, which carried safety inspection assurances. The § 1986 claim was dismissed as untimely under the one-year statute of limitations.

source_file: 10182954_2024_Siguel v. King Farm Citizens Assembly, Inc._mdd
case_name: Edward Siguel v. King Farm Citizens Assembly, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested various reasonable modifications and accommodations purportedly necessary due to his disability, including: (1) construction or use of a roof balcony ('Balcony Requests'); (2) installation of storage sheds on his front porch and in the back of his house; (3) installation of a brick patio over soil ('Yard/Storage Requests'); and (4) installation of a trellis. The court found the balcony, patio, and trellis requests insufficiently pleaded as 'necessary' under the FHA, while the storage shed modification claims survived dismissal as to KFCA and the BFMA Defendants.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's pro se motion for reconsideration of its prior interlocutory order largely dismissing his FHA claims, finding he failed to present new evidence, a change in applicable law, or clear error causing manifest injustice under the Carlson standard.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Edward Siguel brought FHA and ADA claims against his homeowners association (King Farm Citizens Assembly), individual board members, an attorney, and architects, alleging denial of reasonable modifications and accommodations including a roof balcony, storage sheds, a brick patio, and trellis. In an earlier ruling, the court granted in part and denied in part defendants' motions to dismiss, dismissing most counts but allowing Count VI (storage shed modification requests) to proceed against KFCA and the BFMA Defendants. In this opinion, the court denied plaintiff's motion for reconsideration of that prior ruling, holding that plaintiff failed to identify new litigation-produced evidence, a change in applicable law, or a clear error rising to the level of manifest injustice as required by Fourth Circuit precedent.
key_cases_cited: Vorchheimer v. Philadelphian Owner's Ass'n, 903 F.3d 100 (3d Cir. 2018)
Gavin v. Spring Ridge Conservancy, 934 F.2d 605 (4th Cir. 1991)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
U.S. Tobacco Coop., Inc. v. Big S. Wholesale of Va., LLC, 899 F.3d 236 (4th Cir. 2018)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Roof balcony modification/accommodation
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed Count II (reasonable accommodation for roof balcony) under Iqbal/Twombly pleading standard, finding that when construing facts in plaintiff's favor, the balcony accommodation was not 'necessary' as defined by the FHA—it was merely 'preferable' but not 'essential.'

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable modifications for storage sheds on front porch and back of house
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss as to Count VI for storage shed modifications against KFCA and BFMA Defendants, finding that plaintiff sufficiently pleaded necessity of these modifications when facts were construed liberally in plaintiff's favor. Claim survives MTD but merits not yet reached.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Yard/storage requests pertaining to brick patio over soil and trellis
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed portions of Count VI related to patio and trellis modifications, finding that even when liberally construing facts in plaintiff's favor, neither request clearly pleaded necessity as required by the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to allow reasonable modifications (roof balcony) in violation of FHA
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed Count I (reasonable modifications for roof balcony) under Iqbal/Twombly standard, finding that the balcony modification was not 'necessary' as defined by the FHA but merely 'preferable.'

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Disparate impact claim related to roof balcony
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed Count III (disparate impact related to roof balcony) for failure to meet pleading standards of Iqbal and Twombly; plaintiff failed to plausibly allege disparate impact.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Disparate impact claim related to roof balcony (Count IV)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed Count IV (disparate impact) for failure to meet Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards; court found that facts as confusingly pleaded seemed to suggest 24 C.F.R. § 1007 is a separate cause of action, which it is not.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation in violation of FHA for requesting roof balcony accommodation
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed Count V (retaliation) because the balcony requests were not necessary accommodations/modifications, therefore there was no protected activity, and plaintiff's vague and rambling factual assertions did not plausibly demonstrate a causal nexus between the accommodation request and alleged retaliatory actions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Intentional discrimination in violation of FHA
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed Count VIII (intentional discrimination) for failure to meet Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards; plaintiff failed to plausibly allege intentional discrimination based on disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III claims (Counts II and IX); declaratory relief (Count VII); forced labor/trafficking claims under 15 U.S.C. §§ 1589, 1590 (Count X)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed Counts II and IX (ADA claims) because the lawsuit involves a private residence and homeowners association, so the ADA does not apply. Court dismissed Count VII (declaratory relief) for failure to adequately plead any cause of action. Court dismissed Count X (forced labor/trafficking) for failure to sufficiently allege facts establishing a forced labor claim under federal law.

source_file: 10182963_2024_Siguel v. King Farm Citizens Assembly, Inc._mdd
case_name: Edward Siguel v. King Farm Citizens Assembly, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested permission to install storage sheds on his front porch and in the back of his house as a reasonable modification and/or accommodation, asserting that the sheds were causally connected to and necessary due to his disability (handicap status) to afford him full enjoyment of his dwelling under the FHA.
key_holding: The court denied the BFMA Defendants' motion for reconsideration of the interlocutory order denying their motion to dismiss Count VI (reasonable modification claim for storage sheds), finding that the defendants failed to establish substantially different evidence, a change in applicable law, or clear error causing manifest injustice under the Carlson framework.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Edward Siguel sued King Farm Citizens Assembly and numerous other defendants, including architect Laurence Frank and Bennett Frank McCarthy Architects, Inc. (BFMA Defendants), alleging multiple Fair Housing Act violations arising from the denial of his requests to install storage sheds as a reasonable modification/accommodation for his disability. In a prior interlocutory order, the court granted motions to dismiss as to most counts but allowed Count VI (failure to permit reasonable modifications for storage sheds) to survive against Defendant KFCA and the BFMA Defendants. The BFMA Defendants then moved for reconsideration, arguing the court erred in not dismissing Count VI against them; the court denied that motion, finding the defendants were merely relitigating the prior ruling and had not met the high bar required for reconsideration of an interlocutory order.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
U.S. Tobacco Coop., Inc. v. Big South Wholesale of Va., LLC, 899 F.3d 236 (4th Cir. 2018)
Carlson v. Bos. Sci. Corp, 856 F.3d 320 (4th Cir. 2017)
Fair Hous. Ctr. of the Greater Palm Beaches, Inc. v. Sonoma Bay Cmty. Homeowners Ass'n, Inc., 141 F. Supp. 3d 1321 (S.D. Fla. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Balcony modifications
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed Count I (failure to allow reasonable modifications for balcony) at the motion to dismiss stage under Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards without reaching substantive RA analysis.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Balcony accommodations
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed Count II (failure to allow reasonable accommodations for balcony) at the motion to dismiss stage under Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Balcony policy
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed Count III (disparate impact regarding balcony) at the motion to dismiss stage, finding plaintiff failed to clearly plead disparate treatment versus disparate impact and failed to identify a policy or practice resulting in discriminatory impact.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Balcony policy (second disparate impact claim)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed Count IV (disparate impact regarding balcony) at the motion to dismiss stage under Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation for exercising FHA rights
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed Count V (retaliation under § 3617) at the motion to dismiss stage without substantive analysis of retaliation elements.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Storage sheds on front porch and back of house
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss Count VI as to BFMA Defendants and KFCA regarding storage shed modifications, finding plaintiff adequately pleaded disability, causal connection between sheds and disability, and that defendants' actions contributed to denial of the accommodation. Claim survives MTD and proceeds to discovery.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Intentional discrimination regarding balcony and other modifications
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed Count VIII (intentional discrimination) at the motion to dismiss stage, finding plaintiff failed to adequately plead discriminatory purpose under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodations and/or modifications (balcony, sheds, patio, trellis)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed Count IX (failure to allow reasonable accommodations/modifications) at the motion to dismiss stage under Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Trafficking, involuntary servitude, and forced labor under 15 U.S.C. §§ 1589, 1590
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed Count X (trafficking and forced labor claims under 15 U.S.C. §§ 1589, 1590) at the motion to dismiss stage as non-FHA claims lacking plausible factual allegations.

source_file: 10183030_2024_Bailey v. The Queen's Landing Council of Unit Owners, Inc._mdd
case_name: Rosanna Bailey v. The Queen's Landing Council of Unit Owners, Inc.
accommodation_description: Dr. Bailey alleges she was denied repairs, maintenance, and services (including remediation for mold, door replacements, video cameras) because of her disability and race, while similarly situated non-disabled, white neighbors received these services.
key_holding: The court dismissed the sex discrimination claim for failure to state a claim, but denied the motion to dismiss on the race discrimination, disability discrimination, and retaliation claims, finding sufficient timely allegations that the Council treated Dr. Bailey differently because of her race and disability.
brief_summary: Dr. Rosanna Bailey, a Black woman with disabilities, sued her condominium association alleging race and disability discrimination and retaliation under the Fair Housing Act, claiming she received inferior repair services and maintenance compared to white, non-disabled neighbors. The court granted the motion to dismiss the sex discrimination claim as conclusory, but denied dismissal on the race and disability discrimination and retaliation claims, finding she alleged sufficient facts to proceed past the pleadings stage.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Reyes v. Waples Mobile Home Park Ltd. P'ship, 903 F.3d 415 (4th Cir. 2018)
Hall v. Greystar Mgmt. Servs., L.P., 637 F. App'x 93 (4th Cir. 2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's sex discrimination allegations were conclusory and devoid of specific factual averments suggesting disparate treatment because of sex, failing to meet the Iqbal/Twombly pleading standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff plausibly alleged race discrimination through multiple timely factual allegations (delayed repairs compared to white neighbors, differential treatment regarding cameras/lights, disparate insurance coverage, prioritization of white neighbors' repairs), sufficient to survive motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Although disability discrimination allegations were aggregated with race claims and less clearly articulated than race claims, Plaintiff stated sufficient disability-related factual allegations (severe allergies triggered by mold, medical condition known to Defendant, denial of cameras/lights to disabled owner) to survive dismissal with all inferences drawn in her favor.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Remediation and removal of mold from unit; repair of leaking sliding doors; provision of repairs and remediation services
fha_claims.reasoning: Court noted in footnote 2 that Plaintiff may be alleging failure to accommodate disabilities under § 3604(f)(3)(A)-(B) regarding mold remediation and repairs; allegations sufficiently state a failure-to-accommodate claim to proceed past pleadings stage, though many underlying facts appear barred by claim preclusion.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged all four elements of retaliation under § 3617: protected activity (complaints to Association, HUD, MCCR, courts), Defendant's awareness, adverse action (delayed repairs, refusal to discuss repairs post-litigation), and causal connection (repairs scheduled differently and later than neighbors' due to protected activity).

case_name: Tamara Johnson, et al. v. City of Annapolis
accommodation_description: No accommodation request at issue; this is a disparate impact challenge to the City's non-enforcement of rental licensing and inspection requirements for HACA public housing properties
key_holding: The plaintiffs' renewed motion for summary judgment on FHA disparate impact liability was denied because, although the City's non-enforcement policy and the poor conditions at HACA properties are undisputed, the plaintiffs failed to establish the necessary causal link between the City's illegal conduct and the plaintiffs' injury given that the causal inference is not ineluctable and additional discovery is warranted.
brief_summary: Black public housing tenants and the Estate of DaMon R. Fisher sued the City of Annapolis alleging that the City's decades-long non-enforcement of rental licensing and inspection requirements for Housing Authority of the City of Annapolis (HACA) properties violated the Fair Housing Act by disparately impacting almost exclusively Black renters. The court denied the plaintiffs' renewed motion for summary judgment on disparate impact liability because while the City's discriminatory policy and poor housing conditions were undisputed, the plaintiffs failed to establish proximate causation given the debatable causal inference and the need for additional discovery.
key_cases_cited: Bank of Am. Corp. v. City of Miami, 581 U.S. 189 (2017)
City of Oakland v. Wells Fargo & Co., 14 F.4th 1030 (9th Cir. 2021) (en banc)
Pac. Shores Props., LLC v. City of Newport Beach, 730 F.3d 1142 (9th Cir. 2013)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied plaintiffs' renewed motion for summary judgment on FHA disparate impact claim because causation remained a disputed factual question requiring jury determination. Although the City's non-enforcement policy and poor conditions at HACA properties were undisputed, the plaintiffs failed to establish a direct causal link between the policy and the harm suffered, relying instead on debatable inferences that the City could reasonably rebut with competent evidence. The court found that additional discovery was necessary before summary judgment could be granted.

source_file: 10183095_2024_Estate of DaMon R. Fisher v. City of Annapolis_mdd
case_name: Estate of DaMon R. Fisher v. City of Annapolis
accommodation_description: Challenge to City's exemption of public housing from inspection/licensing requirements, alleged to have disparate impact on Black renters
key_holding: The court denied plaintiffs' motion for summary judgment on disparate impact claim because, although the City's non-enforcement policy and poor conditions at HACA properties were largely undisputed, the causal connection between the policy and the alleged harm remained genuinely disputed, precluding summary judgment before adequate discovery.
brief_summary: The Estate of DaMon R. Fisher and other plaintiffs sued the City of Annapolis alleging the City's decades-long policy of exempting Housing Authority of the City of Annapolis (HACA) public housing properties from its rental property inspection/licensing regime violated the Fair Housing Act by having a disparate impact on Black renters. The court denied plaintiffs' renewed motion for summary judgment on disparate impact liability because causation remained genuinely disputed—while evidence showed the non-enforcement policy and poor conditions at HACA properties, plaintiffs failed to establish as a matter of law that the policy directly caused the alleged harm.
key_cases_cited: Bank of Am. Corp. v. City of Miami, 581 U.S. 189 (2017)
City of Oakland v. Wells Fargo & Co., 14 F.4th 1030 (9th Cir. 2021)
Pac. Shores Props., LLC v. City of Newport Beach, 730 F.3d 1142 (9th Cir. 2013)
Spann v. Colonial Vill., Inc., 899 F.2d 24 (D.C. Cir. 1990)
Md. Shall Issue, Inc. v. Anne Arundel Cnty., 662 F. Supp. 3d 557 (D. Md. 2023)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied plaintiffs' renewed motion for summary judgment on their FHA disparate impact claim because, although the non-enforcement policy and poor conditions at HACA properties are undisputed, the causal link between the City's conduct and plaintiffs' injury remains a debatable inference that should be resolved by a jury after adequate discovery, not on summary judgment. The court found that causation is an intensely factual question and that the plaintiffs' evidence, while strong, does not compel only one inference.

case_name: Lynette Cooper v. Housing Authority Baltimore City et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff's complaint does not request a specific accommodation; it broadly alleges retaliation by HABC in violation of 42 U.S.C. § 3617.
key_holding: The court found the complaint frivolous or failing to state a viable claim, noting the retaliation claim was likely barred by res judicata from prior dismissed cases and failed to allege sufficient facts connecting HABC's actions to plaintiff's involvement in a 2015 lawsuit.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Lynette Cooper sued the Housing Authority of Baltimore City and others alleging retaliation under the Fair Housing Act, claiming HABC failed to pay its portion of her rent in retaliation for a 2015 sexual harassment case. The court, conducting initial screening under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B), found the complaint rambling and incoherent with many delusional elements, and concluded the retaliation claim was likely barred by res judicata from two prior dismissed cases, directing plaintiff to show cause why the case should not be dismissed.
key_cases_cited: Hagans v. Lavine, 415 U.S. 528 (1974)
Denton v. Hernandez, 504 U.S. 25 (1992)
Erickson v. Pardus, 551 U.S. 89 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found complaint frivolous or failing to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B). Plaintiff failed to explicitly state the basis for alleged retaliation, alleged only vague connection to 2015 events, and prior identical claims were dismissed as res judicata. Court lacked subject matter jurisdiction over 'obviously frivolous' allegations of chemical attacks and electronic tampering unconnected to any FHA-protected activity.

source_file: 10183208_2024_CMDS Residential, LLC v. Mayor and City Council Of Baltimore_mdd
case_name: CMDS Residential, LLC v. Mayor and City Council of Baltimore
accommodation_description: CMDS, a residential substance-abuse treatment facility, sought a use and occupancy permit to operate, which the City denied based on community opposition to the prospective clients.
key_holding: The motion to stay was denied because the federal discrimination claims focus on whether discriminatory intent motivated the City's permit denial, while the state judicial review proceeding addresses whether the denial was correct under City Code—these are distinct legal questions, and further delay would prejudice CMDS given the existing six-year litigation history.
brief_summary: CMDS Residential, LLC, a substance-abuse treatment facility operator, sued the Mayor and City Council of Baltimore alleging the City wrongfully denied its use and occupancy permit in deference to discriminatory community opposition to its prospective disabled clients. The court denied the City's motion to stay the federal proceedings pending state court judicial review, reasoning that the federal claims focus on discriminatory intent while the state proceeding addresses whether the denial was correct under City Code—distinct legal questions—and that further delay would prejudice CMDS after six years of litigation.
key_cases_cited: Landis v. N. Am. Co., 299 U.S. 248 (1936)
Clinton v. Jones, 520 U.S. 681 (1997)
St. Mary's Honor Ctr. v. Hicks, 509 U.S. 502 (1993)
Martin v. Stewart, 499 F.3d 360 (4th Cir. 2007)
Bryant Woods Inn, Inc. v. Howard County, 124 F.3d 597 (4th Cir. 1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Use and occupancy (U&O) permit to operate a residential substance-abuse treatment facility
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the City's motion to stay pending state court judicial review, finding that the federal discrimination claim (whether the City's decisionmakers were motivated by discrimination in denying the permit) is distinct from the state law question of whether the City correctly interpreted the City Code. The court held that the state proceeding's outcome is not dispositive of the federal discrimination claim because the federal question concerns the process and motivation, not the correctness of the result.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) claims; Equal Protection Clause claim
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the City's motion to stay the ADA and equal protection claims, applying the same reasoning as for the FHA claim: the federal legal questions regarding discriminatory intent and equal protection are distinct from the state law question of correct interpretation of the City Code, and the state proceeding's outcome is not dispositive of whether discrimination motivated the City's decision.

case_name: Antoinette Marie Williams v. Carrington Mortgage Services, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges she was denied fair mortgage servicing and proper notifications based on her race and sex, resulting in foreclosure.
key_holding: The court granted Defendants' motions to dismiss, finding Plaintiff's claims time-barred under the applicable statutes of limitations and precluded by res judicata from the prior foreclosure action.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Antoinette Williams sued Carrington Mortgage Services, Bank of America Corp., and Bank of America, N.A. alleging Fair Housing Act, Truth in Lending Act, and Equal Credit Opportunity Act violations based on race and sex discrimination in mortgage refinancing, assignment, and foreclosure. The court granted Defendants' motions to dismiss, finding all claims time-barred by the applicable statutes of limitations and precluded by res judicata from the prior foreclosure proceeding.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Ashcroft v. Iqbal

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: FHA claims are subject to a two-year statute of limitations beginning on the date of the occurrence or termination of the discriminatory housing practice. Plaintiff's claims arising from the 2009 refinancing and 2011 assignment were time-barred when the initial complaint was filed on April 18, 2022, well after the applicable limitations period had expired. The discovery rule does not apply because Plaintiff offers no adequate explanation for the four-year delay between the 2016 bankruptcy (which allegedly put her on notice) and the filing of her complaint.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: TILA, ECOA violations related to mortgage refinancing and assignment disclosures
fha_claims.reasoning: TILA claims are subject to a one-year statute of limitations and ECOA claims to a five-year statute of limitations. All claims arising from the 2009 refinancing and 2011 assignment were time-barred when filed on April 18, 2022. Additionally, res judicata bars the claims because they arise from the same transaction (foreclosure of the property) as the prior state court foreclosure action, which resulted in a final judgment on the merits when the sale was ratified on March 16, 2023.

case_name: Christine M. Arnold v. Poinsettia Homeowners Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: No specific reasonable accommodation was requested; the plaintiff alleged broadly discriminatory treatment in housing conditions, including failure to address neighbor harassment (nude and inappropriate messages, window peering, physical threats, attempted assault), failure to provide adequate security, and ultimately a discriminatory eviction proceeding filed in Florida state court.
key_holding: The court dismissed the case without prejudice for lack of personal jurisdiction over Poinsettia Homeowners Association, a Florida corporation, finding that neither Michigan's long-arm statute nor constitutional due process requirements were satisfied because all relevant conduct occurred in Florida.
brief_summary: Christine Arnold, a former tenant at a Florida mobile home park, sued Poinsettia HOA in the Eastern District of Michigan alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act, Equal Protection Clause, 42 U.S.C. § 1985, and Title VI/VII, arising from alleged harassment by neighbors, failure to provide adequate security, and discriminatory eviction she experienced in Florida. Poinsettia, a Florida corporation with no Michigan contacts, moved to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction. The court granted the motion, holding that Poinsettia's passive website advertising did not constitute purposeful availment of Michigan, and Arnold's voluntary post-eviction relocation to Michigan did not create jurisdiction over a Florida defendant whose allegedly tortious acts and the resulting injuries both occurred in Florida.
key_cases_cited: Int'l Shoe Co. v. State of Wash., 326 U.S. 310 (1945)
Ford Motor Co. v. Montana Eighth Jud. Dist. Ct., 592 U.S. 351 (2021)
Bristol-Myers Squibb Co. v. Superior Ct. of California, San Francisco Cnty., 582 U.S. 255 (2017)
Miller v. AXA Winterthur Ins. Co., 694 F.3d 675 (6th Cir. 2012)
Neogen Corp. v. Neo Gen Screening, Inc., 282 F.3d 883 (6th Cir. 2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal Protection Clause, 42 U.S.C. § 1985, Title VI of the Civil Rights Act, negligence, intrusion on seclusion, abuse of process
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked personal jurisdiction over the defendant, a Florida corporation with no minimum contacts with Michigan. The plaintiff's claims arose entirely from events in Florida, and the defendant's passive website maintenance did not constitute purposeful availment of Michigan's forum. Dismissal was without prejudice.

case_name: Mattie T. Lomax v. Marketplace Homes Lending, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges race-based housing discrimination and selective repair denial, with no distinct accommodation request.
key_holding: The court dismissed the case because plaintiff's allegations—that she viewed a Section 8 apartment, encountered maintenance issues, and was subjected to unwanted attention from the owner's brother—were insufficient to state a plausible Fair Housing Act claim regardless of the protected class asserted.
brief_summary: Mattie Lomax, proceeding pro se and in forma pauperis, sued Marketplace Homes Lending and two individuals alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on race and economic status discrimination, including failure to make repairs. The court denied her motions for default judgment, set aside the entries of default, and dismissed the case without prejudice for failure to state a claim, finding her factual allegations—summary references to a leaking ceiling, unwanted visits from the property owner's brother, and general assertions of discrimination—insufficient to plead a plausible FHA cause of action.
key_cases_cited: Shellhammer v. Lewallen, No. 84-3573, 1985 WL 14457 (6th Cir. July 31, 1985)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged discrimination based on economic status, race, or color, including failure to provide adequate repairs of ceiling leaking; also alleged harassment by property owner's brother.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to state a plausible claim under the FHA. Plaintiff did not assert facts suggesting discrimination in the rental transaction itself, and allegations regarding harassment by the property owner's brother were too disjointed and unsupported to constitute an FHA violation. The court applied the Iqbal/Twombly pleading standard under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) screening.

case_name: Doll v. Trellis Walnut Towers LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested that the elevator work consistently or that Defendants otherwise secure reliable access to their apartments as an accommodation for their mobility disabilities.
key_holding: The reasonable accommodation claim failed because Plaintiffs' request that the elevator 'work consistently' was not reasonably specific and the complaint did not plausibly allege that the elevator functioned worse than it should for a building of its age.
brief_summary: Shannon Doll and Brittney Mandery, wheelchair-bound tenants in a Mankato, Minnesota apartment building, sued their landlord and related entities alleging the building's repeated elevator outages over thirteen months constituted disability discrimination under the FHAA, Section 504, and Minnesota state law. The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that while the elevator outages affected Plaintiffs more severely, the complaint failed to state a plausible disparate treatment, disparate impact, or failure-to-accommodate claim because the accommodation request was not reasonably specific.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Tex. Dep't of Housing & Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Cmtys. Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Congdon v. Strine, 854 F. Supp. 355 (E.D. Pa. 1994)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint alleges no facts suggesting intentional handicap-based discrimination. Elevator mechanical failures affected all residents, not just disabled tenants, and the complaint contains no allegations that defendants delayed repairs with discriminatory intent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint fails to identify a facially neutral policy or practice susceptible to disparate-impact analysis. Seven elevator outages in thirteen months with no allegation that this frequency is unusually high does not plausibly show a pattern and practice of failing to maintain the elevator.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Elevator repair and consistent operation; alternative access to apartments when elevator inoperable
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint fails to identify a reasonably specific requested accommodation. The request that the elevator 'work consistently' lacks objective measures and is undermined by the complaint's own allegations showing seven outages in thirteen months with no evidence this frequency is unusually high. The alternative-access request is similarly vague, providing no indication how plaintiffs requested such access be provided.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, 29 U.S.C. § 794; Minnesota Human Rights Act, Minn. Stat. §§ 363A.01–363A.50; Minn. Stat. § 504B.211 (unauthorized entry into apartments)
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 504 claim fails for the same reasons as the FHAA claims (failure to allege specific, reasonable accommodation). State-law claims dismissed without prejudice under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3) to allow pursuit in state court after dismissal of all federal claims.

case_name: Stallworth v. Newrez LLC d/b/a Shellpoint Mortgage Servicing Co.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, as pastor of Word and Worship Church, alleged that Trustmark National Bank engaged in discriminatory appraisal practices by using warehouse comparables instead of church comparables, constituting predatory redlining in violation of the FHA.
key_holding: The FHA claim fails because the Fair Housing Act applies only to residential loans, not commercial loans such as the church loan at issue, and the ECOA claim fails because the appraisal did not actually use warehouse comparables but instead used comparable church sales in the Jackson metropolitan area.
brief_summary: Jeffery Stallworth sued Newrez LLC, Bank of America, Trustmark National Bank, and others alleging TILA, FCRA, and FHA violations stemming from a 2007 residential construction loan and a commercial loan for Word and Worship Church, claiming discriminatory appraisal practices and inaccurate credit reporting. The court granted Trustmark's motion in full as time-barred, granted Newrez's and Bank of America's motions in part while allowing limited FCRA § 1681s-2(b) claims to proceed, and denied Stallworth's motion to stay foreclosure proceedings.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly

fha_claims.accommodation_description: TILA disclosure violations, FCRA credit reporting violations, breach of duty of good faith and fair dealing, ECOA redlining/appraisal discrimination, FDCPA debt collection harassment
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's TILA claims against Newrez fail as a matter of law because Newrez is a loan servicer, not a creditor subject to TILA's disclosure requirements. FCRA claim under § 1681s-2(a) fails because there is no private right of action; FCRA claim under § 1681s-2(b) survives because pro se complaints are held to less stringent pleading standards and plaintiff may not yet have knowledge of whether the CRA notified Newrez of the dispute. Breach of duty of good faith and fair dealing claim fails because plaintiff does not allege any contractual relationship with Newrez.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: TILA disclosure violations, FCRA credit reporting violations, breach of duty of good faith and fair dealing
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's TILA claim against Bank of America is time-barred under 15 U.S.C. § 1640(e), which requires suit within one year of the violation; the alleged non-disclosure occurred in 2017 and suit was filed in 2024. Breach of duty of good faith and fair dealing claim is time-barred under Mississippi Code § 15-1-49(1) (three-year statute of limitations) and fails as a matter of law because Bank of America's contractual relationship with plaintiff ended on June 7, 2019, when it assigned the loan to U.S. Bank National Association.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: TILA disclosure violations, FCRA credit reporting violations, breach of duty of good faith and fair dealing
fha_claims.reasoning: All claims against Trustmark relating to the 2007 loan are time-barred. Trustmark assigned the loan to Bank of America in 2012 (twelve years before suit) and plaintiff became aware of the error in the Deed of Trust's legal description in 2014 (ten years before suit). TILA claims are barred by the one-year statute of limitations, FCRA claims by the two or five-year statute of limitations, and breach of duty of good faith and fair dealing claims by the three-year statute of limitations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act redlining claim, Equal Credit Opportunity Act appraisal discrimination claim, Fair Debt Collection Practices Act harassment claim
fha_claims.reasoning: FHA claim fails because the FHA applies only to residential loans, not commercial loans; the Church's loan was commercial. ECOA claim fails because it is based on a factually false premise—Trustmark presented uncontroverted evidence that the appraiser did not use any warehouse as a comparable sale but instead used four churches in the Jackson metropolitan area. FDCPA claim fails as a matter of law because the FDCPA applies only to third-party debt collectors, not to mortgage lenders collecting their own debts. The allegation regarding pressure for sporting event tickets is not linked to any claim for relief.

source_file: 10186174_2024_Baptist Homes, Inc. v. City of Madison, Mississippi_mssd
case_name: Baptist Homes, Inc. v. City of Madison, Mississippi
accommodation_description: Baptist Homes requested a reasonable accommodation from the City's R-1 single-family zoning to house four unrelated adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities who would receive residential support services.
key_holding: Baptist Homes adequately stated a FHA reasonable accommodation claim where the nonprofit alleged it requested a zoning accommodation for a home serving disabled adults but the City refused to process its rental license application and failed to respond to multiple accommodation requests.
