brief_summary: Baptist Homes, a nonprofit providing residential support services to adults with disabilities, sued the City of Madison, Mississippi after the City refused to process its rental license application for a home intended to house four unrelated disabled adults in an R-1 residential zone. The court denied the City's motion to dismiss, holding that Baptist Homes adequately alleged standing and stated plausible FHA and ADA reasonable accommodation claims where the City's zoning ordinance provisions specifically target the type of zoning regulations at issue in disability housing cases.
key_cases_cited: UNDETERMINED

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation to allow four adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities to reside together in a single-family residential (R-1) zoned property with in-home support services, notwithstanding zoning ordinance restrictions on multi-family or commercial uses.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the City's motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6), finding that Baptist Homes plausibly alleged a reasonable accommodation request under the FHA § 3604(f)(3)(B). The court held that even if the intended use violated the zoning ordinance, the FHA and ADA require reasonable accommodations and specifically target zoning regulations of this type. The claim survives the motion to dismiss and proceeds to discovery.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claim for denial of rental license based on disability association; potential state law claims regarding zoning enforcement.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court rejected the City's argument that only a 'qualified individual with a disability' may sue under ADA Title II, holding that the enforcement provision (42 U.S.C. § 12133) authorizes suit by any entity alleging discrimination on the basis of disability, including organizations that associate with or care for individuals with disabilities. The ADA claim survives the motion to dismiss.

case_name: David L. Weik v. Jim Asby, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges Fair Housing Act violations related to being terminated from employment and ousted from his residence, but no specific accommodation request is identified in the opinion.
key_holding: The court dismissed Plaintiff's FHA claims (Counts 2 and 9) as barred by res judicata because they arose from the same transactional nucleus of facts as claims that could have been litigated in a prior action, and failed to state a viable FHA claim.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff David Weik sued his former employer/landlord Jim Asby, attorney Rydel Peterson, and related parties alleging Fair Housing Act violations, Taxpayer First Act retaliation, and state law claims arising from being terminated and evicted after reporting alleged tax fraud. The court dismissed all FHA claims (Counts 2 and 9) with prejudice as barred by res judicata because they arose from the same facts as claims that could have been raised in a prior lawsuit, and dismissed the remaining claims on various grounds including failure to exhaust administrative remedies and violation of vexatious litigant orders.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Stewart v. U.S. Bancorp
Owens v. Kaiser Found. Health Plan, Inc.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination in violation of the Federal Fair Housing Act and Montana Residential Landlord Tenant Act (Count 2); alleged differential treatment based on race (plaintiff is part Hispanic) and denial of ability to file workers' compensation claim and demand to vacate property
fha_claims.reasoning: The FHA claim in Count 2 is barred by res judicata because it arises out of the same transactional nucleus of facts as claims dismissed with prejudice in the prior action (Weik I), and could have been brought in that prior action. A Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal is a judgment on the merits to which res judicata applies.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Violation of the FHA (Count 9); alleged discrimination and retaliation related to employment termination and eviction from residence
fha_claims.reasoning: The FHA claim in Count 9 is barred by res judicata because it arises out of the same set of operative facts as claims dismissed with prejudice in Weik I and could have been litigated at that time. The identity of claims element of claim preclusion is satisfied.

case_name: James L. Bryant, Jr. and Sharon R. Bryant v. Eastwood Construction, LLC
accommodation_description: The complaint references reasonable accommodations as part of FHA claims but the specific accommodation requested is not detailed in the opinion, as the case settled before any merits analysis.
key_holding: The court granted the motion to enforce the settlement agreement, finding the Bryants failed to comply with their obligation to dismiss the federal lawsuit per the Settlement Agreement, entitling Eastwood to attorney's fees.
brief_summary: The Bryants filed federal claims against Eastwood Construction alleging discriminatory and retaliatory housing practices in violation of the FHA, Civil Rights Act, and state law, claiming Eastwood sought to silence them for filing complaints about housing discrimination, reasonable accommodations, and environmental hazards. The parties settled, but when the Bryants failed to dismiss the federal lawsuit as required by the Settlement Agreement, the court granted Eastwood's motion to enforce the settlement, dismissed the claims with prejudice, and awarded attorney's fees to Eastwood.
key_cases_cited: Petty v. Timken Corp., 849 F.2d 130 (4th Cir. 1988)
Smith-Phifer v. City of Charlotte, __ F.4th __, 2024 WL 4280970 (4th Cir. Sept. 25, 2024)
Clayton v. Ameriquest Mortg. Co., No. 1:02cv415, 2004 WL 734978 (M.D.N.C. Apr. 5, 2004)
Malave v. Carney Hosp., 170 F.3d 217 (1st Cir. 1999)
Young v. FDIC, 103 F.3d 1180 (4th Cir. 1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Home maintenance and/or warranty requests; reasonable accommodations related to housing
fha_claims.reasoning: The parties entered into a binding Settlement Agreement on December 29, 2023, resolving all claims in the federal lawsuit, including FHA claims for reasonable accommodations and housing discrimination, without admission of liability. The court enforced the settlement agreement pursuant to its inherent equitable authority.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation for filing complaints about housing discrimination, reasonable accommodations, and environmental hazards
fha_claims.reasoning: The parties entered into a binding Settlement Agreement on December 29, 2023, resolving all claims in the federal lawsuit, including FHA retaliation claims arising from Eastwood's alleged retaliatory conduct in suing the Bryants and obtaining restraining orders, without admission of liability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discriminatory and retaliatory housing practices in violation of the FHA
fha_claims.reasoning: The parties entered into a binding Settlement Agreement on December 29, 2023, resolving all claims in the federal lawsuit, including FHA disparate treatment claims, without admission of liability. The court enforced the settlement agreement pursuant to its inherent equitable authority.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Civil Rights Act of 1866 (42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 & 1982), North Carolina State Fair Housing Act (N.C.G.S. § 41A-1 et seq.), North Carolina Unfair Deceptive Trade Practices Act (N.C.G.S. § 75-1.1 et seq.)
fha_claims.reasoning: The parties entered into a binding Settlement Agreement on December 29, 2023, resolving all claims in the federal lawsuit, including non-FHA statutory claims under the Civil Rights Act of 1866 and state fair housing and consumer protection laws, without admission of liability.

source_file: 10187928_2024_MAK Development LLC v. City of Lincoln, Nebraska_ned
case_name: MAK Development LLC v. City of Lincoln, Nebraska
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs operate a residence for individuals recovering from substance abuse disorders and seek reasonable accommodation from local zoning requirements to allow the facility to continue operating.
key_holding: The court granted a stay of proceedings pending HUD administrative proceedings because the defendant demonstrated hardship in being required to participate in potentially duplicative litigation while HUD investigates nearly identical fair housing complaints.
brief_summary: MAK Development LLC and Michael Corrado sued the City of Lincoln, Nebraska alleging the city violated the Fair Housing Act by refusing to allow a residence for individuals recovering from substance abuse disorders to operate due to zoning requirements and by refusing to grant reasonable accommodations from those zoning requirements. The court granted a partial stay of proceedings pending HUD administrative proceedings to avoid duplicative litigation while HUD investigates the underlying fair housing complaints.
key_cases_cited: Landis v. North American Co., 299 U.S. 248 (1936)
Kansas City S. Ry. Co. v. United States, 282 U.S. 760 (1931)
Doe v. University of Nebraska, 2020 WL 5057767 (D. Neb.)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation to zoning requirements to allow the Residence (a sober living group home for individuals recovering from substance abuse disorders) to operate at 2648 Washington in Lincoln, Nebraska
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted a stay of the federal court proceedings pending completion of parallel HUD administrative investigation and proceedings under 42 U.S.C. § 3610. The court found that Defendant demonstrated specific hardship from duplicative proceedings, and that staying the case would not prevent Plaintiffs from eventually obtaining relief. The merits of the reasonable accommodation claim have not been addressed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) claims related to refusal to allow the Residence to operate and refusal to provide reasonable accommodations to zoning requirements
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted a stay of all proceedings, including ADA claims, pending completion of the HUD administrative investigation. The court did not reach the merits of the ADA claims.

source_file: 10187994_2023_Brookline Opportunities, LLC v. Brookline, NH, Town of_nhd
case_name: Brookline Opportunities, LLC et al. v. Town of Brookline et al.
accommodation_description: Not applicable—this case does not involve a reasonable accommodation or modification request; rather, it involves a challenge to municipal zoning ordinances (a moratorium and a growth management ordinance) alleged to discriminate against families with children, racial minorities, and persons of national origin in connection with a proposed affordable rental housing development.
key_holding: The court denied both parties' cross-motions for summary judgment—granting summary judgment only as to claims against the Selectboard—because genuine disputes of material fact remained on standing, ripeness, and the merits of the familial status discrimination claims under the FHA.
brief_summary: Two real estate development companies (Brookline Opportunities, LLC and Tamposi Brothers Holdings, LLC) sought to build an 80-unit affordable rental housing development in Brookline, NH, but the Town responded by adopting a one-year building permit moratorium and a growth management ordinance that effectively foreclosed the project. The Developers sued under the FHA alleging the Town discriminated against the likely tenants—families with children, Blacks, and Latinos—through disparate treatment, disparate impact, discriminatory statements (§ 3604(c)), and interference with their development efforts (§ 3617). The court denied both cross-motions for summary judgment on the standing/ripeness and merits issues, finding triable facts throughout, while granting judgment for defendants only on claims against the Selectboard whose sole act was a ministerial vote to hold the town meeting.
key_cases_cited: Village of Arlington Heights v. Metropolitan Housing Development Corp., 429 U.S. 252 (1977)
Texas Dept. of Housing & Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Macone v. Town of Wakefield, 277 F.3d 1 (1st Cir. 2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether the moratorium and GMO facially discriminate against families with children. The ordinances are facially neutral and apply evenhandedly to all residential housing; school capacity is analytically distinct from familial status and is not a proxy for it. The court denied summary judgment because the Developers' burden of proof requires conclusive evidence, which the record does not provide.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court rejected the Developers' argument that statements by Town officials regarding school capacity constitute direct evidence of discriminatory intent. The court held that a plaintiff cannot prevail on summary judgment on a disparate treatment claim merely by citing direct evidence of intent; the record must be conclusive. Statements about legitimate government interests in managing school growth do not, in and of themselves, reveal animus against families with children.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Under § 3604(c), the court held that statements expressing concerns about school capacity and public education services do not conclusively indicate a preference against families with children. An ordinary reader may interpret such statements as expressing legitimate concern for educational quality rather than aversion to children. The Developers' burden of proof requires conclusive evidence, which the record does not provide.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted summary judgment on the Developers' claims against the Selectboard under § 3617 (retaliation/interference) because the complaint did not allege any actionable conduct by the Selectboard. The Selectboard's only action was a ministerial vote to hold the Town Meeting where the moratorium was put to a vote, which was required by state law and cannot form the basis for FHA liability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The Developers asserted disparate impact claims under § 3604(a) and (b) but limited their summary judgment motion to disparate treatment. The court did not reach the merits of the disparate impact claim, which remains pending for further proceedings.

source_file: 10188107_2019_BLAKE GARDENS, LLC v. STATE OF NEW JERSEY_njd
case_name: Blake Gardens, LLC v. State of New Jersey
accommodation_description: Developer Blake Gardens challenged New Jersey's 2015 Act requiring use variances for Alzheimer's residences as facially discriminatory against persons with disabilities under the FHA.
key_holding: The 2015 Act facially violates the Fair Housing Act by treating Alzheimer's residences differently from other community residences without justification, as the State failed to demonstrate no alternative less discriminatory course of action was available.
brief_summary: Blake Gardens, LLC, a developer of Alzheimer's residences, sued the State of New Jersey challenging P.L. 2015 c.125, which reclassified dementia care homes as health care facilities requiring use variances in residential zones while allowing similar community residences for other disabilities without such requirements. The court granted Blake Gardens' motion for summary judgment, finding the statute facially discriminates against persons with Alzheimer's disease under the Fair Housing Act because the State failed to justify treating these residences differently from other community residences for disabled persons.
key_cases_cited: Arc of New Jersey, Inc. v. State of N.J., 950 F. Supp. 637 (D.N.J. 1996)
Association for Advancement of the Mentally Handicapped v. City of Elizabeth, 876 F. Supp. 614 (D.N.J. 1994)
Bangerter v. Orem City Corp., 46 F.3d 1491 (10th Cir. 1995)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Zoning approval for development of Alzheimer's/dementia care residences in single-family residential zones
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that New Jersey P.L. 2015 c.125 facially discriminates against individuals with Alzheimer's disease and dementia by requiring a use variance for their residences while permitting similar community residences for persons with head injuries, developmental disabilities, and terminal illnesses without such approval. Although the State has a legitimate governmental interest in protecting vulnerable populations, it failed to demonstrate that no less discriminatory alternative exists, as the Department of Health already regulates dementia care homes through comprehensive safety standards without zoning restrictions.

source_file: 10188344_2021_WR PROPERTY LLC v. TOWNSHIP OF JACKSON, NEW JERSEY_njd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of permits/approvals for construction of Orthodox Jewish religious schools and eruvim (symbolic boundaries for religious observance)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiffs likely to succeed on merits of FHA disparate treatment claim based on evidence that ordinances were adopted with discriminatory purpose targeting Orthodox Jewish community. Court analyzed Arlington Heights factors and found sufficient evidence of discriminatory intent and effect, though final merits determination was reserved pending full litigation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Free Exercise Clause (First Amendment), Equal Protection Clause (Fourteenth Amendment), RLUIPA, Freedom of Association, Establishment Clause, New Jersey Law Against Discrimination, Property Rights, New Jersey Municipal Land Use Law
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiffs likely to succeed on Free Exercise and Equal Protection claims based on evidence that ordinances were not neutral, were adopted with discriminatory purpose targeting Orthodox Jewish religious practices, and defendants failed to articulate any compelling government interest. Court applied strict scrutiny and Arlington Heights framework.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA employment discrimination, Title VII employment discrimination, NJFLA leave entitlement, Rehabilitation Act disability discrimination, wrongful termination, misrepresentation, FMLA retaliation
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to state a claim under ADA, Title VII, NJFLA, and Rehabilitation Act. For ADA and Title VII, plaintiff did not exhaust administrative remedies (no EEOC charge or right-to-sue letter alleged) and failed to allege she was disabled or discriminated against based on protected status. For NJFLA, plaintiff's own health condition is not an eligible reason for leave. For Rehabilitation Act, plaintiff did not allege Advancing Opportunities receives federal financial assistance and failed to allege disability. Wrongful termination and misrepresentation claims also dismissed for failure to allege facts supporting relief.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: FMLA retaliation claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied defendant's motion for a more definite statement regarding FMLA claim. When liberally construed, the complaint sufficiently alleges a prima facie FMLA retaliation claim: plaintiff took protected FMLA leave for COVID-19 recovery, suffered adverse employment action (termination), and the termination was causally related to the leave. Claim survives and proceeds.

case_name: Donnell L. Prince v. Priscilla Pajela
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request was made; plaintiff alleges Fair Housing Act violations related to alleged exposure to toxic substances as retaliation for pursuing other lawsuits.
key_holding: The Court denied Defendant's motion to dismiss on procedural grounds (subject matter jurisdiction and claim preclusion), finding that federal question jurisdiction exists based on Plaintiff's FHA, First Amendment, and § 1983 claims, and that Defendant failed to meet her burden to establish res judicata or collateral estoppel.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Donnell Prince sued his landlord Priscilla Pajela, alleging intentional exposure to toxic fumes, chemicals, and drugs as retaliation for pursuing other lawsuits, asserting claims including Fair Housing Act violations, First Amendment violations, and § 1983 claims. The Court denied Defendant's motion to dismiss, finding federal question jurisdiction exists and that Defendant failed to establish that res judicata or collateral estoppel bars the claims.
key_cases_cited: Const. Party of Pa. v. Aichele, 757 F.3d 347 (3d Cir. 2014)
Bracken v. Matgouranis, 296 F.3d 160 (3d Cir. 2002)
Watkins v. Resorts Int’l Hotel & Casino, Inc., 591 A.2d 592 (N.J. 1991)
In re Docteroff, 133 F.3d 210 (3d Cir. 1997)
Colorado River Water Conservation Dist. v. United States, 424 U.S. 800 (1976)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges he is entitled to reasonable accommodation or protection from intentional exposure to toxic fumes, chemicals, and drugs in his rooming house unit, which he claims was done to prevent him from pursuing civil rights litigation.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied Defendant's motion to dismiss on jurisdictional and preclusion grounds, allowing the Fair Housing Act claim to proceed. The court did not reach the substantive merits of the FHA claim or apply any reasonable accommodation standard, as the motion was decided on procedural grounds (subject matter jurisdiction, res judicata, collateral estoppel).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: First Amendment violation, § 1983 civil rights claims, state law claims including conspiracy, negligent/inadequate security, New Jersey Reprisal Law violations, violations of rooming house regulations, and breach of implied warranty of habitability and covenant of quiet enjoyment.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied Defendant's motion to dismiss on jurisdictional and preclusion grounds. The non-FHA claims survive the motion to dismiss and proceed to the next stage. The court did not reach the merits of these claims, as the motion was decided on procedural grounds.

source_file: 10189170_2023_431 E PALISADE AVENUE REAL ESTATE, LLC v. CITY OF ENGLEWOOD_njd
case_name: 431 E Palisade Avenue Real Estate, LLC v. City of Englewood
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs sought modification of or a variance from the city's zoning ordinance to permit construction of an assisted-living facility in a residential zone (R-AAA or other residential designation), rather than being confined to the single industrial RIM district where such facilities were permitted under the existing code.
key_holding: The court denied the motion to dismiss plaintiffs' FHA, ADA, and RA disparate impact claims (Counts I–III) because the allegations that the city's zoning ordinance confined assisted-living facilities to an industrial district sufficiently pleaded a greater adverse impact on the elderly handicapped without requiring statistical evidence at the pleading stage, but granted dismissal of the § 1983 Equal Protection claim (Count IV) for failure to allege discriminatory intent or adequately identify similarly situated comparators.
brief_summary: Plaintiff LLCs seeking to build an assisted-living facility in a residential zone in Englewood, New Jersey sued the city, alleging its zoning ordinance—which restricted assisted-living facilities to an industrial district—violated the FHA, ADA, RA, and Equal Protection Act by disproportionately burdening the elderly handicapped, including Orthodox Jewish residents who cannot drive or carry objects on Shabbat in industrial areas. The court found plaintiffs' facial disparate impact challenge was ripe for adjudication without requiring a final administrative decision, and that the allegations were sufficient to state a claim under the FHA, ADA, and RA even without statistical evidence at the pleading stage. However, the court dismissed the Equal Protection claim because the Second Amended Complaint contained only conclusory allegations of intentional discrimination and failed to identify similarly situated non-handicapped uses treated more favorably.
key_cases_cited: 431 E. Palisade Ave. Real Estate, LLC v. City of Englewood, 977 F.3d 277 (3d Cir. 2020)
Texas Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Lapid-Laurel v. Zoning Bd. of Adjustment of the Twp. of Scotch Plains, 284 F.3d 442 (3d Cir. 2002)
Mt. Holly Gardens Citizens in Action, Inc. v. Twp. of Mount Holly, 658 F.3d 375 (3d Cir. 2011)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Zoning ordinance restricting assisted-living facilities to industrial zone (RIM district) rather than residential zones (R-AAA and other residential categories)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found Plaintiffs adequately pleaded disparate impact under FHA § 3604(f)(2) by alleging the zoning ordinance has greater adverse impact on elderly handicapped persons than others, without requiring statistical analysis at the pleading stage. Facial challenge to zoning ordinance is ripe for adjudication.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Zoning ordinance restricting assisted-living facilities to industrial zone (RIM district) rather than residential zones
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that FHA analysis applies to ADA claims brought together with FHA claims, and Plaintiffs adequately pleaded disparate impact under 42 U.S.C. § 12132. ADA implementing regulations extend coverage to entities associated with disabled persons, such as assisted-living facility operators.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Zoning ordinance restricting assisted-living facilities to industrial zone (RIM district) rather than residential zones
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that FHA analysis applies to Rehabilitation Act claims brought together with FHA claims, and Plaintiffs adequately pleaded disparate impact under 29 U.S.C. § 794(a). Same allegations sufficient to state claim under RA as under FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal Protection Act claim under 42 U.S.C. § 1983; ADA Title II; Rehabilitation Act § 504
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed Equal Protection claim because Plaintiffs failed to allege discriminatory intent required under rational basis review. Conclusory allegations of intent and lack of legitimate governmental purpose are insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly; disparate impact alone does not satisfy equal protection standard.

source_file: 10189320_2024_FRANKLIN v. THE JERSEY CITY HOUSING AUTHORITY_njd
case_name: Edwina Franklin v. The Jersey City Housing Authority, Secretary, Department of Housing and Urban Development
accommodation_description: The complaint alleges Fair Housing Act violations but the opinion does not describe any specific accommodation request; the court's analysis focuses entirely on procedural requirements for default judgment.
key_holding: The Court dismissed Plaintiff's motion for default judgment because after Plaintiff filed a Consolidated and Amended Complaint against the JCHA following an entry of default, she was required to request a new entry of default against the JCHA before moving for default judgment under Rule 55.
brief_summary: Pro se Plaintiff Edwina Franklin filed a motion for default judgment against the Jersey City Housing Authority and HUD alleging Fair Housing Act and ECOA violations. The Court dismissed the motion without prejudice, holding that Plaintiff failed to obtain a fresh entry of default under Rule 55(a) after filing her Consolidated and Amended Complaint, which was required before moving for default judgment under Rule 55(b)(2).
key_cases_cited: Husain v. Casino Control Comm’n, 265 F. App’x 130 (3d Cir. 2008)
Nationwide Mut. Ins. Co. v. Starlight Ballroom Dance Club, Inc., 175 F. App’x 519 (3d Cir. 2006)

source_file: 10189406_2024_CAREONE AT BIRCHWOOD, LLC v. TOWNSHIP OF EDISON_njd
case_name: CareOne at Birchwood, LLC v. Township of Edison
accommodation_description: Developer sought a use variance and bulk variances to construct a 106-bed, 3-story assisted living facility in a residential zoning district as a reasonable accommodation for elderly and disabled individuals.
key_holding: The court found that the Township's zoning code has a discriminatory disparate impact on disabled individuals by excluding assisted living facilities from all residential zones, but also found genuine disputes of material fact exist as to whether the specific 106-bed, 3-story design of the proposed facility was 'necessary' to provide disabled individuals an equal opportunity to housing under the reasonable accommodation analysis.
brief_summary: CareOne at Birchwood, LLC sued Edison Township and its Zoning Board alleging the municipal zoning code, which excludes assisted living facilities from all residential districts, violates the Fair Housing Act by discriminating against elderly and disabled individuals who require congregate care housing. The court granted partial summary judgment to plaintiffs on the disparate impact claim, finding the zoning ordinance disproportionately affects disabled persons, but denied cross-motions on the reasonable accommodation claim because disputed facts exist regarding whether the specific size and design of the proposed 106-bed facility was necessary to provide disabled individuals an equal opportunity to housing.
key_cases_cited: Lapid-Laurel, LLC v. Zoning Bd. of Adjustment of Twp. of Scotch Plains, 284 F.3d 442 (3d Cir. 2002)
Hovsons, Inc. v. Tower Oaks, Inc., 89 F.3d 1096 (3d Cir. 1996)
Vorchheimer v. Philadelphian Owners Ass'n, 903 F.3d 100 (3d Cir. 2018)
Bryant Woods Inn, Inc. v. Howard County, 124 F.3d 597 (4th Cir. 1997)
Yates Real Est., Inc. v. Plainfield Zoning Bd. of Adjustment, 404 F. Supp. 3d 889 (D.N.J. 2019)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Zoning ordinance prohibition on assisted living facilities in residential districts
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that Plaintiffs established a prima facie disparate impact case through Dr. Beveridge's statistical evidence showing disabled individuals are 34-92 times more likely to live in group quarters, and that Defendants failed to demonstrate a legitimate non-discriminatory reason for excluding assisted living facilities from all residential districts. The Code's failure to list assisted living as a permitted use in any residential district, while allowing single-family homes, has a disproportionate effect on disabled individuals seeking housing.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Use variance and bulk variances (building coverage, lot coverage, floor area ratio, height, stories) to permit construction of 106-bed, 3-story assisted living facility on property in R-A residential district
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found genuine disputes of material fact on both prongs of the burden-shifting test. On Plaintiffs' burden: while a use variance is necessary as a matter of definition, Plaintiffs failed to establish that the specific size (106 beds) and configuration (3 stories) are necessary for financial viability or therapeutic purpose—testimony was conclusory without quantification. On Defendants' burden: while the Board cited legitimate concerns (traffic, noise, height, character), a genuine issue remains whether these constitute a fundamental alteration, particularly given the adjacent nursing facility and country club suggesting compatibility.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II of the ADA, 42 U.S.C. § 12101 et seq.; Rehabilitation Act of 1973, 29 U.S.C. § 791 et seq.; Equal Protection under 42 U.S.C. § 1983
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the same FHAA framework to Title II ADA and Rehabilitation Act claims (Counts Three and Four), denying summary judgment on both because genuine disputes remain on the reasonable accommodation analysis. The court granted summary judgment on the § 1983 Equal Protection claim (Count Five) because Plaintiffs abandoned it by failing to respond to Defendants' arguments or mention it in their opposition and summary judgment briefs.

source_file: 10189729_2024_BORIA v. THE HERITAGE AT ALEXANDER HAMILTON_njd
case_name: Boria v. The Heritage at Alexander Hamilton
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs did not make a formal reasonable accommodation request; rather, they requested that defendants remediate mold and replace the air filter, and—following medical recommendations—sought relocation to another unit free from the environmental hazard caused by mold and rodent infestation.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' negligence per se claim because violations of New Jersey's Hotel and Multiple Dwellings Law regulations, the FHA, and the TSCA cannot form the basis of a negligence per se claim under New Jersey law, and dismissed the res ipsa loquitur claim because it is an evidentiary rule, not a standalone cause of action.
brief_summary: Tenants at a Paterson, New Jersey apartment complex sued after discovering mold, rodent infestation, and other habitability hazards upon move-in, alleging among other claims negligence per se based on alleged violations of HMDL regulations, the FHA, and the TSCA, and a freestanding res ipsa loquitur claim. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss Counts Three and Four under Rule 12(b)(6), holding that none of the cited statutes incorporate the common-law standard of negligence necessary to support a negligence per se theory under New Jersey law, and that res ipsa loquitur is an evidentiary doctrine rather than an independent cause of action. The direct FHA claim (Count Six) was not challenged by defendants and remains pending.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Wartluft v. Milton Hershey School
Braitman v. Overlook Terrace Corporation

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Relocation to another unit to avoid continued mold exposure; remediation of mold in the unit; repair of heating system
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the FHA claim as part of the negligence per se analysis, holding that the FHA does not incorporate common law negligence standards and cannot serve as the basis for a negligence per se claim. The court did not reach the merits of the underlying reasonable accommodation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Negligence (Count 1), breach of warranty of habitability and implied warranty of quiet enjoyment (Count 2), negligence per se based on HMDL and TSCA violations (Count 3), res ipsa loquitur (Count 4)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed Counts 3 and 4 (negligence per se and res ipsa loquitur) for failure to state a plausible claim. HMDL regulations do not provide a private right of action and cannot support negligence per se; TSCA does not permit private citizens to pursue compensation for personal injuries; res ipsa loquitur is an evidentiary rule, not a cognizable claim. Counts 1 and 2 were not addressed in this motion.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges that the Netflix redevelopment plan violates the Fair Housing Act because it fails to require construction of lower-income housing. However, this is a passing reference in the context of a preliminary injunction motion regarding a land sale, not a substantive FHA claim.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court rejected plaintiff's FHA argument in the context of denying preliminary injunctive relief, finding that plaintiff—an incarcerated individual serving a 57-year murder sentence—lacks standing to represent individuals needing lower-income housing and has failed to establish any personal connection to or harm from the land sale. The court did not reach the substantive merits of any FHA claim.

source_file: 10189892_2024_FRANKLIN v. THE JERSEY CITY HOUSING AUTHORITY_njd
case_name: Franklin v. The Jersey City Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested waiver of JCHA's 20-year recapture requirement to sell her two-story home and relocate to a one-story home due to mobility limitations from aging and disability.
key_holding: HUD's Motion to Dismiss was granted because HUD enjoys sovereign immunity, the FHA does not provide a private right of action against HUD for failure to investigate, and Plaintiff lacks Article III standing against HUD.
brief_summary: Pro se Plaintiff Edwina Franklin sued HUD and Jersey City Housing Authority alleging JCHA violated the FHA by denying her request to waive a recapture policy so she could sell her home and move to a one-story residence due to her disability-related mobility limitations. The Court granted HUD's Motion to Dismiss, finding HUD immune from suit under sovereign immunity, that no private right of action exists against HUD under the FHA, and that Plaintiff lacks Article III standing against HUD; Plaintiff's claims against JCHA remain pending.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver of mortgage recapture requirement to allow plaintiff to sell two-story home and purchase one-story home due to aging and existing handicap
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under Article III standing doctrine. Plaintiff's alleged injury (JCHA's denial of recapture waiver) was not traceable to HUD, as 42 U.S.C. § 1437z-4(i) requires HUD to allow JCHA discretion in setting lending terms. Additionally, even if court ruled against HUD, it could not alter the mortgage terms set solely by JCHA, so injury would not be redressed by favorable judicial decision.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to investigate civil rights complaints; procedural due process violation; alleged discrimination in provision of credit under ECOA
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction. FHA does not provide private right of action to sue HUD for failure to investigate FHA violations. ECOA waives sovereign immunity only for discrimination in provision of credit, but HUD did not lend plaintiff money. Procedural due process claim fails because alleged failure to investigate amounts to procedural violation, not concrete injury sufficient for Article III standing, and no cause of action exists for monetary damages from federal agencies.

case_name: Nelson v. Claussen
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege FHA discrimination based on race, religion, and citizenship status in connection with HOA services, but fail to articulate a specific accommodation request.
key_holding: The Fair Housing Act claim was dismissed with prejudice because Plaintiffs' SAC contained only conclusory statements about discrimination based on race, religion, and citizenship with no factual matter to plausibly state a claim, and amendment would be futile and inequitable.
brief_summary: Three homeowners sued over forty defendants including their HOA (Monmouth Hills, Inc.), property management, and individual residents for alleged Fair Housing Act violations based on race, religion, and citizenship status. The Court dismissed the FHA claim with prejudice for failure to state a claim, finding the SAC contained only conclusory allegations devoid of factual support and that amendment would be futile and inequitable.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged discrimination in provision of services or facilities in connection with status as shareholders within planned real estate community, including alleged race-based discrimination in housing sales and alleged redirection of polluted stormwater to plaintiffs' properties.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found the Fair Housing Act claim failed under Iqbal/Twombly because plaintiffs pleaded only conclusory statements with no sufficient factual matter to state a plausible claim. The SAC contained minimal facts supporting the FHA claim—only three paragraphs (74, 89, 127-128)—and plaintiffs failed to articulate any coherent theory of liability under the FHA. The court could not discern what legal theory plaintiffs were advancing.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: RICO Act claims (18 U.S.C. §§ 1962(a)-(d)); New Jersey Civil RICO Act (N.J.S.A. 2C:41 et seq.); common law breach of fiduciary duty; fraud; fraud in the inducement; equitable fraud; professional negligence; breach of contract; conversion; Federal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (15 U.S.C. § 1692)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed all non-FHA claims for failure to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly. RICO claims failed because plaintiffs failed to plead mail and wire fraud predicate acts with the particularity required by Rule 9(b), instead offering only conclusory references to 'misrepresentations' without dates, times, places, or specific details of fraudulent conduct. The SAC and RICO Case Statement contradicted each other regarding who sent communications. State law claims were dismissed without prejudice, and supplemental jurisdiction was declined.

case_name: Ruth T. McLean v. Aimee D. Sumitra, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff's incomprehensible filings reference the Fair Housing Act but do not articulate a valid accommodation request; the case concerns a foreclosure action.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's Operative Complaint for failure to state a claim, finding her filings incomprehensible, confusing, and conclusory, failing to meet the pleading standards under Rules 8 and 12(b)(6).
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Ruth McLean filed multiple incomprehensible complaints against PNC Bank and Secretary of State defendants arising from a New Jersey state foreclosure action on her property. The court dismissed the Operative Complaint for failure to state a claim, finding plaintiff's filings failed to comply with Rule 8 pleading standards and contained no cognizable legal theories.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly

fha_claims.accommodation_description: FDCPA, NJFCRA, fraud, civil conspiracy, and various constitutional/statutory claims (Fair Housing Act sections 837, 245, 701 cited but do not exist; National Currency Act; 4th Amendment; § 1983)
fha_claims.reasoning: The Operative Complaint fails to comply with Rule 8's pleading standards and consists of formulaic recitations of legal elements without sufficient factual allegations. The complaint cites non-existent FHA sections and fails to state plausible claims for relief under any cognizable legal theory. The court found the pleading so confusing and unintelligible that defendants could not discern the conduct complained of.

source_file: 10190254_2024_BIRD BUYS HOUSES LLC v. BRYANT ROGERS_njd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Eviction defense based on alleged Fair Housing Act violation related to disability; specific accommodation not detailed in opinion
fha_claims.disposition: Dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the case sua sponte for lack of federal question jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1331, untimely removal under § 1446 (over two years after state court judgment), and application of the Rooker-Feldman Doctrine barring review of state court judgments. The underlying state court complaint was not provided, preventing assessment of whether a federal question existed on the face of the complaint.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) claim; COVID-19 Eviction Moratorium claim; CARES Act claim
fha_claims.disposition: Dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed all non-FHA federal claims (ADA, CARES Act, COVID-19 Eviction Moratorium) along with the FHA claim for lack of federal question jurisdiction, untimely removal, and Rooker-Feldman bar. No substantive analysis of these claims was conducted.

case_name: Jerry Smith v. Supportive Housing Coalition
accommodation_description: Vague allegations of failure to move plaintiff to safe living conditions due to toxic mold in dwelling unit, with complaint failing to identify any specific disability-related accommodation request.
key_holding: The complaint fails to state a plausible FHA claim because it contains no facts establishing plaintiff's membership in a protected class or a causal connection between protected status and any discriminatory conduct, but plaintiff is granted leave to amend.
brief_summary: Jerry Smith sued Supportive Housing Coalition, the City of Albuquerque, and Laura Chavez alleging Fair Housing Act violations and failure to provide safe living conditions free from toxic mold. The federal court found the complaint deficient for failing to allege facts establishing plaintiff's protected class membership and a causal connection between that status and discriminatory conduct, granting plaintiff fourteen days to amend the complaint or face dismissal and remand to state court.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic v. Twombly

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint fails to allege facts establishing that plaintiff is a member of a protected class or establishing a plausible causal connection between any protected status and the alleged discriminatory conduct (unsafe living conditions/toxic mold). Court applied Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard and found allegations insufficient.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of implied warranty of habitability, New Mexico Owner Resident Relations Act (ORRA)
fha_claims.reasoning: In the absence of a viable federal FHA claim, the court lacks subject matter jurisdiction over plaintiff's state-law claims and will remand to state court upon dismissal of the FHA claim.

case_name: Jerry Smith v. Supportive Housing Coalition
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested to be relocated from his current unit—which suffered from toxic mold, cracked ceilings, water damage, and electrical hazards—to a safer unit, asserting this transfer was a reasonable accommodation for his mental health disability and in connection with his familial status as a parent of minor children.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claims with prejudice because the amended complaint failed to allege any factual causal connection between plaintiff's protected statuses (disability and familial status) and defendants' adverse actions, and remanded the remaining state law claims to state court.
brief_summary: Jerry Smith sued Supportive Housing Coalition, the City of Albuquerque, and an employee under the FHA, alleging failure to accommodate his disability and familial status after requesting relocation from a unit with unsafe conditions including toxic mold, cracked ceilings, water damage, and electrical hazards, and alleging retaliation when defendants terminated his rental assistance after his complaints. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss the FHA claim with prejudice, holding that despite multiple opportunities to amend, plaintiff failed to plead underlying facts establishing a plausible causal link between his mental health disability or familial status and either the denial of accommodation or the termination of rental assistance—the core problem being that the unsafe conditions would affect any tenant regardless of protected status. The court declined supplemental jurisdiction over the state-law warranty of habitability and New Mexico Owner-Resident Relations Act claims and remanded them to the Second Judicial District Court.
key_cases_cited: Morgan v. Carrington Mortg. Servs., 719 F. App'x 735 (10th Cir. 2017)
Cinnamon Hills Youth Crisis Ctr., Inc. v. Saint George City, 685 F.3d 917 (10th Cir. 2012)
Knight v. Mooring Cap. Fund, LLC, 749 F.3d 1180 (10th Cir. 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Relocation to a safer unit without toxic mold, cracked ceilings, water damage, and electrical hazards
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege a plausible causal connection between his disability (mental health condition) and the requested accommodation (transfer to safer unit). The complaint alleges only unsafe living conditions that would affect anyone regardless of disability status, not a disability-specific need for accommodation. Court found the claim was really about landlord-tenant habitability, not FHA discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged discrimination based on familial status in provision of housing and services
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts plausibly supporting a causal connection between his familial status (having minor children) and Defendants' adverse actions (unsafe conditions or termination of rental assistance). Mere allegation of familial status and adverse conditions without linking them is insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation for requesting reasonable accommodations and reporting code violations
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's reliance on temporal proximity between his request for accommodation and termination of rental assistance is insufficient because the underlying request was for transfer due to unsafe conditions affecting anyone, not a disability-specific accommodation. The claim fails to establish that Defendants' actions were motivated by Plaintiff's protected activity under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of implied warranty of habitability, New Mexico Owner-Resident Relations Act
fha_claims.reasoning: Court declined supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims after dismissing all federal FHA claims, as permitted under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3). State courts are better suited to adjudicate landlord-tenant and habitability claims. Case remanded to state court.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 civil rights claim; New Mexico Fair Housing Act claim (state law)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found the § 1983 claim fails to allege deprivation of a federally protected right or action under color of state law, and lacks sufficient factual allegations against the property owner defendants. The court issued an Order to Show Cause requiring plaintiff to show cause why the case should not be dismissed and to file an amended complaint within 21 days.

case_name: Jean Robert Saint-Jean, et al. v. Emigrant Mortgage Company, et al.
accommodation_description: Motion for substitution of administrator for deceased plaintiff Felipe Howell following jury verdict finding defendants liable under the FHA, ECOA, and state human rights laws.
key_holding: The court granted plaintiffs' motion to substitute the estate administrator for the deceased plaintiff, finding that the underlying FHA, ECOA, NYSHRL, and NYCHRL claims survive death as they are remedial rather than penal, and declined to adjudicate the contingent question of whether punitive damages claims survive death.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs moved under Rule 25(a)(1) to substitute the estate administrator for deceased plaintiff Felipe Howell, who died after a jury found defendants liable under the FHA, ECOA, and state human rights laws and awarded compensatory damages. The court granted the motion, finding all claims survive death as they are remedial rather than penal in nature, and declined to adjudicate whether punitive damages claims survive death as that question was not ripe.
key_cases_cited: Kotler v. Jubert, 986 F.3d 147 (2d Cir. 2021)
Estwick v. U.S. Air Shuttle, 950 F. Supp. 493 (E.D.N.Y. 1996)
Int’l Cablevision, Inc. v. Sykes, 172 F.R.D. 63 (W.D.N.Y. 1997)
Barrett v. United States, 689 F.2d 324 (2d Cir. 1982)
Revock v. Cowpet Bay W. Condo. Ass’n, 853 F.3d 96 (3d Cir. 2017)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; opinion does not address substantive FHA claim merits
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted motion to substitute Administrator for deceased plaintiff under Rule 25(a)(1), finding FHA claim survives death as remedial rather than penal. Court declined to address punitive damages ripeness question, leaving substantive FHA claims pending for future adjudication.

case_name: Terrance Dixon v. New York City Housing Development Corporation
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges discrimination in the housing application process based on race and familial status through community preferences and occupancy policies.
key_holding: Plaintiff failed to state FHA claims because he did not plausibly allege discriminatory intent to discriminate based on race, familial status, or national origin, and failed to adequately plead protected activity for his retaliation claim under § 3617.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Terrance Dixon sued the New York City Housing Development Corporation and multiple related defendants alleging Fair Housing Act violations, § 1982 and § 1983 claims, and RICO violations arising from the denial of his application for affordable housing. The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss, finding that plaintiff failed to plausibly allege discriminatory intent, failed to adequately plead protected activity for his retaliation claim, and failed to state any viable federal claim.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Francis v. Kings Park Manor, Inc., 992 F.3d 67 (2d Cir. 2021)
Sykes v. Mel S. Harris & Assocs. LLC, 780 F.3d 70 (2d Cir. 2015)
Reg'l Econ. Cmty. Action Program, Inc. v. City of Middletown, 294 F.3d 35 (2d Cir. 2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege discriminatory intent under § 3604. Mere awareness of plaintiff's family size does not support an inference of family-size discrimination, and plaintiff failed to allege facts showing that defendants' policies regarding self-employed individuals were motivated by discriminatory intent based on protected class status.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege a causal connection between protected activity and adverse action under § 3617. Cavazza's cessation of communication occurred before plaintiff filed his Article 78 petition, and the petition itself did not assert FHA violations or fair housing concerns, so it did not constitute protected activity under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. §§ 1982, 1983; 18 U.S.C. § 1961 (RICO); state law claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 1982 claim failed because plaintiff did not allege facts supporting defendants' intent to discriminate based on race. Section 1983 claim failed because plaintiff did not allege purposeful or intentional discrimination or deprivation of a constitutionally protected property interest. RICO claim failed because plaintiff did not satisfy Rule 9(b)'s heightened pleading requirements for fraud allegations and failed to allege how defendants engaged in witness tampering or retaliation.

source_file: 10192659_2024_Fair Housing Justice Center, Inc. v. 203 Jay St. Associates, LLC_nyed
case_name: Fair Housing Justice Center, Inc. v. 203 Jay St. Associates, LLC
accommodation_description: Fair Housing Justice Center alleges the building known as The Amberly is inaccessible to people with disabilities who use wheelchairs due to design and construction deficiencies
key_holding: The court adopted the Magistrate Judge's recommendation to deny Woods Bagot's motion to amend its third-party complaint because its proposed contribution claim still failed to allege tort liability distinct from contractual obligations, and its implied indemnification claim failed to demonstrate a special relationship warranting indemnification.
brief_summary: Fair Housing Justice Center sued the owners, developers, and architects of The Amberly residential building in Brooklyn for disability discrimination based on alleged inaccessibility for wheelchair users under the FHA. The court adopted the Magistrate Judge's R&R denying Woods Bagot's motion to amend its third-party complaint for contribution and indemnification against JFG Architects, finding the proposed amendments futile because they failed to establish tort liability independent of contractual duties and failed to show a special relationship warranting implied indemnification.
key_cases_cited: Clark-Fitzpatrick, Inc. v. Long Island R. Co., 70 N.Y.2d 382
Morse/Diesel, Inc. v. Trinity Indus., Inc., 859 F.2d 242
Peoples Democratic Rep. of Yemen v. Goodpasture, Inc., 782 F.2d 346
Bd. of Educ. of Hudson City Sch. Dist. v. Sargent, Webster, Crenshaw & Folley, 71 N.Y.2d 21
Clover Communities Beavercreek, LLC v. Mussachio Architects P.C., 676 F. Supp. 3d 82

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible design and construction of residential apartment building (The Amberly) for people with disabilities who use wheelchairs, including accessible common areas, entrances, and units
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss on August 4, 2022, allowing plaintiff's FHA design and construction claims to proceed. The opinion addresses third-party claims and procedural matters but does not reach the merits of the underlying FHA accessibility claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: New York State Human Rights Law (N.Y. Exec. Law § 290 et seq.), New York City Human Rights Law (N.Y.C. Admin. Code § 8-107 et seq.), New York State Civil Rights Law (§ 40 et seq.)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff asserted parallel state and local civil rights claims alongside FHA claims. The court's August 4, 2022 order denying the motion to dismiss allowed these claims to proceed, but the opinion does not address their merits.

source_file: 10193115_2024_Mills Pond Group LLC v. Town of Smithtown, New York_nyed
case_name: Mills Pond Group LLC v. Town of Smithtown, New York
accommodation_description: Developer Mills Pond sought to construct an assisted living facility in a residential zone and alleged Fair Housing Act claims after the Town amended zoning to eliminate assisted living facilities from special exception eligibility.
key_holding: The developer Mills Pond lacks standing to pursue Fair Housing Act and ADA claims because its primary purpose is to develop property for profit, not to operate assisted living facilities for disabled persons, and the zoning challenge is not ripe for adjudication because Mills Pond failed to pursue available remedies such as a variance or zone change application.
brief_summary: Mills Pond Group LLC, a real estate development company, sued the Town of Smithtown and its officials seeking to build an assisted living facility after the Town amended its zoning code to eliminate assisted living facilities from special exception permits in residential zones, asserting Fair Housing Act, ADA, and constitutional claims. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that Mills Pond lacked constitutional standing to pursue discrimination claims because its primary purpose was property development for profit rather than providing housing for disabled persons, and that the zoning challenge was not ripe because the developer failed to exhaust available administrative remedies.
key_cases_cited: Sunrise Development, Inc. v. Town of Huntington, 62 F. Supp. 2d 762 (E.D.N.Y. 1999)
31FO, LLC v. Inc. Vill. of Lloyd Harbor, 2023 WL 6385187 (E.D.N.Y. Sept. 29, 2023)
Sunrise Detox V, LLC v. City of White Plains, 769 F.3d 118 (2d Cir. 2014)
Williamson County v. Regional Housing Auth., 473 U.S. 172 (1985)
Knick v. Township of Scott, 139 S. Ct. 2162 (2019)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act discrimination claims; Americans with Disabilities Act; Equal Protection Clause; Due Process Clause; New York State Constitution provisions; state common law bad faith re-zoning
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs lack Article III standing. The fictional plaintiffs (XYZ, Inc. and John/Jane Does 9-97) lack legal existence and present only hypothetical future claims. The six named individual plaintiffs lack standing as intended future residents of a non-existent facility. Mills Pond Group LLC lacks standing to assert discrimination claims because its primary purpose is revenue generation through property development, not assisting the elderly and disabled; the pivot to assisted living was merely to obtain favorable zoning treatment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Due Process and Equal Protection claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 based on zoning denial
fha_claims.reasoning: The matter is not ripe for adjudication under Williamson County's final-decision requirement. Mills Pond has not received a final decision from the Town and has not exhausted available remedies, including applying for a zoning change or variance. The two-month delay before filing suit undermines any claim that zoning procedures have concluded.

source_file: 10193270_2024_Chestnut Hill NY, Inc. v. City of Kingston_nynd
case_name: Chestnut Hill NY, Inc. v. City of Kingston
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested that the Planning Board waive fire safety requirements and accept the structural engineer's reports regarding the fire escape as a reasonable accommodation to continue operating the group home for persons with disabilities.
key_holding: The reasonable accommodation claim was properly dismissed because plaintiffs failed to allege facts showing how the requested waiver of fire safety requirements was related to their disabilities, as required to demonstrate the accommodation was necessary to afford them an equal opportunity to use and enjoy housing; however, the disparate treatment claim survived because plaintiffs adequately alleged facts supporting a plausible inference of disability-based animus influencing the permit denial.
brief_summary: Chestnut Hill NY, Inc. and individual residents sued the City of Kingston challenging the denial of renewal of a special use permit for a group home serving persons with mental health disabilities and recovering from substance use. The court granted defendant's motion to dismiss the reasonable accommodation claim (brought under the ADA) and the Fourteenth Amendment due process claim, but denied dismissal of the Fair Housing Act disparate treatment claim finding plaintiffs adequately alleged disability-based animus influenced the permit denial.
key_cases_cited: Tsombanidis v. West Haven Fire Dep't, 352 F.3d 565 (2d Cir. 2003)
Mhany Mgmt., Inc. v. Cty. of Nassau, 819 F.3d 581 (2d Cir. 2016)
Olsen v. Stark Homes, Inc., 759 F.3d 140 (2d Cir. 2014)
Innovative Health Sys., Inc. v. City of White Plains, 117 F.3d 37 (2d Cir. 1997)
Laflamme v. New Horizons, Inc., 605 F. Supp. 2d 378 (D. Conn. 2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plausible inference of disability-based animus from disability-based comments at public hearing and lack of credible justification for at least one finding in the Planning Board's denial resolution (fire alarm system compliance finding). Disparate treatment claim survived motion to dismiss under Iqbal/Twombly standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver of fire safety requirements and acceptance of engineer's reports regarding the fire escape as structurally sound and safe
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed reasonable accommodation claim because plaintiffs failed to allege facts showing the requested waiver of fire safety requirements was necessary to afford disabled persons equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling. Plaintiffs did not allege how their disabilities (mental health impairments and mental challenges) prevented enjoyment of the group home or how waiver of fire safety requirements would compensate for diminished use caused by disabilities. The accommodation was unrelated to the residents' disabilities.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II discrimination claim, ADA reasonable accommodation claim, and Fourteenth Amendment substantive due process claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed ADA reasonable accommodation claim on same grounds as FHA claim—failure to allege nexus between disability and requested accommodation. Court dismissed substantive due process claim because Planning Board had discretion to deny renewal if conditions of permit were not being met, meaning plaintiffs lacked clear entitlement to renewal and thus no valid property interest protected by substantive due process.

case_name: Brown v. Community Preservation Partners, LLC
accommodation_description: This is a procedural order addressing party substitution under Rule 25 following plaintiff Beverly Brown's death; no substantive accommodation request is analyzed.
key_holding: The court granted plaintiffs' motion to substitute Roslyn Brown, administrator of decedent Beverly Brown's estate, as plaintiff because Fair Housing Act claims survive a party's death and the estate administrator is a proper substitute party.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs' counsel moved to substitute Roslyn Brown, sister and administrator of deceased plaintiff Beverly Brown's estate, as plaintiff in this Fair Housing Act case commenced in 2017. The court granted the unopposed motion, holding that FHA claims do not extinguish upon a party's death and the estate administrator is a proper substitute party under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 25(a)(1).
key_cases_cited: Saint-Jean v. Emigrant Mortg. Co., 2022 WL 843836 (E.D.N.Y. Mar. 22, 2022)
Natale v. Country Ford Ltd., 287 F.R.D. 135 (E.D.N.Y. 2012)
Graham v. Henderson, 224 F.R.D. 59 (N.D.N.Y. 2004)

case_name: Hendricks v. Urban & Economic Development
accommodation_description: No traditional FHA accommodation was requested. Plaintiff alleged her Section 8 housing voucher (referenced as 'Section 81' in the complaint) was improperly terminated without a pre-termination hearing, raising a Fourteenth Amendment due process claim under § 1983; the FHA and ADA claims were dismissed with leave to amend at initial review but were never amended.
key_holding: The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss without prejudice under Rule 41(b) because plaintiff failed to update her address or take any meaningful action to prosecute the case for over a year, satisfying all five Second Circuit factors favoring dismissal.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Danielle Hendricks filed a § 1983 complaint alleging her Section 8 housing voucher was improperly terminated without a pre-termination hearing, with FHA and ADA claims also raised. After the Magistrate Judge recommended dismissal of the FHA/ADA claims with leave to amend and the sole surviving due process claim moved forward, plaintiff's mail was returned as undeliverable and she completely ceased all participation in the litigation. The district court granted defendants' Rule 41(b) motion to dismiss for failure to prosecute, noting all five Second Circuit factors favored dismissal, but ordered dismissal without prejudice given plaintiff's pro se status.
key_cases_cited: Chambers v. NASCO, Inc., 501 U.S. 32 (1991)
Lyell Theatre Corp. v. Loews Corp., 682 F.2d 37 (2d Cir. 1982)
LeSane v. Hall's Sec. Analyst, Inc., 239 F.3d 206 (2d Cir. 2001)
Lucas v. Miles, 84 F.3d 532 (2d Cir. 1996)
Baptiste v. Sommers, 768 F.3d 212 (2d Cir. 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation related to Section 8 housing voucher termination (specific accommodation not detailed in opinion)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the entire complaint for failure to prosecute under Rule 41(b) due to plaintiff's prolonged noncompliance with court orders and failure to update her address, making it impossible to serve her or conduct litigation. The FHA claim was never reached on the merits.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 due process claim; Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) claim; Fair Housing Act claim (collapsed into single NOT_FHA object per instructions)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the entire complaint for failure to prosecute under Rule 41(b). The magistrate judge's Report-Recommendation had recommended that the § 1983 due process claim against Curley and Grant survive initial review, the due process claim against Urban & Economic Development be dismissed with prejudice, and the FHA and ADA claims be dismissed without prejudice with leave to amend, but the Rule 41(b) dismissal for failure to prosecute superseded all pending claims.

case_name: Amanda David and Rootwork Herbals, LLC v. Robert Whittaker, Jr.
accommodation_description: Neighbor harassment claims based on race and sexuality (not a reasonable accommodation case)
key_holding: The court denied defendant's motion to dismiss, finding plaintiffs plausibly alleged hostile housing environment and retaliation claims under § 3617, disparate treatment under § 3604(c), and claims under §§ 1981 and 1982.
brief_summary: Amanda David and her business Rootwork Herbals sued neighbor Robert Whittaker alleging nearly three years of racial and sexual harassment including epithets, threats, property damage, and vandalism that forced Rootwork to cancel workshops. The court denied Whittaker's motion to dismiss, finding plaintiffs plausibly alleged hostile housing environment and retaliation claims under § 3617, disparate treatment under § 3604(c), and claims under §§ 1981 and 1982.
key_cases_cited: Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 144 S. Ct. 2244 (2024)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009)
Mohamed v. McLaurin, 390 F. Supp. 3d 520 (D. Vt. 2019)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs plausibly alleged disparate treatment under § 3604(c) based on race and sexual orientation. Although the court noted uncertainty regarding neighbor-on-neighbor § 3604(c) claims and post-acquisition conduct, defendant did not develop these arguments, and the motion to dismiss was denied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Hostile housing environment claim under § 3617
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs plausibly alleged a hostile housing environment under § 3617 by alleging severe and pervasive harassment based on race and sexual orientation. The court rejected defendant's argument that constructive eviction is a required element, finding that § 3617 applies to post-acquisition conduct and does not require proof of constructive eviction.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation for reporting harassment to law enforcement
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs plausibly alleged retaliation under § 3617 by alleging protected activity (complaints to law enforcement), defendant's awareness of the protected activity, and a causal connection between the complaints and escalated harassment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 and 1982 claims for racial discrimination in contracting and property rights
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs plausibly alleged claims under §§ 1981 and 1982 by alleging that defendant interfered with their contracts with third-party workshop participants and their ability to use their property for its intended purpose, and that defendant possessed the requisite power or authority to effect such interference as an adjacent neighbor.

source_file: 10193726_2023_Pierre v. United States Office of the Comptroller of Currency_nysd
case_name: Katheline Pierre v. United States Office of the Comptroller of Currency
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation is identified. Plaintiff used the word 'accommodate' in a general, conclusory sense when alleging that financial institutions refused to provide her standard banking and lending services (depository, credit, and fair lending), without articulating any particular disability-related or other accommodation request.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's pro se complaint against the FDIC and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency for failure to state a claim upon which relief can be granted and because sovereign immunity bars monetary suits against federal agencies absent a statutory waiver.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Katheline Pierre sued the FDIC and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency alleging that multiple financial institutions — including Bank of America, Chase, and Citizens Bank — discriminated against her on the basis of race, color, and gender by refusing to provide depository, credit, and fair lending services, and that the federal agency defendants failed to act on her complaints. The court found the complaint fatally unclear, unable to discern why the federal agencies (rather than the banks themselves) were proper defendants, and dismissed it for failure to state a claim under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii). The court additionally dismissed on sovereign immunity grounds because plaintiff had not identified any statutory waiver permitting a money-damages suit against the FDIC or OCC, and denied leave to amend as futile.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
United States v. Mitchell, 445 U.S. 535 (1980)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges discrimination and retaliation based on race, color, and gender in connection with refusal to provide depository, credit, and fair lending services by multiple financial institutions. Claims brought under Equal Credit Opportunity Act (15 U.S.C. § 1691), Fair Housing Act (42 U.S.C. § 3402), Electronic Fund Transfer Act (15 U.S.C. § 1693), and Freedom of Information Act (5 U.S.C. § 552).
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint fails to state a claim upon which relief can be granted because it is wholly unclear what occurred involving the various banks and creditors, why plaintiff sues the FDIC and COC, and how the attachments relate to the claims. Additionally, sovereign immunity bars suits against federal agencies and officers in their official capacities unless immunity is waived, and plaintiff invoked no statute waiving such immunity.

source_file: 10193740_2023_Fair Housing Justice Center, Inc. v. Goldfarb Properties, Inc._nysd
case_name: Fair Housing Justice Center, Inc. v. Pelican Management, Inc.
accommodation_description: Waiver of minimum income requirements (43x monthly rent) for applicants with rental subsidies (Section 8, OHS, HASA), many of whom are disabled, whose rent obligations are calculated based on their income.
key_holding: Defendants' 2015 minimum income policy requiring all applicants to earn 43 times the monthly rent had a disparate impact on disabled subsidy recipients (OHS, HASA, Section 8) in violation of the FHA and NYCHRL, and the 2019 policy's treatment of partial subsidy applicants also had a discriminatory disparate impact.
brief_summary: Fair Housing Justice Center sued Pelican Management/Goldfarb Properties over their minimum income policy (43x monthly rent) that effectively excluded applicants with rental subsidies, many of whom are disabled under the FHA. After a bench trial, the court found for FHJC on all claims under the FHA and NYCHRL, holding the 2015 policy had a discriminatory disparate impact on disabled subsidy recipients and the 2019 policy remained unlawful as to partial subsidy holders, awarding $240,540 in compensatory damages and $750,000 in punitive damages with injunctive relief.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dept. of Housing & Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Mhany Mgmt., Inc. v. County of Nassau, 819 F.3d 581 (2d Cir. 2016)
BMW of N. Am., Inc. v. Gore, 517 U.S. 559 (1996)
Robinson v. Instructional Sys., Inc., 80 F. Supp. 2d 203 (S.D.N.Y. 2000)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied burden-shifting framework for disparate impact under FHA § 3604(f)(3)(B). FHJC established that the 2015 Policy (requiring 43x monthly rent income) had a significantly adverse impact on applicants with OHS, HASA, and Section 8 subsidies, all of whom are disabled. Defendants failed to prove the policy was necessary to achieve their legitimate interest in reducing rent arrears, particularly for full-subsidy applicants where the voucher covers 100% of rent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found the 2019 Policy unlawful as applied to applicants with partial subsidies under disparate impact analysis. Applicants with partial subsidies were approved at 13% rate versus 30% for non-subsidy applicants—a statistically significant adverse impact. Defendants failed to prove the policy was necessary to assess ability to pay rent, as they provided no evidence that partial-subsidy holders fail to pay their required portion.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found intentional discrimination under NYCHRL source-of-income provision. Defendants treated subsidy applicants less favorably: (1) assessed subsidy applicants' income against both their rent share and voucher share (an unreachable standard); (2) applied different reviewers with different standards (Dunn granted 5% variance for non-subsidy applicants; Schaper/Miller rigidly applied 40% ratio to subsidy applicants); (3) had prior notice from Goode settlement and fair housing training that such policies violate law but took no corrective action. Totality of circumstances reflects reckless indifference amounting to intentional discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: NYCHRL disability discrimination claim (disparate impact); NYCHRL source-of-income discrimination claim (disparate impact and disparate treatment)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied same burden-shifting framework under NYCHRL as FHA for disability discrimination claim and found for FHJC. For source-of-income discrimination under NYCHRL § 8-107(5)(a), court found disparate impact: 100% of OHS, 100% of HASA, and 97% of Section 8 applicants could not meet 43x rent requirement. Defendants' justification (reducing rent arrears) was insufficient, particularly for full-subsidy applicants. Court also found intentional discrimination based on totality of circumstances including prior Goode settlement, fair housing training, and differential treatment of subsidy versus non-subsidy applicants.

case_name: Michael O. Williams v. Settle Homes
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges he was refused an apartment because of his income and choice of occupation as a student and stock market trader.
key_holding: Plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claims were properly dismissed because income and source of income are not protected classes under the FHA, and Plaintiff failed to allege membership in any enumerated protected class (race, color, religion, sex, familial status, national origin, or disability).
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Michael Williams sued Settle Homes and two individuals alleging they refused to rent him an apartment because of his income and occupation as a student and stock market trader. The Court dismissed the FHA claims for failure to state a claim because income and source of income are not protected classes under the Fair Housing Act, and the Court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over state law source-of-income discrimination claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Gladstone Realtors v. Vill. of Bellwood, 441 U.S. 91 (1979)
Short v. Manhattan Apartments, Inc., 916 F. Supp. 2d 375 (S.D.N.Y. 2012)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of rental based on income and choice of occupation
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege membership in a protected class under the FHA.
