Income and choice of occupation are not enumerated protected classes under 42 U.S.C. § 3604, and the complaint contains no factual allegations suggesting Plaintiff belongs to any protected class (race, color, religion, sex, familial status, national origin, or disability).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: New York State Human Rights Law claim for discrimination based on lawful source of income
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacks diversity jurisdiction because Plaintiff and Defendant Settle Homes are both New York residents and Plaintiff seeks only $15,000, below the $75,000 statutory minimum. The court declined supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims after dismissing all federal claims.

case_name: Jimmy Avila v. Acacia Network, Inc.
accommodation_description: The specific accommodation requested by plaintiff is not described in this order; the document is limited to directing the service of process on defendants and does not address the substantive nature of plaintiff's disability-related request.
key_holding: The Court directed the Clerk of Court to issue summonses and complete U.S. Marshals Service process forms to effect service on both defendants in this pro se, in forma pauperis FHA disability discrimination and retaliation action.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Jimmy Avila filed suit against Acacia Network, Inc. and Trevor Griffiths—a nonprofit supportive housing organization and its Program Director—asserting claims of disability-based discrimination and retaliation under the Fair Housing Act, the ADA, and state law. Having previously granted plaintiff IFP status, the Court issued an Order of Service instructing the Clerk of Court to prepare USM-285 forms and summonses for both defendants and to deliver the necessary paperwork to the U.S. Marshals Service to effect service at their respective Bronx, New York addresses. The order imposes no substantive ruling on the merits and concerns only the mechanics of service.
key_cases_cited: Walker v. Schult, 717 F.3d 119 (2d Cir. 2013)
Meilleur v. Strong, 682 F.3d 56 (2d Cir. 2012)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not specified in this order
fha_claims.reasoning: This is a procedural order addressing service of process only. The court granted plaintiff's IFP request and ordered the Clerk to issue summonses and arrange service through the U.S. Marshals Service. No substantive claims have been addressed or dismissed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA, state law claims
fha_claims.reasoning: This is a procedural order addressing service of process only. The complaint alleges ADA and state law claims, but no substantive ruling on these claims has been made.

case_name: Avila v. Acacia Network
accommodation_description: Plaintiff asserts disability-based retaliation claim under the Fair Housing Act; specific accommodation request not detailed in this service order.
key_holding: Court granted plaintiff's request to proceed in forma pauperis and ordered the U.S. Marshals Service to effect service on defendants; no substantive ruling on the merits of the FHA retaliation claim.
brief_summary: Jimmy Avila, proceeding pro se and in forma pauperis, filed this action against Acacia Network, Aja Douglas, 1212 Grant Realty LLC, Manny Stein, and Caren Abate asserting disability-based retaliation under the Fair Housing Act. The court ordered service of process on defendants but has not yet reached the merits of the claims.
key_cases_cited: Walker v. Schult
Meilleur v. Strong

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; retaliation claim does not allege failure to provide accommodation
fha_claims.reasoning: This is a service of process order issued after the court granted plaintiff's IFP request. The court has not yet reviewed the complaint on the merits or ruled on any motion to dismiss. The retaliation claim survives at this preliminary stage and remains pending.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Professional negligence and unjust enrichment claims under New York state law for failure to timely file tax returns
fha_claims.reasoning: Accounting malpractice claim survived motion to dismiss under Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard; unjust enrichment claim dismissed as duplicative of the surviving malpractice claim. The court found that the taxpayer's non-delegable duty to file returns does not preclude a malpractice claim against accountants, and the continuous representation doctrine tolls the statute of limitations.

case_name: Elewood Torres v. MMS Group, LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Deaf plaintiff requests installation of high-intensity strobe lights and bed shakers to alert him of fire emergencies, and hiring security staff fluent in ASL or equipped with communication devices.
key_holding: Plaintiff failed to establish likelihood of success on the merits because strobe lights were already installed in the building more than a decade ago and plaintiff submitted no evidence the current strobe lights or security staff communication tools were inadequate, and plaintiff's years-long delay in seeking relief undermined his claim of irreparable harm.
brief_summary: Deaf plaintiff Elewood Torres sued MMS Group LLC and other defendants seeking preliminary injunction for fire alarm strobe lights, bed shakers, and ASL-fluent security staff as disability accommodations at his apartment buildings. The court denied the preliminary injunction because plaintiff failed to show likelihood of success on the merits (strobe lights already existed and no evidence showed current systems were inadequate) and demonstrated undue delay undermining irreparable harm claims, and also granted HPD's motion to dismiss because plaintiff failed to plausibly allege HPD owned the premises.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Henrietta D. v. Bloomberg, 331 F.3d 261 (2d Cir. 2003)
Roberts v. Royal Atl. Corp., 542 F.3d 363 (2d Cir. 2008)
Demirayak v. City of N.Y., 746 F. App'x 49 (2d Cir. 2018)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Installation of high-intensity strobe lights and bed shakers to alert deaf and hearing-impaired persons of fire hazards
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish likelihood of success on the merits because defendants submitted evidence that strobe lights were already installed more than 10 years ago in every unit and common area, and plaintiff provided no evidence that bed shakers are necessary to deny him access to the premises. The court found that the absence of bed shakers does not constitute a barrier to accessibility within the meaning of the ADA and related statutes.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Hiring 24/7 security staff fluent in American Sign Language (ASL) or equipped with devices to communicate effectively with deaf or hearing-impaired individuals
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish likelihood of success on the merits because defendants demonstrated that security staff already have tools to communicate with deaf and hearing-impaired individuals, including written communication via notepads and pens, and emergency communication boards. Plaintiff could not provide evidence of a particular instance in which security staff were unable to communicate during an emergency. The court found that broad complaints about staff quality and availability do not rise to the level of a barrier to accessibility, especially given HUD's recent approval for hiring a second security guard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), 42 U.S.C. § 12181 et seq.; Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973; 42 U.S.C. § 1983; New York State Human Rights Law (NYSHRL); New York City Human Rights Law (NYCHRL)
fha_claims.reasoning: All claims against Defendant HPD were dismissed because plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that HPD owns the Premises. The court took judicial notice of publicly recorded deeds and Land Disposition Agreements showing that HPD conveyed ownership to NYSD Housing Development Fund Corporation and NYSD Forsyth Housing Development Fund Company, Inc. in 1992 and 2000. Plaintiff's argument that HPD retained a future possessory interest or possibility of reverter was rejected because the reverter provision requires a written demand by the City (which plaintiff did not allege occurred) and is not available to non-parties to the LDAs.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Walk-in shower modification to plaintiff's apartment
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for failure to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly because plaintiff did not allege facts showing he requested the accommodation or that defendants denied it based on disability; court granted leave to amend to replead disability discrimination claims under the Fair Housing Act.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III (residential housing discrimination); False Claims Act (qui tam action); state law defamation and harassment claims
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA Title III claims dismissed because residential apartments are not public accommodations; FCA claims dismissed because pro se plaintiff lacks standing to bring qui tam actions; supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims declined after dismissal of all federal claims.

case_name: Ali Moore v. City of New York
accommodation_description: Plaintiff brought claims arising from police arrests and involuntary psychiatric hospitalizations, with an FHA claim dismissed for failure to plead adverse housing action.
key_holding: Plaintiff's § 1983 claims for false arrest, excessive force, unlawful search/seizure, and due process survived dismissal, but his Fair Housing Act claim was dismissed because the complaint failed to plead any adverse housing action caused by his race.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Ali Moore sued New York City, NYPD officers, NYCH+H Harlem Hospital, and medical staff alleging constitutional violations stemming from two incidents in October 2021 where police forcibly arrested him and he was involuntarily transported for psychiatric evaluation. The court granted in part and denied in part defendants' motion to dismiss, allowing Fourth Amendment false arrest, excessive force, and unlawful search/seizure claims to proceed while dismissing the FHA claim for failure to plead adverse housing action and dismissing municipal liability claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Monell v. Dep't of Soc. Servs.
Graham v. Connor

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Civil Rights Act of 1968 (FHA) claim alleging adverse housing action based on race; § 1983 false arrest, excessive force, unlawful seizure, unlawful search, due process, failure to intervene; § 1985 conspiracy; § 1981 racial discrimination; Title VI; state law assault, battery, false arrest, IIED, negligent infliction of emotional distress; respondeat superior
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the FHA claim (construed as Civil Rights Act of 1968) because plaintiff failed to plausibly allege an adverse housing action caused by race. The complaint failed to allege facts suggesting race was a motivating factor in the described incidents. Municipal liability claims were dismissed for failure to allege a municipal policy or custom. Conspiracy claims were dismissed for failure to allege a meeting of the minds or class-based discriminatory animus. § 1981 claims were dismissed because they can only be brought against private actors, not state actors. Title VI claims were dismissed for failure to allege intentional racial discrimination as a substantial or motivating factor.

case_name: Loren Leon v. Mary Kearney, et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; case concerns alleged race-based discriminatory treatment including false accusations of subletting, required escort of cleaning staff, and posting of ID at doorman's desk.
key_holding: The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss plaintiff's FHA race discrimination claims because plaintiff failed to allege sufficient factual matter to support even a minimal inference of discriminatory intent, offering only conclusory assertions without comparator facts or evidence that similarly situated tenants outside her protected class were treated differently.
brief_summary: Loren Leon, a Black female tenant, sued Mary Kearney, Melissa Hines, Joni Hughes, Landing Living LLC, and Related Rentals Corporate alleging Fair Housing Act race discrimination, Fourth Amendment, and state law claims after being accused of subletting her apartment and subjected to what she characterized as discriminatory treatment. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that plaintiff's FHA claims consisted of conclusory allegations of racial profiling without factual support, failed to identify similarly situated comparators treated differently, and did not allege conduct sufficiently severe or pervasive to create a hostile housing environment.
key_cases_cited: Francis v. Kings Park Manor, Inc., 992 F.3d 67 (2d Cir. 2021)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
A.L.M. ex rel. Moore v. Bd. of Managers of Vireum Schoolhouse Condo., 2021 WL 5121137 (2d Cir. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts to support an inference of discriminatory intent under the McDonnell Douglas framework. Plaintiff's allegations that she was accused of subletting 'solely based on her race' and was 'unfairly singled out' were conclusory assertions without factual support, and plaintiff did not allege disparate treatment of similarly situated tenants outside her protected class.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's hostile housing environment claim failed on two grounds: (1) the alleged conduct—accusation of subletting, requirement to escort cleaning staff, and request for proof of lease—was not sufficiently pervasive or severe to alter housing conditions; and (2) plaintiff failed to plead facts showing the harassment occurred because of her race, relying instead on conclusory assertions without factual allegations tending to show discriminatory motivation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 Fourth Amendment claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's § 1983 Fourth Amendment claim failed because defendants are private parties, not state actors. The Constitution regulates only government conduct, and plaintiff did not allege that defendants acted under color of state law or that there was a sufficiently close nexus between the state and defendants' challenged actions.

case_name: Goldstein v. The Bowery Defendants
accommodation_description: Plaintiff claims exclusion from Bowery Mission shelter due to antisemitism (religious discrimination), not a request for disability accommodation.
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA claims against Bowery Mission defendants were dismissed because his allegations do not support an inference of discriminatory motivation based on his Jewish religion, and district courts have concluded the FHA does not apply to shelters.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Jesse Goldstein sued the Bowery Mission and numerous other defendants claiming religious discrimination (antisemitism) when he was excluded from a homeless shelter, invoking the Fair Housing Act. The court dismissed the FHA claims for failure to state a claim, finding no plausible inference of discriminatory intent and noting that courts have held the FHA does not apply to shelters, while also severing unrelated claims against other defendants.
key_cases_cited: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Palmer v. Fannie Mae, 755 F. App’x 43 (2d Cir. 2018)
Littlejohn v. City of New York, 795 F.3d 297 (2d Cir. 2015)
Vega v. Hempstead Union Free School District, 801 F.3d 72 (2d Cir. 2015)
Jenkins v. New York City Dep't of Homeless Servs., 643 F. Supp. 2d 507 (S.D.N.Y. 2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged discrimination based on religion (Jewish identity) in exclusion from shelter. Court found allegations insufficient to support even minimal inference of discriminatory motivation, noting that plaintiff's name suggesting Jewish identity and prior authorized stays at the shelter when defendants were presumably aware of his religion do not plausibly support discriminatory intent. Additionally, court noted that district courts in this circuit have concluded the FHA does not apply to shelters.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Eighth Amendment cruel and unusual punishment claim; § 1983 constitutional rights claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish that Bowery Mission is a state actor required for § 1983 liability. Court applied three-part state action test (compulsion, joint action, public function) and found that provision of low-cost supportive housing is not a public function and no other basis for state attribution exists. Additionally, Eighth Amendment protections apply only to criminal and certain civil punishments imposed by government, not private entities.

source_file: 10195301_2024_MacNeal v. The State of New York_nysd
case_name: Kelly MacNeal v. The State of New York, et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request is identified in this service order; the court does not substantively analyze any Fair Housing Act claim.
key_holding: The court dismissed claims against the DHR as redundant of claims against the State of New York, and dismissed claims against NYPD and FDNY's EMS for failure to state a claim, while directing service on the remaining governmental defendants.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Kelly MacNeal filed an in forma pauperis complaint against the State of New York, City of New York, and various state and city agencies and employees, invoking the Fair Housing Act among other federal statutes. This service order dismisses certain agency defendants for failure to state a claim and directs service on the remaining governmental defendants; the court has not yet conducted any substantive analysis of the FHA claims.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Jenkins v. City of New York, 478 F.3d 76 (2d Cir. 2007)
Valentin v. Dinkins, 121 F.3d 72 (2d Cir. 1997)
Charles v. City of New York, 2023 WL 2752123 (S.D.N.Y. Mar. 31, 2023)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act claim (unspecified); also 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1983, 1985(3), 1986; Title II ADA; state law claims
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed claims against DHR as redundant of claims against the State of New York under Rule 21, and dismissed claims against NYPD and FDNY/EMS for failure to state a claim because these agencies are not separate entities suable under New York law. The court did not reach the merits of any FHA claim; the opinion does not describe the factual allegations supporting the FHA claim or apply any FHA legal standard.

source_file: 10195352_2024_Hall v. Crestwood Lake Section 8 Holding Corporation_nysd
case_name: Lisa Hall v. Crestwood Lake Section 8 Holding Corporation
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request identified; complaint alleges retaliation for race-based claims and participation in state court proceedings.
key_holding: The complaint failed to comply with Rule 8 and did not state a viable FHA claim because plaintiff alleged no facts supporting discrimination based on race, and nothing in the complaint suggested she suffered an adverse housing action because of her race; the court granted leave to amend.
brief_summary: Lisa Hall, proceeding pro se, sued Crestwood Lake Section 8 Holding Corporation and related defendants alleging violations of her civil and housing rights, claiming she was retaliated against because she is Black and because she countersued defendants in state court. The Court dismissed the complaint for failure to comply with Rule 8, finding no plausible FHA claim because plaintiff alleged no facts supporting race-based discrimination, and granted leave to amend.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Gladstone Realtors v. Vill. of Bellwood, 441 U.S. 91 (1979)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged retaliation based on race but provided no factual support for the belief that she was discriminated against on the basis of race, and nothing in the complaint or attachments suggests she suffered an adverse housing action because of her race. The complaint fails to plausibly allege the elements of an FHA retaliation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 due process claims; potential state law tort claims (breach of contract, tortious interference)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's allegations of 'civil rights' violations do not state a viable § 1983 claim because defendants are private parties not acting under color of state law. Plaintiff failed to allege diversity jurisdiction for any state law claims, and the complaint does not comply with Rule 8's requirement for a short and plain statement of relief.

case_name: Samuel Indig, Leah Indig, Meir Kahana, Robert Klein, and Naftali Klein v. The Village of Pomona, Brett Yagel, Louis Zummo, Leon Harris, Doris Ulman, and Ian Banks
accommodation_description: This is not a disability accommodation case; plaintiffs allege religious discrimination in building permit approvals and code enforcement against Orthodox Jewish property owners
key_holding: Summary judgment is granted for defendants on Kahana's claims and against Ulman and Banks, but denied on Indigs' and Kleins' claims against Yagel, Harris, and Zummo because genuine disputes exist regarding whether village officials' permit delays, stop work orders, and code enforcement actions were motivated by anti-Semitic animus rather than legitimate zoning enforcement.
brief_summary: Five Orthodox Jewish homeowners sued the Village of Pomona and individual village officials alleging religious discrimination in building permit approvals and selective enforcement of municipal codes against them. The court granted summary judgment for defendants on plaintiff Kahana's claims and dismissed claims against individual defendants Ulman and Banks, but denied summary judgment on the Indigs' and Kleins' claims against Mayor Yagel, Trustee Harris, and Building Inspector Zummo, finding genuine disputes of material fact regarding discriminatory intent based on recordings and communications revealing anti-Semitic animus.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Reynolds v. Barrett, 685 F.3d 193 (2d Cir. 2012)
Gilead Cmty. Servs., Inc. v. Town of Brookfield, 432 F. Supp. 3d 77 (S.D.N.Y. 2020)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The Indigs established a prima facie case of FHA discrimination by pointing to statements by Zummo and Yagel indicating hostility toward their religion and their construction projects. Although Defendants articulated legitimate non-discriminatory reasons (code violations), the Indigs raised a triable issue of fact regarding whether those reasons were pretext for discrimination based on the discriminatory statements and conduct.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Meir Kahana's FHA discrimination claim fails because the pool violation does not constitute making a dwelling unavailable under § 3604(a), and Kahana failed to establish that Defendants' issuance of appearance tickets was motivated by discriminatory animus. Defendants had a legitimate, non-discriminatory reason (heightened pool safety alert following a child's drowning), and Kahana failed to show pretext.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The Kleins established a prima facie case of FHA discrimination through extensive evidence of discriminatory statements and conduct directly related to their construction projects, including mocking their religion, conducting early-morning inspections, and issuing stop work orders on Jewish holidays. Although Defendants articulated legitimate reasons (code violations, sprinkler requirement), the Kleins raised triable issues regarding pretext and intentional delays.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The Indigs raised a viable FHA retaliation claim by alleging they engaged in protected activity (filing this lawsuit) and Defendants retaliated by slow-walking approval of revised permit applications. Although Defendants articulated legitimate reasons (deficient applications), the Indigs raised a triable issue regarding pretext through discriminatory statements.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Meir Kahana's FHA retaliation claim fails because he did not allege what protected activity he was engaged in when Defendants allegedly retaliated, and Zummo did not know Kahana's religion when the pool violations were discovered. Defendants had a legitimate, non-discriminatory reason (heightened pool safety alert), and Kahana failed to show pretext.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The Kleins raised a viable FHA retaliation claim by alleging Defendants delayed lifting stop work orders after the Board of Review determined the sprinkler requirement did not apply to residential homes. The court found manipulation of municipal processes to delay permit approval sufficient to establish a prima facie case, and the Kleins raised triable issues regarding pretext through discriminatory statements and conduct.

case_name: Charlier v. 21 Astor Place Condominium
accommodation_description: No accommodation request - case involves sexual harassment by building doorman resulting in hostile housing environment claims
key_holding: The Court denied dismissal of sex-based hostile housing environment claims under the FHA, NYSHRL, and NYCHRL against the employer-defendants (Douglas Elliman and 21 Astor Place Condominium), finding the plaintiff plausibly alleged Mr. Proverbs' conduct was sufficiently severe and pervasive, and that employer knowledge could be imputed through the building manager supervisor who witnessed the harassment.
brief_summary: Annabelle Charlier sued 21 Astor Place Condominium, its management company Douglas Elliman, and others alleging that building doorman Ricardo Proverbs sexually harassed her for weeks, including entering her apartment uninvited and making sexually explicit comments and threats. The Court granted in part and denied in part the Condo Defendants' motion to dismiss, dismissing claims against the Board of Managers and its President for lack of vicarious liability, but allowing the sex discrimination and hostile housing environment claims to proceed against the employer-defendants.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Burlington Indus., Inc. v. Ellerth, 524 U.S. 742 (1998)
Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)
A.L.M. ex rel. Moore v. Bd. of Managers of Vireum Schoolhouse Condo., 2021 WL 5121137 (2d Cir. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff plausibly pleaded hostile housing environment based on sexual harassment by doorman, including extraordinarily severe June 29 incident and pattern of conduct depriving plaintiff of use and enjoyment of condominium for seven weeks. Claim survives motion to dismiss against employer defendants under FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: NYSHRL housing discrimination claim analyzed under same framework as FHA. Court found plaintiff plausibly pleaded severe or pervasive harassment and that employer defendants knew or should have known of conduct through building manager supervisor. Claim survives against employer defendants.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: NYSHRL housing discrimination claim (Count Three). Court found plaintiff adequately pleaded facts supporting inference that upper-level supervisors had knowledge of conduct and ignored it, establishing condonation by employer defendants. Claim survives against employer defendants.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff abandoned retaliation claim under NYSHRL by failing to respond to defendants' arguments in opposition brief. Court found plaintiff did not allege any adverse housing action taken in retaliation for complaint.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Aiding and abetting claim under NYSHRL. Court found plaintiff established plausible inference that employer defendants condoned discriminatory conduct by failing to take corrective action after supervisor witnessed harassment. Claim survives against employer defendants.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: NYCHRL housing discrimination claim (Count Six). Court found employer defendants strictly liable for discriminatory conduct of employees under NYCHRL without regard to knowledge or conduct of employer. Claim survives against employer defendants.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: NYCHRL housing discrimination claim (Count Seven). Court applied strict liability standard under NYCHRL and found plaintiff plausibly pleaded basis for employer defendants' liability. Claim survives against employer defendants.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff abandoned interference claim under NYCHRL by failing to respond to defendants' arguments in opposition brief. Court found plaintiff did not allege that defendants threatened her, an essential element of cognizable interference claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Aiding and abetting claim under NYCHRL (Count Nine). Court found plaintiff adequately pleaded factual basis for employer defendants' liability by establishing they condoned discriminatory conduct. Claim survives against employer defendants.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff abandoned interference claim (Count Ten) by failing to respond to defendants' arguments in opposition brief. Court dismissed without substantive analysis of merits.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Negligent hiring, supervision, and retention; intentional infliction of emotional distress; negligence
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff adequately pleaded negligent supervision and retention claim by establishing employer-employee relationship, breach of duty to supervise, and proximate causation. Plaintiff failed to plead negligent hiring because she did not allege defendants knew or should have known of employee's propensity for conduct prior to hiring. IIED claim against Proverbs not addressed in motion. Negligence claims survive against employer defendants.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VII employment discrimination (nationality discrimination); state law claims (unspecified)
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim / 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that defendants discriminated or retaliated against him based on his nationality under Title VII. The factual allegations—interactions with employees of different nationalities, being sent home due to lack of internet, and mandatory lunch breaks—do not suggest discriminatory conduct or adverse employment action based on protected characteristics. Conclusory allegations of unequal pay lack factual support.

case_name: Ronald Cavallo v. HPD Section 8; Goddard Riverside
accommodation_description: Pro se plaintiff appears to seek transfer or improved housing conditions due to disability-related health concerns (tremors, heart disease, hypertension), but no specific accommodation request is clearly articulated.
key_holding: The court dismissed the complaint because plaintiff failed to allege facts showing that defendants discriminated against him because of his disability, as required to state a plausible FHA claim.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Ronald Cavallo sued HPD Section 8 and Goddard Riverside Community Center alleging Fair Housing Act violations for inadequate housing conditions (roach infestation) and disability-related harm, seeking money damages. The court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim because plaintiff failed to allege facts showing defendants discriminated against him because of his disability, granting him 60 days leave to amend.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Gladstone Realtors v. Vill. of Bellwood, 441 U.S. 91 (1979)
Mazzocchi v. Windsor Owners Corp., 2012 WL 3288240 (S.D.N.Y. 2012)
Connick v. Thompson, 563 U.S. 51 (2011)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Transfer to a different SRO unit due to roach infestation caused by neighbor's hoarding and alleged inadequate living conditions including drug trafficking, violence, and lack of social services
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for failure to state a plausible FHA claim under Iqbal/Twombly because plaintiff did not allege that defendants discriminated against him because of his disability, only that he suffered inadequate housing conditions. Plaintiff did not connect his disability to the requested accommodation or explain how defendants' conduct was motivated by his protected status.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 1983 municipal liability claim for alleged violation of civil liberties related to Section 8 housing conditions
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed the Section 1983 claim because there is no constitutional right to housing under the Fourteenth Amendment, and plaintiff failed to allege a municipal policy, custom, or practice that caused a constitutional violation. The claim is legally insufficient as a matter of law.

case_name: Williams v. 647 E. 229th St. Bronx LLC
accommodation_description: No disability-related accommodation request; plaintiff alleges race-based discrimination and retaliation in housing terms, conditions, and tenancy termination proceedings.
key_holding: The complaint fails to state an FHA claim because while plaintiff alleges he is Black and the owner is White, he provides only conclusory allegations about discriminatory motive without factual allegations explaining what defendants did or said that evidenced racial discrimination.
brief_summary: Robert Williams, a pro se Black plaintiff, sued his landlord 647 E. 229th Street Bronx LLC and Eli Weissman alleging race-based housing discrimination under the FHA, claiming defendants disputed his legal tenancy and commenced holdover proceedings against him. The court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim, finding Williams provided only conclusory allegations of discriminatory motive without factual support, and granted him 30 days leave to amend.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Fair Hous. in Huntingon Comm. v. Town of Huntington
Palmer v. Fannie Mae

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged membership in a protected class (race) and adverse treatment (disputing tenancy legality and commencing eviction), but failed to plead sufficient factual allegations to support an inference of discriminatory motivation. The statement that the owner 'believes blacks are stupid' is conclusory and does not explain what conduct evidenced racial animus, failing to meet the plausibility standard under Twombly/Iqbal.

source_file: 10197106_2024_Avila v. New York City Housing Authority_nysd
case_name: Jimmy Avila v. New York City Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiff vaguely requests unspecified accommodations to prevent severe mental and physical health crises due to disability, but court did not analyze any specific accommodation request.
key_holding: The Court dismissed Plaintiff's FHA claims because he failed to allege facts showing he suffered adverse treatment or that NYCHA discriminated against him because of his disability, race, or gender, as required to state a claim of intentional discrimination.
brief_summary: Pro se Plaintiff Jimmy Avila sued NYCHA under the Fair Housing Act, Rehabilitation Act, ADA Title II, and Section 1983, alleging discrimination based on disability, race, and gender in housing application processing. The Court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim because Plaintiff failed to allege any facts showing adverse treatment or discriminatory intent based on his protected classifications, though the Court granted leave to amend within 30 days.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Ctr.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts showing adverse treatment at his current apartment or that NYCHA discriminated against him based on disability, race, or gender. Although the court assumed plaintiff was protected under the FHA, he did not plead sufficient facts to support a minimal inference of discriminatory motivation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rehabilitation Act, Title II ADA, 42 U.S.C. § 1983 equal protection
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts showing denial of services, programs, or activities under the Rehabilitation Act or Title II ADA. For the § 1983 equal protection claim, plaintiff and recently arrived migrants are not similarly situated because plaintiff seeks permanent disability-appropriate housing while migrants seek temporary shelter system housing.

case_name: Annalicia Deandra Pownall El v. S. Realty; Lawrence Spitz; Manny; Mark
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges disability discrimination related to rent payment and eviction proceedings, but does not articulate a specific accommodation request.
key_holding: The Court dismissed Plaintiff's FHA reasonable accommodation claim because she failed to allege facts sufficient to show she has a covered disability or that she requested a reasonable accommodation shaped by her disability that the landlord was required to make.
brief_summary: Annalicia Pownall El, a pro se plaintiff, sued S. Realty and related defendants alleging disability discrimination under the Fair Housing Act related to her eviction from a Mount Vernon apartment for nonpayment of rent. The Court dismissed her federal claims, finding that while she invoked the FHA, she failed to allege facts sufficient to show she has a covered disability or that she requested a reasonable accommodation shaped by her disability that the landlord was required to make.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Salute v. Stratford Greens Garden Apartments, 136 F.3d 293 (2d Cir. 1998)
US Airways, Inc. v. Barnett, 535 U.S. 391 (2002)
Hevner v. Village East Towers, Inc., 2011 WL 666340 (S.D.N.Y. 2011)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unspecified reasonable accommodation related to plaintiff's disabilities; plaintiff alleged defendants were 'impatiently pushing' her around for rent 'knowing of her disabilities'
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts sufficient to show she has a covered disability or to identify any reasonable accommodation shaped by her disability that the landlord was required to make. The court held that economic discrimination (pressure to pay rent) is not cognizable as a failure to make reasonable accommodations under § 3604(f)(3)(B), and plaintiff's allegations were insufficient to state a claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Due process violation under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments); eviction without proper notice
fha_claims.reasoning: Defendants are private parties (landlord and realty agency) not alleged to be acting under color of state law, so they cannot be liable under § 1983. Additionally, even assuming a property interest existed, New York law provides meaningful post-deprivation remedies (continuing jurisdiction of state court to restore tenant to possession), so the alleged failure to provide 14-day notice does not state a constitutional violation.

case_name: Jerry W. Moore v. Capital Realty Group, Inc.
accommodation_description: Request for physical modifications to apartments and common areas to accommodate wheelchair users and tenants with vision impairments
key_holding: The court struck from the Third Amended Complaint the claims against HUD Defendants as immaterial matter in violation of a prior order, while directing the parties to submit proposed scheduling orders for the remaining claims against Capital Realty Group and other non-HUD defendants.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Jerry Moore sued Capital Realty Group, Inc. and other defendants alleging they failed to reasonably modify and maintain St. John Towers Apartments to accommodate tenants with vision impairments and wheelchair accessibility needs. The court struck as immaterial the claims against HUD Defendants that had been previously dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, while permitting the claims against the remaining defendants to proceed.
key_cases_cited: Offor v. Mercy Med. Ctr., 167 F. Supp. 3d 414 (E.D.N.Y. 2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable modification and maintenance of St. John Towers Apartments to accommodate tenants with vision impairments, including accessible design modifications in individual apartments and common areas
fha_claims.disposition: Complaint screened under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2); claims found viable and permitted to proceed
fha_claims.reasoning: The court screened the pro se complaint under § 1915(e)(2) and found all FHA claims viable except as alleged against HUD. The claims were permitted to proceed to amended pleadings without substantive merits analysis at the screening stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Wheelchair accessibility modifications in individual apartments and common areas of St. John Towers Apartments
fha_claims.disposition: Complaint screened under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2); claims found viable and permitted to proceed
fha_claims.reasoning: The court screened the pro se complaint under § 1915(e)(2) and found all FHA claims viable except as alleged against HUD. The claims were permitted to proceed to amended pleadings without substantive merits analysis at the screening stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II and Section 504 Rehabilitation Act claims for failure to provide reasonable accommodations for vision impairments and wheelchair accessibility
fha_claims.disposition: Complaint screened under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2); claims found viable and permitted to proceed
fha_claims.reasoning: The court screened the pro se complaint under § 1915(e)(2) and found all non-FHA claims viable. The claims were permitted to proceed to amended pleadings without substantive merits analysis at the screening stage.

case_name: Chelsea Culver, et al. v. Melissa Churchill, et al.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation was requested in this case; plaintiffs generally alleged FHA violations and 'acts of retaliatory action' arising from their landlords' eviction proceedings for non-payment of rent, without specifying a protected class or any accommodation sought.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiffs' Rule 60(b) motion for relief from the prior dismissal of their FHA claims, holding that plaintiffs failed to identify any protected class or plead the required elements of disparate treatment or retaliation, and that failure to properly plead does not constitute a 'mistake' warranting reopening under Rule 60(b)(1).
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Chelsea Culver and Ben Smith sued their former landlords under the FHA after being evicted for non-payment of rent, but their complaint was dismissed for lack of a cognizable claim because they never identified a protected class or alleged specific discriminatory conduct. Plaintiffs then filed a Rule 60(b) motion asserting eight 'Assignments of Error,' including mistakes of law and fact and judicial bias, and for the first time disclosed that plaintiff Smith is 'an American Indian.' The court denied the motion, finding no grounds to reopen the case and noting that even the newly disclosed racial identity was insufficient without an allegation that defendants acted discriminatorily because of that protected characteristic.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
HDC, LLC v. City of Ann Arbor, 675 F.3d 608 (6th Cir. 2012)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to allege intentional discrimination based on any protected class, either through direct evidence or circumstantial evidence under McDonnell Douglas. The complaint gave no specific basis for FHA violations and named no protected class, which is fatal to an FHA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Although Plaintiffs alleged retaliation under § 3617, they failed to establish a causal connection between protected activity and harm. The complaint merely alleged 'acts of retaliatory action' without connecting them to any exercise of FHA rights.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Defamation claim under 28 U.S.C. § 4101 against Davis Group for rejecting rental application due to eviction
fha_claims.reasoning: 28 U.S.C. § 4101 does not provide a federal cause of action for state law defamation tort claims; it addresses only enforcement of foreign court judgments for defamation and is wholly irrelevant to this case.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege any violation of the Fair Housing Act itself, which is a prerequisite to a § 3617 retaliation claim. The complaint contains no suggestion of an FHA violation and therefore fails to state a plausible claim under § 3617.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (civil rights); 28 U.S.C. § 1654 (pro se appearance); 18 U.S.C. §§ 871-880 (criminal extortion/threats); California Penal Code § 519 (extortion)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to state a plausible § 1983 claim because private defendants (Board, Board Jr., Gambrell) are not state actors; judicial defendants (McKenney, Peck) are entitled to absolute judicial immunity; and court entities (Barberton Municipal Court, Ohio Court of Claims) cannot be sued absent statutory authority or are barred by Eleventh Amendment immunity. Criminal statutes (18 U.S.C. §§ 871-880) provide no private cause of action, and California Penal Code does not apply in Ohio. Allegations regarding § 1654 are too vague and conclusory.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: This case involves civil liability under the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act (TVPRA), 18 U.S.C. § 1595(a), for alleged participation in a venture involving sex trafficking. No FHA claims are alleged.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the defendant's motion to dismiss, finding that the plaintiff sufficiently pleaded direct civil liability under the TVPRA beneficiary theory by alleging: (1) knowing financial benefit from room rentals to traffickers; (2) participation in a venture (the hotel business); and (3) constructive knowledge that the venture involved trafficking based on red flags and industry awareness. The court also found vicarious liability theories (agency and joint employer) sufficiently pleaded at the pleading stage.

case_name: Tasha Chapman v. Justin Davis, et al.
race_if_mentioned: African American or Black, and Native American
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested permission to keep her emotional support animal, a dog named Nemo, despite a no-pet policy in her lease.
key_holding: The housing provider's request for the ESA's vaccination records during the week following notice did not constitute a refusal to make a reasonable accommodation under § 3604(f)(3)(B).
brief_summary: Plaintiff Tasha Chapman, a Section 8 voucher holder, sued her landlord and property manager for failing to reasonably accommodate her disability by allowing her to keep an emotional support animal despite a no-pet policy. The court dismissed her complaint on initial screening, finding that the property manager's request for vaccination records did not constitute a refusal to accommodate.
key_cases_cited: Overlook Mut. Homes, Inc. v. Spencer, 415 F. App'x 617 (6th Cir. 2011)
Miami Valley Fair Hous. Ctr., Inc. v. Connor Grp., 805 F. Supp. 2d 396 (S.D. Ohio 2011)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege any discriminatory statement or action by CMHA and CGI based on family status. The demand for an updated lease removing minor children's names and the termination notice for failure to provide requested information do not constitute statements indicating a preference, limitation, or discrimination based on family status.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege any racially discriminatory action or statement by CMHA and CGI. Merely alleging that plaintiff and her children are African American and defendants are white, without more, is insufficient to state a claim for racial discrimination under Title VIII.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Allowing plaintiff to keep her emotional support animal (ESA), a dog named Nemo, in violation of the lease's no-pets policy
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege that defendants refused to make the reasonable accommodation. The complaint only alleges that defendants requested vaccination records for the ESA, which is not a refusal to allow the ESA as a reasonable accommodation. A request for information does not constitute a denial of the accommodation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to state a retaliation claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3617 based on the initiation of eviction proceedings. The amended complaint alleged no new facts beyond the fact of eviction to support retaliation for exercising FHA rights, and the underlying discrimination claims failed to state a claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Human trafficking claim under Trafficking Victims Protection Act, 18 U.S.C. § 1595; § 1983 conspiracy claim based on First and Fourteenth Amendment deprivation of rights
fha_claims.reasoning: The trafficking claim was devoid of any facts supporting a violation of the Trafficking Victims Protection Act and failed to allege facts showing abuse of legal process. The § 1983 conspiracy claim failed because the underlying discrimination claims did not state a claim for violation of constitutional rights.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Civil liability under the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act (TVPRA), 18 U.S.C. § 1595(a), for benefiting from sex trafficking venture
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff plausibly alleged all three elements of the beneficiary theory under § 1595(a): (1) knowing financial benefit from room rentals to traffickers; (2) participation in ventures with both traffickers and franchisees through continuous business relationship; and (3) constructive knowledge of trafficking through red flags, staff awareness, online reviews, and franchisor's control over training and operations. Court applied Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard and resolved factual disputes in plaintiff's favor at the pleading stage.

case_name: Ronald D. Leonard v. Hocking Metropolitan Housing Authority, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested permission to keep an emotional support dog as a reasonable accommodation for his disability, which Defendants allegedly approved in 2020 but later demanded he sign a pet agreement to retain.
key_holding: The court found that requesting plaintiff sign a pet agreement for his ESA, without evidence that Defendants refused to allow the ESA or questioned its legitimacy, did not constitute a failure to accommodate or discriminatory interference under the FHAA.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Ronald Leonard sued Hocking Metropolitan Housing Authority alleging it violated the Fair Housing Act by demanding he sign a pet agreement for his previously approved emotional support animal, which he claimed constituted constructive eviction. The court granted leave to proceed in forma pauperis but recommended dismissal for failure to state a claim, finding that requesting documentation and a pet agreement does not constitute a refusal to accommodate or discriminatory animus when there was no evidence Defendants refused to allow the ESA to remain.
key_cases_cited: Overlook Mut. Homes, Inc. v. Spencer, 415 F. App'x 617 (6th Cir. 2011)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
HDC, LLC v. City of Ann Arbor, 675 F.3d 608 (6th Cir. 2012)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to keep an emotional support animal (ESA) in the housing unit without signing a separate pet agreement or providing current vaccination records and tags
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege that Defendants refused to allow him to keep his ESA. The complaint only alleged that Defendants requested he sign a pet agreement with unspecified terms and provide vaccination/tag documentation, with no indication the agreement would have deprived Plaintiff of the ability to live with his ESA or that Defendants questioned the legitimacy of his need for the ESA. This does not plausibly allege a refusal to accommodate under the FHAA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged coercion, intimidation, and harassment through threat of losing ESA and housing unless Plaintiff signed a pet agreement by April 18, 2024
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's allegations do not raise a plausible inference of discriminatory animus required for an FHAA interference claim under § 3617. The April 8 letter quoted the lease agreement implying that all residents with pets, disabled or not, were required to sign a pet agreement, suggesting the requirement applied equally to all residents regardless of disability status.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act disability discrimination claim; negligent training and supervision claim under state law
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 504 claim fails for the same reason as the FHAA claims—Plaintiff's allegations do not give rise to a plausible inference of disability discrimination because all residents with pets, regardless of disability, were required to sign a pet agreement. The state negligent training and supervision claim was dismissed for lack of supplemental jurisdiction after dismissal of all federal claims.

source_file: 10198974_2024_Chapman v. Franklin County Board of Commissioners_ohsd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Removal of children from lease at Columbus Metropolitan Housing Authority
fha_claims.disposition: Request for leave to amend denied; claim not addressed on merits
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff sought leave to amend complaint to add FHA claim against Columbus Metropolitan Housing Authority alleging violation based on directive to remove children from lease. Court denied leave to amend under Rule 20(a)(2) for misjoinder and noted plaintiff had already brought substantially similar claims in other cases (2:24-cv-2051 and 24-cv-1789). The proposed FHA claim was not substantively analyzed and remains pending in other proceedings.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. §§ 1983, 1986, 1985; 18 U.S.C. §§ 241, 242; Ohio Revised Code § 2921.45(A) — constitutional claims against various state actors (judges, prosecutors, court officials, sheriff, county commissioners, city of Columbus)
fha_claims.disposition: 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) — failure to state a claim; 12(b)(1) — lack of subject matter jurisdiction
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed all non-FHA claims for failure to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly standard and for lack of subject matter jurisdiction. Claims against state courts and court officials were barred by judicial immunity, Rooker-Feldman doctrine, and the principle that courts are not 'persons' under § 1983. Claims against prosecutor's office failed because the office is not a legal entity capable of being sued. Conspiracy allegations were conclusory and devoid of factual enhancement. Claims under 18 U.S.C. §§ 241 and 242 were barred because no private right of action exists under those criminal statutes.

source_file: 10199087_2024_Metropolitan Fair Housing Council of Oklahoma, Inc v. Feiock_oked
case_name: Metropolitan Fair Housing Council of Oklahoma, Inc. v. Feiock
accommodation_description: The McNamees requested a one-year lease renewal as a reasonable accommodation for James McNamee's disability; the current order analyzes whether Frank Feiock's conduct (approaching James McNamee about his disability and photographing him during move-out) constituted unlawful harassment.
key_holding: The harassment claim fails because Frank Feiock's conduct—asking about James McNamee's disability and photographing him while moving out—was not sufficiently severe or pervasive to constitute unlawful harassment, and the fair housing organization MFH lacks standing to assert harassment claims where it failed to demonstrate concrete injury to its organizational mission.
brief_summary: Metropolitan Fair Housing Council of Oklahoma and James and Marta McNamee sued landlords Frank and Glenna Feiock alleging discriminatory housing practices under the FHA, including denial of a reasonable accommodation request for lease renewal and harassment based on disability. The Court granted summary judgment for defendants, finding that the harassment claim fails because Feiock's alleged conduct (asking about McNamee's disability and photographing him during move-out) was not severe or pervasive enough to constitute unlawful harassment, and MFH lacked standing to bring harassment claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Jackson v. Park Place Condominiums Ass'n, Inc., 619 Fed. Appx. 699 (10th Cir. 2015)
Zhu v. Fisher, Cavanaugh, Smith & Lemon, P.A., 151 F. Supp. 2d 1254 (D. Kan. 2001)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Lease renewal for a one-year term for James McNamee, who is covered as a disabled person under the FHA
fha_claims.reasoning: In the Court's prior order (Docket No. 52), the failure-to-accommodate claim was dismissed on the merits after substantive analysis. The Court found the accommodation request was neither necessary nor reasonable, and Defendants were entitled to summary judgment on this claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged harassment and intimidation by Frank Feiock, including asking about James McNamee's disability, photographing him during move-out, and sending multiple emails and complaints to HUD and the Oklahoma Bar Association
fha_claims.reasoning: Under 42 U.S.C. § 3617, the Court applied the hostile housing environment standard and found that the alleged conduct—a single incident of photographing and questioning during move-out—was not sufficiently severe or pervasive to constitute unlawful harassment. The conduct did not alter the conditions of housing because the lease had already been declined for renewal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Oklahoma Fair Housing Law violation (25 Okla. Stat. § 1452) and state-law negligence claim for want of ordinary care in property management
fha_claims.reasoning: After dismissing all federal FHA claims, the Court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over remaining state-law claims under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c), as there were no exceptional circumstances or compelling reasons to retain jurisdiction. The state-law claim was dismissed without prejudice.

case_name: White v. Matthews
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges the eviction from her federally assisted subsidized housing unit was discriminatory under the Fair Housing Act.
key_holding: The court granted in part Defendants' motion for discovery sanctions, ordering Plaintiff to supplement her discovery responses regarding living arrangements during homelessness, damage calculations, and medical records within five days or face dismissal of claims.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Brandy White sued the Greater Muskogee Community Foundation and the Housing Authority for the City of Muskogee following eviction from federally assisted subsidized housing, alleging Fair Housing Act discrimination. The court granted in part Defendants' motion for discovery sanctions, ordering Plaintiff to supplement deficient discovery responses regarding her living arrangements during homelessness, detailed damage calculations, and clarification of medical records, with failure to comply potentially resulting in dismissal of her claims.
key_cases_cited: Walker v. State Farm Fire and Casualty, 2020 WL 6205841 (E.D. Okla. Oct. 22, 2020)

case_name: Robinson v. Nationstar Mortgage, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff's mother requested loan reinstatement and alternative payment schedule as reasonable accommodation for disability during foreclosure proceedings
key_holding: Plaintiff lacks Article III standing to assert FHA retaliation claim because her injuries from the insurance non-renewal and increased mortgage payments are not fairly traceable to defendants' conduct—the non-renewal decision was made by a non-party insurer AFR based on 'Condition/Upkeep' rather than vacancy, and the causal chain is too attenuated.
brief_summary: Katrina Robinson sued Nationstar Mortgage and Ogden Insurance Agency alleging they retaliated against her late mother in violation of the FHA by causing the mother's homeowner's insurance to be non-renewed after the mother requested a reasonable accommodation for disability during foreclosure proceedings. The district court granted defendants' summary judgment motions, finding Robinson lacked Article III standing because her claimed injuries were not fairly traceable to defendants' allegedly retaliatory conduct—the independent insurer AFR made the non-renewal decision for reasons (property condition) distinct from defendants' vacancy report.
key_cases_cited: Defs. of Wildlife v. Everson, 984 F.3d 918 (10th Cir. 2020)
Habecker v. Town of Estes Park, 518 F.3d 1217 (10th Cir. 2008)
Nova Health Sys. v. Goser, 416 F.3d 1149 (10th Cir. 2005)
Alliance for Hippocratic Med. v. FDA, 602 U.S. 367 (2024)
Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins, 578 U.S. 330 (2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff lacked Article III standing to assert the retaliation claim because she failed to establish the traceability element—the injury (increased mortgage payments due to lender-placed insurance) was not fairly traceable to defendants' conduct but rather depended on the independent action of AFR (a third party not before the court) in declining to renew the insurance policy. The chain of causation was too attenuated and speculative.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Oklahoma Consumer Protection Act, Oklahoma fraud claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims (Counts Two and Three) under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3) after dismissing the only federal claim (Count One) for lack of standing. The court found it prudent to decline jurisdiction based on considerations of comity and convenience.

case_name: Rosemary McVicker v. Muskogee Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiff appeared to argue that MHA should have adopted a written medical marijuana policy as a reasonable accommodation for her disability, but the court did not analyze this as a formal reasonable accommodation claim.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for MHA on Plaintiff's FHA claims because MHA had a policy prohibiting marijuana use, Plaintiff had actual notice of this policy through newsletters and her lease, and Plaintiff failed to demonstrate that MHA intentionally discriminated against her based on disability or sex.
brief_summary: Rosemary McVicker, a tenant with a disability residing at Heritage Park Apartments (a Section 811 supportive housing property operated by Muskogee Housing Authority), sued MHA for Fair Housing Act violations, claiming sex discrimination as a domestic violence victim and disability discrimination based on her medical marijuana use. The court granted summary judgment for MHA on all federal claims, finding no evidence of intentional sex discrimination and that MHA had provided adequate notice of its no-drug policy despite not having a formal written medical marijuana policy.
key_cases_cited: Bostock v. Clayton County, 590 U.S. 644 (2020)
Cinnamon Hills Youth Crisis Ctr., Inc. v. St. George City, 685 F.3d 917 (10th Cir. 2012)
Dornheim v. Sholes, 430 F.3d 919 (8th Cir. 2005)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Sex discrimination based on status as domestic violence victim
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to demonstrate that MHA's actions were motivated by discriminatory animus based on sex. Although some district courts recognize domestic violence victim status as a proxy for sex discrimination in disparate impact cases, plaintiff's disparate treatment claim requires proof of intentional discrimination based on sex, not merely status as a domestic violence victim. The court found no evidence that MHA evicted plaintiff because she is a woman.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to establish written policy and standards regarding medical marijuana use for tenants with disabilities
fha_claims.reasoning: Even assuming plaintiff's theory that lack of written policy constitutes disability discrimination, undisputed facts demonstrate MHA had a policy prohibiting marijuana use, communicated it through monthly newsletters, and plaintiff admitted awareness that marijuana use could result in lease termination. Plaintiff had actual notice of the policy and the consequences of violation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation for invoking VAWA rights and prevailing in 2021 forcible entry and detainer action
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish that she exercised a right protected by the FHA. Because the court determined that domestic violence victim status does not implicate FHA protections against sex discrimination, plaintiff did not exercise any FHA right. Additionally, plaintiff presented no evidence that the 2022 forcible entry and detainer action was filed in retaliation for any FHA-protected activity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 due process violation, Fourth Amendment unreasonable search, Rehabilitation Act § 504 violation
fha_claims.reasoning: Due process claim: plaintiff had actual notice that marijuana use was prohibited and could result in lease termination through newsletters and her own deposition testimony. Fourth Amendment claim: pest control inspection was conducted pursuant to lease consent and with advance notice; items were in open view; photographing paraphernalia did not exceed scope of consent. Rehabilitation Act claim: marijuana is a Schedule I controlled substance; the Rehabilitation Act explicitly excludes individuals currently engaging in illegal drug use from protection.

case_name: Tyeashia M. Blackburn; Lezlie E. Freeman v. Kelly Webb; Rent King, LLC
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED - This order addresses only procedural sanctions for discovery violations and does not analyze the substantive merits of any accommodation request.
key_holding: The court granted Defendants' Motion to Dismiss with prejudice under Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(f), 37(b)(2)(A)(v), and 41(b) after finding plaintiffs engaged in a pattern of delay and noncompliance including discovery violations, missed deadlines, and failure to comply with court orders, and that all Ehrenhaus factors supported dismissal as the appropriate sanction.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs filed a Fair Housing Act lawsuit against their landlord and property management company that was dismissed with prejudice for repeated discovery violations and procedural failures. The court found that plaintiffs failed to provide adequate initial disclosures, incompletely responded to discovery requests, failed to verify interrogatories, and missed multiple court deadlines, warranting dismissal under the Ehrenhaus factors.
key_cases_cited: Ehrenhaus v. Reynolds, 965 F.2d 916 (10th Cir. 1992)
Gripe v. City of Enid, Okla., 312 F.3d 1184 (10th Cir. 2002)
Morris v. Berry, CV-11-456-W, 2012 WL 13168469 (W.D. Okla. May 8, 2012)

case_name: Blackburn v. Webb
accommodation_description: No accommodation is described in this order; the opinion concerns only the post-dismissal attorney's fees motion and does not disclose the specific nature of the underlying FHA claims.
key_holding: The court granted in part defendants' motion for attorney's fees, awarding $5,248.32 (after a 30% lodestar reduction) for fees caused by plaintiffs' repeated procedural noncompliance under Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(f)(2) and 37(b)(2)(C), but denied fees for the frivolous First Amendment claim under 42 U.S.C. § 1988(b) due to defendants' counsel's insufficiently meticulous contemporaneous billing records.
brief_summary: Pro se, in forma pauperis plaintiffs Blackburn and Freeman sued defendants Kelly Webb and Rent King, LLC alleging FHA violations, state housing law violations, and a First Amendment claim; the First Amendment claim was dismissed with prejudice at the pleading stage and the remaining claims were later dismissed with prejudice for pervasive procedural noncompliance. Defendants subsequently moved for $21,586.33 in attorney's fees on two grounds: frivolousness of the First Amendment claim under § 1988(b), and fees caused by plaintiffs' procedural noncompliance under Rules 16(f)(2) and 37(b)(2)(C). The court found both grounds legally valid but denied fees under § 1988 for lack of precise billing records, and awarded a reduced sum of $5,248.32 for the procedural noncompliance, accounting for plaintiffs' pro se status, health issues, in forma pauperis status, and the prior sanction of dismissal with prejudice.
key_cases_cited: Hensley v. Eckerhart, 461 U.S. 424 (1983)
Christiansburg Garment Co. v. EEOC, 434 U.S. 412 (1978)
Mays v. Forsythe, 2023 WL 6307979 (W.D. Okla. 2023)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: First Amendment claim; state housing law claims
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the First Amendment claim with prejudice because defendants are not state actors and therefore cannot be sued for First Amendment violations. Fair Housing Act claims were allowed to proceed at the MTD stage but were subsequently dismissed with prejudice for procedural noncompliance and failure to participate in discovery.

case_name: Zachary Forrest Marquart v. City of Shaniko
accommodation_description: No disability-based accommodation was requested; the case centers on plaintiff's allegations that defendants denied his property access to municipal services including power and water hook-ups, road maintenance, trash collection, and a physical address, while also subjecting him to discrimination and intimidation due to his bisexual identity.
key_holding: The court granted in part and denied in part defendants' motion to dismiss, dismissing with prejudice claims barred by claim preclusion from prior state and federal court judgments, dismissing without prejudice certain insufficiently pled claims, and allowing plaintiff's sexual-orientation discrimination claim against specific named defendants to survive.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Zachary Forrest Marquart sued the City of Shaniko and ten individual defendants—many current or former city council members—alleging they conspired to deny him municipal services (power, water, trash collection, road maintenance, and a physical address) and subjected him to discrimination and intimidation based on his bisexual identity after he purchased rural property within the city's limits in 2021. The court applied claim preclusion based on several prior state and federal court dismissals with prejudice to bar claims arising before certain dates against specified defendants, dismissed without prejudice various insufficiently pled claims (ADA, Oregon Bicycle Bill, conversion, conflict of interest, and all claims against four defendants lacking specific allegations), and denied defendants' request for attorney's fees while granting plaintiff leave to file an amended complaint by August 23, 2024.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Bloomfield v. Weakland, 339 Or. 504 (2005)
Lucas v. Lake County, 253 Or. App. 39 (2012)
Tahoe-Sierra Pres. Council, Inc. v. Tahoe Reg'l Plan. Agency, 322 F.3d 1064 (9th Cir. 2003)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges violations of the Fair Housing Act based on alleged denial of services to his property, but the complaint does not specify what accommodation was requested or denied.
fha_claims.reasoning: The FHA claim against Richard Cereghino, Sandra Cereghino, and Donald Treanor based on conduct before July 19, 2022, is barred by claim preclusion because it could have been brought in the prior federal lawsuit (No. 3:22-cv-1072-MO) filed July 19, 2022, and dismissed with prejudice September 26, 2022. The claim arises from the same nucleus of operative facts as the prior federal action. The FHA claim against the City and other defendants based on conduct before September 28, 2021, is similarly barred by claim preclusion from the state-court lawsuit (No. 21CV38660) dismissed with prejudice January 5, 2022.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination based on sexual orientation under Oregon law (ORS §§ 659A.885, 659A.400, 659A.403); ADA Title II violations (42 U.S.C. § 12132); Oregon Bicycle Bill violations (ORS § 30.275); private nuisance; public nuisance; intentional/negligent infliction of emotional distress; negligence; breach of covenant of quiet enjoyment; common law conflict of interest; conversion; encroachment in public right of way.
fha_claims.reasoning: The ADA claim is dismissed without prejudice because Plaintiff fails to allege that he is a qualified individual with a disability or that he suffered particularized injury from the City's alleged ADA non-compliance. The Oregon Bicycle Bill claim is dismissed without prejudice as time-barred under ORS § 30.275 (180-day notice requirement), based on allegations of conduct in 2007. The conversion claim is dismissed without prejudice because conversion applies only to chattel property, not real property, and Plaintiff does not allege encroachment onto his own property. The conflict of interest claim is dismissed without prejudice because Plaintiff fails to allege particularized injury. The discrimination claim against David Long, Diana Marrs, Scott Marrs, Donald Treanor, Richard Cereghino, and Sandra Cereghino survives the motion to dismiss as to conduct after the applicable preclusion dates, but claims against Andrea Kegel, Sandra Thomas, Nick Nimms, and Goldie Roberts are dismissed without prejudice for lack of specific allegations.

case_name: Wilmore Lee Washington, III v. Farmington Estates Owners Association
accommodation_description: Plaintiff originally filed suit alleging race discrimination in violation of the Fair Housing Act; subsequently sought to amend to add claims under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 and 1982.
key_holding: The court denied Plaintiff's Motion for Leave to Amend to add claims under §§ 1981 and 1982 because Plaintiff failed to establish good cause under Rule 16(b)(4) to modify the scheduling order, and alternatively because Plaintiff's undue delay in moving to add new claims would prejudice Defendants.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Wilmore Lee Washington, III sued Farmington Estates Owners Association and related defendants alleging race discrimination in violation of the Fair Housing Act. Plaintiff filed a motion for leave to amend to add claims under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 and 1982. The court adopted the Magistrate Judge's recommendation and denied the motion, finding Plaintiff failed to demonstrate good cause under Rule 16(b)(4) for modifying the scheduling order and that the undue delay would prejudice Defendants.
key_cases_cited: Johnson v. Mammoth Recreations, Inc., 975 F.2d 604 (9th Cir. 1992)
Thomas v. Arn, 474 U.S. 140 (1985)
Erickson v. Pardus, 551 U.S. 89 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.disposition: Motion for Leave to Amend Denied
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's motion to amend to add FHA race discrimination claims was denied under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 16(b)(4) for failure to establish good cause and diligence in modifying the scheduling order, and alternatively under Rule 15(a)(2) for undue delay and prejudice to defendants. The court found that plaintiff's delay in researching potential claims did not establish the diligence required.

case_name: King Anthony Alvarez v. City of Philadelphia, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges termination from subsidized housing program in retaliation for filing fair housing complaints; no specific accommodation request.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA retaliation claim as barred by claim preclusion because the same termination from TURN-funded housing was already litigated in a prior case, and alternatively because plaintiff failed to allege membership in a protected class as required to state an FHA retaliation claim.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff King Anthony Alvarez sued the City of Philadelphia, HUD, TURN, and CLS alleging FHA retaliation claims based on his termination from a subsidized housing program in November 2022 in retaliation for filing fair housing complaints. The court dismissed the complaint on two grounds: first, the claim was barred by claim preclusion because Alvarez had already litigated the same termination in a prior case (Alvarez v. HUD, No. 22-3631), and second, even on the merits, the claim failed because Alvarez did not adequately allege membership in a protected class.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Beasley v. Howard, 14 F.4th 226 (3d Cir. 2021)
Gimenez v. Morgan Stanley DW, Inc., 202 F. App'x 583 (3d Cir. 2006)
Haefner v. N. Cornwall Twp., 40 F. App'x 656 (3d Cir. 2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the FHA retaliation claim under the doctrine of claim preclusion (res judicata) because Alvarez's 2022 lawsuit (Case No. 22-3631) resulted in a final judgment on the merits of his FHA claims based on the same November 2022 termination from subsidized housing, and the new evidence (Zoom recording) does not overcome preclusive effect. Additionally, even if not barred by claim preclusion, the claim fails on the merits because Alvarez failed to allege that he was discriminated against or that he was a member of a protected class, which is fatal to any FHA claim.

case_name: Parker v. Lee
accommodation_description: Parker alleges defendants issued a notice to vacate in retaliation for filing a complaint with the Philadelphia Commission on Human Relations about alleged race, gender, and disability discrimination
