key_holding: The court denied dismissal of Parker's FHA retaliation claim because he adequately pled protected activity (filing PCHR complaints about discrimination) and causation (the notice to vacate was issued eight days after his PCHR intake form), while dismissing his race/sex discrimination claims for lack of comparator evidence and his disability accommodation claim because he failed to allege any specific accommodation request.
brief_summary: Gordon Parker sued Ronald and Teresa Lee, their trust, Kenneth Baritz, Jeffrey Mai, and Canaan Realty Investment Group, alleging they attempted to illegally evict him and his brother from their Chinatown apartment in retaliation for filing discrimination complaints with the Philadelphia Commission on Human Relations. The court largely granted defendants' motions to dismiss but denied them as to Parker's FHA retaliation claim under § 3617, finding he adequately alleged protected activity and causation based on temporal proximity between his PCHR intake form and the notice to vacate, while dismissing his race/sex discrimination and failure to accommodate claims for failure to plead comparator evidence and failure to request any specific accommodation, respectively.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Wind Gap Mun. Auth. v. Community Servs., 421 F.3d 170 (3d Cir. 2005)
Vorchheimer v. Philadelphian Owners Ass'n, 903 F.3d 100 (3d Cir. 2018)
Qing Qin v. Vertex, Inc., 100 F.4th 458 (3d Cir. 2024)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Parker adequately alleged protected activity (filing complaints with PCHR about race, gender, and disability discrimination), an adverse action (notice to vacate), and a causal link (notice issued eight days after intake form filing, within the 'unusually suggestive' temporal proximity standard). Claim survives motion to dismiss as to Landlord Defendants but fails as to Canaan Defendants.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Parker failed to plausibly allege race or sex discrimination. He did not adequately plead similarly situated comparators treated better; the fact that a nonwhite female tenant paid more for a superior apartment does not support an inference of discrimination. Allegations regarding lease renewal offers, apartment availability, and trespassing incidents lack sufficient factual support for discriminatory motive and rely on speculation and conclusory assertions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Labor Standards Act retaliation (Count II), Americans with Disabilities Act Title III discrimination and retaliation (Count IV), fraudulent and negligent misrepresentation (Count V)
fha_claims.reasoning: FLSA retaliation claim fails due to lack of causal link between 2016 FLSA suit and current events (too speculative). ADA Title III claim fails because apartment complexes are not places of public accommodation and private plaintiffs cannot obtain monetary damages under Title III. ADA retaliation claim fails because complaint to PCHR did not concern conduct unlawful under Title III. Fraudulent/negligent misrepresentation claims fail under Rule 9(b) heightened pleading standard; Parker speculates about intent without alleging sufficient facts.

source_file: 10200545_2024_LERNER v. CITY AND COUNTY OF PHILADELPHIA_paed

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged violations of Fair Housing Act, Americans with Disabilities Act, Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, due process clause, and HUD regulations in connection with eviction proceedings.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked subject matter jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine because plaintiff's claims were essentially appeals from a final state court judgment (eviction and writ of possession) rendered before the federal suit was filed. Plaintiff lost in state court, complained of injuries caused by the state judgment, the judgment was final before federal filing, and plaintiff invited federal court review and rejection of the state judgment. The court also noted that plaintiff's references to FHA, ADA, and FDCPA were merely passing references without factual basis and insufficient to raise cognizable claims.

case_name: Miriam Millan-Heffner, et al. v. Gemcraft Homes Group, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: No disability accommodation request was made; this case involves racial discrimination in the home purchase process, including steering away from a white neighborhood, false information about lot availability, differential treatment, and failure to complete construction repairs.
key_holding: The court denied the motion to dismiss as to the FHA and § 1981 claims, finding plaintiffs adequately alleged intentional race discrimination, including steering away from a white neighborhood and differential treatment of Ms. Millan-Heffner based on her Puerto Rican ethnicity, while granting dismissal of the breach of contract claim for failure to plead specific contract terms.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Gary Heffner and Miriam Millan-Heffner sued Gemcraft Homes Group, Inc. and its employees alleging race discrimination during their home purchase in Winslett, a housing development in Harrisburg, PA, including steering them away from a primarily white section of the neighborhood based on Ms. Millan-Heffner's Puerto Rican ethnicity. The court denied the motion to dismiss the Fair Housing Act and § 1981 claims, finding plaintiffs sufficiently alleged intentional race discrimination and that Gemcraft could be held vicariously liable under the non-delegable duty doctrine, while dismissing the breach of contract claim for failing to allege specific contract terms.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
White v. Barbe
Alexander v. Riga
Castleberry v. STI Group

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiffs plausibly alleged intentional race discrimination under FHA § 3604 by alleging defendants falsely told them a lot was unavailable, then sold it to white purchasers who built identical features, combined with discriminatory statements and differential treatment. Allegations sufficient to survive motion to dismiss under Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1981 race discrimination in contracting; Pennsylvania common law breach of contract
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found § 1981 claim survives MTD because plaintiffs alleged additional conditions imposed on them (spray painting deck location) not imposed on similarly situated white homebuyers, and misrepresentation about lot availability interfered with their right to contract. Breach of contract claim dismissed for failure to specify material terms of alleged oral or written agreement.

source_file: 10201075_2024_Ewideh v. Homesite Insurance Company of the Midwest_pamd
case_name: Ewideh v. Homesite Insurance Company of the Midwest
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege discrimination by homeowners insurance company in adjusting property damage claims based on disability and sexual orientation, without specifying a particular accommodation request.
key_holding: Plaintiffs' FHA claim fails because they have not explained how homeowners insurance claim adjustments fall within the scope of 42 U.S.C. § 3604(a)-(f), and their vague, conclusory allegations of discriminatory motive are insufficient to state a plausible claim; dismissal is also warranted under Rule 41(b) due to plaintiffs' history of dilatoriness and failure to comply with court orders.
brief_summary: Omar Ewideh and Nivertiti Geaith, proceeding pro se, sued their homeowners insurance company, its counsel, and claims adjusters under the Fair Housing Act, alleging discrimination based on disability and sexual orientation in the adjustment of their property damage claims. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding the amended complaint failed to state a plausible FHA claim because plaintiffs did not explain how insurance claim adjustments fall within the FHA's provisions, and alternatively dismissed the case under Rule 41(b) due to plaintiffs' extensive dilatory conduct and failure to prosecute.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Wartluft v. Milton Hershey Sch. & Sch. Tr., 400 F. Supp. 3d 91 (M.D. Pa. 2019)
Wilson v. Hillsborough Twp. Constr. Dep't, 779 F. App'x 969 (3d Cir. 2019)
Mt. Holly Gardens Citizens in Action, Inc. v. Twp. of Mount Holly, 658 F.3d 375 (3d Cir. 2011)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs' FHA claim alleging discrimination based on sexual orientation and disability in the context of homeowners' insurance claim adjustment fails under Iqbal/Twombly because the allegations are vague and conclusory, do not explain how insurance claim adjustment falls within 42 U.S.C. § 3604(a)-(f), and lack sufficient factual matter to state a plausible claim. The court also noted the FHA may not apply to property insurers and claims may be barred by the McCarran-Ferguson Act, but did not reach those arguments.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Negligence per se and civil conspiracy under Pennsylvania state law
fha_claims.reasoning: Negligence per se claim is meritless because anti-discrimination statutes like the FHA cannot serve as the basis for a negligence per se action. Civil conspiracy claim fails because plaintiffs did not plead facts establishing the overt acts of the alleged conspiracy or actual legal damage, rendering the allegations threadbare conclusory statements under Iqbal/Twombly.

case_name: Gabriel Cortez-Villanueva v. Puerta de Tierra, LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought transfer to another apartment with physical modifications including handicap-accessible bathroom features (toilet, shower with hose, seat, grab bars) and designated handicap parking near the new unit.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction based on res judicata because, although the parties exchanged written offers and acceptances through HUD conciliation, the court could not find at this stage that the settlement agreement was signed by both parties as required by Article 1503 of Puerto Rico's 2020 Civil Code.
brief_summary: Gabriel Cortez-Villanueva sued his landlords (Puerta de Tierra, LLC and McCormack Baron Management Puerto Rico) alleging Fair Housing Act violations arising from their failure to provide reasonable accommodations, including transfer to an accessible unit and physical modifications. Defendants moved to dismiss claiming the parties had reached a binding settlement agreement during HUD conciliation proceedings. The court denied the motion, finding insufficient evidence that a valid settlement agreement was signed as required by Puerto Rico's 2020 Civil Code, thus preserving plaintiff's right to litigate his FHA claims.
key_cases_cited: Belsito Commc'ns, Inc. v. Decker, 845 F.3d 13 (1st Cir. 2016)
Valentín v. Hospital Bella Vista, 254 F.3d 358 (1st Cir. 2001)
Rivera-Rosario v. LSREF2 Island Holdings, Ltd., Inc., 79 F.4th 1 (1st Cir. 2023)
Citibank Global Markets, Inc. v. Rodríguez-Santana, 573 F.3d 17 (1st Cir. 2009)
United States v. Zannino, 895 F.2d 1 (1st Cir. 1990)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Handicap toilet, shower with hose, shower seat, and grab bars in bathroom; handicap parking space in proximity to relocated apartment; hotel accommodations with two beds for caregiver during move; clarification of payment responsibility for move duration exceeding 4 days
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss for lack of subject matter jurisdiction based on res judicata, finding that no valid settlement agreement was executed under Puerto Rico Civil Code Article 1503 because the agreement was not signed by both parties in a manner satisfying the statutory requirement. The FHA claims survive the jurisdictional challenge and remain pending.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Puerto Rico general tort statute (P.R. Laws Ann. tit. 31 § 10801)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss for lack of subject matter jurisdiction based on res judicata, finding that no valid settlement agreement was executed. Non-FHA tort claims survive the jurisdictional challenge and remain pending.

source_file: 10201923_2024_Newbury v. United States Department of Housing and Urban Development_rid
case_name: Nancy Newbury, et al. v. United States Department of Housing and Urban Development
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged that HUD's approval of easements allowing 55+ residents of West House II to use common areas and parking of West House I (restricted to 62+ residents) constituted impermissible age-group intermingling without Congressional authorization.
key_holding: The court recommended denying plaintiffs' motion for preliminary/permanent injunction because HUD afforded adequate procedural notice and opportunity to comment, and HUD's determination approving the easements was neither arbitrary nor capricious under the APA; plaintiffs' claims that allowing 55+ residents to use WH I common areas required new legislation failed because existing statutory framework permits age-group intermingling.
brief_summary: Three elderly residents of West House I sued HUD and other defendants seeking to enjoin easements permitting residents of an adjacent West House II (restricted to ages 55+) to use WH I's common areas and parking lot, alleging HUD failed to comply with procedural requirements and that such intermingling requires new legislation. The Magistrate Judge recommended denying plaintiffs' motion for preliminary/permanent injunction and entering judgment for Federal Defendants because HUD afforded proper notice and opportunity to comment, and HUD's decision was neither arbitrary nor capricious under the APA.
key_cases_cited: Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 144 S. Ct. 2244 (2024)
Ohio v. Environmental Protection Agency, 144 S. Ct. 2040 (2024)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
DeSuze v. Sununu, 442 F. Supp. 3d 531 (D.R.I. 2020)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Administrative Procedures Act (APA) challenge to HUD's approval of easements permitting WH II residents (ages 55+) to access WH I common areas and parking lot; also state law defamation claims, gender discrimination under 42 U.S.C. § 3604, breach of contract, and elder abuse claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs lack Article III standing because their alleged injury (breach of quiet enjoyment) is based on speculation regarding future conduct of WH II residents and is redressable in state court. APA claim for procedural violation under 12 U.S.C. § 1715z-1b survives MTD but fails on merits because HUD provided notice, opportunity to comment, and considered tenant comments. Gender discrimination claim under § 3604 fails for insufficient pleading (80% female residents and some male officials does not support sex discrimination). Defamation claims against federal officials in official capacity barred by sovereign immunity; FTCA does not waive immunity for defamation. State law claims against non-federal defendants dismissed for lack of supplemental jurisdiction.

case_name: Larocque v. Spring Green Corporation
accommodation_description: No accommodation request at issue; case involves claims of discriminatory enforcement of community rules, denial of maintenance services, and failure to respond to third-party harassment based on religion (Judaism) and sexual orientation (lesbian)
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for the Spring Green Defendants because Larocque failed to establish a prima facie case of disparate treatment—she offered no evidence of adverse action, no comparison to similarly situated tenants, and no evidence that any differential treatment was motivated by discriminatory intent based on her religion or sexual orientation; additionally, third-party liability for the landlord's failure to respond to harassment by a non-resident nephew was rejected under the Wetzel framework because the landlord lacked sufficient control over the land tenant's nephew.
brief_summary: Lynn Larocque, a Jewish lesbian tenant at a manufactured housing community in Warwick, Rhode Island, sued Spring Green Corporation and related entities alleging they discriminated against her based on religion and sexual orientation by stringently enforcing community rules, ignoring maintenance requests, and failing to respond to harassment by a neighbor's nephew. The court granted summary judgment for defendants, finding Larocque failed to establish a prima facie case of disparate treatment because she offered no evidence of adverse action, no comparison to similarly situated tenants, and no evidence of discriminatory motive; the court also rejected her third-party liability theory for failing to respond to harassment.
key_cases_cited: Gros v. Spring Green Corp., 776 F.3d 38 (1st Cir. 2015)
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Bostock v. Clayton County, 590 U.S. 644 (2020)
Wetzel v. St. Andrew's Resources for People, Animals, & the Environment, Inc., 901 F.3d 856 (7th Cir. 2018)
Hughes v. Magic Sky Homes, LLC, 992 F.3d 67 (2d Cir. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Enforcement of community rules against plaintiff more strictly than other tenants
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish prima facie disparate treatment: she provided no evidence of adverse action (never fined), failed to show differential treatment compared to similarly situated non-protected tenants (admitted no knowledge of how rules enforced against others), and provided no evidence that protected characteristics motivated any alleged disparate enforcement.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to provide maintenance services in response to plaintiff's requests
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish prima facie disparate treatment: defendants provided over thirty documented instances of maintenance services provided to plaintiff, plaintiff failed to show differential treatment compared to similarly situated non-protected tenants, and plaintiff provided no evidence that protected characteristics motivated any alleged maintenance failures.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to intervene in alleged harassment by third party (neighbor's nephew) including noose, bullet casing, and swastika found on plaintiff's property
fha_claims.reasoning: Even assuming FHA imposes third-party liability under the Wetzel standard, defendants fall outside its reach because: (1) alleged harassment occurred on private property lines between land and home tenants, not in common areas under defendants' control; (2) defendants lacked the 'arsenal of incentives and sanctions' over the harasser (a non-resident nephew of a land tenant) that would trigger liability; and (3) defendants had far less supervisory control over the land tenant and her nephew than the landlord had in Wetzel.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rhode Island Fair Housing Practices Act (RIFHPA) claims for discrimination based on religion and sexual orientation
fha_claims.reasoning: RIFHPA claims analyzed under same framework as FHA claims (burden-shifting disparate treatment analysis). Plaintiff failed to establish prima facie case on all three theories (rule enforcement, maintenance, third-party harassment) for the same reasons as federal FHA claims.

case_name: Whisonant v. Exclusive Properties, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff is African American and alleged racial discrimination in rental terms and conditions, including that defendant refused to offer her a discount while offering better terms to a white male applicant
key_holding: The court denied defendant's motion for summary judgment, finding plaintiff established a prima facie case of racial discrimination and that defendant's varying justifications created a genuine issue of material fact regarding pretext
brief_summary: Stacie Whisonant, an African American woman, sued Exclusive Properties, LLC alleging racial discrimination under the Fair Housing Act when the property management company refused to rent her the Sea Palace vacation property while offering more favorable terms to a white male applicant who submitted a lower offer. The court denied defendant's motion for summary judgment, finding sufficient circumstantial evidence of discrimination under the McDonnell Douglas framework including evidence that defendant's stated reasons for refusing plaintiff's rental offer varied over time, supporting an inference of pretext.
key_cases_cited: Murrell v. The Ocean Mecca Motel, Inc., 262 F.3d 253 (4th Cir. 2001)
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Texas Dept. of Cmty. Affairs v. Burdine, 450 U.S. 248 (1981)
E.E.O.C. v. Sears Roebuck & Co., 243 F.3d 846 (4th Cir. 2001)
Hawkins v. PepsiCo, Inc., 203 F.3d 274 (4th Cir. 2000)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff established a prima facie case of race discrimination under the McDonnell Douglas framework by showing defendant was aware of her race and offered a lower price to a white male comparator; defendant's varying explanations over time support an inference of pretext, creating a genuine issue of material fact for trial.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II Civil Rights Act (42 U.S.C. § 2000a), 42 U.S.C. § 1981, South Carolina Code § 45-9-10
fha_claims.reasoning: Non-FHA claims (Title II, § 1981, state law) were analyzed under the same McDonnell Douglas disparate treatment framework as the FHA claim; summary judgment was denied on all claims based on the same prima facie case and pretext evidence.

case_name: Avril Smalls v. RE Carroll Management Company
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, an employee, alleged retaliation for reporting that a tenant was improperly charged pet fees for a service animal.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment to the employer on the FHA retaliation claim because plaintiff failed to show she had a reasonable basis to believe an FHA violation occurred (the tenant was charged pet fees before completing service animal registration) and failed to rebut the employer's legitimate, non-discriminatory reason for termination.
brief_summary: Avril Smalls, an assistant property manager, sued her employer RE Carroll Management Company claiming she was terminated in retaliation for reporting that a tenant was charged improper pet fees for a service animal, in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The court granted summary judgment to the employer, finding Smalls failed to establish a prima facie case of retaliation because she had no reasonable basis to believe an FHA violation occurred (fees were charged before service animal registration was completed) and failed to rebut the employer's legitimate reason for termination.
key_cases_cited: Boyer-Liberto v. Fontainebleau Corp., 786 F.3d 264 (4th Cir. 2015)
EEOC v. Navy Fed. Credit Union, 424 F.3d 397 (4th Cir. 2005)
Roberts v. Glenn Indus. Grp., Inc., 998 F.3d 111 (4th Cir. 2021)
Waters v. Logistics Mgmt. Inst., 716 F. App'x 194 (4th Cir. 2018)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a causal link between protected FHA activity and termination. The court found no reasonable basis for Plaintiff to believe an FHA violation occurred (tenant had not yet registered service animal when charged pet fees), and Plaintiff failed to rebut Defendant's legitimate, non-pretextual reason for termination (Plaintiff's refusal to work with her supervisor following performance issues).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Wrongful discharge under South Carolina public policy exception, FLSA overtime wages, South Carolina Payment of Wages Act unpaid wages and commissions, defamation (libel and slander)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's wrongful discharge claim fails because no retaliatory termination occurred. FLSA overtime claim contradicted by time sheets. SCPWA claim lacks evidence of unpaid commissions. Defamation claims fail due to lack of specificity regarding statements and absence of evidence that written write-up was published to third parties.

case_name: Eshawn Jessica Scipio v. Housing Authority of Hartsville
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request analyzed; this order addresses discovery disputes rather than substantive FHA merits.
key_holding: The court denied Plaintiff's motion to compel regarding quarterly reports, finding Defendants lack possession of requested documents, and denied other discovery requests as improper inquiries; Defendants' motion to amend answer to add qualified immunity defense was granted.
brief_summary: Pro se Plaintiff filed various discovery motions (motion to compel, subpoena, telephone conference) against the Housing Authority of Hartsville in this action alleging Fair Housing Act and civil rights claims; the Magistrate Judge denied the motion to compel regarding quarterly reports for 2022 and other requests as improper discovery inquiries, granted Defendants' motion to amend their answer to add qualified immunity as an affirmative defense, and found the subpoena and telephone conference motions moot.
key_cases_cited: Frasier Healthcare Consulting, Inc. v. Grant Mem'l Hosp. Reg'l Healthcare Ctr., No. 2:12-CV-87, 2014 WL 12701042 (N.D.W. Va. Jan. 9, 2014)
Causey v. Williams, No. 4:22-cv-1475, 2023 WL 4851196 (D.S.C. July 28, 2023)
Equal Rights Ctr. v. Niles Bolton Assocs., 602 F.3d 597 (4th Cir. 2010)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges various claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1982, 42 U.S.C. § 1983, and the Fair Housing Act (§§ 3604 & 3617) related to denial of access to tenant file and grievance hearing procedures at public housing authority.
fha_claims.reasoning: This order addresses discovery disputes and procedural motions (motion to compel, motion for subpoena, motion to amend answer) rather than substantive claims on the merits. The case remains pending with no determination of the underlying FHA or § 1983 claims.

case_name: Murphy v. Brixworth Homeowners Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: No formal FHA reasonable accommodation was requested. Plaintiffs asserted under the ADA that Murphy needed access to the private neighborhood pool to 'cool himself down when his disability flares up,' and under the FHA they claimed protection from discrimination based on their political expression — neither of which constitutes a cognizable accommodation or protected-class claim under the applicable statutes.
key_holding: The court granted defendant HOA's motion for judgment on the pleadings and dismissed all claims, holding that the FHA does not protect against discrimination based on political expression, the ADA does not apply to private residential facilities, the First Amendment claim was collaterally estopped by prior state-court rulings, and the HOA did not breach its CCRs when it enforced its sign restrictions and temporarily suspended community facility access.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs, HOA members living in the Brixworth neighborhood, sued after the HOA enforced its sign restrictions against Murphy's political yard art and temporarily revoked their access to community amenities including the pool and clubhouse. Plaintiffs attempted to invoke the FHA, ADA, First Amendment, and breach of contract, but the court dismissed all claims on judgment on the pleadings, finding that political expression is not a protected class under the FHA, the neighborhood pool is a private residential facility outside the ADA's reach, the First Amendment claim was barred by collateral estoppel from prior litigation, and the HOA's actions were authorized under and consistent with the CCRs. The court also denied plaintiffs' motions to remand and to recuse the presiding judge.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Hollis v. Chestnut Bend Homeowners Ass'n, 760 F.3d 531 (6th Cir. 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Access to private neighborhood pool to cool down when plaintiff's disability flares up
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the FHA claim because plaintiffs failed to state a plausible claim under the FHA, which protects against discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, familial status, or national origin—not political expression or disability-based pool access. The court did not reach the merits of whether the accommodation was reasonable.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III claim for access to private residential pool; breach of contract claim for enforcement of CCRs and revocation of community facility access
fha_claims.reasoning: The ADA claim was dismissed because the private residential pool is not a public accommodation covered by the ADA. The breach of contract claim was dismissed because plaintiffs' own allegations established that Murphy violated the CCRs by displaying signs exceeding the one-square-foot limit, and the BHOA properly enforced the covenant through discretionary suspension of facility access, which constituted no breach by the BHOA.

case_name: Cynthia George v. Overall Creek Apartments, LLC
accommodation_description: Not a reasonable accommodation case; plaintiff alleged design and construction violations under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(C), asserting that the apartment complex was not designed and constructed with accessible and usable features for persons with disabilities, specifically observing and encountering accessibility barriers during a visit to the property as a wheelchair user.
key_holding: The court held that third-party state-law claims for equitable indemnification are preempted by the FHA and must be dismissed, but state-law claims for equitable contribution and breach of contract construed as de facto contribution claims are not preempted and may proceed, resulting in a grant in part and denial in part of the architect's motion to dismiss.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Cynthia George, a wheelchair user, sued multiple defendants alleging that Overall Creek Apartments in Murfreesboro, Tennessee was designed and constructed without accessible features in violation of the FHA. Two defendants, Overall Creek, LLC and Chandler Properties, filed a third-party complaint against the property's architect, Niles Bolton Associates, Inc. (NBA), asserting state-law claims for equitable indemnification, equitable contribution, and breach of contract. The court granted in part and denied in part NBA's Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss, holding that equitable indemnification claims and breach-of-contract claims functioning as de facto indemnification are preempted by the FHA, but equitable contribution claims and breach-of-contract claims functioning as de facto contribution are not preempted and survive dismissal.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
United States v. Murphy Dev., LLC, No. 3:08-0960, 2008 WL 3614829 (M.D. Tenn. Oct. 27, 2009)
Clover Cmty. Beavercreek, LLC v. Mussachio Architects, P.C., 676 F. Supp. 3d 82 (N.D. N.Y. 2023)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: State-law claims for equitable indemnification, equitable contribution, and breach of contract asserted by third-party plaintiffs (Overall Creek and Chandler Properties) against third-party defendant (NBA, the architect). These are derivative claims arising from the underlying FHA design and construction violation alleged by the original plaintiff.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied preemption analysis under the Supremacy Clause to determine whether state-law claims are preempted by the FHA. The court granted dismissal of the equitable indemnification claim and the breach-of-contract claim to the extent it seeks full indemnification (both preempted as obstacles to FHA purposes), but denied dismissal of the equitable contribution claim and the breach-of-contract claim to the extent it seeks only proportionate contribution (not preempted). The court applied Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards and obstacle preemption doctrine.

case_name: George v. Overall Creek Apartments, LLC
accommodation_description: Wheelchair user plaintiff visited an apartment complex and alleged design and construction accessibility barriers that would deter disabled persons from renting units
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA design-and-construction claim is time-barred because the statute of limitations began running when the last rental unit was first rented on March 19, 2021, more than two years before she filed suit on March 31, 2023, and her argument that an unrented model unit should toll the limitations period lacks merit.
brief_summary: Cynthia George, a wheelchair user, sued the designers, developers, and owners of Overall Creek Apartments alleging the complex was not designed and constructed in compliance with FHA accessibility requirements under § 3604(f)(3)(C). The court granted summary judgment for defendants, finding the claim time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations because the last available rental unit was first occupied on March 19, 2021, more than two years before suit was filed.
key_cases_cited: Fair Hous. Council, Inc. v. Vill. of Olde St. Andrews, Inc., 210 F. App'x 469 (6th Cir. 2006)
Miami Valley Fair Hous. Ctr., Inc. v. Preferred Living Real Est. Invs., LLC, 2018 WL 4690790 (S.D. Ohio 2018)
Housing Rsch. & Advoc. Ctr. v. WXZ Residential Grp./Circle Lofts 118 LLC, 2017 WL 1078956 (N.D. Ohio 2017)
Housing Advocs., Inc. v. Berardi & Partners, Inc., 2010 WL 4905547 (N.D. Ohio 2010)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible and adaptable design and construction features for persons with disabilities in multifamily housing development
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that the statute of limitations for FHA design and construction claims begins to run upon the initial rental of the final unit available for rent. The last unit was rented on March 19, 2021, and plaintiff filed suit on March 31, 2023—more than two years later. Unit 1107, which plaintiff argued should toll the limitations period, was undisputedly set aside as a model unit for marketing purposes and never made available for rent, so it does not extend the limitations period.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title III ADA accessibility claim
fha_claims.reasoning: To the extent plaintiff intended to state a Title III ADA claim, it is governed by Tennessee's one-year statute of limitations for personal injury actions under Tenn. Code Ann. § 28-3-104(a)(1)(A), not the two-year FHA period, making any ADA claim time-barred as well.

case_name: Gamane v. Diamond
accommodation_description: Request for an emotional support cat as a reasonable accommodation for Mrs. Gamane's disabilities including stroke effects, depression, and anxiety
key_holding: The court held that Plaintiffs were unlikely to succeed on the merits because they failed to establish that an ESA cat was necessary to afford equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling, as the medical documentation did not establish a causal connection between the disability and the requested accommodation, and the accommodation was unreasonable due to potential burdens on staff and risks to allergic residents.
brief_summary: Mrs. Gamane and her husband sued Bells Retirement Village and its management seeking a preliminary injunction to allow Mrs. Gamane to keep an emotional support cat as a reasonable accommodation for her disabilities. The court denied the motion, finding Plaintiffs unlikely to succeed on the merits because the medical evidence failed to establish that a cat was necessary to afford equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling, and the accommodation was unreasonable due to potential burdens on staff and risks to allergic residents.
key_cases_cited: Overlook Mut. Homes, Inc. v. Spencer, 415 F. App'x 617 (6th Cir. 2011)
Anderson v. City of Blue Ash, 798 F.3d 338 (6th Cir. 2015)
Howard v. City of Beavercreek, 276 F.3d 802 (6th Cir. 2002)
Hollis v. Chestnut Bend Homeowners Ass'n, 760 F.3d 531 (6th Cir. 2014)
Phillips v. Acacia on the Green Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 2022 WL 1692948 (6th Cir. May 26, 2022)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Emotional support animal (cat) for Mrs. Gamane to ameliorate effects of disability (stroke, kidney disease, depression, anxiety) and provide equal opportunity to use and enjoy her dwelling
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied the five-element reasonable accommodation test and found that plaintiffs failed to establish likelihood of success on the merits because: (1) the cat was not necessary—plaintiffs failed to provide evidence of a causal connection between the disability and how the ESA would ameliorate it such that Mrs. Gamane could enjoy her dwelling as a non-disabled person would; and (2) the cat was not reasonable—the burdens on defendants (staff entering apartments five times daily, potential property damage, allergen exposure to other residents and staff) outweighed the benefits, and plaintiffs offered only conclusory statements unsupported by evidence, whereas defendants provided sworn declarations detailing operational impacts.

source_file: 10204105_2024_Brady v. The Evangelical Lutheran Good Samaritan Society_txed
case_name: Mary Brady v. The Evangelical Lutheran Good Samaritan Society
accommodation_description: Brady requested a priority waitlist position, carpet installation, security system installation, mold testing, and a residence free from environmental triggers as accommodations for her autoimmune disease and allergies.
key_holding: The court dismissed Brady's FHA claim with prejudice because she failed to plausibly allege a qualifying disability or that Good Samaritan Society knew of her alleged handicaps and their consequential limitations, and she failed to establish a nexus between her claimed conditions and her requested accommodations.
brief_summary: Mary Brady sued The Evangelical Lutheran Good Samaritan Society, operator of Denton Village senior living community, alleging the defendant denied her reasonable accommodations for her alleged autoimmune disease and allergies when it rejected her rental application and subsequent accommodation requests. The court granted the motion to dismiss with prejudice, finding Brady failed to plausibly allege a qualifying disability under the FHA or that she communicated her disability and its limitations to the defendant with sufficient specificity.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Mueck v. La Grange Acquisitions, L.P., 75 F.4th 469 (5th Cir. 2023)
Windham v. Harris Cnty., 875 F.3d 229 (5th Cir. 2017)
Chavez v. Aber, 122 F. Supp. 3d 581 (W.D. Tex. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Mold testing of Unit #60; installation of carpet due to polyarthralgia; installation of security system; priority placement on waitlist above current residents; assurance that any offered residence be free from triggers
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege a handicap under the FHA because she did not establish that her alleged conditions (autoimmune disease, allergies, joint pain, muscle loss, lumbar strain, bulging discs) substantially limit any major life activity as compared to the general population. The complaint contained only conclusory assertions and vague symptoms without factual support for the severity or causal connection to major life activities. Additionally, plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that defendant knew of her alleged handicaps and their consequential limitations, and failed to articulate how requested accommodations related to her handicaps.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title III ADA claim for injunctive relief seeking accommodations at senior living facility
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff lacked Article III standing to seek injunctive relief under Title III of the ADA because she failed to establish a sufficient likelihood of future injury. Her claims sought redress for past harms (denial of Unit #60) or relied on highly attenuated chains of possibilities (hypothetical future denials of accommodations for units not yet offered). The amended complaint provided no facts suggesting that future denials would occur or that she would be denied admission to alternative units.

case_name: Lakeside of Coppell v. Hurst
accommodation_description: Defendants requested reasonable accommodations in response to plaintiff's eviction action, but the specific accommodation is not described in this jurisdictional ruling.
key_holding: Federal question jurisdiction cannot be established through defenses or counterclaims based on federal law; because the landlord's right to relief depends on state eviction law rather than federal law, the case must be remanded to state court.
brief_summary: Lakeside of Coppell filed an eviction action against tenants Jaycen and Jillian Hurst in Texas state court; defendants removed the case to federal court claiming federal question jurisdiction based on ADA and FHA reasonable accommodation defenses and counterclaims. The district court granted the magistrate judge's recommendation to remand, holding that a plaintiff's right to relief must depend on federal law to establish federal question jurisdiction, and a defense or counterclaim—even one based on federal law—cannot support removal.
key_cases_cited: Borden v. Allstate Insurance Co., 589 F.3d 168 (5th Cir. 2009)
Vaden v. Discover Bank, 556 U.S. 49 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation(s) requested by defendants in response to eviction action; specific accommodation not detailed in opinion
fha_claims.reasoning: The court remanded for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because defendants' FHA reasonable accommodation claim is a defense or counterclaim to the eviction action, not the basis of plaintiff's cause of action. Federal question jurisdiction does not exist when the plaintiff's right to relief does not depend on resolution of federal law; here, plaintiff seeks eviction under state law, and defendants' federal defenses cannot establish jurisdiction.

source_file: 10204970_2024_Haire v. 5445 Caruth Haven Lane Apartments Owner LLC_txnd
case_name: Tiffany Haire v. 5445 Caruth Haven Lane Apartments Owner LLC
accommodation_description: No specific reasonable accommodation or modification request is described in the case text. The FHA claims center on a § 3604 housing discrimination claim (nature unspecified) and a § 3617 claim that defendants interfered with a HUD/Fair Housing investigation by defaming plaintiff, falsifying and concealing evidence, intentionally delaying the investigation, and misleading HUD investigators.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for all defendants and dismissed all of plaintiff's claims with prejudice, finding the FHA § 3604 claim time-barred and the FHA § 3617 interference claim unsupported by competent summary judgment evidence.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Tiffany Haire sued her apartment complex's owners and managers under the Fair Housing Act (§§ 3604 and 3617), as well as for intentional infliction of emotional distress, negligence, and related state-law claims. The FHA § 3604 claim was dismissed because plaintiff failed to provide information sufficient to establish tolling of the two-year statute of limitations, and the § 3617 interference claim failed at summary judgment because plaintiff's allegations that defendants sabotaged a HUD investigation through defamation and fraud were unsupported by competent evidence. The court also rejected the IIED and negligence claims, the former because a defamation remedy was available and the latter because no private cause of action exists under HIPAA.
key_cases_cited: Zhu v. Countrywide Realty Co., 165 F. Supp. 2d 1181 (D. Kan. 2001)
Stelly v. Duriso, 982 F.3d 403 (5th Cir. 2020)
Acara v. Banks, 470 F.3d 569 (5th Cir. 2006)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim involves alleged discrimination under § 3604
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that the two-year statute of limitations under 42 U.S.C. § 3613(a)(1)(B) had expired because plaintiff provided no information regarding the contents of her HUD charge filed in February 2020 or the duration of the investigation, and thus the tolling provision could not be applied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim involves alleged retaliation and interference with HUD investigation
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted summary judgment on the § 3617 retaliation claim because plaintiff's allegations of sabotage, defamation, fraud, and deliberate delay of the HUD investigation were unsupported by any competent summary judgment evidence and plaintiff failed to meet her burden to provide factual support for the claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Intentional infliction of emotional distress, negligence (HIPAA violation), ratification, and retraction claims
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted summary judgment on the intentional infliction of emotional distress claim because defamation is an available remedy for the alleged misconduct, making IIED inappropriate as a gap-filler tort. The negligence claim failed because the only factual allegations related to Jennifer Owen (dismissed from the case) and because there is no private cause of action under HIPAA. Ratification and retraction are not cognizable as causes of action.

source_file: 10205156_2024_Bowman v. SWBC Real Estate Services LLC_txnd
case_name: Bowman v. SWBC Real Estates Services, LLC
accommodation_description: Disabled veteran alleging architectural barriers at 590-unit apartment complex prevented wheelchair access to common areas and unit features.
key_holding: The court found Bowman lacked standing to sue under § 3604(f)(1) for rental discrimination because he did not engage in rental activity, but found he sufficiently alleged standing under § 3604(f)(2) by claiming inability to access privileges of the rental due to architectural barriers; the court granted leave to amend complaint to specify which barriers Bowman encountered.
brief_summary: Dana Bowman, a disabled veteran who lost both legs, sued SWBC Real Estates Services and related entities alleging architectural barriers at a 590-unit apartment complex in Rockwall, Texas prevented wheelchair access to common areas and unit features. The court granted partial dismissal, finding Bowman lacked standing under § 3604(f)(1) because he did not allege sufficient rental activity, but allowed claims under § 3604(f)(2) to proceed, giving Bowman 28 days to amend his complaint to specify which barriers he encountered.
key_cases_cited: Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Laufer v. Mann Hosp., L.L.C., 996 F.3d 269 (5th Cir. 2021)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible design and construction of multifamily dwellings; architectural barriers including inaccessible mailbox center, lack of accessible route to public transportation, thermostats at unreachable heights, and inaccessible bathrooms for wheelchair users
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff lacked standing under § 3604(f)(1) because he failed to allege he engaged in rental activity (leasing, subletting, or granting consideration for right to occupy premises). The provision requires a contractual relationship or rental activity, which plaintiff did not establish.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible design and construction of multifamily dwellings; architectural barriers including inaccessible mailbox center, lack of accessible route to public transportation, thermostats at unreachable heights, and inaccessible bathrooms for wheelchair users
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff stated a plausible claim under § 3604(f)(2) by alleging inability to access privileges of rental dwelling (common use areas), but complaint lacked specificity regarding where barriers were encountered (common use areas vs. private units). Court granted in part and allowed 28 days to replead with clarification of barrier locations.

case_name: Dana Bowman v. Prida Construction, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff challenged lack of accessibility at Waterfront Apartments; an agreed judgment required remediation of 96 categories of barriers to access.
key_holding: Although plaintiff prevailed on the underlying FHA accessibility claims, the court substantially reduced attorneys' fees from the requested $159,308.75 to $79,213.75, finding excessive billing, lack of billing judgment, and an excessive hourly rate.
brief_summary: Dana Bowman sued Prida Construction and Waterfront Housing for Fair Housing Act violations concerning lack of accessibility at Waterfront Apartments in Galveston, resulting in an agreed judgment requiring remediation of 96 accessibility barriers. This opinion addressed Bowman's motion for attorneys' fees, with the court reducing the requested $159,308.75 award to $79,213.75 due to excessive hourly rates, lack of billing judgment, and duplicative billing entries.
key_cases_cited: Hensley v. Eckerhart, 461 U.S. 424 (1983)
Watkins v. Fordice, 7 F.3d 453 (5th Cir. 1993)
LULAC v. Roscoe Indep. Sch. Dist., 119 F.3d 1228 (5th Cir. 1997)
Blum v. Stenson, 465 U.S. 886 (1984)
McClain v. Lufkin Indus., Inc., 649 F.3d 374 (5th Cir. 2011)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessibility barriers at Waterfront Apartments in Galveston; 96 categories of barriers to access requiring remediation
fha_claims.reasoning: Following partial summary judgment, the parties entered into an agreed judgment ordering defendants to remediate 96 categories of accessibility barriers. The court found plaintiff was the prevailing party entitled to recover reasonable attorneys' fees, expert fees, costs and expenses under 42 U.S.C. § 3613(c)(2) and the ADA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) claim for accessibility violations; 42 U.S.C. § 12205
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff brought parallel claims under the ADA. The agreed judgment expressly stated plaintiff was the prevailing party under both 42 U.S.C. §§ 3613(c)(2) and 12205, entitling plaintiff to recover reasonable attorneys' fees, expert fees, and litigation expenses.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation related to failure to timely provide documentation for Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher Program; nature of specific accommodation not detailed in opinion
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found no federal-question jurisdiction because Stewart's state-law claims under the Texas Fair Housing Act do not necessarily require resolution of federal law; the case was remanded to state court before any FHA claim could be substantively analyzed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Texas Fair Housing Act familial discrimination claim; Texas Constitution due process claims (substantive and procedural)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court determined that Stewart's state-law claims do not require interpretation of federal law and therefore lack federal-question jurisdiction; the case was remanded to state court without substantive analysis of the merits.

source_file: 10208849_2022_Parada v. Sandhill Shores Property Owners Association, Inc._txsd
case_name: Cecilia Parada v. Sandhill Shores Property Owners Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that the HOA not construct a beach-access path near her home, which would force her to leave because her Alzheimer's disease leaves her unable to cope with encounters with strangers outside her residence.
key_holding: The court denied the HOA's motion to dismiss, finding that Parada adequately pleaded she is handicapped under the FHA (Alzheimer's disease substantially limits major life activities including caring for herself, learning, communicating, and interacting with others) and that her requested accommodation—refraining from constructing the beach-access path near her home—is facially reasonable and plausibly necessary to afford her equal opportunity to use and enjoy her dwelling.
brief_summary: Cecilia Parada, who suffers from late-onset Alzheimer's disease, sued Sandhill Shores Property Owners Association alleging the HOA violated the Fair Housing Act and ADA by refusing her request to not construct a beach-access path near her home, which construction would force her to leave because her disability prevents her from coping with encounters with strangers. The court denied the HOA's motion to dismiss, finding Parada adequately pleaded Article III standing, survived abstention arguments, and stated a plausible reasonable accommodation claim under § 3604(f)(3)(B) by alleging she is handicapped (Alzheimer's substantially limits major life activities) and her requested accommodation is facially reasonable.
key_cases_cited: Providence Behav. Health v. Grant Rd. Pub. Util. Dist., 902 F.3d 448 (5th Cir. 2018)
Trafficante v. Metro. Life Ins. Co., 409 U.S. 205 (1972)
Gladstone Realtors v. Vill. of Bellwood, 441 U.S. 91 (1979)
Bank of Am. Corp. v. City of Miami, Fla., 137 S. Ct. 1296 (2017)
City of Edmonds v. Oxford House, Inc., 514 U.S. 725 (1995)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request that Sandhill Shores not construct a pedestrian beach-access path behind and to the side of Parada's home, or alternatively, locate the path at a considerable distance from her residence as previously maintained, to prevent constant confrontation with strangers that triggers severe panic attacks due to her late-onset Alzheimer's disease and cognitive impairment.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the motion to dismiss on the FHA reasonable-accommodation claim, finding that Parada adequately pleaded all elements under Iqbal/Twombly: she has a cognizable handicap (Alzheimer's disease substantially limiting major life activities including caring for oneself, learning, working, concentrating, thinking, communicating, and interacting with others), she requested an accommodation and Sandhill Shores denied it, the accommodation is facially reasonable, and it is necessary to afford her equal opportunity to use and enjoy her dwelling. The court rejected Sandhill Shores' argument that Parada's impairment does not substantially limit a major life activity, distinguishing Eastwood and holding that while the effect of her disability is to prevent coping with strangers, that effect is not itself the major life activity—the underlying Alzheimer's disease is.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act Title III claim for failure to make reasonable modifications to policies, practices, or procedures; also alleged ADA Title III public accommodation discrimination based on disability.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the motion to dismiss on the ADA Title III claim, holding that Parada adequately pleaded a reasonable-modification claim under 42 U.S.C. § 12182(b)(2)(A)(ii). The court rejected Sandhill Shores' argument that constructing a beach-access path does not constitute a 'policy, practice, or procedure' and that compliance with the Texas Open Beaches Act insulates the association from ADA liability. The court found that a beach qualifies as a 'place of recreation' under the liberally construed definition of public accommodation in 42 U.S.C. § 12181(7)(I), and that Sandhill Shores' discretionary decision regarding path placement—not merely the obligation to provide access—constitutes a policy or practice subject to the ADA's reasonable-modification requirement.

source_file: 10209181_2022_People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals, Inc. v. Young_txsd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: First Amendment free speech rights; challenge to deletion of PETA's comments from TAMU's social media pages (Facebook and YouTube) during virtual graduation ceremonies in May 2020
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss on jurisdictional grounds (12(b)(1)) and failure to state a claim (12(b)(6)). PETA established Article III standing under Driehaus test for threatened enforcement of unconstitutional policy, Ex parte Young exception applies, and PETA stated a plausible § 1983 claim for First Amendment violation under viewpoint discrimination theory. Claim survives and proceeds.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 1983 claims for excessive force and municipal liability; ADA Title II and Section 504 claims for failure to accommodate mental health disability during arrest by providing mental health professional, backup officer, or scheduling surrender to court
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 1983 municipal liability claims dismissed for failure to plead facts showing pattern of similar incidents or deliberate indifference under Iqbal/Twombly standard. ADA Title II and Section 504 claims survived motion to dismiss; court held that arrest warrant and obtaining of taser do not constitute exigent circumstances excusing disability accommodation obligations, and plaintiffs adequately pleaded that no life-threatening situation existed at initial contact.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Social Security disability benefits claim under Title II of the Social Security Act; service animal medical necessity and vocational impact in RFC determination
fha_claims.reasoning: The ALJ's RFC determination was largely supported by substantial evidence and proper legal standards were applied. However, the ALJ committed reversible error by failing to consider whether plaintiff's service animals were medically necessary and, if so, what vocational impact they would have on his ability to perform work. The case was remanded for the ALJ to determine medical necessity of service animals and adjust RFC accordingly.

case_name: Prinyah El-Bey v. Berkshire Hathaway Home Services
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a wheelchair-bound tenant with asthma, sought injunctive relief to stop a neighbor's marijuana smoking that triggered her asthma, but did not request a specific reasonable accommodation.
key_holding: El-Bey failed to state a plausible FHA reasonable accommodation claim because she did not plead facts showing she requested a particular reasonable, necessary accommodation or that any defendant refused such a request.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Prinyah El-Bey, a wheelchair-bound tenant with asthma, sued Berkshire Hathaway Home Services and related entities alleging discrimination under the ADA and FHA, claiming the landlord failed to address marijuana smoke from a neighbor that triggered her asthma. The court dismissed her federal claims with prejudice under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B) for failure to state a plausible claim, finding she failed to allege that she requested a specific reasonable accommodation or that any defendant refused such a request.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Parada v. Sandhill Shores Property Owners Association, Inc., 604 F. Supp. 3d 567 (S.D. Tex. 2022)
Prim v. Stein, 6 F.4th 584 (5th Cir. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Modification of policies or procedures to address neighbor's marijuana smoking that triggered plaintiff's asthma; plaintiff sought injunctive relief to stop the neighbor from smoking and compensation for emergency room visit and mental anguish.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts to establish a reasonable accommodation claim under the FHA. The court found that plaintiff did not allege that she requested a particular reasonable, necessary accommodation or that such a request was denied. The emails showed only that the property manager consulted with the HOA manager and advised plaintiff to call police, with no allegations or documents showing that any defendant refused a request for reasonable accommodation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III policy modification claim; Texas state law landlord-tenant claims; defamation claims
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA Title III claims dismissed because residential apartments are not 'public accommodations' under the ADA, and plaintiff failed to identify a specific policy, practice, or procedure to modify or show that a modification was requested and denied. State law claims dismissed without prejudice under supplemental jurisdiction doctrine because all federal claims were eliminated before trial.

case_name: Bowman v. Shadowbriar Apartments, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff observed and encountered physical accessibility barriers at Briar Apartments including excessively high thresholds, inadequate clearance on interior doors, and light switches inaccessible from a wheelchair, alleging violations of design and construction accessibility requirements.
key_holding: The court denied third-party defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that third-party plaintiffs have standing to seek contribution from architects and engineers for their own professional negligence in designing inaccessible housing, and that such contribution claims are not preempted by the FHA or ADA.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Dana Bowman sued Shadowbriar Apartments and its principal alleging that the apartment complex contains design and construction accessibility barriers in violation of the FHA and ADA. The original defendants then filed third-party claims against the architects and engineers seeking contribution for any liability. The court denied the third-party defendants' motion to dismiss, holding that third-party plaintiffs had standing to pursue contribution claims and that such claims were not preempted by federal disability law.
key_cases_cited: Equal Rights Ctr. v. Niles Bolton Assocs., 602 F.3d 597 (4th Cir. 2010)
City of Los Angeles v. AECOM Servs., Inc., 854 F.3d 1149 (9th Cir. 2017)
Sewell v. Monroe City Sch. Bd., 974 F.3d 577 (5th Cir. 2020)
Vinmar Overseas, Ltd. v. OceanConnect, LLC, 2012 WL 5989206 (S.D. Tex. 2012)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible design and construction of apartment units, including correction of excessively high thresholds, inadequate clearance on interior doors, and inaccessible light switches
fha_claims.disposition: Motion to Dismiss (Third-Party Defendants' Motion to Dismiss Denied)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the third-party defendants' motion to dismiss the underlying FHA design and construction claim. The opinion addresses only the third-party complaint's preemption and standing issues, not the merits of Bowman's original FHA claim, which survives and remains pending against the original defendants.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II accessibility standards violations; professional negligence claim by third-party plaintiffs against architects and engineers
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the third-party defendants' motion to dismiss the professional negligence claim, finding that contribution claims against third parties for their own wrongdoing in failing to comply with federal disability standards are not preempted by the FHA or ADA, following AECOM Services, Inc.

case_name: Shayla Anderson, et al. v. SunRidge Management Group, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation was requested; the case concerns alleged intentional race and sex discrimination rather than a disability accommodation request.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for defendants because plaintiffs' FHA claims under §§ 3604(a)-(b) failed as a matter of law since the alleged discrimination related to habitability rather than housing availability, and plaintiffs failed to establish prima facie cases of disparate treatment or retaliation.
brief_summary: African American tenants Anderson and Edwards sued SunRidge Management Group and Grand Fountain Apartments alleging race and sex discrimination, Title VII violations, § 1983 claims, and retaliation under the FHA. The court granted summary judgment for defendants on all claims, finding the FHA claims failed because plaintiffs' alleged harms concerned habitability rather than housing availability, and plaintiffs presented no evidence establishing prima facie cases of intentional discrimination or retaliation.
key_cases_cited: Cox v. City of Dallas, 430 F.3d 734 (5th Cir. 2005)
Mandawala v. Struga Mgmt., 2023 WL 2712500 (5th Cir. 2023)
Inclusive Cmtys. Project, Inc. v. Lincoln Prop. Co., 920 F.3d 890 (5th Cir. 2019)
Brown v. Harris Cty. Hous. Auth., 2018 WL 3080880 (S.D. Tex. 2018)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to establish a prima facie case of racial and sex-based discrimination under §§ 3604(a)–(b). The court found that discrimination claims must affect housing availability, not merely habitability; plaintiffs were permitted to live in the apartment for years without paying rent. Additionally, plaintiffs presented no evidence of differential treatment compared to similarly situated tenants, and their allegations were vague and conclusory.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Although Anderson's HUD complaints and Justice of the Peace lawsuit constitute protected activities, the alleged conduct (delayed maintenance requests, lease violation notices for unpaid rent) does not rise to the level of material adversity required for retaliation. Additionally, Anderson failed to establish a causal connection because alleged conduct occurred both before and after the protected activities, and Edwards failed to demonstrate participation in any protected activity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, 42 U.S.C. § 1983
fha_claims.reasoning: Title VII claims fail because plaintiffs were never employed by defendants; Title VII applies only to employment discrimination. Section 1983 claims fail because defendants are private entities, not state actors, and plaintiffs presented no evidence that defendants acted under color of state law, which is a prerequisite for § 1983 liability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III accessibility modifications including curb ramp replacement, additional handicap accessible parking spaces, parking lot and sidewalk regrading, and automatic door openers
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found defendant liable for failure to make readily achievable modification to curb ramp but rejected plaintiff's claims for additional modifications (parking spaces, lot/sidewalk regrading, automatic door openers) as not readily achievable under ADA accessibility standards for existing facilities.

source_file: 10211893_2019_Payne v. City of San Antonio, Texas_txwd
case_name: Payne v. City of San Antonio, Texas
accommodation_description: Request for waiver of fees for covered parking as a reasonable accommodation for disability
key_holding: The court recommended dismissing the reasonable accommodation claim because plaintiffs failed to adequately plead the nature of Mr. Payne's disability, stating there were no facts by which the court could determine whether he suffered from a qualifying disability under the FHA, despite noting the accommodation requested concerned a waiver of fees for covered parking.
brief_summary: Don Albert Payne and Gloria Jean Payne, proceeding pro se, sued the City of San Antonio, San Antonio Housing Authority (SAHA), SAHA employee Amy Carrillo, and various police officers alleging wrongful eviction, disability discrimination, and failure to accommodate under the FHA after Mr. Payne requested a waiver of covered parking fees. The magistrate judge recommended granting SAHA's motion to dismiss all claims against it for failure to state a claim, including dismissing the FHA reasonable accommodation claim because plaintiffs failed to adequately plead Mr. Payne's qualifying disability beyond referencing mental health.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Monell v. Dep't of Soc. Servs. of City of New York, 436 U.S. 658 (1978)
Providence Behavioral Health v. Grant Rd. Pub. Util. Dist., 902 F.3d 448 (5th Cir. 2018)
Bd. of Comm'rs of Bryan County v. Brown, 520 U.S. 397 (1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver of fees for covered parking as a reasonable accommodation for disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Court allowed claim to proceed despite deficiencies because defendants did not move to dismiss on the basis of failure to allege a qualifying disability; court noted that even after opportunity to file More Definite Statement, plaintiffs failed to describe the disability at issue, but declined to dismiss at this early stage given defendants' narrow grounds for dismissal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 1983 due process violation (wrongful eviction without hearing); Section 1983 due process violation (eviction without process); Texas tort claims (intentional infliction of emotional distress, negligence); Texas Deceptive Trade Practices Act; Section 1985 conspiracy; Section 1986 conspiracy to prevent civil rights violation
fha_claims.reasoning: Against SAHA: All Section 1983 claims dismissed for failure to allege official policy or custom required for municipal liability; tort claims dismissed under governmental immunity doctrine; DTPA claim dismissed because governmental entities excluded from DTPA definition of 'person.' Against Carrillo: Section 1983 claims survive qualified immunity defense at pleading stage; DTPA claim survives official immunity defense; Section 1985 conspiracy claim survives; Section 1986, tort claims, and other claims dismissed.

source_file: 10212330_2020_Harmony Haus Westlake, LLC v. Parkstone Property Owners Association, Inc._txwd
case_name: Harmony Haus Westlake, LLC v. Parkstone Property Owners Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: Request for a waiver of the twelve-hour street-parking restriction during the coronavirus pandemic shelter-in-place order.
key_holding: The court granted the motion to dismiss the reasonable accommodation claim because the requested parking restriction waiver was not necessary to ameliorate the disability (it was merely inconvenient) and was not reasonable (a blanket waiver was overbroad compared to the defendant's counter-accommodation offer of four cars on the street), while denying the motion to dismiss the retaliation claim based on the close temporal proximity between the HOA's new enforcement scheme and the plaintiffs' protected FHA activities.
brief_summary: Harmony Haus Westlake, LLC (a transitional sober living residence operator) and the property owners sued Parkstone Property Owners Association seeking reasonable accommodation from parking restrictions during the COVID-19 pandemic and challenging new HOA enforcement schemes as discriminatory and retaliatory. The court dismissed the reasonable accommodation, intentional discrimination, and disparate treatment claims but allowed the retaliation claim to proceed based on the temporal proximity between the HOA's new enforcement actions and the plaintiffs' protected FHA activities.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
City of Edmonds v. Oxford House, Inc., 514 U.S. 725 (1995)
Groome Res., Ltd., L.L.C. v. Par. of Jefferson, 234 F.3d 192 (5th Cir. 2000)
Bryant Woods Inn, Inc. v. Howard Cty. Md., 124 F.3d 597 (4th Cir. 1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Intentional discrimination through new escalating fine structure and enforcement scheme targeting Harmony Haus residents
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege that Defendant's fines and enforcement were imposed 'because of' Plaintiffs' handicap status. The fines were imposed for violating parking restrictions, not because of disability status, and Defendant was following the Court's prior directive permitting strict enforcement of restrictions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Disparate treatment in terms, conditions, or privileges of dwelling through selective enforcement of parking restrictions
fha_claims.reasoning: Under § 3604(f)(2), Plaintiffs failed to plead the fundamental element that Defendant's treatment was 'because of a handicap.' Plaintiffs conceded that Defendant enforced restrictions against other residents, undermining any disparate treatment claim, and provided no evidence of discriminatory intent based on disability status.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver of twelve-hour street parking restriction during COVID-19 pandemic shelter-in-place order; blanket moratorium 'until further order of the Court'
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to show the accommodation was necessary because the pandemic-driven need for residents to remain at home actually reduced the need for street parking, and the twelve-hour restriction itself does not mandate immediate vehicle movement. The requested blanket waiver was unreasonable as it imposed an open-ended burden on the defendant and court, and Defendant's counter-offer of four street parking spaces was a more efficient alternative.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Enactment of new enforcement scheme with escalating fine structure approximately two weeks after Court's judgment in prior case; new deed restriction preemptively disallowing reasonable accommodation requests for single-family use within 1,000 feet of Harmony Haus
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs satisfied the prima facie retaliation framework under § 3617: (1) they engaged in protected activities (requesting reasonable accommodation and filing suit); (2) Defendant took an adverse action (new enforcement scheme with escalating fines); and (3) close temporal proximity (two weeks after judgment) raises a plausible causal connection between the protected activities and the adverse action, even though the actions were not discriminatory on their face.

case_name: Mandawala v. Struga Management
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges landlord's refusal to recognize his occupancy arrangement with other tenants and subsequent eviction was based on racial discrimination.
key_holding: Plaintiff's motion for summary judgment on FHA racial discrimination claim was denied because he failed to present sufficient evidence to prove discriminatory animus or meet his burden of proof on the elements of the claim.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Symon Mandawala sued Struga Management, his former property management company, alleging racial discrimination in violation of the Fair Housing Act when the manager allegedly refused to recognize his occupancy arrangement with other tenants and forced him to vacate. The court denied Mandawala's motion for summary judgment on his FHA claim because he failed to present sufficient evidence demonstrating discriminatory animus or establishing each element of his claim as a matter of law.
key_cases_cited: Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986)
Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242 (1986)
Matsushita Elec. Indus. Co. v. Zenith Radio Corp., 475 U.S. 574 (1986)
Scott v. Harris, 550 U.S. 372 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to present summary judgment evidence proving each element of the FHA disparate treatment claim, specifically failing to establish discriminatory animus or to show that defendants' decision to remove him from the property was based on race rather than lease violation. The court found disputed facts regarding whether a valid 'joining agreement' existed and whether race motivated the defendants' actions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fraudulent practices under 42 U.S.C. § 1981(a)(b) and Texas Business & Commercial Code § 17.46; Conversion under Texas common law
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to present summary judgment evidence proving the elements of fraud or conversion claims as a matter of law, and failed to identify specific evidence in the record or articulate how evidence supported the claims. Disputed facts remained regarding whether defendants engaged in fraudulent practices or wrongfully withheld plaintiff's mail and packages.

case_name: Mandawala v. Struga Management
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges he was forced to move after defendant property management initiated eviction proceedings based on his unauthorized occupancy with the Smith family.
key_holding: The court denied dismissal of plaintiff's racial discrimination claims under the FHA, finding plaintiff pleaded enough facts to qualify as an 'aggrieved person' under 42 U.S.C. § 3602(i) who can pursue discriminatory housing practice claims, while dismissing claims under Texas Property Code § 92.004, § 1981(c)/§ 1983, intentional infliction of emotional distress, and § 1985/§ 1986 conspiracy claims.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Symon Mandawala sued Struga Management alleging racial discrimination after he was forced to move from an apartment where he had paid a $40 joining fee to reside with the Smith family, and defendants subsequently initiated eviction proceedings based on his unauthorized occupancy. The court granted in part and denied in part defendant's motion to dismiss, dismissing claims for fraudulent practices under Texas Property Code § 92.004, deprivation of rights under color of law, intentional infliction of emotional distress, and conspiracy under §§ 1985-1986, while allowing plaintiff's racial discrimination claims under the Fair Housing Act to proceed.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Domino's Pizza, Inc. v. McDonald

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges racial discrimination in denial of occupancy rights and forced eviction based on race.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that plaintiff adequately alleged facts to satisfy the definition of 'aggrieved person' under 42 U.S.C. § 3602(i) by claiming injury from a discriminatory housing practice. Plaintiff need not allege authorization by formal lease; the FHA definition of 'to rent' includes granting the right to occupy for consideration without a lease. Counts 1-3 survive the motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1981(a)-(b) (equal right to make and enforce contracts); Texas Property Code § 92.004 (bad faith suit liability); Texas Business & Commercial Code § 17.46 (TDTPA); 42 U.S.C. § 1981(c) and § 1983 (color of law deprivation); state tort claims (intentional infliction of emotional distress, conversion); 42 U.S.C. § 1985(3) (conspiracy); 42 U.S.C. § 1986 (failure to prevent conspiracy).
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed § 1981(c)/§ 1983 claim (Count 7) as asserting only 'color of law' without cognizable cause of action; dismissed intentional infliction of emotional distress (Count 8) as duplicative gap-filler tort based on same underlying conduct as discrimination claims; dismissed § 1985(3) conspiracy (Count 10) under intracorporate conspiracy doctrine (corporation cannot conspire with its own employees); dismissed § 1986 claim (Count 11) as dependent on invalid § 1985 claim; dismissed Texas Property Code § 92.004 claim (Count 5) as inapplicable (statute provides remedy only for landlord against tenant, not vice versa). Court allowed § 1981(a)-(b) contract claim (Counts 4-6 in part) and TDTPA claim (Count 6) to survive, finding plaintiff adequately alleged he sought to acquire lease of real property as a 'consumer' and that Struga Management provided 'goods' (real property) under the TDTPA.
