case_name: Sophia Loftis v. Progress Residential and Tiffany Green
accommodation_description: No accommodation request described; plaintiff alleges race-based housing discrimination regarding property purchases in Black neighborhoods and withholding of rental deposit.
key_holding: The court dismissed the complaint as frivolous and for failure to state a claim because plaintiff failed to allege sufficient factual details connecting Progress Residential's alleged conduct—purchasing properties in predominantly Black neighborhoods and using race-based statistics to withhold her deposit—to a plausible Fair Housing Act violation.
brief_summary: Sophia Loftis sued Progress Residential and Tiffany Green under the Fair Housing Act, alleging that Progress Residential engaged in racial discrimination by purchasing properties in predominantly Black neighborhoods, making homes unavailable, and driving up prices, and that a leasing agent used race-based statistics to withhold her deposit. The court dismissed the complaint without prejudice for failure to state a plausible FHA claim, finding the allegations too conclusory to establish intentional discrimination or disparate impact.
key_cases_cited: Jackson v. Okaloosa Cnty., 21 F.3d 1531 (11th Cir. 1994)
Bonasera v. City of Norcross, 342 F. App'x 581 (11th Cir. 2009)
Hallmark Devs., Inc. v. Fulton Cnty., 466 F.3d 1276 (11th Cir. 2006)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's complaint alleging that Progress Residential acquired properties in predominantly Black neighborhoods and used race-based statistics to withhold her deposit fails to state a plausible disparate impact claim under the FHA because she provides no details regarding the statistic, how it operates to have discriminatory impact, or how the alleged conduct connects to her claims. The factual allegations are too conclusory and disconnected to survive § 1915(e) frivolity review.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff fails to allege sufficient facts showing intentional racial discrimination by Progress Residential. The complaint lacks details regarding the underlying transaction, how the withholding of deposit or refusal to provide an MLS number constitutes unequal treatment based on race, and how these allegations connect to the claim that Progress Residential targets predominantly Black neighborhoods. The allegations are too vague and conclusory to state a plausible claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint fails to state a claim against defendant Tiffany Green because it contains no allegations of any particular action taken by Green. Although Green is named as a defendant and identified as a real estate broker, the complaint does not refer to her again and provides no factual basis for attributing any discriminatory conduct to her individually.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VII discrimination claim (race, color, age); Connecticut state law discrimination and retaliation claims under Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 46a-58, 46a-60(b)(1), and 46a-60(b)(4)
fha_claims.reasoning: Title VII claims against individual defendants dismissed because individuals are not subject to liability under Title VII. Title VII claim against South Oxford dismissed for failure to allege an employer-employee relationship—plaintiffs alleged they were applying for a lease, not that they were hired or received remuneration from defendant. Remaining state law claims dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction after federal question jurisdiction was eliminated; court declined supplemental jurisdiction. Ms. Williams dismissed for improper service of process under Rule 12(b)(5).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: False Claims Act qui tam action alleging defendant charged rent in excess of Housing Assistance Payments contract; breach of HAP contract
fha_claims.reasoning: Pro se litigant may not bring qui tam action under False Claims Act; complaint not filed in government's name, not under seal, and government not served as required by 31 U.S.C. § 3730(b). Breach of HAP contract claim dismissed for lack of standing because tenant is not a party to or third-party beneficiary of HAP contract between landlord and PHA.

case_name: McGinn v. Broadmead, Inc.
accommodation_description: Request that Broadmead retirement community provide safe, varied gluten-free food options to accommodate celiac disease
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment to Broadmead on the FHA reasonable accommodation claim because Plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie case that Broadmead denied her a reasonable accommodation for her celiac disease, and the court also found many claims time-barred under the two-year FHA statute of limitations.
brief_summary: Eleanor McGinn, an 83-year-old resident with celiac disease at Broadmead, a retirement community in Hunt Valley, Maryland, sued Broadmead under the FHA, Rehabilitation Act, and ADA alleging the community failed to accommodate her need for safe gluten-free food, having experienced multiple gluten exposures from meals served at the community. The court granted Broadmead's motion for summary judgment, finding McGinn failed to establish a prima facie failure-to-accommodate claim and that many of her claims were time-barred under the applicable statutes of limitations.
key_cases_cited: Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242 (1986)
Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986)
Thomas v. The Salvation Army S. Territory, 841 F.3d 632 (4th Cir. 2016)
Ricco v. DeStefano, 557 U.S. 557 (2009)
Lujan v. Defs. of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Safe, varied gluten-free dining options and preparation in a certified gluten-free kitchen with adequately trained staff; alternatively, return of entrance fee and payments for services not rendered
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that Plaintiff's FHA claim accrued in January 2021 when she stopped eating at Broadmead, placing the claim outside the two-year FHA statute of limitations. The court also rejected application of the continuing violation doctrine to failure-to-accommodate claims, finding that discrete incidents of alleged gluten exposure and menu errors do not constitute a systemic practice of recurring unlawful discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title III ADA (injunctive relief for discrimination in public accommodation); Section 504 Rehabilitation Act (damages for failure to accommodate disability); breach of contract; negligence; negligent misrepresentation; breach of express warranty; breach of implied warranty of merchantability; breach of implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted summary judgment on all non-FHA claims. For the ADA claim, Plaintiff lacked Article III standing to seek injunctive relief because she failed to demonstrate a concrete and imminent risk of future injury; she had stopped eating at Broadmead and could verify gluten content by inquiry. For breach of contract and negligence claims, Plaintiff failed to produce sufficient evidence that the chicken marsala incident (the only non-time-barred incident) actually contained gluten; her evidence consisted of speculation and inferences rather than probative proof. For negligent misrepresentation, Plaintiff failed to identify timely false statements of present or past fact. For warranty claims, the R&C Agreement is a contract for services (not goods), so UCC warranty provisions do not apply.

case_name: Shaniqua Newkirk v. Douglas Elliman, Inc.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation requested; plaintiff alleges racial discrimination through refusal to rent based on housing voucher status (source of income) with disparate impact on African Americans
key_holding: The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss plaintiff's FHA claim as time-barred because discriminatory acts occurred in February and June 2021, beyond the two-year limitations period, and neither the discovery rule nor continuing violation doctrine applies; discriminatory advertisements published within the limitations period did not injure plaintiff who merely viewed them.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Shaniqua Newkirk, an African American housing voucher holder, sued Douglas Elliman and individual brokers alleging racial discrimination under the FHA, claiming that defendants' refusal to rent to voucher holders and publication of income-restrictive advertisements disparately impacted Black and Hispanic renters. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss the FHA claim as time-barred, finding the alleged discriminatory acts occurred in 2021, beyond the two-year statute of limitations, and dismissed the remaining state law claims without prejudice for lack of supplemental jurisdiction.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
McDermott v. New York Metro LLC, 664 F. Supp. 2d 294 (S.D.N.Y. 2009)
Ragin v. Harry Macklowe Real Estate Company, 6 F.3d 898 (2d Cir. 1993)
Jordan v. Chase Manhattan Bank, 91 F. Supp. 3d 491 (S.D.N.Y. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged that defendants' refusal to rent to housing voucher holders constitutes racial discrimination under the FHA because voucher holders are disproportionately African American and Hispanic (82% of voucher holders are Black or Hispanic). Plaintiff also alleged that defendants published discriminatory advertisements with high income, credit score, and guarantor requirements that disqualify voucher holders.
fha_claims.reasoning: The FHA has a two-year statute of limitations. Plaintiff's alleged discriminatory acts (refusals to assist in February and June 2021) occurred outside the limitations period (suit filed August 9, 2023). The discovery rule does not apply because plaintiff knew the critical facts of her injury by June 2021, even if she did not appreciate the legal significance until consulting counsel in September 2021. The continuing violation doctrine does not apply because the refusals and advertisements are separate and discrete acts, not a continuous policy. Plaintiff lacks standing to bring a claim based solely on reading discriminatory advertisements without alleging personal injury.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: NYSHRL § 296(5)(a) and NYCHRL § 8-107(5)(a) claims for discrimination based on lawful source of income (housing voucher); NYRPL § 441(d) claim for negligent supervision of brokers and salespersons regarding fair housing training.
fha_claims.reasoning: After dismissing plaintiff's sole federal FHA claim, the district court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the remaining state law claims (NYSHRL, NYCHRL, NYRPL) pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3), as the federal question jurisdiction basis had been eliminated and only state law claims remained.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA) claim for alleged discrimination in loan denial based on race and property location
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish prima facie ECOA claim by not demonstrating he was an 'applicant' under 15 U.S.C. § 1691a(b), as he never submitted a completed application or the financial information Legacy regularly obtains and considers in evaluating loan applications.

source_file: 10296755_2024_South Carolina State Conference of NAACP v. South Carolina Department of Juvenile Justice_scd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (Fourteenth Amendment Due Process violations); Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA); Rehabilitation Act of 1973; and Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA). Allegations concern unlawful conditions of confinement in juvenile detention facilities, failure to protect children, prolonged solitary confinement, failure to provide rehabilitative services, and substandard conditions.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed organizational standing claims under Rule 12(b)(6) for failure to allege that the plaintiff organizations themselves suffered deprivation of constitutional rights; the organizations alleged only that their members' rights were violated and that the organizations suffered resource diversions and mission frustration as a consequence. The court also dismissed associational standing claims as moot because none of the identified constituent juveniles remained in DJJ custody at the time of ruling, and no mootness exception applied.

source_file: 10297777_2024_Plainview Mobile Home Park v. City of Oak Grove, Kentucky_kywd
case_name: Plainview Mobile Home Park v. City of Oak Grove, Kentucky
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested; the underlying claims concern the alleged discriminatory denial of water utility service to manufactured home communities and their residents.
key_holding: The magistrate judge denied defendants' motion to strike plaintiffs' expert accountant Missy DeArk, finding the deficient disclosure was not a fatal surprise warranting exclusion, and instead ordered plaintiffs to supplement their expert disclosure with a written report complying with Rule 26 within thirty days.
brief_summary: Mobile home park owners and individual prospective tenant Sarina Shannon sued the City of Oak Grove, Kentucky and its public works director, alleging that defendants denied water utility service to manufactured home communities with discriminatory intent to eliminate those communities and their residents from the city, in violation of the FHA, equal protection, civil rights statutes, and the Takings Clause. The present opinion addresses defendants' motion to strike plaintiffs' expert accountant Missy DeArk under Fed. R. Civ. P. 26 and 37 for failure to provide a written expert report by the disclosure deadline. The court denied the motion, finding the omission was likely an honest misunderstanding between counsel rather than gamesmanship, and directed plaintiffs to supplement the disclosure with a compliant written report within thirty days.
key_cases_cited: Howe v. City of Akron, 801 F.3d 718 (6th Cir. 2015)
Russell v. Absolute Collection Servs., Inc., 763 F.3d 385 (4th Cir. 2014)
Bisig v. Time Warner Cable, Inc., 940 F.3d 205 (6th Cir. 2019)
Dickenson v. Cardiac & Thoracic Surgery of E. Tenn. P.C., 388 F.3d 976 (6th Cir. 2004)
Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharm., Inc., 509 U.S. 579 (1993)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act violation (42 U.S.C. § 3601 et seq.); Equal Protection Fourteenth Amendment; K.R.S. 278.170 state statutory violation; vested rights doctrine; § 1983 civil rights violations; equitable estoppel; Fifth Amendment takings claim
fha_claims.reasoning: This opinion addresses only a procedural motion to strike an expert witness under Rule 37 and Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(2). The court denied the motion to strike and ordered plaintiffs to supplement their expert disclosure with a written report within 30 days. The underlying FHA and other substantive claims have not been adjudicated on the merits and remain pending.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act claim mentioned in footnote 3 but not briefed or analyzed by either party; court assumes plaintiffs do not move for preliminary injunction on this claim.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court noted in footnote 3 that plaintiffs brought FHA claims along with Fourth Amendment and § 1985 conspiracy claims, but neither party discussed the merits of these claims in their briefs. The court assumed plaintiffs did not move for preliminary injunction based on the FHA claim, leaving it unresolved at this stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of contract and bad faith under Pennsylvania law; Fair Housing Act, Civil Rights Act, and Declaratory Judgment Act claims added in amended complaint
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked subject matter jurisdiction because plaintiff, not a defendant, attempted removal from state court, which is prohibited by 28 U.S.C. § 1441. Additionally, even if removal were proper, complete diversity did not exist because USAA is a reciprocal interinsurance exchange with members in all fifty states, precluding diversity jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1332.

case_name: Andrea Ortiz v. Beverly Valasek, Donald E. Loudner, Douglas County Housing Authority, Gretna Crown, L.L.C.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested installation of a handicap ramp at the rental property for her mother who could not use stairs due to disability.
key_holding: The federal district court dismissed plaintiff's complaint without prejudice, finding it lacked subject matter jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine because plaintiff's claims arose from and sought to reverse a state court eviction judgment, and alternatively would abstain under Younger given the ongoing state court proceedings.
brief_summary: Andrea Ortiz, proceeding pro se, sued Douglas County Housing Authority, its Section 8 manager, an attorney, and a property owner alleging disability discrimination and retaliation under the Fair Housing Act and due process violations under § 1983, arising from her eviction from public housing for unpaid rent; the court dismissed the case without prejudice on jurisdictional grounds, holding that Rooker-Feldman barred review of claims seeking to reverse the state court eviction judgment and that Younger abstention applied given ongoing state proceedings.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Rooker v. Fid. Trust Co., 263 U.S. 413 (1923)
D.C. Court of Appeals v. Feldman, 460 U.S. 462 (1983)
Younger v. Harris, 401 U.S. 37 (1971)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Installation of a handicap ramp to allow plaintiff's mother (who could not use stairs) to access the rental property
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under Rooker-Feldman doctrine because plaintiff's claims arise solely from and seek relief from the state court eviction judgment. The court did not reach the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Change of rent due date to align with when plaintiff and her mother received their disability checks; also request to allow payment plans and emergency rental assistance
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under Rooker-Feldman doctrine. The court did not reach the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim regarding rent payment modifications.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under Rooker-Feldman doctrine. Plaintiff alleged retaliation under § 3617 after complaining to Fair Housing, HUD, and NEOC, but the court did not reach the merits due to jurisdictional barriers.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Due process violation under 42 U.S.C. § 1983
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed the § 1983 due process claim for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under Rooker-Feldman doctrine, as the claim arises from and seeks relief from the state court eviction judgment.

case_name: Michael John Ryall, Sr. v. Normandy Village Apartments, Inc.
accommodation_description: No accommodation requested; plaintiff claims general discrimination from lease non-renewal under the Fair Housing Act.
key_holding: The magistrate recommended dismissal because the plaintiff, a white male with no disabilities, failed to plead that he is a member of a protected class under the Fair Housing Act, and the lease dispute is a state contract matter lacking federal jurisdiction.
brief_summary: Michael John Ryall, Sr. sued Normandy Village Apartments, Inc. claiming the landlord discriminated against him under the Fair Housing Act by failing to properly notify him of lease non-renewal. The magistrate recommended dismissal, finding the plaintiff is a white male with no disabilities and failed to allege membership in any protected class required to state an FHA claim, and the underlying lease dispute is a state contract matter.
key_cases_cited: Roberson v. Dep't of Soc. Servs., No. CV 23-4022, 2023 WL 10406019 (E.D. La. Dec. 12, 2023)
Treece v. Perrier Condo. Owners Ass'n, Inc., 593 F. Supp. 3d 422 (E.D. La. 2022)
L & F Homes & Dev., LLC v. City of Gulfport, Miss., 2012 WL 2863481 (S.D. Miss. July 11, 2012)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found the FHA claim frivolous and insubstantial because plaintiff failed to allege membership in a protected class under the FHA. Plaintiff is a white male who did not allege discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, familial status, national origin, or handicap, and made no credible allegation of disability. The dispute is a lease termination/contract matter, not a federal housing discrimination claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Defamation, slander, and breach of lease contract claims
fha_claims.disposition: 12(b)(1) — Lack of Subject Matter Jurisdiction; Supplemental Jurisdiction Declined
fha_claims.reasoning: Court declined supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims (defamation, slander, breach of contract) because the federal FHA claim was dismissed and no diversity jurisdiction existed. The case is a state contract dispute properly addressed in state court.

source_file: 10299281_2024_Semper v. Hawaii Life Real Estate Services, LLC_hid
case_name: Jehan Semper v. Hawaii Life Real Estate Services, LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: N/A - plaintiff alleges religious discrimination (based on Judaism) in real estate transactions, not an accommodation request
key_holding: The First Amended Complaint failed to state plausible claims for religious discrimination under the FHA because plaintiff's conclusory allegations of discriminatory intent were insufficient without factual allegations supporting an inference that defendants' conduct was motivated by her Jewish faith.
brief_summary: Jehan Semper, who is Jewish, sued multiple real estate agencies and agents alleging they conspired to prevent her from purchasing vacant land in Hawaii County because of her religion, and later retaliated by interfering with her HUD complaint. The court recommended dismissing the First Amended Complaint with prejudice because plaintiff failed to plead sufficient factual allegations to support a plausible inference of discriminatory intent, offering only conclusory assertions that defendants discriminated against her because she is Jewish.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Gamble v. City of Escondido, 104 F.3d 300 (9th Cir. 1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that defendants engaged in conduct prohibited by the FHA or that their conduct was motivated by discriminatory intent based on religion. Conclusory allegations of discriminatory motive without factual support are insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly. Additionally, plaintiff failed to affirmatively link the conduct of most named defendants to any specific injury.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege specific conduct by each defendant related to retaliation and failed to allege any factual allegations that defendants took action to interfere with plaintiff's HUD complaint or otherwise retaliate against her. Plaintiff cannot rely on discovery to cure pleading deficiencies.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Defendant asserted in the Notice of Removal that the complaint alleged Fair Housing Act violations and civil rights discrimination based on race/color, but the actual complaint on file is a straightforward state court eviction action for failure to pay rent with no federal question alleged on its face.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found lack of subject matter jurisdiction because the complaint, as properly pleaded, contains no federal question under the well-pleaded complaint rule. Although Defendant asserted FHA violations in the Notice of Removal, the actual complaint is a state landlord-tenant eviction action, and federal defenses or counterclaims cannot create removal jurisdiction. The case was remanded to state court.

case_name: Brandy White, et al. v. Scott Matthews, et al.
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: The court recommended dismissing the case without prejudice due to the plaintiff's persistent failure to comply with multiple court orders directing discovery responses, finding all five Ehrenhaus factors favored dismissal.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Brandy White, a tenant evicted from federally assisted subsidized housing, brought Fair Housing Act claims against the Greater Muskogee Community Foundation and the Housing Authority for the City of Muskogee. This Report and Recommendation addresses Defendants' Second Motion for Discovery Sanctions, recommending dismissal without prejudice because Plaintiff repeatedly failed to comply with court orders directing her to provide discovery responses, supplement deficient interrogatories, and execute medical authorizations.
key_cases_cited: Ehrenhaus v. Reynolds, 965 F.2d 916 (10th Cir. 1992)
Ocelot Oil Corp. v. Sparrow Indus., 847 F.2d 1458 (10th Cir. 1988)
In re Standard Metals Corp., 817 F.2d 625 (10th Cir. 1987)
Spiller v. U.S.V. Labs., Inc., 842 F.2d 535 (1st Cir. 1988)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges eviction from federally assisted subsidized housing was based on discrimination in violation of the Fair Housing Act, but the specific nature of the discrimination claim is not detailed in this discovery sanctions opinion.
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 37(b)(2)(A) — Dismissal for failure to comply with discovery orders
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claims pursuant to Fed. R. Civ. P. 37(b)(2)(A) for persistent failure to comply with multiple discovery orders, applying the Ehrenhaus factors (prejudice, interference with judicial process, culpability, prior warning, and efficacy of lesser sanctions). The court did not reach the merits of the underlying FHA claim because discovery was incomplete and plaintiff's noncompliance prevented defendants from adequately investigating and defending against the claims.

case_name: Brooklynn C. Clark v. GSL Properties, Inc. et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that defendant not post or stick any information on her door and not place a trash can in front of her entrance, both as accommodations for anxiety disability.
key_holding: Plaintiff fails to state an FHA claim because she did not allege the race, sex, or gender identity of her neighbors to establish that similarly situated individuals outside her protected class were treated more favorably.
brief_summary: Brooklynn Clark, a Black transgender woman with anxiety, sued GSL Properties Inc. and related defendants alleging discrimination during her tenancy including disproportionate rent increases, police contact, and eviction. The court recommends dismissing her FHA claims because she failed to adequately plead that similarly situated individuals outside her protected classes were treated more favorably, and recommends dismissal of her ADA and Title VII claims on separate grounds.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Harris v. Itzhaki, 183 F.3d 1043 (9th Cir. 1999)
Gamble v. City of Escondido, 104 F.3d 300 (9th Cir. 1997)
Molski v. M.J. Cable, Inc., 481 F.3d 724 (9th Cir. 2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request that GSL not post or stick any information on plaintiff's door; request that GSL not place a trash can in front of the front door entrance because it triggered plaintiff's anxiety
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court did not reach the merits of the reasonable accommodation claims. The court dismissed the amended complaint under § 1915(e)(2)(B) screening for failure to state a plausible FHA claim, applying Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards. The court found that Clark failed to allege facts sufficient to support her FHA claims based on race and sex discrimination, and did not separately analyze whether the requested accommodations were reasonable or whether defendants engaged in the interactive process.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged disparate rent increases (30% at each lease renewal compared to neighbors' lower increases) based on race, sex, gender identity, or departure from gender-based norms
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)
fha_claims.reasoning: Clark failed to allege that similarly situated individuals outside her protected class were treated more favorably. Although she alleged that neighbors paid less rent, she did not allege the race, sex, or gender identity of those neighbors, and thus failed to plausibly allege disparate treatment based on a protected status under the Iqbal/Twombly standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation through false police reports, attempted assault, false statements to police, trespass order, and eviction notice following Clark's attempts to address disability-related accommodation requests and other grievances
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed Clark's FHA claims (including any retaliation theory under § 3617) for failure to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly. The court found that Clark did not allege facts suggesting that the negative treatment and eviction were because of a protected status, and did not separately analyze the retaliation claim on its merits.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title I (employment discrimination), ADA Title II (public entity services), ADA Title III (public accommodations), and Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968 (employment discrimination)
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B) and lack of applicability
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the ADA claims because Clark did not allege that defendants were a public entity (Title II) or operated a place of public accommodation (Title III), and residential apartment complexes are not covered by the ADA. The court dismissed the Title VII claim because Clark did not allege that any defendants were her employer, that she suffered an adverse employment action, or that defendants treated other employees more favorably.

case_name: Wilmore Lee Washington, III v. Farmington Estates Owners Association
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged HOA enforced community rules differently against him as an African American homeowner compared to non-Black homeowners, constituting racial discrimination in housing services.
key_holding: The court recommends denying plaintiff's motion to amend because he failed to demonstrate the diligence required under Rule 16 to modify the scheduling order, and even under Rule 15 standards, his undue delay and the prejudice to defendants warranted denial.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Wilmore Lee Washington III, an African American condominium owner, sued the Farmington Estates HOA and its management for racially discriminatory enforcement of community rules compared to non-Black homeowners. The magistrate judge recommends denying plaintiff's motion to amend the complaint to add new claims under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 and 1982, finding plaintiff failed to demonstrate good cause under Rule 16 because he lacked diligence in bringing the claims and defendants would suffer prejudice from the late amendment.
key_cases_cited: Foman v. Davis, 371 U.S. 178 (1962)
AmerisourceBergen Corp. v. Dialysist W., Inc., 465 F.3d 946 (9th Cir. 2006)
Carvalho v. Equifax Info. Servs., LLC, 629 F.3d 876 (9th Cir. 2010)
Jackson v. Bank of Hawaii, 902 F.2d 1385 (9th Cir. 1990)
Sonoma Cty. Ass'n of Retired Employees v. Sonoma Cty., 708 F.3d 1109 (9th Cir. 2013)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied plaintiff's motion to amend to add §1981 and §1982 claims based on lack of diligence under Rule 16(b) and undue prejudice to defendants under Rule 15(a). The underlying FHA disparate treatment claim (racial discrimination in enforcement of HOA rules) survives in the operative Fourth Amended Complaint but has not been substantively decided on the merits.

case_name: Carlos A. Alonso Cano, et al. v. 245 C and C, LLC and CFH GROUP, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested: (1) an assigned handicapped parking space for Angie (Count One); (2) a reasonable modification to Angie's bathroom (Count Three); (3) refinishing Angie's bathtub without toxic substances (Count Four); and (4) removal of noisy equipment near plaintiffs' residence (Count Five).
key_holding: The magistrate judge recommended denial of defendants' motion for attorney's fees and non-taxable costs because plaintiffs' FHA claims, though ultimately unsuccessful, were not frivolous, unreasonable, or without foundation under the Christiansburg standard, and defendants failed to demonstrate that fees incurred defending non-frivolous claims were attributable solely to the arguably frivolous ones.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs, a family including a disabled son (Angie), sued their landlord defendants for multiple FHA violations including denial of reasonable accommodations (handicapped parking, bathtub refinishing, noise removal) and a reasonable modification (bathroom), as well as retaliation and interference/coercion under § 3617. After years of complex litigation—including two motions to dismiss, summary judgment, and a bench trial—final judgment was entered for defendants. Defendants then moved for attorney's fees and non-taxable costs. The magistrate judge recommended denial, finding that while several claims were dismissed early on, the case as a whole was not frivolous given that two counts survived summary judgment and proceeded to trial, defendants made settlement offers weighing against frivolity, and plaintiffs litigated largely pro se; moreover, defendants failed to isolate fees attributable only to the arguably frivolous dismissed claims.
key_cases_cited: Buckhannon Bd. & Care Home, Inc. v. W. Va. Dep't of Health & Hum. Res., 532 U.S. 598 (2001)
Christiansburg Garment Co. v. EEOC, 434 U.S. 412 (1978)
Sullivan v. Sch. Bd. of Pinellas Cnty., 773 F.2d 1182 (11th Cir. 1985)
Scoggins v. Lee's Crossing Homeowners Ass'n, 718 F.3d 262 (4th Cir. 2013)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Assigned handicapped parking space for Angie
fha_claims.reasoning: At Phase One of trial, the Court found that no request for accommodation had been made during the FHA's limitations period, determining that Plaintiff Carlos Cano's testimony regarding when he made the request was not credible based on his embellishment, inconsistent testimony, and conflicting testimony from other credible witnesses.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Pedestrian paths suitable for Angie
fha_claims.reasoning: The Court found that Count Two was not actionable under the FHA and dismissed it with prejudice for failure to state a plausible claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Modification to Angie's bathroom
fha_claims.reasoning: At Phase One of trial, the Court found that no request for accommodation had been made during the limitations period, crediting Defendants' evidence over Plaintiff's testimony that he made a request in 2017, though acknowledging a second request was made in 2018 and granted.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refinish Angie's bathtub without toxic substances
fha_claims.reasoning: The Court held that the undisputed facts established that Plaintiffs' request to repaint the bathtub in a guest room was not a necessary accommodation under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Removing noisy equipment near Plaintiffs' residence
fha_claims.reasoning: The Court found that there was no evidence that Defendants knew Angie suffered from a disability such that the requested accommodation was necessary.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permit Plaintiffs to keep tape on glass doors and windows
fha_claims.reasoning: Count Six was dismissed with prejudice because it required the Court to speculate about the connection between the accommodation and Angie's disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Repair broken laundry machines
fha_claims.reasoning: Count Seven was dismissed with prejudice as a conclusory assertion that did not explain why Angie's disability required Defendants to fix the laundry facilities.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation for instituting a HUD investigation
fha_claims.reasoning: The Court held that no reasonable jury could find that Plaintiffs had an objectively reasonable and good faith belief that the conduct they protested in Count Nine was unlawful, as Plaintiffs failed to establish a prima facie case of retaliation under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Allowing OnCall Parking to harass Plaintiffs
fha_claims.reasoning: The Court found that there was no evidence that Defendants' legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason for the emails and text messages was pretext for a discriminatory motive.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Engaging in intimidation and retaliation by instituting eviction proceedings in retaliation for filing HUD complaint
fha_claims.reasoning: The Court held that the admitted facts and record evidence established that Defendants initiated eviction proceedings before Plaintiffs filed their HUD complaint, and thus the retaliation claim lacked a causal connection.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Engaging in intimidation and retaliation by appealing the state court's judgment of retaliatory eviction
fha_claims.reasoning: The Court found that the premise of Count Twelve was demonstrably false and that Plaintiffs presented no evidence that Defendants appealed the county court judgment to intimidate or retaliate, especially considering that Defendants were successful on appeal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Engaging in intimidation and retaliation by threatening to raise Plaintiffs' rent
fha_claims.reasoning: The Court granted Defendants' Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings on Count 13, determining that the claims and defenses in the prior eviction suit did not allege FHA violations and accordingly could not support the retaliation claim as pled.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Committing familial discrimination by shutting off Plaintiffs' water
fha_claims.reasoning: Count Seventeen was dismissed with prejudice because Plaintiffs failed to allege facts demonstrating a disparate impact to them caused by Defendants' policies.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failing to maintain the laundry facilities
fha_claims.reasoning: Count Eighteen was dismissed with prejudice as a conclusory assertion that did not explain why Angie's disability required Defendants to maintain the laundry facilities.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusing to allow Plaintiffs to tape the apartment's glass doors and windows
fha_claims.reasoning: Count Nineteen was dismissed with prejudice for failure to allege facts demonstrating a disparate impact caused by Defendants' policies.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Florida Statutes Chapter 83 violations (landlord-tenant law); breach of lease covenant of quiet enjoyment; failure to maintain premises; failure to provide notice of entry; failure to repair pedestrian paths; interruption of utilities without notice
fha_claims.reasoning: The Court granted summary judgment on state law claims (Counts 14, 15, and 16) under Florida Statutes Chapter 83, finding insufficient evidence to support Plaintiffs' allegations regarding maintenance obligations, utility interruption, and other landlord-tenant duties.

case_name: Takayujki Hiroto v. Lashunda Smith
accommodation_description: Defendant raised FHA and ADA claims in counterclaims but no specific accommodation request was analyzed; this is a procedural remand ruling.
key_holding: The federal court lacks subject matter jurisdiction because the plaintiff's state court forcible detainer petition did not raise a federal question and the parties are not diverse (both appear to be Texas citizens), so the case must be remanded to state court.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Hiroto, a landlord, filed a forcible detainer action in Texas state court against tenant Lashunda Smith; Smith removed the case to federal court claiming FHA and ADA violations. The court recommends granting Hiroto's motion to remand because the federal court lacks subject matter jurisdiction—the state court petition raised no federal question and the parties are not diverse citizens of different states.
key_cases_cited: Rivet v. Regions Bank of La., 522 U.S. 470 (1998)
Caterpillar v. Williams, 482 U.S. 386 (1987)
Metro Ford Truck Sales, Inc. v. Ford Motor Co., 145 F.3d 320 (5th Cir. 1998)
Howery v. Allstate Ins. Co., 243 F.3d 912 (5th Cir. 2001)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act, ADA, and constitutional claims (due process and equal protection under the Fourteenth Amendment) raised as counterclaims by defendant in removal notice
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked subject matter jurisdiction because the original state court petition raised only a forcible detainer action (state law claim), and federal questions cannot be established by counterclaims or defenses. The defendant's FHA and ADA counterclaims do not confer federal question jurisdiction on the district court, and diversity jurisdiction was lacking because both parties were Texas citizens.

case_name: Stephan A. Ricks v. DMA Companies, Diana McIver, Nichole Guptill, Roxanne Marroquin, and Overland, Pacific & Cutler LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, who is blind, requested numerous modifications and accommodations including: a specific model of Ring Peephole Camera, a first-floor apartment unit, all communications in Braille or accessible format, a mail chute on his door, Braille-modified washer/dryer, accessible toilet, light/horn combination in bathroom, sink and tub levers, tub grab bars, accessible range/oven, rocker light switches, a wheelchair ramp, an orientation and mobility specialist, trash pickup by housekeeping, large address numerals outside his unit, and assistance retrieving his mail.
key_holding: The Magistrate Judge denied the majority of plaintiff's pending motions, recommended denial of his motion for temporary injunction for failure to show likelihood of success on the merits or irreparable injury, and imposed a pre-filing bar requiring court permission before plaintiff could file any additional motions.
brief_summary: Stephan Ricks, a blind pro se plaintiff, brought a disability discrimination suit against DMA Companies and related defendants alleging they denied his requests for reasonable modifications and accommodations to his apartment unit under the ADA and FHA. The court addressed numerous pending motions including requests for subpoenas, reinstatement of a previously dismissed defendant, exclusion of expert testimony, auxiliary aids from the court, a temporary injunction, and recusal of both judges. The Magistrate Judge denied or recommended denial of virtually all motions and imposed a pre-filing bar due to plaintiff's pattern of frivolous and duplicative filings.
key_cases_cited: Koester v. Young Men's Christian Ass'n of Greater St. Louis, 855 F.3d 908 (8th Cir. 2017)
Prim v. Stein, 6 F.4th 584 (5th Cir. 2021)
Winter v. Nat. Res. Def. Council, Inc., 555 U.S. 7 (2008)
Big Tyme Invs., LLC v. Edwards, 985 F.3d 456 (5th Cir. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible communications in Braille or other accessible format; specific Ring camera model; first-floor apartment unit; mail chute; modified washer/dryer with Braille; Ring Peephole Camera; accessible toilet; light/horn combo in bathroom; sink and tub levers; tub grab bars; accessible range/oven; rocker light switches; wheelchair ramp; orientation and mobility specialist
fha_claims.disposition: 12(c) Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings
fha_claims.reasoning: The District Court adopted the Magistrate Judge's recommendation that Ricks failed to allege a plausible FHA claim against OPC because he did not allege that OPC owned, leased, or operated the property; that OPC discriminated against him because of his disability; or that he requested an accommodation from OPC. The court found Ricks' FHA claim failed because he did not allege that he requested an accommodation from OPC, that OPC denied any request, or that OPC had authority to make modifications to his dwelling.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA); Rehabilitation Act, 29 U.S.C. § 794; Title II of the ADA (auxiliary aids and services in court proceedings)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the preliminary injunction motion because Ricks failed to show a substantial likelihood of success on the merits of his Title III ADA and Rehabilitation Act claims. Ricks did not demonstrate that DMA owns, leases, or operates a place of public accommodation, took adverse action based on disability, or failed to make reasonable modifications. For the Rehabilitation Act claim, Ricks failed to show that DMA received federal financial assistance or that it denied him services because of his disability. The court also found no irreparable injury absent the injunction.

case_name: Gonzalez v. Lexington Police Department
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, who has asthma, requested that the landlord enforce the non-smoking lease provision against other tenants who were smoking and affecting her respiratory condition.
key_holding: The FHAA reasonable accommodation claim fails because the complaint does not identify what specific accommodation Plaintiff requested, whether that request was reasonable, or what accommodation (if any) the landlord provided.
brief_summary: Pro se Plaintiff Tania A. Gonzalez sued the Lexington Police Department and Beacon Point Development LLC in Massachusetts state court, alleging disability discrimination under the ADA and FHAA, constitutional violations under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, and other claims related to alleged failures to accommodate her asthma and complaints about police conduct. The magistrate judge recommended dismissing the case because the complaint failed to state viable claims—the FHA reasonable accommodation claim failed because Plaintiff did not identify what specific accommodation was requested, and the § 1983 claims failed because the complaint did not allege violations of clearly established constitutional rights.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Summers v. City of Fitchburg, 940 F.3d 133 (1st Cir. 2019)
Plumhoff v. Rickard, 572 U.S. 765 (2014)
Astralis Condo. Ass'n v. Sec'y, U.S. Dep't of Hous. & Urban Dev., 620 F.3d 62 (1st Cir. 2010)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Removal of other tenants who were smoking in their units, which plaintiff alleged compromised her asthma and respiratory health
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint failed to plausibly allege the elements of a reasonable accommodation claim under the FHAA: while plaintiff alleged a qualifying disability (asthma) and defendant's knowledge thereof, the complaint did not clearly state what specific accommodation was requested, whether removal of other tenants was reasonable, or what accommodation was actually provided. The court found the allegations too conclusory and lacking sufficient factual detail to state a plausible claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 claims against Lexington Police Department and officers; ADA Title II claims; state law claims including G.L. 111 § 127 (building code), G.L. 93A (consumer protection), negligence, tortious interference, intentional infliction of emotional distress, and landlord-tenant dispute regarding failure to disclose Lexington Wine & Spirits lease
fha_claims.reasoning: Claims against Lexington Police Department and officers failed to state a plausible § 1983 claim because the complaint did not adequately allege what specific actions the officers took or that such actions violated a clearly established constitutional or statutory right. Claims against landlord defendants regarding failure to disclose the wine store lease failed because plaintiff did not allege that defendants had any duty to make such disclosure or identify the source of any such duty. All claims were dismissed for failure to provide sufficient factual allegations to meet the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard.

case_name: Frederick Williams v. Toll Brothers Builders
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request identified; complaint alleges FHA violation among other claims related to mortgage fraud and faulty construction
key_holding: The court dismissed all claims, including the FHA claim, because plaintiff's complaint consisted of legal conclusions and bald assertions that failed to state facts plausibly suggesting any defendant violated the cited statutes.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Frederick Williams sued Toll Brothers Builders and others claiming mortgage fraud, faulty construction, and violations of TILA, FHA, ECOA, and RESPA arising from his 2011 home purchase. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding the complaint failed to state plausible claims and consisted of legal conclusions, though plaintiff was granted leave to amend.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly

fha_claims.accommodation_description: TILA, ECOA, RESPA, FHA, breach of contract, negligence, fraud claims arising from alleged mortgage fraud, faulty construction, and mold exposure causing Non-Hodgkin lymphoma
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that the FHA claim, along with TILA, ECOA, and RESPA claims, consisted of legal conclusions and bald assertions that did not amount to more than labels and formulaic recitations, failing to plausibly allege violations against named defendants. The court could not reasonably infer substantively plausible claims from the facts alleged.

case_name: Stephan A. Ricks v. DMA Companies, Diana McIver, Nichole Guptill, and Roxanne Marroquin
accommodation_description: Plaintiff Stephan A. Ricks, who is blind, alleges that DMA Companies denied his requests for reasonable modifications to his apartment unit.
key_holding: The court granted counsel's motion to withdraw due to irreconcilable conflict, denied plaintiff's motion for appointment of new counsel, granted leave to file objections to the magistrate judge's report and recommendation, and denied leave to file an amended complaint as untimely and futile.
brief_summary: Stephan A. Ricks, a blind pro se plaintiff, brought disability discrimination claims against DMA Companies (his property management company) and its employees, alleging they denied his requests for reasonable modifications to his apartment unit in violation of the ADA, FHA, and Rehabilitation Act. This order addresses only procedural matters: the court granted attorneys' motion to withdraw based on irreconcilable differences, denied Ricks' motion for new appointed counsel, and denied leave to file an amended complaint as untimely and futile, while granting leave to file objections to the magistrate judge's prior report and recommendation.
key_cases_cited: Gowdy v. Marine Spill Response Corp., 925 F.3d 200 (5th Cir. 2019)
Lopez v. Reyes, 692 F.2d 15 (5th Cir. 1982)
Naranjo v. Thompson, 809 F.3d 793 (5th Cir. 2015)
Williams v. La. Dep't of Educ., No. CV 21-339-JWD-RLB, 2021 WL 12268243 (M.D. La. Aug. 23, 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable modifications to apartment unit requested by blind plaintiff; specific modifications not detailed in this opinion
fha_claims.disposition: Motion to Amend Denied; Case Pending
fha_claims.reasoning: The opinion addresses procedural motions (counsel withdrawal, amendment of complaint) but does not reach the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim. The case remains pending with a modified scheduling order and trial date set for approximately four months from October 2024.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) and the Rehabilitation Act of 1973
fha_claims.disposition: Motion to Amend Denied; Case Pending
fha_claims.reasoning: Non-FHA claims under ADA Title III and the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 remain pending. The opinion does not address the merits of these claims, focusing instead on procedural matters regarding counsel representation and amendment of the complaint.

source_file: 10301656_2024_Jett v. The Country Acres Association of Columbus County LTD_nced
case_name: Raymond A. Jett, Jr., et al. v. George Parker Coleman, et al.
race_if_mentioned: Interracial couple/biracial children (specific races not explicitly stated in text)
accommodation_description: No specific reasonable accommodation request was made. Plaintiffs alleged that Raymond Jett, a disabled veteran suffering from anxiety, insomnia, chronic kidney disorder, chronic liver disorder, and PTSD, was discriminated against under the FHA and ADA, and speculatively claimed that defendants' failure to maintain the main subdivision road 'will allow' it to fall into disrepair and become inaccessible to persons with disabilities.
key_holding: The court recommends denying plaintiffs' motion for leave to file a second amended complaint because all proposed amendments—including reasserted FHA and ADA claims, a § 242 claim, claims against a state court judge, and reinstated state law claims against previously dismissed defendants—would be futile.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Raymond and Tara Jett, an interracial couple with biracial children, own a home in the Country Acres subdivision in Chadbourn, North Carolina, and allege racial harassment via racial slurs by neighboring defendants and retaliatory conduct by the developer Mitchell Powell for their efforts to enforce HOA covenants. After certain claims were dismissed on frivolity review, Plaintiffs moved for leave to file a second amended complaint seeking to reassert FHA and ADA claims, add a § 242 criminal statute claim, add a state court judge as a defendant, and reinstate previously dismissed defendants. The magistrate judge recommends denying the motion in its entirety because the proposed FHA/ADA claims fail to allege discriminatory motivation sufficiently, the § 242 claim has no private right of action, the judge defendant is entitled to absolute judicial immunity, and the state law claims against other defendants lack a common nucleus of operative fact with the surviving § 1982 claim.
key_cases_cited: Foman v. Davis, 371 U.S. 178 (1962)
Edwards v. City of Goldsboro, 178 F.3d 231 (4th Cir. 1999)
Steinburg v. Chesterfield Cnty. Planning Comm'n, 527 F.3d 377 (4th Cir. 2008)
Warren v. Carroll, No. 1:21-CV-415, 2021 WL 11134946 (M.D.N.C. Aug. 31, 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found proposed FHA and ADA claims would be futile because plaintiffs failed to allege discriminatory purpose (race, disability, etc.) and instead alleged retaliation for enforcing HOA bylaws; allegations that road maintenance failure 'will allow' disrepair to persons with disabilities were speculative and conclusory without supporting facts.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 28 U.S.C. § 242 (criminal statute); ADA Title III; state law negligence and tort claims
fha_claims.reasoning: 28 U.S.C. § 242 is a criminal statute that does not create a private right of action; state law negligence claims against Powell, Scott, and homeowners lack supplemental jurisdiction because they do not share a common nucleus of operative fact with the § 1982 claim against George and Michael Coleman.

case_name: Sinatra Young v. Ben Schwadel
accommodation_description: Plaintiff's complaint is too vague to identify a specific accommodation request; references harassment, eviction threats, refusal to make repairs, and a lower-floor apartment request from DHCR proceedings, but does not clearly plead a defined accommodation request.
key_holding: The court recommended dismissing plaintiff's FHA claim because his complaint was conclusory and failed to state his disability, whether he requested an accommodation from defendant, what accommodation he requested, or how defendant failed to provide a reasonable accommodation.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Sinatra Young sued his landlord Ben Schwadel alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on disability discrimination, harassment, and failure to accommodate; the magistrate judge recommended dismissing the complaint for failure to state a plausible FHA claim because Young's complaint was conclusory and failed to identify his disability, describe a specific accommodation request, or allege how defendant denied a reasonable accommodation.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Olsen v. Stark Homes, Inc., 759 F.3d 140 (2d Cir. 2014)
Calixte v. Susan Ray Equities Inc., No. 21 CV 3623 (RPK), 2022 WL 118738 (E.D.N.Y. Jan. 12, 2022)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges defendant failed to accommodate his disability (heart condition, metal in back, arthritis in knees) and references inability to urinate by the side door of the building as needed due to disability; also references superintendent's refusal to make repairs and placement of garbage bags at his door.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff's FHA claim conclusory and failing to state a claim because the complaint does not clearly identify: (1) plaintiff's specific disability; (2) whether he requested an accommodation; (3) a description of the accommodation requested; or (4) whether defendant failed to provide a reasonable accommodation. The complaint lacks sufficient factual allegations to plausibly allege an FHA violation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Bivens claim for constitutional violation against federal official; landlord-tenant disputes concerning rent and repairs to apartment
fha_claims.reasoning: Bivens claim dismissed because plaintiff named a private landlord, not a federal official, as defendant. Landlord-tenant claims dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because federal courts do not have federal question jurisdiction over state residential landlord-tenant matters such as rent disputes and repair requests.

case_name: Linda Kay Holloway v. Delia SiFuentes
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges race-based discrimination in sale of home she sought to purchase from landlord, where defendant (real estate agent) subsequently purchased the property instead.
key_holding: The court dismissed the case for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction because there was no diversity of citizenship (both parties are Texas citizens) and no federal question jurisdiction, as plaintiff failed to plead facts showing a plausible Fair Housing Act violation even under liberal construction of her race and age discrimination claims.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Linda Kay Holloway sued Delia SiFuentes alleging race and age discrimination after a failed real estate transaction where SiFuentes, a real estate agent Holloway had contacted to help purchase her rented home, ultimately purchased the property herself. The magistrate judge recommended dismissing the case without prejudice for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, finding no diversity of citizenship and that even liberally construed, Holloway's complaint failed to state plausible facts supporting a Fair Housing Act violation.
key_cases_cited: Kokkonen v. Guardian Life Ins. Co. of Am., 511 U.S. 375 (1994)
Howery v. Allstate Ins. Co., 243 F.3d 912 (5th Cir. 2001)
Ruhrgas AG v. Marathon Oil Co., 526 U.S. 574 (1999)
Estelle v. Gamble, 429 U.S. 97 (1976)
Artisan/American Corp. v. City of Alvin, 588 F.3d 291 (5th Cir. 2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court liberally construed pro se plaintiff's allegations as raising a Fair Housing Act disparate treatment claim based on race and age discrimination in a real estate transaction, but dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction because plaintiff failed to allege facts plausibly showing discrimination by the real estate agent, and the claim was not properly pleaded to establish federal question jurisdiction.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of fiduciary duty in real estate transaction
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331 and 1332 because plaintiff and defendant are both Texas citizens (no diversity) and the breach of fiduciary duty claim arises under state law (no federal question).

case_name: Walter Tanner v. Rochdale Village Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges he was discriminated against based on perceived disability (HIV status and sex offender status) including refusal to perform repairs and threats of eviction.
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA disparate treatment claim fails because the complaint contains only speculative and conclusory allegations about discriminatory motive without sufficient factual support to raise an inference of discrimination.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Walter Tanner sued Rochdale Village Inc., a housing cooperative in Jamaica, Queens, alleging disability discrimination under the Fair Housing Act and ADA based on management's alleged belief he was HIV positive and a sex offender. The court granted defendant's motion to dismiss, finding the complaint failed to state a plausible discrimination claim because plaintiff's conclusory allegations lacked sufficient factual detail to raise an inference of discriminatory motive.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Francis v. Kings Park Manor, Inc., 992 F.3d 67 (2d Cir. 2021)
Thompson v. CRF-Cluster Model Program, LLC, 2020 WL 4735300 (S.D.N.Y. 2020)
Camarillo v. Carrols Corp., 518 F.3d 153 (2d Cir. 2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged that management staff directed personnel not to perform maintenance/repair work on plaintiff's unit based on perceived disability (false perception that plaintiff was a sexual offender and HIV positive).
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient factual allegations to give rise to an inference of discrimination. The complaint relied on vague, speculative allegations based on information from a confidential source, without explaining why management perceived plaintiff as having a disability or why they interfered with maintenance requests, and without alleging differential treatment of similarly situated individuals.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III discrimination claim; NYSHRL discrimination claim; NYCHRL disparate treatment claim; New York Not-for-Profit Corporation Law fiduciary duty claim.
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA Title III claim dismissed because Rochdale is a private housing cooperative, not a place of public accommodation; residential facilities are excluded from Title III coverage. State law claims dismissed by declining supplemental jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3) after dismissal of all federal claims.

case_name: Jimmy Avila v. Acacia Network, Inc., Basics, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: No specific reasonable accommodation was formally requested or denied; rather, plaintiff alleged that defendants failed to provide necessary accommodations for his disabilities (schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type, periodontal disease, and stage 2 kidney disorder) and that stable housing and specific accommodations were required to prevent severe mental health crises, but these allegations were conclusory and unsupported by specific facts.
key_holding: The court dismissed pro se plaintiff's amended FHA, Rehabilitation Act, ADA, and § 1983 claims for failure to state a claim because his allegations remained conclusory and failed to allege facts showing his disability was a motivating factor in defendants' conduct, and denied further leave to amend.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Jimmy Avila, a disabled individual residing in supportive housing in the Bronx, filed an amended complaint against a network of non-profit housing providers, state mental health officials, and Adult Protective Services, alleging disability discrimination, retaliation, wrongful arrest, lockout from his apartment, and related civil rights violations under the FHA, Rehabilitation Act, ADA, and 42 U.S.C. § 1983. The court dismissed the amended complaint in its entirety, finding that Avila's allegations remained conclusory and failed to plead facts showing his disability was a motivating factor in the defendants' conduct, that several defendants were entitled to Eleventh Amendment immunity, and that private-entity defendants could not be held liable under § 1983 absent state-actor allegations. Because the deficiencies mirrored those identified in the court's prior April 15, 2024 order and could not be cured by further amendment, the court denied leave to amend a second time.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Palmer v. Fannie Mae
DeShaney v. Winnebago Cnty. Dep't of Soc. Servs.
Rendell-Baker v. Kohn

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged no facts showing that his disability was at least a motivating factor for the alleged discrimination by Acacia, Basics, Griffiths, Douglas, Crow, Staten, 1212 Grant Realty LLC, and 1412 COL LLC. Allegations were conclusory and lacked factual support under Iqbal/Twombly pleading standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation for bringing previous lawsuit against Acacia and other defendants
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to state a plausible claim of retaliation under the FHA. The amended complaint did not cure the deficiencies identified in the prior order.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rehabilitation Act disability discrimination claims against Acacia, Basics, NYSOMH, APS (City of New York), 1212 Grant Realty LLC, and 1412 COL LLC; Title II ADA disability discrimination claims against NYSOMH and City of New York; § 1983 claims against NYSOMH, Ben-Atar (official capacity), APS, City of New York, Glenoy (official capacity), Acacia, Basics, Griffiths, Douglas, Crow, Staten, 1212 Grant Realty LLC, and 1412 COL LLC; state law claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Rehabilitation Act and Title II ADA claims dismissed for conclusory allegations lacking factual support regarding denial of services or discrimination based on disability. § 1983 claims against NYSOMH and Ben-Atar (official capacity) dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction due to Eleventh Amendment immunity. § 1983 claims against private defendants dismissed for failure to allege state action. § 1983 claims against City of New York dismissed for failure to allege municipal policy, custom, or practice. § 1983 claims against Ben-Atar and Glenoy (individual capacities) dismissed for failure to allege personal involvement. State law claims declined under supplemental jurisdiction.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II and Title III claims; § 1983 First Amendment retaliation claim; federal health and safety code violations
fha_claims.disposition: Order to Show Cause under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff failed to state viable federal claims: ADA Title II does not apply to private residential housing; Title III does not cover purely residential dwellings; § 1983 First Amendment claim fails because defendants are private actors, not state actors; federal health and safety claims are too vague to constitute a federal claim. Court issued order to show cause rather than outright dismissal to allow pro se plaintiff opportunity to amend.

case_name: Carey v. Torres
accommodation_description: Plaintiff seeks injunctive relief to access tenant storage area and restrain defendants from filing frivolous lawsuits and physical harassment, framed as FHA claims but lacking any accommodation request under § 3604(f)(3)(B).
key_holding: The amended complaint fails to state an FHA claim because plaintiff did not allege she is a member of a protected class or that defendants discriminated against her based on protected status, warranting dismissal with leave to amend.
brief_summary: Cecilia Carey, a pro se tenant in Oakland, sued private landlord Mauricio Torres and others alleging Fourteenth Amendment violations, Title VII claims, Fair Housing Act violations, and criminal statute claims arising from alleged predatory buyout, lock changes, and unlawful detainer actions. The Court dismissed the FHA claim because plaintiff failed to allege membership in a protected class or discriminatory motivation, granting leave to amend.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged unlawful detainer actions and lock-outs but failed to allege she is a member of a protected class under the FHA or that defendants discriminated against her based on protected status. The court found it possible she could state a claim under the FHA but that she had not done so in the amended complaint, and granted leave to amend.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fourteenth Amendment Due Process and Equal Protection claims; Title VII employment discrimination; 18 U.S.C. §§ 242 and 1341 (criminal statutes)
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii); lack of subject matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1331
fha_claims.reasoning: Fourteenth Amendment claims against private actors fail because plaintiff did not allege state action; Title VII does not apply because plaintiff did not allege she was employed by defendants; criminal statutes 18 U.S.C. §§ 242 and 1341 provide no private cause of action and no basis for civil liability. No federal question jurisdiction exists over these claims.

case_name: Jimmy Avila v. Promesa, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged various disability-based discrimination including refusal to provide keys to his apartment, false arrest, and wrongful hospitalization, with a medical accommodation request for a safety transfer to a one-bedroom apartment at an alternate scatter site.
key_holding: The court dismissed Plaintiff's disparate-treatment disability discrimination claims under the FHA for failure to plead facts showing his disability was a motivating factor in the alleged conduct, and dismissed related Rehabilitation Act, ADA, and Section 1983 claims for failure to state a claim or lack of subject matter jurisdiction.
brief_summary: Jimmy Avila, a pro se plaintiff with schizoaffective disorder residing in rent-stabilized supportive housing, sued Promesa, Inc., Basics, various individual defendants, and 1412 Col LLC alleging disability discrimination under the FHA, Rehabilitation Act, ADA, and Section 1983, claiming they wrongfully withheld apartment keys, caused his arrest and hospitalization, and failed to provide necessary disability accommodations. The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss all claims for failure to state a claim, finding Avila failed to plead facts showing his disability was a motivating factor for the alleged discriminatory conduct.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Carnegie-Mellon Univ. v. Cohill, 484 U.S. 343 (1988)
Ex Parte Young, 209 U.S. 123 (1908)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts showing that his disability was a motivating factor for any of the alleged conduct underlying his claims of disparate-treatment disability discrimination under the FHA against Promesa, Basics, Albors, Douglas, 1412 Col LLC, Crow, Staten, JSAF Management, and Safdie. The complaint does not satisfy the pleading standard under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rehabilitation Act disability discrimination, ADA Title II disability discrimination, § 1983 federal constitutional violations, state law claims
fha_claims.disposition: 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) and (iii); Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(h)(3)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's Rehabilitation Act claims against Promesa, Basics, NYSOMH, JSAF Management, and 1412 Col LLC fail because he did not allege facts showing denial of services by reason of disability or federal funding (where required). ADA Title II claims against NYSOMH fail for the same reason. § 1983 claims against NYSOMH and Abate in official capacity are barred by Eleventh Amendment immunity (jurisdictional dismissal). § 1983 claims against Abate in individual capacity fail because plaintiff did not allege her direct and personal involvement. § 1983 claims against private defendants (Promesa, Basics, Albors, Douglas, 1412 Col LLC, Crow, Staten, JSAF Management, Safdie) fail because plaintiff did not allege they acted as state actors. State law claims are declined under supplemental jurisdiction.

case_name: Zikar Holdings LLC v. Ruhland
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs are developers seeking to build a residential development with a mosque (masjid) in Lino Lakes, claiming the City's development moratorium was enacted with discriminatory animus toward Muslims in violation of the FHA.
key_holding: The court denied the preliminary injunction motion because plaintiffs failed to demonstrate irreparable harm, as their representations about the purchase agreement lacked foundation and constituted mere speculation about theoretical future loss.
brief_summary: Zikar Holdings LLC and individual Muslim developers sued the City of Lino Lakes and two City Council members, alleging that a one-year development moratorium was enacted with discriminatory animus toward Muslims in violation of the FHA and Free Exercise Clause. The court denied the motion for preliminary injunction, finding that plaintiffs failed to demonstrate irreparable harm because their assertions about the purchase agreement lacked evidentiary foundation.
key_cases_cited: Church of Lukumi Babalu Aye, Inc. v. City of Hialeah, 508 U.S. 520 (1993)
Dataphase Sys., Inc. v. C L Sys., Inc., 640 F.2d 109 (8th Cir. 1981)
Gallagher v. Magner, 619 F.3d 823 (8th Cir. 2010)
Planned Parenthood Minn., N.D., S.D. v. Rounds, 530 F.3d 724 (8th Cir. 2008)
Jones v. City of Faribault, 2021 WL 1192466 (D. Minn. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework for indirect-evidence disparate treatment and found that while a reasonable juror could infer the moratorium was pretextual based on council members' anti-Muslim statements and timing, the evidence at the preliminary injunction stage did not satisfy the heightened Rounds standard for enjoining legislation. The court concluded the success-on-the-merits factor was neutral, and the motion was denied on the basis of failure to demonstrate irreparable harm and the balance of equities.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Free Exercise Clause (First Amendment), Equal Protection Clause (Fourteenth Amendment), Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the Free Exercise Clause framework from Church of Lukumi Babalu Aye and concluded that plaintiffs failed to demonstrate a substantial burden on their ability to practice Islam because the moratorium merely delayed development of a specific property but did not restrict their ability to worship elsewhere or build a mosque elsewhere in the city. The court found the moratorium facially neutral and generally applicable, applying to all development in the covered area regardless of religious affiliation.

case_name: United States of America v. Madison Property, L.L.C.
accommodation_description: Boucher requested an accommodation to waive the building's no-pets policy to allow her emotional support animal cat to live with her in her apartment.
key_holding: The court denied both parties' summary judgment motions because genuine disputes of material fact exist regarding whether Boucher was financially qualified to rent, which precludes resolution of both the disparate treatment and reasonable accommodation claims at summary judgment.
brief_summary: The United States sued Madison Property and Andrew Brenner alleging they violated the FHA by refusing to rent to Beverly Boucher because of her disability (Count I - disparate treatment) and by refusing to accommodate her ESA cat under the building's no-pets policy (Count II - reasonable accommodation). The court denied both parties' cross-motions for summary judgment, finding genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether Boucher was financially qualified to rent, which precluded resolution of both claims.
key_cases_cited: Radecki v. Joura, 114 F.3d 115 (8th Cir. 1997)
One Love Housing, LLC v. City of Anoka, Minn., 93 F.4th 424 (8th Cir. 2024)
Huberty v. Wash. Cnty. Hous. & Redevelopment Auth., 374 F. Supp. 2d 768 (D. Minn. 2005)
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242 (1986)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the McDonnell-Douglas burden-shifting framework and found genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether Boucher was financially qualified to rent, precluding summary judgment for either party on the question of whether financial disqualification was pretext for disability discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver of the building's no-pets policy to permit Boucher to live with her emotional support animal (ESA) cat
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether Boucher was qualified to rent (third element of prima facie case), which precluded summary judgment for either party. The court did not reach the remaining elements of the reasonable accommodation claim, including whether the requested accommodation was reasonable and necessary, noting that a jury is best equipped to determine the reasonableness of incurring a $300,000 expense to overhaul the building's ventilation system or other mitigation measures.

case_name: Arlene Johnson-Byrd, et al. v. PennyMac Loan Services, LLC
race_if_mentioned: Not explicitly identified; plaintiff alleges PennyMac promoted foreclosures in 'communities of color'
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested; this case concerns the servicing of a rehabilitation mortgage loan, specifically PennyMac's alleged failure to properly release and administer escrow funds for property repairs.
key_holding: The court granted PennyMac's motion to dismiss all of Johnson-Byrd's claims on res judicata grounds, holding that the state court's dismissal without prejudice became a final judgment on the merits when Johnson-Byrd elected not to refile in state court, and alternatively dismissing counts 1–4 for failure to state a claim.
