brief_summary: Plaintiff Arlene Johnson-Byrd sued PennyMac Loan Services asserting race discrimination (42 U.S.C. § 1981), FHA discrimination in residential lending (§ 3605), FHA interference (§ 3617), fraudulent misrepresentation, breach of contract, and Missouri Merchandising Practices Act violations, all arising from PennyMac's alleged mishandling of escrow funds under her rehabilitation mortgage loan. The court dismissed co-plaintiff Louis Byrd for lack of standing because he was not a party to the loan contract, then dismissed all of Johnson-Byrd's claims under res judicata, reasoning that the state court's prior dismissal without prejudice—entered as a discovery sanction—ripened into a final judgment on the merits when Johnson-Byrd failed to refile in state court. As an alternative basis, the court dismissed Count 1 (§ 1981) for conclusory pleading of discriminatory intent, Counts 2 and 3 as time-barred under the FHA's two-year limitations period, and Count 4 (fraud) under the economic loss doctrine.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Duffner v. City of St. Peters, 930 F.3d 973 (8th Cir. 2019)
Cornice & Rose Int'l, LLC v. Four Keys, LLC, 76 F.4th 1116 (8th Cir. 2023)
Yang v. Robert Half Int'l, Inc., 79 F.4th 949 (8th Cir. 2023)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Count 2 alleges discrimination under § 3605 based on PennyMac's refusal to release escrow funds. The alleged discriminatory conduct ended in September 2021 when plaintiff sold the property. The complaint was filed March 20, 2024, nearly three years later, exceeding the two-year statute of limitations under 42 U.S.C. § 3613.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Count 3 alleges interference under § 3617 based on misconduct during the rehabilitation project. All conduct ended in September 2021. The complaint was filed March 20, 2024, nearly three years later, exceeding the two-year statute of limitations under 42 U.S.C. § 3613.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1981 race discrimination, fraudulent misrepresentation, breach of contract, Missouri Merchandising Practices Act
fha_claims.reasoning: All claims are barred by res judicata because: (1) the prior state court judgment was rendered by a court of competent jurisdiction; (2) the state court's dismissal without prejudice became a final judgment on the merits when plaintiff failed to refile in state court as required; and (3) the same cause of action (PennyMac's alleged mismanagement of the loan) and parties are involved in both cases. The nucleus of operative facts is identical.

case_name: Sinisio Sarafin v. Hawaii Public Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Sarafin, a mobility-impaired tenant using a rollator walker and electric wheelchair, requested transfer from his upstairs apartment to a ground-floor or elevator-accessible unit due to stairs that made his current unit inaccessible.
key_holding: The court denied dismissal of Sarafin's FHA reasonable accommodation claim against HPHA, finding he adequately alleged HPHA failed to timely respond to his transfer requests and improperly transferred him to an even less accessible unit, but dismissed LASH's organizational standing claims and national origin discrimination claims based on language access failures.
brief_summary: Sarafin, a mobility-disabled tenant represented by Legal Aid Society of Hawaii, sued the Hawaii Public Housing Authority and its officials alleging they failed to grant his reasonable accommodation request for transfer to accessible housing for over two years, then improperly transferred him to an even less accessible unit. The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss Sarafin's FHA reasonable accommodation claim, finding he adequately alleged discriminatory conduct, but dismissed LASH's organizational standing claims and national origin discrimination claims based on language access failures.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Olmstead v. L.C., 527 U.S. 581 (1999)
Ex parte Young, 209 U.S. 123 (1908)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Transfer to a ground-floor or elevator-accessible apartment to accommodate Sarafin's mobility impairments and need to use an electric wheelchair
fha_claims.reasoning: Sarafin's disability discrimination claim based on failure to provide reasonable accommodation (transfer to accessible unit) survives the motion to dismiss. The court did not reach the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim itself but allowed it to proceed past the pleading stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to provide interpretation services in Chuukese language to accommodate Sarafin's limited English proficiency
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed national origin discrimination claims based on denial of interpretive services against Ouansafi and Akamine in their individual capacities and against HPHA in Counts I, III, and V because the complaint failed to plead facts showing the injury occurred 'because of' national origin or LEP status, lacking sufficient factual allegations to support a reasonable inference of discriminatory animus. Dismissal was without prejudice.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claim, Title VI Section 601 claim, Rehabilitation Act Section 504 claim, and Hawai'i Fair Housing Act claim
fha_claims.reasoning: After the hearing, the parties stipulated to dismiss without prejudice Counts II (ADA), III (Title VI), and IV (Rehabilitation Act) against Ouansafi and Akamine in their individual capacities. These claims survive as to HPHA and remain pending.

case_name: Anthony George Bell v. Weinreb Management LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that landlord repair or replace building elevators to accommodate his mobility limitations (knee pain requiring him to climb nine flights of stairs) and asthma.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claims without prejudice because his amended complaint failed to allege sufficient facts establishing a disability requiring accommodation, failed to identify which specific defendant was responsible for the elevator failures, and failed to connect any defendant conduct to discriminatory intent.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Anthony Bell sued Weinreb Management LLC and related parties under the FHA and ADA, alleging disability discrimination for failing to repair building elevators causing him knee pain from climbing nine floors, and racial discrimination. The court dismissed the amended complaint without prejudice for failure to state a claim, finding the complaint failed to allege sufficient facts connecting any specific defendant to the discriminatory conduct or establishing plaintiff's disability.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Francis v. Kings Park Manor, Inc., 992 F.3d 67 (2d Cir. 2021)
Reyes v. Fairfield Props., 661 F. Supp. 2d 249 (E.D.N.Y. 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Replacement of non-functioning elevators in the building to provide access to plaintiff's ninth-floor apartment, which plaintiff alleges causes knee pain and exacerbates asthma when forced to use stairs.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that although plaintiff's allegations may state a claim for refusal to make reasonable accommodation, the complaint fails to allege a disability requiring accommodation and fails to identify which specific defendant was responsible for the elevator failure, depriving defendants of fair notice under Rule 8 and Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Provision of used, defective appliances (refrigerator and stove) that infested plaintiff's apartment with roaches, allegedly in violation of Section 8 program requirements.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiff failed to connect the appliance allegation to any protected class under the FHA (race, disability, or other enumerated categories), and that source of income/Section 8 status is not a protected class. Complaint also failed to identify which defendant was responsible for the conduct.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claim for discrimination based on disability; also alleged discrimination based on race and income status.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that the ADA does not apply to private landlords and that plaintiff's amended complaint contained no factual allegations indicating any defendant is a public entity or provides public accommodation. Receipt of federal funds (Section 8) does not bring a private landlord within the reach of the ADA.

case_name: Gregory Kelly v. Elite Roofing, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff's complaint references a Fair Housing Act claim but no specific accommodation request is substantively analyzed due to dismissal for procedural deficiencies.
key_holding: The magistrate judge struck Kelly's second amended complaint as a shotgun pleading that failed to comply with court orders and recommended dismissing his claims with prejudice for failure to comply with court orders and the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.
brief_summary: Pro se Plaintiff Gregory Kelly sued Elite Roofing, LLC, Jimmy Holley, Alfa Mutual Insurance, and Terry McKelvey in a dispute apparently involving roof work, with Kelly referencing Fair Housing Act claims. The magistrate judge struck Kelly's second amended complaint as a shotgun pleading that failed to comply with the court's December 5, 2024 Order and recommended dismissing Kelly's claims with prejudice for his continued failure to comply with court orders and the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.
key_cases_cited: Equity Lifestyle Props., Inc. v. Fla. Mowing & Landscape Serv., Inc., 556 F.3d 1232 (11th Cir. 2009)
Chambers v. NASCO, Inc., 501 U.S. 32 (1991)
Jones v. Graham, 709 F.2d 1457 (11th Cir. 1983)
Goforth v. Owens, 766 F.2d 1533 (11th Cir. 1985)
McKelvey v. AT & T Techs., Inc., 789 F.2d 1518 (11th Cir. 1986)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged violation of the Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3614(a), but the specific accommodation requested is not identifiable from the opinion due to the shotgun pleading defects.
fha_claims.disposition: Struck as shotgun pleading; dismissed with prejudice for failure to comply with court orders and Federal Rules of Civil Procedure
fha_claims.reasoning: The court struck the second amended complaint as a shotgun pleading that violated the December 5, 2024 Order requiring amendment by December 26, 2024, and dismissed all claims with prejudice under Rule 41(b) for failure to comply with court orders and the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure after repeated warnings and a clear record of contumacious conduct.

case_name: Kendrick v. Oakbrook Corporation
accommodation_description: No accommodation requested; plaintiff alleges racial discrimination and disparate impact based on criminal background policy in denial of rental application
key_holding: The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss because plaintiff's FHA claims were time-barred—the discriminatory housing practice occurred on February 4, 2019, the two-year statute of limitations expired on February 4, 2021, and plaintiff did not file his complaint until July 12, 2021, with no basis for tolling since his HUD complaint was filed after the limitations period had already expired.
brief_summary: Suan Kendrick, proceeding pro se, sued Oakbrook Corporation, Rebecca Lindley, Heather Gerensky, and Resident Check LLC alleging racial discrimination after his rental application was denied, claiming the denial violated the Fair Housing Act based on his race and old criminal conviction. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding the claims time-barred because the discriminatory housing practice occurred on February 4, 2019, but Kendrick did not file suit until July 12, 2021—past the two-year statute of limitations—and no equitable tolling applied.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Erickson v. Pardus
Pearle Vision, Inc. v. Romm
Hoskins v. Poelstra

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The plaintiff's FHA claim alleging denial of rental application based on race and criminal conviction occurred on February 4, 2019. The two-year statute of limitations under 42 U.S.C. § 3613(a)(1)(A) expired on February 4, 2021. The plaintiff did not file a HUD complaint until May 5, 2021, which was outside the one-year period required to initiate an administrative proceeding under 42 U.S.C. § 3610(a)(1)(A)(i), and the complaint filed on July 12, 2021 was time-barred. No basis existed to toll the statute of limitations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of housing at low-income senior/disabled subsidized housing facility
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction because plaintiff asserted federal-question jurisdiction but the complaint does not allege discrimination under the FHA or any other federal cause of action. Plaintiff merely alleged denial of subsidized housing eligibility without alleging any discriminatory basis, which is insufficient to invoke federal jurisdiction.

case_name: Hartley v. United Student Rentals
accommodation_description: No formal accommodation request was pleaded. Plaintiff alleged that he notified the owner of a 'paper thin' front door with a lock 'hanging off' upon moving in and requested it be fixed; the unnamed respondent said they would 'get with [plaintiff] sooner or later,' and the door remained unrepaired for approximately one year, during which the apartment was vandalized. The plaintiff's civil cover sheet characterized this as a 'violation of fair housing under disability,' suggesting he viewed the failure to maintain the door as discriminatory based on his mental health impairment.
key_holding: The magistrate judge recommends dismissing all of plaintiff's claims — under § 1983, the Fair Housing Act, and state law — without prejudice and with leave to amend, because the complaint fails to connect defendants' failure to repair the front door to plaintiff's disability, fails to establish state action, and lacks federal jurisdiction over habitability claims.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Michael Hartley sued his landlord United Student Rentals and associated defendants after they failed to repair a broken front door in his apartment for nearly a year despite his requests, alleging violations of § 1983 and the Fair Housing Act based on disability. The magistrate judge recommended dismissing the § 1983 claims because defendants are private parties who do not qualify as state actors, dismissing the FHA claim because plaintiff failed to allege facts connecting the door-repair failure to his mental health disability, and dismissing state law habitability claims for lack of subject matter jurisdiction. Plaintiff was granted leave to amend within thirty days.
key_cases_cited: Francis v. Kings Park Manor, Inc., 992 F.3d 67 (2d Cir. 2021)
Ingraham v. Red Carpet Hous. Corp., 2017 WL 5152343 (N.D.N.Y. 2017)
Robinson v. Soc. Serv., 2013 WL 1122450 (N.D.N.Y. 2013)
Rendell-Baker v. Kohn, 457 U.S. 830 (1982)
Fabrikant v. French, 691 F.3d 193 (2d Cir. 2012)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to repair broken front door of rental apartment
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint fails to allege sufficient facts connecting defendants' alleged failure to repair the door to plaintiff's disability or to establish that defendants took any action regarding the door. Plaintiff alleges mental health impairments generally but does not describe how impairments limit major life activities or connect any defendant action to the disability, failing to state a plausible FHA claim under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (First, Sixth, Eighth, Fourteenth Amendment violations); state law breach of warranty of habitability
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 1983 claims fail because defendants are private parties, not state actors, and complaint alleges no facts supporting any exception (compulsion, joint action, or public function delegation). State law habitability claim dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1331 and § 1332 (no federal question, no diversity, and no supplemental jurisdiction without viable federal claims).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Federal Tort Claims Act negligence claim against HUD for property conditions (water damage, mold, electrical issues, rodent infestation)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to exhaust administrative remedies required under 28 U.S.C. § 2675(a) before filing suit against the United States under the FTCA. The court lacked subject matter jurisdiction because plaintiff's communications with HUD did not constitute proper presentment of a tort claim—they did not reference the FTCA, request monetary damages, or state a sum certain for recovery.

case_name: Angel Lopez and Kazue Koizumi v. Edward Pec, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested that the landlord remediate mold and repair water leaks in their basement apartment to accommodate Angel Lopez's asthma and COPD.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' FHA reasonable accommodation claim because plaintiffs failed to adequately allege what disability entitled them to accommodation, what specific accommodation they requested, whether defendants knew of the disability, or how refusing to repair water leaks constituted discrimination based on disability.
brief_summary: Angel Lopez and Kazue Koizumi, tenants in a Palisades Park, New Jersey apartment, sued their landlord Edward Pec and The Palisades LLC, as well as a law firm, alleging Fair Housing Act claims (including reasonable accommodation), ADA violations, and state law claims arising from habitability disputes. The District of New Jersey granted both motions to dismiss, finding plaintiffs failed to adequately plead their federal claims—the FHA reasonable accommodation claim was dismissed because plaintiffs made only conclusory allegations without stating what accommodation was requested, what disability entitled them to accommodation, or how defendants' failure to repair discriminated against them—and abstained from exercising jurisdiction over related state court matters.
key_cases_cited: Spieth v. Bucks Cnty. Hous. Auth., 594 F. Supp. 2d 584 (E.D. Pa. 2009)
Cmty. Servs., Inc. v. Wind Gap Mun. Auth., 421 F.3d 170 (3d Cir. 2005)
El v. People's Emergency Ctr., 438 F. Supp. 3d 283 (E.D. Pa. 2020)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Butler v. Sundo Cap., LLC, 559 F. Supp. 3d 452 (W.D. Pa. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Removal of mold and repair of water leaks in apartment to accommodate plaintiff Angel Lopez's asthma and severe COPD
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to adequately allege facts supporting a reasonable accommodation claim under the FHA. They provided only conclusory allegations that defendants refused to accommodate Lopez's disability without specifying what disability they have, whether defendants knew of it, or how defendants denied specific accommodation requests. The complaint lacks sufficient factual matter to state a plausible claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged discrimination based on race and national origin in refusing to repair water leaks and remediate mold
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to adequately allege intentional discrimination based on race or national origin under the FHA. They provided only conclusory allegations without specifying how or when discrimination occurred, and a single offensive statement by the landlord about Puerto Ricans does not establish a claim for housing discrimination. The complaint lacks sufficient factual allegations to state a plausible disparate treatment claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title III ADA claim for failure to make reasonable modification; Title II Civil Rights Act claim for discrimination in public accommodation; state law claims for harassment, stalking, invasion of privacy, intentional infliction of emotional distress, and public accommodation violations
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed all non-FHA claims for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under Rooker-Feldman, Younger abstention, and Colorado River abstention doctrines because the claims were identical to or inextricably intertwined with pending state court actions. The court also found that Title II claims failed the mandatory notice requirement under 42 U.S.C. § 2000a-3(c), and Title III ADA claims failed to adequately allege disability discrimination in a public accommodation. State law claims against the Broderick Defendants were dismissed for lack of supplemental jurisdiction.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) and Supplemental Security Income (SSI) benefits determination under 42 U.S.C. §§ 401 et seq. and 1381 et seq.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court affirmed the ALJ's determination that plaintiff was not disabled under the Social Security Act's five-step sequential evaluation process. The ALJ's RFC assessment was supported by substantial evidence, and the ALJ properly weighed medical opinions, considered plaintiff's impairments in combination, and provided sufficient narrative explanation for his conclusions.

source_file: 10308231_2025_Washington v. DHS Department of Homeless Services_nysd
case_name: Sandra A. Washington v. NYC DHS; WIN Shelter
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a Home Bound Individual with a disability residing in a homeless shelter, alleges that DHS failed to secure permanent housing for her and failed to provide adequate services needed for a person with a disability to obtain housing in a timely manner.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's federal claims with leave to amend because she failed to plead facts about what disability she suffers, what services were denied, and whether she alleges intentional discrimination or a failure to accommodate; the court further noted uncertainty about whether the FHA applies to homeless shelters.
brief_summary: Sandra A. Washington, a pro se plaintiff residing at WIN homeless shelter, sued NYC Department of Homeless Services and WIN Shelter alleging disability discrimination, failure to provide adequate services to obtain housing, and constitutional violations under § 1983. The court dismissed all federal claims with leave to amend, finding the complaint failed to allege facts specifying her disability, what accommodations were denied, and the nature of the discrimination claim.
key_cases_cited: Jenkins v. City of New York, 478 F.3d 76 (2d Cir. 2007)
Connick v. Thompson, 563 U.S. 51 (2011)
Monell v. Dep't of Soc. Servs., 436 U.S. 658 (1978)
DeShaney v. Winnebago Cnty. Dep't of Soc. Servs., 489 U.S. 189 (1989)
Loeffler v. Staten Island Univ. Hosp., 582 F.3d 268 (2d Cir. 2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to provide adequate services for person with disability to obtain housing; failure to secure permanent housing in timely manner; inadequate housing voucher funding
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts regarding her disability, what specific services were denied, or whether she alleged intentional discrimination, denial of accommodation, or other theory. Allegations that she did not receive permanent housing within state-law timelines are insufficient to state a claim under ADA Title III or the Rehabilitation Act. Court noted that money damages are unavailable under ADA Title III and that plaintiff failed to allege federal funding for WIN or deliberate indifference required under the Rehabilitation Act.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Constitutional claims for unsanitary shelter conditions, toxic water, physical and mental abuse of residents
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim / § 1915(e)(2)(B); lack of state action
fha_claims.reasoning: WIN is a private party and plaintiff made no allegations showing WIN acts as a state actor under § 1983. Provision of homeless services by a private organization, even under contract with the state, does not convert the organization into a state actor. Additionally, plaintiff cannot pursue claims on behalf of other shelter residents as a non-attorney pro se litigant.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to secure permanent housing; violation of DHS guidelines; alleged abuse and rights violations of other residents
fha_claims.disposition: Dismissal for lack of capacity to be sued / jurisdictional
fha_claims.reasoning: NYC DHS, as an agency of the City of New York, lacks capacity to be sued in its own name under N.Y. City Charter § 396. All actions must be brought in the name of the City of New York. Court granted leave to amend to name the City as defendant and noted that § 1983 claims against the City require pleading a municipal policy, custom, or practice that caused the constitutional violation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act violation alleged in complaint; no specific accommodation identified
fha_claims.reasoning: The District Court lacked jurisdiction to reopen the case after remanding it to state court for lack of diversity jurisdiction. The appellate court affirmed the dismissal on jurisdictional grounds without reaching the merits of any FHA or other federal claims alleged in the complaint.

case_name: Gerald Cymbalsky v. 522 Shore Road Owners, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff did not specifically request a reasonable accommodation but appears to challenge the cooperative's commencement of a state court 'furniture eviction' action against him while he was hospitalized.
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA claim fails because he did not allege that he requested and was denied a reasonable accommodation, and the commencement of the state court eviction action was motivated by profit-seeking rather than discriminatory animus based on his disability.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Gerald Cymbalsky sued his cooperative housing corporation, property managers, and attorneys for Fair Housing Act violations, RICO, constitutional privacy violations, and FDCPA violations arising from a state court action seeking access to clean his apartment while he was hospitalized. The court dismissed all claims, finding that the FHA claim failed because Cymbalsky did not request any accommodation and alleged no discriminatory animus, while the other claims failed for failure to state a viable claim.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Francis v. Kings Park Manor, Inc.
Logan v. Matveevskii

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged discrimination based on disability (severe osteoarthritis requiring walker, persistent open leg wound, anxiety disorder, morbid obesity) in connection with co-op's commencement of state court action to access apartment for cleaning.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege discriminatory intent or causal nexus to disability. Plaintiff alleged he continues to reside in apartment, was not denied housing opportunity, and did not request any accommodation. Court found no plausible interpretation supporting inference of discriminatory animus—plaintiff alleged co-op sought to profit from his equity, not that disability motivated the action.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Civil RICO (18 U.S.C. § 1961 et seq.), Constitutional rights to privacy/property (§ 1983), Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (15 U.S.C. § 1692 et seq.)
fha_claims.reasoning: RICO claim failed because plaintiff did not allege two related predicate acts or effect on interstate commerce. Constitutional claims failed because defendants were not state actors. FDCPA claim failed because defendants were not debt collectors—co-op defendants were creditors collecting rent, and Finkelstein defendants were attorneys providing legal services, not regularly collecting debts.

case_name: Sarah Nathreen v. Denver Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought to halt an imminent eviction and compel the Denver Housing Authority to fulfill its obligations under the Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher Program by paying past-due rent to her landlord, effectively requesting eviction defense relief premised in part on her severe physical and mental health conditions.
key_holding: The court denied Plaintiff's Emergency Motion for TRO and Preliminary Injunction because her seven-month delay in seeking relief undermined a finding of irreparable harm, and her conclusory allegations failed to demonstrate a likelihood of success on the merits of her FHA and civil rights claims.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Sarah Nathreen sued the Denver Housing Authority alleging it failed to pay her Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher rent for the entirety of her lease, resulting in eviction proceedings initiated by her landlord, Holland Residential, LLC (Sabine Apartments). She sought an emergency TRO to halt the eviction, compel DHA to remit past-due rent, and facilitate porting of her voucher, asserting eight claims including FHA violations, Title VI, Section 1981/1982, and constitutional claims. The court denied the TRO, finding that Plaintiff's seven-month delay in seeking relief undercut irreparable harm and that her bare, conclusory allegations—including the absence of specific facts showing DHA was obligated to pay rent or that any failure was discriminatory—failed to establish a likelihood of success on the merits.
key_cases_cited: Haines v. Kerner, 404 U.S. 519 (1972)
Schrier v. Univ. of Colo., 427 F.3d 1253 (10th Cir. 2004)
Heideman v. S. Salt Lake City, 348 F.3d 1182 (10th Cir. 2003)
Petrella v. Brownback, 787 F.3d 1242 (10th Cir. 2015)
Thompson v. Boulder Cnty. Hous. Auth., 2016 WL 852893 (D. Colo. Mar. 4, 2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied TRO on procedural grounds (failure to show irreparable harm due to delay and failure to comply with Rule 65(b) notice requirements) and on merits (plaintiff failed to allege that eviction resulted from discrimination based on race or other protected class). FHA claim survives the TRO motion but has not been substantively decided on the merits.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of contract (Section 8 HAP contract), fraudulent inducement, Title VI Civil Rights Act, Fourteenth Amendment due process and equal protection, Spending Clause violations, intentional and negligent infliction of emotional distress, Section 1981 and Section 1982 Civil Rights Act violations
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied TRO on procedural grounds (delay in seeking relief, failure to comply with Rule 65(b)(1)(B) notice requirements, and failure to clearly show immediate irreparable injury) and on merits (plaintiff failed to plead required elements of fraudulent inducement and failed to establish that DHA was under obligation to pay rent under the lease). Non-FHA claims survive the TRO motion but remain pending.

source_file: 10311847_2025_Fair Hous. Ctr. of Metro. Detroit v. Am. House Grosse Pointe_ca6
case_name: Fair Housing Center of Metropolitan Detroit v. American House Grosse Pointe, LLC
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: The Sixth Circuit vacated the district court's summary judgment and remanded for further proceedings on the issue of standing, in light of FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine (2024), without expressing any view on the merits of the Fair Housing Act claims.
brief_summary: The Fair Housing Center of Metropolitan Detroit sued American House Grosse Pointe, a senior living facility, alleging Fair Housing Act violations. The district court granted summary judgment to the defendant on November 28, 2023. The Sixth Circuit vacated and remanded because the district court's standing analysis predated the Supreme Court's decision in FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine (2024), and the appellate court declined to rule on the merits, leaving standing for the district court to reassess on a fully developed record.
key_cases_cited: FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine, 602 U.S. 367 (2024)
Fair Housing Center of Metro. Detroit v. Singh Senior Living, LLC, No. 23-3969, 2025 WL 16385 (6th Cir. Jan. 2, 2025)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: The opinion does not specify the particular accommodation(s) at issue; it references only 'allegedly unlawful behavior' by the senior living facility.
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court vacated the district court's summary judgment and remanded for reconsideration of standing in light of FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine (2024), which post-dated the district court's November 28, 2023 ruling. The court did not reach the merits of the FHA claims and expressed no view on the district court's merits ruling.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation moves involving household goods transportation by Reliable and Eco Movers, facilitated by KCHA
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the § 1983 claim (which incorporated allegations related to the reasonable accommodation moves) as time-barred under Washington's three-year statute of limitations for taking or detaining personal property. The claim accrued no later than March 8, 2021, when plaintiff became aware property was missing, and the suit was filed June 1, 2024—85 days after the March 8, 2024 deadline. The court did not reach the merits of any reasonable accommodation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (deprivation of property without due process and unreasonable seizure under Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments); § 1981, § 1982, § 1985; Rehabilitation Act of 1973; Americans With Disabilities Act; Uniform Relocation Assistance and Real Property Acquisition Policies Act of 1970
fha_claims.reasoning: The § 1983 claim alleging unlawful deprivation of $177,000 in personal property and documents was time-barred under Washington's three-year statute of limitations. The claim accrued on March 8, 2021, when plaintiff became aware property was missing; the suit was filed June 1, 2024, well after the March 8, 2024 deadline. Amendment would be futile because the underlying chronology cannot be revised.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: RCW 48.30A.070 (duty to investigate, enforce, and prosecute violations); RCW 9A.80.010 (official misconduct); RCW 49.60.178 (Washington Law Against Discrimination—unfair practices with respect to insurance transactions during reasonable accommodations move); WAC 284-30-330 (unfair claims settlement practices)
fha_claims.reasoning: After dismissing the federal § 1983 claim with prejudice, the court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the remaining state-law claims (Second and Third Causes of Action) under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3), finding that principles of economy, convenience, fairness, and comity did not favor retention of jurisdiction at this early stage and that state courts were the proper forum for state-law claims.

case_name: Miriam Millan-Heffner, et al. v. Gemcraft Homes Group, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: Home purchasers alleged race-based steering and discriminatory treatment during home construction process based on Ms. Millan-Heffner's Puerto Rican identity.
key_holding: The court granted in part plaintiffs' motion for leave to amend, finding the proposed breach of contract and UTPCPL claims were not futile, but denied leave to add quasi-contract and third-party beneficiary claims as futile.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Millan-Heffner (Puerto Rican) and her husband sued their homebuilder alleging race-based discrimination, claiming they were treated with less respect than white clients and steered to a separate area of the development. The court granted in part plaintiffs' motion for leave to amend the complaint, allowing breach of contract and UTPCPL claims to proceed while denying leave to add quasi-contract and third-party beneficiary claims as futile.
key_cases_cited: Foman v. Davis, 371 U.S. 178 (1962)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Earl v. NVR, Inc., 990 F.3d 310 (3d Cir. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The FHA disparate treatment claim based on race discrimination (Puerto Rican identity) survived the prior motion to dismiss and remains pending. The court's July 15, 2024 order granted in part and denied in part the motion to dismiss, allowing the FHA claim to proceed. This opinion addresses only the motion to amend, not the merits of the FHA claim itself.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1981 (race-based discrimination), breach of contract, quasi-contract/unjust enrichment/promissory estoppel, third-party beneficiary, UTPCPL
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted leave to amend the breach of contract claim (Count III) and the UTPCPL claim (Count VI), finding them not futile under Rule 15. The court denied leave to amend for the quasi-contract/unjust enrichment/promissory estoppel claim (Count IV) and third-party beneficiary claim (Count V) as futile. The § 1981 claim survived the prior motion to dismiss and remains pending.

source_file: 10313209_2025_Tiffany Simone Fulton v. City of New York_nysd
case_name: Tiffany Simone Fulton v. City of New York
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs, as Black and Brown Harlem residents, allege defendants discriminated against them by failing to offer apartment units at a vacant property for rent to immediate community members instead of migrants.
key_holding: Plaintiffs lack Article III standing because they failed to allege a concrete and particularized injury in fact—the proposed plan to house migrants at the property was abandoned, and plaintiffs' objection is a generalized grievance about keeping housing available for Harlem residents generally rather than a personal injury.
brief_summary: Three Harlem residents sued the City of New York and property owners alleging racial discrimination under the Fair Housing Act for allegedly planning to house migrants at a vacant property instead of offering housing to Black and Brown community members. The court dismissed all claims without prejudice for lack of Article III standing, finding plaintiffs failed to allege a concrete and particularized injury since the proposed plan was abandoned and plaintiffs' grievance was generalized rather than particularized.
key_cases_cited: Warth v. Seldin, 422 U.S. 490 (1975)
Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)
Flast v. Cohen, 392 U.S. 83 (1968)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to offer Property for rent to Black and Brown Harlem residents; alleged discrimination by offering Property to migrants instead
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs lack Article III standing because they failed to allege an injury in fact. They did not identify any actual or imminent injury to themselves individually, only a generalized grievance about housing availability for the Harlem community generally. The alleged discrimination is hypothetical and conjectural, as there are no current plans to rent the Property to migrants.

source_file: 10314069_2025_(PS) Roberts v. Sacramento Housing _ Redevelopment Agency_caed
case_name: Sydney Brooke Roberts and David Tyrone Samuel v. Sacramento Housing and Redevelopment Agency, et al.
accommodation_description: Request for an additional bedroom added to plaintiffs' Housing Choice Voucher to accommodate David Samuel's and AIMS's disabilities, including separate bedrooms for each.
key_holding: Plaintiffs' motion for summary judgment was denied because the evidence was insufficient to establish that defendants violated the FHA, ADA, or Rehabilitation Act, particularly given that the additional bedroom accommodation was ultimately granted in March 2023.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Sydney Brooke Roberts and David Tyrone Samuel, a family with disabilities (David and their minor child AIMS both have qualifying disabilities), sued the Sacramento Housing and Redevelopment Agency under the FHA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act for denying their reasonable accommodation request for an additional bedroom added to their Housing Choice Voucher. The court denied plaintiffs' motion for summary judgment, finding that plaintiffs failed to meet their burden to show they were entitled to judgment as a matter of law, particularly given that the accommodation was ultimately granted in March 2023.
key_cases_cited: Giebeler v. M & B Associates, 343 F.3d 1143 (9th Cir. 2003)
Duvall v. County of Kitsap, 260 F.3d 1124 (9th Cir. 2001)
Zukle v. Regents of Univ. of Cal., 166 F.3d 1041 (9th Cir. 1999)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Extra bedroom(s) to provide separate sleeping space for David Samuel (due to ADHD, Autism, PTSD, and Major Depressive Disorder) and minor child AIMS (Autism Spectrum Disorder, non-verbal); later requests for five bedrooms total, housekeeping services, soundproofing, and blackout curtains
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied the four-part FHA reasonable accommodation test (disability, defendant's knowledge, necessity, and refusal) but found insufficient evidence for summary judgment because defendants granted the initial three-bedroom accommodation in March 2023, making it unclear whether plaintiffs were denied a benefit, and plaintiffs failed to demonstrate entitlement to additional accommodations (five bedrooms, housekeeping) or identify which specific requests remained at issue.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II ADA disability discrimination in housing; Section 504 Rehabilitation Act discrimination; Fourteenth Amendment due process violation; accessibility of services claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied the prima facie elements for Title II ADA (qualified individual, exclusion/discrimination, by reason of disability) and Section 504 (disability, qualified for benefits, denied solely because of disability, federal funding) but found insufficient evidence for summary judgment on the same grounds as the FHA claim—the March 2023 grant of the three-bedroom accommodation created a genuine dispute of material fact regarding whether plaintiffs were denied benefits.

source_file: 10314802_2024_Xi v. BES Kessler Park Fund X11 LLC_txnd
case_name: K'in Way Xi, et al. v. BES Kessler Park Fund X11 LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege employment discrimination based on race and color, claiming they were fired for stealing Amazon packages while a white employee was given the benefit of the doubt.
key_holding: The complaint fails to state a plausible disparate treatment claim because it does not allege that the adverse employment action was taken because of protected status; all employees, regardless of race, were fired for the same conduct after video evidence confirmed their participation.
brief_summary: Four plaintiffs sued their employer under Title VII, Section 1981, and the Fair Housing Act, alleging they were discriminated against based on race and color when they were fired for stealing Amazon packages while a white employee was initially given the benefit of the doubt. The court recommends granting the motion to dismiss because the complaint fails to plausibly allege that the adverse employment action was taken because of a protected status, as all employees were ultimately fired for the same conduct.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Comcast Corp. v. Nat'l Ass'n of Afr. Am.-Owned Media, 589 U.S. 327 (2020)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege that an adverse employment action was taken because of race or protected status. The complaint alleges all employees, regardless of race, were fired for allegedly stealing packages after video footage verified their participation, establishing no causal nexus between race and the adverse action.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VII employment discrimination, 42 U.S.C. § 1981 race discrimination
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plead sufficient facts establishing that adverse employment actions (termination) were taken because of race. The complaint alleges all employees were terminated for the same conduct (stealing packages) regardless of race, failing to establish the ultimate element of causation required under Title VII and § 1981.

case_name: Michael Feliciano v. Andres Aguirre
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested an emergency transfer to a different unit due to worsening medical and mental health conditions caused by unsafe living conditions with his current landlord.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA reasonable accommodation claim because he failed to allege sufficient facts showing he has a covered disability or that he explained the connection between his disability and the requested emergency transfer accommodation.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Michael Feliciano sued Andres Aguirre, a Section 8 program representative, under the Fair Housing Act and ADA, alleging Aguirre refused to process his reasonable accommodation request for an emergency transfer due to medical and mental health issues. The court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim because plaintiff failed to adequately plead a covered disability or explain the nexus between his disability and the requested accommodation.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Salute v. Stratford Greens Garden Apartments, 136 F.3d 293 (2d Cir. 1998)
McElwee v. Cty. of Orange, 700 F.3d 635 (2d Cir. 2012)
Cuoco v. Moritsugu, 222 F.3d 99 (2d Cir. 2000)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Emergency move/transfer from current apartment due to landlord's failure to follow lease agreements and worsening medical and mental health conditions
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to state a plausible FHA reasonable accommodation claim. The complaint does not adequately describe the disability, the specific accommodation sought, or the connection between the disability and the requested accommodation, as required by the FHA and the reasonable accommodation form itself.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II ADA claim for denial of services in Section 8 housing program
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts sufficient to establish that he is a qualified individual with a disability or that he was denied participation in Section 8 housing. The complaint does not clarify whether the form was rejected for incompleteness or on disability grounds, making it impossible to infer discrimination.

case_name: Eyvonne A. Webb v. Carrington Mortgage Services LLC
accommodation_description: This case does not involve a reasonable accommodation request; it challenges mortgage escrow account handling and property tax credit calculations as source-of-income discrimination under the Maryland Fair Housing Act.
key_holding: The court dismissed Plaintiff's Maryland Fair Housing Act claim because property tax credits applied directly to reduce tax obligations do not constitute 'source of income' under the statute, which requires money paid to or on behalf of a buyer or renter.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Eyvonne A. Webb sued Carrington Mortgage Services LLC alleging the mortgage servicer discriminated against her by failing to account for property tax credits in her escrow account statements, violating the Maryland Fair Housing Act's prohibition on source-of-income discrimination. The court granted Carrington's motion to dismiss, finding that property tax credits applied directly to reduce tax liability are not a 'source of income' under the MFH statute because they are not money paid to or on behalf of the homeowner.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to state a claim under Maryland Fair Housing Act § 20-707 because property tax credits do not constitute a 'source of income' under the statute's plain language. Tax credits reduce the amount owed rather than conferring income or transferring new monies to the plaintiff, and thus fall outside the statutory definition of 'source of income' as 'any lawful source of money paid directly or indirectly to or on behalf of a renter or buyer of housing.'

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Maryland Consumer Debt Collection Act (MCDCA) § 14-202(11) and (8); Maryland Consumer Protection Act (MCPA) §§ 13-301 et seq.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege debt collection activity triggering FDCPA/MCDCA protections. The 2022 and 2023 Escrow Statements contained clear disclaimers stating they were 'informational only' and required 'no action,' lacked explicit payment demands, and were not sent for the animating purpose of obtaining payment. Under the commonsense inquiry test, these statements were not attempts to collect a debt. MCPA claims also failed for lack of specificity under Rule 9(b) and failure to allege reasonable reliance on alleged misrepresentations.

case_name: Carmencita María Pedro, et al. v. Hilton Worldwide, Inc., et al.
race_if_mentioned: Pedro is Puerto Rican; Fisher is Afro-Latino
accommodation_description: Request for a $60 laundry credit as a reasonable accommodation for Fisher's schizophrenia
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' FHA claims because the complaint failed to allege facts supporting a plausible inference of race or disability discrimination, including dismissing the $60 laundry credit accommodation request as failing to state a nexus between Fisher's schizophrenia and the requested financial accommodation.
brief_summary: Pedro and Fisher, a mother and son with schizophrenia, sued Hilton and related entities alleging they were ejected from a hotel where Fisher was residing while awaiting permanent supportive housing, claiming discrimination based on race and disability and failure to accommodate. The court dismissed the complaint for failure to state plausible claims, finding no facts supporting an inference of discrimination and that the $60 laundry credit request lacked a nexus to Fisher's disability.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Revock v. Cowpet Bay W. Condominium Ass'n, 853 F.3d 96 (3d Cir. 2017)
Lloyd v. Manbel Devco I LP., No. 23-2261 (E.D. Pa. 2024)
Fair Hous. Rts. Ctr. in Se. Pennsylvania v. Morgan Properties Mgmt. Co., LLC, No. 16-4677 (E.D. Pa. 2018)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Credit of $60.00 to cover laundry costs following bed bug incident, framed as accommodation for Fisher's Schizophrenia
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found no plausible nexus between Fisher's disability and the requested $60 laundry credit accommodation. The FHA does not require financial accommodations for disabled tenants, and plaintiff failed to allege facts showing the accommodation was necessary to afford Fisher equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged arbitrary enforcement of hotel rules against plaintiffs regarding complementary breakfast and cell phone usage in lobby, allegedly not applied to white guests
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found allegations of race discrimination implausible because complaint provided no explanation of when alleged incidents occurred, no factual basis for inferring discriminatory intent, and only conclusory assertions that rules were applied differently to white people.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation for asserting tenancy rights under landlord-tenant law and seeking disability accommodations, including improper charging of credit card and filing of ejectment action
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found no plausible causal link between protected activity and alleged retaliation. Facts as pled showed Hilton filed ejectment case once plaintiffs could no longer pay for lodging, not because of any protected activity. Allegations of retaliation were unsupported conclusory assertions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (constitutional due process and equal protection claims); 42 U.S.C. § 1981 (race discrimination in contract); ADA Title III (public accommodation discrimination); Section 504 Rehabilitation Act (federal financial assistance recipients); Civil Rights Act of 1964 Title II (public accommodation race discrimination); Pennsylvania Constitution and state law claims
fha_claims.reasoning: § 1983 claims dismissed because private defendants (Hilton, hotel entities, legal counsel, Gasperetti) are not state actors; conclusory allegations of conspiracy and municipal assent insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly. ADA Title III and Civil Rights Act Title II claims dismissed as moot because only injunctive relief available and plaintiffs no longer reside at hotel. RA claims dismissed because no allegation defendants receive federal financial assistance. § 1981 claims dismissed for failure to allege facts supporting race discrimination. State law claims dismissed for lack of diversity jurisdiction.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: General failure to accommodate Fisher's Schizophrenia during hotel stay and ejectment process
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found no plausible FHA reasonable accommodation claim. Plaintiffs failed to allege specific accommodations requested or necessary to afford Fisher equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling. Allegations were conclusory and lacked factual support.

case_name: Sydney Ellerbe v. Tuscan Highlands, LLC; Schulman Properties; and Winnie Schulman
accommodation_description: No accommodation request was made; plaintiff alleges race-based disparate treatment and eviction as cover-up for racially motivated removals from a restaurant
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's constructive eviction, disparate impact, negligence, and defamation claims but allowed plaintiff's claim for wrongful eviction under Nevada law and his FHA disparate treatment claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(b) to proceed because plaintiff sufficiently alleged that defendants used false assault allegations as a pretext to evict him in retaliation for or to cover up racially discriminatory conduct.
brief_summary: Sydney Ellerbe, an African American tenant, sued Tuscan Highlands LLC and related defendants alleging he was discriminatorily removed from a restaurant twice due to his race and then wrongfully evicted using false assault allegations as a pretext. The court granted leave to proceed on his wrongful eviction claim under Nevada law and his Fair Housing Act disparate treatment claim, but dismissed his constructive eviction, disparate impact, negligence, and defamation claims.
key_cases_cited: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Under either the McDonnell Douglas framework or direct evidence method, plaintiff plausibly alleged a prima facie case of disparate treatment based on race by showing protected class status, discriminatory conduct (false assault allegations used as pretext), distinct and palpable injury (eviction, reputational and financial harm), and circumstantial evidence of racial animus (timing of allegations after racial incidents, disparate treatment compared to similarly situated non-minority residents).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege that defendants' actions created a discriminatory effect upon a protected class or perpetuated housing segregation; allegations were confined to individual harm to plaintiff rather than class-wide impact.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: NRS 118A.390 wrongful eviction, constructive eviction, negligence, defamation
fha_claims.reasoning: Wrongful eviction claim under NRS 118A.390 survives because plaintiff alleged landlord-tenant relationship, unlawful removal, and blocking of entry. Constructive eviction dismissed because plaintiff alleged actual eviction, not conditions rendering premises unfit. Negligence dismissed because allegations describe intentional conduct, not negligence. Defamation dismissed because plaintiff failed to allege unprivileged publication to third parties and did not allege false statements were included in eviction notice or credit reporting.

case_name: Eugene Davis v. Holly Negaard; Holly Negaard as Trustee of the Holly Negaard Revocable Living Trust; Jessica Purdy a/k/a Jessica Shanafelt; and Purdy Investments, LLC d/b/a/ Western Apartments
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that defendants (landlord and property manager) timely cooperate by providing him with a rent ledger and other tenant information necessary to qualify for the Community Action/Emergency Rent Bridge rental assistance program so he could avoid falling into arrears and face eviction.
key_holding: The court dismissed Count 3 of plaintiff's complaint seeking declaratory relief because the Rooker-Feldman doctrine barred federal review of the state court eviction judgment, and the Declaratory Judgment Act does not provide relief for past conduct where no ongoing or future controversy exists.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Eugene Davis, a tenant at Western Apartments in Minot, North Dakota, sued his landlord and property manager alleging housing discrimination under the FHA and North Dakota law, negligence/property damage, and seeking declaratory relief after defendants allegedly failed to timely provide rental documents needed for the Community Action/Emergency Rent Bridge assistance program, leading to eviction. Defendants moved to partially dismiss Count 3, which sought a court order requiring defendants to file stipulations in state court acknowledging the eviction was wrongfully obtained through discrimination and to satisfy the state court judgment. The federal court granted the motion, holding that such relief would effectively void the state court's eviction ruling in violation of the Rooker-Feldman doctrine and that the Declaratory Judgment Act does not provide a remedy for purely past conduct.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Charchenko v. City of Stillwater, 47 F.3d 981 (8th Cir. 1995)
MSK EyEs LTD v. Wells Fargo Bank, 546 F.3d 533 (8th Cir. 2008)
Simes v. Huckabee, 354 F.3d 823 (8th Cir. 2004)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Declaratory relief seeking order that eviction judgment was obtained wrongfully through discriminatory actions; request for stipulation and satisfaction of judgment in state court docket
fha_claims.reasoning: Federal district court lacks subject matter jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine to hear claims seeking to declare a state court eviction judgment wrongful or to require filing of stipulations in the state court docket, as such relief would effectively void the state court's decision. The state court properly declined to hear discrimination claims due to lack of subject matter jurisdiction in an eviction proceeding.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodations for persons with behavioral/mental health disabilities in response to 911 calls, including deflection to behavioral-health response teams instead of armed police
fha_claims.reasoning: The court has not yet approved the proposed consent decree and has ordered the parties to provide additional factual information regarding the alleged violations and their relationship to the proposed remedies, including clarification on how dispatchers and officers will determine whether a 911 call requires a police response, mental-health response, or both, and what legal standard determines whether deflection of calls to behavioral-health response teams constitutes reasonable accommodations under the ADA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fourth Amendment excessive force claims (lethal and non-lethal), First Amendment retaliation and mass arrest claims, Safe Streets Act disparate impact and alleged sex discrimination claims, Americans with Disabilities Act claims regarding behavioral health emergency response
fha_claims.reasoning: The court has not yet approved the proposed consent decree and has ordered the parties to provide additional factual information regarding the alleged violations under the Fourth Amendment, First Amendment, Safe Streets Act, and Americans with Disabilities Act, including the frequency and nature of alleged excessive force incidents, First Amendment violations since 2021, and the legal basis for sex discrimination allegations not alleged in the complaint.

case_name: Fair Hous. Just. Ctr., Inc. v. Pelican Mgmt., Inc.
accommodation_description: The case involves Goldfarb's minimum income policy (requiring applicants to earn 43 times monthly rent) which allegedly had a disparate impact on renters with rental subsidies, many of whom have disabilities.
key_holding: The Second Circuit affirmed the district court's finding that Goldfarb's 2019 minimum income policy violated the Fair Housing Act and NYCHRL by having a disparate impact on applicants with partial rental subsidies, including many disabled individuals, based on Dr. Steil's statistical analysis showing only 13% of partially subsidized applicants were approved compared to 30% of unsubsidized applicants.
brief_summary: Fair Housing Justice Center sued Pelican Management and related entities (Goldfarb) alleging that their minimum income policy requiring prospective renters to earn 43 times monthly rent violated the FHA and NYCHRL by disparately impacting disabled applicants who rely on rental subsidies. The Second Circuit affirmed the district court's judgment for FHJC, agreeing that Goldfarb's 2019 Policy had a statistically significant disparate impact on partially subsidized applicants based on Dr. Steil's expert analysis.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Minimum income policy (2015 Policy requiring gross annual income of at least 43 times total monthly rent) that excluded renters receiving rental subsidies
fha_claims.reasoning: District court found the 2015 Policy violated the FHA by disparately impacting renters with disabilities and those receiving rental subsidies. The policy excluded virtually all renters receiving certain rental subsidies, a large percentage of whom have disabilities.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Revised minimum income policy (2019 Policy) that maintained 43x income requirement for unsubsidized applicants, eliminated income requirements for fully subsidized applicants, and required 40x income for partially subsidized applicants' share of rent
fha_claims.reasoning: Appellate court affirmed district court's finding that the 2019 Policy violated the NYCHRL by continuing to adversely impact applicants with partial subsidies on the basis of source of income. The court rejected defendant's arguments regarding expert methodology and the proper comparison group, finding the district court did not err in comparing partially subsidized to unsubsidized applicants while excluding fully subsidized applicants who were not subject to the challenged income requirements.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: New York City Human Rights Law (NYCHRL) source of income discrimination claims
fha_claims.reasoning: District court found the 2015 and 2019 Policies violated the NYCHRL's prohibition on housing discrimination based on lawful source of income. Appellate court affirmed, applying NYCHRL's disparate impact framework and rejecting defendant's statistical and legal arguments.

source_file: 10319990_2025_Eddy J. Philippeaux v. Miami Apartments Investors, LLC_ca11
case_name: Eddy J. Philippeaux v. Miami Apartments Investors, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges landlord refused to renew his lease in retaliation for filing a prior fair housing lawsuit against the same defendants
key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed summary judgment for defendants on the FHA retaliation claim, holding that Philippeaux failed to produce sufficient evidence that defendants' legitimate, non-retaliatory reasons for non-renewing his lease—persistent resident complaints about his behavior and his rude conduct toward management—were pretextual.
brief_summary: Eddy J. Philippeaux, a disabled veteran, sued Miami Apartments Investors, LLC, Baron Residential Management, and related defendants alleging they unlawfully refused to renew his lease in retaliation for filing a prior fair housing lawsuit against them. The district court granted summary judgment to defendants on the FHA retaliation claim, and the Eleventh Circuit affirmed, finding that Philippeaux failed to rebut defendants' legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for non-renewal—resident complaints and his disruptive behavior toward property management.
key_cases_cited: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
St. Mary's Honor Ctr. v. Hicks, 509 U.S. 502 (1993)
Ring v. Boca Ciega Yacht Club Inc., 4 F.4th 1149 (11th Cir. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Although plaintiff established a prima facie case of FHA retaliation (protected activity, adverse action, causal link), defendants articulated legitimate, non-retaliatory reasons for non-renewal (resident complaints about loitering and disruptive behavior, documented in warning letters). Plaintiff failed to produce sufficient evidence that these reasons were pretextual; his own deposition testimony partially corroborated the complaints, and temporal proximity alone is insufficient to establish pretext without additional evidence.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III retaliation claim; IIED claim under Florida law
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA claim dismissed because Title III of the ADA does not apply to private residential apartment buildings; plaintiff abandoned the argument that the Monarc was a public accommodation by failing to challenge this ground on appeal. IIED claim dismissed because non-renewal of lease, as a matter of law, constitutes no more than insistence on legal rights in a permissible way and is not conduct 'atrocious and utterly intolerable in a civilized community' under Florida law; allegations about movers' confiscation of belongings were speculative and failed to plausibly connect defendants' conduct to the alleged harm.

case_name: Robert L. Hatcher v. Sylvain Yang and Travis Smith
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges Fair Housing Act claims against landlord Yang arising from forcible entry and detainer action, though specific accommodation request not detailed in this order.
key_holding: Claims against Defendant Smith, an attorney who represented the landlord in state court eviction proceedings, are dismissed with prejudice based on litigation privilege; any discrimination claim against Smith is too conclusory to withstand dismissal.
brief_summary: Robert Hatcher, proceeding pro se, sued his landlord Sylvain Yang and Yang's attorney Travis Smith alleging claims including Fair Housing Act violations arising from a forcible entry and detainer action in state court. The Court granted Smith's motion to dismiss with prejudice, finding that statements made during judicial proceedings are privileged under Oklahoma law and plaintiff's discrimination allegations were too conclusory to state a claim; the FHA claims against Yang remain pending.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Defamation and conspiracy claims arising from attorney's filing of forcible entry and detainer action in state court
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's claims against the attorney defendant are barred by litigation privilege under Oklahoma law, which immunizes attorneys for communications made during or preliminary to judicial proceedings regardless of falsity or malice. Additionally, any discrimination claim is too conclusory and alleges no facts showing discriminatory conduct.

case_name: Latonia Black v. Royal American Management, et al.
accommodation_description: The complaint alleges failure to reasonably accommodate under § 3604(f)(3) but does not specify the accommodation requested; this procedural order does not address the substance of the accommodation claim.
key_holding: The court granted plaintiff's motion for leave to file an amended complaint under Rule 15(a)(2)'s liberal standard despite finding plaintiff's delay resulted from bad faith or carelessness, because there was no undue prejudice to defendants and the amendment was filed before the scheduling order deadline.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Latonia Black, a Black tenant, sued Royal American Management and related defendants alleging Fair Housing Act violations including disparate treatment and failure to reasonably accommodate under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3), along with retaliation claims. This procedural order granted Black's motion for leave to file an amended complaint under Rule 15(a)(2), finding that despite her bad faith or carelessness in delaying amendment, no undue prejudice would result to defendants and the amendment deadline had not passed.

case_name: In re L.D. Ford

The Court denies the petition, holding that it lacks authority under 28 U.S.C. § 1651 to issue writs of mandamus against state officials or courts outside the Third Circuit.

case_name: Kiontay Smith v. Kittle Property Group, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges discriminatory eviction based on race and sex following termination from employment at the property.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for Kittle Property Group on plaintiff's FHA claims because plaintiff failed to establish discriminatory intent in her eviction—she could not identify similarly situated comparators outside her protected class who engaged in comparable conduct (threatening gun violence) yet received more favorable treatment, and plaintiff presented no evidence that the decisionmakers doubted the reports of her threats or acted with discriminatory motive.
brief_summary: Kiontay Smith, an African-American bisexual woman employed as a maintenance technician at Kittle Property Group, sued the company alleging Title VII race and sex discrimination and Fair Housing Act claims after she was terminated for allegedly making threats of gun violence and subsequently evicted from her employee housing within seven days. The court granted summary judgment for Kittle on all claims, finding Smith failed to establish a prima facie case of discrimination because she identified no similarly situated comparators who engaged in comparable conduct—threatening gun violence—yet received more favorable treatment, and presented no evidence that Kittle's stated reason for her termination and eviction was pretextual.
key_cases_cited: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Wrongful eviction based on race and sex discrimination
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to identify similarly situated employees outside her protected class who were treated more favorably. The comparators identified (Loper and Neal) engaged in different conduct (resignation/insubordination) compared to plaintiff's alleged threats of gun violence, and dealt with different decisionmakers or different lease provisions, making them dissimilar. Plaintiff also failed to establish discriminatory intent under McDonnell Douglas framework applied to FHA claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Coercion, intimidation, threats, and interference under § 3617
fha_claims.reasoning: To prevail on § 3617 claim, plaintiff must show defendants were motivated by intent to discriminate. Plaintiff failed to establish discriminatory intent through comparator analysis or holistic record review. No evidence suggested decisionmakers doubted reports of threats or acted with discriminatory motive in evicting plaintiff.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VII race and sex discrimination claims (including sexual orientation)
fha_claims.reasoning: Under McDonnell Douglas framework applied to Title VII claims, plaintiff failed to establish prima facie case of discrimination. Plaintiff could not identify similarly situated employees outside her protected class treated more favorably; comparators engaged in conduct (insubordination, inappropriate bumper sticker, unauthorized home entry, phone use) not comparable in seriousness to alleged threats of gun violence. Plaintiff also failed to establish pretext; defendant maintained consistent reason for termination throughout litigation and no evidence showed decisionmakers disbelieved the threat reports.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act claim regarding public housing eligibility based on criminal history; also § 1983 Equal Protection Clause (federal and state) and Title VII employment discrimination
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the FHA claim in a footnote, holding that the Fair Housing Act does not mandate housing availability to individuals whose tenancy would constitute a direct threat to health or safety, and public housing authorities retain discretion to deny applications based on conviction history. The court also noted plaintiff failed to name the Detroit Housing Commission as a defendant. The primary claims (§ 1983 Equal Protection and Title VII) were dismissed because the State of Michigan is not a 'person' under § 1983, state equal protection claims are barred by Eleventh Amendment immunity, and Title VII does not protect convicted felons.

case_name: Clark v. Blueprint Investments, LLC
accommodation_description: No specific reasonable accommodation was requested in this proceeding. The underlying state court cases involved landlord-tenant disputes including allegations of retaliatory evictions and discriminatory practices by the landlord, but no discrete accommodation request was at issue before the federal court.
key_holding: The court remanded all four state court cases because it lacked subject matter jurisdiction: plaintiff could not remove cases as a plaintiff under 28 U.S.C. § 1441(a) (which permits only defendants to remove), and the Municipal Court eviction and escrow cases were founded on state law without a properly pleaded federal question.
brief_summary: Plaintiff April Clark attempted to remove four Franklin County state court cases — two eviction cases against her, one rent escrow case she filed, and one Common Pleas case she filed alleging breach of contract, retaliation, and discrimination — to federal court, claiming FHA, ADA, RICO, and constitutional violations. The Magistrate Judge recommended remand for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, and the District Court adopted that recommendation over Clark's objections. The court held that removal is statutorily available only to defendants, not plaintiffs, and the Municipal Court cases presented no properly pleaded federal question sufficient to confer jurisdiction.
key_cases_cited: Caterpillar Inc. v. Williams, 482 U.S. 386 (1987)
Beneficial Nat. Bank v. Anderson, 539 U.S. 1 (2003)
Arbaugh v. Y&H Corp., 546 U.S. 500 (2006)
Metropolitan Life Ins. Co. v. Taylor, 481 U.S. 58 (1987)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged Fair Housing Act violations, American Disability Act violations, and Constitutional rights violations in connection with landlord-tenant disputes, eviction cases, and rent escrow matters. Specific accommodations not identified in the opinion.
fha_claims.disposition: 28 U.S.C. § 1447(c) — Remand for lack of subject matter jurisdiction
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked subject matter jurisdiction because the Municipal Court cases were based on state law (eviction and escrow) and the Common Pleas case could not be removed by plaintiff as a party to the action. Federal questions were not essential elements of the properly pleaded claims for relief, and no complete preemption doctrine applied. The case was remanded to state court without reaching the merits of any FHA claim.

case_name: Concern for Independent Living, Inc. v. Town of Southampton, New York
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED - The complaint alleges the Town's denial of a zone change application for a 50-unit supportive housing development for disabled and low-income persons constitutes disability discrimination under the FHA.
key_holding: The court granted the parties' joint motion to stay discovery pending resolution of Defendants' anticipated motion to dismiss, finding that Defendants made a strong showing that Plaintiff's claims may be unmeritorious, discovery would be voluminous and burdensome, and Plaintiff would suffer little prejudice from a stay.
brief_summary: Concern for Independent Living, Inc., a non-profit developer, sued the Town of Southampton and its Town Board alleging the denial of its zone change application to construct Liberty Gardens, a 50-unit affordable supportive housing development for disabled and low-income persons, violated the FHA, ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and NYSHRL. fha_claims.accommodation_description: Zoning change to permit 50-unit affordable supportive housing development for disabled and low-income persons
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found FHA claims likely unripe because plaintiff failed to exhaust alternative administrative remedies (bonus density application, variance application to ZBA) before seeking zoning change, and land use claims require final government decision on application of regulations to property.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II, Section 504 Rehabilitation Act, NYSHRL claims arising from denial of zoning change application
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found ADA and Rehabilitation Act claims likely unripe for same ripeness reasons as FHA claims; NYSHRL claims likely fail because Town and Town Board do not fall within categories of liable actors under Executive Law § 296 (owner, lessee, managing agent of housing accommodation); Article 78 claim lacks subject matter jurisdiction in federal court.

case_name: Naketia Johnson v. FirstKey Homes LLC
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; case involves alleged race-based refusal to rent and lease termination.
key_holding: Johnson adequately stated a claim under the FHA because she alleged the defendant terminated her lease four minutes after she took possession and informed her the cancellation was based on reasons related to her race.
brief_summary: Naketia Johnson sued FirstKeyHomes LLC alleging the landlord violated the Fair Housing Act by canceling her lease four minutes after she took possession, citing reasons related to her race. The court denied the motion to dismiss the FHA claim, finding Johnson adequately alleged race-based discrimination under § 3604(a), while dismissing her § 1983 claim for failure to state that defendant acted under color of law.

Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
