brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Jaezon Ellis sued NAICA Housing Development Fund Company, a nonprofit homeless prevention organization, and two employees for negligence, property loss, and discrimination after being called a slur by a staff member at a transitional housing facility. The court dismissed all federal claims, finding NAICA is a private entity not subject to Section 1983 liability, the single incident of name-calling is insufficient to state a hostile housing environment claim under the Fair Housing Act, and plaintiff has no constitutional due process claim for the property loss.
key_cases_cited: Spavone v. Transitional Servs. of New York Supportive Hous. Program, 2016 WL 2758269 (E.D.N.Y. 2016)
New York by Abrams v. Merlino, 694 F. Supp. 1101 (S.D.N.Y. 1988)
Favourite v. 55 Halley St., Inc., 381 F. Supp. 3d 266 (S.D.N.Y. 2019)
Anonymous v. Goddard Riverside Cmty. Ctr., Inc., 1997 WL 475165 (S.D.N.Y. 1997)
Snell v. Suffolk Cnty., 782 F.2d 1094 (2d Cir. 1986)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Hostile housing environment based on alleged name-calling by staff member
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's allegations of a single incident of name-calling are insufficient to state a hostile housing environment claim under the FHA because the conduct must be severe and pervasive, not isolated or sporadic. Additionally, plaintiff failed to allege a relationship between the alleged harassment and his housing conditions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Negligence claims for failure to protect from other residents, loss of property
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish that defendants are state actors under § 1983; NAICA is a private nonprofit entity and provision of housing is not a public function. Even assuming state actor status, the Constitution does not impose an affirmative duty to protect individuals from harm by private parties absent custody, and property loss claims are adequately remedied under New York state law.

source_file: 10361008_2025_Reese v. Park Place Condominium Homeowners Association I_dcd
case_name: Reese v. Park Place Condominium Homeowners Association I
accommodation_description: Reese alleged that PPCA permitted white unit-owners to use the master insurance policy to cover repairs while denying her similar requests.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for PPCA because Reese failed to produce any evidence rebutting PPCA's legitimate, non-discriminatory reasons for denying her insurance coverage claims, instead relying on unsupported allegations and speculation.
brief_summary: Allison Reese, an African American condominium owner, sued Park Place Condominium Homeowners Association alleging race discrimination under 42 U.S.C. § 3605, claiming the association permitted white unit-owners to use the master insurance policy for repairs but denied her similar requests. The court granted summary judgment for PPCA, finding Reese failed to produce any evidence rebutting PPCA's legitimate, non-discriminatory justification for denying coverage and instead relied on unsupported assertions and speculation about differential treatment.
key_cases_cited: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Reeves v. Sanderson Plumbing Prods., Inc., 530 U.S. 133 (2000)
Brady v. Office of Sergeant at Arms, 520 F.3d 490 (D.C. Cir. 2008)
2922 Sherman Ave. Tenants' Ass'n v. District of Columbia, 444 F.3d 673 (D.C. Cir. 2006)
Holcomb v. Powell, 433 F.3d 889 (D.C. Cir. 2006)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to produce evidence rebutting defendant's legitimate, non-discriminatory reasons for denying insurance coverage and repair requests. Defendant established that its master insurance policy covers only casualty events (not structural/foundational damage), that plaintiff failed to identify specific structural defects requiring repair, and that plaintiff failed to provide comparative evidence of similarly situated white owners receiving favorable treatment. Plaintiff's bald assertions about discriminatory treatment were unsupported by evidence and amounted to speculation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted motion to dismiss on retaliation claim at the motion to dismiss stage, finding that plaintiff failed to state a plausible claim of retaliation for reporting Board members' misconduct. The claim did not survive the pleading-stage scrutiny under Iqbal/Twombly.

case_name: Will J. Belton v. Regions Bank NA, et al.
accommodation_description: This is not a reasonable accommodation case; it involves business partnership disputes, alleged race-based discrimination in financial transactions, RICO claims, and banking regulation violations regarding limited partnerships.
key_holding: The court denied multiple procedural motions (stay of state court proceedings, protective order, motions to consolidate) as the underlying removed state court actions were recommended for remand and the parties were required to communicate through counsel.
brief_summary: Will J. Belton, proceeding pro se and then with counsel, sued Regions Bank NA and related entities alleging race-based discrimination, Fair Housing Act violations, RICO violations, and banking regulation breaches related to limited partnership interests and business opportunities for African American businesses. The court denied all procedural motions including requests to stay state court proceedings, consolidate cases, and obtain a protective order, while remanding improperly removed state court actions and staying discovery pending resolution of pending motions to dismiss.
key_cases_cited: Chick Kam Choo v. Exxon Corp., 486 U.S. 140 (1988)
Smith v. Bayer Corp., 564 U.S. 299 (2011)
Fulford v. Transp. Servs. Co., 412 F.3d 609 (5th Cir. 2005)
In re Terra Int'l, Inc., 134 F.3d 302 (5th Cir. 1998)
United States v. Garrett, 571 F.2d 1323 (5th Cir. 1978)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint alleges systematic racism and discrimination under the Fair Housing Act and Equal Protection Clause, but the motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6) remains pending before the district court. The magistrate judge's order addresses only procedural motions and does not rule on the merits of the FHA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of fiduciary duty, whistleblower retaliation (12 U.S.C. § 4806), Equal Protection Clause, RICO (18 U.S.C. § 1962), Community Reinvestment Act (12 U.S.C. § 2901 et seq.), Equal Credit Opportunity Act (15 U.S.C. § 1691 et seq.), bank fraud, wire fraud, conspiracy
fha_claims.reasoning: Multiple non-FHA claims remain pending, including fiduciary duty breach, whistleblower retaliation, Equal Protection, RICO, banking regulation violations, and criminal fraud allegations. The motions to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6) are pending before the district court.

case_name: Nadia Winston v. HON Partners II LLC et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff raises general discrimination and disability allegations but does not articulate a specific reasonable accommodation request that the court analyzes.
key_holding: The court granted Defendant Mulvaney's motion to dismiss because the plaintiff's complaint and amended complaint failed to allege any cognizable claim against her specifically, as all alleged wrongful conduct was attributed to other parties (HON Partners, Dallas Housing Authority), and plaintiff had already been given an opportunity to amend.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Nadia Winston sued HON Partners II LLC and property manager Marissa Mulvaney in federal court alleging discrimination, retaliation, breach of lease, negligence, defamation, and Violence Against Women Act violations. The court granted Mulvaney's motion to dismiss with prejudice because the plaintiff's amended complaint failed to allege any actions taken by Mulvaney specifically, instead attributing all alleged misconduct to other parties, and plaintiff had already been afforded an opportunity to amend her complaint.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 566 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Brewster v. Dretke, 587 F.3d 764 (5th Cir. 2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged discrimination based on race and disability but failed to articulate a cognizable legal theory or connect any conduct to Defendant Mulvaney.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege a plausible theory of recovery under any statute (FHA, ADA, Fourteenth Amendment) and failed to connect any discriminatory conduct to Defendant Mulvaney, who is not mentioned in the pleadings. The court found Plaintiff did not provide fair notice of the claims against this defendant.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged retaliation for tenant advocacy and complaints to legal authorities, including removal of positive credit standing and imposition of fees.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff made conclusory statements of retaliation without legal basis or factual support and failed to allege any actions by Defendant Mulvaney. The court found Plaintiff did not carry her burden to plausibly allege entitlement to relief.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Defamation of character; Landlord and Tenant Contract Breach; Violation of Lease; Negligence with mold and mildew; Violation of Violence Against Women's Act; Falsified Information/Fraud
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA claims were dismissed for failure to state a plausible claim. Plaintiff failed to allege any conduct by Defendant Mulvaney in connection with any of these causes of action. For defamation, Plaintiff did not allege the required elements. For contract breach, Plaintiff admitted Defendant Mulvaney was not a party to the lease. For negligence, Plaintiff failed to connect the mold inspection findings to Defendant Mulvaney. For VAWA, Plaintiff alleged only HON Partners' conduct. For fraud, Plaintiff failed to plead with particularity under Rule 9(b) and did not allege Defendant Mulvaney's involvement.

case_name: Victor Ortiguerra, et al. v. Grand Isle Shipyard, LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation is at issue; the underlying FHA claim alleges that defendants discriminatorily segregated Filipino workers in employer-provided housing and COVID-19 quarantine facilities and refused to permit them to evacuate during Hurricane Ida, while non-Filipino workers were allowed to leave.
key_holding: The magistrate judge denied defendants' motion to modify the protective order covering T visa applications, holding that the motion was effectively an improperly grounded request for reconsideration of a prior discovery ruling under Rule 54(b) and that defendants failed to present any persuasive justification for revisiting that ruling.
brief_summary: Filipino welders and fitters employed by Grand Isle Shipyard sued their employers under the FLSA, TVPA, and FHA, alleging they were segregated in housing, forced to remain in a hurricane-damaged bunkhouse without utilities while non-Filipino co-workers were permitted to evacuate, and subjected to threats of termination and deportation. During discovery, defendants moved to modify a protective order entered in August 2024 to compel production of plaintiffs' T visa applications and all supporting documents, a request the court had substantially denied in a prior June 2024 ruling. The magistrate judge denied the motion, finding it was a thinly disguised reconsideration motion under Rule 54(b) that lacked new evidence or identification of error in the prior ruling, and that all four factors governing protective order modification weighed in plaintiffs' favor.
key_cases_cited: Austin v. Kroger Texas, L.P., 864 F.3d 326 (5th Cir. 2017)
Cazorla v. Koch Foods of Mississippi, L.L.C., 838 F.3d 540 (5th Cir. 2016)
United States v. Morales, 807 F.3d 717 (5th Cir. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: TVPA (18 U.S.C. § 1589) forced labor claim; FLSA minimum wage and overtime violations; housing segregation and isolation of Filipino workers; denial of evacuation during Hurricane Ida
fha_claims.reasoning: This opinion addresses a discovery dispute regarding production of T visa applications and supporting documents in a case involving TVPA forced labor claims, FLSA wage violations, and alleged housing discrimination. The court denied defendants' motion to modify the protective order and did not reach the merits of any underlying FHA claim. The FHA is cited only as one of the federal statutes alleged in the amended complaint; no substantive FHA analysis occurs in this discovery ruling.

case_name: Yolanda E. Quewon v. Philadelphia Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Request for a handicap-accessible ramp outside her home as a reasonable accommodation for hip and knee pain.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claim because she failed to adequately plead the elements of a reasonable accommodation claim: she did not describe her disability, did not allege whether she requested the accommodation from the defendant, and did not explain how the ramp was necessary for her to use and enjoy her dwelling.
brief_summary: Yolanda Quewon, a public housing tenant with hip and knee pain, sued the Philadelphia Housing Authority alleging harassment about rent payments and requesting a handicap-accessible ramp as a reasonable accommodation. The court dismissed her Amended Complaint without prejudice, finding she failed to state a plausible FHA claim because she did not adequately describe her disability, did not allege whether she requested the accommodation from defendants, and did not explain how the ramp was necessary for her to use and enjoy her dwelling.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2009)
T.W. v. School District of Philadelphia, 284 F.3d 442 (3d Cir. 2002)
In re Ghada F. v. City of Philadelphia, 853 F.3d 96 (3d Cir. 2017)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Handicap-accessible ramp on the outside of plaintiff's home
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege a reasonable accommodation claim because she did not describe her disability or its relationship to knee and hip pain, did not allege whether and to whom she requested the ramp accommodation, and did not allege whether the accommodation was necessary for her to use and enjoy her home. The complaint lacks sufficient factual detail to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged discrimination based on disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege any facts about the alleged discrimination, rendering the claim implausible under Iqbal/Twombly. The complaint does not provide sufficient factual allegations to support an intentional discrimination theory.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 due process claim, breach of contract claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 1983 claim against PHA fails because plaintiff made no allegations about PHA's involvement in any violation, did not allege an unconstitutional policy or custom, and did not allege deliberate indifference. Section 1983 claim against property manager Ukwa fails because plaintiff did not provide sufficient detail about his role, duties, or relationship to the state to establish state action. Breach of contract claim dismissed for lack of supplemental jurisdiction because no independent basis for federal jurisdiction exists.

case_name: Manson v. Fresno Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested that defendants maintain a functioning elevator to provide equal access to their apartments, arguing that 21 months of elevator outages and entrapments constituted a constructive denial of reasonable accommodation for their mobility disabilities.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiffs' motion for summary judgment, finding genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether the 21-month delay in repairing the malfunctioning elevator constituted a constructive denial of reasonable accommodation and whether defendant Cipro had a disability known to defendants.
brief_summary: Three mobility-disabled tenants at a supportive housing project for homeless and disabled veterans in Fresno sued their housing provider for failing to reasonably accommodate their disabilities by delaying over 20 months to repair a frequently malfunctioning elevator that trapped passengers, including plaintiff Manson. The court denied plaintiffs' motion for summary judgment, finding genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether the delay constituted a constructive denial of reasonable accommodation and whether one plaintiff had a disability known to defendants.
key_cases_cited: Giebeler v. M & B Associates, 343 F.3d 1143 (9th Cir. 2003)
Hume v. Guardian Mgmt. LLC, 2022 WL 17834397 (D. Or. Dec. 21, 2022)
Elliott, 2018 WL 2933467
Fraihat v. U.S. Immigr. & Customs Enf't, 16 F.4th 613 (9th Cir. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Timely and sufficient repair of the Renaissance's elevator to provide functioning access to dwelling units for plaintiffs with mobility disabilities
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine disputes of material fact precluding summary judgment: (1) whether defendant knew of Cipro's mobility disability given conflicting evidence (SSI documentation vs. application stating no disability and property manager testimony of frequent stair use); (2) whether the 21-month delay in elevator repair constituted constructive denial of accommodation, as jury could find either that delay was unreasonable or that defendants' efforts with Schindler and reliance on vendor's explanation regarding transient interference were reasonable under the circumstances.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to provide reasonable accommodation under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act by failing to timely and sufficiently repair the elevator
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied Section 504 four-element test and found genuine dispute of material fact as to whether defendants denied plaintiffs services needed to enjoy meaningful access to the Renaissance. The question of whether defendants unreasonably delayed in providing a fixed elevator and thereby constructively denied a reasonable accommodation remains for jury determination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, 29 U.S.C. § 794; Cal. Gov't Code § 11135; Cal. Gov't Code § 12900 et seq. (FEHA); Cal. Civ. Code § 51 et seq. (Unruh Act); Cal. Civ. Code § 54 et seq. (DPA); negligence
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied summary judgment on FEHA reasonable accommodation claim (same elements and analysis as FHA claim); DPA reasonable accommodation claim (same four elements as FHA/FEHA); Unruh Act claim (requires proof of intentional discrimination or willful misconduct, which cannot be established without resolving underlying accommodation denial); Cal. Gov't Code § 11135 claim (identical to Section 504 except requires state rather than federal funding); and violation of California Building Code Title 24 accessibility standards for elevator maintenance and dog park construction (genuine disputes of material fact regarding compliance with ASME standards and causation).

case_name: Anthony Jackson v. S2 Residential
accommodation_description: No accommodation requested; case concerns alleged racial discrimination in leasing an apartment with pest control problems.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for defendant because plaintiff failed to present competent evidence of discriminatory intent or identify a specific policy, procedure, or practice with a discriminatory effect on a protected class; plaintiff's conclusory assertions that defendant leased him an infested apartment because of his race did not constitute competent summary judgment evidence.
brief_summary: Anthony Jackson, a Black pro se plaintiff, sued S2 Residential, the management company for his apartment complex, alleging that defendant racially discriminated against him by renting him an apartment knowing it had a pest control problem, causing him to contract an infectious disease. The court granted defendant's motion for summary judgment and denied plaintiff's cross-motion, dismissing all claims with prejudice because plaintiff failed to present competent evidence creating a genuine issue of material fact on his race-based housing discrimination claim.
key_cases_cited: Tex. Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Cmtys. Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986)
Matsushita Elec. Indus. Co. v. Zenith Radio Corp., 475 U.S. 574 (1986)
Artisan/Am. Corp. v. City of Alvin, 588 F.3d 291 (5th Cir. 2009)
Crain v. City of Selma, 952 F.3d 634 (5th Cir. 2020)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff did not assert a disparate-treatment claim because his grievance stemmed from alleged uninhabitability of the apartment he was leased, not rejection from renting housing. The court construed plaintiff's claims liberally as a pro se litigant but found the disparate-treatment theory inapplicable to the facts alleged.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to identify any discriminatory policy, procedure, or practice by defendant and provided no statistical or other evidence that such a policy had a significantly greater impact on members of a protected class. Plaintiff's bald assertions of racial motivation without competent summary judgment evidence were insufficient to create a genuine issue of material fact.

case_name: C.R., an individual, by and through his next friend Tracey Joffe v. PLB Management, LLC, DBA Park La Brea Management; et al.
accommodation_description: Request to reserve the parking space directly in front of C.R.'s apartment for exclusive use by his mother as caretaker to accommodate his severe autism spectrum disorder.
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit reversed the district court's grant of judgment as a matter of law, holding that substantial evidence supported the jury's verdict that PLB failed to provide a reasonable accommodation, but affirmed the conditional new trial order because the district court did not abuse its discretion in finding the jury's verdict on reasonable alternatives was against the weight of evidence.
brief_summary: C.R., a nonverbal individual with severe autism spectrum disorder, sued PLB Management, LLC under the Fair Housing Act after the property manager refused his mother's request to reserve a parking space directly in front of their apartment for his disability-related needs. Following a jury trial verdict for C.R., the district court granted PLB judgment as a matter of law and conditionally ordered a new trial. The Ninth Circuit reversed the judgment as a matter of law, finding substantial evidence supported the jury's verdict that the reserved parking space further away was not a reasonable alternative, but affirmed the conditional new trial on reasonable alternatives and damages as within the district court's discretion.
key_cases_cited: Pavao v. Pagay, 307 F.3d 915 (9th Cir. 2002)
Harper v. City of Los Angeles, 533 F.3d 1010 (9th Cir. 2008)
Experience Hendrix L.L.C. v. Hendrixlicensing.com Ltd., 762 F.3d 829 (9th Cir. 2014)
Allied Chem. Corp. v. Daiflon, Inc., 449 U.S. 33 (1980)
Morris v. W. Hayden Ests. First Addition Homeowners Ass'n, Inc., 104 F.4th 1128 (9th Cir. 2024)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reserved parking space directly in front of plaintiff's apartment to accommodate his severe Autism Spectrum Disorder and disability-related needs
fha_claims.disposition: Judgment as a Matter of Law (Rule 50(b)) / Conditional New Trial (Rule 59(a))
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed the district court's grant of judgment as a matter of law, finding substantial evidence supported the jury's verdict that a reserved parking space further away was not a reasonable alternative accommodation. However, the court affirmed the conditional grant of a new trial, finding the district court did not abuse its discretion in crediting the defendant's expert testimony over the plaintiff's evidence regarding whether an alternative accommodation was reasonable.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged violations of New Jersey Fair Housing Act, New Jersey Identity Theft Act, intrusion upon seclusion, harassment, assault, negligent infliction of emotional distress, fraud in connection with sale or advertisement of real estate, forgery, and theft. Plaintiff also asserted a 42 U.S.C. § 1983 claim against Judge Richard F. Wells for alleged due process violations in an eviction proceeding.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine because plaintiff sought to challenge a state court eviction judgment. The court found all four Rooker-Feldman criteria were satisfied: plaintiff lost in state court, complained of injuries caused by the state judgment, the judgment was rendered before the federal suit, and plaintiff invited the district court to review and reject the state judgment. Additionally, the § 1983 claim against Judge Wells was barred by judicial immunity because the allegations referred solely to the judge's conduct while acting in his official capacity.

case_name: McGrath v. Dunecrest Condominium Association
accommodation_description: Request for approval to construct a balcony extension with stairs to provide additional space and a secondary exit for adult autistic children
key_holding: The court granted the Association's motion for attorney's fees because the plaintiffs' Fair Housing Act claims were frivolous, unreasonable, or groundless from the outset—the balcony extension accommodation failed because autism was not the but-for cause of the need, the familial status claim failed because disabled adults do not constitute protected familial status, and the retaliation claim failed because the emails did not constitute coercive conduct.
brief_summary: The McGraths sued their condominium association seeking approval for a balcony extension with stairs as a reasonable accommodation for their adult autistic children, plus familial status discrimination and retaliation claims. The court granted summary judgment for the Association in May 2024 and, in this March 2025 ruling, awarded the Association $86,562.50 in attorney's fees after finding the plaintiffs' claims were frivolous and groundless from the outset because the disability accommodation failed the causation requirement, the familial status claim did not fit the FHA's definition, and the retaliation claim lacked evidentiary support.
key_cases_cited: Good Shepherd Manor Found., Inc. v. City of Momence, 323 F.3d 557 (7th Cir. 2003)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Balcony extension with stairs to provide secondary exit and additional space for pacing and feeding tube assistance for adult autistic children (Tim and Martin McGrath)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied the 'but-for' causation test and concluded that the proposed balcony extension was not necessary to ameliorate the effect of Tim and Martin's autism because the problems it addressed (unreliable secondary exit, wear and tear, lack of grilling space, entrapment risk) affect anyone living in the unit, not just those with autism. The accommodation did not directly address needs created by the disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Familial status discrimination claim based on alleged animus toward the McGrath family due to the presence of disabled adult children (Tim and Martin McGrath, both over age 18)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that § 3604(b) familial status discrimination applies only to families with minor children under age 18, not families with disabled adults. The McGraths' theory was based on the presence of disabled adult children, which is not a protected class under the plain language of § 3604(b). Even under McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting, plaintiffs failed to establish a prima facie case because they did not show they had minor children under 18 or identify similarly situated comparators.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation through three emails: (1) notice of lien for unpaid special assessment; (2) request to remove anchors/bolts and repair garage door; (3) forwarding fire marshal report prohibiting grilling on decks less than 10 feet from exterior wall
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied the standard requiring conduct that a person of normal fortitude would view as coercive, intimidating, threatening, or interfering with FHA rights. The three emails, without any further action taken by the Association, caused only trivial harm and inconvenience. No reasonable person would view them as coercive or interfering with protected rights.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination claims against Individual Defendants (Holly Candella, Ruth Palonis, Michael Hernandez, Janet Moran) based on their votes against the balcony extension
fha_claims.reasoning: Court sua sponte granted summary judgment in favor of Individual Defendants because the discrimination claims against them were interrelated with and based on the same statements and conduct as the claims against the Association, which had already been resolved on summary judgment. Plaintiffs had adequate opportunity to oppose the motion.

source_file: 10365173_2025_Dave's Driving School LLC v. Utah Department of Public Safety_utd
case_name: Dave's Driving School, LLC v. Utah Department of Public Safety
accommodation_description: This is not a Fair Housing Act case; it concerns a driving school business license revocation. Plaintiffs asserted a FHA claim under § 3617 which was dismissed because the statute governs housing and residential transactions not applicable to a driving school.
key_holding: The FHA claim under § 3617 was dismissed with prejudice because §§ 3603-3606, which govern the sale or rental of housing and residential real estate transactions, are not addressed in the complaint and have no application to a driving school business license matter.
brief_summary: Dave's Driving School, LLC and its owners sued the Utah Department of Public Safety and related state agencies over the revocation of their driving school business license, asserting claims under § 1983 for due process violations, the ADA, and the Fair Housing Act. The court recommended granting the motion to dismiss all federal claims with prejudice, including dismissing the FHA claim because the statutes governing housing and residential transactions have no applicability to a business licensing dispute.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA claim (42 U.S.C. § 12132); § 1983 due process claims; 42 U.S.C. § 14141; 18 U.S.C. §§ 241-242; 42 U.S.C. § 1981; Title VII; state law claims
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed all federal claims for failure to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly. The ADA claim failed because plaintiffs made only conclusory references to 'ADA status' without identifying which plaintiff was disabled or the nature of the disability. The § 1983 due process claims failed because plaintiffs alleged only state law violations (not constitutional violations) and were afforded adequate procedural process. The § 14141, §§ 241-242, § 1981, and Title VII claims failed because they either lack private rights of action, do not apply to the defendants, or are inapplicable to the facts alleged.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act § 3617 retaliation claim
fha_claims.reasoning: The FHA § 3617 claim was dismissed because it requires an allegation that the plaintiff exercised or enjoyed a right protected by §§ 3603-3606 (governing sale or rental of housing and residential real estate transactions). The complaint does not address housing, residential real estate transactions, or brokerage services, so plaintiffs failed to state a plausible FHA claim.

case_name: Moore v. City of New York
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation request; case involves alleged racial discrimination by property management who called police on plaintiff, leading to his arrest and involuntary psychiatric evaluations.
key_holding: The complaint failed to state a racial discrimination claim under § 1981, Title VI, or the FHA because it did not plead facts showing discriminatory intent, only conclusory assertions about a 'medical industrial complex' exploiting Black men.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Ali Moore sued Morningside Heights Housing Corporation and FirstService Residential (Property Defendants), alleging they called police on him because of his race, leading to his arrest and involuntary psychiatric evaluations on October 1 and 5, 2021. The court granted the Property Defendants' motion to dismiss, finding the complaint failed to plausibly allege discriminatory intent, containing only conclusory assertions about a 'medical industrial complex' without factual support linking the defendants' conduct to racial animus.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Francis v. Kings Park Manor, Inc., 992 F.3d 67 (2d Cir. 2021)
Henry v. Cnty. of Nassau, 6 F.4th 324 (2d Cir. 2021)
Dolan v. Connolly, 794 F.3d 290 (2d Cir. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint fails to plead facts showing the Property Defendants' intent to discriminate on the basis of race under the FHA. The complaint does not link any alleged actions to Plaintiff's race and instead broadly asserts a conspiracy theory about a 'medical industrial complex' without factual basis to infer racial animus.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint fails to identify protected activity under the FHA. Plaintiff alleged retaliation for seeking to complain about Morningside employees but did not describe what violation he sought to complain about, and nothing supports an inference that the complaint concerned a § 3604 or § 3617 FHA violation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1983, 1985, 1986; Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964; state law claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 1983 claims fail because Property Defendants are private actors and complaint does not allege state action. Sections 1985 and 1986 claims fail because complaint does not allege a conspiracy with sufficient factual basis. State law claims dismissed for lack of supplemental jurisdiction after all federal claims are dismissed.

source_file: 10366099_2025_Resources for Human Development, Inc. v. Lower Providence Township_paed
case_name: Resources for Human Development, Inc. v. Lower Providence Township
accommodation_description: RHD requested a zoning permit to use property at Eagleville Hospital as supportive housing for individuals with disabilities, which the Township denied after initially indicating the institutional zoning designation would permit it.
key_holding: The court dismissed RHD's FHA claim without prejudice because RHD failed to identify a specific discriminatory policy or practice necessary for a disparate impact claim, did not frame its claim within the disability discrimination framework under the FHAA, failed to exhaust administrative remedies before pursuing reasonable accommodation claims, and lacked allegations of discriminatory intent.
brief_summary: Resources for Human Development, Inc. (RHD), a non-profit operator, sued Lower Providence Township after being denied a zoning permit to operate supportive housing for individuals with disabilities at Eagleville Hospital. The court dismissed RHD's Fair Housing Act claim for failure to state a claim because RHD did not identify a discriminatory policy causing disparate impact, did not plead within the FHAA's disability discrimination framework, and failed to exhaust administrative remedies for its reasonable accommodation claim.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Texas Dep't of Hous. and Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Lapid-Laurel, L.L.C. v. Zoning Bd. of Adjustment of Twp. of Scotch Plains, 284 F.3d 442 (3d Cir. 2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation in zoning rules, policies, and practices to permit use of property as supportive housing for individuals with disabilities (including those with substance use disorders and homelessness-related disabilities)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege a reasonable accommodation claim under the FHAA framework. The complaint did not identify the specific disability or protected class, did not frame the claim within the disability discrimination framework required by the FHAA, and did not exhaust administrative remedies before pursuing the claim in federal court.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts establishing a causal connection between a specific Township policy or practice and the alleged disparate impact on African Americans. The complaint lacked statistical evidence and identified no facially neutral policy causing the alleged racial disparity; a one-time zoning permit denial does not constitute a 'policy' under disparate impact doctrine.

case_name: Deborah Morris, et al. v. Baltimore City, et al.
accommodation_description: Pro se plaintiffs made general demands for ADA-compliant housing, elevator installation, bathroom remodeling, and housing conditions improvements at 301 McMechen Street, framed as civil rights violations rather than specific accommodation requests.
key_holding: The court dismissed the complaint without prejudice for failure to state a plausible claim and for failing to comply with Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 8 and Local Rule 103.1.d (79-page complaint exceeding the 40-page limit), noting plaintiffs had filed a nearly identical action that was dismissed less than two weeks prior.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Deborah Morris and Arnell Mason filed a 79-page civil rights complaint against Baltimore City and related housing entities alleging Fair Housing Act, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act violations regarding housing conditions at 301 McMechen Street. The court dismissed the complaint without prejudice for failure to state a plausible claim and for violating Rule 8 and Local Rule 103.1.d, noting the complaint was nearly identical to a prior case dismissed just two weeks earlier.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unspecified reasonable accommodations related to housing conditions at 301 McMechen Street for elderly and disabled residents; complaint references need for ADA and Rehabilitation Act compliance, emergency response plans, and protections for elderly and disabled persons
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint dismissed for failure to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly. Plaintiffs rested entirely on conclusory assertions without setting forth plausible factual allegations that could support liability; the complaint provided only generalized assertions of wrongdoing insufficient to state a claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint dismissed for failure to state a plausible claim. Plaintiffs alleged housing conditions violated civil rights but provided no plausible factual allegations demonstrating defendants' liability based on protected class status.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claims under Civil Rights Act of 1866, Civil Rights Act of 1871, Title II of the Americans With Disabilities Act, and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA claims dismissed for failure to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly. Complaint contained only conclusory assertions without factual allegations supporting liability under any of the cited statutes.

case_name: Jennifer Dixon v. Silva-Markham Partners and Koelbel & Co.
accommodation_description: Ms. Dixon sought a live-in aide accommodation for her autoimmune disorder that affects her cognition and mobility, and separately sought a transfer from a one-bedroom to a two-bedroom apartment unit facilitated through her housing voucher from the Colorado Division of Housing.
key_holding: The court adopted the magistrate judge's recommendation granting defendants summary judgment on all FHA claims—discrimination, hostile housing environment, and retaliation—because plaintiff's objections were insufficiently specific to trigger de novo review and the court found no clear error in the recommendation, while dismissing the state law security deposit claim without prejudice.
brief_summary: Jennifer Dixon, a tenant with an autoimmune disorder living in a Colorado apartment complex managed by Silva-Markham Partners and Koelbel & Co., brought FHA claims for housing discrimination under § 3604, hostile housing environment, and retaliation under § 3617, as well as a state law claim for failure to return her security deposit. The magistrate judge recommended—and the district court adopted—summary judgment for defendants, concluding that a prior settlement barred pre-January 2021 conduct, the statute of limitations barred pre-June 2020 conduct, and plaintiff failed to establish genuine disputes of material fact on the merits of any FHA claim. Plaintiff's pro se objections were overruled as too vague and non-specific to warrant de novo review.
key_cases_cited: One Parcel of Real Prop., 73 F.3d 1057
Thomas v. Arn, 474 U.S. 140
Haines v. Kerner, 404 U.S. 519
Hall v. Bellmon, 935 F.2d 1106

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a genuine dispute of material fact that she was treated differently from similarly situated tenants or that defendant's conduct was pretextual. Summary judgment granted on the discrimination claim under § 3604.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Live-in aide accommodation
fha_claims.reasoning: Undisputed facts do not show that defendants interfered with plaintiff's attempts to obtain an accommodation for her medical condition. The conduct was intended to promote the accommodation request during the transfer process, not interfere with it, and cannot sustain a retaliation claim under § 3617.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Hostile housing environment based on disability-related harassment
fha_claims.reasoning: Even considering the full scope of allegedly harassing conduct, plaintiff failed to present evidence of a genuine factual issue whether defendant's conduct was sufficiently severe or pervasive to alter plaintiff's living conditions and create a hostile environment under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Colorado state law claim for failure to return security deposit (Colo. Rev. Stat. § 38-12-103)
fha_claims.reasoning: District court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over plaintiff's state law claim for failure to return security deposit pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3), and dismissed without prejudice.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Emotional support animal (ESA) as part of Social Security disability determination; Fair Housing Act mentioned only in Dr. Daniels's letter as context for ESA recommendation, not as basis for independent FHA claim
fha_claims.reasoning: This is a Social Security Act Title II appeal, not an FHA claim. The court affirmed the ALJ's determination that plaintiff is not disabled under the Social Security Act. Although Dr. Daniels's letter referenced the Fair Housing Amendment Act and plaintiff sought to incorporate an ESA into his RFC calculation, the court analyzed these issues under Social Security disability law (42 U.S.C. § 423(d)(2) and 20 C.F.R. § 416.920), not the FHA. The court found the letter did not constitute a medical opinion under Social Security regulations and that plaintiff failed to establish medical necessity of an ESA for purposes of the RFC assessment.

case_name: Eldridge v. City of Alton, Illinois
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested disability accommodations from the City of Alton related to trash/waste collection services, as co-plaintiff Eldridge is disabled and physically struggles to pull full trash bins back toward the house after collection; they also sought the City's intervention to stop their neighbor from disrupting waste collection and requested that an outstanding trash bill be voided due to the City's failure to provide the paid-for services.
key_holding: The court dismissed the pro se complaint without prejudice for failure to state a claim, finding that plaintiffs' FHA and ADA claims failed because they did not connect the alleged interference with trash collection services or the denial of reasonable accommodations to disability-based discrimination, and their constitutional and other federal claims were similarly deficient.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Elliander Eldridge and Melissa Scharfinski, both disabled homeowners in Alton, Illinois, sued the City of Alton alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act, ADA, and various constitutional and criminal statutes arising from a contentious ongoing dispute involving a well-connected neighbor who allegedly disrupted their trash collection, the City's selective ordinance enforcement against them rather than the neighbor, and the City's failure to provide disability accommodations related to waste collection services. The court granted both plaintiffs IFP status but screened and dismissed the entire complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2), finding that claims under criminal statutes lacked a private right of action, ESA and CAA claims failed for lack of pre-suit notice compliance, and FHA/ADA claims failed because plaintiffs never connected the alleged conduct to disability discrimination. Plaintiffs were granted leave to file an amended complaint by April 28, 2025.
key_cases_cited: East-Miller v. Lake Cnty. Highway Dep't, 421 F.3d 558 (7th Cir. 2005)
Southend Neighborhood Improvement Ass'n v. St. Clair Cnty., 743 F.2d 1207 (7th Cir. 1984)
McDaniel v. Bd. of Educ. of City of Chi., 956 F. Supp. 2d 887 (N.D. Ill. 2013)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation for trash collection services; plaintiff Eldridge has mobility disability and physically struggles to pull full trash bins back toward the house. Plaintiffs requested disability accommodations related to trash collection from the City, alleging the City charged for these services but failed to provide them due to neighbor interference.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiffs failed to allege discrimination based on disability or connect the exclusion from trash collection services to disability discrimination. The complaint alleged the disruption was caused by the neighbor's personal vendetta, not the City's disability discrimination, and plaintiffs did not disclose what specific reasonable accommodation they sought from the City that was denied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claim for discrimination in provision of public services (trash collection); § 1983 equal protection and procedural due process claims; state law tort claims related to smoke hazard, tree damage, and ordinance enforcement disparities
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA Title II claim failed because plaintiffs did not allege they were denied participation in garbage collection services or discriminated against because of disability; the disruption was caused by neighbor interference, not City discrimination. Equal protection claim failed because plaintiffs did not allege their neighbor violated the same ordinances but was treated differently, and did not establish a rational basis for differential treatment. Procedural due process claim failed because all citations were dismissed, so no deprivation of property interest occurred.

case_name: Danell R. Scoggins v. Falcon Court, Turning Point of Central California
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request; plaintiff alleges disability discrimination and retaliation after filing FHA lawsuit
key_holding: The court granted leave to amend the retaliation claim because the three-day notice to quit issued one day after plaintiff filed objections to the magistrate's findings, combined with temporal proximity, may establish a prima facie case of retaliation under the McDonnell Douglas framework.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Danell Scoggins sued her landlords Falcon Court and Turning Point of Central California alleging disability discrimination and retaliation under the Fair Housing Act; the magistrate found her complaint deficient and the court adopted that finding but granted leave to amend, finding that the three-day notice to quit issued one day after she filed objections to the magistrate's findings may constitute sufficient evidence of retaliatory motive to state a retaliation claim.
key_cases_cited: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green
Walker v. City of Lakewood
Washington v. Farmington Estates Owners Ass'n
Elliot v. QF Circa 37, LLC
Donaghey v. Moorpark Bellingham Homeowners Ass'n, Inc.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.disposition: Dismissed without prejudice; leave to amend granted
fha_claims.reasoning: The first amended complaint failed to state a cognizable retaliation claim under the Fair Housing Act because it did not adequately allege the three elements of prima facie retaliation (protected activity, adverse action, and causal link). However, the court found that plaintiff's subsequently-filed objections and notice of the landlord's three-day notice to quit, filed one day after the protected activity, provided sufficient evidence to allow amendment and potential viability of a retaliation claim under McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination based on disability, sexual orientation, and religion
fha_claims.reasoning: The first amended complaint failed to state a cognizable claim of disability discrimination because it did not flesh out the details of any disability or describe how defendants discriminated on that basis. The complaint was dismissed for failure to plausibly allege the elements of disparate treatment discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Eighth Amendment claim
fha_claims.reasoning: The magistrate judge screened the complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915 and found that the Eighth Amendment claim, along with the FHA claims, failed to allege sufficient facts to make out a cognizable claim.

source_file: 10368942_2025_Baez v. New York State Office of Temporary and Disability Assistance_nysd
case_name: Baez v. New York State Office of Temporary and Disability Assistance
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged they were discriminated against in the administration of ERAP funds and in NYCHA's failure to recertify incomes, based on race, national origin, disability, and source of income.
key_holding: The court dismissed all claims against the state and city defendants on procedural grounds, including lack of Article III standing (individual plaintiffs received ERAP benefits or never applied, and the organizational plaintiff lacked sufficient connection to its mission), sovereign immunity for OTDA, qualified immunity for the OTDA commissioner, and the FHA claims were time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations.
brief_summary: Black and Hispanic NYCHA public housing residents and Residents to Preserve Public Housing sued OTDA, NYCHA, and its commissioner alleging racial and disability discrimination in the state's ERAP program, which allegedly deprioritized public housing tenants, and NYCHA's failure to recertify incomes during the pandemic. The court granted all motions to dismiss on standing, sovereign immunity, qualified immunity, and statute of limitations grounds without reaching the merits of the discrimination claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)
National Railroad Passenger Corp. v. Morgan, 536 U.S. 101 (2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A

RPPH lacks associational standing because the connection between income recertification and its core mission of preserving public housing is tenuous, and diversion of resources does not constitute concrete injury.

case_name: Merriilee Turnbull v. Frankenmuth Insurance Company
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, an insurance agent, alleges she was terminated in retaliation for whistleblowing about Defendant's bundled insurance policy requirement that she claimed discriminated against disabled homeowners.
key_holding: The court dismissed Plaintiff's FHA retaliation claim because she failed to plead a causal connection between any protected whistleblowing activity and her termination, and lacked standing to bring a disparate impact claim on behalf of disabled homeowners.
brief_summary: Merriilee Turnbull, an independent insurance agent, sued Frankenmuth Insurance Company and Matthew Hillborg alleging they terminated her agency appointment in retaliation for whistleblowing about a sales policy she claimed discriminated against disabled homeowners, along with state law claims for negligent misrepresentation, promissory estoppel, defamation, and tortious interference. The court dismissed the FHA retaliation claim for failure to plead causation and lack of standing, dismissed most claims against both defendants, but allowed one defamation claim against Hillborg to proceed.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged retaliation for whistleblower activity related to Defendant FIC's January 24, 2024 sales restriction requiring packaged home and automobile policies, which she claimed discriminated against disabled homeowners who could not drive.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead a causal link between any whistleblower activity and her termination. She conceded that Defendant FIC revoked her authority to bind new business on January 4, 2024, twenty days before announcing the sales restriction on January 24, 2024, and she did not specify what whistleblower activity she engaged in or when. Additionally, to the extent Plaintiff alleged a disparate impact claim on behalf of disabled homeowners, she lacked Article III standing because the alleged injury was to third parties, not to Plaintiff herself.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Negligent misrepresentation, promissory estoppel, Michigan Essential Insurance Act violations, defamation, and tortious interference with business relationship.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's negligent misrepresentation and promissory estoppel claims failed because she did not allege detrimental reliance on any promise or misrepresentation; her tortious interference claim failed because neither Defendant FIC nor Defendant Hillborg could be liable as third parties to Plaintiff's business relationship with Defendant FIC under Michigan law; her MEIA claim failed because the MEIA does not create a private right of action for insurance agents; and her defamation claim against Defendant FIC failed because the non-renewal letters were true statements. However, her defamation claim against Defendant Hillborg survived dismissal because intra-corporate communications can constitute third-party publication under Michigan law, and she pleaded facts supporting actual malice.

case_name: Robert Ricketts v. Westwood Condo Assoc.
accommodation_description: Repair of roof leaks and carbon monoxide hazards to allow Plaintiff and his children with asthma to occupy the condo safely
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA reasonable accommodation claim was properly dismissed because he failed to allege sufficient facts showing that his or his children's asthma constitutes a 'handicap' as defined under the FHA, which requires that the condition substantially limit a major life activity such as breathing.
brief_summary: Robert Ricketts, a Connecticut attorney and condo owner, sued Westwood Condominium Association and related parties alleging they violated the FHA by failing to repair roof leaks and carbon monoxide hazards after learning of his and his children's asthma. The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss, finding Ricketts failed to state a plausible FHA claim because his allegations did not establish that his or his children's asthma substantially limits a major life activity as required to qualify as a handicap under the FHA.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Olsen v. Stark Homes, Inc., 759 F.3d 140 (2d Cir. 2014)
Gladstone Realtors v. Bellwood, 441 U.S. 91 (1979)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Repair of leaking roof and ceiling, and remediation of carbon monoxide leaks in plaintiff's condo unit
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to establish the first element of a reasonable accommodation claim—that plaintiff or his children suffered from a handicap as defined by the FHA. Plaintiff's allegations that he and his children suffered from childhood asthma and could not tolerate mildew or black mold were conclusory and failed to establish that asthma substantially limited a major life activity. The court declined to consider other elements of the claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) claims for alleged harassing and abusive debt collection conduct; state law claims for negligence, breach of fiduciary duty, breach of contract, breach of Connecticut Unfair Trade Practices Act (CUTPA), and unjust enrichment
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's FDCPA claims failed under Iqbal/Twombly because he alleged only conclusory statements that defendant Chappell engaged in harassing and oppressive conduct without factual support. The one potentially non-conclusory allegation—that Chappell threatened foreclosure—did not violate the FDCPA because the threatened foreclosure action was legally permissible and actually pursued. State law claims were dismissed without prejudice as to supplemental jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3).

source_file: 10369794_2025_Fair Housing Justice Center, Inc. v. Goldfarb Properties, Inc._nysd
case_name: Fair Housing Justice Center, Inc. v. Pelican Management, Inc.
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation was requested by an individual plaintiff. FHJC, as a fair housing organization, challenged defendants' facially neutral minimum annual income policy (43x monthly rent) as discriminatory in its application to applicants with rental subsidies or vouchers, disproportionately harming disabled persons who rely on such assistance.
key_holding: The court granted in substantial part FHJC's motion for attorneys' fees and costs following its successful bench trial and Second Circuit affirmance on disability discrimination and source of income discrimination claims, applying a 15% across-the-board reduction and reducing paralegal billing rates to $200/hour, while rejecting defendants' remaining objections to the fee application.
brief_summary: Fair Housing Justice Center (FHJC) challenged defendants' 2015 policy requiring prospective renters to earn an annual income of at least 43 times their monthly rent as discriminatory under the FHA and New York City Human Rights Law. After a bench trial, the court found in FHJC's favor on all three claims—disability discrimination under the FHA, disability discrimination under the NYCHRL, and source of income discrimination under the NYCHRL—and awarded $240,540 in compensatory damages, $750,000 in punitive damages, and injunctive relief; the Second Circuit affirmed in January 2025. This opinion resolves FHJC's post-appeal motion for attorneys' fees and costs totaling $1,582,286.61, directing an amended fee application incorporating a reduced paralegal rate of $200/hour, re-rating of entries identified as entirely clerical at $200/hour, and a 15% across-the-board reduction.
key_cases_cited: Farrar v. Hobby
Hensley v. Eckerhart
Fox v. Vice
Green v. Torres
Lilly v. City of New York

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Minimum income policy requiring prospective renters to earn at least 43 times their total monthly rent (2015 Policy) and subsequent 2019 Policy with similar income requirements applied to applicants with rental subsidies or vouchers
fha_claims.disposition: Judgment on merits after bench trial
fha_claims.reasoning: The Court found that Defendants' minimum income policies violated the FHA as disability discrimination (disparate impact) because they disproportionately burdened applicants with disabilities who rely on rental subsidies. The Court awarded compensatory damages, punitive damages, and injunctive relief prohibiting application of minimum income requirements to applicants with rental subsidies or vouchers.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Disability discrimination under New York City Human Rights Law (NYCHRL); source of income discrimination under NYCHRL
fha_claims.disposition: Judgment on merits after bench trial
fha_claims.reasoning: The Court found in favor of FHJC on disability discrimination claims under NYCHRL and source of income discrimination claims under NYCHRL, applying similar standards to the FHA analysis. The Court awarded all requested relief including compensatory damages, punitive damages, and injunctive relief.

source_file: 10369809_2025_Fair Housing Justice Center, Inc. v. Goldfarb Properties, Inc._nysd
case_name: Fair Housing Justice Center, Inc. v. Pelican Management, Inc.
accommodation_description: The case did not involve a traditional reasonable accommodation request; rather, FHJC challenged defendants' company-wide minimum income policy (43x monthly rent) as unlawfully screening out applicants with disabilities who rely on partial rental subsidies or housing vouchers, and sought an injunction prohibiting defendants from applying minimum income requirements to applicants with rental subsidies or vouchers.
key_holding: The court granted FHJC's motion for attorneys' fees and costs, directing submission of an amended fee application reflecting adjustments including reduction of paralegal hourly rates to $200, compensation of fully clerical entries at $200/hour, and a 15% reduction to all pre-settlement fees to account for work performed on behalf of a dismissed co-plaintiff, vague entries, and unrelated work.
brief_summary: Fair Housing Justice Center (FHJC) brought suit against the owners of New York City rental buildings alleging that defendants' minimum income policy—requiring prospective renters to earn at least 43 times monthly rent—unlawfully discriminated based on disability and source of income under the FHA and NYCHRL. After a bench trial, the court found for FHJC on all three claims, awarded $240,540 in compensatory damages, $750,000 in punitive damages, and injunctive relief; the Second Circuit affirmed on January 21, 2025. This amended opinion resolves FHJC's motion for $1,582,286.61 in attorneys' fees and costs, largely granting the award while applying targeted adjustments to paralegal rates, clerical entries, and pre-settlement hours.

case_name: Carol Noe v. Ray Realty et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that defendants perform necessary repairs to her apartment in a manner that accommodated her disability—i.e., that repairs be made in a particular way as a reasonable accommodation for her disability.
key_holding: The court adopted the magistrate judge's Report and Recommendation in its entirety, granting all four motions to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6) and dismissing all claims with prejudice except FHA discrimination and retaliation claims against the Original Defendants (Ray Realty and the Zecevic/Militec individuals), which were dismissed without prejudice with leave to replead within 30 days.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Carol Noe filed suit in 2019 against her landlord Ray Realty and numerous other defendants, alleging violations of the FHA, ADA, and 42 U.S.C. § 1983 based on disability discrimination and retaliation—specifically that defendants refused to perform apartment repairs in a manner accommodating her disability. Magistrate Judge Tarnofsky issued a 51-page Report and Recommendation recommending that all four motions to dismiss be granted, with the specific FHA reasonable accommodation claims dismissed with prejudice and broader FHA discrimination and retaliation claims against the Original Defendants dismissed without prejudice. The district court overruled plaintiff's objections (which merely reiterated prior arguments and did not address particular findings), adopted the R&R in full, and gave plaintiff 30 days to file a second amended complaint limited to FHA discrimination and retaliation claims against the Original Defendants.

case_name: Stern v. Highland Lake Homeowners Association
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege HOA amendments (rental ban, religious structure restrictions, Sunday viewing restrictions) and individualized harassment by HOA members were motivated by religious animus toward Hasidic Jews.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for defendants because plaintiffs failed to establish that the alleged discriminatory conduct—HOA by-law amendments and individualized harassment—was sufficiently severe and pervasive to create a hostile housing environment under § 3604(b), and defendants articulated legitimate non-discriminatory reasons for their policies.
brief_summary: Hasidic Jewish homeowners sued their HOA and individual defendants alleging religious discrimination based on hostile by-law amendments (rental ban, religious structure restrictions, Sunday commercial restrictions) and individualized harassment intended to create a hostile housing environment. The court granted summary judgment for defendants, finding plaintiffs failed to demonstrate the conduct was sufficiently severe and pervasive under § 3604(b), and defendants proffered legitimate non-discriminatory reasons for their policies that plaintiffs did not rebut with sufficient evidence of pretext.
key_cases_cited: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Mitchell v. Shane, 350 F.3d 39 (2d Cir. 2003)
People of State of N.Y. by Abrams v. Merlino, 694 F. Supp. 1101 (S.D.N.Y. 1988)
Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242 (1986)
Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to establish a prima facie case of hostile housing environment discrimination under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(b). The court applied the McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework and found that the alleged discrimination was not pervasive and severe but rather isolated or sporadic, and that defendants articulated legitimate non-discriminatory reasons for their policies (rental bans contemplated before Hasidic residents arrived, residential zoning restrictions, aesthetic concerns, traffic reduction). Plaintiffs provided only conclusory allegations without sufficient evidence of discriminatory intent or unequal enforcement.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs' § 3617 claim for coercion, intimidation, and interference failed under the same hostile housing environment standard. The alleged conduct—being stopped and questioned, stared at, cut pipes by unidentified persons, snowballs thrown by a non-party, and headlights shone into a home—was not sufficiently pervasive and severe to constitute actionable harassment. The court found these incidents isolated or sporadic and failed to establish a causal nexus to protected class membership when viewed from the perspective of a reasonable person in the aggrieved person's position.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: New York Executive Law § 296 (state law religious discrimination claim)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs' state law claim under New York Executive Law § 296 was subject to the same burden-shifting analysis and hostile housing environment standard as the federal FHA claims. The court applied the same McDonnell Douglas framework and found that plaintiffs failed to establish prima facie discrimination, as the alleged conduct was not pervasive and severe and defendants provided legitimate non-discriminatory reasons for their policies.

case_name: CMDS Residential, LLC v. Mayor & City Council of Baltimore
accommodation_description: CMDS sought a use-and-occupancy permit to operate a residential substance-abuse treatment facility, which the City denied based on zoning requirements that CMDS claims were discriminatorily applied.
key_holding: The Court held that punitive damages are unavailable against the City under the FHA and that CMDS cannot recover lost profits if it never had a legal right to open its facility, making the outcome of parallel state-court zoning litigation critical to determining actual damages.
brief_summary: CMDS Residential, LLC sued the City of Baltimore alleging the City discriminatorily denied a use-and-occupancy permit to operate a residential substance-abuse treatment facility in violation of the FHA and ADA. This Court ruling addressed a motion in limine on damages, holding that punitive damages are unavailable against the municipality under the FHA and that CMDS cannot recover lost profits unless it first establishes a legal entitlement to operate the facility in pending parallel state-court zoning litigation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of use-and-occupancy permit to operate a residential substance-abuse treatment facility
fha_claims.reasoning: The court ruled on damages availability (punitive damages barred against municipality under FHA; actual damages contingent on outcome of parallel state-court zoning litigation) but did not reach the merits of the underlying FHA discrimination claim, which remains set for trial on April 28, 2025. The court held that punitive damages are categorically unavailable against municipalities under the FHA, and that actual damages (lost profits) are speculative absent a legal entitlement to operate the facility, which depends on the state court's interpretation of the zoning code.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal protection claims (federal and state constitutional); ADA discriminatory administration and discriminatory requirements claims; state law claims
fha_claims.reasoning: The court addressed damages availability for federal constitutional claims under § 1983, state constitutional claims, and ADA claims, holding that punitive damages are unavailable against municipalities under all three theories. Actual damages remain contingent on the parallel state-court zoning litigation. The underlying merits of these claims remain pending for trial.

case_name: Sherri Strole v. Mark Wirth, et al.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation under § 3604(f)(3)(B) was at issue; plaintiff sought equal enforcement of park policies and equal access to amenities and community events on the same terms afforded to male tenants, constituting a sex/gender disparate-treatment discrimination claim rather than an accommodation request.
key_holding: On IFP screening under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2), plaintiff's FHA sex discrimination (disparate treatment), retaliation, and interference claims state plausible claims for relief and proceed, while her IIED claim is dismissed without prejudice for failure to allege sufficiently extreme and outrageous conduct.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Sherri Strole, a tenant at Fairgrounds RV LLC's RV park, brought FHA claims for sex/gender discrimination, retaliation, and coercion/interference, along with an IIED claim, alleging discriminatory enforcement of park policies, arbitrary rent increases, vandalism to her property, and exclusion from community activities based on her gender as compared to male tenants. The court conducted mandatory IFP screening and found the three FHA claims plausible on their face — allowing them to proceed — but dismissed the IIED claim without prejudice because the alleged conduct did not rise to the level of extreme and outrageous conduct required under Arizona law, granting leave to amend within thirty days. The court also denied plaintiff's motions for permanent anonymity and to compel arbitration without prejudice, while partially granting her motion to compel by ordering service by a U.S. Marshal.

case_name: Robert A. Johnson v. Raven Wood Homeowners Association, et al.
accommodation_description: Request that the HOA provide virtual/remote attendance option via Zoom at annual meetings as an accommodation for disability-related health risks during the COVID-19 pandemic
key_holding: Genuine disputes of material fact exist regarding whether Mr. Johnson is disabled within the FHA's definition, whether the accommodation was necessary and reasonable, and whether the HOA denied his request by failing to provide virtual meeting access, precluding summary judgment.
brief_summary: Disabled combat veteran Robert Johnson sued Raven Wood Homeowners Association alleging failure to provide reasonable accommodation under the FHA by denying his request to attend annual HOA meetings virtually via Zoom due to his health conditions. The court denied Defendants' motion for summary judgment, finding genuine disputes of material fact on all elements of the reasonable accommodation claim including disability status, necessity of the accommodation, reasonableness, and whether the HOA's actions constituted a denial.
key_cases_cited: DuBois v. Assoc. of Apartment Owners of 2987 Kalakaua, 453 F.3d 1175 (9th Cir. 2006)
Giebeler v. M & B Associates, 343 F.3d 1143 (9th Cir. 2003)
Reed v. Goertz, 598 U.S. 230 (2023)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Remote or virtual access to annual HOA meetings via Zoom platform to accommodate plaintiff's underlying health conditions and high-risk status for COVID-19 complications
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine disputes of material fact on all elements of the reasonable accommodation claim: (1) whether plaintiff's condition substantially limits major life activities under FHA definition; (2) whether defendants knew or should have known of the disability; (3) whether the accommodation was necessary to afford equal opportunity; (4) whether the accommodation was reasonable given the undue burden defense (limited resources, rural location, poor internet service); and (5) whether defendants actually denied the request or offered an alternative. Summary judgment was inappropriate where reasonable factfinders could differ on these issues.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: State law claims: violation of Cowlitz County Code 12.10.020 (private road standards), RCW 64.3.025(1) (standard of care), RCW 7.48.020 (nuisance), negligence, and common law infliction of emotional distress
fha_claims.reasoning: Court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over state and county law claims (Counts II, III, IV, VI) because they do not share a common nucleus of operative fact with the FHA claim. The facts regarding HOA governing documents, private road alterations, and stormwater management are distinct from the facts required to establish FHA disability discrimination. Claim V (infliction of emotional distress) was retained as it shares operative facts with the FHA claim.

key_holding: Section 3604(b) applies to post-acquisition HOA conduct affecting housing-related contractual rights under HOA rules, and Watts plausibly stated claims for racial discrimination under the FHA and Civil Rights Act by alleging the HOA selectively enforced rules against her and denied access to community amenities because of her race.
brief_summary: Sara Watts, an African American woman, sued her HOA alleging racial discrimination in post-acquisition enforcement actions including towing her son's car without proper notice, restricting basketball court access citing concerns about people of color, and subjecting her guests to false accusations. The Eleventh Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that Section 3604(b) covers HOA conduct affecting housing-related contractual rights under HOA rules, and Watts sufficiently alleged plausible claims for racial discrimination under the FHA and Civil Rights Act.
