Plaintiff also failed to allege how each defendant discriminated, what reasonable accommodations were requested, when requests were made, or how requests were reasonable.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodations necessary to safeguard health in rental unit; repairs and accommodations for uninhabitable conditions (plumbing issues, mold, vermin infestations)
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 504 claim against HopeLink dismissed because plaintiff failed to allege she was denied benefits solely by reason of disability. Plaintiff failed to describe her disability, how it qualifies under ADA, how she was otherwise qualified for benefits, what benefits were denied, or how denial was because of disability—failing to plead basic elements of § 504 claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, ADA Title III, breach of implied warranty of habitability, negligence per se, constructive eviction, breach of covenant of quiet enjoyment, intentional infliction of emotional distress, negligent infliction of emotional distress, negligence, breach of contract, breach of implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, tortious interference with contractual relations, negligent hiring/retention/supervision, fraudulent misrepresentation, unjust enrichment
fha_claims.reasoning: State law claims dismissed without prejudice due to lack of supplemental jurisdiction after federal claims were dismissed. Court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3) because federal claims were dismissed and it is preferable to remand remaining pendent claims to state court.

case_name: Jacqueline Buckholz v. Kelso Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Request for informal hearing to appeal housing voucher termination, or extension of tenancy, as reasonable accommodation for mental health disabilities affecting ability to meet appeal deadlines
key_holding: Plaintiff demonstrated serious questions going to the merits of her reasonable accommodation claim, irreparable harm from imminent eviction and homelessness, and the balance of hardships and public interest favored granting the preliminary injunction to reinstate her housing voucher.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Jacqueline Buckholz, an individual with mental health disabilities receiving Section 8 housing assistance, sued Kelso Housing Authority alleging the termination of her housing voucher violated the Fair Housing Act's reasonable accommodation requirement because her disability affected her ability to meet the deadline for requesting an informal hearing. The court granted Plaintiff's motion for preliminary injunction, finding she showed serious questions going to the merits, faced irreparable harm from imminent eviction, and the balance of equities and public interest favored enjoining the defendant from refusing to make housing assistance payments while the case proceeds.
key_cases_cited: Giebeler v. M & B Associates, 343 F.3d 1143 (9th Cir. 2003)
Winter v. Natural Res. Def. Council, 555 U.S. 7 (2008)
Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319 (1976)
Nozzi v. Hous. Auth. of City of Los Angeles, 806 F.3d 1178 (9th Cir. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation for mental health disability (anxiety, depression, bipolar disorder) in the form of: (1) granting an informal hearing to appeal the termination of housing voucher despite late filing; (2) extending tenancy until plaintiff could secure new housing; or (3) at minimum, extending tenancy until January 6, 2025. The accommodation was requested to address plaintiff's difficulty understanding procedural deadlines and written communications due to her mental health impairments.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff made a prima facie case under the four-part Giebeler test: (1) plaintiff suffers from a disability (mental impairment substantially limiting ability to concentrate and understand notifications); (2) defendant knew or reasonably should have known of the disability; (3) accommodation was necessary to afford equal opportunity to use and enjoy housing; and (4) defendant refused accommodation. Court applied direct balancing, finding the accommodation reasonable because it imposed no fundamental alteration and minimal burden on defendant, while plaintiff faced irreparable harm (eviction and homelessness).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Due Process Clause claim under the Fourteenth Amendment; Washington Law Against Discrimination (RCW 49.60.222); Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff showed a fair chance of prevailing on Due Process Clause claim by demonstrating: (1) housing voucher is a protected property interest under Mathews v. Eldridge; (2) risk of erroneous deprivation through procedures used (termination notice failed to inform plaintiff of right to reasonable accommodation as required by defendant's own Administrative Plan); and (3) minimal burden on defendant to provide informal hearing. Court did not substantively analyze the Washington Law Against Discrimination or Section 504 claims separately.

case_name: Newman v. State of Delaware
accommodation_description: Plaintiff Newman filed multiple incoherent complaints alleging a 'double dipping' rent scheme and various conspiracies, with one complaint mentioning the Fair Housing Act in connection with housing voucher payments but not asserting a cognizable reasonable accommodation claim.
key_holding: The Court dismissed all five Complaints as frivolous pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(i) because they relied on indisputably meritless legal theories and fantastic or delusional factual scenarios, with Plaintiff Newman having filed twenty-six previously dismissed complaints demonstrating a pattern of groundless litigation.
brief_summary: Pro se Plaintiff Shantell D. Newman filed five separate civil actions against various defendants including the State of Delaware, private landlords, and courthouse security officers, alleging federal criminal statutes, § 1983 civil rights claims, and Fair Housing Act violations stemming from an alleged rent scheme while she was homeless and pregnant. The Court dismissed all five Complaints as frivolous under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(i), finding the allegations were clearly baseless, relied on fantastic or delusional scenarios, and noting Plaintiff had filed twenty-six previously dismissed complaints demonstrating a pattern of groundless litigation.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged denial of housing assistance and rental payment support while pregnant; landlord allegedly denied help from agency that would have paid additional months of rent to allow plaintiff to give birth in peace
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint dismissed as frivolous under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(i) because it relies on indisputably meritless legal theories and arises from fantastic or delusional factual scenarios. The court did not engage substantively with the elements of any reasonable accommodation claim, applying only the frivolousness standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 due process claims, criminal violations under 18 U.S.C. §§ 242 and 245, state tort claims, Fair Debt Collection Practices Act violations, intellectual property claims, human trafficking and genocide allegations, Indian Removal Act claims, First Amendment and Second Amendment claims, Fourth Amendment claims
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA claims across the five consolidated complaints dismissed as frivolous under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(i) because they rely on indisputably meritless legal theories and fantastic or delusional factual scenarios, including allegations of fraudulent birth certificates, corporate slavery, human trafficking by state officials, genocide, and attempts on plaintiff's life.

case_name: Stansly T. Maponga v. Hall Park Hotel, et al.
accommodation_description: Maponga alleged generally that the hotel 'failed to accommodate' his 'back disability and cognitive impairments' under the ADA, but did not identify what specific accommodation was requested, denied, or needed, nor did he allege what major life activity was substantially limited.
key_holding: The court held that pro se plaintiff Maponga's amended complaint failed to state a claim upon which relief could be granted under the ADA, FHA, and all state law claims due to insufficient factual allegations, but granted leave to file a second amended complaint within 30 days.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Stansly Maponga sued Hall Park Hotel and two individuals alleging violations of the ADA and FHA, breach of contract, unjust enrichment, and intentional infliction of emotional distress, arising from his removal from the hotel 21 days into a 32-night stay after paying only $2,000 of a $12,000 agreed rate. Screening the complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B), the court found all claims deficient: the ADA and FHA claims lacked any factual allegations establishing a disability, discriminatory conduct, or how the defendants interfered with fair housing, while the state law claims failed for independent reasons. Rather than dismissing outright, the court afforded Maponga one additional opportunity to amend and cure the identified deficiencies.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged defendants 'failed to accommodate' his disabilities and 'imposed undue hardship' in violation of the FHA, but provided no specific factual allegations regarding what accommodation was requested or denied.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiff failed to allege facts showing he has a disability (did not specify which prong of the disability definition applied or what major life activity was substantially limited) and failed to allege facts showing the defendants failed to accommodate him based on disability. The fact pattern—making a reservation, paying less than agreed, and being removed—does not support a discrimination claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged defendants' 'actions interfered with [his] ability to secure fair housing and stability for his family' but did not point to any particular FHA provision, describe any conduct in violation of the Act, or explain how defendants allegedly discriminated against him. No factual allegations support an FHA violation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of contract, unjust enrichment, intentional infliction of emotional distress
fha_claims.reasoning: Breach of contract claim fails because plaintiff did not allege his own performance (he paid $2,000 of $12,000 owed, suggesting he breached first) or explain contract terms regarding payment timing and damages. Unjust enrichment claim fails because a valid contract already addresses the matter and plaintiff did not specify fraud, duress, or undue advantage. IIED claim fails because complaint alleges no conduct that is atrocious, intolerable, or intended to cause emotional distress—only that plaintiff made a reservation, underpaid, and was removed.

case_name: Quintin J. Ballentine v. Bowery Residence Committee
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: This transfer order does not address the merits of the FHA reasonable accommodation claim; the court transferred venue to the Eastern District of New York because the operative events occurred in Brooklyn, making EDNY a more convenient forum.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Quintin J. Ballentine, a shelter resident, brings Fair Housing Act and ADA claims against Bowery Residence Committee and government officials alleging violations at a Brooklyn shelter. The S.D.N.Y. court transferred this action to the Eastern District of New York, finding that venue was proper in EDNY where the underlying events occurred and that transfer served the convenience of parties and witnesses.
key_cases_cited: Keitt v. N.Y. City, 882 F. Supp. 2d 412 (S.D.N.Y. 2011)
N.Y. Marine and Gen. Ins. Co. v. LaFarge No. Am., Inc., 599 F.3d 102 (2d Cir. 2010)
D.H. Blair & Co. v. Gottdiener, 462 F.3d 95 (2d Cir. 2006)
Coppedge v. United States, 369 U.S. 438 (1962)

case_name: National Urban League et al. v. Trump
accommodation_description: This is not a reasonable accommodation case. Plaintiffs are nonprofit organizations challenging executive orders restricting DEI programs in federal contracts and grants on constitutional grounds (First and Fifth Amendment).
key_holding: Plaintiffs failed to show likelihood of success on the merits of their constitutional challenges to executive orders restricting DEI programs; the government's decision not to fund certain activities does not violate the First Amendment, and the challenged provisions are not facially invalid.
brief_summary: Three nonprofit organizations (National Urban League, National Fair Housing Alliance, AIDS Foundation of Chicago) sued President Trump and federal agencies to preliminarily enjoin enforcement of executive orders restricting DEI programs in federal contracts and grants, alleging First and Fifth Amendment violations. The court denied the preliminary injunction motion, finding plaintiffs lacked standing for some claims and failed to show likelihood of success on their facial constitutional challenges because the government may decline to fund certain activities and the executive orders do not facially violate constitutional rights.
key_cases_cited: Winter v. Nat. Res. Def. Council, 555 U.S. 7 (2008)
Agency for Int'l Dev. v. Alliance for Open Soc'y Int'l, Inc., 570 U.S. 205 (2013)
Rust v. Sullivan, 500 U.S. 173 (1991)
National Rifle Ass'n of Am. v. Vullo, 602 U.S. 175 (2024)
United States v. Hansen, 599 U.S. 762 (2023)

case_name: Sandpiper Residents Association v. United States Department of Housing & Urban Development
accommodation_description: Tenants at a deteriorating Section 8 project-based rental assistance property sought Tenant Protection Vouchers that would allow them to relocate to market-rate housing while continuing to receive HUD rental assistance.
key_holding: Although the D.C. Circuit reversed the district court's mootness holding, it affirmed dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6) because plaintiffs failed to state a plausible claim for voucher relief: the statutory condition requiring 'the owner' to have received a Notice of Default was not satisfied where the current owner Winnie Street had not received such notice.
brief_summary: Sandpiper Cove tenants and the resident association sued HUD seeking to compel issuance of Tenant Protection Vouchers to relocate from uninhabitable conditions at their Section 8 project-based rental assistance property in Galveston, Texas. The D.C. Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal, holding that despite errantly characterizing the issue as moot, the complaint failed to state a viable claim because the current property owner had not received a Notice of Default as required by the Consolidated Appropriations Act for HUD to issue vouchers.
key_cases_cited: Chafin v. Chafin, 568 U.S. 165 (2013)
Marino v. NOAA, 33 F.4th 593 (D.C. Cir. 2022)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Steel Co. v. Citizens for a Better Env't, 523 U.S. 83 (1998)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Issuance of Tenant Protection Vouchers to allow relocation from uninhabitable Section 8 project-based assistance property
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to state a plausible claim for intentional discrimination under the Fair Housing Act because they did not allege facts showing that the current owner (Winnie Street) had received a Notice of Default, which is a statutory prerequisite to HUD's authority to issue vouchers under the Consolidated Appropriations Act. The complaint's allegations were insufficient under the Iqbal/Twombly standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Administrative Procedure Act claim for arbitrary and capricious agency action; Fifth Amendment due process claim for intentional discrimination based on race and ethnicity
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to state a plausible claim under the Administrative Procedure Act or Fifth Amendment because they did not allege facts demonstrating that the current owner had received a Notice of Default, which is the statutory prerequisite for HUD's authority to issue vouchers. The complaint lacked sufficient factual allegations to support relief under these non-FHA theories.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Sex discrimination in membership denial and advertising practices under D.C. Human Rights Act of 1977 (DCHRA), D.C. Code § 2-1401.01 et seq.
fha_claims.disposition: Summary Judgment (Granted in Part); Bench Trial on Damages
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted plaintiff summary judgment on public-accommodation and advertising claims under DCHRA, finding defendant violated the statute by denying membership based on sex and engaging in discriminatory advertising. At bench trial, court awarded $1,000 compensatory damages and $2,000 punitive damages for the violations.

case_name: Katherine Trujillo v. Amity Plaza, LLC, Housing Authority of the City of Littleton, d/b/a South Metro Housing Options, and Frank Martinez
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; claims involve alleged sexual assault/harassment by maintenance employee and individual liability under the FHA for discriminatory housing practices.
key_holding: The court properly granted sua sponte summary judgment in favor of Frank Martinez because he is not a 'housing provider' under the FHA, had no authority over rental decisions as a maintenance employee, and no evidence established any quid pro quo relationship or discriminatory housing practice connected to his role.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Katherine Trujillo sued Amity Plaza LLC, the Housing Authority of the City of Littleton, and maintenance employee Frank Martinez for Fair Housing Act violations under §§ 3604(b) and 3617, alleging discriminatory conduct and seeking individual liability against the employee. The court denied Trujillo's motion to amend judgment and confirmed sua sponte summary judgment in favor of Martinez, finding that as a maintenance employee with no authority over housing decisions, he could not be held individually liable as a 'housing provider' under the FHA.
key_cases_cited: Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242 (1986)
Fielder v. Sterling Park Homeowners Ass'n, 914 F. Supp. 2d 1222 (W.D. Wash. 2012)
Lacour v. A&M Prop. Inv., LLC, No. CIV-23-370-J, 2024 WL 2988961 (W.D. Okla. May 28, 2024)
Metro. Fair Housing Council of Okla. v. Pelfrey, 292 F. Supp. 3d 1250 (W.D. Okla. 2017)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim involves alleged discriminatory conduct by individual maintenance employee, not accommodation request
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish that Frank Martinez, a maintenance employee without ownership or control over rental decisions, participated in, authorized, or ratified any discriminatory housing practice. The court found Martinez's actions were taken in his personal capacity, separate from his role as a maintenance employee, and that no quid pro quo relationship existed between Martinez and plaintiff.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; retaliation claim under § 3617 against individual maintenance employee
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish that Frank Martinez, as a non-housing provider and maintenance employee without authority over rental decisions, engaged in retaliation under § 3617. The court found no evidence that Martinez participated in any discriminatory housing practices or retaliation related to FHA-protected activity.

case_name: Heather Hogrobrooks Harris v. Wells Fargo Bank, N.A.
accommodation_description: This case concerns mortgage foreclosure proceedings and does not involve any disability accommodation request; plaintiff raised claims under Reconstruction Era civil rights statutes (§§ 1981, 1982, 1985(3)) and state consumer protection law.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's claims as barred by res judicata because the same claims had been raised and rejected in two prior lawsuits (Harris I and Harris II), and plaintiff failed to demonstrate any basis to overcome the res judicata bar.
brief_summary: Heather Hogrobrooks Harris filed her third lawsuit against Wells Fargo Bank and Wilson & Associates, raising claims under §§ 1981, 1982, and 1985(3) related to mortgage foreclosure proceedings that she had previously brought and lost in Harris I and Harris II. The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss, finding that the claims were barred by res judicata because they had been raised and rejected in prior litigation, and ordered Harris to show cause why she should not be subject to a pre-filing restriction for her repetitive, frivolous lawsuits.
key_cases_cited: Kane v. Magna Mixer Co., 71 F.3d 555 (6th Cir. 1995)
Federated Dep’t Stores, Inc. v. Moitie, 452 U.S. 394 (1981)
Chapman v. JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., 651 F. App'x 508 (6th Cir. 2016)
Wheeler v. Dayton Police Dep't, 807 F.3d 764 (6th Cir. 2015)
Ullmo ex rel. Ullmo v. Gilmour Acad., 273 F.3d 671 (6th Cir. 2001)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1982, 1985(3); breach of contract; fraudulent misrepresentation; Tennessee Consumer Protection Act; intentional infliction of emotional distress; malicious prosecution; abuse of process; misuse and abuse
fha_claims.reasoning: All claims are barred by res judicata because Harris raised substantially identical claims in Harris I and Harris II, which were adjudicated on the merits and affirmed by the Sixth Circuit. The Court found that Harris I ended in a final judgment on the merits (the Sixth Circuit affirmed on the alternative ground that the claims failed to state a claim), and all elements of res judicata were satisfied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Social Security disability benefits eligibility determination under 42 U.S.C. §§ 405(g) and 1383(c)(3); plaintiff challenged ALJ's residual functional capacity finding, evaluation of medical opinions, and assessment of symptomology
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the deferential substantial evidence standard and found that the ALJ's residual functional capacity determination was supported by medical records, prior administrative medical findings, and activities of daily living evidence; the ALJ properly evaluated medical opinions under 20 C.F.R. § 416.920c(a) focusing on supportability and consistency; and the ALJ's assessment of plaintiff's symptoms under SSR 16-3p was entitled to considerable deference and supported by the record.

case_name: Luis Ricardo Munroe v. New York University, Erin Jane Lynch, Legal Affairs Department, Office of Faculty Housing
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED - complaint asserts FHA claims but specific accommodation request not described in this service order
key_holding: No merits determination; Court granted Plaintiff in forma pauperis status and ordered service of process on Defendants New York University, Erin Jane Lynch, Legal Affairs Department, and Office of Faculty Housing.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Luis Ricardo Munroe, proceeding pro se and in forma pauperis, filed a complaint against New York University and related defendants asserting claims under the Fair Housing Act, Americans with Disabilities Act, and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act regarding faculty housing. The Court granted IFP status and issued this order directing the U.S. Marshals Service to effect service on Defendants — this is a procedural service order that does not address the merits of any claim.
key_cases_cited: Walker v. Schult, 717 F.3d 119 (2d Cir. 2013)
Meilleur v. Strong, 682 F.3d 56 (2d Cir. 2012)

case_name: Green v. Allied First Bank SB
accommodation_description: Plaintiff's complaint references Fair Housing Act but does not articulate a specific reasonable accommodation request; the case concerns mortgage loss-mitigation and foreclosure, not a disability accommodation request.
key_holding: The court granted Servbank's motion to dismiss because claim preclusion bars Green's second lawsuit, which involves the same parties, same court, same judgment on the merits, and the same nucleus of operative facts (loss-mitigation process and foreclosure) as her first lawsuit.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff LaKeisha C. Green filed her second lawsuit against Allied First Bank SB (Servbank) challenging the bank's loss-mitigation process and foreclosure on her home, invoking the Fair Housing Act and Equal Credit Opportunity Act. The court granted Servbank's motion to dismiss with prejudice, holding that claim preclusion bars the lawsuit because it involves the same parties, the same prior judgment on the merits, and the same nucleus of operative facts as Green's earlier lawsuit.
key_cases_cited: Test Masters Educ. Servs., Inc. v. Singh, 953 F.3d 311 (5th Cir. 2020)
Davis v. Wells Fargo, 824 F.3d 333 (3d Cir. 2016)
Oreck Direct, LLC v. Dyson, Inc., 560 F.3d 398 (5th Cir. 2009)
United States v. Davenport, 484 F.3d 321 (5th Cir. 2007)
Green v. Servbank, 2025 WL 777726 (S.D. Miss. Mar. 11, 2025)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act discrimination claim related to loss-mitigation process and foreclosure; also Equal Credit Opportunity Act claim under 15 U.S.C. § 1691e(a) and 18 U.S.C. § 2255 claim for emotional, mental, and physical injury
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the second lawsuit under claim preclusion (res judicata) because all four elements were satisfied: identical parties, competent jurisdiction in prior action, final judgment on the merits in the prior action, and the same nucleus of operative facts (Servbank's loss-mitigation process and foreclosure). The FHA and ECOA claims were barred by the final judgment in the first lawsuit.

case_name: Michael-Zahir David Fleming v. Westwood Apartments, LLC
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation was requested in this case. Fleming challenged a new parking policy requiring residents to park miles away from the apartment complex, framing this as a constitutional taking and due process violation rather than any accommodation request under the FHA.
key_holding: The court granted defendants' Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss because plaintiff failed to allege state action for his constitutional claims and failed to allege membership in a protected class for his FHA and § 1982 claims.
brief_summary: Pro se tenant Michael-Zahir David Fleming sued his apartment complex and property manager alleging violations of the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments, 42 U.S.C. §§ 1982 and 1983, the Fair Housing Act, and state conversion law, primarily challenging a new parking policy that he claimed infringed his property rights. The court dismissed all federal constitutional claims because Westwood, a private company, was not a state actor, and dismissed the FHA and § 1982 claims because Fleming explicitly failed to allege membership in any protected class or any discriminatory animus. The court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the remaining state law conversion claim, and all claims were dismissed without prejudice.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Lugar v. Edmondson Oil Co., 457 U.S. 922 (1982)
Jones v. Alfred H. Mayer Co., 392 U.S. 409 (1968)
Brentwood Academy v. Tenn. Secondary Sch. Athletic Ass'n, 531 U.S. 288 (2001)
White v. City of Annapolis ex rel. City Council, 439 F. Supp. 3d 522 (D. Md. 2020)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged discrimination in terms and conditions of rental (parking policy) but failed to allege membership in a protected class or discriminatory intent based on protected status.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege membership in a protected class (race, color, religion, sex, handicap, familial status, or national origin) as required to state an FHA claim under 42 U.S.C. §§ 3604(b) and 3605(a). The court dismissed for failure to plead a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1982 (racial discrimination in property rights); 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (constitutional claims under Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments); state law conversion claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege state action required for § 1983 claims (Takings Clause and Due Process Clause violations), failed to allege membership in a protected class or racial animus for § 1982 claim, and lacked diversity jurisdiction for state conversion claim, which was dismissed under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3).

source_file: 10548175_2025_Avila v. New York City Housing Authority_nysd
case_name: Jimmy Avila v. New York City Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges NYCHA failed to find him appropriate housing that accommodates his disabilities and that CIDNY terminated disability-related services.
key_holding: The Court dismissed plaintiff's amended complaint for failure to state a claim because plaintiff did not allege facts suggesting defendants violated his federal rights with respect to housing discrimination based on disability, race, or gender.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Jimmy Avila sued NYCHA and CIDNY alleging disability, race, and gender discrimination under the FHA, Rehabilitation Act, ADA, and Section 1983, claiming defendants failed to provide housing accommodating his disabilities and terminated needed services. The Court dismissed the amended complaint for failure to state a claim because plaintiff did not allege sufficient facts showing defendants discriminated against him based on protected characteristics.
key_cases_cited: Ruotolo v. City of New York, 514 F.3d 184 (2d Cir. 2008)
Salahuddin v. Cuomo, 861 F.2d 40 (2d Cir. 1988)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Appropriate housing that addresses plaintiff's disabilities
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) as frivolous because plaintiff failed to allege facts suggesting that NYCHA discriminated against him based on disability or failed to provide reasonable accommodation; the amended complaint's one-paragraph statement of facts was insufficient to state a plausible claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) because plaintiff failed to allege facts suggesting discrimination based on disability, race, or gender; no factual allegations supported intentional discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rehabilitation Act, Title II ADA, 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (Equal Protection Clause)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed non-FHA claims under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) because plaintiff failed to allege facts suggesting violations; the § 1983 Equal Protection claim lacked allegations of adverse treatment compared to similarly situated individuals.

case_name: Noureddine Ecasali v. Scott McMillin, et al.
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: The court dismissed the action under Rule 41(b) and its inherent authority for failure to prosecute after plaintiff failed to file an amended complaint by the court-ordered deadline and ignored an order to show cause, without reaching the merits of any fair housing claim.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Noureddine Ecasali filed suit against eighteen defendants alleging violations of the Federal Fair Housing Act, California Fair Housing Act, and the Fourteenth Amendment, but the court dismissed the action without prejudice for failure to prosecute after plaintiff failed to file an amended complaint despite court-ordered deadlines and ignored an order to show cause.
key_cases_cited: Ferdik v. Bonzelet, 963 F.2d 1258 (9th Cir. 1992)
Link v. Wabash R.R., 370 U.S. 626 (1962)
Edwards v. Marin Park, 356 F.3d 1058 (9th Cir. 2004)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not specified in opinion
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 41(b) dismissal for failure to prosecute
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to file an amended complaint within the court-ordered deadline and failed to respond to the show cause order. The court dismissed the action for failure to prosecute and comply with court orders under its inherent authority, applying the Ferdik factors.

case_name: Charles H.M.S. Sexton v. Department of Homeless Services, et al.
accommodation_description: Pro se plaintiff alleging discrimination and retaliation under the Fair Housing Act at multiple homeless shelters; specific accommodation request not described in detail in this screening order.
key_holding: Court dismissed most claims against city agencies (not suable entities), private shelter operators (not state actors for § 1983), and constitutional claims (no right to housing or investigation), but allowed service on seven defendants for potential FHA and § 1981 discrimination/retaliation claims.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Charles Sexton, a homeless individual, sued the NYC Department of Homeless Services, multiple private shelter operators (VOA, Westhab, Project Renewal, Breaking Ground), and numerous individual defendants claiming constitutional violations, FHA discrimination, and other federal claims arising from his stays at three homeless shelters. The court dismissed most claims on state action, municipal liability, and failure-to-state grounds, but allowed service to proceed on seven defendants for potential FHA and § 1981 discrimination and retaliation claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Rendell-Baker v. Kohn, 457 U.S. 830 (1982)
Fabrikant v. French, 691 F.3d 193 (2d Cir. 2012)
Lindsey v. Normet, 405 U.S. 56 (1972)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff may have alleged claims of discrimination and/or retaliation under the FHA against McBride, Henderson, David or Davis, the VOA, Westhab, Project Renewal, and Breaking Ground, but the court did not substantively analyze any FHA claim in this opinion.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that Plaintiff may have alleged sufficient facts to state claims of discrimination and/or retaliation under the FHA against certain defendants and directed service on those defendants. The court did not reach the merits of any FHA claim, but allowed the claims to proceed past the screening stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (due process, right to housing, duty to protect/investigate), ADA Title II, Rehabilitation Act § 504, HIPAA, Title VII, 18 U.S.C. §§ 1701, 1702, 1708 (criminal prosecution), New York State Human Rights Law, New York City Human Rights Law, § 1981
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed all non-FHA claims for failure to state a claim under the Iqbal/Twombly standard. HIPAA has no private right of action; Title VII does not apply to non-employment housing contexts; Title II ADA and Rehabilitation Act claims lacked factual support; § 1983 claims against municipal agencies and officers in official capacity were improper; § 1983 claims against the City of New York failed because plaintiff did not allege a municipal policy or custom; § 1983 claims based on a purported right to housing or duty to protect/investigate failed as a matter of law; § 1983 claims against private entities and shelter employees failed because they are not state actors; criminal prosecution claims failed for lack of standing; and § 1983 claims against individual NYC officers in individual capacity failed for lack of personal involvement allegations.

case_name: Tyeashia M. Blackburn; Lezlie E. Freeman v. Kelly Webb; Rent King, LLC
accommodation_description: No FHA accommodation was requested or at issue as a substantive claim. Plaintiffs raised for the first time on appeal an argument that the district court should have provided them ADA litigation accommodations for disabilities affecting their capacity to meet procedural requirements during periods of worsening health; this argument was forfeited because plaintiffs never requested such accommodations, a continuance, or any extension of time before the district court.
key_holding: The Tenth Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal with prejudice of plaintiffs' Fair Housing Act racial discrimination and retaliation claims as a sanction for repeated litigation misconduct, including failure to cooperate with discovery and chronic noncompliance with procedural rules and court orders.
brief_summary: Tyeashia Blackburn and Lezlie Freeman sued landlord Kelly Webb and Rent King, LLC under 42 U.S.C. § 3604 alleging racial discrimination and retaliation under the Fair Housing Act. The district court dismissed the case with prejudice pursuant to Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 16(f), 37(b)(2)(A), and 41(b) based on a pattern of discovery failures, unauthorized filings, and repeated noncompliance despite prior warnings. The Tenth Circuit affirmed, finding no abuse of discretion in the district court's application of the Ehrenhaus factors and declining to consider plaintiffs' forfeited ADA-accommodations argument raised for the first time on appeal.
key_cases_cited: Ehrenhaus v. Reynolds, 965 F.2d 916 (10th Cir. 1992)
Richison v. Ernest Grp., Inc., 634 F.3d 1123 (10th Cir. 2011)
Garrett v. Selby Connor Maddux & Janer, 425 F.3d 836 (10th Cir. 2005)
Clark v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 590 F.3d 1134 (10th Cir. 2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court dismissed the case with prejudice as a sanction for litigation misconduct (failure to comply with discovery obligations, procedural rules, and court orders) under Federal Rules 16(f), 37(b)(2)(A), and 41(b). The appellate court affirmed, finding no abuse of discretion in the sanction decision after applying the Ehrenhaus factors. The merits of the racial discrimination claim were never reached.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court dismissed the case with prejudice as a sanction for litigation misconduct. The appellate court affirmed, finding no abuse of discretion. The merits of the retaliation claim were never reached.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) reasonable accommodations for disabilities affecting capacity to meet procedural requirements
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs raised an ADA accommodations argument for the first time on appeal, claiming they should have received accommodations for disabilities affecting their ability to meet procedural requirements. The court held the argument forfeited because plaintiffs never requested ADA accommodations before the district court and never sought a continuance or extension of time. The court declined to consider the argument absent plain-error review.

case_name: Dawn M. Chappel v. Adams County Children's Services, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested injunctive relief preventing enforcement of a state court eviction order and allowing her to return to property at 211 Sunshine Ave., Winchester, Ohio, as relief for alleged FHA retaliation.
key_holding: The court adopted the Magistrate Judge's recommendation to deny preliminary injunction on the FHA retaliation claim because plaintiff failed to establish a substantial likelihood of success on the merits, presented no evidence of discriminatory animus beyond speculation, and the requested relief would not preserve the status quo.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Dawn Chappel, a Section 8 voucher holder, sued Adams County Children's Services, a police chief, and a housing authority official alleging FHA retaliation under § 3617, seeking preliminary injunctions to prevent enforcement of a state court eviction order and to obtain housing-related relief. The court adopted both Magistrate Judge R&Rs, denying the preliminary injunction motions because plaintiff failed to demonstrate a substantial likelihood of success on her retaliation claim, offered only speculation of discriminatory animus related to her status as a recovering drug addict, and sought relief inconsistent with the status quo.
key_cases_cited: Liberty Coins, LLC v. Goodman, 748 F.3d 682 (6th Cir. 2014)
Kooman v. Boulder Bluff Condos., 833 F. App'x 623 (6th Cir. 2020)
HDC, LLC v. City of Ann Arbor, 675 F.3d 608 (6th Cir. 2012)
Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Saudi Basic Indust. Corp., 544 U.S. 280 (2005)
Lawrence v. Welch, 531 F.3d 364 (6th Cir. 2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the Rooker-Feldman doctrine to bar the plaintiff's request for injunctive relief preventing enforcement of a state court eviction order, finding that the source of injury was the state-court judgment itself, placing the matter beyond federal subject-matter jurisdiction. Alternatively, even if Rooker-Feldman did not apply, the plaintiff failed to establish a substantial likelihood of success on the merits of the FHA retaliation claim under the four-factor preliminary injunction test, as she presented no evidence of discriminatory animus and speculation regarding the defendant's motivation was insufficient.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fourteenth Amendment substantive due process claim, Fourteenth Amendment procedural due process claim, Fourth Amendment claim
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that the plaintiff's constitutional claims relating to temporary removal of children and searches/seizures between November 14-23, 2022 could not be redressed through the injunctive relief requested (preventing enforcement of an eviction order from August 2024), as there was a threshold mismatch between the alleged injury and the requested remedy.

source_file: 10581724_2025_U.S. Bank, National Association as legal title trustee v. Valeria Taveras_ca11
case_name: U.S. Bank, National Association as Legal Title Trustee for Truman 2016 SC6 Title Trust v. Taveras
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation was requested. The Fair Housing Act was invoked solely as a predicate for civil-rights removal under 28 U.S.C. § 1443; the Taverases argued that Florida's foreclosure procedures reflected a systemic policy of racial discrimination that denied them rights under the FHA, the Civil Rights Acts of 1866 and 1964, and the Equal Protection Clause.
key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the district court's remand of a state foreclosure action and its award of costs and fees to U.S. Bank, holding that the Taverases failed the second prong of the Rachel test for § 1443 civil-rights removal because they could not demonstrate that their federal civil rights would be predictably denied by Florida courts, and that their second removal attempt on the eve of a dispositive hearing was objectively unreasonable.
brief_summary: The Taverases defaulted on their Florida mortgage in 2008 and faced a state-court foreclosure by U.S. Bank. Two days before a 2023 summary-judgment hearing, they attempted for the second time to remove the case to federal court, asserting jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331, 1332, and 1443, and alleging that Florida's foreclosure system embodied a policy of racial discrimination that violated the Civil Rights Acts and the Fair Housing Act. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the district court's remand, finding the Taverases failed both prongs of the Rachel civil-rights-removal test and that no diversity or federal-question jurisdiction existed, and affirmed the award of costs and fees because the removal lacked an objectively reasonable basis.
key_cases_cited: Georgia v. Rachel, 384 U.S. 780 (1966)
Greenwood v. Peacock, 384 U.S. 808 (1966)
Johnson v. Mississippi, 421 U.S. 213 (1975)
Sofarelli v. Pinellas County, 931 F.2d 718 (11th Cir. 1991)
BP P.L.C. v. Mayor of Balt., 593 U.S. 230 (2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: No accommodation requested. This is a mortgage foreclosure case in which defendants invoked the Fair Housing Act only as one of several federal civil rights statutes in an attempt to establish removal jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1443. The FHA was cited solely to satisfy the first prong of the Georgia v. Rachel test for civil rights removal, not to allege a substantive FHA violation or request any accommodation.
fha_claims.disposition: 28 U.S.C. § 1447(c) remand with costs and fees
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court affirmed the district court's remand because defendants failed to satisfy the second prong of the § 1443 removal test: they did not demonstrate that their federal civil rights (including those under the Fair Housing Act) would be predictably denied by Florida courts. No federal civil rights law grants mortgagors a right to default on loans or immunizes them from foreclosure, and defendants alleged no facts suggesting the facially neutral foreclosure action was filed for a discriminatory purpose. The FHA claim was not a substantive housing discrimination claim but merely one of several statutes cited in a jurisdictional removal argument.

case_name: Tony Cole v. Joseph Faulkner, et al.
accommodation_description: Cole alleged retaliation under the Fair Housing Act for asserting his legal rights related to the property at issue in eviction proceedings.
key_holding: Cole's FHA retaliation claim fails because he failed to allege what specific right under §§ 3603, 3604, 3605, or 3606 he was exercising that triggered the anti-retaliation provision of § 3617, merely alleging he was asserting 'legal rights related to the property' generally.
brief_summary: Tony Cole sued Joseph Faulkner and others alleging retaliatory eviction under the Fair Housing Act and constitutional claims after being evicted from a building in Chicago through state court proceedings. The court granted reconsideration on jurisdictional grounds but ultimately maintained dismissal of Cole's claims, finding his FHA retaliation claim failed because he did not adequately allege the specific right he was exercising under the Act, and his § 1983 claim failed because private defendants did not act under color of state law.
key_cases_cited: Gilbank v. Wood Cnty. Dep't of Hum. Servs., 111 F.4th 754 (7th Cir. 2024)
Johnson v. Pushpin Holdings, LLC, 748 F.3d 769 (7th Cir. 2014)
Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Saudi Basic Industries Corp., 544 U.S. 280 (2005)
Wang v. City of Indianapolis, No. 24-2664, 2025 WL 1000158 (7th Cir. Apr. 3, 2025)
Hu v. Huey, 325 F. App'x 436 (7th Cir. 2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege what specific right under § 3603, 3604, 3605, or 3606 he was exercising when allegedly retaliated against. Mere assertion of 'legal rights related to the property' generally does not satisfy the pleading standard for FHA retaliation under § 3617.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 due process violation, state-law fraudulent transfer, state-law retaliatory eviction, state-law legal malpractice
fha_claims.reasoning: § 1983 claim dismissed for failure to allege defendants acted under color of state law; mere use of state courts by private parties does not constitute state action. State-law claims dismissed for lack of supplemental jurisdiction after federal claims were dismissed.

source_file: 10583019_2025_Dogbe v. The Lakes at Lemmon Valley, LLC_nvd
case_name: John Dogbe and Alberta Dogbe v. The Lakes at Lemmon Valley, LLC
accommodation_description: No accommodation request - case concerns alleged racial discrimination in eviction and enforcement of clubhouse policies
key_holding: The court denied dismissal of plaintiffs' racial discrimination claims under § 1981, § 1982, § 3604(b) disparate treatment, and § 3617 because plaintiffs sufficiently alleged that but-for their race, the party would not have been shut down and they would not have received an eviction notice.
brief_summary: African American tenants John and Alberta Dogbe sued their landlord The Lakes at Lemmon Valley, LLC alleging racial discrimination after their clubhouse party was shut down and they received an eviction notice while similarly-situated white residents had not faced such actions. The court granted in part and denied in part defendant's motion to dismiss, dismissing disparate impact claims but allowing disparate treatment claims under § 3604(b) and § 3617 to proceed because plaintiffs sufficiently alleged race was a but-for cause of the eviction notice.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Morris v. West Hayden Estates First Addition Homeowners Ass'n, Inc., 104 F.4th 1128 (9th Cir. 2024)
Texas Dept. of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Comcast Corp. v. Nat'l Ass'n of African Am.-Owned Media, 589 U.S. 327 (2020)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs sufficiently alleged facts plausibly suggesting that race was a but-for cause of the party shutdown and eviction notice by alleging comparator evidence of similarly situated white and other-race tenants who held similar parties without incident and were not evicted. The claim survives the motion to dismiss under the Iqbal/Twombly standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to allege what specific policies or procedures regarding the Clubhouse or eviction existed, and in fact cast doubt on whether any such policies existed at all. A disparate impact claim requires identification of a specific policy or practice; allegations of unfair application without identifying the underlying policy are insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly. Leave to amend is granted.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Hostile housing environment based on race; party shutdown and eviction notice
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs sufficiently alleged a hostile housing environment claim under § 3604(b) by alleging severe harassment (party shutdown and eviction notice) based on race, with comparator evidence showing white and other-race residents were not similarly treated. The Ninth Circuit recognizes that eviction notices constitute severe harassment sufficient to support a § 3604(b) disparate treatment claim when factually tied to a protected characteristic.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Interference with right to enjoy apartment free from racial discrimination through party shutdown and eviction notice
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs sufficiently alleged a § 3617 violation by alleging that Defendant broke up the party and issued an eviction notice because of Plaintiffs' race, thereby interfering with their right to take and enjoy possession of their home free from racial discrimination. The FAC adds factual allegations supporting this conclusion through comparator evidence.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1981 (equal contracting rights); 42 U.S.C. § 1982 (equal property rights); NRS 118.120 (Nevada fair housing law); NRS 118A.390 (constructive eviction); breach of contract; breach of implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing; IIED; NIED
fha_claims.reasoning: § 1981 and § 1982 claims survive because Plaintiffs alleged facts plausibly suggesting race was a but-for cause of injury under the Comcast standard. NRS 118.120 survives because it mirrors the FHA and Plaintiffs stated a colorable claim. NRS 118A.390 survives because Plaintiffs alleged an unlawful eviction notice based on illegal discrimination. Breach of contract survives because Plaintiffs alleged the four required elements. Breach of implied covenant survives because Plaintiffs alleged conduct distinct from the breach of contract claim (fabrication of the verbal assault allegation and selective enforcement based on race). IIED is dismissed without leave to amend because Plaintiffs failed to allege facts supporting severe emotional distress beyond conclusory statements, but leave to amend is granted. NIED is dismissed because Plaintiffs failed to allege factual allegations establishing what duty of care was owed or how it was breached, but leave to amend is granted.

case_name: Christopher K. Andersen v. Olympus at Daybreak
accommodation_description: Plaintiff seeks TRO to enjoin unlawful detainer action and prevent eviction as reasonable accommodation for disability-related claims (water-heater repair requests and mental health impacts).
key_holding: The court denied the TRO because Andersen failed to demonstrate irreparable harm—he voluntarily surrendered his apartment and obtained alternative housing, undercutting his claim of imminent injury from the pending unlawful detainer action.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Christopher K. Andersen, a tenant facing eviction from Olympus at Daybreak apartments, moved for a temporary restraining order to enjoin the unlawful detainer action, prevent reporting of eviction records, and halt collection of early termination fees, asserting Fair Housing Act and ADA claims based on disability-related repair requests and retaliation. The court denied the motion without prejudice, finding Andersen failed to demonstrate irreparable harm because he voluntarily surrendered the apartment and obtained alternative housing, mooting his claim of imminent injury from the pending state court eviction proceedings.
key_cases_cited: Colorado v. EPA, 989 F.3d 874 (10th Cir. 2021)
Mrs. Fields Franchising, LLC v. MFGPC, 941 F.3d 1221 (10th Cir. 2019)
Diné Citizens Against Ruining Our Env't v. Jewell, 839 F.3d 1276 (10th Cir. 2016)
McNeill v. NYC Hous. Auth., 719 F. Supp. 233 (S.D.N.Y. 1989)
Schiermeyer on Behalf of Blockchain Game Partners, Inc. v. Thurston, 746 F. Supp. 3d 1188 (D. Utah 2024)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Repair of water heater defect; plaintiff alleges defendants ignored eight written requests to repair and encouraged him to move, constituting retaliation and constructive eviction
fha_claims.reasoning: Court declined to opine on likelihood of success on merits of FHA claims and denied TRO/PI motion on grounds that plaintiff failed to demonstrate irreparable injury and that requested relief was not narrowly tailored to remedy discrimination under the FHA. Claims survive but injunctive relief denied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Repair of water heater defect; plaintiff alleges defendants failed to provide reasonable accommodation by ignoring eight written requests to repair a defective water heater
fha_claims.reasoning: Court declined to opine on likelihood of success on merits and denied TRO/PI motion on grounds that plaintiff failed to demonstrate irreparable injury and that requested relief (halting state court action, preventing dissemination of eviction information, enjoining collection of fees) was not narrowly tailored to remedy the alleged accommodation failure.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II/III claim; § 1983 due process claim; state law claims including breach of contract, breach of implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, abuse of process, failure to train, failure to supervise, defamation, negligent infliction of emotional distress, intentional infliction of emotional distress, and wrongful eviction
fha_claims.reasoning: Court declined to opine on likelihood of success on merits of non-FHA claims and denied TRO/PI motion on grounds that plaintiff failed to demonstrate irreparable injury and that requested relief was not narrowly tailored to remedy any alleged violations. Claims survive but injunctive relief denied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III claim for failure to install grab bars in shower to accommodate vertigo; defamation claim against Ms. Hall
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the ADA Title III claim as frivolous because private apartment rentals do not fall within the ADA's definition of public accommodations. The defamation claim against Ms. Hall was also dismissed because plaintiff failed to allege the statement was made to a third person, as required under Wisconsin law.

case_name: United States of America v. Javier Salazar, Jr., et al.
accommodation_description: The underlying accommodation or FHA violation at issue is not described in this order, which addresses only the procedural motion to set aside default judgment; the complaint references enforcement of the FHA on behalf of Angela McGinnis but no specifics of the alleged violation or requested accommodation are disclosed in the text of this order.
key_holding: The court adopted the magistrate judge's findings and recommendations and denied defendants' motion to set aside the default judgment previously entered in favor of the United States in this Fair Housing Act enforcement action, holding that the relevant factors weighed in favor of maintaining the default judgment.
brief_summary: The United States filed a Fair Housing Act enforcement action on behalf of Angela McGinnis against Javier Salazar Jr., Javier Salazar Sr., and Ricardo Covarrubias, and obtained a default judgment against defendants in October 2024. Defendants, through newly retained counsel, moved to set aside the default judgment in November 2024. The court adopted the magistrate judge's findings and recommendations — to which no party filed objections — and denied the motion, concluding that the factors governing relief from a default judgment weighed in favor of maintaining it.
key_cases_cited: Brandt v. Am. Bankers Ins. Co. of Fla., 653 F.3d 1108 (9th Cir. 2011)
U.S. v. Aguilar, 782 F.3d 1101 (9th Cir. 2015)
U.S. v. Signed Personal Check No. 730 of Yubran S. Mesle, 615 F.3d 1085 (9th Cir. 2010)
Wilkerson v. Wheeler, 772 F.3d 834 (9th Cir. 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not specified in opinion; case involves enforcement action by United States on behalf of Angela McGinnis under Title VIII FHA
fha_claims.reasoning: Court adopted magistrate judge's findings and recommendations granting default judgment against defendants who failed to respond to enforcement action. The opinion does not specify the underlying FHA violation alleged, only that the United States brought the action on behalf of Angela McGinnis under Title VIII.

case_name: 8214 Wilson Drive, LLC v. Daugherty
accommodation_description: The underlying eviction dispute allegedly involves disability and familial status discrimination under the FHA, but no specific accommodation request is identified in the record.
key_holding: The court lacked subject-matter jurisdiction because removal under 28 U.S.C. § 1443(1) requires reliance on laws providing equal civil rights in terms of racial equality, and Daugherty's claims of disability and familial status discrimination did not satisfy this requirement; additionally, the Rooker-Feldman doctrine and Younger abstention barred federal review.
brief_summary: Daugherty, acting as trustee of RLD Ministry Trust, removed a Nebraska landlord-tenant eviction proceeding to federal court alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on disability and familial status discrimination, along with constitutional claims. The court granted in forma pauperis status but remanded the case to state court for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, holding that 28 U.S.C. § 1443(1) only authorizes removal for racial equality claims, and alternatively that Rooker-Feldman and Younger abstention doctrines barred federal review of the state court proceedings.
key_cases_cited: Westridge Place Apartments LP v. Delph, 744 F. App'x 333 (8th Cir. 2018)
Neal v. Wilson, 112 F.3d 351 (8th Cir. 1997)
Georgia v. Rachel, 384 U.S. 780 (1966)
Rooker v. Fidelity Trust Co., 263 U.S. 413 (1923)
Younger v. Harris, 401 U.S. 37 (1971)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unspecified reasonable accommodation related to disability; complaint alleges discrimination on the basis of disability in violation of the Fair Housing Act
fha_claims.disposition: Remanded for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked subject-matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1443(1) because the removal was improper; § 1443(1) requires reliance on a law providing for equal civil rights stated in terms of racial equality, and plaintiff alleged discrimination based on disability, familial status, and religion. The court also applied Rooker-Feldman and Younger abstention doctrines, concluding it could not exercise jurisdiction without effectively reviewing state court decisions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination on the basis of familial status in violation of the Fair Housing Act
fha_claims.disposition: Remanded for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked subject-matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1443(1) because removal was improper; § 1443(1) requires reliance on a law providing for equal civil rights stated in terms of racial equality, and plaintiff alleged discrimination based on familial status, disability, and religion. Rooker-Feldman and Younger abstention also barred federal jurisdiction.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Deprivation of property without due process under the Fourteenth Amendment; religious discrimination; violations of 42 U.S.C. §§ 1982 and 1983
fha_claims.disposition: Remanded for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked subject-matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1443(1) because removal was improper; § 1443(1) requires reliance on a law providing for equal civil rights stated in terms of racial equality. The existence of federal defenses to state law claims does not permit removal. Rooker-Feldman and Younger abstention also barred federal jurisdiction.

case_name: Jimmy Avila; Mezie Oduka v. Danisha Davis; Lindsey M. Blackwell; City of New York; NYC Department of Housing Preservation and Development; Jane Doe; John Doe; Symone Elizabeth Sylvester; 1412 Col LLC; Basics, Inc.; JSAF Management LLC; Adult Protective Services; NYC Department of Homeless Services; City FHEPS; Breaking Ground; Harlem YMCA; Andrew Brain Bittens Esq.; Bronx Works; Office of Mental Health
subsidy_program: City Family Homelessness and Eviction Prevention Supplement (City FHEPS)
accommodation_description: This screening order does not substantively analyze any reasonable accommodation request; it addresses municipal liability under state law and service of process issues.
key_holding: The Court dismissed claims against municipal agencies (NYC HPD, DHS, APS, City FHEPS) because NYC agencies are not suable entities under N.Y. City Charter ch. 17, § 396, but ordered service on remaining private and individual defendants.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Jimmy Avila and Mezie Oduka sued numerous defendants including private landlords, property management companies, and NYC municipal agencies for alleged violations of the ADA and Fair Housing Act. The Court dismissed claims against municipal agencies on the ground that NYC agencies cannot be sued as separate entities, while ordering service on remaining named defendants.
key_cases_cited: Valentin v. Dinkins, 121 F.3d 72 (2d Cir. 1997)
Jenkins v. City of New York, 478 F.3d 76 (2d Cir. 2007)
Emerson v. City of New York, 740 F. Supp. 2d 385 (S.D.N.Y. 2010)
Walker v. Schult, 717 F.3d 119 (2d Cir. 2013)
Meilleur v. Strong, 682 F.3d 56 (2d Cir. 2012)

case_name: Pamela Shomo & DeJa Shomo v. Karen Cooksey, et al.
accommodation_description: Request to keep an emotional support animal (dog named King) in the apartment as a reasonable accommodation, which was allegedly not considered before eviction.
key_holding: The FHA failure to accommodate claim was dismissed because the amended complaint failed to allege any qualifying disability, any request for reasonable accommodation, how the accommodation was reasonable and necessary, or that defendants refused any such request.
brief_summary: Pamela and DeJa Shomo sued Columbia Glade Apartments and its manager Karen Cooksey alleging that their eviction violated the Fair Housing Act on both racial discrimination and failure to accommodate an emotional support animal grounds. The court granted Cooksey's motion to dismiss, finding the amended complaint failed to state plausible FHA claims because it did not allege a qualifying disability, did not allege a request for accommodation was made, and did not allege defendants refused such a request.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Bryant Woods Inn, Inc. v. Howard County, Maryland
Greengael, LLC v. Bd. of Supervisors

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged only that she is Black but failed to allege any discriminatory comments, comparator evidence, or facts showing the eviction was motivated by discriminatory purpose. Absent factual allegations of discriminatory intent, the race discrimination claim fails under Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retention of emotional support animal (dog named King) in apartment despite incident with neighbor's dog
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege: (1) any qualifying disability; (2) that she made any request for reasonable accommodation; (3) how the accommodation was reasonable and necessary; or (4) that defendants refused any such request. The complaint lacks the factual allegations necessary to state a plausible failure-to-accommodate claim under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of contract claim for violation of Service Animal Amendment to lease
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege any contract between plaintiff and defendant Cooksey. As an office manager, Cooksey would not be a party to the lease; the lease would be with Columbia Glade. Therefore, no basis exists for a breach of contract claim against Cooksey.

source_file: 10587034_2025_APPELGREN v. ISLAND HOSPITALITY MANAGEMENT VII, LLC_njd
case_name: Mark Appelgren v. Island Hospitality Management VII, LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought a quiet, stress-free environment and room modifications during a hotel stay to manage his anxiety disorder, IBS, and other disabilities, but he did not inform hotel staff of his disabilities.
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA and ADA reasonable accommodation claims fail because he never informed hotel staff of his disabilities, so Defendants could not have known why he made any requests and cannot be liable for refusing accommodations they were unaware were sought.
brief_summary: Mark Appelgren, a federal agent with severe anxiety, depression, and IBS, sued Island Hospitality Management and Hilton alleging discrimination during an attempted hotel stay where he experienced delays, hostile interactions, and a chaotic lobby environment that triggered his anxiety and IBS symptoms. The Court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that because Plaintiff never informed hotel staff of his disabilities, Defendants could not be held liable for failing to accommodate those disabilities.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Revock v. Cowpet Bay W. Condo. Ass'n, 853 F.3d 96 (3d Cir. 2017)
Yates Real Est., Inc. v. Plainfield Zoning Bd. of Adjustment, 404 F. Supp. 3d 889 (D.N.J. 2019)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Quiet, stress-free environment and room modifications to accommodate severe social anxiety, generalized anxiety disorder, panic attacks, severe depression, IBS, and long-haul COVID during hotel check-in and stay
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege that he informed Defendants of his disabilities or made any specific accommodation request that Defendants could understand. Without notice of the disability and a clear request for accommodation, Defendants cannot be held liable for failure to accommodate under the FHA. The vague allegations regarding requests for 'a quiet, stress-free environment' and 'room modifications' do not plausibly allege that Defendants knew why Plaintiff made these requests or that they refused a known accommodation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III public accommodations claim; also state law claims for failure to train and supervise, gross negligence, breach of duty of care, breach of contract, intentional infliction of emotional distress, breach of implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, and unjust enrichment
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA Title III claim dismissed for failure to state a claim (same deficiency as FHA claim—no allegation that Defendants knew of disability) and because Title III defendants cannot be liable for money damages, which is all Plaintiff seeks. State law claims dismissed without prejudice under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3) because all federal claims were dismissed and supplemental jurisdiction was declined.

case_name: Patsy Jay v. Grand Management Services, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff made a verbal request to keep her mobility walker on her porch as a disability accommodation, which defendants did not respond to, and later cited the walker as a lease violation in the eviction notice issued after plaintiff reported McKnight's sexual assault.
key_holding: The court denied summary judgment on plaintiff's hostile living environment and retaliation claims because genuine issues of material fact existed regarding whether defendants' failure to evict McKnight and issuance of an eviction notice to plaintiff constituted disability discrimination and unlawful retaliation under § 3617.
brief_summary: Patsy Jay, a mobility-disabled elderly tenant, sued Grand Management Services and related defendants alleging they failed to protect her from a neighbor who sexually assaulted and stalked her, issued a retaliatory eviction notice after she reported the assault, and discriminated against her based on disability by failing to accommodate her need to keep a walker on her porch. The court denied summary judgment on plaintiff's hostile living environment and retaliation claims, finding genuine disputes of material fact regarding defendants' knowledge of the neighbor's dangerous behavior toward women and whether the eviction notice was retaliation for plaintiff's protected activity.
key_cases_cited: Ellison v. Brady, 924 F.2d 872 (9th Cir. 1991)
San Pedro Hotel Co. v. City of Los Angeles, 159 F.3d 470 (9th Cir. 1998)
Walker v. City of Lakewood, 272 F.3d 1114 (9th Cir. 2001)
Miller v. Tabor W. Inv. Co., 223 Or. App. 700 (2008)
McAlpine v. Multnomah County, 166 Or. App. 472 (2000)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to keep a walker on plaintiff's front patio despite lease provision restricting items on patios; plaintiff sought exception to patio policy due to mobility disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine dispute of material fact as to whether defendants communicated approval of the accommodation request to plaintiff. Defendants failed to provide documentation of communication, making credibility determination necessary at trial. Viewing evidence in light most favorable to plaintiff, court denied summary judgment on the fifth element of the Dubois test (refusal to accommodate).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claim alleges hostile sexual living environment created by co-tenant John McKnight's conduct (sexual assault on July 12, 2021, and subsequent stalking and harassment through August 2021)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied five-part Neudecker test adapted from Eighth Circuit for co-tenant harassment claims. Court found genuine issues of material fact on elements 2 (unwanted harassment), 4 (severity/pervasiveness), and 5 (awareness/failure to remedy). July 12 sexual assault was severe; subsequent daily stalking and threatening gestures created pervasive harassment. Defendants were aware of McKnight's pattern of harassment toward women through AppFolio documentation and direct complaints. Court found conduct resembled or exceeded severity in Ellison v. Brady.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Issuance of August 20, 2021 eviction notice (14/30 notice) alleging multiple lease violations including walker on patio, watching McKnight with binoculars, and caretaker's aggressive conduct toward management
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied three-part San Pedro Hotel test for § 3617 retaliation claims. Court found genuine disputes on all three elements: (1) protected activity (reporting McKnight's assault); (2) adverse housing action (eviction notice constitutes coercion/intimidation/threat); (3) causal nexus (timing three months after initial report, disputed factual basis for notice allegations, and walker issue previously unaddressed). Plaintiff's account of events, if believed, would show retaliatory motive. Temporal proximity and circumstantial evidence of retaliatory intent precluded summary judgment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Issuance of March 2023 eviction notice (14/30 notice) for alleged failure to provide required recertification documents
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted summary judgment on this portion of the retaliation claim because plaintiff offered no evidence linking the March 2023 paperwork miscommunication to her complaints about McKnight from July-August 2021. The temporal gap of one and a half years, combined with no evidence that the new manager (Elrod) was aware of or involved in the McKnight complaints, precluded any reasonable inference of causal nexus.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Oregon common law negligence claim: (1) negligent violation of duty to recognize obligations under law and refrain from discrimination; (2) negligent violation of duty to provide reasonably safe dwelling. Defendants moved for summary judgment only on the second allegation.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied Oregon landlord-tenant law foreseeability standard. Court found genuine issue of material fact as to whether defendants knew or should have known McKnight posed a danger to plaintiff. Defendants were aware through AppFolio and direct complaints of at least ten allegations against McKnight between September 2018 and March 2021, including stalking, window-staring, threatening comments, gun-display, and at least two explicit sexual misconduct allegations. Common threads between past conduct (stalking, following, threatening, displaying gun) and conduct toward plaintiff (same behaviors plus sexual assault) created foreseeable risk. Court rejected 'mere facilitation' defense and found conduct exceeded what was foreseeable in Miller v. Tabor W. Inv. Co.

case_name: Robert L. Hatcher v. Sylvain Yang and Travis Smith
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested to continue parking his vehicle in the back yard of the duplex property due to his disability-related limitations.
key_holding: The court denied Defendant Yang's motion to dismiss because he failed to demonstrate that dismissal was proper, as he submitted unsworn statements outside the pleadings and cited no legal authority addressing the FHA.
brief_summary: Robert L. Hatcher, a 74-year-old disabled African American man, sued his private landlord Sylvain Yang alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act, including that Yang refused to make reasonable accommodations for his disability (allowing him to park in the back yard and be excused from lease maintenance obligations) and discriminated against him based on disability and race by showing favorable treatment to a new tenant. The court denied Yang's motion to dismiss because he failed to meet his burden, submitting only unsubstantiated facts outside the pleadings without supporting legal authority.
key_cases_cited: North Mill Street, LLC v. City of Aspen, 6 F.4th 1216 (10th Cir. 2021)
Cuervo v. Sorenson, 112 F.4th 1307 (10th Cir. 2024)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exemption from or modification of lease requirement to perform maintenance work on the property due to plaintiff's physical disabilities (hypertension, cardiovascular disease, arm/feet/leg pain) and mental health conditions
fha_claims.reasoning: Defendant failed to cite legal authority or explain why plaintiff's FHA reasonable accommodation claim fails under Rule 12(b)(6); court cannot consider facts outside the pleadings, and defendant's unsupported statement of facts does not meet the burden for dismissal. Complaint survives motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Continued permission to park plaintiff's vehicle in the back yard after defendant rented adjacent property to new tenant, based on plaintiff's prior use and disability-related need (vehicle previously hit twice by hit-and-run drivers)
fha_claims.reasoning: Defendant failed to cite legal authority or explain why plaintiff's FHA reasonable accommodation claim for continued parking fails under Rule 12(b)(6); court cannot consider facts outside the pleadings. Complaint survives motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination based on disability and race by showing favorable treatment to new tenant (Mr. Ken) while denying plaintiff reasonable accommodation for parking
fha_claims.reasoning: Defendant failed to cite legal authority or explain why plaintiff's FHA disparate treatment claim based on disability and race fails under Rule 12(b)(6). Complaint survives motion to dismiss.

case_name: Deepa Patel et al. v. City of Stanton et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs are motel business operators challenging revocation of their motel permit and business license by the City of Stanton as violating procedural due process; the case does not involve a reasonable accommodation request.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' procedural due process claim with prejudice because plaintiffs lacked standing to challenge the permit revocation, received constitutionally adequate notice and hearing for the business license revocation, failed to adequately plead a Haas claim regarding hearing officer bias, and had no protected property interest in their business license under the Stanton Municipal Code's discretionary revocation provisions.
brief_summary: Motel operators Ahir and Megha Hospitality LLC sued the City of Stanton alleging violations of their Fourteenth Amendment procedural due process rights when the City revoked their motel permit and business license without adequate notice. The court granted the City's motion to dismiss, finding plaintiffs lacked standing to challenge the permit revocation, received constitutionally adequate process for the business license revocation, failed to state a Haas claim for hearing officer bias, and had no protected property interest in their business license.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Lujan v. Defs. of Wildlife
Mullane v. Cent. Hanover Bank & Tr. Co.
Town of Castle Rock v. Gonzales

source_file: 10590335_2025_Turner v. Autumn Lake Property Owners Association, Inc._txsd
case_name: Dennis Turner and Darlene Brooks v. Autumn Lake Property Owners Association Inc.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request was made; this is an HOA fee overcharge dispute where plaintiffs attempted to invoke the FHA in their objection without pleading any discrimination in the complaint.
key_holding: The case was dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction because plaintiffs failed to plead any discrimination allegations in their complaint, and their objection attempting to invoke the Fair Housing Act was meritless.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Dennis Turner and Darlene Brooks sued Autumn Lake Property Owners Association Inc. alleging the HOA overcharged them fees. The court dismissed the case for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction because plaintiffs failed to plead any discrimination allegations in their complaint, and their attempt to invoke the Fair Housing Act in an objection was insufficient to establish jurisdiction.
key_cases_cited: United States v. Wilson, 864 F.2d 1219 (5th Cir. 1989)
Guillory v. PPG Industries, Inc., 434 F.3d 303 (5th Cir. 2005)
