Douglass v. United Services Automobile Ass'n, 79 F.3d 1415 (5th Cir. 1996)

source_file: 10592491_2025_Turner v. Autumn Lake Property Owners Association, Inc._txsd
case_name: Dennis Turner and Darlene Brooks v. Autumn Lake Property Owners Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request — case concerns HOA fee disputes, not disability accommodations; plaintiffs improperly invoked FHA for fee challenge
key_holding: Plaintiffs' federal claims citing the Fair Housing Act are wholly insubstantial and frivolous because their actual allegations concern homeowners' association fees, which have no connection to the FHA's provisions governing housing discrimination.
brief_summary: Two homeowners sued their property owners association over alleged overcharging of HOA fees for over a decade, invoking the Fair Housing Act as the sole basis for federal jurisdiction. The court recommends granting the motion to dismiss because plaintiffs' Fair Housing Act claims are wholly insubstantial and frivolous — their fee dispute has no connection to the FHA's provisions governing housing discrimination.
key_cases_cited: Kokkonen v. Guardian Life Ins. Co. of Am., 511 U.S. 375 (1994)
Bell v. Hood, 37 U.S. 678 (1946)
Southpark Square Ltd. v. City of Jackson, Miss., 565 F.2d 338 (5th Cir. 1977)
Badgerow v. Walters, 596 U.S. 1 (2022)
Life Partners, Inc. v. United States, 650 F.3d 1026 (5th Cir. 2011)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs cite the Fair Housing Act in conclusory fashion but allege only that defendant overcharged homeowners' association fees; no disability, accommodation request, or fair housing violation is alleged.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiffs' allegations concern only homeowners' association fee disputes, which have nothing to do with the Fair Housing Act's prohibition on discrimination in the sale or rental of housing, lending, or brokering. The FHA citations lack any legal substance and are insufficient to establish federal question jurisdiction.

case_name: Daniel St. Clair v. Leonard Bernard George
accommodation_description: The opinion does not describe any specific accommodation request; it only addresses whether the case was properly removed to federal court.
key_holding: The magistrate judge recommends denying the motion to remand because the defendant timely removed the case within 30 days of receiving the amended petition that first stated a federal claim, and none of the prior exhibits qualified as 'other paper' under 28 U.S.C. § 1446(b)(3) to trigger earlier removal.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Daniel St. Clair sued landlord Leonard Bernard George in Texas justice court; after plaintiff amended his petition to add a Fair Housing Act claim, defendant removed the case to federal court, and plaintiff moved to remand. The magistrate judge recommends denying the remand motion because defendant's removal was timely under 28 U.S.C. § 1446(b)(3).
key_cases_cited: Zea v. Avis Rent a Car Sys., Inc., 435 F. Supp. 2d 603 (S.D. Tex. 2006)
Chapman v. Powermatic, Inc., 969 F.2d 160 (5th Cir. 1992)
Bosky v. Kroger Tex., LP, 288 F.3d 208 (5th Cir. 2002)
Davidson v. Georgia-Pacific, L.L.C., 819 F.3d 758 (5th Cir. 2016)

case_name: Anne Lauren Krause v. KCG Development, LLC and Landsman Real Estate Company
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges Defendants failed to make repairs to her apartment as a reasonable accommodation for her physical and mental impairments under the FHA.
key_holding: Because Defendants filed timely Answers to the Complaint, default has not been entered and Plaintiff's motion for default judgment, treated as a motion for entry of default, is denied; separately, the court found insufficient merit to appoint counsel under the relevant factors.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Anne Lauren Krause, proceeding pro se, sued KCG Development and Landsman Real Estate Company alleging they failed to make repairs to her apartment as a reasonable accommodation for her physical and mental impairments in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The court denied Plaintiff's motion for default judgment because Defendants had filed timely Answers, finding no default had occurred; the court also denied Plaintiff's request for appointed counsel, finding insufficient merit to warrant counsel assignment.
key_cases_cited: Priestley v. Headminder, Inc., 647 F.3d 497 (2d Cir. 2011)
Cooper v. A. Sargenti Co., 877 F.2d 170 (2d Cir. 1989)
Hendricks v. Coughlin, 114 F.3d 390 (2d Cir. 1997)
Hughey v. Wagner, 2024 WL 3647785 (W.D.N.Y. Aug. 5, 2024)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to make repairs to plaintiff's apartment to accommodate plaintiff's physical and mental impairments
fha_claims.reasoning: The court screened the complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) and dismissed plaintiff's ADA and Rehabilitation Act claims for failure to state a claim, but allowed the FHA claim to proceed. The FHA reasonable accommodation claim survives the screening stage and the case is now in discovery.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) and Rehabilitation Act claims for failure to make repairs to accommodate physical and mental impairments
fha_claims.reasoning: District Judge Sinatra dismissed plaintiff's ADA and Rehabilitation Act claims for failure to state a claim pursuant to § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) screening, without prejudice and with leave to amend. Plaintiff did not file an amended complaint, so the action proceeded only on the FHA claim.

case_name: Charity Mainville v. Anna De Santis and De Santis Rentals, LLC
accommodation_description: This opinion addresses a motion to recuse the assigned Magistrate Judge under 28 U.S.C. § 455(a), not a substantive fair housing accommodation claim.
key_holding: The magistrate judge's motion to recuse was denied because plaintiff failed to comply with local rules requiring a supporting brief, and alternatively, plaintiff failed to establish any valid basis for recusal as her dissatisfaction with adverse rulings does not create a reasonable question of impartiality.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Charity Mainville filed a motion seeking recusal of the assigned Magistrate Judge under 28 U.S.C. § 455(a), asserting bias based on his denial of her motion for electronic filing authorization. The court denied the motion to recuse because plaintiff failed to file a required supporting brief under local rules and, alternatively, because plaintiff's disagreement with adverse rulings does not establish a valid basis for recusal under objective standards.
key_cases_cited: Liteky v. United States, 510 U.S. 540 (1994)
United States v. Cherry, 330 F.3d 658 (4th Cir. 2003)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation related to plaintiff's documented complex post-traumatic stress disorder (C-PTSD); specific accommodation not clearly identified in opinion
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied TRO on Anti-Injunction Act grounds (plaintiff sought injunction of ongoing state court proceeding); in the alternative, TRO would be denied on merits because plaintiff's allegations were too conclusory to establish likelihood of success on the merits.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied TRO on Anti-Injunction Act grounds; in the alternative, TRO would be denied on merits because plaintiff's allegations were too conclusory to establish likelihood of success on the merits.

case_name: Mirlande Dina Michel-Wiggins v. Jes Holdings, LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested two apartments under a single housing voucher to accommodate a live-in aide arrangement, because she does not wish to share living space with an aide.
key_holding: The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, holding that requiring two apartments under a single housing voucher imposed an undue financial burden and did not constitute a reasonable accommodation under the FHA.
brief_summary: Mirlande Michel-Wiggins, a disabled individual using a Section 8 housing voucher, sued Jes Holdings LLC and Fairway Management alleging they violated the Fair Housing Act by refusing to rent her two apartments under a single voucher to accommodate a live-in aide, and by declining to provide trash pickup and mail delivery as disability accommodations. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss with prejudice, holding that requiring two apartments under one housing voucher constituted an undue financial burden and was not a reasonable accommodation, and that the ancillary service requests failed because the primary accommodation claim failed.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Klossner v. IADU Table Mound MHP, LLC, 65 F.4th 349 (8th Cir. 2023)
One Love Housing, LLC v. City of Anoka, 93 F.4th 424 (8th Cir. 2024)
Developmental Services of NE v. City of Lincoln, 504 F. Supp. 2d 714 (D. Neb. 2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Renting two apartments under a single housing voucher and lease to accommodate plaintiff's need for a live-in aide while maintaining separate living quarters
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege a reasonable accommodation claim because the requested accommodation (two apartments for one housing voucher) is unreasonable on its face as it would impose an undue financial burden on defendants. The court applied the undue burden defense, finding that HUD regulations cap rent at the lower of possible payments, so defendants would receive no additional compensation for providing two units.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Trash collection and mail delivery to front door or placement of mailbox outside door
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed this claim as derivative of the primary two-apartment claim, finding that because plaintiff is not entitled to reside at the property in the manner she requests (two apartments for one voucher), the secondary accommodations claims also fail as a matter of law.

case_name: Adrian Oree v. Parkchester Condominium Complex, PPC Residential, LLC, Parkchester Preservation Management LLC, Parkchester Preservation Company, LP
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: The court issued an order directing service of process on defendants and referring plaintiff to the Pro Se Clinic, noting the complaint may be construed as asserting Fair Housing Act claims but making no substantive ruling on the merits.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Adrian Oree, proceeding pro se and in forma pauperis, filed this action against Parkchester Condominium Complex and related entities, which the court noted may be construed as asserting claims under the Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3604(b), (f), along with ADA and state/city human rights law claims. The court issued an order of service directing the Clerk to issue summonses and the U.S. Marshals Service to effect service on defendants, and referred plaintiff to the Pro Se Clinic for assistance.
key_cases_cited: Walker v. Schult
Meilleur v. Strong

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unspecified reasonable accommodation related to disability in condominium housing
fha_claims.reasoning: This is an order of service directing the Clerk of Court to issue summonses and effect service on defendants through the U.S. Marshals Service. The court has not yet reviewed the complaint on the merits or addressed any FHA claims substantively. The case is in its initial procedural stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act; New York State and City Human Rights Laws
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint invokes Title III of the ADA and state/local human rights laws. This order addresses only service of process and does not reach the merits of any non-FHA claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges defendants failed to provide reasonable accommodations in the foreclosure process, including accessible communication and adjusted procedures, despite knowledge of plaintiff's disability status disclosed in bankruptcy proceedings and UCC filings.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied TRO without prejudice for failure to comply with Rule 65(b)(1) notice requirements and delay in seeking relief, not on the merits of the FHA claim. The claim survives and may be revived if plaintiff complies with procedural requirements.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges defendants knowingly engaged in unlawful conduct denying plaintiff fair and equal opportunity to maintain residence by refusing to adjust foreclosure practices or communicate through accessible means, constituting intentional or reckless disability-based discrimination.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied TRO without prejudice for procedural defects under Rule 65(b)(1), not on substantive merits of the discrimination claim. The claim survives and may be revived upon proper procedural compliance.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II and Title III violations (42 U.S.C. § 12101 et seq.), § 1983 due process violations (42 U.S.C. § 1983), fraudulent misrepresentation and forgery, wrongful foreclosure, civil RICO violations (18 U.S.C. § 1962), quiet title, and state law claims.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied TRO without prejudice for failure to comply with Rule 65(b)(1) notice and certification requirements and delay in seeking relief. Non-FHA claims survive procedurally and remain pending.

case_name: April Elisha Randle v. Shardai Pearson, et al.
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request identified; complaint broadly alleges housing conditions and retaliation under FHA § 3617.
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA claim fails because she does not claim to belong to any protected class enumerated in the FHA, and her complaint does not identify which FHA rights she seeks to enforce.
brief_summary: April Randle, proceeding pro se, sued her property manager, property management company, and corporate officer over housing conditions (cockroaches, mold, leaking pipes) and alleged Fourth Amendment violations from security cameras. The court dismissed her complaint without prejudice for failure to state a claim, finding her FHA claim deficient because she did not claim membership in a protected class and her Fourth Amendment claim failed for lack of state action.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged that uninhabitable housing conditions (cockroaches, leaking pipes, mold, mice, broken windows, faulty plumbing, lack of security features) constituted retaliatory conduct under § 3617.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed under § 1915(e)(2)(B) as frivolous because plaintiff failed to identify any protected class status under the FHA and failed to identify which FHA rights were allegedly interfered with, making the retaliation claim under § 3617 implausible on its face.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fourth Amendment claim regarding security cameras in garbage area; state law claims regarding uninhabitable housing conditions (cockroaches, leaking pipes, mold, mice, broken windows, faulty plumbing, lack of security features).
fha_claims.reasoning: Fourth Amendment claim dismissed as frivolous because it requires state action and the complaint contains no allegations of government involvement. State law claims dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because there are no allegations of diversity of citizenship and no independent federal question.

case_name: Karla Hunt v. Volare Health LLC
accommodation_description: Employee terminated for advocating against discrimination of a prospective patient with a mental health diagnosis who was denied admission to a nursing facility
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA retaliation claim was dismissed because she did not allege that she aided or encouraged the prospective patient in exercising his FHA rights, as the patient was unaware of the dispute, but she was granted leave to amend; Plaintiff's Oregon whistleblower retaliation claim survived because the close temporal proximity between her advocacy and her termination, combined with the factual setting, was sufficient to plead causation.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Karla Hunt, an employee at a nursing and rehabilitation facility operated by Volare Health LLC, sued alleging she was terminated in retaliation for advocating that the facility admit a prospective patient with a mental health diagnosis, which she believed constituted disability discrimination under the FHA. The court granted Volare's motion to dismiss the FHA retaliation claim because Hunt failed to allege she aided the patient in exercising his FHA rights, but dismissed with leave to amend; the court denied dismissal of Hunt's Oregon whistleblower retaliation claim finding sufficient temporal proximity and factual support for causation.
key_cases_cited: Walker v. City of Lakewood, 272 F.3d 1114 (9th Cir. 2001)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Villiarimo v. Aloha Island Air, Inc., 281 F.3d 1054 (9th Cir. 2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that she 'aided or encouraged' the Patient in exercising FHA rights under § 3617. The court found that Plaintiff's single argument with Drummond, with no allegation that the Patient was involved or aware of the dispute, does not constitute protected activity as contemplated by Walker v. City of Lakewood. Dismissal granted with leave to amend.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Oregon whistleblower retaliation under ORS 659A.199
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff survived the motion to dismiss on her state law whistleblower retaliation claim. The court found that Plaintiff adequately pleaded causation through temporal proximity (four weeks between protected activity and discipline, six days between discipline and termination) and factual context (stated reasons for discipline referencing 'undermining management' and 'insubordination' plausibly linked to the July 25 dispute). The court declined to require allegations that Drummond was the ultimate decision maker, finding that causation can be inferred from timing alone under Ninth Circuit precedent.

case_name: Kenneth Glover v. Elevate Property Management and MFR-XVIII Jones LLC
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: The court lacked subject-matter jurisdiction after plaintiff amended his complaint to remove federal questions, requiring remand to state court.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Kenneth Glover filed suit in federal court against Elevate Property Management and MFR-XVIII Jones LLC, originally raising federal Fair Housing Act claims, but after filing an amended complaint that removed all federal questions, he moved to remand the case to state court.
key_cases_cited: Royal Canin U.S.A., Inc. v. Wullschleger, 604 U.S. 22 (2025)
Gunn v. Minton, 568 U.S. 251 (2013)
Vlaming v. W. Point Sch. Bd., 10 F.4th 300 (4th Cir. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) violation — alleged misrepresentation in debt collection letter regarding authorization to refer medical debt to attorney
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied plaintiff's motion for class certification under Rule 23(b)(3) because putative class members cannot establish Article III standing without individualized evidence of injury and detrimental reliance on the debt collection letter. The court declined to extend Havens Realty (an FHA case) to the FDCPA context, finding that FDCPA violations do not automatically confer standing merely by receipt of a misleading letter, and that determining standing for 747+ class members would require individualized factual development that would overwhelm common questions.

case_name: Delroy Askins v. Prestige Management Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, who receives medical supplies via mail and has a home health aide, alleges he was assaulted by the building superintendent, his medical supplies were taken, and he was denied access to the community room.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claims because he failed to allege facts showing he has a disability as defined by the FHA or that any adverse actions taken against him were motivated by his disability.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Delroy Askins sued Prestige Management Inc. and building superintendent Lowell Hendricks alleging disability discrimination under the FHA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act based on being assaulted, having his medical supplies taken, and being denied access to the community room. The court dismissed all claims for failure to state a claim because plaintiff failed to allege facts establishing he has a disability as defined by the statutes or that any adverse actions were motivated by his disability, though the court granted plaintiff 30 days' leave to amend.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
McElwee v. Cnty. of Orange, 700 F.3d 635 (2d Cir. 2012)
Rodriguez v. Vill. Green Realty, Inc., 788 F.3d 31 (2d Cir. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges discrimination in housing based on disability, including assault by superintendent, loss of medical supplies, and denial of access to community room.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts showing he has a disability as defined by the FHA or that any adverse actions were motivated by his disability. The complaint does not plausibly allege discriminatory motivation at the pleading stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (federal constitutional rights); ADA Title II and Title III; Rehabilitation Act § 504
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 1983 claims fail because defendants are private parties not acting under color of state law; ADA Title III does not apply to residential housing; ADA Title II and Rehabilitation Act claims fail because plaintiff alleges no facts describing the nature of his disability or connecting the adverse actions to disability discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) claim arising from allegedly false proof of claim filed in bankruptcy proceeding
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed for lack of Article III standing, finding that plaintiffs failed to allege a concrete injury-in-fact. The court declined to extend Havens Realty (an FHA case) to the FDCPA context and found that plaintiffs' alleged informational injury lacked the required downstream consequences and nexus to the FDCPA's protective purpose under the three-prong test from Kelly and George.

case_name: Alberto James Santiago Sr. v. Elishia Chill, et al.
accommodation_description: Santiago alleges disability and national origin discrimination based on derogatory comments about Puerto Ricans, eviction threats, and failure to repair a door latch, but no specific accommodation request is substantively analyzed.
key_holding: The court dismissed Santiago's claims with prejudice for improper service of process (Santiago served defendants personally as a party, violating Fed. R. Civ. P. 4(c)(2)) and failure to prosecute (Santiago failed to respond to discovery, ignored court orders, and engaged in contumacious conduct).
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Santiago sued Key Property Management and property manager Chill alleging national origin and disability discrimination under the Fair Housing Act, claiming derogatory comments about Puerto Ricans, eviction threats, and failure to repair his door. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss with prejudice, finding Santiago improperly served process himself as a party and failed to prosecute by ignoring discovery obligations and court orders over three years of litigation.
key_cases_cited: Knoll v. Am. Tel. & Tel. Co., 176 F.3d 359 (6th Cir. 1999)
Schafer v. City of Defiance Police Dept., 529 F.3d 731 (6th Cir. 2008)
Russell v. City of Farmington Hills, 34 F. App'x 196 (6th Cir. 2002)
Lee v. George, No. 3:11-CV-607-CRS, 2012 WL 1833389 (W.D. Ky. May 18, 2012)
Greene v. United States, No. 6:19-CV-00024-GFVT, 2021 WL 1214499 (E.D. Ky. Mar. 30, 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Repair of broken door latch
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's claims were dismissed for improper service of process under Rule 4(m) and failure to prosecute under Rule 41(b). The court did not reach the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim because service was never properly effectuated and plaintiff failed to participate in discovery or comply with court orders over three years of litigation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged discriminatory refusal to repair door and derogatory comments about Puerto Ricans in connection with eviction threat
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's national origin discrimination claim was dismissed for improper service of process and failure to prosecute. The court did not reach the merits because service was defective and plaintiff failed to comply with discovery obligations and court orders.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act
fha_claims.reasoning: Non-FHA claims under Title VI and Section 504 were dismissed along with all FHA claims for improper service of process and failure to prosecute. The court did not reach the merits of these claims.

case_name: Nathaniel Manny Ballantyne v. Guenther Management LLC
accommodation_description: No accommodation request at issue; plaintiff alleges racial discrimination in rental denial based on claim that defendant changed credit score requirement from 600 to 700 after his application.
key_holding: Plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie case of disparate treatment or disparate impact because he was not the first qualified applicant (another applicant applied two days earlier and was approved), the credit score requirement was always 700, and the property was ultimately rented to a Black individual.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Nathanial Ballantyne sued Guenther Management LLC, a property management company, alleging racial discrimination under the Fair Housing Act after he was not selected as a tenant for a rental property in Spokane, Washington. The court granted summary judgment for defendants, finding plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie case because he was not the first qualified applicant, the credit score requirement was always 700, and evidence showed the property was rented to another Black individual.
key_cases_cited: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Texas Dep't of Hous. & Urban Dev. v. Inclusive Communities Project, 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Gamble v. City of Escondido, 104 F.3d 300 (9th Cir. 1997)
Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242 (1986)
Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish prima facie disparate treatment claim under McDonnell Douglas framework. Although plaintiff established membership in protected class (Black), he could not prove he was qualified (credit score 620 vs. 700 requirement), was denied the property (another applicant submitted application first on Dec. 17, two days before plaintiff's Dec. 19 application), or that similarly situated applicant was treated differently (the approved applicant was also Black). Defendants' legitimate nondiscriminatory reason—first-come-first-served policy with earlier qualified applicant—was unrebutted.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish prima facie disparate impact claim. Although plaintiff presented statistical evidence that Black and Hispanic consumers have lower median credit scores than white consumers, he failed to establish 'robust causality' between defendants' credit score requirement and disparate impact on protected class. Plaintiff provided no evidence regarding how many of defendants' properties require 700+ credit scores, how many Black/Hispanic applicants were denied, or whether defendants' practices disproportionately affected protected classes. The property was ultimately rented to a Black applicant, undermining the disparate impact theory.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Washington Law Against Discrimination (RCW 49.60.030(1)(c), RCW 49.60.222, RCW 49.60.220); Intentional Infliction of Emotional Distress; Negligent Infliction of Emotional Distress; Negligent Retention; Negligent Supervision; Breach of Contract; Unfair Business Practices
fha_claims.reasoning: Washington state discrimination claims fail under same McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework as federal FHA claims; plaintiff failed to establish prima facie case. Tort claims for intentional and negligent infliction of emotional distress fail because defendants provided unrebutted evidence they did not manipulate rental criteria and plaintiff was not denied based on credit score but rather because another applicant applied first (not outrageous conduct); negligent infliction requires physical manifestation of injury (none alleged); negligent retention and supervision claims fail because no employee acted outside scope of employment. Breach of contract and unfair business practices claims raised for first time in opposition to summary judgment are disregarded.

case_name: Quintin J. Ballentine v. Bowery Residence Committee
accommodation_description: The case text does not specify the particular accommodation or modification requested; it states only that plaintiff alleges Defendants violated his rights at a shelter operated by BRC in Brooklyn, New York.
key_holding: The Southern District of New York transferred plaintiff's pro se FHA and ADA action to the Eastern District of New York because the events giving rise to the claims occurred in Brooklyn, which falls within the Eastern District, making it the more convenient forum under 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a).
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Quintin Ballentine filed suit under the FHA and ADA against Bowery Residents' Committee (a nonprofit shelter operator), BRC Chair Julie Salamon, NYC Mayor Eric Adams, and NY Governor Kathy Hochul, alleging violations of his rights at a BRC-operated shelter in Brooklyn, New York. The SDNY court did not reach the merits but determined that because the locus of operative facts — the Brooklyn shelter — lies within the Eastern District of New York, transfer was appropriate under 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a) for the convenience of the parties and witnesses and in the interest of justice. The case was transferred to the Eastern District of New York with all further determinations, including in forma pauperis status, left to the transferee court.
key_cases_cited: Keitt v. N.Y. City, 882 F. Supp. 2d 412 (S.D.N.Y. 2011)
N.Y. Marine and Gen. Ins. Co. v. LaFarge No. Am., Inc., 599 F.3d 102 (2d Cir. 2010)
D.H. Blair & Co. v. Gottdiener, 462 F.3d 95 (2d Cir. 2006)

case_name: Claran Lundgren v. Ashton Glenn H.O.A. c/o Wacammaw Management, and Bob Sauthoff
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request; plaintiff alleges harassment, discrimination, retaliation, and selective enforcement by HOA officials
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claims under the doctrine of res judicata, finding the claims arose from the same operative facts and subject matter adjudicated in prior state court proceedings; alternatively, the claims failed to plausibly allege discrimination in the terms, conditions, or privileges of housing.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Claran Lundgren sued the Ashton Glenn HOA and its president Bob Sauthoff alleging Fair Housing Act claims based on harassment, discrimination, retaliation, and selective enforcement related to HOA fines and property violations. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss under res judicata, finding the federal claims were barred because they arose from the same operative facts litigated in prior state court proceedings, and alternatively because the allegations failed to plausibly state a discrimination claim under the FHA.
key_cases_cited: Schronce v. Rear
Diamond v. Colonial Life & Accident Ins. Co.
Thomas v. Arn
Camby v. Davis
Mathews v. Weber

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's factual allegations regarding personal comments made by Defendant Sauthoff fail to state a claim under the Fair Housing Act because they do not plausibly allege discrimination in the terms, conditions, or privileges of housing within the meaning of the statute.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's federal Fair Housing Act claims, including retaliation and selective enforcement allegations, are barred by res judicata because they arise from the same operative facts and subject matter already litigated and decided in prior state court proceedings, and under South Carolina law, res judicata bars not only claims actually litigated but also those that could have been raised in the prior action.

case_name: Scoggins v. Falcon Court
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges retaliation by housing provider for engaging in protected activity, including reporting habitability issues to code enforcement, HUD, and local authorities; plaintiff mentions disabilities (cancer survivor, heart problems, depression) and her son's respiratory issues.
key_holding: The complaint fails to state a retaliation claim under the Fair Housing Act because plaintiff failed to identify specific protected actions she took or any adverse actions by defendants, providing only threadbare conclusory assertions insufficient under the pleading standards.
brief_summary: Danell Scoggins, proceeding pro se, sued Falcon Court and Turning Point of Central California (a permanent supportive housing provider), alleging retaliation under the Fair Housing Act for reporting habitability issues to code enforcement and federal authorities. The magistrate judge recommended dismissal without leave to amend, finding the complaint failed to plead a prima facie retaliation claim because plaintiff did not identify specific protected actions or adverse actions, providing only conclusory allegations insufficient under Twombly and Iqbal standards.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Walker v. City of Lakewood, 272 F.3d 1114 (9th Cir. 2001)
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead a retaliation claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3617 because she did not identify specific protected actions she took or any adverse actions by defendants, providing only threadbare assertions and conclusory statements insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: State law negligence and intentional infliction of emotional distress claims
fha_claims.disposition: Lack of subject matter jurisdiction (12(b)(1)) / Improper amendment (Rule 15)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked subject matter jurisdiction over state law claims because the parties were not diverse and the court could not exercise supplemental jurisdiction without a cognizable federal claim; additionally, plaintiff lacked leave to amend to add these claims under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 15.

case_name: Charlesetta Moore, SR. v. C.F.Y. Development Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request; complaint alleges poor treatment and discriminatory conduct including a racial slur directed at plaintiff.
key_holding: The complaint was dismissed because plaintiff failed to allege membership in a protected class and failed to plead facts showing different treatment because of protected class status, as a single racial slur and generalized allegations of poor treatment are insufficient to state a disparate treatment claim.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Charlesetta Moore, proceeding pro se and in forma pauperis, sued C.F.Y. Development Inc. and individual defendants alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on discriminatory treatment at Galt Place Senior Apartments, including rent increases, service failures, and a racial slur. The court dismissed the first amended complaint for failure to state a claim because plaintiff failed to allege membership in a protected class and failed to plead facts showing she was treated differently because of protected class status.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Gamble v. City of Escondido, 104 F.3d 300 (9th Cir. 1997)
Sw. Fair Hous. Council, Inc. v. Maricopa Domestic Water Improvement Dist., 17 F.4th 950 (9th Cir. 2021)
Fried v. Wynn Las Vegas, LLC, 18 F.4th 643 (9th Cir. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege she is a member of a protected class and failed to allege facts showing she received different treatment because of protected class status. A single racial slur, while deplorable, is insufficient to establish an FHA violation without allegations that the defendants' conduct was motivated by plaintiff's protected status.

case_name: Gorawara v. Caprio
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation or modification was requested in this case. The claims centered on alleged racial intimidation and discrimination by the landlords under FHA § 3617 and deceptive practices under CUTPA in connection with renting and evicting Gorawara from an apartment.
key_holding: The Second Circuit affirmed the district court's judgment, holding that the court properly exercised its inherent docket-management authority, did not err in rejecting jury instructions lacking a factual predicate or proper pleading basis, and did not abuse its discretion in denying leave to amend the complaint for a fourth time at the jury charge conference.
brief_summary: Rahul Gorawara, a pro se attorney, sued his former landlords John and Carolyn Caprio alleging intimidation and racial discrimination under Fair Housing Act § 3617 and deceptive-practices claims under the Connecticut Unfair Trade Practices Act (CUTPA), arising from his tenancy and eviction. Following a jury trial, the jury found for the defendant on all but two state-law claims (slander and negligent infliction of emotional distress against Carolyn Caprio's estate). On appeal, Gorawara challenged the district court's pre-trial scheduling order, rejection of two proposed jury instructions, and denial of leave to file a fourth amended complaint; the Second Circuit rejected all three challenges and affirmed.
key_cases_cited: In re World Trade Ctr. Disaster Site Litig., 722 F.3d 483 (2d Cir. 2013)
Innomed Labs, LLC v. ALZA Corp., 368 F.3d 148 (2d Cir. 2004)
McCardle v. Haddad, 131 F.3d 43 (2d Cir. 1997)
Empire Merchs., LLC v. Reliable Churchill LLLP, 902 F.3d 132 (2d Cir. 2018)
McCarthy v. Dun & Bradstreet Corp., 482 F.3d 184 (2d Cir. 2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Jury found in favor of defendant on the Fair Housing Act § 3617 intimidation and race discrimination claim after trial. The appellate court affirmed the judgment, finding no error in the district court's jury instructions or procedural rulings.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Connecticut Unfair Trade Practices Act (CUTPA) deceptive acts claim; Connecticut anti-intimidation law § 52-571c; 42 U.S.C. § 1983 due process claim; negligent infliction of emotional distress; slander
fha_claims.reasoning: Jury found in favor of defendant on most non-FHA claims, but found in favor of plaintiff on slander and negligent infliction of emotional distress claims against Carolyn Caprio. The appellate court affirmed the district court's denial of leave to amend the CUTPA claim and jury instruction rulings based on fair-notice pleading requirements.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: RESPA claims (failure to respond to qualified written request and notice of error); breach of mortgage agreement; breach of covenant of good faith and fair dealing; FCRA violations; ECOA violations; FHA violations for alleged discrimination in compensation offered to similarly situated white borrowers
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to send qualified written request and notice of error to defendants' designated mailing address as required by RESPA and Regulation X; instead, she emailed the correspondence. The Eleventh Circuit in Bivens held that servicers have no duty to respond when correspondence is not sent to the designated address. Additionally, RESPA and Regulation X do not prohibit servicers from committing errors in the first instance or obligate them to respond to CFPB complaints. State law claims were dismissed without prejudice for lack of supplemental jurisdiction.

source_file: 10599227_2025_Tenn. State Conference of the NAACP v. William Lee_ca6

fha_claims.accommodation_description: This case involves claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (civil rights violations, 8th Amendment, negligent hiring/training/staffing/supervision), California negligence, failure to summon medical aid (Cal. Gov. Code § 845.6), negligent infliction of emotional distress, and intentional infliction of emotional distress. The plaintiff alleges he was assaulted by a fellow inmate at Fresno County Jail due to improper segregation.
fha_claims.reasoning: The parties settled the case for $3 million gross. The court found the settlement fair and reasonable in light of the plaintiff's severe and permanent brain injuries, lifetime care needs, and comparable settlements in similar cases involving traumatic brain injury. The court approved the settlement with a modification reducing attorney's fees from 40% to 33% of the gross amount to protect the incompetent plaintiff's interests.

source_file: 10599504_2025_Calhoun v. The Greens at Lake Overholser_okwd
case_name: Yolanda Calhoun v. The Greens at Lake Overholser
accommodation_description: The case text does not describe any specific accommodation requested; it refers only generically to 'claims of discrimination and retaliation under the Fair Housing Act' without further elaboration on the underlying allegations.
key_holding: The court dismissed the FHA action without prejudice because plaintiff failed to effect timely service of process under Fed. R. Civ. P. 4(m) and failed to respond to the court's order to show cause, with no permissive extension warranted under the Espinoza factors.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Yolanda Calhoun filed a Fair Housing Act complaint against The Greens at Lake Overholser and Jessica Jeffries alleging discrimination and retaliation arising from events beginning in November 2022 and culminating in her eviction in March 2023. After plaintiff failed to serve defendants within the 90-day period required by Rule 4(m), the court issued a show cause order, which plaintiff also failed to answer. The court dismissed the action without prejudice both for failure to effect timely service and for failure to comply with a court order, finding no Espinoza factors favored a permissive extension and that the Ehrenhaus factors supported dismissal.
key_cases_cited: Nasious v. Two Unknown B.I.C.E. Agents at Arapahoe Cty. Justice Ctr., 492 F.3d 1158 (10th Cir. 2007)
Espinoza v. United States, 52 F.3d 838 (10th Cir. 1995)
Ehrenhaus v. Reynolds, 965 F.2d 916 (10th Cir. 1992)
Davis v. Miller, 571 F.3d 1058 (10th Cir. 2009)
McIntosh v. Boatman's First Nat. Bank of Oklahoma, 103 F.3d 144 (10th Cir. 1996)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not specified; complaint alleges discrimination and retaliation under the Fair Housing Act but no details provided in this order
fha_claims.reasoning: Case dismissed without prejudice for failure to effect timely service of process within 90 days and for failure to comply with the Court's Order to Show Cause. The court did not reach the merits of the FHA claims because the case was dismissed on procedural grounds (service of process failure and non-compliance with court orders).

source_file: 10599577_2025_ROSADO v. THE CITY OF CHESTER COUNTY PENNSYLVANIA_paed
case_name: Geronimo F. Rosado, Jr. v. The City of Chester County, Pennsylvania, et al.
accommodation_description: Rosado, who has a visual impairment, alleges he was discriminated against due to his disability and was not provided reasonable accommodation during property retrieval after eviction, but no specific accommodation request is clearly articulated in the opinion.
key_holding: The court dismissed Rosado's federal claims with prejudice for failure to state a claim, including ADA Title II and Section 504 claims which failed because the private defendants (Kurtas Defendants, police officers) are not public entities and do not receive federal financial assistance as required for RA claims.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Geronimo Rosado, a Section 8 HCVP participant with visual impairment, sued the City of Chester, Chester County Housing Authority, private landlords, police officers, and others alleging wrongful eviction and failure to accommodate his disability during property retrieval after an August 2024 eviction. The court dismissed all federal claims with prejudice, finding Rosado failed to state viable ADA Title II or Section 504 claims because the private defendants are not public entities and do not receive federal financial assistance.
key_cases_cited: Furgess v. Pennsylvania Dep't of Corr., 933 F.3d 285 (3d Cir. 2019)
Kokinda v. Pennsylvania Dep't of Corr., 779 F. App'x 938 (3d Cir. 2019)
Bowens v. Wetzel, 674 F. App'x 133 (3d Cir. 2017)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation for visual impairment disability during property recovery on August 30, 2024; plaintiff alleges he was discriminated against due to his visual impairment and was not provided adequate time or assistance to recover personal property from the evicted premises
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the FHA claim for failure to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly. Rosado's allegations that he was discriminated against due to his visual impairment were conclusory and speculative, lacking sufficient factual matter to plausibly allege a violation of the Fair Housing Act. The court did not apply any substantive FHA reasonable accommodation standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II, Section 504 Rehabilitation Act, § 1983 due process and equal protection claims, First Amendment retaliation, state law tort claims (defamation, property damage, breach of contract)
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA federal claims were dismissed for failure to state a plausible claim: ADA Title II and Section 504 claims failed because defendants were not public entities or federal funding recipients; § 1983 claims failed because private landlords are not state actors, the police department is not a proper defendant, the magisterial court has Eleventh Amendment immunity, Judge Hipple has judicial immunity, and the First Amendment claim lacked plausible factual support. State law claims were dismissed for lack of diversity jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a).

case_name: Laurie Thorson v. Hawaii Public Housing Authority, Hakim Ouansafi, Ryan Akamine, and Lyle Matsuura
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested continuation of a two-bedroom voucher reasonable accommodation to permit her son to serve as her live-in aide for epilepsy and transient epileptic amnesia.
key_holding: Defendants are entitled to summary judgment because HPHA's investigation into whether Thorson's son actually resided with her as a live-in aide was motivated by legitimate compliance concerns under HUD regulations, and Thorson failed to present sufficient evidence that this explanation was pretextual for disability-based retaliation.
brief_summary: Laurie Thorson, a Section 8 voucher recipient with epilepsy, sued the Hawaii Public Housing Authority and its officials alleging disability discrimination and retaliation under the Fair Housing Act, claiming HPHA improperly investigated her live-in aide arrangement and used flawed comparables in rent reasonableness determinations. The court granted summary judgment for Defendants, finding Thorson failed to establish that HPHA's legitimate, nondiscriminatory justification for investigating whether her son actually resided with her was pretext for retaliation.
key_cases_cited: Walker v. City of Lakewood, 272 F.3d 1114 (9th Cir. 2001)
Harris v. Itzhaki, 183 F.3d 1043 (9th Cir. 1999)
Kama v. Mayorkas, 107 F.4th 1054 (9th Cir. 2024)
Nozzi v. Hous. Auth. of Los Angeles, 806 F.3d 1178 (9th Cir. 2015)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 120 percent payment standard exception to allow plaintiff to afford housing units not in high-rises or near busy streets due to epilepsy and transient epileptic amnesia
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff never lost the 120 percent payment standard exception accommodation; it was approved for the Hawai'i Kai unit and continues to apply to her current housing. The rent reasonableness test is not itself a reasonable accommodation but a mechanism to ensure fair market rent. Plaintiff received the accommodation she requested and cannot show defendants denied it.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Two-bedroom voucher to accommodate plaintiff's son as a full-time live-in aide to provide 24/7 care for her disabilities
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff herself terminated use of the live-in aide accommodation by informing defendants her son was no longer serving in that role. Defendants consistently maintained plaintiff was approved for the accommodation and could identify a replacement aide. Plaintiff's subsequent requests specified overnight care 'when needed' rather than full-time residence, which does not qualify as a live-in aide under HUD regulations requiring the aide to 'reside' with the recipient.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request to convert two-bedroom Hawai'i Kai unit to one-bedroom by locking or sealing off a bedroom
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish that the requested accommodation was reasonable or necessary. She provided no medical evidence or declaration from a doctor showing her disabilities required conversion of the unit. The burden is on plaintiff to show an accommodation 'seems reasonable on its face,' and she did not meet this burden. Defendants' explanation that they must treat units as designated by city tax records is a legitimate nondiscriminatory reason.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Investigation into plaintiff's live-in aide arrangement, questioning about whether her son actually resided with her, and conditioning inspection on answers to questions about the aide's residency status
fha_claims.reasoning: Although plaintiff established a prima facie case of retaliation (protected activity of threatening HUD complaint, adverse action of investigation with close temporal proximity of two days), defendants articulated a legitimate nondiscriminatory reason: compliance with HUD regulations requiring live-in aides to actually reside with recipients. Plaintiff failed to prove pretext. The information defendants discovered (son's work email, employment status, plaintiff's statement that son would move in 'as soon as' inspection allowed) reasonably raised compliance concerns under any definition of 'reside.' Temporal proximity alone does not overcome defendants' legitimate reason, especially where the nondiscriminatory reason arose during the same period as the protected activity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged denial of request to convert two-bedroom Hawai'i Kai unit to one-bedroom by locking a door during 2024 move
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish prima facie case of retaliation. Evidence consisted only of unauthenticated emails and letters without sworn declarations. Plaintiff provided no affidavit or deposition testimony and failed to submit required counter-concise statement of facts. Plaintiff did not explain how the denial constituted coercion, intimidation, threats, or interference. Even accepting the conduct occurred, defendants' stated reason (required to treat units as designated by City and County) was not shown to be pretext; plaintiff's only evidence was inadmissible hearsay from an alleged city employee.

source_file: 10600430_2025_El Camino, LLC v. City of South Saint Paul, Minnesota_mnd
case_name: El Camino, LLC v. City of South Saint Paul, Minnesota
accommodation_description: Request to house up to ten unrelated adults in recovery from substance use disorders in a single-family residential zone that otherwise limits occupancy to three unrelated persons
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment because El Camino lacked Article III standing, having failed to demonstrate concrete injury in fact—the company sold the property at a profit, and its claims of monetary harm were speculative, while its requests for declaratory and injunctive relief were moot after the property sale.
brief_summary: El Camino, LLC, a group sober home operator, sued the City of South Saint Paul alleging the city violated the Fair Housing Act and ADA by twice denying its requests for a zoning accommodation to house up to ten unrelated adults in recovery from substance use disorders in a single-family residential zone. The court granted the city's motion for summary judgment, holding that El Camino lacked Article III standing because its claims for declaratory and injunctive relief were moot after it sold the property, and El Camino failed to demonstrate any concrete monetary injury attributable to the city.
key_cases_cited: TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
One Love Hous., LLC v. City of Anoka, 93 F.4th 424 (8th Cir. 2024)
Cross v. Fox, 23 F.4th 797 (8th Cir. 2022)
Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins, 578 U.S. 330 (2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request for variance/accommodation to house up to ten unrelated adults with substance use disorders at a single-family residential property, in violation of City Code limiting occupancy to three unrelated persons
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed on mootness/standing grounds without reaching the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim. El Camino no longer owns the property, rendering declaratory and injunctive relief moot. Compensatory damages claims lack concrete injury in fact: El Camino profited from the sale and operated the property as intended despite never receiving formal authorization. Attorneys' fees cannot independently confer standing.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act Title II claim for failure to provide reasonable accommodation
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA claim dismissed on same mootness and standing grounds as FHA claim. Court did not reach merits of either claim, instead finding El Camino lacked Article III standing to pursue any form of relief.

source_file: 10601202_2025_Albert Pickett, Jr. v. City of Cleveland, OH_ca6
case_name: Albert Pickett, Jr. et al. v. City of Cleveland, Ohio
accommodation_description: No accommodation request - case involves disparate impact challenge to municipal water lien policy allegedly making housing unavailable to Black homeowners
key_holding: The Sixth Circuit affirmed class certification, holding that plaintiffs' disparate-impact claim under § 3604(a) presents a common question—whether Cleveland's water lien policy violates the FHA by disproportionately affecting Black homeowners—that predominates over individualized damages issues, and that plaintiffs have Article III standing based on the FHA's congressional authorization of housing discrimination claims.
brief_summary: African American homeowners and residents in Cuyahoga County, Ohio sued the City of Cleveland alleging that its water lien policy, which places liens on properties with delinquent water bills, has a disparate impact on Black homeowners in violation of § 3604(a) of the Fair Housing Act. The Sixth Circuit affirmed class certification under Rules 23(b)(2) and 23(b)(3), finding that plaintiffs' common question—whether the disproportionate placement of water liens on Black homeowners violates the FHA—predominates over individualized damages issues and that plaintiffs have Article III standing based on the cognizable harm of housing discrimination claims.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dept. of Hous. & Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Cmtys. Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. v. Dukes, 564 U.S. 338 (2011)
TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021)
Merck v. Walmart, Inc., 114 F.4th 762 (6th Cir. 2024)
In re Whirlpool Corp. Front-Loading Washer Prods. Liab. Litig., 722 F.3d 838 (6th Cir. 2013)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court affirmed class certification under Rule 23(b)(2) and 23(b)(3) for a disparate-impact claim under FHA § 3604(a), finding that Plaintiffs alleged a common question of whether the City's disproportionate placement of water liens on Black homeowners violates the FHA. The court declined to address the merits of the FHA claim itself, holding that Rule 23(f) appeals are limited to evaluating class certification, not the substantive cause of action.

case_name: Heidi Grossman Lepp v. Conrad Mallet, Jr.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff claims defendants' enforcement actions (denial of lease occupancy, parking lot closure, inspections) constituted discrimination based on religion and disability under the FHA.
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA claims fail because she only conclusorily alleged discrimination on the basis of disability and religion without pleading facts showing defendants acted with discriminatory intent based on those protected classes.
brief_summary: Heidi Grossman Lepp, associated with Sugarleaf Church, sued Detroit officials and private parties alleging defendants conducted raids, inspections, and parking restrictions that violated her constitutional and federal statutory rights. The court denied plaintiff's motion to amend the complaint as futile, finding her FHA claims under §§ 3604 and 3617 failed because she only conclusorily alleged discrimination without factual allegations showing discriminatory intent based on disability or religion.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009)
Brown v. Dominion Mgmt. Servs., LLC, 2023 WL 5608861 (6th Cir. 2023)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges discrimination on the basis of religion and disability regarding Madden's email denying occupancy of John R. Street property and Black and Green's alleged closure of Adelaide Street parking lot.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to support an inference that defendants discriminated against her on the basis of protected classes (religion and disability). Allegations were conclusory without factual support showing discriminatory intent or animus.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges retaliation under § 3617 for asserting FHA rights, claiming Madden's email and Black's warrantless inspection constituted unlawful retaliation.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to specify which FHA rights (§§ 3603-3606) she exercised and failed to allege facts showing defendants acted with discriminatory animus. Conclusory allegations without factual support are insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claim alleging parking closures denied disabled members access; § 1983 claims for First Amendment (Free Exercise and Free Speech), Fourth Amendment, Fifth Amendment (Takings), and Fourteenth Amendment (Equal Protection and Due Process) violations; § 1985(3) conspiracy; RLUIPA; § 504 Rehabilitation Act; civil RICO; state law claims for defamation, false light, intentional infliction of emotional distress, trespass, conversion, and misappropriation of public funds.
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA federal claims failed under Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards due to conclusory allegations, lack of factual support, failure to identify applicable law, and lack of state action (for § 1983 claims against private attorney Madden and private company Woodward). State law claims dismissed for lack of supplemental jurisdiction after all federal claims found futile.

case_name: Oudree Ellis-Sanders, et al v. Guardian Piazza D'Oro LLC, et al
accommodation_description: Pro se plaintiff filed a motion to seal her entire case, including complaint, TRO motion, and documents containing medical records, disabilities, and requests for disability accommodations.
key_holding: The Court denied the motion to seal the entire case as overbroad because plaintiff's generalized privacy concerns about medical conditions did not overcome the strong presumption in favor of public access to court records, but granted limited sealing of the minor daughter's full name, medical records, and email addresses.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Oudree Ellis-Sanders filed a motion to seal her entire case and supporting documents containing sensitive medical and disability-related information, which the court partially granted by sealing the minor daughter's name, medical records, and email addresses while denying the request to seal the entire case. The court ordered plaintiff to resubmit filings using only the minor's initials and restricted access to current filings pending resubmission with proper redactions.
key_cases_cited: Kamakana v. City & Cnty. of Honolulu, 447 F.3d 1172 (9th Cir. 2006)
Harrell v. California Forensic Med. Grp., Inc., No. 2:15-CV-00579 KJN P, 2015 WL 1405567 (E.D. Cal. Mar. 26, 2015)
Rock v. McHugh, 819 F.Supp.2d 456 (D.Md. 2011)
A.C. v. City of Santa Clara, No. 13-CV-03276-HSG, 2015 WL 4076364 (N.D. Cal. July 2, 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Disability accommodations in connection with unlawful detainer action; specific accommodations not detailed in this sealing order
fha_claims.reasoning: This is a procedural order on a motion to seal; the court did not address the merits of the FHA reasonable accommodation claim. The complaint alleges FHA violations related to disability accommodations in the context of an unlawful detainer action, but the court's order concerns only the sealing of sensitive medical and disability information, not the substantive claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983, Titles II and III of the American with Disabilities Act, California Unruh Act, California Fair Employment and Housing Act
fha_claims.reasoning: Non-FHA claims under § 1983, ADA Titles II and III, California Unruh Act, and California Fair Employment and Housing Act survive this procedural sealing order without substantive adjudication.

case_name: Edward Kindle v. Paula Carrey Moore
accommodation_description: Nature of accommodation request not specified in complaint; insufficient factual allegations to identify the accommodation sought.
key_holding: The court dismissed the complaint because Kindle failed to plead sufficient factual content to state a plausible Fair Housing Act claim against Moore, though the court granted him 30 days to file an amended complaint.
brief_summary: Edward Kindle sued Paula Carrey Moore under the Fair Housing Act for housing discrimination. The court dismissed his complaint without prejudice because it lacked sufficient factual allegations to state a plausible claim, granting him 30 days to amend.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not specified in complaint
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff cited the Fair Housing Act but failed to plead sufficient factual content to allow the court to draw a reasonable inference that defendant violated the statute and may be liable. The complaint was dismissed without prejudice under the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard during § 1915 screening, with leave to amend.

case_name: Ivaylo Dodev, et al. v. D.R. Horton Incorporated, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege discrimination in maintenance and repairs based on national origin under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(a); complaint also references § 3604(f)(1) and (f)(2) for disability-based discrimination in housing terms.
key_holding: The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, finding the FHA claim time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations and the MMWA claim legally insufficient because home fixtures constitute real property rather than tangible personal property.
brief_summary: Ivaylo and Nikolina Dodev sued D.R. Horton and Mike Douglas alleging claims under the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act and Fair Housing Act related to their new home purchase, including workmanship defects and discriminatory refusal to make repairs. The court dismissed the case without prejudice for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, finding the FHA claim time-barred and the MMWA claim legally deficient, without reaching the merits of the discrimination allegations.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Warth v. Seldin, 422 U.S. 490 (1975)
Garcia v. Brockway, 526 F.3d 456 (9th Cir. 2008)
Bennett v. CMH Homes, Inc., 770 F.3d 511 (6th Cir. 2014)
Comm. Concerning Cmty. Improvement v. City of Modesto, 583 F.3d 690 (9th Cir. 2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to repair defects in newly constructed home (drywall, electrical systems, plumbing, roofing, floor tiles, cabinetry, countertops, trim, framing, insulation) allegedly based on national origin
fha_claims.reasoning: The FHA claim is time-barred under 42 U.S.C. § 3613(a)(1)(A), which requires filing within two years of the occurrence or termination of the discriminatory practice. The alleged discrimination terminated on May 5, 2022, when defendants stopped communicating with plaintiffs; the two-year statute of limitations expired on May 5, 2024, but plaintiffs did not file until February 3, 2025. The court rejected arguments for tolling based on subsequent health effects or a state-law prerequisite letter, as these do not constitute continuing discrimination or new occurrences.

source_file: 10603130_2025_Ridge Point Apartments v. ThompsonCase remanded to Harris County Court at Lat No. 1._txsd
case_name: Ridge Point Apartments v. Thompson
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request described in this procedural remand order
key_holding: The court remanded the case to state court for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction over Thompson's Fair Housing Act claims, rendering his pending class certification motions moot.
brief_summary: Ridge Point Apartments sued tenant Jim Thompson in Texas state court to evict him; Thompson removed the case to federal court and sought to assert Fair Housing Act claims against Harris County. The district court adopted the magistrate judge's recommendation to remand for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, denying Thompson's class certification motions as moot.
key_cases_cited: Guillory v. PPG Industries Inc
Douglass v. United Services Automobile Association
United States v. Wilson

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Thompson purported to assert claims under the Fair Housing Act against Harris County and others as third-party defendants, but the opinion does not specify the nature of the FHA claims or any accommodation requested.
fha_claims.disposition: Remanded for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction
fha_claims.reasoning: The court adopted the Magistrate Judge's recommendation to remand the matter for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction without reaching the merits of any FHA claims. The opinion does not specify the jurisdictional defect but indicates the federal court lacked authority to hear the case.

source_file: 10603183_2025_JONES v. FEATHERSTONE CONDOMINIUM HOMEOWNERS ASSOCIATION INC_gamd
case_name: Quincy Bernard Jones v. Featherstone Condominium Homeowners Association Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that Defendants remove slippery, wet dirt from his parking spot and the sidewalk connected to his unit because he is afraid he will slip and fall.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's failure-to-accommodate claim because he failed to allege what his disability is or explain how cleaning the parking space and sidewalk would address limitations caused by his disability.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Quincy Jones, proceeding in forma pauperis, sued Featherstone Condominium Homeowners Association alleging failure to accommodate his disability by removing slippery dirt from his parking spot and sidewalk, along with retaliation claims. The court dismissed the complaint without prejudice for failure to state a claim, finding that Jones failed to allege what his disability is or explain how the requested accommodation would address limitations caused by his disability.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Philippeaux v. Apartment Inv. & Mgmt. Co., 598 F. App'x 640 (11th Cir. 2015)
Schwarz v. City of Treasure Island, 544 F.3d 1201 (11th Cir. 2008)
Schaw v. Habitat for Human. of Citrus Cnty., Inc., 938 F.3d 1259 (11th Cir. 2019)
Watts v. Joggers Run Prop. Owners Ass'n, Inc., 133 F.4th 1032 (11th Cir. 2025)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege an adverse action by defendants. Merely informing a landlord of pending legal claims does not constitute coercion, intimidation, threat, or interference under 42 U.S.C. § 3617, and therefore fails to state a plausible retaliation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Same as Claim 1: plaintiff alleged only that defendants informed his landlord of the lawsuit, which does not constitute an adverse action under the FHA's antiretaliation provision.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Removal of slippery, wet dirt from plaintiff's parking spot and sidewalk connected to his unit to prevent slip-and-fall injuries
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege what his disability is or how the requested accommodation (cleaning a parking space and sidewalk) would address a need created by that disability. Under the FHA, an accommodation is only 'necessary' if it alleviates the effects of an impairment that limits a person's ability to walk, see, hear, or work, and plaintiff provided no nexus between his unspecified disability and the requested relief.

case_name: Tasha M. Lester v. Bamboo Broadway, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges lease non-renewal was racially discriminatory; no disability accommodation request is at issue.
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA race discrimination claim was dismissed because she failed to allege any factual content showing she was treated differently due to her race, and she admitted she owed unpaid rent and failed to pay on time.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Tasha Lester sued Bamboo Broadway, LLC alleging racial discrimination under the Fair Housing Act related to the landlord's decision not to renew her lease. The court dismissed her complaint for failure to state a claim because she provided no factual allegations demonstrating discriminatory treatment based on race, and she conceded she owed back rent and failed to pay by the required deadline.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Gallagher v. Magner, 619 F.3d 823 (8th Cir. 2010)
Radecki v. Joura, 114 F.3d 115 (8th Cir. 1997)
Wheatley v. Beasley, 2021 WL 1667503 (E.D. Mo. Apr. 28, 2021)
Wiles v. Capitol Indem. Corp., 280 F.3d 868 (8th Cir. 2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Lease renewal based on alleged racial discrimination
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege any factual information showing she was treated differently due to a protected provision within the FHA. The complaint contains only conclusory allegations of racial discrimination without the 'who, what, when and where' of what happened, and thus fails to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation for complaining about discriminatory housing practices
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to articulate what housing practices she complained about that were protected under the FHA or Constitution. The return of a check under 'suspicious circumstances' does not establish a protected FHA complaint or retaliation nexus.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (First Amendment retaliation, Fifth and Fourteenth Amendment due process); Equal Credit Opportunity Act, 15 U.S.C. §§ 1691 et seq.; state law negligence claim for stolen items from storage unit
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 1983 claims fail because plaintiff did not allege that Bamboo Broadway, LLC acted under color of state law; a private property management company is not a state actor. ECOA claim fails because plaintiff did not allege defendant was a creditor, that she applied for a loan, or that she was rejected based on a protected class. State negligence claim was dismissed as supplemental jurisdiction was declined after federal claims were dismissed.

source_file: 10603332_2025_Kenneth S. Taylor v. Judge Michael C. Martin_cacd
case_name: Kenneth S. Taylor et al. v. Judge Michael C. Martin et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged a general denial of Fair Housing Act and ADA protections in connection with their eviction from Temecula Senior Apartments, but did not specify or detail any particular accommodation request; the claim appears incidental to their broader challenge of the state court's unlawful detainer ruling.
key_holding: The district court denied plaintiffs' TRO and sua sponte dismissed all claims with prejudice as frivolous and violating Rule 8, finding the complaint was essentially an improper attempt to challenge a state court unlawful detainer ruling barred by the Rooker-Feldman doctrine.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Kenneth and Alycia Taylor sued a state court judge, their landlord (FG Temecula Senior Apartments, LP), and various other individuals after losing an unlawful detainer bench trial following their failure to pay rent in February and March 2025. Their shotgun complaint alleged a wide array of violations including Fourteenth Amendment due process, First Amendment retaliation, Fair Housing Act and ADA protections denial, conspiracy to violate civil rights, Monell claims, and intentional infliction of emotional distress, along with a motion for a TRO to halt eviction. The court denied the TRO for failure to show likelihood of success on the merits, dismissed all claims with prejudice as frivolous under Rule 8, and applied the Rooker-Feldman doctrine to bar federal review of the state unlawful detainer proceeding.
key_cases_cited: Winter v. NRDC, Inc., 555 U.S. 7 (2008)
Partington v. Gedan, 961 F.2d 852 (9th Cir. 1992)
Perry v. NP Parc Chateaux, LLC, No. 22-cv-05378 (C.D. Cal. 2022)
Watts v. Santos, 48 F.3d 1230 (9th Cir. 1995)
McHenry v. Renne, 84 F.3d 1172 (9th Cir. 1996)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged denial of Fair Housing Act and ADA protections, along with Fourteenth Amendment due process violations, First Amendment retaliation, conspiracy to violate civil rights, fraud on the court, Monell claims, intentional infliction of emotional distress, equal protection violations, and judicial misconduct.
fha_claims.disposition: Frivolous dismissal under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B); Rule 8 violation
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed all claims as frivolous under § 1915(e)(2)(B) because they lack an arguable basis in law or fact, violate Rule 8's pleading requirements, and constitute an improper collateral attack on a state court unlawful detainer judgment barred by the Rooker-Feldman doctrine. The court found plaintiffs could not possibly win relief.

case_name: Benvin v. City of Inkster
accommodation_description: No accommodation requested; case involves neighbor harassment claims under § 3617 (racial slurs, 'racist' accusations, loud music) rather than a disability accommodation request
key_holding: The court found that plaintiffs' § 3617 interference claims failed because the alleged conduct (three racial comments over five years, loud music) was insufficiently severe or pervasive to establish Fair Housing Act liability, and ordered plaintiffs to show cause why federal claims should not be dismissed for failure to state a claim
brief_summary: Peter and Denise Benvin sued neighbor William Garrett and the City of Inkster alleging that Garrett engaged in racially-motivated harassment (calling Benvin a racist, white trash, and making other racial comments over five years), and that the City failed to respond to complaints. The court denied plaintiffs' motions for default judgment without prejudice and ordered plaintiffs to show cause why their federal claims should not be dismissed, finding the § 3617 claims legally deficient because the alleged conduct did not constitute actionable interference under the Fair Housing Act.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Egan v. Schmock
Ohana v. 180 Prospect Place Realty Corp.
Harris v. Cooley
Monell v. Dep't of Soc. Servs.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges neighbor harassment and racial slurs, not a request for accommodation
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found allegations of racial slurs and harassment spread over five years were too vague, conclusory, and insufficient to establish a violation of § 3617, which requires conduct that is 'sufficiently pervasive and severe' and implicates FHA concerns, not merely neighbor disputes. Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege facts showing more than 'a quarrel among neighbors.'

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 due process and equal protection claims; state law ethnic intimidation claim under Mich. Comp. Laws § 750.147b
fha_claims.reasoning: § 1983 claims against the City failed because plaintiffs did not allege a municipal policy or custom under Monell and did not establish that failure to enforce ordinances constitutes a constitutional violation; DeShaney and Town of Castle Rock establish no affirmative duty to protect citizens from private actors. State law claims dismissed for lack of supplemental jurisdiction.

case_name: Jane Doe v. Spillman Ranch Homes, LP and The NRP Group
accommodation_description: Request to be allowed to leave trash and recycling bins outside her unit without incurring fees as a reasonable accommodation for disability
key_holding: Summary judgment for defendants was proper because plaintiff failed to demonstrate a triable issue of fact as to defendant's knowledge of her disability—she never returned the reasonable accommodation form—and failed to show she requested an accommodation in direct and specific terms as required.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Jane Doe, proceeding pro se, sued Spillman Ranch Homes, LP and The NRP Group, alleging Fair Housing Act claims including failure to accommodate, discrimination based on race, gender, and disability, and retaliation. The court granted defendants' motion for summary judgment, dismissing all claims with prejudice, finding plaintiff failed to provide evidence that defendants knew of her disability or that she properly requested an accommodation in direct and specific terms.
key_cases_cited: Providence Behav. Health v. Grant Rd. Pub. Util. Dist., 902 F.3d 448 (5th Cir. 2018)
Chavez v. Aber, 122 F. Supp. 3d 581 (W.D. Tex. 2015)
Wyndham v. Harris Cnty., 875 F.3d 229 (5th Cir. 2017)
