Inclusive Cmtys. Project, Inc. v. Lincoln Prop. Co., 920 F.3d 890 (5th Cir. 2019)
McDonnell Douglas v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request to leave trash and recycling bins outside unit without incurring fees due to disability preventing plaintiff from moving bins in compliance with lease
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish that defendants knew or reasonably should have known of her disability because she never returned the reasonable accommodation form provided by defendants and never specifically identified her disability to them. Additionally, plaintiff failed to request the accommodation in direct and specific terms as required by law.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination based on race, gender, and disability in refusing to fix sewage pipes, raising rent, and declining to renew lease
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish prima facie case because she provided no evidence that similarly situated residents outside her protected class were treated more favorably. Even if prima facie case were established, defendants articulated legitimate non-discriminatory reasons for their actions (lease violations, failure to enter service requests, unauthorized animals, failure to pay rent), and plaintiff provided only conclusory assertions without evidence that her protected traits were a significant factor in defendants' decisions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation for filing fair-housing complaint through opening garage remotely, sending unrequested maintenance, and raising rent
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish the third element of retaliation—causal connection between protected activity and adverse action. Even assuming protected activity, defendants articulated legitimate non-discriminatory reasons for their actions (holdover rent rate applied when lease expired, not an increase), and plaintiff failed to raise a genuine dispute of material fact that defendants' reasons were pretextual.

case_name: Lynya Cooper v. Chicago Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Request to transfer Ms. Talbert, who had a progressive neurological disease rendering her unable to walk, from a second-floor apartment to a wheelchair-accessible ground floor unit
key_holding: The court approved a $525,000 settlement and allocated 95% to Lynya Cooper individually ($498,750) and 5% to the Estate of Trebora Talbert ($26,250), finding the settlement fair and reasonable after thorough negotiation.
brief_summary: Lynya Cooper sued the Chicago Housing Authority on behalf of herself and her late daughter Trebora Talbert, alleging the CHA failed to provide reasonable alternative housing accommodations (transfer to a wheelchair-accessible unit) for 788 days despite Ms. Talbert's progressive neurological disease rendering her unable to walk. The court approved the parties' $525,000 settlement and allocated 95% to Ms. Cooper individually and 5% to the Estate.
key_cases_cited: Williams v. Rush-Presbyterian St. Luke's Med. Ctr., 899 N.E.2d 1241 (Ill. App. Ct. 2008)
Johnson v. Provena St. Therese Med. Ctr., 778 N.E.2d 298 (Ill. App. Ct. 2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Transfer to a wheelchair-accessible first-floor unit in lieu of second-floor apartment; plaintiff requested reasonable alternative housing accommodation for disabled daughter with progressive neurological disease unable to walk or perform everyday activities
fha_claims.reasoning: Parties settled claims for $525,000 after thorough settlement conference. Plaintiff alleged CHA failed to provide reasonable alternative housing accommodation and failed to properly engage in interactive process for 788 days between July 2020 and daughter's death in September 2022. Settlement approved as fair and reasonable result of negotiation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rehabilitation Act (29 U.S.C. § 701 et seq.), Americans with Disabilities Act (42 U.S.C. § 12101 et seq.), Illinois Human Rights Act (775 ILCS § 5/101 et seq.)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff asserted parallel claims under Rehabilitation Act, ADA, and Illinois Human Rights Act on behalf of herself and Estate of Trebora Talbert. All claims settled as part of single $525,000 settlement agreement approved by court and CHA Board.

case_name: Marcus Hinton, et al. v. County of Cochise, et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request alleged; plaintiffs claim they were illegally evicted and subjected to racial epithets, alleging housing discrimination based on race under § 3604(a).
key_holding: Plaintiffs fail to state a Fair Housing Act claim because they do not plausibly allege that the County Defendants, who are not alleged to have had any authority to sell or rent the property, engaged in housing discrimination based on race; the vague allegation that racial epithets were directed at them does not support an inference of housing discrimination under § 3604(a).
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Marcus, Vanessa, and Veronica Hinton sued Cochise County and numerous other defendants alleging they were illegally evicted from their rental property, subjected to racial slurs, and had their property stolen by law enforcement officials. The Court granted the County Defendants' motion to dismiss the Fair Housing Act claim, finding that plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege that county officials with no authority to rent property engaged in housing discrimination based on race under § 3604(a), though the Court granted leave to amend the complaint.
key_cases_cited: Benavidez v. County of San Diego, 993 F.3d 1134 (9th Cir. 2021)
Monell v. Dep't of Soc. Servs., 436 U.S. 658 (1978)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege that County Defendants, who had no authority to sell or rent the property, engaged in housing discrimination based on race. Vague allegations that racial epithets were directed at Plaintiffs on one occasion do not support an inference of discrimination in the refusal to sell or rent under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(a).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 Fourth Amendment, § 1983 Due Process, RICO
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to state a § 1983 claim against Cochise County for lack of municipal liability allegations; failed to state a claim against the Fire Chief whose conduct was reasonable; failed to state a claim against individual defendants (Sheriff, Watkins, Parker) by referring to them generally without alleging what each defendant specifically did; and failed to state a RICO claim by alleging only threadbare and conclusory allegations of predicate acts without factual support.

case_name: T&R Properties, Inc. v. Berlin Township
accommodation_description: No accommodation request—this case involves a developer's challenge to municipal zoning denial based on racial discrimination and disparate impact under the FHA.
key_holding: The Fair Housing Advocates Association lacks standing to intervene because its alleged injuries—resource diversion and frustration of organizational mission—do not constitute a concrete, particularized injury caused by the Township's actions, and its proposed claims are duplicative of the original plaintiff's claims.
brief_summary: T&R Properties sued Berlin Township alleging the municipality denied zoning approval for affordable housing with discriminatory intent against racial minorities. Fair Housing Advocates Association moved to intervene, asserting its own intentional discrimination and disparate impact claims. The court denied the motion to intervene, finding FHAA lacks Article III standing because its alleged injuries—resource expenditure investigating the Township and frustration of its anti-discrimination mission—do not constitute a concrete injury traceable to the Township's conduct, and its claims are duplicative of T&R's.
key_cases_cited: FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine, 602 U.S. 367 (2024)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Grutter v. Bollinger, 188 F.3d 394 (6th Cir. 1999)
Purnell v. City of Akron, 925 F.2d 941 (6th Cir. 1991)
Fair Housing Ctr. of Metro. Detroit v. Singh Senior Living, 124 F.4th 990 (6th Cir. 2025)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied FHAA's motion to intervene on standing grounds under FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine, finding FHAA lacked a concrete injury in fact and could not manufacture standing through voluntary expenditure of resources to investigate and advocate against the Township's alleged discriminatory denial of T&R's zoning applications. The underlying disparate treatment claim brought by T&R remains pending.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied FHAA's motion to intervene on standing grounds, finding FHAA lacked a concrete injury in fact independent of T&R's injury and could not establish a substantial legal interest in the Township's denial of T&R's zoning applications. The underlying disparate impact claim brought by T&R remains pending.

case_name: Anthony Alexander James v. Matzger Management Company
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: The magistrate recommends dismissal without prejudice because plaintiff, proceeding pro se, failed to file a Second Amended Complaint after being granted leave to amend and failed to respond to an order to show cause regarding failure to prosecute.
brief_summary: Anthony Alexander James, proceeding pro se, sued Matzger Management Company alleging Fair Housing Act violations and other claims. Following a prior order granting defendant leave to amend, the Court issued findings and recommendations recommending dismissal without prejudice because plaintiff failed to file a Second Amended Complaint or respond to an order to show cause for failure to prosecute.
key_cases_cited: Martinez v. Yist, 951 F.2d 1153 (9th Cir. 1991)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act violation (unspecified)
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to amend after leave granted
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff was granted leave to amend his Fair Housing Act claim but failed to file a Second Amended Complaint within the extended deadline despite a show cause order, resulting in dismissal for failure to prosecute.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Negligence, intentional infliction of emotional distress, harassment, fraud
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to amend after leave granted
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff was granted leave to amend his negligence and IIED claims but failed to file a Second Amended Complaint within the extended deadline despite a show cause order, resulting in dismissal for failure to prosecute.

case_name: McLain v. Sedgwick County Sheriff's Office
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs request extended time for filings, clear written instructions, and accommodations for disability-related communication barriers during legal proceedings due to Michael McLain's PTSD, TBI, and cognitive impairments affecting cognitive processing, memory, and communication.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiffs' motion for appointed counsel after evaluating the four relevant factors, finding that while plaintiff Michael McLain has documented cognitive disabilities (PTSD, TBI, stroke-related impairment), his filings in this litigation have been articulate and well-organized, and plaintiffs failed to demonstrate diligent efforts to obtain counsel on their own.
brief_summary: Michael S. McLain and Janette McLain, proceeding pro se, sued Sedgwick County Sheriff's Office and other defendants asserting civil rights claims including ADA and Fair Housing Act violations, and filed a motion seeking appointed counsel and disability accommodations (extended time, clear instructions, communication support) for Michael McLain's PTSD, TBI, and cognitive impairments. The court denied the motion for appointed counsel, finding plaintiffs' filings were articulate and organized despite their claimed disabilities, and declined to issue prospective accommodations, indicating it would address accommodation requests on an as-needed basis.
key_cases_cited: Beaudry v. Corr. Corp. of Am., 331 F.3d 1164 (10th Cir. 2003)
McCarthy v. Weinberg, 753 F.2d 836 (10th Cir. 1985)
Castner v. Colorado Springs Cablevision, 979 F.2d 1417 (10th Cir. 1992)
Hill v. SmithKline Beecham Corp., 393 F.3d 1111 (10th Cir. 2004)
Lane v. Brewer, 2008 WL 3271921 (D. Kan. Aug. 7, 2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Extended time for filings when necessary due to disability-related limitations; clear, written instructions for procedural requirements; accommodation for disability-related communication barriers during proceedings; other accommodations deemed necessary to ensure effective participation in litigation
fha_claims.reasoning: The court declined to provide prospective reasonable accommodations in the litigation context, stating it would address such requests on an 'as needed' basis in real time as circumstances arise, rather than granting blanket prospective relief.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983, Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act, the First Amendment, Fourth Amendment, Fifth Amendment, Fourteenth Amendment, and the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act (RICO), 18 U.S.C. § 1962
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the motion for appointment of counsel on discretionary grounds under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(1), finding that plaintiffs had not demonstrated sufficient diligence in seeking counsel, had adequate financial means, and possessed adequate capacity to present the case pro se based on their demonstrated litigation filings.

case_name: Joy Lucretia Clark v. PNC Bank
accommodation_description: No accommodation requested; case concerns denial of a business trust account application at a bank.
key_holding: The FHA claim was dismissed with prejudice because the statute does not apply to business bank account applications—the FHA applies only to dwellings, and Clark alleged no facts connecting her claim to housing discrimination.
brief_summary: Joy Lucretia Clark sued PNC Bank for denying her business trust account application, invoking the Fair Housing Act, Consumer Financial Protection Act, and Equal Credit Opportunity Act. The court dismissed her complaint with prejudice under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B), finding the FHA inapplicable to banking transactions with no connection to dwellings, the CFP Act provides no private right of action, and the ECOA claim lacked any factual allegations of prohibited discrimination.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Neitzke v. Williams, 490 U.S. 319 (1989)
Deutsch v. United States, 67 F.3d 1080 (3d Cir. 1995)
Grayson v. Mayview State Hosp., 293 F.3d 103 (3d Cir. 2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff cited Fair Housing Act, Consumer Financial Protection Act, and Equal Credit Opportunity Act in connection with denial of business trust account application
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed all statutory claims as frivolous and legally baseless under § 1915(e)(2)(B). The FHA claim was dismissed because it concerns a business trust account application, not a dwelling or housing-related transaction, and contains no allegations of discrimination based on a protected class. The Consumer Financial Protection Act claim was dismissed because it creates no private cause of action. The Equal Credit Opportunity Act claim was dismissed because the complaint alleges no discrimination based on prohibited grounds and fails to state a plausible claim under that statute.

source_file: 10613505_2025_White Lake Caddis, LLC v. White Lake, Charter Township of_mied
case_name: White Lake Caddis, LLC v. Charter Township of White Lake
accommodation_description: Developer seeks to place a three-quarter transitional living facility for individuals recovering from addiction without being required to comply with all ordinances applicable to adult foster care congregate facilities.
key_holding: The court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the breach of contract claim because it did not relate to the federal discrimination claims and would substantially expand the scope of litigation, and therefore denied the preliminary injunction motion without prejudice.
brief_summary: White Lake Caddis, LLC sued Charter Township of White Lake alleging discriminatory zoning practices that prohibited development of a three-quarter transitional living facility for individuals in recovery from addiction. The court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the plaintiff's breach of contract claim and denied without prejudice the motion for preliminary injunction on that state law claim, which the court found unrelated to the federal Fair Housing Act and ADA claims that remain pending.
key_cases_cited: United Mine Workers of Am. v. Gibbs, 383 U.S. 715 (1966)
Moor v. County of Alameda, 411 U.S. 693 (1973)
Michigan Paralyzed Veterans of Am. v. Charter Twp. of Oakland, Mich., No. 14-14601, 2015 WL 4078142 (E.D. Mich. July 2, 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Approval of special use permit for a three-quarter transitional living facility (sober living group home) for individuals in recovery from addiction on multi-family residential zoned property without subjecting the facility to adult foster care congregate facility ordinances
fha_claims.reasoning: The court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the breach of contract claim and deferred ruling on the preliminary injunction motion without prejudice. The FHA claims (including the reasonable accommodation claim for the transitional living facility) remain pending before the court, which retained jurisdiction over all federal discrimination claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act Title II, 42 U.S.C. §§ 1231 et seq.; Michigan Persons with Disabilities Civil Rights Act, Mich. Comp. Laws §§ 37.1301-1303, 27.1501-1507; Substantive Due Process Clauses of US Constitution and Michigan Constitution; Michigan Exclusionary Zoning Statute, Mich. Comp. Laws § 125.3207
fha_claims.reasoning: The court retained supplemental jurisdiction over the state law discrimination claims (Third, Fifth, and Sixth Causes of Action) as they are related to the federal FHA claims and form part of the same case or controversy. These claims survive the preliminary injunction motion and remain pending.

source_file: 10614302_2025_Mills Pond Grp., LLC v. Town of Smithtown_ca2
case_name: Mills Pond Grp., LLC v. Town of Smithtown
accommodation_description: Developer sought special exception approval to build an assisted living facility in a residentially-zoned district, asserting that denial of such approval violates the Fair Housing Act.
key_holding: The Second Circuit affirmed dismissal, holding that the developer's Fair Housing Act claims were unripe because the developer failed to apply for a variance with the Zoning Board of Appeals before seeking federal judicial review, and failed to demonstrate that such an application would be futile.
brief_summary: Mills Pond Group LLC, a real estate developer, and putative future residents of a planned assisted living facility sued the Town of Smithtown after the Town passed an ordinance amendment preventing assisted living facilities in residential zones and denied the developer's special exception application without prejudice. The Second Circuit affirmed dismissal, holding the claims were unripe because the developer failed to apply for a variance with the Zoning Board of Appeals and did not demonstrate that such an application would be futile.
key_cases_cited: Village Green at Sayville, LLC v. Town of Islip, 43 F.4th 287 (2d Cir. 2022)
Sunrise Detox V, LLC v. City of White Plains, 769 F.3d 118 (2d Cir. 2014)
BMG Monroe I, LLC v. Village of Monroe, 93 F.4th 595 (2d Cir. 2024)
Williamson Cnty. Reg'l Planning Comm'n v. Hamilton Bank of Johnson City, 473 U.S. 172 (1985)
Sherman v. Town of Chester, 752 F.3d 554 (2d Cir. 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act claim alleging discrimination in zoning/land use approval for assisted living facility; Americans with Disabilities Act claim; Equal Protection Clause claim; Due Process Clause claim; New York state law claims
fha_claims.disposition: Affirmed on ripeness and standing grounds
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court affirmed the district court's dismissal on ripeness grounds under the final-decision requirement for land use disputes. The court held that Mills Pond failed to exhaust local remedies by not applying for a variance with the Zoning Board of Appeals, and thus the claims were unripe for federal adjudication. The court did not reach the merits of the FHA, ADA, or constitutional claims.

source_file: 10614323_2025_FDA v. R. J. Reynolds Vapor Co._scotus

case_name: Danell R. Scoggins v. Falcon Court and Turning Point of Central California
citation: No reporter citation (E.D. Cal. Case No. 1:24-cv-00188-KES-SKO)
accommodation_description: Pro se plaintiff alleged some form of retaliation by housing providers, but failed to identify protected activity or adverse action with sufficient specificity
key_holding: The second amended complaint was dismissed because plaintiff failed to plead facts sufficient to state a retaliation claim under the Fair Housing Act, specifically failing to identify any protected activity in which she engaged and any sufficiently adverse action taken by defendants.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Danell Scoggins sued Falcon Court and Turning Point of Central California alleging retaliation under the Fair Housing Act. The district court adopted the magistrate judge's findings and recommendations and dismissed the case without leave to amend because the second amended complaint failed to plead facts sufficient to state a retaliation claim under the FHA, as plaintiff did not identify protected activity or sufficiently adverse actions by defendants.
key_cases_cited: Walker v. City of Lakewood, 272 F.3d 1114 (9th Cir. 2001)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead facts sufficient to establish a prima facie retaliation claim under the Fair Housing Act. The complaint did not identify any protected activity in which plaintiff engaged or any sufficiently adverse action taken by defendants, failing to satisfy the three-element test under Walker v. City of Lakewood.

source_file: 10615091_2025_Affinity Recovery Center LLC v. Town Commissioners of Sudlersville_ca4
case_name: Affinity Recovery Center LLC v. Town Commissioners of Sudlersville
accommodation_description: The specific accommodation requested is not described in this brief appellate opinion; however, given the plaintiff's identity as a recovery center LLC suing a municipality under the FHA and ADA, the accommodation likely involved a request for a zoning exception, variance, or permit to operate a substance use recovery/sober living facility within the Town of Sudlersville.
key_holding: The Fourth Circuit affirmed the district court's order granting the Town Commissioners of Sudlersville's motion to dismiss or, in the alternative, for summary judgment on Affinity Recovery Center LLC's claims under Title II of the ADA and the Fair Housing Act, finding no reversible error.
brief_summary: Affinity Recovery Center LLC, a substance use recovery center operator, sued the Town Commissioners of Sudlersville asserting claims under Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act and the Fair Housing Act. The district court granted defendant's motion to dismiss or, in the alternative, for summary judgment. The Fourth Circuit affirmed without oral argument, finding no reversible error in the district court's ruling.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Zoning accommodation or land use exception to permit operation of a sober living/recovery group home facility
fha_claims.disposition: Motion to Dismiss or, in the alternative, Summary Judgment
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court affirmed the district court's order granting the defendant's motion to dismiss or, in the alternative, for summary judgment on the FHA claims without substantive analysis, finding no reversible error in the lower court's disposition.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), 42 U.S.C. §§ 12131-12134
fha_claims.disposition: Motion to Dismiss or, in the alternative, Summary Judgment
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court affirmed the district court's order granting the defendant's motion to dismiss or, in the alternative, for summary judgment on the ADA Title II claims without substantive analysis, finding no reversible error.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 conditions of confinement claim; Eighth Amendment cruel and unusual punishment claim regarding constant overhead lighting in prison cell, mold/feces on ceiling, water intrusion from leaky roof, and stale air in cell; Prison Litigation Reform Act (PLRA) exhaustion requirement
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to exhaust administrative remedies as to mold, feces, water intrusion, and stale air claims. As to the exhausted light claim, the court found no Eighth Amendment violation because: (1) the overhead light remaining on for approximately three months does not constitute a deprivation of a basic human need; (2) defendants responded to plaintiff's grievances and worked with maintenance to fix the issue, demonstrating lack of deliberate indifference; (3) plaintiff's medical records indicate his sleep disturbance was caused by mental health issues (nightmares and anxiety) rather than the light; and (4) the PLRA bars recovery for mental or emotional injury without prior showing of physical injury. Defendants also entitled to qualified immunity because no constitutional violation occurred.

source_file: 10615697_2025_Audette v. Lake of the Woods County_mnd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 12-foot-wide concrete ramp to the lake to provide accessibility for Jennifer Audette, who has multiple sclerosis, to access the lakeshore
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the 'too little, too late' doctrine, holding that the Audettes' request for reasonable accommodation came only after they had completed unpermitted concrete work in violation of county zoning ordinances and state wetland conservation laws, and only after receiving notice of violations. The court found that property owners must engage in an interactive dialogue with regulators before undertaking construction, and the failure to do so is fatal to a reasonable accommodation claim under Title II of the ADA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework and found that although the Audettes established a prima facie case, the defendants articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for denying the permit: environmental concerns (nutrient impairment, shoreline erosion) and the Audettes' willful, egregious violation of zoning ordinances. The Audettes failed to raise a genuine dispute of material fact that these reasons were pretextual for disability discrimination, as the Board's comments reflected hostility toward the Audettes' conduct in flouting zoning rules, not toward Jennifer's disability.

case_name: United States v. AION Management, LLC
accommodation_description: Fair housing testers requested assigned parking spaces as a reasonable accommodation for mobility impairments (inability to walk long distances, use of canes, crutches, or walkers).
key_holding: The court denied Defendants' motion for reconsideration and motion to certify for interlocutory appeal, holding that (1) plaintiffs plausibly alleged necessity for assigned parking accommodations based on specific physical impairments, (2) testers have standing to bring § 3604(f)(3)(B) claims under fair housing law, and (3) § 3604(c) discriminatory statement claims are not duplicative of § 3604(f)(3)(B) claims.
brief_summary: The United States and Fair Housing Partnership of Greater Pittsburgh, Inc. sued AION Management, LLC and related entities for allegedly refusing to provide assigned parking spaces as reasonable accommodations for testers representing mobility-impaired individuals, in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The court denied Defendants' motion for reconsideration and motion to certify for interlocutory appeal, upholding its prior ruling that plaintiffs plausibly pleaded necessity for the accommodations and that fair housing testers have standing to assert § 3604(f)(3)(B) claims.
key_cases_cited: Vorchheimer v. Philadelphian Owners Association, 903 F.3d 100 (3d Cir. 2018)
FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine, 602 U.S. 367 (2024)
Smith v. Pac. Props. & Dev. Corp., 358 F.3d 1097 (9th Cir. 2004)
United States v. Perry Homes, Inc., 2022 WL 2829887 (W.D. Pa. 2022)
Access Living of Metro Chi. v. Prewitt, 111 F. Supp. 3d 890 (N.D. Ill. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Assigned parking space for individuals with mobility impairments (testers' family members using canes, crutches, walkers, unable to walk more than 100 feet, experiencing fatigue after walking long distances)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiffs plausibly alleged necessity for assigned parking space based on specific factual allegations regarding testers' physical impairments, and rejected defendants' argument that testers categorically lack standing under § 3604(f)(3)(B). The pleading standard was satisfied; merits remain for trial.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged discriminatory statements suggesting preference or non-preference for housing based on association with disabled persons
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that plaintiffs need not allege explicit denial of housing or accommodation, but only that defendants' statements would suggest to an ordinary listener that a protected class is preferred or not preferred. Plaintiffs adequately pleaded § 3604(c) discriminatory statement claims at the pleading stage.

case_name: Arocho v. Chicopee Housing Authority
accommodation_description: No accommodation request was made; the case concerns the housing authority's alleged failure to protect tenants from a violent neighbor based on race/national origin discrimination.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' FHA claims because they failed to plead facts showing they were personally subjected to discriminatory conduct, failed to identify similarly situated comparators treated differently based on race, and because the claims were barred by the FHA's two-year statute of limitations.
brief_summary: Relatives and visitors of a murder victim sued the Chicopee Housing Authority and its executive director, claiming the housing authority violated the FHA by failing to evict a violent tenant with a known criminal history while making derogatory comments about Hispanic residents, thereby discriminating based on race and national origin. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding the visitor plaintiffs lacked standing under the FHA, the tenant plaintiffs failed to plead a plausible disparate treatment claim, and all FHA claims were time-barred.
key_cases_cited: Bank of Am. Corp. v. City of Miami, 581 U.S. 189 (2017)
DeShaney v. Winnebago Cty. Dep't of Soc. Servs., 489 U.S. 189 (1989)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Ctr., 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The FHA claim is barred by the two-year statute of limitations under 42 U.S.C. § 3613(a)(1)(A). The final alleged discriminatory act occurred on September 10, 2021, when Urimagua-Guraboa killed Arocho. The complaint was not filed until August 23, 2024, nearly a year beyond the September 10, 2023 deadline. The continuing violation doctrine does not apply because the plaintiffs failed to allege a series of discriminatory acts emanating from the same discriminatory animus within the limitations period, and the tolling provision does not extend to unrelated administrative proceedings or separate civil actions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses); 42 U.S.C. § 1985(3) (Civil Rights Conspiracy)
fha_claims.reasoning: The substantive due process claim fails because the plaintiffs alleged only private violence by a third party (Urimagua-Guraboa), which does not constitute a violation of the Due Process Clause under DeShaney. The state-created danger exception does not apply because the plaintiffs did not allege an affirmative act by defendants that increased the threat of third-party harm; merely relocating Urimagua-Guraboa next to Laracuente is an allegation of rendering her more vulnerable to risk, not an affirmative act. The equal protection claim fails because the plaintiffs made only conclusory assertions without identifying similarly situated non-Hispanic tenants who received different treatment. The conspiracy claim under § 1985(3) fails because the plaintiffs did not provide minimum factual support for the existence of a conspiracy, did not identify co-conspirators, and did not allege facts showing an agreement to deprive plaintiffs of rights based on race or ethnicity.

case_name: Amanda Craven v. Karyn Knaak and Dane County Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested participation in a HUD homeownership program and an 'exception to payment standard grants' as reasonable accommodations for her disability, and requested office space as a reasonable accommodation.
key_holding: The complaint was dismissed for failure to state a plausible claim because plaintiff did not identify what her disability is, what specific actions each defendant took, or how those actions constituted discrimination, though the court assumed her requests to participate in a homeownership program and for office space as reasonable accommodations related to her disability.
brief_summary: Amanda Craven, a disabled resident of Dane County with a Section 8 housing choice voucher, sued Dane County Housing Authority alleging disability discrimination for denying her request to participate in a HUD homeownership program and interfering with her ability to use her voucher. The court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a plausible claim because Craven did not identify what her disability is, what specific acts each defendant committed, or how those acts constituted discrimination, though the court granted her leave to amend.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Oconomowoc Residential Programs v. City of Milwaukee, 300 F.3d 775 (7th Cir. 2002)
Swanson v. Citibank, N.A., 614 F.3d 400 (7th Cir. 2010)
Wagoner v. Lemmon, 778 F.3d 586 (7th Cir. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Participation in HUD homeownership program as a reasonable accommodation
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to state a plausible claim. She did not identify her disability, did not specify what conduct by the Housing Authority violated her rights, and did not provide details about the homeownership program request sufficient to assess whether the accommodation was reasonable or necessary.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Office space as a reasonable accommodation
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to state a plausible claim. Without information about the nature of plaintiff's disability, the court could not assess whether the requested office space accommodation was reasonable or necessary.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exception to payment standard grants for housing voucher; plaintiff alleges she was required to resubmit requests for payment standard exceptions for each new property rather than having a standing exception approved
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to state a plausible claim. She did not provide details about what exception payment standard HUD initially approved or specific instances in which she was told to resubmit requests, making it impossible to assess whether the Housing Authority's conduct violated the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claim for disability discrimination; § 1983 Due Process Clause claim; state law tortious interference claim
fha_claims.reasoning: For the ADA claim, plaintiff failed to identify what specific action or omission by the Housing Authority denied her benefits or subjected her to discrimination. For the § 1983 due process claim, plaintiff failed to identify what property or liberty interest she was deprived of or what action lacked a hearing or appeal. For the tortious interference claim, plaintiff's allegation that the Housing Authority interfered with her doctor's recommendation was entirely speculative, with no allegation of any actual interaction between the Housing Authority and the doctor.

case_name: Donna Calloway v. Kenyon Morgan, as agent of Prime Time Housing, LLC, and individually, et al.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation requested; case involves alleged housing discrimination based on sex and religion, discriminatory statements, and retaliation.
key_holding: The court rejected defendants' attempt to invoke FHA exemptions as a jurisdictional challenge, characterizing the exemptions as affirmative defenses rather than matters affecting subject matter jurisdiction, and found the court has jurisdiction over claims under §§ 3604(c) and 3617 which are not subject to the exemptions at § 3603(b).
brief_summary: Donna Calloway sued Kenyon Morgan and Prime Time Housing, LLC alleging Fair Housing Act violations including sex discrimination, religious discrimination, discriminatory statements, and retaliation in connection with a home purchase arrangement. Defendants moved to dismiss for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, arguing the FHA's exemptions under § 3603(b) applied. The court denied the motion, holding that FHA exemptions are affirmative defenses rather than jurisdictional defects and that the court has jurisdiction over claims under §§ 3604(c) and 3617, which are not subject to the exemptions.
key_cases_cited: United States v. Space Hunters, Inc., 429 F.3d 416 (2d Cir. 2005)
Osborne v. Belton, 131 F.4th 262 (5th Cir. 2025)
Ho v. Donovan, 569 F.3d 677 (7th Cir. 2009)
Rural Water Dist. No. 2 v. City of Glenpool, 698 F.3d 1270 (10th Cir. 2012)
Czerwinski v. Gallagher, 661 F. Supp. 3d 718 (E.D. Mich. 2023)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Housing discrimination on the basis of sex
fha_claims.disposition: 12(b)(1) — Motion to Dismiss for Lack of Subject Matter Jurisdiction
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that FHA exemptions under § 3603(b) are affirmative defenses, not jurisdictional bars. The complaint alleges claims under § 3604(a) which survive the motion to dismiss because subject matter jurisdiction exists under 28 U.S.C. § 1331 and the exemption defense cannot be resolved on the face of the pleadings without factual development.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Housing discrimination on the basis of religion
fha_claims.disposition: 12(b)(1) — Motion to Dismiss for Lack of Subject Matter Jurisdiction
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that FHA exemptions under § 3603(b) are affirmative defenses, not jurisdictional bars. The complaint alleges claims under § 3604(b) which survive the motion to dismiss because subject matter jurisdiction exists under 28 U.S.C. § 1331 and the exemption defense cannot be resolved on the face of the pleadings without factual development.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discriminatory statements
fha_claims.disposition: 12(b)(1) — Motion to Dismiss for Lack of Subject Matter Jurisdiction
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that § 3604(c) claims for discriminatory statements are not subject to the exemptions in § 3603(b) by their plain language. Accordingly, the court has subject matter jurisdiction over this claim regardless of any exemption defense, and the motion to dismiss is denied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unlawful retaliation for exercise of rights protected under the FHA, specifically the issuance of notice to vacate and initiation of eviction proceedings following plaintiff's termination of sexual relationship with defendant
fha_claims.disposition: 12(b)(1) — Motion to Dismiss for Lack of Subject Matter Jurisdiction
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that § 3617 retaliation claims are not subject to the exemptions in § 3603(b) because § 3603(b) explicitly exempts only 'section 3604 of this title' and does not reference § 3617. Accordingly, the court has subject matter jurisdiction over this claim and the motion to dismiss is denied.

case_name: Tekeva Shaw v. Habitat for Humanity, et al.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation request identified; plaintiff alleged discrimination, breach of contract, privacy violations, and construction defects related to home purchase.
key_holding: The court recommended dismissal with prejudice of Shaw's Fair Housing Act claims under 42 U.S.C. § 3605 because Shaw failed to plead membership in any protected class, failed to plead she met all relevant qualifications, and failed to plead defendants continued similar transactions with others of similar qualifications.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Tekeva Shaw filed suit against Habitat for Humanity, Regions Bank, and various other corporate defendants alleging breach of contract, privacy violations, construction defects, and Fair Housing Act claims stemming from her home purchase. The court recommended dismissing Shaw's federal claims with prejudice for failure to state a claim upon which relief may be granted, finding she failed to plead any protected class membership required under § 3605.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ray v. U.S. Bank Nat. Ass'n, 627 F. App'x 452 (6th Cir. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead membership in a protected class under § 3605 with respect to any alleged discrimination. The court found that plaintiff's allegations of discrimination based on age (against Allstate for auto insurance denial) do not constitute a protected class under § 3605, and auto insurance is not a real estate-related transaction. Plaintiff's complaint was dismissed as frivolous under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) for failure to state a claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of contract, breach of property rights, breach of privacy rights, violation of building codes and safety codes, redlining, private inurement, harassment/exploitation
fha_claims.reasoning: Court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over state-law claims because it lacked diversity jurisdiction (plaintiff and most defendants are Tennessee residents, foreclosing complete diversity under 28 U.S.C. § 1332) and had dismissed all federal claims over which it had original subject matter jurisdiction.

case_name: Sehra Waheed v. Molly Wasow Park, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested reasonable accommodation in eviction proceedings due to disability-related medical injuries affecting her ability to work and financial hardship.
key_holding: The court dismissed Plaintiff's FHA reasonable accommodation claim as beyond the scope of the leave to amend granted, without substantive analysis of the accommodation request.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Sehra Waheed sued her former landlord Trinity Bui and various City of New York officials and agencies, asserting claims including Fair Housing Act reasonable accommodation based on her alleged disability affecting her ability to work and pay rent during eviction proceedings. The court dismissed this FHA claim as beyond the scope of the limited leave to amend granted, and dismissed the entire action for failure to state a claim and lack of standing.
key_cases_cited: Palm Beach Strategic Income, LP v. Salzman, 457 F. App'x 40 (2d Cir. 2012)
Grimes v. Fremont Gen. Corp., 933 F. Supp. 2d 584 (S.D.N.Y. 2013)
Ruotolo v. City of New York, 514 F.3d 184 (2d Cir. 2008)
Salahuddin v. Cuomo, 861 F.2d 40 (2d Cir. 1988)
Coppedge v. United States, 369 U.S. 438 (1962)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation for delay in litigation and financial hardship and medical injuries preventing plaintiff's ability to physically stand on her feet for long hours to work
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the FHA reasonable accommodation claim as beyond the scope of the limited leave to amend granted in the prior order. The claim was asserted against Park, French, and the City of New York arising from alleged failure to accommodate plaintiff's disability in state court eviction proceedings, which exceeded the scope of permitted amendment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Defamation, slander, breach of lease, unlawful housing discrimination, violation of Civil Rights Act and ADA, retaliation, and violation of peace and quiet
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed claims against Trinity Bui and Trinity Financing Investments Corporation as beyond the scope of the limited leave to amend, which did not authorize assertion of new defendants or new claims arising from the eviction. The court dismissed without prejudice to refiling in a new civil action.

source_file: 10622451_2025_Gilbert v. Tucson Realty _ Trust Company Management Services LLC_azd
case_name: Shenoa Gilbert v. Tucson Realty & Trust Company Management Services LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested to transfer from an upper-floor unit to a first-floor unit due to her back injury disability.
key_holding: Plaintiff failed to adequately plead the elements of her reasonable accommodation claim under § 3604(f)(3)(B) because she did not sufficiently allege how her back injury and kidney disease substantially limit major life activities, that defendant knew of her disability, or how the denial deprived her of equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling.
brief_summary: Shenoa Gilbert, a Section 8 voucher holder with a back injury and Stage 3 kidney disease, sued her property management company alleging violations of the Fair Housing Amendments Act and Rehabilitation Act for denying her accommodation requests for a first-floor unit and exemption from pesticide use. The Court dismissed the complaint with leave to amend, finding plaintiff failed to sufficiently plead the elements of her reasonable accommodation and retaliation claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Dubois v. Ass'n of Apartment Owners of 2987 Kalakaua, 453 F.3d 1175 (9th Cir. 2006)
Giebeler v. M & B Assocs., 343 F.3d 1143 (9th Cir. 2003)
Howard v. HMK Holdings, LLC, 988 F.3d 1185 (9th Cir. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Transfer to a first-floor apartment unit due to back injury and disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege how her back injury and kidney disease substantially limit major life activities (element 1), failed to clearly allege she informed defendant of her disability (element 2), failed to allege how denial of first-floor unit deprived her of equal opportunity to use/enjoy dwelling (element 3), and failed to allege defendant knew or should have known of her disability. Although plaintiff demonstrated the accommodations were facially reasonable (element 4) and that defendant refused them (element 5), the complaint failed to satisfy all five elements of the reasonable accommodation claim under Dubois.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exemption from use of chemical pesticides in plaintiff's unit due to severe allergies and Stage 3 kidney disease
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege how her allergies and kidney disease substantially limit major life activities (element 1), failed to clearly allege she informed defendant of her disability (element 2), and failed to clearly allege that exemption from pesticides was necessary to afford equal opportunity to use/enjoy dwelling (element 3). Although the accommodation appeared facially reasonable and defendant refused it, the complaint did not satisfy all five elements of the reasonable accommodation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to extend lease, denial of rent payment, and filing of eviction action allegedly in retaliation for requesting accommodations
fha_claims.reasoning: Under 42 U.S.C. § 3617, plaintiff must allege: (1) protected activity, (2) adverse housing consequence causally linked to that activity, and (3) resulting damage. While plaintiff plausibly alleged protected activity (requesting accommodations) and adverse consequences (lease denial, eviction filing) and damages (emotional/financial harm and risk to Section 8 voucher), she failed to clearly allege the causal nexus between her accommodation requests and the subsequent adverse consequences.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act claim for failure to provide reasonable accommodations for first-floor unit and pesticide exemption
fha_claims.reasoning: Under Section 504, plaintiff must show: (1) she is an individual with a disability, (2) she is otherwise qualified to receive the benefit, (3) she was denied benefits solely by reason of disability, and (4) the program receives federal financial assistance. Plaintiff failed to allege how her back injury and kidney disease substantially limit major life activities (element 1), failed to allege the qualifications necessary to live on the first floor and that she meets them (element 2), failed to allege denial was solely based on disability (element 3), and failed to allege sufficient facts that defendant receives federal financial assistance (element 4).

case_name: Valentine v. Granville Realty, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff Valentine, a disabled U.S. Army veteran, requested emergency injunctive relief to halt eviction proceedings, which he alleges were initiated in retaliation for his disability-related ESA and protected activity.
key_holding: The court denied the TRO motion because Plaintiffs failed to comply with procedural requirements (Rule 65(b) and Local Rule 231) by not providing notice or certifying efforts to notify Defendants, and failed to demonstrate likelihood of success on the merits, irreparable harm, or that equities favored injunctive relief.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Valentine and Hubbard, including a disabled U.S. Army veteran with an ESA, moved for a temporary restraining order to halt eviction proceedings at their Fresno residence, alleging disability discrimination, retaliation under the Fair Housing Act, and Civil RICO violations. The court denied the TRO motion for failure to comply with procedural requirements and for failure to demonstrate likelihood of success on the merits, irreparable harm, or favorable balance of equities.
key_cases_cited: Wood v. City of Hayward, 974 F.2d 1344 (9th Cir. 1992)
Salazar v. Moynihan, 2011 WL 6179262 (E.D. Cal. Dec. 12, 2011)
Gruzen v. Henry, 84 Cal. App. 3d 515 (Ct. App. 1978)
Younger v. Harris, 401 U.S. 37 (1971)
Winter v. Nat. Res. Def. Council, Inc., 555 U.S. 7 (2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Emotional support animal (ESA) prescribed by Department of Veterans Affairs on July 9, 2019, as medically necessary equipment to mitigate plaintiff Valentine's disabilities as a permanently disabled U.S. Army veteran.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the TRO motion on procedural grounds (failure to comply with Rule 65(b) and Local Rule 231 notice requirements) and on the merits (plaintiff failed to demonstrate likelihood of success, irreparable harm, or that equities favored relief). The court did not substantively analyze the reasonable accommodation claim under the FHA framework.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliatory eviction initiated on April 23, 2025, fourteen days after plaintiff's ESA was diagnosed with terminal kidney failure on April 8, 2025.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that although plaintiffs alleged the eviction was retaliatory and timed with the ESA's terminal illness, they failed to demonstrate that the eviction was initiated in response to protected activity or that defendants lacked a legitimate, non-retaliatory basis for the notice. The court did not reach the substantive merits of the retaliation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Civil RICO claims alleging pattern of racketeering, housing fraud, wire fraud, obstruction of justice, and fabrication of rental ledgers; California state law retaliatory eviction claim; claim that property was unlawfully rented without Certificate of Occupancy in violation of California Health and Safety Code § 17920.3.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that RICO allegations, while extensive, relied heavily on conclusory assertions of wire fraud and enterprise conduct unsupported by concrete evidence. The court also noted that federal courts lack jurisdiction to review state court eviction proceedings and that Younger abstention applies to this landlord-tenant dispute governed by state law.

source_file: 10623897_2025_Sutton v. Penny Mac Loan Services, LLC_tnmd

case_name: Charugundla v. First, M.D.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs KC and MC requested a service dog (emotional support animal) for MC's undisclosed psychiatric disability as a reasonable accommodation
key_holding: The court denied Defendant's motion for a stay of discovery based on its assessment of the merits of the pending motions to dismiss, suggesting the court found the reasonable accommodation claims have sufficient merit to proceed.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs KC and MC, residents of the Monarch Condominium since 2000, sued the Condo Defendants and a retained psychiatrist after their August 2021 request for a service dog (emotional support animal) was denied in September 2021 following an independent psychiatric evaluation. The court denied Defendant Dr. First's motion for a stay of discovery pending his motion to dismiss, ruling based on its assessment of the merits of the pending motions that discovery should proceed.
key_cases_cited: UNDETERMINED

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request for emotional support animal (service dog) for MC's mental health disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Defendant Dr. First argued that Plaintiffs failed to plead the required elements of discrimination—that Plaintiff MC was disabled and that the requested accommodation was necessary—which was fatal to the claim. The motion to dismiss is pending resolution; this opinion addresses only a stay of discovery request, not the merits of the MTD.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Aiding and abetting violations of FHA, NYCRL § 47, NYSHRL § 296, and NYC Administrative Code § 8-101
fha_claims.reasoning: Defendant Dr. First argued that a precondition to proving aiding and abetting is a finding of the underlying discrimination, and that Plaintiffs failed to plead the required elements of discrimination. The motion to dismiss is pending; this opinion addresses only a stay of discovery request.

case_name: TL Harvey v. Maxwell & Morgan P.C., et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff filed Fair Housing Act claims against a homeowners association and related defendants, but the specific accommodation requested is not detailed in this attorneys' fees order.
key_holding: Defendants' motion for attorneys' fees was denied because plaintiff's FHA claims were not frivolous and defendants failed to identify which fees were incurred exclusively in defending non-frivolous federal claims.
brief_summary: Plaintiff TL Harvey sued a law firm, property management company, and homeowners association alleging multiple federal and state claims including Fair Housing Act violations and racial discrimination under 42 U.S.C. § 1981. This order addresses only defendants' motion for attorneys' fees, denying the motion because plaintiff's federal claims were not frivolous under the demanding federal standard and defendants failed to segregate recoverable from non-recoverable fees.
key_cases_cited: Harris v. Maricopa Cnty. Superior Ct., 631 F.3d 963 (9th Cir. 2011)
Christiansburg Garment Co. v. EEOC, 434 U.S. 412 (1978)
Galen v. Cnty. of Los Angeles, 477 F.3d 652 (9th Cir. 2007)
Green v. Mercy Hous., Inc., 991 F.3d 1056 (9th Cir. 2021)
Gammel v. Kuna Rural Fire Prot. Dist., 2021 WL 5165675 (D. Idaho Nov. 5, 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act claims (specific nature not detailed in this opinion)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed FHA claims for failure to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly but granted leave to amend, indicating the claims were not frivolous. The opinion does not specify which FHA theory (reasonable accommodation, disparate treatment, etc.) was alleged.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1981 (racial discrimination in making or enforcing contracts); breach of contract; constitutional claims; civil RICO; criminal mail fraud; common law fraud; breach of fiduciary duty
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed non-FHA claims including § 1981, breach of contract, constitutional claims, and others for failure to state a plausible claim. § 1981 claim against certain defendants was weak but not wholly frivolous; plaintiff was granted leave to amend.

case_name: Smith v. ResiPro, LLC
subsidy_program: Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher; Choose to Own Homeownership Program
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request; case centers on alleged discriminatory housing practices based on race and disability in connection with home purchase
key_holding: The court dismissed Plaintiff's FHA claim (Count II) as time-barred under the two-year limitations period, finding no basis to apply the continuing violations doctrine to extend the deadline, and dismissed the ADA and Rehabilitation Act claims (Count III) on the same timeliness grounds.
brief_summary: Ronetta Smith, individually and as guardian for two disabled adults, sued ResiPro LLC and ResiCap LP alleging they performed deficient construction work on her home purchased through the CHA Choose to Own program in Chicago's south side, with claims including FHA discrimination, ADA, and state law torts. The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss the FHA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act claims as time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations, finding no continuing violation exception applied, and dismissed most state law claims for factual insufficiency or failure to state a claim.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Copperweld Corp. v. Indep. Tube Corp., 467 U.S. 752 (1984)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged disability-based discrimination in housing transaction and failure to accommodate disabled individuals (Mildred and Doris Smith) in connection with property purchase and construction defects causing respiratory issues due to mold
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed FHA claim (Count II) as barred by the two-year statute of limitations under 42 U.S.C. § 3613(a). Discriminatory practice occurred in 2017; plaintiff filed complaint in September 2024. Continuing violations doctrine did not apply because plaintiff alleged only isolated conduct with no facts showing discrimination extending into the limitations period.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act and Americans with Disabilities Act Title II claims based on disability discrimination in housing transaction
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed ADA and Section 504 claims (Count III) as barred by Illinois' two-year statute of limitations for personal injury actions. Discriminatory conduct occurred in 2017; complaint filed September 2024. Continuing violations doctrine did not apply for same reasons as FHA claim.

case_name: Jason Calderon v. City of New York
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a homeless individual, does not request a disability accommodation but rather challenges the City's housing system for allegedly treating homeless U.S. citizens differently from migrants/asylum seekers, asserting this violates the FHA.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claim, agreeing with the magistrate judge that the FHA does not apply to individuals seeking free government shelter.
brief_summary: Jason Calderon, a pro se plaintiff, sued the City of New York alleging that the City's shelter system violated equal protection and the Fair Housing Act by providing hotels to migrants and asylum seekers while forcing homeless U.S. citizens to use the general shelter system. The court adopted the magistrate judge's recommendation and granted the City's motion to dismiss, holding that the FHA does not apply to individuals seeking free government shelter and that plaintiff failed to state viable constitutional claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged disparate treatment based on immigration status: U.S. citizens were housed in shelters while migrants and asylum seekers were housed in hotels.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court agreed with the magistrate judge that the FHA does not apply to individuals seeking free government shelter, and therefore the FHA disparate treatment claim failed as a matter of law.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal protection claim under 42 U.S.C. § 1983; due process claims; claims regarding alleged harms to migrants.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to infer unequal treatment under the Equal Protection Clause; lacked standing to bring claims on behalf of migrants; and failed to allege a deprivation of liberty or property sufficient to support a due process claim.

source_file: 10626360_2025_Earle v. Manchester Village Owners Association Inc_wied
case_name: Dawn N. Earle v. Manchester Village Owners Association Inc, et al.
accommodation_description: Earle, who is blind with mobility impairments, requested installation of an accessible pathway/sidewalk from her ground-floor patio door across common grassy area to the public parking lot to enable safe egress and access to public transit.
key_holding: The court denied dismissal of the FHA failure-to-accommodate claim, finding Earle sufficiently alleged the installed walkway was too narrow (30 inches) to accommodate her disability needs and her seeing-eye dog, and that whether an accommodation is reasonable requires a fact-specific inquiry.
brief_summary: Dawn N. Earle, a blind woman with mobility impairments, sued her condominium association alleging violations of the ADA and FHA, including claims that the association failed to reasonably accommodate her disability by installing a non-ADA-compliant walkway and retaliated against her for filing housing discrimination complaints. The court dismissed the ADA claim (which Earle conceded) but denied dismissal of the FHA claims, finding Earle pleaded sufficient facts that the installed walkway was too narrow to accommodate her needs.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Watters v. Homeowners' Ass'n at Pres. at Bridgewater, 48 F.4th 779 (7th Cir. 2022)
Oconomowoc Residential Programs v. City of Milwaukee, 300 F.3d 775 (7th Cir. 2002)
Wetzel v. Glen St. Andrew Living Cmty., LLC, 901 F.3d 856 (7th Cir. 2018)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA-compliant sidewalk/pathway from plaintiff's patio door across common area to public parking lot, with adequate width (at least 60 inches) to accommodate plaintiff and her seeing-eye dog walking side-by-side, and proper drainage to prevent water runoff into plaintiff's unit
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff pleaded sufficient factual allegations that the installed walkway was non-ADA compliant (30 inches wide, improper drainage causing mold damage) to survive motion to dismiss. Defendants' attached exhibits did not incontrovertibly contradict plaintiff's allegations because they were not referenced in the complaint and did not confirm actual completion specifications. Whether accommodation is reasonable requires fact-specific balancing inquiry inappropriate for Rule 12(b)(6) stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff sufficiently alleged all three elements of FHA retaliation claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3617: (1) protected activity (filing Wisconsin ERD complaint on May 12, 2022); (2) adverse action (delay in providing sidewalk, cancellation of initial approval, non-compliant final product); and (3) causal connection (temporal proximity between complaint and delay, statements from defendants that complex was not built for disabled). Allegations of delay as retaliation and failure to provide compliant accommodation survive at pleading stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III claim for discrimination and failure to reasonably accommodate disabilities
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff conceded dismissal of ADA Title III claim for lack of available monetary damages. Court granted dismissal without substantive analysis of the claim's merits.

source_file: 10626608_2025_Lost Lake Holdings LLC v. Town of Forestburgh_nysd
case_name: Lost Lake Holdings LLC v. Town of Forestburgh
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege the Town denied building permits for the Lost Lake Resort development out of discriminatory animus against Hasidic Orthodox Jewish developers.
key_holding: Plaintiffs' land use claims were dismissed as unripe because plaintiffs failed to seek a variance from the Town Board as required under Williamson County's final decision requirement and the Second Circuit's decision in BMG Monroe.
brief_summary: Lost Lake Holdings LLC and Hasidic Jewish individuals sued the Town of Forestburgh alleging religious discrimination in denying building permits for a resort development project; the court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, holding plaintiffs' land use claims were unripe because plaintiffs failed to seek a variance from the Town Board as required under Second Circuit precedent.
key_cases_cited: BMG Monroe I, LLC v. Vil. of Monroe, 93 F.4th 595 (2d Cir. 2024)
Williamson Cnty. Reg'l Planning Comm'n v. Hamilton Bank of Johnson City, 473 U.S. 172 (1985)
Murphy v. New Milford Zoning Com'n, 402 F.3d 342 (2d Cir. 2005)
Sunrise Detox V, LLC v. City of White Plains, 769 F.3d 112 (2d Cir. 2014)
Vill. Green at Sayville, LLC v. Town of Islip, 43 F.4th 287 (2d Cir. 2022)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged Fair Housing Act violations related to alleged religious discrimination in land use decisions, zoning enforcement, and building permit denials. Also alleged violations under 42 U.S.C. § 1982, U.S. Constitution (due process and equal protection), New York State Constitution, New York State Civil Rights Law, and state tort claims (trespass, tortious interference with prospective business advantage).
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed plaintiffs' land use claims (including FHA claims) as unripe for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under the final decision requirement of Williamson County Regional Planning Commission v. Hamilton Bank. Plaintiffs failed to obtain a final decision by not seeking a variance from the Town Board after their building permit applications were denied, and the futility and discrimination exceptions to the final decision requirement did not apply.

case_name: Cynthia Exline-Johnson v. Rosser Properties, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested to remain in her apartment as a reasonable accommodation after receiving a sixty-day notice of lease non-renewal due to smoking complaints.
key_holding: Plaintiff failed to establish she was disabled under the FHA because her sleep impairment was not shown to substantially limit a major life activity, and she presented no evidence that defendants regarded her as disabled, so her reasonable accommodation claim failed at the first element.
brief_summary: Cynthia Exline-Johnson sued Rosser Properties LLC and its owner alleging Fair Housing Act violations after they declined to renew her lease following tenant complaints about smoking, and she requested an accommodation to remain in her apartment. The federal court granted summary judgment for defendants on all federal claims, finding Johnson failed to establish she was disabled under the FHA and therefore could not support her reasonable accommodation, discrimination, or retaliation claims, and dismissed her state-law claims without prejudice.
key_cases_cited: Metropolitan Fair Hous. Council of Oklahoma, Inc. v. Fetock
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green
Steele v. Thiokol Corp.
Cinnamon Hills Youth Crisis Ctr., Inc. v. Saint George City
Bloch v. Frischholz

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Statement or advertisement indicating preference, limitation, or discrimination based on religion
fha_claims.reasoning: The statement at issue was not made 'with respect to the sale or rental of a dwelling' as required by § 3604(c), and no ordinary listener would interpret Ms. Rosser's skeptical comment about Ms. Johnson's spirituality as expressing a religion-based preference in housing.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Making housing unavailable because of disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie case of discrimination under McDonnell Douglas because she presented no evidence that she is handicapped under § 3602(h)(1) or (3). Her testimony of poor sleep without medical evidence, severity, permanence, or long-term impact is insufficient to establish substantial limitation of a major life activity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation to remain in apartment despite lease non-renewal
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to satisfy the first element of the five-part reasonable accommodation test because she presented no evidence establishing that she is handicapped under the FHA, and no evidence that defendants knew or reasonably should have known of any disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation for requesting accommodation and exercising FHA rights
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to present evidence satisfying the third element of the § 3617 retaliation claim—that defendants coerced, threatened, intimidated, or interfered with her on account of her protected activity. Her conclusory allegations of harassment and interference lacked factual support and record citations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Oklahoma Discrimination in Housing Act, Oklahoma Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, Oklahoma Consumer Protection Act, state-law libel
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed all state-law claims without prejudice, finding no compelling reasons to retain supplemental jurisdiction over state-law claims that should ordinarily be tried in state court.

case_name: Quentin Ballentine v. Cares for the Homeless
accommodation_description: Plaintiff's complaint, construed to assert FHA claims, does not specify a particular accommodation request in this order.
key_holding: The court dismisses claims against NYC Department of Homeless Services because it is not a suable entity, and orders service on remaining defendants; the FHA reasonable accommodation claim is not substantively analyzed.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Quentin Ballentine sued Cares for the Homeless, City of New York, and NYC Department of Homeless Services under the ADA, federal constitutional law, and Fair Housing Act, alleging violations of his rights in the homeless services system. The court dismissed the NYC DHS as a non-suable entity and ordered service on the remaining defendants, but has not yet substantively analyzed the FHA reasonable accommodation claim.
key_cases_cited: Livingston v. Adirondack Beverage Co., 141 F.3d 434 (2d Cir. 1998)
Harris v. Mills, 572 F.3d 66 (2d Cir. 2009)
Triestman v. Fed. Bureau of Prisons, 470 F.3d 471 (2d Cir. 2006)
Jenkins v. City of New York, 478 F.3d 76 (2d Cir. 2007)
Emerson v. City of New York, 740 F. Supp. 2d 385 (S.D.N.Y. 2010)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges violations of federal constitutional rights, ADA, and New York state law; court construes amended complaint as potentially asserting FHA claims but does not substantively address any FHA theory
fha_claims.reasoning: Claims against New York City Department of Homeless Services dismissed because a municipal agency cannot be sued under New York City Charter § 396; allegations construed as asserted against the City of New York instead. No substantive analysis of any FHA, ADA, or constitutional claims on the merits.

case_name: John May v. Erie County, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges Defendants failed to address reasonable accommodation requests for disabilities and provided substandard housing based on transgender status and disability.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claims because the complaint failed to provide sufficient factual content to support plausible FHA claims, instead relying on conclusory allegations of wrongdoing.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff John May, a homeless individual identifying as physically and mentally disabled and pansexual, sued Erie County and fourteen other defendants alleging Fair Housing Act violations, Section 1983 constitutional claims, ADA violations, and state law claims related to COVID-19 fund misuse, housing discrimination, and retaliation. The court dismissed the complaint without prejudice for failure to state a claim and lack of standing, finding the FHA claims conclusory and lacking sufficient factual allegations to support a plausible cause of action.
key_cases_cited: Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)
Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins, 578 U.S. 330 (2016)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Monell v. Dep't of Social Services, 436 U.S. 658 (1978)
Roman v. Jeffes, 904 F.2d 192 (3d Cir. 1990)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation requests for Plaintiff's disabilities in connection with housing
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found Complaint failed to provide sufficient factual content regarding reasonable accommodation requests and relied instead on conclusory allegations of wrongdoing. No viable cause of action stated under FHA because Plaintiff did not allege facts from which the Court could infer any named Defendant's liability for FHA violations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged discrimination based on transgender status and disability in provision of housing accommodations
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint alleged that ECCM and associated landlords discriminated based on transgender status and disability, providing substandard and unsafe housing, but failed to provide sufficient factual allegations to state a plausible claim. Court could not infer liability from conclusory allegations alone.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged disparate impact based on disability status in housing provision
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint alleged disparate impact violations but failed to provide factual content sufficient to state a plausible claim. Court found conclusory allegations of wrongdoing insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (Equal Protection, Due Process, First Amendment, Takings Clause); Americans with Disabilities Act Title I and Title II; Rehabilitation Act § 504; state law claims (breach of fiduciary duty, fraud, intentional infliction of emotional distress, negligence, unjust enrichment, Pennsylvania Ethics Act)
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim / § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii); Lack of standing / Article III
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed § 1983 claims for failure to establish standing (as to taxpayer and citizen claims), failure to identify proper defendants (county departments lack separate legal status), failure to allege color of state law as to private defendants, failure to allege personal involvement, and failure to state plausible constitutional violations. ADA/Rehabilitation Act claims dismissed for failure to allege disability status, employment relationship, or specific adverse actions. State law claims dismissed without prejudice as supplemental jurisdiction declined after dismissal of federal claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rehabilitation Act disability discrimination, ADEA age discrimination, Rehabilitation Act interference, Rehabilitation Act and ADEA retaliation
fha_claims.reasoning: All five claims brought under the Rehabilitation Act and ADEA, not the FHA. The court applied the McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework to the disability discrimination and age discrimination claims, and found the BOP articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons (performance issues, concerning conduct, mental health concerns) that were not pretextual. The interference claim failed because denial of leave requests does not constitute unlawful interference under 42 U.S.C. § 12203(b), and the retaliation claim failed because plaintiff could not establish causal connection between EEO activity and investigations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Excusal from responding to emergency situations and inmate disturbances; liberal leave and breaks with leave without pay; reassignment to a vacant position at same agency, commuting area, pay grade, and tenure
fha_claims.reasoning: Under the Rehabilitation Act reasonable accommodation framework, plaintiff failed to identify a specific, reasonable accommodation because excusing him from responding to emergencies would strip the correctional counselor role of its essential functions, which the law does not require. Plaintiff's request for reassignment was too amorphous—he never identified a specific vacant position for which he was qualified, failing to meet his burden under Donahue. The court noted that even if the BOP failed to engage in the interactive process, plaintiff's proposed accommodations were facially unreasonable.

case_name: Mendoza-Lebron v. Adams
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs sought disability-based exemptions from the City's policy of shutting off water to delinquent property owners, including adequate notice of exemption eligibility and procedures to apply.
key_holding: Plaintiffs' ADA and FHA reasonable accommodation claims fail because all plaintiffs ultimately received exemptions from water shutoffs, there was no actual deprivation of water service, and plaintiffs failed to allege they were treated differently because of their disabilities—the City's policy actually provides affirmative exemptions for disabled residents.
brief_summary: Homeowners sued New York City and its water utility officials under the ADA and FHA, alleging that the City's policy of shutting off water to delinquent property owners failed to provide adequate notice of disability exemptions and reasonable accommodations for medically vulnerable residents. The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss, finding all plaintiffs' claims moot because they all qualified for exemptions and none had their water actually shut off, and alternatively that the federal damages claims failed on the merits because plaintiffs did not allege they were treated differently because of their disabilities.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
