key_holding: The court denied the TRO because plaintiff failed to show likelihood of success on her reasonable accommodation claims, as her requested accommodations (environmental screening, washer/dryer, restrictions on other residents, and eviction stay) were not shown to be reasonable without undue burden, and the two-month delay in responding did not constitute a constructive denial absent evidence of bad faith.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Jacqueline Peters sued Cafton Towers Owners Corp. alleging the cooperative building violated the Fair Housing Act by failing to provide reasonable accommodations for her disability and by terminating her lease in retaliation for requesting accommodations. The court denied Peters' motion for a temporary restraining order, finding she failed to demonstrate likelihood of success on the merits because she did not show her requested accommodations were reasonable without undue burden and did not adequately plead pretext for the eviction.
key_cases_cited: Austin v. Town of Farmington, 826 F.3d 622 (2d Cir. 2016)
Logan v. Matveevskii, 57 F. Supp. 3d 234 (S.D.N.Y. 2014)
Basank v. Decker, 449 F. Supp. 3d 205 (S.D.N.Y. 2020)
Shang Hai Zhenglang Tech. Co. v. Mengku Tech. Co., 2020 WL 6826257 (E.D.N.Y. 2020)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Screening projects through an environmental expert, providing plaintiff with her own washer and dryer, restricting residents from burning candles and incense, and staying plaintiff's eviction until she completes lengthy medical treatment
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied the reasonableness standard under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(B), finding plaintiff failed to demonstrate that the requested accommodations would not impose unreasonable burdens on defendant. Court also found that plaintiff's allegation of only delayed response (two months), without facts suggesting constructive denial through bad faith or unreasonableness, was insufficient to establish likely success on the merits for preliminary injunction purposes.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Termination of lease based on disability status
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff failed to demonstrate likely success on the merits of a discrimination claim because defendant provided a non-discriminatory reason for lease termination (creating near-daily disturbances, harassing emails, yelling at neighbors and staff), and plaintiff alleged no non-conclusory facts showing this explanation was pretextual.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Termination of lease in retaliation for requesting accommodations and filing discrimination complaints
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff failed to demonstrate likely success on a retaliation claim under the FHA because defendant provided a legitimate, non-retaliatory reason for lease termination (disruptive conduct), and plaintiff's complaint contained only conclusory assertions of retaliation without factual support.

source_file: 10645226_2025_(PS) Roberts v. Sacramento Housing _ Redevelopment Agency_caed
case_name: Sydney Brooke Roberts and David Tyrone Samuel v. Sacramento Housing & Redevelopment Agency
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested an extra bedroom added to their Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher as a reasonable accommodation for disabilities including ADHD, autism, PTSD, and depression.
key_holding: The motion to compel discovery was denied because plaintiffs failed to identify specific discovery responses that were wrongfully withheld, instead making broad challenges to defendants' overall discovery conduct, and defendants had made substantial document productions exceeding 10,000 pages.
brief_summary: Two disabled plaintiffs with two children sued Sacramento Housing and Redevelopment Agency alleging disability discrimination and failure to accommodate under the Fair Housing Act, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act, stemming from the denial of their request to add an extra bedroom to their Section 8 voucher. The court denied plaintiffs' motion to compel discovery, finding they failed to identify specific responses that were wrongfully withheld and that defendants had made substantial document productions.
key_cases_cited: Oppenheimer Fund, Inc. v. Sanders, 437 U.S. 340 (1978)
Dahl v. City of Huntington Beach, 84 F.3d 363 (9th Cir. 1996)
In re Heritage Bond Litigation, 223 F.R.D. 527 (C.D. Cal. 2004)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Extra bedroom added to housing voucher as a reasonable accommodation for family with disabled members (David Tyrone Samuel with ADHD, Autism, PTSD, Major Depressive Disorder; child AIMS with Autism Spectrum Disorder and non-verbal status)
fha_claims.reasoning: This is a discovery order denying plaintiffs' motion to compel. The underlying reasonable accommodation claim (disability discrimination in housing under FHA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act) survives the prior motion to dismiss and remains pending. The court did not reach the merits of the accommodation claim itself; it addressed only whether defendants wrongfully withheld discovery.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II ineffective communication claim; Rehabilitation Act Sections 504 and 508 accessibility claims; Fourteenth Amendment due process violation
fha_claims.reasoning: Non-FHA claims (ADA Title II, Sections 504/508 of Rehabilitation Act, and Fourteenth Amendment) survive the prior motion to dismiss and remain pending. This discovery order does not address the merits of these claims.

case_name: Mary Anne Sause v. Mid America Management, et al.
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation was formally requested; plaintiff, who alleged she is elderly and disabled, sought renewal and recertification of her government-subsidized apartment lease and alleged defendants failed to follow proper eviction procedures before locking her out.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's second amended complaint without prejudice for failure to comply with Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(a) because she listed statutes without connecting them to specific factual allegations or identifying which defendant took which actions.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Mary Anne Sause sued the owners, operators, and managers of Cedar Run Apartments, alleging she was locked out of her government-subsidized apartment and rendered homeless. Her second amended complaint listed a lengthy array of federal and state statutes—including the Fair Housing Act, ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and VAWA—but failed to connect those statutes to specific factual allegations or identify which defendant committed which acts. The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss without prejudice, holding the complaint did not satisfy Rule 8(a)'s pleading requirements despite multiple opportunities to amend.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Renewal and recertification of lease in government-subsidized housing; safe and working fire alarms; freedom from sexual harassment in housing
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly state a claim under the Fair Housing Act by listing the statute without connecting factual allegations to any specific FHA cause of action, failing to identify which defendant took which actions, and providing only conclusory assertions without factual enhancement. The complaint does not explain what each defendant did, when, how it harmed plaintiff, or what specific legal right was violated.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, ADA, First Amendment constitutional claims, Kansas Residential Tenant Act, Housing and Community Development Act § 109, Violence Against Women Act, USDA Rural Development regulations, Civil Rights Act of 1968, 18 U.S.C. § 241
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to comply with Rule 8(a) by listing multiple federal and state statutes without connecting them to specific factual allegations or identifying which defendant violated which statute. The complaint contains only conclusory assertions and does not explain the nature of each claim, the specific legal right allegedly violated, or the factual basis for relief under any particular statute.

case_name: Lillian Gonzalez v. Cheryl Mongo, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges defendants failed to keep premises safe during her tenancy, causing safety risk and emotional distress to herself and her minor child, in violation of the Fair Housing Act.
key_holding: The complaint was dismissed for failure to state a claim because plaintiff failed to articulate specific tortious conduct attributable to any defendant and failed to ascribe any wrongful conduct to named defendants.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Lillian Gonzalez sued multiple defendants alleging Fair Housing Act violations, claiming defendants failed to keep Southlawn Palm Apartments safe during her tenancy, resulting in stalking and assault. The court granted all pending motions to dismiss, finding Gonzalez failed to state a plausible claim because she did not articulate specific tortious conduct attributable to any named defendant or provide facts putting defendants on notice of the claims against them.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Anderson v. U.S. Dep't of Hous. & Urban Dev.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged failure to keep premises safe during tenancy; no specific accommodation requested or identified
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint failed to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly because it contained no factual allegations ascribing any specific tortious conduct to any named defendant and failed to meet the notice pleading standard of Rule 8(a)(2).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Eighth Amendment, VAWA, Fourteenth Amendment due process, and state law tort claims arising from alleged stalking and assault during tenancy
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA claims dismissed for failure to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly due to lack of factual allegations connecting any defendant to specific wrongful conduct.

case_name: K.F., a Minor, by and through His Legal Guardian Sandra Fernandez v. Hines Corporation, et al.
accommodation_description: Specific accommodation request not identifiable from the complaint; the case concerns unsafe housing conditions and 2024 eviction but no specific accommodation is described.
key_holding: The court denied pending motions without prejudice, abstaining from substantive review under Younger and Rooker-Feldman doctrines due to parallel state court proceedings, and ordered plaintiff to file an amended complaint or pay filing fees.
brief_summary: Sandra Fernandez, proceeding pro se on behalf of her minor son K.F., filed a 79-page complaint against Hines Corporation and other defendants alleging unsafe housing conditions and 2024 eviction, invoking the FHA, ADA, and civil rights statutes. The court denied pending motions without prejudice, abstaining under Younger and Rooker-Feldman doctrines from interfering with state court proceedings, and ordered plaintiff to either pay the filing fee or file a fee application and submit an amended complaint by August 29, 2025.
key_cases_cited: Neitzke v. Williams, 490 U.S. 319 (1989)
Younger v. Harris, 401 U.S. 37 (1971)
Geiger v. Foley Hoag LLP Retirement Plan, 521 F.3d 60 (1st Cir. 2008)
Starbucks Corp. v. McKinney, 602 U.S. 339 (2024)
Rossi v. Gemma, 489 F.3d 26 (1st Cir. 2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Complaint alleges unsafe housing conditions and eviction-related claims under the Fair Housing Act, but specific accommodation requests are not clearly articulated in the opinion.
fha_claims.disposition: Denied without prejudice pending amended complaint
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that the complaint challenges state court proceedings and rulings, which are barred by the Rooker-Feldman doctrine and Younger abstention doctrine. The court lacks subject matter jurisdiction over claims that would interfere with ongoing or final state court proceedings. The court denied the motions without prejudice and directed plaintiff to file an amended complaint that states a plausible claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. §§ 1983, 1985; 42 U.S.C. § 12101 (Americans With Disabilities Act); state court tort, contract and consumer claims
fha_claims.disposition: Denied without prejudice pending amended complaint
fha_claims.reasoning: Non-FHA claims under § 1983, § 1985, ADA, and state law are barred by Rooker-Feldman and Younger abstention doctrines to the extent they challenge state court proceedings. The court lacks subject matter jurisdiction over such claims.

case_name: Allen Feingold v. Erie Insurance Exchange
accommodation_description: No housing accommodation was requested; plaintiff merely invoked the Fair Housing Act as a purported basis for federal jurisdiction in an automobile insurance dispute.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's third amended complaint for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, finding plaintiff failed to establish diversity jurisdiction (by not pleading Erie Insurance's citizenship) and failed to plead any valid federal claim, including a Fair Housing Act claim which the court found insufficient because plaintiff did not allege Erie is his landlord or that Erie provides housing covered by the statute.
brief_summary: Allen Feingold sued Erie Insurance Exchange asserting claims arising from an alleged 2018 assignment of his former client's rights to uninsured/underinsured motorist claims from automobile accidents; he invoked the Fair Housing Act and other federal statutes to establish federal question jurisdiction. The court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, finding Feingold failed to plead Erie's citizenship for diversity jurisdiction and failed to state any valid federal claim, including an insufficient Fair Housing Act claim because he did not allege Erie is a landlord or housing provider.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Larsen v. Senate of the Commonwealth, 152 F.3d 240 (3d Cir. 1998)
American Manufacturers Mutual Insurance Co. v. Sullivan, 526 U.S. 40 (1999)
McCann v. Newman Irrevocable Trust, 458 F.3d 281 (3d Cir. 2006)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 due process/equal protection, § 1985 conspiracy, § 1988 attorney's fees, Fair Housing Act § 3604(b), Americans with Disabilities Act Title I/II/III
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because plaintiff failed to establish either diversity jurisdiction (did not plead defendant's citizenship or principal place of business) or federal question jurisdiction (FHA claim lacked factual support showing defendant is a landlord or housing provider; ADA claims did not allege defendant is a public entity or public accommodation; § 1983 claims failed because defendant is a private insurer, not a state actor). The court did not reach the merits of any claim.

case_name: Jasmine Hill v. Philadelphia Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiff seeks damages and injunctive relief for alleged race discrimination (failure to maintain lead-safe housing) and retaliation for complaining about housing conditions.
key_holding: The complaint fails to state a FHA or Title VI claim because plaintiff's allegations of race discrimination are conclusory and provide no factual basis to infer discriminatory intent, and plaintiff's retaliation claim fails because her complaints concerned housing conditions rather than prohibited discrimination.
brief_summary: Jasmine Hill, an African-American Section 8 voucher holder, sued the Philadelphia Housing Authority and HUD alleging she was discriminated against based on race and retaliated against for complaining about lead paint exposure in her subsidized unit. The Court dismissed her complaint for failure to state plausible claims, finding her race discrimination allegations conclusory and her retaliation claim deficient because her complaints concerned housing conditions rather than prohibited discrimination.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Texas Dept. of Hous. & Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Mt. Holly Gardens Citizens in Action, Inc. v. Twp. of Mount Holly, 658 F.3d 375 (3d Cir. 2011)
White v. Barbe, 767 F. App'x 332 (3d Cir. 2019)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged discrimination based on race and socioeconomic status in conclusory fashion without factual allegations connecting the PHA's handling of complaints to her race. Socioeconomic status is not a protected class under the FHA. Conclusory allegations of race discrimination without factual support fail to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege any facts, statistical or otherwise, from which the court could conclude that the PHA adopted practices disproportionately impacting African-Americans. Undeveloped allegations of disparate impact are insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's complaints concerned the condition of the unit (lead hazards) rather than prohibited discrimination. The complaint lacked details about when and to whom complaints were made, and nothing suggested complaints concerned unlawful discrimination. Complaints about general housing conditions do not constitute protected activity under § 3617.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act (42 U.S.C. § 2000d) — discrimination based on race, color, or national origin by recipients of federal funding
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts demonstrating discrimination on the basis of race, color, or national origin. Conclusory allegations of Title VI discrimination without factual support fail to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly.

source_file: 10646262_2025_Chosen Consulting, LLC v. Town Council of Highland, Indiana_ca7

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Issuance of letter confirming zoning compliance for addiction treatment facility; Title II ADA and Section 504 Rehabilitation Act claims for discrimination based on disability (addiction-related ailments)
fha_claims.reasoning: The Seventh Circuit affirmed summary judgment dismissing the ADA Title II and Rehabilitation Act Section 504 claims as not ripe for adjudication under the Williamson County finality requirement. Because Chosen had not exhausted available local zoning procedures (variance application, rezoning petition, or Board of Zoning Appeals review), the Town had not adopted a final, conclusive position on whether to authorize the proposed use, and therefore federal court jurisdiction was premature.

source_file: 10646930_2025_Canoe Creek Neighborhood Association, Inc. v. Douse_flmd

case_name: Sharon Lee, et al. v. Twin Hawks Airpark LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Not determinable from the case text; the order addresses only service-of-process procedure and does not describe the underlying Fair Housing Act claim or any accommodation requested.
key_holding: The court granted plaintiffs' motions for an extension of time to complete service of process and for alternative service by mail to defendants' addresses and their known attorney, finding that unique circumstances including a gated rural property, a frequently absent defendant, and the risk of statute-of-limitations bar on the Fair Housing Act claim constituted good cause or excusable neglect.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Sharon Lee and Tommy Wessel filed a Fair Housing Act complaint against Twin Hawks Airpark LLC and Harold Duane Lambeth in February 2025 but were unable to complete traditional service of process due to a gated rural property accessible only by keypad code and a defendant who frequently traveled by private plane, leaving his home vacant. The court authorized alternative service by First Class Mail to defendants' home and work addresses and by certified mail to attorney Craig Cline, who had represented Twin Hawks in ongoing related litigation and had actual or near-certain notice of the suit. The court also extended the service deadline to September 3, 2025, noting that dismissal would bar plaintiffs' FHA claims under the statute of limitations.
key_cases_cited: Bank of N.Y. Mellon v. Dodev, 433 P.3d 549 (Ariz. Ct. App. 2018)
Lemoge v. United States, 587 F.3d 1188 (9th Cir. 2009)

case_name: Cindy Adams v. Consuelleo Anderson, et al.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation request is identified in the opinion; the complaint alleges general racial discrimination and various tort claims against HUD.
key_holding: The court granted HUD's motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(1) because plaintiff failed to establish subject matter jurisdiction over her claims against HUD, as sovereign immunity bars suits against federal agencies absent an express waiver, and plaintiff did not identify any applicable waiver for her discrimination, tort, or other claims.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Cindy Adams, who alleges she lived in HUD-owned public housing, sued HUD along with nineteen other defendants asserting racial discrimination, premise liability, civil rights, and tort claims. The court granted HUD's motion to dismiss for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, finding that sovereign immunity bars plaintiff's claims against HUD because she failed to identify any statutory waiver of sovereign immunity applicable to her claims for money damages, including under the Fair Housing Act.
key_cases_cited: Kelly v. Wilson, 426 F. App'x 629 (10th Cir. 2011)
Unimex, Inc. v. U.S. Dep't of Hous. & Urb. Dev., 594 F.2d 1060 (5th Cir. 1979)
Ramming v. United States, 281 F.3d 158 (5th Cir. 2001)
Moore v. Bryant, 853 F.3d 245 (5th Cir. 2017)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Racial discrimination, premise liability, color of law violations, civil conspiracy, negligence, tortious conduct, libel and slander, intentional infliction of emotional distress, and claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, Tucker Act, Federal Tort Claims Act, and Louisiana law
fha_claims.reasoning: The United States and its agencies are shielded by sovereign immunity absent an express waiver. Plaintiff failed to identify any applicable waiver of sovereign immunity. Section 1983 does not apply to federal officials; the FHA does not waive sovereign immunity for money damages against the federal government; Title VI does not waive sovereign immunity; Tucker Act claims must be brought in the Court of Federal Claims; and FTCA claims require administrative exhaustion, which plaintiff failed to satisfy as evidenced by unrebutted HUD records showing no claims filed for injury or damages.

case_name: Gregory Austin Gadson v. Riverbay Corporation
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request identified; plaintiff pro se complaint was incomprehensible and failed to allege any specific accommodation request
key_holding: The court dismissed the action for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because plaintiff failed to allege facts demonstrating a federal law claim, and even if FHA retaliation claims were analyzed, plaintiff failed to allege facts showing FHA-protected activity, defendant's awareness, adverse action, and causal connection.
brief_summary: Gregory Austin Gadson, proceeding pro se, sued Riverbay Corporation in federal court seeking injunctive and declaratory relief related to an eviction proceeding in Housing Court, invoking the FHA and other federal statutes. The court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, finding plaintiff's complaint alleged no facts demonstrating a federal law claim, and granted plaintiff 30 days leave to amend.
key_cases_cited: Ruhrgas AG v. Marathon Oil Co., 526 U.S. 574
St. Paul Mercury Indem. Co. v. Red Cab Co., 303 U.S. 283
Hertz Corp. v. Friend, 559 U.S. 77
Wis. Dep't of Corr. v. Schacht, 524 U.S. 381
Livingston v. Adirondack Beverage Co., 141 F.3d 434

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; no accommodation requested or at issue
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because plaintiff alleged no facts demonstrating a federal law claim under the FHA. The court noted in a footnote that even if facts were alleged, plaintiff would fail to state a retaliation claim because he alleged nothing suggesting FHA-protected activity, defendant's awareness, adverse action, or causal connection.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 constitutional violations, § 1985 conspiracy, APA claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed § 1983 claims because plaintiff failed to allege facts showing Riverbay is a state actor; dismissed § 1985 conspiracy claims as vague and unsupported with no identified underlying federal violations; dismissed APA claims because the APA applies only to federal agencies, not private corporations.

case_name: Dominic Son v. Oakmont Properties-Azure, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges disability discrimination related to his adjustment disorder but does not specify what accommodation was requested or needed.
key_holding: The court dismissed the FHA disability claim because plaintiff failed to allege facts showing his adjustment disorder substantially limited major life activities or explaining what accommodation he needed and was refused.
brief_summary: Dominic Son, a Vietnamese-American tenant at Azure Apartments in Sparks, Nevada, sued Oakmont Properties, FPI Management, and the Housing Authority of the City of Reno alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on race and disability discrimination, along with state law claims. The court dismissed the federal claims for failure to state a claim, finding the complaint contained only conclusory allegations of racial discrimination without supporting facts and failed to adequately plead the disability accommodation claim.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Giebeler v. M & B Assocs.
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Ctr.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Count II alleged racial discrimination under § 3604 but contained only conclusory legal assertions without factual support. The court found bare assertions of racial discrimination insufficient to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged he had a diagnosed disability (adjustment disorder) and was enduring financial distress, but failed to specify what accommodation he needed or requested that was refused.
fha_claims.reasoning: Count IV failed to allege that the disability substantially limited a major life activity during the relevant timeframe, and failed to identify any specific accommodation requested and refused. The complaint did not state a plausible claim under § 3604(f).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: False Claims Act (31 U.S.C. § 3729), § 1981 racial discrimination, § 1983 Fourteenth Amendment equal protection (disability and race), First Amendment retaliation
fha_claims.reasoning: Count I (False Claims Act) dismissed for failure to comply with procedural requirements (not brought in name of United States, not filed in camera, not sealed). Count III (§ 1981) dismissed for failure to allege facts supporting race-based discrimination and because RHA is a state actor not subject to § 1981. Count V (§ 1983 equal protection—disability) dismissed because PMDs are private parties without state action and RHA allegations lack sufficient facts for municipal liability. Count VI (§ 1983 equal protection—race) dismissed for same reasons. Count VII (First Amendment retaliation) dismissed because PMDs are not state actors and no nexus exists between Plaintiff's protected activities and RHA's alleged retaliatory actions.

source_file: 10648578_2025_(PS) Holmstrand v. Mercy Housing of California_caed
case_name: Holmstrand v. Mercy Housing of California
accommodation_description: Plaintiff's complaint is too vague to identify a specific accommodation request; plaintiff alleges housing discrimination related to an eviction and prior assault by another resident.
key_holding: Plaintiff's complaint was dismissed for failure to state a claim because it lacked sufficient factual allegations describing the specific actions or omissions by defendants and failed to comply with Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(a)(2) pleading requirements.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Sue Ellen Holmstrand sued Mercy Housing entities alleging Fair Housing Act and VAWA violations related to her eviction from a Section 202 supportive housing property in Encinitas, California, and a prior assault by another resident. The court dismissed the complaint without prejudice for failure to state a claim because the complaint lacked sufficient factual detail to identify specific causes of action or explain what each defendant did to violate her rights, granting plaintiff leave to amend.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Wetzel v. Glen St. Andrew Living Cmty., LLC, 901 F.3d 856 (7th Cir. 2018)
Pardo-Pena v. Kaas Props. LLC, 2024 WL 3298284 (C.D. Cal. 2024)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges hostile living environment based on assault by another resident and management's failure to provide alternative housing; also alleges wrongful eviction using fake documents.
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint fails to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly because it lacks sufficient factual detail regarding who did what, when, and where. Plaintiff's allegations do not provide enough specificity about the assault, management's response, or the eviction to allow the court to draw a reasonable inference of liability under the FHA's hostile living environment or interference provisions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: VAWA housing protections claim; state law eviction defense
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint fails to state a plausible claim under VAWA or state law because it lacks sufficient factual allegations regarding the specific actions taken by defendants and how those actions violated VAWA's protections or state eviction law. The complaint does not provide enough detail for the court to discern the elements of any non-FHA claim.

case_name: Bolima Tafah v. Lake Village Townhomes et al.
accommodation_description: No specific reasonable accommodation was requested; plaintiffs sought a temporary restraining order to prevent their eviction from their residence at 1806 Long Leaf Way, Severn, Maryland, which they characterized as a retaliatory eviction taken in response to their filing of a federal lawsuit.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiffs' emergency TRO motion to stop an eviction because (1) plaintiffs failed to comply with Rule 65(b)(1)'s procedural prerequisites, (2) plaintiffs failed to demonstrate likelihood of success on the merits, and (3) the Anti-Injunction Act and Younger abstention doctrine bar federal courts from enjoining ongoing state court eviction proceedings, even where FHA claims are asserted; the original motion to dismiss was denied as moot following the filing of an amended complaint.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Bolima Tafah and co-plaintiff filed a complaint and subsequently an amended complaint against their landlord, property manager, and a credit reporting company, alleging fifty federal and state law violations spanning 2021–2025, including claims related to ongoing eviction proceedings, vehicle repossession, and negative credit reporting. Plaintiffs filed an emergency TRO motion seeking to halt an eviction scheduled for August 13, 2025, arguing it was retaliatory for having filed their federal lawsuit. The court denied the TRO on procedural grounds under Rule 65(b)(1), for failure to demonstrate the Winter factors, and on jurisdictional grounds under the Anti-Injunction Act and Younger abstention doctrine, which bar federal interference with ongoing state court eviction proceedings even when FHA claims are raised.
key_cases_cited: Hoechst Diafoil Co. v. Nan Ya Plastics Corp., 174 F.3d 411 (4th Cir. 1999)
MicroStrategy Inc. v. Motorola, Inc., 245 F.3d 335 (4th Cir. 2001)
Winter v. Nat. Res. Def. Council, Inc., 555 U.S. 7 (2008)
Centro Tepeyac v. Montgomery Cnty., 722 F.3d 184 (4th Cir. 2013)
Younger v. Harris, 401 U.S. 37 (1971)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Eviction defense; state court eviction proceedings and related claims regarding venue, rent disputes, and alleged fraud/misrepresentation
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied TRO seeking to enjoin state court eviction proceedings under the Anti-Injunction Act (28 U.S.C. § 2283), which deprives the federal court of subject matter jurisdiction to interfere with ongoing state court proceedings. Younger abstention doctrine also applies. The complaint alleges state law claims (fraud, misrepresentation, venue defects) related to state court eviction and rent cases, not FHA violations.

case_name: Chrysanthus v. Stedke
accommodation_description: No coherent disability accommodation request identified; complaint alleges 'terrorism' claims and social media retaliation in connection with a lease
key_holding: Plaintiff's in forma pauperis complaint was dismissed as frivolous under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B) because the allegations were incomprehensible, failed to meet basic pleading standards, and asserted fantastical terrorism theories unrelated to any cognizable legal claim.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Philip Chrysanthus filed an in forma pauperis complaint against Daven E. Stedke alleging terrorism and social media retaliation in connection with a property lease at 4610 South Dixie Highway in Lima, Ohio, invoking Title VIII of the Fair Housing Act but asserting no coherent disability-based claims. The court sua sponte dismissed the complaint as frivolous under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B), finding the allegations were incomprehensible and failed to state any plausible claim upon which relief could be granted.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Neitzke v. Williams, 490 U.S. 319 (1989)
Hill v. Lappin, 630 F.3d 468 (6th Cir. 2010)
Lillard v. Shelby Cnty. Bd. of Educ., 76 F.3d 716 (6th Cir. 1996)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff references Title VIII (Fair Housing Act) and a retaliatory lease agreement but provides no coherent factual allegations or legal theory
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed the complaint as frivolous under § 1915(e)(2)(B) because the allegations are so unclear and incomprehensible that they fail to meet basic pleading requirements and do not state any plausible claim. The complaint's assertions regarding terrorism and social media retaliation in connection with a property lease lack an arguable basis in law or fact.

source_file: 10649340_2025_McBride v. Housing Authority of the County of Jackson, Illinois_ilsd
case_name: Shelby McBride v. Housing Authority of the County of Jackson, Illinois
accommodation_description: McBride requested to remain in her home during repairs rather than transfer, have belongings relocated, stay with her daughters temporarily, and receive expedited repairs with regular progress reports.
key_holding: Because the original complaint contained substantial federal claims under the Fair Housing Act and 42 U.S.C. § 1983, the Housing Authority was required to remove within thirty days of receiving the complaint; their failure to do so rendered the removal untimely, requiring remand.
brief_summary: Shelby McBride sued the Housing Authority of the County of Jackson, Illinois alleging discrimination under the Fair Housing Act after the Authority delayed repairs to her home following storm damage and ignored her written requests for reasonable accommodations. The Court granted McBride's Motion to Remand, finding the removal was untimely because the original complaint contained substantial federal claims under the FHA and 42 U.S.C. § 1983, triggering the thirty-day removal deadline long before the Authority filed its notice of removal.
key_cases_cited: Loper Bright v. Raimondo
Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Allapatthah Services, Inc.
Johnson v. Orr
Williams v. Aztar Indiana Gaming Corp.
Walker v. Trailer Transit, Inc.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that the Housing Authority relocate her belongings to an area out of the repair zone, allow her to remain temporarily residing with her daughters while repair work was ongoing, expedite the repair work and report progress regularly, and return her to her apartment after work completion. Plaintiff also alleges the Housing Authority insisted she transfer to a different unit despite her risk of physical and mental harm.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court remanded the case to state court for lack of timely removal, finding the original complaint contained two federal claims (FHA and § 1983) that triggered the 30-day removal requirement. The court did not reach the merits of the FHA reasonable accommodation claim because the case was remanded on jurisdictional grounds before the motion to dismiss was adjudicated.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges the Housing Authority discriminated against her by refusing to permit her to reside in the three-bedroom apartment, insisting she transfer from her home despite her risk of physical and mental harm, delaying repairs, ignoring written requests, and failing to engage in dialogue about accommodations.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court remanded the case to state court for lack of timely removal, finding the original complaint contained two federal claims (FHA and § 1983) that triggered the 30-day removal requirement. The court did not reach the merits of the FHA disparate treatment claim because the case was remanded on jurisdictional grounds.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 claim alleging the Housing Authority's taking of plaintiff's entitlement to public housing under color of state law without good cause, violating due process.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court remanded the case to state court for lack of timely removal, finding the original complaint contained two federal claims (FHA and § 1983) that triggered the 30-day removal requirement. The court did not reach the merits of the § 1983 claim because the case was remanded on jurisdictional grounds.

case_name: Jimmy Avila v. ACACIA Network, Inc. et al.
accommodation_description: Request to transfer from an apartment with mold that exacerbates tenant's chronic rhinitis and rhinosinusitis, a condition worsened by mold exposure.
key_holding: Avila's claims were properly dismissed because he failed to plead sufficient factual allegations establishing that defendants discriminated against him based on disability or that there was a causal connection between his protected activity (filing lawsuits) and the termination of his tenancy.
brief_summary: Jimmy Avila, a tenant with schizoaffective disorder living in supportive housing managed by ACACIA Network, sued ACACIA and 1212 Grant Realty for disability discrimination and retaliation under the FHA, ADA, and state laws, claiming he was denied a reasonable accommodation in the form of a transfer from a moldy apartment and was evicted in retaliation for filing lawsuits. The court granted motions to dismiss both actions, finding Avila failed to plead sufficient facts to support a causal connection between his lawsuits and tenancy termination, or to support a disability discrimination claim.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell A. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Dodd v. City Univ. of New York, 489 F. Supp. 3d 219 (S.D.N.Y. 2020)
Wise v. JPMorgan Chase, No. 21 Civ. 3718, 2023 WL 5575889 (S.D.N.Y. Aug. 29, 2023)
Palmer v. Fannie Mae, 755 F. App'x 43 (2d Cir. 2018)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Transfer from an apartment alleged to be uninhabitable, moldy, and adversely affecting plaintiff's health due to chronic rhinitis and rhinosinusitis worsened by mold and mildew exposure
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint fails to plead sufficient factual allegations to state a plausible reasonable accommodation claim. The complaint is devoid of factual details regarding defendants' awareness of plaintiff's disability, dates of alleged events, and the specific facts supporting the accommodation request, falling short of the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege a causal connection between filing lawsuits and termination of tenancy. Two lawsuits were filed in 2018 and 2021, several years before the 2023 termination, creating a temporal gap too large to infer causation. As to the 2023 small-claims suit, plaintiff did not allege defendants were aware of it before the eviction notice was issued.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint contains only conclusory allegations of disability discrimination without factual support. The facts pled do not support an inference that defendants discriminated against plaintiff on the basis of his disability, amounting to nothing more than conclusory statements insufficient to state a claim under the FHA and ADA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Intentional infliction of emotional distress claim under New York law; also includes ADA Title II claims, NYSHRL, NYCHRL, and NYSRPL retaliation claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Housing discrimination and retaliation, as a matter of law, do not constitute conduct sufficiently extreme and outrageous to meet the very high standard for pleading an IIED claim under New York law. Sending eviction notices or filing eviction actions, even when contested, does not meet this standard.

case_name: Siddharth Kode v. Joseph Pargin; Kimberly Pargin
accommodation_description: No accommodation request — case involves alleged racially motivated conspiracy to drive plaintiff out of neighborhood
key_holding: The Fifth Circuit affirmed dismissal of Kode's Fair Housing Act and other civil rights claims against the Pargins as time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations, finding no actionable conduct within the limitations period to support his claims of racially motivated conspiracy and racketeering.
brief_summary: Siddharth Kode, proceeding pro se, sued his neighbors Joseph and Kimberly Pargin and others alleging a racially motivated conspiracy and racketeering enterprise to drive him out of his Williamson County, Texas neighborhood, asserting claims under the Fair Housing Act, Civil Rights Acts, Ku Klux Klan Act, and RICO. The Fifth Circuit affirmed dismissal of all claims against the Pargins, agreeing with the district court that the claims were time-barred under the applicable two-year statute of limitations because Kode failed to identify any actionable conduct within the relevant limitations period.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court affirmed dismissal of FHA claims under the two-year statute of limitations, finding that Kode failed to identify any activity by the Pargins within the limitations period to support his civil rights claims. The only alleged act within the period—a statement by Joseph Pargin on October 10, 2021—was insufficient to support any FHA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court affirmed dismissal of FHA § 3617 retaliation claims under the two-year statute of limitations, finding that Kode failed to identify any retaliatory activity by the Pargins within the limitations period. The continuing-violation doctrine did not extend the limitations period because no continuous conduct occurred within the relevant period.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Civil Rights Act of 1866 (§§ 1981, 1982), Ku Klux Klan Act (§§ 1983, 1985), Civil Rights Act of 1964 (§ 2000d), Texas Fair Housing Act (Tex. Pr. Code § 301.021), RICO (18 U.S.C. § 1962)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court affirmed dismissal of non-FHA civil rights claims under the two-year statute of limitations applicable in Texas. For RICO claims, the court also found that Kode failed to meet the heightened pleading standard of Rule 9(b) by presenting only threadbare recitals and conclusory statements without identifying specific fraudulent acts or participation by each defendant.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of contract (VAWA emergency transfer obligation), procedural due process violation, sex discrimination under Ohio Fair Housing Act, warranty of habitability
fha_claims.disposition: Remanded for lack of federal question jurisdiction
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked federal-question jurisdiction because the plaintiff's state-law claims (breach of contract, procedural due process, Ohio FHA sex discrimination, warranty of habitability) did not involve a genuine dispute over the meaning of the federal Violence Against Women Act; both parties agreed CMHA had an obligation to offer emergency transfers, and the dispute concerned only how to prioritize competing requests. Remand to state court was proper.

case_name: Larry Johnson v. Thomas Brenneke; Guardian Management, LLC; Guardian Real Estate Services; Uptown Tower Apartments; Lisa Simonson; Kelly Paine; et al.
accommodation_description: Pro se plaintiff seeks Rule 60 relief to reopen three previously dismissed Fair Housing Act cases
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's Rule 60 motion as untimely, noting the judgment was entered in August 2022 and plaintiff offered no compelling reason for delaying nearly three years to seek reopening.
brief_summary: Larry Johnson, proceeding pro se, filed three consolidated Fair Housing Act actions that were dismissed with prejudice in August 2022; after the Ninth Circuit affirmed the judgment, Johnson filed a Rule 60 motion seeking to reopen the cases. The District Court adopted the Magistrate Judge's Findings and Recommendation and denied the motion as untimely, finding no compelling reason for the nearly three-year delay.
key_cases_cited: Ashford v. Steuart, 657 F.2d 1053 (9th Cir. 1981)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Erickson v. Pardus, 551 U.S. 89 (2007)
Thomas v. Arn, 474 U.S. 140 (1985)

case_name: Larry Johnson and Michelle Hume v. Guardian Management, LLC; Lisa Simonson; Kelly Paine; et al.
accommodation_description: The underlying accommodation request is not described in this document. The order is entirely procedural, addressing only the timeliness of a Rule 60 motion for relief from judgment; no details of the original FHA accommodation or modification claims appear in the text.
key_holding: The court adopts the magistrate judge's Findings and Recommendation and denies plaintiff's Rule 60 motion seeking leave to amend or file an independent action as untimely, finding no extraordinary circumstances to justify relief from a judgment entered nearly three years prior.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Larry Johnson and Michelle Hume brought two consolidated Fair Housing Act actions that were dismissed with prejudice in September 2022, a judgment subsequently affirmed by the Ninth Circuit on appeal. Plaintiff Johnson then filed a Rule 60 motion seeking leave to amend his pleadings, claiming he was unaware until April 2025 that he had been granted leave to amend in a March 2022 order, and that health issues impaired his ability to participate in the litigation. The district court adopted the magistrate judge's Findings and Recommendation denying the motion as untimely under Rule 60(c)(1), concluding that plaintiff's health difficulties did not constitute extraordinary circumstances where he had nonetheless been able to file and vigorously litigate an appeal.
key_cases_cited: Ashford v. Steuart, 657 F.2d 1053 (9th Cir. 1981)
United States v. Alpine Land & Reservoir Co., 984 F.2d 1047 (9th Cir. 1993)
Erickson v. Pardus, 551 U.S. 89 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Housing voucher
fha_claims.reasoning: The court transferred the case to the District of Maryland for improper venue under 28 U.S.C. § 1391 and § 1406, finding no connection between the claims and the Middle District of Pennsylvania. The FHA claim regarding failure to provide a housing voucher was not substantively addressed and remains pending in the transferee court.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act claim for failure to provide housing voucher; tort claim for failure to hire at University of Maryland; tort claim related to Medicare and Medicaid protection
fha_claims.reasoning: The court transferred the case to the District of Maryland for improper venue. Non-FHA claims (ADA, state tort claims) were not substantively addressed and remain pending in the transferee court.

case_name: John L. Roseman v. 1900 Capital Trust II
accommodation_description: Pro se plaintiff seeks temporary restraining order to stay state court eviction order and prevent removal from his home at 24823 Cobblestone Court.
key_holding: The court denied the TRO motion because it lacked subject matter jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine, which bars federal courts from reviewing state court decisions, and because plaintiff failed to comply with Rule 65(b)(1)(B)'s notice certification requirements.
brief_summary: John L. Roseman, proceeding pro se, sued 1900 Capital Trust II seeking a temporary restraining order to prevent his eviction from property in Farmington Hills, Michigan, asserting fraud, contract, and race discrimination claims under the Fair Housing Act. The court denied the TRO motion on procedural grounds (failure to certify notice to defendant) and for lack of jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine, which bars federal courts from reviewing state court eviction orders.
key_cases_cited: Givens v. Homecomings Fin., 278 F. App'x 607 (6th Cir. 2008)
D.C. Ct. of App. v. Feldman, 460 U.S. 462 (1983)
Rooker v. Fid. Tr. Co., 263 U.S. 413 (1923)
Battah v. ResMAE Mortg. Corp., 746 F. Supp. 2d 869 (E.D. Mich. 2010)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Race discrimination in housing
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the motion for temporary restraining order on Rooker-Feldman grounds, holding that federal courts lack subject matter jurisdiction to enjoin state court proceedings or stay state court eviction orders. The FHA claim was not substantively addressed on the merits.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fraud, Misrepresentation, Promissory Estoppel, Contract Reformation, Civil Conspiracy, Slander/Slander of Title/Defamation per quod
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the motion for temporary restraining order on Rooker-Feldman grounds, holding that the request to stay the state court eviction order is barred by the Anti-Injunction Act and the Rooker-Feldman doctrine. Non-FHA claims were not substantively analyzed.

case_name: Damia Bjurling v. Alec Johnson, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges that defendant Alec Johnson denied 'reasonable accommodations related to her disability' (autism); the complaint also references her service dog, which was allegedly injured by defendant Holder. The specific nature of the reasonable accommodation requested is not described with any particularity in the complaint.
key_holding: The court dismisses pro se plaintiff's amended complaint without prejudice and with leave to amend because it fails to plead sufficient facts showing how defendants injured plaintiff and her service dog, instead improperly relying on approximately 500 pages of attached exhibits.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Damia Bjurling filed an amended complaint under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 and the Fair Housing Act against a private individual (Alec Johnson), a police chief (Shelby Parker), and another individual (Calvin Earl Holder III), alleging harassment, intimidation, retaliation for asserting FHA rights, denial of reasonable accommodations related to her autism, and injury to herself and her service dog. The court dismissed the original complaint for failure to state a claim, and the amended complaint likewise failed to articulate specific facts as to each defendant's conduct, instead incorporating roughly 500 pages of exhibits. The court dismissed the amended complaint without prejudice, granting plaintiff leave to file a second amended complaint by August 25, 2025 that specifically pleads the underlying factual bases for her claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
French v. Washington State Dep't of Health

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodations related to plaintiff's disability (autism and service dog)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the amended complaint for failure to plead sufficient facts to state a plausible claim. The complaint lacked factual specificity regarding what each defendant did to harm plaintiff and her service dog, and improperly relied on 500 pages of exhibits rather than allegations within the four corners of the complaint itself.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the retaliation claim for failure to plead sufficient facts. Plaintiff alleged defendants retaliated against her for asserting Fair Housing Act rights and for her autism, but the complaint lacked factual specificity regarding the conduct of each defendant and the circumstances surrounding alleged injuries.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 due process and First Amendment claims; ADA compliance allegations
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed all claims under § 1983 and related statutes for failure to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly. The complaint lacked sufficient factual allegations describing the conduct of each defendant, how and when injuries occurred, and the circumstances surrounding the alleged harm.

case_name: Pamela Crawford v. Douglas M. Milner et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges she was denied rental of an apartment because of her race (African American); no accommodation request is involved.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA disparate treatment claim because she failed to plead facts supporting her belief that defendants rented the apartment to a non-African American tenant, stating only conclusory allegations about motivation without factual support.
brief_summary: African American plaintiff Pamela Crawford sued landlords Douglas and Michelle Milner alleging they refused to rent an apartment to her because of her race, claiming the unit was rented to a non-African American applicant after she submitted documentation. The court dismissed the complaint without prejudice under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B) for failing to state a claim, finding the complaint contained only conclusory allegations without factual support for the discriminatory intent claim.
key_cases_cited: SW. Fair Housing Council, Inc. v. Maricopa Domestic Water Improvement Dist., 17 F.4th 950 (9th Cir. 2021)
Ohio House, LLC v. City of Costa Mesa, 135 F.4th 645 (9th Cir. 2025)
Calhoun v. Stahl, 254 F.3d 845 (9th Cir. 2001)
Lopez v. Smith, 203 F.3d 1122 (9th Cir. 2000)
Watison v. Carter, 668 F.3d 1108 (9th Cir. 2012)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts to support her assertion that the competing applicant was non-African American or to allege facts supporting her claim that defendants were motivated by racial discrimination. The complaint contains only conclusory allegations of discriminatory intent without factual support, failing to meet the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Washington Law Against Discrimination, breach of duty of good faith and fair dealing, negligent and intentional infliction of emotional distress
fha_claims.reasoning: Non-FHA claims dismissed under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) screening for failure to state a claim under the Iqbal/Twombly standard, applying the same pleading requirements as Rule 12(b)(6).

case_name: Dalila Agiza v. Bexar County, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff referenced an emotional support horse named Beautie in her amended complaint; the horse was seized during an alleged unlawful entry on May 30, 2025. No formal accommodation request or denial is described in detail—the FHA claim was included only as a conclusory allegation and was dismissed for failure to state a claim.
key_holding: The magistrate judge recommends dismissal of nearly all claims—including conclusory FHA, ADA, and RICO claims—for failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii), while recommending that a new § 1983 unlawful-seizure claim against a Bexar County constable, accompanying officers, and attorney Alex Perez be allowed to proceed based on the alleged warrantless seizure of personal property, including an emotional support horse named Beautie, from Plaintiff's home on May 30, 2025.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Dalila Agiza brought § 1983 civil rights claims against Bexar County, a county judge, clerk's office staff, private attorneys, and LVNV Funding, LLC, arising from state court eviction and consumer-debt proceedings. After a show-cause order, Plaintiff amended her complaint to add claims under the ADA, FHA, and RICO, but all were dismissed as conclusory and legally deficient. The one surviving claim is a § 1983 cause of action alleging that a Bexar County Precinct 1 Constable (badge 1114), accompanying officers, and attorney Alex Perez unconstitutionally entered Plaintiff's property and seized personal items, including her emotional support horse Beautie, without legal authority.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Ashcroft v. Iqbal

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged violations of the Americans with Disabilities Act, Fair Housing Act, and Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act, but offered only conclusory statements without factual support.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege claims under the ADA, FHA, and RICO, offering only conclusory statements without sufficient factual allegations to state a plausible claim for relief under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) screening standards.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 claims against Bexar County, county judge, county clerk's office staff, private attorneys, and LVNV Funding, LLC arising from eviction and consumer-debt cases in state court.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to overcome absolute immunity of judges, quasi-judicial immunity of court clerks, lack of state action by private attorneys, and failed to plausibly allege § 1983 liability against private parties LVNV Funding, LLC and its counsel.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA claim for alleged failure to accommodate disability-related requests (pond maintenance, insulation repair, tennis court repair, bee invasion, service animal incident cleanup); state-law claims for fraud, conspiracy, intentional misrepresentation, personal injury, breach of covenant of good faith and fair dealing, harassment, and negligence
fha_claims.reasoning: The ADA does not apply to private condominiums, which are not places of public accommodation under 42 U.S.C. § 12182(a). The court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over state-law claims after dismissing the only federal claim.

case_name: Manuel James Gonzalez, as legal guardian of REG, a minor v. Royse Services LLC d/b/a LaVida Vacations
accommodation_description: Request to waive pet deposit fee for minor daughter's service dog trained to prevent panic attacks and destructive tantrums associated with autism
key_holding: The court granted default judgment for plaintiff, finding that Royse Services violated both the ADA and FHA by refusing to waive a pet deposit for the minor daughter's service dog, despite knowledge of her disability and the dog's necessity to mitigate her autism symptoms.
brief_summary: Manuel James Gonzalez sued Royse Services LLC on behalf of his minor daughter R.E.G., who has autism and requires a service dog, alleging the vacation rental company violated the ADA and FHA by refusing to allow the service dog unless he paid a $150 pet deposit. The court granted default judgment for plaintiff, finding Royse Services discriminated against R.E.G. based on her disability by refusing to waive its pet fee policy despite knowing of her disability and the service animal's necessity.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014)
Surtain v. Hamlin Terrace Found., 789 F.3d 1239 (11th Cir. 2015)
Loren v. Sasser, 309 F.3d 1296 (11th Cir. 2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver of pet fee for service dog accompanying disabled minor with autism; service dog is certified and trained to prevent panic attacks and destructive tantrums
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that R.E.G. is disabled under the FHA, requested a reasonable and necessary accommodation (service dog without pet fee), and Royse Services refused. The accommodation is reasonable because the service dog ameliorates R.E.G.'s disability symptoms, and the burden on Royse Services is minimal. By defaulting, defendant admitted well-pleaded factual allegations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III claim for discrimination based on disability in public accommodation; refusal to waive pet fee for service animal
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied ADA Title III standards (42 U.S.C. § 12182(a)) and found that Royse Services' vacation rental is a public accommodation, R.E.G. is disabled, and Royse Services violated the ADA by requiring a pet fee for a service animal (28 C.F.R. § 36.302(c)(8)). Defendant's default admitted all well-pleaded factual allegations.

source_file: 10651719_2025_Joe v. Olive Branch Assisted Living LLC_azd
case_name: Hailei Joe v. Olive Branch Assisted Living LLC
accommodation_description: No formal accommodation was requested by Plaintiff; the issue arose as Defendant argued that its duty to provide a reasonable accommodation was never triggered because Plaintiff made no request. The court rejected this defense, noting that the duty to explore reasonable accommodations can arise without a formal request when the need is obvious, and analyzed whether Defendant should have explored accommodations enabling Plaintiff to remain in the facility following her HIV-positive disclosure rather than discharging her.
key_holding: The court denied both parties' cross-motions for summary judgment on FHA, AFHA, and ADA discrimination claims because a genuine issue of material fact remains as to whether Plaintiff's HIV-positive status was the but-for cause of her discharge, while granting Defendant summary judgment on Plaintiff's retaliation claims (for lack of a distinct and palpable injury), public disclosure of private facts claim (for insufficient publicity), and prayer for punitive damages.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Hailei Joe sued Olive Branch Assisted Living LLC after being discharged from its residential addiction treatment facility three days after disclosing an HIV-positive diagnosis, alleging discrimination under the FHA, AFHA, and ADA, retaliation based on Defendant's threatening emails and defamation counterclaim, and public disclosure of private facts under Arizona common law. On cross-motions for summary judgment, the court found genuine disputes of material fact as to whether HIV status was the but-for cause of Plaintiff's discharge, allowing the discrimination claims to proceed to a jury trial on the FHA and AFHA counts (with ADA injunctive relief reserved for the court). The court granted Defendant summary judgment on retaliation (Plaintiff suffered no distinct and palpable injury from the non-frivolous defamation counterclaim), public disclosure (informing a small group of residents does not satisfy the 'public at large' publicity requirement), and punitive damages (insufficient evidence of reckless indifference or evil mind).
key_cases_cited: Brown v. City of Tucson, 336 F.3d 1181 (9th Cir. 2003)
Pac. Shores Props., LLC v. City of Newport Beach, 730 F.3d 1142 (9th Cir. 2013)
Murray v. Mayo Clinic, 934 F.3d 1101 (9th Cir. 2019)
Bragdon v. Abbott, 524 U.S. 624 (1998)
Bax v. Doctors Med. Ctr. of Modesto, Inc., 52 F.4th 858 (9th Cir. 2022)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges Defendant failed to provide reasonable accommodation for her HIV-positive status and related mental health needs (PTSD, suicidal ideation, substance use disorder). Defendant argues it lacked duty to accommodate because Plaintiff did not request accommodation, and that its facility lacked capacity to treat her elevated care needs.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that liability for failure to provide reasonable accommodation does not hinge on a requirement that plaintiff first request accommodation; duty may be triggered when need is obvious. Court found genuine issue of material fact as to whether Plaintiff's discharge would have occurred absent her HIV diagnosis, precluding summary judgment on either party's motion.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discharge from residential addiction treatment facility based on HIV-positive status
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied 'but for' causation standard under FHA § 3604(f)(2). Although timing of discharge and Appleton's deposition testimony suggested HIV diagnosis was a factor, genuine issue of material fact remained as to whether discharge would have occurred absent the HIV diagnosis, given conflicting evidence about Plaintiff's elevated care needs and facility's capacity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Defendant's defamation counterclaim and threatening emails from counsel
fha_claims.reasoning: Although court found reasonable juror could find threat in counsel's email stating countersuit would proceed if lawsuit not dismissed, Plaintiff failed to establish 'distinct and palpable injury' required under FHA § 3617 and ADA § 12203(b). Defendant's defamation counterclaim was not frivolous as matter of law, so time defending it did not constitute requisite injury.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Public disclosure of private facts (Arizona common law); Title III ADA discrimination claim; Arizona Fair Housing Act discrimination claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Public disclosure claim failed because disclosure of HIV diagnosis to facility residents and staff did not constitute 'publicity' to public at large as required by Restatement § 652D. ADA Title III claim survives summary judgment on discrimination merits but no damages available; only injunctive relief permitted under Title III. AFHA claim mirrors FHA claim and will proceed to trial together.

case_name: Metcalf v. Stapp
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request identified; complaint alleges discriminatory housing acts and retaliation under Colorado Fair Housing Act by HOA members and board.
key_holding: The magistrate recommends granting the motion to dismiss as to six claims (1, 3, 4, 6, 11, 12) for violating Rule 8 shotgun pleading requirements and dismissing the Amended Complaint for insufficient service of process, while denying the motion as to claims 2, 5, 7, 8, 9, and 10 which sufficiently apprise defendants of the allegations.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Matthew Metcalf and Allison Moore sued former neighbors who were members and officers of the Pines at Riva Chase Homeowners Association over neighborhood disputes including parking, snow removal, and HOA board actions. The magistrate judge recommends granting in part defendants' motion to dismiss the Amended Complaint for violating Rule 8 pleading requirements (shotgun pleading) and for insufficient service of process, while denying dismissal of several other claims that sufficiently identify the specific defendants and conduct at issue.
key_cases_cited: Haines v. Kerner, 404 U.S. 519 (1972)
McNamara v. Brauchler, 570 F. App'x 741 (10th Cir. 2014)
Mann v. Boatright, 477 F.3d 1140 (10th Cir. 2007)
Nasious v. Two Unknown B.I.C.E. Agents, 492 F.3d 1158 (10th Cir. 2007)
Sierra Club v. Tri-State Generation & Transmission Ass'n, Inc., 173 F.R.D. 275 (D. Colo. 1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Claim 1 (alleged discrimination against all defendants) was struck as shotgun pleading under Rule 12(f) because it failed to clearly articulate which defendant engaged in each of nine allegedly discriminatory acts, violating Rule 8's requirement for a short and plain statement and failing to provide fair notice.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Claim 2 (retaliation) survived the motion to strike because, despite reincorporating all preceding paragraphs, it sufficiently articulated the specific retaliatory conduct allegedly engaged in by each defendant and identified the protected conduct Plaintiffs engaged in, providing fair notice under Rule 8.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Claim 3 (Colorado Fair Housing Act violations) was struck as shotgun pleading because it listed allegedly discriminatory acts but utterly failed to explain who did what to whom, failing to provide fair notice of which defendant engaged in which conduct.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Claim 4 (retaliation) was struck as shotgun pleading because it referenced protected activity and then stated in blanket fashion that all defendants injured plaintiffs by committing retaliatory acts detailed elsewhere, without clearly identifying which defendant did what.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: State law claim (specific theory unclear from opinion)
fha_claims.reasoning: Claim 5 (asserted against Defendant Stapp only) survived the motion to strike because it specifically explained Defendant Stapp's at-issue conduct and the harm Plaintiffs suffered, though it did not specifically identify when the unlawful conduct occurred, providing sufficient fair notice under Rule 8.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fraud by concealment of material facts
fha_claims.reasoning: Claim 6 (fraud) was struck as shotgun pleading because although it described material facts allegedly not disclosed, it failed to indicate which individual defendants failed to disclose which specific material facts.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: State law claim (specific theory unclear from opinion)
fha_claims.reasoning: Claim 7 (asserted against Defendant Stapp only) survived the motion to strike because it specifically explained Defendant Stapp's at-issue conduct, when it allegedly occurred, and the harm Plaintiffs suffered, providing fair notice under Rule 8.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: State law claim (specific theory unclear from opinion)
fha_claims.reasoning: Claim 8 (asserted against Defendant Stapp only) survived the motion to strike because it specifically explained Defendant Stapp's at-issue conduct, when it allegedly occurred, and the harm Plaintiffs suffered, providing fair notice under Rule 8.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of contract and/or breach of covenant of good faith and fair dealing
fha_claims.reasoning: Claim 9 (breach of contract against Defendants Stapp and Cindy Chudacoff) survived the motion to strike because it explained the at-issue contract and each defendant's specific conduct purportedly violating the contract, providing fair notice under Rule 8.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Interference with performance of contract
fha_claims.reasoning: Claim 10 (interference with contract performance against Defendants Dunlap and Bruce Chudacoff) survived the motion to strike because it sufficiently explained the allegedly unlawful conduct each defendant engaged in, providing fair notice under Rule 8.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Extreme and outrageous conduct (intentional infliction of emotional distress)
fha_claims.reasoning: Claim 11 (extreme and outrageous conduct against all defendants) was struck as shotgun pleading because although it listed allegedly extreme and outrageous conduct, it failed to explain which defendant engaged in which conduct or when the conduct occurred.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Civil conspiracy
fha_claims.reasoning: Claim 12 (civil conspiracy against all defendants) was struck as shotgun pleading because although it reincorporated 545 preceding paragraphs, it utterly failed to explain who did what, failing to provide fair notice of the conspiracy allegations.

case_name: Felicia Rosa v. Administration for Children's Services
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges ACS employee interfered with her housing and lease termination as discriminatory conduct under the FHA.
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA claim against ACS employee Moore was dismissed for failure to state a claim because her allegations were too vague and lacked factual details about what Moore said to the landlord.
brief_summary: Felicia Rosa, proceeding pro se, sued ACS and its employees along with multiple other defendants under the Fair Housing Act, Section 1983, and Section 1985 arising from custody removal and housing voucher termination. The court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim, finding Plaintiff's FHA allegations against ACS employee Moore too vague to survive dismissal, and dismissed claims against Officer Mickey as time-barred, claims against NYPD and ACS for lack of capacity to be sued, with 30 days' leave to replead.
key_cases_cited: Gladstone, Realtors v. Vill. of Bellwood, 441 U.S. 91 (1979)
Rodriguez v. Vill. Green Realty, Inc., 788 F.3d 31 (2d Cir. 2015)
Palmer v. Fannie Mae, 755 F. App'x 43 (2d Cir. 2018)
Littlejohn v. City of New York, 795 F.3d 297 (2d Cir. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged that ACS employee Kiesha Moore contacted her landlord without consent to discuss lease terms and housing voucher terms, resulting in termination of her housing. Plaintiff styled this as an FHA violation.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's vague allegations, which do not include factual details about what Moore said to the landlord, are insufficient to state a claim on which relief may be granted under the FHA. The complaint fails to plausibly allege membership in a protected class, adverse treatment, or discriminatory motivation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 1983 due process and Fourth Amendment seizure of property claims; state law claims for intentional infliction of emotional distress, malicious prosecution, and conspiracy.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's allegations against ACS employees Moore, Morrison, and Wilson fail to state a claim under Section 1983 because they lack factual details and fail to show personal involvement of defendants in alleged constitutional deprivations. State law claims are dismissed for lack of supplemental jurisdiction after dismissal of federal claims.

source_file: 10652700_2025_Cahail v. United States of America, The_ksd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Appointment of counsel in civil rights case; plaintiff alleges severe PTSD with cognitive and emotional impairments affecting legal self-advocacy
fha_claims.disposition: Motion for Appointment of Counsel Denied
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion for appointment of counsel under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(1), finding no constitutional right to counsel in civil cases, case not unusually complex, and allegations of PTSD insufficient basis for appointment under District precedent. Underlying complaint involves § 1983 claims and Fair Housing Act claims but this opinion addresses only the procedural motion for counsel, not the merits of any FHA claim.

case_name: J&S Group Inc., Wanaque Realty Corp., and Mountain Lakes Estates, Inc. v. Borough of Wanaque
accommodation_description: Developer-plaintiffs allege the Borough refused to assign Developer Agreements and created obstacles to development based on the national origin of the developers and their selected builder (Portuguese immigrants).
key_holding: The court denied summary judgment on Plaintiffs' Fair Housing Act claim under an intentional discrimination theory because genuine issues of material fact exist regarding whether the Borough's Administrator made discriminatory statements and took adverse actions against Portuguese immigrant developers, but granted summary judgment on the takings claim and Section 1982 claim which required race-based discrimination rather than national origin discrimination.
brief_summary: Property developer companies owned by a Portuguese immigrant sued the Borough of Wanaque, NJ alleging the municipality discriminated against them based on national origin by refusing to assign developer agreements to their Portuguese-owned builder and creating obstacles to their housing development project. The court granted summary judgment for defendant on takings and Section 1982 claims but denied summary judgment on the Fair Housing Act intentional discrimination claim, finding genuine disputes of material fact regarding discriminatory statements made by the Borough Administrator about Portuguese people.
key_cases_cited: Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Hovsons, Inc. v. Township of Brick, 89 F.3d 1096 (3d Cir. 1996)
Growth Horizons, Inc. v. Delaware County, 983 F.2d 1277 (3d Cir. 1993)
Village of Arlington Heights v. Metro. Hous. Dev. Corp., 429 U.S. 252 (1977)
Eastampton Center L.L.C. v. Township of Eastampton, 155 F. Supp. 2d 102 (D.N.J. 2001)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found genuine issues of material fact regarding whether the Borough's refusal to assign Developer's Agreements to J&J Builders and the Borough Administrator's statements about not wanting Portuguese immigrants to develop the project constitute intentional discrimination based on national origin under the Fair Housing Act. The court applied the Arlington Heights framework for discriminatory intent and found sufficient circumstantial evidence (derogatory comments, differential treatment, refusal to assign agreements) to survive summary judgment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1982 (Civil Rights Act - racial discrimination in property transactions); 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (Fifth Amendment Takings Clause)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted summary judgment on the § 1982 claim because Section 1982 prohibits only race-based discrimination in property transactions, not national origin discrimination. Although Plaintiffs alleged discrimination based on Portuguese heritage, the court held that heritage/national origin is not cognizable under § 1982, which applies only to racial discrimination. The court also granted summary judgment on the Fifth Amendment Takings Clause claim (Count I) because Plaintiffs retained economically viable use of the property (valued at $5.2 million as of March 2024) and could still sell, lease, or develop the property under alternative arrangements; the loss of anticipated profits from a specific development plan does not constitute a regulatory taking under Penn Central.

case_name: Cherry-El v. Blount
accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought to change his status from live-in aide to primary tenant and continue residing in subsidized housing as a reasonable accommodation after his mother passed away.
