key_cases_cited: Village of Arlington Heights v. Metropolitan Housing Development Corp., 429 U.S. 252 (1977)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Tex. Dep't of Hous. and Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Cmtys. Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Cmty. Servs., Inc. v. Wind Gap Mun. Auth., 421 F.3d 170 (3d Cir. 2005)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Certificate of Continuing Occupancy (CCO) for operation of Oxford House sober living facility in a two-family dwelling
fha_claims.reasoning: The First Amended Complaint failed to allege sufficient facts to support a plausible inference of discriminatory intent. The complaint alleged only legal misapplication of zoning ordinances, absence of similar housing, procedural deviation, and conflicting explanations from officials—none of which, without more, support an inference that the Township's denial was motivated by discriminatory animus rather than innocent error or legitimate zoning concerns.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Zoning ordinance prohibiting Community Residences in two-family dwellings
fha_claims.reasoning: Oxford House forfeited its disparate impact arguments by failing to respond to the Township's arguments on this theory in the District Court. The court did not reach the merits of the disparate impact claim because the arguments were not properly preserved for appeal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) Title II claim; New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (NJLAD) claim (removed in First Amended Complaint)
fha_claims.reasoning: The ADA claim was analyzed under the same discriminatory intent framework as the FHA claim and failed for the same reasons—insufficient factual allegations to support a plausible inference of discrimination. The NJLAD claim was voluntarily removed in the First Amended Complaint.

source_file: 10713560_2025_Phillip Pella v. Atlantic County Department of Family and Community Development, New Jersey Department of Human Services, Helen Cheatham, Audrey Alphaeus, John_Jane Does 1-10_njd
case_name: Phillip Pella v. Atlantic County Department of Family and Community Development, New Jersey Department of Human Services, Helen Cheatham, Audrey Alphaeus, John/Jane Does 1-10
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation under the FHA is described in the complaint; plaintiff makes only conclusory references to FHA §§ 3604(f) and 3617 in the context of alleged wrongful denial of New Jersey Emergency Assistance and SNAP benefits.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's IFP application without prejudice and administratively terminated the matter because plaintiff failed to provide sufficient financial detail — including a breakdown of expenses and liabilities — for the court to determine his economic eligibility to proceed in forma pauperis.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Phillip Pella filed a second amended complaint against two New Jersey government agencies (Atlantic County Department of Family and Community Development and New Jersey Department of Human Services) and individual employees, alleging wrongful denial of emergency assistance and SNAP benefits in violation of the FHA (§§ 3604(f) and 3617), ADA, § 1983, the Fourteenth Amendment, the Civil Rights Act, and the Rehabilitation Act. The court found the plaintiff's IFP application deficient because, while he listed income of $2,577/month and claimed $5,000/month in housing costs, he provided no breakdown of expenses or liabilities, and inconsistently described himself as both paying $5,000/month in rent and being homeless. The court dismissed the IFP application without prejudice, ordered plaintiff to file a revised and complete application within 30 days, and warned plaintiff that the complaint itself may be dismissed for failure to state a claim due to its vague, ambiguous, and conclusory allegations.
key_cases_cited: Haines v. Kerner, 404 U.S. 519 (1972)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Sinwell v. Shapp, 536 F.2d 15 (3d Cir. 1976)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of Emergency Assistance and SNAP benefits; alleged ADA, FHA, § 1983, Civil Rights Act Title II/VI, Rehabilitation Act § 504, and state tort claims (gross negligence, reckless endangerment, willful misconduct)
fha_claims.disposition: IFP Application Dismissed Without Prejudice; Complaint Not Yet Screened on Merits
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the IFP application as incomplete due to lack of necessary financial information and cautioned that the complaint itself is vague, ambiguous, and conclusory and may be dismissed under 12(b)(6) for failure to state a claim under Iqbal/Twombly. The court has not yet screened the substantive claims on the merits; the matter is administratively terminated pending resubmission of a complete IFP application.

source_file: 10714020_2025_Preston Jermain Lewis v. Barrons Property Managers Inc._ca11
case_name: Preston Jermain Lewis v. Barrons Property Managers Inc.
accommodation_description: Lewis alleged disability-based discrimination in connection with the unavailability of parking and Barrons's failure to make necessary repairs to his apartment; however, no distinct, formal accommodation request is described—the disability claims appear to overlap with general discriminatory treatment rather than a specific accommodation demand.
key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the district court's sua sponte dismissal of Lewis's second FHA complaint as frivolous under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B) because his prior appeal of identical claims had already been found frivolous by this Court.
brief_summary: Preston Lewis, a pro se Black male tenant, filed a second federal FHA lawsuit against Barrons Property Managers alleging discrimination based on familial status, race, and disability (inadequate parking, unaddressed repairs, and eviction), and retaliation—all arising from the same lease and time period as a prior federal lawsuit that had been dismissed and whose appeal was found frivolous. The district court dismissed the new complaint sua sponte as both barred by res judicata and frivolous under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B). The Eleventh Circuit affirmed solely on frivolity grounds, holding that because the earlier appeal of the same claims had already been deemed frivolous, the district court did not abuse its discretion in dismissing the refiled case.
key_cases_cited: Miller v. Donald, 541 F.3d 1091 (11th Cir. 2008)
Bilal v. Driver, 251 F.3d 1346 (11th Cir. 2001)
Jenkins v. Anton, 922 F.3d 1257 (11th Cir. 2019)
Sapuppo v. Allstate Floridian Ins. Co., 739 F.3d 678 (11th Cir. 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Adequate parking and apartment repairs
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court dismissed Lewis's complaint as frivolous under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B) because Lewis had already litigated identical Fair Housing Act claims against Barrons in a prior federal case, which this Court had previously determined to be frivolous on appeal. The court found that Lewis's history of bringing unmeritorious litigation and the re-litigation of the same claims spanning the same time period and lease supported dismissal without reaching the substantive merits.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Eviction defense based on alleged retaliation for prior complaints
fha_claims.reasoning: The retaliation claim, added in the amended complaint in the first federal case, was part of the same frivolous litigation that this Court had previously determined to lack arguable merit. The district court's sua sponte dismissal as frivolous was not an abuse of discretion given the prior determination and the identical nature of the claims.

source_file: 10714396_2025_Estela Elizabeth Jeffcoat v. Brookings Housing _ Redevelopment Commission_sdd
case_name: Estela Elizabeth Jeffcoat v. Brookings Housing & Redevelopment Commission
accommodation_description: The underlying complaint alleges Fair Housing Act violations including reasonable accommodation claims, but the specific accommodation requested is not described in this order denying appointment of counsel.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's motion to appoint counsel, finding that plaintiff demonstrated ability to litigate her claims through her detailed complaint, successful service of process, and filing of multiple motions.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Estela Elizabeth Jeffcoat filed suit against Brookings Housing & Redevelopment Commission alleging Fair Housing Act, Section 504 Rehabilitation Act, and HUD Regulations violations, and now moves for appointment of counsel. The court denied the motion to appoint counsel, finding that plaintiff demonstrated sufficient ability to litigate through her detailed filings and successful service of process on defendant.
key_cases_cited: Stevens v. Redwing, 146 F.3d 538 (8th Cir. 1998)
Wiggins v. Sargent, 753 F.2d 663 (8th Cir. 1985)
Nelson v. Redfield Lithograph Printing, 728 F.2d 1003 (8th Cir. 1984)
White v. Walsh, 649 F.2d 560 (8th Cir. 1981)
Williams v. Carter, 10 F.3d 563 (8th Cir. 1993)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unspecified reasonable accommodation(s) under Fair Housing Act § 3604(f)
fha_claims.reasoning: The opinion addresses only a motion to appoint counsel and does not reach the merits of any FHA claim. The complaint alleges Fair Housing Act violations but no substantive ruling on the claims themselves has been issued.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 504 Rehabilitation Act (29 U.S.C. § 794) and HUD Regulations (24 C.F.R. §§ 5.609, 5.611)
fha_claims.reasoning: The opinion addresses only a motion to appoint counsel and does not reach the merits of any non-FHA claims. The complaint alleges Section 504 and HUD regulatory violations but no substantive ruling on these claims has been issued.

source_file: 10714653_2025_Daniel Shirley v. Mulberry Properties LLC, et al._gamd
case_name: Daniel Shirley v. Mulberry Properties LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff's FHA claim concerns alleged failure to ensure property managers received fair housing compliance training, not a personal accommodation request.
key_holding: The FHA does not provide a cause of action for failure to ensure fair housing compliance training; to state an FHA claim, a plaintiff must allege unequal treatment on the basis of race affecting housing availability.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Daniel Shirley brought multiple claims including an FHA claim against his employer Mulberry Properties LLC, alleging defendants violated the FHA by failing to ensure property managers received fair housing compliance training. The Court dismissed all claims under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e) for failure to state a cognizable claim, finding the FHA claim fails because there is no private right of action for failure-to-train claims and the plaintiff did not allege unequal treatment on the basis of race affecting housing availability.
key_cases_cited: Hallmark Developers, Inc. v. Fulton Cty., Ga., 466 F.3d 1276 (11th Cir. 2006)
Great American Federal Savings & Loan Ass'n v. Novotny, 442 U.S. 366 (1979)
Eagle v. Viewpoint Invs. LLC, No. 1:20-cv-236-RH-GRJ, 2022 WL 22227628 (N.D. Fla. Mar. 11, 2022)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to ensure property managers continued taking required fair housing compliance and anti-discrimination training
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that failure to train is not a cognizable claim under the FHA, which requires unequal treatment on the basis of a protected class affecting housing availability. The court also noted plaintiff failed to file a complaint with HUD before filing suit, as required by the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VII employment discrimination, § 1985 conspiracy, OSHA workplace safety, FLSA retaliation
fha_claims.disposition: Frivolous dismissal and failure to state a claim under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)
fha_claims.reasoning: Title VII claims were time-barred (filed 92 days after EEOC notice, exceeding the 90-day deadline); § 1985 claim was frivolous as it attempted to circumvent Title VII requirements; OSHA claims were frivolous because no private right of action exists under OSHA; FLSA retaliation claim failed because reporting sexual harassment and discrimination is not protected activity under the FLSA.

source_file: 10715172_2025_Wayne Alexander Howlett v. City of Susanville, et al._caed
case_name: Wayne Alexander Howlett v. City of Susanville, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges defendants harassed him with racial slurs, contaminated his water supply, damaged his property, and attempted to force him to sell his home because of his race.
key_holding: Plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claim fails because he did not adequately allege membership in a protected class or establish the causal link between an existing policy and a disproportionate effect on a protected class necessary to state a prima facie case of disparate-impact discrimination.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Wayne Alexander Howlett sued the City of Susanville and Susanville Sanitary District alleging they harassed him with racial slurs, contaminated his water, and attempted to force him to sell his home in violation of the Fair Housing Act and Fourteenth Amendment. The court granted defendants' unopposed motions to dismiss, finding plaintiff's complaint failed to adequately plead intentional discrimination or disparate impact under the FHA because he did not sufficiently allege membership in a protected class or a causal link between a municipal policy and discriminatory effect.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 129 S. Ct. 1937 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Monell v. Dep't of Soc. Servs., 436 U.S. 658 (1978)
Sw. Fair Hous. Council, Inc. v. Maricopa Domestic Water Improvement Dist., 17 F.4th 950 (9th Cir. 2021)
Pac. Shores Props., Ltd. Liab. Co. v. City of Newport Beach, 730 F.3d 1142 (9th Cir. 2013)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to establish a prima facie case of disparate-impact discrimination under the FHA. The complaint lacks factual allegations showing a causal link between an existing policy and a disproportionate effect on a protected class, and fails to demonstrate that defendants intentionally discriminated based on race.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fourteenth Amendment Equal Protection claim; § 1983 municipal liability claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege that defendants treated him differently from similarly situated individuals based on membership in a protected class, failed to establish he is a member of a protected class, and failed to allege facts showing intentional discrimination by the named defendants. Allegations were vague and conclusory, and plaintiff did not adequately plead Monell municipal liability.

source_file: 10715251_2025_T_R Properties, Inc., et al. v. Berlin Township, et al._ohsd
case_name: T&R Properties, Inc., et al. v. Berlin Township, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff developer challenges zoning denials as racially discriminatory and seeks to add familial status discrimination claim.
key_holding: The court granted plaintiff leave to amend its complaint to add a familial status discrimination claim because the amendment was not futile, would not cause undue prejudice given discovery had just begun, and the new claim was closely related to the existing racial discrimination claims.
brief_summary: T&R Properties, Inc., a developer, sued Berlin Township over denial of zoning approvals for a mixed-use project, alleging intentional racial discrimination and disparate impact under the FHA. The court granted plaintiff leave to amend its complaint to add a familial status discrimination claim, finding the amendment was not futile and would not unduly prejudice defendants given early discovery stage.
key_cases_cited: Foman v. Davis, 371 U.S. 178 (1962)
Inge v. Rock Financial Corp., 388 F.3d 930 (6th Cir. 2004)
Moore v. City of Paducah, 790 F.2d 557 (6th Cir. 1986)
Bear v. Delaware County, 2015 WL 1954451 (S.D. Ohio 2015)
Durthaler v. Accounts Receivable Management, Inc., 2011 WL 5008552 (S.D. Ohio 2011)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.disposition: Motion to Dismiss Denied as Moot
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted plaintiff's motion to amend the complaint to add a familial status discrimination claim under the FHA. The existing motion to dismiss was denied as moot because the amended complaint will be tested on future dispositive motions before the district judge. The court found the amendment was not futile on its face and that allowing amendment was consistent with the liberal amendment policy of Rule 15.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.disposition: Motion to Dismiss Denied as Moot
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted plaintiff's motion to amend the complaint to add a familial status discrimination claim under the FHA. The existing motion to dismiss was denied as moot because the amended complaint will be tested on future dispositive motions before the district judge. The court found the amendment was not futile on its face and that allowing amendment was consistent with the liberal amendment policy of Rule 15.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Familial status discrimination claim based on allegations that defendants denied zoning proposal because of private motives that child safety concerns and preferences for professional and single residents exist in Berlin Township
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted plaintiff's motion for leave to file an amended complaint adding a familial status discrimination claim under the FHA. The court found the amendment was not futile on its face, that little prejudice would result from allowing the amendment given the limited discovery to date, and that the new claim was closely related to existing claims and did not fundamentally alter the nature of the dispute.

source_file: 10715355_2025_Curtis Stowe v. Chalet Capri Condominium Association, Inc., and David Kidd_flmd
case_name: Curtis Stowe v. Chalet Capri Condominium Association, Inc., and David Kidd
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested; this case involves alleged retaliation and interference under FHA § 3617 arising from the plaintiff's use of his condominium unit as a short-term rental and the HOA's and its president's conduct toward him and his tenants.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA and FFHA retaliation claims because he failed to plausibly allege either an underlying violation of a protected FHA right based on a protected classification or that defendants' conduct rose to the level of coercion, intimidation, threats, or interference under 42 U.S.C. § 3617, characterizing the dispute as a neighbor/HOA disagreement over short-term rentals rather than discriminatory retaliation.
brief_summary: Curtis Stowe, who managed a condominium owned by his LLC as a short-term rental, sued the HOA (Chalet Capri Condominium Association) and its president (David Kidd) for retaliation under the FHA (42 U.S.C. § 3617) and the Florida FHA after defendants allegedly harassed him and his tenants—some of whom were Black—called police on them, amended bylaws to prohibit short-term rentals, and engaged in ongoing contentious conduct. The court found Stowe had Article III standing as a person who aided others in exercising FHA rights, but dismissed both counts because he failed to allege that defendants treated him or his tenants differently based on a protected characteristic (Kidd scrutinized all short-term renters regardless of race) and failed to allege conduct severe enough to constitute coercion, intimidation, threats, or interference within the meaning of § 3617. The court dismissed the complaint without prejudice, granting Stowe leave to amend.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Philippeaux v. Miami Apartments Invs., LLC, No. 24-11468 (11th Cir. 2025)
Gourlay v. Forest Lake Ests. Civic Ass'n of Port Richey, Inc., 276 F. Supp. 2d 1222 (M.D. Fla. 2003)
Sofarelli v. Pinellas County, 931 F.2d 718 (11th Cir. 1991)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that defendants violated any FHA-protected right (§§ 3603-3606) or that they coerced, intimidated, threatened, or interfered with plaintiff's exercise of such rights. The FHA does not independently protect an owner's right to use property as a short-term rental, and plaintiff did not allege discrimination based on protected class. The dispute amounts to a contractual and property disagreement outside the scope of FHA retaliation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Florida Fair Housing Act (FFHA), § 760.37, Florida Statutes
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's FFHA claim rises and falls with the FHA claim because the FFHA and FHA are substantively identical and incorporate the same facts. For the same reasons as the FHA retaliation claim, plaintiff failed to allege that defendants coerced, intimidated, threatened, or interfered with any person's exercise of rights granted under the FFHA.

source_file: 10715870_2025_Greater Guide, Inc. d_b_a American Service Pets v. SAPS LLC et al._laed

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Sherman Act antitrust claims, Computer Fraud and Abuse Act claims, RICO claims, and state law claims arising from business competition in the emotional support animal certification industry
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed all federal claims (Sherman Act, CFAA, RICO) and declined supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims. Sherman Act claims were barred by Noerr-Pennington immunity for petitioning activity; CFAA claims failed to plausibly allege the type of technological harm the statute addresses; RICO claims failed because the predicate acts (mail/wire fraud based on regulatory complaints) were immunized under Noerr-Pennington, leaving insufficient predicate acts to establish a pattern of racketeering activity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Defendant asserted disability-based defenses under the Americans with Disabilities Act in response to unlawful detainer action, but the specific accommodation requested is not identified in the opinion.
fha_claims.disposition: Remanded for lack of subject matter jurisdiction
fha_claims.reasoning: The federal court lacked subject matter jurisdiction over the state law unlawful detainer action. Defendant cannot establish federal question jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1331 by relying on potential defenses such as the Fair Housing Act, Rehabilitation Act, or Americans with Disabilities Act. The case was remanded to state court without reaching the merits of any FHA or disability-based claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act, Rehabilitation Act, and First Amendment defenses asserted in unlawful detainer action.
fha_claims.disposition: Remanded for lack of subject matter jurisdiction
fha_claims.reasoning: Federal court lacked subject matter jurisdiction. Defendant cannot establish jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1331, § 1343, or § 1443 based on potential defenses or counterclaims. The case was remanded to state court without addressing the merits of non-FHA federal claims.

source_file: 10716332_2025_Damia Bjurling v. Alec Johnson, et al._wawd
case_name: Damia Bjurling v. Alec Johnson, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges she and her service dog were injured when a fellow tenant attacked her; the court analyzes whether defendants violated FHA provisions regarding disability discrimination rather than analyzing a specific accommodation request.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claims because Mr. Holder, as a fellow tenant, is not a proper defendant under the FHA which only regulates individual tenants through traditional agency principles, and plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that Mr. Holder was acting as an agent for her landlord.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Damia Bjurling sued former defendant Alec Johnson, Police Chief Shelby Parker, and fellow tenant Calvin Earl Holder III under the ADA, FHA, and constitutional provisions, alleging defendants' conduct—including recording an assault and failing to properly investigate—violated her rights as an adult with autism and injured her and her service dog. The court granted Chief Parker's motion to dismiss and dismissed all federal claims against all defendants with prejudice, finding plaintiff failed to state plausible claims including FHA claims against Mr. Holder because he is a fellow tenant not acting as an agent of a landlord.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Dubois v. Ass'n of Apartment Owners of 2987 Kalakaua, 453 F.3d 1175 (9th Cir. 2006)
Morris v. W. Hayden Ests. First Addition Homeowners Ass'n, Inc., 104 F.4th 1128 (9th Cir. 2024)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation related to plaintiff's status as an adult with autism in connection with housing or services
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed under § 1915(e)(2)(B) because plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that Mr. Holder, a private individual fellow tenant, is directly or vicariously liable for a discriminatory housing practice under § 3604(f). The court applied the pleading-stage standard without substantive analysis of the reasonable accommodation framework.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged discriminatory harassment based on disability (autism) by fellow tenant
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed under § 1915(e)(2)(B) because plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that Mr. Holder was acting as an agent of the landlord (necessary for vicarious liability) and did not sufficiently allege that the attack was motivated by discriminatory intent based on a protected characteristic.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II and Title III claims; § 1983 constitutional claims (First, Eighth, Tenth, Fourteenth Amendments); state law claims under RCW 10.109, RCW 7.105, RCW 74.34
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed ADA Title II claim because Mr. Holder is a private individual, not a public entity. ADA Title III claim failed because Mr. Holder does not own, lease, or operate a place of public accommodation. § 1983 claims failed for failure to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly. State law claims dismissed without prejudice due to decline of supplemental jurisdiction.

case_name: Alfey Ramdhan v. Morgan Stonehill, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff did not articulate a specific accommodation request; he alleged only that defendant Morgan Stonehill, LLC was 'unwilling to work with him to resolve the issue of' eviction and 'becoming homeless,' implying a request that the landlord make some adjustment to the eviction process or outcome in light of his medical and mental health disabilities.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's ADA claim with prejudice because a residential apartment is not a place of public accommodation, and dismissed the FHA disability discrimination claim without prejudice with leave to amend because the complaint failed to plead sufficient facts to state a plausible claim for relief.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Alfey Ramdhan, who suffers from medical and mental health disabilities, sued his landlord Morgan Stonehill, LLC in the District of Nevada alleging violations of the ADA and FHA in connection with an eviction proceeding. The court granted IFP status, dismissed the ADA claim with prejudice because residential apartments are not places of public accommodation under 42 U.S.C. § 12182(a), and dismissed the FHA claim without prejudice with leave to amend, finding the complaint provided only conclusory allegations that the defendant was 'unwilling to work with' plaintiff regarding eviction without sufficient facts to state a plausible disability discrimination claim. The court also explained that the Rooker-Feldman doctrine bars it from staying or reviewing a state court eviction order.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Harris v. Itzhaki, 183 F.3d 1043 (9th Cir. 1999)
Turner v. Crawford Square Apartments III, L.P., 449 F.3d 542 (3d Cir. 2006)
Independent Housing Servs. v. Fillmore Center Assocs., 840 F. Supp. 1328 (N.D. Cal. 1993)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges discrimination based on disability in connection with eviction; seeks stay of eviction.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege discriminatory conduct under the FHA. The complaint contains only conclusory allegations that defendant was 'unwilling to work with' plaintiff regarding eviction and homelessness, without factual allegations demonstrating discriminatory animus or conduct based on disability. The complaint is ambiguous as to whether plaintiff seeks to challenge a state court eviction order (which would implicate Rooker-Feldman) or allege an independent FHA violation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claim for discrimination in housing based on disability.
fha_claims.reasoning: The ADA prohibits discrimination only in 'places of public accommodation' under 42 U.S.C. § 12182(a), and an apartment does not constitute a place of public accommodation. Therefore, the ADA claim is dismissed with prejudice as a matter of law.

source_file: 10716560_2025_Felice Lazae Martin, et al. v. Michael Castillo, et al._caed
case_name: Felice Lazae Martin, et al. v. Michael Castillo, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested to be excused from rent payments during a search period for alternative housing while relocating from a property with toxic mold and no functioning heat; plaintiffs also alleged they sought electronic filing accommodations from the Kern County Superior Court due to their disabilities during a 43-day e-filing shutdown.
key_holding: The court found that pro se plaintiffs failed to plead any cognizable federal claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, the ADA, or the Fair Housing Act, and granted leave to file an amended complaint within 21 days.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Felice Lazae Martin and Hector Joseph Borges sued their landlord Michael Castillo and his attorney for toxic mold habitability violations, an illegal lockout, and disability discrimination under the FHA, ADA, and constitutional provisions. On IFP screening, the court found the complaint failed to state any cognizable federal claim, noting plaintiffs made only cursory references to the FHA without supporting facts, failed to identify a proper ADA defendant, and did not adequately allege any constitutional violations under § 1983. The court ordered plaintiffs to file an amended complaint or a notice of voluntary dismissal within 21 days.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Lopez v. Smith, 203 F.3d 1122 (9th Cir. 2000)
United States v. Cal. Mobile Home Park Mgmt., 107 F.3d 1374 (9th Cir. 1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs sought to relocate safely and requested to be excused from rent payments during the search period due to toxic mold conditions and resulting health effects (pneumonia, neurological deterioration from mold exposure). The accommodation was framed as relief from rent obligations during constructive eviction.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that Plaintiffs made only two cursory references to the Fair Housing Act and asserted no specific facts to establish a cognizable claim under the FHA. The complaint failed to plausibly allege the elements of a failure to accommodate claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(B), including whether defendants knew of the handicap, whether accommodation was necessary, and whether defendants refused the accommodation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 (First, Fourth, Fourteenth Amendment claims including due process, equal protection, access to courts); ADA Title II (denial of electronic filing accommodations); state law claims (Bane Act, Unruh Act, infliction of emotional distress, California Civil Code § 789.3)
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim / Lack of subject matter jurisdiction
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that § 1983 claims failed because neither Castillo (private landlord) nor Schneider (private attorney) acted under color of state law; Plaintiffs failed to adequately plead state action under the public function or joint action tests. ADA Title II claims failed because the County of Kern was not named as a defendant and Plaintiffs failed to adequately allege denial of reasonable accommodations or what specific accommodations were requested and denied. State law claims could not be addressed because no cognizable federal claim existed to support supplemental jurisdiction.

source_file: 10730094_2025_Eric Crouse v. Housing Works, Deschutes County, and the State of Oregon_ord
case_name: Eric Crouse v. Housing Works, Deschutes County, and the State of Oregon
accommodation_description: Request that payment standard be increased and utility allowance be raised to allow access to suitable housing under the Section 8 voucher program
key_holding: The State of Oregon's motion to dismiss was granted because the court lacks subject matter jurisdiction under Oregon's APA (which provides the exclusive remedy for review of final agency orders) and because Plaintiff failed to allege any affirmative acts by the State that caused injury, as opposed to mere failures to act.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Eric Crouse, a person with disabilities represented by the Deschutes County IDD program, sued Housing Works (the local housing authority), Deschutes County, and the State of Oregon alleging failures to provide reasonable housing accommodations including increased payment standards and utility allowances under Section 8. The State of Oregon moved to dismiss, and the court granted the motion on jurisdictional grounds (Oregon APA provides exclusive review mechanism) and for failure to state a claim because Plaintiff alleged no affirmative acts by the State causing injury.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Wyatt B. v. Kotek, 146 F.4th 1267 (9th Cir. 2025)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Increased payment standard to allow access to suitable housing and higher utility allowance; plaintiff's housing costs exceeded the approved standard, requiring payment of more than 30% of income towards rent
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege any affirmative action by the State of Oregon causing injury; claims rest solely on alleged failures to act and do not allege that plaintiff was denied services actually offered by the State, rendering the complaint implausible under Twombly/Iqbal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II, Section 504 Rehabilitation Act, and 42 U.S.C. § 1983 claims based on alleged failure to provide housing accommodations and equal access to services
fha_claims.reasoning: To the extent claims are based on the February 21, 2025 ODDS letter (a final agency order under Oregon's Administrative Procedures Act), federal court lacks subject matter jurisdiction; judicial review of final orders must proceed exclusively in Oregon state court under ORS 183.484.

source_file: 10730134_2025_Mikel James Gueltzau v. Derek Warehime, Property Manager and Owner; and Cathy Warehime, Property Manager and Owner_ned
case_name: Mikel James Gueltzau v. Derek Warehime, Property Manager and Owner; and Cathy Warehime, Property Manager and Owner
accommodation_description: The specific accommodation request is not described in this procedural order.
key_holding: The court struck two improperly filed documents, revoked the pro se plaintiff's CM/ECF electronic filing privileges due to persistent non-compliance with procedural rules, and ordered plaintiff to show cause why future submissions should not be pre-screened by the court.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Mikel James Gueltzau, who alleges Fair Housing Act discrimination against private landlords Derek and Cathy Warehime, filed additional improperly docketed documents despite prior court warnings; the court struck the filings, revoked plaintiff's electronic filing privileges, and ordered plaintiff to show cause why future submissions should not require pre-filing court review due to abusive litigation practices.
key_cases_cited: In re Tyler, 839 F.2d 1290 (8th Cir. 1988)
Williams v. McKenzie, 834 F.2d 152 (8th Cir. 1987)
Kurkowski v. Volcker, 819 F.2d 201 (8th Cir. 1987)
Eckert v. Lane, 678 F. Supp. 773 (W.D. Ark. 1988)

source_file: 10730290_2025_Yifan Shen v. Commissioner, Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services_ca11
case_name: Yifan Shen v. Commissioner, Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege SB 264's purchase restriction, registration requirement, and affidavit requirement constitute discriminatory housing practices under the Fair Housing Act based on race and national origin, though no individualized accommodation request is at issue.
key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the denial of preliminary injunction as to registration and affidavit requirements but reversed as to the purchase restriction because no plaintiff had standing to challenge it; the court applied rational basis review under Terrace v. Thompson, finding the purchase restriction did not violate Equal Protection as applied to noncitizens, and rejected federal preemption arguments regarding CFIUS.
brief_summary: Chinese citizens and a real estate brokerage firm sued Florida officials to enjoin enforcement of SB 264, which restricted Chinese noncitizens from purchasing Florida real property, required registration of property owned by Chinese persons, and mandated compliance affidavits. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the denial of preliminary injunction for the registration and affidavit requirements but reversed and remanded for the purchase restriction because no plaintiff had standing to challenge it, applying rational basis review and finding the statute did not facially violate Equal Protection.
key_cases_cited: Village of Arlington Heights v. Metro. Hous. Dev. Corp., 429 U.S. 252 (1977)
Plyler v. Doe, 457 U.S. 202 (1982)
Yick Wo v. Hopkins, 118 U.S. 356 (1886)
Terrace v. Thompson, 263 U.S. 197 (1923)
Crosby v. Nat'l Foreign Trade Council, 530 U.S. 363 (2000)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged that Florida's registration requirement and affidavit requirement for real property purchases violated the Fair Housing Act by discriminating based on race and national origin.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that the registration and affidavit requirements do not constitute discriminatory housing practices under FHA § 3604(a) because they do not restrict anyone from owning property and do not require or permit refusal to sell, rent, or negotiate with anyone. The provisions are administrative registration and attestation requirements, not restrictions on housing transactions themselves, and therefore fall outside the scope of FHA § 3604(a).

source_file: 10730691_2025_Maria Guadalupe Aguilera v. Capital One, N.A., Jack Johnson, Kristina Nevel, Joanne Tucker, Suzanne Drotman, and Judith Williams_oknd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VII race discrimination, Title VII/PDA pregnancy discrimination, Title VII retaliation, FMLA retaliation, negligent infliction of emotional distress, wrongful termination
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead sufficient non-conclusory factual allegations to support Title VII race discrimination and Title VII retaliation claims within the applicable 300-day limitations period. Pregnancy discrimination claim dismissed for failure to exhaust administrative remedies. Negligent infliction of emotional distress and wrongful termination claims have no cognizable basis under Oklahoma law and are preempted by the OADA and OWCA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: FMLA retaliation claim based on placement on Performance Improvement Plan (PIP) while on FMLA leave
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff adequately pleaded FMLA retaliation claim as to the PIP placement by alleging protected FMLA leave, an adverse employment action (PIP with heightened scrutiny and weekly meetings), and sufficient temporal proximity and circumstantial facts (no prior discipline, interference with FMLA approval, selective metric application) to infer retaliatory motive. Claim survives motion to dismiss and proceeds to discovery.

source_file: 10730883_2025_Mikel James Gueltzau v. Derek Warehime, Property Manager and Owner; and Cathy Warehime, Property Manager and Owner_ned
case_name: Mikel James Gueltzau v. Derek Warehime, Property Manager and Owner; and Cathy Warehime, Property Manager and Owner
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested permission to file documents via email or fax and to attend hearings via Zoom or telephone as ADA accommodations to court filing requirements.
key_holding: The Court denied Plaintiff's ADA accommodation requests for email/fax filing and remote hearings because such accommodations are not reasonably necessary—email and fax filing would be inappropriate given Plaintiff's past abuse of electronic filing privileges, and the Court already considers parties' circumstances when setting hearings.
brief_summary: Pro se Plaintiff filed multiple improper and frivolous documents in a Fair Housing Act discrimination case, prompting the Court to impose filing restrictions requiring paper submissions by mail. Plaintiff then sought ADA accommodations to file documents via email or fax and attend hearings remotely, which the Court denied because such accommodations were not reasonably necessary given his past abuse of electronic filing and his demonstrated ability to file documents quickly in person.
key_cases_cited: In re Tyler, 839 F.2d 1290 (8th Cir. 1988)
Williams v. McKenzie, 834 F.2d 152 (8th Cir. 1987)
Hall v. Higgins, 77 F.4th 1171 (8th Cir. 2023)
Fletcher v. Brown Cnt'y, 2008 WL 752661 (D. Neb. 2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to file documents via email or fax as a reasonable accommodation for health and financial hardship
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied a direct balancing test under the ADA/Rehabilitation Act meaningful access standard and concluded that email and fax filing are not reasonably necessary given plaintiff's past abuse of electronic filing privileges and his demonstrated ability to personally deliver documents to the clerk's office.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Conducting future hearings or conferences via Zoom or telephone when in-person appearance in Omaha would create an undue burden
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied a meaningful access standard and found no reasonable necessity for the accommodation because the court already considers location and circumstances of parties in setting proceedings, and plaintiff's ability to personally deliver documents to the clerk's office in Lincoln undermined his claim of undue burden.

source_file: 10731021_2025_Asya Weston, et al. v. WIP 800 J Lofts, et al._caed
case_name: Asya Weston, et al. v. WIP 800 J Lofts, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege the unlawful detainer action and eviction were retaliatory and discriminatory based on race, familial status, and disability, but do not specify a particular accommodation request being denied.
key_holding: The FHA claim was dismissed because plaintiffs failed to sufficiently allege they suffer from a qualifying handicap under § 3602(h), that defendants knew of their impairments, or that defendants refused to make an accommodation.
brief_summary: Two Black tenants sued WIP 800 J Lofts and associated individuals alleging the unlawful detainer action against them was fraudulent and retaliatory, targeting their race, familial status, and disabilities in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The court dismissed the complaint with leave to amend, finding plaintiffs failed to state an FHA claim because they did not adequately allege a qualifying handicap or discriminatory conduct based on protected characteristics.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Harris v. Itzhaki
United States v. Cal. Mobile Home Park Mgmt. Co.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs alleged only conclusory statements that defendants engaged in discriminatory conduct based on race without providing sufficient facts. The court found the allegations insufficient under the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard and noted that plaintiffs' claims were primarily centered on the unlawful detainer action.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accommodation related to disability (ADHD, hypertension for Weston; asthma for Marshall) in connection with housing
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to sufficiently allege that they suffered from a handicap as defined under the FHA, that defendants knew or should have known about the handicap, that accommodation might be necessary, or that defendants refused to make an accommodation. The court found these elements were not plausibly alleged.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to sufficiently plead a discrimination claim based on familial status, as they did not allege that defendants created discriminatory rules treating families with children less favorably than adult-only households. Additionally, plaintiff Marshall was no longer a minor at the time of the order.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to sufficiently allege what housing or disability rights they asserted, failed to show that asserting such rights caused defendants to initiate the unlawful detainer action, and failed to show that the action resulted from coercion, intimidation, or threats as required under § 3617.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (due process, property rights, denial of access to courts), 42 U.S.C. § 1985 (conspiracy), 18 U.S.C. § 1962(c) (RICO), 18 U.S.C. § 1503 (obstruction of justice), state law claims
fha_claims.reasoning: § 1983 claims failed because plaintiffs did not allege defendants acted under color of state law; § 1985 conspiracy claim failed for the same reason; RICO claim failed due to conclusory allegations and Rooker-Feldman bar; § 1503 obstruction claim failed because it is a criminal statute with no private right of action. State law claims were dismissed without supplemental jurisdiction.

source_file: 10731555_2025_Daniel Reeves v. United States of America et al._gasd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges amorphous violations of federal statutes including the Fair Housing Act, Equal Credit Opportunity Act, and Religious Freedom Act, but does not tie any alleged violations to specific actions by any particular defendant.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege concrete injury sufficient to establish Article III standing. Although plaintiff mentioned the Fair Housing Act among other federal statutes, he made no specific allegations connecting any defendant to any FHA violation and failed to establish a personal stake in the outcome distinct from a generalized grievance about government operations.

source_file: 10731564_2025_United States of America v. Five Properties, LLC et al._laed
case_name: United States of America v. Five Properties, LLC et al.
accommodation_description: Request to keep an emotional support dog as a reasonable accommodation for a mental disability
key_holding: The Government's action is not barred by res judicata because the Government has an independent interest in enforcing the FHA and seeks broader public interest remedies beyond what the private plaintiff sought, and laches does not apply to bar the Government's suit.
brief_summary: The United States government filed suit on behalf of Dory Turnipseed against Five Properties, LLC and Tonti Management alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act for refusing to accommodate Turnipseed's mental disability by denying her emotional support dog. The court denied the defendants' motion for summary judgment, holding that the Government's action is not barred by res judicata because the Government has independent enforcement interests seeking broader public remedies, and laches does not apply to bar suits brought by the United States in its sovereign capacity.
key_cases_cited: Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986)
E.E.O.C. v. Waffle House, Inc., 534 U.S. 279 (2002)
United States v. East Baton Rouge Par. Sch. Bd., 594 F.2d 56 (5th Cir. 1979)
United States v. Popovich, 820 F.2d 134 (5th Cir. 1987)
Test Masters Educ. Servs., Inc. v. Singh, 428 F.3d 559 (5th Cir. 2005)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to accommodate plaintiff's mental disability by allowing her to live in the apartment with her emotional support dog
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied defendants' motion for summary judgment on res judicata and laches grounds, finding that the Government has an independent interest in enforcing the FHA distinct from the original tenant's suit, and that laches cannot be asserted against the United States when acting in its sovereign capacity to enforce public rights. The substantive FHA reasonable accommodation claim on the merits was not addressed.

source_file: 10731635_2025_Troy King v. Julia Owner LLC, et al._azd
case_name: Troy King v. Julia Owner LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation request; plaintiff alleges intentional racial discrimination in rental terms, lease renewal denial, and eviction proceedings.
key_holding: Plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claims were properly dismissed because his amended complaint failed to allege sufficient facts connecting the defendant's alleged discriminatory statements and actions to his race, despite having been given specific guidance on what factual allegations were required.
brief_summary: Troy King, a Black tenant at an apartment complex managed by Julia Owner LLC and later Greystar Management, sued alleging racial discrimination under the Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 1981, and the Arizona Civil Rights Act, claiming he witnessed staff quote a White family a lower rate, was denied lease renewal, and faced retaliatory eviction and fraudulent court filings. The court dismissed his claims without leave to amend, finding his amended complaint still failed to allege sufficient facts showing the defendant's alleged discriminatory conduct was connected to his race.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
In re Cloudera, Inc., 121 F.4th 1180 (9th Cir. 2024)
United States v. United Healthcare Ins. Co., 848 F.3d 1161 (9th Cir. 2016)
Kendall v. Visa U.S.A., Inc., 518 F.3d 1042 (9th Cir. 2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged racial discrimination under the FHA but failed to plausibly allege that the defendant's statements or actions were actually connected to his race. The court found the allegations conclusory and insufficient under the Iqbal/Twombly standard to state a plausible claim for intentional discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1981 discriminatory contracting claim; Arizona Civil Rights Act (ACRA) claim; fraud claim under state law; civil conspiracy claim under state law
fha_claims.reasoning: The § 1981 and ACRA claims failed for the same reason as the FHA claim—failure to allege intentional discrimination connected to a protected class. The fraud claim failed to meet Fed. R. Civ. P. 9(b)'s heightened pleading standard because plaintiff provided no specific details regarding time, place, and content of alleged false representations. The conspiracy claim failed because plaintiff did not allege an underlying tort.

source_file: 10731728_2025_Irish Horton v. Beacon Woods East Master Association, Inc., Ronnie Armstrong, and Christopher Skene_flmd
case_name: Irish Horton v. Beacon Woods East Master Association, Inc., Ronnie Armstrong, and Christopher Skene
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a Black man with a physical disability requiring a service dog, alleged he was expelled from the clubhouse when Defendants refused entry based on his service animal.
key_holding: The Court dismissed Plaintiff's race-based discrimination claims under the FHA, 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 and 1982, finding that the Amended Complaint failed to plead sufficient facts showing that Defendants' discriminatory conduct stemmed from racial animus rather than animus toward Plaintiff's disability and use of a service dog.
brief_summary: Irish Horton, a Black/African American man with a physical disability who uses a service dog, sued Beacon Woods East Master Association, Inc. and two HOA officers alleging they expelled him from a clubhouse in May 2023 because of both his race and disability. The Court granted Defendants' motions to dismiss, finding that Plaintiff's factual allegations showed discriminatory animus stemmed from his disability and use of a service dog rather than his race, and that Plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts showing he was treated differently than similarly situated non-Black residents.
key_cases_cited: Watts v. Joggers Run Prop. Owners Ass'n, Inc., 133 F.4th 1032 (11th Cir. 2025)
Ziyadat v. Diamondrock Hosp. Co., 3 F.4th 1291 (11th Cir. 2021)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Plowright v. Miami Dade Cnty., 102 F.4th 1358 (11th Cir. 2024)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Access to clubhouse facilities and HOA meeting
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that defendants' conduct was motivated by racial animus. All factual allegations concerning the expulsion from the clubhouse relate to plaintiff's disability and use of a service animal, not his race. The court found no facts suggesting race played any role in defendants' actions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Access to clubhouse facilities and HOA meeting with service animal
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts showing that any interference by defendants was connected to plaintiff's race. The court found that interference requires a pattern of harassment invidiously motivated by race, and plaintiff's allegations describe only a one-time incident concerning use of a service animal, not a pattern of race-based harassment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1982; Florida common law IIED
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to adequately allege intentional racial discrimination under § 1981 or § 1982, either directly or circumstantially. Plaintiff did not allege any racial slurs or racially charged language, and failed to identify similarly situated comparators of a different race who were treated differently. For IIED, plaintiff's allegations of verbal abuse and denial of clubhouse access do not rise to the level of outrageousness required under Florida law; Florida courts reject IIED claims based on mere insults, indignities, or threats.

source_file: 10731759_2025_Toby Masse v. Clark County, et al._wawd
case_name: Toby Masse v. Clark County, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges discrimination based on race, sex, and sexual orientation, denial of homeless services, and seizure of personal property, claiming Fair Housing Act violations.
key_holding: The Court found the complaint deficient under Rule 8 for failing to provide factual allegations showing the who, what, where, when, and why of each claim, and granted plaintiff 21 days to file an amended complaint.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Toby Masse filed an in forma pauperis complaint against Clark County, City of Vancouver, and others alleging discrimination based on race, sex, and sexual orientation, denial of homeless services, and unconstitutional seizure of property in violation of the Fair Housing Act, Civil Rights Act, and Fourteenth Amendment. The Court screened the complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B) and found it deficient for failing to provide sufficient factual allegations to state plausible claims, ordering plaintiff to file an amended complaint within 21 days or face dismissal.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges discrimination based on race, sex, and sexual orientation; deprivation of homeless services; and taking of personal property without due process. Claims brought under Fair Housing Act, Civil Rights Act of 1964, Fourteenth Amendment, City of Vancouver Emergency Homeless Declaration, and executive order prohibiting illegal discrimination.
fha_claims.disposition: Order to Amend or Dismiss under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found complaint fails to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly because plaintiff provides only conclusory allegations of discrimination without factual detail regarding who, what, where, when, and why. Plaintiff did not identify which defendant committed which act or explain the factual basis for discrimination claims. Court granted leave to amend rather than dismiss with prejudice.

source_file: 10732345_2025_Ronald Satish Emrit and Presidential Committee_Political Action Committee_Separate Segregated Fund Number C00569897 d_b_a United Emrits of America v. Erin Burnett, et al._nmd
case_name: Ronald Satish Emrit and Presidential Committee/Political Action Committee/Separate Segregated Fund Number C00569897 d/b/a United Emrits of America v. Erin Burnett, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges defendants failed to provide Section 8 housing voucher and violated Fair Housing Act
key_holding: The complaint failed to state Fair Housing Act or ADA claims because it did not identify the specific statutory provisions violated or allege sufficient facts showing the claims arose under those statutes, and plaintiff failed to comply with the court's order to show cause.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Ronald Satish Emrit sued television personalities, BMW Cars of North America, and Congresswoman Nancy Mace alleging Fair Housing Act and ADA violations based on defendants' failure to provide a Section 8 housing voucher and defamatory statements. The court dismissed the case without prejudice for failure to state a claim upon which relief could be granted and for plaintiff's failure to comply with the magistrate judge's order to show cause.
key_cases_cited: Schaffer v. Salt Lake City Corp., 814 F.3d 1151 (10th Cir. 2016)
Davison v. Grant Thornton LLP, 582 Fed.Appx. 773 (10th Cir. 2014)
Varnell v. Dora Consol. School Dist., 756 F.3d 1208 (10th Cir. 2014)
Dental Dynamics, LLC v. Jolly Dental Group, LLC, 946 F.3d 1223 (10th Cir. 2020)
Gustafson v. Luke, 696 Fed.Appx. 352 (10th Cir. 2017)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to provide Section 8 housing voucher; alleged defamatory statements regarding President Donald J. Trump and others; § 1983 equal protection and due process claims; ADA claims
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint fails to state a claim under § 1983 (no allegations of state action), FHA (no identification of specific statutory provisions or sufficient factual allegations), and ADA (same deficiency). The court applied the pleading standard requiring identification of the statutory provision and sufficient facts showing the case arises under federal law, finding the complaint deficient on its face.

source_file: 10732441_2025_Anthony George Bell v. Weinreb Management LLC; Abraham Reiss of Weinreb Management LLC; Pitor Piwowarczyk of 455 Ocean Associates LLC; 455 Ocean Associates LLC_nyed
case_name: Anthony George Bell v. Weinreb Management LLC; Abraham Reiss of Weinreb Management LLC; Pitor Piwowarczyk of 455 Ocean Associates LLC; 455 Ocean Associates LLC
accommodation_description: No accommodation requested; plaintiff alleges housing quality issues (roach infestation, inoperable vents, electrical problems) without requesting any disability-related accommodation or alleging discrimination based on his HIV and asthma
key_holding: The complaint fails to state a Fair Housing Act claim because plaintiff does not allege any acts of discrimination—merely mentioning health conditions (HIV and asthma) without linking defendants' conduct to discriminatory treatment based on disability is insufficient to invoke FHA protections.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Anthony George Bell sued Weinreb Management LLC and 455 Ocean Associates LLC alleging housing quality issues including roach infestation, broken vents, and electrical problems at his Brooklyn apartment; Bell mentioned having HIV and asthma but did not request any disability accommodation. The court dismissed the complaint for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, finding that merely citing the Fair Housing Act is insufficient where plaintiff fails to allege any discriminatory conduct based on his protected characteristics.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Rivera v. Inc. Vill. of Farmingdale, 784 F. Supp. 2d 133 (E.D.N.Y. 2011)
Gamarra v. Paul, 2024 WL 4515286 (E.D.N.Y. Oct. 17, 2024)
Scoggins v. Turning Point of Cent. Cal., Inc., 2023 WL 2354820 (E.D. Cal. Mar. 3, 2023)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Repair of non-functioning bathroom and kitchen vents and correction of electrical socket issues in plaintiff's apartment unit
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, finding that plaintiff failed to allege facts establishing discrimination based on disability. Plaintiff merely mentioned the FHA by name but did not allege that defendants discriminated against him because of his HIV or asthma, nor did he allege that defendants declined repairs because of his disability status. The complaint concerns housing quality generally, not discrimination, which the FHA does not regulate.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: RICO Act (alleged conspiracy to infest apartment with roaches and extort money); false advertising; bait and switch; state law claims regarding housing conditions, lease violations, and threatened eviction
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction. Plaintiff's bare reference to RICO failed to establish federal question jurisdiction because he did not plead any facts establishing the seven required elements of a civil RICO claim. State law claims and false advertising claims do not invoke federal question jurisdiction. Diversity jurisdiction was not established because all parties listed New York addresses.

source_file: 10734040_2025_Elewood Torres, on behalf of himself and all others similarly situated v. MMS Group LLC. d_b_a MMS Group, New York City Housing Preservation and Development, New York State Division of Housing and Community
case_name: Elewood Torres, on behalf of himself and all others similarly situated v. MMS Group LLC. d/b/a MMS Group, New York City Housing Preservation and Development, New York State Division of Housing and Community Renewal
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs sought accessible building features and accommodations necessary for deaf and hearing-impaired individuals to independently use and access the residential premises, including modifications and design features at two residential buildings that would enable deaf or hard-of-hearing residents and visitors to use the buildings without barriers.
key_holding: The district court adopted the Magistrate Judge's Report and Recommendation in full, granting class certification under Rule 23 for a class of deaf and hearing-impaired residents and visitors as to Counts Three, Four, Five, Six, Seven, Eight, Ten, and Eleven with modifications narrowing the class period to on or after July 19, 2019 (or 2020 for Count Ten), while denying certification as to Counts One and Two.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Elewood Torres filed FHA and state law claims on behalf of himself and similarly situated individuals, alleging that Defendants—including property owners, managers, and related entities—failed to maintain two residential buildings to be independently usable by deaf and hearing-impaired persons and failed to provide access to housing for individuals with disabilities. Magistrate Judge Figueredo issued a Report and Recommendation recommending class certification as to most counts with modifications to the proposed class period and class definition. The district court reviewed Defendants' and Plaintiff's objections, applying de novo review to newly raised arguments and clear error review to rehashed arguments, and adopted the R&R in full, certifying the class with the narrowed time period and also granting Defendants' motion to seal sensitive medical information.
key_cases_cited: City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, Inc., 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Comcast Corp. v. Behrend, 569 U.S. 27 (2013)
Amchem Products, Inc. v. Windsor, 521 U.S. 591 (1997)
Consolidated Rail Corp. v. Town of Hyde Park, 47 F.3d 473 (2d Cir. 1995)
Tyson Foods, Inc. v. Bouaphakeo, 577 U.S. 442 (2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to maintain buildings to be independently usable by deaf or hearing-impaired individuals; failure to provide access to housing for individuals with disabilities
fha_claims.reasoning: The court adopted the magistrate judge's recommendation to certify a class action on Counts Three through Eight, Ten, and Eleven, which allege failures to provide reasonable accommodations and accessible housing for deaf and hearing-impaired residents. The opinion addresses class certification requirements under Rule 23, not the substantive merits of the FHA claims themselves. The claims survive the procedural motion and proceed to discovery and trial.

source_file: 10734407_2025_Farrial Mercer v. Kristopher Brewer, et al._almd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: FHA violations raised by defendant in counterclaim (not specified in plaintiff's complaint)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked subject matter jurisdiction because plaintiff's complaint raised only a state-law eviction claim. Defendants' FHA counterclaim cannot create federal question jurisdiction under the well-pleaded complaint rule. The case was remanded to state court.

source_file: 10734421_2025_Valery Kantsepolsky v. River Shores Association, Inc._flsd
case_name: Valery Kantsepolsky v. River Shores Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a condominium owner with medical conditions limiting her tolerance to demolition-related environmental hazards, requests a 90-day extension of pretrial and trial deadlines in the underlying state court action as a reasonable accommodation for her disability.
key_holding: The Anti-Injunction Act bars the federal court from granting the requested injunction because neither the Fair Housing Act nor the Americans with Disabilities Act expressly authorizes injunctive relief to stay state court proceedings, and the Plaintiff's objection regarding the court's consideration of medical evidence is without merit since the AIA prohibition is a legal threshold issue independent of the quantum of disability evidence.
brief_summary: Valery Kantsepolsky, a condominium owner with health conditions affecting her tolerance to environmental hazards from demolition, sued the River Shores Association, Inc. (her HOA) under the FHA and ADA seeking a preliminary injunction to enjoin the HOA from proceeding with exploratory demolition in her unit and to obtain a 90-day extension of trial deadlines in a related state court action. The federal court denied the TRO because the Anti-Injunction Act prohibits enjoining state court proceedings, and neither the FHA nor ADA expressly authorizes such relief as an exception to the AIA's general prohibition.
key_cases_cited: Mitchum v. Foster, 407 U.S. 225 (1972)
Mercer v. Sechan Realty, Inc., 569 F. App'x 652 (11th Cir. 2014)
Atl. Coast Line R. Co. v. Bhd. of Locomotive Eng'rs, 398 U.S. 281 (1970)
Schiavo ex. rel. Schindler v. Schiavo, 403 F.3d 1223 (11th Cir. 2005)
Burr & Forman v. Blair, 470 F.3d 1019 (11th Cir. 2006)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 90-day extension of pretrial and trial deadlines in pending state court action; accommodation for exploratory demolition and repairs subject to plaintiff's medical conditions; engagement in interactive process regarding accommodation requests
fha_claims.reasoning: The Anti-Injunction Act, 28 U.S.C. § 2283, prohibits federal courts from enjoining state court proceedings unless an exception applies. Neither the FHA nor ADA are expressly authorized exceptions to the AIA. The court did not reach the substantive merits of the reasonable accommodation claim because the jurisdictional bar under the AIA was dispositive.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claim for failure to accommodate disability in residential condominium context
fha_claims.reasoning: The ADA does not apply to residential condominiums, which are not 'places of public accommodation' under Title II. Additionally, the ADA is not an expressly authorized exception to the Anti-Injunction Act, so federal court cannot enjoin the state court proceeding on this basis.

source_file: 10734581_2025_N. Clark LLC, ET AL v. UNITED STATES DEPARTMENT OF HOUSING AND URBAN DEVELOPMENT, ET AL_laed
case_name: N. Clark LLC v. United States Department of Housing and Urban Development
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs (property owners accused of FHA violations) requested that HUD dismiss the discrimination complaint and charge against them and issue a corrective press release vindicating them.
key_holding: The court lacked subject matter jurisdiction because plaintiffs failed to exhaust their FTCA claims (no sum-certain monetary claim presented), their intentional tort claims were barred by the FTCA's intentional tort exception, HUD's decision to close the case without determination was committed to agency discretion, and HUD's press release was not a final agency action subject to APA review.
brief_summary: N. Clark LLC and Kathleen Cresson sued HUD and DOJ under the FTCA and APA seeking to have HUD dismiss a discrimination complaint and charge filed against them by the Louisiana Fair Housing Action Center, and to compel HUD to issue a corrective press release. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, finding plaintiffs failed to exhaust FTCA administrative remedies, their intentional tort claims were barred, and HUD's actions were either committed to agency discretion or did not constitute final agency action subject to judicial review.
key_cases_cited: Hui v. Castaneda, 559 U.S. 799 (2010)
FDIC v. Meyer, 510 U.S. 471 (1994)
Millbrook v. U.S., 569 U.S. 50 (2012)
Bennett v. Spears, 520 U.S. 154 (1997)
Texas v. Cardona, 743 F. Supp. 3d 824 (N.D. Tex. 2024)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA) claims for slander, defamation, and intentional torts arising from HUD's issuance of a press release regarding a charge of discrimination; Administrative Procedure Act (APA) claims for equitable relief (injunction and declaratory relief) challenging HUD's administrative closure of a discrimination investigation and the press release.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked subject matter jurisdiction over FTCA claims because plaintiffs failed to exhaust the administrative presentment requirement (no sum-certain monetary claim presented to HUD/DOJ) and because intentional tort claims are barred by the FTCA's intentional tort exception. The court also lacked jurisdiction over APA equitable relief claims because HUD's administrative closure and press release do not constitute final agency actions subject to judicial review, and HUD's discretionary decisions fall outside the scope of APA review.

source_file: 10734649_2025_Michael Troy Wilkes v. San Mateo County Transit District (SAMTRANS), et al._cand
case_name: Michael Troy Wilkes v. San Mateo County Transit District (SAMTRANS), et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested court facility access accommodations and modifications to security policies to allow use of prosthetic inline skates as a mobility aid rather than wheelchair.
key_holding: The court dismissed the case as frivolous under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2) because plaintiff failed to file an amended complaint curing deficiencies, failed to establish subject matter jurisdiction, violated local rules by filing motions without leave, and repeatedly ignored court orders despite warnings.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Michael Troy Wilkes, who uses prosthetic inline skates as a mobility aid for severe pelvic injuries, sued San Mateo County Transit District and numerous other defendants alleging ADA and Fair Housing Act violations related to access denials. The court dismissed the case with prejudice as frivolous under § 1915(e)(2) screening because plaintiff failed to file an amended complaint establishing jurisdiction, violated local procedural rules, and repeatedly ignored court orders despite warnings.
key_cases_cited: Denton v. Hernandez, 504 U.S. 25 (1992)
Neitzke v. Williams, 490 U.S. 319 (1989)
Lopez v. Smith, 203 F.3d 1122 (9th Cir. 2000)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Franklin v. Murphy, 745 F.2d 1221 (9th Cir. 1984)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Use of prosthetic inline skates as a mobility aid; access to housing and public accommodations without removal or carrying of mobility aid
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the FHA claim as frivolous under § 1915(e)(2) because the complaint failed to establish subject matter jurisdiction, contained scattered allegations that did not provide fair notice to defendants, and plaintiff failed to file an amended complaint after the initial dismissal with leave to amend. The court did not engage substantively with the reasonable accommodation framework.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title I (employment discrimination), ADA Title II (public services discrimination), ADA Title III (public accommodation denial), ADA Title V (retaliation), due process violation
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed all non-FHA claims as frivolous under § 1915(e)(2) for failure to establish subject matter jurisdiction, lack of coherent allegations providing fair notice, and plaintiff's repeated failure to cure deficiencies after being granted leave to amend. The court found the complaint's scattered allegations regarding surveillance, subpoenas, and administrative complaints did not establish a proper federal case or controversy.

source_file: 10735679_2025_Delroy Askins v. Prestige Management Inc.; Lowell Hendricks_nysd
case_name: Delroy Askins v. Prestige Management Inc.; Lowell Hendricks
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges he was assaulted by building superintendent, denied access to community room, and had medical supplies stolen, all because of his disability (paraplegia/wheelchair use); no specific accommodation request was made.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claims because, even assuming he has a disability, he alleged no facts suggesting his disability motivated any adverse actions—the claim that the assault occurred 'because of his disability' was speculative without supporting facts from which a reasonable inference of discriminatory motivation could be drawn.
brief_summary: Delroy Askins, a paraplegic wheelchair user, sued Prestige Management and building superintendent Lowell Hendricks alleging assault, denial of community room access, and theft of medical supplies as discrimination because of his disability. The court dismissed the amended complaint, finding that plaintiff failed to allege facts suggesting his disability motivated any adverse action—his conclusory assertion that the assault occurred 'because of his disability' was speculative and insufficient to state a FHA claim.
key_cases_cited: Palmer v. Fannie Mae, 755 F. App'x 43 (2d Cir. 2018)
Rodriguez v. Vill. Green Realty, Inc., 788 F.3d 31 (2d Cir. 2015)
Gladstone, Realtors v. Vill. of Bellwood, 441 U.S. 91 (1979)
Amato v. McGinty, 2022 WL 226798 (N.D.N.Y. 2022)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged no facts suggesting that his disability was a motivating factor in the alleged assault by the superintendent, the missing medical supplies, or the denial of access to the community room. Plaintiff's assertion that the assault occurred 'because of' his disability was purely speculative without factual support that disability motivated the adverse action.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II, Rehabilitation Act § 504
fha_claims.reasoning: Although the court assumed plaintiff had a disability under the ADA and Rehabilitation Act, plaintiff alleged no facts suggesting that defendants discriminated against him because of his disability. The allegations that bad things happened to a disabled person are insufficient without facts showing the adverse actions occurred because of disability.

source_file: 10736151_2025_Jana Smith v. Mark Downey; Charles Olsen; Ariell Hartwell; Mark Simon; and Sherman Smith_ord
case_name: Jana Smith v. Mark Downey; Charles Olsen; Ariell Hartwell; Mark Simon; and Sherman Smith
accommodation_description: Not described in this order; the specific nature of the housing discrimination or accommodation at issue is not detailed in this procedural ruling, which addresses only the summary judgment motion and scheduling.
key_holding: The court denied Defendant Downey's motion for summary judgment because genuine disputes of material fact exist regarding plaintiff's housing rights claims, and denied the parties' joint motion for a trial extension, maintaining the December 15, 2025 trial date limited to plaintiff's two federal claims under the Fair Housing Act and § 1985.
brief_summary: Jana Smith brought suit against Mark Downey and others alleging violation of the Fair Housing Act under 42 U.S.C. § 3604 and conspiracy to interfere with civil rights under 42 U.S.C. § 1985, among twelve total claims. Defendant Downey moved for summary judgment, arguing that Smith followed a pattern of destroying residences and then claiming housing rights violations, supporting his motion with declarations from a plumber, handyman, neighbor, and real estate agent. The court denied summary judgment because Smith's competing declaration created genuine disputes of material fact, denied the joint motion for a trial extension due to the age of the case, and ordered trial to proceed on December 15, 2025 limited to the two federal law claims.
key_cases_cited: Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986)
Clicks Billiards, Inc. v. Sixshooters, Inc., 251 F.3d 1252 (9th Cir. 2001)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not specified in opinion
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied defendant's motion for summary judgment because genuine disputes of material fact exist regarding plaintiff's allegations. Court found factual disputes inappropriate for resolution at summary judgment stage and required case to proceed to trial on FHA claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3604.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Conspiracy to interfere with civil rights under 42 U.S.C. § 1985
