fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied defendant's motion for summary judgment on the § 1985 conspiracy claim, allowing it to proceed to trial along with the FHA claim. Factual disputes precluded summary judgment.

source_file: 10737079_2025_Lawrence Bryant v. Jonathan Lagos, Et al._flsd
case_name: Lawrence Bryant v. Jonathan Lagos, Et al.
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: The complaint was dismissed as a shotgun pleading because the counts generally alleged all defendants were liable for the same acts and multiple causes of action were improperly combined within single counts, without prejudice to filing an amended complaint.
brief_summary: Lawrence Bryant filed suit in Florida state court against Jonathan Lagos and unnamed defendants alleging Fair Housing Act violations and related state law claims, including a claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3604 for discriminatory housing practices. The federal court denied the plaintiff's motions to remand and granted the defendants' motions to dismiss, finding the complaint constituted an improper shotgun pleading that failed to separate causes of action and specify which defendants were responsible for which allegedly discriminatory acts.
key_cases_cited: Caterpillar, Inc. v. Williams, 482 U.S. 386 (1987)
Parker v. Scrap Metal Processors, Inc., 468 F.3d 733 (11th Cir. 2006)
Weiland v. Palm Beach Cnty. Sheriff's Office, 792 F.3d 1313 (11th Cir. 2015)
Grupo Dataflux v. Atlas Global Grp., L.P., 541 U.S. 567 (2004)
Stone v. Bank of N.Y. Mellon, N.A., 609 Fed. App'x 979 (11th Cir. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Count IV alleges violations of section 760, Florida Statutes, and 42 U.S.C. § 3604 (Fair Housing Act), but the complaint does not specify the nature of the alleged housing discrimination or any requested accommodation.
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint was dismissed as a shotgun pleading for failing to separate causes of action into different counts and for asserting multiple claims against multiple defendants without specifying which defendants are responsible for which acts. The court did not reach the substantive merits of the FHA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act, IRS Code § 6103, section 213.053 Florida Statutes (Count I); 26 U.S.C. § 42, 26 C.F.R. § 1.42, 24 C.F.R. § 882.511, IRS Revenue Ruling 2004-82 (Count II); breach of implied warranty of habitability under Florida law (Count III); retaliation under Florida law (Count V); waiver of right to terminate lease by acceptance of rent under Florida law (Count VI); 42 U.S.C. § 1983 civil rights violation (Count VII).
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA claims were dismissed as part of the shotgun pleading defect. The court did not reach the substantive merits of any non-FHA claim, dismissing on pleading grounds for failure to separate causes of action and specify which defendants are responsible for which acts.

source_file: 10737104_2025_Dyshawn Underwood, individually, and as guardian of minor child K.U. v. Blue Leaf Residential Management, LLC, et al._ohsd
case_name: Dyshawn Underwood, individually, and as guardian of minor child K.U. v. Blue Leaf Residential Management, LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: The complaint alleges refusal to accommodate K.U.'s disabilities but the specific accommodation request is not described in this procedural ruling.
key_holding: The court granted Cyclone's motion for leave to file a counterclaim because futility determinations are better made through a motion to dismiss than at the pleading stage.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Dyshawn Underwood, on behalf of herself and minor child K.U., sued defendants Blue Leaf Residential Management and Cyclone Columbus Park for refusing to accommodate K.U.'s disabilities and for retaliation under the Fair Housing Act. This opinion only addresses Cyclone's motion for leave to file a counterclaim for breach of contract and declaratory judgment, which the court granted without reaching the merits of the FHA claims.
key_cases_cited: Leary v. Daeschner, 349 F.3d 888 (6th Cir. 2003)
Inge v. Rock Fin. Corp., 281 F.3d 613 (6th Cir. 2002)
Carson v. U.S. Off. of Special Counsel, 633 F.3d 487 (6th Cir. 2011)
Durthaler v. Accounts Receivable Mgmt., Inc., 2011 WL 5008552 (S.D. Ohio Oct. 20, 2011)
Andretti v. Borla Performance Indus., Inc., 426 F.3d 824 (6th Cir. 2005)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accommodation for K.U.'s disabilities (specific nature not detailed in opinion)
fha_claims.disposition: Motion for Leave to File Counterclaim Granted
fha_claims.reasoning: The opinion addresses only a procedural motion for leave to file a counterclaim and does not reach the merits of the plaintiff's FHA claims. The complaint alleges refusal to accommodate K.U.'s disabilities, but the court's ruling concerns only whether the defendant may file a counterclaim for breach of contract and declaratory judgment regarding jury trial waiver.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation for exercising son's rights under the Fair Housing Act
fha_claims.disposition: Motion for Leave to File Counterclaim Granted
fha_claims.reasoning: The opinion addresses only a procedural motion for leave to file a counterclaim and does not reach the merits of the plaintiff's FHA retaliation claim. The complaint alleges retaliation for exercising the son's FHA rights, but the court's ruling concerns only the defendant's procedural request to file a counterclaim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of contract for refusing to make essential repairs; state law property maintenance claims
fha_claims.disposition: Motion for Leave to File Counterclaim Granted
fha_claims.reasoning: The opinion addresses only a procedural motion for leave to file a counterclaim and does not reach the merits of the plaintiff's non-FHA claims for refusing to make essential repairs. The court's ruling concerns only the defendant's procedural request to file a counterclaim.

source_file: 10737236_2025_Alicia Paschall v. Amber Andrade and Julie Hardison_waed
case_name: Alicia Paschall v. Amber Andrade and Julie Hardison
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation request was made; the case involves a child custody dispute and constitutional claims against CPS and probation officials, with a brief FHA retaliation claim dismissed for failure to plead protected activity.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA retaliation claim because she failed to adequately plead she engaged in protected FHA activity or that defendants caused an adverse housing consequence causally linked to such activity, and failed to plausibly allege retaliatory motive.
brief_summary: Alicia Paschall, proceeding pro se, sued Federal Probation Officer Amber Andrade and CPS Supervisor Julie Hardison alleging constitutional violations, civil rights claims, and federal statutory claims stemming from the removal of her child in a Washington dependency proceeding. The district court dismissed her Third Amended Complaint for failure to state a claim, finding defendants immune from suit, plaintiff's claims barred by Rooker-Feldman doctrine and lack of standing, and her FHA retaliation claim deficient for failure to plead protected activity.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Food & Drug Admin. v. All. for Hippocratic Med.
San Pedro Hotel Co. v. City of Los Angeles

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged retaliation for reporting child abuse, including loss of Section 8 housing voucher and business interference
fha_claims.reasoning: Under § 1915(e)(2) screening, plaintiff failed to allege facts plausibly showing retaliation under FHA § 3617. She did not allege she was retaliated against for engaging in activity protected by the FHA, failed to specifically allege how defendants interfered with her housing, and failed to plausibly allege a retaliatory motive. The court found the allegations too vague and lacking the required nexus between protected activity and adverse housing consequence.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II retaliation (42 U.S.C. § 12203, § 12132), CAPTA, 18 U.S.C. § 1512(b), Medicaid Act (42 U.S.C. § 1396a), FFPSA, § 1983 First Amendment retaliation, § 1983 Fifth Amendment takings, § 1983 Fourteenth Amendment due process/equal protection, § 1985(3) conspiracy
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to state cognizable claims under multiple non-FHA statutes. ADA § 12203 does not apply (no employment relationship); § 12132 claim failed because plaintiff did not allege denial of benefits based on disability. CAPTA creates no private right of action for retaliation. § 1512(b) is criminal and creates no private civil cause of action. Medicaid Act § 1396a creates no private cause of action. FFPSA creates no identifiable private cause of action. § 1983 claims for First Amendment retaliation, Fifth Amendment takings, and Fourteenth Amendment due process all failed for vagueness and lack of nexus. § 1985(3) conspiracy claims failed because plaintiff did not allege deprivation motivated by racial animus.

source_file: 10739169_2025_Asia Martin, et al. v. Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp. and Ansonia Property Management, LLC_ilnd
case_name: Asia Martin, et al. v. Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp. and Ansonia Property Management, LLC
accommodation_description: No specific reasonable accommodation request is identified in the opinion. The FHA and Rehabilitation Act claims are framed as disability discrimination arising from the allegedly uninhabitable and poorly maintained conditions of the apartment complex, with plaintiffs seeking injunctive relief to ensure they are not discriminated against due to their disabilities or left 'unable to sufficiently utilize the Property.'
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion to stay proceedings, finding that neither Burford nor Colorado River abstention applied because the parallel state court building code enforcement action could not provide plaintiffs with monetary relief, eviction protection, or redress for disability discrimination and retaliation claims, and because defendants had themselves chosen the federal forum by removing several plaintiffs' cases.
brief_summary: Over twenty tenants of Ellis Lakeview Apartments in Chicago's Kenwood neighborhood sued Freddie Mac (the owner) and Ansonia Property Management for allegedly failing to maintain the complex in habitable condition, asserting claims under the Fair Housing Act (disability discrimination), the Rehabilitation Act, the Illinois Human Rights Act, the Chicago RLTO (including retaliation and security deposit violations), the Illinois Landlord Retaliation Act, the Illinois Consumer Fraud Act, breach of implied warranty of habitability, and breach of lease. Defendants moved to stay the federal action pending a longstanding City of Chicago building code enforcement lawsuit in state court, invoking Burford and Colorado River abstention doctrines. The court denied the stay, finding no real risk of disrupting the state proceeding, no adequacy of state-court relief for plaintiffs' monetary and disability-related claims, and noting that defendants had affirmatively chosen the federal forum by removing several plaintiffs' cases.
key_cases_cited: Burford v. Sun Oil Co., 319 U.S. 215 (1943)
Colorado River Water Conservation District v. United States, 424 U.S. 800 (1976)
Tyrer v. City of S. Beloit, 456 F.3d 744 (7th Cir. 2006)
Hartford Cas. Ins. Co. v. Borg-Warner Corp., 913 F.2d 419 (7th Cir. 1990)
Int'l Coll. of Surgeons v. City of Chicago, 153 F.3d 356 (7th Cir. 1996)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Injunctive relief to ensure plaintiffs are not discriminated against due to their disabilities and are able to sufficiently utilize the property; specific accommodations not detailed in the opinion
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the defendants' motion to stay the case and did not reach the merits of the Fair Housing Act disability discrimination claim. The claim survives the procedural challenge and remains pending for substantive adjudication.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to maintain premises in violation of Chicago RLTO; breach of implied warranty of habitability; breach of lease terms; retaliation under RLTO and Illinois Landlord Retaliation Act; violation of Illinois Consumer Fraud and Deceptive Business Practices Act; violation of security deposit requirements; violation of Rehabilitation Act; violation of Illinois Civil Rights Remedies Restoration Act; violation of Illinois Human Rights Act
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the defendants' motion to stay the case on Burford and Colorado River abstention grounds. All non-FHA claims survive the procedural challenge and remain pending for substantive adjudication.

source_file: 10739282_2025_Trestle Creek Association v. Stephen R. Schooley, Jody F. Schooley_mtd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Defendants asserted in their notice of removal that plaintiff's easement enforcement actions violate § 3604(f) of the Fair Housing Act, but no specific accommodation was requested or analyzed.
fha_claims.disposition: 28 U.S.C. § 1447(c) — Remand for lack of subject matter jurisdiction
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that federal question jurisdiction does not exist because the FHA claim was raised only as a defense/counterclaim by defendants, not on the face of plaintiff's well-pleaded complaint. Federal defenses and counterclaims cannot support removal jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1331. The case was remanded to state court without addressing the merits of any FHA claim.

source_file: 10740192_2025_Connie D. Parker v. PulteGroup, Inc., et al._mdd
case_name: Connie D. Parker v. PulteGroup, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation request; case involves allegations of racial discrimination in home pricing and terms, with plaintiff claiming she was charged more than white neighbors for comparable homes.
key_holding: The court granted defendants' motions to compel arbitration, finding the Home Purchase Agreement's broad arbitration clause enforceable and applicable to all of Parker's claims, including her Fair Housing Act and Civil Rights Act discrimination claims, despite Parker's arguments that she did not intend to arbitrate statutory discrimination claims.
brief_summary: Connie D. Parker, a 74-year-old Black U.S. Army veteran, sued PulteGroup, Inc. and related defendants alleging racial and age-based discrimination in the sale of a townhome in the Watershed community, claiming she was charged higher prices and down payments than white neighbors for comparable homes. The court granted defendants' motions to compel arbitration, finding the Home Purchase Agreement's broad arbitration clause was enforceable and covered all of Parker's claims including her Fair Housing Act and Civil Rights Act discrimination claims.
key_cases_cited: Adkins v. Lab. Ready, Inc., 303 F.3d 496 (4th Cir. 2002)
Green Tree Fin. Corp.-Ala. v. Randolph, 531 U.S. 79 (2000)
Hill v. Peoplesoft USA, Inc., 412 F.3d 540 (4th Cir. 2005)
Cheek v. United Healthcare of the Mid-Atlantic, Inc., 835 A.2d 656 (Md. 2003)
Stone v. Wells Fargo Bank, N.A., 361 F.3d 539 (D.Md. 2019)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's FHA disparate treatment claim based on alleged race and age discrimination in pricing and down payment terms falls within the broad scope of the arbitration clause in the Home Purchase Agreement, which covers 'any controversy, claim or dispute that arises out of or is related to' the agreement or property. The claim was not dismissed on the merits but rather stayed pending arbitration.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Maryland Consumer Protection Act (Md. Code Ann., Com. § 13-301); Civil Rights Act (42 U.S.C. § 1981 et seq.); intentional misrepresentation; constructive fraud; intentional infliction of emotional distress
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA claims, including state consumer protection claims, fraud claims, and CRA § 1981 claims, fall within the scope of the broad arbitration clause and are subject to mandatory arbitration. The court did not reach the merits of any non-FHA claim but rather compelled arbitration of all claims.

source_file: 10740678_2025_John R. Fouts v. United States of America et al._kywd
case_name: John R. Fouts v. United States of America et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought ADA housing accommodations including prevention of eviction while holding a valid mainstream housing voucher, remediation of toxic mold and water leakage in his unit, safe housing with storage of medications and oxygen equipment outside a homeless shelter, housing for two certified registered emotional support animals, and access to medically necessary treatment and diet.
key_holding: The court dismissed the entire pro se action under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e) for failure to state a claim, finding FHA and ADA allegations conclusory and lacking specific factual support, constitutional claims barred by sovereign and judicial immunity, and § 1983 claims against private defendants unsupported by state-actor allegations.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff John R. Fouts filed suit against a sprawling list of defendants—including the United States, Commonwealth of Kentucky, Louisville Metro Housing Authority, a private apartment complex (Station J-Town/New Chestnut Ridge Apts LLC), multiple technology companies, and three federal judges—alleging violations of the FHA, ADA, § 1983, Bivens, RICO, the False Claims Act, and state law, arising from his alleged eviction while holding a valid mainstream housing voucher, denial of ADA housing accommodations, and a wide range of other grievances including medical denial and digital surveillance. The court dismissed all federal claims on initial review under § 1915(e): claims against the United States and Commonwealth of Kentucky were barred by sovereign immunity; Bivens claims against the three federal judges were barred by judicial immunity; § 1983 claims against private defendants failed for lack of state-actor allegations; the Louisville Metro Housing Authority was not a suable 'person' under § 1983; and FHA/ADA claims against the housing authority and apartment complex were dismissed for being purely conclusory without supporting factual allegations. State-law claims were dismissed without prejudice for lack of supplemental jurisdiction.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Haines v. Kerner
Monell v. New York City Department of Social Services
McGore v. Wrigglesworth

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Safe housing with remediation of toxic mold and water leakage; ADA housing accommodations; housing with relocation costs; safe storage of medications and oxygen equipment; housing suitable for certified emotional support animals
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff made only conclusory allegations of FHA violation without specific factual allegations to support a reasonable accommodation claim. The complaint failed to plead factual content with facial plausibility under Iqbal/Twombly, offering only labels and conclusions devoid of factual enhancement.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 claims against state and local defendants; Bivens claims against federal defendants; ADA Title II claims; state law medical negligence, malpractice, and intentional/negligent infliction of emotional distress
fha_claims.reasoning: § 1983 claims against Commonwealth of Kentucky dismissed for sovereign immunity; claims against Louisville Metro Housing Authority dismissed for failure to allege municipal policy or custom; claims against private defendants dismissed for failure to allege state action; Bivens claims against United States dismissed for sovereign immunity; judicial immunity barred claims against judges; ADA claims dismissed for conclusory allegations without factual support; state-law claims dismissed without prejudice due to lack of supplemental jurisdiction.

source_file: 10740712_2025_United States of America ex rel. Eric J. Russell v. The City of Columbus_ohsd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: False Claims Act qui tam claims (Counts I-IV): presenting false claims for payment, use of false statements and false certifications, failure to return misused CDBG funds, and whistleblower retaliation under 31 U.S.C. § 3729 et seq.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead with particularity that the City submitted false certifications (express or implied) that were material to HUD's decision to award CDBG funds. The complaint lacked specific allegations regarding when certifications were submitted, their content, and which regulatory provisions were violated. Materiality was not adequately pleaded under the demanding standard requiring consideration of express conditions of payment, government's past response, and whether noncompliance goes to the essence of the bargain.

source_file: 10740783_2025_Hlevictor A. Hoskins, Jr. and Tracey R. Young v. Plaza Place Owners Association, Inc. and Associa Principal Management Group of Houston_txsd
case_name: Hlevictor A. Hoskins, Jr. and Tracey R. Young v. Plaza Place Owners Association, Inc. and Associa Principal Management Group of Houston
accommodation_description: The order does not detail the specific accommodation request; the complaint alleges FHA and ADA violations but the ruling only addresses procedural requirements for TRO.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiffs' emergency motion for temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction because plaintiffs failed to demonstrate substantial likelihood of success on the merits through unsubstantiated allegations and failed to show irreparable harm beyond speculative consequences from non-payment of disputed charges.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Hlevictor Hoskins and Tracey Young sued their homeowners association and property management company for ADA and FHA violations, also bringing state law claims for breach of fiduciary duty and negligence. The court denied their emergency motion for temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction, finding they failed to meet the requirements for extraordinary relief.
key_cases_cited: Guillory v. PPG Industries Inc, 434 F.3d 303 (5th Cir. 2005)
United States v. Wilson, 864 F.2d 1219 (5th Cir. 1989)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unspecified reasonable accommodation related to disability; complaint alleges FHA violation but specific accommodation not detailed in opinion
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied TRO/preliminary injunction motion because plaintiffs failed to demonstrate substantial likelihood of success on the merits and irreparable harm; unsubstantiated allegations in the motion failed to meet the standard. The underlying FHA claims survive but have not been substantively adjudicated.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act claim; breach of fiduciary duty; negligence
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied TRO/preliminary injunction motion on all claims (ADA, breach of fiduciary duty, negligence) because plaintiffs failed to demonstrate substantial likelihood of success on the merits and irreparable harm; claims survive but have not been substantively adjudicated.

source_file: 10741156_2025_Jessica Berk v. Ritz Condominium Association, et al._njd
case_name: Jessica Berk v. Ritz Condominium Association, et al.
accommodation_description: The specific accommodation or modification requested by plaintiff is not described in this opinion; the court dismissed the matter on procedural grounds and noted that a fuller recounting of plaintiff's allegations appears at ECF No. 40.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA and 42 U.S.C. § 3617 claims with prejudice for lack of prosecution under Rule 41(b) because plaintiff willfully abandoned her case by repeatedly failing to appear for court conferences and comply with court orders, rendering Poulis balancing unnecessary.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Jessica Berk filed suit against Ritz Condominium Association and Stanley Maragoudakis asserting claims under 42 U.S.C. § 3617, fraud, Fair Housing Act violations, and civil rights violations. Over a six-month period, plaintiff failed to attend multiple court-ordered conferences, failed to respond to an order to show cause, and failed to move to reinstate the case within the court's 90-day deadline. The court dismissed the case with prejudice for lack of prosecution under Rule 41(b), finding that plaintiff's willful abandonment rendered the Poulis balancing analysis unnecessary.
key_cases_cited: Poulis v. State Farm Fire & Cas. Co., 747 F.2d 863 (3d Cir. 1984)
Spain v. Gallegos, 25 F.3d 439 (3d Cir. 1994)
Ricks v. Udijohn, No. 14-04079, 2017 WL 53706 (D.N.J. Jan. 4, 2017)
Mindek v. Rigatti, 964 F.2d 1369 (3d Cir. 1992)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not specified; complaint alleges violations of the Fair Housing Act and § 3617 retaliation claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Case dismissed for lack of prosecution due to plaintiff's willful abandonment and repeated failure to appear for court-ordered conferences and comply with court orders, rendering adjudication impossible. The court did not reach the merits of any FHA claim.

source_file: 10741255_2025_Jimmy Keels Williamson v. Christian Recovery Centers, Inc._nced
case_name: Jimmy Keels Williamson v. Christian Recovery Centers, Inc.
accommodation_description: Pro se plaintiff's complaint, which was screened for failure to state a claim, referenced disability accommodation in housing context at a recovery center.
key_holding: Upon reviewing the magistrate judge's recommendation with no objections filed, the district court dismissed plaintiff's FHA disability discrimination claim without prejudice for failure to state a claim, while allowing plaintiff's FHA racial discrimination claim to proceed.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Jimmy Keels Williamson sued Christian Recovery Centers, Inc., a recovery center operator, alleging race discrimination and disability discrimination under the Fair Housing Act, Title VII, and ADA. Upon screening under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e), the court dismissed plaintiff's disability discrimination claims (including FHA reasonable accommodation claim) without prejudice for failure to state a claim, but allowed the FHA racial discrimination claim to proceed.
key_cases_cited: Diamond v. Colonial Life & Acc. Ins. Co., 416 F.3d 310 (4th Cir. 2005)
Camby v. Davis, 718 F.2d 198 (4th Cir. 1983)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Disability-based housing accommodation (specific accommodation not detailed in opinion)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court adopted magistrate judge's recommendation to dismiss plaintiff's FHA disability discrimination claim as frivolous under § 1915(e)(2)(B) screening without substantive analysis of the reasonable accommodation elements.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Housing discrimination on the basis of race
fha_claims.reasoning: Magistrate judge recommended and court adopted dismissal of Title VII and ADA claims, but allowed plaintiff's FHA racial discrimination claim to proceed past § 1915(e) screening.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VII race discrimination and hostile work environment claim; ADA disability discrimination claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Court adopted magistrate judge's recommendation to dismiss Title VII hostile work environment claim and ADA disability discrimination claim as frivolous under § 1915(e)(2)(B) screening.

source_file: 10741283_2025_Concern for Independent Living, Inc. v. Town of Southampton, New York, and Town Board of the Town of Southampton_nyed
case_name: Concern for Independent Living, Inc. v. Town of Southampton, New York, and Town Board of the Town of Southampton
accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought permission and the opportunity to construct Liberty Gardens, an affordable housing development intended for persons with disabilities, in the unincorporated community of Tuckahoe within the Town of Southampton—construction that Defendants allegedly blocked through unlawful and discriminatory conduct.
key_holding: The magistrate judge denied plaintiff's motion to lift the stay of discovery, finding no change in circumstances justified vacating the stay while the motion to dismiss remained pending with oral argument already scheduled.
brief_summary: Concern for Independent Living, Inc., a non-profit organization, sued the Town of Southampton and its Town Board for allegedly using unlawful and discriminatory conduct to prevent the construction of Liberty Gardens, an affordable housing development in the unincorporated community of Tuckahoe, in violation of the FHA, ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and New York Human Rights Law. Discovery had been stayed pending resolution of a motion to dismiss. The magistrate judge denied plaintiff's motion to lift the stay, concluding that no changed circumstances existed to warrant vacating it, particularly given that oral argument on the motion to dismiss was already scheduled before the district judge for January 9, 2026.
key_cases_cited: New York by James v. Puff Bar, No. 25-CV-01445 (MMG), 2025 WL 2607635 (S.D.N.Y. Aug. 29, 2025)
In re Kind LLC “Healthy & All Natural” Litig., No. 15-MC-02645 (WHP), 2019 WL 542834 (S.D.N.Y. Feb. 11, 2019)
Brinkmann v. Town of Southold, New York, No. 21-CV-02468 (LDH)(JMW), 2022 WL 3912974 (E.D.N.Y. Aug. 31, 2022)
Chesney v. Valley Stream Union Free Sch. Dist. No. 24, 236 F.R.D. 113 (E.D.N.Y. 2006)
Chechele v. Standard Gen. Master Fund L.P., No. 20-CV-03177 (JLR), 2023 WL 1796371 (S.D.N.Y. Feb. 7, 2023)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Approval or accommodation for construction of Liberty Gardens, an affordable housing development in the unincorporated community of Tuckahoe in the Town of Southampton, allegedly prevented by unlawful and discriminatory conduct
fha_claims.reasoning: The motion to dismiss is fully briefed and pending before the District Judge with oral argument scheduled for January 9, 2026. The court has not yet ruled on the merits of the FHA claims, and discovery remains stayed pending resolution of the dispositive motion.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (42 U.S.C. § 12131 et seq.), Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act (29 U.S.C. § 794 et seq.), and New York Human Rights Law (N.Y. Exec. Law § 296)
fha_claims.reasoning: Non-FHA claims under ADA, Section 504, and state law are pending resolution of the motion to dismiss, with no substantive merits analysis conducted to date.

source_file: 10742406_2025_David D. Crossett v. Douglas Shumway, and Carriage Crossing Homeowners Association, Inc._utd
case_name: David D. Crossett v. Douglas Shumway and Carriage Crossing Homeowners Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: Request for two additional live-in aides beyond the one already approved by the HOA, to assist with daily movement, glucose monitoring, insulin preparation, and safety needs due to legal blindness, diabetes, and bipolar disorder.
key_holding: The court denied Crossett's emergency motions for injunctive relief because he failed to show the requested accommodation of two additional live-in aides is reasonable, a required element of an FHA reasonable accommodation claim under § 3604(f)(3)(B).
brief_summary: Plaintiff David Crossett, a condominium owner with legal blindness, diabetes, and bipolar disorder, sued his homeowners association seeking to compel approval of two additional live-in aides beyond the one already permitted. The court denied Crossett's emergency motions for temporary injunctive relief, finding he failed to establish a likelihood of success on the merits because he did not demonstrate the requested accommodation of two additional live-in aides is reasonable under the Fair Housing Act.
key_cases_cited: Carlson v. Carrington Square LLC, 2025 WL 1017536 (D. Utah Apr. 4, 2025)
Courage to Change Ranches Holding Co. v. El Paso Cnty., 73 F.4th 1175 (10th Cir. 2023)
Arnal v. Aspen View Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 226 F. Supp. 3d 1177 (D. Colo. 2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Approval of two additional live-in aides (for a total of three) to assist with daily movement, glucose monitoring, insulin preparation, and safety needs related to legal blindness, diabetes, and bipolar disorder. Plaintiff's physician stated three live-in aides were medically necessary.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the five-element FHA reasonable accommodation test but found plaintiff failed to establish the fourth element—that the accommodation is reasonable—because he provided no authority showing that approval of one aide establishes the reasonability of three aides. The court declined to address the other Rule 65 factors or remaining FHA elements because plaintiff failed to show likelihood of success on the merits. The underlying claim survives but the TRO motion was denied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) claim for failure to provide reasonable accommodations (live-in aides). The court noted the legal framework for reasonable accommodation under the ADA and FHA is identical and that the ADA claim rises and falls with the FHA claim.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court treated the ADA claim as coterminous with the FHA claim, applying identical legal standards. Because the FHA claim failed on the reasonability element, the ADA claim also fails. The underlying claim survives but the TRO motion was denied.

source_file: 10743592_2025_JAMES B. HERRERA v. MADDOX MANAGEMENT, LLC_nmd
case_name: James B. Herrera v. Maddox Management, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges Defendant submitted false rental verifications to prospective landlords, interfering with his Section 8 voucher use, and ignored his requests for reasonable accommodations for his disabilities.
key_holding: Plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claims fail because he failed to plausibly allege a connection between his disability or protected activity and the alleged adverse action, and he did not adequately plead disability status, causation, or discriminatory intent.
brief_summary: James Herrera sued Maddox Management, LLC alleging Fair Housing Act violations, procedural due process claims, and Rehabilitation Act claims stemming from the landlord's alleged submission of false rental verifications and failure to accommodate his disabilities. The court denied Defendant's motion to dismiss but ordered Plaintiff to show cause why his case should not be dismissed for failure to state plausible claims, finding the complaint failed to adequately plead disability, causation, or discriminatory intent.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Morgan v. Carrington Mortg. Servs., 719 F. App'x 735 (10th Cir. 2017)
Cinnamon Hills Youth Crisis Ctr., Inc. v. St. George City, 685 F.3d 917 (10th Cir. 2012)
Hatfield v. Cottages on 78th Cmty. Ass'n, No. 21-4035 (10th Cir. 2022)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges Defendant submitted false or misleading rental verification information to prospective landlords, interfering with his ability to relocate using his Section 8 voucher.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege discrimination under § 3604(f)(1) because he did not allege that Defendant denied him a dwelling because of his disability, did not specify what false or misleading statements were made, and failed to allege a causal connection between his disability and the alleged adverse action. The court found the allegations conclusory and vague.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges Defendant retaliated against him for asserting housing rights by pursuing inflated damages claims, refusing to apply rent credits, and contributing to an unlawful eviction.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege a § 3617 retaliation claim because he did not identify protected activity under the FHA, did not allege Defendant was motivated by intent to discriminate, failed to allege causation, and did not establish that Defendant's pursuit of damages in the eviction proceeding was because of protected activity rather than unpaid rent and property damage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Procedural Due Process claim under the Fourteenth Amendment (Count II) and Rehabilitation Act Section 504 claim (Count III).
fha_claims.reasoning: The Rooker-Feldman doctrine bars the federal court from reviewing the state court's judgment in the eviction proceeding. Alternatively, Plaintiff failed to allege Defendant was a state actor acting under color of law, and failed to allege any facts showing how Defendant violated his due process rights. As to the Rehabilitation Act claim, Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege he was disabled (no factual allegations regarding the nature or extent of his impairment), failed to allege Defendant was a recipient of federal financial assistance, and failed to allege he was otherwise qualified for the Section 8 program.

source_file: 10743632_2025_Raphael Jackson, et al. v. Mills Properties, Inc., et al._moed
case_name: Raphael Jackson, et al. v. Mills Properties, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs' email to landlord requesting accommodation for high-risk pregnancy and suicidal ideation, characterizing it as a request for reasonable accommodation to avoid eviction.
key_holding: The Court dismissed the federal action without prejudice under Rooker-Feldman doctrine and other abstention doctrines because parallel state-court proceedings involving the same eviction and FHA claims were already pending, depriving the federal court of subject-matter jurisdiction.
brief_summary: Individual tenants Raphael Jackson and Chaley Grant sued Mills Properties, Inc. and related entities alleging Fair Housing Act violations arising from eviction proceedings they claim were discriminatory retaliation for requesting accommodations related to high-risk pregnancy and suicidal ideation. The Court dismissed the federal action without prejudice under Rooker-Feldman, Younger, and Colorado River abstention doctrines because parallel state-court proceedings involving identical eviction and FHA claims were already pending, depriving the federal court of jurisdiction.
key_cases_cited: Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Saudi Basic Indus. Corp., 544 U.S. 280 (2005)
Hageman v. Barton, 817 F.3d 611 (8th Cir. 2016)
Jacobs v. Gear Prop., 2 F. App'x 617 (8th Cir. 2001)
Newell v. Rolling Hills Apartments, 134 F. Supp. 2d 1026 (N.D. Iowa 2001)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accommodation for pregnancy-related disability and suicidal ideation; plaintiff characterized email requesting accommodation as protected activity under FHA
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction under Rooker-Feldman doctrine because plaintiffs sought to collaterally attack an unfavorable state-court eviction judgment and raised identical FHA claims in parallel state litigation. The court did not reach the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction under Rooker-Feldman, Colorado River, and Younger abstention doctrines. Plaintiffs alleged retaliation for requesting accommodations via email, but the court abstained without reaching the merits due to parallel state-court proceedings.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction. Plaintiffs alleged discrimination based on familial status, race (African American), and disability, but the court abstained without reaching the merits due to Rooker-Feldman and other abstention doctrines triggered by parallel state litigation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Missouri Human Rights Act, Missouri common law claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed all claims, including state-law claims under the Missouri Human Rights Act and common law, for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction under Rooker-Feldman and abstention doctrines due to parallel state-court proceedings.

case_name: Desiree Knight v. Macon Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Request for minimum rent hardship adjustment as a reasonable accommodation for anxiety and ADHD
key_holding: Knight's FHA failure-to-accommodate claim was dismissed because she failed to plausibly allege how her requested accommodations (special inspection, rent hardship adjustment) were necessary to alleviate the effects of her anxiety and ADHD, as she did not explain how these impairments limit her major life activities.
brief_summary: Desiree Knight, a Section 8 voucher holder with anxiety and ADHD, sued Macon Housing Authority alleging failures to accommodate, FHA retaliation, Section 504 discrimination, and due process violations. The court dismissed her FHA failure-to-accommodate and retaliation claims without prejudice, finding she failed to plead sufficient facts showing how her requested special inspection, rent hardship adjustment, and VAWA transfer were necessary accommodations for her disabilities.
key_cases_cited: Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condo. Ass'n, 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Philippeaux v. Apartment Inv. & Mgmt. Co., 598 F. App'x 640 (11th Cir. 2015)
Wright v. City of Roanoke Redevelopment & Housing Auth., 479 U.S. 418 (1987)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Special Inspection Request for unit defects (inadequate air circulation, cracks around doors, hazardous trees) and minimum rent hardship adjustment
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) / 12(b)(6)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege how her ADHD and anxiety were affected by the requested accommodations or how the accommodations were necessary to alleviate the effects of her disabilities. The nexus between disability and accommodation was not plausibly alleged.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) / 12(b)(6)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege an adverse action sufficient to deter a reasonable person from engaging in protected activity. Mere delay in responding to requests and a biased hearing do not constitute coercion, intimidation, threat, or interference under § 3617.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 504 Rehabilitation Act disability discrimination claim; Due Process Clause violation under 42 U.S.C. § 1437d(k) and 24 C.F.R. § 966.56(a) regarding impartial hearing officer requirement
fha_claims.disposition: Section 504 claim dismissed under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) / 12(b)(6); Due Process claim survives
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 504 claim dismissed because plaintiff failed to identify any major life activity substantially limited by ADHD and anxiety, and failed to allege MHA was aware of or motivated by her disabilities. Due Process claim survives because plaintiff plausibly alleged that a hearing was presided over by an MHA employee rather than an impartial hearing officer, violating the statutory requirement.

source_file: 10744240_2025_Irvin G. Murray v. U.S. Treasury, et al._paed
case_name: Irvin G. Murray v. U.S. Treasury, et al.
accommodation_description: No specific reasonable accommodation was requested. Murray sought restoration of his housing voucher and housing rights at 5138 Reno Street in Philadelphia, claiming he had been denied housing and evicted in retaliation for attempting to reclaim a purported $43 million inherited FHA judgment, not based on any disability or other protected characteristic.
key_holding: The court dismissed Murray's complaint in its entirety as factually frivolous and for failure to state a claim, including his FHA retaliation claim, because Murray failed to allege that he was discriminated against or retaliated against on account of membership in a protected class rather than for attempting to reclaim a purported $43 million inheritance.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Irvin Murray sued numerous federal, state, and local government entities and private individuals alleging a broad conspiracy to steal his claimed $43 million inheritance and to retaliate against him—including by denying him housing—for attempting to recover it. The court screened the complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915 and dismissed all claims as factually frivolous, finding the allegations wholly incredible, and alternatively as legally baseless on sovereign immunity, Eleventh Amendment, Monell, statute of limitations, and state-action grounds. The court also dismissed a liberally construed FHA retaliation claim because Murray predicated it solely on retaliation for pursuing an inheritance rather than on discrimination tied to a protected class, which is an essential element of any FHA claim.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Holley v. Dep't of Veteran Affairs, 165 F.3d 244 (3d Cir. 1999)
Lloyd v. Presby's Inspired Life, 251 F. Supp. 3d 891 (E.D. Pa. 2017)
Davis v. Rubin, 2020 WL 7624833 (E.D. Pa. Dec. 22, 2020)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Restoration of housing voucher/rights; plaintiff alleged denial of housing assistance in retaliation for attempting to recover alleged stolen inheritance
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege discrimination based on a protected class under the FHA. FHA retaliation claims require a nexus to protected activity (exercise of FHA rights based on protected class membership). Plaintiff's allegations concerned only retaliation for attempting to recover an alleged inheritance, not discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, handicap, familial status, or national origin. Dismissal was with prejudice as amendment would be futile.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 constitutional claims (due process, equal protection); Bivens claims against federal officials; FOIA requests; claims for criminal prosecution
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's allegations were factually frivolous and wholly incredible, rising to the level of the irrational. Allegations of a $43 million stolen inheritance, conspiracy by multiple government agencies and private entities to murder plaintiff, and mind-control harassment lacked any plausible factual basis. Additionally, claims against DHS were barred by Eleventh Amendment immunity; claims against PHA and SEPTA failed to allege municipal policy or custom; claims against U.S. Treasury and HUD were barred by sovereign immunity absent waiver; claims against Senator Santorum were time-barred under Pennsylvania's two-year statute of limitations for personal injury torts; claims against private individuals failed to establish state action; claims against District Attorney Krasner and Representative Brown failed to allege personal involvement; and due process claims against Councilmembers Brooks and Gaultier were barred by availability of adequate state remedy under Pennsylvania Tort Claims Act.

source_file: 10744257_2025_Robert A. Johnson v. Raven Wood Homeowners Association, et al._wawd
case_name: Robert A. Johnson v. Raven Wood Homeowners Association, et al.
accommodation_description: Request to participate in HOA meetings virtually as a reasonable accommodation for disability
key_holding: The court set aside the entry of default against Mr. Krieger, finding he did not act in bad faith or with culpable intent, has a meritorious defense (including an argument that he reasonably accommodated plaintiff's request to participate in HOA meetings virtually), and plaintiff would not suffer prejudice.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Robert Johnson brought Fair Housing Act claims against the HOA and its former president Mr. Krieger; after default was entered against Krieger, he moved to set aside the default. The Court granted Krieger's motion, finding no culpable conduct, a meritorious defense that he reasonably accommodated Johnson's request to participate in meetings virtually, and no prejudice to Johnson.
key_cases_cited: United States v. Signed Personal Check No. 730 of Yubran S. Mesle, 615 F.3d 1085 (9th Cir. 2010)
Community Dental Services v. Tani, 282 F.3d 1164 (9th Cir. 2002)
Meadows v. Dominican Republic, 817 F.2d 517 (9th Cir. 1987)
Mendoza v. Wight Vineyard Mgmt., 783 F.2d 941 (9th Cir. 1986)
Azam v. Brown, 714 F. App'x 663 (9th Cir. 2017)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Virtual participation in HOA meetings
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted defendant's motion to set aside the entry of default, finding no bad faith, a meritorious defense (defendant asserts he reasonably accommodated plaintiff's request for virtual HOA meeting participation), and no prejudice to plaintiff. The FHA claim remains pending for trial on February 9, 2026.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Common law infliction of emotional distress
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted defendant's motion to set aside the entry of default. The infliction of emotional distress claim survives and remains pending for trial on February 9, 2026.

source_file: 10745098_2025_K.D., a minor, by and through his Guardian ad Litem, LaQuantae Davis v. CALIBER CHANGEMAKERS, et al._caed

case_name: Anthony Alfieri v. Cortland Management LLC
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; plaintiff alleges discrimination based on familial status (having a minor child) and retaliation for filing a HUD complaint.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claims under § 3604(b) and § 3617 because plaintiff failed to allege sufficient factual facts showing concrete adverse action or causal link between the alleged harms and his protected class status.
brief_summary: Anthony Alfieri sued Cortland Management LLC alleging the landlord discriminated against him based on familial status by targeting his four-year-old daughter with repeated noise complaints and threatened eviction, and retaliated against him by raising his rent after he filed a HUD complaint. The court dismissed the complaint with leave to amend, finding Alfieri failed to allege sufficient facts showing concrete adverse action or a causal connection between the alleged harms and his protected class status.
key_cases_cited: Morris v. W. Hayden Ests. First Addition Homeowners Ass'n, Inc., 104 F.4th 1128 (9th Cir. 2024)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
United States v. City of Hayward, 36 F.3d 832 (9th Cir. 1994)
Ohio House, LLC v. City of Costa Mesa, 135 F.4th 645 (9th Cir. 2025)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege a prima facie case of disparate treatment based on familial status under § 3604(b). Although plaintiff adequately alleged membership in a protected class (parent with minor child), he did not identify concrete adverse impacts or provide factual allegations linking any alleged harms to his familial status, falling short of the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's retaliation claim under § 3617 failed at the pleading stage because although he alleged protected activity (filing a HUD complaint), he did not provide factual allegations establishing a causal link between the complaint and any alleged adverse actions, such as temporal proximity or statements by defendant's employees suggesting retaliation.

source_file: 10745833_2025_Mekal Faruki v. Housing Authority for the County of Sacramento, et al._caed
case_name: Mekal Faruki v. Housing Authority for the County of Sacramento, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested reasonable accommodation in processing his Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher application, including consideration of his certified disability, after defendants allegedly lost his application and failed to respond for years.
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA claim was dismissed for failure to state a claim because his allegations were speculative and lacked specific supporting facts necessary to state a claim for relief, and his claim that a similarly situated friend was treated more favorably failed to suggest disability discrimination since that friend is also disabled.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Mekal Faruki, an elderly individual with Multiple Myeloma, sued the Housing Authority for the County of Sacramento and related entities alleging they violated the Fair Housing Act by losing his Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher application and failing to accommodate his disability over years of follow-up. The magistrate judge recommended dismissing the complaint without leave to amend for failure to state a plausible FHA claim, finding the allegations speculative and failing to plead facts showing disability-based discrimination since plaintiff's friend who received more favorable treatment was also disabled.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Lovell v. Chandler, 303 F.3d 1039 (9th Cir. 2002)
Duvall v. County of Kitsap, 260 F.3d 1124 (9th Cir. 2001)
Budnick v. Town of Carefree, 518 F.3d 1109 (9th Cir. 2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accommodation for disability in processing Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher application; plaintiff alleges defendants refused to accommodate his disability and claimed his application was lost despite proof of delivery.
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found plaintiff's allegations speculative and lacking specific supporting facts necessary to state a claim. Plaintiff's allegation that a similarly situated disabled friend was treated more favorably does not plausibly suggest disability discrimination, and the complaint fails to plead adequate factual content allowing the court to infer discrimination because of plaintiff's disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's claim that loss of his application and non-receipt of Section 8 Vouchers constituted discrimination because of disability is speculative and lacks specific supporting facts. The comparison to a similarly situated disabled friend does not support an inference of disability-based discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II, Unruh Civil Rights Act, California Disabled Persons Act, and Fraud claims
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim; supplemental jurisdiction declined
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found the ADA Title II claims failed to state a claim under the Iqbal/Twombly standard. Because no federal question claims survived, the court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3).

source_file: 10746118_2025_Sean Murphy v. Brixworth Homeowners Ass'n, Inc._ca6
case_name: Sean Murphy; Denise Pagels, et al. v. Brixworth Homeowners Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation was requested; Murphy alleged that the HOA violated the FHA and ADA by enforcing its covenant prohibiting yard signs and banning him from community amenities (pool and common spaces) as a result of his non-compliance, claiming membership in a protected class under the FHA.
key_holding: The Sixth Circuit affirmed the district court's judgment on the pleadings, holding that Murphy's complaint's explicit invocation of the Fair Housing Act and ADA gave the district court proper federal-question jurisdiction, and that the district judge committed no reversible error in accepting the related case or refusing to recuse.
brief_summary: Sean Murphy sued the Brixworth HOA after it told him to remove large political yard signs and banned him and his family from community amenities until he complied. Murphy's complaint in Tennessee state court alleged breach of contract and violations of the Fair Housing Act and Americans with Disabilities Act; the HOA removed the case to federal court. The Sixth Circuit affirmed the district court's grant of judgment on the pleadings, rejecting Murphy's arguments that no federal claims existed in his complaint, that reassignment to Chief Judge McDonough was improper, and that the judge should have recused himself.
key_cases_cited: Smolarek v. Chrysler Corp., 879 F.2d 1326 (6th Cir. 1989)
Davet v. City of Cleveland, 456 F.3d 549 (6th Cir. 2006)
Liteky v. United States, 510 U.S. 540 (1994)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exception to homeowners association covenant prohibiting yard signs; plaintiff sought to display large political banners in front yard without losing access to neighborhood amenities (pool, common spaces)
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court granted the Association's motion for judgment on the pleadings, finding that Murphy failed to state a viable claim. The appellate court affirmed on jurisdictional grounds (federal question jurisdiction existed based on FHA/ADA claims) without substantively analyzing the merits of the FHA reasonable accommodation claim itself.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of contract claim under Tennessee state law; Americans with Disabilities Act claim
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court granted judgment on the pleadings dismissing all claims. The appellate court affirmed without reaching the merits of the non-FHA claims, focusing instead on jurisdictional authority and procedural issues.

source_file: 10746417_2025_T_R PROPERTIES, INC., et al. v. BERLIN TOWNSHIP, et al._ohsd
case_name: T&R Properties, Inc., et al. v. Berlin Township, et al.
accommodation_description: This discovery ruling does not involve a reasonable accommodation request; the underlying case involves challenges to zoning decisions allegedly motivated by racial discrimination and familial status.
key_holding: The court denied Defendants' motion to stay discovery because their Rooker-Feldman jurisdictional arguments were fairly debatable rather than certain to bar the case, and Defendants overstated the hardship of resuming limited depositions.
brief_summary: T&R Properties sued Berlin Township alleging the Township engaged in intentional and disparate impact racial discrimination in zoning decisions and denied housing to families with children in violation of the Fair Housing Act. This Opinion & Order denies Defendants' motion to stay discovery, finding their jurisdictional objections were fairly debatable and did not warrant pausing the case.
key_cases_cited: Ohio Valley Bank Co. v. MetaBank
Shanks v. Honda of Am. Mfg.
Hahn v. Star Bank
Seattle House, LLC v. City of Delaware
Ohio Bell Tel. Co., Inc. v. Global NAPs Ohio, Inc.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs alleged intentional racial discrimination in violation of the FHA. The motion to dismiss is pending before the court; this opinion addresses only a motion to stay discovery and does not resolve the merits of the discrimination claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs alleged disparate impact racial discrimination in violation of the FHA. The motion to dismiss is pending before the court; this opinion addresses only a motion to stay discovery and does not resolve the merits of the disparate impact claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of zoning plan to keep out families with children
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs added a familial status FHA claim alleging Defendants denied their zoning plan based on familial status. The motion to dismiss is pending before the court; this opinion addresses only a motion to stay discovery and does not resolve the merits of the familial status claim.

case_name: Manal Farhan v. 2715 NMA LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested to display a Palestinian flag in her apartment window to express her heritage, and was evicted when she refused to comply with defendants' neutrality policy.
key_holding: The Seventh Circuit affirmed dismissal, holding that Farhan's complaint failed to plausibly allege that defendants enforced a neutrality policy against her because of her national origin rather than her political expression in support of the Palestinian cause, and that her disparate impact claim failed without any statistical evidence showing the policy disproportionately affected Palestinian tenants.
brief_summary: Manal Farhan, a Palestinian American, sued her apartment building's owner and operator after they ordered her to remove a Palestinian flag from her window pursuant to a neutrality policy regarding the Israel-Palestine conflict and then terminated her tenancy when she refused. The Seventh Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal, finding Farhan's complaint failed to plausibly allege intentional national origin discrimination or disparate impact because the eviction was motivated by her political expression rather than her protected status, and she provided no statistical evidence of disparate impact.
key_cases_cited: Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009)
Texas Dept. of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Swanson v. Citibank, N.A., 614 F.3d 400 (7th Cir. 2010)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff challenged defendants' enforcement of a 'neutrality' policy requiring her to remove a Palestinian flag from her apartment window, alleging this constituted national origin discrimination under § 3604(b).
fha_claims.reasoning: At the pleading stage, plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to plausibly infer discriminatory intent. The complaint did not allege that the neutrality policy applied only to Palestinian flags, that other non-Palestinian tenants were permitted to fly Israeli or Palestinian flags, or that defendants were aware of plaintiff's national origin prior to enforcing the policy. The court held that plaintiff's allegations, viewed as a whole, described punishment for political viewpoint rather than national origin discrimination, which is not protected under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged that defendants' neutrality policy regarding the Israel-Palestine conflict had a disproportionate impact on Palestinian tenants by preventing them from expressing national pride through flag display.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead facts establishing a causal connection between the policy and disparate impact on a protected class. The complaint contained no allegations about how many tenants or Palestinian tenants were affected, no comparative data on enforcement against Palestinians versus non-Palestinians, and no factual basis for inferring that the policy had a disproportionate effect. The court noted that to the extent the policy facially discriminated, disparate treatment rather than disparate impact was the proper theory.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged that defendants coerced, intimidated, or interfered with her exercise of fair housing rights under § 3617 by enforcing the neutrality policy and evicting her.
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 3617 requires a showing of a 'pattern of harassment' motivated by discriminatory intent. Plaintiff alleged only a single action—enforcement of the neutrality policy and eviction—which does not constitute a pattern. Additionally, plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts to infer that this action was motivated by intent to discriminate based on a protected status, as discussed in the disparate treatment analysis.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Illinois Consumer Fraud and Deceptive Business Practices Act; Chicago Residential Landlord and Tenant Ordinance
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims after dismissing all federal FHA claims with prejudice. The court followed the usual practice in the Seventh Circuit of dismissing state supplemental claims without prejudice when all federal claims are dismissed prior to trial. The appellate court found no abuse of discretion in this decision.

case_name: Manal Farhan v. 2715 NMA LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff is a Palestinian American who was told to remove a Palestinian flag from her apartment window and was subsequently evicted under a 'neutrality' policy.
key_holding: The Seventh Circuit affirmed dismissal because Farhan failed to plead facts showing defendants' neutrality policy was created or applied 'because of' her national origin rather than viewpoint neutrality regarding the Israel-Palestine conflict, and she effectively pleaded herself out of court by characterizing her claim as viewpoint discrimination.
brief_summary: Manal Farhan, a Palestinian American tenant, sued her landlord under the Fair Housing Act alleging national origin discrimination after being told to remove a Palestinian flag from her apartment window and subsequently evicted under a 'neutrality' policy. The Seventh Circuit affirmed dismissal, holding that Farhan failed to plead facts showing defendants enforced the policy because of her national origin rather than viewpoint neutrality, and that she effectively pleaded herself out of court by characterizing her claim as viewpoint discrimination rather than protected-class discrimination.
key_cases_cited: Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009)
Texas Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Swanson v. Citibank, N.A., 614 F.3d 400 (7th Cir. 2010)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff challenged defendants' enforcement of a 'neutrality' policy requiring her to remove a Palestinian flag from her apartment window, alleging this constituted national origin discrimination under § 3604(b).
fha_claims.reasoning: At the pleading stage, plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to plausibly infer discriminatory intent based on national origin. The complaint did not allege that the neutrality policy applied only to Palestinian flags, that other non-Palestinian tenants were permitted to fly Israeli or Palestinian flags, or that defendants were aware of plaintiff's Palestinian national origin prior to enforcing the policy. The court held that plaintiff's allegations, viewed as a whole, described viewpoint discrimination based on political expression in support of the Palestinian cause, not intentional discrimination based on national origin, which is not protected under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged that defendants' neutrality policy regarding the Israel-Palestine conflict had a disproportionate impact on Palestinian tenants by preventing them from expressing national pride through flag display.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead facts establishing a causal connection between the policy and disparate impact on a protected class. The complaint contained no allegations about how many tenants were affected, how many Palestinian tenants were affected, or comparative data showing the policy impacted Palestinians more than non-Palestinians. The court held that plaintiff's bare assertion that the policy 'negatively impacts Palestinians' was insufficient; she was required to allege that it negatively impacts Palestinians more by proportion than non-Palestinians. Additionally, to the extent the policy facially discriminates, disparate treatment is the proper theory, not disparate impact.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged that defendants coerced, intimidated, threatened, or interfered with her exercise of fair housing rights under § 3617 by enforcing the neutrality policy and evicting her.
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 3617 interference claims require a showing of a 'pattern of harassment' motivated by discriminatory intent. Plaintiff alleged only a single action—enforcement of the neutrality policy and eviction—which does not constitute a pattern. Additionally, plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts to infer that this action was motivated by intent to discriminate based on national origin, for the same reasons the disparate treatment claim failed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Illinois Consumer Fraud and Deceptive Business Practices Act; Chicago Residential Landlord and Tenant Ordinance
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over plaintiff's state law claims after dismissing all federal FHA claims with prejudice. The court followed the usual practice in the Seventh Circuit of dismissing without prejudice state supplemental claims when all federal claims have been dismissed prior to trial. Plaintiff provided no argument that this exercise of discretion constituted an abuse of discretion.

source_file: 10748104_2025_61 East Main Street Associates, LLC, and Moche Halpern v. The Village of Washingtonville, Thomas Devinko, in his official and individual capacities, Donna Jacaruso, in her official and individual capacities
case_name: 61 East Main Street Associates, LLC, and Moche Halpern v. The Village of Washingtonville
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs, an Orthodox Jewish developer and LLC, allege discriminatory denial of approval for a multi-unit residential development based on anti-Semitic animus.
key_holding: The Court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that Plaintiffs' claims were not ripe because no final determination was issued on their site plan application and Plaintiffs failed to demonstrate that the futility exception applied to excuse the finality requirement.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs, an Orthodox Jewish real estate developer and his LLC, sued the Village of Washingtonville and individual officials alleging Fair Housing Act, Equal Protection, Due Process, and civil conspiracy claims based on alleged anti-Semitic animus motivating delays and denial of their multi-unit residential development project. The Court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss, finding the claims were not ripe because the Village had not issued a final determination on the site plan application and Plaintiffs failed to meet the high standard required to invoke the futility exception to the finality requirement.
key_cases_cited: Williamson County Regional Planning Commission v. Hamilton Bank, 473 U.S. 172 (1985)
Vill. Green at Sayville, LLC v. Town of Islip, 43 F.4th 287 (2d Cir. 2022)
Murphy v. New Milford Zoning Comm'n, 402 F.3d 342 (2d Cir. 2005)
Sherman v. Town of Chester, 752 F.3d 554 (2d Cir. 2014)
Sunrise Detox V, LLC v. City of White Plains, 769 F.3d 118 (2d Cir. 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the FHA discrimination claim as unripe under Williamson County because plaintiffs failed to obtain a final, definitive decision from the municipality on their site plan application. The court found that the futility exception to the finality requirement did not apply, as the five-year delay and moratorium extensions were not sufficiently egregious to constitute farcical conduct, and plaintiffs' own project modifications contributed to the delay.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal Protection claim (Fourteenth Amendment), due process claim (Fourteenth Amendment), conspiracy to interfere with civil rights claim (42 U.S.C. § 1983 and § 1985)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the non-FHA claims on two independent grounds: (1) lack of third-party standing because plaintiffs sought to vindicate the rights of the Orthodox Jewish community without identifying specific injured third parties or establishing a close relationship to them; and (2) ripeness, as the claims were unripe under Williamson County's finality requirement and the discriminatory animus exception did not apply because plaintiffs failed to establish standing to assert injury on behalf of the Orthodox Jewish community.

source_file: 10748138_2025_Williams Victor Funes Nunez v. Morgan Properties LLC, et al._njd
case_name: Williams Victor Funes Nunez v. Morgan Properties LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Request to be moved to a first-floor unit for five-year-old child with autism
key_holding: The court denied the TRO/preliminary injunction because the Anti-Injunction Act bars federal courts from enjoining state court eviction proceedings, and plaintiff failed to demonstrate irreparable harm for his other requested relief.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Williams Victor Funes Nunez filed an emergency motion seeking to halt state court eviction proceedings and obtain FHA/ADA accommodations for his autistic child, including transfer to a first-floor unit. The court denied the motion under the Anti-Injunction Act, which bars federal courts from enjoining state eviction proceedings absent narrow statutory exceptions that do not apply here, and found plaintiff failed to demonstrate irreparable harm.
key_cases_cited: In re Prudential Ins. Co. of Am. Sales Pracs. Litig., 314 F.3d 99 (3d Cir. 2002)
Poussaint v. Mendlowitz, No. 24-5387, 2024 WL 4543062 (E.D. Pa. Oct. 22, 2024)
In re Diet Drugs, 282 F.3d 220 (3d Cir. 2002)
Reilly v. City of Harrisburg, 858 F.3d 173 (3d Cir. 2017)
Ferring Pharms., Inc. v. Watson Pharms., Inc., 765 F.3d 205 (3d Cir. 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Transfer to first-floor unit for child with autism; unspecified housing adjustments to provide stable sensory environment; measures to protect child's health and disability-related needs
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied preliminary injunction on threshold grounds (failure to show irreparable harm absent preliminary relief) without reaching merits of FHA reasonable accommodation claim. Plaintiff alleged defendants approved but failed to implement accommodations, but court did not analyze whether accommodations were reasonable or required.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged retaliatory eviction action in response to civil action brought against defendants for administrative harassment and housing conditions. Court denied preliminary injunction on threshold grounds without reaching merits of retaliation claim under FHA § 3617.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 privacy claim regarding disclosure of minor child's name in state court proceedings
fha_claims.reasoning: Court noted that § 1983 privacy claim fails on merits because defendants are private entities with no allegation of state action, but did not formally dismiss; claim survives preliminary injunction denial on threshold irreparable harm grounds.

source_file: 10748519_2025_Karen Denise Price, individually and as executor and sole beneficiary of the Estate of Dennis H. Buie v. FCI Lender Services, et al._gand
case_name: Karen Denise Price, individually and as executor and sole beneficiary of the Estate of Dennis H. Buie v. FCI Lender Services, et al.
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED - No reasonable accommodation claim analyzed; this is a transfer order addressing venue.
key_holding: The Court transferred the action to the Northern District of Georgia because the property at issue is located there, all defendants are found or transact business there, and a substantial portion of alleged events occurred in that district, making it the proper and more convenient venue.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Karen Denise Price, proceeding pro se and seeking in forma pauperis status, filed this action in the Southern District of New York against 50 defendants asserting eleven federal claims including Fair Housing Act claims arising from real property located in Atlanta, Georgia. The Court transferred the action to the Northern District of Georgia under 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a) because venue was proper there (property location, defendant contacts, and locus of operative facts) and that forum was more convenient for all parties and witnesses.
key_cases_cited: Keitt v. N.Y. City, 882 F. Supp. 2d 412 (S.D.N.Y. 2011)
N.Y. Marine and Gen. Ins. Co. v. LaFarge N. Am., Inc., 599 F.3d 102 (2d Cir. 2010)
D.H. Blair & Co. v. Gottdiener, 462 F.3d 95 (2d Cir. 2006)
Coppedge v. United States, 369 U.S. 438 (1962)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: RICO, Securities and Exchange Act, Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, Truth in Lending Act, RESPA, § 1983, § 1985, ADA, Lanham Act, and state law claims arising from real property conveyance
fha_claims.reasoning: The court transferred the action to the Northern District of Georgia for venue and convenience purposes under 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a), finding that the property at issue is located in Atlanta, Georgia, all defendants are found or transact affairs there, and a substantial portion of alleged events occurred in that district. The court did not reach the merits of any claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unspecified reasonable accommodation related to disability under the Fair Housing Act
fha_claims.reasoning: The Fair Housing Act claim was transferred along with all other claims to the Northern District of Georgia without substantive analysis. The court did not apply any reasonable accommodation standard or reach the merits of the FHA claim.

source_file: 10748536_2025_Lance Frazier v. Justin Luther, Individually and d_b_a Luther Properties, LLC, Phillip Kennedy, and Angie Kennedy_msnd
case_name: Lance Frazier v. Justin Luther, Individually and d/b/a Luther Properties, LLC, Phillip Kennedy, and Angie Kennedy
accommodation_description: Racial discrimination claim under the Fair Housing Act, not a reasonable accommodation request
key_holding: The court granted the motion to quash because the subpoenas seeking all text messages, phone calls, photos, and videos over a six-month period were grossly overly broad and sought irrelevant information that would capture private communications entirely unrelated to the case.
brief_summary: Lance Frazier sued Luther Properties, LLC and others for racial discrimination under the Fair Housing Act, along with state law claims for conversion, trespass, and negligent infliction of emotional distress. This order grants the motion to quash overly broad subpoenas served on telecommunications companies seeking six months of all text messages, calls, photos, and videos from multiple phone numbers, as the subpoenas captured volumes of irrelevant private communications unrelated to the case.
key_cases_cited: Crescent City Remodeling, LLC v. CMR Constr. & Roofing, LLC, 643 F. Supp. 3d 613 (E.D. La. 2022)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Racial discrimination claim under the Fair Housing Act
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted defendant's motion to quash four subpoenas seeking telecommunications records over a six-month period, finding them grossly overbroad and seeking irrelevant information unrelated to the FHA claim. The underlying FHA racial discrimination claim remains pending but was limited to an 11-day period (September 2-13, 2022) by prior order. This ruling addresses discovery procedure, not the merits of the FHA claim itself.

source_file: 10748635_2025_Duc L. Trinh and Sally Y. Ly v. La Jolla Racquet Club Condominium Owners’ Association, Inc., et al._casd
case_name: Duc L. Trinh and Sally Y. Ly v. La Jolla Racquet Club Condominium Owners' Association, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested reasonable accommodations for safe ingress and egress due to Plaintiff Ly's wheelchair-bound disability after the parking garage—the sole accessible route to her unit—was closed.
