fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination in the sale or rental of housing under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(b) and (f)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court identified discrimination claims under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(b) and (f) as surviving § 1915(e)(2) screening and ordered plaintiff to file a third amended complaint addressing these surviving claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Defamation (28 U.S.C. § 4101), disclosure of personal information (15 U.S.C. § 6802), retaliation under ADA (42 U.S.C. § 12203), Title III ADA violation (42 U.S.C. §§ 12181, 12182)
fha_claims.reasoning: Defamation claim dismissed because the SPEECH Act does not confer a private right of action. Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act claim dismissed because it does not confer a private right of action. ADA retaliation claim dismissed because plaintiff failed to allege opposition to a statutorily protected activity. Title III ADA claim dismissed because plaintiff's claims relate to his personal residence, not a place of public accommodation.

source_file: 10765288_2025_Johnny Moffett v. Columbia Manor et al._wawd
case_name: Johnny Moffett v. Columbia Manor et al.
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation requested; plaintiff alleges racial harassment by white supremacy group and failure of property manager to intervene.
key_holding: Plaintiff's amended complaint fails to state an FHA claim because it contains only conclusory allegations of racial bias without specific facts from which the court could infer that defendants were motivated by racial discrimination or engaged in conduct prohibited by 42 U.S.C. § 3604(a).
brief_summary: Johnny Moffett, an African American man with disabilities, sued Columbia Manor (Smith Towers) and individual defendants alleging racial harassment by a white supremacy group and claiming the property manager failed to intervene. The court dismissed the amended complaint sua sponte under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) for failure to state a claim, finding the complaint contained only conclusory allegations of race-based discrimination without specific facts demonstrating discriminatory intent or conduct prohibited by the FHA.
key_cases_cited: Barren v. Harrington, 152 F.3d 1193 (9th Cir. 1998)
Missouri ex rel. Koster v. Harris, 847 F.3d 646 (9th Cir. 2017)
Watison v. Carter, 668 F.3d 1108 (9th Cir. 2012)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's amended complaint fails to allege specific facts supporting a claim of race-based discrimination in violation of 42 U.S.C. § 3604(a). The complaint relies on conclusory allegations and assumptions rather than factual allegations showing defendants engaged in conduct prohibited by the FHA or were motivated by racial bias. Leave to amend is denied as futile because plaintiff has already been given one opportunity to cure the deficiencies and failed to do so.

source_file: 10766204_2025_Mary E. Martinez v. ABQ Code Enforcement, Angelo Matzer, Ray Velarde, and William (Josh) Gallegos_nmd
case_name: Mary E. Martinez v. ABQ Code Enforcement, Angelo Matzer, Ray Velardez, and William (Josh) Gallegos
accommodation_description: Unable to determine; complaint too incoherent and non-compliant with Rule 8(a) to identify any specific accommodation request
key_holding: Magistrate recommended declining to accept plaintiff's 64-page filing as an amended complaint and dismissing all federal claims without prejudice for failure to comply with Rule 8(a) pleading requirements, remanding remaining state-law claims to state court.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Mary E. Martinez filed suit against ABQ Code Enforcement and city employees alleging Fair Housing Act, ADA, and constitutional claims related to code enforcement actions and her Section 8 housing. The Magistrate recommended dismissing all federal claims without prejudice because plaintiff's complaint failed to comply with Rule 8(a), being rambling, non-compliant with formatting requirements, and failing to identify specific claims or factual allegations against defendants.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Nasious v. Two Unknown B.I.C.E. Agents
McNamara v. Brauchler
Robbins v. Oklahoma
Smith v. City of Enid ex rel. Enid City Comm'n

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges that her disability affects her ability to read, write, and comprehend things, and that defendants' refusal to make allowances for this constitutes a violation of the Americans with Disabilities Act and Fair Housing Act.
fha_claims.reasoning: The operative complaint (Doc. 1-2) fails to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly because it does not clearly identify which defendant took which actions, does not specify the nature of the disability, and does not provide fair notice of the factual basis for the claim. The court declined to accept the subsequent 64-page filing as an amended complaint because it failed to comply with Rule 8(a) and the court's explicit instructions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: First Amendment religious freedom claims (mocking of religious beliefs and crosses on windows); ADA Title II claims; state law animal abuse claims; and other constitutional and statutory claims.
fha_claims.reasoning: The operative complaint fails to state a plausible claim for any non-FHA federal or state law cause of action because it lacks clear factual allegations, does not identify which defendant did what, and does not provide fair notice of the basis for relief. The court found that although plaintiff alleged mocking of religious beliefs, she did not allege that defendants placed a substantial burden on her religious exercise as required by First Amendment doctrine.

source_file: 10766223_2025_Maurice Dosso v. The Coventry Group Community Management, Inc. et al._vawd
case_name: Maurice Dosso v. The Coventry Group Community Management, Inc. et al.
accommodation_description: Vehicle towing enforcement; plaintiff alleges selective enforcement of parking rules against him as a Black homeowner compared to white homeowners, constituting race-based housing discrimination.
key_holding: The court transferred the case to the Northern District of West Virginia because venue was improper in the Western District of Virginia—all alleged events (towing, HOA citations, property management decisions) occurred in West Virginia, and the court lacked personal jurisdiction over defendant ZZ Auto, a West Virginia corporation.
brief_summary: Maurice Dosso, a Black homeowner in Stonebrook Village, West Virginia, sued Coventry Group Community Management, Stonebrook Village HOA, property manager Keila Navarro, and ZZ Auto alleging race-based discrimination after his vehicle was towed while white neighbors' similarly parked vehicles were not towed. The court transferred the case to the Northern District of West Virginia because venue was improper in the Western District of Virginia—all events occurred in West Virginia and the court lacked personal jurisdiction over defendant ZZ Auto—and declined to reach the merits of any claims.
key_cases_cited: Atlantic Marine Constr. Co. v. U.S. Dist. Court, 571 U.S. 49 (2013)
Goldlawr, Inc. v. Heiman, 369 U.S. 463 (1962)
Bristol-Myers Squibb Co. v. Superior Court, 582 U.S. 255 (2017)
Goodyear Dunlop Tires Operations, S.A. v. Brown, 564 U.S. 915 (2011)
Mitrano v. Hawes, 377 F.3d 402 (4th Cir. 2004)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges racial discrimination in vehicle towing and HOA enforcement, not failure to provide accommodation.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found venue improper in the Western District of Virginia under 28 U.S.C. § 1391(b) and transferred the entire case to the Northern District of West Virginia without addressing the merits of the FHA discrimination claim. The court declined to reach the substantive arguments in the motion to dismiss, leaving those for the transferee court.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Civil Rights Act of 1866 (42 U.S.C. §§ 1981-82); West Virginia state law claims including tortious breach of contract, negligent breach of contract, breach of covenant of good faith and fair dealing, negligent failure to comply with West Virginia notice requirements (W. Va. Code § 17C-14-13), negligence, conversion, trespass to chattel, invasion of privacy, unjust enrichment, intentional infliction of emotional distress, and negligent infliction of emotional distress.
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA claims were transferred along with the FHA claim to the Northern District of West Virginia due to improper venue. The court did not address the merits of any claims, leaving all substantive arguments for the transferee court.

source_file: 10766369_2025_Justin Baker v. The Emerald Condos et al._wawd
case_name: Justin Baker v. The Emerald Condos et al.
citation: UNDETERMINED (W.D. Wash. Order, Case No. C25-1989JLR)
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested an exception to the condominium building's policy requiring residents to break down cardboard boxes before disposal, which he characterized as a reasonable accommodation for his disability. He claimed he had such an accommodation 'on file with the city of Seattle,' but defendants, particularly Mr. Page, told him he was 'not allowed to have his reasonable accommodation for the cardboard.'
key_holding: The court dismissed with prejudice pro se plaintiff's third amended FHA complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B) for failure to comply with Rule 8(a) and failure to state claims for disparate treatment, reasonable accommodation, interference/coercion, and harassment, finding further amendment futile after four opportunities to plead.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Justin Baker, proceeding in forma pauperis, filed a third amended complaint against property management company CWD Group and individual defendants Joe Majewski and Zach Page, alleging violations of the FHA (42 U.S.C. § 3604(b) and (f)) and related regulations concerning disability-based discrimination at his condominium. Baker's central allegation was that defendants refused to honor his reasonable accommodation—an exemption from the building's policy requiring residents to break down cardboard boxes for disposal—despite his claim of federal disability status. The court dismissed all claims with prejudice, finding the complaint violated Rule 8(a)'s pleading requirements and failed to allege sufficient facts to support any of the asserted claims, and denied further leave to amend as futile.
key_cases_cited: Becker v. Orchard Hills Apts., No. CV-11-5108RMP, 2012 WL 3776975 (E.D. Wash. Aug. 29, 2012)
Foman v. Davis, 371 U.S. 178 (1962)
Ebner v. Fresh, Inc., 838 F.3d 958 (9th Cir. 2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discriminatory terms and conditions of tenancy under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(b)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that defendants applied different terms, conditions, or privileges to him compared to others. The complaint lacks sufficient factual allegations to state a claim for discriminatory terms and service under § 3604(b).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Disability discrimination under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege the required elements: disability, qualification to rent, different terms/conditions applied, and causation. The complaint lacks sufficient factual detail regarding his disability and how defendants' conduct was causally linked to it.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination in terms, conditions, privileges, services and facilities under 24 C.F.R. § 100.65
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts showing he is a protected class member, was qualified to rent, defendants imposed different terms or limited services compared to others, and causation. The complaint lacks the necessary factual allegations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exception to building policy requiring breakdown of cardboard boxes; plaintiff alleged he had a reasonable accommodation on file with the city of Seattle
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege the required elements: (1) insufficient detail about the nature and severity of his disability; (2) unclear what accommodation was actually requested or communicated to defendants; (3) unclear whether defendants were the appropriate parties to receive the request; and (4) no allegation that cardboard disposal accommodation was necessary to afford equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Prohibited interference, coercion, or intimidation under 24 C.F.R. § 100.400 related to refusal to accommodate cardboard disposal and alleged false HOA violation charges
fha_claims.reasoning: Although plaintiff alleged he reported the accommodation refusal to authorities and that defendants attempted to charge him for HOA violations, he failed to plausibly allege sufficient facts to state a claim for prohibited interference, coercion, or intimidation against the current defendants.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Quid pro quo harassment under 24 C.F.R. § 100.600
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege that he was subject to an unwelcome request or demand made a condition of housing access, or that harassment occurred because of protected class membership. The complaint lacks the necessary factual allegations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Hostile environment harassment under 24 C.F.R. § 100.600
fha_claims.reasoning: Although plaintiff alleged CWD Group required written communication, imposed penalties for cardboard non-compliance, and showed security footage, he failed to allege that such conduct was based on protected class membership or sufficiently severe or pervasive to interfere with his ability to use and enjoy the dwelling.

source_file: 10766412_2025_Randy Dewayne Pittman v. Landsphere Property Management, et al._cand
case_name: Randy Dewayne Pittman v. Landsphere Property Management, et al.
accommodation_description: Creation of an accessible parking space for the plaintiff at his apartment building.
key_holding: The court dismissed the plaintiff's FHA claim with prejudice for failure to state a claim after the plaintiff failed to file an amended complaint, and dismissed the state-law claims without prejudice for lack of supplemental jurisdiction.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Randy Dewayne Pittman sued his landlord and property manager under the FHA and California state law, alleging they failed to create an accessible parking space at his apartment building. The court had previously dismissed his complaint with leave to amend after screening it pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2), finding it failed to state an FHA claim. Because Pittman did not file an amended complaint by the December 1, 2025 deadline, the court dismissed the federal FHA claim with prejudice and the state-law claims without prejudice.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic v. Twombly

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible parking space at apartment building
fha_claims.reasoning: The court screened the complaint under § 1915(e)(2) and determined that the FHA claim failed to state a plausible claim. The complaint was dismissed with leave to amend, and upon plaintiff's failure to file an amended complaint by the deadline, the case was dismissed with prejudice.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (Cal. Gov't Code §§ 12927, 12955), California Civil Code § 54.1, and California Code of Civil Procedure §§ 526 and 1060
fha_claims.reasoning: The court determined that the complaint failed to articulate an independent basis for subject-matter jurisdiction over the state-law claims and declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction, dismissing those claims without prejudice.

source_file: 10766939_2025_Blakelick Properties, LLC v. The Village of Glen Ellyn_ilnd
case_name: Blakelick Properties, LLC v. The Village of Glen Ellyn
accommodation_description: This is not a disability accommodation case; Blakelick Properties challenges a municipal ordinance banning short-term rentals as a regulatory taking, with FHA cited as one of several claims but not substantively analyzed.
key_holding: The Court granted preliminary injunction against Glen Ellyn's short-term rental ban as applied to Blakelick, finding Blakelick likely succeeded on its regulatory takings claim and would suffer irreparable harm from loss of its short-term rental business.
brief_summary: Blakelick Properties LLC, owner of a short-term rental property in Glen Ellyn, Illinois, sued the Village of Glen Ellyn challenging Ordinance No. 7180-VC which bans short-term rentals, arguing it constitutes a regulatory taking under the Fifth Amendment. The Court granted preliminary injunction, finding Blakelick demonstrated likelihood of success on the merits of its regulatory taking claim, would suffer irreparable harm from loss of its entire short-term rental business, and the balance of equities favors enjoining enforcement against Blakelick while litigation proceeds.
key_cases_cited: Whitaker v. Kenosha Unified Sch. Dist. No. 1 Bd. of Educ., 858 F.3d 1034 (7th Cir. 2017)
Valencia v. City of Springfield, 883 F.3d 959 (7th Cir. 2018)
Murr v. Wisconsin, 582 U.S. 383 (2017)
Morgan v. City of Chicago, 115 F.4th 841 (7th Cir. 2024)
Lucas v. S.C. Coastal Council, 505 U.S. 1003 (1992)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fifth Amendment regulatory takings claim; First Amendment free speech claim; Contracts Clause claim; Due Process claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found Blakelick likely to succeed on the merits of its regulatory takings claim, that it would suffer irreparable harm without adequate legal remedy, and that the balance of equities favors Blakelick. The court granted a preliminary injunction against Glen Ellyn's enforcement of the short-term rental ban ordinance as to Blakelick only, finding the ordinance would deprive Blakelick of economically viable use of the property.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act claim (mentioned in complaint but not substantively analyzed by court)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court noted that Blakelick alleged a Fair Housing Act violation but did not analyze the merits of this claim, instead focusing its preliminary injunction analysis on the regulatory takings claim. The FHA claim remains pending and unresolved.

source_file: 10766941_2025_Valery Kantsepolsky v. River Shores Association, Inc._flsd
case_name: Valery Kantsepolsky v. River Shores Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested a 90-day extension of pretrial and trial deadlines in the pending state court action as a reasonable accommodation for her medical conditions affecting her ability to tolerate demolition-related environmental hazards.
key_holding: The court adopted the magistrate judge's recommendation to stay the federal case pending resolution of the state court action under Colorado River abstention, while allowing the FHA reasonable accommodation claim to proceed and dismissing the ADA claim for failure to state a claim.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Valery Kantsepolsky, a condominium unit owner with medical conditions limiting her tolerance for demolition-related environmental hazards, sued the River Shores Association, Inc. alleging the HOA failed to provide reasonable accommodations and engaged in retaliation when she sought a 90-day extension of deadlines in underlying state court litigation. The court adopted the magistrate judge's report, staying the federal case under Colorado River abstention doctrine while allowing the FHA reasonable accommodation claim to survive dismissal and dismissing the ADA claim for failure to state a claim.
key_cases_cited: Colorado River Water Conservation District v. United States, 424 U.S. 800 (1976)
A.L. by and through D.L. v. Walt Disney Parks & Resorts US, Inc., 900 F.3d 1270 (11th Cir. 2018)
Thomas v. Arn, 474 U.S. 140 (1985)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation for medical conditions limiting ability to tolerate environment created by demolition (chemicals, dust, mold, breathing hazards); 90-day extension of pretrial and trial deadlines in state court action; accommodation for exploratory demolition and repairs subject to plaintiff's medical conditions; engagement in interactive process regarding accommodation requests
fha_claims.reasoning: The court stayed the FHA reasonable accommodation claim based on Colorado River abstention doctrine to prevent piecemeal litigation, finding that at least three of seven abstention factors weighed strongly in favor of abstention pending resolution of the parallel state court action. The court found plaintiff sufficiently alleged an FHA violation to survive Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal but abstained from exercising jurisdiction rather than dismissing on the merits.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Part of Count II alleging retaliation under the FHA was stayed based on Colorado River abstention doctrine pending resolution of the state court action. The court did not reach the merits of the retaliation claim but allowed it to proceed if plaintiff files an amended complaint.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act Title III claims (Counts I and II)
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA Title III claims were dismissed for failure to state a claim because Title III applies only to private entities offering commercial services to the public, and plaintiff did not allege that the condominium association offers commercial services to the public. Dismissal was without prejudice, allowing plaintiff to file an amended complaint by January 23, 2026.

source_file: 10767062_2025_Marcos Isaac Rojas v. Shelter Corporation and Kyle Didier_mnd
case_name: Marcos Isaac Rojas v. Shelter Corporation and Kyle Didier
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation requested; claims involve race-based tenant harassment and alleged retaliation via camera installation.
key_holding: The court dismissed Rojas's FHA disparate impact and retaliation claims because he failed to allege sufficient facts to plausibly support either claim, failing to adequately plead that defendants' policies disproportionately harmed minorities or that the camera installation constituted actionable retaliation.
brief_summary: Rojas, a Mexican national origin tenant, sued his property manager and company president alleging they failed to protect him from race-based tenant harassment and retaliated by installing a camera near his parking spot. The court dismissed his FHA claims (disparate impact and retaliation) without prejudice, finding he failed to plead sufficient facts to state plausible claims under either theory.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Texas Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Ellis v. City of Minneapolis, 860 F.3d 1106 (8th Cir. 2017)
Gallagher v. Magner, 619 F.3d 823 (8th Cir. 2010)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that defendants knew about mistreatment by other tenants and failed to act, or that such inaction rose to the level of creating a policy or practice adversely impacting minorities. Plaintiff did not allege sufficient facts to support a prima facie case of disparate impact under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's vague allegation regarding installation of a camera trained at his parking spot was insufficient to support a plausible claim for retaliation under 42 U.S.C. § 3617. The allegation lacked sufficient factual content to allow reasonable inference of retaliation for exercising FHA rights.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Minnesota Human Rights Act (Minn. Stat. §§ 363A.09, et seq.) and Minnesota personnel records statute (Minn. Stat. §§ 181.960–181.965)
fha_claims.reasoning: State law claims were remanded to state court under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3) because all federal question claims were dismissed, leaving no basis for the district court's original jurisdiction. The court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the remaining state law claims.

source_file: 10767770_2025_Maurice Dosso v. The Coventry Group Community Management, Inc. et al._wvnd
case_name: Maurice Dosso v. The Coventry Group Community Management, Inc. et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges racial discrimination in towing of his vehicle from HOA community parking, claiming Black residents are selectively targeted compared to White residents.
key_holding: The court found venue improper in the Western District of Virginia because ZZ Auto (a West Virginia corporation) was not subject to personal jurisdiction there, and a substantial part of the events giving rise to the claims occurred in West Virginia; accordingly, the court transferred the case to the Northern District of West Virginia rather than dismissing it.
brief_summary: Maurice Dosso, a Black homeowner in Stonebrook Village HOA community in West Virginia, sued Coventry Group Community Management, Inc., Stonebrook Village HOA, HOA agent Keila Navarro, and ZZ Auto Service Center alleging racial discrimination under the Civil Rights Act and Fair Housing Act after his vehicle was towed from community parking. The court transferred the case to the Northern District of West Virginia after finding that venue in the Western District of Virginia was improper because defendant ZZ Auto was a West Virginia corporation not subject to personal jurisdiction in Virginia and the events giving rise to the claims occurred in West Virginia.
key_cases_cited: Atlantic Marine Const. Co. v. U.S. Dist. Court for Western Dist. of Texas, 571 U.S. 49 (2013)
Bristol-Myers Squibb Co. v. Superior Ct. of Cal., S.F. Cnty., 582 U.S. 255 (2017)
Goodyear Dunlop Tires Operations, S.A. v. Brown, 564 U.S. 915 (2011)
Walden v. Fiore, 571 U.S. 277 (2014)
Blue Rhino Glob. Sourcing, Inc. v. Best Choice Prod., No. 1:17-cv-69, 2018 WL 4784006 (M.D.N.C. June 20, 2018)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court did not reach the merits of the FHA discrimination claim (Count XI alleging race discrimination under the Civil Rights Act of 1866 and Fair Housing Act). The case was transferred to the Northern District of West Virginia for improper venue under 28 U.S.C. § 1391(b), leaving all substantive motions to dismiss for decision by the transferee court.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Civil Rights Act of 1866 (42 U.S.C. §§ 1981-82), West Virginia state law claims (tortious breach of contract, negligent breach of contract, breach of covenant of good faith and fair dealing, negligent failure to comply with notice requirements, negligence, conversion, trespass to chattel, invasion of privacy, unjust enrichment, intentional infliction of emotional distress, negligent infliction of emotional distress)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court transferred the entire case to the Northern District of West Virginia for improper venue without addressing the merits of the non-FHA claims (Counts I-X, XII-XIII). The transferee court will decide all outstanding motions to dismiss.

source_file: 10767804_2025_Estela Elizabeth Jeffcoat v. Brookings Housing _ Redevelopment Commission_sdd
case_name: Estela Elizabeth Jeffcoat v. Brookings Housing & Redevelopment Commission
accommodation_description: Request that the housing authority extend and preserve plaintiff's Housing Choice Voucher without interruption and process her portability packet as an accommodation for disability
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's emergency TRO and preliminary injunction motion because she failed to establish a likelihood of success on the merits of her disability accommodation claims against the housing authority.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Estela Elizabeth Jeffcoat sued Brookings Housing & Redevelopment Commission alleging Fair Housing Act violations, seeking an emergency TRO and preliminary injunction to prevent expiration of her Housing Choice Voucher and to compel the housing authority to process her portability request as a disability accommodation. The court denied the motion, finding that Jeffcoat failed to demonstrate a likelihood of success on the merits of her claims.
key_cases_cited: Winter v. Nat. Res. Def. Council, Inc.
Mgmt. Registry, Inc. v. A.W. Cos., Inc.
Dataphase Sys., Inc. v. C L Sys., Inc.
Home Instead, Inc. v. Florance

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Disability accommodation related to Housing Choice Voucher administration; plaintiff requested defendant refrain from denying her disability accommodations letter and maintain/extend her voucher
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied preliminary injunction because plaintiff failed to establish likelihood of success on the merits; plaintiff made only conclusory assertions regarding disability law violations without substantive legal analysis connecting her disability accommodation request to the applicable legal standards.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rehabilitation Act, HUD program requirements, HUD portability rules (24 C.F.R. § 982.355), income rules (24 C.F.R. § 5.609; HOTWIA)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied preliminary injunction on all non-FHA claims (Rehabilitation Act and HUD program requirements) because plaintiff failed to establish likelihood of success on the merits through conclusory assertions without legal analysis.

source_file: 10767808_2025_James E. Jacobson, Jr. v. AH Gresham Park, LLC; AH Albion House, LLC; TMG Property Management Services NW, LLC; and Atlas Property Management_ord
case_name: James E. Jacobson, Jr. v. AH Gresham Park, LLC; AH Albion House, LLC; TMG Property Management Services NW, LLC; and Atlas Property Management
accommodation_description: Jacobson requested a 'simple space swap' to obtain a wheelchair-accessible parking spot that GPA management had assigned to other tenants.
key_holding: The Court dismissed Jacobson's federal action with prejudice because his claims were barred by res judicata, as they arose from the same factual transactions underlying his previously filed state court action that resulted in a final judgment with prejudice.
brief_summary: Jacobson, a wheelchair-using tenant at Gresham Park Apartments, sued his landlords and property managers claiming they denied his request for a wheelchair-accessible parking spot and engaged in various retaliatory and discriminatory conduct. The federal court dismissed the case with prejudice based on res judicata, finding that Jacobson's claims arose from the same factual transactions that were or could have been litigated in a prior state court action that resulted in a final judgment with prejudice.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Wheelchair-accessible parking spot; plaintiff requested reassignment of accessible parking spot that defendants had assigned to other tenants
fha_claims.disposition: Dismissed with prejudice under res judicata
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the FHA reasonable accommodation claim on res judicata grounds under Oregon law, finding that the same factual transactions and claims were raised or could have been raised in plaintiff's prior state court action that resulted in a final judgment with prejudice. The court did not reach the substantive merits of the accommodation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III accessibility claims, ORLTA habitability claims, Oregon financial abuse statute, fraud, negligence, conversion, trespass to chattels, breach of implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, intentional infliction of emotional distress
fha_claims.disposition: Dismissed with prejudice under res judicata
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA claims were dismissed on res judicata grounds under Oregon law. The court found that plaintiff's federal and state law claims in this action were based on the same underlying transactions and events as those raised in his prior state court action, which resulted in a final judgment with prejudice. The court did not reach the substantive merits of any non-FHA claims.

source_file: 10767966_2025_Angel Lopez and Kazue Koizumi v. Edward Pec, et al._njd
case_name: Angel Lopez and Kazue Koizumi v. Edward Pec, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff Angel Lopez requested a handicapped parking space near his apartment as a reasonable accommodation for his asthma and COPD disability.
key_holding: The court dismissed Lopez's FHA reasonable accommodation claim with prejudice because his allegations were conclusory—he failed to plead specific facts showing how a handicapped parking space was necessary to afford him an equal opportunity to use and enjoy his dwelling, as opposed to merely being something he would prefer.
brief_summary: Angel Lopez and Kazue Koizumi sued their landlord Edward Pec and The Palisades LLC, as well as attorneys Brandon Broderick and Christopher Karounos, alleging Fair Housing Act violations including failure to provide a reasonable accommodation (handicapped parking space) for Lopez's asthma and COPD, along with claims of harassment, invasion of privacy, and discrimination based on race and disability. The Court granted both motions to dismiss, dismissing the FHA reasonable accommodation claim with prejudice because Lopez failed to plead specific facts demonstrating how the requested parking accommodation was necessary to afford him an equal opportunity to use and enjoy his dwelling.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Lapid-Laurel, L.L.C. v. Zoning Bd. of Adjustment of Twp. of Scotch Plains
Vorchheimer v. Philadelphian Owners Ass'n
Sporn v. Ocean Colony Condo. Ass'n

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Handicapped parking space for Plaintiff Lopez due to asthma and COPD; plaintiff alleges he was forced to park far away and walk long distances, impacting his breathing, especially when carrying groceries
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff failed to plead specific facts showing how the requested accommodation was necessary to afford equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling, as opposed to merely preferable. Plaintiff alleged only conclusory statements that walking long distances 'impacts' asthma without medical evidence or detailed factual support.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Repairs to water leaks and mold remediation in apartment to accommodate Plaintiff Lopez's asthma and COPD
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found allegations conclusory and failed to sufficiently allege how refusal to repair water leaks and mold constituted discrimination based on disability or denial of reasonable accommodation under the FHA. Claims were barred by Rooker-Feldman doctrine as relating back to original state court allegations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged discrimination in refusing repairs and refusing to provide handicapped parking based on race, national origin, and disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff failed to sufficiently allege intentional discrimination based on race or national origin. The sole non-conclusory allegation (defendant's offensive statement about Polish heritage and Puerto Ricans) was insufficient to state a claim for FHA discrimination. No plausible facts supported inference that disability was a motivating factor.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title III ADA discrimination claim; Title II Civil Rights Act 1964 discrimination claim; state law harassment, stalking, cyber stalking, privacy violations, intentional infliction of emotional distress, public accommodation denial
fha_claims.reasoning: Title III ADA claims dismissed with prejudice because residential apartment complexes do not constitute 'places of public accommodation' under the ADA. Title II Civil Rights Act claims dismissed with prejudice for failure to satisfy mandatory notice requirement under 42 U.S.C. § 2000a-3(c) and because apartment is not a public accommodation. State law claims dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction and/or barred by Rooker-Feldman doctrine as relating to pending state court actions.

source_file: 10768029_2025_Scott Robert Moore v. Amy C. Yerkey, et al._cacd
case_name: Scott Robert Moore v. Amy C. Yerkey, et al.
accommodation_description: The underlying accommodation request is not described in this order; the opinion only references that plaintiff raised housing discrimination and retaliation claims against his landlord following an eviction proceeding.
key_holding: The Court accepted the Magistrate Judge's Report, dismissing Claims One through Four without further leave to amend, while authorizing service on Defendant Rosanna Domingo as to Claim Two (housing discrimination and retaliation) only.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Scott Robert Moore, a tenant, filed a pro se complaint against his landlord and state court officials following an eviction proceeding, raising Fair Housing Act and ADA claims. The Magistrate Judge recommended dismissing most claims based on Eleventh Amendment immunity, judicial immunity, and the Anti-Injunction Act, but recommended allowing Claim Two (housing discrimination and retaliation against the landlord) to proceed. The District Court accepted this Report and Recommendation, dismissing Claims One through Four without leave to amend while authorizing service on Defendant Domingo as to the surviving Claim Two.
key_cases_cited: Warda v. Santee Apartments LP, 2017 WL 1336843 (S.D. Cal. 2017)
Moore v. Capital Realty Group, Inc., 2023 WL 4699915 (W.D.N.Y. 2023)
Mitchum v. Foster, 407 U.S. 225 (1972)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claims under Title II of the ADA, Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, and other non-FHA statutes related to alleged violations during unlawful detainer proceeding in state court
fha_claims.disposition: 12(b)(1) / Eleventh Amendment / Judicial Immunity / Anti-Injunction Act
fha_claims.reasoning: Claims against Judge Yerkey and state courts were barred by the Eleventh Amendment, judicial immunity, and the Anti-Injunction Act. The ADA Title II and Rehabilitation Act claims do not satisfy the Mitchum v. Foster exception to the Anti-Injunction Act, and the state court's receipt of federal funding was insufficient to waive Eleventh Amendment immunity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claims against Sheriff Luna for failure to investigate challenges to the eviction order and alleged failure to engage in interactive process regarding disability accommodations
fha_claims.reasoning: Sheriff had a mandatory duty to serve the writ of possession and no duty to investigate challenges to the state court's eviction order. Plaintiff failed to allege exclusion from any benefit or service offered by the Sheriff's Department, and the Sheriff has no authority to delay enforcement of a judgment. Claims attacking the implementation of a state court order by suing individuals responsible for effecting that decision are barred under Rooker-Feldman.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claim seeking an accounting of Defendant Domingo's assets
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff lacks standing to demand an accounting because he does not allege he would be entitled to any funds that Defendant Domingo allegedly obtained wrongfully.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claim for housing discrimination and retaliation against landlord (Claim Two); injunctive relief under the Fair Housing Act
fha_claims.disposition: Partial dismissal of injunctive relief component; claim against landlord survives
fha_claims.reasoning: The injunctive relief component of Claim Two is barred by the Anti-Injunction Act because the Fair Housing Act claim is enforceable in both state and federal court and does not satisfy the Mitchum exception. However, the underlying housing discrimination and retaliation claim against the landlord (Defendant Rosanna Domingo) survives the motion to dismiss and proceeds to service.

case_name: Charles Ray Johnson v. Norman Rinehart
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request was described; plaintiff's complaint was too vague and conclusory to identify any particular accommodation sought.
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA and ADA claims were dismissed without prejudice because his complaint contained only conclusory statements and general legal references without specific factual allegations establishing that he is disabled, that he was discriminated against based on race, or that defendant took retaliatory action against him.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Charles Ray Johnson sued landlord Norman Rinehart alleging ADA discrimination, race-based housing discrimination, disability discrimination, and retaliation under the Fair Housing Act. The court granted in forma pauperis status but dismissed all claims without prejudice under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) for failure to state a claim, finding Johnson's complaint contained only conclusory legal assertions and highlighted sections from a judicial system overview without any specific factual allegations supporting his claims.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Gallagher v. Magner, 619 F.3d 823 (8th Cir. 2010)
Martin v. Sargent, 780 F.2d 1334 (8th Cir. 1985)
Stone v. Harry, 364 F.3d 912 (8th Cir. 2004)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination based on race and disability in housing
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege specific facts establishing disparate treatment based on race. Underlining phrases on a general housing discrimination overview and references in the civil cover sheet (which is not a pleading) do not provide sufficient factual allegations to raise a right to relief above the speculative level under Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation related to disability in housing (plaintiff referenced refusing to allow disabled person to make reasonable accommodations to dwelling but provided no specific facts)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish that he meets the definition of a disabled individual under the FHA. Without establishing disability status, any reasonable accommodation claim cannot proceed. Plaintiff provided no facts establishing his alleged disability meets the FHA definition.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation for filing a complaint; defendant banned plaintiff from property and prevented him from seeing his family
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to establish a prima facie retaliation claim. Plaintiff did not provide details about the complaint made, who it was made to, how it constitutes protected activity, whether defendant was aware of it, or facts establishing retaliatory motive.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) Title II and Title III discrimination claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff named only a private individual defendant, against whom Title II ADA claims are not cognizable (Title II applies only to public entities). Title III claims require plaintiff to establish disability status under the ADA, which plaintiff failed to do. Plaintiff provided no facts establishing his alleged disability meets the ADA definition.

source_file: 10769132_2026_Judy Shaw Foundation v. City of Howard, South Dakota_sdd
case_name: Judy Shaw Foundation v. City of Howard, South Dakota
accommodation_description: The City enacted zoning ordinances requiring a special exception for group homes and residential chemical dependency treatment centers, allegedly discriminating against disabled individuals with substance use disorders.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for JSF on the issue that a residential chemical dependency treatment center was a permissible use under existing zoning ('service establishment') without needing a special exception, denied the City's motion on the FHA disparate treatment claim finding evidence of discriminatory intent in enacting the ordinances, and denied JSF's motion on the City's advice-of-counsel defense which remains for jury determination.
brief_summary: Judy Shaw Foundation (JSF), which owned property in Howard, South Dakota, sued the City of Howard after the city enacted ordinances requiring a special exception to operate a residential chemical dependency treatment center on property JSF was selling to iRecover US, Inc. The court granted summary judgment for JSF on its ADA claim (for lack of standing), denied summary judgment for both parties on JSF's FHA disparate treatment claim (finding evidence of discriminatory intent), granted JSF partial summary judgment on the interpretive question of whether the treatment center was a permissible use under existing zoning, and denied JSF's motion on the City's advice-of-counsel defense.
key_cases_cited: Gallagher v. 56 Lean Corp., 619 F.3d 823 (8th Cir. 2010)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, Inc., 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Durand v. Fairview Health Servs., 902 F.3d 836 (8th Cir. 2018)
Hernon v. Revere Copper & Brass, Inc., 494 F.2d 705 (8th Cir. 1974)
Stockwell v. McCook Cnty. Bd. of Comm'rs, 2 N.W.3d 236 (S.D. 2024)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of use of property as residential chemical dependency treatment center; alleged discrimination against future residents with disabilities (individuals recovering from chemical dependency)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found sufficient evidence of proximate causation under the FHA's Miami framework. The record showed a direct relation between JSF's monetary damages (from iRecover's withdrawal) and the City's adoption of Ordinances 745 and 746, which iRecover's CEO testified was a 'significant' factor in the decision to abandon the purchase agreement. Summary judgment was denied because a genuine issue of material fact exists regarding causation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (regulatory takings under Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments); South Dakota tortious interference with business relations or expectancy; ADA Title II and Section 504 Rehabilitation Act (associational standing claim)
fha_claims.reasoning: On the § 1983 takings claim, the court found sufficient evidence of causation under the Penn Central balancing test. iRecover's CEO testified that Ordinance 746 was a 'significant' factor in the decision to withdraw, creating a genuine issue of material fact. On the tortious interference claim, the court similarly found that the City's passage of Ordinance 746 was a 'significant' factor that would have complicated the proposed use, satisfying the but-for causation standard. The ADA/RA claim was dismissed on standing grounds (lack of associational standing), not on the merits.

source_file: 10769187_2026_Judy Shaw Foundation v. City of Howard, South Dakota_sdd
case_name: Judy Shaw Foundation v. City of Howard, South Dakota
accommodation_description: JSF alleged the City enacted discriminatory zoning ordinances (745 and 746) to exclude residential chemical dependency treatment centers serving disabled individuals (those recovering from substance use disorders), requiring them to obtain a special exception permit.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for the City on JSF's ADA claim for lack of standing, but denied the City's motion on JSF's FHA disparate treatment claim, finding genuine issues of material fact exist regarding the City's discriminatory intent in enacting the zoning ordinances, including what advice of counsel the City received and whether the treatment center was already a permitted use under the existing ordinance.
brief_summary: Judy Shaw Foundation (JSF), which owned the Howard Hotel property in Howard, South Dakota, sued the City of Howard after iRecover backed out of purchasing the property to operate a residential chemical dependency treatment center, allegedly due to the City's enactment of zoning Ordinances 745 and 746 requiring a special exception permit for group homes and treatment facilities. The court granted summary judgment for the City on JSF's ADA claim (lack of standing), but denied summary judgment on JSF's FHA disparate treatment claim, finding genuine disputes of material fact exist regarding the City's discriminatory intent, including whether the treatment center was already a permitted use under existing zoning and what advice of counsel the City received before enacting the ordinances.
key_cases_cited: City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, Inc., 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Gallagher v. Catholic Health Initiatives, 619 F.3d 823 (8th Cir. 2010)
Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)
Durand v. Fairview Health Servs., 902 F.3d 836 (8th Cir. 2018)
McCullum v. Orlando Reg'l Healthcare Sys., Inc., 768 F.3d 1135 (11th Cir. 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges the City discriminated against the Property's future residents (individuals recovering from chemical dependency) by adopting Ordinances 745 and 746, which required a special exception permit for residential chemical dependency treatment centers, thereby preventing the Property from being used as a residential treatment facility.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found a genuine issue of material fact regarding causation. The record shows a direct relation between JSF's monetary damages (from iRecover's withdrawal) and the City's adoption of Ordinances 745 and 746, as iRecover's CEO testified the ordinance was a 'significant' factor in the decision to withdraw. The court applied the FHA proximate cause standard from Bank of America v. Miami and found sufficient evidence of direct relation to survive summary judgment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (regulatory takings violation under Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments); South Dakota tortious interference with business relations or expectancy; Americans with Disabilities Act Title II; Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act
fha_claims.reasoning: On the § 1983 takings claim, the court found the claim ripe under the Bannum exception because the City enacted ordinances targeting iRecover's purchase agreement after JSF had already signed a contract, imposing an additional burden on a previously contemplated use. On tortious interference, the court found a genuine issue of material fact regarding causation because iRecover's CEO testified the ordinance was a 'significant' factor in withdrawing from the contract, and but-for causation does not require the defendant's conduct to be the sole cause. On ADA/RA, the court granted summary judgment for the City because JSF lacked associational standing—JSF had only a contractual relationship with iRecover, not an association with disabled persons as required under Loeffler or McCullum.

source_file: 10769217_2026_Gerard Torres, + 2 Children v. Alexis Winnell, Property Manager, et al._mad
case_name: Gerard Torres, + 2 Children v. Alexis Winnell, Property Manager, et al.
accommodation_description: Torres requested accommodations for participation in court proceedings—specifically, clear plain-language explanations of filings, motions, and orders; extra time to read, understand, and respond to court documents; assistance from court staff or an appointed advocate if necessary; and any other accommodations the court deemed appropriate—asserting a mental impairment and invoking Title II of the ADA and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act.
key_holding: The court lacks subject matter jurisdiction over the plaintiff's complaint because his pleading fails to identify any disability, discriminatory conduct, or how he exercised rights under the Fair Housing Act or other federal statutes, and complete diversity of citizenship is absent.
brief_summary: Gerard Torres, a self-represented disabled tenant in Roslindale, Massachusetts, filed suit against his property manager and fellow residents alleging harassment, defamation, car tampering, and—in a later TRO motion—retaliation under the FHA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act after receiving a 7-Day Notice to Quit. The court found it lacked both federal question and diversity subject matter jurisdiction because Torres's complaint contained no well-pleaded federal claim (he identified no disability, no discriminatory conduct tied to that disability, and no exercise of federal statutory rights), and the parties lacked complete diversity. The court denied Torres's motions for IFP status, a temporary restraining order, and court-proceeding accommodations, and directed him to file an amended complaint within 28 days if he wished to proceed.
key_cases_cited: Castillo Condo. Ass’n v. U.S. Dep't of Hous. & Urb. Dev., 821 F.3d 92 (1st Cir. 2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1331 because the complaint does not contain a well-pleaded claim arising under federal law. Although Mr. Torres invoked the FHA in his motion for a temporary restraining order, alleging retaliation for asserting FHA rights, the original complaint did not identify any disability, describe discrimination based on disability, or explain how he exercised FHA rights, and thus did not establish federal question jurisdiction.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodations in housing-related rules, policies, or practices related to alleged disability (mental impairment); specific accommodation not identified in complaint
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because the complaint does not plausibly allege a failure to provide reasonable accommodations under the FHA. Mr. Torres did not identify his disability, how defendants discriminated against him based on that disability, or what specific accommodations were requested or denied in the housing context.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II and Section 504 Rehabilitation Act claims for accommodations in legal proceedings (clear language explanations, extra time, court staff assistance)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that Title II of the ADA and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act do not apply to federal courts. Title II applies only to state and local government entities, and Section 504 applies only to programs receiving federal financial assistance or conducted by Executive agencies; federal courts do not fall within either category. The court noted that Mr. Torres may request case-specific accommodations by motion as necessitated by his asserted mental impairment.

source_file: 10769390_2026_Dewanna Johnson, et al. v. Providence Homeowners Association and FirstService Residential Texas, Inc.; McKinney Housing Authority v. Providence Homeowners Association and FirstService Residential Texas, Inc
case_name: Dewanna Johnson, et al. v. Providence Homeowners Association and FirstService Residential Texas, Inc.; McKinney Housing Authority v. Providence Homeowners Association and FirstService Residential Texas, Inc.
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested; this is a discriminatory policy case involving a ban on rentals to tenants who use Section 8 Housing Choice Vouchers to pay rent, which the court analyzes as a facially neutral policy alleged to be motivated by racial animus against the predominantly Black voucher-holding population.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motions to dismiss plaintiffs' disparate treatment, hostile housing environment harassment, racial intimidation, and retaliation claims, finding plaintiffs plausibly alleged that the Section 8 voucher ban was racially motivated, while dismissing with prejudice the disparate impact claims of the Johnson Plaintiffs and McKinney Housing.
brief_summary: Three consolidated Fair Housing Act cases challenge a 2022 Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher ban enacted by the Providence Homeowners Association (PHOA) and managed by FirstService Residential Texas in a Dallas suburb, which displaced a predominantly Black voucher-holding tenant population. The court denied most motions to dismiss, holding that plaintiffs plausibly alleged racial discriminatory intent behind the facially neutral voucher ban based on Board members' use of racially coded language, procedural departures in rule-making, and the fact that 93% of affected voucher holders were Black—distinguishing the case from the Fifth Circuit's Lincoln Property decision. The disparate impact claims of the Johnson Plaintiffs and McKinney Housing were dismissed with prejudice, while all other claims, including hostile housing environment harassment, racial intimidation, and retaliation, survived.
key_cases_cited: Lincoln Property Co. v. Rankin, 920 F.3d 900 (5th Cir. 2019)
Village of Arlington Heights v. Metropolitan Housing Development Corp., 429 U.S. 252 (1977)
Cicalese v. Univ. of Tex. Med. Branch, 924 F.3d 762 (5th Cir. 2019)
Swierkiewicz v. Sorema North America, 534 U.S. 506 (2002)
Ames v. Ohio Dep't of Youth Servs., 605 U.S. 303 (2025)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Under Lincoln Property's robust causality requirement, plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege that the Voucher Ban policy caused black or female tenants to be the dominant group of voucher holders in Providence, or that a change in enforcement caused a disparate impact. The statistical disparities relied upon preexisted the policy's enactment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs plausibly alleged that race motivated the Voucher Ban's enactment despite its facially neutral application, through allegations of racially coded language by Board members, procedural departures from normal decision-making, and the substantially disparate impact on a 93% black voucher-holder population already residing in Providence. The complaint states sufficient facts to nudge the claim from conceivable to plausible under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Hostile housing environment harassment and racial intimidation
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs alleged hostile housing environment harassment and racial intimidation through social media posts, Board member participation in discriminatory discussions, and failure to address threatening conduct. The court found plausible claims for relief under Rule 12(b)(6) without detailed analysis of the specific legal theory.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation for exercising FHA rights
fha_claims.reasoning: McKinney Housing alleged retaliation claims. The court found plausible claims for relief under Rule 12(b)(6) without detailed substantive analysis, denying the motion to dismiss.

accommodation_description: Not applicable. This is not a reasonable accommodation or modification case. The central issue is defendants' categorical ban on renting to tenants who use federal Housing Choice Vouchers (Section 8) to pay rent, which plaintiffs allege was enacted because of the race of the voucher-holding population (93% Black) rather than the payment mechanism itself.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motions to dismiss disparate treatment, hostile housing environment, and retaliation claims, finding plaintiffs plausibly alleged that racial animus motivated the HOA's Section 8 voucher ban, but dismissed disparate impact claims for the Johnson and McKinney plaintiffs with prejudice.
brief_summary: Three consolidated Fair Housing Act cases arise from a 2022 decision by Providence Homeowners Association and its property manager FirstService to implement a ban on rentals to tenants using Housing Choice Vouchers (Section 8) in Providence Village, Texas, where 93% of voucher-holding households were Black. Individual tenants, fair housing nonprofits, and two government housing authorities allege the ban was racially motivated, supported by Board members' racially coded social media comments, procedural departures from normal voting processes, and continued racial hostility after the ban's enactment. The court denied the bulk of defendants' Rule 12(b)(6) motions, holding that plaintiffs plausibly alleged intentional race discrimination under a flexible pleading standard, while dismissing disparate impact claims for the Johnson and McKinney plaintiffs.

The complaint states sufficient facts to nudge the claim from conceivable to plausible under Iqbal/Twombly.

brief_summary: Current and former Providence Village tenants and two public housing authorities sued the HOA and its property manager alleging the HOA's ban on Section 8 voucher holders (implemented in 2022) constituted intentional race discrimination under § 3604(a). The court denied defendants' motions to dismiss the disparate-treatment claims, finding plaintiffs plausibly alleged racially coded language and procedural irregularities suggesting race motivated the policy, while dismissing the disparate-impact claims with prejudice.

The complaint sufficiently pleads the ultimate elements of disparate treatment to survive Rule 12(b)(6).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Hostile housing environment harassment and racial intimidation related to voucher holders

The court found plausible claims for relief and denied dismissal, though noting uncertainty about whether a hostile housing environment claim is viable in the Fifth Circuit.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation for exercising FHA rights

source_file: 10769863_2026_Marceline Hope Engler v. The Salvation Army_arwd
case_name: Marceline Hope Engler v. The Salvation Army
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a transgender woman, alleges she was prevented from using the women's bathroom and was evicted from The Salvation Army facility based on gender identity.
key_holding: The complaint was dismissed because it failed to allege sufficient facts establishing that The Salvation Army's facility qualified as a 'dwelling' under the FHA, and the damages claim of $900 fell below the jurisdictional minimum for diversity jurisdiction.
brief_summary: Marceline Hope Engler, a pro se transgender plaintiff, sued The Salvation Army alleging sex/gender-identity discrimination after being prevented from using the women's bathroom and being evicted from the facility. The court dismissed the complaint without prejudice, finding the plaintiff failed to allege facts establishing the Salvation Army facility qualified as a 'dwelling' under the Fair Housing Act, and the claim fell below the jurisdictional threshold for diversity jurisdiction.
key_cases_cited: Hunter ex rel. A.H. v. D.C., 64 F.Supp.3d 158 (D.D.C. 2014)
Intermountain Fair Hous. Council v. Boise Rescue Mission Ministries, 717 F. Supp. 2d 1101 (D. Idaho 2010)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Access to women's bathroom; not dismissed on accommodation grounds but on jurisdictional/pleading grounds
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed under § 1915(e)(2) screening for failure to state a plausible FHA claim. Although plaintiff alleged sex/gender-identity discrimination, the complaint failed to allege sufficient facts regarding the nature of the housing relationship, location, and duration of stay at the alleged Salvation Army shelter to permit analysis of whether the facility qualifies as a 'dwelling' under 42 U.S.C. § 3602(b), which is a threshold requirement for FHA coverage.

source_file: 10769944_2026_James B. Herrera v. Maddox Management, LLC_nmd
case_name: James B. Herrera v. Maddox Management, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged in his Amended Complaint that he suffered from documented medical and psychological disabilities and had requested reasonable accommodations from Defendant, which were ignored; however, he did not specify in either the Amended Complaint or the Second Amended Complaint the nature or content of the accommodations requested.
key_holding: The court dismissed all claims in Plaintiff's Second Amended Complaint with prejudice for failure to state a claim under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e), finding that Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege disability discrimination or retaliation under the Fair Housing Act and the Rehabilitation Act, with the sole exception that the portion of Count I challenging the state court damages award was dismissed without prejudice under Rooker-Feldman.
brief_summary: Plaintiff James Herrera sued his former landlord, Maddox Management, LLC, alleging that during eviction proceedings Defendant responded to rental verification inquiries from prospective landlords with false or misleading information, causing him to lose housing at Tesoro Apartments and forfeit his Section 8 voucher, and that Defendant retaliated against him by seeking inflated damages in state court. The court conducted a sua sponte review under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e) and found that Plaintiff's Second Amended Complaint failed to plausibly allege causation (the rental verification predated his HUD complaint by months), failed to plead sufficient factual allegations of disability status or Defendant's discriminatory intent, and failed to allege that the rental verification forms actually contained the false information Plaintiff claimed. After two prior opportunities to amend, the court dismissed all claims with prejudice, declining to grant a third leave to amend.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Morgan v. Carrington Mortg. Servs., 719 F. App'x 735 (10th Cir. 2017)
Wilkerson v. Shinseki, 606 F.3d 1256 (10th Cir. 2010)
Hall v. Bellmon, 935 F.2d 1106 (10th Cir. 1991)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged Defendant retaliated by providing adverse rental verification information to prospective landlords and seeking inflated damages in eviction proceedings after Plaintiff filed a HUD complaint in May 2024.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege causation because the rental verification was signed on January 3, 2024, months before the alleged protected activity (HUD complaint filed in May 2024), making temporal sequence impossible. Plaintiff also failed to plausibly allege Defendant's intent to discriminate or awareness of protected activity with only conclusory allegations unsupported by factual allegations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged Defendant discriminated based on disability by providing misleading or false rental verification information to prospective landlords, denying him housing.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege disability discrimination under § 3604(f)(1) because he provided only conclusory allegations of disability without factual allegations describing the impairment or its substantial limitation on major life activities. Plaintiff also failed to allege that Defendant denied him a dwelling because of disability; rather, Defendant merely responded to rental verification inquiries from prospective landlords, which does not fall under the FHA's prohibition on denying dwellings.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act (29 U.S.C. § 794(a)); Plaintiff alleged Defendant discriminated based on disability by providing adverse rental verification information.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie case under the Rehabilitation Act by failing to plausibly allege: (1) disability with factual allegations describing the impairment and its substantial limitation on major life activities; (2) that Defendant is a recipient of federal financial assistance or a 'program or activity' under § 794(b)(3); and (3) that Defendant denied Plaintiff benefits or excluded him from a federally-funded program, as opposed to merely responding to a rental verification request.

source_file: 10770206_2026_Telvon Taylor v. Westland Real Estate Group, LLC., et al._nvd
case_name: Telvon Taylor v. Westland Real Estate Group, LLC., et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges he was evicted despite paying rent in violation of the Fair Housing Act because of his disabilities, requesting that the eviction be prevented as a reasonable accommodation.
key_holding: At the § 1915(e) screening stage, the court found that plaintiff adequately alleged a plausible FHA reasonable accommodation claim because he sufficiently alleged he is disabled, defendants knew of his disability, the accommodation to address hazardous conditions was necessary to afford equal enjoyment of the dwelling, and defendants refused to make such accommodation.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Telvon Taylor, a disabled tenant, sued Westland Real Estate Group, LLC and Hacienda Hills Apartment alleging disability discrimination under the Fair Housing Act and wrongful eviction after he complained about hazardous conditions including mold exposure. The court granted Taylor's in forma pauperis application and, at the § 1915(e) screening stage, found his complaint stated a plausible FHA reasonable accommodation claim sufficient to proceed past screening.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Dubois v. Ass'n of Apartment Owners of 2987 Kalakaua, 453 F.3d 1175 (9th Cir. 2006)
United States v. Cal. Mobile Home Park Mgmt. Co., 107 F.3d 1374 (9th Cir. 1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Remediation of hazardous conditions (mold exposure) at the rental property to accommodate plaintiff's disability
fha_claims.reasoning: At the initial § 1915(e) screening stage, the court found that plaintiff plausibly alleged all four elements of a prima facie reasonable accommodation claim under the Iqbal/Twombly standard: disability, defendant's knowledge, necessity of accommodation, and refusal. The complaint survived screening and proceeds to the next stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Wrongful eviction claim under NRS 118A.390 (Nevada state law); due process violation (federal)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court liberally construed plaintiff's due process claim as a wrongful eviction claim under Nevada state law and found that plaintiff stated a colorable claim at the screening stage, allowing it to proceed past § 1915(e) review.

source_file: 10770715_2026_Cincinnati Insurance Company v. Lost Run Farm Community Association, Inc., Armour Property Management, LLC, Vincent Kroon, Ben Wheat, Scott Bruns, Ashlee Wheat, Edward Kowlowitz, Rebecca Kiell, John Garcia,
case_name: Cincinnati Insurance Company v. Lost Run Farm Community Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: The Garcias requested a fence to contain their dogs as an accommodation for Mary Kay Garcia's disability, which the Board denied.
key_holding: The insurer had no duty to defend or indemnify because the CGL coverage did not apply (the intentional discriminatory acts were not an 'occurrence') and the Wrongful Acts coverage exclusions barred coverage (dishonest/malicious acts, civil rights violations, emotional distress).
brief_summary: Cincinnati Insurance Company sought declaratory judgment that it had no duty to defend or indemnify Lost Run Farm HOA, its board members, and property management company Armour against the Garcias' discrimination claims in underlying state litigation. The court granted Cincinnati's summary judgment motion, finding no coverage under the CGL policy (intentional discriminatory acts did not constitute an 'occurrence') and no coverage under the Wrongful Acts policy (exclusions for dishonest/malicious acts and civil rights violations applied).
key_cases_cited: Jim Barna Log Sys. Midwest, Inc. v. Gen. Cas. Ins. Co. of Wisconsin, 791 N.E.2d 816 (Ind. Ct. App. 2003)
Auto-Owners Ins. Co. v. Harvey, 842 N.E.2d 1279 (Ind. 2006)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request for exception to fence prohibition to contain dogs and address steepness of 27-foot hill on property due to Mary Kay Garcia's disability
fha_claims.reasoning: The court did not reach the merits of the FHA reasonable accommodation claim because it was analyzing an insurance coverage dispute. The underlying FHA claims in the Garcias' counterclaim were not directly adjudicated in this federal insurance case; rather, the court determined Cincinnati Insurance had no duty to defend the HOA defendants under the insurance policy's exclusions for intentional/malicious acts and civil rights violations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination based on race and national origin (John Garcia) and disability (Mary Kay Garcia) in enforcement of restrictive covenants
fha_claims.reasoning: The court did not reach the merits of the FHA disparate treatment claims because it was analyzing insurance coverage. The court determined Cincinnati had no duty to defend under the policy's exclusion for violations of civil rights laws and malicious acts, but did not adjudicate the underlying discrimination claims on their merits.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Civil Rights Act of 1866 (42 U.S.C. § 1982), Indiana Fair Housing Act, intentional infliction of emotional distress, breach of fiduciary duty, breach of duty of loyalty, breach of duty to act in good faith, enforcement of restrictive covenants, breach of contract, declaratory judgment
fha_claims.reasoning: The court determined Cincinnati Insurance had no duty to defend the HOA defendants on any of the Garcias' non-FHA and FHA claims because the insurance policy excluded coverage for intentional/malicious acts, civil rights violations, emotional distress, and abuse of process. The court did not reach the merits of these underlying claims.

source_file: 10770839_2026_United States of America v. Juliet Payseur and 20-22 McGregor Avenue, LLC_njd
case_name: United States of America v. Juliet Payseur and 20-22 McGregor Avenue, LLC
accommodation_description: No accommodation request at issue; case involves race-based housing discrimination and retaliation claims.
key_holding: The court granted in part Doyle's motion to strike, striking Defendants' second, fifth, eighth (unclean hands portion), thirteenth, and fourteenth affirmative defenses as insufficient, while denying the motion as to the first (failure to state a claim) defense and denying Defendants' request for sanctions.
brief_summary: Brittany Doyle, a Black woman, intervened as a plaintiff in this Fair Housing Act enforcement action alleging that Defendants discriminated against her based on race by imposing discriminatory lease terms and retaliating against her after she filed a HUD complaint. The court ruled on Doyle's motion to strike Defendants' affirmative defenses, striking several as legally insufficient while denying others and also denying Defendants' request for sanctions.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Ashcroft v. Iqbal

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court ruled on a motion to strike affirmative defenses, not on the merits of the FHA claim itself. Doyle's disparate treatment claim (based on race and discriminatory lease terms) survives the procedural challenge and remains pending. The court struck several affirmative defenses (causation, failure to mitigate, unclean hands, and punitive damages defenses) but did not reach the substantive merits of the underlying FHA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Doyle alleged retaliation under § 3617 for filing an FHA complaint with HUD, including harassment, surveillance cameras, and deprivation of heating oil. The court's opinion addresses only affirmative defenses, not the merits of the retaliation claim, which survives and remains pending.

source_file: 10770867_2026_Hector Salvatori v. The Huntington National Bank_ohsd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Mortgage loan approval based on immigration status discrimination (42 U.S.C. § 1981 and 15 U.S.C. § 1691 ECOA)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's § 1981 claim for discrimination in contract formation falls under § 1981(a), which predates the 1991 amendment, and thus is subject to Ohio's one-year statute of limitations under O.R.C. § 4112.055(A)(1). The claim was filed over two years after the September 17, 2021 denial, making it time-barred. No tolling provision applies because the Fair Housing Act tolling provision cited by plaintiff does not apply to § 1981 claims, and the Sixth Circuit has held there are no tolling provisions for administrative complaints filed with OCRC.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Mortgage loan denial under Equal Credit Opportunity Act (15 U.S.C. § 1691; 12 C.F.R. § 1002.6)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead the required elements of an ECOA claim. Although plaintiff alleged denial based on immigration status, he failed to allege explicitly in the complaint that he is a member of a protected class (race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, or age). The assertion of Venezuelan nationality and asylum status appears only in the opposition motion, not in the complaint itself, and plaintiff's allegation that denial was based 'solely' on immigration status does not establish discrimination based on a protected characteristic.

source_file: 10772814_2026_Karen Sam _ Robert Sam v. Dekalb Housing Authority, et al._ilnd
case_name: Karen Sam & Robert Sam v. DeKalb Housing Authority, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs did not specifically identify what reasonable accommodations were requested, beyond vague references to accommodations that could have prevented their eviction and delay in processing a port request for their Section 8 voucher.
key_holding: The court dismissed the FHA reasonable accommodation claim because plaintiffs failed to allege what specific accommodations were requested or how their disabilities connected to the alleged wrongs, and failed to state plausible disparate treatment or disparate impact claims.
brief_summary: Karen and Robert Sam, proceeding pro se, sued the DeKalb Housing Authority, HUD, and the City of Sycamore alleging Fair Housing Act violations and other claims arising from their eviction from Section 8 voucher housing and alleged delays in processing their request to port their voucher. The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss, finding the complaint failed to state what specific accommodations were requested or how they related to plaintiffs' disabilities, and failed to adequately plead disparate treatment, disparate impact, or reasonable accommodation claims.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Tex. Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Cmtys. Project, Inc.
Valencia v. City of Springfield, Ill.
Monell v. Dep't of Soc. Servs. Of City of New York
Trimuel v. Chicago Hous. Auth.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Port (transfer) of Housing Choice Voucher to a safer home in another jurisdiction; delay in processing port request
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to allege what reasonable accommodations could have prevented eviction and failed to connect their disabilities (multiple chronic medical conditions) to the alleged wrong (delay in processing port request). The court found no nexus between disability and the requested accommodation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs alleged intentional and retaliatory delay in processing port request but provided no basis for inference that delay was motivated by discriminatory intent. Mere delay without discriminatory motive is insufficient to state a disparate treatment claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to allege facts or produce statistical evidence demonstrating a causal connection between HACD's delay in processing port requests and disparate impact on a protected class. Complaint alleged bureaucratic delay but not discriminatory impact.
