fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 504 Rehabilitation Act, Title II ADA, § 1983 due process (substantive and procedural), Monell negligence and deliberate indifference, intentional infliction of emotional distress
fha_claims.reasoning: Substantive due process claim failed because loss of housing without violation of fundamental constitutional right is insufficient. Procedural due process claim failed because nexus between HUD/City of Sycamore and loss of housing was insufficiently pled; actual deprivation was by nonparty landlord. Monell claim failed because single incident without evidence of widespread practice is insufficient. IIED claim failed because unsuccessful calls, ignored emails, and slow governmental processes constitute mere indignities, not conduct beyond all bounds of decency.

source_file: 10773145_2025_Valery Kantsepolsky v. River Shores Association, Inc._flsd
case_name: Valery Kantsepolsky v. River Shores Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff with chemical sensitivities requested that defendant use disability-related precautions during any entry into her unit for exploratory demolition and repairs.
key_holding: The court recommended staying the FHA claims under Colorado River abstention doctrine rather than dismissing them, finding the parallel state proceedings involve substantially similar parties and issues, while dismissing the ADA claim because residential condominiums are not places of public accommodation subject to ADA Title III.
brief_summary: Valery Kantsepolsky, a condominium owner with chemical sensitivities, sued the River Shores Association alleging the HOA violated the FHA by denying her requests for disability-related precautions during unit inspections and by refusing to engage in an interactive process. The magistrate judge recommended granting the motion to dismiss in part, dismissing the ADA claim and staying the FHA claims pending resolution of parallel state court proceedings involving the same parties and substantially similar issues.
key_cases_cited: Hunt v. Aimco Props., L.P., 814 F.3d 1213 (11th Cir. 2016)
Colorado River Water Conservation District v. United States, 424 U.S. 800 (1976)
Taveras v. Bank of Am., N.A., 89 F.4th 1279 (11th Cir. 2024)
Ambrosia Coal & Constr. Co. v. Morales, 368 F.3d 1320 (11th Cir. 2004)
Moorer v. Demopolis Waterworks & Sewer Bd., 374 F.3d 994 (11th Cir. 2004)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Disability-related precautionary measures (approximately $3,000 in cost) to be used during exploratory demolition and potential repairs in plaintiff's condominium unit, including precautions against environmental exposures (chemicals, dust, mold, VOCs) that substantially limit plaintiff's ability to tolerate such exposures.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that the FHA claims survive the motion to dismiss under Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards when plaintiff's allegations are taken as true and liberally construed (pro se standard). However, the court stayed the FHA claims pending resolution of parallel state proceedings under the Colorado River abstention doctrine, finding that the state and federal cases involve substantially the same parties and issues, and that multiple Colorado River factors (piecemeal litigation risk, order of jurisdiction, reactive nature of federal suit) weigh heavily in favor of abstention.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act Title III claim based on same operative facts as FHA claims
fha_claims.reasoning: The ADA Title III claim was dismissed because residential condominiums are not places of public accommodation subject to ADA Title III compliance, and plaintiff failed to allege that defendant offers commercial services to the public. The court noted that Title III applies only to private entities offering commercial services, and residential facilities are explicitly excluded.

source_file: 10773598_2026_Brittany M. Chandler v. LoanCare, LLC; Lakeview Loan Servicing, LLC; and Trustee Corps_ord
case_name: Brittany M. Chandler v. LoanCare, LLC; Lakeview Loan Servicing, LLC; and Trustee Corps
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges LoanCare refused to provide financial assistance (forbearance, loan modification, or other mortgage relief) after learning of her disability, while offering such assistance to her non-disabled ex-boyfriend for the same property.
key_holding: The court found that plaintiff raised serious questions as to the merits of her Fair Housing Act disability discrimination claim alleging that the mortgage servicer offered financial assistance to her ex-boyfriend but refused to extend such assistance to her after learning of her disability, warranting a TRO to prevent foreclosure.
brief_summary: Brittany Chandler, a disabled homeowner with a neuromuscular autoimmune disease and mental health conditions, sued her mortgage servicer and foreclosure trustee alleging Fair Housing Act disability discrimination after LoanCare refused to provide financial assistance following her disability disclosure while offering assistance to her non-disabled ex-boyfriend. The court granted a temporary restraining order enjoining the foreclosure sale after finding serious questions on the merits of her disability discrimination claim and that the balance of hardships favored the plaintiff.
key_cases_cited: Winter v. Nat. Res. Def. Council, Inc., 555 U.S. 7 (2008)
All. for the Wild Rockies v. Cottrell, 632 F.3d 1127 (9th Cir. 2011)
Planned Parenthood Great Nw., Haw., Alaska, Ind., Ky. v. Labrador, 122 F.4th 825 (9th Cir. 2024)
Park Vill. Apartment Tenants Ass'n v. Mortimer Howard Tr., 636 F.3d 1150 (9th Cir. 2011)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Financial assistance or loan modification to address mortgage payment difficulties due to disability-related injury and inability to pay
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff raised serious questions as to the merits of disability discrimination claim under FHA by alleging defendant extended financial assistance to co-owner but not to plaintiff after learning of her disability. Court did not conduct full merits analysis but found sufficient serious questions to warrant preliminary relief pending further proceedings.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Differential treatment in offering financial assistance based on disability status
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff raised serious questions as to merits of disability discrimination claim by alleging LoanCare offered financial assistance to non-disabled co-owner but refused same assistance to plaintiff after learning of her disability, suggesting intentional discrimination based on protected status.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Wrongful foreclosure, fraud, and other federal law violations
fha_claims.reasoning: Court noted plaintiff raised serious questions as to merits of other claims beyond FHA but did not need to reach those claims to issue the TRO based on FHA discrimination questions alone.

source_file: 10774111_2026_Jacob O’Connor v. Collett’s Mountain Resorts, Inc. d_b_a Flaming Gorge Resort and Maretta Bair_utd
case_name: Jacob O'Connor v. Collett's Mountain Resorts, Inc. d/b/a Flaming Gorge Resort and Maretta Bair
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested to keep his trained diabetic alert dog, Smokey, in employer-provided shared employee housing. Smokey was trained to alert O'Connor or another human when O'Connor's blood glucose levels dropped or spiked, and O'Connor contended the dog was medically necessary to prevent unnoticed nocturnal hypoglycemic episodes that could result in coma or death.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss all seven causes of action, holding that plaintiff plausibly alleged ADA and FHA claims for failure to accommodate, wrongful termination/denial of housing, discriminatory statement, and retaliation based on defendants' refusal to allow his diabetic alert service dog in employer-provided housing and his subsequent termination.
brief_summary: Jacob O'Connor, a front desk clerk with Type 1 diabetes, sued his former employer Collett's Mountain Resorts after it refused to allow his trained diabetic alert dog in employer-provided employee housing and then terminated his employment when he protested the denial and mentioned seeking legal advice. The court held that employer-provided housing qualifies as a 'privilege of employment' under the ADA, that O'Connor's requests to multiple managers constituted protected activity, and that the close temporal connection between his accommodation requests and his firing supported plausible claims. The court denied defendants' Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss all seven causes of action arising under the ADA, the FHA, and the Utah Fair Housing Act.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Courage to Change Ranches Holding Co. v. El Paso
Cinnamon Hills Youth Crisis Ctr., Inc. v. Saint George City
Arnal v. Aspenview Condo. Ass'n

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to keep a trained diabetic alert service dog (Smokey) in employer-provided employee housing to alert plaintiff of dangerous blood glucose fluctuations
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff plausibly alleged all five elements of FHA failure-to-accommodate claim: disability, defendant's knowledge, necessity (trained dog prevents coma/death from nocturnal blood sugar drops), reasonableness (guests and other employees allowed pets), and refusal. Court rejected defendant's arguments that dog was unnecessary because plaintiff spent nights without it and that no certification requirement exists.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discriminatory statements by management regarding plaintiff's service animal and disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Court rejected defendant's argument that discriminatory statement claim should be dismissed for same reasons as reasonable accommodation claim, finding the elements are not identical and defendant provided no analysis or citations supporting dismissal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of housing (removal from employee housing)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court rejected defendant's argument that denial of housing claim should be dismissed for same reasons as reasonable accommodation claim, finding the arguments were unavailing.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Termination of employment and denial of housing in retaliation for requesting service animal accommodation and protesting its denial
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff plausibly alleged all three elements of § 3617 retaliation claim: protected activity (requesting accommodation for service dog), adverse action (termination and housing denial), and causal link (Ms. Bair stated protesting denial was reason for termination). Court found plaintiff need not use magic words to request accommodation and that Ms. Bair's statements directly connected protected activity to adverse action.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA claims: failure to accommodate, wrongful termination, retaliation; Utah Fair Housing Act claims (parallel to FHA claims)
fha_claims.reasoning: Under ADA, employer-provided housing qualifies as a 'privilege of employment' protected by 42 U.S.C. § 12112(a), and EEOC regulations confirm reasonable accommodations apply to non-work facilities provided by employers. Plaintiff plausibly alleged failure to accommodate (all four elements), wrongful termination (close timing and disability-related explanations support inference), and retaliation (protected activity of requesting accommodation, materially adverse termination, causal connection). UFHA claims survive for same reasons as FHA claims.

source_file: 10775296_2026_Jennifer Phillips v. Beckley Police Department and Officer Gregory and Officer Atterson and Officer Murray and Officer Birchfield and Officer Christian, in their individual and official capacities._wvsd
case_name: Jennifer Phillips v. Beckley Police Department et al.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation or modification was requested; the FHA claim was based on allegations that the Beckley Police Department's pattern of inaction in response to racially motivated harassment by neighbors, and Officer Murray's falsified or delayed police reports submitted to the Beckley Housing Authority, interfered with and discriminated against Phillips in the enjoyment of her federally protected housing rights.
key_holding: The court dismissed Jennifer Phillips' complaint against the Beckley Police Department and five officers, finding she failed to state a claim for § 1983 municipal liability, constitutional defamation, or Fair Housing Act violations, and overruled all objections to the magistrate judge's proposed findings and recommendation.
brief_summary: Jennifer Phillips, a pro se tenant at a Beckley Housing Authority property, sued the Beckley Police Department and five officers under § 1983 and the Fair Housing Act, alleging that officers falsified police reports, failed to protect her from racially motivated harassment by neighbors, subjected her to unlawful detention, and ignored her requests to correct official reports. The district court adopted the magistrate judge's recommendation, finding that Phillips failed to plead an official policy or custom for municipal liability, failed to allege a constitutionally cognizable deprivation for her defamation/stigma claim, and failed to allege a sufficient causal connection between any protected FHA activity and an adverse housing action. The court dismissed the complaint but held dismissal in abeyance until January 30, 2026, to allow Phillips an opportunity to file a curative amended complaint.
key_cases_cited: Paul v. Davis, 424 U.S. 693 (1976)
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Bank of Am. Corp. v. City of Miami, 581 U.S. 189 (2017)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Bd. of County Commis of Bryan County v. Brown, 520 U.S. 397 (1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged that the Beckley Police Department failed to properly investigate and respond to racial harassment by neighbors and that Officer Murray delayed amending police reports, which she characterized as retaliation for exercising FHA rights.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiff failed to allege a sufficient causal connection between any protected activity under the FHA and the alleged adverse action (police inaction, delayed report amendments, or housing instability). The court applied the four-part retaliation test from Title VII jurisprudence and found the nexus between the alleged protected activity and the asserted harm was too attenuated to state a plausible claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (Equal Protection, Unlawful Seizure/Detention, Retaliation for Exercising Rights and Reporting Misconduct, Negligent or Intentional Misrepresentation in Official Reports, Failure to Intervene/Supervisory Liability); defamation claim based on false police reports.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts showing constitutional violations by individual officers or an official policy or custom by the municipality. Regarding the defamation claim, reputational injury alone does not constitute a deprivation of liberty or property under the Fourteenth Amendment absent a tangible loss such as government employment. The court found no plausible allegations of constitutional harm.

source_file: 10776090_2026_Ernesto Varela, et al. v. William Harold Hill, et al._moed
case_name: Ernesto Varela, et al. v. William Harold Hill, et al.
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request; this case concerns alleged race-based harassment and threats (§ 3617 retaliation claim) rather than a reasonable accommodation request.
key_holding: The court sua sponte identified a potential statute of limitations bar for Count III under the FHA (§ 3617) because plaintiffs filed their action approximately five years after the alleged discriminatory conduct ended, beyond the two-year limitations period, and ordered plaintiffs to show cause why the claim should not be dismissed.
brief_summary: Ernesto Varela and others sued William Harold Hill and others alleging race-based harassment and threats that made their housing unavailable and caused them to move; Count III under the Fair Housing Act's anti-retaliation provision survived earlier motions but the court sua sponte ordered plaintiffs to show cause why this claim should not be dismissed as untimely because it was filed approximately five years after the alleged discriminatory conduct ended, beyond the two-year FHA statute of limitations.
key_cases_cited: Buckley v. Ray, 848 F.3d 855 (8th Cir. 2017)
Smith v. Boyd, 945 F.2d 1041 (8th Cir. 1991)
Smithrod v. City of St. Paul, 746 F.3d 391 (8th Cir. 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Count III under § 3617 alleges race-based harassment and threats. The complaint was filed July 12, 2023, nearly five years after plaintiffs moved on July 14, 2018, exceeding the FHA's two-year statute of limitations under 42 U.S.C. § 3613(a)(1)(A). The court issued an order to show cause why Count III should not be dismissed as untimely.

source_file: 10776210_2026_Bolima Tafah et al. v. Lake Village Townhomes et al._mdd
case_name: Bolima Tafah et al. v. Lake Village Townhomes et al.
accommodation_description: The complaint contains only conclusory allegations including 'refusal to accommodate postpartum recovery' and 'retaliation after request for accommodation' without specifying the nature of any accommodation request.
key_holding: The court dismissed the amended complaint for failure to state plausible claims because plaintiffs' allegations were merely conclusory statements lacking sufficient factual content to support any cause of action, including FHA reasonable accommodation claims.
brief_summary: Bolima Tafah and Akwi Suna Epse Tafah sued Lake Village Townhomes, Orchards at Severn, LLC, RentGrow, Inc., and Equifax alleging over 50 violations of federal and state law including Fair Housing Act claims. The court granted all defendants' motions to dismiss, finding the amended complaint failed to state plausible claims because it contained only conclusory legal conclusions without supporting factual allegations.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Postpartum recovery accommodation
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs alleged '[r]efusal to accommodate postpartum recovery violated FHA reasonable accommodation requirements' but provided only conclusory assertions without factual detail sufficient to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly. The court found the allegation was a bare legal conclusion lacking sufficient factual content.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation after request for accommodation
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs alleged '[r]etaliation after request for accommodation' but provided only conclusory assertions without factual allegations sufficient to state a plausible retaliation claim. The court found the allegation lacked the requisite factual content to allow reasonable inference of liability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rejection of public housing assistance (source-of-income discrimination)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs alleged '[r]ejection of public housing assistance' and '[r]efusing source-of-income assistance from ACDS' but provided only conclusory assertions without factual allegations. The court found these bare assertions failed to meet the pleading standard for discrimination claims under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) § 1681s-2(b) false reporting to credit bureaus; Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) 15 U.S.C. § 1692 et seq.; intentional infliction of emotional distress (IIED); fraud; due process violation under Fourteenth Amendment
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plead the required elements of FCRA, FDCPA, IIED, and fraud claims. For FCRA § 1681s-2(b), plaintiffs provided no factual allegations supporting the three required elements. For FDCPA, plaintiffs did not allege Lake Village was a debt collector. For IIED, plaintiffs provided only bare assertion of emotional distress without allegations of extreme and outrageous conduct. For fraud, plaintiffs failed to state with particularity the circumstances constituting fraud as required by Rule 9(b). The due process claim against a private company fails as a matter of law because the Fourteenth Amendment applies only to state actors.

source_file: 10776283_2026_Akosua AaeBo-Akhan v. Kwesi Akhan, et al._ksd
case_name: Akosua Aaebo-Akhan v. Kwesi Akhan, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought one million dollars in damages and reinstatement of her Section 8 housing status after the cancellation of her Section 8 voucher in 2022.
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA claim against HUD was dismissed because the United States has not waived sovereign immunity for claims under § 3617, and Plaintiff failed to allege facts sufficient to state a claim that HUD violated the Fair Housing Act.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Aaebo-Akhan, proceeding pro se, sued HUD seeking $1 million in damages and reinstatement of her Section 8 housing status after her voucher was cancelled in 2022, alleging her traffickers prevented her from submitting documents to HUD. The court dismissed her complaint against HUD under § 3617 of the Fair Housing Act because the United States has not waived sovereign immunity for such claims and Plaintiff failed to state facts sufficient to allege a FHA violation.
key_cases_cited: Kelly v. Wilson, 426 F. App'x 629 (10th Cir. 2011)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 8 housing voucher reinstatement; alleged cancellation due to third-party interference preventing submission of identity documents to HUD
fha_claims.disposition: Dismissal under § 1915(e)(2)(B) for failure to state a claim; sovereign immunity bar
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts supporting a Fair Housing Act violation under 42 U.S.C. § 3617, and the United States has not waived sovereign immunity for FHA claims. Plaintiff's allegations that a third party prevented her from submitting documents do not establish HUD's violation of the FHA.

source_file: 10776300_2025_Min Huang, Qiong Dai, and Jiayin Dong v. Ken Paxton, Attorney General of Texas, in his Official Capacity_txwd
case_name: Min Huang, Qiong Dai, and Jiayin Dong v. Ken Paxton, Attorney General of Texas, in his Official Capacity
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested; this case involves a constitutional and statutory preemption challenge to Texas Senate Bill 17, which prohibits non-U.S. citizens and non-permanent residents domiciled in designated countries (including China) from purchasing or renting property in Texas for more than one year.
key_holding: The court dismissed the claims of the two foreign-domiciled plaintiffs (Min Huang and Quiong Dai) because foreign citizens outside U.S. territory lack standing to assert constitutional rights under both Rule 12(b)(1) and Rule 12(b)(6), denied the preliminary injunction for lack of irreparable harm as to plaintiff Jiayin Dong, and stayed Dong's remaining claims pending the Fifth Circuit's ruling in Wang v. Paxton.
brief_summary: Three Chinese nationals challenged Texas Senate Bill 17, which makes it unlawful for non-U.S. citizens or permanent residents domiciled in China and certain other countries to purchase or rent property in Texas for more than one year, asserting claims including FHA preemption, Equal Protection, and Supremacy Clause violations. The court dismissed the claims of plaintiffs Min Huang and Quiong Dai—both domiciled outside the United States—holding that foreign citizens outside U.S. territory cannot assert constitutional rights under either 12(b)(1) or 12(b)(6), and rejected their argument that Supremacy Clause and Equal Protection claims could survive on alternative facts. The court denied the preliminary injunction as to plaintiff Jiayin Dong, a Baylor University student on an F-1 visa whose lease is not yet expired, finding no irreparable harm at the time, and stayed his remaining claims pending the Fifth Circuit's opinion in the related case Wang v. Paxton.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Agency for Int'l Dev. v. All. for Open Soc'y Int'l, Inc., 591 U.S. 430 (2020)
United States v. Verdugo-Urquidez, 494 U.S. 259 (1990)
Boumediene v. Bush, 553 U.S. 723 (2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act preemption claim (Count Three); also Equal Protection Clause (Count Two), Supremacy Clause/CFIUS-FIRMA preemption (Count One), and Equal Credit Opportunity Act preemption (Count Four)
fha_claims.reasoning: Foreign citizens outside U.S. territory do not possess rights under the U.S. Constitution. Plaintiffs Min Huang and Quiong Dai, who are not present in the United States, lack standing to bring constitutional challenges, including any claim premised on FHA preemption of SB 17. The court found no present injury in fact and declined to recognize standing based on future, speculative property purchases.

source_file: 10776301_2025_Rosanna Barrera v. LDG Riverstone LP, ET AL._txwd
case_name: Rosanna Barrera v. LDG Riverstone LP, ET AL.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that defendants provide accessible design and construction including safe, accessible routes from the parking garage to her residential unit, and requested a reserved accessible parking spot in front of her unit due to her mobility limitations.
key_holding: The magistrate recommended dismissing plaintiff's Section 1983 claims for failure to plead state action, but found she stated non-frivolous FHA claims for design and construction violations under § 3604(f)(3)(C) and for failure to accommodate under § 3604(f)(3)(B) by denying her request for an accessible parking spot.
brief_summary: Rosanna Barrera, a tenant with mobility impairments, sued LDG Riverstone LP and related entities alleging the apartment complex's design lacked accessible routes from the parking garage to her unit and that defendants denied her request for a reserved accessible parking spot in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The magistrate recommended dismissing her Section 1983 constitutional claims for failing to plead state action, but found she adequately stated claims under the FHA for design and construction violations and failure to accommodate, allowing those FHA claims to proceed past in forma pauperis screening.
key_cases_cited: Providence Behav. Health v. Grant Rd. Pub. Util. Dist., 902 F.3d 448 (5th Cir. 2018)
Bowman v. RLB Inv. Partners, LLC, 2016 WL 7326622 (E.D. Tex. 2016)
Whitaker v. W. Vill. Ltd. P'ship, 2004 WL 2008502 (N.D. Tex. 2004)
Neitzke v. Williams, 490 U.S. 319 (1989)
Priester v. Lowndes Cnty., 354 F.3d 414 (5th Cir. 2004)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible route from shared parking garage to residential units; accessible paths of travel and compliant parking
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff sufficiently pleaded a claim for design and construction violations under § 3604(f)(3)(C) by alleging that defendants intentionally approved and constructed site features (garage placement, inaccessible paths, noncompliant parking) that created no safe accessible route from parking to units, which is sufficient to survive § 1915(e) screening.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reserved accessible parking spot in front of plaintiff's unit to allow access between vehicle and residential unit
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff sufficiently pleaded a failure-to-accommodate claim under § 3604(f)(3)(B) by alleging she is a qualified individual with a known mobility disability, requested an accessible parking accommodation, and defendants denied it despite knowledge of her limitations, satisfying the three-element test for reasonable accommodation claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 1983 claims alleging enforcement of FHA rights and violation of right to access courts during TWCCRD proceeding
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed § 1983 claims as frivolous because plaintiff failed to allege that any defendant was a state actor or to plausibly allege specific facts showing an agreement between private defendants and the TWCCRD to violate her rights, which is required to establish state action necessary for § 1983 liability.

source_file: 10776422_2026_Daniel T. Doria v. Yavapai College District Governing Board, et al._azd
case_name: Daniel T. Doria v. Yavapai College District Governing Board, et al.
accommodation_description: The case text does not specify the particular accommodation requested in the underlying FHA claim; the opinion addresses only the attorneys' fees motion following dismissal, noting the FHA claim arose from defendants' enforcement of a lease governing plaintiff's tenancy at the Verde Valley RV Park and subsequent eviction proceedings.
key_holding: The court granted in part defendants' motion for attorneys' fees under 42 U.S.C. § 1988(b) and A.R.S. § 12-349, awarding $7,500 of the requested $31,446 after finding plaintiff's FHA, ADA, retaliation, and Due Process claims were frivolous and brought without substantial justification, but reducing the award due to plaintiff's pro se status and limited financial resources.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Daniel Doria brought claims under the FHA, ADA, Arizona state law retaliation, and Due Process arising from defendants' enforcement of a lease and eviction proceedings at the Verde Valley RV Park. The court had previously dismissed all claims with prejudice based on res judicata and collateral estoppel because the same claims had already been adjudicated in state court. Defendants then sought $31,446 in attorneys' fees, which the court reduced to $7,500 based on plaintiff's in forma pauperis status, pro se status, and minimal income of approximately $300/month.
key_cases_cited: Christiansburg Garment Co. v. Equal Emp. Opportunity Comm'n, 434 U.S. 412 (1978)
Miller v. L.A. Cnty. Bd. of Educ., 827 F.2d 617 (9th Cir. 1987)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: FHA claim, ADA claim, state law retaliation claim, and Due Process Clause claim arising from enforcement of lease and eviction proceedings at Verde Valley RV Park
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the FHA and retaliation claims as barred by res judicata because a prior state jury verdict in an eviction proceeding had already adjudicated the same claims between the same parties. The ADA and Due Process claims were dismissed under collateral estoppel based on the same prior judgment.

source_file: 10776430_2026_Nicole Furnas v. Tierra Luna and Sol Enterprises, LLC; et al._azd
case_name: Nicole Furnas v. Tierra Luna and Sol Enterprises, LLC; et al.
accommodation_description: Sexual harassment claim - tenant alleges maintenance worker demanded sexual favors in exchange for lease renewal
key_holding: The court granted the motion for protective order in part, limiting discovery to relevant topics and requiring each party to bear their own costs.
brief_summary: Nicole Furnas sued Tierra Luna and Sol Enterprises and its maintenance worker Jesus Santos Caceres, alleging sexual harassment in violation of the Federal Fair Housing Act after Caceres allegedly demanded sexual favors in exchange for lease renewal. The court resolved a discovery dispute by granting in part the defendants' motion for protective order to limit the scope of depositions and discovery requests to relevant matters.
key_cases_cited: Phillips ex rel. Ests. of Byrd v. Gen. Motors Corp., 307 F.3d 1206 (9th Cir. 2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Sexual harassment claim under Federal Fair Housing Act; negligence for failing to train and supervise; assault and battery under Arizona law
fha_claims.reasoning: This opinion addresses a discovery dispute via motion for protective order, not a ruling on the merits of any FHA or non-FHA claim. The court ruled on the scope of discovery permitted, not on the substantive claims themselves. The sexual harassment claim is labeled as FHA but involves quid pro quo sexual coercion unrelated to disability accommodation; the negligence, assault, and battery claims are state law torts. No merits determination has been made.

source_file: 10776572_2026_Steven E. Hobbs, Sr. v. Igor Goncharko, et al._ilnd
case_name: Steven E. Hobbs, Sr. v. Igor Goncharko, et al.
accommodation_description: Hobbs requested expedited rodent remediation as a disability accommodation because his mobility impairment prevented him from cleaning infested areas without re-injury risk, and eviction settlement/payment plan due to disability-related financial hardship.
key_holding: The court granted Coldwell Banker's motion to dismiss the racial disparate impact claim with prejudice, but denied Landlord Defendants' motion on the failure-to-accommodate claim, finding that rodent remediation is plausibly a service accommodation rather than a modification, while eviction-related requests fail because financial hardship is not unique to disabled persons.
brief_summary: Steven Hobbs, an African American tenant with a mobility disability from spinal fractures, sued his Chicago landlords and Coldwell Banker under the Fair Housing Act alleging racial discrimination, disability discrimination, and retaliation. The court granted Coldwell Banker's motion to dismiss his disparate impact racial discrimination claim with prejudice for failure to plead causation, but denied the landlords' motion on Hobbs's failure-to-accommodate claim regarding rodent remediation, which the court found plausibly alleges a service accommodation necessary due to his disability.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dept. of Hous. & Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Watters v. Homeowners' Ass'n at Pres. at Bridgewater, 48 F.4th 779 (7th Cir. 2022)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Hunt v. Aimco Props., L.P., 814 F.3d 1213 (11th Cir. 2016)
Oconomowoc Residential Programs v. City of Milwaukee, 300 F.3d 775 (7th Cir. 2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts establishing a causal connection between Coldwell Banker's alleged practice of concealing affordable housing requirements and charging above-cap rents and a disparate impact on minorities. The complaint lacks statistical or factual support showing that minority tenants suffer disproportionately from nondisclosure, and the alleged policy appears to be a one-off affecting only plaintiff rather than a pattern affecting large groups.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Expedited rodent remediation services due to plaintiff's disability-caused inability to clean infested areas without risking re-injury to his spinal fractures
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that requests for doorbell, locks, entry system, and window guards constitute modifications rather than accommodations. However, the request for expedited rodent remediation survives as a plausible accommodation because it is a service (not construction) and plaintiff plausibly alleged that his disability made him unable to self-mitigate the infestation, distinguishing him from non-disabled residents. Eviction-related requests fail because financial hardship is not unique to disabled persons.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Settlement on eviction proceedings or a payment plan due to disability-related financial hardship
fha_claims.reasoning: Financial hardship is not unique to people with disabilities and therefore does not satisfy the requirement that an accommodation be necessary because of the disability. The court applied the equal-opportunity limitation, holding that a rule affecting all residents equally does not require accommodation merely because disabled residents are disproportionately affected.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff adequately pleaded all three elements of retaliation: (1) protected activity (complaints of discrimination and filing lawsuits to enforce FHA rights); (2) adverse actions (escalated conduct, bad-faith notice to enter, accelerated eviction); and (3) causal connection (conduct escalated after complaints and filings). Defendants' arguments regarding plaintiff's motive and timing are factual disputes inappropriate for resolution at the pleading stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Racial discrimination claim alleging inferior maintenance and living conditions compared to non-Black tenants and use of racial slur
fha_claims.reasoning: The court's prior order dismissed the disparate-treatment theory against Landlord Defendants but allowed the claim to survive. The current opinion does not re-address this claim against Landlord Defendants, indicating it survives the second motion to dismiss. The claim is based on allegations of inferior maintenance conditions and discriminatory conduct (racial slur) compared to non-Black tenants.

source_file: 10776617_2026_Daniel T. Doria v. Happy Jack Lodge LLC, et al._azd
case_name: Daniel T. Doria v. Happy Jack Lodge LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Accommodation request for disability; specific accommodation not identified in complaint.
key_holding: The complaint was dismissed because plaintiff failed to allege any non-conclusory facts establishing he has a disability under the FHA or describing what discriminatory housing practice occurred when defendants allegedly ignored his accommodation request.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Daniel T. Doria sued Happy Jack Lodge LLC and others alleging Fair Housing Act violations for failing to accommodate his disability and for retaliation after requesting accommodation. The Court granted IFP status but dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim, finding Doria alleged only conclusory statements that he is disabled and that defendants ignored his accommodation request without providing factual details about his disability or the nature of the alleged discriminatory act.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Gilligan v. Jamco Dev. Corp., 108 F.3d 246 (9th Cir. 1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unspecified accommodation for disability; plaintiff alleged defendants 'ignored' his request for an accommodation but provided no factual details about what accommodation was requested
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint dismissed for failure to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly because plaintiff alleged only conclusory statements that he is disabled and that defendants ignored his accommodation request, without any non-conclusory factual allegations about what his disability is, which major life activities it substantially limits, or what specific accommodation was requested.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Retaliation claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3617 dismissed because plaintiff failed to adequately allege a handicap or discriminatory housing practice, which are prerequisites to any FHA retaliation claim; without establishing an underlying FHA violation, the retaliation claim cannot proceed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Arizona RV Long-Term Rental Space Act, A.R.S. § 33-2101
fha_claims.reasoning: Court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the state-law claim under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3) after dismissing all federal FHA claims, finding no judicial economy or other factor warranting continued jurisdiction over the remaining state-law claim.

source_file: 10776828_2025_FDA v. R. J. Reynolds Vapor Co._scotus
10777793_2026_Kevin Brown v. Cornerstone Realtors, LLC, et al._moed
case_name: Kevin Brown v. Cornerstone Realtors, LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Claim that developers, architects, builders, contractors, and/or owners of an apartment complex violated the FHAA's design and construction accessibility requirements.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss for failure to prosecute, finding that while plaintiff's counsel engaged in improper conduct by allowing deadlines to lapse due to a busy schedule, dismissal would be a disproportionate sanction where there was no bad faith and defendants had not been prejudiced by failure to engage in discovery.
brief_summary: Kevin Brown sued Cornerstone Realtors, LLC, LC Lafayette Partners, LLC, and The Hinrichs Group, Inc. under the Fair Housing Act alleging that the developers, architects, builders, contractors, and/or owners of an apartment complex at 2200 LaSalle Street in St. Louis, Missouri violated the FHAA's accessibility and usability requirements. The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss for failure to prosecute under Rule 41(b), finding that dismissal would be too harsh a sanction absent a clear record of delay or contumacious conduct and warning plaintiff that future dilatory conduct would result in sanctions including dismissal.
key_cases_cited: Bergstrom v. Frascone, 744 F.3d 571 (8th Cir. 2014)
Skelton v. Rapps, 187 F.3d 902 (8th Cir. 1999)
Arnold v. ADT Sec. Servs., Inc., 627 F.3d 716 (8th Cir. 2010)
Chorosevic v. MetLife Choices, 600 F.3d 934 (8th Cir. 2010)
Giles v. Saint Luke's Northland-Smithville, 908 F.3d 365 (8th Cir. 2018)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged violations of the Fair Housing Act's accessibility and usability requirements at an apartment complex located at 2200 LaSalle Street in St. Louis, Missouri
fha_claims.disposition: Motion to Dismiss for Failure to Prosecute
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the defendants' motion to dismiss for failure to prosecute, finding that while plaintiff's counsel's conduct was improper, it did not warrant dismissal as a sanction. The claim itself was not addressed on the merits and remains pending; the court's ruling concerned only the procedural sanction of dismissal for dilatory conduct.

source_file: 10777846_2026_Edward Siguel v. King Farm Citizens Assembly, Inc., et al._mdd
case_name: Edward Siguel v. King Farm Citizens Assembly, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: Siguel requested, as a reasonable modification under the FHA, that he be permitted to leave the roof of his front porch without a decorative balustrade (a fake balcony composed of columns, posts, and railings), or alternatively, that King Farm install and maintain the balustrade for him, on the ground that his physical disability causes pain, bleeding, and fatigue that make installing and maintaining the structure burdensome and harmful.
key_holding: The court denied Siguel's motion to vacate the dismissal of his 2025 lawsuit because both his 2022 and 2025 complaints arise from the same ongoing dispute over King Farm's demand that he reinstall a balustrade, and under the doctrine against claim splitting, all claims arising out of a single wrong must be presented in one action.
brief_summary: Edward Siguel, a disabled homeowner in a planned community, filed a second federal lawsuit in 2025 against his HOA, King Farm Citizens Assembly, alleging FHA violations related to the association's repeated demands that he reinstall a decorative balustrade on his front porch roof, which he removed in 2019 due to roof damage and the difficulty of maintaining it given his disability. The court sua sponte dismissed the 2025 case as duplicative of Siguel's still-pending 2022 lawsuit, which involved substantively identical allegations about the same balustrade dispute. Siguel's motion to vacate the dismissal and for leave to amend were denied because the 2025 claims arise from the same continuing wrong as the 2022 case and must be pursued in that proceeding, whether through a motion to supplement or for reconsideration.
key_cases_cited: Colorado River Water Conservation Dist. v. United States, 424 U.S. 800 (1976)
Sensormatic Sec. Corp. v. Sensormatic Elecs. Corp., 452 F. Supp. 2d 621 (D. Md. 2006)
Katyle v. Penn Nat'l Gaming, Inc., 637 F.3d 462 (4th Cir. 2011)
JTH Tax, Inc. v. Aime, 984 F.3d 284 (4th Cir. 2021)
Hodges v. Meletis, 109 F.4th 252 (4th Cir. 2024)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request to be exempted from or not required to install and maintain a balustrade (decorative balcony) on the front porch roof, or alternatively, for King Farm to install and maintain the balustrade on plaintiff's behalf
fha_claims.reasoning: In the 2022 case, Judge Simms dismissed the balustrade-related FHA claims under the Iqbal/Twombly standard because plaintiff failed to sufficiently plead that the requested accommodations were necessary, as the FHA requires, because they would not 'directly ameliorate' the effects of plaintiff's disability. The 2025 complaint raising the same balustrade claims was dismissed as duplicative of the pending 2022 case.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Intentional discrimination by rejecting plaintiff's request not to install a balustrade
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's disparate treatment claim regarding the balustrade was dismissed in the 2022 case as part of the pleading-stage dismissal for failure to state a plausible claim. The 2025 complaint reasserting this claim was dismissed as duplicative.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged adverse discriminatory effects from King Farm's balustrade requirement
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's disparate impact claim regarding the balustrade was dismissed in the 2022 case at the pleading stage. The 2025 complaint reasserting this claim was dismissed as duplicative of the pending 2022 case.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of contract claim based on alleged promises in King Farm Charter to protect owners from onerous maintenance and to provide reasonable accommodations; claim that King Farm's rights to enforce exterior appearances are void; claim for involuntary labor
fha_claims.reasoning: Non-FHA claims including breach of contract and related state law theories were dismissed in the 2025 case as part of the overall dismissal for duplicativeness with the pending 2022 case. The court did not reach the merits of these claims.

source_file: 10778453_2026_New Beginning Sanctuary, A Missouri Not-For-Profit Corporation, Jaam Properties LLC, A Missouri Limited Liability Company, and Alon Fisch, An Individual v. City of Springfield, Missouri, A Missouri Municipa
case_name: New Beginning Sanctuary, A Missouri Not-For-Profit Corporation, Jaam Properties LLC, A Missouri Limited Liability Company, and Alon Fisch, An Individual v. City of Springfield, Missouri, A Missouri Municipal Corporation
accommodation_description: Request to operate a residential recovery home for persons in recovery from substance use addiction in an R-SF residential zone as a reasonable accommodation from the City's zoning ordinance that prohibits group homes within a quarter mile of an existing group home.
key_holding: Plaintiffs' expert testimony may be admitted under Daubert for disparate impact and disparate treatment claims, but must be excluded from the failure to accommodate claim under One Love Housing because the experts' opinions were not presented to the City as part of Plaintiffs' accommodation request.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs New Beginning Sanctuary and Jaam Properties sued the City of Springfield seeking to operate a residential recovery home for individuals recovering from substance use addiction, requesting a reasonable accommodation from the City's zoning ordinance that prohibited group homes within a quarter mile of an existing group home. The Court ruled on a motion to exclude expert testimony, allowing the experts' opinions to be considered for disparate impact and disparate treatment claims but excluding them for the failure to accommodate claim because the plaintiffs did not present this evidence to the City during the administrative process.
key_cases_cited: One Love Hous., LLC v. City of Anoka, Minnesota, 93 F.4th 424 (8th Cir. 2024)
Lapid-Laurel, L.L.C. v. Zoning Bd. of Adjustment, 284 F.3d 442 (3d Cir. 2002)
Tsombanidis v. W. Haven Fire Dep't, 352 F.3d 565 (2d Cir. 2003)
Gallagher v. Magner, 619 F.3d 823 (8th Cir. 2010)
Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals, 509 U.S. 479 (1993)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request for reasonable accommodation to operate a home for residents in recovery from drug or alcohol addiction in an R-SF Zone, notwithstanding the City's zoning ordinance prohibiting group homes within ¼ mile of another group home.
fha_claims.disposition: Expert testimony excluded from reasonable accommodation claim
fha_claims.reasoning: The court excluded expert testimony on the reasonable accommodation claim under One Love Housing because the evidence was not presented to the City during the administrative request process, and the plaintiffs were given a meaningful opportunity to resubmit but chose not to address the City's concerns. The claim itself survives and proceeds to trial, but expert testimony is barred.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.disposition: Expert testimony admitted; claim proceeds to trial
fha_claims.reasoning: The court admitted expert testimony on the disparate treatment claim because One Love Housing's administrative record limitation applies only to reasonable accommodation claims, not disparate treatment claims. The claim proceeds to trial with expert evidence permitted.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.disposition: Expert testimony admitted; claim proceeds to trial
fha_claims.reasoning: The court admitted expert testimony on the disparate impact claim because One Love Housing's administrative record limitation applies only to reasonable accommodation claims, not disparate impact claims. The claim proceeds to trial with expert evidence permitted.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) claim arising from the same facts as the FHA claims—denial of reasonable accommodation to operate a sober living group home.
fha_claims.disposition: Expert testimony admitted; claim proceeds to trial
fha_claims.reasoning: The ADA claim is treated similarly to the FHA claims. Expert testimony is excluded on the reasonable accommodation component under One Love Housing but admitted on disparate treatment and disparate impact components. The claim proceeds to trial.

source_file: 10779646_2026_Orane M. Cornish Jr. v. Cheyanne Tripp et al._ctd
case_name: Orane M. Cornish Jr. v. Cheyanne Tripp et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges his landlord conditioned continued housing on submission to unwanted sexual advances, creating a hostile housing environment.
key_holding: The court denied Defendant Tripp's motion to dismiss Plaintiff's FHA hostile housing environment claim, finding Plaintiff sufficiently alleged that his landlord conditioned housing on submission to unwanted sexual advances on the basis of sex, but granted Defendant Paris's motion to dismiss because Paris, as a non-landlord associate, lacked sufficient connection to Plaintiff’s housing arrangement.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Orane Cornish, proceeding pro se, sued Defendant Tripp (his landlord) and Defendant Paris (Tripp's associate) under the Trafficking Victims Protection Act and Fair Housing Act, alleging he was coerced into unpaid labor and sex trafficking, and that his landlord created a hostile housing environment by conditioning housing on submission to unwanted sexual advances. The court denied both defendants' motions to dismiss the TVPA claims and denied Tripp's motion to dismiss the FHA hostile housing environment claim, but dismissed the FHA claim against Paris without leave to amend because he was not the plaintiff's landlord.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Texas Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Cain v. Rambert, No. 13-CV-5807 (MKB), 2014 WL 2440596 (E.D.N.Y. May 30, 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff sufficiently alleged a hostile housing environment claim under FHA § 3604(b) against Defendant Tripp based on sexual harassment and conditioning continued housing on submission to unwanted sexual advances. The claim survived the motion to dismiss as Plaintiff established all three elements: severe harassment, based on sex, and imputable to the landlord.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to state a plausible FHA hostile housing environment claim against Defendant Paris because Paris was not Plaintiff's landlord and Plaintiff did not sufficiently tie Paris's alleged threats of physical harm to Plaintiff's housing arrangement. The claim lacked the required nexus between discriminatory conduct and housing.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: TVPA (18 U.S.C. §§ 1589, 1590, 1591), § 1983 (previously dismissed)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff sufficiently alleged TVPA claims under §§ 1589 (forced labor), 1590 (trafficking/harboring), and 1591 (sex trafficking) with particularized facts showing coercion to perform unpaid labor under threat of eviction and false criminal charges, and conditioning housing on sexual acts. The motions to dismiss were denied as to all three TVPA provisions.

source_file: 10779681_2026_Justin Thomas Fanty v. Greater Dayton Premier Management, et al._ohsd
case_name: Justin Thomas Fanty v. Greater Dayton Premier Management, et al.
accommodation_description: The opinion does not describe the specific accommodation request; the complaint alleging Fair Housing Act violations was dismissed as time-barred and failing to state a claim.
key_holding: Plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claims fail because they are time-barred and fail to state a claim upon which relief can be granted, and the case was dismissed with prejudice for failure to prosecute after plaintiff failed to respond to the motion for judgment on the pleadings despite being given multiple opportunities to do so.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Justin Thomas Fanty, proceeding pro se, sued Greater Dayton Premier Management (a public housing authority) and individual defendants alleging Fair Housing Act violations during his tenancy. The court granted defendants' motion for judgment on the pleadings on the merits, finding the claims time-barred and insufficient, and also dismissed the case with prejudice for failure to prosecute after Fanty failed to respond to the motion despite receiving multiple extensions.
key_cases_cited: Link v. Wabash R.R., 370 U.S. 626 (1962)
Carpenter v. City of Flint, 723 F.3d 700 (6th Cir. 2013)
Fair Hous. Council, Inc. v. Vill. of Olde St. Andrews, Inc., 210 F. App’x 469 (6th Cir. 2006)
Jourdan v. Jabe, 951 F.2d 108 (6th Cir. 1991)
Erickson v. Pardus, 551 U.S. 89 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not specified in opinion
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 12(c) — Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed plaintiff's pro se FHA claims as time-barred and failing to state a claim upon which relief can be granted. The opinion does not specify the nature of the FHA claims alleged, but the court found them time-barred under applicable statute of limitations.

source_file: 10779805_2026_Ellen Burke v. AP Atherton Limited Partnership, Tomlinson _ Associates Inc., Teri Giacomino, Glen Kyle, Tim Beery and Tom Mannschreck_mtd
case_name: Ellen Burke v. AP Atherton Limited Partnership, Tomlinson & Associates Inc., Teri Giacomino, Glen Kyle, Tim Beery and Tom Mannschreck
accommodation_description: The opinion does not describe any specific accommodation request; the court merely notes plaintiff was granted leave to amend her Fair Housing Act claims.
key_holding: The court denied Defendants' Motion to Dismiss as moot because plaintiff filed an amended complaint, which superseded the original complaint and rendered the pending motion to dismiss non-justiciable.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Ellen Burke sued AP Atherton Limited Partnership, Tomlinson & Associates Inc., and individual defendants for Fair Housing Act claims. The court initially dismissed all defendants except AP Atherton Limited Partnership and Tomlinson & Associates Inc. and granted leave to amend, then denied the pending Motion to Dismiss as moot upon the filing of an Amended Complaint.
key_cases_cited: CDK Global LLC v. Brnovich, 16 F.4th 1266 (9th Cir. 2021)
Morgan v. LexisNexis Risk Solutions, Inc., 2025 WL 2986630 (E.D. Cal. Oct. 23, 2025)

source_file: 10780289_2026_Heidi Erickson v. Michael Inman, et al._ilcd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested accommodations for ZBA hearing including that the hearing be set early enough in the day so she could travel back to where she was living by train during daylight, and that the hearing be held in a wheelchair-accessible room. Plaintiff alleges she never received a response to these accommodation requests and the hearing was conducted without her presence.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that Erickson sufficiently alleged that the City violated the ADA by failing to make reasonable accommodations for her in the zoning appeals process, allowing the claim to proceed against the City under Title II of the ADA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II discrimination claim based on alleged seizure of service dog and therapy animals, obtaining of administrative search warrant, and seeking involuntary commitment because of discriminatory animus towards plaintiff's disability or in retaliation for asserting ADA rights; ADA Title III claim against Lake Behavioral Hospital for refusing to release plaintiff due to her use of a wheelchair; § 1983 Fourth Amendment claims for unlawful search, seizure of property, excessive force, and wrongful arrest/seizure of person; Illinois state law claims for false imprisonment, replevin, malicious prosecution, fraud, and due process violations.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court allowed multiple non-FHA claims to proceed including ADA discrimination and failure to accommodate claims against the City and Lake Behavioral Hospital, Fourth Amendment claims for unlawful search and seizure, excessive force, and wrongful arrest against various police officers and the City, false imprisonment claims against Herrick, Clemens, and Lake Behavioral Hospital, replevin claim against McDonough County, and due process claims. The court dismissed other non-FHA claims including defamation, breach of contract, malicious prosecution, and conspiracy claims for failure to state a claim under Iqbal/Twombly.

source_file: 10781059_2026_Christine Carroll, individually and on behalf of residents of “A Fortress,” v. Town of Manchester, City of Hartford, Roger Thrall, Nancy Navarretta, and Advanced Behavioral Health, Inc._ctd
case_name: Christine Carroll, individually and on behalf of residents of "A Fortress," v. Town of Manchester, City of Hartford, Roger Thrall, Nancy Navarretta, and Advanced Behavioral Health, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought to enjoin enforcement of zoning, building, and fire code ordinances against her substance abuse recovery group homes, arguing that selective enforcement against facilities housing individuals with disabilities (persons recovering from addiction) constituted discrimination, and she requested that defendants be enjoined from enforcing any directives or ordinances requiring cessation of operations at 510 New Britain Avenue, Hartford and 101-103 Cedar Street, Manchester.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's motion for a preliminary injunction because she failed to demonstrate irreparable harm or a clear likelihood of success on the merits of her FHA and ADA claims alleging discriminatory enforcement of municipal zoning, building, and fire codes against her substance abuse recovery group homes.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Christine Carroll, owner and operator of multiple substance abuse recovery group homes operating as 'A Fortress,' sued the Town of Manchester, City of Hartford, state DMHAS commissioner, and a behavioral health contractor, alleging they enforced zoning, building, and fire codes in a discriminatory manner against her properties in violation of the FHA, ADA, and the Fourteenth Amendment. Plaintiff sought a TRO and preliminary injunction to prevent enforcement of ordinances that could result in closure of her properties and eviction of disabled residents. The court denied the motion, finding no irreparable harm (residents remained housed with no imminent eviction) and no clear likelihood of success on the merits, and further concluding the balance of equities favored defendants given the compelling public interest in ensuring safe, code-compliant housing.
key_cases_cited: Stewart B. McKinney Found., Inc. v. Town Plan & Zoning Comm'n of Town of Fairfield, 790 F. Supp. 1197 (D. Conn. 1992)
Step By Step, Inc. v. City of Ogdensburg, 176 F. Supp. 3d 112 (N.D.N.Y. 2016)
Gresham v. Windrush Partners, Ltd., 730 F.2d 1417 (11th Cir. 1984)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Enforcement of zoning, building, and fire codes at substance abuse recovery properties allegedly applied in discriminatory manner against individuals with substance use disorder disabilities
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied preliminary injunction on grounds of failure to demonstrate irreparable harm and likelihood of success on merits, without reaching substantive merits of the FHA disparate treatment claim. Court noted that plaintiff failed to show code enforcement actions were pretext for discrimination and that a forthcoming ruling on motions to dismiss would address cognizability of claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (Title III), Equal Protection Clause (Fourteenth Amendment), Due Process Clause (Fourteenth Amendment)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court noted that constitutional claims must be brought under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, not directly under the Fourteenth Amendment, and indicated these claims will be dismissed in forthcoming ruling on motions to dismiss. Court found plaintiff failed to demonstrate likelihood of success on merits of any claims.

source_file: 10781103_2026_KORTNEY DONAVON v. RICHMOND-HENRICO ARMS LIMITED PARTNERSHIP_vaed
case_name: Kortney Donavon v. Richmond-Henrico Arms Limited Partnership
accommodation_description: The specific accommodation requested is not described in the federal court opinion; plaintiff invoked FHA § 3604(f) as a defense to eviction in state court proceedings, suggesting a disability-related accommodation was asserted before the state court, but the nature of the accommodation is not detailed in this federal court record.
key_holding: The court dismissed the action for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because the state court eviction proceeding was not properly removable, the claims were moot after execution of the writ of eviction, and the Anti-Injunction Act barred the requested injunctive relief.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Kortney Donavon attempted to remove a state court eviction proceeding to federal court after a writ of eviction issued by Henrico County General District Court, asserting Fair Housing Act claims under 42 U.S.C. §§ 3604(f) and 3617 and civil rights claims under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1983 and 1985(3). The federal court dismissed the action on three independent grounds: the writ had already been executed rendering the matter moot, the state court action was not removable because no pending controversy existed when plaintiff filed, and the Anti-Injunction Act precluded the court from enjoining state court proceedings. The court granted plaintiff's IFP application but dismissed without reaching the merits of any claims.
key_cases_cited: Porter v. Clarke, 852 F.3d 358 (4th Cir. 2017)
Atlantic C. L. R. Co. v. Bhd. of Locomotive Eng'rs, 398 U.S. 281 (1970)
Denny's Inc. v. Cake, 364 F.3d 521 (4th Cir. 2004)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Arbaugh v. Y & H Corp., 546 U.S. 500 (2006)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff asserted Fair Housing Act claims (§ 3604(f) and § 3617) in opposition to eviction in state court; specific accommodation or theory not articulated in the opinion.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked subject matter jurisdiction because the state court had already issued the Writ of Eviction, making the case moot, and the Anti-Injunction Act precluded federal court intervention in pending state court proceedings. The court did not reach the merits of the FHA claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. §§ 1983, 1985(3) civil rights claims
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked subject matter jurisdiction over the entire action due to mootness and the Anti-Injunction Act's prohibition on enjoining state court proceedings. The court did not reach the merits of any claims.

source_file: 10781650_2026_Sharon Lee, et al. v. Twin Hawks Airpark LLC, et al._azd
case_name: Sharon Lee, et al. v. Twin Hawks Airpark LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege Twin Hawks filed an easement lawsuit in retaliation for Lee's housing discrimination complaint filed with the Arizona Attorney General.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' retaliation claims with leave to amend, finding plaintiffs failed to plead facts showing Twin Hawks' easement lawsuit would not have occurred without intentional race-based retaliation, particularly when a plausible nonretaliatory explanation (enforcing prescriptive easements) was supported by deposition testimony, the timing of events, and the large number of community members believing easements existed.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Sharon Lee and Tommy Wessel sued Twin Hawks Airpark LLC and Managing Committee member Harold Duane Lambeth, alleging Twin Hawks filed state court easement litigation in retaliation for Lee's housing discrimination complaint filed with the Arizona Attorney General, asserting claims under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1982, and 3617. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege but-for causation for their retaliation claims given the compelling alternative explanation that Twin Hawks legitimately pursued easement enforcement against community members who had barricaded roads and obstructed property.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Comcast Corp. v. Nat'l Ass'n of Afr. Am.-Owned Media, 589 U.S. 327 (2020)
Starr v. Baca, 652 F.3d 1202 (9th Cir. 2011)
Edwards v. Marin Park, Inc., 356 F.3d 1058 (9th Cir. 2004)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege a causal link between protected activity (Lee's discrimination complaint to Arizona Attorney General) and adverse action (Twin Hawks's easement lawsuit). The complaint alleged only temporal proximity (six months) and vague deposition quotes, which are insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly. The court found a convincing alternative nonretaliatory explanation: the underlying easement dispute unrelated to race, supported by deposition testimony and the fact the lawsuit continued after the discrimination complaint was dismissed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 and 1982 claims for retaliation based on race and national origin discrimination
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege intentional race-based retaliation under §§ 1981 and 1982. The complaint lacked sufficient facts showing that but-for race or retaliation, the lawsuit would not have occurred. Temporal proximity alone (six months) is insufficient, and the complaint itself provided a convincing alternative nonretaliatory explanation: the underlying easement dispute involving a large number of community members, unrelated to race.

source_file: 10782307_2026_Jesse Lewis Walker v. Lukrom REIT LLC, et al._azd
case_name: Jesse Lewis Walker v. Lukrom REIT LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff's dog was left in the apartment during eviction; the accommodation request is not clearly articulated as a reasonable accommodation but is framed as familial status discrimination and retaliation for requesting repairs.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claims for failure to state a claim because the conclusory allegations of familial status discrimination and retaliation lacked sufficient factual matter to make the claims plausible under Ashcroft v. Iqbal and Bell Atlantic v. Twombly; the court granted leave to amend the FHA claims but denied leave to amend the PTFA claim as futile.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Jesse Walker, who was evicted for non-payment of rent, sued his landlord Lukrom REIT LLC alleging Fair Housing Act claims for familial status discrimination and retaliation for requesting repairs. The court screened the complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2) and dismissed it for failure to state a claim, finding the FHA allegations were conclusory and unsupported by sufficient factual matter, but granted leave to amend the FHA claims against Lukrom while denying leave to amend the PTFA claim as futile.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ferdik v. Bonzelet, 963 F.2d 1258 (9th Cir. 1992)
Lyons v. Gene B. Glick Company, Inc., 844 F. App'x 866 (7th Cir. 2021)
Logan v. U.S. Bank Nat. Ass'n, 722 F.3d 1163 (9th Cir. 2013)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged refusal to remedy hazardous conditions and denial of safe conditions; retaliation for requesting repairs and asserting rights related to serious health and safety hazards
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint contains only conclusory statements that Walker was retaliated against for requesting repairs, without substantial factual allegations supporting the retaliation claim. The court found the allegations insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged discrimination or disparate treatment on the basis of familial status as a custodial parent of minor children; denial of safe conditions
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint contains only conclusory statements that Walker was targeted due to his status as a custodial parent, without factual allegations supporting the discrimination claim. The justice court judgment stating the eviction was for non-payment of rent further undermines the claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act (PTFA), 12 U.S.C. § 5220 — claim that Lukrom failed to provide 90 days' notice to vacate
fha_claims.reasoning: The PTFA claim fails because there is no private right of action under the PTFA, and the PTFA is inapplicable to the facts alleged (the PTFA protects tenants when a landlord defaults on a mortgage and a successor landlord seeks to evict bona fide tenants, which is not the case here).

source_file: 10783818_2026_Tami Huston; Justin Huston v. Willamette Valley Rentals, LLC; Nick Sharifi; Roya Sharifi_ord
case_name: Tami Huston; Justin Huston v. Willamette Valley Rentals, LLC; Nick Sharifi; Roya Sharifi
accommodation_description: No accommodation requested; case involves refusal to rent to foster parents with disabled children based on familial status and disability
key_holding: Plaintiffs, who are foster parents of children with disabilities, are entitled to summary judgment on their Fair Housing Act claims because the landlord's treatment of their rental application changed adversely after learning of their familial status and children's disabilities, while a similarly situated applicant without children or disabilities was offered more favorable terms.
brief_summary: Foster parents with disabled children sued a property management company for housing discrimination after their rental application was denied following disclosure of their family composition and children's disabilities. The court granted plaintiffs' motion for partial summary judgment on federal and state Fair Housing Act claims, finding that defendants discriminated against plaintiffs based on familial status and disability by refusing to rent and offering less favorable terms compared to applicants without children or disabilities.
key_cases_cited: Morris v. West Hayden Estates First Addition Homeowners Ass'n, Inc., 104 F.4th 1128 (9th Cir. 2024)
Pacific Shores Props., LLC v. City of Newport Beach, 730 F.3d 1142 (9th Cir. 2013)
Harris v. Itzhaki, 183 F.3d 1043 (9th Cir. 1999)
City of Edmunds v. Oxford House, Inc., 514 U.S. 725 (1995)
Conlon v. United States, 474 F.3d 616 (9th Cir. 2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs submitted the first application, met all criteria, and were denied without explanation. WVR's communication slowed after learning of Plaintiffs' familial status and the property was rented to someone with a smaller household, establishing discrimination in refusal to rent based on familial status under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(a).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: WVR offered Ms. Collins (who did not disclose familial status) more favorable terms including quick turnaround and application fee refund, while denying these same terms to Plaintiffs, establishing discrimination in terms, conditions, or privileges of rental based on familial status under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(b).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: After Plaintiffs disclosed familial status, WVR falsely represented that there was new activity surrounding the property and encouraged them to consider other properties, while later telling Ms. Collins there was only one applicant and that Plaintiffs' application was unlikely to work, establishing false representation of unavailability based on familial status under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(d).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: WVR discouraged Plaintiffs from renting the property after learning of their familial status by encouraging them to look elsewhere, establishing an attempt to discourage rental based on familial status under ORS 659A.421(d).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: WVR represented the Sharifi Defendants and retained the listing despite Ms. Sharifi's discriminatory comments about familial status, then assisted in rejecting Plaintiffs' application and finding an alternative renter with a smaller household, establishing unlawful retention of listing under ORS 659A.421(4).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: WVR assisted the Sharifi Defendants in violating fair housing law by discriminating against Plaintiffs based on familial status, establishing liability for assisting another in violation under ORS 659A.421(2)(f).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs met all criteria but their application was denied without explanation and WVR's treatment worsened after they disclosed their children's disabilities. The property was subsequently rented to individuals without disabilities, establishing discrimination in refusal to rent based on disability under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(1)(B).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Shortly after Plaintiffs disclosed their children's disabilities, WVR falsely represented that there was new activity surrounding the property and encouraged them to rent elsewhere, establishing false representation of unavailability based on disability under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(d).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: WVR falsely represented new activity and encouraged Plaintiffs to rent elsewhere shortly after they disclosed their children's disabilities, establishing an attempt to discourage rental based on disability under ORS 659A.145(2)(d).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: WVR represented the Sharifi Defendants and retained the listing despite Ms. Sharifi's discriminatory comments about Plaintiffs' disabled children, then assisted in rejecting Plaintiffs' application and finding an alternative renter without disabilities, establishing unlawful retention of listing under ORS 659A.145(5).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: WVR assisted the Sharifi Defendants in violating fair housing law by discriminating against Plaintiffs based on disability, establishing liability for assisting another in violation under ORS 659A.145(7).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Negligence claim under Oregon state law
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs represented they intend to dismiss their negligence claim in the event that the summary judgment motion on fair housing claims is granted, and the court did not address the merits of the negligence claim.

source_file: 10784337_2026_Shasta Partee, on behalf of herself and all other occupants v. Powers Properties_scd
case_name: Shasta Partee, on behalf of herself and all other occupants v. Powers Properties
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested accommodation to allow her son with mental health disabilities (ADHD, bipolar disorder, emotional dysregulation) to remain in the apartment despite behavioral incidents rather than having her lease non-renewed.
key_holding: The court held that plaintiff failed to establish the accommodation was necessary to afford an equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling because the requests neither specified what accommodation was sought nor identified how it would ameliorate the son's mental impairments, and alternatively that the direct threat exception applied given documented evidence of the son posing safety risks.
brief_summary: Shasta Partee sued Powers Properties, the property manager of Briar Grove Apartments, alleging the landlord failed to accommodate her adult son's mental health disabilities and retaliated against her after she requested accommodations to prevent lease non-renewal based on the son's behavioral incidents. The court granted summary judgment for the defendant, finding plaintiff failed to establish the requested accommodation was necessary and that the direct threat exception applied given evidence of the son pointing a realistic weapon at people, jumping from a balcony, and committing arson.
key_cases_cited: Olsen v. Stark Homes, Inc., 759 F.3d 140 (2d Cir. 2014)
Bryant Woods Inn, Inc. v. Howard Cnty., 124 F.3d 597 (4th Cir. 1997)
Scoggins v. Lee's Crossing Homeowners Ass'n, 718 F.3d 262 (4th Cir. 2013)
Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014)
Lapid-Laurel, L.L.C. v. Zoning Bd. of Adjustment, 284 F.3d 442 (3d Cir. 2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested accommodation for her adult son's mental health disabilities (ADHD, bipolar disorder, oppositional defiant disorder, emotional dysregulation) to allow him to remain in the apartment and receive medical treatment; the specific accommodation was not clearly defined beyond avoiding eviction or obtaining more time to move.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the five-element Olsen test and found that plaintiff failed to establish the third element: that the accommodation was likely necessary to afford the disabled person an equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling. The court determined that plaintiff's requests neither specified what accommodation was sought nor identified how it would directly ameliorate the effect of the son's mental impairments.
