Additionally, the court found that defendant established the direct threat exception under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(9) based on objective evidence of the son's dangerous conduct (pointing a realistic firearm, jumping from a third-floor balcony, and attempting to set fires to the building).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the four-element prima facie test for retaliation and found that plaintiff failed to establish a causal connection between the protected activity (October 6, 2022 email to defendant) and the alleged retaliatory action (false eviction filing on October 12, 2022). Although temporal proximity was close, defendant provided a legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason for its actions, and plaintiff offered no evidence that the reasons were pretextual. Additionally, the court found that a nine-month gap between the alleged protected activities in October 2022 and purported retaliatory actions beginning in July 2023 was too remote to establish sufficient causal connection.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of contract (South Carolina habitability statute, S.C. Code Ann. § 27-40-440), constructive eviction (South Carolina common law), and intentional infliction of emotional distress (South Carolina tort law)
fha_claims.reasoning: For breach of contract: plaintiff failed to identify evidence of defendant's failure to maintain habitability (smoke detectors, sprinkler system, electrical safety) and the notice of non-renewal was issued in accordance with the lease term, not as a breach requiring a fourteen-day cure notice. For constructive eviction: the twenty-one-month delay between the notice of non-renewal and plaintiff's departure in July 2024 failed to constitute abandonment within a reasonable time as required under South Carolina law. For IIED: plaintiff failed to offer evidence that defendant's conduct was extreme and outrageous enough to exceed all possible bounds of decency.

source_file: 10784366_2026_Laura Saitta v. Greystar Real Estate Partners, LLC; et al._casd
case_name: Laura Saitta v. Greystar Real Estate Partners, LLC; et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; claim is for gender-based discrimination in housing terms and conditions
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act sex discrimination claim because the SAC contained only conclusory allegations without factual content sufficient to plausibly infer gender-based discriminatory animus, and plaintiff was currently renting a two-bedroom penthouse unit contradicting her theory that women were being forced into one-bedroom apartments.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Laura Saitta, proceeding pro se, sued Greystar Real Estate Partners (property manager), Kilroy Realty (property owner), and individual defendants alleging Fair Housing Act sex discrimination and Section 1985 conspiracy claims related to her rental at One Paseo Village in San Diego, claiming she was discriminatorily subjected to unequal housing terms and pricing because she is a woman. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss without leave to amend, finding plaintiff's FHA sex discrimination claim conclusory and factually unsupported, and declined supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
In re Gilead Scis. Secs. Litig., 536 F.3d 1049 (9th Cir. 2008)
Karim-Panahi v. Los Angeles Police Dep't, 839 F.2d 621 (9th Cir. 1988)
Griffin v. Breckenridge, 403 U.S. 88 (1971)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's allegations of gender-based discrimination were conclusory and unadorned by facts supporting a reasonable inference of discriminatory animus. The court found no factual allegations plausibly supporting discrimination based on protected class membership, particularly where female managers allegedly implemented the challenged policies and plaintiff currently occupies a two-bedroom unit despite alleging women were forced into one-bedroom apartments.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1985 Conspiracy to Interfere with Civil Rights
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 1985 conspiracy claim was inextricably intertwined with the failed FHA claim and lacked factual specificity showing defendants conspired with invidiously discriminatory animus. Without factual content supporting a conspiracy allegation, the claim failed under the Iqbal/Twombly standard.

source_file: 10784453_2026_Lori Robins v. Waterford at Aberdeen Association, Inc., et al._flsd
case_name: Lori Robins v. Waterford at Aberdeen Association, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: Visually impaired plaintiff requested to submit HOA work orders via email as an alternative to the inaccessible website.
key_holding: The court granted plaintiff summary judgment on her reasonable accommodation claim for email work order submission, finding that Waterford constructively rejected the request by ignoring it after reviewing it; however, the court denied summary judgment on her pool gate lock modification claim because she failed to offer to pay for the modification as required under § 3604(f)(3)(A).
brief_summary: Plaintiff Lori Robins, who is visually impaired, sued Waterford at Aberdeen Association, Inc. (an HOA) for discrimination and retaliation under the Fair Housing Act, alleging the HOA failed to accommodate her disability by refusing to provide accessible alternatives to its inaccessible website. The court granted partial summary judgment for Robins on her claim that the HOA constructively rejected her reasonable accommodation request to submit work orders via email, while denying her modification claim for the pool gate lock because she failed to offer to pay for it as required under § 3604(f)(3)(A).
key_cases_cited: Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014)
Schwarz v. City of Treasure Island, 544 F.3d 1201 (11th Cir. 2008)
Wood v. Briarwinds Condo. Ass'n Bd. of Directors, 2009 WL 10668944 (S.D. Fla. Mar. 20, 2009)
Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242 (1986)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request for large-print physical copy of ACH automatic withdrawal form to be mailed to plaintiff to enable payment of HOA fees
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found a genuine dispute of material fact whether Waterford actually mailed the accessible ACH form as claimed, precluding summary judgment on whether Waterford refused the accommodation request.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request to submit work orders via email instead of through inaccessible website due to visual impairment
fha_claims.reasoning: Waterford constructively rejected the accommodation request by failing to respond after reviewing it. The accommodation was necessary (plaintiff could not access website due to visual impairment) and reasonable (minimal burden to allow email submission), entitling plaintiff to judgment as a matter of law under § 3604(f)(3)(B).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request to modify pool gate lock to make it accessible to visually impaired resident
fha_claims.reasoning: Under § 3604(f)(3)(A), modifications must be made at the handicapped person's expense. Plaintiff failed to allege or offer to pay for the modification, which is a prerequisite to stating a modification claim. Plaintiff's failure to offer payment means she did not properly make a modification request under the statute.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges Waterford retaliated by ignoring unrelated maintenance requests, refusing to inform her of safety hazards, and ignoring residents' harassment after she requested accommodations
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted partial summary judgment on the first element of retaliation (protected activity and defendant's awareness) only as to the work-order accommodation request, since plaintiff prevailed on the underlying discrimination claim. Whether other requests constituted protected activity and whether any adverse actions were causally related remain questions of fact for the jury.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Florida Fair Housing Act (FLFHA) § 760.20 et seq. claims for discrimination and retaliation
fha_claims.reasoning: Court noted that FLFHA adopted FHA provisions almost verbatim, such that violations of FHA also constitute FLFHA violations. Plaintiff's FLFHA claims track her FHA claims and receive identical treatment on summary judgment.

source_file: 10784485_2026_My Thi Nhu Tran, et al. v. Gulf Coast Bank _ Trust Co., et al._laed
case_name: My Thi Nhu Tran, et al. v. Gulf Coast Bank & Trust Co., et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged defendants engaged in mortgage fraud against Vietnamese immigrants with limited English proficiency, and during settlement negotiations, defendants threatened foreclosure to coerce plaintiffs into abandoning their federal housing claims.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiffs' motions for reconsideration and leave to supplement because plaintiffs failed to plead sufficient facts to support a § 3617 retaliation claim (no causal connection between protected activity and adverse action), failed to allege state action for § 1983 claims, and failed to state a cognizable claim under § 1985 for conduct at a settlement conference.
brief_summary: Vietnamese immigrant homeowners sued Gulf Coast Bank, their mortgage broker, realty company, and closing agent alleging mortgage fraud and seeking to add claims for Fair Housing Act retaliation under § 3617 based on alleged foreclosure threats during settlement conference. The court denied plaintiffs' motions for reconsideration, finding plaintiffs failed to plead causation for the § 3617 retaliation claim, failed to allege state action for § 1983 claims, and failed to state a cognizable claim under § 1985 for settlement conduct.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Lugar v. Edmondson Oil Co.
Montoya v. FedEx Ground Package Sys., Inc.
Kush v. Rutledge

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plead a causal nexus between the protected activity (asserting federal housing rights via litigation) and the adverse action (threat of foreclosure). Under the retaliation framework, plaintiffs must allege (1) protected activity, (2) adverse action, and (3) causal connection. The court found only conclusory allegations of retaliation without specific facts establishing causation, which is insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (deprivation of constitutional rights under color of state law); 42 U.S.C. §§ 1985(2) and 1986 (conspiracy to deter witness/party from federal court); 18 U.S.C. § 1962(d) (RICO conspiracy)
fha_claims.reasoning: For § 1983: Plaintiffs failed to allege any person acting under color of state law or deprivation of constitutional rights. Merely pursuing a state foreclosure action does not constitute state action. For §§ 1985(2) and 1986: Plaintiffs' theory that settlement conference conduct constitutes a cognizable injury under § 1985 is not supported by Fifth Circuit precedent, which limits the statute to deterrence of witnesses/parties from attending or testifying in federal court, not settlement negotiations. The court found the legal theory not cognizable as a matter of law.

source_file: 10785316_2026_Hilda Kennedy v. New Jersey Court System_ca3

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged denial of access to courts and failure to implement ADA Title II measures, including failure to provide 'extra assistance,' speak slowly/loudly/clearly, assistive listening systems, Braille materials, and disability services centers. Also alleged adverse judicial rulings (dismissal of complaint, denial of stay, denial of fee waivers) as discriminatory.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege a Title II ADA claim because she did not allege that denial of accommodations or adverse judicial rulings were based on her disability, provided only conclusory allegations of discrimination, and failed to connect the lack of resources or services to her ability to access courts or participate in proceedings. The court applied the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard at the motion to dismiss stage.

source_file: 10785321_2026_Hemphill v. St. Mary's County Housing Authority_dcd
case_name: Hemphill v. St. Mary's County Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested permission to appear virtually in all court proceedings as a reasonable accommodation for her disability.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's TRO and reasonable accommodation motions because plaintiff failed to establish likelihood of success on the merits—she did not adequately demonstrate she has a disability, that defendant knew of her disability, or that any adverse action was caused by her disability status.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Larisha Hemphill, proceeding pro se, filed for a temporary restraining order and reasonable accommodation under the ADA and FHA against St. Mary's County Housing Authority. The court denied both motions because Hemphill failed to establish a likelihood of success on the merits—her filings did not adequately establish her disability status, causation linking any adverse action to disability, or imminent irreparable harm warranting emergency relief.
key_cases_cited: Giebeler v. M & B Assocs., 343 F.3d 1143 (9th Cir. 2003)
United States v. Georgia, 546 U.S. 151 (2006)
Alston v. District of Columbia, 561 F. Supp. 2d 29 (D.D.C. 2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unspecified reasonable accommodation related to disability; plaintiff references failure to test unit for mold, moisture levels, rent payment disputes, and denial of legally required accommodations, but does not clearly articulate what specific accommodation was requested or refused.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiff failed to establish a nexus between her disability and any alleged adverse action or accommodation request. The record does not show what plaintiff's disability is, what accommodation was requested, or how any alleged wrongs (mold testing, moisture levels, rent disputes) are connected to her disability status rather than being harms any tenant could suffer.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found no facts or direct evidence that St. Mary's County Housing Authority made decisions based on plaintiff's disability status, and thus lacked a basis to connect any adverse action to plaintiff's disability, which is required to establish disability-based discrimination under Title II of the ADA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II ADA claim for disability discrimination by public housing authority; eviction defense claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiff failed to establish that her eviction is based on discriminatory reasons or that her occupancy is an accommodation tied to her disability. An eviction is not, by itself, a violation of the ADA or FHA without facts showing discriminatory intent or disability-based causation.

source_file: 10785456_2026_New Hampshire Youth Movement v. David M. Scanlan, in his official capacity as New Hampshire Secretary of State; Coalition for Open Democracy et al. v. David Scanlan in his official capacity as New Hampshire
10785621_2026_Vladik Uchikura, et al. v. Clark County Properties LP, et al._azd
case_name: Vladik Uchikura, et al. v. Clark County Properties LP, et al.
accommodation_description: Wheelchair user plaintiff requested accommodation to access the leasing office, laundry room, and ground floor apartments which were allegedly inaccessible to people with physical disabilities.
key_holding: The court granted CPA's motion to dismiss because the TAC failed to allege any facts establishing successor liability—CPA purchased the property over three years after plaintiffs' tenancy ended, and there were no allegations of CPA's specific conduct, express assumption of liabilities, consolidation, mere continuation, or fraudulent transfer.
brief_summary: Vladik Uchikura and Cindy Mateer, individuals with disabilities including wheelchair use, sued Clark County Properties LP, management companies, and successor owner Copper Point Apartments LLC alleging Fair Housing Act violations for discrimination based on disability and failure to accommodate accessibility barriers at CopperPoint Apartments during their 2019-2021 tenancy. The court granted CPA's motion to dismiss on successor liability grounds, finding the TAC failed to allege any facts plausibly establishing that CPA assumed liability for the predecessor owners' alleged misconduct occurring years before CPA's 2024 property purchase.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Warne Investments, Ltd. v. Higgins

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessibility modifications to leasing office, laundry room, and ground floor apartment units to accommodate wheelchair use; assistance entering leasing office
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to allege sufficient facts establishing successor liability against Copper Point Apartments, LLC, which purchased the property in December 2024, over three years after Plaintiffs' tenancy ended in 2021. The TAC contains no allegations of CPA's specific conduct, no allegations that CPA assumed liabilities, and no factual basis for holding CPA liable for events predating its ownership.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged discrimination based on disability; exclusion from community events; multiple eviction attempts
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to allege sufficient facts establishing successor liability against Copper Point Apartments, LLC. The TAC lacks any allegations of CPA's specific conduct or involvement in discriminatory acts, which all occurred years before CPA's December 2024 purchase of the property.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claims; Arizona Disabilities Act (AzDA); Arizona Fair Housing Act (AFHA); Arizona Contract Law; Arizona Material Affect on Health and Safety of Occupants; Article 8 (Public Accommodations and Services) of Arizona's Civil Rights Laws
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to allege sufficient facts establishing successor liability against Copper Point Apartments, LLC. The TAC is devoid of allegations establishing an ADA, state statutory claim, or other basis for holding Defendant liable for events that transpired years before its purchase of the property.

source_file: 10785674_2026_Kathleen Bankhead, individually and on behalf of all others similarly situated v. Wintrust Financial Corporation and Barrington Bank _ Trust Co., N.A._ilnd
case_name: Kathleen Bankhead v. Wintrust Financial Corporation and Barrington Bank & Trust Co., N.A.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; case involves alleged race discrimination in mortgage lending terms and access to favorable loan products (float-down option, interest rates).
key_holding: The court dismissed the Second Amended Complaint with prejudice because plaintiff failed to plausibly allege intentional discrimination (no factual allegations of discriminatory animus connecting Wintrust's policies to racial disparities) or disparate impact (statistics alone, without identifying a specific 'artificial, arbitrary, and unnecessary' policy causing the disparity, cannot satisfy the robust causality requirement under Texas Dept. of Housing v. Inclusive Communities Project).
brief_summary: African American plaintiff Kathleen Bankhead sued Wintrust Financial Corporation and Barrington Bank alleging racial discrimination in mortgage lending, claiming she was denied favorable loan terms (float-down option, lower interest rates) because of her race and because she was purchasing property in Bronzeville, a majority-Black Chicago neighborhood. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss with prejudice, finding the complaint failed to plausibly allege intentional discrimination (no allegations of discriminatory animus connecting policies to disparities) and disparate impact (statistics alone, without identifying a specific policy causing disparity, cannot satisfy the causal requirements under Inclusive Communities).
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Texas Dept. of Housing and Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Swanson v. Citibank, N.A., 614 F.3d 400 (7th Cir. 2010)
McCauley v. City of Chicago, 671 F.3d 611 (7th Cir. 2011)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege intentional discrimination under the FHA by relying solely on statistical disparities without alleging facts suggesting discriminatory animus in loan officers' exercise of discretion or connecting disparities to defendant's intent. The pattern-and-practice claim required more detailed factual allegations than provided.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Under Inclusive Communities, plaintiff must allege a specific policy that is artificial, arbitrary, and unnecessary and show a causal connection between that policy and the statistical disparity. Plaintiff alleged only statistics controlling for objective factors without identifying any specific challenged policy or practice, failing to satisfy the robust causality requirement.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ECOA (Equal Credit Opportunity Act), 42 U.S.C. § 1981, 42 U.S.C. § 1982, state law claims (Counts I, II, III, V, VI, VII)
fha_claims.reasoning: ECOA and § 1981/§ 1982 disparate treatment claims failed for the same reasons as the FHA claim—insufficient factual allegations of intentional discrimination. State law claims were dismissed for lack of supplemental jurisdiction after federal claims were dismissed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodations for left-hand fracture sustained while working as registered nurse, including lifting/boosting restrictions and BLS/CPR accommodation; reassignment to Infection Preventionist position at lower pay and different schedule
fha_claims.reasoning: Pre-resignation reasonable accommodation claims survive motion to dismiss because the Release is disputed and may not be considered at the pleading stage; the court denied the motion to dismiss pre-resignation claims based solely on the Release.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of incentive shift/payment and differential treatment regarding accommodations compared to white colleague with arthritis
fha_claims.reasoning: Pre-resignation race discrimination claims survive motion to dismiss because the Release is disputed and may not be considered at the pleading stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Post-resignation retaliation based on filing EEOC charge in August 2024 and alleged adverse actions in February 2025 settlement negotiations
fha_claims.reasoning: Post-resignation retaliation claim fails because plaintiff did not allege any materially adverse action; offering a settlement agreement with release of EEOC claims is not facially retaliatory under Third Circuit law, and plaintiff was not denied any earned benefits. Additionally, the six-month temporal gap between the EEOC charge (August 2024) and settlement offer (February 2025) is insufficient to establish causal connection.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Post-resignation claims under Title VII retaliation, ADA retaliation, PHRA retaliation, 42 U.S.C. § 1981 race discrimination, and ADA § 12203(b) interference
fha_claims.reasoning: Post-resignation § 1981 claim dismissed because plaintiff failed to allege that the settlement offer was based on racial discrimination; racial discrimination allegations relate only to pre-resignation conduct. ADA interference claim dismissed because Reading Hospital's mere offer to settle the workers' compensation claim conditioned on withdrawal of EEOC charge does not constitute 'interference' under 42 U.S.C. § 12203(b), which requires meddling or hampering activity, not merely offering settlement terms.

source_file: 10785877_2026_Linda C. Chase v. Arbor Properties Development Inc., et al._flnd
case_name: Linda C. Chase v. Arbor Properties Development Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation requested; plaintiff alleges retaliation for having filed a prior fair housing complaint alleging disability discrimination.
key_holding: Plaintiff fails to state a plausible FHA retaliation claim because the temporal sequence—Arbor decided in June 2021 not to lease to Plaintiff before she filed her discrimination complaint in August 2021—irrefutably negates causation, and the ten-month gap between the protected activity and the adverse action is insufficient without additional factual allegations.
brief_summary: Linda C. Chase sued Arbor Properties Development Inc. and individual property managers alleging defendants denied her lease application at Arbor Landing Mill Bayou in retaliation for her having filed a fair housing complaint based on disability. The magistrate judge recommends dismissal, finding the second amended complaint is an impermissible shotgun pleading and alternatively that plaintiff failed to state a retaliation claim because the timeline negates causation.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Philippeaux v. Apartment Inv. & Mgmt. Co., 598 F. App'x 640 (11th Cir. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege a plausible causal connection between her protected activity (filing a fair housing complaint on August 28, 2021) and the adverse action (denial of lease application on June 15, 2022). The temporal sequence negates causation: Arbor decided not to lease to Plaintiff on June 25, 2021—before the complaint was filed—based on hostile conduct during her prior residency, and the ten-month gap between complaint and application, without additional facts suggesting causation, is insufficient to state a retaliation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Defamation claim under Florida law
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege the essential element of publication required for defamation: statements made to Plaintiff herself do not constitute publication under Florida law, and statements made to a fellow corporate employee are protected by the intra-corporate communications exception and qualified privilege for statements made by employees to other employees in the course of business.

source_file: 10786318_2026_Lorin Grossman v. B_J Services of Miami, LLC, et al._flsd
case_name: Lorin Grossman v. B&J Services of Miami, LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a wheelchair user, alleges landlord refused to show or lease property to her because of her physical disability.
key_holding: The court entered default judgment on Counts III–XI (Florida FHA claims and federal § 3604(c), (d), and (f)(1) claims) based on disability discrimination, but denied default judgment on Counts I and II because federal § 3604(a) and (b) do not cover disability-based discrimination.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Lorin Grossman, a wheelchair user, sued B&J Services of Miami and its agent alleging they refused to show or lease a rental property to her because of her disability after representing the property was unavailable while showing it to able-bodied prospective tenants. The court adopted the magistrate judge's recommendation to enter default judgment on most claims under the Florida Fair Housing Act and federal § 3604(c), (d), and (f)(1), awarding $132,200 in damages, but denied default judgment on federal § 3604(a) and (b) claims because those provisions do not cover disability discrimination.
key_cases_cited: Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)
Banai v. Sec'y, U.S. Dept. of Hous. & Urban Dev., 102 F.3d 1203 (11th Cir. 1997)
Eagle Hosp. Physicians, LLC v. SRG Consulting, Inc., 561 F.3d 1298 (11th Cir. 2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Count I under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(a) fails to state a claim because this subsection does not cover discrimination based on disability; plaintiff's allegations of disability-based discrimination cannot support relief under this provision.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Count II under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(b) fails to state a claim because this subsection does not cover discrimination based on disability; plaintiff's allegations of disability-based discrimination cannot support relief under this provision.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Count III under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c) states a plausible claim for making discriminatory statements in rental advertisements; plaintiff alleges defendant's written communications reflected that plaintiff's disability was the motivating factor in refusing to show and lease the property.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Count IV under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(d) states a plausible claim for misrepresentation regarding housing availability; plaintiff alleges defendants misrepresented that the property could not be toured on a day when able-bodied persons were allowed to tour, based on her disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Count V under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(1) states a plausible claim for disability discrimination; plaintiff alleges adverse action (refusal to show and rent property) was taken because of her disability, supported by allegations that able-bodied renters were allowed to tour and lease the property.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Count VI under Fla. Stat. § 760.23(1) states a plausible claim for disability discrimination; plaintiff alleges defendants had knowledge of her disability, she was qualified and willing to rent, and defendants used subterfuge and refused her the opportunity to view and lease the property because of her disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Count VII under Fla. Stat. § 760.23(2) states a plausible claim for discrimination in terms, conditions, or privileges of rental; plaintiff alleges she was denied equal opportunity to rent on the same terms as able-bodied prospective renters because of her disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Count VIII under Fla. Stat. § 760.23(3) states a plausible claim for discriminatory statements; plaintiff alleges defendant's written communications reflected that plaintiff's disability was the motivating factor in refusing to show and lease the property.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Count IX under Fla. Stat. § 760.23(4) states a plausible claim for misrepresentation regarding housing availability; plaintiff alleges defendants misrepresented that the property could not be toured on a day when able-bodied persons were allowed to tour, based on her disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Count X under Fla. Stat. § 760.23(7) states a plausible claim for disability discrimination; plaintiff alleges adverse action (refusal to show and rent property) was taken because of her disability, supported by allegations that able-bodied renters were allowed to tour and lease the property.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Count XI under Fla. Stat. § 760.23(8) states a plausible claim for discrimination in terms, conditions, or privileges of rental; plaintiff alleges she was denied equal opportunity to rent on the same terms as able-bodied prospective renters because of her disability.

source_file: 10786786_2026_Laquita Oliver v. Navy Federal Credit Union_ca4
case_name: Oliver v. Navy Federal Credit Union
accommodation_description: Class action alleging Navy Federal Credit Union's semi-automated underwriting algorithm produces discriminatory results against African American, Latino, and other minority mortgage applicants through disparate treatment and disparate impact.
key_holding: The Fourth Circuit held that district courts may deny class certification before discovery only if the complaint's allegations fail to satisfy Rule 23(a) and (b) as a matter of law, affirmed the denial of Rule 23(b)(3) class certification for lack of commonality due to significant variation across mortgage products, minority groups, and adverse outcomes, but vacated the Rule 23(b)(2) denial as premature.
brief_summary: Nine minority mortgage applicants sued Navy Federal Credit Union individually and on behalf of a putative class alleging that its semi-automated underwriting algorithm produces discriminatory results against African Americans, Latinos, and other racial minorities in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The Fourth Circuit affirmed the district court's denial of Rule 23(b)(3) class certification, finding the proposed class lacked commonality because statistical evidence showed disparate impact varied significantly across different mortgage products, minority groups, and adverse outcomes with no single practice uniformly affecting all class members, but vacated the Rule 23(b)(2) certification denial as premature.
key_cases_cited: Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. v. Dukes, 564 U.S. 338 (2011)
Goodman v. Schlesinger, 584 F.2d 1325 (4th Cir. 1978)
General Telephone Co. of Southwest v. Falcon, 457 U.S. 147 (1981)
Eisen v. Carlisle & Jacquelin, 417 U.S. 156 (1974)
Microsoft Corp. v. Baker, 582 U.S. 23 (2017)

source_file: 10786933_2026_Judy Shaw Foundation, Inc. v. City of Howard, South Dakota_sdd
case_name: Judy Shaw Foundation, Inc. v. City of Howard, South Dakota
accommodation_description: This is a procedural order striking defendant's untimely motion for partial summary judgment; no accommodation is analyzed as the court addressed only statutory standing and Rule 16(b) good cause.
key_holding: The City of Howard's partial summary judgment motion raised only statutory standing arguments (whether JSF qualifies as an 'aggrieved person' under the FHA and third-party standing under § 1983), which are non-jurisdictional merits issues subject to procedural deadlines; because the City failed to show good cause for filing nine months after the dispositive-motion deadline and was not diligent, the motion was properly stricken.
brief_summary: Judy Shaw Foundation, a fair housing organization, sued the City of Howard, South Dakota, under the Fair Housing Act (and § 1983); this order grants JSF's motion to strike the City's partial summary judgment motion as untimely. The court held that the City's motion raised only statutory standing issues (whether JSF is an 'aggrieved person' under the FHA) that are non-jurisdictional and subject to scheduling deadlines, and because the City failed to demonstrate good cause or diligence in filing nine months late, the motion was properly stricken.
key_cases_cited: Arbaugh v. Y & H Corp., 546 U.S. 500 (2006)
Bank of Am. Corp. v. City of Miami, 581 U.S. 189 (2017)
Steel Co. v. Citizens for a Better Env't, 523 U.S. 83 (1998)
Sherman v. Winco Fireworks, Inc., 532 F.3d 709 (8th Cir. 2008)
FW/PBS, Inc. v. City of Dallas, 493 U.S. 215 (1990)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not specified; the opinion addresses only procedural standing and does not describe the underlying FHA claim's substantive nature
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted plaintiff's motion to strike defendant's untimely partial summary judgment motion as procedurally barred under Rule 16(b). The court held that defendant's statutory standing arguments were non-jurisdictional and subject to ordinary procedural deadlines, which defendant failed to meet. The underlying FHA claims survive and remain pending.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 claim; defendant argued plaintiff improperly asserts rights of third parties
fha_claims.reasoning: The court struck defendant's untimely partial summary judgment motion challenging plaintiff's statutory standing under § 1983 as procedurally barred. The court held that statutory standing arguments are non-jurisdictional and subject to ordinary procedural rules, which defendant violated by filing nine months after the dispositive-motion deadline.

fha_claims.reasoning: This order grants plaintiff's request for pro bono counsel and does not address the merits of any non-FHA claims. The court noted that plaintiff alleges constitutional and statutory violations but made no substantive ruling on these claims.

source_file: 10787023_2026_United States of America v. Douglas S. Waterbury, Carol A. Waterbury, E_A Management Co., and Ontario Realty, Inc._nynd
case_name: United States of America v. Douglas S. Waterbury, Carol A. Waterbury, E&A Management Co., and Ontario Realty, Inc.
accommodation_description: This is a procedural motion to dismiss based on the expiration of a consent decree, not a reasonable accommodation case; the underlying discrimination allegations are not substantively analyzed in this order.
key_holding: The consent decree, which was entered on August 9, 2019 with a five-year effective period, expired on August 9, 2024, and neither party moved to extend it, so the case must be dismissed with prejudice.
brief_summary: The United States government sued landlords and property management companies for Fair Housing Act violations, a consent decree was entered in 2019, and defendants were later held in contempt for violating it. On defendants' motion, the court dismissed the case with prejudice because the five-year consent decree expired on August 9, 2024, and neither party sought to extend it.
key_cases_cited: J.G. v. Bd. of Educ. of Rochester City Sch. Dist., 193 F. Supp. 2d 693 (W.D.N.Y. 2002)
Balark v. City of Chicago, 81 F.3d 658 (7th Cir. 1996)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: The complaint alleged discriminatory ownership, management, and/or operation of properties in Oswego, New York, but the opinion does not specify the nature of the discrimination or any particular accommodation request.
fha_claims.reasoning: The parties entered into a signed consent decree on August 9, 2019, which resolved the FHA claims without adjudication on the merits. The case was subsequently dismissed with prejudice on February 9, 2026, after the five-year term of the consent decree expired and neither party sought extension.

source_file: 10793996_2026_Chelsie Nitschke and Cynthia George v. 326 Welch Partners; Avenue Construction, LLC; Barnett Design Studio, LLC_tnmd
case_name: Chelsie Nitschke and Cynthia George v. 326 Welch Partners; Avenue Construction, LLC; Barnett Design Studio, LLC
accommodation_description: This is a design and construction accessibility case, not an individual accommodation request case; the plaintiffs alleged the apartment complex failed to meet FHA accessibility requirements.
key_holding: The court granted judgment on the pleadings and found defendants liable for violating 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(C) and the ADA by failing to design and construct the apartment complex in compliance with federal accessibility standards.
brief_summary: Two disabled Tennessee residents sued the owner, construction company, and architectural firm of a Nashville apartment complex, alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act's design and construction requirements. The defendants admitted most allegations and acknowledged violations of the FHA and Fair Housing Act Accessibility Guidelines, with the court granting judgment on the pleadings and finding defendants liable for failing to design and construct accessible covered multifamily dwellings under § 3604(f)(3)(C).
key_cases_cited: Meyer Nat. Foods, LLC v. Liberty Mut. Fire Ins. Co., 218 F. Supp. 3d 1034 (D. Neb. 2016)
Grindstaff v. Green, 133 F.3d 416 (6th Cir. 1998)
Tucker v. Middleburg-Legacy Place, 539 F.3d 545 (6th Cir. 2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible design and construction of covered multifamily dwellings, including ground-floor units and upper-floor units served by elevators, and public and common-use areas in compliance with FHA accessibility guidelines and ADA standards
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 12(c) — Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted plaintiffs' motion for judgment on the pleadings and found defendants liable for FHA violations under § 3604(f)(3)(C). Defendants admitted the apartment complex contains covered multifamily dwellings built after March 13, 1991, and admitted certain elements do not comply with FHA accessibility guidelines and standards. The court applied the design and construction standard and found defendants failed to design and construct dwellings in compliance with the FHA and applicable regulations.

source_file: 10794074_2026_Scott William Marston v. Bellsouth Communications, LLC_alsd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA failure to accommodate (additional leave beyond FMLA), ADA hostile work environment, ADA retaliatory hostile work environment, ADA retaliation, FMLA retaliation, FMLA interference, ADA interference, constructive discharge
fha_claims.reasoning: All eight claims brought under the ADA and FMLA (not the FHA). The court granted summary judgment on all claims, finding that plaintiff failed to establish prima facie cases or that defendant established affirmative defenses (Faragher-Ellerth for hostile work environment, legitimate nonretaliatory reasons for adverse actions, failure to exhaust administrative remedies for accommodation and interference claims, and lack of causation for retaliation claims).

source_file: 10795232_2026_Rosalind Holmes v. Warren County Metropolitan Housing Authority_ohsd
case_name: Rosalind Holmes v. Warren County Metropolitan Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Request for a two-bedroom unit to permit plaintiff's mother, a disability-related live-in caregiver, to be included in the household
key_holding: The court recommended denying the TRO and preliminary injunction because plaintiff failed to demonstrate a substantial likelihood of success on the merits, irreparable harm, or that the requested affirmative relief fell within the proper scope of preliminary injunctive relief.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Rosalind Holmes sued Warren County Metropolitan Housing Authority under the Fair Housing Act alleging the agency denied her reasonable accommodation request for a two-bedroom unit to permit her mother to live with her as a disability-related live-in caregiver. The court recommended denying plaintiff's motion for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction, finding she failed to demonstrate a substantial likelihood of success on the merits or irreparable harm warranting extraordinary relief.
key_cases_cited: Liberty Coins, LLC v. Goodman, 748 F.3d 682 (6th Cir. 2014)
Winter v. Nat. Res. Def. Council, Inc., 555 U.S. 7 (2008)

Jones v. City of Monroe, 341 F.3d 474 (6th Cir. 2003)
Chabad of S. Ohio & Congregation Lubavitch v. City of Cincinnati, 363 F.3d 427 (6th Cir. 2004)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation to permit inclusion of plaintiff's mother as a disability-related live-in caregiver in a two-bedroom unit within the Rapid Re-Housing program
fha_claims.disposition: Motion for TRO and Preliminary Injunction Denied
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the TRO and preliminary injunction motion because plaintiff failed to demonstrate a substantial likelihood of success on the merits of her FHA claim or to show irreparable harm. The court did not reach the substantive merits of the reasonable accommodation claim itself, only the preliminary injunction factors.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II (42 U.S.C. § 12132), Rehabilitation Act (29 U.S.C. § 794), Due Process (42 U.S.C. § 1983)
fha_claims.disposition: Motion for TRO and Preliminary Injunction Denied
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the TRO and preliminary injunction motion, finding plaintiff failed to demonstrate a substantial likelihood of success on the merits of her ADA Title II, Rehabilitation Act, and due process claims, and failed to connect those claims to the injunctive relief sought or show irreparable harm.

source_file: 10795873_2026_Bianca Bates v. Amin Habeeb, Marisol Bassit, and Iron Valley Real Estate_pamd
case_name: Bianca Bates v. Amin Habeeb, Marisol Bassit, and Iron Valley Real Estate
accommodation_description: No accommodation request is described; the amended complaint is completely devoid of any factual allegations about what the defendants did.
key_holding: The court dismissed the amended complaint with prejudice because it failed to state any claims—the complaint was devoid of factual allegations detailing what the defendants allegedly did to violate the Fair Housing Act, ADA, Rehabilitation Act, or constitutional rights.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Bianca Bates sued Amin Habeeb, Marisol Bassit, and Iron Valley Real Estate for alleged violations of the Fair Housing Act, ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and constitutional rights. fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not specified; complaint devoid of factual allegations
fha_claims.reasoning: The amended complaint failed to state a claim because it was completely devoid of any facts detailing what defendants allegedly did to plaintiff. Pro se pleadings must still comply with the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and plausibility standards.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act, 42 U.S.C. § 12101 et seq.; Rehabilitation Act, 29 U.S.C. § 701 et seq.; constitutional rights violations
fha_claims.reasoning: Non-FHA claims (ADA, Rehabilitation Act, constitutional claims) were dismissed along with the FHA claim for failure to state a claim due to complete absence of factual allegations.

case_name: Eleanor McGinn v. Broadmead, Inc.
accommodation_description: Request for gluten-free meals at a continuing care retirement community due to celiac disease
key_holding: The Fourth Circuit held that McGinn forfeited review of her Fair Housing Act claim by failing to address the district court's alternate ground for dismissal, and alternatively that her FHA claim was barred by the two-year statute of limitations since the alleged failure to accommodate occurred in January 2019 and she filed suit in September 2023.
brief_summary: Eleanor McGinn, who has celiac disease, sued Broadmead, Inc., her continuing care retirement community, alleging it failed to accommodate her dietary needs by repeatedly serving her meals containing gluten. The Fourth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for Broadmead on McGinn's Fair Housing Act claim, holding that she forfeited review by failing to address the district court's alternative reasoning and that her claim was untimely under the two-year statute of limitations; the court vacated summary judgment on state law breach of contract and negligence claims arising from a January 2021 incident involving allegedly contaminated chicken marsala.
key_cases_cited: Laufer v. Naranda Hotels, LLC, 60 F.4th 156 (4th Cir. 2023)
Nanni v. Aberdeen Marketplace, Inc., 878 F.3d 447 (4th Cir. 2017)
Hill v. Hampstead Lester Morton Ct. Partners LP, 581 F. App'x 178 (4th Cir. 2014)
Frederick Rd. Ltd. P'ship v. Brown & Sturm, 756 A.2d 963 (Md. 2000)
Clapper v. Amnesty Int'l USA, 568 U.S. 398 (2013)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Gluten-free meal preparation and accommodation for celiac disease; failure to provide safe gluten-free meals at retirement community dining facilities
fha_claims.reasoning: The Fair Housing Act claim accrued in January 2019 when plaintiff first informed defendant of the alleged failure to accommodate her disability. The two-year FHA limitations period expired in January 2021. Plaintiff did not file suit until September 2023, making the claim time-barred. The continuing violation doctrine does not apply to failure-to-accommodate claims outside the hostile workplace context.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (injunctive relief claim); Rehabilitation Act (failure to accommodate); state law breach of contract and negligence claims
fha_claims.disposition: Standing / Statute of Limitations / Summary Judgment
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff lacked standing to seek injunctive relief under the ADA because she failed to demonstrate a real or immediate threat of future wrongdoing. Past injury alone is insufficient; plaintiff must show a plausible intent to return for the service. At summary judgment, plaintiff could not point to evidence she would ever eat again at defendant's facilities, and she refused to eat there even after defendant implemented the changes she requested.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rehabilitation Act claim for failure to accommodate celiac disease
fha_claims.reasoning: The Rehabilitation Act claim accrued in January 2019 when plaintiff first informed defendant of the alleged failure to accommodate. Applying Maryland's three-year limitations period, the claim expired in January 2022. Plaintiff did not file suit until September 2023, making the claim time-barred. Plaintiff forfeited appellate review by failing to address the district court's alternate ground that the continuing violation doctrine does not apply to failure-to-accommodate claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: State law breach of contract and negligence claims arising from alleged gluten exposure in February 2018 crab cake incident
fha_claims.reasoning: The three-year Maryland statute of limitations for breach of contract and negligence claims ran in February 2021 from the February 2018 incident. Maryland's discovery rule does not apply because plaintiff had actual knowledge of the need to inquire into the crab cake's ingredients and made only a limited inquiry without diligence. Plaintiff did not file suit until September 2023. Additionally, on the merits, plaintiff's speculation that the 2021 chef's use of Rice Krispies proves the 2018 chef did the same is insufficient; the evidence shows the 2018 chef used gluten-free bread crumbs.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: State law breach of contract and negligence claims arising from alleged gluten exposure in January 2021 chicken marsala incident
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court erred in granting summary judgment because it overlooked the defendant administrator's statements that she instructed the dining director 'to determine how this process failed' and '[s]omewhere along the line there was a failure and we will find it.' These statements create a genuine issue of material fact as to whether they constitute admissions of wrongdoing or mere promises to investigate. A jury must weigh these statements against other evidence.

case_name: Connecticut Fair Housing Center and Carmen Arroyo v. CoreLogic Rental Property Solutions, LLC
accommodation_description: Arroyo requested that CoreLogic accept her conservatorship certificate as proof of authority to access her son Mikhail's consumer file, rather than requiring a power of attorney which Mikhail, as a conservatee, could not execute.
key_holding: The Second Circuit affirmed that CoreLogic did not violate the Fair Housing Act because it did not proximately cause the denial of housing, and Arroyo failed to establish a prima facie case of disparate impact or failure to accommodate since she never provided a facially valid conservatorship certificate even after being informed of the documentation requirement.
brief_summary: Connecticut Fair Housing Center and Carmen Arroyo sued CoreLogic Rental Property Solutions, which provides tenant screening reports to housing providers, alleging that CoreLogic violated the Fair Housing Act by facilitating housing denials based on criminal history and by refusing to accept a conservatorship certificate as documentation for accessing a disabled conservatee's consumer file. The Second Circuit affirmed dismissal of the FHA claims, holding that CoreLogic did not proximately cause housing denials because landlords made independent discretionary decisions, and that Arroyo's failure-to-accommodate claim failed because she never provided a facially valid conservatorship certificate despite being informed of the requirement.
key_cases_cited: Staub v. Proctor Hospital, 562 U.S. 411 (2011)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Texas Dept. of Housing & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Bank of America Corp. v. City of Miami, 581 U.S. 189 (2017)
FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Med., 144 S. Ct. 1540 (2024)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Disparate impact claim based on CrimSAFE criminal history screening platform's effect on African American and Hispanic rental applicants
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish proximate cause—a required element of the prima facie case—because CoreLogic did not directly cause the denial of housing. The housing provider (WinnResidential) made all discretionary decisions regarding application of screening criteria, configuration of the platform, and ultimate approval or denial. The attenuated connection between CoreLogic's provision of a tool and the provider's independent decision falls short of the required 'direct relation' between conduct and harm under the FHA's proximate cause standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Disparate impact claim based on CoreLogic's policy requiring power of attorney documentation for third-party disclosure of consumer reports, allegedly affecting handicapped individuals under conservatorship
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie case of disparate impact because the record showed CoreLogic had never encountered a request from a conservator for a conservatee's consumer file, and plaintiff presented no statistical evidence of disparate impact. The written policies referred uncommon scenarios to a supervisor; the failure of an employee to follow written policies in one instance does not establish a policy causing disparate impact. At step two, CoreLogic established a legitimate business justification: the FCRA requires proper identification before disclosure, and the conservatorship certificate itself stated it was invalid without an impressed seal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request that CoreLogic accept a conservatorship certificate without a visible impressed seal as proper identification for disclosure of consumer report
fha_claims.reasoning: The requested accommodation was not reasonable because it would have required CoreLogic to ignore the certificate's own express requirement that it be valid only with an impressed seal. The FCRA requires CoreLogic to adopt reasonable procedures regarding confidentiality and proper identification. Requiring valid documentation was a legitimate business justification, and the cost and burden of accepting an invalid document exceeded what could be considered a reasonable accommodation. Additionally, delay in communicating requirements was not constructive denial because Arroyo's own conduct contributed to the delay, and she failed to submit proper identification even after receiving clear instructions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) claims under 15 U.S.C. § 1681g and § 1681h; Connecticut Unfair Trade Practices Act (CUTPA) claims
fha_claims.disposition: Judgment after bench trial; reversed on appeal
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court imposed FCRA liability for the June-November 2016 period, finding CoreLogic willfully violated the statute by making it 'impossible' for Arroyo to request Mikhail's file. However, on appeal, the court reversed because Arroyo never furnished proper identification—a condition precedent to any right to disclosure under the FCRA. Even after receiving clear instructions that a conservatorship certificate with a visible seal would be acceptable, Arroyo did not submit one. The undisputed evidence showed she could not establish that absent CoreLogic's conduct, she would have submitted proper identification. Therefore, she failed to show her inability to obtain disclosure resulted from CoreLogic's conduct rather than her own failure to provide valid documentation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Disparate impact claim on basis of race and national origin regarding CrimSAFE criminal history screening platform (brought by Connecticut Fair Housing Center)
fha_claims.disposition: Vacated and dismissed for lack of standing
fha_claims.reasoning: The Connecticut Fair Housing Center lacked Article III standing to bring the claim. Under FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine, an organization cannot manufacture standing by diverting resources to investigate and advocate against a defendant's conduct. The CFHC alleged only frustration of mission and diversion of resources—precisely the theory rejected by the Supreme Court. Unlike Havens, where the organization operated a core business service (housing counseling) directly impaired by the defendant's conduct, the CFHC engaged in advocacy and informational programming. The choice to focus resources on CoreLogic to the detriment of other priorities does not constitute an injury in fact conferring Article III standing.

source_file: 10797116_2025_Kiara S. Jones v. Chad Chronister, ET AL._flmd
case_name: Kiara S. Jones v. Chad Chronister, ET AL.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff challenges the legitimacy of a writ of possession issued while her eviction appeal was pending, seeking to have her eviction reversed or enjoined.
key_holding: The Rooker-Feldman doctrine bars federal review of state court judgments, and Florida law permitted the trial court to issue the writ of possession while the underlying order was on appeal absent a stay.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Kiara Jones, proceeding pro se, sued Sheriff Chad Chronister, Deputy Harrison, landlord Earl B. Mason Sr., and attorney Jason Kao challenging the validity of a writ of possession executed during her appeal of an eviction judgment. The Magistrate Judge recommends denying Jones's in forma pauperis motion and dismissing the amended complaint with prejudice because the Rooker-Feldman doctrine bars federal review of the state court judgment and Florida law permitted issuance of the writ pending appeal absent a stay.
key_cases_cited: Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Saudi Basic Indus. Corp., 544 U.S. 280 (2005)
Siegel v. LePore, 234 F.3d 1163 (11th Cir. 2000)
Carr v. U.S. Bank, 793 F. App'x 971 (11th Cir. 2019)
Mann-Stack v. Homeside Lending, Inc., 982 So. 2d 72 (Fla. 2nd DCA 2008)
Fonseca v. Taverna Imports, Inc., 193 So. 3d 92 (Fla. 3rd DCA 2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged violations of Fourth Amendment, Fourteenth Amendment, Fair Housing Act, and Violence Against Women Act arising from state court eviction proceedings and execution of writ of possession.
fha_claims.disposition: Recommended dismissal under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B) and Rooker-Feldman doctrine
fha_claims.reasoning: The Rooker-Feldman doctrine divests federal courts of jurisdiction to review final judgments of state courts. All of Plaintiff's claims, including any FHA claim, require the Court to rule that the state court improperly issued the writ of possession, which is barred. Additionally, under Florida law, the trial court retained power to enforce a judgment on appeal absent a stay, so the claims lack merit independently.

source_file: 10797202_2026_Leonor E Canales v. Phoenix Housing Authority, et al._azd
case_name: Leonor E Canales v. Phoenix Housing Authority, et al.
accommodation_description: Request that PHA accept alternative medical documentation instead of required physician-signed accommodation form to process her Section 8 reasonable accommodation request
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's failure to accommodate claim because she failed to allege sufficient facts about what specific accommodation she requested, how it was necessary to afford her equal opportunity to use and enjoy her dwelling, and why it was reasonable, though granting leave to amend.
brief_summary: Leonor Canales, a Section 8 participant with multiple mental health disabilities including depression, anxiety, PTSD, and bipolar disorder, sued the Phoenix Housing Authority alleging it failed to provide reasonable accommodations by refusing to accept her medical records instead of a required physician-signed form and failed to engage in an interactive process. The court dismissed her reasonable accommodation claim without prejudice for failure to state a claim, finding she did not adequately allege what accommodation she requested or why it was necessary and reasonable, though it allowed her retaliation claim to proceed.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Howard v. HMK Holdings, LLC, 988 F.3d 1185 (9th Cir. 2021)
Salisbury v. City of Santa Monica, 998 F.3d 852 (9th Cir. 2021)
Gamble v. City of Escondido, 104 F.3d 300 (9th Cir. 1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Acceptance of alternative medical documentation (comprehensive medical records) in lieu of a specific housing authority form signed by a physician; relief from rigid enforcement of internal procedures requiring physician signature on accommodation request form
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff insufficiently pleaded the reasonable accommodation claim because she failed to allege facts showing how the requested accommodation may be necessary to afford her equal opportunity to use and enjoy her dwelling, or that it was reasonable. Court granted leave to amend.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff plausibly alleged all three elements of FHA and ADA retaliation: (1) protected activity (requesting reasonable accommodations and expressing intent to file HUD complaint); (2) adverse action (rejection of accommodation form and dismissive statement from employee Cole); and (3) causal link (Cole's statement that complaint would be denied again, which plaintiff experienced as retaliatory and intended to discourage her from exercising fair housing rights). Claim survives screening and defendants must answer.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 due process claim; ADA Title II disability discrimination claim; Rehabilitation Act § 504 disability discrimination claim; state law negligence claim
fha_claims.reasoning: § 1983 claim dismissed for failure to identify a constitutional right or federal law upon which the claim is predicated. ADA Title II and Rehabilitation Act § 504 claims dismissed because plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts showing she was denied accommodations solely/because of her disability, which is a required element. Negligence claim dismissed because plaintiff was not yet a tenant (only a Section 8 program participant applying for housing) and thus no duty of care was owed; court granted leave to amend on ADA/RA claims but dismissed negligence without prejudice.

source_file: 10797228_2026_Tyrone K. White v. Harvard Security, LLC_paed

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VII retaliation, harassment, and constructive discharge claims based on race
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's grievances fail to raise a reasonable expectation that discovery will reveal evidence of retaliation, harassment, or constructive discharge based on race. The complaint makes virtually no connection between the alleged adverse employment actions (broken gate, work duties, scheduling) and race discrimination, and the scant references to race appear only in supplemental filings at the motion-to-dismiss stage. Even construing liberally, the allegations do not plausibly suggest severe or pervasive discrimination or intolerable working conditions required for these Title VII claims.

source_file: 10799433_2026_Joyce Ann Jefferson v. Landmark Apartment Associates; Ross Financial Services, Inc.; Cris Barnett_ilcd
case_name: Joyce Ann Jefferson v. Landmark Apartment Associates; Ross Financial Services, Inc.; Cris Barnett
accommodation_description: Not applicable — this case does not involve a request for reasonable accommodation or modification; the FHA claims concern hostile housing environment and constructive eviction based on race and disability discrimination.
key_holding: The court granted Jefferson's motion for leave to amend her complaint to add six individual defendants and three state-law claims, finding the proposed amendments were not futile because the amended complaint stated plausible claims for FHA racial and disability discrimination, § 3617 interference/intimidation, conversion, constructive eviction, Illinois Landlord Retaliation Act violation, and negligence.
brief_summary: Joyce Ann Jefferson, a tenant in a federally subsidized apartment in Peoria managed by Landmark Apartment Associates and Ross Financial Services, alleged that employees stole her belongings and sold them on Facebook Marketplace, then launched a campaign of racial slurs, harassment, threats, and intimidation that drove her from the property. She brought FHA claims for racial and disability discrimination (§§ 3604(b) and 3604(c)) and unlawful intimidation (§ 3617), along with state-law claims for conversion. Jefferson moved to amend her complaint to add six individual employee defendants and three additional state-law claims (constructive eviction, Illinois Landlord Retaliation Act, and negligence). The court granted leave to amend in full, rejecting defendants' futility arguments on every count.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009) (en banc)
Wetzel v. Glen St. Andrew Living Community, LLC, 901 F.3d 856 (7th Cir. 2018)
Runnion ex rel. Runnion v. Girl Scouts of Greater Chi. & Nw. Ind., 786 F.3d 510 (7th Cir. 2015)
Grieveson v. Anderson, 538 F.3d 763 (7th Cir. 2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that Jefferson's § 3604(b) racial discrimination claim alleging hostile housing environment and constructive eviction states a plausible claim. The theft of property was only the first chapter; the subsequent threats, racial slurs, and harassment created the alleged hostile environment sufficient to survive futility review on motion to amend.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that Jefferson's § 3604(c) disability discrimination claim, combined with allegations of unlawful intimidation under § 3617, states a plausible claim. The court rejected Landmark's argument that Jefferson failed to allege a causal connection between disability and the alleged conduct, finding that the complaint adequately alleges harassment and intimidation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Conversion (state law), Constructive Eviction (state law), Illinois Landlord Retaliation Act (state law), Negligence (state law)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that all four state-law claims survive futility review. Conversion claim survives because property can be converted when lawfully acquired but later unjustifiably withheld. Constructive eviction claim survives because intent to deprive can be inferred from harassment and threats. Illinois Landlord Retaliation Act claim survives despite novel interpretation questions. Negligence claim survives because foreseeability of harm and lack of true abandonment establish a legal duty.
