10800666_2026_Estela Elizabeth Jeffcoat v. Brookings Housing _ Redevelopment Commission_sdd
case_name: Estela Elizabeth Jeffcoat v. Brookings Housing & Redevelopment Commission
accommodation_description: Plaintiff filed a motion for protective order prohibiting defendant from contacting her employer about employment, income, or medical limitations, which the court analyzed as unrelated to discovery.
key_holding: The magistrate judge's denial of plaintiff's protective order motion was not clearly erroneous or contrary to law because the motion was unrelated to discovery requests and plaintiff failed to meet and confer with defendant before filing.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Estela Elizabeth Jeffcoat filed an objection to Magistrate Judge Duffy's order denying her motion for a protective order to prevent defendant housing authority from contacting her employer about her employment, income, or medical limitations. The district court overruled her objection, finding the protective order motion was not related to any discovery requests in the case and plaintiff failed to meet and confer with defendant before filing.
key_cases_cited: Ferguson v. United States, 484 F.3d 1068 (8th Cir. 2007)
Gateway, Inc. v. Companion Prods., Inc., 384 F.3d 503 (8th Cir. 2004)
United States v. Red Bird, 2020 WL 6129634 (D.S.D. Oct. 19, 2020)

case_name: Brown v. Nationwide Mutual Insurance Company
accommodation_description: Plaintiff with disability affecting executive function requested that insurance claims adjuster explain water remediation procedures in simplified terms.
key_holding: All of plaintiff's claims, including FHA reasonable accommodation claims, were dismissed with prejudice as time-barred because the alleged discriminatory conduct occurred in 2016 but plaintiff did not file suit until 2024, well beyond the applicable statutes of limitations.
brief_summary: Randy Brown sued Nationwide Mutual Insurance Company eight years after a 2016 water damage claim, alleging violations of the ADA and FHA based on the insurer's failure to provide effective communication accommodations about water remediation procedures. The court dismissed all claims with prejudice as time-barred, finding no basis for statutory tolling or equitable exception.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Firestone v. Firestone, 76 F.3d 1205 (D.C. Cir. 1996)
Smith-Haynie v. District of Columbia, 155 F.3d 575 (D.C. Cir. 1998)
Reese v. Park Place Condo. Homeowners Ass’n I, 2023 WL 5833678 (D.D.C. 2023)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Effective communication about water damage remediation procedures in simple terms to accommodate plaintiff's impaired executive functioning
fha_claims.reasoning: The FHA claim accrued in 2016 when plaintiff knew or had reason to know of Nationwide's alleged denial of his request for effective communication. The two-year FHA statute of limitations expired before plaintiff filed suit in 2024. No continuing violation was adequately pleaded, and no tolling applied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged creation of hostile environment through misrepresentation of water damage procedures
fha_claims.reasoning: The FHA hostile environment claim based on alleged misrepresentations in 2016 is barred by the two-year FHA statute of limitations. Plaintiff's allegations of ongoing requests from 2016 to 2024 do not establish a continuing violation because the complaint fails to specify the timing, nature, or Nationwide's response to any requests beyond 2016.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III claim for failure to provide reasonable accommodations for effective communication; D.C. Consumer Protection Procedures Act claim for unfair/deceptive trade practices; intentional infliction of emotional distress; breach of contract
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA claims accrued in 2016 based on Nationwide's alleged statements to plaintiff. The ADA claim is time-barred under the applicable statute of limitations (three or four years depending on the theory), and D.C. law claims are barred by the three-year limitations period. No statutory tolling or equitable tolling (including the D.C. 'lulling doctrine') applies because plaintiff has not alleged affirmative misconduct or inducement to delay.

source_file: 10802670_2026_Sandy Phillips v. Stoddard County Circuit Court, et al._moed
case_name: Sandy Phillips v. Stoddard County Circuit Court, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested telephonic appearance at court hearings as an ADA Title II accommodation due to a documented disability that prevents her from driving; she alleged she had previously requested this accommodation from the Missouri state court but was denied, and she renewed the request before the federal court. In the housing context, she also alleged denial of 'reasonable modifications and telephonic accommodations' in state court proceedings where she sought to litigate her housing claims.
key_holding: The court grants plaintiff in forma pauperis status but orders her to file a second amended complaint on the court-provided form, finding the amended complaint legally deficient for misjoining unrelated claims against different defendant groups and failing to plead essential elements for each cause of action under the FHA, ADA Title II, and § 1983.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Sandy Phillips brought claims under the FHA, ADA Title II, 42 U.S.C. § 1983, and Missouri law against her landlord and associated agents (for habitability issues and retaliatory conduct) and against state court defendants (for denying telephonic hearing accommodations). The court granted IFP status and conducted an initial § 1915 review, identifying multiple deficiencies including misjoinder of unrelated claims arising from two separate factual situations, and failure to allege essential elements for each legal theory. The court ordered plaintiff to file a second amended complaint choosing which set of claims to pursue in this action, warning that failure to comply would result in dismissal.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Monell v. Dep't of Soc. Servs., 436 U.S. 658 (1978)
Rooker v. Fidelity Trust Co., 263 U.S. 413 (1923)
George v. Smith, 507 F.3d 605 (7th Cir. 2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged retaliation for complaining about housing conditions (roaches, nonfunctioning stove, mold, lack of hot water, broken doors/smoke detectors), including threats of eviction, removal of doors, wiretapping, defamatory statements, and denial of relocation or repairs.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiff failed to allege facts establishing a nexus between protected FHA activity and retaliatory conduct. Plaintiff complained about apartment conditions (roaches, hot water, broken equipment, mold, stove) but did not allege that any condition failed to accommodate her disability, and thus did not engage in protected activity under the FHA. Without protected activity, any allegedly retaliatory actions are not prohibited by the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested reasonable modifications and telephonic accommodations from the Missouri state court system to provide meaningful access to court proceedings where she was attempting to bring her housing claims.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts to state a Title II ADA claim. Plaintiff alleged only that she called the courthouse and spoke with a court clerk to request telephone access to a hearing but never heard back, which is insufficient to state a plausible claim for exclusion from participation in court services by reason of disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of Implied Warranty of Habitability/Constructive Eviction (state law); Illegal Wiretapping and Invasion of Privacy (state law); § 1983 due process and civil rights claims against state and private defendants.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found multiple pleading deficiencies: (1) § 1983 claims against private defendants (Gill Family Properties, Chad Gill, Kyle Orf, Cortney Bass, Kayse Soule) fail because they are not state actors; (2) § 1983 claims against state courts fail due to Eleventh Amendment state sovereign immunity; (3) state law claims lack sufficient factual pleading; (4) joinder of unrelated claims (housing and court access) violates Federal Rule 20 and must be brought in separate suits.

source_file: 10803192_2026_Jermaine Capel v. Norfolk Redevelopment _ Housing Authority_ca4
case_name: Jermaine M. Capel v. Norfolk Redevelopment & Housing Authority
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: The Fourth Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B), finding no reversible error in the dismissal of plaintiff's Fair Housing Act and § 1983 claims.
brief_summary: Jermaine M. Capel, proceeding pro se, appealed the Eastern District of Virginia's dismissal of his Fair Housing Act and 42 U.S.C. § 1983 claims against Norfolk Redevelopment & Housing Authority. The Fourth Circuit affirmed, finding no reversible error in the district court's § 1915(e)(2)(B) dismissal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 due process claim; FHA claims not substantively described in opinion
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court dismissed the amended complaint under § 1915(e)(2)(B) as frivolous or failing to state a claim. The appellate court affirmed without identifying specific deficiencies, indicating the claims were deemed clearly baseless or indisputably meritless at the screening stage.

source_file: 10803438_2026_Tanesha A. Turner v. 3526-28 E 9TH AVE TRUST, et al._innd
case_name: Tanesha A. Turner v. 3526-28 E 9TH AVE TRUST, et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; plaintiff alleges discrimination based on familial status, sex, and domestic violence history, and retaliation for reporting housing violations.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA discrimination claim for failing to allege facts connecting defendants' actions to her protected characteristics, and dismissed her retaliation claim for failing to adequately plead protected activity under Rule 8 and Twombly.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Tanesha A. Turner sued her landlord, a housing assistance organization (Continuum of Care Network), and related individuals alleging Fair Housing Act discrimination based on familial status, sex, and domestic violence history, as well as retaliation for reporting housing violations. The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss, finding the complaint failed to state a plausible claim because it lacked factual allegations connecting defendants' conduct to any protected characteristic and failed to adequately plead protected activity for the retaliation claim.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Rooker v. Fidelity Trust Co., 263 U.S. 413 (1923)
District of Columbia Court of Appeals v. Feldman, 460 U.S. 462 (1983)
Wetzel v. Glen St. Andrew Living Cmty., LLC, 901 F.3d 856 (7th Cir. 2018)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that defendants' actions were connected to any protected characteristic under the FHA. The complaint contained only conclusory allegations of discrimination based on familial status, sex, and domestic violence history without factual allegations connecting defendants' conduct to these protected characteristics, failing to meet the Twombly plausibility standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to adequately allege protected activity under the FHA retaliation standard. Reporting general housing conditions, fraud, and domestic violence issues does not constitute protected activity under the FHA, and plaintiff failed to allege facts showing a causal connection between any protected activity and defendants' actions, failing the Twombly plausibility test.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Violence Against Women Act (34 U.S.C. § 12491), Indiana state law claims for fraud, fraudulent concealment, breach of habitability, negligence, retaliatory eviction, wrongful eviction, abuse of process, constructive eviction, intentional infliction of emotional distress, negligent infliction of emotional distress, and violations of the Indiana Deceptive Consumer Sales Act
fha_claims.reasoning: The court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3) because all federal claims were disposed of prior to trial. The VAWA claim was also dismissed because it does not provide a private right of action against the defendants in this case under United States v. Morrison.

source_file: 10804321_2026_Memphis Street Academy Charter School at J.P. Jone v. Philadelphia School District_ca3
10804696_2026_Karen DeMoor v. Freeman Webb Company, Realtors, et al._tnmd
case_name: Karen DeMoor v. Freeman Webb Company, Realtors, et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request was made; the plaintiff alleged disability-related discrimination in housing maintenance and eviction without requesting any accommodation.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claims because, although she alleged she was disabled and discriminated against, she failed to allege that she requested a reasonable accommodation related to her disability, and she did not allege that defendants' actions were taken in response to any accommodation request.
brief_summary: Karen DeMoor, a tenant in Lebanon, Tennessee receiving Social Security Disability benefits, sued Freeman Webb Company (property manager) and individuals alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on delayed repairs to her window and smoke detectors and subsequent eviction. The court dismissed all claims with prejudice, finding that while plaintiff adequately alleged disability, she failed to state a plausible FHA claim because she never requested a reasonable accommodation related to her disability.
key_cases_cited: Hollis v. Chestnut Bend Homeowners Ass'n, 760 F.3d 531 (6th Cir. 2014)
Overlook Mut. Homes, Inc. v. Spencer, 415 F. App'x 617 (6th Cir. 2011)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Repair of broken living room window and inoperable smoke detectors in plaintiff's townhome
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged disability but failed to allege that she requested a reasonable accommodation related to her disability. The court found that plaintiff's allegations of requesting window and smoke detector repairs were not connected to any disability-based accommodation request, rendering the claim implausible under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege that she exercised an FHA right (requesting reasonable accommodation based on disability) or that defendants' conduct (eviction, banning from property) was taken in response to such exercise. Without the requisite causal nexus between FHA-protected activity and defendant conduct, the interference claim fails under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II and 42 U.S.C. § 1983 civil rights claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's ADA and § 1983 claims are barred by Tennessee's one-year statute of limitations (Tenn. Code Ann. § 28-3-104(a)(3)). The alleged wrongful acts occurred between March 31, 2022, and January 23, 2023, but the lawsuit was filed on September 13, 2024, more than one year after the latest alleged act.

case_name: Shannon Perry v. Encore At Boulevard One LLC
accommodation_description: The specific accommodation request is not described in this appellate order; the opinion focuses on procedural issues rather than the merits of the FHA claim.
key_holding: The Tenth Circuit affirmed the dismissal of the Fair Housing Act claim, holding that the tenant's substantive challenges to the dismissal were waived for being raised only in the reply brief and lacked merit even if considered.
brief_summary: Shannon Perry appealed the dismissal of her Fair Housing Act claim arising from an eviction dispute against Encore At Boulevard One LLC and individual defendants. The Tenth Circuit affirmed the dismissal, holding that Perry waived her substantive challenges by raising them only in a reply brief, and rejected her remaining procedural arguments regarding the TRO denial as moot, the ADA and Double Jeopardy claims, the timing of dismissal before discovery, and the denial of a guardian ad litem.
key_cases_cited: Tymiak v. Omodt, 676 F.2d 306 (8th Cir. 1982)
Becker v. Kroll, 494 F.3d 904 (10th Cir. 2007)
Buchheit v. Green, 705 F.3d 1157 (10th Cir. 2012)
Garewal v. Sliz, 611 F. App'x 926 (10th Cir. 2015)
Nixon v. City & Cnty. of Denver, 784 F.3d 1364 (10th Cir. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Tenant sought a temporary restraining order to prevent eviction, implicitly asserting a disability-related defense to the eviction proceedings.
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court granted defendants' motion to dismiss the Fair Housing Act claim for failure to state a valid claim under the pleading standard. The appellate court affirmed, finding the tenant failed to adequately plead the FHA claim and noting that screening survival does not preclude later dismissal on a motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act Title III claim (public accommodation); Double Jeopardy Clause claim under 42 U.S.C. § 1983; Violence Against Women Act claim
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court summarily dismissed the ADA claim because an apartment residence is not a place of public accommodation, the Double Jeopardy Clause claim because it applies only to state actors and criminal proceedings (not civil evictions), and the § 1983 claim for the same reason. The appellate court affirmed, finding the tenant waived appellate challenge by failing to explain why the rulings were erroneous.

source_file: 10805225_2026_Elhadj Alpha Mahmound Souare v. Akron Metropolitan Housing Authority, et al._ohnd
case_name: Elhadj Alpha Mahmound Souare v. Akron Metropolitan Housing Authority, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff challenges his eviction from public housing, asserting claims under the Fair Housing Act without specifying a particular accommodation request.
key_holding: The federal district court lacks subject matter jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine to review a state court eviction judgment, and therefore dismissed plaintiff's complaint without addressing the merits of his Fair Housing Act claims.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Elhadj Alpha Mahmound Souare sued Akron Metropolitan Housing Authority and Stephanie Pence in federal court, challenging his September 2024 eviction and raising Fair Housing Act claims. The federal court dismissed the complaint sua sponte for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, holding that the Rooker-Feldman doctrine bars federal district courts from reviewing state court judgments, and denied all pending motions as moot.
key_cases_cited: Hall v. Callahan, 727 F.3d 450 (6th Cir. 2013)
Higgs v. Dupuis, 2021 WL 2270707 (W.D. Ky. 2021)
Kafele v. Lerner, Sampson & Rothfuss, L.P.A., 161 F. App'x 487 (6th Cir. 2005)
District of Columbia Court of Appeals v. Feldman, 460 U.S. 462 (1983)
Rooker v. Fid. Tr. Co., 263 U.S. 413 (1923)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff challenged eviction based on alleged failure to properly credit rent payments and procedural defects in eviction hearing.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine because plaintiff's claims challenge a final state court eviction judgment, which only the U.S. Supreme Court may review. The complaint also cited 42 U.S.C. § 1983, the Fourteenth Amendment, and Ohio landlord-tenant law, but the court did not reach the merits of any claim.

source_file: 10805293_2026_Darrell Bilbrey v. Oceana Oceanfront Condominium Association, Inc._flmd
case_name: Darrell Bilbrey v. Oceana Oceanfront Condominium Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: This order does not analyze the merits of any accommodation request; it is a discovery ruling denying Defendant's motions to compel.
key_holding: The court denied Defendant's motions to compel discovery because Defendant failed to provide legal authority in support of its requests, exceeded the 25-interrogatory limit without court approval, propounded overbroad document requests, and sought production of tax returns irrelevant to the damages actually claimed.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Darrell Bilbrey sued Oceana Oceanfront Condominium Association under the Fair Housing Act for claims including reasonable accommodation denial after being recalled from the Board of Directors, and Defendant removed the case to federal court. This order denies Defendant's motions to compel discovery responses because Defendant failed to provide legal authority, exceeded interrogatory limits, and propounded procedurally defective discovery requests.
key_cases_cited: Commodores Ent. Corp. v. McClary, 2015 WL 12843874 (M.D. Fla. 2015)
Border Collie Rescue, Inc. v. Ryan, 2005 WL 662724 (M.D. Fla. 2005)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act claims and Florida Statute § 718.1224(3) claims (state condominium law regarding board recall)
fha_claims.reasoning: This opinion addresses only discovery disputes (motions to compel) and does not reach the merits of any FHA or state law claims. The operative pleading asserts FHA violations and Florida Statute § 718.1224(3) claims, but the court's order concerns only procedural discovery compliance and does not analyze or resolve any substantive claim on the merits. The case remains pending with discovery closing October 5, 2026.

source_file: 10805317_2026_Jameerah Ware, Amira Ware, and Cheryl Vaughn v. A and K Properties of SC, Inc. and Sheriff Phillip E. Thompson_scd
case_name: Jameerah Ware, Amira Ware, and Cheryl Vaughn v. A and K Properties of SC, Inc. and Sheriff Phillip E. Thompson
accommodation_description: Request that the eviction and ejectment process accommodate Plaintiff Amira Ware's disabilities as required under the Fair Housing Act
key_holding: Plaintiffs' FHA claim against Sheriff Thompson was dismissed because Plaintiffs failed to respond to his arguments for dismissal and therefore conceded the claim, and Plaintiffs failed to allege facts plausibly demonstrating that Sheriff Thompson deprived Plaintiff Amira Ware of due process or otherwise discriminated against her on the basis of disability.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Jameerah Ware, Amira Ware, and Cheryl Vaughn sued their landlord A&K Properties and Sheriff Phillip Thompson alleging, inter alia, that the eviction process failed to accommodate Plaintiff Amira Ware's disabilities under the Fair Housing Act. The district court granted Sheriff Thompson's motion to dismiss, adopting the magistrate judge's recommendation, because Plaintiffs failed to respond to his dismissal arguments and thus conceded the FHA claim, and because Plaintiffs failed to state a plausible claim for relief against him.
key_cases_cited: Mathews v. Weber, 423 U.S. 261 (1976)
Thomas v. Arn, 474 U.S. 140 (1985)
Diamond v. Colonial Life & Accident Ins. Co., 416 F.3d 310 (4th Cir. 2005)
Roseboro v. Garrison, 528 F.2d 309 (4th Cir. 1975)
United States v. Schronce, 727 F.2d 91 (4th Cir. 1984)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accommodation of Plaintiff Amira Ware's disabilities in the eviction process
fha_claims.reasoning: The Magistrate Judge found that Plaintiffs failed to respond to Sheriff Thompson's arguments regarding the FHA claim and therefore conceded it, warranting dismissal for failure to state a plausible claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II ADA claim and Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment claim
fha_claims.reasoning: The Magistrate Judge concluded that Sheriff Thompson is an arm of the State entitled to Eleventh Amendment immunity; Title II ADA abrogates sovereign immunity only to the extent conduct violates the Fourteenth Amendment; Plaintiffs failed to allege facts sufficient to state a viable equal protection or due process violation attributable to Sheriff Thompson; and the Complaint fails to allege facts plausibly showing Sheriff Thompson excluded Plaintiff Amira Ware from a public service or discriminated against her on the basis of disability.

source_file: 10805479_2026_Jlyn Bryant et al. v. Tinker Federal Credit Union_okwd
case_name: Jlyn Bryant et al. v. Tinker Federal Credit Union
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation was requested in this case. The dispute involved plaintiffs' application for a $1.5 million residential mortgage loan that defendant denied, and plaintiffs' theory that the signed loan application itself constituted a financial asset owed back to them.
key_holding: The court granted defendant's motion to dismiss with prejudice, finding plaintiffs' claims—premised on the legally frivolous 'vapor money' theory—failed to state a plausible claim under the FHA, ECOA, or any other cited statute, and that amendment would be futile.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Jlyn Bryant and Joecelyne Acuna applied to Tinker Federal Credit Union for a $1.5 million residential mortgage loan, which was denied due to delinquent payment history and insufficient income. Plaintiffs sued alleging breach of fiduciary duty, fraud, and violations of ECOA and FHA, advancing the 'vapor money' theory that their signed loan application was a financial asset they lent to defendant, which defendant was obligated to credit back to them. The court dismissed all claims with prejudice under Rule 12(b)(6), holding that the vapor money theory has been universally rejected by federal courts, and that plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege disparate treatment under the FHA or ECOA because they did not allege membership in a protected class or differential treatment compared to similarly qualified applicants.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
McLaughlin v. CitiMortgage, Inc., 726 F. Supp. 2d 201 (D. Conn. 2010)
Baldwin v. Glob. Lending Servs., LLC, No. CIV-25-121-D, 2025 WL 1426564 (W.D. Okla. May 16, 2025)
Burnett v. Mortg. Elec. Registration Sys., Inc., 706 F.3d 1231 (10th Cir. 2013)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of loan application; plaintiffs sought $1.5 million residential loan
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege that defendant treated them differently because of membership in a protected class or that they were qualified for the loan but rejected despite qualifications while similarly situated applicants were approved. The complaint lacks factual allegations sufficient to raise a plausible claim for disparate treatment under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of fiduciary duty, fraud, violation of Federal Credit Union Act Section 206(2)(B), violation of Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs' claims rest on the rejected 'vapor money' theory and fail to establish any violation of the cited federal statutes. The Federal Credit Union Act Section 206(2)(B) provides no private right of action; the fiduciary duty claim fails under Oklahoma law absent a written agreement; and the fraud claim lacks particularity under Rule 9(b) and plausibility under Rule 12(b)(6).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Defendant alleged Plaintiff did not provide reasonable accommodations (specific accommodation not detailed in removal notice)
fha_claims.disposition: Remand for lack of subject matter jurisdiction
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked federal question jurisdiction because the underlying state court complaint filed by Plaintiff made no reference to federal statutes and did not articulate a federal claim. Federal question jurisdiction is based on the complaint filed by the Plaintiff in state court, not allegations in the Notice of Removal filed by Defendant.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Defendant alleged Plaintiff retaliated against Defendant for protected activity
fha_claims.disposition: Remand for lack of subject matter jurisdiction
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked federal question jurisdiction because the underlying state court complaint filed by Plaintiff made no reference to federal statutes and did not articulate a federal claim. Federal question jurisdiction is based on the complaint filed by the Plaintiff in state court, not allegations in the Notice of Removal filed by Defendant.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Defendant alleged Plaintiff failed to make repairs to the leased premises and harassed Defendant (state law claims for breach of warranty of habitability and harassment)
fha_claims.disposition: Remand for lack of subject matter jurisdiction
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked federal question jurisdiction because the underlying state court complaint filed by Plaintiff made no reference to federal statutes and did not articulate a federal claim. The complaint details a simple lease dispute that resulted in an unlawful detainer case—a quintessential state law claim.

source_file: 10806862_2026_William M. Pickard, III v. American Pride Properties, LLC, et al._alnd
case_name: William M. Pickard, III v. American Pride Properties, LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges APP Defendants refused to sell him property due to his disability-related criminal and litigious history (depression and mania).
key_holding: The court dismissed SPM Defendants' claims because plaintiff's FHA claims were conclusory and failed to allege SPM took prohibited discriminatory action; the court dismissed APP Defendants' claims under Colorado River abstention because parallel state court proceedings involving the same parties and substantially similar issues regarding the property sale were already pending.
brief_summary: William Pickard sued American Pride Properties (APP) and SPM LLC (his former landlord) alleging they discriminated against him due to his mental health disability by refusing to sell him property and by sharing derogatory information. The court abstained from the APP claims under Colorado River due to pending state litigation, and dismissed SPM claims for failure to state an FHA claim because plaintiff provided only conclusory allegations without facts showing SPM took prohibited discriminatory action.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Taveras v. Bank of Am., N.A., 89 F.4th 1279 (11th Cir. 2024)
Jackson-Platts v. Gen. Elec. Cap. Corp., 727 F.3d 1127 (11th Cir. 2013)
Colorado River Water Conservation Dist. v. United States, 424 U.S. 800 (1976)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to sell property and refusal to negotiate based on disability (mental health)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court abstained from deciding claims against APP Defendants under Colorado River doctrine because substantially similar issues and parties were pending in state court ejectment action. Court found that allowing plaintiff to relitigate the same dispute in federal court after state court proceedings reached appellate stage would constitute improper piecemeal litigation and circumvention of abstention through creative pleading.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 due process claim; collusion to violate settlement agreement (state contract law)
fha_claims.reasoning: SPM Defendants are not state actors under § 1983 because plaintiff failed to allege any of the three conditions (state compulsion, public function, or nexus/joint action) required to establish state actor status. Plaintiff's bare assertion that SPM was established as a state actor in prior settled litigation does not bind this court and is unsupported by the record.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged FHA violation by SPM for divulging derogatory information about plaintiff's tenancy and litigation history to APP, which APP then used to refuse to sell property
fha_claims.reasoning: Claim against SPM is conclusory and fails to state a plausible FHA violation. Plaintiff alleges only that SPM provided information about his litigation history, but provides no support for the proposition that the FHA prohibits disclosure of litigation history or that such disclosure constitutes discrimination based on disability. The claim lacks factual allegations sufficient to raise a plausible right to relief.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Collusion to violate settlement agreement (state contract law claim)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court lacks subject matter jurisdiction over state contract law claims for breach of settlement agreement or civil conspiracy based on breach of contract. Plaintiff is an Alabama resident and SPM is an Alabama LLC, so complete diversity does not exist. No federal question jurisdiction applies to state contract claims. Court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction after dismissing all federal claims.

source_file: 10806870_2026_Metropolitan Fair Housing Council of Oklahoma, Inc., James McNamee, and Marta McNamee v. Frank Feiock and Glenna Feiock, both d_b_a Rockford Garden Apartments_oked
case_name: Metropolitan Fair Housing Council of Oklahoma, Inc., James McNamee, and Marta McNamee v. Frank Feiock and Glenna Feiock, both d/b/a Rockford Garden Apartments

key_holding: The court granted defendants' motion to enforce the prior attorney's fees and costs award, ordering plaintiffs to pay $6,055.50 in fees and $2,151.65 in costs plus post-judgment interest within 45 days.

The court granted the motion to enforce, finding the award was joint and undisputed, and ordered plaintiffs to pay within 45 days plus post-judgment interest at the applicable Treasury rate.

fha_claims.reasoning: On April 8, 2024, the Court granted Defendants' motion for partial summary judgment and dismissed the failure to accommodate claims. The Court applied the summary judgment standard to the evidentiary record, constituting a merits determination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Oklahoma Fair Housing Law claims and Oklahoma state-law negligence claim
fha_claims.reasoning: On August 7, 2024, the Court granted Defendants' second summary judgment motion as to all remaining claims (Oklahoma Fair Housing Law and state negligence) and entered Judgment for Defendants. The Court applied the summary judgment standard to the evidentiary record.

source_file: 10806920_2026_Harmony Home of Huntington, Inc. v. Executive Director, Indiana Department of Homeland Security, The Members of the Fire Prevention and Building Safety Commission, Indiana Department of Homeland Security_in
case_name: Harmony Home of Huntington, Inc. v. Executive Director, Indiana Department of Homeland Security
accommodation_description: Request for governmental exemption from Class 1 building code requirements applied to group recovery home for persons with substance use disorders
key_holding: The court found DHS engaged in intentional discrimination by classifying the Home as a Class 1 structure while treating similarly situated nuclear family and foster homes as Class 2, using a flexible yet targeted definition of 'tenant' that functions as a proxy for discrimination against persons with disabilities.
brief_summary: Harmony Home of Huntington, Inc., which operates a group recovery home for men with substance abuse disorders, sued the Indiana Department of Homeland Security and the Fire Prevention and Building Safety Commission alleging that DHS unlawfully classified the Home as a Class 1 structure under Indiana building codes while treating similarly situated nuclear family and foster homes as Class 2, violating the Fair Housing Amendments Act, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act. The court granted summary judgment for Plaintiff, finding that DHS engaged in intentional discrimination by applying a facially neutral 'tenant' definition in a manner designed to impose Class 1 building requirements on group homes for persons with disabilities while exempting comparable family homes, and entered a permanent injunction requiring DHS to treat the Home as a Class 2 structure.
key_cases_cited: New Horizons Rehabilitation, Inc. v. State, 400 F. Supp. 3d 751 (S.D. Ind. 2019)
Next Step, 755 F. Supp. 3d 1078 (S.D. Ind. 2024)
Valencia v. City of Springfield, 883 F.3d 959 (7th Cir. 2018)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Gresham v. Windrush Partners, Ltd., 730 F.2d 1417 (11th Cir. 1984)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that Defendants' classification of Plaintiff's group recovery home as a Class 1 structure, while treating similarly-situated foster homes and nuclear family homes as Class 2 structures, constitutes intentional discrimination under the FHAA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act. Defendants' facially neutral definition of 'tenant' was applied as a proxy to discriminate against persons with disabilities, with no legitimate justification for the disparate treatment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Variance from Class 1 sprinkler system requirement; treatment of the Home as a Class 2 structure
fha_claims.reasoning: The court declined to reach Plaintiff's failure to accommodate claims because Plaintiff had already prevailed on disparate treatment claims, which provided an independent basis for relief. The court dismissed the failure to accommodate claims without prejudice, stating that no further analysis was necessary once intentional discrimination was established.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act Title II, 42 U.S.C. § 12132; Rehabilitation Act, 29 U.S.C. § 794
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the same analytical framework to ADA Title II and Rehabilitation Act claims as it did to the FHAA claims, finding that Defendants' classification of the Home as a Class 1 structure violated all three statutes through intentional discrimination. The court noted that 'the same analysis generally applies under all three statutes.'

source_file: 10806943_2026_Gabriella Collette, for herself and on behalf of Channin Collette, an incapacitated person v. Utah State Developmental Center; Utah State Department of Human Services; State of Utah; Jarod Squire_utd
case_name: Gabriella Collette, for herself and on behalf of Channin Collette, an incapacitated person v. Utah State Developmental Center; Utah State Department of Human Services; State of Utah; Jarod Squire
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges State Defendants violated the FHA by failing to prevent and protect Plaintiff from sexual assault at the Center, but does not identify a specific accommodation request.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claim (Count II) on Eleventh Amendment sovereign immunity grounds because Congress did not abrogate states' immunity when enacting the FHA, and Utah has not waived immunity under the circumstances.
brief_summary: Gabriella Collette, as legal guardian of incapacitated Channin Collette with intellectual disabilities and autism, sued Utah State Developmental Center, the Utah Department of Health and Human Services, the State of Utah, and employee Jarod Squire alleging, inter alia, an FHA violation for failure to protect Channin from sexual assault by a caregiver. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss the FHA claim on Eleventh Amendment sovereign immunity grounds, holding Congress did not abrogate state immunity in the FHA and Utah has not waived immunity where the injury arose from assault and battery.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Will v. Mich. Dep't of State Police, 491 U.S. 58 (1989)
Melton v. Okla. ex rel. Univ. of Okla., 532 F. Supp. 3d 1080 (W.D. Okla. 2021)
McCardell v. U.S. Dep't of Hous. & Urb. Dev., 794 F.3d 510 (5th Cir. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to prevent sexual assault and provide safe, accessible environment; failure to provide reasonable accommodations and protection
fha_claims.reasoning: The FHA claim was dismissed on Eleventh Amendment immunity grounds. Congress did not abrogate States' Eleventh Amendment immunity in the FHA, and Utah has not waived immunity. The claim arises from assault and battery, which is specifically retained under Utah's Governmental Immunity Act. The court did not reach the merits of the FHA claim itself, dismissing on jurisdictional/immunity grounds rather than on the substantive elements of an FHA violation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 due process violation; Title IX sex discrimination; ADA Title II discrimination; premise liability; negligence; gross negligence; sexual battery
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA claims (§ 1983, Title IX, ADA Title II, premise liability, negligence, gross negligence, sexual battery) were dismissed. § 1983 and premise liability claims were dismissed on Eleventh Amendment immunity grounds. Title IX and ADA Title II claims were dismissed for failure to plausibly allege the requisite elements (actual knowledge/deliberate indifference for Title IX; nexus to disability for ADA). Negligence, gross negligence, and sexual battery claims were dismissed on immunity grounds as vicarious liability claims against state defendants.

source_file: 10808207_2026_Edward Siguel v. King Farm Citizens Assembly, Inc., et al._mdd
case_name: Edward Siguel v. King Farm Citizens Assembly, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that the HOA (KFCA) accommodate his disability by excusing him from its requirement to reinstall the decorative columns and railings (a 'fake balcony' or 'balustrade') on the flat roof above his open front porch, citing that maintaining the structure caused him physical pain and organ damage due to the need to clear accumulated snow and ice. He also sought accommodations/modifications allowing him to build a brick patio in his backyard, construct a backyard shed, install a 'horizontal shed' on his front porch, and install a plant trellis — all of which KFCA denied.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's motion for a preliminary injunction/stay because plaintiff failed to establish likelihood of success on the merits, finding that the Fourth Circuit's Gibson Island Corp. decision did not alter the Bryant Woods causation/amelioration standard for 'necessity' under the FHA, and that plaintiff's request to avoid reinstalling decorative columns and railings on his porch roof did not plausibly provide direct amelioration of the effects of his disability.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Edward Siguel, a disabled homeowner in an HOA community, sought a preliminary injunction to prevent KFCA from requiring him to reinstall decorative columns and railings ('fake balcony' or 'balustrade') on the flat roof above his front porch, contending the reinstallation requirement violated the FHA's reasonable accommodation and modification provisions and arguing that the Fourth Circuit's 2025 Gibson Island Corp. decision established new, more favorable legal standards. The court carefully analyzed Gibson Island Corp. and concluded it did not overrule or modify the Bryant Woods requirement that a proposed accommodation must provide 'direct amelioration' of a disability's effects in order to be 'necessary' under the FHA. Because plaintiff could not demonstrate likelihood of success on the merits under that standard, the court denied the motion without reaching the other Winter preliminary injunction factors.
key_cases_cited: Bryant Woods Inn, Inc. v. Howard Cnty, Md., 124 F.3d 597 (4th Cir. 1997)
Grp. Home on Gibson Island, LLC v. Gibson Island Corp., 144 F.4th 522 (4th Cir. 2025)
Acosta v. A&G Mgmt. Co., Inc., 2014 WL 1236918 (D. Md. 2014)
Gavin v. Spring Ridge Conservancy, Inc., 934 F. Supp. 685 (D. Md. 1995)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to maintain flat roof on front porch without reinstalling columns and railings (balustrade); alternatively, HOA to reinstall columns, provide contractors, or allow alternative visual obstruction such as plants or planters
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied Bryant Woods 'direct amelioration' test and found plaintiff failed to establish that not reinstalling the balustrade provides direct amelioration of his disability's effects. The accommodation does not provide equal opportunity to use and enjoy the home; it merely seeks to avoid compliance with facially neutral HOA regulations. Gibson Island Corp. did not change this legal standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to build brick patio on soil in backyard, construct shed in backyard, install horizontal shed on front porch, and install plant trellis
fha_claims.reasoning: Claims were dismissed at motion to dismiss stage for failure to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly standard. Court found insufficient pleading of nexus between disability and requested accommodations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Disparate impact claims were dismissed at motion to dismiss stage for failure to state a plausible claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Retaliation claim was dismissed at motion to dismiss stage for failure to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Intentional discrimination claim was dismissed at motion to dismiss stage for failure to state a plausible claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II, § 504 Rehabilitation Act, state law claims related to housing discrimination and civil rights violations
fha_claims.reasoning: Non-FHA claims including ADA and state law claims were dismissed at motion to dismiss stage for failure to state a plausible claim.

source_file: 10808242_2026_Keith David Nizwantowski v. Monarch, et al._nced

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.disposition: Jurisdictional dismissal under Rooker-Feldman and failure to state a claim
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found it lacked subject matter jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine because plaintiff's alleged injuries (homelessness, property damage, emotional distress, financial hardship) resulted directly from the state court eviction judgment, and plaintiff explicitly sought to vacate that judgment. Additionally, plaintiff failed to allege membership in a protected class or engagement in protected FHA activity, failing to state a claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3617.

source_file: 10808764_2026_Terry Rockette v. Carpenter Management Company, et al._msnd
case_name: Terry Rockette v. Carpenter Management Company, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff's vague reference to a request for mail-in recertification when the accommodation was allegedly provided to an out-of-state female tenant, though this was not substantively analyzed as a reasonable accommodation claim.
key_holding: Plaintiff failed to establish the required causal connection between his protected HUD complaints and defendants' alleged adverse conduct, and his claims of harassment and discrimination rested solely on conclusory assertions insufficient to survive summary judgment.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Terry Rockette sued Carpenter Management Company and its employees alleging racial and gender discrimination in violation of the Fair Housing Act, retaliation for filing HUD complaints, and other federal and state claims. The court granted defendants' motion for summary judgment, dismissing all federal claims with prejudice because plaintiff failed to establish causation between his protected activity and any alleged adverse action, and his conclusory assertions were insufficient to support his discrimination and harassment claims.
key_cases_cited: Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242 (1986)
Scruggs v. Marshall Hous. Auth., 232 F.3d 210 (5th Cir. 2000)
Hood v. Pope, 627 F. App'x 295 (5th Cir. 2015)
Inclusive Communities Project, Inc. v. Lincoln Prop. Co., 920 F.3d 890 (5th Cir. 2019)
Cox v. City of Dallas, 430 F.3d 734 (5th Cir. 2005)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of apartment D4 and assignment to apartment B08 based on race
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish prima facie case of racial discrimination under § 3604(a)-(b) because he was never denied an apartment, successfully leased apartment B08, other African Americans resided in the complex, and he renewed his lease without differential terms. The fact that he did not obtain the specific apartment he toured does not constitute an adverse action under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of apartment D4 and assignment to apartment B08 based on sex/gender
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's gender discrimination claim under § 3604(a)-(b) fails because assignment to a different apartment (B08 instead of D4) does not constitute an adverse action necessary to invoke § 3604, and plaintiff successfully leased and renewed his lease without differential terms compared to other tenants.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged discrimination in housing conditions and habitability
fha_claims.reasoning: The Fifth Circuit has expressly limited § 3604 discrimination claims to alleged discrimination related to sale, rental, or eviction from housing, not the habitability or value of the housing itself. Plaintiff's remaining discrimination claims relating to housing conditions fall outside the scope of § 3604.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation for filing HUD fair housing complaints, including improper infractions, ignored maintenance requests, and lack of accommodation for mail-in income recertification
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a causal connection between his protected activity (filing HUD complaints) and the alleged adverse actions (improper infractions, ignored maintenance requests, lack of accommodation). Harassment claims under § 3617 must be connected to attempts to exercise FHA rights, and plaintiff's allegations were unorganized and failed to plead a causal nexus except for the sexual harassment claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Sexual harassment by Ms. Ashford allegedly offered in exchange for dropping HUD complaint
fha_claims.reasoning: Although plaintiff alleged that Ms. Ashford offered sexual favors if he dropped his HUD complaint, plaintiff failed to produce any evidence supporting this assertion and confirmed in deposition that he had no evidence of sexual harassment. Conclusory assertions alone are insufficient to support a § 3617 retaliation claim, and plaintiff failed to meet his burden after defendants established no genuine dispute of material fact.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 Fourth Amendment violation (unlawful search/seizure based on police officer presence during apartment inspection); state law claims including unlawful entry, disturbance of peace, false imprisonment, threats, intentional infliction of emotional distress, defamation, invasion of privacy under Miss. Code Ann. §§ 97-3-55, 97-7-75
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 1983 does not apply to private parties absent state action under color of law. Plaintiff failed to allege an agreement between Ms. Ashford and the police officer that would constitute state action; Ms. Ashford's request that a police officer be present as a neutral observer during a routine inspection authorized by the lease does not constitute state action. State law claims were dismissed without prejudice under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3) after all federal claims were dismissed.

source_file: 10808878_2026_Plainview Mobile Home Park, et al. v. City of Oak Grove, et al._kywd
case_name: Plainview Mobile Home Park, et al. v. City of Oak Grove, et al.
accommodation_description: Mobile home park operators and prospective resident allege city denied water service to new mobile-home hookups as discriminatory treatment in violation of the FHA.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiffs' Rule 59(e) motion because plaintiffs failed to establish grounds for reconsideration, and their FHA claim lacked evidence of disparate treatment and sufficient statistical evidence of disparate impact.
brief_summary: Plainview Mobile Home Park and a prospective resident sued the City of Oak Grove and its public-works director alleging the city unlawfully refused to extend water service to new mobile-home hookups in violation of the Fair Housing Act and constitutional provisions. The court denied plaintiffs' motion to alter judgment under Rule 59(e), finding they failed to establish grounds for reconsideration and had previously lacked sufficient evidence of disparate treatment or statistical evidence of disparate impact to support their FHA claims.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dept. of Housing & Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Reeves v. Sanderson Plumbing Products, Inc., 530 U.S. 133 (2000)
Michigan Flyer LLC v. Wayne County Airport Authority, 860 F.3d 425 (6th Cir. 2017)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Extension of water service to new mobile-home hookups
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiffs lacked evidence of disparate treatment and failed to establish statistical evidence of disparate impact under the FHA. The record supported the defendant's nondiscriminatory reason (water lines out of code) and plaintiffs' pretext allegations created only a weak issue of fact that was overcome by corroborating evidence.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal Protection Clause (14th Amendment), Due Process Clause (5th and 14th Amendments)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that equal protection claims failed because the city's water-hookup decisions survived rational-basis review, and due-process claims failed because the record revealed adequate process that did not implicate fundamental rights or liberty interests requiring higher scrutiny.

case_name: Dickerson v. BPP PCV Owners LLC
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation request; this is an appeal from dismissal of racial discrimination and retaliation claims arising from a baseless theft accusation by a building security officer.
key_holding: The Second Circuit affirmed dismissal, holding that the complaint failed to plead intentional racial discrimination under the FHA because the security guard's accusation was based on the plaintiff's resemblance to the person in security footage, not racial animus, and the FHA retaliation claim failed for lack of allegations connecting the incident to prior complaints.
brief_summary: Gloria D. Dickerson, a 72-year-old Black woman residing at Peter Cooper Village in Manhattan, sued BPP PCV Owners LLC alleging racial discrimination after a building safety officer accused her of theft based on security camera footage. The Second Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal, finding that Dickerson failed to plead intentional discrimination because the accusation was based on physical resemblance to the person in the footage rather than racial animus, and her retaliation claim failed for lack of causal connection to any prior protected activity.
key_cases_cited: Francis v. Kings Park Manor, Inc., 992 F.3d 67 (2d Cir. 2021)
Gilead Comm. Servs., Inc. v. Town of Cromwell, 112 F.4th 93 (2d Cir. 2024)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court affirmed dismissal of the FHA disparate treatment claim because the SAC failed to plausibly allege intentional racial discrimination. The allegations suggested only that the security guard's accusation was based on Dickerson's resemblance to the person in security footage, not racial animus.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court affirmed dismissal of the FHA retaliation claim because the SAC contained no allegations about prior complaints by Dickerson or any causal connection between protected activity and the November 2020 incident, failing to satisfy the pleading standard for retaliation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 due process claim, ADA Title II discrimination claim
fha_claims.reasoning: The § 1983 claim failed because Dickerson alleged a constitutional violation by a private entity without alleging a close nexus between BPP's conduct and state action; the mere fact that a safety officer called the NYPD did not convert private conduct into state action. The ADA claim failed because the original complaint lacked any allegations concerning the prima facie elements of disability discrimination.

case_name: Steven Ray Collins; Sharon Lavette Collins v. Wells Fargo & Company; Wells Fargo Bank, N.A.
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested or at issue in this case; the action was dismissed on res judicata grounds without reaching the merits of any FHA claim.
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal of plaintiffs' Fair Housing Act claims against Wells Fargo as barred by res judicata, because the action involved the same cause of action between the same parties after a final judgment on the merits in a prior state court proceeding.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Steven Ray Collins and Sharon Lavette Collins appealed the dismissal of their Fair Housing Act claims against Wells Fargo & Company and Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. The district court dismissed the action under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6) on the ground that it was barred by res judicata, applying California's claim preclusion doctrine to give effect to a prior state court judgment involving the same cause of action and the same parties. The Ninth Circuit affirmed, also rejecting plaintiffs' procedural objections regarding the lack of oral argument and the alleged consideration of matters outside the pleadings.
key_cases_cited: Holcombe v. Hosmer, 477 F.3d 1094 (9th Cir. 2007)
DKN Holdings LLC v. Faerber, 352 P.3d 378 (Cal. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not specified in opinion
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court affirmed the district court's dismissal under res judicata, holding that the FHA claims were barred by a prior final judgment on the merits in state court involving the same cause of action between the same parties under California law.

source_file: 10813080_2026_Monique Davis v. Post Woods Townhomes, LLC, et al._ohsd
case_name: Monique Davis v. Post Woods Townhomes, LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: The case text does not specify the particular accommodation or modification requested; it states only that Plaintiff alleged disability discrimination and retaliation while a tenant at Post Woods Apartments, without further detail on the underlying accommodation claim.
key_holding: The district court adopted the Magistrate Judge's Report and Recommendation and dismissed Plaintiff's complaint for failure to prosecute under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 41(b) after Plaintiff failed to meet deadlines, respond to court orders, and object to the Report and Recommendation.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Monique Davis brought claims under the Fair Housing Act and state law against Post Woods Townhomes and related defendants, alleging disability discrimination and retaliation she experienced as a tenant. After Davis repeatedly failed to meet court deadlines and did not respond to a Show Cause Order, the Magistrate Judge recommended dismissal for failure to prosecute, concluding Davis had abandoned her lawsuit. The district court adopted the recommendation and dismissed the complaint under Rule 41(b).
key_cases_cited: United States v. Walters, 638 F.2d 947 (6th Cir. 1981)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unspecified reasonable accommodation related to disability discrimination as a tenant
fha_claims.reasoning: Case dismissed for failure to prosecute due to plaintiff's failure to meet deadlines and respond to Court orders and Show Cause Order, not on the merits of the FHA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation for exercising FHA rights as a tenant
fha_claims.reasoning: Case dismissed for failure to prosecute due to plaintiff's failure to meet deadlines and respond to Court orders and Show Cause Order, not on the merits of the FHA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: State law claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Case dismissed for failure to prosecute due to plaintiff's failure to meet deadlines and respond to Court orders and Show Cause Order, not on the merits of the claims.

source_file: 10813290_2026_Daniel K. Miller, Elizabeth D. Wilhour, and Sean M. Wilhour v. Asset Living, LLC, AMFP V Central Park LLC, and Shanna Martinez_cod
case_name: Miller v. Asset Living, LLC
accommodation_description: The case does not involve a discrete reasonable accommodation or modification request. Plaintiffs' disability-related claims arise from alleged failure to maintain habitable conditions—including functional elevators—that affected residents with disabilities, brought under the ADA (Title III) and the Fair Housing Amendments Act.
key_holding: The Magistrate Judge recommends granting defendants' partial motions to dismiss, dismissing Claims One (ADA) and Five (Denver Municipal Code) with prejudice on substantive legal grounds, and Claims Three (CCPA) and Eight ("Colorado CARES Act") without prejudice for pleading deficiencies and duplicativeness, while allowing Claims Two (FHA), Four (CADA), Six (warranty of habitability), and Seven (retaliation) to proceed.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs residing at Avantus Apartments in Denver sued their property owner and manager for severe habitability failures—including sewage backups, mold, pest infestations, and non-functional elevators—and for alleged retaliation after complaining about those conditions, bringing eight claims under federal and state law. Defendants filed partial motions to dismiss Claims One (ADA), Three (CCPA), Five (Denver Municipal Code), and Eight ("Colorado CARES Act"). The Magistrate Judge recommended granting all four dismissals: the ADA claim failed because residential apartment complexes are not "places of public accommodation"; the Denver Municipal Code claim failed because the cited provisions were reserved or conferred enforcement rights only on a government manager; the CCPA claim failed to meet Rule 9(b)'s heightened pleading particularity standard; and Claim Eight was both insufficiently pleaded and duplicative of surviving warranty-of-habitability and retaliation claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Hall v. Bellmon
Phibbs v. Am. Prop. Mgmt.
Coe v. Cross-Lines Ret. Ctr.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA claim for accessibility of residential apartment complex common areas; CCPA claim for misrepresentation of apartment condition and failure to make repairs; Denver Municipal Code claim for violations of health, safety, and habitability standards
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA does not apply to residential apartment complexes; CCPA claim fails to meet Rule 9(b) particularity standard for fraud allegations; Denver Municipal Code sections cited are reserved/nonexistent and no private right of action exists for municipal code violations.

source_file: 10813488_2026_United States of America v. Five Properties, LLC et al._laed
case_name: United States of America v. Five Properties, LLC et al.
accommodation_description: Request to keep an emotional support dog as a reasonable accommodation for mental disability
key_holding: Turnipseed's motion to intervene was denied because all elements of res judicata were met: Five Properties and Tonti Management were in privity through a principal/agent relationship, and the Government's suit arose from the same nucleus of operative facts as Turnipseed's original suit, which was dismissed with prejudice for failure to prosecute.
brief_summary: Dory Turnipseed sought to intervene in the United States' Fair Housing Act lawsuit against Five Properties, LLC and Tonti Management Corporation, which alleged the defendants refused to accommodate her mental disability by prohibiting her emotional support dog. The district court sustained Defendants' objection, reversed the magistrate judge's order granting intervention, and denied Turnipseed's motion based on res judicata, finding that Turnipseed's dismissed suit and the Government's suit arose from the same nucleus of operative facts, and that the defendants were in privity through their principal/agent relationship.
key_cases_cited: Test Masters Educ. Servs., Inc. v. Singh, 428 F.3d 559 (5th Cir. 2005)
Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)
Lubrizol Corp. v. Exxon Corp., 871 F.2d 1279 (5th Cir. 1989)
Meza v. Gen. Battery Corp., 908 F.2d 1262 (5th Cir. 1990)
Eubanks v. F.D.I.C., 977 F.2d 166 (5th Cir. 1992)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Emotional support dog for tenant with mental disability
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied res judicata doctrine to bar the Government's suit on behalf of Turnipseed because all four elements were satisfied: identical parties (or privity via principal-agent relationship), competent jurisdiction, final judgment on the merits in the prior action, and same nucleus of operative facts. The original FHA claim was dismissed with prejudice for lack of prosecution, and the Government's subsequent suit arises from the identical alleged discriminatory conduct.

source_file: 10814487_2026_Ronald Yocca, Rachel Estates, L.P., My Brother's House v. Allegheny County Health Department_pawd
case_name: Ronald Yocca, Rachel Estates, L.P., My Brother's House v. Allegheny County Health Department
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested exemption from ACHD Rooming House permitting and inspection requirements based on the Oxford House model, arguing the recovery house residents live as a family unit and should be treated as a single-family residence.
key_holding: The court dismissed the disparate treatment and disparate impact claims but denied dismissal of the reasonable accommodation claim, finding plaintiffs sufficiently alleged all three elements of a § 3604(f)(3)(B) claim: refusal, reasonable accommodation, and necessity for equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs My Brother's House (a drug and alcohol recovery house), its Executive Director Ronald Yocca, and property owner Rachel Estates sued Allegheny County Health Department seeking to be treated as a single-family residence rather than a Rooming House under ACHD regulations. The court granted ACHD's motion to dismiss the disparate treatment and disparate impact claims for failure to plead discriminatory animus or statistical disparity, but denied dismissal of the reasonable accommodation claim, finding plaintiffs plausibly alleged that exemption from permitting requirements was necessary for residents to maintain their recovery in a family-like community setting.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Vorchheimer v. Philadelphian Owners Assoc., 903 F.3d 100 (3d Cir. 2018)
City of Edmonds v. Oxford House, Inc., 514 U.S. 725 (1995)
Lapid-Laurel, LLC v. Zoning Bd. of Adjustment, 284 F.3d 442 (3d Cir. 2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plead facts showing that the residents' disability was a motivating factor in ACHD's enforcement of the Permitting Requirements. The regulations are facially neutral and ACHD's letters contain no mention of the residents' recovery or sober status, only neutral reasoning about permit violations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to provide statistical or other data plausibly suggesting that the Permitting Requirements have a disparate impact on disabled individuals. They did not allege that disabled people are more likely to live in high-occupancy homes, be subjected to these requirements, or be burdened more than non-disabled people.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exemption from rooming house permitting and inspection requirements; treatment as a single-family residence rather than a rooming house
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs plausibly pled all three elements of a reasonable accommodation claim under § 3604(f)(3)(B): (1) refusal—ACHD denied the request to treat the residence as a single-family home; (2) reasonableness—the accommodation is fact-specific and at this stage there is no indication it would impose undue burdens or fundamentally alter ACHD's enforcement of health and safety standards; and (3) necessity—the residents need stable family-like community-based residency to recover from substance use disorder, and the permit could be suspended at any time, destabilizing that community.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), 42 U.S.C. § 12131 et seq.; Rehabilitation Act of 1973, 29 U.S.C. § 794
fha_claims.reasoning: ACHD did not move to dismiss the ADA and Rehabilitation Act claims. The court declined to address them sua sponte and allowed them to proceed. The court noted that the governing standards for claims under the FHA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act are essentially the same.

source_file: 10815083_2026_Mark Heimkes v. Fairhope Motorcoach Resort Condominium Owners Association, Inc.; Shearldine Marie Allfrey v. Fairhope Motorcoach Resort Condominium Owners Association, Inc._alsd
case_name: Mark Heimkes v. Fairhope Motorcoach Resort Condominium Owners Association, Inc.; Shearldine Marie Allfrey v. Fairhope Motorcoach Resort Condominium Owners Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: Both plaintiffs requested accommodation to bring their service/assistance dogs into the pool and Owner's Lodge areas where pets were prohibited: Mr. Heimkes for his PTSD service dogs (Logan, Rex, Tatanka) and Mrs. Allfrey for her seizure alert dog (Dewey).
key_holding: The accommodation claims failed because plaintiffs refused to provide FMRCOA with reliable disability-related information linking their disabilities to the need for service animals, and Mr. Heimkes' dog Rex was properly excluded under the direct threat exception; additionally, Mrs. Allfrey failed to demonstrate Dewey was trained to perform a specific alerting task for her seizure condition.
brief_summary: Two condominium unit owners sued Fairhope Motorcoach Resort Condominium Owners Association seeking reasonable accommodations under the FHA to bring their service/assistance dogs into restricted common areas, and also brought ADA and interference claims. After a twelve-day bench trial, the court found for the defendant on all claims, holding that plaintiffs' refusal to provide reliable disability-related information prevented the defendant from conducting a meaningful review of the accommodation requests, one dog's behavior justified exclusion under the direct threat exception, and the facility was not a place of public accommodation under the ADA.
key_cases_cited: Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condo. Ass'n, 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014)
Schwarz v. City of Treasure Island, 544 F.3d 1201 (11th Cir. 2008)
Cordoves v. Miami-Dade Cnty., 92 F. Supp. 3d 1221 (M.D. Fla. 2015)
Warren v. Delvista Towers Condo. Ass'n, 49 F. Supp. 3d 1082 (S.D. Fla. 2014)
Peklun v. Tierra Del Mar Condo. Ass'n, 2015 WL 8029840 (S.D. Fla. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff Heimkes requested accommodation to have his service dog Logan off-leash in common areas (pool, Owner's Lodge) and throughout the property without leash restrictions
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 52(a) Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to provide FMRCOA with necessary disability-related information showing the relationship between his PTSD disability and the need for the service dog accommodation until after filing suit. FMRCOA was entitled to conduct a meaningful review and request verification before granting the accommodation. By the time verification was provided during discovery, Logan had passed away, making retroactive accommodation impossible.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff Heimkes requested accommodation to have his service dog Rex off-leash in common areas and throughout the property
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 52(a) Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law
fha_claims.reasoning: Even if Rex was trained to perform tasks for Heimkes' disability, FMRCOA was permitted to exclude Rex under the direct threat exception to the FHA. Multiple credible witnesses testified that Rex's behavior posed a direct threat (barking, growling, lunging, bearing teeth, pulling aggressively), and Heimkes himself conceded Rex could not pass the canine good citizenship test, ultimately giving the dog away.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff Allfrey requested accommodation to have her seizure alert dog Dewey in all common areas (Lodge, pool deck, and other common elements) where other owners' visitors are allowed
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 52(a) Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff Allfrey failed to provide FMRCOA with information demonstrating that Dewey was trained to perform a specific task to ameliorate her seizure disability. By her own admission, Dewey does not alert consistently or in the same manner each time. The court observed Allfrey during a purported seizure and did not observe Dewey performing any of the described alerting behaviors. FMRCOA's request for verification was reasonable and necessary to conduct meaningful review.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff Heimkes alleged FMRCOA used litigation and fines to coerce, intimidate, threaten, or interfere with his exercise of FHA rights
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 52(a) Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law
fha_claims.reasoning: Fines issued to Heimkes for violations (smoking in common areas, bringing dogs to pool and lodge) were warranted because he had not been granted accommodations and knowingly violated the rules. The fines were not retaliatory. Conduct by individual owners (not being friendly, taking photographs) was not attributable to FMRCOA and did not constitute interference, coercion, intimidation, or threats under § 3617.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff Allfrey alleged FMRCOA treated her differently based on disability and accommodation request, harassed, retaliated, and intimidated her through stalking, photographing, threatening fines, and threatening eviction
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 52(a) Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law
fha_claims.reasoning: Allfrey presented no evidence that FMRCOA threatened eviction or attempted to make housing unavailable. Fines for bringing dog to pool and lodge were warranted because accommodation was properly denied. Conduct by individual owners (photographing, reduced friendliness) was not attributable to FMRCOA and resulted from litigation disputes, not retaliation for exercising FHA rights. The FHA is not a civility statute.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III claims by both Heimkes and Allfrey; ADA claim by Allfrey only
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 52(a) Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law
fha_claims.reasoning: FMR is not a place of public accommodation under the ADA. Although FMR has short-term rental units, it lacks on-site management/reservation services, walk-up/call-in availability, housekeeping/linen service, and renters are guaranteed specific units. Additionally, FMRCOA is not an 'owner' of the common elements or units under the ADA because the Declaration provides that each unit owner has an undivided interest in common elements, not FMRCOA.

source_file: 11161991_2023_Evelyn Rivera v. Jimmy Ducharme et al._nhd
case_name: Evelyn Rivera v. Jimmy Ducharme et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges defendant interfered with her housing rights through racially discriminatory harassment including use of racial slurs and snow plowing onto her vehicle.
key_holding: Defendant's motion for summary judgment on plaintiff's FHA claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3617 is denied because genuine disputes of material fact exist as to whether defendant engaged in severe or pervasive harassment based on plaintiff's race and national origin, including direct evidence of defendant's use of racial slurs.
brief_summary: Evelyn Rivera, a Puerto Rican woman, sued her neighbor Jimmy Ducharme claiming he violated the Fair Housing Act by harassing her because of her race and national origin, including using racial slurs and plowing snow onto her vehicle. The court denied Ducharme's motion for summary judgment on Rivera's § 3617 interference claim, finding genuine disputes of material fact exist as to whether his conduct constituted severe or pervasive harassment motivated by discriminatory intent.
key_cases_cited: Watters v. Homeowners' Ass'n at Pres. at Bridgewater, 48 F.4th 779 (7th Cir. 2022)
Chamberlin v. 101 Realty, Inc., 915 F.2d 777 (1st Cir. 1990)
Ortiz v. Sch. Bd. of Broward Cnty., Fla., 780 F. App'x 780 (11th Cir. 2019)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied summary judgment on Rivera's § 3617 hostile environment harassment claim because direct evidence of racial slurs ('spic') and intentional snow plowing onto her vehicle could support a finding of severe or pervasive harassment based on race/national origin, creating a jury question on both the severity of conduct and discriminatory intent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: State law claims: trespass, nuisance, negligence, intentional infliction of emotional distress
fha_claims.reasoning: Summary judgment granted on trespass and nuisance claims because Rivera failed to produce evidence of ownership interest in the disputed driveway and no easement by implication, necessity, or prescription existed. Negligence claim survived summary judgment due to triable issues of fact regarding duty, breach, and causation. Intentional infliction of emotional distress claim was dismissed by agreement.

source_file: 11260497_2026_Eaton Corp. v. Angstrom Auto. Group, LLC_ca6
11267540 - Yocca v. ALLEGHENY COUNTY HEALTH DEPARTMENT
case_name: Ronald Yocca, Rachel Estates, L.P., My Brother's House v. Allegheny County Health Department
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested exemption from ACHD's Rooming House permitting and inspection requirements, arguing the recovery house should be treated as a single-family residence since residents live in a family-like setting.
key_holding: The court denied dismissal of the reasonable accommodation claim because Plaintiffs plausibly pled all three elements under § 3604(f)(3)(B): ACHD denied their request to be treated as a single-family residence, the accommodation is reasonable since ACHD could apply health and safety standards without the permitting scheme, and the accommodation is necessary because permit suspension would destabilize the recovery community essential to residents' sobriety.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs My Brother's House (a drug and alcohol recovery residence operator), its director Ronald Yocca, and property owner Rachel Estates sued Allegheny County Health Department after ACHD classified their Turtle Creek residence as an unlicensed Rooming House subject to permitting and inspection requirements.
