The court granted ACHD's motion to dismiss the disparate treatment and disparate impact claims for failure to plead sufficient facts, but denied dismissal of the reasonable accommodation claim, finding Plaintiffs adequately alleged that being treated as a single-family residence was a reasonable and necessary accommodation to afford recovery house residents equal opportunity to use and enjoy their housing.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Vorchheimer v. Philadelphian Owners Assoc., 903 F.3d 100 (3d Cir. 2018)
City of Edmonds v. Oxford House, Inc., 514 U.S. 725 (1995)
Lapid-Laurel, LLC v. Zoning Bd. of Adjustment, 284 F.3d 442 (3d Cir. 2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to allege facts plausibly showing that the residents' disability status was a motivating factor in ACHD's enforcement of the Permitting Requirements. The complaint alleged only neutral reasoning (garbage complaint, permit violation) with no mention of discriminatory animus or the residents' recovery status in ACHD's enforcement letters.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to provide statistical or other data plausibly suggesting that the Permitting Requirements have a disparate impact on disabled individuals. The complaint did not allege that disabled people are more likely to live in high-occupancy homes, be subjected to these requirements, or be burdened more than non-disabled people.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exemption from rooming house permitting and inspection requirements; treatment as a single-family residence despite having four or more unrelated residents, based on the Oxford House model where recovery homes operate as family units
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs plausibly alleged all three elements of a reasonable accommodation claim under § 3604(f)(3)(B): (1) refusal—ACHD denied the request to treat the residence as a single-family home; (2) reasonableness—the court found no indication at the pleading stage that the accommodation would impose undue burdens or fundamentally alter ACHD's enforcement, particularly since ACHD enforces health and safety in single-family homes through other means; and (3) necessity—plaintiffs alleged that family-like community-based residency is essential for residents' recovery and that permit suspension risk destabilizes that community. The motion to dismiss was denied and the claim proceeds to discovery.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), 42 U.S.C. § 12131 et seq.; Rehabilitation Act of 1973, 29 U.S.C. § 794
fha_claims.disposition: Not addressed on motion to dismiss
fha_claims.reasoning: ACHD did not move to dismiss the ADA and Rehabilitation Act claims. The court declined to address them sua sponte, noting that the governing standards for claims under the FHA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act are essentially the same. These claims proceed forward.

case_name: Herbozo v. Fernandez
accommodation_description: The opinion does not identify a specific accommodation request; the complaint references Fair Housing Act claims but focuses on procedural deficiencies rather than any particular accommodation.
key_holding: The court dismissed the second amended complaint as an impermissible shotgun pleading and denied motions to remand, declining to reach the merits of the Fair Housing Act claims due to standing issues and failure to comply with Rule 8 pleading standards.
brief_summary: Pro se tenants Joseph Herbozo and Meghan Liesenfeld sued landlord Debbie Fernandez and others asserting Fair Housing Act claims related to an apartment complex. The court denied the plaintiffs' motions to remand the removed case to state court and dismissed their second amended complaint as an impermissible shotgun pleading that was 787 paragraphs and 200 pages long, contained claims for alleged discrimination against non-parties, and failed to separate causes of action into distinct counts.
key_cases_cited: Weiland v. Palm Beach Cnty. Sheriff's Off., 792 F.3d 1313 (11th Cir. 2015)
Pretka v. Kolter City Plaza II, Inc., 608 F.3d 744 (11th Cir. 2010)
Citizens Concerned About Our Children v. Sch. Bd. of Broward Cnty., 193 F.3d 1285 (11th Cir. 1999)
Chavez v. Sec'y Fla. Dep't of Corr., 647 F.3d 1057 (11th Cir. 2011)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Second amended complaint dismissed as impermissible shotgun pleading under Rule 8(a) for excessive, conclusory, and immaterial factual allegations not obviously connected to causes of action, and for failure to separate distinct claims into separate counts. The court did not reach the merits of the § 3617 retaliation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Second amended complaint dismissed as impermissible shotgun pleading under Rule 8(a) for excessive, conclusory, and immaterial factual allegations not obviously connected to causes of action. The court did not reach the merits of the § 3604(f)(2)(A) or (C) disparate treatment claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unspecified reasonable accommodation related to alleged discrimination against disabled residents
fha_claims.reasoning: Second amended complaint dismissed as impermissible shotgun pleading under Rule 8(a) for excessive, conclusory, and immaterial factual allegations not obviously connected to causes of action. The court did not reach the merits of the § 3604(b) reasonable accommodation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Second amended complaint dismissed as impermissible shotgun pleading under Rule 8(a) for excessive, conclusory, and immaterial factual allegations not obviously connected to causes of action. The court did not reach the merits of the § 3604(a) disparate treatment claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: State law claims and other non-FHA federal claims (Counts II through VI)
fha_claims.reasoning: Second amended complaint dismissed as impermissible shotgun pleading under Rule 8(a) for excessive, conclusory, and immaterial factual allegations not obviously connected to causes of action, and for failure to separate distinct claims into separate counts. Additionally, plaintiffs lack standing to assert claims for discrimination inflicted upon other residents they do not live in or seek to live in.

source_file: 11267542 - Robinson v. BRAZOS VALLEY COUNCIL OF GOVERNMENTS
case_name: Robinson v. Brazos Valley Council of Governments
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: The court denied plaintiffs' motions for court-appointed counsel under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(1) because plaintiffs had neither sought nor been granted in forma pauperis status and had not demonstrated exceptional circumstances warranting appointment.
brief_summary: Anthony and Latoya Robinson sued the Brazos Valley Council of Governments, BVCOG employees, Heritage Apartments employees, and a former neighbor, alleging Fair Housing Act violations and that the termination of their Section 8 housing voucher was arbitrary and capricious. The court denied plaintiffs' motions for court-appointed counsel, finding the motions premature (no IFP application filed) and that plaintiffs failed to demonstrate exceptional circumstances justifying appointment.
key_cases_cited: Ulmer v. Chancellor, 691 F.2d 209 (5th Cir. 1982)
Lopez v. Reyes, 692 F.2d 15 (5th Cir. 1982)
Naranjo v. Thompson, 809 F.3d 793 (5th Cir. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Due process rights (U.S. Const. Amend. XIV, Tex. Const. Art. I § 19), Violence Against Women Act (34 U.S.C. § 12491), Texas Penal Code § 42.092, and arbitrary and capricious termination of Section 8 housing voucher (24 C.F.R. § 982.555(e)(6))
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied plaintiffs' request for court-appointed counsel under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(1), finding no exceptional circumstances warranting appointment. The underlying claims remain pending; this order addresses only the procedural request for counsel.

source_file: 11267543 - PLACE OF GRACE, INC. v. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR
case_name: Place of Grace, Inc. v. Executive Director
accommodation_description: Plaintiff Place of Grace operates group recovery homes for women with substance use disorders; the discriminatory treatment involves DHS classifying these group homes as Class 1 (commercial) structures rather than Class 2 (residential) structures, subjecting them to stricter building requirements like sprinkler systems that are not imposed on foster homes or nuclear family residences.
key_holding: DHS engaged in intentional discrimination under the FHAA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act by classifying group recovery homes as Class 1 structures while not applying the same classification to foster homes or nuclear family homes, resulting in disparate treatment of persons with disabilities without legitimate justification.
brief_summary: Place of Grace, Inc., a non-profit operating group recovery homes for women with substance use disorders in Huntington, Indiana, sued the Indiana Department of Homeland Security, alleging that DHS's classification of its group homes as Class 1 (commercial) structures under Indiana building codes, while not applying the same classification to foster homes or nuclear family homes, violated the Fair Housing Amendments Act, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act. The court granted summary judgment for Place of Grace, issued a permanent injunction requiring DHS to treat the Guilford Street Home as a Class 2 structure, and awarded $206,232.11 in monetary damages under the Rehabilitation Act, finding that DHS engaged in intentional discrimination without legitimate justification.
key_cases_cited: New Horizons Rehabilitation, Inc. v. State, 400 F. Supp. 3d 751 (S.D. Ind. 2019)
Next Step, Inc. v. City of Evansville, 755 F. Supp. 3d 1071 (S.D. Ind. 2024)
Valencia v. City of Springfield, 883 F.3d 959 (7th Cir. 2018)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Olmstead v. L.C., 527 U.S. 581 (1999)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that Defendants intentionally discriminated against Plaintiff's group recovery homes by classifying them as Class 1 structures (requiring sprinkler systems and heightened construction standards) while treating similarly situated foster homes and nuclear family homes as Class 2 structures. Defendants' facially neutral definition of 'tenant' was applied as a proxy to discriminate against persons with disabilities, with no legitimate justification based on fire safety.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Variance from Class 1 sprinkler system requirement and other Class 1 building requirements; treatment of group recovery homes as Class 2 structures instead of Class 1 structures
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed Plaintiff's failure to accommodate claims without prejudice because Plaintiff had already prevailed on disparate treatment claims, which provided a complete remedy. The Court stated it need not reach the failure to accommodate claims or related requests for equitable relief because the disparate treatment violation was sufficient to entitle Plaintiff to an injunction.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act Title II (42 U.S.C. § 12132), Rehabilitation Act (29 U.S.C. § 794)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied the same disparate treatment analysis under the ADA and Rehabilitation Act as under the FHAA, finding intentional discrimination. Plaintiff was awarded monetary damages of $206,232.11 under the Rehabilitation Act based on the difference between Class 1 and Class 2 construction costs for the Superior Street Homes.

source_file: 11267544 - HARMONY HOME OF HUNTINGTON, INC. v. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR
case_name: Harmony Home of Huntington, Inc. v. Executive Director
accommodation_description: Group recovery home operator seeking to be classified as a Class 2 residential structure rather than Class 1 commercial structure under Indiana building codes, alleging discriminatory classification based on disability
key_holding: The court found that DHS's definition of 'tenant' was designed and interpreted to impose Class 1 building requirements on the group recovery home for persons with disabilities while not applying the same requirements to nuclear family or foster homes, constituting intentional discrimination with no legitimate justification.
brief_summary: Harmony Home of Huntington, Inc., a nonprofit operating group recovery homes for men with substance abuse disorders, sued the Indiana Department of Homeland Security and Fire Prevention and Building Safety Commission alleging that classifying its group home as a Class 1 structure under Indiana building codes, rather than a Class 2 residential structure like nuclear family or foster homes, constituted disability discrimination in violation of the FHAA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act. The court granted summary judgment for Plaintiff, finding intentional discrimination because DHS's definition of 'tenant' was designed to target group homes for persons with disabilities while excluding similarly situated family homes, with no legitimate justification.
key_cases_cited: New Horizons Rehabilitation, Inc. v. State, 400 F. Supp. 3d 751 (S.D. Ind. 2019)
Next Step, Inc. v. City of Ogdensburg, 176 F. Supp. 3d 112 (N.D.N.Y. 2016)
Valencia v. City of Springfield, 883 F.3d 959 (7th Cir. 2018)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Courage to Change, Inc. v. Joaquin, 73 F.4th 1184 (9th Cir. 2024)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that DHS's classification of the Home as a Class 1 structure, while treating similarly situated foster homes and nuclear family homes as Class 2 structures, constitutes intentional disparate treatment under the FHAA. DHS's definition of 'tenant' was applied in a discriminatory manner as a proxy to impose heightened building requirements exclusively on group homes for persons with disabilities, with no legitimate justification based on actual fire risk differences.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Variance from Class 1 sprinkler system requirement; treatment of Home as Class 2 structure instead of Class 1
fha_claims.reasoning: The court declined to reach the failure to accommodate claims because Plaintiff had already prevailed on disparate treatment claims, which provided a sufficient basis for the requested injunction. The court dismissed the failure to accommodate claims without prejudice, stating that no further analysis was necessary once intentional discrimination was established.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act Title II (42 U.S.C. § 12132) and Rehabilitation Act (29 U.S.C. § 794) claims based on same facts as FHAA disparate treatment claim
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the same disparate treatment analysis under the ADA and Rehabilitation Act as under the FHAA, finding that the same analysis generally applies under all three statutes. Plaintiff prevailed on intentional discrimination claims under both non-FHA statutes based on DHS's discriminatory classification of the Home.

case_name: Ramone Taylor v. Lisa Royal
accommodation_description: Unspecified medical and disability accommodation request denied during eviction proceedings
key_holding: The court dismissed Taylor's FHAA reasonable accommodation claims because his complaint contained only conclusory allegations that he 'repeatedly requested medical and disability accommodation' without pleading sufficient factual content to state a plausible claim for relief.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Ramone Taylor sued his landlord and related entities under the ADA, FHAA, and federal Constitution alleging he is blind and suffers from PTSD, was subjected to eviction, and was denied unspecified disability accommodations. The court dismissed the FHAA reasonable accommodation claims for failure to state a plausible claim because Taylor's complaint contained only conclusory allegations without factual content allowing the court to draw a reasonable inference that any defendant violated the Fair Housing Act.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Revock v. Baypointe W. Condo. Ass'n, 853 F.3d 96 (3d Cir. 2017)
City of Edmonds v. Oxford House, Inc., 514 U.S. 725 (1995)
Monell v. Dep't of Soc. Servs., 436 U.S. 658 (1978)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unspecified medical and disability accommodations related to plaintiff's blindness and chronic PTSD
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient factual content to allow the court to draw a reasonable inference that any defendant violated the FHA. The complaint contained only conclusory allegations that plaintiff requested accommodations and was denied, without describing the circumstances, events, or specific accommodations at issue, falling short of the plausibility standard under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claims (unspecified), § 1983 due process claims, and state law legal malpractice claims
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA Title II claims against private defendants and individuals dismissed because Title II applies only to public entities; § 1983 claims against Robinson dismissed for failure to allege personal involvement and sufficient facts; Monell claim against City dismissed as conclusory and contradicted by state court records showing judicial authorization for eviction; state law claims dismissed for lack of diversity jurisdiction.

source_file: 11267546 - NEXT STEP RECOVERY HOME, INC. v. Indiana
case_name: Next Step Recovery Home, Inc. v. State of Indiana
accommodation_description: Plaintiff operates a substance abuse recovery home and challenges DHS's classification of the home as a Class 1 (commercial) structure rather than a Class 2 (residential) structure under Indiana building laws, which the court finds constitutes intentional discrimination against persons with disabilities.
key_holding: DHS's facially neutral definition of 'tenant,' which requires each occupant to enter an independent occupancy agreement, is applied in a discriminatory manner to impose Class 1 building requirements on group homes for persons with disabilities while the same requirements are not imposed on nuclear family or foster homes, constituting intentional discrimination under the FHAA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act.
brief_summary: Next Step Recovery Home, Inc., a substance abuse recovery home operator, sued the State of Indiana and DHS, challenging the classification of its group recovery home as a Class 1 (commercial) structure under Indiana building laws that would require sprinkler systems and other commercial requirements not imposed on family homes. The court granted summary judgment for Plaintiff, finding DHS engaged in intentional disability discrimination by applying a facially neutral definition of 'tenant' that effectively targets group homes for persons with disabilities while the same classification is not applied to nuclear family or foster homes.
key_cases_cited: New Horizons Rehabilitation, Inc. v. State, 400 F. Supp. 3d 751 (S.D. Ind. 2019)
Pacific Shores Properties, LLC v. City of Newport Beach, 730 F.3d 1142 (9th Cir. 2013)
Pyke v. Cuomo, 258 F.3d 107 (2d Cir. 2001)
Courage to Change Ranches Holding Co. v. El Paso County, 73 F.4th 1175 (10th Cir. 2023)
Valencia v. City of Springfield, 883 F.3d 959 (7th Cir. 2018)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that Defendants intentionally discriminated against the Home by classifying it as a Class 1 structure subject to heightened building requirements (including sprinkler systems) while treating similarly situated foster homes and nuclear family homes as Class 2 structures. Defendants' facially neutral definition of 'tenant' was applied as a proxy to discriminate against persons with disabilities, with no legitimate justification based on fire safety or other factors.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Variance from Class 1 sprinkler system requirement and other Class 1 building requirements; treatment of the Home as a Class 2 structure
fha_claims.reasoning: Court declined to reach the failure to accommodate claims because Plaintiff had already prevailed on disparate treatment claims, which provided a complete basis for relief. The Court stated that Plaintiff's failure to accommodate claims could be dismissed without prejudice.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act Title II (42 U.S.C. § 12132) and Rehabilitation Act (29 U.S.C. § 794) claims based on same facts as FHAA disparate treatment claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied the same disparate treatment analysis under the ADA and Rehabilitation Act as under the FHAA, finding that the same analysis generally applies under all three statutes. Plaintiff prevailed on intentional discrimination claims under both statutes based on Defendants' classification of the Home as Class 1 while treating similarly situated non-disabled housing as Class 2.

case_name: Lisa R. Wrighten v. Old Linco LLC
accommodation_description: Request to keep an emotional support/service animal (Bella, a dog) as a reasonable accommodation for disability
key_holding: Both cross-motions for summary judgment are denied because genuine disputes of material fact exist regarding whether Plaintiff's emotional support animal was necessary to afford her an equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling, as the accommodation support letter did not sufficiently connect Bella to Plaintiff's specific disability-related need.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Lisa Wrighten sued her landlords, Old Linco LLC and Charlie Oliver, alleging disability discrimination under the FHA arising from their handling of her service/emotional support animal Bella and related eviction actions. The Court denied both parties' cross-motions for summary judgment, finding genuine disputes of material fact exist regarding whether the animal accommodation was necessary to afford Plaintiff equal use and enjoyment of the dwelling.
key_cases_cited: Coots v. Tankersley, 2021 WL 3617841 (E.D. Tex. June 25, 2021)
Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242 (1986)
Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation for a service dog (Bella) as an emotional support animal necessary to afford plaintiff equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found a genuine dispute of material fact exists regarding whether the service animal is necessary to afford plaintiff equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling. The accommodation support letter was not self-authenticating and did not establish the nexus between the animal and plaintiff's use of the dwelling, precluding summary judgment for either party.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged failure to repair home and provide heat from November 2022-March 2023 in retaliation for requesting service animal accommodation
fha_claims.reasoning: The court did not substantively analyze the retaliation claim on the merits. The opinion focuses on the reasonable accommodation claim and denies summary judgment for both parties without reaching the retaliation theory.

case_name: Karen DeMoor v. Freeman Webb Company, Realtors, et al.
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation was requested; plaintiff alleged she was treated worse than other tenants regarding repairs and eviction due to her disability.
key_holding: The plaintiff's FHA claims were dismissed because she failed to allege that she requested a reasonable accommodation related to her disability, and her interference claim failed because she did not allege she exercised her right to request an accommodation under the FHA.
brief_summary: Karen DeMoor, a disabled tenant on Social Security Disability, sued Freeman Webb Company and related defendants for Fair Housing Act violations after being evicted from her townhome, alleging she was discriminated against regarding repairs and eviction. The court dismissed all claims with prejudice, finding she failed to state viable FHA claims because she did not request any reasonable accommodation related to her disability and failed to allege a causal connection between any protected activity and the defendants' conduct.
key_cases_cited: Hollis v. Chestnut Bend Homeowners Ass'n, 760 F.3d 531 (6th Cir. 2014)
Overlook Mut. Homes, Inc. v. Spencer, 415 F. App'x 617 (6th Cir. 2011)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Repair of broken living room window and inoperable smoke detectors in plaintiff's townhome
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged she is disabled and requested repairs to a broken window and smoke detectors, but failed to allege that she requested a reasonable accommodation related to her disability or that the defendants refused to make such an accommodation. The complaint does not plausibly allege the elements required for an FHA reasonable accommodation claim under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged coercion, intimidation, and interference through eviction proceedings and banning from property
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege that she exercised or enjoyed a right guaranteed by the FHA (such as requesting a reasonable accommodation based on disability) or that the defendants' conduct was taken in response to such exercise. The allegations of eviction and property banning, without connection to FHA-protected activity, do not state a plausible interference claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3617.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) Title II claims and 42 U.S.C. § 1983 civil rights claims
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA and § 1983 claims are subject to Tennessee's one-year statute of limitations under Tenn. Code Ann. § 28-3-104(a)(3). Plaintiff's alleged wrongful acts occurred between March 31, 2022 and January 23, 2023, but the lawsuit was filed on September 13, 2024, more than one year after the latest alleged wrongful act, rendering the claims time-barred.

source_file: 11267549 - BITTENBENDER v. FAMILY SERVICES ASSOCIATION OF BUCKS COUNTY
case_name: Cynthia Bittenbender v. Family Services Association of Bucks County
accommodation_description: Request to keep emotional support animals (cat and bearded dragon) in emergency medical housing at Extended Stay America
key_holding: The court dismissed Bittenbender's FHA claims because Extended Stay America did not constitute a 'dwelling' under the FHA under the Columbus Country Club framework, and because she failed to name a proper defendant subject to FHA liability; her ADA claims failed because emotional support animals are explicitly excluded from ADA service animal protections.
brief_summary: Cynthia Bittenbender, a pro se plaintiff with multiple disabilities including autism and PTSD, sued Family Services Association of Bucks County, Extended Stay America, and others alleging Fair Housing Act and ADA violations after being ejected from emergency medical housing for keeping emotional support animals. The court dismissed her complaint with prejudice, finding that Extended Stay America was not a 'dwelling' under the FHA because she lacked intent to remain and did not view it as a residence, and that emotional support animals are not protected as service animals under the ADA.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
United States v. Columbus Country Club, 915 F.2d 877 (3d Cir. 1990)
Lakeside Resort Enters., LP v. Bd. of Supervisors of Palmyra Twp., 455 F.3d 154 (3d Cir. 2006)
Growth Horizons, Inc. v. Delaware County, 983 F.2d 1277 (3d Cir. 1993)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Emotional support animals (cat and bearded dragon)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege that her conditions substantially limit any major life activity, which is required to establish disability under the FHAA. Conclusory allegations of disability without factual support are insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Emotional support animals (cat and bearded dragon) at Extended Stay America hotel
fha_claims.reasoning: Extended Stay America hotel room does not constitute a 'dwelling' under the FHA. Under the Columbus Country Club framework, plaintiff failed to allege she intended to remain for a significant period of time or viewed the hotel as a place to return to, as her placement was temporary emergency housing pending issuance of a Housing Choice Voucher.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 due process and equal protection claims; ADA Title II, Title III, and § 504 Rehabilitation Act disability discrimination claims
fha_claims.reasoning: § 1983 claims fail because FSABC and Stewart are not state actors; plaintiff lacks a protected property interest in emergency housing services. ADA Title II claims fail because FSABC is a private nonprofit, not a public entity. ADA Title III and RA claims fail because emotional support animals are explicitly excluded from the ADA definition of service animals, and plaintiff failed to allege disability substantially limits a major life activity.

source_file: 11267550 - Pella v. ATLANTIC COUNTY DEPARTMENT OF FAMILY AND COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT
case_name: Pella v. Atlantic County Department of Family and Community Development
subsidy_program: Work First New Jersey; Emergency Assistance; SNAP
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, found 'overhoused' and denied Emergency Assistance benefits for refusing to downsize from three bedrooms to one, challenged the benefits determination under disability discrimination theories without requesting a specific accommodation.
key_holding: The Fair Housing Act does not apply to the administration of state public benefits programs, and plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that benefit denials occurred by reason of his disability or that he requested and was denied a reasonable accommodation.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Phillip Pella, who is disabled, sued Atlantic County and New Jersey state agencies alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act, ADA, Section 1983, and Rehabilitation Act based on the denial of Emergency Assistance and SNAP benefits and a determination that he was 'overhoused.' The court dismissed all federal claims, holding that the FHA does not govern the administration of state public assistance benefits and that plaintiff failed to plausibly allege disability-based discrimination or a failure to accommodate.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Ctr., 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Goldberg v. Kelly, 397 U.S. 254 (1970)
Oxford House, Inc. v. Twp. of N. Bergen, 158 F.4th 486 (3d Cir. 2025)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exception to 'overhoused' policy determination; plaintiff sought to retain three-bedroom housing rather than downsize to one bedroom in connection with Emergency Assistance benefits determination
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiff failed to allege facts showing that defendants refused to rent him a dwelling, imposed discriminatory rental terms, or acted as housing providers. The FHA's scope is narrow and regulates only discriminatory practices in the sale, rental, or making unavailable of dwellings; the conduct challenged involved administration of state emergency assistance benefits, not housing discrimination. Court could not draw reasonable inference that housing determinations were made with discriminatory animus based on disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claim for denial of state benefits (EA and SNAP) based on disability; § 504 Rehabilitation Act claim for denial of benefits solely by reason of disability; Civil Rights Act Title II and VI claims for discrimination in public assistance programs; § 1983 claims for deprivation of constitutional rights (procedural due process, substantive due process, equal protection, retaliation)
fha_claims.reasoning: For ADA Title II and § 504: plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that denial of benefits occurred 'by reason of' disability; SNAP denial notice explained gross income calculation, and plaintiff offered no facts showing denial was disability-based or that he requested and was denied reasonable accommodation. For § 1983: plaintiff adequately alleged state action but failed to plausibly allege deprivation of constitutional right; procedural due process claim failed because administrative and judicial review were available; substantive due process claim failed because public assistance is statutory entitlement, not fundamental right, and allegations of delay/error do not shock conscience; equal protection claim failed because no similarly situated non-disabled individuals identified and no discriminatory intent alleged; retaliation claim failed because no protected activity or causal connection alleged. For Civil Rights Act: Title II does not apply to state agencies administering public assistance; Title VI does not encompass disability discrimination and plaintiff failed to allege protected class membership.

case_name: Keith David Nizwantowski v. Monarch, et al.
accommodation_description: Pro se plaintiff alleging disability discrimination, retaliation, and hostile housing environment but no specific accommodation request identified in the complaint.
key_holding: The court found plaintiff's complaint failed to state a viable FHA claim because it contained only conclusory allegations parroting the statute without factual support for the nature of the disability, specific discriminatory acts, or the link between disability and alleged wrongful conduct, but allowed amendment to particularize the complaint.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Keith David Nizwantowski sued Monarch NC (property management) and The Ark of North Carolina Inc. (apartment owner) alleging disability discrimination, retaliation, and hostile housing environment under the Fair Housing Act. The court conducted frivolity review under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B) and found the complaint failed to state a claim because it contained only conclusory allegations without factual support for the disability, discriminatory acts, or causal connection, but allowed plaintiff to file an amended complaint to particularize his claims.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Affinity Recovery Ctr., LLC v. Town Commissioners of Sudlersville, No. 23-CV-00714-LKG, 2024 WL 149835 (D. Md. Jan. 12, 2024)
Martin v. Brondum, 535 F. App'x 242 (4th Cir. 2013)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Disability discrimination in terms, conditions, or privileges of rental housing
fha_claims.disposition: Complaint subject to dismissal under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e); opportunity to amend granted
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint contains only conclusory allegations parroting the statute without factual support regarding the nature of disability, specific discriminatory acts, or nexus between disability and alleged wrongful conduct. Court found complaint fails to meet Twombly pleading standard but granted pro se plaintiff opportunity to amend.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation for asserting FHA rights, objecting to discriminatory conduct, and requesting fair treatment
fha_claims.disposition: Complaint subject to dismissal under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e); opportunity to amend granted
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint contains only conclusory allegations without factual support identifying the nature of disability, specific retaliatory acts, or causal connection between protected activity and alleged retaliation. Court found complaint fails Twombly pleading standard but granted pro se plaintiff opportunity to amend.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Harassment, intimidation, increased scrutiny, and adverse treatment creating hostile housing environment
fha_claims.disposition: Complaint subject to dismissal under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e); opportunity to amend granted
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint alleges hostile housing environment through harassment and intimidation but lacks factual allegations regarding specific conduct, disability, and nexus. Court found complaint fails Twombly pleading standard but granted pro se plaintiff opportunity to amend.

source_file: 11267552 - Phillips v. STODDARD COUNTY CIRCUIT COURT
case_name: Sandy Phillips v. Stoddard County Circuit Court, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested telephonic participation in court hearings as an ADA/disability accommodation due to documented inability to drive to court proceedings.
key_holding: The Court found multiple deficiencies in Plaintiff's amended complaint including failure to state a prima facie FHA retaliation claim, improper joinder of unrelated claims, and insufficient facts to support Title II ADA claim; Plaintiff was ordered to file a second amended complaint on the proper form.
brief_summary: Self-represented Plaintiff Sandy Phillips filed an amended complaint against private landlords and state court entities alleging disability discrimination, FHA violations, and Title II ADA violations arising from substandard housing conditions and denial of telephonic court access. The Court conducted an initial review under 28 U.S.C. § 1915 and found Plaintiff's pleading legally deficient on multiple grounds, including failure to state a prima facie FHA retaliation claim, improper joinder of unrelated claims, and insufficient facts to support Title II ADA denial of access claims; the Court ordered Plaintiff to file a second amended complaint on the proper form.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
George v. Smith, 507 F.3d 605 (7th Cir. 2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Repairs and relocation related to uninhabitable housing conditions (roaches, nonfunctioning stove, mold, lack of hot water, broken doors/smoke detectors); unclear whether disability-related accommodation was requested
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiff failed to allege facts connecting the housing conditions to her disability or demonstrating that she requested a disability-related accommodation. The complaint alleged only general habitability defects (roaches, hot water, equipment) unrelated to any alleged disability, and did not plead sufficient facts to state a reasonable accommodation claim under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiff failed to allege a protected activity under the FHA. To state an FHA retaliation claim, plaintiff must allege engagement in a protected activity (such as complaining about disability-related discrimination) and a causal link between that activity and defendant's retaliatory conduct. Plaintiff's allegations of threatening eviction, removing doors, wiretapping, and spreading defamatory statements were not connected to any protected FHA activity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II ADA claim for denial of telephonic accommodations and meaningful access to court system; § 1983 claims for constitutional violations; Missouri state law claims for breach of implied warranty of habitability, constructive eviction, harassment, illegal wiretapping, and invasion of privacy
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found multiple deficiencies in pleading non-FHA claims. For Title II ADA: plaintiff alleged only that she called the courthouse requesting telephone access and never heard back, insufficient to state a claim. For § 1983: most defendants are private parties, not state actors, and plaintiff failed to identify which defendants she sued under § 1983 or what constitutional rights were violated. For state law claims: plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts to support each claim or demonstrate they arise from the same case or controversy as federal claims.

case_name: Nitschke v. 326 Welch Partners
accommodation_description: Design and construction of apartment complex allegedly failed to meet FHA accessibility requirements for covered multifamily dwellings.
key_holding: The court granted judgment on the pleadings finding defendants violated § 3604(f)(3)(C) by failing to design and construct the apartment complex in compliance with FHA accessibility requirements, with defendants admitting most allegations and acknowledging liability.
brief_summary: Cynthia George and Chelsie Nitschke sued 326 Welch Partners, Avenue Construction, LLC, and Barnett Design Studio alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on the inaccessibility of a 129-unit apartment complex they attempted to access. The court granted judgment on the pleadings, finding defendants violated § 3604(f)(3)(C) by failing to design and construct the dwellings in compliance with FHA accessibility requirements, with the court reserving determination of damages and injunctive relief while parties proceed to mediation.
key_cases_cited: Grindstaff v. Green, 133 F.3d 416 (6th Cir. 1998)
Tucker v. Middleburg-Legacy Place, 539 F.3d 545 (6th Cir. 2008)
Iowa Beef Processors, Inc. v. Amalgamated Meat Cutters, 627 F.2d 853 (8th Cir. 1980)
Meyer Nat. Foods, LLC v. Liberty Mut. Fire Ins. Co., 218 F. Supp. 3d 1034 (D. Neb. 2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible design and construction of covered multifamily dwellings, including ground-floor units and upper-floor units served by elevators, in compliance with FHA accessibility guidelines and 24 C.F.R. Part 100.205
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that the apartment complex is a covered multifamily dwelling built after March 13, 1991, subject to § 3604(f)(3)(C) design and construction requirements. Defendants admitted violations of the FHA and applicable accessibility standards. Court granted judgment on the pleadings in favor of plaintiffs on liability, finding defendants failed to design and construct dwellings in compliance with FHA requirements and applicable regulations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Maintenance of public and common-use areas of the apartment complex in compliance with ADA accessibility requirements
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that public and common-use areas are subject to design and construction requirements under both § 3604(f)(3)(C) and the ADA. Defendants' admitted violations of accessibility standards in these areas constitute discrimination against disabled persons. Court granted judgment on the pleadings in favor of plaintiffs on liability.

source_file: 11267554 - GRACE L. HERNANDEZ TRUST v. Lozano

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Defendant asserted FHA discrimination as a defense to unlawful detainer, claiming plaintiff discriminated against him and co-tenant in violation of FHA § 3604(f)(3)(A), (C)(ii), and (C)(iii); specific accommodation or relief not identified in opinion.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court lacked subject matter jurisdiction because unlawful detainer actions are purely state law matters, and a defendant cannot create federal jurisdiction by asserting FHA defenses or claims in a removal notice. Case remanded to state court.

source_file: 11267555 - Grossman v. B&J SERVICES OF MIAMI, LLC
case_name: Lorin Grossman v. B&J Services of Miami, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff who uses a wheelchair sought to tour and rent a property, but defendants refused based on the property's allegedly unsuitable stone pathway for wheelchairs, renting it to others instead.
key_holding: Because defendants defaulted, the court accepted the complaint's well-pleaded facts as true, finding plaintiff plausibly alleged disability-based discrimination under § 3604(f)(1) and violations of §§ 3604(c) and (d), warranting default judgment and $132,200 in damages.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Lorin Grossman, who uses a wheelchair, sued B&J Services of Miami and its agent Carla Rodas for refusing to show or lease a rental property to her based on her physical disability, despite her offering to demonstrate the allegedly unsuitable stone pathway posed no issue. The court entered default judgment against defendants for violations of Fair Housing Act provisions prohibiting disability discrimination, discriminatory advertising, and misrepresentation, awarding $132,200 in actual and punitive damages.
key_cases_cited: Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)
Eagle Hosp. Physicians, LLC v. SRG Consulting, Inc., 561 F.3d 1298 (11th Cir. 2009)
Nishimatsu Const. Co. v. Houston Nat'l Bank, 515 F.2d 1200 (5th Cir. 1975)
Banai v. Sec'y, U.S. Dept. of Hous. & Urban Dev. on Behalf of Times, 102 F.3d 1203 (11th Cir. 1997)
Miller v. Paradise of Port Richey, Inc., 75 F. Supp. 2d 1342 (M.D. Fla. 1999)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to show or lease property based on disability (wheelchair mobility)
fha_claims.reasoning: Counts I and II under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(a) and (b) fail to state a claim because these subsections do not cover discrimination based on disability; plaintiff's disability-based discrimination claim cannot proceed under these provisions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to show or lease property based on disability; denial of equal opportunity to rent on same terms as able-bodied renters
fha_claims.reasoning: Count VI under Fla. Stat. § 760.23(1) states a plausible claim for disability discrimination in rental; plaintiff alleged defendants had knowledge of her disability, she was qualified and willing to rent, and defendants refused her the opportunity because of her disability while allowing able-bodied renters to view and lease the property.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination in terms, conditions, or privileges of rental based on disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Count VII under Fla. Stat. § 760.23(2) states a plausible claim; plaintiff alleged she has a disability, defendants knew about it, she was qualified to rent, and defendants deprived her of the opportunity to rent on the same terms as able-bodied renters because of her disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discriminatory statements and communications indicating preference, limitation, or discrimination based on disability in housing advertisement and rental communications
fha_claims.reasoning: Count III under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c) states a plausible claim; plaintiff alleged that defendant Carla Rodas's written communications reflected that plaintiff's disability was the motivating factor behind defendants' refusal to show and lease the property.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discriminatory statements and communications indicating preference, limitation, or discrimination based on disability in housing rental communications
fha_claims.reasoning: Count VIII under Fla. Stat. § 760.23(3) states a plausible claim; the provisions in Counts III and VIII can be interpreted together, and plaintiff's allegations of discriminatory written communications support liability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Misrepresentation regarding availability of housing based on disability; false statements that property could not be toured on dates when able-bodied persons were allowed to tour
fha_claims.reasoning: Count IV under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(d) states a plausible claim; plaintiff alleged defendants misrepresented that the property could not be toured on a day when able-bodied persons were allowed to tour, violating the right to truthful information about available housing.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Misrepresentation regarding availability of housing based on disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Count IX under Fla. Stat. § 760.23(4) states a plausible claim; the provisions in Counts IV and IX can be interpreted together, and plaintiff's allegations of misrepresentation support liability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to show or lease property and denial of equal opportunity to rent based on disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Count V under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(1) states a plausible claim; plaintiff alleged adverse action was taken because of her disability, that the property was toured by and rented to non-disabled renters, and that defendants refused her the ability to tour and rent because of her disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to show or lease property and denial of equal opportunity to rent based on disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Count X under Fla. Stat. § 760.23(7) states a plausible claim; plaintiff's allegations are sufficient to plausibly state that defendants' adverse actions were taken because of plaintiff's disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination in terms, conditions, or privileges of rental based on disability; denial of equal opportunity to rent on same terms as able-bodied renters
fha_claims.reasoning: Count XI under Fla. Stat. § 760.23(8) states a plausible claim; plaintiff's allegations plausibly support an inference that because of her disability, she was denied an equal opportunity to rent the property on the same terms and conditions as available to able-bodied prospective renters.

source_file: 11267556 - Robins v. ABERDEEN AT GOLF & COUNTRY CLUB, INC.
case_name: Lori Robins v. Waterford at Aberdeen Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: Visually impaired homeowner requested to email work orders to the property manager instead of submitting them through the inaccessible HOA website, and requested large-print copies of HOA documents mailed to her.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for plaintiff on her FHA reasonable accommodation claim because Waterford constructively rejected her request to email work orders by ignoring it after review, which is legally equivalent to denial; however, summary judgment was denied on her ACH form request (fact dispute exists) and her pool gate modification request (plaintiff failed to offer to pay as required under § 3604(f)(3)(A)).
brief_summary: Lori Robins, a visually impaired homeowner, sued her HOA alleging it discriminated against her by refusing reasonable accommodations for her disability, including refusing to let her email work orders instead of using the inaccessible website. The court granted summary judgment for Robins on the work-order email accommodation claim, finding Waterford constructively rejected her request by ignoring it, while denying summary judgment on other accommodation claims due to factual disputes or failure to follow statutory requirements.
key_cases_cited: Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014)
Schwarz v. City of Treasure Island, 544 F.3d 1201 (11th Cir. 2008)
Wood v. Briarwinds Condo. Ass'n Bd. of Directors, 2009 WL 10668944 (S.D. Fla. 2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request for large-print physical copy of ACH automatic withdrawal form to be mailed to plaintiff so she could pay HOA fees via direct deposit without accessing the inaccessible website
fha_claims.reasoning: Whether Waterford actually mailed the accessible ACH form is a genuine question of fact for the jury; Waterford's property manager testified it was mailed, but plaintiff disputes receipt, precluding summary judgment on this claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request to submit work orders via email instead of through the inaccessible website due to visual impairment
fha_claims.reasoning: Waterford constructively rejected the request by never responding after reviewing it; the accommodation was necessary (plaintiff could not access website due to disability) and reasonable (minimal burden to allow email submission); plaintiff entitled to judgment as matter of law under FHA § 3604(f)(3)(B).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request to modify the pool gate lock to make it accessible to plaintiff with visual impairment
fha_claims.reasoning: Under FHA § 3604(f)(3)(A), a modification request requires the disabled person to offer to pay for the modification at their own expense; plaintiff never alleged she offered to pay, so she failed to properly make a modification request and is not entitled to relief.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claim that Waterford retaliated against plaintiff for requesting accommodations by ignoring unrelated maintenance requests, refusing to inform her of safety hazards, and ignoring residents' harassment
fha_claims.reasoning: Partial summary judgment granted on the first element (protected activity and defendant's awareness) as to the work-order accommodation request only, because the court found that claim meritorious; whether other requests constituted protected activity and whether adverse actions were causally related remain questions of fact for the jury.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Florida Fair Housing Act (FLFHA) § 760.20 et seq. claims for discrimination and retaliation; claims under state law parallel to FHA claims
fha_claims.reasoning: FLFHA adopted FHA provisions almost verbatim; violations of FHA also constitute violations of FLFHA; same outcomes apply to state law claims as to federal FHA claims (plaintiff prevails on work-order accommodation, defendant prevails on modification claim, ACH form claim proceeds to jury).

source_file: 11267557 - Huston v. WILLAMETTE VALLEY RENTALS, LLC
case_name: Huston v. Willamette Valley Rentals, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs sought to rent a property for their family including disabled foster children requiring DSP assistance, but were denied housing based on familial status and disability.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for plaintiffs because WVR admitted through failed requests for admission that it received plaintiffs' complete application first, plaintiffs met all financial criteria, WVR falsely told plaintiffs there was new activity on the property after learning about their disabled foster children, and WVR subsequently rented to an applicant with a smaller household who did not have disabled persons.
brief_summary: Tami and Justin Huston, foster parents with disabled children, sued Willamette Valley Rentals, LLC for refusing to rent them a property based on familial status and disability after learning about their children and their disabilities. The court granted plaintiffs' motion for partial summary judgment, finding that WVR admitted to discriminatory conduct including falsely representing competing interest in the property after learning about plaintiffs' family composition and subsequently renting to an applicant with a smaller household who had no disabled persons.
key_cases_cited: Pacific Shores Props., LLC v. City of Newport Beach, 730 F.3d 1142 (9th Cir. 2013)
Morris v. West Hayden Estates First Addition Homeowners Ass'n, Inc., 104 F.4th 1128 (9th Cir. 2024)
Harris v. Itzhaki, 183 F.3d 1043 (9th Cir. 1999)
Wilson v. Guardian Management, 383 F. Supp.3d 1105 (D. Or. 2019)
Conlon v. United States, 474 F.3d 616 (9th Cir. 2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs submitted the first application, met all financial criteria, and were denied without explanation after disclosing familial status. WVR's communication slowed after learning of children and the property was rented to someone with a smaller household. Court found discriminatory motive was a motivating factor in the refusal to rent under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(a) and ORS 659A.421(2).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: WVR offered Ms. Collins (who did not disclose familial status) more favorable terms including quick turnaround and application fee refund, while denying Plaintiffs the same terms. This constitutes discrimination in terms, conditions, or privileges of rental under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(b) and 24 C.F.R. § 100.65(a).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: After Plaintiffs disclosed familial status, WVR falsely represented that new activity surrounded the rental and encouraged them to consider other properties, while later telling Ms. Collins there was only one applicant (Plaintiffs) whose application 'doesn't look like it will work.' This violates 42 U.S.C. § 3604(d) and ORS 659A.421(2)(i).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: WVR discouraged Plaintiffs from renting the property after learning of their familial status by falsely representing new activity and encouraging them to look elsewhere, violating ORS 659A.421(d).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: WVR represented the Sharifi Defendants and retained the listing despite Ms. Sharifi's discriminatory comments about familial status. After Plaintiffs communicated concerns to WVR, WVR retained the listing, assisted in rejecting Plaintiffs' application, and found an alternative renter with a smaller household, violating ORS 659A.421(4).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: WVR assisted the Sharifi Defendants in violating ORS 659A.421 by participating in the discriminatory rejection of Plaintiffs' application based on familial status.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs met all criteria but were denied after disclosing their children's disabilities. WVR's treatment worsened after disability disclosure and the property was rented to individuals without disabilities, violating 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(1)(B) and ORS 659A.145(2)(a).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: After Plaintiffs disclosed their children's disabilities, WVR falsely represented that new activity surrounded the property and encouraged them to rent elsewhere, violating 42 U.S.C. § 3604(d) and 24 C.F.R. § 100.80(a).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: WVR discouraged Plaintiffs from renting after they disclosed their children's disabilities by falsely representing new activity and encouraging them to rent elsewhere, violating ORS 659A.145(2)(d).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: WVR represented the Sharifi Defendants and retained the listing despite Ms. Sharifi's discriminatory comments about Plaintiffs' disabled children. After Plaintiffs communicated concerns, WVR retained the listing, assisted in rejecting Plaintiffs' application, and found an alternative renter without disabilities, violating ORS 659A.145(5).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: WVR assisted the Sharifi Defendants in discriminating against Plaintiffs because of disability by participating in the rejection of Plaintiffs' application, violating ORS 659A.145(7).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Negligence claim under Oregon state law
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs did not move for summary judgment on their negligence claim and represented their intent to dismiss it in the event the fair housing claims were granted. The claim remains pending.

case_name: Doe v. 2001 ARTHUR LLC
accommodation_description: HIV-positive shelter resident's request for repairs to unit conditions (broken sink, nonfunctional stove, cleanup of hazardous needles) as reasonable accommodation for disability-related vulnerability to infection
key_holding: Plaintiff fails to state a reasonable accommodation claim because he never requested a disability-related accommodation from defendants, and his FHA claim fails because he does not 'rent' his shelter unit within the meaning of the Act.
brief_summary: John Doe, an HIV-positive individual, sued the owner and operator of an emergency temporary shelter for families with HIV/AIDS, claiming the deplorable unit conditions (including used needles that injured him) constituted denial of reasonable accommodations under the FHA and ADA. The court denied Doe's default judgment motion, finding he failed to state a claim because he never requested a disability-related accommodation—he merely complained about general repairs—and his FHA claim failed because he did not 'rent' the shelter unit within the meaning of the Act.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Levine v. Project Renewal
PGA Tour v. Martin
Bragdon v. Abbott

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Repair of unit conditions including broken sink, nonfunctional stove, dead roaches, puddles of water, damaged door lock, and removal of used needles from the shelter unit
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to state a claim under the FHA because he did not 'rent' his shelter unit within the meaning of the Act—he made no allegation of furnishing consideration and was placed in the temporary shelter by the City's Human Resources Administration. Courts in the Second Circuit consistently hold that the FHA applies only to renters and buyers, not to someone seeking free government shelter.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III failure to accommodate claim for unit conditions; NYSHRL discrimination claim; New York statutory warranty of habitability; negligence claim
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA Title III claim dismissed because plaintiff failed to allege he requested a reasonable accommodation or that defendants refused one; he complained about repairs unrelated to his disability and sought only monetary damages, which are unavailable under Title III. State-law claims dismissed without prejudice under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c) because court declined supplemental jurisdiction after dismissing federal claims and parties reside in the same state.

source_file: 11267559 - Holmes v. WARREN COUNTY METROPOLITAN HOUSING AUTHORITY
case_name: Holmes v. Warren County Metropolitan Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested a reasonable accommodation to obtain a two-bedroom unit to allow her mother, a disability-related live-in caregiver, to live with her.
key_holding: The court recommended denying the TRO and preliminary injunction because plaintiff failed to demonstrate a substantial likelihood of success on the merits of her Fair Housing Act and ADA claims, failed to show irreparable harm, and sought affirmative relief beyond the scope of preliminary injunctive relief.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Rosalind Holmes sued Warren County Metropolitan Housing Authority alleging the public housing authority denied her reasonable accommodation requests under the Fair Housing Act, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act for a two-bedroom unit to accommodate her disability-related live-in caregiver (her mother). The court recommended denying plaintiff's motion for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction because she failed to demonstrate a substantial likelihood of success on the merits or irreparable harm warranting such extraordinary relief.
key_cases_cited: Liberty Coins, LLC v. Goodman, 748 F.3d 682 (6th Cir. 2014)
Overstreet v. Lexington Fayette Urban Cnty. Gov't, 305 F.3d 566 (6th Cir. 2002)
Winter v. Nat. Res. Def. Council, Inc., 555 U.S. 7 (2008)
Chabad of S. Ohio & Congregation Lubavitch v. City of Cincinnati, 363 F.3d 427 (6th Cir. 2004)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Two-bedroom unit to permit plaintiff's mother to reside as a disability-related live-in caregiver
fha_claims.disposition: Motion for TRO and Preliminary Injunction Denied
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied preliminary injunction on the ground that plaintiff failed to demonstrate a substantial likelihood of success on the merits of her FHA claim and failed to show irreparable harm, without reaching the substantive elements of the reasonable accommodation claim. The underlying FHA claim survives and remains pending.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II (42 U.S.C. § 12132), Rehabilitation Act (29 U.S.C. § 794), Due Process (42 U.S.C. § 1983)
fha_claims.disposition: Motion for TRO and Preliminary Injunction Denied
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied preliminary injunction on the ground that plaintiff failed to demonstrate a substantial likelihood of success on the merits of her ADA Title II, Rehabilitation Act, and due process claims and failed to show irreparable harm. The underlying non-FHA claims survive and remain pending.

source_file: 11267560 - DONAVON v. RICHMOND-HENRICO ARMS LIMITED PARTNERSHIP
case_name: Kortney Donavon v. Richmond-Henrico Arms Limited Partnership
accommodation_description: Pro se plaintiff seeks to challenge a state court eviction as a Fair Housing Act violation, though no specific accommodation request is articulated in the operative filings.
key_holding: The district court dismissed the removed state court eviction action for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, finding the case moot (eviction already executed), the removal improper, and the Anti-Injunction Act precluded federal injunctive relief against the state proceeding.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Kortney Donavon attempted to remove a state court eviction proceeding to federal court, asserting Fair Housing Act claims against Richmond-Henrico Arms Limited Partnership, along with civil rights claims under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1983 and 1985(3). The district court granted in forma pauperis status but dismissed the action for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, finding the case moot (the eviction had already been executed), the removal procedurally improper, and that the Anti-Injunction Act barred any injunctive relief against the state court proceedings.
key_cases_cited: Porter v. Clarke, 852 F.3d 358 (4th Cir. 2017)
Atlantic C. L. R. Co. v. Bhd. of Locomotive Eng'rs, 398 U.S. 281 (1970)
Denny's Inc. v. Cake, 364 F.3d 521 (4th Cir. 2004)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff asserted Fair Housing Act claims in opposition to Writ of Eviction but specific accommodation or relief sought is not identified in the opinion.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction on multiple grounds: (1) mootness—the Writ of Eviction was already executed and plaintiff evicted before federal court could act; (2) the unlawful detainer action was not removable because state court had already issued final judgment; and (3) Anti-Injunction Act barred federal court from enjoining state court proceedings.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. §§ 1983, 1985(3) civil rights claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction on the same grounds as FHA claims: mootness, non-removability of the underlying state court action, and Anti-Injunction Act bar.

source_file: 11267561 - Taylor v. WESTLAND REAL ESTATE GROUP, LLC
case_name: Telvon Taylor v. Westland Real Estate Group, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges that despite paying rent, he was evicted in violation of the FHA because the landlord failed to accommodate his disability related to mold exposure and hazardous conditions at the rental property.
key_holding: At the § 1915(e) screening stage, the court found plaintiff sufficiently alleged a prima facie FHA reasonable accommodation claim by pleading he is disabled, defendants knew of his disability, he raised disability-related concerns about hazardous mold conditions requiring accommodation to afford equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling, and defendants refused to make such accommodations.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Telvon Taylor, alleging disability and receipt of SSI benefits, filed suit against his landlord Westland Real Estate Group, LLC and Hacienda Hills Apartment claiming disability discrimination under the Fair Housing Act and wrongful eviction under Nevada state law. The court granted Taylor's in forma pauperis application and screened his complaint, finding at this preliminary stage that he stated a plausible FHA reasonable accommodation claim where he alleged the landlord failed to accommodate his disability by refusing to fix hazardous mold conditions and proceeding with an eviction despite his disability-related complaints.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Dubois v. Ass'n of Apartment Owners of 2987 Kalakaua, 453 F.3d 1175 (9th Cir. 2006)
United States v. Cal. Mobile Home Park Mgmt. Co., 107 F.3d 1374 (9th Cir. 1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Remediation of hazardous mold conditions at the rental property to accommodate plaintiff's disability-related health concerns
fha_claims.reasoning: At the initial § 1915(e) screening stage, the court accepted plaintiff's allegations as true and found that he had plausibly alleged all four elements of a reasonable accommodation claim: disability, defendant's knowledge, necessity of accommodation, and refusal. The court did not apply the substantive RA balancing test or undue burden analysis, but allowed the claim to survive screening and proceed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Wrongful eviction claim under NRS 118A.390 (Nevada state law); due process violation (federal)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court liberally construed plaintiff's due process claim as a wrongful eviction claim under Nevada state law (NRS 118A.390) and found that plaintiff had stated a colorable claim by alleging unlawful eviction without a hearing despite paying rent and interruption of mold remediation services. The claim survived § 1915(e) screening and proceeds.

source_file: 11267562 - ROCKERS v. HAVERFORD TOWNSHIP ZONING HEARING BOARD
case_name: Rockers v. Haverford Township Zoning Hearing Board
accommodation_description: Parents sought zoning accommodation to construct a two-story addition to their home to create ADA-accessible corridors, an enlarged bedroom, and accessible bathroom for their non-ambulatory disabled son.
key_holding: The Zoning Board capriciously disregarded uncontroverted medical evidence that the second-floor addition was therapeutically necessary for the disabled child to use and enjoy the home, and the Board lacked authority to condition approval on limiting the accommodation to a single story when the requested modification was proven necessary.
brief_summary: Lindsey and Scott Rockers appealed a zoning board's decision conditioning its grant of a reasonable accommodation on limiting construction to a first-floor addition only, despite their request for a two-story addition to accommodate their non-ambulatory disabled son with cerebral palsy. The Commonwealth Court reversed, holding the Board capriciously disregarded uncontroverted medical testimony establishing the second-floor addition was therapeutically necessary for the child to safely sleep near his parents and accommodate his medical equipment.
key_cases_cited: Vorchheimer v. Philadelphian Owners Association, 903 F.3d 100 (3d Cir. 2018)
Lapid-Laurel, L.L.C. v. Zoning Board of Adjustment, 284 F.3d 442 (3d Cir. 2002)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Evans v. Zoning Hearing Board of Borough of Spring City, 732 A.2d 686 (Pa. Cmwlth. 1999)
Carunchio v. Swarthmore Borough Council, 237 A.3d 1183 (Pa. Cmwlth. 2020)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Two-story, 476-square-foot addition to the side of the home, including an ADA-accessible corridor, enlarged first-floor bedroom and bathroom for the disabled child, and enlarged second-floor bedroom and bathroom to accommodate the child's medical bed, equipment, and bathing needs, plus a 40-square-foot ADA-compliant ramp.
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court applied the Lapid-Laurel burden-shifting framework and found that the Rockers established necessity for both the first-floor and second-floor additions through uncontroverted testimony regarding the disabled child's medical needs (seizure monitoring, specialized medical equipment, bathing assistance) and the pediatrician's letter supporting therapeutic necessity. The court held the Zoning Board capriciously disregarded evidence and lacked authority under the FHA to condition the accommodation to the first floor only, as the statute does not contemplate conditions on accommodations once necessity is established.

case_name: Steven E. Hobbs, Sr. v. Igor Goncharko, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested expedited rodent remediation as a reasonable accommodation because his mobility disability prevented him from bending or squatting to clean infested areas without risking re-injury.
key_holding: The court held that requests for doorbell/locks/entry system/window guards constitute modifications requiring physical changes to the premises, not accommodations; eviction-related financial hardship accommodation fails because financial difficulty is not unique to disabled persons; but rodent remediation survives because Hobbs adequately alleged his disability left him uniquely unable to self-mitigate the infestation.
brief_summary: Steven Hobbs, an African American man with mobility disabilities from spinal fractures, sued his landlord defendants and Coldwell Banker alleging racial discrimination, disability discrimination (failure to accommodate), and retaliation after he was evicted from his Chicago apartment. The court granted Coldwell Banker's motion to dismiss the disparate impact claim with prejudice but denied the landlord defendants' motion, allowing Hobbs's reasonable accommodation claim for rodent remediation to proceed past the pleading stage while dismissing his structural modification and eviction-related accommodation requests.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Texas Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Oconomowoc Residential Programs v. City of Milwaukee, 300 F.3d 775 (7th Cir. 2002)
Good Shepherd Manor Found., Inc. v. City of Momence, 323 F.3d 557 (7th Cir. 2003)
Watters v. Homeowners' Ass'n at Pres. at Bridgewater, 48 F.4th 779 (7th Cir. 2022)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Nondisclosure of affordable housing requirements and charging above-cap rents
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead facts alleging a causal connection between Coldwell Banker's alleged practice of concealing affordable housing requirements and a disparate impact on minorities. The complaint lacked statistical or factual support demonstrating that minority tenants suffer disproportionately from nondisclosure, and the alleged policy appeared to be a one-time decision affecting only plaintiff rather than a pattern affecting large groups.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Expedited rodent remediation due to plaintiff's inability to clean infested areas without risking re-injury from spinal fractures; doorbell, entry locks, secure entry system, and window guards for security; settlement or payment plan on eviction proceedings due to disability-related financial hardship
fha_claims.reasoning: Doorbell, locks, intercom, and window guards are modifications, not accommodations, and therefore not actionable. Eviction-related requests fail because financial hardship is not unique to disabled persons. However, expedited rodent remediation survives as a plausible accommodation because it is a service that plaintiff requested be provided faster due to his disability-caused inability to self-mitigate, drawing a reasonable inference that non-disabled residents could temporarily endure infestation through self-help. Fact-intensive questions of necessity and reasonableness remain for later stages.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged escalation of conduct, accelerated eviction proceedings, and bad-faith notice to enter following plaintiff's complaints of discrimination and filing of lawsuits
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff adequately pleaded all three elements of retaliation: (1) protected activity (complaints of discrimination and filing of federal and City of Chicago housing complaints); (2) adverse action (escalated conduct, accelerated eviction, bad-faith notice to enter); and (3) causal connection (allegations that conduct escalated 'because' of protected activities). Defendants' arguments regarding plaintiff's motive and timing are not proper considerations at the motion to dismiss stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged provision of inferior maintenance and living conditions compared to non-Black tenants; use of racial slur
fha_claims.reasoning: The court's prior opinion dismissed the disparate-treatment theory against Coldwell Banker for failure to plead facts sufficient to infer racial motivation, but the court permitted Hobbs to proceed with his racial discrimination claim against Landlord Defendants (Goncharko and 5120 South) on the basis of allegations of inferior maintenance and use of a racial slur. The current opinion does not address dismissal of this claim against Landlord Defendants, indicating it survives.

source_file: 11267564 - Cincinnati Insurance Company v. LOST RUN FARM COMMUNITY ASSOCIATION, INC.
case_name: Cincinnati Insurance Company v. Lost Run Farm Community Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: Request for fence to contain dogs as accommodation for Mary Kay Garcia's disability
key_holding: The court granted Cincinnati Insurance's motion for summary judgment, finding no duty to defend under the CGL coverage because the HOA's intentional enforcement of restrictive covenants did not constitute an 'occurrence' (accident), and no duty to indemnify under the Wrongful Acts coverage because the exclusion for dishonest, malicious, or fraudulent acts applied to the breach of fiduciary duty claims.
brief_summary: This is an insurance coverage declaratory judgment action where Cincinnati Insurance sought to avoid defending or indemnifying the Lost Run Farm HOA and Armour Property Management against the Garcias' Fair Housing Act claims. The Garcias alleged the HOA discriminated against them based on race, national origin, and disability by refusing accommodations including a fence for Mary Kay Garcia's disability and selectively enforcing restrictive covenants. The court granted Cincinnati summary judgment, finding no coverage under the CGL policy because the intentional enforcement of covenants was not an 'accident,' and no coverage under the Wrongful Acts policy because exclusions for malicious and dishonest acts applied.
key_cases_cited: Jim Barna Log Sys. Midwest, Inc. v. Gen. Cas. Ins. Co. of Wisconsin, 791 N.E.2d 816 (Ind. Ct. App. 2003)
Auto-Owners Ins. Co. v. Harvey, 842 N.E.2d 1279 (Ind. 2006)
Knight v. Ind. Ins. Co., 871 N.E.2d 357 (Ind. Ct. App. 2007)
Erie Ins. Exch. v. Sams, 20 N.E.3d 182 (Ind. Ct. App. 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request for exception to restrictive covenants to allow a fence to contain dogs, based on Mary Kay Garcia's disability and the steepness of a 27-foot hill on the property
fha_claims.reasoning: The court did not reach the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim because it was analyzing an insurance coverage dispute, not the underlying FHA claims themselves. The court determined that the insurer had no duty to defend based on policy exclusions and the definition of 'occurrence,' without substantively analyzing whether the accommodation request was reasonable or whether the interactive process was followed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination based on race and national origin (John Garcia) and disability (Mary Kay Garcia) in the enforcement of restrictive covenants
fha_claims.reasoning: The court did not reach the merits of the FHA discrimination claims because it was analyzing insurance coverage. The court determined that the insurer had no duty to defend the underlying FHA claims under the policy's exclusions for civil rights violations and malicious acts, without substantively analyzing whether discrimination occurred.
