The Court granted summary judgment for the Township, finding no evidence of discriminatory intent and no genuine dispute that the accommodation request was reasonable or necessary when the Township offered alternative paths for expansion.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Cmtys. Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Vill. of Arlington Heights v. Metro. Hous. Dev. Corp., 429 U.S. 252 (1977)
One Love Hous., LLC v. City of Anoka, 2021 WL 3774567 (D. Minn. Aug. 25, 2021)
Meraki Recovery Hous., LLC v. City of Coon Rapids, 2021 WL 5567898 (D. Minn. Nov. 29, 2021)
Peebles v. Potter, 354 F.3d 761 (8th Cir. 2004)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to present evidence of discriminatory statements, discriminatory motive, or discriminatory animus by the Township Board. The Board's decision was exclusively related to the number of residents the property could accommodate under zoning rules, and plaintiffs provided no evidence of bias or discriminatory intent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Amendment to zoning ordinance to allow accommodation of up to ten residents at a sober house (instead of the five allowed under existing R-1 Suburban Residential zoning)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to demonstrate that the requested accommodation (zoning amendment to allow ten residents) was reasonable and necessary. The Township Board reasonably concluded the sober house could achieve its purpose with five residents, and the Board offered alternative accommodations (conditional use permit and duplex conversion). No genuine dispute of material fact existed regarding reasonableness or necessity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act Title II claim (42 U.S.C. § 12132) alleging discrimination by municipality in zoning decision
fha_claims.reasoning: The ADA claim was analyzed under the same framework as the FHA claims (disparate treatment and reasonable accommodation). The court found no evidence of discriminatory intent and no genuine dispute regarding the reasonableness or necessity of the requested accommodation.

case_name: Abraham Shitrai Israel and Sarah Iris Israel v. Barbara Guinn, et al.
accommodation_description: Emergency public housing assistance, home repair funds, and healthcare services from Department of Social Services due to disability
key_holding: The court adopted the Report-Recommendation and dismissed Plaintiffs' Fair Housing Act claim without prejudice because the complaint was devoid of any allegations of discrimination based on protected characteristics including disability.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Israel sued New York State social services officials and police officers under the Fair Housing Act and constitutional claims, alleging they were wrongfully denied emergency housing assistance, home repair funds, and healthcare services. The court dismissed the FHA claim for failure to state a claim because the complaint lacked any factual allegations demonstrating discrimination based on a protected characteristic.
key_cases_cited: Sinisgallo v. Town of Islip Hous. Auth., 865 F. Supp. 2d 307 (E.D.N.Y. 2012)
Vialez v. New York City Hous. Auth., 783 F. Supp. 109 (S.D.N.Y. 1991)
Goldberg v. Kelly, 397 U.S. 254 (1970)
Kapps v. Wing, 404 F.3d 105 (2d Cir. 2005)
DeShaney v. Winnebago Cnty. Dep't of Soc. Servs., 489 U.S. 189 (1989)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 due process claims; ADA Title III; § 504 Rehabilitation Act; state law claims for denial of emergency housing assistance, water pipe repair assistance, and public benefits
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs' § 1983 procedural due process claims were dismissed because they failed to exhaust available Article 78 remedies in state court. The court found that New York law provides adequate post-deprivation remedies (fair hearings and Article 78 proceedings) to challenge adverse determinations regarding public assistance benefits, and Plaintiffs did not allege they pursued these remedies.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act claim for denial of housing assistance based on disability
fha_claims.reasoning: The FHA claim was dismissed because the complaint was devoid of any allegations of discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, familial status, or national origin. Although the FHA also prohibits discrimination based on disability under § 3604(f)(2), Plaintiffs failed to allege facts showing disability-based discrimination in the denial of housing assistance or emergency housing.

source_file: 11267595 - Chavous v. HOUSING VISIONS UNLIMITED, INC.
case_name: Priscilla Chavous v. Housing Visions Unlimited, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a disabled tenant under a HUD-sponsored rent-to-own program, alleges defendant denied her the opportunity to purchase the property, failed to maintain habitable conditions, and retaliated against her because of her disability.
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA claim was dismissed for failure to state a claim because she failed to allege any facts showing that her disability was at least a motivating factor in the alleged discriminatory conduct.
brief_summary: Priscilla Chavous, a pro se plaintiff with disabilities, sued Housing Visions Unlimited, Inc. alleging the defendant denied her the opportunity to purchase a property under a rent-to-own program, failed to maintain habitable conditions, and discriminated against her because of her disability in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The court dismissed the complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B), finding the claims barred by res judicata from a prior action and, alternatively, that plaintiff failed to state a plausible FHA claim because she did not allege facts showing disability was a motivating factor for the alleged discrimination.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Gladstone Realtors v. Vill. of Bellwood, 441 U.S. 91 (1979)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged failure to honor rent-to-own contract and maintain property in habitable condition; alleged disability (glaucoma and cancer) but did not clearly specify what accommodation was requested or necessary
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that disability was a motivating factor in any adverse action by defendant; allegations were conclusory and lacked factual support connecting disability to any specific accommodation request or denial.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of contract (rent-to-own agreement), breach of implied warranty of habitability, retaliatory eviction, fraud, deceptive practices, TILA, RESPA, federal housing regulations, unjust enrichment
fha_claims.reasoning: Court declined supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims after dismissing all federal claims; res judicata also barred the action based on prior dismissal in Chavous I.

source_file: 11267596 - Castellanos v. MANZANO MESA LIMITED PARTNERSHIP
case_name: Castellanos v. Manzano Mesa Limited Partnership
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges disability-based housing discrimination due to exposure to unsafe housing conditions, but no specific accommodation request is identified in the complaint.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claims because the complaint failed to allege facts showing defendants treated plaintiff differently from non-disabled tenants in providing housing and services, as required to state a discrimination claim under 24 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(2)(A).
brief_summary: Plaintiff Tekisha Castellanos, a pro se tenant with disabilities at Manzano Mesa Apartments, sued the property owner, management company, and Bernalillo County Housing Department alleging Fair Housing Act, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act discrimination claims based on exposure to unsafe housing conditions. The court granted leave to proceed in forma pauperis but ordered plaintiff to amend her complaint, finding the FHA claims failed because she did not allege defendants treated her differently from non-disabled tenants in providing housing services.
key_cases_cited: Menefee v. Werholtz, 368 Fed.Appx. 879 (10th Cir. 2010)
Bangerter v. Orem City Corp., 46 F.3d 1491 (10th Cir. 1995)
Cinnamon Hills Youth Crisis Center, Inc. v. Saint George City, 685 F.3d 917 (10th Cir. 2012)
Nasious v. Two Unknown B.I.C.E. Agents, 492 F.3d 1158 (10th Cir. 2007)
J.V. v. Albuquerque Public Schools, 813 F.3d 1289 (10th Cir. 2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged discrimination based on disability in the provision of housing and services due to exposure to unsafe housing conditions
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found no allegations showing that defendants treated plaintiff differently from non-disabled tenants in providing housing and services, failing to state a plausible disparate treatment claim under the Fair Housing Act.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claim for discrimination in public entity services; Section 504 Rehabilitation Act claim for discrimination in federally funded programs; 42 U.S.C. § 1983 due process, equal protection, and privacy claims; state law breach of warranty of habitability, negligence, and infliction of emotional distress
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff failed to allege that defendants discriminated against her by reason of disability under ADA and Rehabilitation Act; § 1983 claims lacked factual support for deprivation of federally protected rights and conclusory allegations of conspiracy; Bernalillo County Housing Department is not a separately suable entity under § 1983.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Coverage for gender-affirming chest surgery (mastectomy/breast reduction) for transgender youth under age 18; also involves age discrimination claim under ACA § 1557 and Title IX
fha_claims.reasoning: Premera's categorical exclusion of gender-affirming chest surgery for transgender youth under 18 violates ACA § 1557 by facially discriminating on the basis of sex under Title IX. The policy treats adolescents differently based on natal sex (covering mastectomy for gynecomastia in cisgender males but not for transgender females) and uses gender dysphoria as a proxy for transgender status. Medical necessity cannot justify facial discrimination on a protected basis.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Age discrimination claim under ACA § 1557 incorporating the Age Discrimination Act of 1975 (AgeDA); categorical age-based exclusion of gender-affirming surgery for individuals under 18
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to exhaust administrative remedies required by the AgeDA. They did not file complaints with HHS within 180 days of learning of the alleged discrimination, did not provide 30-day notice to HHS Secretary and Attorney General until over 18 months after litigation commenced, and did not wait 180 days after HHS closed their complaints before suing. No substantial compliance or waiver of exhaustion requirements was demonstrated. Age discrimination claims are dismissed with prejudice because plaintiffs have already received surgery and reached adulthood, leaving no basis for injunctive relief (the only remedy available under AgeDA).

source_file: 11267598 - BE THE BUSH RECOVERY MINISTRIES v. COFFEE COUNTY, TENNESSEE
case_name: Be the Bush Recovery Ministries v. Coffee County, Tennessee
accommodation_description: BTB sought zoning approval to operate a residential addiction recovery ministry at the Riley Creek Property in an RS-1 Low Density Residential District.
key_holding: The RS-1 zoning ordinance does not facially discriminate against the handicapped because it contains no mention of disability and treats BTB's facility the same as all other non-single-family residential uses; BTB's exclusion was not 'because of' its residents' handicap but rather due to its non-family residential character.
brief_summary: Be the Bush Recovery Ministries, a faith-based residential addiction recovery program, sued Coffee County, Tennessee after the County denied its requests to operate a recovery facility in an RS-1 Low Density Residential District, prompting BTB to relocate to Bedford County. The Sixth Circuit affirmed the district court's rulings, holding that the County's RS-1 zoning ordinance does not facially discriminate against the handicapped because it neutrally limits residential uses to single-family dwellings and duplexes without targeting disabled persons or group homes specifically.
key_cases_cited: Larkin v. Mich. Dep't of Soc. Servs., 89 F.3d 285 (6th Cir. 1996)
Smith & Lee Assocs., Inc. v. City of Taylor, 13 F.3d 920 (6th Cir. 1993)
MX Group, Inc. v. City of Covington, 293 F.3d 326 (6th Cir. 2002)
Livingston Christian Schs. v. Genoa Charter Township, 858 F.3d 996 (6th Cir. 2017)
Living Water Church of God v. Charter Township of Meridian, 258 F. App'x 729 (6th Cir. 2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that the RS-1 zoning ordinance does not facially discriminate against the handicapped because it employs a neutral distinction between single-family homes and other residential uses, applies equally to all non-family residential uses regardless of disability status, and contains no mention of handicapped persons. The exclusion was based on building size and commercial character, not disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Zoning variance or amendment to RS-1 ordinance to permit operation of faith-based residential rehabilitation facility for recovering addicts
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court allowed the reasonable accommodation claim to proceed to trial after denying summary judgment. The jury returned a verdict for the County on this claim, which BTB did not challenge on appeal, leaving the verdict undisturbed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claim for failure to provide reasonable accommodation; RLUIPA claim for substantial burden on religious exercise; Equal Protection Clause claim for class-of-one disparate treatment
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted summary judgment on the ADA reasonable accommodation claim (applying same framework as FHAA), RLUIPA claim (no substantial burden on religious exercise shown; inconvenience insufficient; alternative property available four miles away; success rate of 95% indicates no substantial impairment of core religious functions), and Equal Protection claim (no similarly situated comparators; rational basis for zoning classifications exists).

case_name: Amy Burnett v. Rutledge Flats, LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a wheelchair user, alleges that defendants failed to design and construct the property in compliance with FHA accessibility requirements, causing her to be deterred from renting.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motions to dismiss, finding that the plaintiff sufficiently alleged Article III standing as an individual plaintiff and that her complaint plausibly stated a claim under the FHA's design and construction requirements.
brief_summary: Amy Burnett, a wheelchair user, sued Rutledge Flats, LLC and related defendants (developers, contractors, architects, engineers) alleging the 174-unit apartment complex was not designed and constructed in compliance with the FHA's accessibility requirements under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(C). The court denied defendants' motions to dismiss, finding plaintiff adequately alleged Article III standing as an individual and plausibly stated a design-and-construction claim.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Food & Drug Admin. v. Alliance for Hippocratic Med.
Chapuis v. Forest Hill Grp. LLC
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible design and construction of multifamily dwelling units and common-use areas in compliance with FHA accessibility and usability requirements; plaintiff alleges numerous barriers and lack of accessible features at the 174-unit apartment complex
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiff plausibly alleged that defendants, including architect Hastings, violated the FHA's design and construction requirements under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(C) by failing to design and construct the property in compliance with accessibility standards. Complaint survived motion to dismiss under Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination in rental of dwellings and in terms, conditions, or privileges of rental based on disability; plaintiff alleges she was deterred from renting at the property due to inaccessible design
fha_claims.reasoning: Court accepted plaintiff's allegations that defendants discriminated against her because of her disability in the rental of dwellings and in the terms, conditions, or privileges of rental. Complaint survived motion to dismiss as plausibly alleging discriminatory conduct.

case_name: Weston v. WIP 800 J Lofts
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs' complaint does not clearly articulate a specific accommodation request, though it references disability-related housing rights; the court found plaintiffs failed to sufficiently allege defendants refused to make an accommodation.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' FHA claims because their allegations were conclusory, they failed to sufficiently plead their disabilities (ADHD, hypertension, asthma) substantially limit major life activities, and they did not adequately allege defendants knew of their impairments or refused to make an accommodation.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Weston and Marshall sued WIP 800 J Lofts and individual defendants alleging Fair Housing Act discrimination based on race, familial status, and disability arising from an allegedly fraudulent and retaliatory unlawful detainer action. The court dismissed the first amended complaint with leave to amend, finding plaintiffs' FHA claims conclusory and insufficiently pled because they failed to adequately allege their disabilities substantially limit major life activities or that defendants refused to accommodate their impairments.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Harris v. Itzhaki
United States v. Cal. Mobile Home Park Mgmt. Co.
Lopez v. Smith

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs alleged only conclusory statements that defendants' unlawful detainer action was fraudulent and retaliatory based on race, without providing sufficient facts to demonstrate discriminatory conduct. The court found the allegations insufficient under the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unspecified accommodation related to disability (ADHD, hypertension, asthma)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs alleged disabilities (ADHD, hypertension, asthma) but failed to allege that these impairments substantially limit major life activities, that defendants knew or should have known of the impairments, or that defendants refused to make an accommodation. The complaint lacked the factual specificity required to state a plausible reasonable accommodation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Familial status discrimination claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to allege that defendants created facially discriminatory rules treating families with children less favorably than adult-only households. Additionally, plaintiff Marshall was no longer a minor at the time of the order, undermining the familial status claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation for asserting housing and disability rights
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to sufficiently allege what specific housing or disability rights they asserted, failed to show a causal link between assertion of those rights and the unlawful detainer action, and failed to demonstrate that the action resulted from coercion, intimidation, or threats as required under § 3617.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 due process violations, § 1985 conspiracy, § 1503 obstruction of justice, RICO, state law claims
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim (§ 1915(e)(2)(B)); Rooker-Feldman jurisdictional bar
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs' claims are primarily based on the unlawful detainer action pending in Sacramento County Superior Court and are barred by the Rooker-Feldman doctrine, which prohibits federal courts from exercising appellate jurisdiction over state court judgments. Additionally, § 1983 claims fail because defendants are private parties not acting under color of state law, § 1985 conspiracy claims fail for the same reason, § 1503 obstruction claims fail because no private right of action exists under that criminal statute, and RICO claims rest on conclusory allegations insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly.

source_file: 11267601 - PLACE OF GRACE, INC. v. Indiana
case_name: Place of Grace, Inc. v. Indiana
accommodation_description: Place of Grace, operator of faith-based group recovery homes for individuals with substance use disorders, seeks classification of its homes as Class 2 (residential) structures rather than Class 1 (commercial), and requests variance from sprinkler requirements.
key_holding: The court found Place of Grace lacks standing to pursue failure-to-accommodate claim against IDHS because the Commission, not IDHS, denied the variance request; however, Place of Grace's intentional discrimination claim survives because IDHS's classification of the homes as Class 1 structures is fairly traceable to IDHS and redressable by prospective injunctive relief.
brief_summary: Place of Grace, a nonprofit operating faith-based group recovery homes for individuals with substance use disorders in Huntington, Indiana, sued IDHS and the Fire Prevention Commission alleging that classifying its homes as Class 1 (commercial) structures rather than Class 2 (residential) violates the ADA, FHAA, and Rehabilitation Act. The court granted partial dismissal, finding Place of Grace lacks standing against IDHS on the failure-to-accommodate claim because the Commission, not IDHS, denied the variance, but allowed the intentional discrimination claim to proceed based on IDHS's discriminatory classification of the homes.
key_cases_cited: New Horizons Rehabilitation, Inc. v. State, 400 F. Supp. 3d 751 (S.D. Ind. 2019)
Church of Our Lord & Savior Jesus Christ v. City of Markham, 913 F.3d 670 (7th Cir. 2019)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss the intentional discrimination claim for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction and failure to state a claim. Place of Grace established standing and ripeness by alleging IDHS discriminatorily classified its group homes as Class 1 structures (imposing commercial building standards) while not classifying identical single-family structures housing nuclear families the same way, and by establishing a credible threat of enforcement by IDHS. The allegations satisfy Rule 8 pleading standards under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Variance from sprinkler system requirement for Class 1 structures; exemption from Class 1 building code requirements
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted motion to dismiss the failure to accommodate claim against IDHS for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction because the Commission, not IDHS, denied the variance application. IDHS's referral of the variance request to the Commission was a lawful delegation of authority under state law and did not cause Place of Grace's injuries; only the Commission's denial caused the alleged harm. Therefore, only the Commission can redress the injury by granting the variance, and IDHS lacks the power to do so.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Variance from sprinkler system requirement for Class 1 structures; exemption from Class 1 building code requirements
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss the failure to accommodate claim against the Commission. The claim survives the motion to dismiss and shall proceed to the next stage. The court did not reach the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim at the MTD stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act § 12132, Rehabilitation Act § 504, state law claims related to building code classification and variance denial
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss ADA and Rehabilitation Act claims for injunctive relief against IDHS on sovereign immunity grounds. Congress expressly waived sovereign immunity for Section 504 Rehabilitation Act violations by programs receiving federal funding. Ex parte Young exception applies to suit against the Executive Director seeking prospective injunctive relief for ongoing violations of federal law.

source_file: 11267602 - GROUP HOME ON GIBSON ISLAND v. Gibson Island Corp.
case_name: Group Home on Gibson Island, LLC v. Gibson Island Corp.
accommodation_description: Request for exemption from the Gibson Island business-purpose covenant to permit operation of an assisted living group home for elderly people with disabilities
key_holding: The district court erred by analyzing whether removal of the Corporation's proposed conditions was 'necessary' rather than whether Lussi's requested exemption from the business-purpose covenant was necessary to provide equal housing opportunities, and genuine disputes of material fact exist as to whether the Corporation's stated justifications for its conditions were pretextual, precluding summary judgment.
brief_summary: Group Home on Gibson Island, LLC and Assisted Living Well Compassionate Care 2, LLC (operated by Craig Lussi) sued Gibson Island Corporation (a private HOA) alleging violations of the FHA and Maryland fair housing law for refusing to exempt Lussi's assisted living group home from the community's business-purpose covenant, and for retaliation and discrimination based on disability. The Fourth Circuit vacated the district court's summary judgment for the Corporation, holding that the district court applied the wrong legal standard to the necessity element of the reasonable accommodation claim and that genuine issues of material fact exist regarding whether the Corporation's imposed conditions on approving the accommodation were reasonable or pretextual for discriminatory and retaliatory motives.
key_cases_cited: Bryant Woods Inn, Inc. v. Howard County, 124 F.3d 597
Scoggins v. Lee's Crossing Homeowners Ass'n, 718 F.3d 262
Oconomowoc Residential Prog. v. City of Milwaukee, 300 F.3d 775
Hovsons, Inc. v. Township of Brick, 89 F.3d 1096
Texas Dep't. of Cmty. Affs. v. Burdine, 450 U.S. 248

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exemption from Gibson Island's business-purpose covenant to allow operation of an assisted living group home for elderly persons with disabilities on residential property
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court erred by analyzing whether removal of the Corporation's four disputed conditions was 'necessary' rather than whether the requested exemption itself was necessary to provide equal housing opportunity. The necessity element is satisfied as a matter of law—without the exemption, disabled elderly persons cannot live on Gibson Island. However, the reasonableness element presents genuine factual disputes regarding whether the Corporation's conditions (septic monitoring, arbitration, escrow, guarantor) are justified by legitimate burdens or are pretextual, requiring jury resolution.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court erred in finding no evidence of adverse action or causal nexus to protected activity. The Corporation's efforts to revoke Lussi's permit, delay the project, and refuse accommodation constitute adverse actions. A jury could infer retaliation from the Corporation's stated rationale that dealing with Lussi is burdensome due to his history of FHA litigation threats and discrimination allegations—conduct that itself constitutes protected activity under the FHA. Personal retaliation against Lussi and his family may also support the LLCs' retaliation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court erred in finding no evidence of discriminatory intent. Circumstantial evidence supports a jury inference of disability-based discrimination: the Corporation's stated rationales (septic concerns, litigation risk) may be pretextual; community members expressed hostility to disabled elderly residents and stereotypes about their needs; the Corporation President promised a '360 degree' strategy to block the project 'even if the group home is by right consistent with FHA'; and the Corporation may have acted in response to community animus. Whether these statements and actions reflect genuine concerns or discriminatory motive is a jury question.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Maryland fair housing law claims under Md. Code, State Gov't § 20-706(b)(4) (reasonable accommodation), § 20-708 (retaliation), and § 20-706(b)(1)-(2) (discrimination)
fha_claims.reasoning: Maryland fair housing law claims parallel the FHA claims and are analyzed together by the court. The district court's summary judgment on state law claims is vacated and remanded on the same grounds as the federal claims, with the note that Maryland law shifts the burden of proving reasonableness to the defendant after plaintiff establishes a prima facie case, unlike the FHA.

case_name: Group Home on Gibson Island v. Gibson Island Corp.
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: UNDETERMINED
brief_summary: UNDETERMINED

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that summary judgment was not appropriate because the plaintiff presented evidence that the defendant's litigation updates could have dissuaded a reasonable person from exercising FHA rights, creating a genuine dispute of material fact on whether the defendant's conduct was sufficiently adverse to constitute retaliation under § 3617.

case_name: Ruth Castro v. Lancaster Loft, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, who has asthma and is allergic to smoke, requested that defendant landlord enforce the non-smoking provisions in the lease agreement to provide her a smoke-free apartment as an accommodation for her disability.
key_holding: The Court granted Plaintiff's FHA claims survive screening under § 1915(e), finding her allegations sufficient to state claims for discrimination under § 3604(f)(3)(B) and retaliation under § 3617, but dismissed her constitutional claims for failure to state a claim.
brief_summary: Ruth Castro, a pro se Hispanic plaintiff with asthma, sued her landlord and property management entities alleging they violated the Fair Housing Act by refusing to accommodate her disability-related need for a smoke-free apartment and by retaliating against her with adverse actions including eviction after she requested accommodations and filed complaints with government agencies. The Court screened her complaint and allowed her FHA discrimination and retaliation claims to proceed while dismissing her constitutional claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Wetzel v. Glen St. Andrew Living Cmty., LLC, 901 F.3d 856 (7th Cir. 2018)
Mehta v. Beaconridge Improvement Ass'n, 432 Fed. App'x 614 (7th Cir. 2011)
Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009)
Cole v. Faulkner, No. 24 C 12117, 2025 WL 1359054 (N.D. Ill. May 9, 2025)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Enforcement of non-smoking provisions in lease agreement; smoke-free living environment to accommodate plaintiff's severe asthma and extreme smoke allergies
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiff's allegations—that she has a serious health condition (asthma) requiring accommodations, that she requested enforcement of non-smoking lease provisions, and that defendants refused to accommodate her—are sufficient under the liberal pleading standard for pro se complaints to survive § 1915 screening without applying the substantive reasonable accommodation balancing test.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiff's allegations—that she engaged in protected activity by requesting accommodations under the FHA, suffered adverse actions (eviction, lease non-renewal, overcharging, interference with mail), and that there was a causal connection between the two—satisfy the three-element retaliation test at the pleading stage and survive § 1915 screening.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiff's allegations that defendants singled her out for eviction based on her Hispanic descent, while non-Hispanic tenants who also complained about smoking were not evicted, are sufficient to survive § 1915 screening as a discrimination claim based on protected class status.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (First and Fourteenth Amendment rights); state criminal statutes (perjury, criminal recklessness, mischief); clean hands doctrine
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed § 1983 claims because defendants are private persons and entities who did not act under color of state law; mere use of state courts for eviction proceedings does not transform private actors into state actors. State criminal statutes and the clean hands doctrine do not support private causes of action.

source_file: 11267605 - LEGGE v. CLARKE COUNTY ZONING DEPARTMENT
case_name: Brian K. Legge v. Clarke County Zoning Department et al.
accommodation_description: Property owner with cancer and chronic anemia sought waiver of zoning setback requirements and continued garage use as accommodation for his physical and financial inability to dismantle the structure due to his medical conditions.
key_holding: Plaintiff failed to establish a likelihood of success on his FHA claims because he did not demonstrate any nexus between his medical conditions and his accommodation requests, and he failed to allege facts showing he engaged in protected activity under the FHA.
brief_summary: Brian Legge sued Clarke County, Virginia and its officials seeking to enjoin demolition of his nonconforming garage and alleging violations of the Equal Protection Clause, Fair Housing Act, and procedural and substantive due process based on the County's zoning enforcement actions. The court denied Legge's motion for preliminary injunction, finding he failed to demonstrate a likelihood of success on any claim, including FHA claims where he could not establish that his accommodation requests were connected to his medical conditions or that he engaged in protected FHA activity.
key_cases_cited: Bryant Woods Inn, Inc. v. Howard Cnty., 124 F.3d 597 (4th Cir. 1997)
Vill. of Willowbrook v. Olech, 528 U.S. 562 (2000)
SAS Assocs. 1, LLC v. City Council for City of Chesapeake, Va., 91 F.4th 715 (4th Cir. 2024)
MLC Auto., LLC v. Town of So. Pines, 532 F.3d 269 (4th Cir. 2008)
Rockville Cars, LLC v. City of Rockville, 891 F.3d 141 (4th Cir. 2018)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request for variance or exception to zoning setback requirement; request for County to reconsider enforcement of zoning ordinance despite alleged disability (stomach and prostate cancer, gastrointestinal complications, chronic anemia)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a nexus between his disability and the requested accommodation. The court found no indication that plaintiff's requests for a variance or other accommodations had any connection to his medical condition, and plaintiff did not inform the County of his medical condition until March 2023, well after the state court judgment. Without demonstrating a direct linkage between the proposed accommodation and equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling, plaintiff cannot establish an FHA failure-to-accommodate claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts establishing protected activity under the FHA. Plaintiff claimed only that defendants interfered with his FHA rights after he exercised his right to file appeals and participate in zoning hearings, but did not allege that he exercised or advocated for his FHA rights during any proceedings. The record does not indicate plaintiff even informed the County of his medical condition until March 2023, well after the state court judgment, negating any inference of retaliation for protected FHA activity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 Equal Protection Clause (class-of-one selective enforcement); § 1983 Procedural Due Process; § 1983 Substantive Due Process; Virginia statute governing fines for zoning violations (Eighth Amendment Excessive Fines Clause)
fha_claims.reasoning: For Equal Protection: Plaintiff failed to identify highly similar properties receiving more favorable treatment; structures on comparator properties may predate the zoning ordinance and be grandfathered in, and plaintiff did not demonstrate that comparator structures similarly violated Certificates of Appropriateness. For Procedural Due Process: Plaintiff failed to exhaust available administrative and state court remedies, including appeals of the April 9, 2020 Notice of Violation to the BZA and appeal of the BZA's August 31, 2020 decision to state circuit court. For Substantive Due Process: County had rational basis for finding garage violated zoning ordinance (as-built survey confirmed setback violation); plaintiff did not identify specific procedural irregularities and failed to exhaust available state procedures. For Excessive Fines: Claim barred by Rooker-Feldman doctrine as it seeks to challenge state court judgment imposing fines.

case_name: Gregory R. Marlor v. The Housing Company
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a wheelchair user, requested that the housing provider install a doorbell at the building's main entrance to enable visitors to contact residents with mobility disabilities.
key_holding: The court found that Marlor stated one plausible reasonable accommodation claim—THC's denial of his July 2023 request to install a doorbell at the building entrance—while dismissing all other claims (including earlier denials of accessible housing, transfer requests, and rent-related disputes) as time-barred under the FHA's two-year statute of limitations.
brief_summary: Gregory Marlor, a wheelchair user receiving Social Security disability benefits, sued The Housing Company (manager of Thomas Logan Apartments, a Low-Income Housing Tax Credit property in Boise, Idaho) alleging Fair Housing Act discrimination based on disability. The court screened Marlor's complaint and found that while most claims were time-barred under the FHA's two-year statute of limitations, Marlor stated a plausible claim that THC denied his July 2023 request for a reasonable accommodation—specifically, installation of a doorbell at the building's main entrance to enable visitors to contact residents with mobility disabilities.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Dubois v. Ass'n of Apartment Owners of 2987 Kalakaua, 453 F.3d 1175 (9th Cir. 2006)
Garcia v. Brockway, 526 F.3d 456 (9th Cir. 2008)
Nat'l R.R. Passenger Corp. v. Morgan, 536 U.S. 101 (2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Installation of a doorbell at the main entrance of the building to allow visitors to contact residents, as required by ADA/HUD regulations and necessitated by the key-card entry system that impeded access for persons with disabilities
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that Marlor's April 2023 request for doorbell installation stated a plausible claim under the FHA reasonable accommodation framework (he alleged disability, knowledge of disability, necessity of accommodation, reasonableness, and refusal), and this claim falls within the two-year statute of limitations period. The court did not apply the substantive RA balancing test but rather determined the complaint survived § 1915(e)(2) pleading-stage screening.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Transfer to an accessible one-bedroom apartment at the original qualifying rent of $520 per month (or substantially lower than the $879 offered in July 2023)
fha_claims.disposition: Dismissed under § 1915(e)(2) for failure to state a plausible claim
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that Marlor's allegations regarding the July 2023 offer of an accessible unit at $879/month and the January 2024 income-based denial failed to plausibly allege disability discrimination because Marlor did not allege that the higher rent was applied differently to him than to non-disabled tenants, that non-disabled tenants received preferential pricing, or that the rent increase was motivated by disability rather than market conditions. The court also found that the income eligibility denial was facially neutral and applied uniformly, with no allegation that it was applied differently to disabled residents or used as a pretext for discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Various accommodations related to initial housing application and placement, including accessible one-bedroom apartment with grab bars and side-by-side laundry, and proper processing of transfer requests
fha_claims.disposition: Dismissed under § 1915(e)(2) for failure to state a plausible claim and statute of limitations
fha_claims.reasoning: All claims arising from acts occurring before November 27, 2022 (initial application denial in September 2021, recertification in November 2021, appeal denial in December 2021, placement in non-accessible unit and key-card implementation in February 2022, and transfer request mishandling in July 2022) are time-barred under the FHA's two-year statute of limitations. The court rejected arguments based on the continuing violation doctrine, tolling provisions, equitable tolling, and equitable estoppel, finding that these discrete acts occurred outside the limitations period and their continuing effects cannot revive time-barred claims.

source_file: 11267607 - Terry v. YWCA OF NORTHESTERN NEW YORK
case_name: Elizabeth Marie Terry v. YWCA of Northeastern New York
accommodation_description: Pro se plaintiff raises disability discrimination and Fourteenth Amendment claims relating to YWCA's policy prohibiting residents from operating businesses and not being eligible for full-time employment, but no specific accommodation request under § 3604(f)(3)(B) is identified.
key_holding: The complaint was dismissed without prejudice because plaintiff failed to satisfy Rule 8's pleading requirements, failed to demonstrate she obtained a right-to-sue letter or exhausted EEOC prelitigation requirements, and failed to state a prima facie claim for disability discrimination under the ADA because she did not adequately allege what her disability is or how it limits a major life activity.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Elizabeth Marie Terry, a YWCA resident since mid-2022, sued the YWCA of Northeastern New York alleging disability discrimination under the ADA and violations of her Fourteenth Amendment rights because YWCA policies prohibit residents from operating businesses and allegedly render disabled residents ineligible for full-time employment. The magistrate judge recommended dismissing the complaint without prejudice because plaintiff's pleading failed to comply with Rule 8, did not demonstrate exhaustion of EEOC prelitigation requirements, and failed to adequately allege the elements of a disability discrimination claim, including failing to identify her specific disability.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Scalercio-Isenberg v. Morgan Stanley Servs. Grp. Inc., 2020 WL 4547317 (S.D.N.Y. Aug. 6, 2020)

source_file: 11267608 - THE COMFY COTTAGE, INC. v. Pasco County
case_name: The Comfy Cottage, Inc. v. Pasco County
accommodation_description: Comfy Cottage requested that Pasco County waive the automatic fire sprinkler system requirement under the Florida Building Code to permit operation of a community residential group home for individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities.
key_holding: Pasco County's sprinkler system requirement does not facially discriminate against disabled individuals because it applies equally to care facilities and owner-occupied lodging houses regardless of whether occupants are disabled, and Comfy Cottage failed to establish that waiving the requirement was necessary to afford disabled residents an equal opportunity to use and enjoy housing.
brief_summary: The Comfy Cottage, Inc., a not-for-profit operator of a community residential group home for individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities, sued Pasco County, Florida, alleging the County's requirement that care facilities install automatic fire sprinkler systems violates the Fair Housing Act and ADA. The court granted summary judgment for Pasco County, finding the sprinkler requirement does not facially discriminate because it applies equally to all care facilities regardless of disability status, and Comfy Cottage failed to establish that waiving the requirement was necessary to afford disabled residents an equal opportunity to use and enjoy housing.
key_cases_cited: Sailboat Bend Sober Living, LLC v. City of Fort Lauderdale, 46 F.4th 1268 (11th Cir. 2022)
Schaw v. Habitat for Humanity of Citrus County, Inc., 938 F.3d 1259 (11th Cir. 2019)
Schwarz v. City of Treasure Island, 544 F.3d 1201 (11th Cir. 2008)
Texas Dept. of Housing & Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that the sprinkler system requirement does not facially discriminate against disabled individuals because it treats disabled residents of the group home the same as similarly situated non-disabled individuals in the same occupancy category (owner-occupied lodging houses with five or fewer guest rooms). The requirement is imposed by the Florida Building Code on all such structures regardless of occupant disability status.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish that disabled individuals were treated less favorably than similarly situated non-disabled individuals. The sprinkler requirement applies equally to care facilities and small lodging houses regardless of occupant disability status, so no disparate treatment occurred.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie case of disparate impact because it presented no statistical or comparative evidence showing that disabled individuals are disparately impacted by the sprinkler system requirement. The court noted that disparate impact claims typically require statistical evidence.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver of the requirement to install an automatic fire sprinkler system in the group home for individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish the necessity element of the failure-to-accommodate claim. The court found that plaintiff provided no evidence that the waiver of the sprinkler requirement was necessary to afford disabled residents an equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling, and failed to show that residents' income would not permit them to afford rent covering the cost of installing and maintaining a sprinkler system.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act, 42 U.S.C. § 12101 et seq.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court analyzed the ADA claims under the same legal framework as the FHA claims, applying identical standards for facial discrimination, disparate treatment, disparate impact, and failure to accommodate. All ADA claims were resolved on summary judgment in favor of the defendant using the same reasoning as the FHA claims.

source_file: 11267609 - Doria v. YAVAPAI COLLEGE DISTRICT GOVERNING BOARD
case_name: Daniel T Doria v. Yavapai College District Governing Board, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, citing psychological disabilities, requested accommodation of lease terms to operate a pet-sitting business from his RV site, which the lease prohibited.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claim with prejudice because the same disability discrimination claim had been previously litigated to final judgment in state court proceedings, and thus was barred by res judicata; the remaining claims were dismissed under collateral estoppel.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Daniel Doria sued Yavapai College District and related defendants alleging Fair Housing Act and other claims arising from lease termination and eviction for operating a pet-sitting business from his RV site, which he claimed was a reasonable accommodation for his psychological disabilities. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss with prejudice, finding the FHA claim was barred by res judicata because Doria had previously litigated identical disability discrimination claims in state court proceedings that resulted in final judgments against him.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Campbell v. SZL Props., Ltd., 204 Ariz. 221 (App. 2003)
Falcon ex rel. Sandoval v. Maricopa County, 213 Ariz. 525 (2006)
Phoenix Newspapers, Inc. v. Dep't of Corr., 188 Ariz. 237 (App. 1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accommodation of lease terms to permit plaintiff to operate a pet-sitting business from his RV, allegedly necessary due to psychological disabilities including anxiety, depression, and minor paranoid delusions
fha_claims.reasoning: The FHA claim (Count I) was barred by res judicata because plaintiff had previously asserted identical FHA disability discrimination allegations in Superior Court (dismissed) and as a counterclaim in the Eviction Suit (rejected by jury). All three res judicata elements were satisfied: identity of claims, final judgment on the merits, and privity between parties.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Count III (Arizona retaliation claim) was dismissed on two independent grounds: (1) failure to comply with Arizona's notice-of-claim requirement (A.R.S. § 12-821.01), which requires service on each governing board member and public employees within 180 days; and (2) res judicata, as the retaliation claim had been litigated and rejected in the Eviction Suit, Justice Court Suit, and Superior Court Suit.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claim for disability discrimination in access to public services; Due Process Clause claim alleging deprivation of property without opportunity to be heard
fha_claims.reasoning: Counts II (ADA) and IV (Due Process) were dismissed under collateral estoppel because they were predicated on the identical issue decided against plaintiff in prior litigation—whether Yavapai College discriminately or arbitrarily enforced the lease. The jury's verdict in the Eviction Suit resolved this issue against plaintiff, and all five collateral estoppel elements were satisfied.

source_file: 11267610 - HALL-JOHNSON v. City and County of San Francisco
case_name: Hall-Johnson v. City and County of San Francisco
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation was requested; the case concerns alleged racial discrimination in housing prioritization under a city housing lottery program.
key_holding: The Fair Housing Amendments Act claim was dismissed because the complaint contained no factual allegations that Hall-Johnson has a disability or that the City discriminated against her on that basis, and the Section 1983 equal protection, Title VI, and Section 1981 claims failed for lack of sufficient allegations that the decisionmaker knew Hall-Johnson was Black or acted with discriminatory intent.
brief_summary: Hall-Johnson, a Black woman experiencing homelessness in San Francisco, sued the City and County of San Francisco alleging racial discrimination after a leasing agent allegedly told her that being Black must be the only reason she was not prioritized for housing under a city housing lottery program. The district court granted the motion to dismiss, finding that the complaint failed to plausibly allege intentional discrimination because it lacked allegations that the actual decisionmaker knew Hall-Johnson was Black, and dismissed the Fair Housing Amendments Act claim for failure to allege any disability.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Thornton v. City of St. Helens
Pers. Adm'r of Mass. v. Feeney
Robinson v. Adams

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts that the City was aware of her race or that the decision-maker who reviewed her application knew she was Black and intentionally discriminated against her on that basis. The leasing agent's speculative comments, without more, do not plausibly allege intentional discrimination under the Fair Housing Act.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal Protection (42 U.S.C. § 1983), Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, 42 U.S.C. § 1981
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts plausibly showing intentional discrimination based on race under equal protection, Title VI, and § 1981 standards. The complaint lacks allegations that the City decision-maker was aware of plaintiff's race or that the decision was made because of, not merely in spite of, its adverse effects on plaintiff as a member of a protected class.

case_name: Maple Tree LP, II, et al. v. Rachel Rebollo
accommodation_description: Rebollo requested permission to install handrails/grab bars in her bathtub to assist with mobility due to arthrogryposis, which the court characterized as requiring an exception to the lease's no-screws policy.
key_holding: The appellate court affirmed the trial court's denial of landlords' summary judgment motion, finding genuine issues of material fact exist as to whether Rebollo submitted a valid reasonable accommodation request for handrails and whether landlords' 52-day delay in responding constituted a constructive denial of the accommodation.
brief_summary: Rachel Rebollo sued her landlords alleging they violated the Fair Housing Amendments Act by failing to approve her request to install handrails in her bathroom as a reasonable accommodation for her arthrogryposis-related mobility limitations. The appellate court affirmed the trial court's denial of summary judgment, finding genuine issues of material fact exist regarding whether Rebollo's inquiry about handrails constituted a valid accommodation request and whether the landlords' 52-day failure to respond constituted a constructive denial of the accommodation.
key_cases_cited: Sanders v. AHEPA 78 VI Apartments, Inc., 237 N.E.3d 1126 (Ind. Ct. App. 2024)
Furbee v. Wilson, 144 N.E.3d 801 (Ind. Ct. App. 2020)
Valencia v. City of Springfield, Ill., 883 F.3d 959 (7th Cir. 2018)
Wis. Cmty. Servs., Inc. v. City of Milwaukee, 465 F.3d 737 (7th Cir. 2006)
Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condo. Ass'n, 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exception to lease prohibition on driving screws/fasteners into walls to permit installation of handrails/grab bars in bathroom
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine issues of material fact as to whether plaintiff submitted a request for reasonable accommodation (not merely a modification) and whether defendant engaged in meaningful review and good faith determination of the request. Delay of 52 days without follow-up or communication regarding the request's status could constitute constructive denial, a fact-intensive inquiry requiring jury determination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Negligence claim for failure to approve handrail request; Indiana Code § 32-31-8-5 landlord-tenant statutory duty claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that genuine issues of material fact exist regarding duty (whether FHAA or statutory landlord-tenant duties imposed obligation to approve accommodation request) and proximate cause (whether failure to install handrails was proximate cause of plaintiff's injuries). Proximate cause is ordinarily a question of fact not properly resolved on summary judgment; plaintiff's testimony that handrails might have prevented or reduced injury severity creates factual dispute.

case_name: Dwane Cherry-El v. Belinda Blount, DCHA, Housing Specialist, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested to change his status from live-in aide to primary tenant and continue residing in subsidized housing as a reasonable accommodation for his disability after his mother's death.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's complaint sua sponte under Rules 8 and 12(b)(6) because his pleadings failed to provide fair notice of the nature and substance of his claims, including whether he was challenging his live-in aide designation, his housing list status, or a denied accommodation.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Dwane Cherry-El sued the District of Columbia Housing Authority seeking to remain in his mother's subsidized unit as a primary tenant rather than being required to leave as a live-in aide upon her death, alleging disability discrimination and reasonable accommodation violations. The court dismissed the complaint sua sponte under Rules 8 and 12(b)(6) for failing to state a plausible claim, finding the complaint too vague and conclusory to provide defendants fair notice of the claims against them.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Winter v. Natural Res. Def. Council, Inc., 555 U.S. 7 (2008)
Erickson v. Pardus, 551 U.S. 89 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Change of status from live-in aide to primary tenant in subsidized housing following mother's death; continuation of residency in subsidized housing unit
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for failure to state a plausible claim under Rule 8 and 12(b)(6). Complaint was too vague and conclusory to provide fair notice of the claim; it was unclear whether plaintiff was challenging his designation as live-in aide, whether he was on the housing list, whether he sought to move ahead on the list due to disability, or what specific accommodation was allegedly denied. Court could not discern the essential elements of any FHA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II (42 U.S.C. § 12132), Rehabilitation Act (29 U.S.C. § 794 et seq.), D.C. Municipal Regulation 14-5316, Civil Rights Act of 1965, Eighth Amendment, Fifth Amendment, Fourteenth Amendment
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed non-FHA claims for failure to state a plausible claim under Rule 8 and 12(b)(6). Complaint failed to identify what allegedly happened or how events violated the statutes or constitutional provisions cited. Court noted that Eighth Amendment addresses punishment and does not provide for basic needs of non-incarcerated persons, and that complaint was too vague to permit meaningful analysis of any legal theory.

source_file: 11267613 - Joe v. OLIVE BRANCH ASSISTED LIVING LLC
case_name: Hailei Joe v. Olive Branch Assisted Living LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff was discharged from an addiction treatment facility after disclosing her HIV-positive status; the court analyzes whether this discharge constituted intentional discrimination because of disability.
key_holding: Genuine issues of material fact remain as to whether Plaintiff's HIV-positive status was the 'but for' cause of her discharge from the facility, precluding summary judgment on her discrimination claims under the FHA, AFHA, and ADA; however, Plaintiff's retaliation claims and public disclosure claim fail as a matter of law.
brief_summary: Hailei Joe sued Olive Branch Assisted Living LLC, an addiction treatment facility, alleging she was unlawfully discharged because of her HIV-positive status in violation of the Fair Housing Act, Arizona Fair Housing Act, and Americans with Disabilities Act, along with retaliation and state law claims. The court denied both parties' cross-motions for summary judgment on the discrimination claims, finding genuine disputes of material fact remain regarding causation, but granted summary judgment to Defendant on the retaliation and public disclosure claims.
key_cases_cited: Murray v. Mayo Clinic, 934 F.3d 1101 (9th Cir. 2019)
Pac. Shores Props., LLC v. City of Newport Beach, 730 F.3d 1142 (9th Cir. 2013)
Bax v. Doctors Med. Ctr. of Modesto, Inc., 52 F.4th 858 (9th Cir. 2022)
Bragdon v. Abbott, 524 U.S. 624 (1998)
Brown v. City of Tucson, 336 F.3d 1181 (9th Cir. 2003)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine issue of material fact as to whether plaintiff's HIV-positive status was the 'but for' cause of her discharge. Although timing and deposition testimony suggested causation, defendant presented evidence that discharge was based on plaintiff's need for higher level of care and lack of facility experience, precluding summary judgment for either party on the discrimination claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Continued residence and treatment at facility despite HIV-positive diagnosis and alleged need for higher level of care
fha_claims.reasoning: Court rejected defendant's argument that plaintiff's failure to request accommodation triggered no duty. Court held that duty to provide reasonable accommodation may be triggered when need is obvious even without explicit request, citing Bax v. Doctors Med. Ctr. However, genuine factual disputes remain regarding whether plaintiff's needs fell within facility's scope of services and whether accommodation was reasonable, precluding summary judgment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Although court found prima facie case for retaliation based on threatening emails from defendant's counsel conditioning dismissal of lawsuit on dropping claims, plaintiff failed to establish 'distinct and palpable injury' required under Brown v. City of Tucson. Court held defendant's defamation counterclaim was not frivolous as matter of law, so time spent defending it did not constitute requisite injury.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Public disclosure of private facts (Arizona common law); Title III ADA discrimination claim; AFHA discrimination claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Public disclosure claim failed because plaintiff did not establish 'publicity' as required by Restatement § 652D—disclosure to facility residents and staff does not constitute communication to public at large or substantial certainty of public knowledge. Title III ADA claim survives summary judgment on discrimination merits but plaintiff cannot recover monetary damages under Title III, only injunctive relief.

source_file: 11267614 - Yocca v. TURTLE CREEK ZONING HEARING BOARD
case_name: Ronald Yocca v. Turtle Creek Zoning Hearing Board
accommodation_description: Operator of a seven-resident sober recovery house seeks a reasonable accommodation under the FHA to exceed the borough's three-person occupancy limit for group homes in a residential zone.
key_holding: The court held that the Board and trial court erred by treating the special exception for group homes as an adequate accommodation under the FHA without conducting the proper Lapid-Laurel analysis, and erred by not recognizing that the three-person group home occupancy limit does not fall under the FHA's absolute exception for occupancy limits because it is not uniformly applied to all residences.
brief_summary: Ronald Yocca, operator of a seven-resident sober recovery house in Turtle Creek, Pennsylvania, appealed the denial of his request for a special exception and reasonable accommodation under the FHA to exceed the borough's three-person occupancy limit for group homes. The Commonwealth Court affirmed the special exception denial but vacated the reasonable accommodation denial, holding that the Board and trial court failed to apply the proper Lapid-Laurel legal framework for determining whether the accommodation was necessary and reasonable.
key_cases_cited: City of Edmonds v. Oxford House, Inc., 514 U.S. 725 (1995)
Lapid-Laurel, L.L.C. v. Zoning Board of Adjustment of Township of Scotch Plains, 284 F.3d 442 (3d Cir. 2002)
Carunchio v. Swarthmore Borough Council, 237 A.3d 1183 (Pa. Cmwlth. 2020)
Albert v. Zoning Hearing Board of North Abington Township, 854 A.2d 401 (Pa. 2004)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exemption or modification of the zoning ordinance's three-person occupancy limit for group homes to permit operation of a sober recovery house with up to seven residents; alternatively, a lesser accommodation permitting occupancy greater than three but less than seven residents.
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court held that the trial court and Board failed to apply the correct legal framework under Lapid-Laurel for evaluating reasonable accommodation requests. The court found that the three-person occupancy limit for group homes is not a neutral, uniformly-applicable occupancy restriction under City of Edmonds and therefore does not fall within the FHA's absolute exception for occupancy limits. The court vacated and remanded for the Board to conduct fact-finding on whether Applicant demonstrated necessity (financial viability or therapeutic benefit) and, if so, whether the Borough could show the accommodation unreasonable under the undue burden/fundamental alteration test.

source_file: 11267615 - Drews v. GOLDOLLAR REAL ESTATE INVESTMENTS
case_name: Wendy Marie Drews v. Goldollar Real Estate Investments; Lynmark Group-Orange Avenue Apartments, LLC; Carla Hines-Melcher
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a domestic violence survivor with familial status, alleged defendants discriminated against her by pursuing eviction, refusing lease renewal, denying parking, and creating a hostile housing environment based on her protected status.
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA claims were dismissed because her amended complaint failed to allege facts giving rise to an inference that any adverse actions by defendants were motivated by her protected status as a domestic violence survivor with familial status, and plaintiff failed to adequately allege protected activity for her retaliation claim.
brief_summary: Wendy Marie Drews, proceeding pro se, sued her former landlord entities and property manager alleging Fair Housing Act claims based on discrimination as a domestic violence survivor with familial status and retaliation for engaging in protected activity. The court dismissed all federal claims with prejudice, finding that plaintiff failed to state plausible claims for FHA discrimination or retaliation because her allegations did not give rise to an inference that adverse housing actions were motivated by her protected status and she failed to adequately plead the elements of a retaliation claim.
key_cases_cited: Gladstone Realtors v. Vill. of Bellwood, 441 U.S. 91 (1979)
Palmer v. Fannie Mae, 755 Fed. App'x 43 (2d Cir. 2018)
Lynn v. Vill. of Pomona, 373 F. Supp. 2d 418 (S.D.N.Y. 2005)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged discrimination based on familial status and domestic violence survivor status, but failed to allege facts giving rise to an inference that adverse actions (eviction, non-renewal of lease) were motivated by her protected status. The court found the allegations insufficient under the pleading standard to support a minimal inference of discriminatory motivation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts showing she engaged in protected activity under the FHA (opposing statutorily prohibited discrimination), that defendants were aware of such activity, or that a causal connection existed between protected activity and adverse action. The complaint lacked the required elements of an FHA retaliation claim under § 3617.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (Fourth and Fourteenth Amendment), RICO (18 U.S.C. §§ 1961-1968), FCRA (15 U.S.C. §§ 1681s-2(a) and (b))
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 1983 claims failed because plaintiff did not allege sufficient facts to show Hines-Melcher acted under color of state law or shared a common goal with state actors to violate constitutional rights; allegations of body-camera gaps were conclusory and insufficient. RICO claims failed because allegations of misconduct did not plausibly allege predicate acts or a pattern of racketeering activity. FCRA claim under § 1681s-2(b) failed because plaintiff did not allege sufficient facts about timing, notice, or the furnisher's investigation to show unreasonableness.

source_file: 11267616 - NATIONAL FAIR HOUSING ALLIANCE v. US DEP'T OF HOUSING AND URBAN DEVELOPMENT
case_name: National Fair Housing Alliance v. U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development
accommodation_description: Fair housing organizations seek judicial order requiring HUD to complete FHIP grantmaking process before statutory deadline, not a traditional housing accommodation
key_holding: The court found plaintiffs established likelihood of success on APA unreasonable delay claims and constitutional claims, granted TRO ordering HUD to comply with statutory obligations and file detailed compliance plan, but reserved judgment on multi-year grant claims and declined to order funds remain available through litigation at this time.
brief_summary: National Fair Housing Alliance and Tennessee Fair Housing Council sued HUD under the APA and Constitution, challenging HUD's failure to award FHIP grants for fiscal year 2024 and to implement multi-year grants. The court granted in part a temporary restraining order, finding plaintiffs likely to succeed on claims that HUD's delay in grantmaking was unreasonable and violated statutory obligations, ordering HUD to file a compliance plan but reserving judgment on multi-year grant claims.
key_cases_cited: Winter v. Nat. Res. Def. Council, Inc., 555 U.S. 7 (2008)
Lincoln v. Vigil, 508 U.S. 182 (1993)
City of Houston v. Dep't of Hous. & Urban Dev., 24 F.3d 1421 (D.C. Cir. 1994)
Nken v. Holder, 556 U.S. 418 (2009)
League of Women Voters of U.S. v. Newby, 838 F.3d 1 (D.C. Cir. 2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Administrative Procedure Act claims (5 U.S.C. § 706(1) unreasonable delay; 5 U.S.C. § 706(2) arbitrary and capricious); Appropriations Clause violation; Separation of Powers violation; procedural due process violation
fha_claims.disposition: Temporary Restraining Order Granted in Part
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found a likelihood of success on the merits on at least two claims: (1) Separation of Powers violation because HUD must follow statutory mandates to disburse appropriated FHIP funds by September 30, 2025, and (2) unreasonable delay under APA § 706(1) because HUD's delay in processing FY2024 FHIP grants is unreasonable under the TRAC factors, particularly given the compressed statutory timeline and concrete harm to fair housing enforcement organizations. The court rejected HUD's threshold arguments (Tucker Act, agency discretion under Lincoln, ripeness, and standing) and found the plaintiffs established organizational standing, imminent injury, irreparable harm, and favorable balance of equities.

source_file: 11267617 - MILLERBORG v. BLUE BONNET TRAIL LLC
case_name: Millerborg v. Blue Bonnet Trail LLC
accommodation_description: Wheelchair user seeks removal of physical accessibility barriers (insufficient doorway widths, lack of wheelchair maneuvering space, inaccessible routes to trash dumpsters and mailbox, elevated thermostats and light switches) to access and use the dwelling and common areas.
key_holding: A plaintiff asserting claims about physical accessibility must at least have personally experienced an accessibility issue to have standing; merely observing accessibility barriers without any direct personal effect is insufficient to plead a concrete injury in fact.
brief_summary: Casey Millerborg, a wheelchair user, sued Blue Bonnet Trail LLC, owner of an apartment complex in Waxahachie, Texas, alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on physical accessibility barriers he observed at the property. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss for lack of Article III standing, finding the complaint failed to allege sufficient facts showing Millerborg personally experienced any accessibility barriers rather than merely observing them, and failed to establish likelihood of future injury sufficient for injunctive relief.
key_cases_cited: Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman
Laufer v. Mann Hospitality, L.L.C.
Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife
Deutsch v. Annis Enterprises, Inc.
Frame v. City of Arlington

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible design and construction of multifamily dwelling, including accessible routes to trash dumpsters and public streets, accessible central mailbox, lever-style doorknobs, wheelchair maneuvering space near exterior gates and inside bathrooms, thermostats and light switches at accessible heights, and sufficiently wide doorways.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff lacked Article III standing because his complaint failed to allege concrete injury in fact. Although plaintiff visited the property and observed accessibility barriers, he did not sufficiently allege that he personally experienced (as opposed to merely observed) any specific accessibility challenges, and his allegations regarding future injury were insufficient because he stated he would only return after remediation, negating any future harm an injunction could remedy.

source_file: 11267618 - McCready v. UNITY SOBER LIVING HOMES, LLC
case_name: John McCready v. Unity Sober Living Homes, LLC
accommodation_description: Request to pay rent on the same weekly schedule as non-disabled residents, rather than being required to pay monthly as an SSDI recipient
key_holding: Unity's written rent policy explicitly distinguishing SSDI recipients from other residents by requiring monthly payment from disabled tenants while allowing non-disabled tenants to pay weekly constitutes facial discrimination under the Fair Housing Amendments Act, as disability is the dispositive trait singled out for different treatment.
brief_summary: John McCready, a recovering addict suffering from depression who received SSDI benefits, sued Unity Sober Living and property manager Re/Max Achievers, alleging Unity's written rent policy requiring SSDI recipients to pay rent monthly while non-disabled residents could pay weekly constituted disability discrimination under the Fair Housing Amendments Act, and that he was wrongfully evicted without proper notice or judicial process. The court granted partial summary judgment for McCready, finding Unity's facially discriminatory policy violated the FHAA as a matter of law and that the landlord-tenant relationship triggered liability for wrongful eviction under Pennsylvania law, with damages to be assessed at trial.
key_cases_cited: 431 E. Palisade Ave. Real Estate, LLC v. City of Englewood, 977 F.3d 277 (3d Cir. 2020)
Assouline v. Reynolds, 219 A.3d 1131 (Pa. 2019)
Lakeside Resort Enters., LP v. Bd. of Supervisors, 455 F.3d 154 (3d Cir. 2006)
Sharpvisions, Inc. v. Borough of Plum, 475 F. Supp. 2d 514 (W.D. Pa. 2007)
Lapid-Laurel v. Zoning Bd. of Adjustment, 284 F.3d 442 (3d Cir. 2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rent payment policy requiring SSDI recipients to pay monthly in full on the first of the month, while non-disabled residents could pay weekly
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that Unity's written rent policy facially discriminated against individuals receiving SSDI by explicitly singling them out for different payment terms. The policy's language was unambiguous, and Unity's post-hoc testimony about an unwritten policy applying to all fixed-income residents was uncorroborated and contradicted by the record. Unity failed to demonstrate that no less discriminatory alternatives were available, so the burden did not shift back to plaintiff.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Pennsylvania Landlord Tenant Act wrongful eviction claim; Pennsylvania Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Law claims (seven separate violations); Pennsylvania intentional infliction of emotional distress claim; negligence claim against Re/Max; UTPCPL and FHAA claims against Re/Max
fha_claims.reasoning: On the LTA wrongful eviction claim, the court found Unity liable as a matter of law because it failed to provide the required fifteen-day written notice before removal and had no judicial order. On UTPCPL claims, the court found that a reasonable jury could find violations based on false representations about Unity's status, misrepresentations of policies, failure to return security deposit, and unlawful eviction. On IIED, the court granted summary judgment to Unity because the alleged conduct, while serious, did not meet Pennsylvania's extremely high bar of being 'so outrageous in character, and so extreme in degree, as to go beyond all possible bounds of decency.' On Re/Max's negligence claim, the court found that a reasonable jury could find Re/Max liable based on its contractual duties as property manager and its knowledge of the sober living facility. On Re/Max's FHAA and UTPCPL claims, the court found that a reasonable jury could find liability based on Re/Max's control over the property and knowledge of conditions.

case_name: Mendoza-Lebron v. Adams
accommodation_description: Individual homeowners requested that the City of New York provide accurate information about disability and medical exemptions from water shutoffs and meaningful access to accommodation procedures.
key_holding: The court found no reasonable expectation of recurrence to overcome mootness for forward-looking claims because all plaintiffs qualified for exemptions and no water was actually shut off; the damages claims failed because mere threats without actual termination do not constitute a due process deprivation, and the ADA and FHA claims failed because the City's existing policies already provide exemptions for disabled residents and plaintiffs did not plausibly allege they were treated differently by reason of disability.
brief_summary: Individual homeowners sued the City of New York over its 2024 water shutoff policy targeting delinquent property owners, alleging constitutional, ADA, and FHA violations based on inadequate notice of exemptions for disabled residents. The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss, finding the forward-looking claims moot since all plaintiffs qualified for exemptions and no water was actually shut off, and rejecting the damages claims on the merits because threats without actual termination do not constitute a cognizable due process deprivation and the City's policies already accommodate disabled homeowners without evidence of discrimination by reason of disability; the court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over state and local claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
McElwee v. Cnty. of Orange, 700 F.3d 635 (2d Cir. 2012)
Pinckney v. Carroll, No. 18-cv-12198, 2019 WL 6619484 (S.D.N.Y. Dec. 4, 2019)
Henrietta D. v. Bloomberg, 331 F.3d 261 (2d Cir. 2003)
