fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exemption from water shutoff for households with disabled residents or residents with medical conditions; also alleged failure to provide meaningful notice and information regarding exemption procedures and eligibility criteria
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege that they were denied a reasonable accommodation or treated differently because of their disabilities. The complaint does not allege that any plaintiff's water was actually shut off, and all plaintiffs received notice of exemptions and subsequently qualified for them. Alleged confusion about how to access an accommodation without more is insufficient to state a claim under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: City's water shutoff policy and notice procedures allegedly disproportionately burdening disabled residents
fha_claims.reasoning: Under a disparate impact theory, plaintiffs must allege that the challenged policy denied them meaningful access to water services because of their disabilities. Plaintiffs alleged only deficiencies in notice and exemption process but did not plausibly allege that these deficiencies disproportionately burdened them as individuals with disabilities or that defendants refused to accommodate their needs once eligibility was demonstrated.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 1983 due process claims (Fourteenth Amendment), ADA Title II claims, state and local law claims (CAPA, New York Constitution, New York State Human Rights Law, New York City Human Rights Law)
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 1983 due process claims failed because plaintiffs alleged only threats of water shutoff, not actual deprivation of property; a mere threat without actual termination does not constitute a deprivation. ADA claims failed on the same grounds as FHA claims—no allegation of differential treatment because of disability. State and local law claims were dismissed without prejudice as the court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction.

case_name: Manuel James Gonzalez, as legal guardian of R.E.G. v. Royse Services LLC d/b/a LaVida Vacations
accommodation_description: Request to waive the pet deposit fee for R.E.G.'s service dog that mitigates her autism symptoms of panic attacks and destructive tantrums
key_holding: The court recommended granting default judgment because Royse Services admitted (by default) to discriminating against R.E.G. by refusing to waive its pet fee policy for her service animal despite knowing of her disability and the necessity of the accommodation, thereby denying her use and enjoyment of the vacation rental property.
brief_summary: Manuel James Gonzalez sued Royse Services LLC d/b/a LaVida Vacations on behalf of his minor daughter R.E.G. (who has autism and requires a service dog) after the vacation rental company refused to allow the service animal on the property unless he paid a $150 pet deposit, ultimately requiring his family to leave. The court granted default judgment in favor of Gonzalez, finding that Royse Services violated the ADA and FHA by discriminating against R.E.G. based on her disability and refusing to waive its pet fee policy for her necessary service animal.
key_cases_cited: Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Surtain v. Hamlin Terrace Found., 789 F.3d 1239 (11th Cir. 2015)
Norkunas v. Seahorse NB, LLC, 444 F. App'x 412 (11th Cir. 2011)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to use a certified service dog for autism-related panic attacks and destructive tantrums without payment of an additional pet fee
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied the FHA reasonable accommodation framework, finding that R.E.G. is disabled, requested a necessary and reasonable accommodation (service dog without surcharge), and Royse Services refused. The court analyzed whether the accommodation was reasonable (efficacious and proportional) and necessary (ameliorates disability effects), concluding both elements were satisfied. Royse Services' default admitted all well-pleaded factual allegations supporting the claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act Title III claim for discrimination based on disability at a place of public accommodation; Florida Fair Housing Act claim (substantively identical to FHA claim)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied Title III of the ADA, finding Royse Services is a public accommodation, R.E.G. is disabled, and Royse Services discriminated by requiring a pet fee for a service animal in violation of 28 C.F.R. § 36.302(c)(1) and (c)(8). Florida Fair Housing Act claim analyzed under identical legal standard as FHA claim. Default judgment entered on both claims.

source_file: 11267621 - Gilbert v. TUCSON REALTY & TRUST COMPANY
case_name: Shenoa Gilbert v. Tucson Realty & Trust Company Management Services LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested to transfer to a first-floor apartment due to her back injury and disability.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHAA reasonable accommodation claim because her complaint failed to allege sufficient facts showing her disability substantially limits major life activities, that defendant knew of her disability, and that the accommodation was necessary to afford her equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Shenoa Gilbert, a Section 8 voucher holder with a documented disability (back injury and Stage 3 kidney disease), sued her property management company alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act for denying her accommodation requests for a first-floor apartment transfer and exemption from pesticide use in her unit. The court dismissed her complaint with leave to amend, finding she failed to allege sufficient facts to state a plausible claim under the FHAA's reasonable accommodation elements.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Howard v. HMK Holdings, LLC, 988 F.3d 1185 (9th Cir. 2021)
Dubois v. Ass'n of Apartment Owners of 2987 Kalakaua, 453 F.3d 1175 (9th Cir. 2006)
Giebeler v. M & B Assocs., 343 F.3d 1143 (9th Cir. 2003)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Transfer to a first-floor apartment unit due to back injury and disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege how her back injury and kidney disease substantially limit major life activities (element 1), failed to clearly allege she informed defendant of her disability (element 2), and failed to allege how denial of first-floor unit deprived her of equal opportunity to use/enjoy dwelling (element 3). Although facial reasonableness and refusal were adequately pleaded, failure on multiple elements renders the claim implausible under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exemption from use of chemical pesticides in plaintiff's unit due to severe allergies and Stage 3 kidney disease
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege how her allergies and kidney disease substantially limit major life activities (element 1), failed to clearly allege she informed defendant of her disability (element 2), and failed to clearly allege how pesticide exemption was necessary to afford equal opportunity to use/enjoy dwelling (element 3). Implications of anaphylactic reaction do not clearly state a claim upon which relief can be granted.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation for requesting reasonable accommodations, manifested by refusal to extend lease, return of payment, and filing of eviction action
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff adequately alleged protected activity (requesting accommodations) and adverse housing consequences (lease denial, eviction filing) and damages, but failed to clearly allege the causal nexus between her accommodation requests and defendant's subsequent adverse actions. The complaint lacks sufficient factual allegations to plausibly connect the refusal to extend the lease to the prior accommodation requests.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act claim for failure to provide reasonable accommodations
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege how her back injury and kidney disease substantially limit major life activities (element 1), failed to allege the qualifications necessary to live on first floor and that she meets them (element 2), failed to allege she was denied accommodations solely based on disability (element 3), and failed to allege sufficient facts that defendant receives federal financial assistance (element 4). Multiple elements are insufficiently pleaded under the Iqbal/Twombly standard.

source_file: 11267622 - United States v. FAIR HOUSING PARTNERSHIP OF GREATER PITTSBURGH, INC.
case_name: United States of America v. AION Management, LLC
accommodation_description: Assigned accessible parking space for individuals with mobility impairments who use canes, crutches, or walkers
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion for reconsideration and motion to certify for interlocutory appeal, holding that fair housing testers can assert § 3604(f)(3)(B) claims and that plaintiffs adequately pleaded the necessity element by alleging specific physical impairments from which an assigned parking space would be necessary.
brief_summary: The United States and fair housing organizations sued AION Management and affiliated property entities alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act, including failure to provide assigned parking as a reasonable accommodation under § 3604(f)(3)(B). The court denied defendants' motion for reconsideration and motion to certify for interlocutory appeal, concluding that testers have standing to bring § 3604(f)(3)(B) claims and that plaintiffs plausibly alleged the necessity element of the reasonable accommodation claim.
key_cases_cited: Vorchheimer v. Philadelphian Owners Association, 903 F.3d 100 (3d Cir. 2018)
FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine, 602 U.S. 367 (2024)
Smith v. Pac. Props. & Dev. Corp., 358 F.3d 1097 (9th Cir. 2004)
Access Living of Metro Chi. v. Prewitt, 111 F. Supp. 3d 890 (N.D. Ill. 2015)
United States v. Perry Homes, Inc., 2022 WL 2829887 (W.D. Pa. 2022)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Assigned parking space for individuals with mobility impairments (testers' family members using canes, crutches, walkers, unable to walk more than 100 feet, experiencing fatigue after walking long distances)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiffs plausibly alleged necessity for assigned parking space based on specific factual allegations regarding testers' physical impairments and that testers have standing to assert Section 3604(f)(3)(B) claims despite being fictional; the pleading gap between alleged necessity and ability to prove necessity does not defeat allegations at the motion to dismiss stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged discriminatory statements indicating preference or non-preference for housing based on association with disabled persons
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that Section 3604(c) claims are distinct from Section 3604(f)(3)(B) reasonable accommodation claims and do not require explicit denial of housing or accommodation; plaintiffs need only allege statements that would suggest to an ordinary listener that a protected class is preferred or not preferred, which plaintiffs adequately pleaded.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodations under Section 3604(f)(1) and (f)(2) (specific accommodations not detailed in this opinion, which addresses only the motion to dismiss and reconsideration)
fha_claims.reasoning: Defendants did not move to dismiss Section 3604(f)(1) and (f)(2) claims; these claims survive the motion to dismiss stage and remain pending.

source_file: 11267623 - Watts v. THE IRVINE COMPANY LLC
case_name: Watts v. The Irvine Company LLC
citation: No reporter citation (Report and Recommendation, C.D. Cal. June 20, 2025)
accommodation_description: Plaintiff submitted three formal accommodation requests that were denied, but the Third Amended Complaint does not specify what accommodations were requested (prior versions mentioned carpet replacement and relocation).
key_holding: The Third Amended Complaint fails to comply with Rule 8 because it does not identify which defendant each cause of action is asserted against, and even liberally construed, fails to plausibly allege any viable federal claim, including failure to state a plausible FHA reasonable accommodation claim.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Candi-Rachelle Watts, an African American woman in HUD-subsidized housing owned by The Irvine Company LLC, filed a Third Amended Complaint alleging disability discrimination, failure to accommodate, and retaliation under the FHA, along with ADA, RICO, and state law claims. The magistrate judge recommended dismissing the complaint without leave to amend for failing to comply with Rule 8's pleading requirements and for failing to state any viable federal claim, finding the allegations conclusory and insufficient to give defendants fair notice of the claims against them.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Dubois v. Ass'n of Apartment Owners of 2987 Kalakaua, 453 F.3d 1175 (9th Cir. 2006)
Walker v. City of Lakewood, 272 F.3d 1114 (9th Cir. 2001)
Roman v. Jefferson at Hollywood LP, 495 F. App'x 804 (9th Cir. 2012)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested three formal accommodations (specific nature not clearly specified in complaint; prior versions alleged carpet replacement and relocation to another property)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege she is handicapped within the meaning of § 3602(h) with sufficient factual detail; allegations were conclusory and did not specify what accommodations were requested or why they were denied, failing to establish necessity and reasonableness elements required under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged retaliation under § 3617 based on reduction of utility allowance following accommodation requests, but the allegation was conclusory and lacked factual support for causal connection; complaint also alleged the reduction was caused by fraudulent income statements, undermining any inference of retaliation for accommodation requests.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II and Title III claims; § 1983 and § 1985 civil rights claims; RICO claim; whistleblower retaliation claim; HUD regulatory violations; California state law claims (negligence, intentional infliction of emotional distress, constructive eviction, fraud, Unruh Civil Rights Act, Government Code § 815.6, Health and Safety Code violations, habitability, Penal Code § 186)
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA Title II and III claims failed because plaintiff did not adequately allege disability or that she was denied accommodations because of disability; § 1983/§ 1985 claims failed because complaint did not specify which federal right was violated or identify conduct under color of state law; RICO claim failed because allegations of racketeering activity were conclusory and did not satisfy Rule 9(b) heightened pleading standard for fraud, and no association-in-fact enterprise was alleged; whistleblower claim cited non-whistleblower statutes; HUD regulatory violations lack private cause of action; state law claims lack jurisdictional basis absent viable federal question.

case_name: Cooper v. Chicago Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Request for transfer to wheelchair-accessible ground floor unit for disabled daughter with progressive neurological disease who could no longer navigate second-floor apartment
key_holding: The court approved a $525,000 settlement and 95%/5% allocation between the individual plaintiff and the decedent's estate, finding the settlement fair and reasonable given CHA's failure to provide accessible housing for 788 days.
brief_summary: Lynya Cooper, individually and as administrator of her deceased daughter Trebora Talbert's estate, sued the Chicago Housing Authority for failing to provide reasonable alternative housing accommodations in a wheelchair-accessible unit for 788 days despite the daughter's progressive neurological disease rendering her unable to walk. The court approved a $525,000 settlement with 95% allocated to Ms. Cooper personally and 5% to the estate.
key_cases_cited: Williams v. Rush-Presbyterian St. Luke's Med. Ctr., 899 N.E.2d 1241 (Ill. App. Ct. 2008)
Johnson v. Provena St. Therese Med. Ctr., 778 N.E.2d 298 (Ill. App. Ct. 2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Transfer to a wheelchair-accessible first-floor unit in lieu of second-floor apartment; failure to provide reasonable alternative housing accommodation for 788 days (July 6, 2020 to September 3, 2022) and failure to engage in interactive process
fha_claims.reasoning: Parties settled the reasonable accommodation claim for $525,000 after a thorough settlement conference. The court approved the settlement as fair and reasonable, finding that plaintiff was entitled to 95% of the settlement amount ($498,750) for her personal damages as the sole primary caregiver for her disabled daughter during the 788-day period when CHA failed to provide accessible housing or engage in the interactive process.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rehabilitation Act (29 U.S.C. § 701 et seq.), Americans with Disabilities Act (42 U.S.C. § 12101 et seq.), and Illinois Human Rights Act (775 ILCS § 5/101 et seq.)
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA statutory claims (Rehabilitation Act, ADA, and Illinois Human Rights Act) were resolved as part of the same $525,000 settlement agreement approved by the court on June 13, 2025.

source_file: 11267625 - Jones v. FEATHERSTONE CONDOMINIUM HOMEOWNERS ASSOCIATION INC.
case_name: Quincy Bernard Jones v. Featherstone Condominium Homeowners Association Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that the HOA have a contractor remove slippery, wet dirt from his parking spot and sidewalk because he is afraid he will slip and fall due to his disability.
key_holding: The court dismissed the failure-to-accommodate claim because Plaintiff failed to allege what his disability is or how cleaning the parking space and sidewalk would address limitations caused by his impairment.
brief_summary: Pro se Plaintiff Quincy Jones, a disabled individual receiving disability payments, sued Featherstone Condominium Homeowners Association alleging failure to accommodate and retaliation claims under the Fair Housing Act. The court granted IFP status but dismissed the amended complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e) for failure to state a claim, finding that the accommodation claim failed because Plaintiff did not allege what his disability is or explain how removing dirt from his parking spot would address his impairment.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Neitzke v. Williams, 490 U.S. 319 (1989)
Philippeaux v. Apartment Inv. & Mgmt. Co., 598 F. App'x 640 (11th Cir. 2015)
Schwarz v. City of Treasure Island, 544 F.3d 1201 (11th Cir. 2008)
Schaw v. Habitat for Human. of Citrus Cnty., Inc., 938 F.3d 1259 (11th Cir. 2019)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege an adverse action by defendants. Merely informing a landlord of pending legal claims does not constitute coercion, intimidation, threat, or interference under 42 U.S.C. § 3617, and therefore fails to state a plausible retaliation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege an adverse action by defendants. Merely informing a landlord of pending legal claims does not constitute coercion, intimidation, threat, or interference under 42 U.S.C. § 3617, and therefore fails to state a plausible retaliation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Removal of slippery, wet dirt from parking spot and sidewalk connected to plaintiff's unit
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege what his disability is or how cleaning a parking space and sidewalk would address a need created by that disability. Without establishing the nexus between the disability and the requested accommodation, plaintiff fails to state a claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(B).

case_name: Lepp v. Mallet
accommodation_description: Plaintiff Heidi Lepp, affiliated with Sugarleaf Church, alleges that government and private defendants discriminated against her based on disability and religion in connection with church property occupancy and alleged enforcement actions.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's motion to amend as futile because her proposed amended complaint failed to state plausible Fair Housing Act claims; plaintiff only offered conclusory allegations of discrimination without factual allegations showing defendants acted with discriminatory animus based on religion or disability.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Heidi Lepp, proceeding pro se and affiliated with Sugarleaf Church, sued Conrad Mallet Jr. and other defendants alleging a coordinated campaign of government harassment based on religion and disability in connection with church property at 2627 John R. Street in Detroit. The court denied plaintiff's motion to amend her complaint as futile, finding her Fair Housing Act claims failed to state plausible allegations of discriminatory intent because she only offered conclusory assertions without factual content showing defendants acted because of her protected characteristics.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Fulton v. City of Philadelphia, 593 U.S. 522 (2021)
Church of Lukumi Bablu Aye, Inc. v. City of Hialeah, 508 U.S. 520 (1993)
Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges discrimination based on religion and disability in connection with Madden's email denying occupancy of John R. Street property and Black and Green's alleged closure of Adelaide Street parking lot.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient factual matter to support an inference of discrimination based on protected class. Madden's email made no mention of disability and was rooted in concern for civil/criminal liability, not religion. No allegations show Black or Green knew of or acted with animus toward Plaintiff's disability or religion.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges retaliation under § 3617 for asserting FHA rights through Madden's email and Black's warrantless inspection.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to specify which FHA right (§§ 3603-3606) she exercised and failed to allege discriminatory animus. Madden's email explained refusal based on civil/criminal liability concerns, not retaliation. Black's inspection allegations lack sufficient factual detail to infer discriminatory animus.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claim alleging parking closures denied disabled members access; Section 504 Rehabilitation Act claim referenced in reply brief but not in proposed amended complaint; § 1983 constitutional claims (First Amendment Free Exercise and Free Speech, Fourth Amendment, Fifth Amendment Takings, Fourteenth Amendment Equal Protection and Due Process); RLUIPA; civil RICO; state law claims (defamation, false light, intentional infliction of emotional distress, trespass, conversion, misappropriation of public funds); civil conspiracy under § 1985(3); municipal liability under § 1983.
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA federal claims failed under Rule 12(b)(6) for lack of plausible factual allegations. ADA Title II claim failed because Plaintiff did not identify a public program, did not allege federal financial assistance, and did not allege Black and Green knew of or acted with discriminatory intent based on disability. Constitutional claims failed for various reasons: Free Exercise claims lacked identification of the law allegedly violated; Free Speech claims lacked factual allegations about protected speech and forum analysis; Fourth Amendment claims failed because Plaintiff lacked legitimate expectation of privacy (lease was to LLC, not Plaintiff; occupancy was unlawful); Takings Clause claim failed because Plaintiff lacked property interest in Adelaide Street lot and alleged no final decision; Equal Protection claim failed because Plaintiff alleged no disparate treatment of similarly situated persons; Due Process claim was conclusory. RLUIPA claim failed because Plaintiff lacked property interest and Madden acted as private attorney, not under color of state law. RICO claim failed because Plaintiff did not plausibly allege predicate acts or pattern of racketeering. State law claims were declined on supplemental jurisdiction grounds under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3) after all federal claims were found futile.

source_file: 11267627 - COMM'N ON HUMAN RIGHTS v. MANSIONS, LLC

case_name: Karla Hunt v. Volare Health LLC
accommodation_description: Employee retaliation claim — plaintiff was terminated after advocating for a patient with mental health diagnosis whose admission to nursing facility was denied based on disability
key_holding: Plaintiff failed to state a retaliation claim under § 3617 because she did not allege she 'aided or encouraged' the patient in exercising his FHA rights — she only had a single argument with her supervisor about the patient's admission without involving or informing the patient — but dismissal was with leave to amend; her Oregon whistleblower claim survived because temporal proximity and circumstantial evidence supported causation
brief_summary: Karla Hunt, an employee at French Prairie Nursing and Rehabilitation Center operated by Volare Health LLC, sued claiming she was retaliated against under the FHA after advocating for a patient's admission despite the patient's mental health diagnosis; the court dismissed her FHA retaliation claim with leave to amend because she failed to adequately allege she aided or encouraged the patient in exercising his fair housing rights, but declined to dismiss her Oregon whistleblower retaliation claim finding sufficient temporal proximity and circumstantial evidence of causation.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Walker v. City of Lakewood, 272 F.3d 1114 (9th Cir. 2001)
Macon v. Proud Ground Organization, 2021 WL 3354157 (D. Or. 2021)
University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center v. Nassar, 570 U.S. 338 (2013)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that she 'aided or encouraged' the Patient in exercising FHA rights under § 3617. The complaint alleges only a single argument between Plaintiff and Drummond with no allegation that the Patient was involved or aware of the dispute, and no allegation that Plaintiff ever spoke with the Patient or his caregivers about FHA rights or discrimination concerns. Dismissal granted with leave to amend.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Oregon whistleblower retaliation under ORS 659A.199
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff adequately pleaded a prima facie case of retaliation under ORS 659A.199 by alleging protected activity (reporting alleged FHA discrimination), adverse action (discipline and termination), and causal link (very close temporal proximity of four weeks to discipline and six days to termination, supported by factual allegations that stated reasons for discipline referenced 'undermining management' and 'insubordination' relating to the July 25, 2023 dispute). Ninth Circuit precedent permits causation to be inferred from timing alone when temporal proximity is very close and supported by factual context.

source_file: 11267632 - Watts v. JOGGERS RUN PROPERTY OWNERS ASSOCIATION
case_name: Sara Watts v. Joggers Run Property Owners Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged HOA engaged in racial discrimination including selective enforcement of HOA rules, restrictions on access to community amenities like basketball courts, towing of vehicles, harassment, and unwarranted fees because of her race as an African American woman.
key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that Section 3604(b) covers post-acquisition discriminatory conduct by an HOA against a homeowner because the mandatory HOA contract creates rights and privileges directly connected to the sale of the dwelling, and Watts plausibly alleged racially motivated discrimination in the terms, conditions, and privileges of her HOA membership.
brief_summary: Sara Watts, an African American woman, sued the Joggers Run Property Owners Association alleging that the HOA engaged in racially discriminatory conduct including selectively enforcing parking and pet rules against her while excusing violations by White residents, restricting access to basketball courts because too many Black children used them, harassing her family, and improperly towing her son's car. The Eleventh Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that Section 3604(b) of the Fair Housing Act covers post-acquisition discriminatory conduct by an HOA against homeowners because mandatory HOA membership creates contractual rights directly connected to the sale of a dwelling.
key_cases_cited: Loper Bright Enters. v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024)
Ga. State Conf. of the NAACP v. City of La-Grange, 940 F.3d 627 (11th Cir. 2019)
Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009) (en banc)
Hunt v. Aimco Props., L.P., 814 F.3d 1213 (11th Cir. 2016)
Curto v. A Country Place Condo. Ass'n, 921 F.3d 405 (3d Cir. 2019)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed the district court's dismissal of the § 3604(b) claim, holding that post-acquisition discriminatory conduct by an HOA regarding terms, conditions, and privileges of homeownership (basketball court access, parking enforcement, pet policies, yard sale enforcement, roof repairs) falls within the scope of § 3604(b) when HOA membership is mandatory and the rights are directly connected to the sale of the dwelling. The court applied the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard and found Watts' allegations of race-based discrimination in the provision of services and facilities sufficiently plausible to survive dismissal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed the dismissal of the § 3617 retaliation/interference claim, holding that because Watts plausibly stated a § 3604(b) violation, she necessarily satisfied the requirement to allege an underlying violation of §§ 3603-3606. Section 3617 prohibits coercion, intimidation, threat, or interference with the exercise of rights granted under those sections, and Watts' allegations of harassment and discriminatory treatment constitute plausible interference with her § 3604(b) rights.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1981 (Civil Rights Act — equal contract rights); 42 U.S.C. § 1982 (Civil Rights Act — equal property rights)
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed dismissal of both § 1981 and § 1982 claims. For § 1981, the court held that Watts need only identify an impaired contractual relationship (the HOA Rules contract) under which she had rights; she need not identify specific contractual provisions. For § 1982, the court held that the statute protects not merely the acquisition of property but the right to use property on an equal basis with White citizens, and Watts' allegations that the HOA created a dual property system denying her equal access to amenities and services sufficiently stated a claim.

source_file: 11267633 - BAK REALTY, LLC v. City of Fitchburg
case_name: BAK Realty, LLC v. City of Fitchburg
accommodation_description: Crossing Over, Inc. (a nonprofit operating a 13-resident sober house in a three-family dwelling) requested reasonable accommodation under the FHA and Massachusetts zoning law to permit occupancy exceeding the four-unrelated-person limit applicable to families under Fitchburg's zoning code.
key_holding: The Massachusetts Zoning Act's anti-discrimination provision requires that groups of unrelated disabled persons be treated the same as either families OR similar-sized groups of unrelated persons, not necessarily both; because Fitchburg's zoning code treated the sober house residents the same as any other boarding house use, it did not discriminate against disabled persons.
brief_summary: BAK Realty and Crossing Over, Inc. (operator of a 13-resident sober house) challenged Fitchburg's determination that their three-family dwelling was operating as a prohibited boarding house under the zoning code. The Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts reversed the lower court, holding that G. L. c. 40A, § 3, fourth par., which prohibits discrimination against disabled persons in zoning, requires that unrelated disabled persons be treated the same as either families OR similar-sized groups of unrelated persons (in the disjunctive), not both simultaneously; because the sober house did not meet Fitchburg's local definition of family and was treated the same as any other similar-sized group of unrelated persons under the boarding house prohibition, there was no discrimination.
key_cases_cited: Edmonds v. Oxford House, Inc., 514 U.S. 725 (1995)
Crossing Over, Inc. v. Fitchburg, 98 Mass. App. Ct. 822 (2020)
Peabody Props., Inc. v. Sherman, 418 Mass. 603 (1994)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Pulsifer v. United States, 601 U.S. 124 (2024)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request for reasonable accommodation under FHA to allow sober house residents to occupy a three-unit dwelling without conforming to zoning code restrictions on unrelated persons per unit and single housekeeping unit requirements; specifically, allowing irregular distribution of residents across units and exemption from boarding house prohibition.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that Massachusetts Zoning Act § 3, fourth par., does not require municipalities to treat disabled persons in congregate living arrangements as 'families' regardless of local definition, but only requires equal treatment as comparable groups of nondisabled unrelated persons. The sober house residents were treated the same as any similar-sized group of unrelated nondisabled persons (boarding house classification) and thus no discrimination occurred. Although the zoning board granted a reasonable accommodation allowing up to 12 residents with flexible distribution, the Superior Court's annulment of that decision was reversed because the statutory standard was satisfied without the accommodation.

case_name: Curtis K. Jackson, Sr. v. Chicago Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a person with disabilities receiving a Project-Based Voucher, alleged denial of access to programs and services at Lake Street Studios, including an accessible parking space, and discriminatory housing conditions.
key_holding: Jackson's FHA claim failed because he provided no allegations that the Authority and its employees denied him a housing accommodation or otherwise interfered with his right to rent or enjoy property, let alone that they acted with discriminatory intent.
brief_summary: Curtis Jackson sued the Chicago Housing Authority and Lake Street Studios Limited Partnership under the FHA, ADA, and § 1983, alleging that Lake Street employees engaged in discriminatory conduct against him as a disabled voucher holder, and that CHA employees failed to address his complaints. The Seventh Circuit affirmed dismissal of the Authority defendants and the $10,000 default judgment against Lake Street, holding that Jackson failed to state an FHA claim because he did not adequately allege that defendants denied him a housing accommodation or acted with discriminatory intent based on disability.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Monell v. Dep't of Soc. Servs., 436 U.S. 658 (1978)
Valencia v. City of Springfield, 883 F.3d 959 (7th Cir. 2018)
Stanek v. St. Charles Cmty. Unit Sch. Dist. No. 303, 783 F.3d 634 (7th Cir. 2015)
Williams v. Shah, 927 F.3d 476 (7th Cir. 2019)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Access to programs and services at Lake Street Studios, including laundry room and accessible parking space; housing transfer through Housing Choice Voucher program
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege that the Authority defendants denied him a housing accommodation or otherwise interfered with his right to rent or enjoy property. The complaint provided no allegations connecting the Authority's conduct to a failure to provide reasonable accommodation, only that Lake Street employees engaged in discriminatory conduct and that plaintiff informed Authority employees about it.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's allegation that Burns and Steinbuck acted in a 'conspiratorial manner' to allow or ratify illegal actions was too vague and conclusory to plausibly plead retaliation under § 3617. Plaintiff did not specify what illegal actions the Authority employees allowed to stand or how their conduct constituted interference or coercion.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (constitutional rights), Americans with Disabilities Act § 12131-12213
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege personal involvement of Authority employees in constitutional violations under § 1983 and failed to allege a Monell policy, custom, or practice. ADA claim failed because plaintiff did not allege facts permitting a reasonable inference that Authority defendants discriminated against him because of his disability; disability alone does not establish causal connection.

case_name: Gordon Roy Parker v. Panphil Realty, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges credit score requirements in apartment advertisements deter disabled persons from applying and seeks waiver of credit score policies as an accommodation for disability.
key_holding: The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss because plaintiff lacks Article III standing—he never applied for any apartment, failed to plead a specific disability, and his conclusory futility allegations and tester theory were insufficient to establish concrete, particularized injury-in-fact under controlling Supreme Court precedent.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Gordon Roy Parker sued multiple Philadelphia apartment owners and their attorney alleging their credit score requirements in rental advertisements violated the Fair Housing Act by deterring disabled persons from applying. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding Parker lacks Article III standing because he never applied for any apartment, failed to plead a specific disability, and his generalized futility allegations and tester standing theory were legally insufficient under controlling Supreme Court precedent.
key_cases_cited: Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Carney v. Adams, 592 U.S. 53 (2020)
Ellison v. Am. Bd. of Orthopaedic Surgery, 11 F.4th 200 (3d Cir. 2021)
Int'l Bhd. of Teamsters v. United States, 431 U.S. 324 (1977)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges credit score requirements disproportionately exclude disabled persons; does not request specific accommodation.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff lacks Article III standing because he did not apply for any apartment, did not allege a specific disability, and failed to plead sufficient facts showing he was 'able and ready' to apply but for the credit score requirements. The court applied the Carney/Ellison framework requiring concrete, particularized injury, not abstract generalized grievance.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges credit score requirements disproportionately exclude disabled persons; asserts standing as a 'tester' under Havens Realty.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff does not qualify as a 'tester' under Havens Realty because he did not allege apartment owners discriminated in the sale or rental or 'otherwise made unavailable or denied' a dwelling because of handicap. The alleged conduct—communicating credit score requirements—does not constitute denial of a dwelling or violation of § 3604(d)'s requirement to provide truthful information about available housing.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges retaliation by Attorney Barsky and AMC Delancey for sending cease-and-desist email directing plaintiff to communicate through counsel rather than directly with represented clients.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff lacks standing for retaliation claim because he did not allege protected activity under the FHA. Attorney Barsky's email enforcing Model Rule of Professional Conduct 4.2 (prohibiting direct communication with represented parties) does not constitute coercion, intimidation, threats, or interference with a protected right under § 3617. Plaintiff did not allege he made a complaint, testified, assisted in a proceeding, or reported a discriminatory practice to a housing provider or authority.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Philadelphia Code § 9-810 claim prohibiting credit exclusions by prospective landlords.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3) because all federal FHA claims were dismissed for lack of standing, eliminating the court's original jurisdiction. Plaintiff may pursue state law claims in state court if he does not further pursue federal claims.

source_file: 11267636 - APPELGREN v. ISLAND HOSPITALITY MANAGEMENT VII, LLC
case_name: Mark Appelgren v. Island Hospitality Management VII, LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff allegedly requested 'a quiet, stress-free environment' and 'room modifications' during hotel check-in, but never disclosed his disabilities (severe social anxiety, panic attacks, IBS) to hotel staff.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA and ADA reasonable accommodation claims because he failed to allege that defendants knew of his disabilities, and his vague references to wanting a 'quiet, stress-free environment' and unspecified 'room modifications' did not give defendants sufficient notice of what accommodation he sought.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Mark Appelgren sued Island Hospitality Management VII, LLC and Hilton alleging disability discrimination under the FHA and ADA after a difficult hotel check-in experience where he experienced delays, hostile interactions, and a chaotic lobby that allegedly triggered his anxiety and IBS symptoms. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that plaintiff failed to state a failure-to-accommodate claim because he never alleged that defendants knew of his disabilities, and his vague references to wanting a quieter environment and room modifications were insufficient to put defendants on notice of what accommodation he sought.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Revock v. Cowpet Bay W. Condo. Ass'n, 853 F.3d 96 (3d Cir. 2017)
Yates Real Est., Inc. v. Plainfield Zoning Bd. of Adjustment, 404 F. Supp. 3d 889 (D.N.J. 2019)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Quiet, stress-free environment and room modifications to accommodate severe social anxiety, generalized anxiety disorder, panic attacks, severe depression, IBS, and long-haul COVID symptoms during hotel check-in and stay
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that defendants were aware of his disabilities or the specific accommodations he sought. The court held that under the FHA, defendants must have 'an idea of what accommodation [the plaintiff] sought' to be liable for failure to accommodate, and plaintiff's allegations regarding requests were too vague and did not establish that hotel staff knew why plaintiff made those requests.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III public accommodations claim; also state law claims for failure to train and supervise, gross negligence, breach of duty of care, breach of contract, intentional infliction of emotional distress, breach of implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, and unjust enrichment
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA Title III claim dismissed for failure to state a plausible claim and because Title III defendants cannot be liable for money damages, which was plaintiff's sole remedy sought. State law claims dismissed without prejudice due to court's decline to exercise supplemental jurisdiction after dismissal of all federal claims.

source_file: 11267637 - Doe v. Department of Veterans Affairs
case_name: Jane Doe v. Department of Veterans Affairs
accommodation_description: Doe alleged that Bozzuto Management Co. failed to continue an accommodation granted to her disabled husband by the prior property owner (Equity Residential), and that Friendship Place retaliated against her for reporting discrimination concerns.
key_holding: The court dismissed Doe's FHA claim because she lacked standing to sue on behalf of her disabled husband—she failed to allege that he cannot protect his own interests—and dismissed her ADA and Rehabilitation Act claims with prejudice because none of the defendants qualify as public entities.
brief_summary: Jane Doe, a combat disabled veteran, sued the Department of Veterans Affairs, Friendship Place, Equity Residential, Bozzuto Management Co., federal judges, court clerks, and others, alleging they colluded to deny accommodations for her disabled husband and obstruct her access to courts. The court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim, holding that Doe lacked standing to sue on her husband's behalf because she did not allege he cannot protect his own interests, and that her ADA and Rehabilitation Act claims failed because the defendants are not public entities.
key_cases_cited: Thomas v. The Salvation Army of S. Territory, 841 F.3d 632 (4th Cir. 2016)
Wicomico Nursing Home v. Padilla, 910 F.3d 739 (4th Cir. 2018)
Freilich v. Upper Chesapeake Health, Inc., 313 F.3d 205 (4th Cir. 2002)
Gibson v. Goldston, 85 F.4th 218 (4th Cir. 2023)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accommodation for disabled husband that was granted by Equity Residential but not transferred to or provided by Bozzuto Management Co. upon property transfer
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege that she personally was denied benefits or subjected to adverse action because of her disability; she alleged only that her husband was denied accommodations. Plaintiff lacked standing to sue on behalf of her husband because she did not allege he was unable to protect his own interests.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II, ADA Title III, Rehabilitation Act § 504, § 1983 constitutional claims (due process, equal protection, access to courts)
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim / § 1915(e)(2)(B); Judicial immunity; Lack of state action; Lack of standing
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege she personally suffered an adverse action because of disability (ADA/Rehabilitation Act claims); defendants are not public entities subject to Title II (ADA/Rehabilitation Act); private defendants are not state actors (§ 1983); judges and clerks are protected by judicial immunity; Administrative Office of U.S. Courts and court clerk offices are not 'persons' under § 1983; plaintiff lacked standing to sue on behalf of her husband.

case_name: Park Crossing Homeowners Association, Inc. v. Suarez
accommodation_description: The Suarezes alleged the Association's pre-suit mediation demand threatened to evict their adult son Gabriel based on his autism-related behaviors, constituting discrimination under § 3604(f)(1); the Suarezes also raised a failure-to-accommodate claim (Count II) which the jury rejected.
key_holding: The Association's pre-suit mediation letter demanding that the Suarezes arrange 'proper care and supervision' for Gabriel or face removal from the property did not constitute the kind of actual eviction threat required to support a discrimination claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(1), as the Association never filed an eviction action and the pre-suit mediation demand was not a realistic or genuine threat of housing loss.
brief_summary: Park Crossing HOA sued the Suarezes for covenant violations alleging Gabriel's autism-related noises disturbed neighbors; the Suarezes counterclaimed under the FHA, alleging the HOA's pre-suit mediation letter threatening Gabriel's removal constituted disability discrimination under § 3604(f)(1) and failure to accommodate. The appellate court reversed the new trial order on Count I, holding the mediation letter was not a realistic eviction threat sufficient to support an FHA discrimination claim, while affirming the permanent injunction requiring the Suarezes to maintain noise limits.
key_cases_cited: Hunt v. Aimco Props., L.P., 814 F.3d 1213 (11th Cir. 2016)
Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009)
Wells v. Willow Lake Ests., Inc., 390 F. App'x 956 (11th Cir. 2010)
Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)
Watts v. Joggers Run Prop. Owners Ass'n, 133 F.4th 1032 (11th Cir. 2025)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of housing or making dwelling unavailable based on disability (autism spectrum disorder); alleged threat of eviction of Gabriel from the property in pre-suit mediation demand
fha_claims.disposition: Directed verdict granted at trial; new trial granted by trial court; reversed on appeal
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court held that the pre-suit mediation demand did not constitute an actual, realistic, or concrete threat of eviction sufficient to render the property 'unavailable' under § 3604(f)(1). The conditional threat was merely a hyperbolic negotiating tactic embedded in a mediation demand, not an action that would lead to eviction but for an intervening cause. No landlord-tenant relationship existed, and no expedited procedural pathway was available to the Association to evict Gabriel.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to provide reasonable accommodation for Gabriel's autism spectrum disorder; jury found that Suarezes had not requested a reasonable accommodation
fha_claims.reasoning: The jury found that the Suarezes had not requested a reasonable accommodation to address the noise and mail interference issues. The trial court's injunction was upheld as narrowly tailored to the proven violation of the Association's governing documents, and the court retained jurisdiction to modify the injunction if the Suarezes propose a reasonable accommodation in the future based on changed circumstances.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: State law claims under Florida Homeowners' Association Act (Chapter 720) and common law nuisance; Association's claim for declaratory judgment and injunctive relief for violation of governing documents
fha_claims.reasoning: The jury found that the Suarezes violated Article 10(F) of the Declaration by permitting disturbing noises and interfering with the reasonable rights of other owners. The trial court entered a permanent prohibitory injunction limiting noise to decibel levels specified in the Pembroke Pines ordinance and prohibiting mail interference, which was upheld on appeal as narrowly tailored to the proven violation and not violating the FHA on its face.

source_file: 11267639 - Faruki v. HOUSING AUTHORITY FOR THE COUNTY OF SACRAMENTO
case_name: Faruki v. Housing Authority for the County of Sacramento
accommodation_description: Request that the housing authority process plaintiff's Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher application after providing notice of his Multiple Myeloma disability, alleging constructive denial of the application due to disability.
key_holding: The complaint fails to state a plausible FHA claim because plaintiff's allegations are speculative and conclusory, and because plaintiff's friend who was allegedly treated more favorably was also disabled, negating an inference of disability discrimination.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Mekal Faruki, who has Multiple Myeloma cancer, sued the Housing Authority for the County of Sacramento, Sacramento Housing Regional Authority, and the County of Sacramento, alleging they constructively denied his Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher application after he submitted disability documentation in 2017. The court recommends dismissal of plaintiff's federal claims under the ADA and FHA for failure to state a plausible claim, finding plaintiff's allegations speculative and insufficient to show disability-based discrimination.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Duvall v. County of Kitsap, 260 F.3d 1124 (9th Cir. 2001)
Lovell v. Chandler, 303 F.3d 1039 (9th Cir. 2002)
Budnick v. Town of Carefree, 518 F.3d 1109 (9th Cir. 2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation for disability in processing Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher application; plaintiff alleges defendants failed to accommodate his disability and denied him equal opportunity to use and enjoy housing by refusing to locate his lost application and process his voucher request.
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found plaintiff's allegations speculative and lacking specific supporting facts necessary to state a plausible claim. Plaintiff's comparison to a similarly situated disabled friend does not plausibly suggest disability discrimination, and the SAC does not plead adequate factual content allowing the court to infer discrimination because of plaintiff's disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found plaintiff's allegations that loss of his application and non-receipt of Section 8 Vouchers constituted discrimination because of disability to be speculative and lacking specific supporting facts. The comparison to a similarly situated disabled friend does not plausibly suggest intentional discrimination based on disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II, Unruh Civil Rights Act, California Disabled Persons Act, Fraud
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B); supplemental jurisdiction declined
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed plaintiff's ADA Title II claim for failure to plead adequate factual content showing intentional discrimination or deliberate indifference. The court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3) after dismissing all federal claims.

source_file: 11267640 - United States v. LETTIRE CONSTRUCTION CORP.
case_name: United States of America v. Lettire Construction Corp.
accommodation_description: Retrofitting 185-unit apartment building (The Tapestry) to correct inaccessible design and construction features including door widths, thresholds, kitchen and bathroom layouts, environmental controls, mailboxes, and fitness center accessibility.
key_holding: The government and defendant East 124th Street LLC entered into a Consent Decree requiring substantial retrofits to address alleged violations of the FHA's accessible design and construction requirements at the Tapestry, including physical modifications to common areas and individual units, a $20,000 settlement fund for aggrieved persons, and compliance monitoring over two and a half years.
brief_summary: The United States brought this enforcement action against East 124th Street LLC alleging that The Tapestry, a 185-unit multifamily building completed in 2009, was designed and constructed with accessibility deficiencies in violation of 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(C). The parties settled via Consent Decree requiring defendant to retrofit common areas and dwelling units to meet Fair Housing Act accessibility requirements, establish a $20,000 fund for aggrieved persons, and implement compliance monitoring and training protocols.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible design and construction features in a covered multifamily dwelling, including: accessible lobby counter, accessible outdoor terrace thresholds, accessible mailbox placement, accessible terrace doors, accessible bathroom thresholds, adequate bathroom floor space, adequate kitchen maneuvering space, and accessible environmental control locations.
fha_claims.reasoning: The United States alleged that the Tapestry, a covered multifamily dwelling designed and constructed for first occupancy in 2009, failed to comply with the accessible design and construction requirements of 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(C). The parties resolved the claim through a consent decree in which East 124th agreed to retrofit the building to address identified accessibility deficiencies without admitting liability, and to comply with FHA design standards for future construction.

source_file: 11267641 - LB EX REL. AB v. PREMERA BLUE CROSS

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Coverage for gender-affirming chest surgery (mastectomy/breast reduction) for transgender youth under age 18; claims brought under Section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act (ACA § 1557), which incorporates Title IX and the Age Discrimination Act (AgeDA)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted summary judgment in favor of plaintiffs on their sex discrimination claim under ACA § 1557, holding that Premera's categorical exclusion of gender-affirming chest surgery for transgender youth under age 18 constitutes facial discrimination on the basis of sex. The policy violates ACA § 1557 because it treats adolescents differently based on natal sex (allowing mastectomy for gynecomastia in cisgender males but not for gender-affirming purposes in transgender females under 18) and uses gender dysphoria as a proxy for transgender status. The court rejected Premera's justifications based on minor maturity and lack of scientific evidence, noting Premera had approved 28 of 63 requests using secret exceptions, undermining its stated rationale.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Age discrimination claim under ACA § 1557 (incorporating the Age Discrimination Act of 1975) challenging the categorical age-18 cutoff for coverage of gender-affirming chest surgery
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed plaintiffs' age discrimination claims under ACA § 1557 for failure to exhaust administrative remedies required by the Age Discrimination Act. Plaintiffs failed to file complaints with HHS within 180 days of learning of the alleged discrimination, did not provide 30 days' notice to the HHS Secretary and Attorney General until January 2025 (over a year and a half after litigation commenced), and did not wait the requisite 180 days after filing HHS complaints before initiating suit. The court found no substantial compliance and rejected plaintiffs' request to waive exhaustion, noting that monetary damages are unavailable under the AgeDA and plaintiffs lack standing to seek injunctive relief (A.B. and J.M. have already had surgery; J.M. has reached adulthood).

source_file: 11267642 - Watts v. JOGGERS RUN PROPERTY OWNERS ASSOCIATION, INC.
case_name: Sara Watts v. Joggers Run Property Owners Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff was forced to give up her service dog due to HOA enforcement of pet policies following a neighbor complaint, though disability accommodation is not the primary theory
key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that HOA conduct occurring after a homeowner's purchase—including discriminatory enforcement of community rules regarding amenities, parking, and fees—falls within the scope of Section 3604(b) as discrimination in the terms, conditions, or privileges related to the sale of a dwelling.
brief_summary: Sara Watts, an African American homeowner, sued her HOA alleging racially discriminatory enforcement of community rules including restrictions on basketball court access, selective parking enforcement, and penalties for minor infractions. The district court dismissed her claims under Section 3604(b) and Section 3617 of the Fair Housing Act and Sections 1981 and 1982 of the Civil Rights Act. The Eleventh Circuit reversed, holding that discriminatory HOA conduct regarding contractual rights flowing from mandatory membership—including access to community amenities and services—constitutes discrimination in the terms, conditions, or privileges of homeownership under Section 3604(b).
key_cases_cited: Ga. State Conf. of the NAACP v. City of LaGrange, 940 F.3d 627 (11th Cir. 2019)
Hunt v. Aimco Props., L.P., 814 F.3d 1213 (11th Cir. 2016)
Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009) (en banc)
Curto v. A Country Place Condo. Ass'n, 921 F.3d 405 (3d Cir. 2019)
Loper Bright Enters. v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed the district court's dismissal of the § 3604(b) claim, holding that the FHA's language is broad and inclusive and covers post-acquisition discriminatory conduct by an HOA affecting the terms, conditions, and privileges of homeownership, including access to amenities and services. The court found Watts plausibly alleged race-based discrimination in the HOA's selective enforcement of rules, restricted access to basketball courts, and harassing treatment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed the dismissal of the § 3617 claim, holding that because Watts plausibly stated a § 3604(b) violation, she necessarily satisfied the requirement of alleging an underlying violation of one of the protected sections. Section 3617 prohibits coercion, intimidation, threat, or interference with the exercise of rights granted under § 3604.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1981 (Civil Rights Act - equal contract rights), 42 U.S.C. § 1982 (Civil Rights Act - equal property rights)
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed dismissal of § 1981 and § 1982 claims, holding that Watts plausibly identified a contractual relationship with the HOA under the HOA Rules and alleged intentional racial discrimination that caused contractual injury. Section 1982 protections extend to the use of property on an equal basis with White citizens, including access to community membership benefits and recreational facilities.

source_file: 11267643 - CMDS RESIDENTIAL, LLC v. Mayor & City Council of Baltimore
case_name: CMDS Residential, LLC v. Mayor & City Council of Baltimore
accommodation_description: CMDS sought a use-and-occupancy permit from the City of Baltimore to operate a residential substance-abuse treatment facility, which the City denied based on zoning-related grounds.
key_holding: The court held that punitive damages are unavailable against a municipality under the Fair Housing Act, consistent with City of Newport v. Fact Concerts, and that CMDS cannot recover lost profits if it never had a legal entitlement to operate its facility under the applicable zoning law.
brief_summary: CMDS Residential, LLC, a developer seeking to operate a residential substance-abuse treatment facility, sued the City of Baltimore after the City denied a use-and-occupancy permit; the court ruled on the City's motion in limine that punitive damages are unavailable against a municipality under the FHA and that CMDS cannot recover lost profits if it had no legal right to operate under the zoning code, with the outcome of parallel state litigation on the zoning interpretation potentially affecting actual damages availability.
key_cases_cited: City of Newport v. Fact Concerts, Inc., 453 U.S. 247 (1981)
Barnes v. Gorman, 536 U.S. 181 (2002)
CMDS Residential, LLC v. Mayor & City Council of Balt., 714 F. Supp. 3d 583 (D. Md. 2024)
Gilead Cmty. Servs., Inc. v. Town of Cromwell, 112 F.4th 93 (2d Cir. 2024)
Jennings v. Hous. Auth. of Balt. City, 2014 WL 346641 (D. Md. 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Issuance of use-and-occupancy permit to operate a residential substance-abuse treatment facility
fha_claims.reasoning: The court did not reach the merits of the FHA disparate treatment claim on the motion in limine; the claim survived summary judgment and remains pending for trial. The court's order addresses only damages availability, not the underlying discrimination claim's viability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal protection claims under federal and state constitutions; ADA discriminatory administration and discriminatory requirements claims; state constitutional claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Non-FHA claims (§ 1983 equal protection, ADA §§ 12132-33, state constitutional claims) survived summary judgment and remain pending for trial. The court's order addresses only damages availability, not the underlying claims' merits.

case_name: Danny Carlson v. Carrington Square LLC
accommodation_description: Carlson requested grab bars be installed in his apartment bathroom to prevent falls due to his multiple sclerosis, which requires wheelchair use.
key_holding: Summary judgment for defendants was appropriate because Carlson failed to make his grab bar request in writing as required by the lease agreement, and his failure-to-accommodate claim regarding lease non-renewal failed because defendants demonstrated legitimate, non-discriminatory reasons for the renovation-related non-renewal that applied uniformly to all tenants.
brief_summary: Danny Carlson, a wheelchair user with multiple sclerosis, sued Carrington Square Apartments, its property manager, and its eviction attorneys claiming violations of the Fair Housing Act based on defendants' refusal to install grab bars and the non-renewal of his lease during apartment renovations. The court granted summary judgment for all defendants, finding that Carlson's grab bar request was properly denied because he failed to make the request in writing as required by the lease, and that the lease non-renewal was part of a facially neutral renovation policy applied to all tenants rather than disability-based discrimination.
key_cases_cited: Cinnamon Hills v. St. George City, 685 F.3d 897 (10th Cir. 2012)
Wilson v. Glenwood Intermountain Properties, Inc.
Smith v. Cedars, Inc., 2013 WL 5819342 (D. Utah 2013)
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Hollis v. Chestnut Bend Homeowners Ass'n, 760 F.3d 531 (6th Cir. 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Non-renewal of lease allegedly timed to coincide with unavailability of wheelchair-accessible apartments
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to present direct evidence of discriminatory intent or sufficient circumstantial evidence under McDonnell Douglas. Defendants provided nondiscriminatory rationale (neutral renovation policy applied to all tenants) that plaintiff could not rebut as pretextual, particularly given plaintiff's seven-year tenancy and defendants' unsuccessful attempt to procure alternative housing.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Lease non-renewal policy and apartment availability procedures
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to present statistical evidence or any evidence showing defendants' policies had significant disparate effect on disabled individuals. Even assuming prima facie case, defendants' justifications (substantial business need for renovations not completed since 1998) outweighed any disparate impact, and plaintiff sought to compel affirmative provision of housing rather than merely restrain interference.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Transfer to a remodeled wheelchair-accessible apartment before lease expiration; extended occupancy pending relocation; permission to stay in fitness center
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to demonstrate requested accommodations were 'necessary' to afford equal opportunity to use and enjoy dwelling. Additionally, plaintiff's own admissions that he requested to be 'treated differently' based on disability and source of income—seeking benefits not afforded to others—goes beyond what FHA requires, which does not mandate 'more or better opportunities.'

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Installation of grab bars in bathroom
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish modification was necessary. Additionally, plaintiff never agreed to restore premises to original condition as required by lease, and defendants could condition permission on restoration. Plaintiff's argument that federal law trumps contractual written-request requirement lacks legal authority.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair housing claims against Cullimore Defendants (law firm and attorneys)
fha_claims.reasoning: Cullimore Defendants are not covered by fair housing statutes as they do not rent to anyone, do not provide housing or rental services, and never received reasonable accommodation or modification requests from plaintiff. Plaintiff admitted all material facts establishing defendants' non-involvement and failed to provide legal authority for liability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Third-party harassment (FHA claim); ADA Title II/III; negligence; negligent employment; breach of contract; fraudulent misrepresentation; conspiracy; § 1983; § 504 Rehabilitation Act
fha_claims.reasoning: Third-party harassment claim failed because plaintiff did not establish severe, pervasive, or abusive harassment and failed to cite legal authority supporting that delivery of Notice to Vacate constitutes harassment. ADA does not apply to residential apartment complexes (long-term housing, not public accommodation). Negligence claim failed due to lack of expert testimony on causation. Negligent employment claim failed due to lack of clarity on harm. Breach of contract failed because lease expressly permitted non-renewal and plaintiff failed to request grab bars in writing as required. Fraudulent misrepresentation and conspiracy claims failed due to insufficient evidence and lack of legal authority.

case_name: Robert Ricketts v. Westwood Condo Assn.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that defendants repair the leaking roof, ceiling, and carbon monoxide leaks in his condo unit as a reasonable accommodation for his and his children's asthma.
key_holding: The court dismissed Plaintiff's FHA reasonable accommodation claim because he failed to allege sufficient facts showing his or his children's asthma substantially limits a major life activity as required to establish a handicap under the FHA.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Robert Ricketts, a condominium owner at Westwood Condominiums in West Hartford, Connecticut, sued the Westwood Condo Association, its members, property manager, and attorneys alleging they violated the Fair Housing Act by failing to repair a leaking roof and carbon monoxide leaks as a reasonable accommodation for his and his children's asthma. The court dismissed the FHA claim for failure to state a claim because Plaintiff did not adequately plead that his asthma constitutes a handicap substantially limiting a major life activity under the FHA definition.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Olsen v. Stark Homes, Inc., 759 F.3d 140 (2d Cir. 2014)
Gladstone Realtors v. Bellwood, 441 U.S. 91 (1979)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Repair of leaking roof and ceiling, and remediation of black mold resulting from water damage; repair of carbon monoxide leak from failing water boiler
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to establish that he or his children have a handicap as defined under the FHA. Plaintiff's allegation that he and his children suffered from childhood asthma and could not tolerate exposure to mildew or black mold was insufficient to establish that asthma substantially limits a major life activity. The court declined to consider the remaining elements of the reasonable accommodation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: FDCPA debt collection claims; state law negligence, breach of contract, breach of fiduciary duty, breach of CUTPA, and unjust enrichment claims
fha_claims.reasoning: FDCPA claims dismissed for failure to allege non-conclusory facts supporting harassing or abusive conduct by debt collector; plaintiff alleged only conclusory statements without factual support. Threat of foreclosure was not an FDCPA violation because the threatened litigation could legally be pursued and was actually pursued. State law claims declined for supplemental jurisdiction after dismissal of all federal claims.

case_name: Larry Johnson v. Lisa Simonson and Kelly Paine
accommodation_description: Plaintiff primarily alleged retaliation claims under § 3617, though underlying disputes involved requests to deliver recertification paperwork to his door as a health accommodation and prior live-in aide/spouse accommodation requests.
key_holding: Plaintiff's retaliation claims fail because his own refusal to sign required HUD recertification documents caused the adverse actions, severing any causal link between protected activity and alleged retaliation, and plaintiff's parking space claim is barred by res judicata from prior settlement.
brief_summary: Larry Johnson, a pro se plaintiff and Section 8 tenant at Uptown Tower Apartments, sued property manager Lisa Simonson and portfolio manager Kelly Paine alleging multiple FHA retaliation claims arising from disputes over HUD recertification paperwork and prior housing litigation. The court granted defendants' motion for summary judgment, finding no evidence of retaliation because plaintiff's own refusal to sign required recertification documents directly caused the eviction proceedings and subsidy termination, and plaintiff's parking accommodation claim was barred by res judicata from prior settlement.
key_cases_cited: Brown v. City of Tucson, 336 F.3d 1181 (9th Cir. 2003)
Budnick v. Town of Carefree, 518 F.3d 1109 (9th Cir. 2008)
Walker v. City of Lakewood, 272 F.3d 1114 (9th Cir. 2001)
Johnson v. Guardian Mgmt., 535 F. Supp. 3d 1004 (D. Or. 2021)
Owens v. Kaiser Found. Health Plan, Inc., 244 F.3d 708 (9th Cir. 2001)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish the causal link required for a prima facie retaliation claim because the eviction proceedings were caused by plaintiff's failure to sign recertification documents, and the proceedings were immediately terminated once plaintiff signed. No evidence of pretext disguising retaliatory intent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish causal link between protected activity and alleged retaliatory actions regarding 2023 recertification. Defendants actually posted recertification paperwork to plaintiff's door as requested, yet plaintiff still refused to sign. No evidence of pretext or retaliatory motive regarding child care deduction instructions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Claim is duplicative of retaliation claims and fails for same reasons. To the extent claim asserts § 1983 violation for First Amendment rights, defendants are not state actors and § 1983 does not apply to private landlords.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Restoration of on-site management services (office manager, assistance manager, maintenance workers, services coordinator)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to explain how allegations fit into any particular cause of action or provide legal authority in support of the claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Wheelchair accessible parking space with signage
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff cannot establish that the requested accommodation is necessary to afford equal opportunity because he previously agreed in a settlement that the commercial parking space met his accessibility needs. Claim is also barred by res judicata as it was adjudicated on the merits in prior litigation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: No REAC or pre-REAC inspection was ever conducted of plaintiff's unit. Plaintiff cannot sustain a retaliation claim based on an inspection that never occurred because there is no adverse action.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Claim is duplicative of Claim 2 and fails for the same reasons regarding the 2023 recertification and child care deduction dispute.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Allegations regarding removal of bulletin board postings and attendance at tenant meetings are not specific enough to establish that defendants took an adverse action or that there is a causal link to retaliatory intent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Claim appears to be a reservation of the right to assert additional causes of action and does not assert any specific basis for recovery on any cognizable legal claim.

source_file: 11267648 - Resources for Human Development, Inc. v. LOWER PROVIDENCE TOWNSHIP
case_name: Resources for Human Development, Inc. v. Lower Providence Township
accommodation_description: Zoning permit to operate supportive housing for disabled individuals at Eagleville Hospital property
key_holding: The court dismissed RHD's FHA claim because the complaint failed to properly frame it as a disability discrimination claim under the FHAA and failed to allege sufficient facts showing a causal link between the Township's zoning permit denial and any discriminatory impact, though the court acknowledged that FHAA reasonable accommodation claims can be applied to local land use board decisions.
brief_summary: Resources for Human Development, Inc. sued Lower Providence Township after being denied a zoning permit to operate supportive housing for disabled individuals, alleging the denial violated the FHA through disparate impact on African American homeless persons and constituted a failure to reasonably accommodate disability under the FHAA. The court granted the Township's motion to dismiss, finding RHD failed to state an FHA claim because the complaint did not properly invoke disability discrimination law and failed to allege sufficient facts demonstrating a causal connection between the zoning denial and any discriminatory effect.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Texas Dep't of Hous. and Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Allentown Victory Church v. City of Allentown, No. 22-2817 (3d Cir. July 17, 2024)
Lapid-Laurel, L.L.C. v. Zoning Bd. of Adjustment of Twp. of Scotch Plains, 284 F.3d 442 (3d Cir. 2002)
Gwynedd Properties, Inc. v. Lower Gwynedd Twp., 970 F.2d 1195 (3d Cir. 1992)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation in zoning rules, policies, and practices to permit use of property as supportive housing for individuals with disabilities (including those with substance use disorders and mental health conditions)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead a reasonable accommodation claim within the FHAA framework and did not identify the protected class or specific disability-based need for accommodation. The complaint alleged only a generic reversal of zoning determination without framing the claim as a failure to make reasonable accommodations for persons with disabilities.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
