fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts showing a causal connection between a specific Township policy or practice and the alleged disparate impact on African Americans. A single zoning permit denial is a one-time decision, not a policy or practice, and cannot support a disparate impact claim without identifying the underlying policy causing the disparity.

source_file: 11267649 - Bowman v. SWBC REAL ESTATE SERVICES, LLC
case_name: Dana Bowman v. SWBC Real Estate Services, LLC et al.
accommodation_description: Bowman, a paraplegic veteran who lost the lower half of both legs, toured apartment complexes as a prospective tenant and seeks to challenge physical accessibility barriers including curbs without ramps, narrow doors, and fixtures placed too high.
key_holding: The court dismissed Bowman's § 3604(f)(2) claims for lack of standing because he failed to plead that he uses a wheelchair or was impeded by the alleged accessibility barriers during his property tour, instead merely reciting statutory requirements without connecting them to his own injury.
brief_summary: Dana Bowman, a disabled veteran who lost both legs, sued SWBC Real Estate Services and Jordan Foster Construction alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on physical accessibility barriers he encountered while touring their apartment complexes as a prospective tenant. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(1) for lack of standing, finding Bowman failed to plead that he uses a wheelchair or was personally impeded by the barriers, merely reciting statutory accessibility requirements without showing concrete injury to himself.
key_cases_cited: Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins, 578 U.S. 330 (2016)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessibility barriers in multifamily dwelling common and public use areas, including curbs without ramps on exterior sidewalks, inaccessible toilet and sink dimensions, narrow doors and pantry doors, thermostats and mailboxes placed too high on walls
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff lacked Article III standing because he failed to allege an injury in fact. Although FHA testers can sue under § 3604(f)(2), plaintiff did not plead that he used a wheelchair or that his access to or use of facilities was actually impeded. Plaintiff cannot sue on behalf of abstract class members; he must allege concrete, particularized harm to himself.

case_name: Ronald S. Deitch v. Medstar Medical Group, Southern Maryland LLC, et al.
subsidy_program: St. Mary's County Department of Housing affordable housing program for disabled veterans
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged disability discrimination stemming from landlord's allegedly false police report that led to his arrest and eviction; accommodation request not clearly articulated.
key_holding: The court dismissed the FHA claim because Deitch's own allegations negated any plausible inference that the adverse action (false police report leading to eviction) was taken because of his disability—it was allegedly motivated by retaliation for his activism against the landlord unrelated to his disability.
brief_summary: Ronald Deitch, a tenant with multi system atrophy, sued his former landlord Habitat America, LLC and its employees, alleging they made a false police report (claiming he was building a bomb) in retaliation for his complaints about the lease and assistance to neighbors, which led to his arrest. The court granted the Habitat defendants' motion to dismiss, finding Deitch failed to state an FHA discrimination claim because his own allegations established the alleged retaliation was unrelated to his disability.
key_cases_cited: Thomas v. The Salvation Army of S. Territory, 841 F.3d 632 (4th Cir. 2016)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Indep. Hous. Srvs. of S.F. v. Fillmore Ctr. Assocs., 840 F. Supp. 1328 (N.D. Cal. 1993)
Want v. Shindle Props., LLC, No. PWG-18-2833 (D. Md. Oct. 29, 2018)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges removal from apartment based on false police report; does not allege failure to provide a specific accommodation.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that the adverse action (false report leading to eviction) was taken because of his disability. Plaintiff's own allegations show the false report was made in retaliation for conduct unrelated to his handicap—holding defendants to the lease and helping neighbors fight the landlord. No sufficient nexus of causation between handicap and adverse action.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Intentional infliction of emotional distress (state tort); § 1983 due process claim; ADA Title III discrimination claim
fha_claims.reasoning: IIED claim fails because making a false police report is not extreme and outrageous conduct under Maryland law and plaintiff does not allege severe emotional distress caused by Habitat defendants. § 1983 claim fails because Habitat defendants are not persons acting under color of state law. ADA Title III claim fails because residential apartment complex is not a place of public accommodation and plaintiff does not allege discrimination because of disability.

source_file: 11267651 - COMMISSION ON HUMAN RIGHTS & OPPORTUNITIES EX REL. PIZZOFERRATO v. THE MANSIONS,
case_name: Commission on Human Rights and Opportunities ex rel. Wendy Pizzoferrato et al. v. The Mansions, LLC et al.
accommodation_description: Request for accommodation of Wendy's no-pet policy to keep two emotional support dogs for her generalized anxiety disorder
key_holding: The plaintiffs failed to prove that two emotional support dogs were necessary (indispensable) for Wendy's equal use and enjoyment of the dwelling, as evidence that both dogs alleviated her anxiety in different ways merely demonstrated that both were helpful or preferable, which is insufficient to establish necessity under the FHA.
brief_summary: The Connecticut Commission on Human Rights and Opportunities and the Pizzoferratos sued The Mansions, LLC for housing discrimination under state fair housing laws, alleging the defendants constructively denied Wendy's request to keep two emotional support dogs as a reasonable accommodation for her anxiety. The trial court found for the plaintiffs, but the Appellate Court of Connecticut reversed, holding that plaintiffs failed to prove both dogs were necessary for Wendy's equal use and enjoyment of the dwelling, as evidence that both dogs alleviated her anxiety in different ways merely showed the accommodation was preferable, not indispensable.
key_cases_cited: Vorchheimer v. Philadelphian Owners Assn., 903 F.3d 107 (3d Cir. 2018)
Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condominium Assn., Inc., 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014)
Hollandale Apartments & Health Club, LLC v. Bonesteel, 173 App. Div. 3d 55 (N.Y. App. Div. 2019)
Howard v. HMK Holdings, LLC, 988 F.3d 1185 (9th Cir. 2021)
Davis v. Echo Valley Condominium Assn., 945 F.3d 483 (6th Cir. 2019)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request for accommodation of defendants' no-pets policy to allow two emotional support dogs (Chloe and Mitsie) for Wendy's generalized anxiety disorder
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court held that while Wendy established a disability (record of generalized anxiety disorder), the plaintiffs failed to prove that TWO emotional support dogs were necessary to afford her equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling. The court applied the 'necessity' standard requiring that an accommodation be essential and indispensable, not merely preferable. Evidence showed both dogs ameliorated her anxiety but in different ways; however, there was no evidence that one dog could not be effective or that both were required. The trial court improperly applied an overly broad definition of 'necessary' that included preference rather than requiring proof of essential need.

case_name: Jennifer Dixon v. Silva-Markham Partners and Koelbel & Co.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that her daughter Cesca be designated as a live-in aide to enable her to transfer from a one-bedroom to a two-bedroom apartment due to her autoimmune disease causing cognitive impairment and mobility limitations.
key_holding: The court found that Ms. Dixon failed to demonstrate a genuine dispute of material fact on her FHA claims because the undisputed evidence showed SMP engaged in the accommodation process by sending paperwork to her physician and working with her on rent balance issues, while her settlement of prior state court claims and the applicable statute of limitations barred many claims.
brief_summary: Jennifer Dixon sued Silva-Markham Partners and Koelbel & Co. (owner and manager of Ash Street Apartments in Denver, Colorado) alleging Fair Housing Act violations for disability discrimination, including failure to accommodate her request for a live-in aide and transfer to a two-bedroom unit, and a hostile housing environment. The magistrate judge recommended granting defendants' motion for summary judgment, finding that Dixon's FHA claims were barred by a prior settlement agreement or the statute of limitations, and that she failed to demonstrate triable issues on her disparate treatment and hostile environment claims.
key_cases_cited: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Cinnamon Hills Youth Crisis Ctr., Inc. v. Saint George City, 685 F.3d 917 (10th Cir. 2012)
Hatfield v. Cottages on 78th Cmty. Ass'n, No. 21-4035 (10th Cir. July 6, 2022)
Peterson v. Martinez, 707 F.3d 1197 (10th Cir. 2013)
Throupe v. Univ. of Denver, 988 F.3d 1243 (10th Cir. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested transfer from one-bedroom to two-bedroom apartment to accommodate live-in aide (her daughter Cesca) due to autoimmune disease causing cognitive impairment and mobility disability requiring use of cane or wheelchair.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish that defendants refused the accommodation. The undisputed facts show that SMP offered the two-bedroom unit and held it available until May 15, 2020, but plaintiff chose not to transfer because the Division of Housing declined to increase her rent subsidy. The decision not to transfer was plaintiff's choice, not a refusal by defendants. Additionally, the claim is time-barred as the matter was resolved in May 2020, outside the two-year statute of limitations period measured from June 22, 2020.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged intentional discrimination based on disability in connection with: (1) rent collection efforts in July-September 2020; (2) entries into plaintiff's apartment in February and July 2021; and (3) attempt to access medical records in April 2020.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie disparate treatment claim under the McDonnell-Douglas burden-shifting framework. She presented no direct evidence of differential treatment based on disability and no evidence that similarly situated non-disabled tenants received more favorable treatment regarding rent collection or apartment access. The rent collection emails reflected legitimate business purposes and professional communication. The apartment entries were authorized under the lease terms and were for maintenance purposes (furnace filter changes). Plaintiff's single comment from Duran about not needing an aide was insufficient to demonstrate pretext, particularly given the temporal distance from the alleged discriminatory acts.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation and interference with plaintiff's exercise of fair housing rights in requesting a live-in aide accommodation, including: (1) Duran's attempt to access medical records without consent; (2) Duran's comment that plaintiff did not need an aide; (3) rent collection efforts; and (4) entries into plaintiff's apartment.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a § 3617 retaliation claim. The undisputed facts show that Duran's actions were geared toward promoting, not interfering with, plaintiff's accommodation request. Duran sent accommodation paperwork to the physician to expedite the process during pandemic office closures. Duran worked with plaintiff to correct the outstanding rent balance through a payment plan. The entries into the apartment long post-dated the accommodation process and were authorized under lease terms. Plaintiff presented no evidence that defendants treated her differently from other residents or that they were motivated by intent to discriminate. The conduct constituted 'trivial or isolated disputes' insufficient to meet the § 3617 standard requiring conduct that a person of normal fortitude would view as coercive, intimidating, or threatening.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Colorado Revised Statute § 38-12-103 claim for failure to return security deposit within 30 days of move-out.
fha_claims.reasoning: Defendants complied with Colorado law requiring return of security deposit within 30 days. The undisputed facts show that defendants retained the $450 deposit to cover $120 in unpaid rent and $841 in cleaning and removal costs, which were properly documented in the Final Account Statement. Defendants mailed the statement to plaintiff's last-known address (Ash Street) within 30 days of move-out on August 6, 2021. Colorado law requires only mailing to the last-known address, not actual receipt. Plaintiff provided no forwarding address and failed to contest the accuracy of the charges or the photographs documenting the condition of the unit.

source_file: 2769474_2015_Batista v. Cooperativa De Vivienda Jardines De San Ignacio_ca1
case_name: Priscilla Batista v. Cooperativa de Vivienda Jardines de San Ignacio, et al.
accommodation_description: Batista requested to remain in her three-bedroom apartment rather than transfer to a two-bedroom unit, asserting that her disabilities require separate rooms for physical therapy, reading, and crafts, and that she cannot tolerate the noise levels in the proposed two-bedroom unit.
key_holding: The court affirmed summary judgment for the Cooperativa on the reasonable accommodation claim because the Section 8 subsidy determination that made Batista ineligible for the three-bedroom unit was made by the Puerto Rico Housing Finance Authority, not the private landlord, and the requested accommodation of continuing to receive a Section 8 subsidy for a unit she no longer qualified for was not a reasonable accommodation the Cooperativa could provide.
brief_summary: Priscilla Batista, a disabled tenant with osteoporosis, fibromyalgia, and other conditions, sued a San Juan housing cooperative and its board members alleging the cooperative failed to reasonably accommodate her disability by allowing her to remain in her three-bedroom apartment when Section 8 over-housing rules required her to transfer to a smaller unit. The First Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the cooperative on the accommodation claim, holding that because the Section 8 subsidy determination rested with the Puerto Rico Housing Finance Authority rather than the private landlord, the requested accommodation was not one the cooperative could reasonably provide.
key_cases_cited: Astralis Condo. Ass'n v. Sec'y, U.S. Dep't of Hous. & Urban Dev., 620 F.3d 62 (1st Cir. 2010)
Salute v. Stratford Greens Garden Apartments, 136 F.3d 293 (2d Cir. 1998)
Howard v. City of Beavercreek, 276 F.3d 802 (6th Cir. 2002)
Smith & Lee Assocs. v. City of Taylor, 102 F.3d 781 (6th Cir. 1996)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested to remain in her three-bedroom apartment (Unit 1714A) rather than transfer to a smaller two-bedroom unit, claiming her disability (osteoporosis, fibromyalgia, severe fatigue, depression, migraines, blood anemia, colon irritability, and hypersensitivity to sound) required the larger unit for physical therapy, reading, and crafts, and that the proposed two-bedroom unit was noisier.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the reasonableness standard and found that plaintiff failed to establish a reasonable accommodation because the Cooperativa (private landlord) is not responsible for administering Section 8 subsidies—that responsibility lies with the Puerto Rico Housing Finance Authority. The requested accommodation (continued occupancy in an over-sized unit) was not reasonable because it required the private landlord to provide or reinstate a federal subsidy, which is beyond the landlord's authority and would impose an undue financial burden. The court noted plaintiff's inability to pay rent arose solely from loss of federal rental support, not from any Cooperativa policy.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the disparate treatment framework requiring either direct evidence or indirect evidence of discriminatory intent based on disability. Although the court assumed plaintiff's factual allegations were true (multiple claims against her, disallowing voting, preventing visitors, threatening eviction), plaintiff produced no evidence that disability-based discriminatory purpose motivated the Cooperativa's actions. Plaintiff's own argument framed the Cooperativa's intent as eliminating Section 8 beneficiaries, not discriminating based on disability status.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged the Cooperativa retaliated against her after she prevailed in a prior HUD proceeding regarding denial of a key to the garbage depository, by initiating collection proceedings and denying her reasonable accommodation request.
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court dismissed the retaliation claim for lack of jurisdiction, interpreting it as an attempt to enforce a Consent Order (which only the appellate court can enforce under 42 U.S.C. § 3612(m)). The appellate court reversed, holding that the complaint's reference to 42 U.S.C. § 3613(c)(1) (private enforcement) and § 3617 (retaliation provision) indicates plaintiff was asserting a retaliation claim under the Fair Housing Act's anti-retaliation guarantee, not seeking to enforce the Consent Order itself. The district court has jurisdiction to decide the merits of the retaliation claim, and the case was remanded for that determination.

source_file: 2770244_2015_Eddy Jean Philippeaux v. Apartment Investment and Management Company_ca11
case_name: Eddy Jean Philippeaux v. Apartment Investment and Management Company
accommodation_description: Disabled veteran requested an assigned, handicapped parking space on the ground level of the parking garage as a reasonable accommodation for his mobility limitations following hernia surgery.
key_holding: The requested ground-level parking space was not a reasonable accommodation because it would provide preferential treatment over non-disabled residents, and imposing the obligation to break a third-party lease or pay valet fees would constitute an undue financial burden on the landlord.
brief_summary: A disabled veteran sued his apartment complex alleging the landlord violated the Fair Housing Act by refusing to assign him a ground-level handicapped parking space as a reasonable accommodation. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed dismissal, holding that the request was not reasonable because it would grant preferential treatment over all other residents and impose an undue financial burden on the landlord who had leased the ground level to a third-party valet vendor.
key_cases_cited: Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014)
Schwarz v. City of Treasure Island, 544 F.3d 1201 (11th Cir. 2008)
Loren v. Sasser, 309 F.3d 1296 (11th Cir. 2002)
Dixon v. Hallmark Cos., 627 F.3d 849 (11th Cir. 2010)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Assigned, handicapped parking space on the ground level of the parking garage at no cost or reduced rate
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the four-element reasonable accommodation test and concluded that the requested accommodation was not reasonable because: (1) it would provide preferential treatment compared to non-disabled residents; and (2) it would impose an undue financial burden on the landlord by requiring breach of a lease with a third-party valet vendor or payment of hourly valet fees. Equal opportunity does not require preferential treatment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the prima facie retaliation framework and found that plaintiff failed to establish protected activity because his belief that denial of the ground-level parking space violated the FHA was not objectively reasonable. The eviction was triggered by failure to pay rent, not by the accommodation request, and handicapped spaces were available on upper levels.

case_name: Glenn J. Hopkins v. Springfield Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Hopkins alleged the Housing Authority failed to accommodate his disability when it reduced his Section 8 subsidy, though the specific accommodation requested is not detailed in the record.
key_holding: The Seventh Circuit affirmed dismissal because Hopkins failed to allege differential treatment based on disability—he conceded the subsidy reduction was for a nondiscriminatory reason—and because he did not allege that he requested any accommodation or that a requested accommodation was linked to his disability.
brief_summary: Glenn Hopkins, a Section 8 voucher recipient, appealed the dismissal of his claims against the Springfield Housing Authority alleging disability discrimination and failure to accommodate under the FHA and ADA after his housing subsidy was reduced. The Seventh Circuit affirmed, finding Hopkins failed to state a discrimination claim because he conceded the reduction was based on a change in household size rather than disability, and failed to state an accommodation claim because he did not allege he requested any accommodation linked to his disability.
key_cases_cited: Wigginton v. Bank of Am. Corp., 770 F.3d 521 (7th Cir. 2014)
Kampmier v. Emeritus Corp., 472 F.3d 930 (7th Cir. 2007)
Stone v. City of Indianapolis Pub. Utils. Div., 281 F.3d 640 (7th Cir. 2002)
Logan v. Wilkins, 644 F.3d 577 (7th Cir. 2011)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unspecified accommodation related to disability; plaintiff alleged Housing Authority failed to accommodate his disability when it reduced his Section 8 housing subsidy based on undisclosed income
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege a reasonable accommodation claim because he did not allege that he sought any accommodation or that a requested accommodation was linked to his disability. The complaint did not identify the specific disability or any accommodation request.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's disparate treatment claim lacked an essential element: that someone else was treated differently. Plaintiff conceded the Housing Authority reduced his subsidy for a nondiscriminatory reason (household size change), and he did not allege he was treated differently than other voucher recipients because of his disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Retaliation claim failed because the Housing Authority reduced plaintiff's subsidy and ordered repayment before he complained to Senator Durbin and HUD, breaking the temporal nexus required for retaliation. Additionally, plaintiff did not explain why the subsequent apartment inspections constituted adverse actions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act § 12132 (discrimination), ADA § 12203(a) (retaliation), 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (conspiracy to violate ADA and FHA rights), state law claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff could not state ADA discrimination or retaliation claims because the subsidy reduction was based on household membership change, not disability or protected activity. Section 1983 conspiracy claim failed because plaintiff had no underlying viable claim under the ADA or FHA. District court properly declined supplemental jurisdiction over state-law claims after dismissing all federal claims.

source_file: 2803230_2015_Forziano v. Indep. Grp. Home Living Program, Inc._ca2
case_name: Forziano v. Indep. Grp. Home Living Program, Inc.
accommodation_description: Developmentally disabled married couple sought to cohabitate in one of the defendants' publicly funded group homes, requesting waiver of the policy prohibiting couples from cohabitating.
key_holding: The court affirmed dismissal because plaintiffs lacked standing to seek permanent injunctive relief (they had since obtained alternative placement at East End Disability Associates) and could not recover damages for non-intentional FHA violations, and also rejected their intentional discrimination claims because defendants did not provide cohabitation benefits to anyone.
brief_summary: Paul Forziano and Hava Samuels, a developmentally disabled married couple represented by their guardians, sued Independent Group Home Living Program, Maryhaven Center of Hope, and New York State officials for denying their request to cohabitate in one of the defendants' publicly funded group homes, alleging violations of the ADA, Rehabilitation Act, FHA, and other laws. The Second Circuit affirmed dismissal of all claims, holding that plaintiffs lacked standing to seek injunctive relief (having since obtained alternative placement) and could not recover damages for non-intentional discrimination claims, and alternatively that the intentional discrimination claims failed because cohabitation was not provided to any couples.
key_cases_cited: McElwee v. Cnty. of Orange, 700 F.3d 635 (2d Cir. 2012)
Tsombanidis v. W. Haven Fire Dep't, 352 F.3d 565 (2d Cir. 2003)
Rodriguez v. City of New York, 197 F.3d 611 (2d Cir. 1999)
Doe v. Pfrommer, 148 F.3d 73 (2d Cir. 1998)
Sybalski v. Indep. Grp. Home Living Program, Inc., 546 F.3d 255 (2d Cir. 2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege intentional discrimination because cohabitation was not provided to any couples in the defendant group homes, so defendants could not have discriminated against plaintiffs based on disability by denying a benefit provided to no one.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Ability to cohabitate as a married couple in one of the defendants' group home facilities
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs lacked standing to seek injunctive relief (the only available remedy for non-intentional violations of the ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and FHA) because after filing suit they obtained residential placement at East End where they received all requested services, making any future harm speculative and insufficient to confer standing.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II, Rehabilitation Act § 504, § 1983 Medicaid Act and Fourteenth Amendment claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs' § 1983 damages claims against the State were barred by the Eleventh Amendment; claims against IGHL and Maryhaven failed because plaintiffs did not plausibly allege state action; and plaintiffs lacked standing to seek injunctive relief, the only available remedy under the ADA and Rehabilitation Act.

case_name: Rodriguez v. Village Green Realty, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs sought to remain in their rental housing and not be forced to relocate due to their minor child A.R.'s disability; no formal accommodation request was made as the dispute arose from discriminatory text messages.
key_holding: The Second Circuit held that there was sufficient evidence for a reasonable factfinder to conclude that A.R. qualifies as disabled under the FHA, and that the district court erred in granting summary judgment for defendants on claims that the landlord's agent made housing unavailable and imposed different terms because of disability.
brief_summary: Heidi and Juan Rodriguez, parents of minor child A.R. who has autism and epilepsy, sued Village Green Realty, Inc. and its agent Blanca Aponte under the FHA, alleging disability discrimination when Aponte sent text messages indicating the new property owner would not rent to them because of A.R.'s medical condition. The Second Circuit vacated summary judgment for defendants, holding that sufficient evidence existed that A.R. is disabled under the FHA and that Aponte's statements indicating a preference against renting to tenants with A.R.'s disability could support claims under §§ 3604(f)(1), (f)(2), (c), and (d).
key_cases_cited: Ragin v. New York Times Co., 923 F.2d 995 (2d Cir. 1991)
Toyota Motor Mfg., Ky., Inc. v. Williams, 534 U.S. 184 (2002)
School Bd. of Nassau Cnty., Fla. v. Arline, 480 U.S. 273 (1987)
Reeves v.升降床 Corp., 140 F.3d 147 (2d Cir. 1998)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Made housing unavailable on the basis of disability
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed the district court's grant of summary judgment, holding that there was sufficient evidence that A.R. qualifies as disabled under the FHA (either actually disabled or regarded as disabled), creating a genuine dispute of material fact precluding summary judgment on the claim that defendants made housing unavailable based on disability under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(1).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Provided different terms, conditions, and privileges of rental housing on the basis of disability
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed the district court's grant of summary judgment on the claim that defendants discriminated in the terms, conditions, and privileges of rental housing under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(2), based on the same finding that A.R. qualifies as disabled and that genuine disputes of material fact exist regarding the defendants' discriminatory conduct.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Expressed a preference, limitation, or discrimination based on disability in statements regarding housing
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed the district court's dismissal of the § 3604(c) claim, holding that statements directed at an individual may violate the FHA's prohibition against statements indicating a preference or discrimination based on handicap even if the individual is not disabled under the FHA, and that an ordinary listener could understand Aponte's statements as classifying A.R. as disabled and indicating discrimination on that basis.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Misrepresented the availability of rental housing on the basis of disability
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed the district court's dismissal of the § 3604(d) claim, holding that the 'ordinary listener' standard does not apply to misrepresentation claims under § 3604(d), and that the 'actually disabled' or 'regarded as disabled' standards apply instead; because sufficient evidence exists that A.R. is disabled, the claim survives summary judgment.

source_file: 2809229_2015_Dick Lalowski v. City of Des Plaines_ca7

fha_claims.accommodation_description: First Amendment retaliation claim under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 and Illinois Administrative Review Law claim
fha_claims.disposition: Summary Judgment (affirmed on § 1983 claim; vacated and remanded on administrative review claim)
fha_claims.reasoning: On appeal, the court affirmed summary judgment on the First Amendment retaliation claim, holding that none of Lalowski's statements were constitutionally protected under the Connick-Pickering test because the state's interests in running an efficient police department outweighed his speech interests under the Pickering balancing test. The court vacated and remanded the administrative review claim because the district court failed to comply with Rule 56(f) procedural requirements by granting summary judgment sua sponte without notice or opportunity to brief.

source_file: 2811844_2015_Texas Dept. of Housing and Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc._scotus
case_name: Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc.
court: SUPREME COURT OF THE UNITED STATES
accommodation_description: No individual accommodation request; ICP, a nonprofit housing organization, brought a disparate-impact challenge to TDHCA's allocation of low-income housing tax credits allegedly perpetuating racial segregation
key_holding: The Supreme Court held that disparate-impact claims are cognizable under the Fair Housing Act, adopting a robust causality requirement and limiting liability to policies that are artificial, arbitrary, and unnecessary barriers, but remanded for the Fifth Circuit to reconsider the merits using the proper burden-shifting framework under HUD's regulation.
brief_summary: The Inclusive Communities Project sued the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs alleging that its allocation of low-income housing tax credits perpetuated racial segregation by concentrating credits in predominantly black inner-city areas rather than predominantly white suburban neighborhoods. The Supreme Court affirmed that disparate-impact claims are cognizable under the Fair Housing Act, establishing important limitations including a robust causality requirement and requiring that plaintiffs identify a specific policy causing the disparity, while remanding for proper application of HUD's burden-shifting framework.
key_cases_cited: Griggs v. Duke Power Co., 401 U. S. 424 (1971)
Smith v. City of Jackson, 544 U. S. 228 (2005)
Ricci v. DeStefano, 557 U. S. 557 (2009)
Huntington v. Huntington Branch, NAACP, 488 U. S. 15 (1988)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U. S. 432 (1985)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The Supreme Court held that disparate-impact claims are cognizable under the Fair Housing Act under §§ 804(a) and 805(a). The Court applied the Griggs/Smith framework, finding that the FHA's results-oriented language ('otherwise make unavailable' and 'discriminate') encompasses disparate-impact liability, consistent with statutory purpose and Congress's 1988 ratification of such claims. The case was affirmed and remanded for application of the proper burden-shifting framework.

case_name: Marcia L. Jackson v. Park Place Condominiums Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: This is a race-based hostile housing environment claim, not a disability accommodation request; Ms. Jackson alleged the HOA discriminated against her because of her race through mailbox delays, noise complaints, and other incidents.
key_holding: The Tenth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the HOA because Ms. Jackson failed to present sufficient evidence that the alleged harassment (delayed mailbox name, noise complaints, decal theft, nameplate removal) was based on her race rather than legitimate property management concerns.
brief_summary: Marcia L. Jackson, an African-American woman, sued Park Place Condominiums Association alleging racial discrimination and a hostile housing environment during her tenancy, claiming the HOA harassed her because of her race through mailbox delays, noise complaints, and property incidents. The Tenth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the HOA, finding Jackson failed to present sufficient evidence that the alleged harassment was motivated by race rather than legitimate property management concerns.
key_cases_cited: Honce v. Vigil, 1 F.3d 1085 (10th Cir. 1993)
Asbury v. Brougham, 866 F.2d 1276 (10th Cir. 1989)
Johnson v. Weld Cty., Colo., 594 F.3d 1202 (10th Cir. 2010)
Morris v. City of Colo. Springs, 666 F.3d 654 (10th Cir. 2012)
Hampton v. Dillard Department Stores, Inc., 247 F.3d 1091 (10th Cir. 2001)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie case of hostile housing environment under the Fair Housing Act § 3604(b) because she could not show that the alleged harassment was based on her race (no racial slurs, no direct reference to race, and the 'loud black music' comment was about volume, not race) and could not show the harassment altered the conditions of her housing by unreasonably interfering with use and enjoyment (isolated and minor incidents over months, including mailbox delays, nameplate removal, and noise complaints, do not rise to the level of unlawful harassment).

source_file: 2827459_2015_Anderson Ex Rel. C.A. v. City of Blue Ash_ca6
case_name: Ingrid Anderson, individually and parent on behalf of C.A.; Housing Opportunities Made Equal, Inc. v. City of Blue Ash
accommodation_description: Request to keep a miniature horse at residence as a service animal for C.A., who has disabilities affecting her balance and mobility, enabling independent recreation and exercise in her backyard.
key_holding: The Sixth Circuit reversed summary judgment for the City on the FHAA reasonable accommodation claim, finding genuine factual disputes whether a miniature horse was necessary to afford C.A. equal opportunity to use and enjoy her dwelling and whether permitting it was reasonable, while affirming summary judgment for the City on ADA intentional discrimination and FHAA disparate treatment and impact claims.
brief_summary: Ingrid Anderson, on behalf of her disabled daughter C.A., and Housing Opportunities Made Equal sued the City of Blue Ash, Ohio, challenging the City's ordinance banning horses from residential property and seeking a reasonable accommodation under the Fair Housing Amendments Act to keep a miniature horse as a service animal at their home. The Sixth Circuit reversed the district court's grant of summary judgment to the City on the reasonable accommodation claim, finding genuine disputes of material fact regarding necessity and reasonableness, while affirming summary judgment for the City on ADA intentional discrimination and FHAA disparate treatment and impact claims.
key_cases_cited: Smith & Lee Assocs. v. City of Taylor, Mich., 102 F.3d 781 (6th Cir. 1996)
Hollis v. Chestnut Bend Homeowners Ass'n, 760 F.3d 531 (6th Cir. 2014)
Howard v. City of Beavercreek, 276 F.3d 802 (6th Cir. 2002)
HDC, LLC v. City of Ann Arbor, 675 F.3d 608 (6th Cir. 2012)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to keep a miniature horse (Ellie) at plaintiff's residential property as a service animal to assist C.A. with mobility, balance, and independent recreation in her backyard
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether the miniature horse was individually trained to perform tasks for C.A.'s disability and whether the four ADA assessment factors (type/size/weight, handler control, housebreaking, safety) were satisfied. The court reversed summary judgment, finding the reasonableness inquiry was highly fact-specific and could not be resolved on the record before trial.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claim that the City intentionally discriminated against C.A. based on her disability when enacting and enforcing Ordinance 2013-1
fha_claims.reasoning: Under the McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework, the court found that even viewing facts in plaintiff's favor, the evidence showed the City's actions were motivated by citizen complaints about unsanitary conditions, not by discriminatory animus against C.A.'s disability. The sequence of events—initial complaints, Council's decision not to enforce after receiving physician's letter, subsequent health complaints, and ordinance with federal-law exception—was entirely consistent with legitimate, non-discriminatory response to sanitation concerns.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claim that Ordinance 2013-1 had a disparate impact on C.A. and other disabled individuals who require miniature horses
fha_claims.reasoning: The ordinance explicitly exempted animals protected by federal law, including those protected under the FHAA. By its own terms, the ordinance had less impact on disabled individuals relying on assistance animals than on the general population, defeating the disparate-impact claim which requires showing that disabled individuals suffered disproportionately.

case_name: Nina Shahin v. Andrew Rogan
accommodation_description: Application for home equity loan allegedly denied due to plaintiffs' national origin
key_holding: The Third Circuit affirmed dismissal of the Shahins' FHA and ECOA claims because the complaint failed to allege non-conclusory factual matter establishing a plausible inference that PNC Bank denied their loan application based on national origin discrimination.
brief_summary: Nina and Mazen Shahin sued PNC Bank and branch managers alleging that the bank discriminated against them on the basis of national origin in denying a home equity loan, in violation of the Fair Housing Act and Equal Credit Opportunity Act. The Third Circuit affirmed the District Court's dismissal of the FHA/ECOA claims, finding the complaint failed to state plausible facts supporting an inference of discrimination, though the court vacated and remanded for the plaintiffs to potentially amend their TILA claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Tex. Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Cmties. Project, Inc.
16630 Southfield Ltd. P'ship v. Flagstar Bank

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of home equity loan based on national origin
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint's allegation that defendants were 'well aware of the Plaintiffs' foreign origins' and treated them poorly does not plausibly establish an inference of discrimination under the FHA § 3604(a) or ECOA. At the Rule 12(b)(6) stage, the complaint must contain non-conclusory factual allegations sufficient to nudge the claim from conceivable to plausible; bare assertions of discriminatory intent based on national origin are insufficient.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Closure of all bank accounts allegedly in retaliation for loan application
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint does not plausibly allege that the closure of accounts constituted retaliation under FHA § 3617 for exercising FHA rights. The allegations lack non-conclusory factual support for a causal connection between any protected activity and the alleged adverse action.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: RESPA § 2604(c)-(d) Good Faith Estimate disclosure requirements; TILA § 1640 disclosure requirements; ECOA § 1691(a) credit discrimination
fha_claims.reasoning: RESPA § 2604(c)-(d) claims were affirmed as dismissed because no private right of action exists under those sections. TILA claims were vacated and remanded because the complaint could be construed as alleging failure to provide required disclosures, but the complaint does not allege actual damages linked to the disclosure failure, and statutory damages eligibility is unclear at the pleading stage. The court remanded for opportunity to amend unless amendment would be futile.

source_file: 2832679_2015_City of Miami v. Bank of America Corp._ca11
case_name: City of Miami v. Wells Fargo & Co.
accommodation_description: This case involves discriminatory mortgage lending claims (redlining and reverse redlining), not a reasonable accommodation request under § 3604(f)(3)(B).
key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal of Miami's FHA claim, finding the City had Article III standing, fell within the FHA's zone of interests, and adequately pled proximate cause, while affirming dismissal of the state law unjust enrichment claim.
brief_summary: The City of Miami sued Wells Fargo alleging the bank engaged in discriminatory mortgage lending by targeting Black and Latino borrowers for predatory loans (redlining and reverse redlining), causing increased foreclosures that reduced property tax revenue and increased municipal costs. The Eleventh Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding the City had Article III standing, the FHA's zone of interests extends as broadly as Article III permits, and the City adequately alleged proximate cause between Wells Fargo's discriminatory lending and the City's financial injuries.
key_cases_cited: Gladstone Realtors v. Village of Bellwood, 441 U.S. 91 (1979)
Trafficante v. Metropolitan Life Insurance, 409 U.S. 205 (1972)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)
Nasser v. City of Homewood, 671 F.2d 432 (11th Cir. 1982)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed the district court's dismissal on standing and proximate cause grounds, holding that the City has Article III standing under Gladstone Realtors v. Village of Bellwood and that the FHA's zone of interests extends as broadly as permitted by Article III. The court found the City adequately alleged proximate cause linking the Bank's discriminatory lending to reduced tax revenue.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed the district court's dismissal of the disparate impact claim on the same standing and proximate cause grounds, finding the City adequately alleged that the Bank's facially neutral lending practices had a disproportionate impact on minority borrowers and neighborhoods, resulting in elevated foreclosure rates.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unjust enrichment claim under Florida law
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court affirmed dismissal of the unjust enrichment claim, holding that missing tax revenue is not a benefit conferred on the Bank and that municipal expenditures are not recoverable under Florida law without express legislative authorization, nor are they direct benefits as required for unjust enrichment.

source_file: 2832680_2015_City of Miami v. Wells Fargo _ Co._ca11
case_name: City of Miami v. Citigroup Inc.
accommodation_description: This is not a reasonable accommodation case; it is a discriminatory lending case where the City of Miami alleges Citigroup engaged in redlining and reverse redlining, targeting minority borrowers for predatory loans in violation of the FHA.
key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal of the City's FHA claims, holding that (1) the City had Article III standing based on lost tax revenue from foreclosed properties, (2) the FHA's zone of interests extends as broadly as Article III permits, and (3) the City adequately alleged proximate cause; however, the court affirmed dismissal of the state law unjust enrichment claim.
brief_summary: The City of Miami sued Citigroup Inc. and affiliated entities under the Fair Housing Act, alleging the bank engaged in discriminatory mortgage lending by targeting Black and Latino borrowers for predatory loans, resulting in higher foreclosure rates that reduced the City's property tax base. The Eleventh Circuit reversed the dismissal of the FHA claims, holding the City had standing and adequately alleged proximate cause under the FHA, but affirmed dismissal of the state law unjust enrichment claim.
key_cases_cited: Gladstone, Realtors v. Village of Bellwood, 441 U.S. 91 (1979)
Trafficante v. Metropolitan Life Insurance, 409 U.S. 205 (1972)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)
Nasser v. City of Homewood, 671 F.2d 432 (11th Cir. 1982)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed the district court's dismissal on standing and proximate cause grounds, holding that the City has Article III standing under Gladstone and that the FHA's zone of interests extends as broadly as Article III permits. The court found the City adequately alleged proximate cause at the pleading stage and remanded for further proceedings.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed the district court's dismissal of the disparate impact claim on the same standing and proximate cause grounds applicable to the intentional discrimination claim, finding the City's statistical allegations of disproportionate foreclosure rates in minority neighborhoods adequately pleaded a disparate impact theory.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unjust enrichment claim under Florida law
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court affirmed dismissal of the unjust enrichment claim, holding that the City failed to allege that it conferred a direct benefit on the Bank and that municipal expenditures for governmental services are not recoverable benefits under Florida law absent express legislative authorization.

source_file: 2832681_2015_City of Miami v. Bank of America Corporation_ca11
case_name: City of Miami v. Bank of America Corporation
accommodation_description: This is not a reasonable accommodation case; it involves claims of discriminatory mortgage lending practices targeting minority borrowers resulting in foreclosures that harmed the City.
key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal of Miami's FHA claims, finding the City has standing under the FHA's zone of interests, adequately alleged proximate cause, and may invoke the continuing violation doctrine for discriminatory lending claims.
brief_summary: The City of Miami sued Bank of America alleging the bank engaged in discriminatory mortgage lending by targeting black and Latino borrowers for predatory loans, causing minority property foreclosures that deprived the City of tax revenue and increased municipal costs. The Eleventh Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding the City has statutory standing under the FHA's broad zone of interests, adequately alleged proximate cause, and may invoke the continuing violation doctrine, while affirming dismissal of the state unjust enrichment claim.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dept. of Housing & Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 135 S. Ct. 2507 (2015)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed the district court's dismissal on zone of interests and proximate cause grounds, holding that the City has Article III standing and has adequately pled proximate causation under the FHA's foreseeability standard. The court found the City's allegations of intentional discrimination in mortgage lending practices sufficiently plausible to survive the motion to dismiss and remanded for further proceedings.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed the district court's dismissal of the disparate impact claim on the same grounds as the intentional discrimination claim. The court noted that the Supreme Court's decision in Texas Department of Housing & Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc. (2015) confirmed that disparate-impact claims are cognizable under the FHA, and remanded for the City to file an amended complaint consistent with that decision.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unjust enrichment claim under Florida law
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court affirmed the district court's dismissal of the unjust enrichment claim under Florida law, finding that the City failed to allege that it conferred a direct benefit on the Bank as required under Florida law. Municipal services and tax laws are not direct benefits conferred on the Bank, and the City failed to cite any Florida case supporting recovery of municipal expenditures on an unjust enrichment theory.

case_name: Brenda Miles v. David Wesley
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs, disabled tenants, challenge the Los Angeles Superior Court's consolidation of unlawful detainer (eviction) proceedings into centralized hub courts as having a disparate impact on disabled and minority residents who rely on public transportation.
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed dismissal under O'Shea abstention, holding that federal courts must abstain from interfering with state judicial administration because the plaintiffs' challenge to the court consolidation plan seeks heavy federal interference in the state's management of its shrinking judicial resources.
brief_summary: Brenda Miles, Dane Sullivan, and several nonprofit organizations sued the State of California and Los Angeles Superior Court officials, challenging the consolidation of unlawful detainer actions into centralized hub courts as having a disparate impact on disabled and minority residents. The Ninth Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal, holding that O'Shea abstention required federal courts to refrain from interfering with state judicial administration because the plaintiffs sought injunctive relief that would effectively place federal courts in the role of supervising state court resource allocation decisions.
key_cases_cited: O'Shea v. Littleton, 414 U.S. 488 (1974)
Younger v. Harris, 401 U.S. 37 (1971)
Tennessee v. Lane, 541 U.S. 509 (2004)
L.A. Cty. Bar Ass'n v. Eu, 979 F.2d 697 (9th Cir. 1992)
Courthouse News Serv. v. Planet, 750 F.3d 776 (9th Cir. 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Access to neighborhood unlawful detainer courthouses; consolidation of unlawful detainer cases into five hub courts across Los Angeles County
fha_claims.reasoning: The Ninth Circuit affirmed the district court's O'Shea abstention, holding that federal court interference with LASC's resource allocation and judicial administration would violate principles of federalism and comity. The court declined to reach the merits of the FHA disparate impact claim because the relief sought—an injunction preventing courthouse closures and requiring ongoing federal supervision—would constitute impermissible federal interference in state judicial administration.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II ADA, Rehabilitation Act § 504, First Amendment, Fifth Amendment, Fourteenth Amendment § 1983
fha_claims.reasoning: The court abstained from deciding all statutory and constitutional claims on O'Shea grounds, finding that adjudication would require ongoing federal supervision of state judicial resource allocation and administration, which violates federalism principles regardless of the underlying legal theory.

source_file: 2959750_2015_Texas Dept. of Housing and Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc._scotus
case_name: Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc.
court: SUPREME COURT OF THE UNITED STATES
accommodation_description: Tax credit allocation policy challenged as perpetuating segregated housing patterns through disparate impact rather than individual accommodation request
key_holding: Disparate-impact claims are cognizable under the Fair Housing Act, and the Court adopted HUD's burden-shifting regulation while cautioning that liability must be properly limited with robust causality requirements to avoid constitutional concerns and prevent liability based on mere statistical disparity.
brief_summary: The Inclusive Communities Project sued the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs alleging that the Department's disproportionate allocation of low-income housing tax credits to predominantly black inner-city areas rather than white suburbs violated the Fair Housing Act's disparate-impact prohibition. The Supreme Court held that disparate-impact claims are cognizable under the FHA, affirmed the Fifth Circuit's judgment remanding the case, and established limiting principles requiring robust causality requirements and caution against racial quotas in remedial orders.
key_cases_cited: Griggs v. Duke Power Co., 401 U.S. 424 (1971)
Smith v. City of Jackson, 544 U.S. 228 (2005)
Ricci v. DeStefano, 557 U.S. 557 (2009)
Huntington v. Huntington Branch, NAACP, 488 U.S. 15 (1988)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Allocation of low-income housing tax credits; plaintiff alleged defendant allocated too many credits to predominantly black inner-city areas and too few to predominantly white suburban neighborhoods
fha_claims.reasoning: Supreme Court held that disparate-impact claims are cognizable under the FHA based on the results-oriented language 'otherwise make unavailable' and 'discriminate,' consistent with Title VII and ADEA precedent. Court affirmed the Fifth Circuit's holding that disparate-impact claims are cognizable but remanded for application of proper burden-shifting framework with safeguards including robust causality requirement, legitimate interest defense, and race-neutral remedies.

case_name: Shana Freedman v. SunTrust Banks, Inc. and SunTrust Mortgage, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff challenged SunTrust's policy requiring loan applicants with disability income (SSDI) to obtain documentation from a doctor or Social Security confirming benefits would continue, which plaintiff alleged constituted disability discrimination in lending.
key_holding: The court lacked personal jurisdiction over defendants (Georgia and Virginia corporations without sufficient contacts with D.C.) and transferred the case to the Middle District of Florida in the interest of justice to avoid time-barring plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claims.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Shana Freedman, a Florida resident receiving Social Security Disability Insurance, sued SunTrust Banks and SunTrust Mortgage alleging that their policy requiring documentation that disability benefits would continue constituted disability discrimination under the Fair Housing Act and ECOA. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction and transferred the case to the Middle District of Florida in the interest of justice to prevent plaintiff's FHA claims from being time-barred.
key_cases_cited: Daimler AG v. Bauman, 134 S. Ct. 746 (2014)
Goodyear Dunlop Tire Operations, S.A. v. Brown, 131 S. Ct. 2846 (2011)
Goldlawr, Inc. v. Heiman, 369 U.S. 463 (1962)
Sinclair v. Kleindienst, 711 F.2d 291 (D.C. Cir. 1983)
Gorman v. Ameritrade Holding Corp., 293 F.3d 506 (D.C. Cir. 2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exception to SunTrust's policy requiring firm assurances that disability benefits would continue; plaintiff sought to submit loan application with SSDI income without providing documentation that Social Security Administration cannot provide (guarantee of future benefits continuation)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked personal jurisdiction over defendants under Daimler AG v. Bauman because defendants' contacts with the District of Columbia, though continuous and systematic, did not render them 'essentially at home' in the forum when viewed against their nationwide operations. The court transferred the case to the Middle District of Florida where jurisdiction and venue were proper, preserving plaintiff's FHA claims from statute of limitations bar.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA) claim regarding discriminatory lending practices based on disability status
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked personal jurisdiction over defendants and transferred the case to the Middle District of Florida where jurisdiction and venue were proper, preserving plaintiff's ECOA claims from statute of limitations bar.

source_file: 3004697_2015_County of Westchester v. United States Department of Housing _ Urban Development_ca2
case_name: County of Westchester v. U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development
accommodation_description: This is not an individual accommodation case; the County of Westchester challenges HUD's decision to withhold CPD grant funds because the County's Analysis of Impediments failed to adequately assess impediments to fair housing caused by local zoning ordinances.
key_holding: HUD acted within its statutory authority when it required Westchester County to analyze whether local zoning laws impeded fair housing and withheld CPD funds after the County's Analysis of Impediments was found inadequate and unsupported by the evidentiary record.
brief_summary: Westchester County appealed the District Court's grant of summary judgment upholding HUD's decision to withhold Community Planning and Development Formula Grant funds for fiscal years 2011, 2013, and 2014 because the County's required Analysis of Impediments failed to adequately assess whether local zoning ordinances impeded fair housing. The Second Circuit affirmed, holding that HUD acted within its statutory authority under the APA and applicable fair housing statutes by requiring jurisdictions receiving federal funds to analyze impediments to fair housing, including those caused by exclusionary zoning practices.
key_cases_cited: Tex. Dept. of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 135 S. Ct. 2507 (2015)
United States v. Yonkers Bd. of Educ., 837 F.2d 1181 (2d Cir. 1987)
Rufo v. Inmates of Suffolk Cty. Jail, 502 U.S. 367 (1992)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Administrative Procedure Act (APA) challenge to HUD's withholding of Community Planning and Development (CPD) funds for fiscal years 2011, 2013, and 2014; also challenges under 42 U.S.C. §§ 12705 and 12711 regarding HUD's authority to condition funding on zoning analysis and policy changes
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court affirmed the district court's grant of summary judgment for HUD, holding that HUD's decision to withhold CPD funds was neither arbitrary nor capricious under the APA, and that HUD did not violate §§ 12705 or 12711 by requiring the County to analyze whether local zoning laws impeded fair housing. HUD was authorized to require such analysis as a condition of federal funding and to reject the County's inadequate analysis based on the administrative record.

case_name: Anthony Hood; Princess Williams v. Tessa Pope, et al.
accommodation_description: N/A - case involves alleged race-based housing discrimination, not a disability accommodation request
key_holding: The Fifth Circuit affirmed dismissal because plaintiffs failed to allege sufficient facts to create a plausible inference that race was a significant factor in defendants' conduct; the speculative explanations for the in-person denial did not isolate race as a motivating factor.
brief_summary: Anthony Hood and Princess Williams sued Asset Plus Corporation and its employees alleging race-based housing discrimination under the Fair Housing Act, claiming they were denied an apartment based on their race and subsequently harassed. The Fifth Circuit affirmed dismissal, finding plaintiffs failed to state plausible claims because their allegations did not isolate race as a factor in the denial and subsequent conduct was unrelated to the initial refusal.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Lincoln v. Case, 340 F.3d 283 (5th Cir. 2003)
Cox v. City of Dallas, 430 F.3d 734 (5th Cir. 2005)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to allege sufficient facts to plausibly suggest that the in-person refusal to rent or subsequent actions were based on race. The discrepancy between the phone offer and in-person denial had many race-neutral explanations, and plaintiffs alleged nothing isolating race as a factor in the defendant's motivations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to state a claim under § 3617 because they voluntarily rented the apartment without alleging threatening or intimidating behavior, and they did not allege facts suggesting that post-move-in harassment was connected to exercise of FHA rights or that they had exercised any right granted under § 3604.

source_file: 3007122_2015_Mark Hibbert, Sr. v. Bellmawr Park Mutual Housing_ca3
case_name: Mark E. Hibbert, Sr. v. Bellmawr Park Mutual Housing Corporation
accommodation_description: Hibbert alleged defendants exploited his deafness to acquire his property through coercive conduct during the sale process.
key_holding: The Third Circuit affirmed summary judgment for defendants on the breach of contract claim, finding Hibbert voluntarily moved to Maine rather than being coerced, and separately waived the FHA and NJLAD claims by failing to brief them on appeal.
brief_summary: Mark Hibbert, a deaf resident of Bellmawr Park Mutual Housing Corporation, sued the housing corporation and its managers alleging breach of contract and Fair Housing Act violations, claiming defendants exploited his disability to coerce him into selling his property and moving to Maine. The Third Circuit affirmed summary judgment for defendants on appeal, finding Hibbert voluntarily moved after purchasing property in Maine, and separately held that Hibbert waived his FHA and NJLAD claims by failing to brief them on appeal.
key_cases_cited: Blunt v. Lower Merion Sch. Dist., 767 F.3d 247 (3d Cir. 2014)
Frederico v. Home Depot, 507 F.3d 188 (3d Cir. 2007)
Skretvedt v. E.I. DuPont De Nemours, 372 F.3d 193 (3d Cir. 2004)
Kost v. Kozakiewicz, 1 F.3d 176 (3d Cir. 1993)
Quiroga v. Hasbro, Inc., 943 F.2d 346 (3d Cir. 1991)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged defendants took advantage of his deafness and engaged in a scheme to acquire his property; no specific accommodation was requested or at issue.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff waived the FHA claim on appeal by failing to present any argument in support of it in his opening brief, and the District Court granted summary judgment on the merits. The record showed no evidence that defendants discriminated against plaintiff based on his disability; rather, plaintiff voluntarily moved to Maine after purchasing property there and receiving payment for improvements.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of contract claim under New Jersey law; NJLAD claim under N.J. Stat. Ann. § 10:5-12(g)(2).
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to present sufficient evidence of breach of contract or coercion. The record showed plaintiff voluntarily left his New Jersey property after signing an agreement to purchase Maine property, receiving $20,000 from McCormick for improvements, and using those funds to close on the Maine purchase. No evidence supported plaintiff's claim that defendants interfered with his peaceful use and enjoyment of the property or coerced him to leave.

case_name: Donavette Ely v. Mobile Housing Board
accommodation_description: Request for an extension of the term of her Section 8 housing voucher as a reasonable accommodation for her son's asthma
key_holding: The court affirmed summary judgment for the Board because Ely never explained to the Board that she needed a voucher extension as a reasonable accommodation for her son's disability, and mere knowledge of the son's asthma from a prior bedroom-size request did not obligate the Board to treat her extension request as an accommodation request.
brief_summary: Donavette Ely, a single mother, sued the Mobile Housing Board alleging the Board violated the Fair Housing Act by refusing to extend her Section 8 housing voucher as a reasonable accommodation for her son's asthma. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the Board, holding that Ely failed to establish a reasonable accommodation claim because she never informed the Board that she needed a voucher extension to accommodate her son's disability, and the Board therefore could not be liable for refusing to grant an accommodation it did not know was necessary.
key_cases_cited: Schwarz v. City of Treasure Island, 544 F.3d 1201 (11th Cir. 2008)
Keys Youth Servs., Inc. v. City of Olathe, 248 F.3d 1267 (10th Cir. 2001)
Bd. of Regents of State Colls. v. Roth, 408 U.S. 564 (1972)
Town of Castle Rock v. Gonzales, 545 U.S. 748 (2005)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Extension of housing voucher term to accommodate son's asthma disability; alternatively, increase in voucher amount
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to actually request a voucher extension as a reasonable accommodation for her son's disability; she never explained to the Board that the extension was necessary to accommodate the disability. Under FHA law, a plaintiff must actually request an accommodation and be refused to bring a reasonable accommodation claim, and the housing authority cannot be liable for refusing an accommodation it never knew was necessary.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (due process); HUD regulations 24 C.F.R. § 982.303, § 982.555; 42 U.S.C. § 1437d; Americans with Disabilities Act 42 U.S.C. § 12132; Rehabilitation Act 29 U.S.C. § 794
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff had no constitutionally protected property interest in the voucher extension because the voucher expired by its own terms and extensions were discretionary under HUD regulations; no constitutional entitlement by estoppel; HUD regulations do not require notice or hearing for denial of extension requests; regulations explicitly state PHA may grant extensions at its discretion and is not required to provide hearing for determination not to approve extension.

source_file: 3132420_2015_Anderson Group, LLC v. City of Saratoga Springs_ca2
case_name: The Anderson Group, LLC v. City of Saratoga Springs
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; developer TAG challenged city's zoning rezoning as having discriminatory disparate impact on African-Americans and families with children.
key_holding: The City waived its objection to inconsistencies in the 2010 jury verdict by failing to raise it before the jury was discharged, and any inconsistencies did not constitute fundamental error; however, the $900,000 developer fee portion of the damages award was impermissibly speculative and must be remitted to $100,000.
brief_summary: The Anderson Group (TAG), a real estate developer, sued the City of Saratoga Springs challenging the city's 2005 rezoning of TAG's property as having a disparate impact on African-Americans and families with children under the Fair Housing Act. The Second Circuit reinstated the 2010 jury verdict finding the City liable on the disparate impact claim, reversed the district court's order granting a new trial, and remanded for a new trial on damages only unless TAG accepted remittitur of the $1 million award to $100,000 because the $900,000 developer fee was too speculative.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dept. of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 135 S. Ct. 2507 (2015)
Story Parchment Co. v. Patterson Parchment Paper Co., 282 U.S. 555 (1931)
Casella v. Equifax Credit Info. Servs., 56 F.3d 469 (2d Cir. 1995)
Shcherbakovskiy v. Da Capo Al Fine, Ltd., 490 F.3d 130 (2d Cir. 2007)
Stampf v. Long Island R.R. Co., 761 F.3d 192 (2d Cir. 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed the district court's order for a new trial, holding that the City waived its inconsistency objection by failing to raise it before jury discharge. The court reinstated the July 2010 jury verdict finding the City liable on the disparate impact claim, applying the burden-shifting framework under which plaintiffs must prove substantial discriminatory impact and defendants must prove legitimate governmental interest with no less discriminatory alternative.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Perpetuation of segregation claim (subspecies of disparate impact)
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court held that the jury's verdict finding the City liable on disparate impact but not on perpetuation of segregation was not fundamentally inconsistent because Huntington Branch left open the possibility that a policy could be invalidated on one ground but not the other. The court remanded for a new trial on damages only, as the 2012 jury had found for the City on both claims.

case_name: Parham v. CIH Properties, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff made vague references to wanting a first-floor apartment and accessible parking, but the court found she failed to properly request or document any reasonable accommodation.
key_holding: Even assuming the ADA or FHA applied to private apartment complexes, plaintiff failed to demonstrate she had a qualifying disability, that defendants knew of it, or that she made a cognizable accommodation request that defendants denied.
brief_summary: Evelyn Parham sued her landlord alleging that her car with a handicap tag was improperly towed from the apartment complex parking lot and never returned; she brought claims for breach of contract, fraudulent misrepresentation, violations of the D.C. Consumer Protection Act, and reasonable accommodation under the ADA and FHA. The court granted summary judgment to defendants on all claims, finding that plaintiff failed to present competent evidence on any element of her claims, including that she made a cognizable request for reasonable accommodation under disability statutes.
key_cases_cited: Celotex Corp. v. Catrett
Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc.
Good Shepherd Manor Found., Inc. v. City of Momence
Flemmings v. Howard Univ.
Twin Towers Plaza Tenants Ass'n, Inc. v. Capitol Park Assocs., L.P.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation for disability-related parking needs; plaintiff alleged she requested a first-floor apartment and easy access parking space for years but defendants denied the request by towing her handicapped-tagged vehicle
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to present competent evidence of any of the four elements required for a reasonable accommodation claim: (1) she did not adequately establish a disability as defined by the FHA; (2) she did not demonstrate defendants knew or should have known of the disability; (3) she did not show an accommodation was necessary; and (4) most critically, she failed to demonstrate she made a specific request for accommodation that defendants denied. Her bare allegations of past car accidents, a handicap tag since 1998, and last-minute claims of written requests for first-floor apartment and easy access parking were insufficient to survive summary judgment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of contract, fraudulent misrepresentation, D.C. Consumer Protection Procedures Act, Americans with Disabilities Act Title III
fha_claims.reasoning: Breach of contract claim failed because plaintiff presented no evidence of a contract covering parking; the 1972 lease explicitly excluded parking. Fraudulent misrepresentation claim failed because plaintiff did not establish that the rental office employee knew the statement was false or made it with intent to deceive, and the inconvenience of a trip to the police station did not constitute the substantial pecuniary loss required. CPPA claim failed because the statute does not apply to landlord-tenant relations and the misrepresentation was not a 'trade practice' as defined. ADA Title III claim failed because private apartment complexes do not qualify as public accommodations.

source_file: 3171091_2016_Richard Wolf v. Bank of America, N.A., et a_ca5
case_name: Richard B. Wolf; Marcia A. Wolf v. Bank of America National Association; Marvin Blankenship; Kianie King; Jimmy Widdle; Phil Gonzalez
accommodation_description: Mortgage lending dispute where plaintiffs alleged discrimination but failed to specify any accommodation request related to disability.
key_holding: The Fifth Circuit affirmed dismissal because the Wolfs failed to allege discriminatory intent or a significant discriminatory effect required to state a Fair Housing Act claim.
brief_summary: Richard and Marcia Wolf sued Bank of America and several employees challenging the bank's refusal to refinance their residence and related foreclosure actions, asserting fraud, breach of contract, RICO, and Fair Housing Act claims. The Fifth Circuit affirmed dismissal, finding the Wolfs' complaint failed to state a claim because they did not allege discriminatory intent or a significant discriminatory effect as required under the Fair Housing Act.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Simms v. First Gibraltar Bank, 83 F.3d 1546 (5th Cir. 1996)
Martins v. BAC Home Loans Serv., L.P., 722 F.3d 249 (5th Cir. 2013)
Warren v. Bank of America, N.A., 566 F. App'x 379 (5th Cir. 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court affirmed dismissal of the FHA claim under the Iqbal/Twombly standard, finding that plaintiffs failed to allege either discriminatory intent or a significant discriminatory effect as required under 42 U.S.C. § 3604. The complaint's allegations regarding refinancing and note securitization do not plausibly state a discrimination claim based on a protected class.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fraud, breach of contract, RICO (18 U.S.C. § 1962)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court affirmed dismissal of fraud, breach of contract, and RICO claims under the Iqbal/Twombly standard. Plaintiffs failed to allege material misrepresentation (fraud), specific contractual breach or damages (breach of contract), or an enterprise and pattern of racketeering activity (RICO).

case_name: Dyan Hunt v. Aimco Properties, L.P.
accommodation_description: Dyan Hunt asked Aimco to allow the family to remain in their apartment while she arranged for offsite daytime care for her son Karl, requesting an exception to Aimco's apparent policy of non-renewing leases for tenants who make threats.
key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit reversed the dismissal of the reasonable accommodation claim, finding that the complaint adequately pleaded Dyan requested an accommodation by explaining Karl's disability-caused misunderstandings and offering to arrange offsite daytime care, and that Aimco refused to consider this accommodation, thereby failing to reasonably accommodate Karl's disability.
brief_summary: Dyan Hunt sued Aimco Properties on behalf of herself and her son Karl, who has Down Syndrome, alleging that Aimco violated the FHA by threatening eviction and refusing to renew their lease based on Karl's disability-related behavior (perceived threats stemming from his intellectual disability). The Eleventh Circuit reversed the dismissal, holding that the complaint adequately pleaded claims for making housing unavailable, discriminatory terms and conditions, and failure to reasonably accommodate Karl's disability by disregarding Dyan's explanation of his disability and her offer to arrange offsite daytime care as an alternative to eviction.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014)
Schwarz v. City of Treasure Island, 544 F.3d 1201 (11th Cir. 2008)
McDonald v. Verble, 622 F.2d 1227 (6th Cir. 1980)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court reversed the district court's dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6), holding that the Hunts adequately pleaded a disparate treatment claim under § 3604(f)(1) by alleging Karl has Down Syndrome, Aimco had actual knowledge of his disability, Aimco took adverse action (non-renewal of lease) because of the disability, and the Hunts were willing and qualified to continue renting. The court rejected the argument that the claim failed because the Hunts ultimately remained in the apartment, holding that the FHA protects renters from discriminatory actions that would lead to eviction but for an intervening cause.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court reversed the district court's dismissal of the § 3604(f)(2) claim for discriminating in terms, conditions, or privileges of rental.
