source_file: 4274256_2018_Collington v. District of Columbia Housing Authority_dcd
case_name: William Hugh Collington v. District of Columbia Housing Authority et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges defendants failed to comply with HUD pre-inspection guidelines resulting in leasing a substandard apartment, but does not request a specific accommodation.
key_holding: The complaint against HUD is dismissed for lack of standing since HUD does not administer Section 8 programs locally, and the FHA claim fails because the complaint does not allege discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, familial status, or national origin as required under 42 U.S.C. §§ 3604, 3605, 3606, or 3617.
brief_summary: William Hugh Collington, a District of Columbia resident participating in the Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher Program, sued the District of Columbia Housing Authority and HUD alleging that defendants failed to comply with pre-inspection guidelines, resulting in his leasing of a substandard apartment. The court dismissed the claims against HUD for lack of standing and dismissed the Fair Housing Act claim for failure to state a claim because the complaint did not allege discrimination based on any protected class covered by the FHA.
key_cases_cited: Kokkonen v. Guardian Life Ins. Co. of Am., 511 U.S. 375 (1994)
Honig v. Doe, 484 U.S. 305 (1988)
Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)
Haase v. Sessions, 835 F.2d 902 (D.C. Cir. 1987)
Robbins v. United States Dep't of Hous. & Urban Dev., 72 F. Supp. 3d 1 (D.D.C. 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged defendants failed to comply with HUD pre-inspection guidelines, resulting in leasing of substandard apartment
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege discrimination based on any protected class under the FHA (race, color, religion, sex, familial status, or national origin). The complaint alleged only a failure to comply with pre-inspection guidelines, which does not state a plausible FHA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claims against HUD under Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher Program administration
fha_claims.reasoning: HUD lacks subject matter jurisdiction because the Section 8 Program is administered by local housing authorities (DCHA), not HUD. HUD is not a party to housing assistance contracts and cannot provide relief for local implementation matters.

source_file: 4278555_2018_Holly Geraci v. Union Square Condominium Assoc_ca7
case_name: Holly B. Geraci v. Union Square Condominium Association
accommodation_description: Request to keep her dog as a reasonable accommodation for her PTSD diagnosis
key_holding: The Seventh Circuit affirmed the jury verdict for Union Square, finding no triable issue of fact as to whether the HOA's litigation updates and open forum constituted retaliatory conduct that would coerce, intimidate, threaten, or interfere with a person of reasonable fortitude, and upholding the district court's admission of expert testimony challenging whether Geraci had a qualifying handicap.
brief_summary: Holly Geraci sued Union Square Condominium Association alleging the HOA failed to accommodate her PTSD and retaliated against her for filing the lawsuit by publishing litigation updates and holding an open forum about the case. The jury returned a verdict for the HOA, and the Seventh Circuit affirmed, finding no evidence that the HOA's communications constituted retaliatory conduct and that the district court properly allowed expert testimony challenging whether Geraci had a qualifying handicap.
key_cases_cited: Burlington N. & Santa Fe Ry. v. White, 548 U.S. 53 (2006)
Stuhlmacher v. Home Depot U.S.A., Inc., 774 F.3d 405 (7th Cir. 2014)
Schneiker v. Fortis Ins. Co., 200 F.3d 1055 (7th Cir. 2000)
Dadian v. Vill. of Wilmette, 269 F.3d 831 (7th Cir. 2001)
Good Sheperd Manor Found., Inc. v. City of Momence, 323 F.3d 557 (7th Cir. 2003)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation for PTSD resulting from elevator incident; specific accommodation not detailed in opinion
fha_claims.reasoning: Jury found against plaintiff on failure to accommodate claim after trial. The court allowed defendant to present expert testimony challenging whether plaintiff qualified as handicapped under the FHA, which is a permissible defense to the first element of the reasonable accommodation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court affirmed the jury verdict on retaliation, finding no triable issue because the defendant's conduct (publishing litigation updates and holding an open forum to discuss the lawsuit) did not constitute coercion, intimidation, threat, or interference under § 3617 when evaluated from the perspective of a reasonable person. The conduct was merely factual representation of the public record and reasonable measures to inform co-owners.

source_file: 4303545_2018_Traci Berardelli v. Allied Services Institute of R_ca3

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission for M.B. to be accompanied by her service dog (Buddy) to school to alert during seizures and provide safety and comfort during epileptic episodes
fha_claims.disposition: Jury verdict for defendant; reversed on appeal
fha_claims.reasoning: The District Court gave erroneous jury instructions by requiring plaintiffs to prove reasonableness when, under the ADA service animal regulations applicable to the RA, the accommodation was per se reasonable as a matter of law absent enumerated exceptions. The court conflated the separate requirements of reasonableness and necessity. On remand, the appellate court found compelling evidence of necessity in the record and held that no reasonable jury could rule for the School if properly instructed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Pennsylvania Human Relations Act (PHRA) claim for failure to accommodate service animal; also Title III ADA claim (dismissed for lack of damages remedy)
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 56 (summary judgment granted on ADA; PHRA dismissed)
fha_claims.reasoning: The District Court dismissed the ADA claim on the ground that damages are unavailable under Title III of the ADA. The PHRA claim was dismissed on the erroneous reasoning that the ADA analysis applied equally and that damages were therefore unavailable. The appellate court reversed, holding that while the liability standard is the same, the PHRA expressly permits damages and the PHRA itself prohibits denial of accommodations based on use of a guide or support animal.

case_name: National Fair Housing Alliance v. Carson
accommodation_description: This case does not involve an individual reasonable accommodation request; it is an APA challenge to HUD's withdrawal of the AFFH Assessment Tool, which was administrative guidance for local governments conducting fair housing planning.
key_holding: The court granted HUD's motion to dismiss because plaintiffs lacked Article III standing—they failed to establish concrete injury sufficient to challenge HUD's withdrawal of the AFFH Assessment Tool and reversion to the prior Analysis of Impediments process.
brief_summary: National Fair Housing Alliance and other fair housing organizations sued HUD and Secretary Carson challenging the withdrawal of the AFFH Assessment Tool and HUD's reversion to the prior Analysis of Impediments process as arbitrary and capricious under the APA. The court granted HUD's motion to dismiss, finding plaintiffs lacked Article III standing because they failed to demonstrate concrete, particularized injury resulting from HUD's administrative action.
key_cases_cited: NAACP v. Sec'y of Hous. & Urban Dev., 817 F.2d 149 (1st Cir. 1987)
Shannon v. U.S. Dep't of Hous. & Urban Dev., 436 F.2d 809 (3d Cir. 1970)
Heckler v. Chaney, 470 U.S. 821 (1985)
Texas Dept. of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 135 S. Ct. 2507 (2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Challenge to HUD's withdrawal of the LG2017 Assessment Tool and reversion to Analysis of Impediments process under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA); claims that withdrawal violated APA notice-and-comment requirements and was arbitrary and capricious
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs (fair housing nonprofits) lacked Article III organizational standing because they failed to establish injury in fact: withdrawal of the Assessment Tool did not perceptibly impair their mission-driven activities since key portions of the AFFH Rule remained active (definitions, recordkeeping, certification, community participation requirements), and plaintiffs failed to show diversion of operational costs beyond those normally expended on their advocacy missions. Causation and redressability were also speculative because redress depended on independent choices of third-party local governments.

source_file: 4307711_2018_Marsha Wetzel v. Glen St. Andrew Living Communi_ca7
case_name: Marsha Wetzel v. Glen St. Andrew Living Community, LLC
accommodation_description: Not applicable; this case concerns landlord liability for tenant-on-tenant harassment based on sexual orientation and retaliation for complaining about such harassment, not a reasonable accommodation request.
key_holding: A landlord with actual notice of tenant-on-tenant harassment based on a protected characteristic who chooses not to take reasonable steps within its control to stop that harassment may be held directly liable under the Fair Housing Act for creating a hostile housing environment.
brief_summary: Marsha Wetzel, a lesbian resident of Glen St. Andrew senior living community, sued the management defendants alleging they failed to protect her from severe and pervasive verbal and physical harassment by other residents based on her sexual orientation, and retaliated against her for complaining about the harassment. The Seventh Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that a landlord may be held directly liable under the FHA when it has actual knowledge of harassment based on a protected characteristic and is deliberately indifferent to it.
key_cases_cited: Bloch v. Frischholz
Davis v. Monroe Cnty. Bd. of Educ.
DiCenso v. Cisneros
Halprin v. Prairie Single Family Homes
Texas Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to stop tenant-on-tenant harassment based on sexual orientation (sex discrimination); hostile housing environment created by other residents' verbal abuse, physical violence, and threats, with management's deliberate indifference
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed the district court's dismissal under 12(b)(6), holding that the FHA imposes liability on a landlord with actual notice of tenant-on-tenant harassment based on a protected characteristic (sexual orientation/sex) when the landlord is deliberately indifferent and fails to take reasonable steps within its control to stop the harassment. The court applied a hostile housing environment standard derived from Title VII and Title IX analogues, requiring: (1) unwelcome harassment based on protected characteristic; (2) severe or pervasive interference with residency; and (3) basis for imputing liability to defendant. The court found Wetzel plausibly alleged all three elements and that the harassment was severe and pervasive over 15 months, but remanded for further proceedings on the liability question.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation for complaining about harassment: relegation to less desirable dining location, barring from lobby except for coffee, halting cleaning services, false accusations of smoking, physical assault by staff (slapping), withholding rent-due notice, and building case for eviction
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed the district court's dismissal of the retaliation claim under § 3617, holding that proof of discriminatory animus is not required for a retaliation claim. The court applied the three-element retaliation standard: (1) protected activity (complaints about harassment); (2) adverse action (restrictions on facilities, downgraded dining, halted services, false accusations, physical assault, withheld notice); and (3) causal connection. The court found Wetzel plausibly alleged all elements and rejected the argument that § 3617 retaliation claims require discriminatory animus, noting that anti-retaliation provisions protect based on conduct, not status.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: State law claims (not specified in opinion; dismissed for lack of supplemental jurisdiction)
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court dismissed state law claims for lack of supplemental jurisdiction after dismissing the federal FHA claims. The appellate court reversed the FHA dismissals and instructed the district court to reinstate the state law claims on remand.

case_name: Darryl O. Mason v. Adams County Recorder, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, an African-American, sought injunctive relief compelling Ohio county recorders to stop printing, publishing, or permitting public access to historical documents containing racially restrictive covenants under § 3604(c).
key_holding: Mason lacked Article III standing because his alleged injury was not particularized to him—he failed to allege any concrete, personal economic harm or that any racially restrictive covenant affected him individually—and his generalized grievance about government record-keeping practices cannot support standing.
brief_summary: Mason, an African-American Ohio resident, sued all 88 Ohio county recorders alleging they violate § 3604(c) by maintaining and providing public access to historical land records containing racially restrictive covenants, which he claims discourage Black buyers from purchasing property. The Sixth Circuit affirmed dismissal, holding that Mason lacked Article III standing because he failed to allege any particularized injury distinct from any other Ohio resident, and his claim presented an undifferentiated generalized grievance about government conduct.
key_cases_cited: Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)
Warth v. Seldin, 422 U.S. 490 (1975)
Shelley v. Kraemer, 334 U.S. 1 (1948)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Gladstone, Realtors v. Village of Bellwood, 441 U.S. 91 (1979)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff lacked Article III standing because he failed to allege a particularized, concrete injury. Although the FHA permits standing to the full limits of Article III, plaintiff must still satisfy the constitutional minimum: he did not allege intent to purchase or rent property, did not identify any specific property affected by covenants, and his alleged injury (feeling unwelcome) was generalized and shared by all Ohio residents rather than particularized to him personally.
Plaintiff lacked Article III standing for the same reasons as the FHA claim. The standing doctrine applies uniformly across all federal claims brought in the complaint.

source_file: 4308092_2018_Providence Behavioral Health v. Grant Rd. Pub. Util. Dist._ca5
case_name: Providence Behavioral Health v. Grant Road Public Utility District
accommodation_description: Request for water, drainage, and septic utility services for a psychiatric facility serving minors with mental health disabilities, framed as a reasonable accommodation under the FHA and ADA.
key_holding: Providing water, drainage, and septic services is not a reasonable accommodation under § 3604(f)(3)(B) because the need for utilities is not unique to a psychiatric facility—it exists regardless of whether disabled individuals occupy the building—and failing to provide utilities does not create unequal ability to use and enjoy a dwelling compared to non-disabled individuals.
brief_summary: Providence Behavioral Health and Texas Providence Investments sued Grant Road Public Utility District after it denied annexation for a psychiatric facility serving minors with mental health disabilities, alleging the denial of water, drainage, and septic services violated the FHA and ADA. The Fifth Circuit affirmed the district court's judgment for Grant Road, finding that Providence failed to prove intentional discrimination and that providing utilities did not constitute a reasonable accommodation because the need for utilities exists regardless of disability and does not create unequal access.
key_cases_cited: Good Shepherd Manor Found., Inc. v. City of Momence, 323 F.3d 557 (7th Cir. 2003)
Doe v. Columbia-Brazoria Indep. Sch. Dist., 855 F.3d 681 (5th Cir. 2017)
Jin Choi v. Univ. of Tex. Health Sci. Ctr. of San Antonio, 633 F. App'x 214 (5th Cir. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.disposition: Judgment for defendant after bench trial
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court found that Providence failed to prove intentional discrimination by a preponderance of the evidence. Grant Road Board members testified they based their decision on financial considerations (tax abatements, project viability, revenue impact) rather than the disabilities of potential psychiatric patients. The trial court credited Grant Road's testimony over Providence's speculative evidence of discriminatory motives based on community pressure and politics.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Access to water, drainage, and septic services for a psychiatric treatment facility
fha_claims.disposition: Judgment for defendant after bench trial
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that providing water and wastewater services has no nexus to accommodating the disabilities of psychiatric patients. The need for utilities is not unique to a psychiatric facility and would be required for any building (office, condo, etc.). Denial of utilities does not create unequal ability for disabled individuals to use and enjoy the facility compared to non-disabled individuals, which is the purpose of FHA/ADA reasonable accommodation provisions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II, TFHA, Fourteenth Amendment claims
fha_claims.disposition: Judgment for defendant after bench trial
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court dismissed Providence's ADA Title II, Texas Fair Housing Act, and Fourteenth Amendment claims on the same factual and legal bases as the FHA claims. Providence failed to prove intentional discrimination or that denial of utilities constituted a failure to provide reasonable accommodations under these statutes.

case_name: Darryl O. Mason v. Adams County Recorder, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff seeks to compel Ohio county recorders to stop printing and publishing historical documents containing racially restrictive covenants, to remove such records from public view, and to permit inspection and redaction of such documents.
key_holding: The Sixth Circuit affirmed dismissal for lack of standing because Mason failed to allege a particularized injury—his complaint contained no allegations that he intended to buy or rent property, and his generalized grievance about government maintenance of historical records with restrictive covenants was insufficient to establish Article III standing.
brief_summary: Darryl Mason, an African-American Ohio resident, sued all 88 Ohio county recorders seeking injunctive relief to stop them from maintaining and making publicly available historical land records containing racially restrictive covenants, alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act's prohibition on discriminatory statements. The Sixth Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal, holding that Mason lacked Article III standing because he failed to allege any particularized injury—he never claimed to have suffered actual or threatened harm from encountering these historical covenants when seeking to purchase or rent property.
key_cases_cited: Warth v. Seldin, 422 U.S. 490 (1975)
Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Gladstone, Realtors v. Village of Bellwood, 441 U.S. 91 (1979)
Shelley v. Kraemer, 334 U.S. 1 (1948)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff lacked Article III standing because he failed to allege a particularized, concrete injury. Mason did not allege he intended to purchase or rent any specific property, and any alleged injury (feeling unwelcome) was generalized and shared by all Ohio residents, not particularized to him personally. The court affirmed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing.

Plaintiff lacked Article III standing for all claims, including non-FHA claims under § 1983 and § 1985, for the same reasons: no particularized injury and failure to allege intent to purchase or rent property.

case_name: Carol Vorchheimer v. The Philadelphian Owners Association; June Idzal; Frank J. Bonom
accommodation_description: Request to leave a rolling walker in the lobby common area instead of requiring staff to retrieve it from storage upon her return
key_holding: A requested accommodation is not 'necessary' under § 3604(f)(3)(B) if the landlord offers alternative accommodations that afford the disabled person equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling; the statute requires accommodations that are essential, not merely preferable.
brief_summary: Carol Vorchheimer, a mobility-disabled condominium owner, sued The Philadelphian Owners Association and its managers for refusing to let her leave her rolling walker in the lobby, claiming a failure to accommodate under the Fair Housing Act. The Third Circuit affirmed dismissal, holding that Vorchheimer did not plausibly plead necessity because the building had offered four alternative accommodations that equally satisfied her medical need for ready access to her walker without requiring her to stand unsupported.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Lapid-Laurel, L.L.C. v. Zoning Bd. of Adjustment, 284 F.3d 442 (3d Cir. 2002)
Hovsons, Inc. v. Township of Brick, 89 F.3d 1096 (3d Cir. 1996)
Revock v. Cowpet Bay W. Condo. Ass'n, 853 F.3d 96 (3d Cir. 2017)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to leave rolling walker in building lobby for independent retrieval upon return from car
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly plead necessity under § 3604(f)(3)(B) because her own complaint pleaded four alternative accommodations that satisfied her medical needs (ready access to walker and minimized unsupported standing). The necessity element requires that an accommodation be essential to achieve equal housing opportunity measured against alternatives offered; preference is not necessity. Plaintiff's own exhibits (doctors' letters and building correspondence) contradicted her claim that lobby storage was necessary rather than merely preferable.

case_name: Carol Vorchheimer v. The Philadelphian Owners Association; June Idzal; Frank J. Bonom
accommodation_description: Disabled tenant requested permission to store her rolling walker in the building lobby to independently retrieve it upon returning home.
key_holding: Under § 3604(f)(3)(B), an accommodation is 'necessary' only if it is required to achieve equal housing opportunity; when a landlord offers alternatives that satisfy the disabled person's disability-related needs, the tenant cannot demand her preferred accommodation.
brief_summary: Carol Vorchheimer, a disabled condominium owner at The Philadelphian, sued the Owners Association under the Fair Housing Amendments Act, claiming the building's refusal to let her store her rolling walker in the lobby violated § 3604(f)(3)(B). The Third Circuit affirmed dismissal, holding that Vorchheimer failed to plausibly plead that her preferred accommodation was 'necessary' because the four alternatives offered by the building—staff retrieval, delivery to her car, doorman loading, or valet parking—all satisfied her stated disability-related needs for ready walker access without unsupported standing.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Lapid-Laurel, L.L.C. v. Zoning Bd. of Adjustment, 284 F.3d 442 (3d Cir. 2002)
Cinnamon Hills Youth Crisis Ctr. v. St. George City, 685 F.3d 917 (10th Cir. 2012)
Wisconsin Cmty. Servs., Inc. v. City of Milwaukee, 465 F.3d 737 (7th Cir. 2006)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to leave rolling walker in building lobby for independent retrieval, rather than storing it with front-desk staff
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly plead necessity under Iqbal/Twombly standard. The court held that 'necessary' means 'required' or 'essential,' and necessity must be gauged against alternatives offered. Plaintiff's own complaint pleaded four alternative accommodations that satisfied her medical needs (ready access to walker and minimized unsupported standing), making the requested lobby accommodation merely preferable, not necessary. The court applied the necessity element as a legal standard amenable to dismissal when alternatives are pleaded in the complaint itself.

source_file: 4313320_2018_Tree of Life Christian Sch. v. City of Upper Arlington, Ohio_ca6

case_name: Lindsey Jones v. CitiMortgage, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff raised a Fair Housing Act claim (Count Three) under 42 U.S.C. § 3604, but the claim was abandoned on appeal and the court did not substantively analyze any reasonable accommodation or modification request; the complaint alleged the foreclosure-related actions were discriminatory but did not articulate a specific accommodation request.
key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the dismissal of Jones's complaint in all respects except Count Five (bankruptcy discharge injunction), which was vacated and remanded because the district court lacked jurisdiction to enforce a discharge injunction issued by the bankruptcy court; the court also held that Jones's Fair Housing Act claim was abandoned on appeal and failed because Jones did not allege unequal treatment affecting housing availability.
brief_summary: Lindsey Jones, proceeding pro se, appealed the dismissal of his lawsuit challenging a second foreclosure by CitiMortgage and related defendants, raising claims under the Fair Housing Act, bankruptcy discharge injunction, and constitutional provisions. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed dismissal of all claims except Count Five (bankruptcy discharge injunction), which was vacated and remanded because the district court lacked jurisdiction to enforce an injunction issued by the bankruptcy court, while noting Jones abandoned his FHA claim on appeal.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Alderwoods Group, Inc. v. Garcia
In re McLean

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Jones alleged discrimination based on disability (disabled, elderly, African-American man) in connection with foreclosure proceedings and state court case management.
fha_claims.reasoning: Jones failed to allege sufficient factual content to support a prima facie FHA violation. Under § 3604, a plaintiff must allege unequal treatment on the basis of a protected class affecting the availability of housing. Jones's conclusory assertions of discrimination were not supported by factual allegations and were insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly. Jones abandoned the claim on appeal by not addressing it.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. §§ 1983 and 1985(3) (constitutional due process and equal protection claims); 11 U.S.C. § 524(a)(2) (bankruptcy discharge injunction); 15 U.S.C. § 1681 (Fair Credit Reporting Act); O.C.G.A. § 16-8-3 (Georgia theft by deception statute)
fha_claims.reasoning: Jones failed to state plausible claims under § 1983 and § 1985(3) because he did not allege sufficient factual content showing that CitiMortgage and the Phelan firm were state actors or that they reached an understanding with state officials to deny his rights. For § 1985(3), Jones failed to allege racial or class-based animus. The bankruptcy discharge injunction claim was dismissed for lack of jurisdiction (only the bankruptcy court that issued the discharge could enforce it). The FCRA claim was withdrawn by Jones. The state law theft claim does not appear to create a civil cause of action.

source_file: 4330677_2016_Hardaway v. District of Columbia Housing Authority_cadc
case_name: Hardaway v. District of Columbia Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Angelene Hardaway requested approval for her sister Lena to serve as her live-in aide to provide disability-related care under the Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher Program.
key_holding: The D.C. Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing and mootness, finding that Angelene Hardaway established injury-in-fact by demonstrating the Authority's revocation of her live-in aide approval stripped her of a legal entitlement to a two-bedroom voucher, and that her claims remain live because the Authority's subsequent retention of the voucher was merely administrative grace subject to revocation.
brief_summary: Angelene Hardaway, a disabled Section 8 voucher holder, sued the District of Columbia Housing Authority after it revoked approval of her sister Lena as a live-in aide, threatening her legal entitlement to a two-bedroom voucher and round-the-clock care. The D.C. Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal on standing and mootness grounds, holding that Angelene demonstrated cognizable injury by losing a statutory entitlement and that her claims remain live because the Authority's permissive retention of the voucher was an act of administrative grace rather than a binding determination.
key_cases_cited: Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)
Friends of the Earth, Inc. v. Laidlaw Environmental Services (TOC), 528 U.S. 167 (2000)
Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins, 136 S. Ct. 1540 (2016)
United States v. Hubbard, 650 F.2d 293 (D.C. Cir. 1980)
EEOC v. National Children's Center, Inc., 98 F.3d 1406 (D.C. Cir. 1996)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Approval for Lena Hardaway to serve as a live-in aide to care for Angelene, which would entitle Angelene to a two-bedroom housing voucher under the Housing Choice Voucher Program
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court erred in dismissing on standing and mootness grounds. The appellate court found that Angelene had standing at the time of filing because the Authority's July 9 letter rescinding her live-in aide approval constituted a concrete injury—loss of a government benefit to which she claimed legal entitlement. The case was not moot because the Authority's September 26 letter reaffirming the denial of the live-in aide request meant Angelene retained only a one-bedroom voucher entitlement, making her vulnerable to revocation of the two-bedroom voucher she was occupying. The court reversed and remanded for further proceedings on the merits.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act, 42 U.S.C. § 12132; Rehabilitation Act, 29 U.S.C. § 794
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court's dismissal on standing and mootness grounds was erroneous as to all claims, including the ADA and Rehabilitation Act claims. The appellate court reversed the standing dismissal and found the claims not moot, remanding for further proceedings on the merits of all claims.

case_name: Robyn G. Edwards; Mikki Adams v. Gene Salter Properties and Salter Construction Inc.; Brittany Pringle
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested that defendants accept alternative documentation (proof of government benefits, retirement benefits, and rental income) to verify income qualification instead of requiring standard documentation (pay stubs, offer letter, or tax returns).
key_holding: The Eighth Circuit held that plaintiffs sufficiently alleged a reasonable accommodation claim under § 3604(f)(3)(B) by alleging defendants refused to make a reasonable exception to their income documentation policy, which may be necessary to afford plaintiffs equal opportunity to rent, regardless of whether plaintiffs' inability to provide standard documentation was caused by their disability.
brief_summary: Robyn Edwards and Mikki Adams attempted to rent an apartment from Gene Salter Properties but were denied when the landlord refused to accept alternative documentation of their income sources (government disability benefits, retirement benefits, and rental income) and insisted on standard documentation. The Eighth Circuit vacated the dismissal of plaintiffs' reasonable accommodation claim under § 3604(f)(3)(B), holding that plaintiffs adequately alleged defendants failed to make a reasonable accommodation in their income-verification policy necessary to afford plaintiffs equal opportunity to rent.
key_cases_cited: Peebles v. Potter, 354 F.3d 761 (8th Cir. 2004)
Ricci v. DeStefano, 557 U.S. 557 (2009)
US Airways, Inc. v. Barnett, 535 U.S. 391 (2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege disparate treatment because they alleged differential treatment based on form of income, not because of handicap. A disparate treatment claim requires showing that a similarly situated disabled individual was treated differently because of disability than non-disabled individuals.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege disparate impact because they did not sufficiently allege that handicapped persons are or will be disproportionately impacted by the income-verification policy.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exception to income-verification policy to allow plaintiffs to prove sufficient income through documentation of government disability benefits and rental income instead of pay stubs, offer letters, or tax returns
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that plaintiffs sufficiently alleged a reasonable accommodation claim under § 3604(f)(3)(B). The requested accommodation—accepting alternative income documentation—may be reasonable even if the inability to comply with the policy was not caused by the disability itself, as a reasonable accommodation may involve making an exception to a facially neutral rule. The dismissal was vacated and the case remanded for further proceedings.

case_name: Robyn G. Edwards; Mikki Adams v. Gene Salter Properties and Salter Construction Inc.; Brittany Pringle
accommodation_description: Request to provide alternative income documentation (government benefits, retirement benefits, rental income) in lieu of pay stubs, offer letters, or tax returns to qualify for rental housing
key_holding: The Eighth Circuit held that the district court erred in dismissing plaintiffs' reasonable accommodation claim under § 3604(f)(3)(B) because the inability to comply with the income documentation policy could potentially be a disability-related limitation warranting accommodation, even if not caused by the disability.
brief_summary: Robyn Edwards and Mikki Adams sued Gene Salter Properties after being told they could only qualify for an apartment by providing pay stubs, offer letters, or tax returns, despite having only disability benefits, retirement income, and rental income as sources. The Eighth Circuit affirmed dismissal of plaintiffs' disparate treatment and disparate impact claims but vacated dismissal of their reasonable accommodation claim under § 3604(f)(3)(B), holding that plaintiffs sufficiently alleged defendants failed to accommodate their disability-related need to use alternative income documentation.
key_cases_cited: US Airways, Inc. v. Barnett, 535 U.S. 391 (2002)
Peebles v. Potter, 354 F.3d 761 (8th Cir. 2004)
Ricci v. DeStefano, 557 U.S. 557 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege disparate treatment because they alleged differential treatment based on form of income, not because of handicap. A disparate treatment claim requires showing that a similarly situated disabled individual was treated differently because of disability than non-disabled individuals.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege disparate impact because they did not sufficiently allege that handicapped persons are or will be disproportionately impacted by the income-verification policy.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exception to income-verification policy to allow plaintiffs to prove sufficient income through documentation of government disability benefits and rental income instead of pay stubs, offer letters, or tax returns
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that plaintiffs sufficiently alleged a reasonable accommodation claim under § 3604(f)(3)(B). The court noted that plaintiffs may be able to show the requested accommodation was reasonable even if the inability to comply with the income-documentation policy was not caused by the disability, citing US Airways v. Barnett for the proposition that reasonable accommodations may involve exceptions to facially neutral rules.

source_file: 4343397_2018_Angela Riley v. City of Kokomo, Indiana, Housi_ca7
case_name: Angela Riley v. City of Kokomo, Indiana Housing Authority
accommodation_description: No accommodation request was the subject of the FHA claim; the claim involved alleged retaliation for reporting to HUD what plaintiff perceived as procedural violations by her employer.
key_holding: Riley's FHA retaliation claim failed because she presented no evidence that she called HUD to report a discriminatory housing practice—she admitted she called to report her CEO's alleged fraud—and she conceded she did not know whether anyone was treated differently because of a protected characteristic.
brief_summary: Angela Riley, a former employee of the Kokomo Housing Authority who also resided in KHA-assisted housing, sued claiming the housing authority terminated her employment in retaliation for requesting FMLA leave and ADA accommodations, and later took adverse housing actions against her as a tenant. The Seventh Circuit affirmed summary judgment for KHA on all claims, finding (1) the ADA reasonable accommodation claim was outside the scope of her EEOC charge, (2) no evidence of discriminatory or retaliatory intent, and (3) no protected activity under the FHA because Riley admitted she called HUD to report alleged fraud by her CEO, not any discriminatory housing practice.
key_cases_cited: Green v. Nat'l Steel Corp., 197 F.3d 894 (7th Cir. 1999)
East-Miller v. Lake Cty. Highway Dep't, 421 F.3d 558 (7th Cir. 2005)
Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009)
White v. U.S. Dep't of Hous. & Urban Dev., 475 F.3d 898 (7th Cir. 2007)
Lord v. High Voltage Software, Inc., 839 F.3d 556 (7th Cir. 2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation for disabilities (seizures, anxiety disorder, PTSD, bipolar disorder, depression) requiring periodic breaks; plaintiff requested FMLA leave and accommodations but claim was not developed in EEOC charge
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's ADA reasonable accommodation claim was barred because it was not raised in her EEOC charge and is not reasonably related to the charges actually raised (which alleged only discriminatory termination based on disability, not failure to accommodate). The court held that failure to accommodate claims are separate and distinct from discrimination claims and cannot be expected to develop from an investigation into a termination claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish protected activity under the FHA. She called HUD to report alleged mismanagement and procedural violations by her employer (the housing authority's CEO), not to report a discriminatory housing practice. The court held that reporting apparent mismanagement is not equivalent to reporting housing discrimination, and plaintiff admitted she did not know whether the tenants in question were treated differently based on a protected class characteristic. No rational jury could find plaintiff reasonably believed she was reporting a discriminatory housing practice.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: FMLA interference and retaliation, ADA discrimination and retaliation, Title VII retaliation
fha_claims.reasoning: On FMLA claims: employer decided to terminate plaintiff on May 7, 2014, before plaintiff requested leave on May 9, 2014, breaking the causal chain. Five-month gap between FMLA leave in October 2013 and March 2014 written warning, combined with employer's allowance of additional leave in February 2014, insufficient to establish pretext for retaliation. On ADA and Title VII claims: plaintiff failed to develop coherent arguments in opposition to summary judgment, merely listing 25 facts without explaining how they defeated summary judgment; no evidence of discriminatory or retaliatory intent; temporal proximity alone insufficient; no similarly situated comparators; no evidence undermining employer's stated reasons for discipline and termination.

case_name: Francis v. Kings Park Manor, Inc.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request was made; the claim concerns landlord liability for failing to address tenant-on-tenant racial harassment.
key_holding: A landlord may be liable under § 3604(b) and § 3617 of the FHA for failing to take prompt action to address a racially hostile housing environment created by one tenant targeting another, where the landlord knew of the discriminatory conduct and had the power to correct it.
brief_summary: Donahue Francis, a Black tenant with a Section 8 voucher, sued Kings Park Manor and its property manager alleging they violated the FHA by failing to address repeated racial harassment by a neighboring tenant who called Francis racial slurs and made death threats over several months. The Second Circuit vacated the district court's dismissal, holding that landlords may be liable under §§ 3604(b) and 3617 for post-acquisition hostile housing environment claims when they knew of tenant-on-tenant racial harassment and had the power to address it but failed to act.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dept. of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 135 S. Ct. 2507 (2015)
Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009)
City of Edmonds v. Oxford House, Inc., 514 U.S. 725 (1995)
Trafficante v. Metro. Life Ins. Co., 409 U.S. 205 (1972)
Neudecker v. Boisclair Corp., 351 F.3d 361 (8th Cir. 2003)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The Second Circuit vacated the district court's dismissal of plaintiff's FHA § 3604(b) claim for hostile housing environment based on tenant-on-tenant racial harassment. The court held that § 3604(b) reaches post-acquisition conduct and that a landlord may be liable under § 3617 for failing to take prompt action to address tenant-on-tenant racial harassment of which it knew or should have known and had the power to correct. The claim survives the motion to dismiss and proceeds on remand.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The Second Circuit vacated the district court's dismissal of plaintiff's FHA § 3617 interference/coercion claim. The court held that § 3617 creates an independent cause of action for interference with rights protected by § 3604(b), and that a landlord's failure to intervene in tenant-on-tenant racial harassment can constitute such interference. The claim survives the motion to dismiss and proceeds on remand.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1982 (Civil Rights Act of 1866); N.Y. Exec. Law § 296 (New York State Human Rights Law); negligent infliction of emotional distress under New York common law
fha_claims.reasoning: The Second Circuit vacated the district court's dismissal of plaintiff's claims under §§ 1981 and 1982 and under N.Y. Exec. Law § 296, holding that a defendant's deliberate indifference to racial discrimination can violate these provisions and that plaintiff adequately alleged such indifference. The court affirmed dismissal of the negligent infliction of emotional distress claim because the landlord's breach did not directly cause the emotional distress; the harassing tenant's conduct was the direct cause. All non-FHA claims proceed on remand except the NIED claim.

source_file: 4375755_2017_M.R.G. v. Marsh Harbour Maintenance Association, Inc._ca11
case_name: Fair Housing Center of the Greater Palm Beaches, Inc. v. Sonoma Bay Community Homeowners Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs challenged HOA policies (Curfew Rule, Loitering Rule, Proper Attire Rule, Report Card Requirement) alleged to discriminate against families with children under familial status discrimination theory, not disability accommodation.
key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the district court's denial of plaintiffs' motion for a new trial, finding no reversible error in the jury instructions or verdict form despite plaintiffs' contention that the court improperly allowed the jury to decide liability issues that had been partially resolved at summary judgment.
brief_summary: The Fair Housing Center and individual residents sued condominium homeowner associations alleging that four policies (Curfew Rule, Loitering Rule, Proper Attire Rule, Report Card Requirement) discriminated against families with children in violation of 42 U.S.C. §§ 3604(b) and (c). After a seven-day jury trial resulted in a verdict for defendants, the Eleventh Circuit affirmed the district court's denial of plaintiffs' motion for a new trial, finding no prejudicial error in the jury instructions or verdict form.
key_cases_cited: City of Miami v. Bank of Am. Corp., 800 F.3d 1262 (11th Cir. 2015)
Gu<|reserved_200419|>|zman v. City of Chicago, 689 F.3d 740 (7th Cir. 2012)
Ragin v. N.Y. Times Co., 923 F.2d 995 (2d Cir. 1991)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: District court granted partial summary judgment finding the Loitering and Curfew Rules violated § 3604(b) on their face as a matter of law. However, the jury was asked to determine liability based on enforcement and causation. The jury found no liability, and the appellate court affirmed, holding that proximate cause is a required element of an FHA damages claim and the plaintiffs failed to prove the rules were enforced against families with children in a manner that caused damages.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: District court granted partial summary judgment finding the Loitering and Curfew Rules violated § 3604(c) on their face as a matter of law under the 'ordinary reader' standard. The jury was asked to determine liability. The jury found no liability, and the appellate court affirmed, holding that even if proximate cause is not required for § 3604(c), the plaintiffs failed to prove causation of damages.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: District court denied plaintiffs' motion for partial summary judgment as to the Report Card Requirement, finding sufficient ambiguity in whether it was used as a means of identification or character vetting that a trier of fact must resolve. Plaintiffs did not appeal this ruling.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: District court denied plaintiffs' motion for partial summary judgment as to the Proper Attire Rule, finding the language was ambiguous as to whether it applied only to children or to all males and females, requiring a trier of fact to resolve. Plaintiffs did not appeal this ruling.

case_name: Constante P. Barot et al. v. Aldon Management
citation: No official citation (unpublished order, Case No. 18-140 (TJK))
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; plaintiffs allege disparate treatment in housing based on national origin (Filipino) and age, claiming they received inferior housing compared to American counterparts.
key_holding: Plaintiffs' Fair Housing Act claim for disparate treatment based on national origin survived dismissal because their allegations—that Aldon provided them smaller, inferior housing units on account of their Filipino national origin while American counterparts received larger, standard two-bedroom apartments—were sufficient to create a plausible inference of discriminatory intent.
brief_summary: Pro se tenants Constante and Dolores Barot sued their employer-landlord Aldon Management for housing discrimination based on national origin and age, alleging they received inferior housing (an illegally constructed second bedroom, higher rent) compared to American counterparts who received standard two-bedroom apartments. The court denied Aldon's motion to dismiss as to the Fair Housing Act national origin discrimination claim, finding plaintiffs' allegations sufficient to plausibly infer discriminatory intent, but dismissed several D.C. law claims and the age discrimination claim under the ADEA.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
2922 Sherman Ave. Tenants' Ass'n v. District of Columbia, 444 F.3d 673 (D.C. Cir. 2006)
Halprin v. Prairie Single Family Homes of Dearborn Park Ass'n, 388 F.3d 327 (7th Cir. 2004)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs plausibly alleged that Aldon discriminated against them on the basis of national origin by providing inferior housing (a smaller, illegally constructed two-bedroom apartment with a substandard window) compared to similarly situated American counterparts, satisfying the prima facie elements of disparate treatment under § 3604(b).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VII national origin discrimination, ADEA age discrimination, DCHRA housing discrimination, breach of implied warranty of habitability, D.C. Code § 42-3505.2, D.C. Code §§ 42-3502.13(d) and 42-3502.22, intentional infliction of emotional distress
fha_claims.reasoning: Title VII national origin discrimination and ADEA age discrimination claims survived MTD under the liberal pleading standard for pro se complaints; breach of implied warranty of habitability survived MTD based on allegations of code violations and safety defects; but claims under D.C. Code §§ 42-3502.13(d), 42-3502.22, and 42-3505.2 were dismissed as either providing no independent cause of action or lacking factual allegations; intentional infliction of emotional distress was dismissed for failure to allege extreme or outrageous conduct.

source_file: 4385539_2019_Inclusive Cmtys. Project, Inc. v. Lincoln Prop. Co._ca5
case_name: Inclusive Communities Project, Inc. v. Lincoln Property Co.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; case involves landlord's 'no vouchers' policy challenged as discriminatory based on race rather than any disability accommodation.
key_holding: The Fifth Circuit affirmed dismissal of FHA claims against landlords who refuse to participate in the Section 8 voucher program, concluding that even assuming disparate impact from the 'no vouchers' policy on Black renters, the complaint failed to adequately plead that the policy was the cause of the pre-existing racial disparity in voucher distribution.
brief_summary: The Inclusive Communities Project, a fair housing organization, sued Lincoln Property Company and apartment owners alleging their blanket 'no vouchers' policy disparately impacts Black renters in the Dallas metro area where over 80% of Section 8 voucher holders are Black. The Fifth Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal, holding that even accepting the statistical allegations, ICP failed to adequately plead robust causation between the 'no vouchers' policy and the pre-existing racial disparity in voucher distribution.
key_cases_cited: Inclusive Communities Project, Inc. v. Tex. Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs, 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Huntington Branch, NAACP v. Town of Huntington, 844 F.2d 926 (2d Cir. 1988)
Knapp v. Eagle Prop. Mgmt. Corp., 54 F.3d 1272 (7th Cir. 1995)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that ICP failed to allege facts demonstrating robust causation required under ICP v. Texas Department of Housing & Community Affairs. ICP did not show that defendants' 'no vouchers' policy caused the racial composition of voucher holders in Dallas; rather, the disparity resulted from pre-existing conditions not attributable to defendants. Without showing defendants caused the disparity, the claim fails at the pleading stage under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: ICP's allegations that defendants' refusal to rent to voucher holders constitutes disparate treatment based on race were conclusory and lacked factual support. ICP failed to allege facts supporting a reasonable inference that race motivated the challenged action; awareness that voucher holders are disproportionately Black cannot alone establish intentional discrimination without well-pleaded factual allegations of discriminatory intent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: ICP's claim that Lincoln refused to negotiate with or rent to voucher holders in majority white areas while accepting them in minority areas was insufficiently pleaded. The complaint failed to clearly allege that Lincoln accepts vouchers at properties in minority areas outside of those mandated by law or contract, making the claim too vague to provide fair notice of the disparate treatment alleged.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: ICP's claim that Lincoln's advertisements stating 'Our community is not authorized to accept housing vouchers' violate § 3604(c) failed because the advertisements contain no explicit reference to race. An ordinary reader would not infer a racial preference from statements about voucher acceptance policies; the supposition that such an inference would be drawn is entirely speculative and unwarranted under Iqbal/Twombly.

case_name: Barbara Moody v. Harry Gongloff, et al.
accommodation_description: Request to transfer from a two-story house to a single-story house due to inability to climb stairs as a disability accommodation
key_holding: The district court did not abuse its discretion in refusing Moody's proposed jury instruction on unreasonable delay because Moody herself caused much of the 87-day delay by failing to respond to phone calls and letters and missing appointments, and the evidence did not support a finding that the housing authority's delay was unreasonable.
brief_summary: Barbara Moody, a Section 8 voucher recipient, sued the Lorain Metropolitan Housing Authority alleging it failed to reasonably accommodate her disability by delaying approval of her request to transfer from a two-story house to a single-story house for 87 days. After a jury returned a verdict for the housing authority, Moody appealed the rejection of her proposed jury instruction on unreasonable delay. The Sixth Circuit affirmed, finding no abuse of discretion because Moody caused much of the delay herself through missed appointments and failure to respond to communications.
key_cases_cited: Overlook Mut. Homes, Inc. v. Spencer, 415 F. App'x 617 (6th Cir. 2011)
Tuttle v. Metro. Gov't of Nashville, 474 F.3d 307 (6th Cir. 2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request to transfer to a single-story house due to inability to navigate stairs; plaintiff alleged the housing authority unreasonably delayed in granting this accommodation over an 87-day period.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court affirmed the jury verdict in favor of the housing authority, finding that although delay in responding to an accommodation request may constitute a denial, the 87-day delay here was not unreasonable because plaintiff caused much of it through her own failures to respond to communications and attend meetings, and the delay actually benefitted her by allowing the authority to verify utility restoration.

source_file: 4387735_2017_Victoria Laney v. Thomas Ray Slaten, Jr._ca11
case_name: Victoria Laney v. Thomas Ray Slaten, Jr.
accommodation_description: Laney vaguely alleged the defendants perceived or regarded her as emotionally or mentally impaired, but did not specify what accommodation, if any, she requested or was denied.
key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed dismissal because Laney's FHA complaint failed to allege sufficient facts showing how the defendants' conduct impacted her housing accessibility or how they refused reasonable modifications for handicapped persons, merely asserting she was perceived as mentally ill.
brief_summary: Victoria Laney, a homeowner in The Hammocks HOA community in Ocoee, Florida, appealed the dismissal of her Fair Housing Act claims against the HOA, property manager, and board president, alleging they discriminated against her by publicly disclosing her debt and regarding her as mentally ill. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the dismissal, finding Laney failed to plead sufficient factual content to state a plausible FHA claim because she did not allege how the conduct impacted her housing accessibility or how defendants refused reasonable accommodations for handicapped persons.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condo. Ass'n, 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014)
Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Saudi Basic Industries Corp., 544 U.S. 280 (2005)
Rooker v. Fidelity Trust Co., 263 U.S. 413 (1923)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege plausible facts showing how defendants' conduct impacted her accessibility to housing or refused reasonable modifications for handicapped persons. Complaint contained only conclusory allegations of perceived mental impairment without factual content supporting a Fair Housing Act claim under § 3604(a) or (f).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: FDUTPA, FCCPA
fha_claims.reasoning: Claims under Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act and Florida Consumer Collections Practices Act were barred by Rooker-Feldman doctrine because they were inextricably intertwined with prior state court judgments on the same conduct and would effectively nullify the state court's decision.

source_file: 4389389_2019_Marie Curto v. Country Place Condominium Assn_ca3
case_name: Marie Curto v. A Country Place Condominium Association
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs challenged a condominium association's sex-segregated pool schedule that allocated substantially more favorable evening swimming hours to men than women, with plaintiff Diana Lusardi needing pool therapy for stroke-related disabilities.
key_holding: The pool schedule's allocation of substantially more evening swimming hours to men (16.5 hours after 5 p.m.) compared to women (3.5 hours) constitutes facial discrimination against women in violation of the FHA's prohibition on sex discrimination in the terms, conditions, or privileges of dwelling, even though the schedule provided roughly equal aggregate swimming time to each gender.
brief_summary: Marie Curto and Steve and Diana Lusardi sued A Country Place Condominium Association over its sex-segregated pool schedule, which allocated significantly more favorable evening swimming hours to men (16.5 hours after 5 p.m.) than women (3.5 hours). The Third Circuit reversed the District Court's summary judgment for the Association, finding the schedule facially discriminated against women in violation of 42 U.S.C. § 3604(b), and remanded for entry of summary judgment for the plaintiffs.
key_cases_cited: Community Services, Inc. v. Wind Gap Mun. Auth., 421 F.3d 170 (3d Cir. 2005)
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
United States v. Virginia, 518 U.S. 515 (1996)
Loving v. Virginia, 388 U.S. 1 (1967)
Brown v. Board of Education, 347 U.S. 483 (1954)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal access to communal pool facilities; challenge to sex-segregated swimming schedule that allocated unequal evening hours to men and women
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied explicit facial discrimination analysis under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(b) and held that the pool schedule discriminates against women by allocating unequal favorable swimming times (only 3.5 hours after 5:00 p.m. on weeknights for women vs. 16.5 hours for men), reflecting overbroad generalizations about gender roles, even though aggregate hours were roughly equal. The court reversed the district court's summary judgment and entered judgment for plaintiffs.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: New Jersey state law claims regarding discrimination and condominium association rules
fha_claims.reasoning: The District Court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the state law claims after granting summary judgment on the FHA claim. The appellate court left to the District Court's discretion whether to exercise supplemental jurisdiction on remand.

source_file: 4393705_2019_City of Miami v. Wells Fargo _ Co._ca11
case_name: City of Miami v. Wells Fargo & Co.
accommodation_description: Discriminatory mortgage lending practices (redlining and reverse redlining) allegedly targeted Black and Latino Miami residents for predatory loans
key_holding: The City adequately pled proximate cause for its tax-base injury because discriminatory lending practices bear a direct relation to reduced property values and tax revenue, but failed to adequately plead proximate cause for increased municipal expenditures because the causal chain was too attenuated
brief_summary: The City of Miami sued Wells Fargo and Bank of America alleging the banks engaged in discriminatory mortgage lending practices (redlining and reverse redlining) that intentionally targeted Black and Latino residents, resulting in disproportionate foreclosures, diminished property values, and reduced tax revenue for the City. The Eleventh Circuit reversed the dismissal, holding that Miami adequately pled proximate cause for its tax-base injury because the connection between discriminatory lending practices and reduced property values was direct and logical when considered in the aggregate, but affirmed that the City failed to plead proximate cause for increased municipal expenditures because the causal chain was too attenuated.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Bank of America Corp. v. City of Miami, 137 S. Ct. 1296 (2017)
Holmes v. Securities Investor Protection Corp., 503 U.S. 258 (1992)
Lexmark International, Inc. v. Static Control Components, Inc., 572 U.S. 118 (2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The City adequately pled proximate cause for its tax-revenue injury under the FHA by alleging discriminatory lending practices (redlining and reverse-redlining) that caused disproportionate foreclosures on minority-owned properties, reducing property values and the City's tax base. The court found 'some direct relation' between the Banks' conduct and the City's fiscal injury when measured in the aggregate, applying the Holmes factors and finding the injury calculable via hedonic regression analysis.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The City's allegations of disparate impact from the Banks' predatory lending practices—targeting minority borrowers with worse loan terms and resulting in disproportionate foreclosures—survive the motion to dismiss on proximate cause grounds. The court found the City plausibly alleged a causal connection between the facially neutral lending policies and their disparate impact on minority neighborhoods.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Increased municipal expenditures for police, fire, sanitation, and building code enforcement at foreclosed properties
fha_claims.reasoning: The City failed to adequately plead proximate cause for its increased municipal expenditures injury. The court found the causal chain too attenuated and the City's pleadings too conclusory, lacking any explanation of how to isolate which expenditures were attributable to the Banks' conduct or how damages would be calculated, failing the first Holmes factor regarding ascertainability of damages.

source_file: 4402335_2017_Affordable Recovery Housing v. City of Blue Island_ca7
case_name: Affordable Recovery Housing v. City of Blue Island
accommodation_description: Affordable Recovery Housing operates a faith-based residential recovery home for men with drug/alcohol addiction and sought to operate in a single-family residential zone without installing a sprinkler system.
key_holding: The Seventh Circuit affirmed that Blue Island's fire safety code requiring sprinklers did not substantially burden Affordable's religious exercise under RFRA because the expulsion resulted from Affordable's own disregard of applicable regulations, not from religious discrimination.
brief_summary: Affordable Recovery Housing, a faith-based operator of a residential recovery home for men with substance use disorders, sued the City of Blue Island and its fire chief after being forced to evict residents due to the city's requirement that it install a sprinkler system. The Seventh Circuit affirmed the district court's judgment for the defendants, finding that Affordable's Religious Freedom Restoration Act and RLUIPA claims failed because the city acted on legitimate fire safety concerns rather than religious animus, and Affordable's own failure to research applicable regulations caused the hardship rather than government burden on religious exercise.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exception from sprinkler system requirement for residential recovery housing facility serving men with substance use disorders
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that Affordable failed to establish that the sprinkler requirement was applied because of the disability status of its residents. The exclusion was based on fire safety code compliance, not disability discrimination, and was quickly undone when state law preemption was discovered. The FHA claim lacked the requisite nexus between the housing denial and disability.

source_file: 4403305_2019_Paula Casillas v. Madison Avenue Associates, Inc_ca7

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) § 1692g disclosure violation; defendant failed to notify plaintiff that debt dispute and creditor information requests must be made in writing
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff lacked Article III standing because she alleged only a bare procedural violation of the FDCPA with no concrete injury-in-fact. She did not allege that she attempted or intended to dispute the debt or verify the creditor, and thus suffered no actual or imminent risk of harm to the substantive interests the statute protects. Under Spokeo, a statutory violation divorced from concrete harm is insufficient to confer federal jurisdiction.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Under the Wards Cove burden-shifting framework for disparate-impact claims, plaintiff failed to demonstrate that either of his proposed alternatives to the NCAA's felon-exclusion policy (reverting to the pre-2011 policy or conducting individualized assessments) would be equally effective at serving the NCAA's legitimate interests in protecting youth safety and preserving recruiting integrity while producing less disparate impact. The court applied the three-step Wards Cove analysis and found plaintiff's evidence insufficient at step three.

case_name: Borum v. Brentwood Village, LLC
accommodation_description: This is a class action challenging a redevelopment plan that would eliminate three-, four-, and five-bedroom apartments, allegedly causing disparate impact on families with children and discriminatory statements by defendants.
key_holding: The court found that proposed substitute representative Moore brings typical and adequate claims for the class's disparate impact discrimination claims but not for the discriminatory statements claims, and accordingly decertified the class as to discriminatory statements claims while granting substitution as to disparate impact claims.
brief_summary: Brookland Manor tenants and One D.C. sued Brentwood Village LLC, Mid-City Financial Corporation, and Edgewood Management Corporation alleging that the planned redevelopment reducing family-sized apartments would have a disparate impact on families with children in violation of the FHA. The court granted in part plaintiffs' motion to substitute Marita Moore as class representative, finding her claims typical and adequate for disparate impact claims, but decertified the class as to discriminatory statements claims because Moore lacked standing to bring those claims.
key_cases_cited: Borum v. Brentwood Vill., LLC (Borum I), 218 F. Supp. 3d 1
Borum v. Brentwood Vill., LLC (Borum II), 324 F.R.D. 1
Borum v. Brentwood Vill., LLC (Borum III), 329 F.R.D. 90
DL v. District of Columbia, 312 F.R.D. 1
Reynolds v. Sheet Metal Workers, Local 102, 702 F.2d 221

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court certified a class on disparate impact discrimination claims alleging that the planned redevelopment would reduce three-bedroom units and eliminate four- and five-bedroom units, having a disparate impact on families with children based on familial status. The court found Moore to be a typical and adequate class representative on these claims and granted her substitution, allowing the disparate impact claims to proceed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discriminatory statements made in connection with the redevelopment under FHA § 3604(c)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that the proposed substitute class representative Moore lacked standing to bring discriminatory statements claims because she failed to allege a concrete and particularized injury. The court noted that Moore, lacking protected familial status under the FHA, could not establish that her civil rights were violated by discriminatory statements, and mere awareness of such statements without more discrete injury is insufficient to establish standing. The class was decertified as to these claims.

source_file: 4412459_2017_Oregon Bureau of Labor _ Industries Ex Rel. Fair Housing Council of Oregon v. Chandler Apartments, LLC_ca9
case_name: Oregon Bureau of Labor and Industries, ex rel Fair Housing Council of Oregon v. Chandler Apartments, LLC
accommodation_description: Prospective tenants requested to keep service dogs or therapy dogs as reasonable accommodations to the property's no-pet policy.
key_holding: Defendants violated the FHA by categorically denying testers' accommodation requests for service animals without engaging in the interactive process to determine whether the requested accommodations were reasonable and reasonably related to the claimed handicap.
brief_summary: BOLI and FHCO sued Chandler Apartments for housing discrimination based on denials of reasonable accommodation requests for service animals made by testers posing as prospective tenants. The Ninth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for plaintiffs, holding that defendants violated the FHA by refusing to grant the requested accommodations without engaging in the interactive process to evaluate whether the requests were reasonable and necessary.
key_cases_cited: Dubois v. Ass'n of Apartment Owners of 2987 Kalakaua, 453 F.3d 1175 (9th Cir. 2006)
Fair Hous. Council of San Fernando Valley v. Roommate.com, LLC, 666 F.3d 1216 (9th Cir. 2012)
Consumer Fin. Prot. Bureau v. Gordon, 819 F.3d 1179 (9th Cir. 2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation for service animals/therapy dogs for prospective tenants with disabilities
fha_claims.reasoning: Defendant failed to engage in the interactive process by immediately denying the accommodation request without inquiring whether the requested accommodation was reasonable or reasonably related to the claimed handicap. The court found all five elements of the FHA reasonable accommodation claim satisfied: plaintiff had standing despite testers not being actually disabled; defendant knew or should have known of the disability; accommodation was necessary; accommodation was reasonable; and defendant refused the accommodation.

source_file: 4417289_2017_Civil Rights Education _ Enforcement Center v. Hospitality Properties Trust_ca9
case_name: Civil Rights Education and Enforcement Center v. Hospitality Properties Trust
accommodation_description: Wheelchair users requested equivalent accessible shuttle transportation services at hotels owned by defendant REIT, which delegates hotel operations to independent management companies.
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed denial of class certification, holding that plaintiffs had Article III standing under the ADA's deterrent effect doctrine but failed to establish commonality because HPT did not maintain a uniform policy regarding shuttle services, requiring 142 individualized determinations of whether each hotel violated the ADA.
brief_summary: The Civil Rights Education and Enforcement Center and three wheelchair-using plaintiffs sued Hospitality Properties Trust (a REIT owning hotels across the U.S.) under ADA Title III, alleging hotels failed to provide equivalent shuttle transportation services for mobility-impaired guests. The Ninth Circuit affirmed that plaintiffs established Article III standing under the deterrent effect doctrine, but upheld denial of class certification because HPT's delegation of hotel operations to independent contractors meant there was no common policy to challenge, requiring individualized determinations for each hotel.
key_cases_cited: Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. v. Dukes, 564 U.S. 338 (2011)
Chapman v. Pier 1 Imports (U.S.) Inc., 631 F.3d 939 (9th Cir. 2011)
Pickern v. Holiday Quality Foods Inc., 293 F.3d 1133 (9th Cir. 2002)
Lujan v. Defs. of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title III ADA claim for failure to provide equivalent accessible transportation services (fixed route and demand responsive systems) at hotels
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 23(f) interlocutory appeal of class certification denial
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court affirmed the district court's denial of class certification on the ground that plaintiffs failed to satisfy Rule 23(a)(2) commonality requirement because HPT lacks a uniform policy regarding ADA compliance across its independently-operated hotels. The underlying Title III ADA claims survive the procedural ruling and remain pending on the merits.

case_name: Kirschenbaum v. Assa Corp.
accommodation_description: Not an FHA case — this is an appeal concerning attachment and execution of Iranian corporate assets to satisfy terrorism judgments under FSIA and TRIA.
key_holding: The Second Circuit affirmed that Assa Corporation, as Iran's alter ego and agency/instrumentality, is subject to the district court's jurisdiction and its property is subject to attachment and execution under both the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act and the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act.
brief_summary: Hundreds of terrorism victims holding default judgments against Iran sought to attach assets of Assa Corporation (a New York corporation owned by Bank Melli, ultimately owned by the Government of Iran) under the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act and Terrorism Risk Insurance Act. The Second Circuit affirmed, holding that Assa is Iran's alter ego as a matter of law and is therefore subject to the district court's jurisdiction, and that Assa's property constitutes blocked assets subject to attachment and execution under both statutes.
key_cases_cited: Kirschenbaum v. 650 Fifth Ave. & Related Props., 830 F.3d 107 (2d Cir. 2016)
Rubin v. Islamic Republic of Iran, 138 S. Ct. 816 (2018)
First National City Bank v. Banco Para El Comercio Exterior de Cuba (Bancec), 462 U.S. 611 (1983)
EM Ltd. v. Banco Central de la Republica Argentina, 800 F.3d 78 (2d Cir. 2015)

case_name: National Fair Housing Alliance v. Carson
accommodation_description: This case does not involve an individual reasonable accommodation request; rather, fair housing organizations challenge HUD's withdrawal of the Assessment Tool for the Affirmatively Further Fair Housing (AFFH) Rule as arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiffs' Rule 59(e) motion to alter the judgment, finding no clear error in the prior determination that plaintiffs lacked organizational standing because HUD's withdrawal of the Assessment Tool did not perceptibly impair their mission-driven activities given the AFFH Rule's remaining components.
brief_summary: Fair housing organizations sued HUD challenging the agency's withdrawal of the Assessment Tool used for the Affirmatively Further Fair Housing rule as arbitrary and capricious under the APA; the court had previously dismissed the case for lack of organizational standing and denied plaintiffs' motion to alter that judgment, finding that the withdrawal did not cause cognizable injury to plaintiffs' mission-driven activities.
key_cases_cited: Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Action Alliance of Senior Citizens of Greater Philadelphia v. Heckler, 789 F.2d 931 (D.C. Cir. 1986)
People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals v. U.S. Department of Agriculture, 797 F.3d 1087 (D.C. Cir. 2015)
Exxon Shipping Co. v. Baker, 554 U.S. 471 (2008)
Firestone v. Firestone, 76 F.3d 1205 (D.C. Cir. 1996)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; this is an administrative law challenge to HUD's withdrawal of the Assessment Tool and suspension of the Affirmatively Furthering Fair Housing (AFFH) Rule's Assessment of Fair Housing (AFH) process, not a claim for failure to provide a reasonable accommodation to an individual with a disability.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because the organizational plaintiffs failed to establish standing. The plaintiffs could not demonstrate a cognizable injury in fact because HUD's withdrawal of the Assessment Tool and AFH process did not perceptibly impair the plaintiffs' mission-driven activities; key portions of the AFFH Rule remained in effect, including the definition of affirmatively furthering fair housing, community participation requirements, and recordkeeping obligations that still applied to Consolidated Plans.

source_file: 4439165_2019_Albert Schaw v. Habitat for Humanity of Citrus County, Inc._ca11
case_name: Albert Schaw v. Habitat for Humanity of Citrus County, Inc.
accommodation_description: Request that Habitat count food stamps and familial support as income toward its minimum-income requirement, given that Schaw's quadriplegia prevents him from working.
key_holding: The court held that the district court improperly granted summary judgment on the reasonable accommodation claim because it applied an overly restrictive 'necessity' test that divorced Schaw's financial inability to meet the income threshold from his disability-related inability to work; the accommodation request was facially reasonable and raised genuine issues of material fact as to whether it was necessary to afford Schaw equal opportunity to obtain housing.
