fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation claim under § 3617 for exercising FHA rights
fha_claims.reasoning: The retaliation claim remained pending before the district court, preventing the appellate court from exercising jurisdiction over the appeal of the dismissal orders.

case_name: George Friedel v. Sun Communities, Inc.
citation: 747 F. App'x 775 (11th Cir. 2018) [Friedel I referenced]; No. 20-12275 (11th Cir. Aug. 24, 2021) [current appeal unpublished]
accommodation_description: George Friedel requested that Sun Communities and Park Place allow him to keep his golden retriever Maggie, an emotional support animal for his depression, despite the community's rule prohibiting dangerous or aggressive animals.
key_holding: The eviction notice issued October 18, 2017 was motivated by the jury verdict in Friedel I, not George Friedel's disability, and the requested accommodation of keeping Maggie was not reasonable because a prior jury found Maggie posed a direct threat to other residents.
brief_summary: George and Kathleen Friedel appealed the dismissal of their second lawsuit against Sun Communities and Park Place Community, LLC regarding their emotional support dog Maggie, after a prior jury found the dog posed a direct threat. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed, finding that the eviction notice was issued the day after the first trial ended (not because of disability) and that the requested accommodation was not reasonable on its face given the jury's direct-threat finding.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014)
Hunt v. Aimco Properties, L.P., 814 F.3d 1213 (11th Cir. 2016)
Schwarz v. City of Treasure Island, 544 F.3d 1201 (11th Cir. 2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint failed to plausibly allege that the October 2017 notice to vacate was issued because of George's disability. The factual allegations directly contradicted the discrimination claim and were more likely explained by Park Place's success in the prior jury trial, which occurred the day before the eviction notice was issued.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Allowing Maggie, an emotional support animal, to remain on the property despite prior aggressive behavior; plaintiff alleged Maggie had received nine months of professional training by the time of the October 2017 notice to vacate
fha_claims.reasoning: The Friedels failed to allege sufficient facts showing the requested accommodation was reasonable on its face. The prior jury verdict found no reasonable accommodation would have eliminated the risk Maggie posed; the Friedels did not explain why allowing Maggie was efficacious and proportional to costs; they sought their preferred accommodation rather than a reasonable one; and they did not pursue alternative accommodations or engage forthrightly with Park Place about training before claiming it was complete.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The Friedels' conclusory allegation that eviction resulted from their prior lawsuit and accommodation requests was contradicted by the circumstances: they had notice of eviction risk before filing suit, secretly returned Maggie to the property, the jury found Maggie was a direct threat, and the post-trial eviction notice was consistent with that verdict. The Friedels alleged no retaliatory animus or improper motive and failed to show the protected conduct played a role in the defendants' decision.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing; tortious interference with contract (Florida state law claims)
fha_claims.reasoning: Under Florida law, breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing must attach to a specific express contractual obligation, not the lease as a whole; the Friedels failed to identify any specific breached obligation. For tortious interference, the Friedels failed to allege the interference was unjustified, as the jury verdict and lease terms authorized removal of dangerous animals and eviction for rule violations.

source_file: 5091876_2021_Yellowstone Womens First Step v. City of Costa Mesa_ca9
case_name: Yellowstone Women's First Step House, Inc. v. City of Costa Mesa
accommodation_description: Operators of group homes for women in recovery from substance abuse sought reasonable accommodation from municipal zoning ordinances requiring special use permits for group homes.
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed the jury verdict rejecting plaintiffs' disparate impact and disparate treatment claims, vacated the costs award and remanded for reconsideration under the Christiansburg frivolousness standard applicable to Fair Housing Act plaintiffs.
brief_summary: Yellowstone Women's First Step House, California Women's Recovery, and Sober Living Network sued the City of Costa Mesa challenging municipal ordinances regulating group homes for women recovering from substance abuse, alleging the ordinances violated the Fair Housing Act. After a two-week jury trial, the Ninth Circuit affirmed the judgment rejecting plaintiffs' disparate impact and disparate treatment claims but vacated the costs award and remanded for reconsideration under the proper standard for assessing fees against FHA plaintiffs.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dept. of Hous. & Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Cmtys. Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Green v. Mercy Housing, Inc., 991 F.3d 1056 (9th Cir. 2021)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Christiansburg Garment Co. v. EEOC, 434 U.S. 412 (1978)
Pac. Shores Properties, LLC v. City of Newport Beach, 730 F.3d 1142 (9th Cir. 2013)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request for reasonable accommodation regarding zoning or land use restrictions affecting sober living group homes under Ordinance 17-05 special use permit provisions
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court denied SLN's motion for partial summary judgment on its reasonable accommodation claim because the complaint failed to provide proper notice of specific individualized accommodation denials; the claim was characterized as a repackaged facial discrimination claim lacking notice of discrete instances of accommodation denial.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: A reasonable jury could conclude that the substantial, legitimate, nondiscriminatory interests supporting Ordinance 14-13 would not be served by another practice with less discriminatory effect, and the jury verdict that plaintiffs failed to establish disparate impact by a preponderance of the evidence was supported by substantial evidence.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: A reasonable jury could conclude that passage of Ordinance 14-13 was not more likely than not motivated by a discriminatory reason, and the jury verdict that plaintiffs failed to establish disparate treatment by a preponderance of the evidence was supported by substantial evidence.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: California Government Code § 65008 claim; Americans with Disabilities Act
fha_claims.disposition: Judgment as a Matter of Law
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court's finding that Yellowstone did not meet its burden of proving that the City discriminated against Boston House because of disability was neither clearly erroneous nor predicated on legal or factual error.

case_name: Alice Hicks v. Thomas Skaar
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; case involves claim that landlord declined to renew lease based on plaintiff's race (African American).
key_holding: Summary judgment was appropriate because plaintiff failed to raise a genuine issue of material fact that the defendants' proffered reason for nonrenewal (her repeated, unsubstantiated, racially-tinged complaints) was pretextual for race discrimination.
brief_summary: Alice Hicks, an African American tenant, sued her landlord and property management company alleging race discrimination under the Fair Housing Act after they declined to renew her apartment lease. The Ninth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for defendants, finding Hicks failed to raise a genuine issue that the landlord's proffered reason for nonrenewal (her repeated unsubstantiated complaints about neighbors) was pretextual for discrimination.
key_cases_cited: Ave. 6E Invs., LLC v. City of Yuma, 818 F.3d 493 (9th Cir. 2016)
Harris v. Itzhaki, 183 F.3d 1043 (9th Cir. 1999)
Gamble v. City of Escondido, 104 F.3d 300 (9th Cir. 1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Even assuming plaintiff established a prima facie case of race discrimination in lease nonrenewal, summary judgment was appropriate because plaintiff failed to raise a genuine issue of material fact that defendants' proffered reason (repeated, unsubstantiated, racially-tinged complaints about neighbors) was pretextual. Plaintiff presented no colorable evidence of pretext.

case_name: City of Oakland v. Wells Fargo & Company
accommodation_description: This case does not involve a reasonable accommodation request; it is a municipal government's claim that Wells Fargo's discriminatory mortgage lending practices caused economic harm to the city through reduced property tax revenue and increased municipal expenditures.
key_holding: The en banc court held that Oakland's claimed economic injuries from Wells Fargo's discriminatory lending were too attenuated to establish proximate cause under the FHA—the 'ripples of harm' flowing from discriminatory loans to minority borrowers to higher foreclosure rates to depressed property values to reduced tax revenue and increased municipal expenditures traveled too far beyond the alleged misconduct to satisfy the direct-relation standard articulated in Bank of America Corp. v. City of Miami.
brief_summary: The City of Oakland sued Wells Fargo alleging that the bank's discriminatory mortgage lending practices against African-American and Latino borrowers caused higher default and foreclosure rates, which in turn depressed property values and resulted in lost property tax revenue and increased municipal expenditures for blight remediation. The en banc Ninth Circuit reversed the district court's denial of Wells Fargo's motion to dismiss, holding that Oakland's economic injuries were too remotely caused by the discriminatory lending to satisfy the FHA's proximate cause requirement, applying the direct-relation standard from Bank of America Corp. v. City of Miami.
key_cases_cited: Bank of America Corp. v. City of Miami, 137 S. Ct. 1296 (2017)
Holmes v. Securities Investor Protection Corp., 503 U.S. 258 (1992)
Lexmark International, Inc. v. Static Control Components, Inc., 572 U.S. 118 (2014)
Texas Dept. of Housing & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Bridge v. Phoenix Bond & Indemnity Co., 553 U.S. 639 (2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discriminatory lending practices: steering minority borrowers into adjustable-rate mortgages with higher costs and risk features than fixed-rate mortgages offered to similarly situated white borrowers
fha_claims.reasoning: Under Bank of America Corp. v. City of Miami, 137 S. Ct. 1296 (2017), the court applied the proximate-cause requirement and held that foreseeability alone is insufficient; there must be a direct relation between the injury asserted and the injurious conduct alleged. Oakland's theory of harm—from discriminatory lending to higher defaults to foreclosures to depressed property values to reduced tax revenue—extends too far beyond the first step of the causal chain (harm to minority borrowers) to satisfy the FHA's proximate-cause requirement.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discriminatory lending practices causing increased municipal expenditures: alleged need for increased police, fire, building services, code enforcement, and city attorney resources to remediate blighted conditions resulting from foreclosures
fha_claims.reasoning: The increased municipal expenditure claim introduces even more independent variables and intervening actors into the causal chain than the reduced tax revenue claim, making it even more attenuated from the alleged FHA violation. The claim relies on speculation that individual actors will commit civil and criminal violations necessitating city resources, lacking any direct relation between the FHA violation and the purported harm.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Injunctive and declaratory relief based on discriminatory lending practices
fha_claims.reasoning: The proximate-cause requirement under Miami applies to all FHA claims, including those seeking injunctive and declaratory relief, not merely damages claims. Oakland's injunctive and declaratory relief claims fail for the same proximate-cause reasons as the damages claims: the alleged injuries are too remote from the discriminatory lending conduct to satisfy the direct-relation standard.

case_name: Southwest Fair Housing Council v. Maricopa Domestic Water Improvement District
citation: SW. FAIR HOUSING V. MARICOPA DOMESTIC WATER (9th Cir. 2021)
race_if_mentioned: African American, Native American, Hispanic, White
accommodation_description: This case does not involve a reasonable accommodation request; it challenges a water utility security deposit policy as having disparate impact on racial and familial status protected classes.
key_holding: Although the district court erred in its prima facie analysis, the Ninth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the District because it established that the security deposit policy served legitimate business interests and the plaintiffs failed to demonstrate equally effective, less discriminatory alternatives; the disparate treatment claim also failed for lack of evidence of discriminatory animus.
brief_summary: Southwest Fair Housing Council and two public housing tenants sued Maricopa Domestic Water Improvement District challenging a policy requiring a $180 security deposit from new public housing customers (who are disproportionately African American, Native American, and Hispanic) while non-public housing customers paid only $55. The Ninth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the District, holding that although the district court erred in its prima facie analysis, the District established legitimate business justifications for the policy and plaintiffs failed to show equally effective less discriminatory alternatives.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dept. of Housing & Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Wards Cove Packing Co. v. Aida, 490 U.S. 642 (1989)
Watson v. Fort Worth Bank & Trust, 487 U.S. 977 (1988)
Hardie v. County of RDC, 876 F.3d 312 (9th Cir. 2017)
Ave. 6E Invs., LLC v. City of Yuma, 818 F.3d 493 (9th Cir. 2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Although the court held that plaintiffs established a prima facie disparate-impact case (correcting the district court's error on robust causation), the defendant demonstrated a legitimate business interest in the security deposit policy and plaintiffs failed to identify an equally effective, less discriminatory alternative, resulting in summary judgment for the defendant on the disparate-impact claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to adduce sufficient evidence of discriminatory animus or intent. The statement about 'influx of people and tenants' was not code for protected-class membership, and knowledge of disparate impact alone is insufficient to establish discriminatory motive absent evidence of pretext.

case_name: Cynthia Gatling v. Jubilee Housing, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: Wheelchair user tenant requested that defendant repair or replace an unsafe wheelchair ramp and inoperable wheelchair lift to provide safe building access.
key_holding: The court denied dismissal of the Rehabilitation Act failure-to-accommodate claim because factual questions remained about whether plaintiff's November 2020 request constituted a new accommodation request or a request for reconsideration, potentially restarting the statute of limitations, while dismissing plaintiff's DCHRA design-and-construction claim because the applicable provisions apply only to dwellings first occupied after 1999 and the Mozart was built in the 1930s.
brief_summary: Cynthia Gatling, a wheelchair user residing at the Mozart apartment building owned by Jubilee Housing, sued alleging the wheelchair ramp and lift were unsafe and inoperable, causing her to fall. She brought claims under the Rehabilitation Act, DCHRA, and for breach of contract. The court dismissed most claims including the DCHRA design/construction claim (building predates applicable requirements), breach of contract, and breach of implied covenant of good faith, but allowed the Rehabilitation Act reasonable accommodation claim to proceed because factual disputes existed about when the accommodation was requested.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Owens-Hart v. Howard Univ.
Floyd v. Lee
Tobin v. Liberty Mutual Ins. Co.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Repair or replacement of wheelchair ramp at building entrance and repair or replacement of inoperable wheelchair lift on side of building
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss without prejudice on statute of limitations grounds because the complaint did not clearly establish whether Plaintiff's November 2020 request for accommodations was a new discrete request (restarting the statute of limitations clock) or merely a request for reconsideration of a prior denial. The court adopted the Owens-Hart framework requiring factual development to determine whether requests were new or reconsiderations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Compliance with DCHRA adaptive design requirements for wheelchair accessibility (D.C. Code § 2-1402.21(d)(3)(D))
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted motion to dismiss because the DCHRA adaptive design requirements in subsection (d)(3)(D) apply only to multifamily dwellings first occupied after April 20, 1999. The Mozart was constructed in the 1930s, so the design and construction provisions do not apply. The court interpreted subsections (d)(3)(C) and (d)(3)(D) as referring to the same set of dwellings and applied the effective date restriction from (d)(3)(C) to (d)(3)(D) based on statutory interpretation principles and analogy to the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rehabilitation Act § 504 claim for failure to provide reasonable accommodations; DCHRA aiding and abetting claim; breach of contract; breach of implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed aiding and abetting claim (Count III) because there was no underlying DCHRA violation for defendants to aid and abet. Court dismissed breach of contract claim (Count IV) because the lease contained no provision obligating defendants to provide reasonable accommodations or refrain from discrimination, and HUD regulations were not incorporated into the lease despite plaintiff's argument. Court dismissed breach of implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing (Count V) because reasonable accommodations were not a 'fruit of the contract' and plaintiff failed to allege bad faith or arbitrary conduct beyond declining to provide accommodations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III violation for failure to provide accessible information about hotel accessibility features in online reservation system
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff lacked Article III standing because she failed to allege a concrete and particularized injury in fact. Although she alleged a statutory violation of the ADA Title III regulation requiring accessible information in online reservation systems, she disclaimed any intent to book a room at the hotel and therefore suffered no concrete harm from the alleged regulatory violation, distinguishing her from FHA testers in Havens Realty who received discriminatory misrepresentations.

case_name: Webb v. United States Veterans Initiative
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a disabled veteran, alleges that U.S. VETS discriminated against him based on sex by refusing to offer him a one-bedroom apartment while offering one to a less-qualified female applicant.
key_holding: The plaintiff's Fair Housing Act sex discrimination claim is not time-barred because the administrative tolling during the OHR proceeding preserved his right to sue, and the complaint was filed within the remaining limitations period.
brief_summary: Stanley Webb, a disabled veteran, sued U.S. VETS under the Fair Housing Act alleging sex discrimination in housing placement, claiming he was denied a one-bedroom apartment while a less-qualified female applicant received one. The court denied U.S. VETS's motion to dismiss the FHA claim as untimely, finding that the limitations period was tolled during the administrative proceeding before the D.C. Office of Human Rights, and the lawsuit was filed within the applicable deadline.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Bregman v. Perles, 747 F.3d 873 (D.C. Cir. 2014)
Webb v. United States Veterans Initiative, 993 F.3d 970 (D.C. Cir. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: One-bedroom apartment placement in Shelter Plus Care program
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss on statute of limitations grounds, finding that the claim was timely filed within two years of the most recent discriminatory conduct (February 1, 2017) and that the administrative proceeding tolled the limitations period. The FHA claim survives the motion to dismiss and proceeds on the merits.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: D.C. Consumer Protection Procedures Act, common law fraud, breach of contract
fha_claims.reasoning: Court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over non-federal claims under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3) and denied plaintiff's motion to file a second amended complaint as futile because it merely restated facts in different terms and reasserted claims on which the court had previously ruled.

source_file: 5294785_2021_A.L.M. v. Board of Managers of the Vireum Schoolhouse Condominium_ca2
case_name: A.L.M. v. Board of Managers of the Vireum Schoolhouse Condominium
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested; the case concerns alleged post-acquisition harassment based on protected characteristics.
key_holding: The Second Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the Board because A.L.M. failed to raise a material question of fact that the alleged harassing conduct—excessive noise and 'intersecting behavior'—occurred because of her protected characteristics rather than pre-existing interpersonal conflicts between the Moore Family and Vireum residents.
brief_summary: A.L.M., a minor suing through her parent, sued the Board of Managers of the Vireum Schoolhouse Condominium alleging that the Board and Vireum residents subjected her to a hostile housing environment based on her race (Chinese), national origin, sex, and age in violation of the FHA and Civil Rights Act. The Second Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the Board, finding that while there was evidence of pervasive harassing conduct (noise and intersection behavior), A.L.M. presented no evidence beyond conclusory assertions that the conduct occurred because of her protected characteristics rather than general interpersonal conflicts.
key_cases_cited: Francis v. Kings Park Manor, Inc., 992 F.3d 67 (2d Cir. 2021)
Pierre v. Lantern Grp. Found., Inc., 2016 WL 3461309 (S.D.N.Y. June 20, 2016)
Haber v. ASN 50th St. LLC, 847 F. Supp. 2d 578 (S.D.N.Y. 2012)
Littlejohn v. City of New York, 795 F.3d 297 (2d Cir. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to adduce evidence sufficient to establish that the hostile housing environment harassment occurred because of membership in a protected class (race, national origin, sex, or age). Under McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting, plaintiff presented only conclusory assertions and self-serving testimony of discriminatory animus, which cannot support a prima facie case. The record contained ample evidence of non-discriminatory reasons for the conduct, including long-standing antagonistic relations between the parties over building operations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Civil Rights Act claims under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 and 1982 (racial discrimination in contracts and real property)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to present evidence sufficient to raise a question of fact as to whether race, national origin, sex, or age was a motivating factor in the alleged conduct. Under the three-element test for §§ 1981 and 1982 claims, plaintiff could not establish discriminatory intent by the defendant.

case_name: Julie Ballou v. James McElvain
accommodation_description: Julie Ballou, a police officer, alleges that Police Chief James McElvain denied her promotion to sergeant on the basis of her sex and subjected her to repeated internal affairs investigations as pretext for sex discrimination.
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit held that Ballou established a prima facie case for sex discrimination under the Equal Protection Clause and that McElvain was not entitled to qualified immunity because discriminatorily denying a promotion based on sex violates clearly established law under Lindsey v. Shalmy and Bator v. State of Hawai'i.
brief_summary: Julie Ballou, a Vancouver, Washington police officer, sued Police Chief James McElvain under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 alleging that he violated her Equal Protection rights by discriminatorily denying her promotion to sergeant based on her sex and violated her First Amendment rights by retaliating against her for opposing sex discrimination. The Ninth Circuit affirmed the denial of qualified immunity, holding that Ballou presented sufficient circumstantial evidence of discriminatory intent and that any reasonable officer would have known that sex-based denial of promotion violates clearly established constitutional law.
key_cases_cited: Lindsey v. Shalmy, 29 F.3d 1382 (9th Cir. 1994)
Bator v. State of Hawai'i, 39 F.3d 1021 (9th Cir. 1994)
Village of Arlington Heights v. Metro. Hous. Dev. Corp., 429 U.S. 252 (1977)
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Pac. Shores Props., LLC v. City of Newport Beach, 730 F.3d 1142 (9th Cir. 2013)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal Protection Clause disparate treatment claim (sex discrimination in employment promotion); First Amendment retaliation claim (Petition Clause); Equal Protection Clause retaliation claim. All claims brought under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, not the Fair Housing Act.
fha_claims.disposition: Qualified immunity denial affirmed on appeal
fha_claims.reasoning: Appellate court affirmed denial of qualified immunity on Equal Protection disparate treatment claim and First Amendment retaliation claim, finding McElvain's conduct violated clearly established constitutional rights. Court lacked jurisdiction to address Equal Protection retaliation claim because district court did not deny qualified immunity on that theory. Claims proceed to trial on merits.

source_file: 5296771_2021_City of Oakland v. Wells Fargo _ Company_ca9
case_name: City of Oakland v. Wells Fargo & Company
accommodation_description: Discriminatory mortgage lending practices that steered African-American and Latino borrowers into predatory loans with worse terms than similarly situated white borrowers
key_holding: Under Bank of America Corp. v. City of Miami, the en banc court held that Oakland's claimed economic injuries—lost property tax revenue and increased municipal expenditures—were too attenuated from Wells Fargo's discriminatory lending practices to satisfy the FHA's proximate cause requirement, as the downstream ripples of harm traveled too far beyond the first-step injury to minority borrowers.
brief_summary: The City of Oakland sued Wells Fargo alleging that its discriminatory mortgage lending practices against African-American and Latino borrowers caused higher default and foreclosure rates, which in turn decreased property values and resulted in lost tax revenue and increased municipal expenditures. The Ninth Circuit en banc, applying the Supreme Court's decision in Bank of America Corp. v. City of Miami, held that these downstream economic injuries were too attenuated from the discriminatory lending to establish proximate cause under the Fair Housing Act, reversing the district court's denial of Wells Fargo's motion to dismiss as to the tax revenue and injunctive/declaratory relief claims.
key_cases_cited: Bank of America Corp. v. City of Miami, 137 S. Ct. 1296 (2017)
Lexmark International, Inc. v. Static Control Components, Inc., 572 U.S. 118 (2014)
Holmes v. Securities Investor Protection Corp., 503 U.S. 258 (1992)
Hemi Group, LLC v. City of New York, 559 U.S. 1 (2010)
Bridge v. Phoenix Bond & Indemnity Co., 553 U.S. 639 (2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discriminatory lending practices: steering minority borrowers into adjustable-rate mortgages with higher costs and risk features than fixed-rate mortgages offered to similarly situated white borrowers
fha_claims.reasoning: Under Bank of America Corp. v. City of Miami, 137 S. Ct. 1296 (2017), the City failed to adequately plead proximate cause because its theory of harm—from discriminatory loans to higher defaults and foreclosures to depressed property values to reduced tax revenue—extends too far beyond the first step of the causal chain (harm to borrowers) and involves too many independent intervening factors (borrower default decisions, third-party foreclosure decisions, property value fluctuations) to satisfy the 'direct relation' standard required by the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discriminatory lending practices causing increased municipal expenditures: City alleged that foreclosures required increased spending by police, fire, building services, code enforcement, and city attorney's office to remediate blighted conditions
fha_claims.reasoning: The increased municipal expenditures claim fails the proximate cause test because it introduces even more independent factors into the causal chain than the tax revenue claim, relying on speculation that individual actors will commit civil and criminal violations necessitating city resources, creating no direct relation between the FHA violation and the purported harm.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discriminatory lending practices causing non-economic injury: City alleged that discriminatory lending undermined its racial-integration goals
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court dismissed the non-economic injury claim on standing grounds, which the appellate court did not revisit on appeal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discriminatory lending practices: claims for injunctive and declaratory relief based on alleged steering of minority borrowers into predatory loans
fha_claims.reasoning: The proximate-cause requirement under Miami applies to all FHA claims, including injunctive and declaratory relief, not just damages claims. The City failed to plead proximate cause for these claims for the same reasons it failed on the damages claims—the causal chain extends too far beyond the first step and involves too many independent intervening factors.

case_name: Southwest Fair Housing Council, Inc. v. Maricopa Domestic Water Improvement District
race_if_mentioned: African American, Native American, Hispanic, White
accommodation_description: The case concerns a water utility district's security deposit policy that imposed a $180 deposit on public housing customers versus $55 for other customers, alleged to discriminate based on race, national origin, sex, and familial status.
key_holding: Although the Ninth Circuit held the district court erred in its prima facie disparate impact analysis, it affirmed summary judgment for the District because the Security Deposit Policy served legitimate business interests in recovering unpaid water bills from public housing tenants whose landlord (Pinal County) refused to pay, and plaintiffs failed to demonstrate an equally effective, less discriminatory alternative.
brief_summary: Southwest Fair Housing Council and two public housing residents appealed summary judgment against the Maricopa Domestic Water Improvement District, challenging as discriminatory under the Fair Housing Act a policy requiring a $180 refundable security deposit from public housing customers versus $55 for other customers. The Ninth Circuit affirmed, holding that although plaintiffs established a prima facie disparate impact case, the District proved the policy served its legitimate business interest in recovering delinquent water bills from tenants whose public-entity landlord refused to pay, and plaintiffs failed to present evidence of an equally effective, less discriminatory alternative.
key_cases_cited: Tex. Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Wards Cove Packing Co. v. Aida, 490 U.S. 642 (1989)
Watson v. Fort Worth Bank & Trust, 487 U.S. 977 (1988)
Arlington Heights v. Metropolitan Hous. Dev. Corp., 429 U.S. 252 (1977)
Ojo v. Farmers Grp., Inc., 600 F.3d 1201 (9th Cir. 2010)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Although the court held that plaintiffs established a prima facie disparate-impact case (policy applied only to public housing residents, disproportionately affecting African Americans, Native Americans, and single mothers, with robust causality), the District established by undisputed evidence that the $180 security deposit policy served its legitimate business interest in protecting against unrecoverable delinquencies from Pinal County tenants, and plaintiffs failed to identify an equally effective, less discriminatory alternative. Summary judgment affirmed for defendant.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to adduce evidence sufficient to establish a genuine dispute of material fact that discriminatory animus was a motivating factor in the District's decision to implement the security deposit policy. A single statement about 'influx of people and tenants' was not code for protected classes, and knowledge of potential disparate impact alone is insufficient to prove discriminatory intent absent evidence of pretext.

case_name: McNeil v. Yale University et al
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege they were denied housing opportunities at same-sex fraternities because of their sex, as membership is restricted based on sex.
key_holding: Plaintiffs lack Article III standing to bring FHA claims because they failed to allege any concrete injury related to housing—the SAC contains no allegations that any plaintiff ever sought, inquired about, or expressed interest in housing at any defendant fraternity, only that they sought membership.
brief_summary: Female Yale students sued fraternities and their housing corporations alleging sex discrimination in membership practices that prevented them from accessing fraternity housing, in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The Second Circuit affirmed the dismissal, holding that plaintiffs lacked Article III standing because they failed to allege any actual or imminent injury related to housing—they sought only fraternity membership, not housing, and never inquired about or expressed interest in housing opportunities.
key_cases_cited: Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)
Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins, 578 U.S. 330 (2016)
Katz v. Donna Karan Co., 872 F.3d 114 (2d Cir. 2017)
United States v. Space Hunters, Inc., 429 F.3d 416 (2d Cir. 2005)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of fraternity membership and housing based on sex
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs lacked Article III standing under FHA § 3604(a) because they failed to allege they ever sought housing, applied for housing, expressed interest in housing, or discussed housing with fraternity defendants. The complaint alleged only attempts to gain fraternity membership, not housing injury.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discriminatory statements regarding housing based on sex
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs lacked Article III standing under FHA § 3604(c) because they failed to allege any housing-related injury or that defendants made any discriminatory statements about housing. The only alleged statements concerned denial of fraternity membership based on sex, not housing.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Connecticut Discriminatory Housing Practices Act claims
fha_claims.reasoning: State law housing discrimination claims under Connecticut law failed because they were derivative of the deficient FHA claims and plaintiffs lacked Article III standing.

case_name: Gatling v. Jubilee Housing, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that defendants repair or replace the wheelchair ramp at the front entrance of the Mozart apartment building (which was too steep, non-compliant with architectural standards, and had caused plaintiff to fall from her wheelchair) and repair or replace the wheelchair lift on the side of the building that had been inoperable for years, so that plaintiff—a wheelchair user—could safely access and exit her building and reach the mailroom.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss the Rehabilitation Act reasonable accommodation claim because it could not determine at the pleading stage whether plaintiff's November 2020 request was a new discrete accommodation request (restarting the limitations clock) or merely a reconsideration of a prior denial, but granted dismissal of the DCHRA design and construction claims because those adaptive-design provisions apply only to multifamily buildings first occupied after April 20, 1999, and the Mozart was built in the 1930s.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Cynthia Gatling, a wheelchair user, sued her landlord Jubilee Housing for failing to repair an unsafe, overly steep wheelchair ramp and an inoperable wheelchair lift despite her repeated requests spanning several years, including a specific request following a November 2020 fall requiring emergency medical care. The court granted in part and denied in part defendants' motion to dismiss: it allowed the Rehabilitation Act failure-to-accommodate claim to survive because it was unclear whether the November 2020 accommodation request was a new discrete act restarting the statute of limitations or a mere reconsideration of a prior denial, while dismissing the DCHRA design and construction claims because those provisions do not apply to a building constructed in the 1930s. The breach of contract and covenant of good faith and fair dealing claims were also dismissed because the lease contained no provision obligating defendants to provide reasonable accommodations.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Owens-Hart v. Howard Univ., 220 F. Supp. 3d 81 (D.D.C. 2016)
Floyd v. Lee, 968 F. Supp. 2d 308 (D.D.C. 2013)
Borum v. Brentwood Village, LLC, 218 F. Supp. 3d 1 (D.D.C. 2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Repair or replacement of wheelchair ramp at building entrance and repair or replacement of wheelchair lift on side of building
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss Count I (Rehabilitation Act claim) without prejudice on statute of limitations grounds, finding the complaint insufficiently alleged whether the November 2020 request for accommodations was a new discrete request or merely a request for reconsideration of prior denials. The court applied the Owens-Hart framework requiring factual development to determine whether a new limitations clock began running, but did not reach the substantive merits of the reasonable accommodation claim itself.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Violation of District of Columbia Human Rights Act (DCHRA), D.C. Code § 2-1402.21(d)(3)(D); breach of lease agreement; breach of implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing; violation of Rehabilitation Act of 1973, 29 U.S.C. § 701 et seq.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted motion to dismiss Count II (DCHRA design and construction claim) because the adaptive-design requirements of D.C. Code § 2-1402.21(d)(3)(D) apply only to dwellings first occupied after April 20, 1999, and the Mozart was constructed in the 1930s. The court interpreted subsections (d)(3)(C) and (d)(3)(D) in concert, relying on statutory interpretation canons and parallel FHA language to conclude the effective-date restriction applies to both provisions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Violation of D.C. Code § 2-1402.62 (aiding and abetting discrimination); breach of contract; breach of implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing; Rehabilitation Act claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted motion to dismiss Count III (aiding and abetting under DCHRA § 2-1402.62) because there is no underlying violation of D.C. Code § 2-1402.21 for defendants to aid and abet, as the adaptive-design subsection does not apply to the Mozart.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of lease agreement; breach of implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing; Rehabilitation Act claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted motion to dismiss Count IV (breach of contract) because the lease contains no contractual provision obligating defendants to provide reasonable accommodations or refrain from disability discrimination. The court rejected plaintiff's argument that HUD regulations were incorporated into the lease, finding the lease's integration clause precluded such incorporation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing; Rehabilitation Act claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted motion to dismiss Count V (breach of implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing) because defendants had no contractual duty to provide reasonable accommodations, so the receipt of such accommodations was not a 'fruit of the contract' that defendants could injure by refusing to provide them.

case_name: Josephine Guion v. Bonner Homeless Transitions
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request is described in the case text; the claims sound in general FHA discrimination (disparate treatment and disparate impact) and retaliation, without reference to a particular accommodation sought.
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for defendants on all of Guion's FHA claims (retaliation, disparate treatment, and disparate impact) and state law tort claims because she failed to raise a genuine dispute of material fact as to whether defendants' actions were discriminatory.
brief_summary: Josephine Guion, proceeding pro se, appealed the district court's grant of summary judgment in favor of Bonner Homeless Transitions on her Fair Housing Act claims of discrimination and retaliation, as well as state law claims for fraud, defamation, and intentional infliction of emotional distress. The Ninth Circuit affirmed on all counts, finding Guion failed to create a genuine factual dispute regarding the discriminatory nature of defendants' conduct under any FHA theory and that her fraud claim likewise lacked evidentiary support. Her defamation and IIED claims were separately barred by Idaho's two-year statute of limitations, with no basis for equitable tolling.
key_cases_cited: Walker v. City of Lakewood, 272 F.3d 1114 (9th Cir. 2001)
Harris v. Itzhaki, 183 F.3d 1043 (9th Cir. 1999)
Pfaff v. U.S. Dep't of Hous. & Urban Dev., 88 F.3d 739 (9th Cir. 1996)
Guatay Christian Fellowship v. County of San Diego, 670 F.3d 957 (9th Cir. 2011)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to raise a genuine dispute of material fact as to whether defendants' actions were discriminatory under the FHA retaliation standard articulated in Walker v. City of Lakewood.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to raise a genuine dispute of material fact as to whether defendants' actions were discriminatory under the FHA disparate treatment standard articulated in Harris v. Itzhaki.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to raise a genuine dispute of material fact as to whether defendants' actions were discriminatory under the FHA disparate impact standard articulated in Pfaff v. U.S. Dep't of Hous. & Urban Dev.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: State law fraud, defamation, and intentional infliction of emotional distress claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Fraud claim failed because plaintiff did not raise a genuine dispute of material fact as to falsity; defamation and IIED claims were time-barred under Idaho Code § 5-219(4)-(5) with no extraordinary circumstances justifying equitable tolling.

source_file: 5298765_2021_Constance George v. House of Hope Recovery_ca9
case_name: Constance George v. House of Hope Recovery
accommodation_description: George alleges she was terminated from the recovery home because of her race and religion.
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed summary judgment on George's religious discrimination claim because she failed to present any legitimate comparator evidence showing disparate treatment, and her attempt to raise a new 'reasonable inferences' theory on appeal relied on evidence not presented to the district court.
brief_summary: Constance George appealed the district court's summary judgment in favor of House of Hope Recovery and Patricia Barcroft on her Fair Housing Act claims alleging discrimination based on race and religion. The Ninth Circuit affirmed summary judgment on the religious discrimination claim because George failed to present comparator evidence showing disparate treatment, and dismissed the appeal as to other defendants for lack of jurisdiction due to insufficient service of the notice of appeal.
key_cases_cited: Gamble v. City of Escondido, 104 F.3d 300 (9th Cir. 1997)
Bodett v. CoxCom, Inc., 366 F.3d 736 (9th Cir. 2004)
Lyons v. England, 307 F.3d 1092 (9th Cir. 2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie case of religious discrimination under the McDonnell-Douglas framework because she presented no evidence that similarly situated non-Jehovah's Witness residents were treated differently. On appeal, plaintiff offered a new 'reasonable inferences' theory based on evidence not presented to the district court, which the court rejected.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's racial discrimination claim against Barcroft and House of Hope was affirmed on summary judgment. Plaintiff failed to assert any colorable argument on appeal as to why remand for a new trial on the racial discrimination claim was warranted.

source_file: 5299117_2021_Dayton Veterans Residences v. Dayton Metro. Housing Auth._ca6
case_name: Dayton Veterans Residences Limited Partnership v. Dayton Metropolitan Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Freedom's Path requested that GDPM amend its Administrative Plan to allow GDPM to apply for VASH project-based vouchers on Freedom's Path's behalf to enable development of supportive housing for disabled homeless veterans.
key_holding: A reasonable jury could find that GDPM's refusal to amend its Administrative Plan to enable it to seek VASH vouchers deprived disabled veterans of an equal opportunity to access housing in the Dayton community available to non-disabled persons, making the accommodation necessary under § 3604(f)(3)(B).
brief_summary: Freedom's Path, a developer seeking to build supportive housing for homeless disabled veterans, sued Dayton Metropolitan Housing Authority under the FHA and ADA for refusing to amend its Administrative Plan to apply for VASH vouchers on Freedom's Path's behalf. The Sixth Circuit reversed the district court's sua sponte summary judgment for the housing authority, holding that a reasonable jury could find the accommodation was necessary to afford disabled veterans an equal opportunity to access housing near the VA campus in Dayton.
key_cases_cited: Smith & Lee Associates, Inc. v. City of Taylor, 102 F.3d 781 (6th Cir. 1996)
Overlook Mut. Homes, Inc. v. Spencer, 415 F. App'x 617 (6th Cir. 2011)
Howard v. City of Beavercreek, 276 F.3d 802 (6th Cir. 2002)
Oconomowoc Residential Programs, Inc. v. City of Milwaukee, 300 F.3d 775 (7th Cir. 2002)
Anderson v. City of Blue Ash, 798 F.3d 338 (6th Cir. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Amendment to GDPM's Administrative Plan to allow GDPM to apply for VASH (Veterans Affairs Supportive Housing) project-based vouchers on behalf of Freedom's Path, or alternatively, commitment of 25-60 project-based Section 8 vouchers for a 60-unit affordable housing development for homeless disabled veterans near the VA Medical Center
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court (Judge Rose) granted summary judgment to GDPM on the ground that Freedom's Path failed to establish the necessity element—that the accommodation was necessary to afford disabled veterans equal opportunity to enjoy housing. The appellate court reversed, holding that a reasonable jury could find the accommodation necessary because disabled homeless veterans faced a shortage of supportive housing in the Dayton community and the VASH program was designed to provide supportive services enabling disabled veterans to live independently in the community. The court applied the 'equal opportunity' framework from Smith & Lee, asking whether disabled and non-disabled persons would have equal opportunity to enjoy housing of their choice but for the accommodation, and found a genuine factual dispute on whether the accommodation was necessary to achieve that equality.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Judge Rice granted summary judgment to GDPM on Freedom's Path's intentional discrimination claim, finding that Freedom's Path did not demonstrate that GDPM intentionally discriminated against disabled persons. The appellate court did not address this ruling on appeal, as the parties focused only on the reasonable accommodation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Judge Rice granted summary judgment to GDPM on Freedom's Path's disparate impact claim. The appellate court did not address this ruling on appeal, as the parties focused only on the reasonable accommodation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA)
fha_claims.reasoning: Freedom's Path also alleged violations of Title II of the ADA. The appellate court applied the same legal framework as the FHA reasonable accommodation claim, noting that the requirements for reasonable accommodation under the ADA are the same as those under the FHA. The court reversed the summary judgment on the ADA claim on the same basis as the FHA claim—that a reasonable jury could find the accommodation necessary.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act violation claim (substantive nature not detailed in this appellate opinion addressing only jurisdictional finality)
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court lacked subject-matter jurisdiction because the bankruptcy court's clarification order was not a final order—it merely interpreted the scope of prior orders without resolving any discrete dispute or modifying any prior judgment. The order did not finally dispose of the Clarks' FHA claims or any other discrete dispute within the bankruptcy proceeding.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Bivens claims under First, Second, Fourth, Fifth, Eighth, Ninth, Tenth, and Fourteenth Amendments; claims for excessive force and handcuffing accommodation due to spinal injury
fha_claims.reasoning: Official capacity claims barred by sovereign immunity (12(b)(1) jurisdictional dismissal). Individual capacity Bivens claims dismissed because: (1) plaintiff failed to allege specific actions by named defendants (Iqbal/Twombly pleading standard); (2) claims arise in new contexts not covered by existing Bivens doctrine; (3) special factors (national security, separation of powers, congressional silence) counsel against extending Bivens; (4) qualified immunity bars claims even if Bivens remedy were available.

source_file: 5310802_2021_S. Baxter Jones v. City of Detroit, Mich._ca6
case_name: S. Baxter Jones v. City of Detroit, Michigan
accommodation_description: Request for wheelchair-accessible transportation vehicle rather than cargo van to safely transport plaintiff who uses a wheelchair during arrest by police officers
key_holding: The Sixth Circuit held that vicarious liability (respondeat superior) is not available for Title II of the ADA claims, because Title II incorporates the remedial framework of Title VI of the Civil Rights Act, which does not permit vicarious liability following Gebser v. Lago Vista.
brief_summary: Baxter Jones, a wheelchair user, sued the City of Detroit alleging police officers failed to provide reasonable accommodation when they transported him in a cargo van rather than an accessible vehicle during his 2014 arrest, causing injuries. The Sixth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the City, holding that Title II of the ADA does not permit vicarious liability claims because it incorporates Title VI's remedial framework, which Gebser held does not allow respondeat superior liability.
key_cases_cited: Gebser v. Lago Vista Ind. Sch. Dist., 524 U.S. 274 (1998)
Barnes v. Gorman, 536 U.S. 181 (2002)
Hiler v. Brown, 177 F.3d 542 (6th Cir. 1999)
Foster v. Michigan, 573 F. App'x 377 (6th Cir. 2014)
Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible transportation for a wheelchair user during police arrest and transport to police station; specifically, a vehicle equipped with wheelchair lift and proper restraints, and adequate interior space to allow the plaintiff to sit upright
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that Title II of the ADA does not permit vicarious liability claims against the City. Because the plaintiff's failure-to-accommodate claim was premised solely on vicarious liability (respondeat superior) and the statute incorporates Title VI's remedial regime, which does not allow vicarious liability, the claim fails. The court did not reach the substantive merits of the reasonable accommodation claim itself.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claims under Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act, the Rehabilitation Act (29 U.S.C. § 701 et seq.), Michigan state disability law (Mich. Comp. Laws § 37.1101 et seq.), and § 1983 excessive force claim under the Fourth Amendment
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court affirmed the district court's grant of summary judgment on the non-FHA claims (ADA Title II, Rehabilitation Act, state law, and § 1983 excessive force) on the same vicarious liability ground: these statutes do not permit vicarious liability under the remedial framework they incorporate from Title VI or other sources. The excessive force claim against individual officers was separately resolved by qualified immunity at an earlier interlocutory appeal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act claim (forfeited on appeal); Fair Debt Collection Practices Act claim (forfeited on appeal); Truth in Lending Act claim; Illinois Interest Act claim; RICO conspiracy claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff forfeited challenges to Fair Housing Act and Fair Debt Collection Practices Act claims by failing to make arguments on appeal. All other claims were barred by claim preclusion and issue preclusion based on prior state court judgment, or were time-barred.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III violation for failure to provide accessible information about hotel accessibility features in online reservation system (ORS) in compliance with 28 C.F.R. § 36.302(e)(1)(ii)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff lacked Article III standing because she failed to allege a concrete and particularized injury in fact. Although she alleged a statutory violation of the ADA's ORS regulation, she disclaimed any intent to book a room at the hotel and therefore suffered no concrete harm from the noncompliant online reservation system. Under Spokeo and TransUnion, a statutory violation alone does not establish injury in fact; plaintiff must demonstrate concrete, personal harm.

source_file: 5343691_2022_Constance George v. House of Hope Recovery_ca9
case_name: Constance George v. House of Hope Recovery
accommodation_description: George alleges Barcroft and House of Hope Recovery discriminated against her on the basis of her race and religion in violation of the Fair Housing Act.
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for Barcroft and House of Hope because George failed to present any comparator evidence establishing a prima facie case of religious discrimination under the McDonnell Douglas framework.
brief_summary: Constance George sued Patricia Barcroft, House of Hope Recovery, and other defendants alleging discrimination on the basis of race and religion under the Fair Housing Act. The Ninth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for Barcroft and House of Hope because George failed to present comparator evidence establishing a prima facie case of religious discrimination, and dismissed her appeal against Bridges to Change and Washington County for lack of jurisdiction due to inadequate notice of appeal.
key_cases_cited: Gamble v. City of Escondido, 104 F.3d 300 (9th Cir. 1997)
Bodett v. CoxCom, Inc., 366 F.3d 736 (9th Cir. 2004)
Lyons v. England, 307 F.3d 1092 (9th Cir. 2002)
Smith v. Barry, 502 U.S. 244 (1992)
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green framework

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court affirmed summary judgment on the religious discrimination claim because plaintiff failed to present comparator evidence of disparate treatment of similarly situated non-Jehovah's Witness residents, which is required to establish a prima facie case under the McDonnell-Douglas framework.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court affirmed summary judgment on the racial discrimination claim because plaintiff failed to assert any colorable argument as to why remand was warranted and did not present evidence of disparate treatment on the basis of race.

source_file: 6225633_2022_Karen C. Yeh Ho v. Valencia Isles Homeowners Association, Inc._ca11
case_name: Karen C. Yeh Ho v. Valencia Isles Homeowners Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: Nature of accommodation request is undeterminable; complaint dismissed on procedural grounds before substantive FHA analysis.
key_holding: The district court did not abuse its discretion in dismissing the complaint without prejudice for failure to timely respond to the motion to dismiss, where the plaintiff continued to file other documents and was properly warned of potential dismissal.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Karen Yeh-Ho appealed the dismissal without prejudice of her Fair Housing Act complaint against Valencia Isles Homeowners Association and related defendants; the Eleventh Circuit affirmed, holding the district court did not abuse its discretion in dismissing the complaint for the plaintiff's failure to timely respond to the motion to dismiss despite continued filings and proper notice.
key_cases_cited: Betty K Agencies v. M/V Monada, 432 F.3d 1333 (11th Cir. 2005)
Rance v. Rocksolid Granit USA, Inc., 583 F.3d 1284 (11th Cir. 2009)
Dynes v. Army Air Force Exch. Serv., 720 F.2d 1495 (11th Cir. 1983)
Timson v. Sampson, 518 F.3d 870 (11th Cir. 2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges discrimination under § 3604(b), not failure to accommodate
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court dismissed the complaint for failure to timely respond to the motion to dismiss and failure to cure the default despite explicit warning. The appellate court affirmed under abuse of discretion review, finding no clear error in the district court's procedural dismissal. The merits of the FHA claim were never reached.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges retaliation under § 3617, not failure to accommodate
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court dismissed the complaint for failure to timely respond to the motion to dismiss and failure to cure the default despite explicit warning. The appellate court affirmed under abuse of discretion review, finding no clear error in the district court's procedural dismissal. The merits of the FHA retaliation claim were never reached.

case_name: Gatling v. Jubilee Housing, Inc.
accommodation_description: Wheelchair user tenant requests repair/replacement of building's wheelchair ramp and wheelchair lift to provide accessible entry and exit from the building.
key_holding: The court granted leave to amend for DCHRA reasonable accommodation claims under § 2-1402.21(d)(2)(A) and (d)(3)(B) because Gatling adequately alleged she is disabled, defendants knew of her disability, the requested accommodations (wheelchair ramp and lift repair) are necessary for equal use and enjoyment of the property, and defendants refused the accommodation; but the court denied claims requiring intentional discrimination or aiding-and-abetting theories as futile.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Cynthia Gatling, a wheelchair user, sued Jubilee Housing, Inc. and Jubilee Housing Limited Partnership alleging they failed to accommodate her disability by refusing to repair or replace an unsafe wheelchair ramp and inoperable wheelchair lift at her low-income apartment building. The court granted in part and denied in part her motion to file a second amended complaint, allowing her to proceed on DCHRA reasonable accommodation and breach of warranty of habitability claims but rejecting claims requiring intentional discrimination or aiding-and-abetting as futile.
key_cases_cited: United States v. District of Columbia, 538 F. Supp. 2d 211 (D.D.C. 2008)
Parham v. CIH Properties, Inc., 148 F. Supp. 3d 5 (D.D.C. 2015)
Hunter v. District of Columbia, 64 F. Supp. 3d 158 (D.D.C. 2014)
Killingham v. Wilshire Inv. Corp., 739 A.2d 804 (D.C. 1999)
Javins v. First Nat'l Realty Corp., 428 F.2d 1071 (D.C. Cir. 1970)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Repair and replacement of wheelchair ramp to comply with architectural standards and ANSI accessibility requirements; repair and operation of wheelchair lift
fha_claims.reasoning: The court allowed plaintiff to amend her complaint to add a claim under D.C. Code § 2-1402.21(d)(2)(A) and (d)(3)(B) for failure to provide reasonable accommodations. The court found that plaintiff adequately alleged all four elements of a failure-to-accommodate claim: existence of disability, defendant's knowledge of disability, necessity of accommodation, and refusal to accommodate. The claim survives the futility analysis and proceeds to the next stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: D.C. Code § 2-1402.21(a)(4) (intentional disability discrimination); D.C. Code § 2-1402.62 (aiding and abetting discrimination); breach of implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing; breach of covenant of quiet enjoyment
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied amendment to add D.C. Code § 2-1402.21(a)(4) because plaintiff failed to allege discriminatory animus or intent based on disability—she alleged only refusal to make improvements without showing intentional discrimination. The aiding and abetting claim under § 2-1402.62 was futile because defendants are principal actors, not aiders and abettors of their own conduct. The implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing claim was futile as a reassertion of a previously dismissed claim. The covenant of quiet enjoyment claim failed because plaintiff did not allege actual eviction or constructive eviction—she retained possession and could enter/exit with assistance.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: D.C. Code § 7-1006 (full and equal access for disabled persons); implied warranty of habitability under D.C. Housing Code
fha_claims.reasoning: The court allowed amendment to add a claim for breach of the implied warranty of habitability. The court found that D.C. Code § 7-1006 imposes an obligation on rental housing providers to provide full and equal access for disabled persons, and that failure to provide wheelchair access constitutes a breach of the implied warranty of habitability under Killingham v. Wilshire Inv. Corp. Plaintiff adequately alleged denial of full and equal access based on the inoperable wheelchair lift and non-compliant ramp.

case_name: Doe v. Tonti Management Company, L.L.C.
accommodation_description: Request for accommodation from the one-animal-per-apartment policy to keep a second cat (GiGi) as an emotional support animal for major depressive disorder and anxiety.
key_holding: The Fifth Circuit dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction, holding that the district court's order denying Doe’s motion to re-open the case and sever the cost-splitting provision of the arbitration agreement was an unappealable interlocutory order under § 16 of the FAA, and neither the collateral order doctrine nor mandamus jurisdiction applied.
brief_summary: Jane Doe sued Tonti Management Company, the operator of her apartment complex, under the Fair Housing Act seeking to keep a second emotional support animal despite a one-animal-per-apartment policy. After the district court compelled arbitration and denied Doe’s motion to sever the arbitration agreement’s cost-splitting provision, Doe appealed. The Fifth Circuit dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction, holding that the district court’s order was an unappealable interlocutory order under § 16 of the FAA.
key_cases_cited: Al Rushaid v. Nat’l Oilwell Varco, Inc., 814 F.3d 300 (5th Cir. 2016)
Apache Bohai Corp., LDC v. Texaco China, B.V., 330 F.3d 307 (5th Cir. 2003)
Green v. Serv. Corp. Int’l, 236 F. App’x 898 (5th Cir. 2007)
Vantage Health Plan, Inc. v. Willis-Knighton Med. Ctr., 913 F.3d 443 (5th Cir. 2019)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request to accommodate a second emotional support animal (cat named GiGi) as an exception to the one-animal-per-apartment policy in the lease, to provide emotional support for plaintiff's major depressive disorder and anxiety.
fha_claims.disposition: Arbitration Compelled; Motion to Reconsider Denied
fha_claims.reasoning: The Fifth Circuit dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction under 9 U.S.C. § 16(b)(3) of the Federal Arbitration Act. The district court's order compelling arbitration was interlocutory and unappealable, and the plaintiff's motion to reconsider that order was equally unappealable. The court never reached the merits of the FHA reasonable accommodation claim because the case was stayed and administratively closed pending arbitration.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Louisiana Equal Housing Opportunity Act; Louisiana state-law tort claims
fha_claims.disposition: Arbitration Compelled; Motion to Reconsider Denied
fha_claims.reasoning: The Fifth Circuit dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction. The district court compelled arbitration of all claims, including state-law claims, pursuant to the arbitration clause in the lease. The merits of these claims were never addressed because the case was stayed pending arbitration.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III claim for failure to provide accessibility information on hotel website reservation system (28 C.F.R. § 36.302(e)(1)(ii))
fha_claims.reasoning: District court dismissed for lack of Article III standing, finding plaintiff suffered no concrete injury. Eleventh Circuit reversed, holding that plaintiff adequately alleged stigmatic injury (frustration and humiliation from discrimination) sufficient to confer standing, and remanded for factual determination of whether plaintiff actually suffered the alleged emotional distress.

source_file: 6342877_2022_Sandpiper Residents Association v. United States Department of Housing and Urban Development_dcd
case_name: Sandpiper Residents Association v. United States Department of Housing and Urban Development
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs sought Tenant Protection Vouchers to relocate from substandard housing conditions, alleging racial discrimination in HUD's withholding of this assistance.
key_holding: The court lacked jurisdiction because intervening events—the transfer of the property to a new owner who had not received a Notice of Default—rendered plaintiffs' claims moot and made it impossible to grant effective relief, as HUD no longer had statutory authority to issue Tenant Protection Vouchers based on the prior owner's Notice of Default.
brief_summary: Tenants and a tenant association at Sandpiper Cove sued HUD alleging the agency violated the Fair Housing Act and Fifth Amendment by intentionally discriminating on the basis of race in withholding Tenant Protection Vouchers that would allow tenants to relocate from substandard housing conditions. The court dismissed the case for lack of jurisdiction, holding that the transfer of the property to a new owner who had not received a Notice of Default rendered plaintiffs' claims moot and stripped the court of authority to order the relief sought.
key_cases_cited: United States v. Sanchez-Gomez, 138 S. Ct. 1532 (2018)
City of Los Angeles v. Lyons, 461 U.S. 95 (1983)
Trudeau v. Fed. Trade Comm'n, 456 F.3d 178 (D.C. Cir. 2006)
Marino v. Nat'l Oceanic and Atmospheric Admin., No. 20-5151 (D.C. Cir. May 17, 2022)
Steel Co. v. Citizens for a Better Env't, 523 U.S. 83 (1998)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Tenant Protection Vouchers for relocation from substandard housing
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs' Fair Housing Act § 3604(a) intentional discrimination claim is moot because HUD lacks statutory authority to issue the requested Tenant Protection Vouchers after the property transferred to a new owner who has not received a Notice of Default. The court found that intervening events made it impossible to grant effective relief, depriving the court of jurisdiction under Article III.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Administrative Procedure Act challenge to HUD's withholding of Tenant Protection Vouchers; Fifth Amendment equal protection claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs' APA claims are moot because one of two statutory preconditions for issuing Tenant Protection Vouchers—that the current owner has received a Notice of Default—is no longer satisfied after the property transferred to a new owner. The court held that the Notice of Default issued to the previous owner lapsed upon transfer and HUD has not issued a new Notice of Default to the new owner, making the requested relief impossible to grant.

case_name: Ahmad Ajaj v. Federal Bureau of Prisons
accommodation_description: Prisoner requests religious accommodations including adjusted medication delivery during Ramadan fasting, halal diet, access to an imam, and ability to pray with others five times daily
key_holding: The Tenth Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal of the group-prayer claim as moot because the court's finding that the plaintiff could pray with others five times daily was clearly erroneous, and reversed dismissal of individual-capacity RFRA damages claims because Tanzin v. Tanvir held such damages are available, though qualified immunity applies to RFRA damages claims.
brief_summary: Ahmad Ajaj, a Muslim prisoner at ADX Florence Colorado, sued BOP and individual BOP officials under RFRA alleging violations of his free exercise rights through denial of Ramadan fasting accommodation, halal diet, access to an imam, and group prayer. The Tenth Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal of his group-prayer claim as moot (finding the record did not support that he could pray five times daily in the Life Connections Program) and reversed dismissal of individual-capacity damages claims under RFRA, holding that qualified immunity applies to RFRA damages claims.
key_cases_cited: Tanzin v. Tanvir, 141 S. Ct. 486 (2020)
Harlow v. Fitzgerald, 457 U.S. 800 (1982)
City of Boerne v. Flores, 521 U.S. 507 (1997)
Employment Division v. Smith, 494 U.S. 872 (1990)
Werner v. McCotter, 49 F.3d 1476 (10th Cir. 1995)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Petitioners alleged that the FCC's amendment to antenna regulations would violate the Fair Housing Act and Americans with Disabilities Act by increasing radiofrequency exposure to individuals with radiofrequency sensitivity.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court rejected petitioners' facial challenge to the FCC order on FHA and ADA grounds, holding that petitioners failed to show the regulation would be invalid in all circumstances, as there would necessarily be situations where no adversely affected individual was in the vicinity of an antenna. The court also found the FHA/ADA arguments premature because they were premised on radiofrequency health impacts that the Commission properly directed to a separate rulemaking.

source_file: 6377422_2022_Smita Sanghvi v. County of San Bernardino_ca9
case_name: Smita Sanghvi and Mountain View Centers, Inc. v. County of San Bernardino
accommodation_description: Appellants alleged the County's decision to remove conservatees from Mountain View Centers was discriminatory, but the court found no protected status under the FHA was alleged.
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed dismissal because Appellants' complaint failed to allege how the County's decision to remove residents was based on a protected status under the FHA, and the complaint itself demonstrated non-discriminatory reasons (an alleged sexual assault report) for the removal.
brief_summary: Smita Sanghvi and Mountain View Centers, Inc. (a conservatorship facility operator) appealed the dismissal of their claims against San Bernardino County, which had removed conservatees from their facility based on an alleged sexual assault report. The Ninth Circuit affirmed, finding that Appellants failed to allege how the County's decision was based on a protected status under the Fair Housing Act, and the complaint itself demonstrated non-discriminatory reasons for the removal.
key_cases_cited: Lujan v. G & G Fire Sprinklers, Inc., 532 U.S. 189 (2001)
Monell v. Department of Social Services, 436 U.S. 658 (1978)
Zadrozny v. Bank of New York Mellon, 720 F.3d 1163 (9th Cir. 2013)
Sinaloa Lake Owners Ass'n v. City of Simi Valley, 882 F.2d 1398 (9th Cir. 1989)
Marsh v. County of San Diego, 680 F.3d 1148 (9th Cir. 2012)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 1983 claims for Fourth Amendment, Due Process, and Equal Protection violations; Monell vicarious liability
fha_claims.reasoning: The court affirmed dismissal of all Section 1983 theories: no deprivation of due process because California law provides adequate remedy; substantive due process claim failed because decision to remove residents did not shock the conscience; Equal Protection claim was waived on appeal; Monell claim failed for lack of specific policy or custom; Fourth Amendment claim failed because appellants had no property interest in the residents.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Removal of residents from facility based on alleged protected status under the Fair Housing Act
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint contained no allegations that the County's decision to remove residents was based on a protected status under the FHA; instead, the complaint itself demonstrated the removal was based on a non-discriminatory reason—an incorrect report of sexual assault—thus failing to state a plausible FHA claim.

source_file: 6433397_2022_Secretary, United States Department of Housing v. Welch_ca10
case_name: The Secretary, United States Department of Housing and Urban Development, on behalf of Denver Metro Fair Housing Center v. David B. Welch, et al.
accommodation_description: Not a reasonable accommodation case; the complaint alleged discrimination against families with children based on familial status, with respondents marketing the property as an 'adult condominium community' and making dwellings unavailable to families with children.
key_holding: The Tenth Circuit granted HUD's Petition for Enforcement of the administrative consent order, requiring respondents to pay $800 to the Denver Metro Fair Housing Center, adopt a non-discrimination policy, undergo fair housing training, and engage in affirmative advertising indicating families with children are welcome.
brief_summary: The Secretary of HUD, on behalf of the Denver Metro Fair Housing Center, petitioned the Tenth Circuit to enforce an administrative consent order against David B. Welch, John H. Welch, and Ruth E. Welch, who allegedly discriminated against families with children at their Westwood Cove Condominiums in Gunnison, Colorado. The court granted the enforcement petition, ordering respondents to comply with all terms of the consent order including monetary payment, adoption of non-discrimination policies, fair housing training, and affirmative advertising welcoming families with children.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: HUD and Denver Metro Fair Housing Center alleged discrimination against families with children in violation of FHA §§ 3604(a), (b), and (c). The parties resolved the matter by consent order without admission of liability by respondents. Respondents agreed to pay $800, implement non-discrimination policies, provide fair housing training, and maintain compliance records for three years.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Petitioners alleged that the FCC's amendment to antenna regulations would violate the Fair Housing Act and Americans with Disabilities Act by increasing radiofrequency exposure to individuals with radiofrequency sensitivity; also alleged violations of U.S. Constitution protections of private property and personal autonomy.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that petitioners mounted a facial challenge to the FCC regulation and failed to show that there are no circumstances in which the amendment would be valid. The court noted that petitioners' FHA and ADA claims necessarily depend on the presence of an individual adversely affected by radiofrequency radiation within range of a hub or relay antenna, and therefore there will be circumstances in which the amendment has no adverse consequences. The court also found that petitioners lacked standing to bring the claims because their allegations were premised on speculative future harm and the presence of affected individuals in the vicinity.

source_file: 6444370_2022_Abolfazl Hosseinzadeh v. Bellevue Park Homeowners Assn._ca9
case_name: Abolfazl Hosseinzadeh v. Bellevue Park Homeowners Association
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; claims involve alleged race, national origin, and religion discrimination through document withholding and board election invalidation
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for defendants because plaintiff failed to establish pretext for discrimination, presenting no facts showing BPHOA's legitimate reasons for withholding documents and invalidating the board election were pretextual.
