brief_summary: Plaintiff Hosseinzadeh, an Iranian immigrant and Muslim, sued the Bellevue Park Homeowners Association alleging race, national origin, and religion discrimination under the FHA, CRA, and WLAD based on BPHOA's withholding of personal records and invalidation of a board election in which he was elected. The Ninth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for defendants, finding Hosseinzadeh failed to demonstrate that BPHOA's legitimate, non-discriminatory reasons for these actions were pretextual.
key_cases_cited: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green
Gamble v. City of Escondido
Phiffer v. Proud Parrot Motor Hotel, Inc.
Mikkelsen v. Pub. Util. Dist. No. 1 of Kittitas Cnty.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Under the McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework, plaintiff failed to submit facts demonstrating that defendant's legitimate reason for withholding personal records (precautions due to ongoing litigious relationship) was mere pretext for discrimination based on race, national origin, or religion.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Under the McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework, plaintiff failed to submit facts demonstrating that defendant's legitimate reason for invalidating the March 2016 election (lack of necessary quorum under bylaws) was mere pretext for discrimination based on race, national origin, or religion.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Defamation, false light, Washington Consumer Protection Act, 42 U.S.C. § 1982 Civil Rights Act, Washington Law Against Discrimination
fha_claims.reasoning: Defamation claims fail under the common interest privilege; false light claims fail because plaintiff submitted no facts showing defendants knew of or recklessly disregarded falsity; CPA claims fail because WLAD claims fail and judicially sanctioned foreclosure actions are not recognized as CPA violations under Washington law.

case_name: Minnie McCall v. Montgomery Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged discriminatory inspection practices, unannounced apartment entry, and interference with 'porting out' (transferring to another apartment) based on her race and in retaliation for prior litigation against the Housing Authority.
key_holding: Summary judgment was proper because the racially derogatory comments were made by a third-party inspector and apartment maintenance worker—not Housing Authority employees—and the Housing Authority could not be held vicariously liable for their statements; moreover, McCall failed to establish an adverse action for her retaliation claim as her Section 8 benefits were never terminated and she never submitted a written request to transfer.
brief_summary: Minnie McCall, a Section 8 voucher holder, appealed the district court's summary judgment for the Montgomery Housing Authority on her Fair Housing Act claims alleging racial discrimination in inspection practices and retaliation for her prior lawsuit. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed, finding that racially derogatory comments by a third-party inspector and apartment maintenance worker were not attributable to the Housing Authority under vicarious liability principles, and that McCall failed to establish an adverse action for her retaliation claim.
key_cases_cited: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)
Dixon v. Hallmark Cos., Inc., 627 F.3d 849 (11th Cir. 2010)
Schwarz v. City of Treasure Island, 544 F.3d 1201 (11th Cir. 2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish unequal treatment on the basis of race affecting availability of housing. The derogatory comments were made by a third-party inspector and maintenance worker employed by the private apartment complex, not agents of the Housing Authority, and thus are not attributable to the defendant under the control test established in Meyer v. Holley.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish an adverse action by the Housing Authority or its executive director. Although the Housing Authority threatened to remove plaintiff from the program if she did not attend meetings, it never executed the threat. Plaintiff's claim that she was prevented from 'porting out' failed because she never submitted the mandatory written request to do so.

source_file: 6449993_2022_Kenny Simelton v. Alexander County Housing Auth_ca7
case_name: Kenny Wayne Simelton v. Alexander County Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged the housing authority discriminated against him and other former residents based on race and familial status at two Alexander County housing developments.
key_holding: The Seventh Circuit affirmed the district court's denial of Simelton's Rule 60(b) motion to reinstate, finding no abuse of discretion in dismissing the case for failure to prosecute after Simelton repeatedly failed to comply with discovery requests and court orders.
brief_summary: Kenny Simelton sued the Alexander County Housing Authority and four former directors under the Fair Housing Act, Title VI, and the Illinois Civil Rights Act, alleging discrimination based on race and familial status at two county housing developments. The case was dismissed under Rule 41(b) for Simelton's failure to comply with discovery requests and court orders, and the Seventh Circuit affirmed the district court's denial of his Rule 60(b) motion to reinstate, finding no abuse of discretion in the dismissal.
key_cases_cited: Krivak v. Home Depot U.S.A., Inc., 2 F.4th 601 (7th Cir. 2021)
Shaffer v. Lashbrook, 962 F.3d 313 (7th Cir. 2020)
Kasalo v. Harris & Harris, Ltd., 656 F.3d 557 (7th Cir. 2011)
United States v. Hassebrock, 21 F.4th 494 (7th Cir. 2021)
Sroga v. Huberman, 722 F.3d 980 (7th Cir. 2013)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination based on race and familial status in housing developments
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 41(b) dismissal for failure to prosecute
fha_claims.reasoning: The case was dismissed for failure to prosecute and comply with discovery orders and court directives, not on the merits of the FHA discrimination claim. The appellate court affirmed the dismissal as a sanction for Simelton's repeated non-compliance over six months despite warnings.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VI Civil Rights Act claim and Illinois Civil Rights Act claim for discrimination based on race and familial status
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 41(b) dismissal for failure to prosecute
fha_claims.reasoning: Non-FHA claims (Title VI and Illinois Civil Rights Act) were dismissed along with the FHA claim as a sanction for failure to prosecute and comply with discovery orders, not on substantive merits.

case_name: Jean Paraison v. Nationstar Mortgage, LLC
accommodation_description: N/A - case involves claim of race/nationality discrimination in real estate auction transaction rather than reasonable accommodation request
key_holding: The court affirmed dismissal of Paraison's FHA discrimination claim because his allegations were conclusory and speculative, failing to establish any factual connection between his race/nationality and the real estate agent's statements advising him to back out of the deal.
brief_summary: Jean Paraison, an African American male with a Haitian accent, sued Nationstar Mortgage alleging the company's real estate agent attempted to dissuade him from completing a real estate purchase based on his race and national origin. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed dismissal, finding Paraison's discrimination allegations were conclusory and speculative under Twombly/Iqbal standards, failing to allege facts connecting his protected characteristics to the agent's conduct.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's allegations of discrimination based on race and nationality were conclusory and speculative, failing to allege facts establishing a connection between his protected status and the real estate agent's statements, thus falling short of the Twombly plausibility standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of contract claim under Georgia law
fha_claims.reasoning: The purchase agreement's plain language did not impose any duty on Nationstar to provide a title report or obtain a survey; those obligations fell on the buyer, and the contract language was clear and unambiguous.

source_file: 6455250_2022_Eddie Hatch, Jr. v. City of Milwaukee_ca7
case_name: Eddie L. Hatch, Jr. and Michelle Davis-Hatch v. City of Milwaukee
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged defendants gave unfair preference to a white developer over Black entrepreneurs in sale of city-owned commercial building.
key_holding: The appellate court vacated the dismissal with prejudice because the district court erred in not giving pro se plaintiffs at least one opportunity to amend their complaint to cure deficiencies in pleading intentional race-based discrimination under § 1982.
brief_summary: Black plaintiffs sued the City of Milwaukee and other defendants alleging racial discrimination in the sale of a city-owned commercial building under the Fair Housing Act and 42 U.S.C. § 1982. The district court dismissed with prejudice, finding the commercial property was not a "dwelling" under the FHA and plaintiffs failed to allege intentional race-based discrimination. The Seventh Circuit vacated and remanded, holding that pro se plaintiffs should have been given leave to amend to attempt to cure the pleading deficiencies.
key_cases_cited: Jones v. Alfred H. Mayer Co., 392 U.S. 409 (1968)
Shaikh v. City of Chicago, 341 F.3d 627 (7th Cir. 2003)
Becker v. Montgomery, 532 U.S. 757 (2001)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged discrimination in the sale/purchase of a city-owned commercial building based on race.
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court dismissed the FHA claim because the property was a commercial building, not a 'dwelling' as defined by the FHA (42 U.S.C. § 3602(b)). The appellate court affirmed that the FHA does not apply to non-residential property, but vacated and remanded on the ground that plaintiffs should have been given an opportunity to amend to allege a viable legal theory under 42 U.S.C. § 1982.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1982 claim for racial discrimination in the purchase of property (commercial building).
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court dismissed the § 1982 claim for failure to allege intentional, race-based discrimination. The appellate court agreed the complaint was deficient but held that dismissal with prejudice was improper; pro se plaintiffs are entitled to at least one opportunity to amend, and the defect was not so obviously incurable as to preclude amendment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III claim for failure to provide accessibility information on hotel website reservation system; alleged violation of 28 C.F.R. § 36.302(e)(1)(ii) requiring hotels to identify and describe accessible features in enough detail to permit individuals with disabilities to assess independently whether rooms meet their accessibility needs.
fha_claims.reasoning: District court dismissed for lack of Article III standing, finding plaintiff lacked concrete and particularized injury. Eleventh Circuit vacated and remanded, holding that plaintiff adequately alleged stigmatic injury (frustration, humiliation, sense of isolation and segregation) sufficient to confer standing under narrower reading of Sierra v. City of Hallandale Beach, which survives TransUnion's requirement that intangible injuries be concrete. Court remanded for district court to determine as factual matter whether plaintiff actually suffered requisite emotional distress.

case_name: Hawkins v. United States Department of Housing and Urban Development
accommodation_description: African-American Section 8 tenants sought relocation assistance (tenant protection vouchers) from HUD to move from substandard housing conditions at Coppertree Village, alleging the denial of such assistance constituted race-based discrimination.
key_holding: The Fifth Circuit affirmed dismissal, holding (1) it lacked jurisdiction over the APA and FHA claims because tenants failed to allege a final agency action, and (2) the Fifth Amendment equal protection claim failed because the allegations showed at most that HUD was aware of varying housing conditions but did not support an inference that HUD made decisions 'because of' race.
brief_summary: African-American tenants at Coppertree Village, a Section 8 project in Houston, sued HUD alleging that the agency's failure to provide relocation assistance (tenant protection vouchers) while maintaining a HAP contract with a substandard housing complex violated the Fair Housing Act and Fifth Amendment equal protection. The Fifth Circuit affirmed dismissal, holding it lacked jurisdiction over the APA and FHA claims due to no final agency action, and that the equal protection claim failed because the tenants did not plausibly allege discriminatory purpose—only that HUD was aware of disparate housing conditions, which is insufficient to show decisions were made 'because of' race.
key_cases_cited: Bennett v. Spear, 520 U.S. 154 (1997)
Washington v. Davis, 426 U.S. 229 (1976)
Village of Arlington Heights v. Metro. Hous. Dev. Corp., 429 U.S. 252 (1977)
Personnel Adm'r of Mass. v. Feeney, 442 U.S. 256 (1979)
Veasey v. Abbott, 830 F.3d 216 (5th Cir. 2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Relocation assistance / Tenant Protection Vouchers to move from substandard Section 8 housing
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked jurisdiction over the FHA claim because plaintiffs failed to allege a final agency action reviewable under the APA. HUD's continued work to salvage its contract with Coppertree did not constitute a consummation of the agency's decisionmaking process regarding relocation assistance.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Administrative Procedure Act claim for arbitrary and capricious agency action; Fifth Amendment equal protection claim for intentional racial discrimination
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to state a plausible claim of intentional racial discrimination under the Fifth Amendment. Allegations that HUD was aware of disparities in housing conditions across projects, without more, do not support an inference that HUD made decisions 'because of' rather than 'in spite of' adverse effects on a protected group, and plaintiffs alleged no procedural irregularities or comparative treatment of similarly situated non-minority occupants.

case_name: Birch Family Services, Inc. v. Wlody
accommodation_description: Neighboring homeowners allegedly harassed a group home for disabled adults by photographing and videotaping residents and staff based on disability and race animus.
key_holding: Affirming summary judgment for defendants because Birch failed to establish pretext—the Wlodys' legitimate reasons for photographing and videotaping (documenting alleged staff misconduct) were supported by evidence, and the discriminatory animus evidence (derogatory texts and epithets) combined with failure to show pretext was insufficient to survive summary judgment.
brief_summary: Birch Family Services, Inc., operator of a group home for disabled adults, sued neighboring homeowners under the FHA, alleging the neighbors' extensive photographing and videotaping of residents and staff constituted disability and race-based housing discrimination. The Second Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the defendants, finding that Birch failed to meet its burden of demonstrating pretext—the neighbors articulated legitimate reasons (documenting staff misconduct, noise, blocked driveway) supported by evidence, and Birch's evidence of discriminatory animus was insufficient to create a genuine dispute of material fact.
key_cases_cited: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green
Mhany Mgmt., Inc. v. County of Nassau
Mitchell v. Shane
Frazier v. Rominger
McElwee v. County of Orange

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged that defendants' five-year campaign of photographing and videotaping disabled residents and African-American staff, combined with complaints to local government and state agencies, constituted harassment and interference based on disability and race.
fha_claims.reasoning: Under the McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework, defendants articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for their conduct (documenting alleged staff abuse, noise, parking violations, and supervision failures), supported by evidence in the video log and affidavits. Plaintiff failed to meet its burden of proving pretext; while some evidence of discriminatory animus existed (derogatory comments about a 'psych ward' and alleged use of racial epithets), this was insufficient to overcome defendants' credible, documented reasons for the videotaping and complaints.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: New York City Administrative Code § 8-107(19) housing discrimination claim based on disability and race
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court properly exercised supplemental jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(a) and dismissed the state law claim on the merits because the legal standard for adjudicating a housing discrimination claim under New York City Administrative Code § 8-107(19) is identical to the FHA standard, and plaintiff failed to establish pretext under that standard.

source_file: 6470766_2022_Sandpiper Residents Association v. United States Department of Housing and Urban Development_dcd
case_name: Sandpiper Residents Association v. United States Department of Housing and Urban Development
accommodation_description: Tenants sought Tenant Protection Vouchers to transfer from substandard Sandpiper Cove apartments to decent, safe, and sanitary housing elsewhere.
key_holding: The court dismissed all claims—including APA and intentional discrimination claims under § 3604(a)—as moot because the transfer of ownership to a new owner resolved the Notice of Default, eliminating HUD's statutory authority to issue Tenant Protection Vouchers and making the requested relief unavailable.
brief_summary: Two tenants and the Sandpiper Cove tenant association sued HUD seeking Tenant Protection Vouchers to relocate from substandard project-based Section 8 housing in Galveston, Texas, alleging HUD's refusal to issue vouchers violated the APA and constituted intentional race discrimination under § 3604(a). The court granted HUD's motion to dismiss, holding that intervening events—the sale to a new owner who had not received a Notice of Default—mooted the claims and rendered the requested relief unavailable.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
City of Los Angeles v. Lyons
Steel Co. v. Citizens for a Better Environment
Marino v. Nat'l Oceanic & Atmospheric Admin.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Tenant Protection Vouchers for relocation assistance to obtain decent, safe, and sanitary housing
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs' Fair Housing Act § 3604(a) intentional discrimination claim is moot because HUD lacks statutory authority to issue Tenant Protection Vouchers after the property transferred to a new owner who has not received a Notice of Default. The statutory precondition for issuing vouchers—that 'the owner has received a Notice of Default'—is no longer satisfied, making effective relief impossible.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Administrative Procedure Act claim challenging HUD's failure to issue Tenant Protection Vouchers as arbitrary and capricious; Fifth Amendment equal protection claim for intentional discrimination based on race and ethnicity
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs' APA claims are moot because the statutory preconditions for issuing Tenant Protection Vouchers—a Notice of Default to the current owner and imminent health and safety risks—are no longer satisfied after the property transferred to a new owner. The court also noted a potential standing problem under Marino v. NOAA regarding redressability of discretionary agency action.

source_file: 6471218_2022_Michael Earl Van Cleve v. U.S. Secretary of Commerce_ca11
6472320_2022_Gene Phillips v. Acacia on the Green Condo Ass'n_ca6
case_name: Gene B. Phillips; Babette R. Krause v. Acacia on the Green Condominium Association, Inc.; Scott D. Cohen; Richard N. Dettlebach; John F. Klein; James N. Kleinfelter; Diane E. Lombardy; Nina H. Rothman; Amy W. Wachs
accommodation_description: Two disabled residents requested permission to use personal gas grills on their patios despite the condominium association's rule prohibiting grills on patios and balconies.
key_holding: The Sixth Circuit affirmed that Phillips's requested accommodation was not 'necessary' because she regularly walked to the pool next to the grilling area despite her arthritis, and Acacia offered an alternative accommodation; further, neither Phillips's nor Weiss's requested accommodation was 'reasonable' because permitting individual patio grills would impose significant administrative burdens on the association, including insurance liability risks.
brief_summary: Gene Phillips and Stephen Weiss, disabled residents of the Acacia on the Green Condominium Association in Lyndhurst, Ohio, sued the association after being denied permission to use personal gas grills on their patios, alleging violations of the Fair Housing Amendments Act. The Sixth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the association, holding that Phillips's request was not necessary to afford her equal opportunity to use and enjoy her dwelling because she regularly walked past the grilling area to reach the pool, and both residents' requests were not reasonable because permitting individual patio grills would impose significant administrative and insurance burdens on the condominium association.
key_cases_cited: Vorchheimer v. Philadelphian Owners Ass'n, 903 F.3d 100 (3d Cir. 2018)
Howard v. City of Beavercreek, 276 F.3d 802 (6th Cir. 2002)
Anderson v. City of Blue Ash, 798 F.3d 338 (6th Cir. 2015)
Hollis v. Chestnut Bend Homeowners Ass'n, 760 F.3d 531 (6th Cir. 2014)
Groner v. Golden Gate Gardens Apts., 250 F.3d 1039 (6th Cir. 2001)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to use a personal gas grill on the patio of her ground-floor unit, rather than using the two common-area grills located approximately 600 feet away
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the three-part FHAA test and found that Phillips's requested accommodation was not 'necessary' because she demonstrated the ability to walk to the common grilling area multiple times per week despite her arthritis, and Acacia offered an alternative accommodation (employee assistance with transporting supplies) that would ameliorate her disability-related limitations. Even if necessary, the accommodation was not 'reasonable' because granting it would impose substantial administrative and financial burdens on Acacia, including fire safety concerns, nuisance issues, and significant insurance liability risks.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to use a personal gas grill on the patio of his ground-floor unit, rather than using the two common-area grills located approximately 600 feet away
fha_claims.reasoning: Although the court acknowledged a potential genuine dispute of material fact regarding whether the accommodation was 'necessary' (given Weiss's statements that he could only walk a few steps during extreme exhaustion episodes), the court held that the accommodation was not 'reasonable' under the FHAA because granting it would impose significant administrative burdens on the condominium association and undermine its legitimate justifications for the grill prohibition, including fire safety, nuisance, and substantial insurance liability concerns.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Violation of Ohio Rev. Code § 4112.02(H)(4) for unlawful discrimination in furnishing facilities, services, or privileges in connection with housing accommodations
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the same FHAA reasonable accommodation framework to the analogous Ohio state law claim and reached the same conclusion that the requested accommodations were neither necessary nor reasonable under Ohio law.

source_file: 6472707_2022_Commissiong v. US Dept. Housing _ Urban Development_ca2
case_name: Commissiong v. US Dept. Housing & Urban Development
accommodation_description: Undetermined; Commissiong filed a HUD administrative complaint alleging discrimination in violation of the FHA regarding her apartment, but the specific accommodation requested is not detailed in the opinion.
key_holding: The court affirmed dismissal based on sovereign immunity, holding that HUD and its officials are immune from suit under the FHA and that Commissiong failed to identify a valid waiver of sovereign immunity.
brief_summary: Carol Commissiong filed a HUD administrative complaint alleging housing discrimination in violation of the FHA regarding her apartment; after HUD issued a finding of no reasonable cause, she filed an Article 78 petition against HUD and HUD employees in state court. The court affirmed dismissal, holding that sovereign immunity bars suit against HUD and its officials because the FHA does not create a private right of action against federal agencies and Commissiong failed to identify any valid waiver of sovereign immunity.
key_cases_cited: Green v. Dep't of Educ. of New York, 16 F.4th 1070 (2d Cir. 2021)
FDIC v. Meyer, 510 U.S. 471 (1994)
Makarova v. United States, 201 F.3d 110 (2d Cir. 2010)
United States v. King, 395 U.S. 1 (1969)
Marinoff v. U.S. Dep't of Hous. & Urb. Dev., 78 F.3d 64 (2d Cir. 1996)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged discrimination in violation of the Fair Housing Act against individuals and entities involved in ownership or management of her apartment
fha_claims.reasoning: The court affirmed dismissal on jurisdictional grounds, holding that the FHA does not create a private right of action against HUD and HUD officials, and that HUD and federal officers are protected by sovereign immunity absent an unequivocal waiver. The plaintiff bore the burden of establishing a waiver and failed to do so.

case_name: Mary E. Chambers v. District of Columbia
accommodation_description: This is a Title VII employment discrimination case, not a Fair Housing Act reasonable accommodation case. The accommodation at issue is a job transfer request.
key_holding: The D.C. Circuit sitting en banc overruled Brown v. Brody, holding that discriminatory denial of a job transfer request violates Title VII's antidiscrimination provision without requiring proof of 'objectively tangible harm' because the statutory requirement that the discrimination relate to 'terms, conditions, or privileges of employment' provides the necessary limiting principle.
brief_summary: Mary Chambers sued the District of Columbia under Title VII alleging sex discrimination, claiming her employer denied her repeated transfer requests while granting similar requests to male employees. The en banc court overruled Brown v. Brody, holding that discriminatory denial of job transfers violates Title VII without requiring proof of 'objectively tangible harm' because the statutory text already provides the necessary limiting principle through the requirement that discrimination relate to 'terms, conditions, or privileges of employment.'
key_cases_cited: Brown v. Brody, 199 F.3d 446 (D.C. Cir. 1999)
Burlington Northern & Santa Fe Railway Co. v. White, 548 U.S. 53 (2006)
Burlington Industries, Inc. v. Ellerth, 524 U.S. 742 (1998)
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Bostock v. Clayton County, 140 S. Ct. 1731 (2020)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation claim under New York City Human Rights Law (NYCHRL) § 8-107(7) for alleged retaliation following plaintiff's complaint about a passenger's racist remark and pilot's response; also vicarious liability claim under NYCHRL § 8-107(13)(b) for actions of pilot and supervisors
fha_claims.reasoning: The Second Circuit affirmed dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6), holding that plaintiff failed to allege facts supporting a plausible retaliation claim because she did not adequately allege that Delta engaged in discrimination. The court applied the Iqbal/Twombly pleading standard and concluded that plaintiff could not have had a good-faith, reasonable belief that Delta's conduct was unlawful, as the passenger's single comment was not an employment practice and the pilot's response did not constitute a discriminatory employment practice.

case_name: Mercer v. N.Y.C. Hous. Auth.
accommodation_description: NYCHA tenant with asthma sought accommodation from mold conditions in his apartment, allegedly requiring remediation as a disability-related accommodation.
key_holding: The Second Circuit affirmed the denial of leave to amend because plaintiff waived any challenge to the dismissal of his disability discrimination claim by failing to meaningfully argue it on appeal, despite having raised the issue below.
brief_summary: Robert Mercer, a pro se public housing tenant with asthma allegedly triggered by mold in his NYCHA apartment, appealed the denial of leave to amend his complaint after the district court dismissed his FHAA disability discrimination claim. The Second Circuit affirmed, holding that Mercer waived any challenge to the dismissal by failing to meaningfully argue the disability discrimination claim on appeal, instead abandoning it to focus on procedural issues about case management deadlines.
key_cases_cited: McLeod v. Jewish Guild for the Blind, 864 F.3d 154 (2d Cir. 2017)
LoSacco v. City of Middletown, 71 F.3d 88 (2d Cir. 1995)
Bogle-Assegai v. Connecticut, 470 F.3d 498 (2d Cir. 2006)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Remediation or accommodation related to mold presence in apartment following May 2019 NYCHA inspection; plaintiff developed mild intermittent asthma and was hospitalized
fha_claims.reasoning: District Court dismissed for failure to state a claim under the FHAA disability discrimination theory. On appeal, plaintiff waived challenge to the dismissal of his disability discrimination claim by not mentioning or challenging it in his appellate brief, and the Second Circuit affirmed the dismissal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Violation of 24 C.F.R. § 5.703(f) (HUD regulation requiring dwelling units to be free of mold); possible state law claims
fha_claims.reasoning: District Court dismissed the HUD regulation claim on the ground that 24 C.F.R. § 5.703(f) does not provide a private right of action, and declined supplemental jurisdiction over possible state law claims. Plaintiff did not challenge this basis for dismissal on appeal and waived the issue.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Age discrimination claim under the FHAA
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff explicitly relinquished his age discrimination claim in his notice of appeal, stating he asked the court to 'remove the FHAA claim' from the Second Amended Complaint. The claim was abandoned on appeal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Eighth Amendment challenge to method of execution (lethal injection); prisoner sought injunction to prevent execution by lethal injection and proposed alternative method of execution by firing squad
fha_claims.reasoning: Supreme Court reversed the Eleventh Circuit's dismissal on jurisdictional grounds. The Court held that a prisoner's method-of-execution claim under the Eighth Amendment can proceed under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (not habeas) even when the proposed alternative method is not authorized by state law, because the relief sought does not necessarily prevent the State from carrying out the execution—the State retains the pathway of amending its statute. The case was remanded for consideration of timeliness and other remaining issues.

case_name: Tony Staton v. Vesta Corporation
accommodation_description: Request for an apartment suitable for plaintiff's disability, suggesting plaintiff sought transfer to an accessible unit
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's reasonable accommodation claim because he failed to plead any factual content regarding the nature of his disability, what accommodation he sought, when he requested it, or how his current apartment fails to accommodate his disability, though the dismissal was without prejudice allowing plaintiff to re-plead.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Tony Staton sued Vesta Corporation alleging the defendant denied him an accessible apartment suitable for his disability under the Fair Housing Act. The court granted defendant's motion to dismiss without prejudice, finding plaintiff's complaint failed to state a plausible housing discrimination claim because he provided no factual content about his disability, the accommodation sought, or how his current unit fails to accommodate his needs.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
City of Edmonds v. Oxford House, Inc., 514 U.S. 725 (1995)
FTC v. Compagnie de Saint-Gobain-Pont-a-Mousson, 636 F.2d 1300 (D.C. Cir. 1980)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible apartment suitable for plaintiff's disability; nature of disability and specific accommodation sought not pleaded
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff failed to plead sufficient factual content under Iqbal/Twombly to state a plausible reasonable accommodation claim, as he did not allege the nature of his disability, what accommodation he sought, when he sought it, or how his apartment fails to accommodate his disability. However, dismissal was without prejudice and plaintiff was permitted to file an amended complaint.

case_name: Hatfield v. Cottages on 78th Community Association
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged HOA retaliated against her for filing housing discrimination complaints with UALD and threatened legal action.
key_holding: The HOA's communications (September 6th Letter, September 10th Letter, notice of assessment, and statements at annual meeting) did not constitute coercive, threatening, intimidating, or interfering conduct under § 3617 because a person of normal fortitude would not find them objectively coercive.
brief_summary: Wendi Hatfield, a homeowner, sued her HOA and related defendants alleging FHA retaliation under § 3617 based on communications (cease-and-desist letter, fines, September letters, and meeting statements) that she claimed were coercive responses to her filing housing discrimination complaints. The Tenth Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal, holding that the HOA's conduct did not rise to the level of coercive, threatening, intimidating, or interfering conduct required for a § 3617 claim because the communications were merely informational and not objectively severe enough to deter a person of normal fortitude from exercising fair housing rights.
key_cases_cited: Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009)
Geraci v. Union Square Condo. Ass'n, 891 F.3d 274 (7th Cir. 2018)
Revock v. Cowpet Bay Western Condominium Ass'n, 853 F.3d 96 (3d Cir. 2017)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that defendants' conduct (September 6th Letter, September 10th Letter, notice of assessment, and statements at annual meeting) rose to the level of coercive, intimidating, threatening, or interfering conduct that would violate § 3617. The conduct was less pervasive and derogatory than comparable cases and would not be viewed as coercive by a person of normal fortitude.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Invasion of privacy/intrusion upon seclusion, defamation, tortious interference with economic relations, civil conspiracy (state law claims)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege intrusion upon seclusion (September 6th Letter was not a physical invasion or prying conduct and would not be highly offensive to a reasonable person); defamation (statements were not false or defamatory when considered in context; statements about legal costs, not plaintiff); tortious interference (conclusory allegations lacking factual support for interference with economic relations); and civil conspiracy (no plausible underlying tort and intracorporate conspiracy doctrine bars conspiracy claims against agents acting within scope of authority).

case_name: Tony Staton v. Vesta Corporation
accommodation_description: Request for an accessible apartment unit suitable for his disability
key_holding: The court denied the motion to dismiss on procedural process grounds but dismissed the FHA reasonable accommodation claim for failure to state sufficient factual allegations, granting plaintiff leave to amend.
brief_summary: Tony Staton, proceeding pro se, sued Vesta Corporation alleging the defendant denied him an accessible apartment suitable for his disability under the Fair Housing Act. The court denied the motion to dismiss on procedural process grounds but dismissed the FHA claim without prejudice for failure to plead sufficient factual content, including the nature of his disability and what accommodation he sought.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
City of Edmonds v. Oxford House, Inc., 514 U.S. 725 (1995)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible apartment suitable for plaintiff's disability; nature of disability and specific accommodation sought not specified in complaint
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead sufficient factual content to state a plausible reasonable accommodation claim under Iqbal/Twombly. The complaint did not specify the nature of plaintiff's disability, what accommodation was sought, when it was sought, or how the apartment failed to accommodate the disability. Court permitted re-pleading due to pro se status.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) violation — failure to provide required validation notice and dispute procedures within five days of initial communication; specifically failure to state amount of debt and failure to identify debt collector (rather than creditor) as entity assuming validity of debt, obtaining verification, and providing original creditor information.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted plaintiff's cross-motion for summary judgment on liability under 15 U.S.C. § 1692g(a) because defendant failed to include the amount of debt in the validation notice and failed to state that the debt collector (not the creditor) would assume validity of the debt, verify it, and provide original creditor information. The FDCPA is a strict liability statute, and these technical violations are sufficient to establish liability regardless of actual damages or whether plaintiff read the letter.

source_file: 7229354_2015_Montano v. Bonnie Brae Convalescent Hospital, Inc._cacd
case_name: Montano v. Bonnie Brae Convalescent Hospital, Inc.
accommodation_description: Quadriplegic wheelchair user requested physical modifications including widened bathroom doorways, lever-style door handles, accessible sink fixtures, lighter doors, and temperature control to access his room and bathroom independently.
key_holding: The nursing home operator violated the FHA by failing to provide reasonable accommodations for a quadriplegic tenant's disability, including refusing to widen bathroom doorways, install accessible door handles and fixtures, and maintain adequate room temperature, while also failing to engage in the required interactive process with the resident.
brief_summary: Hector Montano, a quadriplegic wheelchair user residing at Bonnie Brae Convalescent Hospital since 2009, sued the nursing home operator for failing to accommodate his disability by refusing to modify his bathroom (widen doorways, install lever handles, adjust sink fixtures) and provide adequate room temperature. After a bench trial, the court found the facility violated the Fair Housing Act by failing to provide reasonable accommodations and failing to engage in the required interactive process, awarding $65,000 in compensatory damages, $10,000 in punitive damages, and injunctive relief requiring ADA compliance modifications.
key_cases_cited: Giebeler v. M & B Assoc., 343 F.3d 1143 (9th Cir.2003)
California Mobile Home Park Mgmt. Co., 29 F.3d 1413 (9th Cir.1994)
Jankowski Lee & Assoc. v. Cisneros, 91 F.3d 891 (7th Cir.1996)
Dadian v. Vill. of Wilmette, 269 F.3d 831 (7th Cir.2001)
United States v. California Mobile Home Park Mgmt. Co., 29 F.3d 1413 (9th Cir.1994)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible room with sufficient space for wheelchair; widened bathroom doorways; accessible door handles (levers instead of knobs); accessible bathroom fixtures (sinks, faucets, mirrors, towel dispensers); insulated pipes under sinks; lighter doors; moderate room temperature; accessible shower; accessible hallway sink as interim accommodation
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied the four-part reasonable accommodation test under FHA § 3604(f)(3)(B): plaintiff has a disability, defendant knew of it, the accommodations were necessary to afford equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling, and defendant refused to provide them. Court found accommodations were reasonable and necessary, defendant failed to engage in interactive process, and defendant did not meet its burden of demonstrating undue hardship or fundamental alteration.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to engage in interactive process regarding reasonable accommodation requests
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found defendant violated FHA by failing to engage in the interactive process with plaintiff regarding his accommodation requests. Defendant never had a conversation with plaintiff about his needs, never took measurements of his wheelchair, never discussed problems with sinks, and never explained cost concerns. This failure to engage in dialogue constitutes a separate FHA violation under the interactive process requirement.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to remove architectural barriers including inaccessible bathroom doorways, door handles, sink fixtures, exposed uninsulated pipes, high towel dispensers, and temperature control issues
fha_claims.reasoning: Under ADA Title III § 12182(b)(2)(A)(iv), defendant violated the duty to remove architectural barriers where removal is readily achievable. Court found modifications were readily achievable because defendant had already made some of the requested modifications to other rooms/sinks during the relevant period, demonstrating feasibility. Defendant failed to meet its burden of proving modifications were not readily achievable or would fundamentally alter the facility.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: FEHA reasonable accommodation claim; ADA Title III barrier removal claim; Rehabilitation Act § 504 discrimination claim; Unruh Civil Rights Act violation; California Disabled Persons Act (CDPA) reasonable accommodation claim; California Business & Professions Code § 17200 unfair competition claim; state tort claims (intentional infliction of emotional distress, reckless neglect, tort per se, negligence)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found defendant violated FEHA (Cal. Gov't Code § 12927(c)(1)) using the same reasonable accommodation standard as FHA; violated ADA Title III (42 U.S.C. § 12182) by failing to remove readily achievable barriers; violated Rehabilitation Act § 504 (29 U.S.C. § 794(a)) because defendant receives federal funds (Medicare/Medi-Cal) and discriminated based on disability; violated Unruh Civil Rights Act (Cal. Civ. Code § 51(f)) because ADA violation constitutes violation thereof; violated CDPA (Cal. Civ. Code § 54.1) using same standard as FEHA; violated § 17200 because violations of FHA, FEHA, and Unruh Act constitute unlawful competition. Court declined to address tort claims because civil rights violations were established.

source_file: 7229993_2015_Alboniga v. School Board of Broward County Florida_flsd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permit student A.M. to attend school accompanied by his seizure alert and response service dog (Stevie) without requiring plaintiff to provide a separate handler, pay additional liability insurance, or obtain vaccinations exceeding Florida law requirements. School Board must assist A.M. in taking the service dog outside school premises to urinate when necessary during the school day.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied 28 C.F.R. § 35.136 and found that the School Board's policies requiring additional liability insurance and excess vaccinations constitute impermissible surcharges under § 35.136(h). The court further held that permitting A.M. to attend school with his service dog tethered to him (with A.M. as handler) and requiring school staff to assist A.M. in taking the dog outside to urinate are reasonable accommodations that do not fundamentally alter the school's educational services and comply with §§ 35.136(d) and (e). The court rejected the School Board's argument that it could substitute its preferred accommodation (school staff providing seizure care) for the plaintiff's requested accommodation (service dog access), reasoning that individuals with disabilities have the most accurate knowledge of their needs.

source_file: 7230169_2015_United States v. East River Housing Corp._nysd
case_name: United States v. East River Housing Corp.
accommodation_description: Three complainants (Aaron, Eisenberg, Gilbert) requested permission to keep emotional support or service dogs in their apartments as reasonable accommodations for psychiatric disabilities (depression, PTSD, anxiety).
key_holding: The court granted the government's motion to strike East River's second affirmative defense (challenging HUD procedures) and denied East River's motions for partial summary judgment on res judicata grounds and to dismiss the pattern-or-practice claim, ruling that DHR's no-probable-cause determination was unreviewed and thus cannot have preclusive effect, and that the government adequately pled a pattern-or-practice claim under § 3614.
brief_summary: The United States government sued East River Housing Corporation, a Manhattan housing cooperative, alleging that it discriminated against three disabled residents by refusing to allow them to keep emotional support/service dogs as reasonable accommodations for their psychiatric disabilities, and retaliated against one resident by threatening to impose attorneys' fees as 'additional rent.' The court denied East River's motions for partial summary judgment (based on res judicata from an unreviewed state agency determination) and to dismiss the pattern-or-practice claim, and granted the government's motion to strike East River's affirmative defense challenging HUD's investigative procedures.
key_cases_cited: Kosakow v. New Rochelle Radiology Associates, P.C., 274 F.3d 706 (2d Cir. 2001)
Ste. Marie v. Riverside Memorial Cemetery, 650 F.2d 395 (2d Cir. 1981)
De-Cintio v. Westchester County Medical Center, 821 F.2d 111 (2d Cir. 1987)
Kirkland v. City of Peekskill, 828 F.2d 108 (2d Cir. 1987)
Mitchell v. Cellone-P.R. Properties, Inc., 389 F.3d 82 (3d Cir. 2004)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to keep a service dog or emotional support animal (Rosie) in apartment as reasonable accommodation for chronic major depression, anxiety, and PTSD
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied defendant's motion for partial summary judgment on Aaron's reasonable accommodation claim based on res judicata and collateral estoppel, finding no privity between Government and Aaron, no final DHR determination, and Aaron lacked full and fair opportunity to litigate before DHR without discovery or hearing.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to keep a trained, registered service dog (Ruby) in apartment as reasonable accommodation for PTSD with depression, anxiety, panic attacks, and insomnia
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied defendant's motion to sever Eisenberg's claims from the action; claims survive and proceed to discovery and potential trial on merits.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to keep a dog (Olive Oil) in apartment as reasonable accommodation for chronic psychiatric conditions limiting social interaction and stress coping
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied defendant's motion to sever Gilbert's claims from the action; claims survive and proceed to discovery and potential trial on merits.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation against Gilbert for requesting reasonable accommodation and filing FHA complaint, including threatening to pursue attorney's fees, requesting excessive medical information, and seeking to bill legal fees as additional rent
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied defendant's motion to sever Gilbert's retaliation claim; claim survives and proceeds to discovery and potential trial on merits.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Pattern or practice of discrimination and denial of rights to a group of persons with disabilities requesting reasonable accommodations for assistance animals
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied defendant's motion to dismiss the Fifth Cause of Action under § 3614(a) for pattern or practice and group of persons claims, finding that the Government adequately pleaded a plausible claim without requiring statistical evidence, minimum number of incidents, or a single overarching policy; discovery is ongoing and necessary to develop the factual record.

case_name: Donahue Francis v. Kings Park Manor, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, an African-American tenant, alleges the landlord failed to intervene in co-tenant's racial harassment, creating a hostile housing environment.
key_holding: The court granted the motion to dismiss the FHA claims because the plaintiff failed to allege specific facts showing the landlord acted with intentional racial discrimination or failed to intervene on account of the plaintiff's race, as required to state a hostile housing environment claim under the FHA against a landlord for co-tenant harassment.
brief_summary: Donahue Francis, an African-American tenant with a Section 8 voucher, sued Kings Park Manor and its property manager alleging the landlord failed to intervene in racial harassment by a co-tenant who repeatedly used racial slurs and threats. The court granted the motion to dismiss the Fair Housing Act claims, holding that the plaintiff failed to adequately plead that the landlord acted with intentional racial discrimination or failed to intervene on account of the plaintiff's race, as required to state a hostile housing environment claim against a landlord for co-tenant harassment under the FHA.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Neudecker v. Boisclair Corp.
Cain v. Rambert
Haber v. ASN 50th St. LLC

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege specific facts sufficient to support an inference that KPM Defendants intentionally discriminated based on race. The complaint contained only naked assertions without fact-specific allegations of a causal link between KPM's conduct and plaintiff's race, insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged failure to intervene in tenant-on-tenant racial harassment and threats
fha_claims.reasoning: Under § 3617, plaintiff must allege intentional discrimination by the defendant. The court found no plausible allegation that KPM Defendants failed to intervene due to discriminatory animus toward plaintiff based on race; the harassment was perpetrated by co-tenant Endres, not KPM agents, and plaintiff alleged no basis for imputing Endres's conduct to KPM or showing KPM's own racial animus.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Civil Rights Act of 1866 (§§ 1981, 1982), New York Executive Law § 296(5) and § 296(6), negligent infliction of emotional distress, breach of contract (HAP contract and lease warranty of habitability)
fha_claims.reasoning: Sections 1981/1982 claims dismissed for failure to allege intentional discrimination by KPM Defendants with specific facts showing racial animus. Section 296(5) and 296(6) claims dismissed under same framework as FHA claims—no plausible allegation that KPM actually participated in or failed to intervene in Endres's discriminatory conduct due to racial animus. Negligent infliction of emotional distress dismissed because landlord had no common law duty to prevent one tenant from harassing another absent authority, ability, and opportunity to control the assailant; mere knowledge did not trigger a duty to investigate and intervene.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of implied warranty of habitability under New York Real Property Law § 235-b
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss as to KPM on the warranty of habitability claim, finding that under New York law, a tenant may state a claim for breach of the implied warranty of habitability against a landlord for failure to intervene in response to harassing behavior by a co-tenant. Plaintiff adequately pleaded that KPM breached this warranty by failing to respond to documented racial harassment. Claim dismissed as to individual defendant Downing because she signed the lease as an agent for KPM, not in her personal capacity.

case_name: DeCambre v. Brookline Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Request for reasonable accommodation to exclude certain trust disbursements (car purchase, phone/cable bills, veterinary costs for cats as emotional support animals) from calculation of annual income for Section 8 eligibility
key_holding: The BHA's determination to count trust disbursements as income for Section 8 purposes was a reasonable application of HUD regulations, and there was no evidence the BHA acted in a discriminatory manner based on DeCambre's disability status; the court deferred to HUD's regulatory interpretation under Chevron principles.
brief_summary: Kimberly DeCambre, a disabled Section 8 participant, sued the Brookline Housing Authority alleging it unlawfully calculated her annual income by counting distributions from her special needs trust, and that this violated the Fair Housing Act, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act. The court denied her preliminary injunction motion and held that the BHA's income calculation was a reasonable interpretation of HUD regulations, rejecting her discrimination claims but remanding for further consideration of certain expense exclusions.
key_cases_cited: Gammons v. Mass. Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Dev., 523 F. Supp. 2d 76 (D. Mass. 2007)
Finley v. City of Santa Monica, No. BS127077, 2011 WL 7116184 (Cal. Super. Ct. May 25, 2011)
Lewis v. Alexander, 685 F.3d 325 (3d Cir. 2012)
Sullivan v. County of Suffolk, 174 F.3d 282 (2d Cir. 1999)
Chevron U.S.A., Inc. v. Natural Res. Def. Council, Inc., 467 U.S. 837 (1984)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exclusion of special needs trust disbursements from annual income calculation for Section 8 eligibility; exclusion of car purchase, phone/landline bills, and veterinary costs for companion animals from income calculation
fha_claims.disposition: Motion for Preliminary Injunction Denied; Remanded
fha_claims.reasoning: The court upheld the BHA's initial determination that trust disbursements should be counted as income under 24 C.F.R. § 5.603(b)(2), finding the BHA's interpretation reasonable. However, the court remanded for further analysis of specific expense categories (cable/internet, travel, veterinary costs for emotional support animals, and car-related medical transportation) under the medical expense and temporary/nonrecurring income exclusions, directing the BHA to conduct a more thorough interactive process analysis on remand.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Disability-based discrimination in income calculation and denial of Section 8 benefits
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found no evidence that the BHA calculated DeCambre's Section 8 income in a discriminatory manner based on disability status. The court noted that the regulations apply equally to all non-revocable trusts (not just special needs trusts), and that the BHA provided multiple opportunities for DeCambre to submit medical certification. The court concluded that the BHA did not act in a discriminatory manner and that the income calculation rule does not tend to screen out disabled tenants.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 substantive due process claim; 29 U.S.C. § 701 Rehabilitation Act claim; 42 U.S.C. § 12131 Americans with Disabilities Act Title II claim; breach of lease; interference with quiet use and enjoyment
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that DeCambre failed to establish a substantive due process violation under § 1983 because she did not demonstrate a constitutionally protected property interest in Section 8 assistance and the BHA's conduct did not 'shock the conscience.' The court also found no procedural due process violation, as DeCambre received timely notice and a hearing with counsel present. The court did not reach the merits of the ADA and Rehabilitation Act claims on the basis that the income calculation rule applies equally to all non-revocable trusts and does not discriminate based on disability.

case_name: Mosdos Chofetz Chaim, Inc. v. Village of Wesley Hills
accommodation_description: Religious institutions and affiliated individuals allege municipalities used environmental review laws as pretext to block development of Kiryas Radin, an Orthodox Jewish religious school and community center.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for defendants because plaintiffs failed to establish discriminatory intent or that they were selectively treated compared to similarly-situated development projects, as defendants were unaware of comparator sites and had legitimate environmental concerns.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs, Orthodox Jewish religious institutions and individuals, sued four New York municipalities and their officials alleging the Villages filed SEQRA-based litigation against Kiryas Radin, an adult student housing project affiliated with their community, based on discriminatory animus toward Orthodox Jews rather than legitimate environmental concerns. The court granted summary judgment for defendants, finding plaintiffs failed to establish discriminatory intent or that comparator development projects were treated more favorably, as defendants lacked knowledge of the comparator sites.
key_cases_cited: Village of Arlington v. Collet
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center
LeBlanc-Sternberg v. Fletcher
LaTrieste v. Town of Oyster Bay
Chabad Lubavitch of Litchfield Cnty., Inc. v. Litchfield Historic Dist. Comm'n

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1982, 1983, 1985(3); N.Y. Const. Art. I, §§ 3, 11; N.Y. Civil Rights Law § 40-c; RLUIPA 42 U.S.C. § 2000cc et seq.; FHA 42 U.S.C. § 3604 et seq.
fha_claims.reasoning: Defendants entitled to qualified immunity under Noerr-Pennington doctrine for filing the Chestnut Ridge Action. Even if immunity did not apply, plaintiffs failed to establish similarly-situated comparator sites or discriminatory intent required for Equal Protection claims. Plaintiffs also failed to establish discriminatory animus for § 1985(3) conspiracy claim and failed to allege property interest in § 1982 claim. State constitutional and civil rights law claims dismissed for failure to file Notice of Claim or for applying same standards as § 1983 claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: RLUIPA claims (42 U.S.C. §§ 2000cc(a)(1) and 2000cc(b)(2)) alleging substantial burden on religious exercise and nondiscrimination in land use regulation
fha_claims.reasoning: Filing of Chestnut Ridge Action does not constitute imposition or implementation of a land use regulation under RLUIPA. The Villages, as interested agencies without jurisdiction over the Nike Site, merely filed suit to ensure Ramapo (the involved agency) complied with SEQRA. RLUIPA does not extend to litigation seeking enforcement of land use regulations by another municipality. The term 'government practice' in RLUIPA refers to manner of implementing regulations, not filing lawsuits.

case_name: Hoostein v. Mental Health Ass'n
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs (landlords) attempted to use FHA to compel MHA to continue providing Shelter Plus Care subsidy for Ms. Hoostein after her change in family size made her ineligible under the single-person eligibility requirement.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' FHA claims because plaintiffs are landlords seeking to use the FHA against their tenant, but the statute by its text does not provide landlords with a cause of action against tenants; the FHA provisions cited (§§ 3604(a-c), 3604(f)(1)(c), 3617) apply to potential landlords and property owners, not to the plaintiffs who own the property.
brief_summary: Michael Hoostein and Kathlyn Stein (as landlords) sued Mental Health Association Inc., Jerome Ray, the City of Northampton, and Margaret Keller alleging FHA discrimination and retaliation arising from MHA's decision to discontinue Ms. Hoostein's Shelter Plus Care subsidy after she had a child and was no longer a single individual. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, holding that the FHA claims failed because plaintiffs, as landlords, cannot state a claim under the FHA's anti-discrimination provisions against their own tenant, and the court declined supplemental jurisdiction over remaining state law claims.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Ashcroft v. Iqbal

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Continuation of Shelter Plus Care subsidy following birth of child; transition to alternative subsidy (Mobile Rental Voucher)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs lack standing to bring FHA claims because they are the property owners, not tenants or prospective tenants. The FHA's anti-discrimination provisions apply only to landlords and property owners, not to tenants suing their landlords. Plaintiffs attempted to use the FHA to compel defendants (their tenants) to provide a housing subsidy, which is not a cognizable FHA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation for filing FHA complaint with HUD regarding cancellation of Shelter Plus Care subsidy
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 3617 retaliation claims require a prerequisite that the plaintiff attempted or manifested a desire to exercise rights under §§ 3603-3606. Because plaintiffs cannot state a claim under those underlying sections (as they are property owners, not tenants), they cannot establish the necessary predicate for a § 3617 retaliation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Mass. Gen. Laws § 93A unfair/deceptive acts and implied covenant of good faith; breach of lease for non-payment of rent
fha_claims.reasoning: After dismissing all FHA claims over which the court had original federal question jurisdiction, the court exercised its discretion under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3) to decline supplemental jurisdiction over the remaining state law claims (Mass. Gen. Laws § 93A and breach of lease), dismissing them without prejudice.

source_file: 7230918_2015_Holy Ghost Revival Ministries v. City of Marysville_wawd
case_name: Holy Ghost Revival Ministries v. City of Marysville
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs operate group housing for released convicts, some recovering from substance abuse; they submitted a reasonable accommodation request to permit occupancy in a commercially-zoned area.
key_holding: The court dismissed Plaintiffs' FHA claims for failure to state a claim because the amended complaint failed to allege discriminatory purpose—the City officials' emails attached to the complaint showed their concern was based on the population being registered sexual offenders, not on disability or religion.
brief_summary: Holy Ghost Revival Ministries and its pastors sued the City of Marysville challenging zoning enforcement actions against their group housing residences for released convicts, alleging discrimination based on religion and disability under the FHA, RLUIPA, and constitutional provisions. The court granted in part Defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that Plaintiffs failed to adequately plead discriminatory purpose since the City's emails showed its enforcement concern was based on housing for registered sexual offenders, not on Plaintiffs' religious beliefs or residents' disabilities.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Middlesex County Sewerage Authority v. National Sea Clammers Association, 453 U.S. 1 (1981)
Blessing v. Freestone, 520 U.S. 329 (1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation request to allow group housing residence (Smokey Point Property) for recovering substance abusers in a General Commercial zone, submitted via revised floorplan proposing caretaker's unit use
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to allege what the proposed accommodation was, whether it was reasonable, or that the accommodation was necessary to afford handicapped residents equal opportunity to use and enjoy dwellings in General Commercial zones. The complaint lacks factual allegations supporting the third and fourth elements of the reasonable accommodation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 1983 claims for violations of First Amendment (free exercise and equal protection), Fourteenth Amendment (equal protection and due process), FHA, RLUIPA, and Washington State Constitution; Section 1988 conspiracy claim; Washington Constitution claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 1983 claims for First Amendment violations (free exercise and equal protection) and due process failed because the complaint did not allege discriminatory purpose or identify which due process protections were violated. Section 1988 does not provide a cause of action; it only provides for attorney's fees. Section 1983 claim based on Washington Constitution was dismissed because Section 1983 does not vindicate state constitutional violations. The court declined to address whether FHA and RLUIPA violations are enforceable under Section 1983 because defendants did not raise that issue.

source_file: 7231034_2015_Fairchild Semiconductor Corp. v. Power Integrations, Inc._ded
7231257_2015_Palm Partners, LLC v. City of Oakland Park_flsd
case_name: Palm Partners, LLC v. City of Oakland Park
accommodation_description: Request for zoning accommodation to either treat the proposed behavioral health facility as an existing non-conforming use in the Community Facilities district or grant conditional use approval as a hospital.
key_holding: The requested accommodation was not reasonable because the zoning rule prohibiting residential use of property zoned for non-residential use and designated as a non-receiving site is essential to the City's zoning scheme, and granting the accommodation would fundamentally alter that scheme; the City had no obligation to provide preferential treatment when non-disabled individuals have no greater opportunity for residential use of the Property.
brief_summary: Palm Partners, LLC, a behavioral and mental health treatment facility operator, sued the City of Oakland Park alleging the City violated the ADA and FHA by denying its conditional use application and reasonable accommodation request to develop a residential treatment facility in a Community Facilities zoning district. The court granted summary judgment for the City, finding no evidence of discriminatory animus and concluding that the accommodation request was not reasonable because granting it would fundamentally alter the City's zoning scheme by requiring the City to waive residential density requirements for a non-receiving site.
key_cases_cited: Schwarz v. City of Treasure Island, 544 F.3d 1201 (11th Cir. 2008)
Village of Arlington Heights v. Metro. Hous. Dev. Corp., 429 U.S. 252 (1977)
Caron Found. of Florida, Inc. v. City of Delray Beach, 879 F. Supp. 2d 1353 (S.D. Fla. 2012)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework and found no direct evidence of discriminatory intent. The City Commission's stated reason for denial—that the proposed facility would operate as a residential treatment center, not a hospital as represented in the application—was legitimate and nondiscriminatory. The court rejected the argument that community opposition or the discrepancy between the application and actual use constituted evidence of discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request to treat the proposed residential treatment facility as an existing nonconforming use in the Community Facilities district, or alternatively, to grant conditional use approval as a hospital despite the facility's actual operation as a residential treatment center
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the Schwarz framework and found that the zoning rule prohibiting residential use of non-receiving sites in Community Facilities zones is essential to the City's zoning scheme. The proposed treatment facility is incompatible with surrounding land uses (industrial, medical, single-family residential), and the City has not routinely waived the rule. Requiring the City to waive the rule would constitute a fundamental alteration of its zoning scheme. The court also rejected treating the facility as a hospital or as an existing nonconforming use, and found no violation of the equal opportunity requirement.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claims for disparate treatment and failure to provide reasonable accommodation
fha_claims.reasoning: The court analyzed ADA Title II claims using the same legal standards as the FHA claims (McDonnell Douglas for disparate treatment and Schwarz framework for reasonable accommodation) and reached identical conclusions that the City's decision was based on legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons and that the requested accommodation was not reasonable.

case_name: Germain v. M & T Bank Corp.
accommodation_description: Commercial real estate loan applications submitted by Muslim Albanian investors allegedly denied based on religion and national origin rather than creditworthiness.
key_holding: The court dismissed Plaintiffs' FHA claims because Plaintiffs failed to adequately plead that Defendants had knowledge of Plaintiffs' religion or that discriminatory intent was a motivating factor in denying loan discussions, as Plaintiffs' own allegations suggested legitimate, non-discriminatory reasons for Walz's conduct.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs David Germain, Selim Zherka (a Muslim of Albanian descent), and associated business entities sued M & T Bank alleging the bank discriminated against them in commercial lending based on religion and national origin, including claims that a bank officer cancelled a loan meeting upon learning of Zherka's identity and made anti-Muslim statements. The court dismissed the FHA claims without prejudice, finding the complaint failed to adequately plead that the bank had knowledge of Zherka's religion or that discriminatory animus was a but-for cause of the lending decisions, as the allegations suggested Walz's conduct was based on Zherka's notoriety rather than protected characteristics.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed FHA claims for failure to state a claim because plaintiffs sought financing for commercial multi-family rental properties, not for their own residential use. The discrimination alleged was directed at plaintiffs as commercial applicants, not at prospective residents, placing the transaction outside the scope of § 3605's protection of 'residential real estate-related transactions.'

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ECOA discrimination claims (religion, national origin); ECOA notification provision violation; NYHRL discrimination claims; § 1985(3) conspiracy claim; slander per se claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Germain and Lexington Capital's ECOA and NYHRL discrimination claims dismissed for lack of statutory standing (not applicants for credit). Zherka, Zherka Trust, and Silas Investments' ECOA discrimination claims dismissed for failure to adequately allege prima facie elements (failed to allege qualifications for credit and that defendant engaged in similar transactions with similarly qualified applicants). § 1985(3) conspiracy claim dismissed for failure to allege factual basis for meeting of the minds. Zherka's ECOA notification claim and slander claim survived motion to dismiss.

source_file: 7232003_2015_Access Living of Metropolitan Chicago v. Prewitt_ilnd
case_name: Access Living of Metropolitan Chicago v. Prewitt
accommodation_description: Fair housing test by deaf individual using IP Relay service was met with hung-up call, failure to provide apartment showing information, and email stating the apartment was not 'handicapped safe.'
key_holding: The court denied the motion to dismiss, holding that the plaintiff adequately pleaded Fair Housing Act violations by alleging the defendant made statements to a deaf tester indicating a preference against disabled tenants and misrepresented housing availability based on disability.
brief_summary: Access Living of Metropolitan Chicago, a fair housing organization, sued Bill Prewitt d/b/a Best Rents after a fair housing test revealed that a deaf tester calling via IP Relay was hung up on, told information was 'all online,' not offered an apartment showing, and sent an email stating the apartment was not 'handicapped safe,' while a non-disabled tester received full information and an apartment showing invitation. The court denied the motion to dismiss, finding the complaint adequately pleaded violations of the Fair Housing Act's prohibitions on discriminatory statements and misrepresentation of housing availability.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
White v. U.S. Dept. of Housing & Urban Dev., 475 F.3d 898 (7th Cir. 2007)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Gladstone Realtors v. Vill. of Bellwood, 441 U.S. 91 (1979)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6), finding that Access Living adequately pleaded a Section 3604(c) violation by alleging that Defendant made statements indicating a preference against disabled individuals. The complaint identified the type of discrimination (disability-based), the discriminator (Best Rents/Prewitt), and the timeframe, satisfying the plausibility standard under Twombly/Iqbal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6), finding that Access Living adequately pleaded a Section 3604(d) violation by alleging that Defendant misrepresented housing availability to the Deaf tester while offering availability to the Non-Disabled tester. The complaint sufficiently alleged disparate treatment based on disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6), finding that Access Living adequately pleaded violations of Section 3604(f)(1)(A) and 3604(f)(2) by alleging intentional discrimination in the sale or rental of the dwelling and in the terms and conditions of rental based on disability. The complaint identified the type of discrimination, the discriminator, and the timeframe.

source_file: 7232139_2015_Viens v. America Empire Surplus Lines Ins._ctd
case_name: Viens v. America Empire Surplus Lines Insurance Co.
accommodation_description: Insurance underwriting practices that allegedly penalize landlords for renting to Section 8 voucher holders — this is not a reasonable accommodation request but rather a challenge to insurance discrimination practices.
key_holding: The court denied defendant's motion to dismiss, holding that plaintiffs (landlords and fair housing organization) have standing to challenge insurance underwriting criteria that allegedly discriminate against Section 8 tenants based on lawful source of income and have a disparate impact on racial minorities.
brief_summary: Landlords and the Connecticut Fair Housing Center sued an insurance company alleging that its underwriting criteria charging higher premiums or denying coverage to landlords who rent to Section 8 tenants violates the Fair Housing Act (disparate impact on racial minorities) and Connecticut Fair Housing Act (lawful source of income discrimination). The court denied the motion to dismiss, holding that disparate impact claims are cognizable under the FHA, insurance qualifies as a residential real-estate-related transaction, and plaintiffs have standing to bring these claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Texas Dept. of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center
Olmstead v. L.C.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Landlords' right to rent to Section 8 tenants without financial penalty or insurance cancellation
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that CFHA § 46a-64c(a)(9) protects third parties (landlords) who aid protected class members (Section 8 tenants) in exercising their rights, and plaintiffs adequately alleged that defendant interfered with landlords' right to rent to Section 8 tenants by charging higher premiums and canceling coverage as financial penalties for compliance with CFHA obligations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Publication of statements indicating preference against Section 8 tenants in insurance underwriting
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that CFHA § 46a-64c(a)(3) prohibits publication of statements indicating discrimination based on lawful source of income, and the statement need not target a single identifiable individual or result in actual denial of housing; plaintiffs adequately alleged defendant made and printed statements conveying prohibited preference against Section 8 tenants.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination in terms, conditions, or privileges of rental and in residential real-estate-related transactions based on lawful source of income (Section 8 vouchers)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that plaintiffs adequately alleged injury to Section 8 tenants can be plausibly inferred because if landlords are forced to pay financial penalties for renting to Section 8 tenants, they will be less likely to participate in the program, resulting in less housing available to Section 8 participants; this satisfies the requirement that plaintiffs' injuries be linked to discrimination against protected class members.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Insurance underwriting criteria charging higher premiums or denying coverage to landlords who rent to Section 8 tenants, resulting in disparate impact on African-American and Latino households who are 12 times more likely to participate in Section 8
