fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that disparate impact claims are cognizable under the FHA based on Second Circuit precedent in Huntington Branch, and that the logic of Salute (exempting landlords' voluntary non-participation in Section 8) does not extend to insurers; plaintiffs adequately alleged disparate impact on race and national origin.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Connecticut Fair Housing Act claims under Conn. Gen.Stat. § 46a-63 et seq. for discrimination based on lawful source of income; standing and substantive discrimination claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that CFHA standing provision § 46a-98a confers standing 'as broadly as is permitted by Article III' and requires only 'injury in fact'; plaintiffs (landlords and fair housing organization) adequately alleged economic injury and organizational harm from defendant's alleged discrimination against Section 8 tenants.

case_name: Austin v. Town of Farmington
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs request that the Town not require removal of the above-ground pool and protective fence when their disabled son no longer resides at the property or upon sale of the home.
key_holding: The Town's condition requiring plaintiffs to remove the pool and fence when their disabled son no longer resides there or upon sale does not violate the FHA because the restoration requirement applies equally to non-disabled homeowners, plaintiffs failed to allege discriminatory intent, and the Town properly granted the variance recognizing the FHA requirements.
brief_summary: Colleen and John Austin sued the Town of Farmington, New York seeking to enjoin enforcement of a variance condition requiring removal of an above-ground pool and fence they installed for their son with cerebral palsy upon sale of their home or when their son no longer resides there. The court granted the Town's motion to dismiss, finding that the restoration requirement does not violate the FHA because it applies equally to all homeowners, plaintiffs failed to allege discriminatory intent, and the Town properly accommodated the disability by granting the variance itself.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Bangerter v. Orem City Corp.
Oxford House, Inc. v. Township of Cherry Hill
Huntington Branch, N.A.A.C.P. v. Town of Huntington
Cason v. Rochester Housing Authority

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Installation of above-ground pool with protective fencing for disabled son's safety and rehabilitation; plaintiffs challenge the restoration condition requiring removal of pool and fence upon sale of property or when disabled son no longer resides there
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiffs failed to allege facts sufficient to plausibly state a claim that the restoration requirement was based on disability or constituted a refusal to make a reasonable accommodation. The variance was granted knowing the son was disabled, and plaintiffs made only conclusory assertions that the removal requirement was disability-based without factual support.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiffs failed to allege facts showing the restoration requirement had a greater impact on disabled housing applicants than non-disabled ones, as there was no showing that the restoration condition did not apply equally to non-disabled individuals.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Although plaintiffs cited 42 U.S.C. § 3617 in their complaint, the court's analysis focused on whether the restoration requirement constituted discrimination or a refusal to accommodate under § 3604(f)(3), not retaliation. The court found no facts alleged that the restoration requirement was retaliatory or based on disability.

source_file: 7232353_2015_County of Cook v. Wells Fargo _ Co._ilnd
case_name: County of Cook v. Wells Fargo & Co.
accommodation_description: This is not a reasonable accommodation case; it involves a county government's challenge to mortgage lending practices (reverse redlining) under the FHA's general anti-discrimination provisions.
key_holding: The district court dismissed Cook County's FHA reverse redlining claim because the county lacks statutory standing, as its alleged injuries (urban blight and reduced property tax base) are purely derivative of harm to minority borrowers and fall outside the zone of interests the FHA was designed to protect.
brief_summary: Cook County sued Wells Fargo alleging the lender engaged in reverse redlining by steering minority borrowers into subprime loans, causing concentrated foreclosures and urban blight in minority neighborhoods. The court dismissed the case, holding that Cook County lacks statutory standing under the FHA's zone-of-interests test because its injuries are purely derivative of harm to the minority borrowers, not the type of injury the FHA was designed to protect.
key_cases_cited: Thompson v. North American Stainless, LP, 562 U.S. 170 (2011)
Lexmark International, Inc. v. Static Control Components, Inc., 572 U.S. 118 (2014)
Gladstone Realtors v. Village of Bellwood, 441 U.S. 91 (1979)
Texas Dept. of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Trafficante v. Metropolitan Life Insurance Co., 409 U.S. 205 (1972)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges reverse redlining (disparate impact in mortgage lending terms and conditions based on race).
fha_claims.reasoning: Cook County lacks standing under the FHA's zone-of-interests test. Although the county alleged Article III standing based on injury to its tax base and resources from urban blight, the court held that Cook County falls outside the zone of interests protected by §§ 3604 and 3605, which are designed to protect individual borrowers and housing consumers, not municipalities suffering derivative economic injuries. The court applied the zone-of-interests test as the controlling legal standard under Thompson v. North American Stainless and Lexmark International, rejecting Cook County's argument that Article III standing is coextensive with FHA statutory standing.

source_file: 7232396_2015_County of Westchester v. United States Department of Housing _ Urban Development_nysd
case_name: County of Westchester v. United States Department of Housing and Urban Development
accommodation_description: This is not a reasonable accommodation case; it is an APA challenge by a county government to HUD's withholding of CPD grant funds based on the County's failure to produce an adequate Analysis of Impediments to fair housing, including race-based impediments.
key_holding: HUD acted within its discretion and lawfully withheld CPD Funds from the County because the County failed to provide accurate certifications and adequate Analyses of Impediments to fair housing as required by federal law, and HUD's demands for amendments to address race-based impediments did not violate statutory limitations in 42 U.S.C. §§ 12705 and 12711.
brief_summary: The County of Westchester sued HUD under the APA, challenging HUD's withholding of Community Planning and Development Formula Grant Funds for fiscal years 2011, 2013, and 2014 because the County failed to provide adequate Analyses of Impediments to fair housing that addressed race-based impediments. The court granted HUD's motion for summary judgment, holding that HUD acted lawfully in withholding the funds and that HUD's demands for amendments to the County's Analysis of Impediments did not violate statutory limitations in the HOME program statute.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 135 S.Ct. 2507 (2015)
United States ex rel. Anti-Discrimination Ctr. of Metro N.Y., Inc. v. Westchester Cnty., 668 F. Supp. 2d 548 (S.D.N.Y. 2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Administrative Procedure Act (APA) challenge to HUD's denial of Community Planning and Development (CPD) Funds; Fifth Amendment Due Process and Equal Protection claims (abandoned by plaintiff)
fha_claims.reasoning: HUD's decisions to withhold CPD Funds were not arbitrary and capricious under the APA standard. HUD acted within its statutory authority and discretion in rejecting the County's Affirmatively Further Fair Housing (AFFH) certifications and Analysis of Impediments (AI) submissions because the County's conclusions regarding exclusionary zoning were unsupported by data and lacked adequate disparate impact analysis. The County failed to demonstrate entitlement to federal funds under 42 U.S.C. §§ 12705(c)(1) and 12711, which do not prohibit HUD from requiring accurate AFFH certifications based on fair housing (as opposed to affordable housing) considerations.

case_name: Chavez v. Aber
accommodation_description: Request to waive the duplex's no-pet policy to allow plaintiff Yvonne Chavez's minor son to keep a mixed-breed pit bull as an emotional support animal for his mental health disabilities.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss, finding plaintiffs sufficiently pleaded that defendants had knowledge of the minor son's disability, that the emotional support animal accommodation request was reasonable, and that defendants directly and constructively denied the request by engaging in a campaign of harassment including eviction proceedings and Animal Control complaints.
brief_summary: Yvonne Chavez sued her landlord Dick Aber and Fairview Court, LLC alleging they discriminated against her minor son M.C. by refusing to accommodate his mental health disability with an emotional support animal (a pit bull named Chato), and retaliated against her for requesting the accommodation. The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss, finding plaintiffs adequately pleaded the elements of a reasonable accommodation denial claim and a retaliation claim under the FHA.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condo. Ass'n, Inc.
City of Edmonds v. Oxford House Inc.
Groome Res. v. Parish of Jefferson

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to keep a mixed-breed pit bull as an emotional support animal in a rental duplex with a 'no pets' policy to address the minor child's mental health disabilities
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiffs sufficiently pleaded all five elements of a § 3604(f)(3)(B) reasonable accommodation claim: (1) disability of resident; (2) defendant's knowledge of disability; (3) necessity of accommodation; (4) reasonableness of accommodation (waiving no-pet rule for emotional support animal is per se reasonable absent direct threat, which plaintiffs pleaded was absent); and (5) refusal to accommodate. Plaintiffs alleged both express denial and constructive denial through delay and harassment. Motion to dismiss denied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiffs sufficiently pleaded discrimination under § 3604(f)(1) and (f)(2) by alleging defendants made the dwelling unavailable and discriminated in terms and conditions of rental based on the child's disability. The reasonable accommodation claim under § 3604(f)(3)(B) encompasses these theories. Motion to dismiss denied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiffs sufficiently pleaded a § 3617 retaliation claim by alleging: (1) protected activity (request for reasonable accommodation in September 2012); (2) adverse actions (notice to vacate on September 14, 2012; eviction filing on September 24, 2012; two additional eviction proceedings; two Animal Control calls; refusal to renew lease on non-discriminatory terms); and (3) causal connection (close temporal proximity between accommodation request and retaliatory conduct). Court rejected defendant's argument that offering alternatives negated retaliation, applying Iqbal/Twombly standard. Motion to dismiss denied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Texas Fair Housing Act (TFHA) § 301.025(a), (b), (c)(2) and Texas Property Code § 92.331 retaliation claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiffs sufficiently pleaded TFHA claims because the statutory language is nearly identical to the FHA and plaintiffs alleged the same facts supporting their federal claims. Court also found plaintiffs pleaded a § 92.331 retaliation claim by alleging defendants filed eviction proceedings in retaliation for plaintiffs' exercise of rights under federal law, with close temporal proximity between accommodation request and eviction filing. Court rejected defendant's argument that no lease existed after 2010, finding plaintiffs alleged a valid lease through December 31, 2012. Motion to dismiss denied.

source_file: 7234036_2015_County of Cook v. HSBC North America Holdings Inc._ilnd
case_name: County of Cook v. HSBC North America Holdings Inc.
accommodation_description: N/A - This is a discriminatory lending case challenging racially discriminatory mortgage lending practices, not a reasonable accommodation request
key_holding: The court held that Cook County established Article III standing to bring FHA claims based on injuries from discriminatory lending practices that caused foreclosures in minority communities, and adequately stated claims for intentional discrimination and disparate impact.
brief_summary: Cook County sued HSBC and its subsidiaries alleging that Defendants intentionally targeted minority borrowers for predatory subprime mortgage loans, resulting in thousands of foreclosures that caused economic and noneconomic harm to the County. The court denied Defendants' motion to dismiss, holding that the County had standing to pursue its Fair Housing Act claims and adequately stated claims for intentional discrimination and disparate impact under the FHA.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Texas Dept. of Hous. & Cmmy. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc.
Gladstone Realtors v. Vill. of Bellwood
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: County adequately pleaded intentional discrimination/disparate treatment claim by alleging Defendants intentionally targeted and marketed predatory subprime loans to minority borrowers with higher pricing and terms than similarly situated nonminority borrowers. Allegations satisfy Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard at pleading stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: County adequately pleaded disparate impact claim by alleging Defendants' facially neutral pricing policies had discriminatory effect on minority borrowers, reducing home equity and causing mortgage delinquencies. Disparate impact is cognizable under FHA per Texas Dept. of Housing & Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc. Discretionary pricing policy can support disparate impact claim despite Wal-Mart Stores v. Dukes.

source_file: 7234061_2015_Fair Housing Center of the Greater Palm Beaches, Inc. v. Sonoma Bay Community Homeowners Ass'n, Inc._flsd
case_name: Fair Housing Center of the Greater Palm Beaches, Inc. v. Sonoma Bay Community Homeowners Ass'n, Inc.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation request - case involves policies allegedly discriminating against families with children (report card requirement, attire rule, loitering rule, curfew rule)
key_holding: The court granted partial summary judgment for plaintiffs on the Loitering and Curfew Rules under § 3604(b) and (c), finding they facially discriminate against children without legitimate non-discriminatory justification, but denied summary judgment on the Report Card Requirement and Proper Attire Rule because genuine disputes of material fact existed regarding whether those policies discriminated based on familial status.
brief_summary: Fair Housing Center of the Greater Palm Beaches and residents of Sonoma Bay and Marsh Harbour condominiums sued the HOA defendants alleging familial status discrimination based on policies requiring children's report cards, dress codes for children, no-loitering restrictions, and curfews for minors. The court granted partial summary judgment for plaintiffs on the curfew and loitering rules under § 3604(b) and (c), finding them facially discriminatory without legitimate justification, but denied summary judgment on the report card requirement and proper attire rule, finding genuine disputes of material fact requiring trial resolution.
key_cases_cited: Bangerter v. Orem City Corp., 46 F.3d 1491 (10th Cir. 1995)
Community House, Inc. v. City of Boise, 490 F.3d 1041 (9th Cir. 2007)
Iniestra v. Cliff Warren Inv., Inc., 886 F.2d 1161 (C.D. Cal. 2012)
Pack v. Fort Washington II, 689 F.2d 1287 (E.D. Cal. 2009)
Fair Hous. Congress v. Weber, 993 F.2d 1286 (C.D. Cal. 1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Report Card Requirement — rental applications required prospective tenants to provide copies of report cards for persons under age 18
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine dispute of material fact regarding whether the Report Card Requirement discriminates based on familial status under § 3604(a). Plaintiffs failed to provide evidence of actual refusal to rent, and the requirement could be construed as vetting for character (similar to adult background checks) or identification purposes, requiring jury determination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Proper Attire Rule — required all residents to wear proper clothing; specified no boys shirtless and girls must wear cover-up over bathing suit when walking to pool
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found ambiguity in the rule's wording. Although the rule references 'Boys' and 'Girls,' when read in conjunction with the first sentence requiring proper attire for all residents, an ordinary reader could reasonably interpret it as applying to all males and females regardless of age. Genuine dispute of material fact requires jury determination under § 3604(b).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Loitering Rule — prohibited loitering/congregating on streets at any time; stated 'after dark all children should be in their home or on their patio'
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted summary judgment under § 3604(b) because the rule explicitly treats children differently than adults by confining them to home after dark. Plaintiffs established prima facie case of intentional discrimination. Defendants' proffered justifications (safety and crime prevention) were not legitimate because they relied on stereotypes and general crime prevention rather than tangible safety threats, and the rule was not the least restrictive means to achieve legitimate goals.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Curfew Rule — required all persons under age 18 to be in their home or back patio after sunset
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted summary judgment under § 3604(b) because the rule explicitly applies only to children and treats them differently than adults. Plaintiffs established prima facie case. Defendants' safety and crime prevention justifications were not legitimate (based on stereotypes, not concrete evidence) and not the least restrictive means. Rule would prevent children from exiting burning apartments, attending night school, or working at night.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Report Card Requirement — analyzed under § 3604(c) as published notice/statement indicating preference or discrimination based on familial status
fha_claims.reasoning: Under § 3604(c) 'ordinary reader' standard, court found genuine dispute. An ordinary reader could interpret the requirement as indicating preference for families without children, but could also reasonably construe it as character vetting (parallel to adult background checks) or identification purposes. Imperfect correlation does not mandate summary judgment when facts viewed favorably to defendants.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Proper Attire Rule — analyzed under § 3604(c) as published notice/statement indicating preference or discrimination based on familial status
fha_claims.reasoning: Under § 3604(c) 'ordinary reader' standard, court found the wording ambiguous. An ordinary reader could interpret 'Boys' and 'Girls' as referring to male and female children, but could also reasonably interpret it as applying to all males and females of any age. Genuine dispute of material fact requires jury determination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Loitering Rule — analyzed under § 3604(c) as published notice/statement indicating preference or discrimination based on familial status
fha_claims.reasoning: Under § 3604(c) 'ordinary reader' standard, court granted summary judgment. An ordinary reader would clearly conclude the rule discriminates against children because it only affects children and treats them differently than adults. No reasonable alternative reading exists. Defendants' evidence of intent is irrelevant to § 3604(c) analysis.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Curfew Rule — analyzed under § 3604(c) as published notice/statement indicating preference or discrimination based on familial status
fha_claims.reasoning: Under § 3604(c) 'ordinary reader' standard, court granted summary judgment. An ordinary reader would clearly conclude the rule discriminates against children because it explicitly applies only to persons under 18 and treats them differently than adults. No reasonable alternative reading exists.

source_file: 7234161_2015_Congregation Rabbinical College of Tartikov, Inc. v. Village of Pomona_nysd
case_name: Congregation Rabbinical College of Tartikov, Inc. v. Village of Pomona
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs challenge zoning laws restricting educational institutions and dormitories, alleging discriminatory effect on Orthodox Jewish community seeking to build rabbinical college with family housing
key_holding: The court denied summary judgment on Plaintiffs' FHA disparate impact and equal protection claims regarding zoning laws restricting dormitories and educational institutions, finding genuine disputes of material fact exist regarding discriminatory intent and whether the laws have a discriminatory effect on the Orthodox Jewish community.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs, an Orthodox Jewish congregation and affiliated rabbis, sued the Village of Pomona challenging zoning and wetlands laws that restrict educational institutions, dormitories, and development, alleging violations of RLUIPA, the Fair Housing Act, and equal protection. The court granted summary judgment for defendants on free speech and state common law claims, granted plaintiffs' motion for sanctions due to spoliation of evidence, but denied all parties' summary judgment motions on the FHA and equal protection claims, finding genuine disputes of material fact regarding discriminatory intent.
key_cases_cited: Arlington Heights v. Metropolitan Housing Development Corp., 429 U.S. 252 (1977)
Village of Arlington Heights v. Metropolitan Housing Development Corp., 429 U.S. 252 (1977)
Tenafly Eruv Ass'n v. Borough of Tenafly, 309 F.3d 144 (3d Cir. 2002)
Cornell Univ. v. Bagnardi, 68 N.Y.2d 583 (1986)
Congregation Mischkots Lavier Yakov, Inc. v. Bd. of Tr. of Vill. of Airmont

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discriminatory enforcement of housing policies against Orthodox Hasidic Jewish community seeking to build rabbinical college with multi-family student housing
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found sufficient evidence of discriminatory purpose and effect regarding facially neutral zoning laws that prevented construction of rabbinical college with family housing; material fact disputes remain regarding whether laws were motivated by animus against religious group and whether they have disparate impact on housing availability for Orthodox Jewish community.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: First Amendment Free Exercise Clause, Free Speech Clause, Free Association Clause; RLUIPA substantial burden and equal terms provisions; New York Constitution Articles 1 §§ 3, 8, 9, 11; Berenson doctrine (New York common law); Equal Protection Clause Fourteenth Amendment
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied summary judgment on most constitutional and statutory claims (Free Exercise, RLUIPA substantial burden, Equal Protection, Berenson) due to material fact disputes regarding discriminatory purpose and effect; granted summary judgment only on Free Speech claim, finding construction of rabbinical college does not constitute protected speech.

source_file: 7234475_2015_Fair Housing Center of the Greater Palm Beaches, Inc. v. Sonoma Bay Community Homeowners Ass'n, Inc._flsd
case_name: Fair Housing Center of the Greater Palm Beaches, Inc. v. Sonoma Bay Community Homeowners Ass'n, Inc.
accommodation_description: Policies targeting families with children including report card requirements for applicants with minors, proper attire rules for minors, no-loitering rules, and curfew rules for residents under 18
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for the property management company on the report card requirement claim because Emanuel's purely ministerial role in processing applications was insufficient to establish personal liability, but denied summary judgment on the Proper Attire, Loitering, and Curfew Rules claims because genuine disputes of fact existed regarding whether Emanuel personally enforced those discriminatory policies.
brief_summary: The Fair Housing Center sued the HOA and its property management company alleging that policies requiring report cards for minor applicants and rules restricting children's attire, loitering, and curfew discriminated against families with children in violation of the FHA. The court granted summary judgment for the property management company on the report card requirement claim (finding insufficient personal involvement) but denied summary judgment on the other rules claims (finding genuine disputes of material fact regarding enforcement).
key_cases_cited: Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)
Sabal Palm Condos. of Pine Island Ridge Ass'n, Inc. v. Fischer, 6 F. Supp. 3d 1272 (S.D. Fla. 2014)
Dillon v. AFBIC Dev. Corp., 597 F.2d 556 (5th Cir. 1979)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Report Card Requirement — Rental Applications required prospective tenants to submit copies of report cards for persons under age 18
fha_claims.reasoning: Although the Report Card Requirement itself may violate the FHA as discrimination based on familial status, Emanuel and EMS cannot be held liable because Emanuel had no authority to grant or deny rental applications; her role was purely ministerial (checking for required documents and submitting applications to the screening committee). Under Sabal Palm and common law agency principles, an agent cannot be liable for a principal's discriminatory decision when the agent had no authority over that decision.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Proper Attire Rule — Rule requiring all residents to wear proper attire when walking on streets; no shirtless boys; girls must wear cover-up over bathing suit when walking to pool
fha_claims.reasoning: A genuine dispute of material fact exists regarding whether Emanuel personally enforced the Proper Attire Rule against the individual plaintiffs. Emanuel had authority to issue notices of violation and did so on multiple occasions; evidence shows she was present during at least one enforcement action and read rules to a plaintiff. A reasonable jury could conclude Emanuel personally committed or contributed to the FHA violation by enforcing the allegedly discriminatory rule.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Loitering Rule — Rule prohibiting loitering (congregating on streets) at any time
fha_claims.reasoning: A genuine dispute of material fact exists regarding whether Emanuel personally enforced the Loitering Rule against the individual plaintiffs. Emanuel had authority to issue notices of violation and did so on multiple occasions; evidence shows she discussed a loitering violation notice with plaintiff Leann Carr regarding her grandson. A reasonable jury could conclude Emanuel personally committed or contributed to the FHA violation by enforcing the allegedly discriminatory rule.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Curfew Rule — Rule requiring persons under age 18 to be in their home or on their patio after sunset
fha_claims.reasoning: A genuine dispute of material fact exists regarding whether Emanuel personally enforced the Curfew Rule against the individual plaintiffs. Emanuel had authority to issue notices of violation and did so on multiple occasions. A reasonable jury could conclude Emanuel personally committed or contributed to the FHA violation by enforcing the allegedly discriminatory rule based on familial status.

case_name: Johnson v. Macy
citation: No reporter citation provided (C.D. Cal. unpublished order)
accommodation_description: Landlord allegedly pressured disabled tenant to relocate to a first-floor unit and attempted to evict her because of her disability, making discriminatory statements about her medical conditions
key_holding: The court found plaintiff demonstrated a strong likelihood of success on her disability discrimination claims because defendant Macy's own written notes—mentioning Johnson's 'medical problems,' suggesting her life would be 'easier' in a downstairs apartment, and referencing her body 'not getting better'—constitute direct evidence of discriminatory intent to steer and evict a disabled tenant, and defendant's shifting justifications for rent increases and eviction notices raised serious questions of pretext.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Norma Johnson sued her private landlord Elaine Macy alleging disability discrimination under the FHA, claiming Macy repeatedly pressured her to relocate from her second-floor unit and issued discriminatory eviction notices because of her knee and neck injuries. The court granted Johnson's motion for preliminary injunction, finding she established a strong likelihood of success on the merits based on direct evidence in Macy's own notes showing discriminatory intent to evict a disabled tenant, and rejecting Macy's pretextual justifications.
key_cases_cited: Community Services Inc. v. Wind Gap Mun. Auth., 421 F.3d 170 (3d Cir. 2005)
Pack v. Fort Washington II, 689 F. Supp. 2d 1237 (E.D. Cal. 2009)
Fair Housing Congress v. Weber, 993 F. Supp. 1286 (C.D. Cal. 1997)
Gilligan v. Jamco Dev. Corp., 108 F.3d 246 (9th Cir. 1997)
Lowe v. City of Monrovia, 775 F.2d 998 (9th Cir. 1985)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of equal terms, conditions, and privileges of housing; steering to first-floor unit based on disability; rent increases and eviction based on disability status
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found strong likelihood of success on merits under FHA §§ 3604(f)(1) and (f)(2) based on direct evidence of discriminatory intent in defendant's written notes referencing plaintiff's disability, medical problems, and physical condition, combined with pattern of rent increases and eviction notices following plaintiff's refusal to relocate to first-floor unit and complaints to housing authorities.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Written statements indicating preference against tenants with disabilities; notes referencing plaintiff's medical problems, medical situation, and physical impairment
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found strong likelihood of success on FHA § 3604(c) claim (unlawful written statements indicating preference based on handicap) because defendant's written notes facially indicate a preference against plaintiff's tenancy based on her perceived physical impairment, and discriminatory intent is not required under this provision; notes clearly show defendant's preference for tenants without disabilities.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rent increases and eviction notices following plaintiff's complaints to Housing Rights Center and Department of Building and Safety
fha_claims.reasoning: Court noted that defendant did not present evidence to refute plaintiff's retaliation claim; temporal proximity between plaintiff's complaints to housing authorities and subsequent rent increases and eviction notices supports likelihood of success on retaliation claim under FHA § 3617.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA), Unruh Civil Rights Act, Disabled Persons Act, negligence, and retaliation claims under state law
fha_claims.reasoning: Court noted that standards under California FEHA and federal FHA are the same; plaintiff likely to succeed on state law claims under FEHA using same discriminatory conduct analysis as FHA claims; court did not separately analyze negligence or other state tort claims but granted preliminary injunction based on likelihood of success on discrimination and retaliation theories.

source_file: 7235405_2016_Louis ex rel. G.A.H. v. New York City Housing Authority_nysd
case_name: Mesline Louis ex rel. G.A.H. v. New York City Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Request that NYCHA provide meaningful assistance in locating suitable accessible housing and grant emergency transfer as reasonable accommodations under Section 8 tenant-based program
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' ADA Title II claims because Section 8 is a tenant-based voucher program that does not require NYCHA to provide modified housing or substantive additional benefits, and plaintiffs failed to adequately allege they were denied meaningful access to the program because of their disabilities.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Mesline Louis and her children sued NYCHA alleging it failed to provide reasonable accommodations in administering their Section 8 voucher, including modified housing and meaningful assistance in locating suitable accessible housing. The court granted NYCHA's motion to dismiss, holding that Section 8 is a tenant-based program providing vouchers for private housing that does not obligate NYCHA to supply modified housing, and plaintiffs failed to adequately allege they were denied meaningful access to the program because of their disabilities.
key_cases_cited: Alexander v. Choate, 469 U.S. 287 (1985)
Henrietta D. v. Bloomberg, 331 F.3d 261 (2d Cir. 2003)
Wright v. Giuliani, 230 F.3d 543 (2d Cir. 2000)
Taylor ex rel. Wazyluk v. Hous. Auth. of City of New Haven, 645 F.3d 152 (2d Cir. 2011)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Modification of common use portions of dwelling to accommodate Louis's and N.V.S.'s disabilities (mental illness, stroke, seizures, and lung disease requiring monitors and ventilators)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiffs conflated NYCHA's role as public housing operator with its role administering Section 8 tenant-based program. The Section 8 program provides vouchers and subsidies, not housing or modifications to private dwellings. Plaintiffs' demand for modified housing would substantively alter the benefits provided by the program and does not state a cognizable claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Meaningful assistance in obtaining accessible housing for a family with disabled members participating in Section 8 tenant-based program
fha_claims.reasoning: Although HUD regulations (24 C.F.R. § 8.28(a)) may require PHAs to provide certain assistance in locating accessible housing, plaintiffs failed to allege any factual connection between their inability to find housing and their disabilities. Plaintiffs alleged only that they lacked suitable housing and that NYCHA failed to provide meaningful assistance, without alleging that obstacles to locating housing resulted from disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodations under Title II ADA and Section 504 Rehabilitation Act in administration of Section 8 program
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs raised Section 504 and Fair Housing Act claims in opposition brief, which the court declined to consider as new claims. Even if considered, they fail for the same reason as Title II claims: plaintiffs did not sufficiently plead that they were denied meaningful access to the Section 8 program because of disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodations based on Louis's alleged disability (mental illness, stroke, seizures) under Title II ADA
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to adequately plead that Louis suffered from a qualifying disability under the ADA. Although the complaint alleged mental illness, stroke, and seizures, it did not allege that these conditions substantially limited any major life activities or major bodily functions during the relevant time period, as required by 42 U.S.C. § 12102.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: New York State Executive Law § 296.18(2) disability discrimination; negligence and breach of contract claims related to NYCHA's failure to grant emergency transfer when Louis was sexually harassed by landlord; breach of statutory duties under Housing Act and HUD regulations; breach of 1996 Voluntary Compliance Agreement with HUD; § 1983 procedural due process claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs abandoned non-FHA claims by failing to respond to NYCHA's arguments in opposition brief. Court found no private right of action under Housing Act or HUD regulations; 1996 VCA explicitly disclaims private right of action and applies only to NYCHA-owned housing, not Section 8 administration. Negligence and breach of contract claims were inadequately pleaded and time-barred. § 1983 due process claims lacked factual support and failed to identify protected liberty or property interest. Court declined supplemental jurisdiction over remaining state-law claims.

case_name: Pelot v. Criterion 3, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged retaliation for complaining about housing practices (failure to exclude sex offenders) that he believed endangered women; no disability accommodation was requested
key_holding: Plaintiff's complaints about defendant's failure to conduct background checks on sex offenders did not constitute protected activity under the Fair Housing Act because such complaints relate to habitability rather than availability of housing, and even if the reasonable belief standard applied, plaintiff's belief that such practices violated the FHA was unreasonable under Fifth Circuit precedent.
brief_summary: Justin Bradley Pelot sued Criterion 3, LLC and Gary Conner for evicting him and terminating his employment after he wrote a letter complaining that Criterion's failure to conduct background checks on sex offenders endangered female residents at The Pointe apartments. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, holding that plaintiff's retaliation claim under § 3617 failed because his complaints related to habitability rather than availability of housing and, under Fifth Circuit precedent, his belief that such practices violated the Fair Housing Act was not reasonable.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Cox v. City of Dallas, Tex., 430 F.3d 734 (5th Cir. 2005)
Hidden Village, LLC v. City of Lakewood, Ohio, 734 F.3d 519 (6th Cir. 2013)
McZeal v. Ocwen Financial Corp., 252 F.3d 1355 (5th Cir. 2001)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege protected activity under § 3617. His complaints about failure to conduct background checks and the presence of sex offenders relate to habitability, not availability of housing, and thus do not constitute a cognizable Fair Housing Act violation under settled Fifth Circuit law. Even under a 'reasonable belief' standard, no reasonable person could believe that such habitability concerns violate the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: State law claims for eviction and termination
fha_claims.reasoning: The opinion addresses only the FHA retaliation claim and grants the motion to dismiss on that claim. State law claims are mentioned but not substantively analyzed or ruled upon in this opinion.

case_name: West v. DJ Mortgage, LLC
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; case involves sexual harassment by property manager Gene Andrews who grabbed plaintiff's genitals, demanded nude photos, and conditioned repairs on sexual favors.
key_holding: The court denied the motion to dismiss, finding that West sufficiently alleged hostile housing environment sexual harassment, quid pro quo sexual harassment, and unlawful interference under the FHA, where the property manager grabbed her genitals, demanded nude photos in exchange for repairs, and the landlord failed to address complaints before evicting her.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Kayla West, a single mother of four, sued DJ Mortgage LLC and its property manager Gene Andrews for sexual harassment under the FHA, alleging Andrews grabbed her genitals when she signed her lease, demanded nude photos in exchange for repairs, and conditioned housing benefits on sexual favors. The court denied defendant's motion to dismiss, finding West adequately pleaded hostile housing environment sexual harassment, quid pro quo harassment, and unlawful interference claims.
key_cases_cited: Mendoza v. Borden, Inc., 195 F.3d 1238 (11th Cir. 1999)
Tagliaferri v. Winter Park Hous. Auth., 486 Fed. Appx. 771 (11th Cir. 2012)
Quigley v. Winter, 598 F.3d 938 (8th Cir. 2010)
Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009)
Bell Atlantic v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss, finding that plaintiff plausibly alleged hostile housing environment sexual harassment under FHA § 3604(b) by alleging unwelcome sexual advances, grabbing of genitals, and pattern of conduct severe and pervasive enough to alter terms and conditions of tenancy.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss, finding that plaintiff plausibly alleged quid pro quo sexual harassment under FHA § 3604(b) by alleging that housing benefits (repairs) were implicitly conditioned on sexual favors, with pattern of delayed or failed repairs following plaintiff's rejection of sexual advances.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss, finding that plaintiff plausibly alleged interference and retaliation under FHA § 3617 by alleging that defendant failed to respond to complaints about sexual harassment, continued to direct harasser to contact plaintiff, failed to make repairs after plaintiff complained, and evicted plaintiff in retaliation for withholding rent due to uninhabitable conditions caused by harassment-related repair failures.

case_name: Schwarz v. Villages Charter School, Inc.
accommodation_description: Thirty-two deaf residents of The Villages retirement community requested sign language interpreters as auxiliary aids to access recreational and educational programs offered by the Districts and Charter School.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for the Districts on all claims, finding they were not 'dwellings' under the FHA and lacked public accommodation status; the court denied the Charter School's motion regarding whether its Deaf Network Services program constitutes a reasonable accommodation, finding genuine issues of material fact exist.
brief_summary: Thirty-two deaf residents of The Villages retirement community sued the Village Center and Sumter Landing Community Development Districts and The Villages Charter School, Inc. under the ADA, FHA, and Rehabilitation Act, alleging failure to provide sign language interpreters for recreational and educational programs. The court granted summary judgment for the Districts on all claims, finding they were not dwellings under the FHA and lacked public accommodation status; the court denied the Charter School's summary judgment motion on the reasonable accommodation claim regarding its Deaf Network Services program, finding genuine disputes of material fact.
key_cases_cited: Chevron U.S.A. Inc. v. Natural Res. Defense Council Inc.
Onishea v. Hopper
Edison v. Douberly

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Sign language interpreters for Resident Lifestyle Group (RLG) activities and events held at District recreation facilities
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that RLG activities are not services, programs, or activities of the Districts themselves because the Districts do not control the content or presentation of RLG programs, receive no income from them, and the RLGs are operated independently by private residents. The Districts' involvement is limited to facilitating facility use and ensuring compliance with facility guidelines. Therefore, the Districts cannot be held liable under the FHA for the RLGs' alleged failure to provide sign language interpreters, as the RLGs are not instrumentalities of the Districts and participation in them is not a service connected to the dwelling within the meaning of the FHA.

source_file: 7236712_2016_Lowman v. Platinum Property Management Services, Inc._gand
case_name: Lowman v. Platinum Property Management Services, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges defendant denied his rental application and imposed different qualification standards based on his race.
key_holding: The court denied defendant's motion to dismiss, finding that plaintiff sufficiently alleged his application was rejected (satisfying the third element of a prima facie FHA case) and that subsequent approval of the application does not negate a prior denial for purposes of establishing a violation.
brief_summary: Eleanor Lowman, an African American male, sued Platinum Property Management Services alleging the company denied his rental application and subjected him to different qualification standards because of his race. The court denied defendant's motion to dismiss, finding plaintiff sufficiently pled a prima facie case under the Fair Housing Act despite defendant's argument that the subsequent approval of the application negated any prior denial.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
U.S. Dep't of Hous. & Urban Dev. v. Blackwell

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of rental application based on race
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff plausibly alleged that his rental application was rejected based on race under the prima facie framework of § 3604(a). The subsequent approval of the application does not negate the prior discriminatory denial, and Plaintiff alleged injury (forced to rent elsewhere at higher rate). Complaint survives motion to dismiss under Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Imposition of different qualification standards and criteria based on race (differing financial criteria, criminal background investigation)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff plausibly alleged that Defendant imposed different qualification criteria and standards based on race, which constitutes a violation of § 3604(a) as enumerated in 24 C.F.R. § 100.60(b)(4). The regulation provides a list of discriminatory actions that give rise to a § 3604(a) violation. Complaint survives motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1982 (racial discrimination in property rights); Georgia Fair Housing Act, O.C.G.A. § 8-3-200 et seq.
fha_claims.reasoning: Claims under § 1982 and Georgia FHA are interpreted under the same prima facie standard as the Federal FHA. Because Plaintiff survived dismissal on the Federal FHA claims, the parallel state and federal statutory claims must also survive. Motion to dismiss denied as to all claims.

case_name: United States v. Noble Homes, Inc.
accommodation_description: This is a design-and-construction accessibility case; no individual accommodation request is at issue. The United States alleges defendants failed to design and construct covered multifamily dwellings with accessible features including accessible entrances, accessible routes, reinforcements for grab bars, and usable kitchens and bathrooms for wheelchair users.
key_holding: Both parties' motions for summary judgment are denied because genuine issues of material fact exist as to whether deviations from HUD's safe harbor guidelines resulted in violations of the FHA's design and construction requirements; the government's expert established deviations from safe harbors, but defendants' experts provided competing testimony that the units are accessible, creating jury questions.
brief_summary: The United States sued Noble Homes, Inc., Guardian Property Management, and Dean Windham alleging that the defendants failed to design and construct 13 four-unit buildings at Windham Bridge and Hampton Court in compliance with the FHA's design and construction requirements under § 3604(f)(3)(C), including inaccessible building entrances, common areas, and units lacking adaptive design features for wheelchair users. The court denied both parties' summary judgment motions because genuine issues of material fact remain as to whether deviations from HUD's accessibility guidelines constituted FHA violations, given competing expert testimony.
key_cases_cited: Chevron U.S.A., Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc., 467 U.S. 837 (1984)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986)
Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242 (1986)
United States v. JPI Const., L.P., 2011 WL 6963160 (N.D. Tex. 2011)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible building entrances on accessible routes; accessible public and common use portions; accessible routes into and through dwellings; reinforcements in bathroom walls for grab bars; usable kitchens and bathrooms for wheelchair users; accessible mailboxes; door widths sufficient for wheelchairs; door thresholds at appropriate heights; adequate clear floor space in kitchens and bathrooms
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found genuine issues of material fact regarding whether deviations from HUD Guidelines constituted FHA violations. Although defendants' experts testified all properties were accessible, the court determined the question of whether alleged barriers created a pattern or practice of discrimination was ordinarily a question of fact for the jury, precluding summary judgment for either party.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Pattern or practice of resistance to full enjoyment of FHA rights; denial to a group of persons of rights granted by the FHA raising an issue of general public importance
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied summary judgment on the pattern or practice claim because genuine issues of material fact remained regarding whether the alleged accessibility barriers, even if they deviated from HUD Guidelines, constituted unlawful discrimination under the FHA, given that alternative means of achieving compliance existed and defendants presented expert testimony of accessibility.

case_name: Logan v. Matveevskii
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested transfer from third-floor to first-floor apartment as reasonable accommodation for heart condition and mobility disability.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA reasonable accommodation claims because he failed to plausibly allege he was disabled within the meaning of the FHA, that defendants knew of his disability, and that a reasonable accommodation was necessary to afford him an equal opportunity to use and enjoy his dwelling.
brief_summary: Thomas Logan, a disabled Black tenant of the Tuckahoe Housing Authority, sued the housing authority and individual defendants alleging they violated the Fair Housing Act by failing to reasonably accommodate his disability through transfer to a first-floor apartment and by discriminating against him based on race and disability. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss the Third Amended Complaint with prejudice, finding the complaint failed to state plausible FHA claims because plaintiff's disability allegations were conclusory, he did not adequately plead discriminatory intent, and many claims were time-barred.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Sunrise Detox V, LLC v. City of White Plains

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request for transfer to a first-floor or lower-level apartment to accommodate plaintiff's heart condition and mobility difficulties (walking up and down three flights of stairs)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege constructive denial of reasonable accommodation. Although plaintiff alleged a 2.5-year delay from August 2008 email to March 2011 offer, courts require more than silence to establish constructive denial; plaintiff offered no factual basis to conclude defendants acted with discriminatory intent or bad faith in the delay, only conclusory allegations that the request was 'ignored.'

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to establish disparate treatment based on disability. Plaintiff provided only conclusory allegations of discrimination without factual support that animus against the disabled was a significant factor in defendants' actions. The complaint lacked plausible factual allegations connecting any adverse action to plaintiff's disability status.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged racial discrimination based on defendant Matveevskii's reference to plaintiff having a 'gang' of people coming after her at a tenants meeting
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's racial discrimination claim failed under Iqbal/Twombly. A single reference to 'gang' at a meeting, even if it could have racial connotations, is insufficient to establish discriminatory animus as a significant factor. The word 'gang' has innocuous meanings and plaintiff provided no other factual support for racial animus. Remaining allegations were pure legal conclusions unsupported by facts.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Violations of Architectural Barriers Act (42 U.S.C. §§ 4151-57), Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, ADA Title II, HUD regulations, state law claims (negligence, breach of contract, interference with tenant rights, improper lease termination, improper rent calculations, intentional infliction of emotional distress, violations of Real Property Law and Apartment Law)
fha_claims.reasoning: ABA claim dismissed because plaintiff did not exhaust administrative remedies with the Architectural and Transportation Barriers Compliance Board (ATBCB); the ABA provides no private right of action without first presenting claims to the ATBCB. Rehabilitation Act disparate treatment claim dismissed because it requires showing defendants denied benefits 'solely' because of disability, and plaintiff failed to allege this higher standard. Remaining state law claims dismissed for lack of federal question jurisdiction after federal claims were dismissed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rent overcharge claims based on alleged miscalculation of rent, failure to allow medical deductions, and failure to provide rent calculation breakdowns
fha_claims.reasoning: Rent overcharge claims barred by res judicata doctrine. Plaintiff's rent claims arose from the same transaction or series of transactions as a prior New York State Supreme Court judgment (Index No. 50208/2014) that dismissed plaintiff's rent overcharge claim on the merits pursuant to CPLR 3211(a)(1). Under New York's transactional approach to res judicata, all claims arising from the same transaction are barred even if based on different theories.

source_file: 7237438_2016_Step by Step, Inc. v. City of Ogdensburg_nynd
case_name: Step by Step, Inc. v. City of Ogdensburg
accommodation_description: Step by Step, Inc. sought City approval to rezone property from single-family residential to Planned Development District to establish supportive housing, respite housing, and mental health services for individuals with mental illness.
key_holding: The court found plaintiff demonstrated substantial likelihood of success on its intentional discrimination claim because the City Council failed to articulate any legitimate non-discriminatory reasons for denying the PDD application, while community opposition was based on impermissible stereotypes about mentally ill individuals, and the City improperly ceded decision-making authority to a biased public.
brief_summary: Step by Step, Inc., a not-for-profit mental health provider, sued the City of Ogdensburg, New York alleging the City's denial of its application to rezone property for a supportive housing facility for mentally ill individuals violated the Fair Housing Act. The court granted plaintiff's motion for preliminary injunction, finding plaintiff showed substantial likelihood of success on its intentional discrimination claim because the City Council denied the application without articulating legitimate reasons while community opposition was based on impermissible stereotypes about the mentally ill.
key_cases_cited: Innovative Health Systems, Inc. v. City of White Plains
Forest City Daly Hous., Inc. v. Town of N. Hempstead
Tsombanidis v. West Haven Fire Dept.
Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Approval of Planned Development District (PDD) application to establish supportive housing, respite/hospital diversion housing, and mental health services for individuals with mental illness
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework and found plaintiff established prima facie case of intentional discrimination based on sequence of events, strong community opposition rooted in stereotypes about mental illness, City Council's failure to articulate any non-discriminatory rationale for denial, and departure from normal procedures. City failed to provide legitimate non-discriminatory reason, so discriminatory animus must have been significant factor in denial.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Approval of PDD application; plaintiff challenged ARD law as facially neutral but disproportionately impacting mentally ill individuals seeking housing
fha_claims.disposition: Preliminary Injunction Motion - Disparate Impact Claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff failed to establish substantial likelihood of success on disparate impact claim because plaintiff provided no quantitative or qualitative evidence of disproportionate impact on mentally ill persons; plaintiff merely asserted that if it cannot use the Site, there must be disparate impact, which is insufficient at this stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) Title II claim for discrimination in municipal zoning decisions
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied same McDonnell Douglas disparate treatment framework under ADA § 12132 as applied to FHA claims; plaintiff established substantial likelihood of success on intentional discrimination theory under ADA based on same factual record and reasoning as FHA disparate treatment claim.

source_file: 7237902_2015_County of Cook v. Bank of America Corp._ilnd
case_name: County of Cook v. Bank of America Corp.
accommodation_description: Not applicable - this is a reverse redlining/discriminatory lending case, not a reasonable accommodation case under § 3604(f)(3)(B)
key_holding: Cook County adequately alleged Article III standing to sue for reverse redlining under the FHA based on injuries to its tax base and property tax revenues; the complaint states plausible disparate treatment and disparate impact claims under §§ 3604(a)-(c) and 3605.
brief_summary: Cook County sued Bank of America alleging the bank engaged in reverse redlining by targeting African American and Hispanic borrowers with discriminatory loan terms, causing foreclosures that injured the County's tax base and property tax revenues. The court denied Bank of America's motion to dismiss, holding that the County had Article III standing, its claims fell within the FHA's zone of interests, the claims were not time-barred under the continuing violation doctrine, and the complaint stated plausible disparate treatment and disparate impact claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Swanson v. Citibank, N.A.
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman
Texas Dept. of Housing and Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The County adequately alleged a disparate treatment claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3605(a) by identifying the type of discrimination (reverse redlining), the defendants, and the timeframe. The court found the allegations sufficient to state a plausible claim under Twombly/Iqbal and denied the motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that disparate impact claims are cognizable under the FHA under binding Seventh Circuit precedent, and the County adequately alleged specific practices (discretionary pricing, credit approval decisions, appraisal practices) that had disparate impact on minority borrowers. Whether the statistics establish a prima facie case is not decided at the pleading stage.

case_name: Castellano v. Access Premier Realty, Inc.
accommodation_description: Request to keep a house cat as an emotional support animal to alleviate anxiety, depression, panic attacks, and PTSD
key_holding: The court found that defendants violated § 3604(f)(3)(B) by refusing to permit plaintiff to keep an emotional support animal despite receiving adequate medical documentation establishing her disability-related need, and that defendants' issuance of eviction notices in response to her accommodation request also violated § 3617.
brief_summary: LaVonna Castellano and fair housing organization Project Sentinel sued Access Premier Realty and related defendants after Castellano was denied permission to keep her cat as an emotional support animal for her mental health disabilities despite providing medical documentation. The court granted plaintiffs' motion for partial summary judgment, finding defendants violated the Fair Housing Act by refusing the reasonable accommodation and by issuing eviction notices that interfered with her FHA rights.
key_cases_cited: Dubois v. Ass'n of Apartment Owners of 2987 Kalakaua, 453 F.3d 1175 (9th Cir. 2006)
Giebeler v. M & B Associates, 343 F.3d 1143 (9th Cir. 2003)
Smith v. Powdrill, 2013 WL 5786586 (C.D. Cal. Oct. 28, 2013)
Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)
United States v. California Mobile Home Park Mgmt. Co., 29 F.3d 1413 (9th Cir. 1994)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exception to no-pets policy to allow plaintiff to keep an emotional support cat (Mr. Munchkin) as a reasonable accommodation for mental health disabilities including anxiety, depression, panic attacks, psychotic disorder, and PTSD
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied the five-element Dubois test and found all elements satisfied: (1) plaintiff has FHA-qualifying handicap (mental and physical impairments substantially limiting major life activities); (2) defendants knew or should have known of disability (multiple letters and rental application disclosed SSI benefits); (3) accommodation was necessary (uncontroverted evidence that emotional support animal alleviated anxiety, depression, and stress, which reduced symptoms of other impairments); (4) accommodation was reasonable (no fundamental alteration or undue burden; defendants had previously granted similar accommodations; cat was well-behaved and plaintiff offered pet deposit); (5) defendants refused accommodation (despite receiving adequate medical documentation, defendants issued cure-or-quit notice and termination notice, and explicitly denied the request). Court applied HUD Notice FHEO-2013-01 with deference and found defendants' concerns about fleas and safety were speculative and not based on individualized assessment of the specific animal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Defendants interfered with plaintiff's right to request and obtain a reasonable accommodation by issuing cure-or-quit and termination notices in response to accommodation requests
fha_claims.reasoning: Under 42 U.S.C. § 3617, defendants violated the FHA by interfering with plaintiff's exercise of her right to obtain a reasonable accommodation. The court found that defendants' issuance of a cure-or-quit notice and termination notice in response to plaintiff's accommodation requests constituted meddling with and hampering her exercise of FHA rights. The approach taken would give a person in plaintiff's position pause in seeking to enforce her right to accommodation. Defendants did not contest these facts, and plaintiff's departure from the apartment due to fear of eviction demonstrated the chilling effect of defendants' conduct.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Vicarious liability of property owner (Defendant Addison) for violations of § 3604(f) and § 3617 committed by her agents (APM, Akulow, Valenzuela)
fha_claims.reasoning: Under Meyer v. Holley, property owners may be vicariously liable for FHA violations committed by their agents or property managers. Defendants admitted that APM, Akulow, and Valenzuela acted as agents of Defendant Addison and that Addison directly paid Valenzuela. Defendants presented no evidence suggesting vicarious liability was inappropriate and failed to respond to plaintiff's vicarious liability arguments. Court found Addison vicariously liable for the § 3604(f) and § 3617 violations.

source_file: 7238253_2016_Dyer v. Maryland State Board of Education_mdd

case_name: Mehta v. Village of Bolingbrook
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; claim concerns police harassment, selective enforcement, and failure to investigate crimes based on religion and national origin.
key_holding: The court denied summary judgment for defendants, finding plaintiffs adduced sufficient evidence from which a jury could reasonably conclude police acted with discriminatory intent based on religion and national origin when stopping, searching, and harassing the Mehtas over twenty years.
brief_summary: Kirti Mehta and his four children sued the Village of Bolingbrook and its police officers, alleging that police systematically discriminated against them on the basis of religion (Hindu) and national origin (Indian) through racially motivated traffic stops, harassment, use of ethnic slurs, and inadequate investigation of crimes against them. The court denied defendants' motion for summary judgment, finding plaintiffs presented sufficient direct and circumstantial evidence—including officer testimony, use of ethnic slurs, and pretextual explanations—to permit a reasonable jury to find discriminatory purpose under the Equal Protection Clause and interference with FHA rights under § 3617.
key_cases_cited: East-Miller v. Lake Cty. Highway Dep't, 421 F.3d 558 (7th Cir. 2005)
Chavez v. Ill. State Police, 251 F.3d 612 (7th Cir. 2001)
McCleskey v. Kemp, 481 U.S. 279 (1987)
Rossi v. City of Chicago, 790 F.3d 729 (7th Cir. 2015)
Monell v. Dept. of Social Services, 436 U.S. 658 (1978)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Right to enjoy dwelling free from interference, coercion, intimidation, and threats based on religion and national origin; alleged pattern of police harassment, selective enforcement, and intimidation designed to force family to abandon property
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether defendants acted with discriminatory intent to interfere with plaintiffs' FHA-protected right to enjoy their dwelling. Evidence of repeated ethnic slurs, selective enforcement, pattern of harassment over 20 years, and explicit statements that police wanted family to leave Bolingbrook supported inference that conduct was frequent and severe enough to constitute interference under § 3617.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 equal protection claim; 42 U.S.C. § 1982 property rights claim; alleged discriminatory denial of police services, selective enforcement of traffic and municipal regulations, and unlawful stops and seizures based on religion and national origin
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found sufficient evidence of discriminatory intent and effect to survive summary judgment on equal protection and § 1982 claims. Statistical evidence of disparate traffic stops, testimony of ethnic slurs and derogatory language, pattern of selective enforcement, and evidence of pretextual explanations for police conduct supported inference that defendants acted with discriminatory purpose and that selective withdrawal of police protection violated clearly established constitutional rights.

case_name: Handy v. City of New Rochelle
accommodation_description: Plaintiff allegedly requested to be accommodated with a one-bedroom apartment following termination of her Section 8 benefits after her disabled mother's death.
key_holding: Plaintiff's reasonable accommodation claim fails because she presented no evidence that she requested any accommodation of her disability, and while defendants knew or should have known of her disability, they never refused to afford her an accommodation.
brief_summary: Dale Handy sued the City of New Rochelle Section 8 Program and its officials after her housing benefits were terminated for allegedly not residing in her apartment; the court granted summary judgment for defendants, finding the hearing officer's decision was supported by substantial evidence and that Handy failed to establish she requested a reasonable accommodation for her documented mental disability (Major Depressive Disorder and Panic Disorder).
key_cases_cited: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Logan v. Matveevskii, 57 F. Supp. 3d 234 (S.D.N.Y. 2014)
Tsombanidis v. W. Haven Fire Dep't, 352 F.3d 565 (2d Cir. 2003)
Goldberg v. Kelly, 397 U.S. 254 (1970)
Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242 (1986)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff established prima facie case of discrimination (member of protected class, sought housing, was rejected, housing remained available), but defendants provided legitimate nondiscriminatory reason for termination: plaintiff violated Section 8 regulations by not living in the apartment, as supported by substantial evidence (minimal utility usage, vacant apartment conditions, address discrepancies). Plaintiff failed to demonstrate disability was real reason for termination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested accommodation to remain in two-bedroom apartment or transfer to one-bedroom apartment to accommodate her mental disability (Major Depressive Disorder, Panic Disorder)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish prima facie reasonable accommodation claim because she never requested any accommodation of her disability. Although defendants knew or should have known of her disability, plaintiff did not request a one-bedroom apartment as an accommodation for her mental disability; she merely alleged she needed to move to a one-bedroom apartment after her mother's death. Without a request for accommodation, defendants could not refuse to provide one, and plaintiff incurred no liability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fourth Amendment unreasonable search and seizure claim; Due Process claim under Fourteenth Amendment (Goldberg v. Kelly procedural safeguards for termination of public benefits)
fha_claims.reasoning: Fourth Amendment: Plaintiff consented to search of apartment; consent was voluntary and extended to closets, drawers, and refrigerator as areas that would contain evidence of residency. Due Process: Hearing officer's determination that plaintiff did not live in apartment was supported by substantial evidence (minimal utility usage, vacant conditions, address discrepancies), and plaintiff was afforded proper Goldberg procedural safeguards including notice, pre-termination hearing, representation by counsel, and impartial decisionmaker.

case_name: Thurmond v. Bowman
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges defendant refused to show property at 11 Union Street in Geneva, NY because she had two minor children, constituting familial status discrimination under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(a)
key_holding: Magistrate Judge correctly determined that plaintiff did not engage in sanctionable spoliation of Facebook evidence, as posts were merely hidden by privacy settings rather than deleted, and defendants failed to demonstrate relevance of any deleted posts; motion for preliminary injunction denied for failure to satisfy Rule 65 standard.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Amayla Thurmond sued defendants Wilfred Toombs and Margaret Bowman alleging they violated the Fair Housing Act by refusing to show her rental property because she had minor children. This decision addressed defendants' motions for sanctions based on alleged spoliation of plaintiff's Facebook posts and for a preliminary injunction preventing plaintiff from accessing social media during litigation. The court adopted the Magistrate Judge's Report and Recommendation, denying sanctions because plaintiff's Facebook posts were hidden by privacy settings rather than deleted, and defendants failed to demonstrate the deleted posts were relevant.
key_cases_cited: Residential Funding Corp. v. DeGeorge Fin. Corp., 306 F.3d 99 (2d Cir. 2002)
Arista Records LLC v. Usenet.com, Inc., 608 F. Supp. 2d 409 (S.D.N.Y. 2009)
Zubulake v. UBS Warburg LLC, 220 F.R.D. 212 (S.D.N.Y. 2003)
Toussie v. Cty. of Suffolk, 2007 WL 4565160 (E.D.N.Y. 2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.disposition: Motion for Sanctions and Preliminary Injunction
fha_claims.reasoning: The opinion addresses only procedural motions for sanctions and preliminary injunction related to alleged spoliation of Facebook evidence. The underlying FHA claim for disparate treatment based on familial status (refusal to show property due to plaintiff having two minor children) remains pending; the court did not reach the merits of the FHA claim itself.

source_file: 7239557_2016_Poole v. Housing Authority for the Town of Vinton_lawd
case_name: Poole v. Housing Authority for the Town of Vinton
accommodation_description: Request for Ken Bielecki to serve as a live-in aide to assist with daily living activities (showering, bathroom use, cleaning, getting in/out of bed) due to osteoarthritis-related mobility limitations
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for Poole on Housing Act pretermination grievance procedure violations (§ 1437d(k) and (l)) but denied summary judgment on the FHA reasonable accommodation claim because genuine disputes of material fact exist regarding when Poole notified VHA of her need for a live-in aide; additionally, the court found Section 3(A) of the lease contains facially ambiguous language that has the effect of substantially impairing disabled persons' access to public housing by failing to clearly explain their right to live-in aides.
brief_summary: Susan Poole, a tenant with osteoarthritis and bipolar disorder, sued the Housing Authority for the Town of Vinton and its Executive Director alleging they violated the Fair Housing Act, ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and Housing Act by failing to allow her to have a live-in aide to assist with disability-related daily living needs and by initiating eviction proceedings without proper pretermination grievance procedures. The court granted summary judgment for Poole on the Housing Act claims (violations of § 1437d(k) and (l) procedural requirements) and found the lease's Section 3(A) facially ambiguous regarding disabled persons' rights to live-in aides, but denied summary judgment on the FHA reasonable accommodation claim due to genuine factual disputes about when Poole notified VHA of her need for assistance.
key_cases_cited: Bennett-Nelson v. Louisiana Bd. of Regents, 431 F.3d 448 (5th Cir. 2005)
Neely v. PSEG Texas, Ltd. P'ship, 735 F.3d 242 (5th Cir. 2013)
Van Velzor v. City of Burleson, 43 F. Supp. 3d 746 (N.D. Tex. 2014)
Groome Res. Ltd., L.L.C. v. Parish of Jefferson, 234 F.3d 192 (5th Cir. 2000)
eBay Inc. v. MercExchange, L.L.C., 547 U.S. 388 (2006)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested permission for Ken Bielecki to serve as a live-in aide to assist with activities of daily living due to plaintiff's osteoarthritis and mobility limitations requiring wheelchair use.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found the accommodation reasonable and imposed no undue financial or administrative burdens, but denied summary judgment because genuine dispute exists as to when plaintiff notified VHA of the need for a live-in aide, which affects whether VHA had knowledge of the disability and accommodation need.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Violations of 42 U.S.C. § 1437d(k) and (l) (Housing Act pretermination grievance procedures); Fourteenth Amendment due process; Americans with Disabilities Act Title II; Rehabilitation Act § 504; meaningful access claims.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted summary judgment on Housing Act § 1437d(k) and (l) claims, finding unequivocal evidence that lease was terminated in violation of statutory requirements: notice was insufficient (less than 30 days required) and no pretermination grievance procedures were afforded. Court denied summary judgment on due process and ADA/Rehabilitation Act failure-to-accommodate claims due to genuine factual disputes.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Lease Section 3(A) contains language that singles out tenants with disabilities for eviction threat if they cannot live independently and cannot arrange for someone to aid them, creating discriminatory effect under ADA Title II and Rehabilitation Act § 504.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found lease language in Section 3(A) ambiguous and discriminatory under 28 C.F.R. § 35.130(b)(3)(ii), as it has the effect of substantially impairing disabled persons' ability to access and maintain public housing by obfuscating their rights to live-in aides and creating fear of eviction. The ambiguity violated federal law despite no evidence of purposeful intent to mislead.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) violations: failure to provide proper disclosure of debt validation rights and demanding payment before expiration of 30-day validation window
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff lacked Article III standing because he failed to allege a concrete and particularized injury resulting from alleged FDCPA violations. The court found bare procedural violations of the FDCPA's disclosure requirements, without more, do not constitute injury in fact under Spokeo v. Robins, and plaintiff never intended to dispute the debt or exercise the rights he claimed were violated.

case_name: Thurmond v. Bowman
accommodation_description: No accommodation request was made; this case involves intentional discrimination based on familial status when defendant refused to rent to plaintiff because she had two minor children.
key_holding: The court found direct evidence of familial status discrimination where defendant Toombs admitted stating he would not rent to plaintiff because of her two small children, and this statement violated both § 3604(a) (making dwelling unavailable) and § 3604(c) (discriminatory statement) regardless of defendant's claimed motivations.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Amayla Thurmond sued landlords Wilfred Toombs and Margaret Bowman alleging familial status discrimination when Toombs refused to rent an apartment to her after learning she had two minor children.
