fha_claims.accommodation_description: First Amendment petition rights, age discrimination (42 U.S.C. § 6102), conspiracy under 42 U.S.C. § 1985(3), § 1986, § 1983, 18 U.S.C. §§ 241, 242, torture statute (18 U.S.C. § 2340B), RICO (18 U.S.C.), D.C. common law claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Conspiracy claims based on vague and conclusory allegations; criminal causes of action fail as matter of law (no private right of action under criminal statutes, no judicially cognizable interest in prosecution, § 1983 applies only to state actors, torture statute precludes civil remedy); age discrimination claim lacks plausible factual support; supplemental jurisdiction declined over D.C. and common law claims.

case_name: Horne v. Harbour Portfolio VI, LP
accommodation_description: Reverse redlining: predatory contract-for-deed financing allegedly targeting African-American homebuyers with abusive credit terms including 9.9-10% interest rates and forfeiture clauses.
key_holding: The court denied dismissal of plaintiffs' FHA claims, finding plaintiffs adequately alleged both intentional discrimination (reverse redlining targeting African-Americans) and disparate impact under the Inclusive Communities framework, surviving the motion to dismiss stage.
brief_summary: African-American plaintiffs sued Harbour Portfolio VI and VII, LP and related entities alleging reverse redlining—predatory contract-for-deed financing that targeted African-American communities with unfair terms including excessive interest rates and forfeiture clauses. The court denied the defendants' motion to dismiss the Fair Housing Act claims, finding plaintiffs sufficiently alleged both intentional discrimination through targeted marketing and disparate impact through statistical evidence of lending patterns in majority African-American census tracts.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dept. of Housing & Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 135 S. Ct. 2507 (2015)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Steed v. EverHome Mortg. Co., 308 Fed. Appx. 364 (11th Cir. 2009)
Hargraves v. Capital City Mortg. Corp., 140 F. Supp. 2d 7 (D.D.C. 2000)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs adequately pleaded intentional targeting of African-Americans through reverse redlining allegations (targeting via yard signs and word-of-mouth in predominantly African-American neighborhoods), satisfying Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard. Court found direct evidence of intentional targeting on basis of race sufficient to state claim without requiring comparative treatment showing.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs pleaded sufficient facts to invoke disparate impact theory under Texas Department of Housing & Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project: (1) statistically imbalanced lending patterns (71.37% African-American in Fannie Mae tracts vs. 48.37% in other tracts); (2) facially neutral policies (purchasing only from Fannie Mae, advertising via yard signs and word-of-mouth); (3) arbitrariness of policy (Fannie Mae properties were less than one-quarter of available foreclosures); and (4) causal connection (policy of purchasing in high-minority areas caused disproportionate impact on African-American borrowers).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA), Georgia Fair Housing Act, Truth in Lending Act (TILA), Georgia Fair Business Practices Act (FBPA), Unfair and Deceptive Practices Towards the Elderly Act (UDPTEA), Georgia Residential Mortgage Act (GRMA), equitable mortgage, declaratory judgment, unjust enrichment, breach of contract, breach of implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, negligence, malicious eviction, Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act (RESPA)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied Iqbal/Twombly standard to non-FHA claims. ECOA claims survived (same reverse redlining allegations as FHA); Georgia FHA survived (interpreted under same standard as federal FHA); TILA appraisal and escrow claims dismissed as time-barred (one-year limitations period), ability to repay claim survived (three-year period); FBPA and UDPTEA claims survived (contracts for deed distinguished from mortgages, disability adequately alleged for Johnson and Butts); GRMA claim survived (private cause of action recognized); equitable mortgage and declaratory judgment claims survived in part (tender requirement not applicable where plaintiffs seek equitable mortgage rather than cancellation); unjust enrichment survived (pled in alternative to breach of contract where contract validity disputed); breach of contract and implied covenant survived; negligence survived; malicious eviction dismissed (barred by res judicata and compulsory counterclaim waiver); RESPA and negligence claims against NAA limited by statute of limitations; equitable mortgage and declaratory judgment against NAA dismissed (NAA had no ownership interest); unjust enrichment against NAA survived in part (limited to property taxes); breach of contract against NAA dismissed (NAA not party to CFD).

case_name: Evans v. ForKids, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a wheelchair-bound disabled mother, requested installation of a wheelchair ramp and grab bars in her bathroom and hallway to access her elevated unit.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for defendant, finding no constructive denial of reasonable accommodation or modification because defendant immediately began investigating solutions, reasonably needed time to obtain multiple contractor quotes and HUD funding approval for the costly ramp, and within approximately six weeks had arranged either a ramp installation or an accessible three-bedroom unit for plaintiff—during which time plaintiff herself repeatedly suggested she was leaving the program.
brief_summary: Veda Evans, a disabled mother in ForKids, Inc.'s permanent supportive housing program, sued the nonprofit housing provider alleging it constructively denied her reasonable accommodation and modification requests when it failed to promptly install a wheelchair ramp and grab bars after she became wheelchair-bound in January 2016. The court granted summary judgment for defendant, finding that defendant immediately began investigating solutions, reasonably sought multiple contractor quotes and HUD funding approval for the approximately $8,000 ramp, and within six weeks arranged either structural modifications or an accessible three-bedroom unit for plaintiff, while plaintiff herself repeatedly suggested she was leaving the program.
key_cases_cited: Scoggins v. Lee's Crossing Homeowners Ass'n, 718 F.3d 262 (4th Cir. 2013)
Anderson v. Liberty Lobby Inc., 477 U.S. 242 (1986)
Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986)
Thomas v. The Salvation Army S. Territory, 841 F.3d 632 (4th Cir. 2016)
Prindable v. Association of Apartment Owners of 2987 Kalakaua, 304 F. Supp. 2d 1245 (D. Haw. 2003)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Transfer to a handicapped accessible unit (ground floor or three-bedroom unit with wheelchair ramp)
fha_claims.reasoning: Defendant immediately investigated transfer options, had no accessible units available in late January 2016, but within six weeks secured a three-bedroom accessible unit with existing ramp and grab bars for Plaintiff. Plaintiff was offered two reasonable options and chose to wait for the three-bedroom unit. No reasonable juror could find Plaintiff was denied a reasonable accommodation in the form of a transfer.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Installation of wheelchair ramp, grab bars in bathroom, and tub transfer bench at Plaintiff's current residence
fha_claims.reasoning: Under FHA § 3604(f)(3)(A), a tenant must personally fund reasonable modifications. Plaintiff never offered to pay for the modifications and was not capable of paying. However, under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, Defendant may have been obligated to fund modifications. Defendant immediately responded to Plaintiff's January 25, 2016 request, obtained three contractor quotes, secured HUD funding approval, and within six weeks offered Plaintiff two viable options: structural modification of her current unit or transfer to an accessible three-bedroom unit. Plaintiff elected to wait for the three-bedroom unit. No reasonable juror could conclude Plaintiff was denied a reasonable modification.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Constructive denial of reasonable accommodation/modification through unreasonable delay
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff argued she was constructively denied accommodation through unreasonable delay. The Fourth Circuit recognizes constructive denial when a defendant delays responding to an accommodation request. Here, Defendant immediately began investigation on January 25, 2016, stayed in contact with Plaintiff weekly and almost daily, obtained three contractor quotes, consulted with HUD and Virginia Fair Housing Office, and by March 7, 2016 (within six weeks) had finalized two reasonable options. The delay was not indeterminate; it was driven by legitimate need to investigate Plaintiff's medical condition, obtain funding approvals, and secure contractor estimates. No reasonable juror could find constructive denial based on the temporal analysis and absence of evidence of discriminatory animus.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act claim for failure to provide reasonable modifications/accommodations
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff also brought a claim under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, which applies to programs receiving federal funding. The Rehabilitation Act has a stricter causation standard, requiring plaintiff to demonstrate that exclusion from benefits resulted solely by reason of disability. Defendant acknowledged potential obligation under Section 504 to fund structural modifications. However, applying the same factual analysis as the FHA claim, Defendant did not deny Plaintiff a reasonable modification; rather, Defendant offered two reasonable options within six weeks, and Plaintiff chose the option with the longer timeline. Summary judgment is warranted.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: False Claims Act (FCA), New Mexico Medicaid False Claims Act (MFCA), New Mexico Fraud Against Taxpayers Act (FATA), ADA Title I, Title VII, NMHRA
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied summary judgment on FCA, MFCA, and FATA claims against Family Smiles, finding genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether Dr. Shafer knowingly submitted false claims and whether Family Smiles is vicariously liable. Court also denied summary judgment on reverse false claims, finding questions of fact regarding whether Family Smiles received overpayments and failed to exercise reasonable diligence in identifying and reporting them.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested to bring Boscoe, a service dog in training, to the dental clinic to assist with his Generalized Anxiety Disorder and PTSD. The dog was trained to detect panic attacks and provide cues to alert Plaintiff. Plaintiff proposed housing the dog in an office where he could see it; Defendants proposed a cage in a back office.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether Boscoe was a service animal (despite being in training, evidence showed he was trained to perform tasks for Plaintiff's disability), whether the accommodation was reasonable, whether it imposed undue hardship, and whether Defendants engaged in the interactive process in good faith. Court found that Khurram Hussain refused to consider documentation and closed off discussion of accommodations, suggesting bad faith.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Termination based on disability (Generalized Anxiety Disorder and PTSD)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that timing of termination very shortly after disclosure of disability, combined with evidence of pretext (Defendants' stated reasons contradicted by company policy and evidence), created genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether Plaintiff was fired because of his disability under the ADA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation for requesting reasonable accommodation for disability under ADA, Title VII, and NMHRA
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that Plaintiff engaged in protected opposition to discrimination by requesting accommodation for his disability and complaining about sexual harassment. Temporal proximity between protected activity and termination (within days) created inference of causation. Genuine disputes of material fact exist regarding whether termination was in retaliation for protected conduct.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Termination based on sexual orientation (sex discrimination under Title VII and NMHRA)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that Plaintiff established prima facie case of sex discrimination based on sexual orientation. Defendants' stated reasons (refusal to stop bringing dog, unprofessional behavior) were pretextual: Family Smiles had a policy permitting service dogs, Defendants acted contrary to that policy, and evidence of patient/staff complaints was created after termination. Temporal proximity to disclosure of sexual orientation supported inference of discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation for reporting fraudulent billing practices (FCA, MFCA, FATA whistleblower protection)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that Plaintiff took action in furtherance of FCA enforcement by reporting fraudulent billing practices to managers, using words 'fraud' and 'illegal,' and requesting audit. Temporal proximity between protected activity (reports made within days of termination) and adverse action created inference of causation. Genuine disputes of material fact exist regarding whether Khurram Hussain knew of protected activity and whether it motivated the termination.

case_name: Tejada v. Littlecity Realty LLC
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; case involves alleged race/national origin discrimination targeting Latino tenants through harassment, lease addenda requiring immigration status disclosure, and frivolous eviction proceedings.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss, finding plaintiffs adequately pled a continuing violation of the Fair Housing Act based on alleged intentional race and national origin discrimination aimed at displacing Latino tenants from rent-stabilized apartments.
brief_summary: Latino tenants sued landlords LittleCity Realty LLC and owners Adel and Linda Eskander alleging they intentionally discriminated against Latino residents through lease addenda requiring proof of immigration status, frivolous eviction proceedings, and harassment from 2001-2017 to displace rent-stabilized tenants and illegally deregulate apartments. The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss, finding plaintiffs adequately alleged a continuing violation under the Fair Housing Act and that supplemental jurisdiction over state rent stabilization and city human rights law claims was proper.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman
Trafficante v. Metropolitan Life Insurance Co.
United Mine Workers of Am. v. Gibbs

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied defendants' motion to dismiss under Iqbal/Twombly, finding that plaintiffs plausibly alleged intentional discrimination based on race, color, and national origin through a pattern of discriminatory practices including requiring only Latino tenants to disclose immigration status, filing frivolous evictions against them, and engaging in harassment to displace them.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: New York City Human Rights Law § 8-107(5) (discrimination based on perceived national origin, alienage, citizenship status); New York City Housing Maintenance Code § 27-2004(a)(48) (harassment); New York Rent Stabilization Law § 26-516(a)(2) (overcharges in rent-stabilized apartments)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied defendants' motion to dismiss state and local law claims, finding supplemental jurisdiction appropriate under 28 U.S.C. § 1367 because the federal and state claims derive from a common nucleus of operative fact (the alleged discriminatory scheme to displace Latino tenants and deregulate apartments). Court also found continuing violations doctrine applicable to extend statute of limitations for all claims through 2017, and found fraud adequately pled for rent stabilization overcharge claims.

case_name: Blake Gardens, LLC v. New Jersey
accommodation_description: Plaintiff developer sought to develop community residences for persons with head injuries including those with Alzheimer's disease and dementia as a permitted use in residential zones under New Jersey law.
key_holding: The court denied the State's motion to dismiss under the Eleventh Amendment and for failure to state a claim, finding that Blake Gardens adequately alleged that the 2015 Act's exclusion of Alzheimer's and dementia care homes from permitted residential uses states a plausible Fair Housing Act claim based on facially discriminatory treatment of disabled persons.
brief_summary: Blake Gardens, LLC, a developer of community residences for persons with head injuries and dementia, sued the State of New Jersey challenging a 2015 Act amendment that removed community residences for people with Alzheimer's disease and related dementia disorders from permitted uses in residential zones, arguing this violated the Fair Housing Act's prohibition on disability discrimination. The court denied the State's motion to dismiss, holding that the plaintiff adequately stated a plausible FHA claim by alleging that the statute's exclusion of dementia care homes from residential zones as of right constitutes facially discriminatory treatment of disabled persons without sufficient justification.
key_cases_cited: Association for Advancement of the Mentally Handicapped v. City of Elizabeth, 876 F. Supp. 614 (D.N.J. 1994)
ARC of New Jersey v. New Jersey, 950 F. Supp. 637 (D.N.J. 1996)
Doe v. City of Butler, 892 F.2d 315 (3d Cir. 1989)
Larkin v. State of Mich. Dept. of Social Services, 89 F.3d 285 (6th Cir. 1996)
Resident Advisory Bd. v. Rizzo, 564 F.2d 126 (3d Cir. 1977)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exclusion of dementia care homes from permitted-as-of-right residential zoning; requirement that such facilities undergo local municipal land use review rather than being automatically permitted in residential districts
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff stated a plausible claim of facial discrimination under the FHA by alleging that the 2015 Act applies different rules to persons with dementia (requiring local zoning approval) than to other persons with head injuries (permitted as of right). The court applied the burden-shifting framework for disparate treatment and found the complaint adequately alleged discriminatory effect, denying the motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act Title II claim alleging discrimination in housing based on disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Court noted that ADA and FHA claims overlapped and applied FHA analysis, finding the standards similar. The ADA claim survives the motion to dismiss on the same factual basis as the FHA claim.

case_name: Sanders v. SWS Hilltop, LLC
accommodation_description: Jo Sanders requested to rent an apartment with her VA-registered service dog trained to detect insulin changes and assist with balance and mobility.
key_holding: The court found direct evidence of discriminatory intent where the landlord admitted he would only offer the apartment with inflated deposit and worn carpet 'since [Jo Sanders] has a large service animal,' and instructed staff to 'make it difficult' for plaintiffs and not return their calls, establishing that defendants' actions were motivated by discriminatory intent rather than income concerns.
brief_summary: Sarah and Jo Sanders sued SWS Hilltop, LLC and William Seidl for housing discrimination under the Fair Housing Act after being denied an apartment at Hilltop Apartments due to Jo Sanders' service dog. The court granted summary judgment for plaintiffs, finding direct evidence of discriminatory intent where the landlord admitted conditioning the offer on the service animal, imposed an inflated deposit and refused to replace carpet, and instructed staff to make it difficult for the applicants to proceed.
key_cases_cited: Gamble v. City of Escondido, 104 F.3d 300 (9th Cir. 1997)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Harris v. Itzhaki, 183 F.3d 1043 (9th Cir. 1999)
Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242 (1986)
McGinest v. GTE Service Corp., 360 F.3d 1103 (9th Cir. 2004)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found direct evidence of discriminatory intent: defendants explicitly stated they would impose conditions (inflated deposit, refusal to replace carpet) because Jo Sanders owned a service animal. Defendants' conduct of imposing more burdensome application procedures and delaying tactics violated 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(1). Even viewing evidence in light most favorable to defendants, no rational trier of fact could find defendants' actions were motivated by anything other than discriminatory intent based on disability.

source_file: 7248134_2018_Barry Farm Tenants v. D.C. Hous. Auth._cadc
case_name: Barry Farm Tenants and Allies Ass'n v. D.C. Hous. Auth.
accommodation_description: This is not a reasonable accommodation case; it concerns redevelopment plan's unit mix affecting families with children (familial status discrimination) and alleged constructive demolition.
key_holding: The court dismissed all claims for lack of ripeness—the plaintiffs' allegations about the unit mix were based on a proposed housing mix in a 2014 letter that had not been incorporated into any final plan, and the Zoning Commission retained authority over second-stage applications to determine final unit composition.
brief_summary: Barry Farm public housing tenants sued the D.C. Housing Authority and private developers alleging that the approved redevelopment plan's proposed unit mix (increasing one-bedroom units while reducing larger units) would have a disparate impact on families with children in violation of the FHA and DCHRA, and that DCHA's failure to maintain the property constituted constructive demolition under the USHA. The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss, finding the familial status claims unripe because the proposed unit mix had not been adopted and final unit composition would be determined in future zoning applications, and dismissing the constructive demolition claim for lack of an enforceable federal right.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Gonzaga Univ. v. Doe
Blessing v. Freestone

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unit mix composition (number of one-, two-, three-, four-, and six-bedroom units) in replacement public housing units
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under Rule 12(b)(1) on ripeness grounds. The alleged discriminatory unit mix was not final—it was merely a 'possible' mix in a July 2014 letter that was not incorporated into the Zoning Commission's Order. The unit mix will be determined in future second-stage PUD applications subject to Zoning Commission approval, making the claim premature and unfit for judicial review.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unit mix composition (number of one-, two-, three-, four-, and six-bedroom units) in replacement public housing units under D.C. Human Rights Act
fha_claims.reasoning: Same ripeness analysis as Count I. The court lacked supplemental jurisdiction over the state law claim after dismissing the federal FHA claim, and declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c) based on judicial economy and comity considerations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Constructive demolition claim under United States Housing Act (USHA), 42 U.S.C. § 1437p and 24 C.F.R. § 970.25; also alleged under D.C. Human Rights Act
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that 42 U.S.C. § 1437p(a)(1)(A) and (a)(3) do not confer a federal right enforceable through Section 1983 under the Blessing/Gonzaga framework. The relevant subsections lack 'right-creating language' focused on the benefitted class, are directed at the HUD Secretary rather than public housing residents, and Congress removed the post-Edwards clarifying language in the 1998 amendments without including alternative rights-creating language.

case_name: El v. People's Emergency Ctr.
accommodation_description: No disability-related accommodation request; plaintiff alleges discrimination based on religion (Islamic faith) and race (Moor/Urban Indian identity) including refusal to allow move-in and harassment
key_holding: Plaintiff adequately pleaded intentional religious and racial discrimination by alleging a PEC employee stated the Christian-based organization does not want Islamic persons in their programs, which is direct evidence of discriminatory animus sufficient to survive dismissal under § 3604(b), and adequately pleaded harassment sufficient to state an interference claim under § 3617.
brief_summary: Plaintiff El, proceeding pro se, sued People's Emergency Center, 4050 Apartments LP, and property manager Dawn Burrous alleging they refused to let him move into a promised artist loft based on his Islamic religion and Moor/Urban Indian identity, subjected him to harassment with repeated lease infractions, and denied him building amenities. The court denied the motion to dismiss the FHA disparate treatment claim (Count One) finding plaintiff pleaded direct evidence of religious discrimination, denied dismissal of the interference claim (Count Five), dismissed the criminal civil rights statute claim (Count Two) with prejudice, dismissed the ADA claim (Count Four) without prejudice for failure to plead public accommodation or public entity status, and dismissed claims on behalf of plaintiff's wife and children for lack of standing.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Doe v. City of Butler, 892 F.2d 315 (3d Cir. 1989)
Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009)
Revock v. Cowpet Bay West Condo. Ass'n, 853 F.3d 96 (3d Cir. 2017)
Disability Rights N.J., Inc. v. Comm'r, New Jersey Dep't of Human Servs., 796 F.3d 293 (3d Cir. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged that PEC employee stated PEC 'does not care to have folks of Islamic religion' in their programs and that Plaintiff was denied lease signing on ribbon-cutting day while other tenants were permitted to sign. The alleged discriminatory statement is 'so revealing of discriminatory animus' as to survive the motion to dismiss under the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Under 42 U.S.C. § 3617, Plaintiff alleged harassment through continual lease infractions and denial of community room use based on discriminatory animus. Liberally construing pro se allegations and accepting them as true, Plaintiff alleged harassment 'sufficiently severe or pervasive as to create a hostile environment,' satisfying the four-element test for interference claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 3631 (criminal statute prohibiting use of force or threat of force); 18 U.S.C. § 112 (criminal statute protecting internationally protected persons); 42 U.S.C. § 12101 et seq. (ADA Title II and Title III)
fha_claims.reasoning: 42 U.S.C. § 3631 does not create a private right of action; 18 U.S.C. § 112 does not provide a private right of action and Plaintiff alleged no facts showing he is an 'internationally protected person'; ADA Title II and Title III do not apply because Plaintiff did not allege Defendants are a public entity or place of public accommodation (apartments and condominiums are not public accommodations under Title III).

source_file: 7249733_2018_City of Miami Gardens v. Wells Fargo _ Co._flsd
case_name: City of Miami Gardens v. Wells Fargo & Co.
accommodation_description: This case involves discriminatory lending claims under the Fair Housing Act, not a reasonable accommodation request; the City alleges Wells Fargo issued more expensive loans to minority borrowers than to white borrowers.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for Wells Fargo because the City of Miami Gardens failed to establish a prima facie case of discriminatory lending under either disparate impact or disparate treatment theories—the loan comparators identified by the City's expert were not 'nearly identical' due to differences in origination dates, lender credits, and promotional offerings, and even if a prima facie case could be made, Wells Fargo established legitimate nondiscriminatory reasons for the pricing differences that the City could not prove were pretextual.
brief_summary: The City of Miami Gardens sued Wells Fargo alleging the bank issued discriminatory and more expensive loans to African-American and Hispanic borrowers compared to white borrowers in Miami Gardens during the two-year limitations period (June 2012 to June 2014), causing higher default rates, foreclosures, and reduced property tax revenue. The court granted summary judgment for Wells Fargo, finding the City failed to establish a prima facie case because the loan comparators were not 'nearly identical'—they had different origination dates, lender credits, and promotional offerings—and Wells Fargo provided legitimate nondiscriminatory reasons for the pricing differences that the City could not prove were pretextual.
key_cases_cited: City of Miami v. Bank of America Corp., 800 F.3d 1262 (11th Cir. 2015)
Bank of America Corp. v. City of Miami, 137 S.Ct. 1296 (2017)
Texas Dept. of Housing & Comm. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, 135 S.Ct. 2507 (2015)
Boykin v. Bank of Am. Corp., 162 F. App'x 837 (11th Cir. 2005)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged Wells Fargo's Product Validation Process and practice of allowing lender credits on FHA loans caused disparate impact on minority borrowers by steering them into higher-cost loans.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff failed to establish prima facie case of disparate impact because: (1) only two loans alleged to be higher-cost, insufficient to show statistically-imbalanced lending patterns; (2) no evidence of robust causality linking neutral policies to statistical disparity; (3) struck plaintiff's key expert declaration as unreliable; (4) plaintiff failed to identify facially-neutral policy causing the disparity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged Wells Fargo issued loans to minority borrowers at higher rates than similarly-situated non-minority borrowers (two matched pairs: HC6 vs. NHW8, and HC2 vs. NHW8).
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff failed to establish prima facie case because the loan comparators were not 'nearly identical' as required by Boykin: minority borrowers received substantially different lender credits ($1,878 and $8,000) compared to non-minority borrower ($479), originated at different times, and received different promotional discounts. Even if prima facie case could be made, defendant established legitimate nondiscriminatory reasons (lender credits, promotional pricing, origination timing) and plaintiff presented no evidence that these reasons were pretextual for discrimination.

case_name: Nat'l Fair Hous. Alliance v. Carson
accommodation_description: Not a reasonable accommodation case; fair housing organizations challenge HUD's withdrawal of the Assessment Tool for Local Governments as arbitrary and capricious under the APA
key_holding: Plaintiffs lack Article III standing to challenge HUD's withdrawal of the LG2017 Assessment Tool because they cannot demonstrate concrete, particularized injury fairly traceable to the challenged agency action and likely to be redressed by favorable judicial relief.
brief_summary: National Fair Housing Alliance and other fair housing organizations sued HUD and Secretary Carson challenging two May 2018 HUD notices that withdrew the Assessment Tool for Local Governments and directed program participants to revert to the prior Analysis of Impediments process, alleging these actions violated the APA. The court granted HUD's motion to dismiss, finding the plaintiffs lacked Article III standing because they failed to demonstrate concrete injury fairly traceable to HUD's withdrawal of the Assessment Tool.
key_cases_cited: NAACP v. Sec'y of Hous. & Urban Dev., 817 F.2d 149 (1st Cir. 1987)
Texas Dept. of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 135 S.Ct. 2507 (2015)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Olmstead v. L.C., 527 U.S. 581 (1999)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Administrative Procedure Act challenge to HUD's withdrawal of the LG2017 Assessment Tool and reversion to the Analysis of Impediments process; claims that withdrawal violated notice-and-comment requirements and was arbitrary and capricious
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs lacked Article III organizational standing because they failed to establish a cognizable injury in fact. Although HUD's withdrawal of the LG2017 Tool suspended certain AFH procedures, key portions of the AFFH Rule remained active (definitions, community participation requirements, recordkeeping, certification), and plaintiffs' mission-driven activities were not perceptibly impaired. Plaintiffs also failed to show they diverted resources beyond normal operational costs, and any redressability was too speculative because it depended on third-party (local government) conduct.

source_file: 7249823_2018_273 Lee Ave. Tenants Ass'n v. Steinmetz_nyed
case_name: 273 Lee Avenue Tenants Association v. Steinmetz
accommodation_description: Latino tenants allege they received inferior repairs and maintenance compared to Hasidic Jewish tenants, and that vacant apartments were rented exclusively to Hasidic residents.
key_holding: The court denied summary judgment on plaintiffs' repair discrimination claims because genuine disputes of material fact existed regarding whether defendants' failure to provide adequate maintenance was motivated by plaintiffs' Latino ethnicity, while dismissing vacancy claims because plaintiffs failed to actually apply for vacant apartments and thus could not establish the futility exception to the application requirement.
brief_summary: Latino tenants at 273 Lee Avenue in Brooklyn sued landlord Naftali Steinmetz and his LLC, alleging racial discrimination in housing maintenance and apartment rentals compared to Hasidic Jewish tenants. The court granted partial summary judgment, dismissing vacancy discrimination claims because plaintiffs never formally applied for vacant units, but denied summary judgment on repair discrimination claims because disputed facts regarding the landlord's motivations required trial.
key_cases_cited: Mitchell v. Shane, 350 F.3d 39 (2d Cir. 2003)
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Patterson v. County of Oneida, 375 F.3d 206 (2d Cir. 2004)
Grimes v. Fremont Gen. Corp., 785 F. Supp. 2d 269 (S.D.N.Y. 2011)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to provide adequate repairs and maintenance services (heating, water, plumbing, doors, fixtures) in violation of FHA § 3604(b)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiffs established prima facie case of race-based discrimination in provision of repairs and maintenance services. Material issues of fact remain regarding defendants' intent and whether alleged disparate treatment was motivated by race. Summary judgment denied; case proceeds to trial.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to lease vacant apartments to plaintiffs based on race (FHA § 3604(d) and 42 U.S.C. § 1982)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to establish prima facie case under McDonnell Douglas framework. Plaintiffs never sought to rent vacant apartments and were denied; Oyola's 2011-2012 inquiry was outside statute of limitations. Futile gesture doctrine does not apply because plaintiffs lacked direct contact with defendants regarding leasing policies and were not reliably informed of discriminatory rental practices.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: NYHRL § 296(5) and NYCHRL § 8-107(5)(a) claims for race-based discrimination in repairs and maintenance; 42 U.S.C. § 1982 claim for race-based discrimination in leasing
fha_claims.reasoning: NYHRL and NYCHRL repair claims analyzed under same standard as FHA § 3604(b) and survive summary judgment on same basis. § 1982 leasing claim dismissed on same grounds as FHA § 3604(d) claim—failure to establish prima facie case.

source_file: 7250227_2018_Martinez v. Lexington Gardens Assocs., Dennis Ovalle, L.A. Equities Corp._ilsd
case_name: Martinez v. Lexington Gardens Assocs., Dennis Ovalle, L.A. Equities Corp.
accommodation_description: Request to allow Thelma Martinez, plaintiff's sister and court-appointed guardian, to live in plaintiff's apartment full-time as her primary caretaker for intellectual and developmental disabilities
key_holding: A landlord violates the FHA when it refuses to modify its tenant screening policies to allow a disabled tenant's family member to live in the apartment as a caretaker, provided the accommodation is necessary for the tenant to have an equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling and does not impose an undue hardship on the landlord.
brief_summary: Blanca Martinez, a developmentally and intellectually disabled woman receiving Section 8 vouchers, sued her landlord seeking to have her sister Thelma permitted to live with her as a full-time caretaker after their mother's death. The court granted plaintiff's motion for summary judgment, holding that the landlord violated the FHA by unreasonably refusing to accommodate Martinez's disability by denying the live-in aide request based on Thelma's credit and rental history, when the accommodation was necessary for Martinez to use and enjoy her dwelling.
key_cases_cited: Tsombanidis v. W. Haven Fire Dep't, 352 F.3d 565 (2d Cir. 2003)
Tuman v. VL GEM LLC, 2017 WL 781486 (S.D.N.Y. Feb. 27, 2017)
Austin v. Town of Farmington, 826 F.3d 622 (2d Cir. 2016)
Salute v. Stratford Greens Garden Apartments, 136 F.3d 293 (2d Cir. 1998)
U.S. Airways, Inc. v. Barnett, 535 U.S. 391 (2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission for Thelma Martinez, Blanca's sister and primary caretaker, to live in Blanca's Section 8 apartment to provide full-time care and assistance with activities of daily living (cooking, eating, using restroom, dressing). Blanca is intellectually and developmentally disabled with Cerebral Palsy and cannot live alone.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied the five-element reasonable accommodation test and found no genuine dispute of material fact: (1) Blanca is disabled within the FHA definition; (2) defendants knew of her disability; (3) the accommodation is necessary because Blanca cannot live alone and has no other willing/able caretakers; (4) the accommodation is reasonable because the cost to defendants is modest (same Section 8 rent regardless of occupancy), Thelma has demonstrated ability to pay rent, and the burden on defendants does not outweigh Blanca's critical need for full-time care; and (5) defendants refused the accommodation. The court rejected defendants' reliance on neutral screening policies (credit/rental history), holding that FHA § 3604(f)(3)(B) expressly requires deviations from neutral rules when necessary and reasonable.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rehabilitation Act § 504 (29 U.S.C. § 794), New York State Human Rights Law (N.Y. Exec. Law. § 296 et seq.), New York City Human Rights Law (N.Y.C. Admin. Code § 8-107(5))
fha_claims.reasoning: Court analyzed Rehabilitation Act and state/local human rights law claims under the same reasonable accommodation framework as the FHA, finding that the standards are nearly identical. The court noted that NYCHRL claims must be analyzed separately and independently but that defendants' conduct violates all applicable statutes. The court applied the same balancing analysis and reached the same conclusion: defendants must permit Thelma to live in the apartment as a reasonable accommodation.

source_file: 7250229_2018_S_R Dev. Estates, LLC v. Town of Greenburgh_ilsd
case_name: S & R Development Estates, LLC v. Sisters of the Blessed Sacrament, Inc.
accommodation_description: S & R alleged the Sisters selectively enforced a restrictive covenant against its housing development in violation of the FHA's prohibition on making housing unavailable; the Sisters counterclaimed for state-law compensation if their covenant enforcement violated the FHA.
key_holding: The Sisters' state-law claim under RPAPL § 1951(2) for compensation if their restrictive covenant enforcement violated the FHA is preempted because allowing a violator to recover compensation from the victim would undermine the regulatory and deterrent purposes of the FHA.
brief_summary: S & R Development Estates sued Sisters of the Blessed Sacrament, a religious order owning an adjacent convent, alleging the Sisters selectively enforced a restrictive covenant to block S & R's housing development in violation of the Fair Housing Act; the Sisters counterclaimed under New York state law seeking compensation if their enforcement was deemed unlawful. The court granted S & R's motion to dismiss the counterclaim, holding that the Sisters' state-law claim for compensation is preempted by the FHA because allowing a covenant violator to recover damages from the party asserting FHA rights would frustrate the statute's regulatory and deterrent purposes.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Tex. Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 135 S.Ct. 2507 (2015)
Equal Rights Ctr. v. Niles Bolton Assocs., 602 F.3d 597 (4th Cir. 2010)
City of Los Angeles v. AECOM Servs., 854 F.3d 1149 (9th Cir. 2017)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: State law claim for damages under New York Real Property Actions and Proceedings Law (RPAPL) § 1951(2) for monetary value of restrictive covenant deemed unenforceable due to FHA violation
fha_claims.reasoning: The Sisters' counterclaim under RPAPL § 1951(2) is preempted by the FHA because allowing state law compensation to an FHA violator would undermine Congress's regulatory and deterrent purposes. The FHA's broad, results-oriented language and legislative focus on housing availability preclude state law claims that would compensate violators or make housing less available to protected persons.

case_name: Saint-Jean v. Emigrant Mortg. Co.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; case concerns alleged reverse redlining and predatory mortgage lending targeting Black homeowners.
key_holding: The court denied Emigrant's motion for judgment as a matter of law on liability, finding sufficient evidence that Emigrant engaged in racially discriminatory lending practices through the STAR NINA program, but granted a new trial on damages due to inconsistent jury awards that failed to adequately compensate plaintiffs for their losses.
brief_summary: Black homeowners sued Emigrant Mortgage Company alleging that its STAR NINA (No Income No Asset) loan program constituted reverse redlining and predatory lending that targeted minority communities, resulting in discriminatory loan terms including 18% default interest rates. After a jury found Emigrant violated the Fair Housing Act, Equal Credit Opportunity Act, and New York City Human Rights Law, the court denied Emigrant's motion for judgment as a matter of law on liability but ordered a new trial on damages due to inconsistent jury awards that failed to fully compensate plaintiffs for economic and emotional losses.
key_cases_cited: Barkley v. Olympia Mortg. Co., 2007 WL 2437810
Trafficante v. Metropolitan Life Ins. Co., 409 U.S. 205 (1972)
Ragin v. Harry Macklowe Real Estate, 6 F.3d 898 (2d Cir. 1993)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Jury found that Emigrant intentionally discriminated by offering STAR NINA loans that were grossly unfavorable and intentionally targeted certain communities based in part on race, color, or national origin. The court upheld the jury's verdict against Emigrant's post-trial motion for judgment as a matter of law, finding sufficient evidence of targeting through advertising, broker recruitment, and loan product design.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Jury found that Emigrant's practice of making STAR NINA loans had a discriminatory effect on African-American and Hispanic borrowers. The court rejected Emigrant's argument that the instruction relieved plaintiffs of their burden to show causality, finding that the instruction properly required plaintiffs to establish that the STAR NINA loan product itself (not mere economic disparities) caused the adverse impact.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal Credit Opportunity Act (15 U.S.C. § 1691 et seq.), New York City Human Rights Law, Truth in Lending Act (15 U.S.C. § 1601 et seq.)
fha_claims.reasoning: Jury found violations of ECOA and NYCHRL on the same intentional discrimination and disparate impact theories as the FHA claims. The TILA claim (Edith Saint-Jean only) survived motion to dismiss and was strengthened by trial evidence showing the 18% default interest rate was not unanticipated. Court granted new trial on damages for all claims due to inability to determine how jury calculated awards across different types of losses (equity loss, home ownership loss, emotional distress).

source_file: 7250319_2018_Heine v. Comm'r of the Dep't of Cmty. Affairs of State_njd
case_name: Heine v. Comm'r of the Dep't of Cmty. Affairs of State
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs challenge the DCA's regulation of their property as a 'rooming house' as discriminatory under the FHA, alleging it discriminates against unmarried individuals and nontraditional living arrangements.
key_holding: Summary judgment is granted because the City of Garfield—not the DCA—closed the property based on imminent health and safety hazards unrelated to discriminatory rooming house regulations, and plaintiffs failed to establish a nexus between their injury and the DCA's actions; alternatively, res judicata bars the claims and plaintiffs failed to prove FHA familial status discrimination.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Heine and others sued the New Jersey Commissioner of the Department of Community Affairs under § 1983 and the Fair Housing Act, challenging the regulation of their Garfield property as an unlicensed rooming house and seeking injunctive relief. The court granted summary judgment for the Commissioner, finding no evidence that the DCA—rather than the City of Garfield acting on fire safety violations—closed the property, and that the rooming house regulations do not constitute familial status discrimination under the FHA.
key_cases_cited: Monell v. Dep't of Soc. Servs. of City of New York
Bank of Am. Corp. v. City of Miami, Fla.
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green
Village of Belle Terre v. Boraas
Salvation Army v. Dep't of Cmty. Affairs

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged that the DCA's regulation of the Property as a rooming house and enforcement of fire safety and health code violations discriminated against occupants based on familial status (unrelated individuals and non-traditional family configurations).
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that plaintiffs failed to establish a prima facie case of FHA discrimination. The regulations at issue were facially neutral health and safety requirements (fire codes, smoke detectors, egress requirements) that did not target families with children and applied equally to all occupants regardless of family status. The court found no evidence that the enforcement disproportionately impacted families with children, the only protected class under FHA's familial status provision.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 claims for constitutional violations (due process, property rights, equal protection) related to the closure of the Property and enforcement of rooming house regulations.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that plaintiffs failed to establish personal involvement of the Commissioner in the alleged constitutional violations. The Property was closed by the City of Garfield based on imminent fire and safety hazards, not by the DCA. The court found no evidence that the DCA or Commissioner, through policy or direct action, caused the closure or eviction. Additionally, the § 1983 claims were vague, failed to specify which constitutional provisions were violated, and were not tied to any occupant's family status.

source_file: 7250489_2018_Zhou v. Villa De Paz Apartments, LLC_azd
case_name: Zhou v. Villa De Paz Apartments, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege discriminatory notices targeting families with children through mandatory adult supervision rules for minors.
key_holding: The court granted partial summary judgment for plaintiffs, finding that Villa de Paz's rules requiring constant adult supervision of minor children at the apartment complex are facially discriminatory under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c) as they indicate a preference to limit housing based on familial status.
brief_summary: Families with minor children sued their apartment complex in Phoenix, Arizona, alleging that rules requiring constant adult supervision of minors and prohibiting ball playing and unstructured play discriminated against families with children under the Fair Housing Act's familial status protections. The court granted partial summary judgment for plaintiffs, holding that the supervision and play restrictions are facially discriminatory under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c) as discriminatory notices indicating a preference against families with children.
key_cases_cited: Iniestra v. Cliff Warren Investment, Inc., 886 F. Supp. 2d 1161 (C.D. Cal. 2012)
Pack v. Washington II, 689 F. Supp. 2d 1237 (E.D. Cal. 2009)
Community House, Inc. v. City of Boise, 490 F.3d 1041 (9th Cir. 2007)
Blomgren v. Ogle, 850 F. Supp. 1427 (E.D. Wash. 1993)
Fair Housing Congress v. Weber, 993 F. Supp. 1286 (C.D. Cal. 1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that Villa de Paz's published notices requiring supervision of minor children at all times constitute facial discrimination under FHA § 3604(c) as a matter of law, following precedent in Iniestra, Pack, and related cases. Plaintiffs need not show injury to establish the violation; the discriminatory nature of the policy itself is sufficient.

source_file: 7250709_2018_Panjiva, Inc. v. U.S. Customs _ Border Prot._ilsd
7251032_2018_City of Grand Rapids v. Grand Rapids Police Command Officers Ass'n_miwd

case_name: Phyllis Davis v. Echo Valley Condominium Association
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that the condominium association ban smoking throughout the complex, including within private residences, to accommodate her asthma and multiple-chemical sensitivity disorder caused by secondhand smoke exposure.
key_holding: The requested accommodation—a building-wide smoking ban including private residences—is unreasonable because plaintiff failed to demonstrate it was necessary to afford her equal opportunity to enjoy her unit, and imposing such a ban would require the association to violate Michigan law by restricting lawful activity on property owners' own premises without proper consent.
brief_summary: Phyllis Davis, an asthmatic condominium owner with multiple-chemical sensitivity, sued the Echo Valley Condominium Association alleging the association failed to reasonably accommodate her disability by refusing to ban smoking throughout the complex. The court granted summary judgment for the defendants, holding that the requested accommodation was unreasonable because Davis failed to show a complete smoking ban was necessary to afford her equal opportunity to use and enjoy her dwelling, and because enforcing such a ban would violate Michigan condominium law requiring proper consent from property owners.
key_cases_cited: Matarese v. Archstone Pentagon City, 808 F.3d 961 (4th Cir. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Smoking ban throughout the entire Echo Valley condominium complex, including private residential units, to prevent secondhand smoke infiltration into plaintiff's unit
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the three-part reasonable accommodation test (equal opportunity, necessity, reasonableness) and found that plaintiff failed to establish the accommodation was necessary because she offered only conclusory medical opinion without expert testimony showing the smoking ban would ameliorate her disability specifically (not just general burden shared by all exposed to smoke). More critically, the court found the accommodation unreasonable as a matter of law because it would require the HOA to impose a use restriction on co-owners' lawful activity in their own homes without the two-thirds consent required by Michigan law, which the co-owners had already rejected in a vote. The court balanced the burden on defendants (violation of state law and co-owner rights) against the benefit to plaintiff and found the accommodation imposed a fundamental alteration and undue burden.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Michigan Persons with Disabilities Civil Rights Act (PWDCRA) claim; private nuisance claim under Michigan common law; breach of contract claim under condominium bylaws
fha_claims.reasoning: The PWDCRA claim was analyzed under the same reasonable accommodation framework as the FHAA and failed for identical reasons. The private nuisance claim failed because the remaining defendants (HOA and property manager) lacked control over the smoking conduct; under Michigan law, a landlord cannot be held liable for a nuisance created by a tenant, and a condominium association cannot be liable for lawful conduct by co-owners within their own units absent a bylaw violation. The breach of contract claim failed because plaintiff offered no evidence that smoking increases insurance rates, that units were not maintained in safe/clean/sanitary condition, or that smoking constitutes an 'annoyance or nuisance' under the bylaws absent a controlling rule or statute.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Administrative Procedure Act (APA) challenge to asylum eligibility rule; no FHA claim present. Plaintiffs challenge the validity of a Department of Justice and Department of Homeland Security interim final rule that categorically bars asylum eligibility for aliens who enter the United States outside designated ports of entry in violation of a presidential proclamation.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found the Immigration Organizations likely to succeed on the merits of their APA claim that the Rule violates 8 U.S.C. § 1158(a)(1) by creating a categorical bar to asylum eligibility based on manner of entry, which Congress explicitly stated should not disqualify an alien from applying for asylum. The court also found serious questions going to the merits regarding the Rule's compliance with APA notice-and-comment requirements and granted a temporary restraining order pending preliminary injunction hearing.

source_file: 7251500_2019_Walsh v. Friendship Vill. of S. Cnty._moed
case_name: Walsh v. Friendship Village of S. Cnty.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs Mary Walsh and Beverly Nance, a married same-sex couple, were denied housing at Friendship Village senior community because the facility's Cohabitation Policy only permitted opposite-sex married couples, related family members, or siblings to share a unit.
key_holding: The court granted Defendants' motion for judgment on the pleadings, holding that Plaintiffs' claims of discrimination based on sexual orientation were not actionable under the Fair Housing Act because the Eighth Circuit has held that sexual orientation is not a protected characteristic, and Plaintiffs' sex-stereotyping theory was based solely on their sexual orientation rather than gender non-conformity independent of orientation.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Mary Walsh and Beverly Nance, a married same-sex couple, sued Friendship Village senior living community for sex discrimination under the FHA after being denied housing based on the facility's Cohabitation Policy restricting shared units to opposite-sex married couples and related family members. The court granted Defendants' motion for judgment on the pleadings, holding that sexual orientation discrimination is not actionable under the FHA and that Plaintiffs' sex-stereotyping claim was based solely on sexual orientation rather than gender non-conformity independent of that orientation.
key_cases_cited: Williamson v. A.G. Edwards & Sons, Inc., 876 F.2d 69 (8th Cir. 1989)
Price Waterhouse v. Hopkins, 490 U.S. 228 (1989)
Pambianchi v. Arkansas Tech University, 2014 WL 11498236 (E.D. Ark. 2014)
Zarda v. Altitude Express, Inc., 883 F.3d 100 (2d Cir. 2018)
Wetzel v. Glen St. Andrew Living Community, LLC, 901 F.3d 856 (7th Cir. 2018)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that plaintiffs' claim of sex discrimination based on the 'but-for' sex argument (that if Ms. Walsh had been a man married to Ms. Nance, they would not have been denied housing) fails because the claim is fundamentally based on sexual orientation, which is not a protected class under the FHA under Eighth Circuit precedent. The court found the allegations boil down to discrimination based on sexual orientation rather than sex alone.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court rejected plaintiffs' associational discrimination theory (that they were treated less favorably because of association with a same-sex spouse) because sexual orientation is an unprotected class under the FHA, and plaintiffs presented no evidence that associational discrimination claims are actionable with respect to unprotected classes.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that plaintiffs' sex-stereotyping claim fails because the alleged gender non-conforming behavior is based solely on sexual orientation. The court found that sexual orientation alone cannot be the basis for an actionable sex-stereotyping claim under the FHA, as this would impermissibly bootstrap protection for sexual orientation into the statute contrary to binding Eighth Circuit precedent.

source_file: 7252515_2019_Greater New Orleans Fair Hous. Action Ctr. v. Kelly_laed
case_name: Greater New Orleans Fair Housing Action Center v. Kelly
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; case involves landlord's alleged preference for renting to women over men based on sex.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that plaintiff fair housing organization had Article III standing and adequately pleaded claims for sex discrimination under § 3604(b) (including hostile housing environment) and § 3604(c) (discriminatory statements).
brief_summary: Greater New Orleans Fair Housing Action Center sued private landlord Jerry W. Kelly and his LLCs alleging sex-based housing discrimination, claiming Kelly preferred to rent to women, sexually harassed female tenants, and made discriminatory statements. The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss, finding the fair housing organization had standing and adequately pleaded claims under § 3604(b) for hostile housing environment and § 3604(c) for discriminatory statements.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman
Quigley v. Winter
OCA-Greater Houston v. Texas

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to rent and making housing unavailable based on sex; differential treatment of male and female testers regarding availability of rental units
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff sufficiently pleaded a disparate treatment claim under § 3604(a) by alleging a pattern of treating male and female testers differently with respect to unit availability, responsiveness to inquiries, and appointment confirmations. The pattern of differential treatment moves allegations from speculative to plausible under Iqbal/Twombly, particularly when viewed alongside other allegations of Kelly's preference for renting to women.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination in terms, conditions, and privileges of rental; different application requirements (credit check waived for female tester but required for male tester)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff sufficiently pleaded a § 3604(b) claim by alleging Kelly placed different conditions on application materials for male and female testers seeking the same rental unit. The allegation that Kelly told female tester #4 he would forego her credit check because she was a 'grown woman' isolates sex as a factor in his decision, satisfying the plausibility standard when viewed in context of other allegations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Sexual harassment creating hostile housing environment; unwanted touching, sexually suggestive comments, and repeated unauthorized entry into tenant's apartment
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff sufficiently pleaded a hostile housing environment claim under § 3604(b) by alleging Kelly's harassment of tenant B.C. was sufficiently severe and pervasive to alter conditions of her housing arrangement. Allegations of unwanted touching, sexually suggestive comments, and repeated unauthorized apartment entry—viewed in context of similar harassment of other female tenants—satisfy the plausibility standard for hostile environment discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Oral statements indicating preference for renting to women; statements made during lease signing and apartment tours indicating sex-based rental preferences
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff sufficiently pleaded a § 3604(c) claim by alleging Kelly made statements indicating sex-based rental preferences 'with respect to the sale or rental of a dwelling.' Kelly's statement to B.C. that he returned her call because she sounded attractive, and his statements to female tester #4 about her appearance and credit check waiver, were made during rental transactions and would suggest to an ordinary listener a preference for renting to women.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Louisiana Equal Housing Opportunity Act claims under La. R.S. 51:2606(A)(1), (A)(2), and (A)(3), which contain language nearly identical to FHA §§ 3604(a), (b), and (c)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied the same analysis to state law claims as to federal FHA claims, finding that because the language in the relevant sections of the Louisiana Equal Housing Opportunity Act is nearly identical to the FHA, plaintiff's allegations sufficiently state claims under state law as well.

case_name: Sanzaro v. Ardiente Homeowners Ass'n, LLC
accommodation_description: Mrs. Sanzaro, a mobility-impaired homeowner, requested permission to be accompanied by her service dog Angel in the HOA clubhouse.
key_holding: The court found that the HOA violated the FHA by refusing to allow Mrs. Sanzaro's service dog Angel to accompany her in the clubhouse, because the accommodation request was reasonable given her documented mobility disability and the nexus between her disability and the services Angel provided.
brief_summary: Deborah and Michael Sanzaro sued the Ardiente Homeowners Association and related defendants after being denied access to the HOA clubhouse with Mrs. Sanzaro's service dog Angel on three occasions between 2009 and 2011. After a bench trial, the court found in favor of Plaintiffs, holding that the HOA violated the Fair Housing Act by improperly requiring documentation and certification for the service animal and refusing to reasonably accommodate Mrs. Sanzaro's disability.
key_cases_cited: City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, Inc., 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Olmstead v. L.C., 527 U.S. 581 (1999)
Fair Housing Council of San Diego v. Penasquitos Casablanca Owners' Ass'n, 381 Fed. Appx. 674 (9th Cir. 2010)
Bragdon v. Abbott, 524 U.S. 624 (1998)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission for Mrs. Sanzaro to bring her service dog (Angel, a Chihuahua) into the Ardiente HOA clubhouse. Angel was trained to assist Mrs. Sanzaro with her mobility disability by retrieving her walker and helping her manage acute pain attacks.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the five-element FHA reasonable accommodation test and found: (1) Mrs. Sanzaro is handicapped; (2) defendants knew or should have known of her handicap; (3) accommodation was necessary for equal enjoyment of the dwelling; (4) allowing Angel in the clubhouse was reasonable because the dog was not disruptive, posed no risk, and defendants provided no legitimate reason why the accommodation would be unreasonable; and (5) defendants refused the accommodation on three separate occasions despite receiving sufficient documentation of Angel's assistance tasks.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of access to the Ardiente clubhouse based on disability (refusal to allow Mrs. Sanzaro to enter with her service animal while similarly situated non-disabled persons were permitted to use the clubhouse).
fha_claims.reasoning: The court's analysis of the reasonable accommodation claim under § 3604(f)(3)(B) necessarily established disparate treatment: Mrs. Sanzaro was denied access to a common facility available to other homeowners solely because of her disability and her use of a service animal, despite providing documentation of the disability and the animal's assistance function.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III public accommodation claim; NRS § 651.075 Nevada state law claim for denial of service to person with disability accompanied by service animal.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that the Ardiente clubhouse does not qualify as a place of public accommodation under the ADA or Nevada law because the community and clubhouse were private establishments with restricted access. Although members of the public could participate in 'Stay and Play' and 'Taste of the Good Life' marketing programs, access was conditioned on explicit written indication of interest in purchasing a home and was not advertised or available to the general public as a hotel or lodging facility would be. Therefore, neither the ADA nor NRS § 651.075 applied.

source_file: 7252923_2019_Conn. Fair Hous. Ctr. v. Corelogic Rental Prop. Solutions, LLC_ctd
case_name: Connecticut Fair Housing Center v. CoreLogic Rental Property Solutions, LLC
accommodation_description: Ms. Arroyo requested that defendant provide her with her conservator ward Mikhail Arroyo's tenant screening report, which she needed to challenge the housing disqualification decision and request reasonable accommodation.
key_holding: The court denied defendant's motion to dismiss, finding that plaintiffs sufficiently stated a claim that CoreLogic's CrimSAFE product violated the FHA by disqualifying Mr. Arroyo based on arrest records without individualized assessment and by refusing to accept Ms. Arroyo's conservatorship documentation in lieu of power of attorney.
brief_summary: CFHC and the Arroyos sued CoreLogic alleging its CrimSAFE tenant screening product violated the FHA by disqualifying Mr. Arroyo based on arrest records without individualized assessment and refusing to provide his screening report to his conservator without power of attorney. The court denied defendant's motion to dismiss, finding plaintiffs stated claims for disparate treatment, disparate impact, and failure to accommodate under the FHA.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Tex. Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Aff. v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc.
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman
Olsen v. Stark Homes, Inc.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Automatic criminal record screening without individualized assessment or disclosure of underlying records; disparate impact on racial minorities (African Americans and Latinos)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs sufficiently alleged a facially neutral policy (automated CrimSAFE screening without individualized assessment) with disproportionate impact on minorities, supported by allegations that minorities are more likely to be arrested and charged. Court found allegations satisfy prima facie burden at motion to dismiss stage under Inclusive Communities Project framework.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Intentional discrimination based on race through use of automated criminal record screening without individualized assessment
fha_claims.reasoning: Under Swierkiewicz, plaintiffs need not allege prima facie case under McDonnell Douglas at pleading stage. Plaintiffs sufficiently alleged membership in protected class (race), adverse treatment (disqualification without individualized assessment), and minimal facts suggesting inference of discriminatory intent (defendant's knowledge of racial disparities in criminal justice system and HUD guidance, yet continued offering automated product).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Policies requiring power of attorney from conserved individuals and refusing to accept conservatorship documentation; disparate impact on disabled individuals more likely to be conserved and unable to execute power of attorney
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs alleged two facially neutral policies with disproportionate impact on disabled individuals. Court rejected defendant's argument that statistical evidence was required at pleading stage, finding allegations sufficient to satisfy prima facie burden under Inclusive Communities Project framework.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request for disclosure of underlying tenant screening report to conservator (Ms. Arroyo) in lieu of power of attorney requirement; necessary to allow conservator to challenge disqualification and request individualized assessment from housing provider
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs alleged all five elements of failure to accommodate: (1) Mikhail Arroyo had significant disabilities; (2) defendant knew of disabilities; (3) accommodation was necessary to afford equal opportunity to use and enjoy dwelling; (4) accommodation was reasonable because conservatorship gave Ms. Arroyo more power than power of attorney; (5) defendant refused. Defendant's argument that no different treatment of non-disabled individuals was alleged lacks support at pleading stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Connecticut Unfair Trade Practices Act (CUTPA) claim based on unfair and deceptive practices: failure to make individualized assessment of criminal records, failure to disclose underlying records, marketing CrimSAFE as improving fair housing compliance while knowing of discriminatory effect, requiring power of attorney instead of accepting conservatorship, and discrimination based on race and disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs sufficiently alleged unfair or deceptive practices under CUTPA's cigarette rule by showing practices offend public policy (FHA, FCRA, conservatorship statute), are unethical and unscrupulous, and cause substantial injury. Plaintiffs alleged ascertainable loss (housing denial, deprivation of FCRA rights) proximately caused by defendant's conduct. File disclosure practices sufficiently related to defendant's commercial relationship with WinnResidential to constitute trade or commerce.

source_file: 7253536_2019_Nat'l Ass'n of the Deaf v. Harvard Univ._dcd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Captioning and audio description for online video content; auxiliary aids and services to provide meaningful access to deaf and hard of hearing individuals to online educational content, lectures, videos, and other audiovisual materials
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 12(c) - Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied Harvard's motion for judgment on the pleadings on Title III ADA and Section 504 claims. Court held that plaintiffs adequately pleaded a nexus between online content and physical locations at Harvard, and that auxiliary aids/services obligations apply to online content. CDA immunity applies only to embedded third-party content not created or developed by Harvard; claims as to Harvard-created content and third-party content hosted on Harvard platforms survive.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege a distinct and palpable injury under ADA § 12203(b). The defendant's statement that the State Bar would be interested in plaintiff's conduct was not conditioned on plaintiff forgoing ADA rights, and plaintiff did not allege he was forced to abandon any ADA claims or suffered injury from the alleged threat.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III public accommodations access claim; Hawaii state law accessibility claims; unfair and deceptive practices; nondisclosure; negligence
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff and defendant KLC filed a stipulation to dismiss with prejudice all claims against KLC on April 26, 2019, resolving the non-FHA claims by agreement.

source_file: 7253788_2019_Poursaied v. Reserve at Research Park LLC_alnd
case_name: Shahnaz Poursaied v. Reserve at Research Park LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought a quiet, soundproof apartment as an accommodation for alleged noise sensitivity, which the court found was not a recognized disability and the requested accommodation was not reasonable.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claim because she failed to allege any facts establishing she is disabled within the meaning of the FHA, failed to show she requested a specific reasonable accommodation, and admitted the defendant offered her options (move out or wait for another unit) without refusing accommodation.
brief_summary: Shahnaz Poursaied, proceeding pro se, sued her landlord Reserve at Research Park LLC alleging the landlord violated the FHA by failing to accommodate her alleged noise sensitivity by providing a soundproof apartment. The court granted defendant's motion to dismiss, finding plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts establishing she is disabled under the FHA, failed to request a specific reasonable accommodation, and admitted the defendant offered her options to address her concerns.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condominium Ass'n, 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014)
Schwarz v. City of Treasure Island, 544 F.3d 1201 (11th Cir. 2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged that defendant's apartment personnel promised a quiet, sound-proof apartment and failed to accommodate her for a disability related to noise sensitivity. Plaintiff requested either a move-out option or transfer to another unit.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff failed to allege any facts establishing she was disabled within the meaning of the FHA or that she had a disability involving noise sensitivity. The court also found plaintiff failed to allege facts showing defendant refused to accommodate her within the 19-day window between lease signing and filing suit, noting defendant offered her options (move out in 30 days or wait 6 months for another unit). Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege the four elements of a failure-to-accommodate claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alabama Uniform Residential Landlord Tenant Act (AURLTA) claim for failure to maintain apartments in good repair to prevent noise penetration; invasion of privacy claim based on alleged criminal noise torture from neighbors and traffic.
fha_claims.reasoning: Under AURLTA, plaintiff failed to allege defendant violated any applicable building or housing codes; no codes require sound-proof apartments and the lease contained no warranties regarding sound. Under invasion of privacy, plaintiff failed to allege defendant caused the intrusion or failed to remedy it; defendant is not liable for unforeseeable criminal actions of third parties (neighbors and traffic). Court could not draw reasonable inference of liability from facts pleaded.

case_name: Noah v. Assor
accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought to be free from sexual harassment by her landlord; no disability accommodation request was made in this case.
key_holding: The court denied dismissal of plaintiff's § 3617 interference claim, finding that plaintiff's allegations plausibly stated quid pro quo and hostile environment sexual harassment claims sufficient to survive a motion to dismiss, while dismissing plaintiff's § 3604(f)(1)-(2) claims for failure to plead she was 'ready, willing, and able' to renew her lease.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Marlen Noah sued her former landlord Isaac Assor alleging pervasive sexual harassment in violation of the federal and Florida Fair Housing Acts, including quid pro quo harassment (conditioning lease renewal on sexual relations) and hostile environment harassment (unwanted propositions, trespass, stalking, and sexually explicit communications). The court denied defendant's motion to dismiss the § 3617 interference claim, finding plaintiff's allegations sufficient to state quid pro quo and hostile environment sexual harassment claims, but granted dismissal of the § 3604(f)(1)-(2) discrimination claims for failure to plead the 'ready, willing, and able' element.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Lawrence v. Courtyards at Deerwood Ass'n, Inc., 318 F. Supp. 2d 1133 (S.D. Fla. 2004)
West v. DJ Mortg., LLC, 164 F. Supp. 3d 1393 (N.D. Ga. 2016)
Quigley v. Winter, 598 F.3d 938 (8th Cir. 2010)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff plausibly alleged quid pro quo and hostile environment sexual harassment under § 3617 interference theory, applying HUD regulations and totality of circumstances test. Defendant's motion to dismiss this claim was denied; claim survives and proceeds.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege she is disabled, which is required to state a claim under § 3604(f)(1)-(2). Court granted motion to dismiss but allowed plaintiff leave to amend to correct inadvertent pleading error by citing §§ 3604(b)-(c) instead.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Count II under Fla. Stat. § 760.37 (state counterpart to § 3617) survives motion to dismiss on identical reasoning as federal § 3617 claim. Court found plaintiff plausibly alleged interference through quid pro quo and hostile environment sexual harassment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Count III under Fla. Stat. § 760.23(3) survives motion to dismiss. Court found plaintiff adequately pleaded that defendant made oral and written statements indicating sex-based preference/limitation with respect to rental (lease renewal), satisfying all three elements of the claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
