Miami v. Wells Fargo & Co., 923 F.3d 1260 (11th Cir. 2019)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: County's disparate-impact claim based on alleged 'equity stripping scheme' and facially neutral loan origination policies failed because the County's expert testimony was excluded as unreliable under Daubert/Rule 702, and without that statistical evidence, the County could not establish the causal link between the banks' policies and the alleged disparate impact on minority borrowers required by Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: County's second disparate-impact claim based on facially neutral mortgage servicing and foreclosure practices failed for the same reason as Count I: exclusion of expert testimony left no evidentiary basis to establish the causal link between the banks' policies and disparate impact on minority borrowers.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: County's disparate-treatment claim based on an alleged integrated equity-stripping scheme failed because the summary judgment record showed individual banks developed their own programs at different times for different reasons, and the County's own expert conceded such a coordinated scheme would not have made economic sense for the banks.

case_name: James Nathaniel Douse v. Sabrina Traeger
accommodation_description: Complaint was inadequate and incomprehensible, failing to articulate a specific accommodation request; claims related to HOA assessments and property deposit disputes rather than a discrete accommodation.
key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed dismissal because plaintiff's FHA complaint was wholly insubstantial and frivolous, containing no factual allegations establishing a violation of any FHA provision, and even construing the complaint generously, the claims regarding HOA fees and property deposits did not relate to discriminatory conduct on a protected basis.
brief_summary: James Douse, proceeding pro se, appealed the sua sponte dismissal of his Fair Housing Act complaint against private individuals and a homeowners association for lack of subject matter jurisdiction. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed, finding Douse's complaint wholly insubstantial and frivolous because it failed to allege any factual content establishing that defendants engaged in conduct prohibited by the FHA, instead raising only contract claims regarding HOA assessments and a pool construction deposit.
key_cases_cited: Univ. of S. Ala. v. Am. Tobacco Co., 168 F.3d 405 (11th Cir. 1999)
Blue Cross & Blue Shield of Ala. v. Sanders, 138 F.3d 1347 (11th Cir. 1998)
Barnett v. Okeechobee Hosp., 283 F.3d 1232 (11th Cir. 2002)
Lawrence v. Dunbar, 919 F.2d 1525 (11th Cir. 1990)
Diaz v. Sheppard, 85 F.3d 1502 (11th Cir. 1996)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court affirmed the district court's sua sponte dismissal for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because plaintiff's complaint failed to allege any factual allegations under the FHA count and did not relate to the sale or rental of a dwelling. The court found the FHA claims wholly insubstantial and frivolous, and plaintiff did not allege discriminatory conduct based on a protected class.

source_file: 9425247_2023_Reese v. Park Place Condominium Homeowners Association I_dcd
case_name: Allison Reese v. Park Place Condominium Homeowners Association I
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged racial discrimination in the denial of access to the HOA's master insurance policy for foundation repairs, not a reasonable accommodation request.
key_holding: The court found Reese's racial discrimination claim under § 3605 survived PPCA's motion to dismiss because she alleged sufficient facts showing PPCA denied her insurance coverage while allowing White owners to make similar repairs, but dismissed her retaliation claim under § 3617 because reporting fraud and waste is not protected activity under the FHA.
brief_summary: Allison Reese, an African-American condo owner, sued her HOA alleging racial discrimination when PPCA denied her six requests to use the master insurance policy for foundation repairs while allowing White owners to make similar claims. The court granted MCM's motion to dismiss as time-barred, dismissed Reese's retaliation claim for failing to allege protected activity, but allowed her race discrimination claim to proceed finding she alleged sufficient facts supporting an inference of discrimination.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Use of condominium association's master insurance policy to fund repairs to plaintiff's unit for foundation defects
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged sufficient facts to survive motion to dismiss under Iqbal/Twombly standard by alleging she is African-American, qualified for coverage under the master policy, and PPCA denied her coverage while allowing White residents to invoke the same policy for identical repairs. The fact that one other African-American resident received coverage does not negate the inference of racial discrimination at the pleading stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation for reporting fraud and waste of association financial resources while serving on the board
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege protected activity under § 3617 because reporting fraud and waste are not protected activities under the FHA's anti-retaliation provision unless the fraud/waste involved discriminatory housing practices. Additionally, plaintiff failed to allege causation because the initial denial occurred in December 2014 before her board service began in 2015, and the alleged retaliatory denials (2018-2021) occurred two years after her board service ended (2016), which is too attenuated to suggest causal connection.

source_file: 9426420_2023_LA Fair Housing Action v. Azalea Garden_ca5
case_name: Louisiana Fair Housing Action Center, Inc. v. Azalea Garden Properties, LLC
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request was analyzed; the case concerned organizational standing to bring a race-based disparate impact claim challenging Azalea Garden's criminal background check policy.
key_holding: LaFHAC lacks organizational standing because it failed to allege facts showing that its diversion of resources to counteract Azalea Garden's alleged discriminatory practices perceptibly impaired its ability to achieve its mission of eradicating housing discrimination.
brief_summary: LaFHAC sued Azalea Garden Properties, LLC alleging that its criminal background check policy had a disparate impact on African American rental applicants in violation of the FHA. The Fifth Circuit dismissed the appeal after finding that LaFHAC, a nonprofit fair housing organization with no members, lacked organizational standing because its alleged injuries—diversion of resources to investigate and counteract the defendant's practices—did not constitute cognizable Article III injury.
key_cases_cited: Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Texas Dept. of Housing & Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)
OCA-Greater Houston v. Texas, 867 F.3d 604 (5th Cir. 2017)
N.A.A.C.P. v. City of Kyle, 626 F.3d 233 (5th Cir. 2010)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The Fifth Circuit held that LaFHAC, a nonprofit fair housing organization without members, lacked Article III standing to bring the disparate impact claim because it failed to allege a cognizable injury in fact. The court found that LaFHAC's diversion of resources to counteract Azalea Garden's alleged criminal background check policy did not perceptibly impair its ability to achieve its mission, as the counteraction efforts fell within its routine activities and LaFHAC failed to allege concrete impairment such as reaching fewer people or conducting fewer activities.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Disability discrimination claim (mentioned in complaint but not substantively addressed)
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court dismissed LaFHAC's disability discrimination claim at the motion to dismiss stage. The appellate court did not reach the merits of this claim because it determined LaFHAC lacked standing to bring any claims, including the disability claim, due to failure to allege a cognizable organizational injury in fact.

case_name: Orlando Garcia v. Gateway Hotel L.P.
accommodation_description: ADA claim regarding hotel reservation policies and website accessibility for persons with disabilities (not an FHA reasonable accommodation case)
key_holding: The ADA's fee- and cost-shifting provision (42 U.S.C. § 12205) does not 'provide otherwise' than Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 54(d)(1), and therefore a prevailing ADA defendant may be awarded costs at the district court's discretion without a finding that the plaintiff's action was frivolous, unreasonable, or without foundation.
brief_summary: Orlando Garcia sued Gateway Hotel L.P. under the Americans with Disabilities Act, challenging the hotel's reservation policies and website practices regarding accessible rooms. After the district court dismissed the case and awarded costs to Gateway, Garcia appealed arguing ADA defendants should only receive costs if the action was frivolous. The Ninth Circuit affirmed, holding that 42 U.S.C. § 12205 does not limit Rule 54(d)(1)'s discretionary cost award standard, effectively overruling prior precedent in Brown, and concluding the district court properly exercised discretion in awarding costs to the prevailing defendant.
key_cases_cited: Brown v. Lucky Stores, Inc., 246 F.3d 1182 (9th Cir. 2001)
Marx v. General Revenue Corp., 568 U.S. 371 (2013)
Green v. Mercy Housing, Inc., 991 F.3d 1056 (9th Cir. 2021)
Christiansburg Garment Co. v. EEOC, 434 U.S. 412 (1978)
Miller v. Gammie, 335 F.3d 889 (9th Cir. 2003) (en banc)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Website information regarding accessible hotel rooms; ADA Title III claim regarding failure to provide information on website permitting determination of accessible accommodations
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court affirmed the district court's award of costs to the prevailing ADA defendant under Rule 54(d)(1), holding that the ADA's fee- and cost-shifting provision (42 U.S.C. § 12205) does not 'provide otherwise' and thus does not displace Rule 54(d)(1)'s discretionary cost-award standard. The court held that Marx v. General Revenue Corp. effectively overruled Brown v. Lucky Stores, Inc., which had applied the Christiansburg standard to ADA cost awards.

source_file: 9427143_2023_National Association of Mutual Insurance Companies v. United States Department of Housing and Urban Development_dcd
case_name: National Association of Mutual Insurance Companies v. United States Department of Housing and Urban Development
accommodation_description: This is not a reasonable accommodation case; NAMIC challenges HUD's Disparate-Impact Rule as exceeding statutory authority under the FHA.
key_holding: HUD's Disparate-Impact Rule does not conflict with the Fair Housing Act as applied to insurers' underwriting and rating practices; NAMIC's four arguments—that the Rule causes pervasive consideration of protected characteristics, is invalidated by state insurance laws, allows claims based solely on statistical disparities, and permits displacement of valid priorities—are all unpersuasive.
brief_summary: The National Association of Mutual Insurance Companies, a trade association whose members sell homeowners insurance, challenged HUD's Disparate-Impact Rule (which establishes a burden-shifting framework for disparate-impact claims under the FHA) as exceeding HUD's statutory authority under the APA and FHA as interpreted by Inclusive Communities. The court denied NAMIC's motion for summary judgment and granted HUD's cross-motion, finding the Rule does not conflict with the FHA and is a permissible construction of the statute.
key_cases_cited: Chevron U.S.A., Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc., 467 U.S. 837 (1984)
Texas Dept. of Housing & Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Griggs v. Duke Power Co., 401 U.S. 424 (1971)
Wards Cove Packing Co. v. Atonio, 490 U.S. 642 (1989)
Am. Ins. Ass'n v. HUD, 74 F. Supp. 3d 30 (D.D.C. 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that HUD's 2023 Disparate-Impact Rule, which reinstates the 2013 Rule, is a permissible construction of the FHA and does not conflict with the limitations imposed by Inclusive Communities. The Rule does not require pervasive consideration of protected characteristics, is not invalidated by state insurance law limitations, does not allow claims based solely on statistical disparities without causation, and does not impermissibly displace valid priorities. HUD's cross-motion for summary judgment was granted.

source_file: 9428257_2023_Sonya Youvett McNeal v. Navy Federal Credit Union_ca11
case_name: Sonya Youvett McNeal v. Navy Federal Credit Union
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request was substantively analyzed; the plaintiff alleged FHA violations in a foreclosure/mortgage dispute, but the case was dismissed for failure to state a claim and the court did not reach the merits of any accommodation request.
key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit lacked jurisdiction to review the district court's dismissal of the complaint and denial of preliminary injunction due to procedural defects (untimely appeal and mootness), and affirmed the denial of the motion to recuse and first motion to reconsider on the merits.
brief_summary: Sonya McNeal, proceeding pro se, appealed from a district court dismissal of her suit against Navy Federal Credit Union over a foreclosure dispute, alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act, CARES Act, and Due Process Clause. The Eleventh Circuit dismissed for lack of jurisdiction over the dismissal order (untimely appeal) and preliminary injunction denial (mootness), and affirmed the denial of the motion to recuse and first motion to reconsider.
key_cases_cited: AT&T Mobility, LLC v. Nat'l Ass'n for Stock Car Auto Racing, Inc., 494 F.3d 1356 (11th Cir. 2007)
Green v. Drug Enf't Admin., 606 F.3d 1296 (11th Cir. 2010)
Bogle v. Orange Cnty. Bd. of Cnty. Comm'rs, 162 F.3d 653 (11th Cir. 1998)
Campbell v. United States, 26 F.4th 860 (11th Cir. 2022)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act claim (nature unspecified in opinion); also CARES Act and Fifth Amendment Due Process Clause claims
fha_claims.disposition: Jurisdictional dismissal; no timely appeal of underlying MTD ruling
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to timely appeal the district court's dismissal of her complaint within 30 days; subsequent motions to reconsider filed six months later did not toll the appeal deadline. The appellate court lacked jurisdiction to review the underlying dismissal order.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: First Amendment retaliation claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 arising from police investigation of arsons; Fourth Amendment claims related to search warrants
fha_claims.disposition: Qualified immunity granted; summary judgment reversed in part
fha_claims.reasoning: Appellate court held that plaintiffs failed to show defendants' conduct violated clearly established law under the First Amendment. Neither a right to remain silent during police questioning nor a right to be free from retaliatory investigations was clearly established at the time of the alleged conduct, so defendants were entitled to qualified immunity.

case_name: Rosemarie Vargas; et al. v. Facebook, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege Facebook's ad platform allowed housing advertisers to exclude protected classes from seeing housing advertisements, limiting access to housing opportunities.
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that plaintiffs adequately alleged Article III standing and that Facebook is not immune from liability under Section 230(c)(1) because Facebook actively developed the discriminatory ad targeting tools rather than merely publishing third-party content.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs filed a class action against Facebook alleging that its advertising platform allowed housing advertisers to exclude protected classes from viewing housing ads, causing concrete injury. The Ninth Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, finding that plaintiffs adequately alleged Article III standing and that Facebook is not immune from liability under Section 230(c)(1) because Facebook materially contributed to the alleged discrimination through its development of ad targeting categories and tools rather than acting as a mere publisher.
key_cases_cited: Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Fair Housing Council of San Fernando Valley v. Roommates.com, LLC, 521 F.3d 1157 (9th Cir. 2008) (en banc)
Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins, 578 U.S. 330 (2016)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Access to housing advertisements on Facebook Marketplace; plaintiffs allege Facebook's targeting methods excluded them from viewing housing ads available to non-protected class members
fha_claims.reasoning: The Ninth Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of Article III standing, holding that plaintiffs adequately alleged a concrete and particularized injury—deprivation of truthful information and housing opportunities—by alleging that Facebook's targeting methods prevented them from viewing housing ads that similarly situated non-protected class members received, even without identifying specific ads. The court rejected the district court's requirement that plaintiffs identify specific ads they could not see when their claim is that an algorithm restricted access in the first place.

source_file: 9433324_2023_Southwest Fair Housing Council v. Wg Scottsdale LLC_ca9
case_name: Southwest Fair Housing Council v. WG Scottsdale LLC
accommodation_description: Request for an American Sign Language interpreter to assist a deaf applicant in understanding and signing a lease at an assisted-living facility.
key_holding: The court held that Southwest Fair Housing Council had organizational standing, sufficient evidence supported the jury's finding that an ASL interpreter was a necessary accommodation to provide a deaf applicant an equal opportunity to enjoy the housing, and the punitive damages award and permanent injunction were appropriate.
brief_summary: Southwest Fair Housing Council sued WG Scottsdale LLC (operator of Atria Sierra Pointe assisted-living facility) after testers were denied an ASL interpreter for a fictional deaf applicant, alleging Fair Housing Act violations. The Ninth Circuit affirmed the jury verdict in favor of Southwest, holding that the organization had standing, the ASL interpreter request was a necessary accommodation under § 3604(f)(3)(B), and the punitive damages award and permanent injunction were supported by evidence of the defendant's reckless indifference to disability accommodation requirements.
key_cases_cited: Giebeler v. M & B Assocs., 343 F.3d 1143 (9th Cir. 2003)
Karczewski v. DCH Mission Valley LLC, 862 F.3d 1006 (9th Cir. 2017)
Fair Hous. of Marin v. Combs, 285 F.3d 899 (9th Cir. 2002)
Valle del Sol Inc. v. Whiting, 732 F.3d 1006 (9th Cir. 2013)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Provision of American Sign Language (ASL) interpreter for deaf applicant during housing application process and lease signing
fha_claims.reasoning: Court affirmed jury verdict that ASL interpreter was a necessary accommodation because, absent the interpreter, the deaf applicant likely would have been denied equal opportunity to enjoy the housing. Substantial evidence supported that complex conversations regarding lease consideration required an interpreter, and defendant knew of the applicant's ASL use and the legal requirement to accommodate.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) Title III claim for failure to provide communication accommodation
fha_claims.reasoning: Court affirmed jury verdict on ADA claim using same necessity standard as FHA claim. Evidence supported that ASL interpreter was necessary accommodation under 42 U.S.C. § 12182(b)(2)(A)(ii).

case_name: Mamberto Real v. Judith Moran
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged national origin discrimination during the rental process, but no specific accommodation request is described.
key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed dismissal of the complaint as a shotgun pleading because each of the seven counts reincorporated vague factual allegations and legal conclusions, making it impossible to determine which allegations supported which claims, and plaintiff forfeited any challenge to dismissal without leave to amend.
brief_summary: Mamberto Real, proceeding pro se, appealed the dismissal of his Fair Housing Act claims alleging national origin discrimination and retaliation against Judith Moran, Frank Diaz Gines, and Presbyterian Homes & Housing Foundation of Florida, Inc. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed, finding the complaint was properly dismissed as a shotgun pleading because each count reincorporated the same vague factual allegations and legal conclusions, failing to give defendants adequate notice of the claims against them.
key_cases_cited: Weiland v. Palm Beach Cty. Sheriff's Off., 792 F.3d 1313 (11th Cir. 2015)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Vibe Micro Inc. v. Shabanets, 878 F.3d 1291 (11th Cir. 2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: National origin discrimination claim under FHA § 3604
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint was dismissed as a shotgun pleading containing multiple counts that reincorporated all preceding allegations, conclusory and vague language, and legal conclusions merged throughout, failing to give defendants adequate notice of the claims and grounds under Iqbal/Twombly standards.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation claim under FHA § 3617 for alleged coercion, intimidation, threat, or interference with exercise of FHA rights during rental process
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint pleaded elements of § 3617 retaliation without explaining how facts correlated to the elements, and failed to give defendants adequate notice of the claim and grounds, constituting a shotgun pleading under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Civil Rights Act of 1964 (Title VI), 42 U.S.C. § 2000d
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint was dismissed as a shotgun pleading containing conclusory and vague allegations that failed to give defendants adequate notice of the claims and grounds.

case_name: Women's Elevated Sober Living L.L.C. v. City of Plano
accommodation_description: Request for a zoning accommodation to exceed the eight-resident capacity limit to allow 15-20 residents in a women's sober living home for individuals recovering from substance use disorders.
key_holding: The Fifth Circuit held that the district court applied the wrong legal standard by accepting that proof of greater therapeutic benefit from larger occupancy was sufficient to establish necessity under § 3604(f)(3)(B); rather, plaintiffs must prove the requested accommodation is indispensable or essential—not merely preferable—to ameliorate their disabilities.
brief_summary: Women's Elevated Sober Living LLC and its owner sued the City of Plano challenging the denial of a zoning accommodation request to allow 15-20 residents in their sober living home beyond the eight-person limit in the SF-7 zoning ordinance. The Fifth Circuit vacated the district court's finding of an FHA violation, holding that the district court improperly applied a standard accepting that therapeutically beneficial treatment constitutes necessity under the FHA, when plaintiffs must instead prove the accommodation is indispensable to recovery.
key_cases_cited: Providence Behav. Health v. Grant Rd. Pub. Util. Dist., 902 F.3d 448 (5th Cir. 2018)
Bryant Woods Inn v. Howard County, 124 F.3d 597 (4th Cir. 1997)
Vorchheimer v. Philadelphian Owners Ass'n, 903 F.3d 100 (3d Cir. 2018)
Cinnamon Hills Youth Crisis Ctr. v. Saint George City, 685 F.3d 917 (10th Cir. 2012)
Harmony Haus Westlake, L.L.C. v. Parkstone Property Owners Ass'n, 851 F. App'x 461 (5th Cir. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: District court determined that plaintiffs failed to prove their disparate treatment claim. The appellate court did not disturb this finding on appeal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: District court determined that plaintiffs failed to prove their disparate impact claim. The appellate court did not disturb this finding on appeal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request to allow occupancy of 15-20 residents in a sober living home, exceeding the zoning ordinance limit of 8 unrelated disabled individuals plus 2 caretakers. Plaintiffs argued the higher capacity was therapeutically necessary for residents recovering from substance use disorders.
fha_claims.reasoning: The Fifth Circuit held that the district court applied an incorrect legal standard by accepting that therapeutically beneficial treatment constitutes necessity. The court held that necessity requires proof that the accommodation is indispensable or essential—that without it, residents receive no ameliorative effect—not merely that it provides greater therapeutic benefit. The testimony that 15 residents provided increased therapeutic benefit over 8 was insufficient to meet this standard. The court vacated the district court's injunction and remanded.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request to allow occupancy of 15-20 residents in a sober living home under a theory of financial necessity, exceeding the zoning ordinance limit of 8 unrelated disabled individuals plus 2 caretakers.
fha_claims.reasoning: District court determined that plaintiffs failed to prove their failure-to-accommodate claim under a theory of financial necessity. The appellate court did not disturb this finding.

source_file: 9443643_2023_Dayton Veterans Residences Ltd. v. Dayton Metro. Housing Authority_ca6
case_name: Dayton Veterans Residences Ltd. Partnership v. Dayton Metro. Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Request for Dayton Metropolitan Housing Authority to amend its Administrative Plan to permit project-based HUD-VASH vouchers for a veteran homeless housing development serving disabled veterans.
key_holding: The Sixth Circuit affirmed that the district court properly instructed the jury using the 'was necessary' standard for reasonable accommodation claims and that Freedom's Path failed to prove its accommodation claim; the court also upheld evidentiary rulings permitting testimony about whether GDPM knew or should have known its prospective tenants were disabled.
brief_summary: Dayton Veterans Residences Limited Partnership (Freedom's Path), a developer of housing for homeless veterans, sued Dayton Metropolitan Housing Authority alleging GDPM failed to reasonably accommodate disabled veterans by refusing to amend its Administrative Plan to permit project-based HUD-VASH vouchers. After a remand from the Sixth Circuit, a jury found for GDPM, and Freedom's Path appealed challenging jury instructions and evidentiary rulings. The Sixth Circuit affirmed, holding the district court properly used the 'was necessary' standard and that GDPM's late disclosure of a witness and admission of evidence about prospective tenants' disabilities did not warrant reversal.
key_cases_cited: Dayton Veterans Residences Ltd. P'ship v. Dayton Metro. Hous. Auth., No. 21-3090, 2021 WL 5411220 (6th Cir. Nov. 19, 2021)
Howard v. City of Beavercreek, 276 F.3d 802 (6th Cir. 2002)
Smith & Lee Associates, Inc. v. City of Taylor, 102 F.3d 781 (6th Cir. 1996)
Anderson v. City of Blue Ash, 798 F.3d 338 (6th Cir. 2015)
Overlook Mut. Homes, Inc. v. Spencer, 415 F. App'x 617 (6th Cir. 2011)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Amendment of GDPM's administrative plan to allow issuance of project-based Section 8 vouchers for Freedom's Path's HUD-VASH supportive housing project for homeless disabled veterans without requiring a competitive bidding process initiated by GDPM
fha_claims.reasoning: On remand after reversal of summary judgment, the jury found that Freedom's Path failed to prove that the requested accommodation (amendment of GDPM's administrative plan) was necessary to afford disabled veterans an equal opportunity to access housing. The jury applied the 'was necessary' standard and the 'equality of opportunity' framework, finding that Freedom's Path did not establish that GDPM knew or should have known the prospective tenants were disabled or that the accommodation was necessary for that purpose.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: On initial summary judgment motion (before reversal in Dayton I), the district court granted summary judgment on Freedom's Path's disparate impact claim. The claim was not revisited on remand and was not tried.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: On initial summary judgment motion (before reversal in Dayton I), the district court granted summary judgment on Freedom's Path's intentional discrimination claim. The claim was not revisited on remand and was not tried.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Freedom's Path alleged claims under both the ADA and FHA. The trial was limited to the reasonable-accommodation claim, which was analyzed under both statutes. The jury verdict applied to both the FHA and ADA theories, with the jury finding that Freedom's Path failed to prove the accommodation was necessary.

source_file: 9447936_2023_Lawrence T. Newman v. Heritage Village West Condominium Association, Inc._ca11
case_name: Lawrence T. Newman v. Heritage Village West Condominium Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: Request for advance notice of toxic chemical use so Beverly Newman can avoid exposure due to her chemical sensitivity disability.
key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed dismissal of retaliation and discriminatory harassment claims as barred by res judicata and statute of limitations, but reversed dismissal of the reasonable accommodation claim (requiring proof of different facts than retaliation) and religious discrimination claim regarding housing services, which were allowed to proceed.
brief_summary: Lawrence and Beverly Newman, tenants in a Florida condominium, sued the Heritage Village West Condominium Association and board members under the Fair Housing Act alleging religious discrimination and failure to accommodate Beverly Newman's chemical sensitivity. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed dismissal of retaliation and discriminatory harassment claims as barred by res judicata and the statute of limitations, but reversed dismissal of the reasonable accommodation and religious discrimination claims regarding housing services, remanding for further proceedings.
key_cases_cited: Lozman v. City of Riviera Beach, 713 F.3d 1066 (11th Cir. 2013)
Albrecht v. State, 444 So. 2d 8 (Fla. 1984)
Tyson v. Viacom, Inc., 890 So. 2d 1205 (Fla. Dist. Ct. App. 2005)
Saadeh v. Stanton Rowing Found., Inc., 912 So. 2d 28 (Fla. Dist. Ct. App. 2005)
United States v. Campbell, 26 F.4th 860 (11th Cir. 2022)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Notice of toxic chemical use; reasonable accommodation for Beverly Newman's extreme sensitivity to toxic chemicals
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court determined that the reasonable accommodation claim was not barred by res judicata because it required proof of different facts than the retaliation claim (comparing § 3604(f) to § 83.64), and remanded for further proceedings on claims not clearly barred by the statute of limitations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of housing services (property maintenance and clean up, participation in committees and meetings, community notices) based on religion
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court held that the disparate treatment claim based on denial of housing services was not barred by res judicata because it required proof of different facts than the state defamation claim (comparing § 3604(a)-(b) to defamation elements), and remanded claims based on undated or post-April 2019 conduct.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliatory eviction and harassment for complaints about toxic chemical use and based on Jewish religion/heritage
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court affirmed dismissal of the retaliation claim (Count V) as barred by res judicata because it relied on the same facts as the retaliatory eviction counterclaim adjudicated on the merits in the prior state court judgment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Harassment through misuse of litigation process, including requesting medical records, serving subpoenas, and demanding proof of chemical sensitivity
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court held that claims of harassment through abuse of court process were barred by res judicata to the extent they relied on conduct before the state court judgment (March 2020), but remanded claims based on undated or post-April 2019 conduct not clearly barred by the two-year statute of limitations.

source_file: 9448201_2023_Inner City Contracting LLC v. Charter Twp. of Northville_ca6

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Disclosure of accessible room information on hotel websites under the ADA Reservation Rule (28 CFR §36.302(e)(1)(ii))
fha_claims.reasoning: The Supreme Court vacated the First Circuit's judgment as moot after plaintiff voluntarily dismissed her suit following sanctions against her attorney. The Court did not reach the merits of the standing question, though Justice Thomas's concurrence argued plaintiff lacked standing because the ADA does not create a statutory right to information (unlike the Fair Housing Act in Havens Realty), and plaintiff had no intent to visit the hotel, thus no concrete injury.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Short breaks and reduced stress; also challenged the district court's ruling that the January 2018 Letter (which sought changes to the daily office environment including compliance with Code of Ethics, adherence to defined roles, end to threats of termination, courtesy in communications, equal treatment, improved gender diversity, acknowledgment of team management, and written policies) was not an accommodation request
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that although Kelly informed the Town of his disabilities (anxiety, depression, high blood pressure), the January 2018 Letter did not adequately communicate a desire for accommodation because it lacked a logical bridge connecting the requested workplace changes to his disabilities. The letter's substance—focused on workplace governance, ethics, and personnel matters—did not make clear that Kelly was seeking assistance for his disabilities rather than addressing workplace grievances and personality conflicts. The court affirmed that to trigger the employer's duty to accommodate, an employee must communicate both his disability and his desire for an accommodation related to that disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Kelly failed to allege facts warranting a reasonable inference of disability discrimination. Although he plausibly alleged constructive discharge and that he was fulfilling the employer's legitimate expectations, he alleged no facts suggesting the Town harbored a discriminatory motive. The court held that temporal proximity between EEOC filings and adverse action supports retaliation claims but not discrimination claims, which require proof that disability was a but-for cause of the adverse action. Kelly's allegations that the Town mistreated multiple employees (not just him) undermined any inference that his disability motivated the conduct.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court did not address the merits of the retaliation claim on appeal because Kelly's retaliation claim survived the motion to dismiss and proceeded to summary judgment. The district court had limited the scope of the retaliation claim by ruling that the January 2018 Letter was not an accommodation request, restricting the claim to allegations of escalating harassment following Kelly's EEOC filings. The court affirmed this limitation but did not reach the ultimate merits of the retaliation claim itself.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Kelly failed to allege that the Town coerced, threatened, intimidated, or interfered with his exercise of ADA rights, or that the Town was motivated by an intent to discriminate. Although the Town's hostile conduct exacerbated his disabilities, he made no allegation that the Town engaged in this behavior to prevent him from filing EEOC charges, requesting accommodations, or pursuing other protected ADA actions. The court held that mere adverse effects on health do not constitute unlawful interference under 42 U.S.C. § 12203(b).

case_name: Nagla Abdelhalim v. Andrew McDevitt
accommodation_description: N/A - harassment/interference claim under § 3617 alleging neighbors violated the FHA through a year-long campaign to force her out of her neighborhood based on her race, national origin, and religion; no reasonable accommodation was requested.
key_holding: The district court abused its discretion in awarding attorneys' fees to defendants because it applied post hoc reasoning, concluding the plaintiff's case was 'without foundation' merely because she did not prevail on summary judgment, without considering the circumstantial evidence she presented supporting her belief that defendants' harassment was motivated by discrimination.
brief_summary: Nagla Abdelhalim, an Egyptian Muslim woman who wears hijab, sued her neighbors alleging they violated the Fair Housing Act by engaging in a year-long campaign of harassment including threats, intimidation, and interference intended to drive her out of her neighborhood based on her race, national origin, and religion. The district court granted summary judgment to defendants and awarded them attorneys' fees. On appeal, the Fourth Circuit vacated the fee award, holding the district court applied the wrong legal standard by engaging in post hoc reasoning and concluding the case was 'without foundation' merely because plaintiff did not prevail at summary judgment.
key_cases_cited: Christiansburg Garment Co. v. EEOC, 434 U.S. 412 (1978)
EEOC v. Propak Logistics, Inc., 746 F.3d 145 (4th Cir. 2014)
EEOC v. Great Steaks, Inc., 667 F.3d 510 (4th Cir. 2012)
Bryant Woods Inn, Inc. v. Howard Cnty., 124 F.3d 597 (4th Cir. 1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges interference with enjoyment of home through harassment, threats, and intimidation based on protected class status (race, national origin, religion).
fha_claims.reasoning: District court granted summary judgment to defendants on the merits, finding plaintiff failed to produce evidence of intentional discrimination based on protected ground. On appeal, the court vacated only the fee award (not the summary judgment itself), holding the district court abused its discretion by applying post hoc reasoning in awarding fees, but the underlying FHA claim was decided against plaintiff at summary judgment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1982 (Civil Rights Act); 42 U.S.C. § 1985(3) (conspiracy to violate Civil Rights Act)
fha_claims.reasoning: District court granted summary judgment on all claims, including non-FHA claims under § 1982 and § 1985(3), based on plaintiff's failure to produce evidence of intentional discrimination. Appeal addressed only fee award, not merits of underlying claims.

case_name: Nagla Abdelhalim v. Aaron Lewis
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation or modification was requested. This case involves interference and coercion claims under FHA § 3617, based on neighbors' alleged discriminatory harassment of plaintiff because of her race, national origin, and religion.
key_holding: The Fourth Circuit vacated the district court's attorneys' fees award to the prevailing defendants because the district court abused its discretion by applying post hoc reasoning—concluding plaintiff's FHA § 3617 claims were 'without foundation' solely because she did not prevail at summary judgment—rather than independently analyzing whether she knew or should have known her claims were groundless when filed.
brief_summary: Nagla Abdelhalim, an Egyptian immigrant and Muslim woman wearing a hijab, sued her neighbors under the FHA (42 U.S.C. § 3617), the Civil Rights Act (§ 1982), and 42 U.S.C. § 1985(3), alleging a year-long campaign of threats, intimidation, and harassment designed to drive her from her home because of her race, national origin, and religion. The district court granted summary judgment to the defendants for lack of evidence of discriminatory intent and then awarded them attorneys' fees, finding Abdelhalim's claims were 'without foundation.' The Fourth Circuit vacated the fee award, holding that the district court failed to engage with Abdelhalim's specific circumstantial evidence of discriminatory motive and improperly equated losing on the merits with having filed a frivolous or unfounded claim.
key_cases_cited: Christiansburg Garment Co. v. E.E.O.C., 434 U.S. 412 (1978)
EEOC v. Propak Logistics, Inc., 746 F.3d 145 (4th Cir. 2014)
Bryant Woods Inn, Inc. v. Howard Cnty., 124 F.3d 597 (4th Cir. 1997)
EEOC v. Great Steaks, Inc., 667 F.3d 510 (4th Cir. 2012)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges interference with enjoyment of home through harassment, threats, and intimidation based on protected class status (race, national origin, religion).
fha_claims.reasoning: District court granted summary judgment to defendants on the merits, finding plaintiff failed to produce evidence of intentional discrimination based on protected ground. On appeal, the court vacated only the fee award (not the summary judgment itself), holding the district court abused its discretion in awarding fees under the Christiansburg standard by applying post hoc reasoning rather than assessing whether the claim was without foundation at the time of filing.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1982 (Civil Rights Act); 42 U.S.C. § 1985(3) (conspiracy to violate Civil Rights Act)
fha_claims.reasoning: District court granted summary judgment on all non-FHA claims on the same basis as the FHA claim—failure to produce evidence of intentional discrimination based on protected ground. The appeal addresses only the fee award, not the merits of the summary judgment.

case_name: Nagla Abdelhalim v. Aaron Lewis
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation or modification was requested; the case involves claims of interference, threats, and intimidation under 42 U.S.C. § 3617 based on the plaintiff's race, national origin, and religion.
key_holding: The Fourth Circuit vacated the district court's award of attorneys' fees to the prevailing defendant-neighbors, holding that the district court abused its discretion by applying impermissible post hoc reasoning—equating plaintiff's failure to survive summary judgment with her claims being 'without foundation'—when plaintiff had presented sufficient circumstantial evidence to establish a reasonable basis for her FHA interference claim.
brief_summary: Nagla Abdelhalim, an Egyptian Muslim immigrant and homeowner, sued her immediate neighbors under the FHA (42 U.S.C. § 3617) and related civil rights statutes, alleging a year-long campaign of harassment intended to drive her from her home because of her race, national origin, and religion. The district court granted summary judgment for defendants on the merits (finding insufficient evidence of discriminatory intent) and then awarded defendants approximately $124,000 in attorneys' fees on the ground that plaintiff's claims were 'without foundation.' On appeal—limited solely to the fee award—the Fourth Circuit vacated the fee award, finding the district court had engaged in prohibited post hoc reasoning by failing to engage with plaintiff's circumstantial evidence arguments and instead inferring lack of foundation merely from her failure to prevail.
key_cases_cited: Christiansburg Garment Co. v. E.E.O.C., 434 U.S. 412 (1978)
Bryant Woods Inn, Inc. v. Howard Cnty., 124 F.3d 597 (4th Cir. 1997)
E.E.O.C. v. Propak Logistics, Inc., 746 F.3d 145 (4th Cir. 2014)
E.E.O.C. v. Great Steaks, Inc., 667 F.3d 510 (4th Cir. 2012)
James v. Jacobson, 6 F.3d 233 (4th Cir. 1993)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges interference with enjoyment of home through harassment, threats, and intimidation based on protected class status (race, national origin, religion).
fha_claims.reasoning: District court granted summary judgment to defendants on the merits, finding plaintiff failed to produce evidence of intentional discrimination based on protected ground. Appellate court vacated only the fee award, not the underlying summary judgment, finding the district court applied post hoc reasoning in awarding fees but affirming that plaintiff's FHA claim lacked evidentiary support at summary judgment stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1982 (Civil Rights Act); 42 U.S.C. § 1985(3) (conspiracy to violate Civil Rights Act)
fha_claims.reasoning: District court granted summary judgment on all non-FHA claims on the same basis as FHA claims—failure to produce evidence of intentional discrimination based on protected ground. Appellate court did not separately address these claims, focusing only on the fee award issue.

case_name: Emmanuel Adewale Adeyinka v. Project Home, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff's incoherent complaint references Fair Housing Act claims and subsidized housing but fails to articulate any specific accommodation request.
key_holding: The complaint was dismissed without prejudice for failing to comply with Rule 8(a)'s minimal pleading standard, as it was too incoherent and deficient to provide defendants adequate notice of the legal claims against them.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Emmanuel Adeyinka filed suit against Project Home and others alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on disability, race, color, and national origin in connection with subsidized housing, but the District Court for the District of Columbia dismissed the complaint without prejudice because it failed to meet Rule 8(a)'s minimal pleading standard, providing no coherent statement of claims or adequate notice to defendants.
key_cases_cited: Haines v. Kerner, 404 U.S. 519 (1972)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges discrimination based on disability in connection with defendants' efforts to find plaintiff subsidized housing; specific accommodation not clearly articulated in complaint
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint fails to meet minimal pleading standard under Rule 8(a); plaintiff fails to allege cogent facts sufficient to give defendants adequate notice of the legal claims, mixing discussion of medications and unrelated case law with vague housing discrimination allegations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint alleges discrimination based on disability, race, color, and national origin but fails to articulate any specific discriminatory conduct or harm; insufficient factual allegations to state a plausible claim.

source_file: 9459326_2024_Vision Warriors Church, Inc. v. Harry Johnston_ca11
case_name: Vision Warriors Church, Inc. v. Harry Johnston
accommodation_description: Vision Warriors requested zoning approval to house up to 55 men in recovery from substance abuse as a reasonable accommodation to operate its faith-based residential rehabilitation center.
key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the County on the FHA reasonable accommodation claim because Vision Warriors failed to demonstrate necessity—specifically, it did not explain why housing 55 residents was therapeutically or economically essential rather than the eight residents legally permitted.
brief_summary: Vision Warriors Church, a faith-based residential ministry for men recovering from substance abuse, sued Cherokee County, Georgia after the County revoked its tenant occupancy permit and denied zoning approval to house up to 55 residents at its rehabilitation center. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the County on the FHA reasonable accommodation claim, finding Vision Warriors failed to establish the requested accommodation was necessary because it offered no evidence explaining why 55 residents was therapeutically or economically essential compared to the eight residents permitted under existing zoning.
key_cases_cited: Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014)
Schwarz v. City of Treasure Island, 544 F.3d 1201 (11th Cir. 2008)
Sailboat Bend, 46 F.4th 1266 (11th Cir. 2022)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Ctr., 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Thai Meditation Ass'n of Alabama, Inc. v. City of Mobile, 980 F.3d 821 (11th Cir. 2020)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish intentional discrimination through direct or circumstantial evidence under the McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework. No direct evidence of discriminatory animus; circumstantial evidence factors (discriminatory effect, historical background, sequence of events, departures from normal criteria) were insufficient to establish that disability played a role in the County's zoning decisions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Housing up to 55 residents (later conceded to 25-30 residents) in a residential zoning district; Vision Warriors legally permitted to house only 8 unrelated persons under existing zoning (4 per parcel plus domestic workers)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish necessity of the requested accommodation. Although the court did not reach the reasonableness/fundamental alteration question, it held that Vision Warriors did not demonstrate that housing 55 (or 25-30) residents would 'alleviate the effects' of residents' disability or that the accommodation was 'crucial to economic viability' compared to the 8 residents legally permitted. The necessity inquiry requires evidence that the accommodation would 'affirmatively enhance quality of life by ameliorating the effects of disability,' which plaintiff failed to provide.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: This case involves claims under Oregon's Unlawful Trade Practices Act (UTPA) for misleading pricing representations on clothing items, not Fair Housing Act claims. The case concerns consumer fraud and false advertising in retail sales, not housing discrimination or reasonable accommodations.
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed the district court's dismissal of monetary damages claims under the UTPA, holding that Clark adequately pleaded ascertainable loss under a 'purchase price theory' where she was induced to purchase items in reliance on misrepresented price history. The court affirmed dismissal of disgorgement/restitution claims for failure to plead inadequate remedy at law, and reversed dismissal of injunctive relief claim, finding Clark has Article III standing based on Davidson v. Kimberly-Clark Corp., though a dissent argued TransUnion undermined that precedent.

source_file: 9467925_2024_Estados Unidos Mexicanos v. Smith _ Wesson Brands Inc._ca1
9468692_2024_Jose Reyes v. Waples Mobile Home Park Limited Partnership_ca4
case_name: Jose Reyes v. Waples Mobile Home Park Limited Partnership
accommodation_description: Mobile home park policy requiring all adult occupants to provide proof of legal status in the United States, challenged as disproportionately ousting Latino families
key_holding: The Fourth Circuit reversed summary judgment for the defendant, holding that the defendant's business necessity defense failed because the anti-harboring statute does not apply to landlords merely entering lease agreements with undocumented immigrants, and the record was insufficient to support the defense.
brief_summary: Latino families residing in Waples Mobile Home Park sued the park operators challenging a policy requiring all adult occupants to provide proof of legal status as having a disparate impact on Latino residents, leading to lease conversions, rent surcharges, and eventual eviction. The Fourth Circuit reversed the district court's summary judgment for the defendant, holding that the anti-harboring statute does not apply to ordinary landlord-tenant leasing relationships and that the record was insufficient to establish a business necessity defense.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dept. of Housing & Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
United States v. Aguilar, 477 F. App'x 1000 (4th Cir. 2012)
United States v. McClellan, 794 F.3d 743 (7th Cir. 2015)
United States v. Vargas-Cordon, 733 F.3d 366 (2d Cir. 2013)
DelRio-Mocci v. Connolly Props. Inc., 672 F.3d 241 (3d Cir. 2012)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed summary judgment for the defendant, holding that the anti-harboring statute does not plausibly create criminal liability for landlords merely leasing to undocumented immigrants in the ordinary course of business. The statute requires active concealment or harboring with intent to shield from detection, not passive housing. The court found Waples failed to meet its burden at Step Two of the Inclusive Communities framework because the policy did not serve a legitimate, plausible interest in avoiding prosecution, and the record was too thin to support a business necessity defense given Waples's inconsistent enforcement and failure to evict noncompliant tenants.

source_file: 9470569_2024_Oxford House, Inc. v. City of Dothan, Alabama_ca11
case_name: Oxford House, Inc. v. City of Dothan, Alabama
accommodation_description: Oxford House sought waiver of the City of Dothan's business license requirement for opening utility accounts at three sober living group homes for recovering addicts.
key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed that Oxford House's requested accommodation—waiving the business license requirement for utility accounts—was not necessary because plaintiffs failed to establish that the business license requirement actually affected residents' therapeutic recovery or created financial hardship directly tied to their addiction disabilities.
brief_summary: Oxford House, Inc. and three sober living group homes sued the City of Dothan, Alabama, alleging the City violated the Fair Housing Act by requiring them to obtain business licenses to open utility accounts. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the City, holding that the requested accommodation was not necessary because plaintiffs failed to produce evidence that the business license requirement actually addressed the needs created by residents' substance use disabilities.
key_cases_cited: Sailboat Bend Sober Living, LLC v. City of Fort Lauderdale, 46 F.4th 1268 (11th Cir. 2022)
Schaw v. Habitat for Humanity of Citrus County, Inc., 938 F.3d 1259 (11th Cir. 2019)
Gundy v. City of Jacksonville, 50 F.4th 60 (11th Cir. 2022)
Hornsby-Culpepper v. Ware, 906 F.3d 1302 (11th Cir. 2018)
Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver of business license requirement to open utility accounts in the name of the Oxford House group homes
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the four-element failure-to-accommodate test and found that plaintiffs failed to establish the necessity prong. The accommodation (waiver of business license requirement) was not necessary to address the effects of residents' substance use disability because: (1) therapeutic arguments lacked evidentiary support—residents would not be the ones filing licenses, and no evidence showed that filing a license would harm familial bonds or the Oxford House model; and (2) financial arguments were speculative and lacked concrete evidence that residents' addiction created inability to afford potential rent increases.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs asserted an intentional discrimination claim but did not appeal the district court's grant of summary judgment in the City's favor on this claim; the appellate opinion does not substantively address the merits of the disparate treatment theory.

source_file: 9471209_2024_Jane Doe v. Allegheny County Housing Authority_ca3
case_name: Jane Doe v. Allegheny County Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Pro se tenant in public housing alleging harassment and retaliation for filing HUD complaints, with claims under FHA and ADA regarding violation of address confidentiality protections
key_holding: The Third Circuit vacated in part the District Court's dismissal with prejudice, holding that the District Court erred in dismissing without granting leave to amend, while agreeing that Doe failed to adequately plead FHA retaliation for lack of causal connection between protected activity and adverse actions
brief_summary: Jane Doe, a pro se tenant in public housing managed by Allegheny County Housing Authority, appealed the District Court's sua sponte dismissal with prejudice of her amended complaint alleging violations of Pennsylvania's Address Confidentiality Program, the Fair Housing Act, and the ADA. The Third Circuit vacated in part and remanded, holding that while Doe failed to adequately plead an FHA retaliation claim under § 3617 for lack of causal connection, the District Court erred in dismissing without granting leave to amend.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Revock v. Cowpet Bay W. Condo. Ass'n
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to adequately plead an FHA retaliation claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3617 because, although filing a complaint with HUD may have been protected activity, the amended complaint lacked sufficient allegations beyond conclusory assertions of a causal connection between that protected activity and the defendants' complained-of actions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Maintenance issues and safety complaints
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's amended complaint failed to plausibly allege discrimination because of race, sex, disability, or any other legally cognizable protected class; the allegations regarding maintenance and safety issues did not illustrate discrimination based on a protected characteristic.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claims; Pennsylvania Address Confidentiality Program (ACP) violations under 23 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 6707
fha_claims.reasoning: The District Court sua sponte dismissed the ACP claim without analyzing whether the statute implies a private right of action; the appellate court vacated and remanded for the District Court to consider in the first instance whether § 6707 implies a private right of action and whether plaintiff plausibly stated a claim. ADA claims were not separately analyzed on appeal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessibility information on hotel websites regarding accessible rooms, as required by the ADA Reservation Rule (28 CFR § 36.302(e)(1)(ii))
fha_claims.reasoning: The Supreme Court vacated the First Circuit's judgment as moot after Laufer voluntarily dismissed her case with prejudice following sanctions against her attorney. The Court did not reach the merits of the standing question, though Justice Thomas's concurrence argues Laufer lacked Article III standing because she alleged no violation of her own rights—the ADA prohibits discrimination based on disability, not failure to provide information, and Laufer disclaimed any intent to visit the hotel.

source_file: 9475346_2024_One Love Housing, LLC v. City of Anoka, MN_ca8
case_name: One Love Housing, LLC v. City of Anoka, Minnesota
accommodation_description: Request for waiver of zoning restriction limiting occupancy to four unrelated persons to allow a seven-resident sober living home for recovering alcoholics and substance abusers.
key_holding: The Eighth Circuit reversed summary judgment for plaintiffs because genuine issues of material fact existed on whether the requested zoning accommodation was reasonable and necessary, and the district court erred in considering expert evidence not presented to the City Council during its initial review of the accommodation request.
brief_summary: One Love Housing, LLC sued the City of Anoka, Minnesota, alleging the City violated the FHA and ADA by denying its request for a reasonable accommodation to waive the four-unrelated-person zoning limit to operate a seven-resident sober living home for recovering addicts. The Eighth Circuit reversed the district court's summary judgment for plaintiffs, holding that genuine issues of material fact existed on whether the accommodation was reasonable and necessary, and the district court erred in considering expert testimony not presented to the City Council during its initial review.
key_cases_cited: Bryant Woods Inn, Inc. v. Howard Cnty., 124 F.3d 597 (4th Cir. 1997)
Lapid-Laurel, L.L.C. v. Zoning Bd. of Adjustment, 284 F.3d 442 (3d Cir. 2002)
Keys Youth Services, Inc. v. City of Olathe, 248 F.3d 1267 (10th Cir. 2001)
Oxford House-C v. City of St. Louis, 77 F.3d 249 (8th Cir. 1996)
Klossner v. IADU Table Mound MHP, LLC, 65 F.4th 349 (8th Cir. 2023)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver of zoning ordinance limiting occupancy to four unrelated persons to allow seven unrelated recovering alcoholics and substance abusers to reside together in a single-family home in an R-1 zone
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed the district court's grant of summary judgment for plaintiffs, holding that genuine issues of material fact existed regarding whether the requested accommodation was reasonable and necessary. The court found that plaintiffs failed to present sufficient evidence to the City Council demonstrating that seven residents were indispensable (rather than merely preferable) for therapeutic purposes, and that financial viability of the business alone cannot justify an accommodation without proof that sober homes as a category need such accommodations. The court applied the burden-shifting framework requiring plaintiffs to prove reasonableness and necessity, with defendant able to rebut by showing undue burden or fundamental alteration.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court did not rule on the disparate treatment claim, noting only that genuine issues of material fact existed. The appellate court declined to grant summary judgment in favor of the City on appeal, holding that the district court should have the initial opportunity to address this claim on remand, and that disputed factual issues preclude summary judgment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court did not rule on the disparate impact claim, noting only that genuine issues of material fact existed. The appellate court declined to grant summary judgment in favor of the City on appeal, holding that the district court should have the initial opportunity to address this claim on remand, and that disputed factual issues preclude summary judgment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) Title II claims for failure to provide reasonable accommodation and disparate treatment/disparate impact discrimination
fha_claims.reasoning: The court analyzed FHA and ADA claims together under the same legal framework, as both statutes apply to municipal zoning decisions and use nearly identical language regarding disability and reasonable accommodations. The ADA reasonable accommodation claim was reversed on the same grounds as the FHA claim—genuine issues of material fact regarding necessity and reasonableness precluded summary judgment for plaintiffs.

source_file: 9475745_2024_BMG Monroe I, LLC v. Village of Monroe_ca2
case_name: BMG Monroe I, LLC v. Village of Monroe
accommodation_description: BMG Monroe I, LLC, a residential developer, claimed the Village of Monroe denied building permits for a 181-unit subdivision motivated by discriminatory animus toward the Hasidic Jewish community to whom the developer intended to market the development.
key_holding: The Second Circuit affirmed dismissal, holding that the developer's FHA and Equal Protection claims were unripe because the developer failed to exhaust administrative remedies by not appealing to the Zoning Board of Appeals for Lots 1, 2, and 3 and not submitting a meaningful variance application after seeking to modify the conditions of its initial variance.
brief_summary: BMG Monroe I, LLC, a residential developer, sued the Village of Monroe under the Fair Housing Act and Equal Protection Clause, alleging discriminatory animus toward the Hasidic Jewish community motivated denials of building permits for a 181-unit subdivision. The Second Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal, finding the claims unripe because the developer failed to exhaust administrative remedies by not appealing permit denials to the Zoning Board of Appeals for all lots and not submitting a meaningful variance application after seeking to modify the conditions of its initial variance.
key_cases_cited: Murphy v. New Milford Zoning Comm'n, 402 F.3d 342 (2d Cir. 2005)
Pakdel v. City & County of San Francisco, 141 S. Ct. 2226 (2021)
Williamson County Regional Planning Commission v. Hamilton Bank of Johnson City, 473 U.S. 172 (1985)
Village Green at Sayville, LLC v. Town of Islip, 43 F.4th 287 (2d Cir. 2022)
Southview Assocs., Ltd. v. Bongartz, 980 F.2d 84 (2d Cir. 1992)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court affirmed dismissal on ripeness grounds, holding that BMG failed to exhaust administrative remedies by not submitting a meaningful second variance application after the Village Planning Board found non-compliance with the SEQRA Findings' architectural conditions. The court found no futility exception applied because the Village had not definitively rejected a variance request and administrative avenues remained available.

source_file: 9476170_2024_Jennifer Akridge v. Alfa Mutual Insurance Company_ca11
case_name: Jennifer Akridge v. Alfa Mutual Insurance Company
accommodation_description: Employment termination allegedly to avoid healthcare costs for employee's multiple sclerosis and migraines — not a housing accommodation case
key_holding: Plaintiff failed to establish causation under the ADA because there was no evidence that the decisionmakers who terminated her knew her individual healthcare costs, and her proffered comparators were not similarly situated since their job responsibilities were not automated to the same extent.
brief_summary: Jennifer Akridge sued her former employer Alfa Mutual Insurance Company under the Americans with Disabilities Act, alleging that Alfa terminated her to avoid paying healthcare costs for her multiple sclerosis and severe migraines. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed summary judgment for Alfa, finding that Akridge presented insufficient evidence that the decisionmakers knew her individual healthcare costs or that her disability was a but-for cause of her termination.
key_cases_cited: Gross v. FBL Financial Services, Inc., 557 U.S. 167 (2009)
Bostock v. Clayton County, 140 S. Ct. 1731 (2020)
City of Hollywood v. Hoch
Price Waterhouse v. Hopkins, 490 U.S. 228 (1989)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA employment discrimination claim for termination allegedly motivated by disability-related healthcare costs; also includes reasonable accommodation claim under ADA Title I
fha_claims.reasoning: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed summary judgment on the disparate treatment claim, holding that Akridge failed to establish but-for causation under the ADA because no evidence showed the decisionmakers knew her individual healthcare costs. The court also affirmed summary judgment on the reasonable accommodation claim because Akridge abandoned it by failing to raise it in her opposition brief below, and she forfeited any challenge to that abandonment finding on appeal.

source_file: 9476529_2024_Miller v. First United Bank and Trust_ca10
case_name: Miller v. First United Bank and Trust Co.
accommodation_description: This is not an FHA reasonable accommodation case; it concerns credit discrimination claims under ECOA and 42 U.S.C. § 1981 arising from denial of a commercial loan application for an apartment complex. The district court dismissed the FHA claim, and Plaintiffs did not appeal that ruling.
key_holding: The Tenth Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal of Plaintiffs' ECOA and § 1981 claims, holding that individual guarantors lack statutory standing to bring ECOA claims because Regulation B's definition of 'applicant' includes guarantors only for purposes of the signature rules, which were not violated here, and that Plaintiffs' § 1981 injuries were derivative of CDMR's harm rather than their own.
brief_summary: Black individuals and their LLC sued First United Bank under ECOA and § 1981 alleging racial discrimination in the denial of a commercial loan to purchase an apartment complex. The district court dismissed their claims for lack of standing, and the Tenth Circuit affirmed, holding that guarantors lack ECOA standing absent a signature-rule violation and that plaintiffs' § 1981 injuries were derivative of the LLC's harm rather than their own.
key_cases_cited: Domino's Pizza, Inc. v. McDonald, 546 U.S. 470 (2006)
RL BB Acquisitions, LLC v. Bridgemill Commons Development Group, 754 F.3d 380 (6th Cir. 2014)
Guides, Ltd. v. Yarmouth Grp. Prop. Mgmt., Inc., 295 F.3d 1065 (10th Cir. 2002)
Regions Bank v. Legal Outsource PA, 936 F.3d 1184 (11th Cir. 2019)
Chevron, U.S.A., Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc., 467 U.S. 837 (1984)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court dismissed the FHA claim for failure to state a plausible claim under the Iqbal/Twombly standard, reasoning that the FHA did not apply under the alleged circumstances (credit discrimination in loan denial). The Individuals did not challenge this ruling on appeal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ECOA (Equal Credit Opportunity Act, 15 U.S.C. § 1691(a)); 42 U.S.C. § 1981 (civil rights contract claim)
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court dismissed the Individuals' ECOA and § 1981 claims for failure to state a plausible claim. The court held that guarantors are not 'applicants' under the ECOA except for purposes of the signature rules, which were not alleged here. For § 1981, the court found the Individuals lacked statutory standing because they failed to identify injuries flowing from their own contractual relationship with the bank, only from CDMR's proposed relationship. The appellate court affirmed on all grounds.

case_name: Amia L. Bryant v. Darrell Steinburg
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed the dismissal because Bryant failed to allege facts sufficient to show that defendants discriminated against her on the basis of a protected status under 42 U.S.C. § 3604, lacking either allegations of intentional discrimination because of a protected characteristic or a discriminatory effect on a protected class.
brief_summary: Amia L. Bryant, proceeding pro se, appealed the district court's dismissal of her Fair Housing Act claims against the Mayor of Sacramento, Sacramento Housing and Redevelopment Agency officials, and others in connection with a government housing program. The Ninth Circuit affirmed, holding that Bryant failed to plead facts sufficient to establish either intentional discrimination because of a protected characteristic or a discriminatory effect on a protected class under 42 U.S.C. § 3604.
key_cases_cited: Watison v. Carter, 668 F.3d 1108 (9th Cir. 2012)
Avenue 6E Investments, LLC v. City of Yuma, 818 F.3d 493 (9th Cir. 2016)
Padgett v. Wright, 587 F.3d 983 (9th Cir. 2009)
United States v. Elias, 921 F.2d 870 (9th Cir. 1990)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges discrimination based on protected status in connection with government housing program
fha_claims.reasoning: District court properly dismissed FHA claims under § 1915(e)(2) because plaintiff failed to allege facts sufficient to show defendants discriminated against her on the basis of a protected status as required by 42 U.S.C. § 3604. The complaint did not establish either intentional discrimination because of a protected characteristic or a discriminatory effect on a protected class.

source_file: 9484516_2024_Francine Arthur v. Windsor Shadows Homeowner's Association_ca9
case_name: Francine M. Arthur v. Windsor Shadows Homeowner's Association
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for defendant because plaintiff failed to provide admissible evidence of disparate treatment, or of an adverse action that more likely than not was motivated by discrimination.
brief_summary: Francine M. Arthur, proceeding pro se, appealed the district court's summary judgment and dismissal of her Fair Housing Act claims against Windsor Shadows Homeowner's Association, alleging discrimination based on race and disability. The Ninth Circuit affirmed, finding that Arthur failed to present admissible evidence establishing disparate treatment or that an adverse action was motivated by discrimination.
key_cases_cited: Budnick v. Town of Carefree, 518 F.3d 1109 (9th Cir. 2008)
Canady v. Prescott Canyon Ests. Homeowners Ass'n, 60 P.3d 231 (Ariz. Ct. App. 2002)
Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination based on race and disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to provide admissible evidence of disparate treatment or an adverse action motivated by discrimination under the prima facie framework established in Budnick v. Town of Carefree.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Arizona Fair Housing Act, breach of covenant of quiet enjoyment, breach of fiduciary duty, fraud, harassment claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to provide admissible evidence supporting her non-FHA claims: no evidence of landlord-tenant relationship for quiet enjoyment claim; no evidence supporting breach of fiduciary duty or fraud claims; harassment claims dismissed for failure to identify a statute providing a private cause of action.

case_name: Frank C. Briggs v. James D. Campbell
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege Defendants failed to maintain their apartments and discriminated against them based on race and disability in the provision of housing services.
key_holding: The court dismissed Plaintiffs' FHA claim because they failed to allege a facially neutral policy or practice with disparate impact on a protected class, and their bare allegations of intentional discrimination were insufficient to state a disparate treatment claim.
brief_summary: Black disabled tenants sued their private landlords alleging the failure to maintain their apartments and discriminatory housing practices violated the Fair Housing Act. The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss, finding Plaintiffs failed to allege a facially neutral policy with discriminatory effect or factual allegations supporting intentional discrimination based on race or disability.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Boykin v. Fenty, 650 F. App'x 42 (D.C. Cir. 2016)
Tex. Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Cmtys. Project, 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
