fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to allege that Defendants had a facially neutral practice or policy of failing to maintain apartments or that such a policy had a disparate impact on a protected class. Plaintiffs pleaded only individual experiences without statistical or comparative evidence showing disparate impact on Black or disabled tenants versus others.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to allege facts supporting intentional discrimination based on race or disability. The complaint contained only legal conclusions (that the failure to maintain was 'disparate treatment') and bare allegations of protected class membership without factual allegations connecting Defendants' conduct to discriminatory intent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Violations of D.C. housing laws (Counts III, IV, V); violations of 18 U.S.C. §§ 241, 242, 371, 1341 (Counts I, VI, VII, VIII)
fha_claims.reasoning: Criminal statutes (§§ 241, 242, 371, 1341) do not create private causes of action. D.C. law claims lack federal question jurisdiction and diversity jurisdiction is absent because plaintiffs and defendants share D.C. citizenship. Court declined supplemental jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3).

case_name: Smith v. AMH 2014-1 Borrower, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested additional time to vacate/move from his rental unit as a reasonable accommodation for his Crohn's disease.
key_holding: The court affirmed dismissal because plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts showing his Crohn's disease substantially limits a major life activity to qualify as a disability under the FHA, and because his requested accommodation (delay of eviction) did not address the needs created by his alleged disability.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Dwight Smith sued American Homes 4 Rent alleging the landlord failed to reasonably accommodate his Crohn's disease by refusing to grant additional time to vacate the premises, and unlawfully retaliated by continuing eviction proceedings after he requested accommodations. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal, finding Smith failed to adequately plead a disability under the FHA and that his requested accommodation (delay of eviction) did not address his alleged disability needs.
key_cases_cited: Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condo. Ass'n, 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014)
Schaw v. Habitat for Human. of Citrus Cnty., Inc., 938 F.3d 1259 (11th Cir. 2019)
Schwarz v. City of Treasure Island, 544 F.3d 1201 (11th Cir. 2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request for more time to move/delay of eviction due to disability (Crohn's disease)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts showing he was disabled within the FHA definition (did not allege how Crohn's disease substantially limits major life activities beyond hospitalization and transfusion). Additionally, even if disability were established, the requested accommodation (delay of eviction) is not facially reasonable because it does not address the needs created by the disability and would constitute a fundamental alteration requiring removal of the 'hump' rather than merely saddling the camel.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Retaliation claim fails due to temporal sequence: AMH initiated eviction proceedings on March 4, 2021, and sent multiple move-out notices on March 9, 10, 15, and 19, but plaintiff did not send his accommodation request until March 20, 2021. Because the allegedly retaliatory action (eviction notices) preceded the protected activity (accommodation request), plaintiff failed to allege facts sufficient to support a retaliation claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3617.

source_file: 9493619_2024_Kalvin Schanz v. City of Otsego, Mich._ca6
case_name: Kalvin Schanz v. City of Otsego, Michigan et al.
accommodation_description: Schanz alleged that city officials' comments opposing his plan to house immigrant workers at JBS constituted racial discrimination and retaliation under the FHA
key_holding: The Sixth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for defendants because Schanz failed to create a triable issue on the first element of his § 3617 claim—he presented no evidence that he actually aided or encouraged JBS's immigrant employees in exercising their FHA rights, as his speculative housing plan never progressed beyond idle comments to city officials.
brief_summary: Kalvin Schanz sued the City of Otsego, Michigan and city officials under the Fair Housing Act, claiming that officials' opposition to his speculative plan to house immigrant workers at JBS constituted discrimination and retaliation under § 3617. The Sixth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for defendants, holding that Schanz failed to establish that he actually aided or encouraged JBS's immigrant employees in exercising their FHA rights, as his housing plan never progressed beyond idle comments to officials who were not even decisionmakers at the time.
key_cases_cited: Linkletter v. W. & S. Fin. Group, Inc., 851 F.3d 632 (6th Cir. 2017)
Hood v. Midwest Sav. Bank, 95 F. App'x 768 (6th Cir. 2004)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish the first element of a § 3617 'aided or encouraged' claim because he presented no evidence that he actually aided or encouraged JBS immigrant employees in exercising FHA rights. His speculative conversations with city officials about a hypothetical housing plan, untethered from any practical action or contact with prospective tenants, do not constitute protected conduct under § 3617.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 procedural due process claim; Fourth Amendment claim (not renewed on appeal)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a constitutionally protected property interest necessary for a procedural due process claim. The building was never demolished, and plaintiff has no property interest in procedures themselves or in market consequences of a notice of an appealable building-code order.

case_name: Ashley Christina McClendon v. Peter Bresler
accommodation_description: Request to waive landlord's 'no dogs' policy to permit McClendon's emotional support animal to reside in the rental unit as a reasonable accommodation for disability.
key_holding: The district court did not clearly err in finding that the landlord had constructive knowledge of the prospective tenant's disability based on the rental application disclosing a 'registered support animal' and subsequent emails identifying the dog as a verified emotional support animal, and thus violated the FHAA by denying the accommodation request due to his blanket 'no dogs' policy.
brief_summary: Ashley McClendon sued landlord Peter Bresler after he denied her rental application because of his 'no dogs' policy, despite her disclosing an emotional support animal as a reasonable accommodation. The Ninth Circuit affirmed the district court's judgment that Bresler violated the Fair Housing Amendments Act, finding sufficient evidence that Bresler knew or should have known of McClendon's disability based on her rental application and follow-up emails identifying the animal as a verified emotional support animal.
key_cases_cited: Dubois v. Ass'n of Apartment Owners of 2987 Kalakaua, 453 F.3d 1175 (9th Cir. 2006)
Oregon Bureau of Labor & Industries ex rel. Fair Hous. Council of Or. v. Chandler Apartments, LLC, 702 F. App'x 544 (9th Cir. 2017)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation to allow plaintiff to keep a registered emotional support animal (dog) in rental property despite landlord's 'no dogs' policy
fha_claims.reasoning: District court found that defendant had constructive knowledge of plaintiff's disability based on rental application disclosing 'registered support animal' and subsequent emails identifying it as an emotional support animal; defendant's blanket 'no dogs' policy violated FHAA § 3604(f)(3)(B) by failing to provide reasonable accommodation. Appellate court affirmed, finding no clear error in the district court's factual findings regarding defendant's knowledge and the violation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) § 12955 violation; state negligence law claim
fha_claims.reasoning: District court held that defendant violated FEHA § 12955 (parallel to FHAA) and state negligence law by denying rental application based on no-dogs policy; appellate court affirmed the judgment without separately analyzing the non-FHA claims, indicating they were resolved on the same factual and legal basis as the FHAA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: This case involves claims under the Communications Decency Act § 230(c)(1), not the Fair Housing Act. The claims are: (1) negligence, (2) breach of contract, (3) breach of covenant of good faith and fair dealing, (4) violation of California's Unfair Competition Law (UCL), and (5) unjust enrichment, all arising from Meta's alleged failure to prevent fraudulent third-party advertisements on its platform.
fha_claims.reasoning: The Ninth Circuit affirmed dismissal of non-contract claims (negligence, unjust enrichment, UCL) under CDA § 230(c)(1) immunity because they seek to treat Meta as a publisher or speaker of third-party content and do not require Meta to materially contribute to the unlawfulness. The court vacated dismissal of contract claims (breach of contract and breach of covenant of good faith and fair dealing) because they derive from Meta's contractual duty to moderate advertisements, not from its status as a publisher, and thus § 230(c)(1) does not apply.

case_name: Victorio Campos v. 1169 Palms LLC
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: The court issued an order to show cause why it should not decline supplemental jurisdiction over plaintiff's state law claims because they substantially predominate over the Fair Housing Act and Civil Rights Act claims over which the court has original jurisdiction.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Victorio Campos filed a First Amended Complaint against 1169 Palms LLC and related defendants alleging Fair Housing Act, California Fair Employment and Housing Act, and numerous state law claims. The court issued an order to show cause why it should not decline to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the state law claims, finding they appear to substantially predominate over the federal claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not specified in opinion
fha_claims.reasoning: Court issued an Order to Show Cause regarding supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims, finding that plaintiff's state law claims substantially predominate over the FHA claim. The FHA claim itself was not addressed on the merits; the opinion concerns only jurisdictional analysis under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c).

brief_summary: Plaintiffs United African-Asian Abilities Club and Jessie James Davis IV sued Defendant 1939 Wallace, LP alleging violations of the ADA, Fair Housing Act, and California's Unruh Act. The court issued an order to show cause regarding supplemental jurisdiction over the Unruh Act claims, ordering plaintiffs to demonstrate why the court should not decline jurisdiction given concerns about high-frequency litigants circumventing California state procedural requirements.

fha_claims.reasoning: Court issued an Order to Show Cause regarding supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims; no substantive analysis of FHA claims was conducted. The opinion addresses only jurisdictional issues, not the merits of any FHA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA claims and California Unruh Civil Rights Act claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Court issued an Order to Show Cause regarding supplemental jurisdiction over Unruh Act claims; no substantive analysis of non-FHA claims was conducted. The opinion addresses only jurisdictional issues under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c).

case_name: Neway Mengistu v. Forestview Apartments, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that defendants apply to HACLA for a Section 8 exception payment standard—a government subsidy mechanism that could increase the monthly voucher payment above the standard—so that defendants could finance approximately $30,840 in wheelchair-accessibility modifications (including bathroom modifications and other alterations) and recoup those costs over time from the elevated subsidy payments, rather than paying for the modifications out-of-pocket.
key_holding: The court granted defendants' motion for summary judgment on two independent grounds: plaintiff's FHA and related claims were time-barred because they accrued on May 11, 2017—more than two years before suit was filed—and, on the merits, defendants were not required under the FHA to apply for a Section 8 exception payment standard as a reasonable accommodation, nor did plaintiff present evidence of discriminatory motive.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Neway Mengistu, a wheelchair user, applied to rent an apartment from Forestview Apartments using a Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher and requested that defendants apply for a Section 8 exception payment standard to fund approximately $30,840 in accessibility modifications; defendants cancelled his application after determining they could not cover the modification costs and HACLA would not directly fund them. The court granted defendants' motion for summary judgment on two independent grounds: the claims accrued on May 11, 2017 when the application was cancelled—over two years before the June 12, 2019 filing date—making them time-barred, and the court further held that no case law supports requiring a landlord to apply for federal exception payment standards as a reasonable accommodation under the FHA. The court also found no evidence of discriminatory animus, as defendants had repeatedly offered plaintiff the unit and cancelled only after he refused to sign the lease in a timely manner and neither party could cover the modification costs.
key_cases_cited: Dubois v. Ass'n of Apartment Owners of 2987 Kalalaua, 453 F.3d 1175 (9th Cir. 2006)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Garcia v. Brockway, 526 F.3d 456 (9th Cir. 2008)
Ledbetter v. Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co., 550 U.S. 618 (2007)
Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242 (1986)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request for Exception to Payment Standard under Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher program to increase the subsidy cap above the standard payment amount, allowing the landlord to finance accessibility modifications (bathroom and structural modifications) and recoup costs from the increased subsidy payments.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that as a matter of law, landlords are not required under the FHA to apply for government funding or exception payment standards as a reasonable accommodation. The court rejected the expansion of FHA obligations to require landlords to petition housing authorities for such accommodations, finding no case law or regulatory support for this theory.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged refusal to rent the unit to plaintiff based on his disability status.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found no genuine dispute of material fact regarding discriminatory motive. Defendants established a legitimate, non-discriminatory reason for cancellation (inability to afford $30,840 in modifications and lack of government funding), and plaintiff failed to present evidence beyond speculation that this reason was pretextual or that animus against disabled persons motivated the decision.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) disability discrimination claim, Unruh Civil Rights Act § 51 claim, retaliation claims under FHA and FEHA, and negligence claim.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court analyzed FEHA and Unruh Act claims coextensively with FHA claims under the same reasonable accommodation framework and applied the same legal standards. All state law claims failed on the same bases as the FHA claims: the requested accommodation was not legally required, and there was no evidence of discriminatory motive. Retaliation and negligence claims were not separately analyzed but were encompassed in the summary judgment ruling.

case_name: C.R. v. PLB Management LLC et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested assignment of the unassigned parking space directly in front of his apartment as a reasonable accommodation for his disabilities affecting his ability to ambulate safely.
key_holding: The court denied the preliminary injunction motion because plaintiff failed to demonstrate immediate and irreparable injury, noting plaintiff's years-long delay in seeking injunctive relief undermined his claimed urgency and irreparable harm, and his monetary requests for parking and window upgrades were compensable in damages.
brief_summary: C.R., a minor with physical, mental, and emotional disabilities, sued Park La Brea apartment complex through his guardian, seeking a preliminary injunction to require defendants to assign him a specific parking space and fund upgraded windows as reasonable accommodations for his disabilities. The court denied the motion, finding plaintiff failed to establish immediate and irreparable injury because his years-long delay in seeking injunctive relief and the compensable nature of his monetary requests undercut any claim of urgency.
key_cases_cited: Winter v. Nat. Res. Def. Council, Inc., 555 U.S. 7 (2008)
Garcia v. Google, Inc., 786 F.3d 733 (9th Cir. 2015)
Marlyn Nutraceuticals, Inc. v. Mucos Pharma GmbH & Co., 571 F.3d 873 (9th Cir. 2009)
Oakland Trib., Inc. v. Chron. Publ'g Co., 762 F.2d 1374 (9th Cir. 1985)
Benisek v. Lamone, 138 S. Ct. 1942 (2018)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Assignment of the unassigned street parking space immediately in front of Plaintiff's apartment unit as a reserved parking space
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the preliminary injunction motion on the ground that Plaintiff failed to demonstrate immediate and irreparable injury due to unreasonable delay in seeking relief (more than five years from initial move-in, fourteen months through DFEH process, nearly one year in federal court before filing the motion). The court did not reach the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim itself, noting that dispositive motions are under submission and trial is forthcoming.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Upgrade of Plaintiff's apartment windows to double-paned windows to reduce noise intrusion as an accommodation for his disabilities
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the preliminary injunction for the window upgrade on the ground that the cost of windows is easily calculable and compensable in damages, and thus does not constitute irreparable harm warranting mandatory injunctive relief. The court did not reach the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim itself.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: California Civil Code § 54.1 (disability discrimination) and negligence claims
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the preliminary injunction motion on procedural grounds (failure to demonstrate irreparable injury and unreasonable delay) without reaching the merits of the state law claims. The claims survive and remain pending.

case_name: Jason Emer v. Nicole Spearman, et al.
accommodation_description: Defendant tenant raised FHA disability discrimination counterclaims (including failure to accommodate), though the specific accommodation request is not detailed in this order.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's partial motion for summary judgment on his state law claims for unpaid rent and fraudulent inducement, finding genuine disputes of material fact regarding habitability issues (gas leak) and defendant's intent that preclude summary judgment.
brief_summary: Plaintiff landlord Jason Emer sued tenant Nicole Spearman for unpaid rent and fraud arising from a lease for a single-family home at 737 North Fuller Avenue in Los Angeles; the tenant asserted Fair Housing Act counterclaims. The court denied the landlord's partial motion for summary judgment, finding genuine issues of material fact exist regarding habitability defenses related to a gas leak and whether the tenant fraudulently induced the lease agreement.
key_cases_cited: Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986)
Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242 (1986)
Matsushita Elec. Indus. Co. v. Zenith Radio Corp., 475 U.S. 574 (1986)
Gruber v. Gruber, 48 Cal. App. 5th 529 (2020)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff's claims for unpaid rent under California Civil Code § 1951.2 and fraudulent inducement/promissory fraud. Defendant's counterclaims for Fair Housing Act violations (42 U.S.C. § 3604), violation of 42 U.S.C. § 1982, and state law claims for discrimination, stalking, and intentional infliction of emotional distress.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied plaintiff's partial motion for summary judgment on his state law claims (unpaid rent and fraud) because genuine issues of material fact exist regarding the gas leak's impact on habitability and rent obligation, and fraud claims involve fact-intensive issues of intent and reliance unsuitable for summary judgment. Defendant's FHA counterclaims were not addressed in this opinion as the motion targeted only plaintiff's claims.

case_name: C.R. v. PLB Management LLC
accommodation_description: Request that defendant assign Plaintiff a reserved parking space directly in front of his unit as an accommodation for mobility-related disability
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for defendants on the window upgrade claim because Plaintiff refused to bear the expense as required under § 3604(f)(3)(A), but denied summary judgment on the parking space claim because defendants failed to properly serve the unredacted motion and failed to establish the absence of genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether the parking accommodation was necessary and reasonable.
brief_summary: Minor plaintiff C.R., through his guardian, sued PLB Management LLC alleging disability discrimination under the FHA, claiming the landlord failed to reasonably accommodate his mobility disability by refusing to upgrade his apartment windows and by refusing to assign him a preferred parking space. The district court granted summary judgment for defendants on the window upgrade claim (finding it a modification requiring plaintiff to pay) but denied summary judgment on the parking space claim due to defendants' procedural failures in their summary judgment briefing.
key_cases_cited: Giebeler v. M&B Assocs., 343 F.3d 1143 (9th Cir. 2003)
Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986)
Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242 (1986)
Fagundes v. Charter Builders, Inc., 2008 WL 268977 (N.D. Cal. 2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Upgrade of windows in plaintiff's apartment unit to reduce external noise exacerbating plaintiff's disability
fha_claims.reasoning: The court classified the window upgrade request as a reasonable modification under § 3604(f)(3)(A) rather than an accommodation under § 3604(f)(3)(B), because it requires a physical change to the premises. Under the FHA, the tenant bears the expense of modifications, and it is undisputed that plaintiff refused to pay for the windows, so the claim fails as a matter of law.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Assignment of the Preferred Parking Space (located directly in front of plaintiff's unit) as reserved parking to accommodate plaintiff's mobility disability
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied summary judgment on the parking accommodation claim on two independent grounds: (1) defendants failed to serve plaintiff with the unredacted moving memorandum, depriving plaintiff of notice of defendants' arguments; and (2) defendants failed to meet their burden as the moving party by not including material facts in their Statement of Uncontroverted Facts necessary to support their argument that alternative parking was offered at no cost and that relocation was reasonable.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Upgrade of windows in plaintiff's apartment unit to reduce external noise exacerbating plaintiff's disability (California Disabled Persons Act claim)
fha_claims.reasoning: Under the California Disabled Persons Act § 54.1(b)(4), modifications of property are explicitly not required, so plaintiff's DPA claim based on the window upgrade request fails as a matter of law.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Assignment of the Preferred Parking Space as reserved parking to accommodate plaintiff's mobility disability (California Disabled Persons Act claim)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied summary judgment on the DPA parking accommodation claim on the same grounds as the FHA claim: defendants failed to serve the unredacted memorandum and failed to meet their burden by not including necessary material facts in their Statement of Uncontroverted Facts.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Negligence and negligence per se claims under California common law
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted summary judgment on the negligence and negligence per se cause of action because the duty to provide reasonable accommodations is premised on statutory obligations under the FHA and DPA, not on common law theories of negligence, and plaintiff abandoned the issue by not opposing it.

case_name: Ashley Christina McClendon v. Peter Bresler
accommodation_description: Failure to reasonably accommodate disability in rental housing (specific accommodation request not detailed in judgment).
key_holding: The court found that Plaintiff proved Defendant reasonably should have known of her disability and violated the reasonable accommodation provisions of the FHAA (42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(B)) by failing to accommodate her disability.
brief_summary: Ashley McClendon sued Peter Bresler, individually and as trustee of the Bresler Trust, alleging he failed to reasonably accommodate her disability in violation of the Fair Housing Amendments Act. After remand from the Ninth Circuit and a court trial on the briefs, the court found in favor of Plaintiff, awarding $14,800 in compensatory damages for out-of-pocket losses incurred in securing alternative housing.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation for plaintiff's disability in connection with rental of a dwelling

Plaintiff awarded $14,800 in compensatory damages for out-of-pocket losses in securing alternative housing.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) failure to reasonably accommodate claim; negligence claim
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 52(a) - Court Trial on the Briefs
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff proved violation of Cal. Gov't Code § 12955(c) (FEHA reasonable accommodation) and negligence claim. Both claims resulted in judgment in favor of plaintiff with compensatory damages award.

source_file: 9516404_2023_Wilmington Savings Fund Society, FSB v. Bersadeh Bagheri_cacd
case_name: Wilmington Savings Fund Society, FSB v. Bersadeh Bagheri
accommodation_description: This is an unlawful detainer action; no reasonable accommodation claim was analyzed on the merits
key_holding: The court granted plaintiff's motion to remand because defendant failed to establish federal question jurisdiction—the CARES Act, FHA, and PTFA were raised as potential defenses, not as basis for plaintiff's state-law unlawful detainer claim.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Wilmington Savings Fund Society filed an unlawful detainer action in Los Angeles Superior Court against defendants including VRG, who removed the case to federal court arguing federal question jurisdiction based on the CARES Act, Fair Housing Act, and PTFA. The district court granted the motion to remand, finding no federal question jurisdiction because defendant raised these federal statutes as defenses rather than as basis for plaintiff's complaint.
key_cases_cited: Caterpillar, Inc. v. Williams, 482 U.S. 386 (1987)
Kokkonen v. Guardian Life Ins. Co., 511 U.S. 375 (1994)
Valles v. Ivy Hill Corp., 410 F.3d 1071 (9th Cir. 2005)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Defendant VooRooGoo raised Fair Housing Act noncompliance as a potential defense to an unlawful detainer action, but no specific accommodation was requested or at issue.
fha_claims.disposition: Remand (12(b)(1) — lack of subject matter jurisdiction)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that defendant's allegation of FHA violation constitutes a potential defense or counterclaim, not a federal question presented on the face of plaintiff's properly pleaded complaint. Under the well-pleaded complaint rule and Caterpillar, federal law defenses do not confer federal question jurisdiction, and the court remanded for lack of subject matter jurisdiction without reaching the merits of any FHA claim.

case_name: Mark A. Baird, et al. v. PulteGroup, Inc. et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation requested; case involves veteran status discrimination in housing under California FEHA, not a disability accommodation claim
key_holding: Court granted plaintiffs' motion to remand because defendants failed to establish by clear and convincing evidence that Mr. Picano was a fraudulently joined sham defendant, as the law on individual liability under Cal. Gov. Code § 12955 is unsettled and ambiguities must be resolved in plaintiffs' favor.
brief_summary: Individual veterans and their spouse sued PulteGroup, Inc. and its employee alleging discrimination based on veteran status under California's Fair Employment and Housing Act, claiming the developer imposed discriminatory caps on home purchase options for VA loan borrowers and canceled their purchase agreement in retaliation for complaining to the DFEH. The Court granted plaintiffs' motion to remand, finding defendants failed to establish the employee defendant was a fraudulently joined sham defendant.
key_cases_cited: Grancare, LLC v. Thrower, 889 F.3d 543 (9th Cir. 2018)
Hunter v. Phillip Morris USA, 582 F.3d 1039 (9th Cir. 2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination based on veteran status under California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA), Cal. Gov. Code § 12955, relating to VA loan financing and options cap on home upgrades
fha_claims.reasoning: The court remanded the case to state court for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, finding that defendants failed to meet their burden of proving fraudulent joinder of the non-diverse defendant (Mr. Picano) by clear and convincing evidence. The court concluded there remained a non-fanciful possibility that a state court could find plaintiffs could state a claim against Mr. Picano under California law, thus diversity jurisdiction was lacking.

case_name: C.R. v. PLB Management LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested an assigned reserved parking space in front of his apartment unit at Park La Brea for disability-related purposes.
key_holding: The court granted JMOL on causation and damages, finding no evidence PLB's failure to assign the requested parking space caused C.R. emotional harm and no evidence to support the $250,000 damages award, while also finding PLB's reserved parking alternative was reasonable; the court conditionally granted a new trial on these issues and on whether C.R.'s request was an accommodation rather than a modification.
brief_summary: C.R., a minor with a disability, sued PLB Management LLC alleging disability discrimination for refusing to assign him an assigned parking space at Park La Brea apartments; a jury found for C.R. and awarded $250,000 in emotional distress damages. The court granted judgment as a matter of law on causation and damages, finding insufficient evidence that PLB caused C.R. emotional harm or that the damages award was supported, and conditionally ordered a new trial on these issues plus whether C.R.'s request was a reasonable accommodation rather than a modification.
key_cases_cited: Reeves v. Sanderson Plumbing Prods., Inc., 530 U.S. 133 (2000)
Escriba v. Foster Poultry Farms, Inc., 743 F.3d 1236 (9th Cir. 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Assigned handicapped parking space in front of plaintiff's apartment (the 'Requested Space'), which was located in a General (unassigned) parking area
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted judgment as a matter of law on the issue of whether the Reserved Parking Option (the alternative accommodation offered by defendant) was reasonable. The court found that substantial evidence established C.R. was capable of walking to the Reserved Parking Option space, which posed no greater risks than his routine community outings, and that Joffe's testimony to the contrary was inconsistent and amounted only to a scintilla of evidence. The court also granted JMOL on causation and damages, finding no legally sufficient evidence that PLB's refusal caused C.R. emotional harm or that any damages award was supported by evidence.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Move to a different apartment unit with all desired amenities, including a Reserved parking space immediately near the unit (the 'Move Option')
fha_claims.reasoning: The court upheld the jury's verdict that the Move Option was not a reasonable alternative accommodation. Drawing all inferences in favor of C.R., substantial evidence supported that moving would be too traumatic for C.R., given his prior move in 2011 led to a partial six-month hospitalization and that changes to his routine or environment trigger dysregulation. The jury could credit Joffe and Curcio's testimony over the defendant's expert's contrary opinion regarding causation of the prior hospitalization.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Whether plaintiff's request for an assigned handicapped parking space constituted a request for an 'accommodation' (change to rules/policies) versus a 'modification' (physical alteration to premises)
fha_claims.reasoning: On the Rule 50(b) motion, the court upheld the jury's verdict that C.R.'s request was for an accommodation, not a modification, finding substantial evidence in testimony that Joffe wanted PLB to change its parking policy to allow her to reserve the Requested Space based on proximity, not handicap accessibility. However, on the Rule 59(a) motion for new trial, the court found the verdict against the clear weight of evidence, noting Joffe's written requests expressly sought 'an assigned handicapped parking space' with supporting medical documentation, and that Joffe's later testimony that she meant only a policy change was not credible given her education and sophistication.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Defendant withheld rent claiming plaintiff discriminated against defendant in violation of the Fair Housing Act and 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(A)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked subject matter jurisdiction because the plaintiff's complaint presented only a state law unlawful detainer claim; any federal FHA defense or counterclaim by the defendant cannot serve as a basis for federal question jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1331, as federal jurisdiction must appear on the face of the plaintiff's complaint.

source_file: 9519145_2024_Sosa Guerrero v. Camp Pendelton and Quantico Housing, LLC_cacd
case_name: Luis Sosa Guerrero, Ashley Sosa, and A.S. v. Camp Pendelton & Quantico Housing, LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation for a minor child's learning disability in military family housing (specific accommodation request not detailed in this post-trial order).
key_holding: The court denied plaintiffs' motion for permanent injunction because they failed to show monetary damages were inadequate, the balance of hardships did not favor them, and imposing an injunction would disserve the public interest by impeding military operations, while granting in part the attorney's fees motion.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Luis Sosa Guerrero, Ashley Sosa, and their minor daughter A.S. sued Camp Pendelton & Quantico Housing, LLC for refusing to provide a reasonable accommodation for A.S.'s learning disability in military family housing; after a jury found defendants violated the FHA and awarded $98,000 in compensatory damages, the court denied plaintiffs' motion for permanent injunction but granted in part their motion for attorney's fees totaling $351,780 plus costs.
key_cases_cited: eBay Inc. v. MercExchange, LLC, 547 U.S. 388 (2006)
Silver Sage Partners v. City of Desert Hot Springs, 251 F.3d 814 (9th Cir. 2001)
Kerr v. Screen Guild Estras, Inc., 526 F.2d 67 (9th Cir. 1975)
Farrar v. Hobby, 506 U.S. 103 (1992)
Ketchum v. Moses, 24 Cal. 4th 1122 (2001)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation for plaintiff's minor daughter's learning disability in military housing
fha_claims.reasoning: Jury found that defendants violated the FHA by refusing to provide a reasonable accommodation for the minor daughter's learning disability, awarding $98,000 in compensatory damages to the daughter.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) claim; Unruh Civil Rights Act, Unfair Business Practices, and Negligence claims were voluntarily dismissed before trial
fha_claims.reasoning: Jury found that defendants violated FEHA, awarding $98,000 in compensatory damages to the minor daughter. Unruh, Unfair Business Practices, and Negligence claims were voluntarily dismissed on the eve of trial.

source_file: 9519328_2024_Highland Creek Associates v. Claudia M. Bica_cacd
9519849_2024_David Roy Winters v. West Oaks Housing LLC_cacd
case_name: David Winters v. West Oaks Housing LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: The opinion does not describe the specific accommodation request alleged in the complaint.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claim with prejudice because plaintiff failed to file a Second Amended Complaint by the deadline and the court concluded any further leave to amend would be futile.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff David Winters filed suit against his landlord West Oaks Housing LLC and property manager David Nemanpour alleging Fair Housing Act violations. The court dismissed the FHA claim with prejudice after plaintiff failed to file an amended complaint following two prior dismissals for failure to state a viable claim, concluding that any further leave to amend would be futile.
key_cases_cited: Exec. Software v. U.S. Dist. Court for the Cent. Dist. of Cal., 24 F.3d 1545 (9th Cir. 1994)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not specified; complaint allegations not detailed in opinion
fha_claims.reasoning: Court reviewed amended complaint under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) and concluded it did not state a viable FHA claim over which the court possessed subject matter jurisdiction. After multiple opportunities to amend and warning of futility, plaintiff failed to file a second amended complaint by the deadline, and the court dismissed the FHA claim without leave to amend.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: State law fraud claim; also references California Unruh Act (Cal. Civil Code § 51) and FEHA (Cal. Gov't Code §§ 12955-12956.2)
fha_claims.disposition: Dismissal; supplemental jurisdiction declined under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims (fraud, Unruh Act, FEHA) under § 1367(c)(3) because all federal claims over which it had original jurisdiction were resolved. Claims dismissed without prejudice; statute of limitations tolled for 30 days.

source_file: 9520664_2021_Thomason v. Deutsche Bank National Trust Company_almd
9521123_2022_Hammonds v. Montgomery Children's Specialty Center, LLC_almd
case_name: Frankie Hammonds v. Montgomery Children's Specialty Center, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a minor with paraplegia and traumatic brain injury placed in a residential facility for children with disabilities, alleges he was subjected to abuse and neglect and was evicted or forced out after complaining about mistreatment, raising a retaliation claim under the FHA.
key_holding: The FHA retaliation claim was properly dismissed because Hammonds failed to allege facts showing he engaged in protected activity under the FHA by complaining about abuse and neglect, as his complaints did not address discrimination based on disability but rather the quality of medical care received.
brief_summary: Frankie Hammonds, an individual with paraplegia and traumatic brain injury who was placed in a residential facility for children with disabilities, sued Montgomery Children's Specialty Center, LLC alleging the facility failed to protect him from abuse and neglect and evicted him after he complained about mistreatment. The court granted MCSC's partial motion to dismiss, dismissing the FHA retaliation claim because Hammonds failed to allege facts showing his complaints constituted protected activity under the statute.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Olmstead v. L.C. ex rel. Zimring, 527 U.S. 581 (1999)
Silva v. Baptist S. Fla., Inc., 856 F.3d 824 (11th Cir. 2017)
Philippeaux v. Apartment Inv. & Mgmt. Co., 598 F. App'x 640 (11th Cir. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged retaliation for complaining about neglect, mistreatment, exploitation, and abuse; claims he was either evicted or treated so harshly he had to leave for his own safety.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts supporting an inference that he engaged in activity protected under the FHA. The complaint does not allege that his complaints addressed conduct that could reasonably be believed to constitute unlawful discrimination based on disability under the FHA, which is required to establish protected activity for a retaliation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 504 Rehabilitation Act discrimination and harassment claims; ADA Title III discrimination, harassment, and retaliation claims; state law negligence, negligent hiring/retention/training/supervision, felonious injury, and menacing claims.
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA Title III claims dismissed for lack of Article III standing to seek injunctive relief (no allegation of likelihood to return to facility) and unavailability of damages under Title III. § 504 discrimination and harassment claims dismissed because plaintiff failed to allege facts showing denial of services or discrimination 'by reason of' disability—allegations focused on quality of medical care rather than equal opportunity to participate in services. § 504 retaliation claim failed because plaintiff did not allege protected activity under the Rehabilitation Act. State criminal statute claims (felonious injury, menacing) dismissed because the statutes establish only criminal offenses without creating private civil causes of action.

source_file: 9521475_2022_Oxford House, Inc. v. City of Dothan, Alabama_almd
case_name: Oxford House, Inc. v. City of Dothan, Alabama
accommodation_description: Request that Oxford House-Dothan and future Oxford Houses be exempted from the City's business license requirement to open utilities accounts in their associational names using federal employer identification numbers.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for the City because Oxford House failed to establish that the requested business license exemption was necessary under the FHA, as the claimed therapeutic need (honesty in recovery) lacked evidentiary support and the accommodation did not directly address the effects of residents' disabilities or address disability-created needs.
brief_summary: Oxford House, Inc. and three Dothan-based Oxford Houses sued the City of Dothan, Alabama alleging the City discriminated against them based on disability by requiring them to obtain business licenses to open utilities accounts in their associational names. The court granted summary judgment for the City, finding Oxford House failed to establish that exempting them from the business license requirement was necessary under the FHA because the claimed therapeutic and financial needs were either unsupported by evidence or failed to show the accommodation would directly alleviate the effects of residents' disabilities.
key_cases_cited: Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014)
Schwarz v. City of Treasure Island, 544 F.3d 1201 (11th Cir. 2008)
Sailboat Bend Sober Living, LLC v. City of Fort Lauderdale, 46 F.4th 1268 (11th Cir. 2022)
Vill. of Arlington Heights v. Metro. Hous. Dev. Corp., 429 U.S. 252 (1977)
Oxford House-C v. City of St. Louis, 77 F.3d 249 (8th Cir. 1996)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish prima facie case of intentional discrimination under McDonnell Douglas framework. No evidence of selective enforcement or disparate treatment compared to similarly situated non-disabled groups applying for utilities accounts in associational names with EINs. City applied business license requirement evenly to all unrelated groups, and twelve other group homes obtained utilities accounts while procuring business licenses.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exemption from City's business license requirement for utilities account applications in Oxford House associational names
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish that requested accommodation was necessary to afford equal opportunity to use and enjoy dwelling. Therapeutic need claim was strained because OHI employees, not residents, completed applications, and residents had no knowledge of business license contents. Direct liability argument failed because complying with business license requirement does not create the problem. Financial need claim lacked evidentiary support—business license was free, and insurance cost comparison was not apples-to-apples; speculation that landlords would pass costs to residents was insufficient.

source_file: 9523061_2020_FSI Green Park South Property LLC v. Pelham, City of, The_alnd
case_name: FSI Green Park South Property, LLC v. City of Pelham, Alabama
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; case involves challenge to municipal zoning enforcement allegedly targeting Latino residents of manufactured home park
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's takings claim and FHA interference claim but found plaintiff sufficiently alleged viable claims for discrimination under § 3604(a), equal protection, and substantive due process where plaintiff alleged the City's manufactured home park enforcement campaign was motivated by discrimination against its Latino residents.
brief_summary: FSI Green Park South Property, LLC, operator of a manufactured home park in Pelham, Alabama, sued the City of Pelham alleging that the City's zoning enforcement campaign—including denying permits, issuing citations, and pursuing condemnation—was motivated by discriminatory intent against its predominantly Latino residents in violation of the Fair Housing Act and Equal Protection Clause. The court dismissed plaintiff's regulatory takings claim and FHA interference claim but allowed plaintiff's claims for housing discrimination under § 3604(a), equal protection, and substantive due process to proceed, finding sufficient factual allegations to state plausible claims at the motion to dismiss stage.
key_cases_cited: Village of Arlington Heights v. Metro. Hous. Dev. Corp., 429 U.S. 252 (1977)
Tex. Dept. of Hous. & Comm. Affairs v. Inclusive Comms., 135 S. Ct. 2507 (2015)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Hallmark Dev., Inc. v. Fulton Cty, Ga., 466 F.3d 1276 (11th Cir. 2006)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found Green Park adequately alleged facts to state a discrimination claim under the FHA by alleging that the City's zoning enforcement disproportionately impacts Latino residents and lacks rational justification, satisfying the pleading standard under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged interference with FHA rights through blocking electrical permits, refusing written permit denials, refusing direct communication, and issuing citations under repealed ordinance
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed the interference claim because the alleged conduct was not 'so severe or pervasive' as to cause abandonment of housing rights, and Green Park failed to identify the specific FHA right (§§ 3603–3606) with which the City interfered, failing to state a plausible claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fifth Amendment takings claim (just compensation), Fourteenth Amendment due process claim (substantive), and § 1983 Equal Protection claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Just compensation takings claim dismissed because Green Park failed to allege deprivation of all economically viable use and did not establish reasonable investment-backed expectations given the City's published Comprehensive Plan and Redevelopment Plan prior to purchase. Due process and Equal Protection claims survived MTD as Green Park adequately alleged legislative adoption of zoning ordinances with discriminatory intent and disproportionate impact on Latino residents.

case_name: Michael C. Threatt v. Sylacauga Housing Authority, et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested in this case; this is an employment retaliation and race discrimination action brought by a former housing authority CEO who was terminated after reporting discriminatory housing practices and segregation issues to the SHA Board and external agencies.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion to disqualify plaintiff's counsel Richard Rice, finding that even assuming an attorney-client relationship existed between Rice and the SHA, defendants failed to demonstrate that the prior quasi-representation was substantially related to plaintiff's current employment discrimination and FHA retaliation lawsuit.
brief_summary: Michael Threatt, former CEO of the Sylacauga Housing Authority (SHA), filed suit alleging race discrimination, race retaliation under Title VII and § 1981, retaliation under the Fair Housing Act, and retaliation under the False Claims Act after the SHA terminated his employment following his complaints about the agency's discriminatory housing practices and HUD-identified segregation risks. Defendants moved to disqualify plaintiff's attorney Richard Rice, arguing Rice had previously represented the SHA in a civil rights assessment and had switched sides in violation of Alabama Rules of Professional Conduct 1.9 and 1.7. The court denied disqualification, holding that the preliminary civil rights assessment discussions never ripened into a formal representation on a substantially related matter and that no current attorney-client relationship existed between Rice and the SHA.
key_cases_cited: Herrmann v. Gutterguard, Inc.
In re BellSouth Corp.
Ex parte Tiffin
Freund v. Butterworth
Ex parte Regions Bank

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.disposition: Motion to Disqualify Counsel (not on merits)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the motion to disqualify plaintiff's counsel and did not address the merits of the FHA retaliation claim. The claim survives the procedural challenge and remains pending.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VII race discrimination, § 1981 race discrimination via § 1983, Title VII race retaliation via § 1983, False Claims Act retaliation
fha_claims.disposition: Motion to Disqualify Counsel (not on merits)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the motion to disqualify plaintiff's counsel. The non-FHA claims (Title VII, § 1981, § 1983, False Claims Act) survive the procedural challenge and remain pending on the merits.

source_file: 9524190_2022_Miller v. Blue Cross Blue Shield of Alabama_alnd
case_name: Fredrika M. Miller v. Blue Cross Blue Shield of Alabama
accommodation_description: No housing accommodation was requested. Miller asked Blue Cross to investigate pesticide use on her property and to provide specialized medical care for her and her mother following pesticide exposure and domestic violence; there was no request for a reasonable accommodation or modification in a housing context.
key_holding: The court dismissed all of Miller's claims because the cited ACA provisions lack private rights of action, her FHA claim failed to plead any discrimination in housing terms based on a protected class and was time-barred, and her Alabama Fair Housing Law claim similarly failed on the merits and was time-barred.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Fredrika Miller sued her health insurer, Blue Cross Blue Shield of Alabama, under the ACA, the FHA, and the Alabama Fair Housing Law, alleging that Blue Cross's failure to investigate pesticide overuse and domestic violence reports caused her and her mother to lose their home and that her mother subsequently died. The court dismissed the ACA claims because §§ 300gg-17 and 300gg-12 provide no express or implied private right of action and enforcement authority is vested in HHS and state agencies. The FHA and state housing law claims were dismissed both for failure to plead any discrimination in housing transactions based on a protected characteristic — Miller's theory was that unpaid medical bills caused her homelessness, not that Blue Cross discriminated against her as a housing provider — and because the claims were filed seven years after the 2014 events, well outside the applicable limitations periods.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ACA violations (§§ 300gg-17 and 300gg-12) and Alabama Fair Housing Law violations
fha_claims.reasoning: The court screened the complaint under § 1915(e)(2) and dismissed the ACA claims because §§ 300gg-17 and 300gg-12 do not provide express or implied private rights of action; Congress vested enforcement authority in the Secretary of HHS and state authorities. The Alabama Fair Housing Law claim was also dismissed as failing to allege discriminatory housing practices and as time-barred (occurring in 2014, suit filed in 2021, exceeding the one-year statute of limitations under Ala. Code § 24-8-14(a)).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged discrimination in housing based on disability or other protected class status
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiff failed to plead facts establishing that Blue Cross discriminated against her in the terms of her residence, engaged in discriminatory real estate transactions, or interfered with financing based on a protected class characteristic. The alleged loss of housing resulted from medical bills following Blue Cross's inaction regarding insurance coverage, not from discriminatory housing practices. Additionally, the FHA claim was time-barred under 42 U.S.C. § 3613(a)(1)(A) (2-year statute of limitations), as the alleged housing loss occurred in 2014, seven years before the 2021 filing.

case_name: Kaislee McCoy, et al. v. Cypress Landing, LP, et al.
accommodation_description: Mother requested multiple accommodations from April 2018 through October 2019 to ensure safety for her autistic, deaf, and blind daughter inside the home, though specific accommodation requests are not detailed in the opinion.
key_holding: The court denied dismissal of the retaliation claims because the close temporal proximity between Vinson's accommodation requests and the eviction, combined with allegations that other tenants were not evicted for missed rent, plausibly alleged pretext for retaliation.
brief_summary: Vinson sued on behalf of herself and her two minor daughters against their former landlord and property manager, alleging disability discrimination for denying over twenty requests to accommodate her autistic, deaf, and blind daughter Kaislee, and retaliation for evicting them after they made these requests. The court granted the motion to dismiss as to most of Vinson's individual claims as time-barred under the two-year FHA limitations period, but denied dismissal of the minor daughters' claims and the retaliation claims, finding sufficient temporal proximity and pretext allegations to survive dismissal.
key_cases_cited: Hunt v. Aimco Props., L.P., 814 F.3d 1213 (11th Cir. 2016)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
McCullum v. Orlando Reg'l Healthcare Sys., Inc., 768 F.3d 1135 (11th Cir. 2014)
Dixon v. The Hallmark Companies, Inc., 627 F.3d 849 (11th Cir. 2010)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodations related to Kaislee's extreme autism, deafness, and blindness to ensure her safety inside the home; plaintiffs made twenty-plus requests from April 2018 through October 2019, denied through undue delay and/or outright denial
fha_claims.reasoning: Under the FHA's strict two-year limitations period (42 U.S.C. § 3613(a)(1)), which does not incorporate state tolling provisions for minors, discrimination claims accruing before October 18, 2019 are time-barred. Only claims accruing after October 18, 2019 may proceed. Vinson's claims are barred; Kaislee's and Kharsyn's claims survive because they are minors and tolling applies under state law to their Rehabilitation Act claims, but the FHA's federal limitations period applies to their FHA claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Under the FHA's retaliation provision (42 U.S.C. § 3617), plaintiffs plausibly alleged a prima facie case: (1) they engaged in protected activity by requesting reasonable accommodations from April 2018 through October 2019; (2) they suffered an adverse action (eviction notice on October 9, 2019, and eviction proceedings in November 2019); and (3) close temporal proximity between final accommodation requests and the non-renewal/eviction notice supports a causal link. Plaintiffs also plausibly alleged pretext by claiming Cypress Landing did not evict other residents who missed multiple rent payments but evicted Vinson after her first missed payment. The ultimate success of the eviction does not defeat the retaliation claim at the pleading stage because the court lacks information about the lease terms and full eviction proceedings.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act discrimination claims (denial of reasonable accommodations) and retaliation claims under the Rehabilitation Act (eviction in retaliation for accommodation requests)
fha_claims.disposition: 12(b)(6) - Statute of Limitations (in part); Survives MTD (in part)
fha_claims.reasoning: Under Alabama's two-year statute of limitations for personal injury actions (Ala. Code § 6–2–38), which applies to Rehabilitation Act claims, each individual denial of an accommodation request constitutes a discrete discriminatory action. Vinson's discrimination claims for denials prior to October 18, 2019 are time-barred; however, her claims for denials after that date may proceed. Kaislee's and Kharsyn's discrimination claims survive because the tolling provision for minors (Ala. Code § 6–2–8) applies to them. All retaliation claims under the Rehabilitation Act survive dismissal under the Title VII retaliation framework because plaintiffs established a prima facie case with sufficient causal nexus between accommodation requests and eviction.

source_file: 9524475_2022_Cash v. US Department of Housing and Urban Development_alnd
case_name: Don Cash v. U.S. Department of Housing & Urban Development
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation was clearly articulated; plaintiff's complaint vaguely referenced air conditioner maintenance failures at his apartment, which the court characterized as possibly a state-law breach of contract claim rather than a cognizable FHA claim.
key_holding: The court granted all defendants' motions to dismiss because plaintiff's amended complaint failed to comply with the court's prior pleading order and failed to state a federal cause of action upon which relief could be granted.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Don Cash filed a largely indecipherable amended complaint against HUD, a property management company, and related defendants, vaguely invoking the Fair Housing Act, the Fourteenth Amendment, and the Civil Rights Act of 1964 in connection with alleged air conditioner maintenance failures at his apartment. The court had previously ordered plaintiff to file a compliant amended complaint with clear, specific allegations, but the amended pleading still failed to comply with Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 8(a), 8(d)(1), 10(b), and 11(b) and did not assert facts plausibly supporting any federal cause of action. All three motions to dismiss were granted, with the court noting plaintiff may have a viable state-court breach of contract claim.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of lease regarding air conditioning unit maintenance; challenge to jury trial waiver clause; alleged inattentiveness of Housing Authority and HUD
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's amended complaint failed to state a plausible claim under Twombly/Iqbal standards. The complaint vaguely referenced the Fair Housing Act, Fourteenth Amendment, and Civil Rights Act of 1964 but contained no factual allegations plausibly alleging a violation of any federal statute. The court found the complaint nearly indecipherable and failed to comply with the court's prior order requiring clear statement of claims with supporting facts.

case_name: Larry Arnold v. Elmington Property Management LLC
accommodation_description: Arnold requested a waiver of Elmington's policy not to accept housing choice vouchers so he could continue renting his apartment using his Section 8 voucher.
key_holding: The court denied Elmington's motion to dismiss Arnold's reasonable accommodation claim, finding Arnold's request that Elmington accept his Section 8 voucher facially reasonable and that Elmington had not demonstrated undue hardship at the pleading stage, emphasizing that the reasonableness inquiry is highly fact-specific and Elmington's motion was premature without discovery into specific hardships.
brief_summary: Larry Arnold, a disabled veteran with COPD, neuropathy, and heart disease who uses a Section 8 housing voucher, sued Elmington Property Management after it decided to no longer accept housing vouchers, effectively threatening his tenancy. The court denied Elmington's motion to dismiss Arnold's reasonable accommodation claim, finding Arnold adequately pleaded that his request for a voucher policy waiver was facially reasonable and that the undue hardship inquiry required discovery into Elmington's specific circumstances rather than a categorical rule.
key_cases_cited: Schaw v. Habitat for Humanity of Citrus Cty., Inc., 938 F.3d 1259 (11th Cir. 2019)
Salute v. Stratford Greens Garden Apartments, 136 F.3d 293 (2d Cir. 1998)
U.S. Airways v. Barnett, 535 U.S. 391 (2002)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver of defendant's policy refusing to accept Section 8 housing vouchers; plaintiff requested that defendant continue to accept his Housing Choice Voucher as a reasonable accommodation necessary to afford him equal opportunity to use and enjoy his dwelling
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff established a prima facie case by alleging disability, request for accommodation, necessity for equal opportunity, and defendant's refusal. The burden shifted to defendant to demonstrate undue hardship, but defendant failed to meet this burden at the pleading stage through conclusory assertions and reliance on outdated precedent. The court found the undue hardship inquiry fact-specific and premature for dismissal, requiring discovery into defendant's specific circumstances.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff adequately pleaded a prima facie disparate impact claim by alleging that defendant's policy of refusing to accept Section 8 vouchers makes housing options significantly more restrictive for disabled tenants unable to work. The court rejected defendant's argument that plaintiff failed to allege facts about other disabled tenants, finding that discovery would reveal such information. Defendant's categorical bar argument was rejected as unsupported.

case_name: Michael C. Threatt v. Sylacauga Housing Authority
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation requested; plaintiff was an employee who claimed SHA retaliated against him for raising fair housing compliance issues.
key_holding: The court denied summary judgment on the FHA retaliation claim (Count Three) because plaintiff raised a good-faith, reasonable belief that SHA improperly designated Sylavon Court as elderly-only housing to the exclusion of families, which constitutes protected activity under the FHA's anti-retaliation provision.
brief_summary: Michael Threatt, former Executive Director of the Sylacauga Housing Authority, sued SHA and its commissioners alleging race discrimination, Title VII and FHA retaliation, False Claims Act retaliation, and Equal Protection violations. The court granted summary judgment for defendants on most claims but denied summary judgment on the FHA retaliation claim because Threatt raised a reasonable belief that SHA's elderly-only housing designation excluded families in violation of the Fair Housing Act.
key_cases_cited: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Fox v. Gaines, 4 F.4th 1293 (11th Cir. 2021)
Philippeaux v. Apartment Inv. & Mgmt. Co., 598 F. App'x 640 (11th Cir. 2015)
Jenkins v. Nell, 26 F.4th 1243 (11th Cir. 2022)
Hickman v. Spirit of Athens, Ala., Inc., 985 F.3d 1284 (11th Cir. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiff engaged in protected activity under the Fair Housing Act by raising concerns about improper designation of Sylavon Court as elderly/disabled housing to the exclusion of families, and that he had a good faith reasonable belief this violated the FHA's anti-discrimination provisions. Because defendant made no argument regarding causation or legitimate non-retaliatory reasons for the administrative leave, summary judgment was denied and the claim proceeds.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VII race discrimination, Title VII retaliation, § 1981 race discrimination, § 1981 retaliation, False Claims Act retaliation, § 1983 Equal Protection
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish prima facie case of race discrimination under McDonnell Douglas (no similarly situated comparator) and presented insufficient circumstantial evidence of a convincing mosaic. On retaliation claims, plaintiff failed to rebut defendant's legitimate, non-retaliatory reasons for termination. On False Claims Act claim, plaintiff did not engage in protected activity because his complaints concerned general mismanagement of funds, not submission of false claims to the government.

case_name: Mueller v. Sylacauga Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs are former SHA executive officers who were fired after reporting alleged discriminatory housing practices and financial mismanagement to HUD and DOJ.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for SHA on the FHA retaliation claim because the plaintiffs failed to establish causation—they could not show the decision-maker (Royster) was aware of their protected complaints, and their cat's paw theory was unsupported by evidence showing Lozito's alleged financial motives were connected to retaliatory animus based on the plaintiffs' FHA-related reports.
brief_summary: Former executive officers of Sylacauga Housing Authority sued for retaliation under the FHA, alleging they were terminated after reporting discriminatory housing practices and financial mismanagement to HUD and DOJ. The court granted summary judgment for SHA, finding plaintiffs failed to establish causation because the decision-maker testified he was unaware of their complaints, and their cat's paw theory linking board influence to retaliatory animus was unsupported.
key_cases_cited: Gross v. FBL Fin. Servs., Inc., 557 U.S. 167 (2009)
Staub v. Proctor Hosp., 562 U.S. 411 (2011)
Martin v. Fin. Asset Mgmt. Sys., Inc., 959 F.3d 1048 (11th Cir. 2020)
Nesbitt v. Candler Cnty., 945 F.3d 1355 (11th Cir. 2020)
Chapman v. AI Transp., 229 F.3d 1012 (11th Cir. 2000)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that plaintiffs failed to establish a prima facie case of FHA retaliation under § 3617 because they could not demonstrate causation. The decision-maker (Royster) was unaware of the plaintiffs' reports of FHA discrimination regarding the Sylavon properties' designation, and temporal proximity alone is insufficient to establish pretext without additional evidence of retaliatory animus. The cat's paw theory does not apply because FHA retaliation requires but-for causation, not merely a motivating factor.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that plaintiffs failed to establish a prima facie case of False Claims Act retaliation under 31 U.S.C. § 3730(h)(1) because their complaints involved mismanagement of federal funds and lack of internal controls, not submission of false or fraudulent claims to the government. Under Hickman v. Spirit of Athens, FCA liability requires a false claim to the government, not merely regulatory noncompliance or improper internal procedures. The audits and forensic review did not show SHA made any false statement to HUD.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of contract and conversion claims relating to failure to return SHA-issued electronic devices and artwork (Jim Nabors pencil drawing)
fha_claims.reasoning: SHA's counterclaim for breach of contract and conversion was not addressed on the merits in this opinion. The court declined to rule on the counterclaim and instead ordered the parties to submit arguments regarding whether the court should exercise supplemental jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3), as all claims over which the court had original jurisdiction (FCA and FHA retaliation) were dismissed.

source_file: 9524837_2022_Huntsville Senior Services, LLC v. Alabama Department of Public Health_alnd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Declaratory relief and preliminary injunction against enforcement of Alabama hospice licensure statute; § 1983 due process claim challenging Department's determination that facility is unlicensed hospital
fha_claims.reasoning: Counts I and II dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1331 because the federal question (FHA defense) arises only as a defense to anticipated state-law enforcement action, not as an independent cause of action. Count III (§ 1983 due process claim) dismissed under 12(b)(6) as implausible because plaintiff failed to allege direct deprivation of a protected interest; any harm to plaintiff's property interests resulted indirectly from state action directed at third-party hospice providers, not at plaintiff itself, following O'Bannon v. Town Court Nursing Center.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act defense to anticipated state enforcement action; claim that compliance with Department demands to evict residents receiving hospice care or ADL would constitute disability discrimination
fha_claims.reasoning: FHA allegation cannot support federal-question jurisdiction because it presents a federal defense to anticipated state-law action, not an independent federal cause of action. The court cannot exercise jurisdiction over a declaratory judgment action where the federal question would arise only as a defense in hypothetical state-court litigation. State-law determination that facility is not a hospital would obviate need for federal law defense.

case_name: United States v. Hames
accommodation_description: This is a sexual harassment case alleging landlord demanded sexual favors from female tenants in exchange for housing and subjected them to unwelcome sexual contact, comments, and intrusions.
key_holding: The court granted the government's motion for partial summary judgment on vicarious liability but denied defendants' motion for summary judgment, finding the government's § 3614(a) pattern-or-practice claim is not time-barred and genuine issues of material fact exist as to whether the landlord engaged in a pattern of sexual harassment.
brief_summary: The United States brought a pattern-or-practice claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3614(a) against Randy Hames and Hames Marina, alleging the landlord sexually harassed female tenants by demanding sexual favors in exchange for rent and subjecting them to unwelcome sexual contact and intrusions. The court granted the government's motion for partial summary judgment on vicarious liability and denied defendants' motion for summary judgment, finding the government's claim was not time-barred and genuine disputes of material fact existed regarding the pattern-or-practice of discrimination.
key_cases_cited: International Brotherhood of Teamsters v. United States, 431 U.S. 324 (1977)
United States v. Tanski, 2007 WL 1017020 (N.D.N.Y. 2007)
United States v. Balistrieri, 981 F.2d 916 (7th Cir. 1992)
Askins & Miller Orthopaedics, P.A. v. United States, 924 F.3d 1348 (11th Cir. 2019)
Sheely v. MRI Radiology Network, P.A., 505 F.3d 1173 (11th Cir. 2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found a genuine issue of material fact regarding whether Randy Hames engaged in a pattern or practice of sexual harassment and discrimination against female tenants in exchange for rent or housing benefits. Testimony from private plaintiffs directly contradicted Hames's denial, creating a factual dispute that must be resolved at trial rather than on summary judgment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The government's claim for injunctive relief against Hames Marina and its successor entity Marina Management Company was not mooted by the dissolution of Hames Marina. The court applied the voluntary cessation doctrine and found that the timing of dissolution (shortly after suit was filed), the transfer of assets to Hames's daughter, and the lack of acknowledgment of liability all weighed against finding mootness. The court reserved decision on whether injunctive relief is ultimately necessary.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The government's claim for compensatory damages is not barred by the two-year statute of limitations in 42 U.S.C. § 3613(a)(1)(A), which applies only to private individuals. Government actions under § 3614(a) are subject to the three-year statute of limitations in 28 U.S.C. § 2415(b) for tort claims, and the government did not know or reasonably could not have known of the pattern until February 2018 when media reports surfaced.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The government's claim for civil penalties under 42 U.S.C. § 3614(d)(1)(C) is not time-barred under the five-year statute of limitations in 28 U.S.C. § 2462. In a pattern or practice case, the claim accrues upon completion of the final incident making up the pattern, and so long as one incident occurred within the limitations period, the pattern claim is timely. Defendants conceded that claims by three female tenants are not barred.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted the government's motion for partial summary judgment on the issue of vicarious liability of Hames Marina, L.L.C. The court found that if Randy Hames is found to have violated the Fair Housing Act, Hames Marina is vicariously liable for his conduct as the entity's agent and manager. Defendants did not oppose this motion and tacitly consented to its entry.

case_name: Larry Arnold v. Elmington Property Management, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that defendant make an exception to its no-subsidy policy and continue accepting his Section 8 vouchers as an accommodation for his disabilities.
key_holding: Plaintiff's request for defendant to accept his Section 8 vouchers was facially reasonable under the low bar established in Schaw, and defendant failed to produce evidence demonstrating that granting the accommodation would impose an undue burden or fundamental alteration of its program.
brief_summary: Larry Arnold, a 72-year-old disabled veteran with COPD, neuropathy, and heart disease, sued Elmington Property Management after the company adopted a no-subsidy policy and refused his request for an exception to continue accepting his Section 8 vouchers as a reasonable accommodation for his disabilities. The court denied defendant's motion for summary judgment, finding that the accommodation request was facially reasonable under Schaw because Arnold was simply asking defendant to accept the same payment from a different source, and defendant failed to produce evidence of undue burden.
key_cases_cited: Schaw v. Habitat for Humanity of Citrus Cnty., Inc., 938 F.3d 1259 (11th Cir. 2019)
Barnett v. U.S. Air, Inc., 535 U.S. 391 (2002)
Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014)
Willis v. Conopco, Inc., 108 F.3d 282 (11th Cir. 1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exception to no-subsidy policy to allow acceptance of Section 8 housing vouchers as payment source for rent
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff established facial reasonableness of accommodation under Schaw standard (requesting same total payment in different form, not a waiver of basic requirements). Defendant failed to provide evidence of undue burden or fundamental alteration; speculative risk of other tenants' discrimination claims, unsupported financial cost arguments, and unquantified administrative costs are insufficient to meet defendant's burden of proof on affirmative defense.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff voluntarily waived the disparate impact claim in his brief before summary judgment.

case_name: John Doe v. RHOC, Inc.
accommodation_description: No traditional reasonable accommodation request is at issue in this case. The case centers on allegations that RHOC staff and owners physically abused and neglected a profoundly disabled group home resident, excluded him from therapeutic programs, and failed to report the abuse to authorities, all purportedly because of his intellectual and psychological disabilities.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment to RHOC only on Plaintiff's Rehabilitation Act retaliation claim for lack of evidentiary support, but denied summary judgment on all remaining claims, finding sufficient evidence of intentional disability-based discrimination and that Alabama's disability tolling provision saved the claims from a statute of limitations bar.
brief_summary: John Doe, a severely disabled adult involuntarily committed to RHOC's group home, alleged repeated physical abuse and neglect by an owner and staff, asserting claims under the Rehabilitation Act, Fair Housing Act, ADA, and state law. The plaintiff conceded and the court dismissed the FHA and ADA claims prior to the summary judgment ruling.
