fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the non-habitable conditions claim against the County for failure to state a plausible claim because the County does not own, rent, manage, or control Golden Gate Village. The deliberate indifference claim failed because the County had no duty to remedy conditions at the property and the complaint did not plausibly allege facts supporting a state-created danger exception. The negligence claim was dismissed for failure to comply with the California Tort Claims Act's exhaustion requirement and because public employees are statutorily immune from liability for negligent inspection.

source_file: 9602950_2021_Melton v. Regional Center of the East Bay, Inc._cand
case_name: Melton v. Regional Center of the East Bay, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, who is deaf-blind and uses Tactile American Sign Language, requested a staff member at her group home who could communicate with her in Tactile ASL.
key_holding: The court dismissed the FHA claim with prejudice for failure to exhaust administrative remedies, but allowed claims under the ADA, Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, and California civil rights statutes to proceed, finding the plaintiff adequately alleged she was denied meaningful access to services due to her disability.
brief_summary: Selena Melton, a deaf-blind woman who uses Tactile ASL, sued the California Department of Developmental Services, the Regional Center of the East Bay, and Arleen's Residential Care under the ADA, Section 504, the FHA, and California civil rights laws, alleging defendants failed to provide communication accommodations in her group home. The court granted in part defendants' motions to dismiss, dismissing the FHA claim with prejudice for failure to exhaust administrative remedies under the Lanterman Act's fair hearing procedure, while denying dismissal of the ADA and Section 504 claims based on systemic discrimination.
key_cases_cited: Olmstead v. Zimring, 527 U.S. 581 (1999)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Kokkonen v. Guardian Life Ins. Co. of Am., 511 U.S. 375 (1994)
Bragdon v. Abbott, 524 U.S. 624 (1998)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Effective communication accommodations (Tactile American Sign Language interpreter/staff member) and systemic accessibility policies for deaf and deaf-blind consumers; Title II ADA, Title III ADA, Section 504 Rehabilitation Act, California Government Code § 11135, Unruh Civil Rights Act, California Disabled Persons Act, Elder Abuse and Dependent Adult Civil Protection Act, negligence
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed fourth cause of action (Fair Housing Act claim against Arleen's), eighth cause of action (Elder Abuse Act), and ninth cause of action (negligence) for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under 12(b)(1) because plaintiff failed to exhaust the Lanterman Act's mandatory fair hearing procedure for claims based on specific IPP-service issues. These claims were either IPP-service based (requiring fair hearing exhaustion) or not raised in the DRC complaint letter (failing to exhaust the Section 4731 complaint process).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Systemic accessibility policies and effective communication accommodations for deaf and deaf-blind consumers; Title II ADA against DDS, Title III ADA against RCEB, Section 504 Rehabilitation Act against DDS and RCEB, California Government Code § 11135 against RCEB, Unruh Civil Rights Act against RCEB, California Disabled Persons Act against RCEB
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motions to dismiss the systemic discrimination claims (causes of action 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7) under 12(b)(6), finding that plaintiff adequately pleaded: (1) denial of meaningful access to services by reason of disability; (2) deliberate indifference (notice and failure to act) for Title II monetary relief; (3) Title III applicability to RCEB as a coordinator of public accommodations; (4) Section 504 applicability based on federal funding allegations; (5) California Government Code § 11135 applicability; (6) Unruh Act applicability to RCEB as a business establishment; and (7) CDPA applicability. Claims survived pleading-stage scrutiny and proceed to discovery.

source_file: 9603198_2021_Filho v. Chinatown Community Development Center, Inc._cand
case_name: Roberto Filho v. Chinatown Community Development Center, Inc.
accommodation_description: Request to transfer to a one-bedroom apartment with private kitchen and bathroom to accommodate disabilities including traumatic brain injury, HIV, and bladder/prostate damage.
key_holding: The court denied the motion for default judgment and set aside the entry of default because CCDC was not properly served under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 4(h) or California law, and CCDC demonstrated readiness to defend on the merits.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Roberto Filho sued CCDC and Jason Bermak alleging they violated the Fair Housing Act by denying his request to transfer to an apartment that better accommodates his disabilities (TBI, HIV, and bladder/prostate damage). The court denied Filho's motion for default judgment and set aside the entry of default because service of process was improper under Rule 4(h) and California law, finding CCDC was not properly served on its registered agent.
key_cases_cited: Eitel v. McCool, 782 F.2d 1470 (9th Cir. 1986)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request to transfer to a one-bedroom apartment with a private kitchen and bathroom to accommodate disabilities including traumatic brain injury (TBI), HIV, and damage to bladder and prostate tissues
fha_claims.reasoning: The court did not reach the merits of the FHA reasonable accommodation claim because it found that the defendant was not properly served with the summons and complaint under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 4(h) and California law, rendering the court without jurisdiction to proceed against the defendant at that time. The court set aside the entry of default and denied the motion for default judgment on jurisdictional grounds, allowing the case to proceed upon proper service.

source_file: 9604396_2022_National Fair Housing Alliance, Inc. v. Carson_cand
case_name: National Fair Housing Alliance, et al. v. Marcia L. Fudge, et al.
accommodation_description: This is not a reasonable accommodation case; fair housing organizations challenge HUD's disparate impact rulemaking under the APA, not an individual accommodation request.
key_holding: The court granted the parties' joint request to stay proceedings for 90 days to allow HUD to complete its review of the discriminatory effects rule challenged in the APA complaint.
brief_summary: Fair housing organizations sued HUD challenging a 2020 HUD rule on the Fair Housing Act's disparate impact standard as arbitrary and capricious under the APA. The court granted the parties' joint request to stay proceedings for 90 days to allow HUD to complete its ongoing review of the discriminatory effects rule following a Presidential Memorandum directing HUD to examine the rule's effects.
key_cases_cited: Mass. Fair Hous. Ctr. v. United States Dep't of Hous. & Urban Dev., No. CV 20-11765-MGM, 2020 WL 6390143 (D. Mass. Oct. 25, 2020)

case_name: Tate-Austin v. Miller
accommodation_description: African American homeowners allege discriminatory home appraisal based on race under § 3605; no accommodation request is at issue.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' FHA claims under § 3604(a) and (c) but allowed claims under § 3605 (discriminatory appraisal) and § 3617 (interference) to proceed, finding plaintiffs pleaded sufficient facts of racial discrimination in the appraisal of their Marin City home.
brief_summary: Tenisha Tate-Austin and Paul Austin, an African American couple, along with Fair Housing Advocates of Northern California, sued Janette Miller and Perotti Real Estate Appraisals, Inc. alleging racial discrimination in a home appraisal of their Marin City, California residence that valued the property nearly $500,000 below comparable appraisals. The court granted in part defendants' motion to dismiss, dismissing claims under § 3604 but allowing claims under § 3605 (discriminatory appraisal) and § 3617 (interference) to proceed, finding plaintiffs sufficiently alleged Miller knew they were African American and may have relied on the racial demographics of Marin City in conducting a discriminatory appraisal.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Harris v. Itzhaki
Steptoe v. Sav. of Am.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs' FHA claim under § 3604(a) and (c) was dismissed because refinancing does not constitute a 'sale or rental' transaction and did not make any dwelling 'unavailable' to the Austins, who owned the property before and after the refinance. § 3604 applies only to sale/rental transactions or those making housing unavailable; § 3605 is the appropriate vehicle for refinancing discrimination claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs' FHA claim under § 3605 survived the motion to dismiss. The court found plaintiffs pleaded sufficient facts to support a plausible claim of disparate treatment based on race in the appraisal of residential real property in connection with refinancing, including allegations that Miller knew the Austins were African American, selected comparable properties in a racially disparate manner, made downward adjustments, used coded racial language, and deviated from USPAP standards.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs' FHA claim under § 3617 survived the motion to dismiss. To state a § 3617 claim, a plaintiff need only allege discrimination because of a protected class. Plaintiffs sufficiently alleged that Miller Defendants interfered with their rights under § 3605 by discriminating against the Austins on the basis of race in appraising the property.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) §§ 12955(c), (d), (i), 12955.7, 12955.8; Civil Rights Act of 1866 §§ 1981, 1982; California Unruh Civil Rights Act § 51; California Unfair Competition Law § 17200 et seq.; California Negligent Misrepresentation § 1710
fha_claims.reasoning: FEHA claims (§§ 12955(i), 12955.7) survived MTD because they protect substantially the same rights as FHA §§ 3605 and 3617 and are subject to the same analysis. Civil Rights Act §§ 1981 and 1982 claims survived MTD; the court rejected defendants' arguments that denial of loan is required and that overvaluation/undervaluation distinction matters, finding that use of equity in already-owned property for refinancing is a protected use under § 1982. Unruh Act claim survived MTD as appraisers are 'business establishments' and the claim protects substantially the same rights as the FHA. UCL claim was dismissed for failure to plead with requisite specificity. Negligent Misrepresentation claim was dismissed because plaintiffs failed to allege reasonable reliance, as they obtained a second appraisal and refinanced based on that appraisal.

source_file: 9604967_2022_West v. City and County of San Francisco_cand
case_name: West v. City and County of San Francisco
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested reasonable accommodations to extend curfew hours at two homeless shelters (10 p.m. curfew waiver at Sanctuary shelter; arrival one hour after 10 p.m. curfew at Jazzie's Place shelter) due to mental and physical health conditions.
key_holding: The court dismissed the FHA reasonable accommodation claim against ECS with leave to amend, finding the pleading deficient on one or more elements of a § 3604(f)(3)(B) claim, while denying ECS's motion to dismiss the hostile environment claims under the FHA.
brief_summary: James West, a disabled homeless African American man, sued Episcopal Community Services, Dolores Street Community Services, and the City and County of San Francisco alleging Fair Housing Act violations including failure to provide reasonable accommodations for curfew rules at homeless shelters. The court granted in part and denied in part defendants' motions to dismiss, dismissing the reasonable accommodation claim against ECS with leave to amend while allowing hostile environment claims to proceed.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corporation v. Twombly
Community House, Inc. v. City of Boise
United States v. California Mobile Home Park Mgmt. Co.
Gamble v. City of Escondido

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege that the City owns, operates, or runs the shelters or has direct authority to make housing unavailable. The City's receipt of federal funding to grant to independent contractors does not establish FHA liability without a plausible allegation of direct authority over housing decisions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts showing DSCS discriminated based on race, color, religion, sex, familial status, or national origin. Allegations of harassment by other residents and denial of transfer based on 'annoying behavior' do not plausibly allege discrimination on a protected basis.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Transfer to disabled men's section of shelter
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege that he suffers from a cognizable handicap under the FHA, that ECS knew of his disability, or that accommodation of his handicap was necessary to afford equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling. Bare assertion of disability without connection to the requested accommodation is insufficient.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Hostile environment claim based on racial, sexual, and homophobic harassment by other residents
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that allegations of constant racial, sexual, and homophobic slurs coupled with ECS's failure to hear or address Plaintiff's concerns stated a plausible hostile housing environment claim under the FHA, applying Title VII discrimination analysis.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation for filing complaints about harassment and discrimination
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege the second and third prongs of FHA retaliation: an adverse housing consequence causally linked to protected activity and resulting damages. Allegations of threats by unidentified third parties and staff inaction do not clearly connect to protected activity or establish causation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation for complaining about harassment and discrimination
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to clearly connect protected activity to adverse housing consequences or allege resulting damages. Allegations that staff declined to set up a meeting, refused to accept written complaint, and failed to provide security do not plausibly establish retaliatory adverse housing consequences.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title I of Housing and Community Development Act of 1974; Title VI of Civil Rights Act of 1964; California Fair Employment and Housing Act; negligence; breach of mandatory duty
fha_claims.reasoning: Title I claim dismissed with prejudice—no private right of action under HCDA. Title VI claim against City dismissed without leave to amend—no plausible allegation of City's direct discrimination or supervisory duty over contractors. Title VI claim against DSCS survives MTD on hostile environment theory. Title VI claim against ECS survives MTD on deliberate indifference theory. Title VI claims against individual defendants dismissed with prejudice—Title VI applies only to entities receiving federal funds. FEHA hostile environment claim against ECS survives; FEHA claims against DSCS and City dismissed with/without leave to amend. Negligence claims against all defendants dismissed with leave to amend—failure to allege injury/damages. Breach of mandatory duty claim against City dismissed with leave to amend—failure to identify specific ordinance imposing mandatory duty.

source_file: 9605525_2022_Filho v. Chinatown Community Development Center, Inc._cand
case_name: Roberto Filho v. Chinatown Community Development Center, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested to transfer to an apartment that better accommodates his disabilities.
key_holding: The court denied Bermak's Rule 54(b) motion for partial final judgment because it was not an unusual case warranting piecemeal review, finding no pressing need for immediate judgment and no prejudice from waiting.
brief_summary: Roberto Filho sued Bermak and Chinatown Community Development Center (CCDC) alleging Fair Housing Act violations for denying his request to transfer to an apartment that better accommodates his disabilities. The court denied Bermak's motion for entry of partial final judgment under Rule 54(b), finding this was not an unusual case warranting piecemeal review and that Bermak would not be prejudiced by waiting for final judgment.
key_cases_cited: Wood v. GCC Bend, LLC, 422 F.3d 873 (9th Cir. 2005)
Stewart v. U.S. Bancorp, 297 F.3d 953 (9th Cir. 2002)
Morrison-Knudsen Co. v. Archer, 655 F.2d 962 (9th Cir. 1981)
Tsyn v. Wells Fargo Advisors, LLC, No. 14-CV-02552-LB, 2016 WL 7635883 (N.D. Cal. June 27, 2016)
Sarmiento v. Fresh Harvest, Inc., No. 20-CV-07974-BLF, 2022 WL 179685 (N.D. Cal. Jan. 20, 2022)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request to move to an apartment that better accommodates plaintiff's disabilities
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to adequately allege that defendant Bermak was aware of plaintiff's disability or that he had any authority or role in CCDC's decision-making process regarding the accommodation request. The complaint contained only conclusory allegations insufficient to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly.

case_name: Karlen v. Wells Fargo Bank, N.A.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege race-based discriminatory housing practices by mortgage servicer, including interference with property sale, surveillance, harassment, and refusal to provide mortgage statements.
key_holding: The court granted the motion to transfer to the District of Connecticut because the convenience factors—including that the property is located in Connecticut, plaintiffs reside there, and the alleged harassment occurred there—weighed in favor of transfer.
brief_summary: Ms. Karlen (who is Black) and her husband sued Wells Fargo Bank alleging race-based discriminatory housing practices related to mortgage servicing of their Connecticut home, including interference with property sale and harassment. The court granted Wells Fargo's motion to transfer the case to the District of Connecticut, finding that the convenience factors favored transfer where the property is located, plaintiffs reside, and the alleged harassment occurred.
key_cases_cited: Van Dusen v. Barrack, 376 U.S. 612 (1964)
Jones v. GNC Franchising, Inc., 211 F.3d 495 (9th Cir. 2000)
Lou v. Belzberg, 834 F.2d 730 (9th Cir. 1987)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges race discrimination in mortgage servicing and property-related conduct, not a request for reasonable accommodation.
fha_claims.disposition: Motion to Transfer Granted; Motion to Dismiss Not Ruled Upon
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted the motion to transfer to the District of Connecticut and declined to rule on the motion to dismiss, leaving the FHA disparate treatment claim on the merits unresolved pending transfer.

source_file: 9605535_2022_Filho v. Chinatown Community Development Center, Inc._cand
case_name: Roberto Filho v. Chinatown Community Development Center, Inc.
accommodation_description: Request to transfer from current unit to a one-bedroom apartment with private kitchen and bathroom at Derek Silva Apartments for disability-related reasons including ability to prepare healthy meals and manage uncontrolled urination.
key_holding: The court found plaintiff adequately alleged the accommodation is necessary for use and enjoyability of the dwelling, but converted the motion to dismiss to summary judgment because CCDC submitted evidence that no contract exists between CCDC and DAH obligating CCDC to forward accommodation requests, creating a material factual dispute.
brief_summary: Roberto Filho, a pro se plaintiff with physical disabilities including traumatic brain injury and HIV, sued Chinatown Community Development Center (CCDC) alleging it violated the FHA by refusing to forward his transfer request to Direct Access to Housing (DAH) for relocation to a one-bedroom apartment with private kitchen and bathroom. The court found Filho adequately pleaded the accommodation was necessary but converted the motion to dismiss to summary judgment because CCDC submitted evidence showing no current contract exists between CCDC and DAH, creating a material factual dispute about whether CCDC had any obligation to forward such requests.
key_cases_cited: McGary v. City of Portland, 386 F.3d 1259 (9th Cir. 2004)
Dubois v. Ass'n of Apartment Owners of 2987 Kalakaua, 453 F.3d 1175 (9th Cir. 2006)
Wolf v. City of Millbrae, No. 21-CV-00967-PJH, 2021 WL 3727072 (N.D. Cal. Aug. 23, 2021)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Transfer to a one-bedroom apartment with a private kitchen and bathroom at Derek Silva Apartments (20 Franklin Street), allegedly necessary to accommodate plaintiff's disabilities (traumatic brain injury, HIV, chronic fibrosis, bladder and prostate issues) by enabling him to prepare healthy meals and address uncontrolled urination issues.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff adequately alleged disability, necessity of accommodation, and reasonableness of the requested transfer under the Dubois burden-shifting framework. However, the dispositive issue—whether CCDC has a contractual relationship with DAH obligating it to forward accommodation requests—remains factual and requires summary judgment proceedings. Defendant submitted evidence (declaration) that no current contract exists, but plaintiff is given opportunity to present evidence of a contract or practice of forwarding requests to create a genuine dispute of material fact.

case_name: Hassan Salehi v. Lakeview Terrace Homeowners Association
accommodation_description: Condominium owner with mobility impairment requested assignment of a parking space closer to his unit as an accommodation for his disability, instead of his assigned space located behind the building across uneven grassy terrain.
key_holding: The court denied the motion to dismiss and granted preliminary injunction because plaintiff sufficiently alleged all elements of a reasonable accommodation claim under § 3604(f)(3)(B), including that the Association's failure to grant the parking reassignment for over five months constituted a constructive denial of the requested accommodation.
brief_summary: Hassan Salehi, a condominium owner with limited mobility following knee surgery, sued his homeowners association seeking a reasonable accommodation to reassign his parking space from behind his building (requiring traversal of uneven grass) to one of four spaces in front of the building. The court denied the Association's motion to dismiss and granted Salehi's motion for preliminary injunction, ordering the Association to make a front parking space available for Salehi's exclusive use pending resolution of the case.
key_cases_cited: Giebeler v. M & B Assocs., 343 F.3d 1143 (9th Cir. 2003)
Astralis Condo. Ass'n v. Sec'y, U.S. Dep't of Housing & Urban Dev., 620 F.3d 62 (1st Cir. 2010)
Howard v. HMK Holdings, LLC, 988 F.3d 1185 (9th Cir. 2021)
Salisbury v. Caritas Acquisitions V, LLC, 2018 WL 10483437 (S.D. Cal. 2018)
Dubois v. Ass'n of Apt. Owners of 2987 Kalakaua, 453 F.3d 1175 (9th Cir. 2006)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Assignment of one of four unreserved parking spaces located on the front side of the building (instead of the assigned space behind the building with a grassy strip) for exclusive use, marked as reserved, without requiring plaintiff to bear costs of modification.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff plausibly alleged all five elements of a reasonable accommodation claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(B): disability (knee surgery, limited mobility, handicapped placard), defendant's knowledge, necessity (uneven surfaces prevent safe use of assigned space), reasonableness (handicapped parking spaces are recognized reasonable accommodations), and denial (unreasonable delay since February 2022 constitutes constructive refusal). Motion to dismiss denied; claim survives to preliminary injunction and merits stages.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: California Unruh Act claim for disability discrimination in business establishment (condominium association).
fha_claims.reasoning: Court rejected defendant's argument that condominium association is not a business establishment under the Unruh Act, citing O'Connor v. Village Green Owners Ass'n, 33 Cal. 3d 790 (1983). Motion to dismiss the Unruh Act claim denied; claim survives.

case_name: Sydney Skochko v. Mercy Housing, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: Request for a hospital bed (either transported from her apartment or rented from a vendor) during temporary hotel relocation while the building's wheelchair-accessible lift was being repaired.
key_holding: Plaintiff was entitled to summary judgment on her failure-to-accommodate claims because the requested hospital bed was reasonable on its face and defendants failed to demonstrate it would cause undue hardship, particularly because they never contacted any relocation facilities about renting a hospital bed.
brief_summary: Sydney Skochko sued Mercy Housing entities under the Fair Housing Act, alleging defendants failed to reasonably accommodate her mobility disabilities by refusing to provide or facilitate a hospital bed during two temporary relocations while the building's wheelchair lift was repaired. The court granted partial summary judgment to plaintiff, finding as a matter of law that her hospital bed requests were reasonable and that defendants failed to carry their burden of showing undue hardship, while denying defendants' summary judgment motion and allowing remaining claims to proceed.
key_cases_cited: Giebeler v. M & B Associates, 343 F.3d 1143 (9th Cir. 2003)
Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986)
Matsushita Elec. Indus. Co. v. Zenith Radio Corp., 475 U.S. 574 (1986)
Fair Hous. of Marin v. Combs, 285 F.3d 899 (9th Cir. 2002)
Kolstad v. Am. Dental Ass'n, 527 U.S. 526 (1999)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Hospital bed (personal or rented) during June 2019 relocation lasting 66 days while wheelchair-accessible lift was repaired
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied Giebeler burden-shifting framework and found plaintiff established all four elements of failure to accommodate: disability, defendant's knowledge, necessity of accommodation, and refusal. Plaintiff met her burden showing rented hospital bed was reasonable on its face and possible; defendants failed to produce evidence of undue hardship or unreasonableness. Court granted plaintiff's motion for partial summary judgment on FHA claim for June 2019 relocation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Hospital bed (rented) during November 2019 relocation lasting 15 days while wheelchair-accessible lift was repaired
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied Giebeler framework and found plaintiff established all elements for November 2019 relocation. Plaintiff met burden showing rented hospital bed was reasonable and possible; defendants failed to produce evidence of undue hardship or unreasonableness despite 15-day relocation period. Court granted plaintiff's motion for partial summary judgment on FHA claim for November 2019 relocation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Intentional discrimination in failure to provide reasonable accommodation under Unruh Act
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied defendants' summary judgment motion on Unruh Act claim, finding sufficient evidence from which a reasonable jury could conclude defendants' conduct amounted to intentional discrimination. Plaintiff's disabilities were obvious and known; she directly requested accommodations that were refused; defendants' property manager recommended approval; and plaintiff suffered 81 days without accommodation in pain. Evidence supported inference of willful, affirmative misconduct.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA), California Disabled Persons Act (DPA), and California Unruh Act claims for failure to provide reasonable accommodation and punitive damages
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted plaintiff's motion for partial summary judgment on FEHA and DPA failure to accommodate claims, applying substantially similar elements to FHA claim. Court also denied defendants' summary judgment motion on punitive damages under both FHA and FEHA, finding sufficient evidence that defendants' conduct was motivated by reckless or callous indifference (FHA) and was oppressive (FEHA), satisfying standards for punitive damages liability.

source_file: 9606295_2022_Filho v. Chinatown Community Development Center, Inc._cand
case_name: Roberto Filho v. Chinatown Community Development Center, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested to transfer to a one-bedroom apartment with private kitchen and bathroom at a different property (Derek Silva Apartments at 20 Franklin Street) for disability-related reasons.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for CCDC because Filho failed to establish a genuine dispute of material fact regarding whether CCDC had a contract or relationship with DAH obligating CCDC to forward his accommodation request; without such a relationship, CCDC cannot be liable under the FHA for refusing to refer his transfer request.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Roberto Filho sued CCDC for failing to accommodate his disability by refusing to refer his request for a transfer to another housing program, alleging CCDC had a contract with DAH. The court granted summary judgment for CCDC because Filho failed to produce evidence of any contractual or relational obligation between CCDC and DAH after 2017 that would require CCDC to forward his accommodation request; without such a relationship, CCDC had no duty to accommodate under the FHA.
key_cases_cited: Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986)
Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, 477 U.S. 242 (1986)
Thornhill Publ'g Co., Inc. v. GTE Corp., 594 F.2d 730 (9th Cir. 1979)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Transfer to a one-bedroom apartment with a private kitchen and bathroom at Derek Silva Apartments (20 Franklin Street), allegedly necessary due to plaintiff's disabilities (traumatic brain injury, HIV, chronic fibrosis, bladder and prostate issues)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted summary judgment because plaintiff failed to establish a genuine dispute of material fact regarding whether defendant CCDC had a contract or relationship with DAH (the entity controlling the destination property) that would obligate CCDC to forward the accommodation request. Without such a relationship, CCDC cannot be liable under the FHA for refusing to refer the request.

source_file: 9606801_2022_Hall-Johnson v. City and County of San Francisco_cand
case_name: Hall-Johnson v. City and County of San Francisco
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges she was denied housing at Five88 affordable housing complex based on her race and disability status.
key_holding: The court denied CCDC's motion to dismiss the Fair Housing Amendments Act claim, finding plaintiff's allegations that she was denied housing because she was disabled, receiving SSI, and Black — and that 'only Chinese people' qualified — sufficiently established a prima facie case of discrimination at the pleading stage.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Hall-Johnson sued CCDC, the manager of Five88 affordable housing, alleging she was denied housing because of her race and disability. The court denied CCDC's motion to dismiss the FHA claim, finding plaintiff adequately alleged she was qualified, applied, was denied, and that discriminatory reasons were given for the denial.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Harris v. Itzhaki, 183 F.3d 1043 (9th Cir. 1999)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff adequately alleged a prima facie case of discrimination under the FHA based on race and disability at the pleading stage. The court found allegations that she was denied housing because she was Black, disabled, and received SSI, while only Chinese people qualified, sufficient to survive the motion to dismiss under the Iqbal/Twombly standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (Equal Protection and Due Process), Title II of the ADA, Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, Title VI of the Civil Rights Act, 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 and 1982, California Disabled Persons Act
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff survived dismissal of § 1983 claims (Claim One), Section 504 claims (Claim Three), and Title VI claims (part of Claim Five) after CCDC conceded it receives federal funding. Section 1981 claim (part of Claim Six) survived because plaintiff adequately alleged all prima facie elements including that similarly-situated non-protected individuals received the housing. Title II ADA claim (Claim Two) was dismissed with prejudice because CCDC is not a public entity. Section 1982 claim (part of Claim Six) was dismissed with prejudice for failure to plead qualification with specificity. CDPA claim (part of Claim Five) was dismissed with prejudice because it concerns only physical access and plaintiff alleged no barrier to physical access based on asthma.

source_file: 9606994_2022_Christian v. Rancho Grande Manufactured Home Community_cand
case_name: Emory D. Christian v. Rancho Grande Manufactured Home Community
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request was analyzed; plaintiff raised general disability discrimination claim under FHA but failed to allege defendants acted because of her disability.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's federal claims with prejudice because she failed to plausibly allege race discrimination or disability-based discrimination, noting her FHA disability claim would fail since she does not allege defendants acted because of any handicap of hers.
brief_summary: Emory D. Christian, an African-American woman, sued Rancho Grande Manufactured Home Community and related defendants alleging race discrimination, conspiracy, and Fair Housing Act violations based on disability. The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss with prejudice, finding Christian failed to plausibly allege race discrimination or that defendants acted because of any disability, and denied leave to amend as futile.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unspecified accommodation related to alleged disability; plaintiff alleged defendants' conduct caused physical and mental injuries resulting in disability status, but did not allege defendants acted because of any handicap or what specific accommodation was sought.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed the proposed Fair Housing Act § 3604(f) disability discrimination claim as futile amendment because plaintiff failed to allege that defendants acted because of any handicap of hers, which is the required element for such a claim. The complaint alleged only that defendants' conduct caused injuries resulting in disability status, not that discrimination was based on disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed race discrimination claims (causes of action 2-5) for failure to plausibly allege that defendants acted on the basis of plaintiff's race. Allegations consisted largely of conclusory statements and instances of subpar responsiveness by management that do not support an inference of racial animus under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed conspiracy claim (first cause of action) because allegations of meetings between defendants and their failure to do what plaintiff wanted do not plausibly allege a conspiracy. Opportunities to conspire and shared frustration are insufficient under Bell Atlantic v. Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 due process claims against state inspectors; state law tort claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed § 1983 due process claims against state inspectors (causes of action 2-5) because negligent conduct does not violate the Due Process Clause. Court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over remaining state law claims (causes of action 6-21) and dismissed without leave to amend.

source_file: 9607428_2023_Rice v. City and County of San Francisco_cand
case_name: Allison Barton Rice v. City and County of San Francisco
accommodation_description: Request for permission to have a rent-paying roommate in his below-market-rate condominium as a reasonable accommodation for his service-connected depression and paranoid schizophrenia.
key_holding: Triable issues of fact exist about whether the CCSF understood the request was for a rent-paying roommate, whether a rent-paying roommate was necessary as a reasonable accommodation given the plaintiff's mental health needs, and whether it would be reasonable given the program's restrictions.
brief_summary: Allison Barton Rice, a disabled veteran with service-connected depression and paranoid schizophrenia, sued the City and County of San Francisco after the agency denied his request to have a rent-paying roommate as a reasonable accommodation under the Fair Housing Act. The court denied the CCSF's summary judgment motion, finding genuine disputes of material fact on whether the agency understood the request was for a rent-paying roommate, whether such an accommodation was necessary given the plaintiff's mental health needs, and whether it would be reasonable under the below-market-rate program.
key_cases_cited: Budnick v. Town of Carefree, 518 F.3d 1109 (9th Cir. 2008)
Giebeler v. M & B Assocs., 343 F.3d 1143 (9th Cir. 2003)
Dubois v. Ass'n of Apartment Owners of 2987 Kalakaua, 453 F.3d 1175 (9th Cir. 2006)
Vorchheimer v. Philadelphian Owners Ass'n, 903 F.3d 100 (3d Cir. 2018)
United States v. Cal. Mobile Home Park Mgmt. Co., 29 F.3d 1413 (9th Cir. 1994)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to have a rent-paying roommate in a below-market-rate condominium, where the purchase agreement required written consent to lease any portion of the property. Plaintiff sought to have a roommate who would pay rent as a necessary accommodation for his service-connected depression and paranoid schizophrenia.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found genuine disputes of material fact on all three elements of the reasonable accommodation claim: (1) whether the CCSF understood the request was for a rent-paying roommate; (2) whether a rent-paying roommate was necessary given expert testimony that non-paying roommates would exacerbate plaintiff's symptoms; and (3) whether the accommodation was reasonable, as the CCSF already had a process for temporary rentals and resale prices would not be affected by allowing disabled tenants this exception. Summary judgment was denied and the claim proceeds to trial.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged interference with plaintiff's Fair Housing Act rights through issuance of a notice to cure default in response to plaintiff's accommodation request.
fha_claims.reasoning: Under 42 U.S.C. § 3617, interference encompasses issuing a notice to quit or cure in response to an accommodation request. The agency's October 26, 2017 letter warned of enforcement action if plaintiff did not cure the default, and this was issued in response to plaintiff's accommodation request. A genuine factual dispute exists as to whether this constitutes unlawful interference, precluding summary judgment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equitable defenses of good faith, unclean hands, proper conduct, and acting in good faith asserted by CCSF.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted plaintiff's motion for judgment on the pleadings, holding that equitable defenses of good faith, unclean hands, proper conduct, and acting in good faith are not valid defenses to liability under the Fair Housing Act. However, the court noted that the parties' relative conduct may be considered in evaluating equitable remedies.

source_file: 9607470_2023_In re Wells Fargo Mortgage Discrimination Litigation_cand
case_name: In re Wells Fargo Mortgage Discrimination Litigation
race_if_mentioned: Black and/or African American, other minorities
accommodation_description: Putative class of Black and other minority mortgage applicants allege Wells Fargo engaged in race-based discriminatory lending practices in mortgage origination and refinance transactions.
key_holding: The court consolidated six related cases alleging Wells Fargo discriminated against non-white mortgage customers into a single action and declined to appoint interim lead counsel without prejudice, directing plaintiffs to refile a consolidated proposal.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs in six putative class actions sued Wells Fargo alleging the bank discriminated against Black and other minority mortgage applicants through race-based practices in loan origination and refinancing. The court consolidated all six cases into a single action and denied interim lead counsel appointment without prejudice, ordering plaintiffs to file a renewed consolidated proposal.
key_cases_cited: Ortiz v. Fibreboard Corp., 527 U.S. 815 (1999)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim involves mortgage lending discrimination, not housing accommodation
fha_claims.reasoning: This is a consolidation order addressing procedural matters (consolidation of six putative class actions and appointment of interim lead counsel) rather than ruling on the merits of any FHA claim. The opinion identifies that plaintiffs allege disparate treatment and disparate impact in residential mortgage and refinance practices based on race, but does not address the substantive merits of these claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim involves mortgage lending discrimination, not housing accommodation
fha_claims.reasoning: This is a consolidation order addressing procedural matters rather than ruling on the merits of any FHA claim. The opinion identifies that plaintiffs allege disparate impact in residential mortgage and refinance practices based on race, but does not address the substantive merits of these claims.

case_name: Wayne Weatherspoon v. Reza Arfaei
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested permission to keep a trained assistance dog to protect him during seizures as a reasonable accommodation for his epilepsy.
key_holding: Although the court denied the motion to dismiss (finding plaintiff alleged sufficient facts to state plausible claims), the case was dismissed at an earlier stage; the order on the motion to dismiss did not result in a merits determination on the RA claim but rather a procedural ruling.
brief_summary: Wayne Weatherspoon, who has epilepsy and uses an assistance dog, sued his landlord Reza Arfaei after the landlord raised rent and issued a tenancy termination notice citing a no-pet policy after learning of the assistance animal. The court denied Arfaei's motion to dismiss, finding that Weatherspoon alleged sufficient factual matter to state plausible Fair Housing Act claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Lee v. City of Los Angeles, 250 F.3d 668 (9th Cir. 2001)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested accommodation for a trained assistance dog to protect him during seizures related to his epilepsy; defendant denied the accommodation and cited a no-pet policy as reason for termination.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's allegations, taken as true, state a plausible claim for relief under the Fair Housing Act by alleging epilepsy, use of a trained assistance dog, disclosure to landlord, and subsequent rent increase and termination notice citing a no-pet policy. The complaint provides sufficient factual matter beyond naked assertions to survive the motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges that after disclosing his assistance animal, defendant threatened to raise rent and subsequently terminated the tenancy, citing the no-pet policy.
fha_claims.reasoning: The allegations that defendant raised rent and terminated tenancy after plaintiff disclosed his assistance animal state a plausible claim for retaliation under the Fair Housing Act. The temporal proximity and causal connection between the disclosure and adverse actions support the claim at the pleading stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (Cal. Gov. Code §§ 12900–96) and Unruh Civil Rights Act (Cal. Civ. Code § 51) claims based on same factual allegations regarding assistance animal accommodation and retaliation.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's state law claims survive the motion to dismiss on the same basis as the FHA claims—the allegations, taken as true, state plausible claims for relief under California's Fair Employment and Housing Act and the Unruh Civil Rights Act.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA retaliation claim; ADA discrimination claim; ADA interference/coercion claim under 42 U.S.C. § 12203(b)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege adverse employment actions or causal connection required for ADA retaliation, discrimination, and interference claims. The court found that dissatisfaction with the interactive process itself, removal of flexible schedule accommodation, and complaints about fitness-for-duty exams do not constitute adverse employment actions under ADA law, and plaintiff provided only conclusory allegations without factual enhancement.

source_file: 9608564_2023_Tidwell v. Kaiser Foundation Health Plan, Inc._cand

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Twelve state law claims relating to medical care provided by Kaiser to plaintiff's deceased daughter; plaintiff scattered citations to federal criminal statutes (18 U.S.C. § 1001, 26 U.S.C. §§ 7206–07), Internal Revenue Code (26 U.S.C. § 501), False Claims Act (31 U.S.C. §§ 3729–3733), and Fair Housing Act (42 U.S.C. § 3604), but none of the enumerated claims arise under federal law.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court lacks subject-matter jurisdiction because all twelve claims arise under state law, not federal law. Plaintiff's scattered citations to federal statutes do not confer jurisdiction; plaintiff lacks standing to bring claims under criminal statutes, tax-exempt status, or False Claims Act procedures. Fair Housing Act citation is patently without merit because claims have nothing to do with housing.

case_name: Julia Hayer v. Alex Liverant
accommodation_description: Request to keep an emotional support dog in her rental home to manage symptoms of her mental health disability
key_holding: The court granted Plaintiff's motion to compel discovery regarding Defendant's No-Pet Policy and communications with a forensic psychologist because such discovery is relevant to her reasonable accommodation and disparate treatment claims, while denying Defendant's request to inspect Plaintiff's unit and dog as irrelevant since Plaintiff seeks an emotional support animal, not a service animal, and no inspection of the dog is permissible under California law.
brief_summary: Julia Hayer sued her landlord Alex Liverant alleging he refused to provide a reasonable accommodation by denying her request to keep an emotional support dog to manage her mental health disability. The court granted Plaintiff's motion to compel discovery responses regarding the landlord's No-Pet Policy and communications with a forensic psychologist consulted regarding the accommodation request, finding such evidence relevant to Plaintiff's reasonable accommodation and disparate treatment claims, while denying Defendant's request to inspect Plaintiff's apartment and dog as irrelevant to an emotional support animal claim.
key_cases_cited: Village of Arlington Heights v. Metropolitan Housing Corp., 429 U.S. 252 (1977)
Pac. Shores Properties, LLC v. City of Newport Beach, 730 F.3d 1142 (9th Cir. 2013)
Johnson v. Birks Properties, LLC, No. 21-CV-01380-GPC-DEB, 2022 WL 104736 (S.D. Cal. Jan. 11, 2022)
Auburn Woods I Homeowners Assn. v. Fair Employment & Housing Com., 121 Cal. App. 4th 1578 (2004)
Atari Corp. v. Sega of America, 161 F.R.D. 417 (N.D. Cal. 1994)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to keep an assistance dog (emotional support animal, with potential future training as psychiatric service dog) in violation of landlord's No-Pet Policy
fha_claims.reasoning: This is a discovery order, not a merits ruling. The court granted plaintiff's discovery requests regarding the no-pet policy and defendant's communications with a forensic psychologist, finding the information relevant to plaintiff's reasonable accommodation claim. The underlying claim survives and proceeds to discovery.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination in the terms, conditions, and privileges of tenancy based on disability
fha_claims.reasoning: The court recognized that plaintiff's complaint may be construed to allege disparate treatment liability based on discrimination in terms, conditions, and privileges offered because of disability. The court granted discovery requests to develop evidence of discriminatory motive and treatment of similarly situated non-disabled tenants.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) disability discrimination claim; intentional infliction of emotional distress (state tort)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court addressed plaintiff's FEHA claim and intentional infliction of emotional distress claim in the context of discovery relevance, finding that information regarding implementation of the no-pet policy and defendant's practices could bear on whether conduct was extreme or outrageous. Claims survive and proceed to discovery.

case_name: Kai Lu v. Vivente 1, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested a live-in aide as a reasonable accommodation for her disability to assist with daily living activities.
key_holding: The court denied the TRO because Defendant Vivente approved Plaintiff's reasonable accommodation requests twice (for a live-in aide and for a two-bedroom unit transfer), but Plaintiff never hired a live-in aide or provided the required documentation, and the requested injunction would constitute a collateral attack on a valid state court judgment.
brief_summary: Kai Lu sued Vivente 1, Inc. alleging Fair Housing Act violations after the landlord sought to evict her for failing to return to her original unit following a temporary relocation. The court denied Lu's motion for a temporary restraining order because Vivente approved her reasonable accommodation requests twice, but Lu never hired a live-in aide or provided the required documentation, and the TRO would improperly constitute a collateral attack on the state court eviction judgment.
key_cases_cited: Winter v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc., 555 U.S. 7 (2008)
Southeastern Community College v. Davis, 442 U.S. 397 (1979)
Updike v. Multnomah Cnty., 870 F.3d 939 (9th Cir. 2017)
Glasby v. Mercy Housing, Inc., 2017 WL 4808634 (N.D. Cal. 2017)
Marina Point, Ltd. v. Wolfson, 30 Cal. 3d 721 (1982)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation for a live-in aide and transfer to a two-bedroom unit
fha_claims.reasoning: Defendant approved plaintiff's reasonable accommodation request for a live-in aide twice (March 31, 2022 and May 27, 2022), conditioned on plaintiff completing required documentation. Plaintiff never hired a live-in aide or provided required information. Because defendant did not deny the accommodation request, plaintiff failed to show likelihood of success on the merits.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation claim under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973
fha_claims.reasoning: Under Section 504, plaintiff must show she was denied a reasonable accommodation. Because defendant approved plaintiff's accommodation requests, plaintiff failed to establish denial of a reasonable accommodation and thus cannot show likelihood of success on the merits.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation claim under California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) for live-in aide and unit transfer
fha_claims.reasoning: Under FEHA, discrimination includes refusal to make reasonable accommodations. Defendant approved plaintiff's accommodation requests twice; plaintiff never hired a live-in aide or provided required documentation. Defendant did not deny the accommodation, so plaintiff failed to show likelihood of success on the merits.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation claim under Unruh Civil Rights Act Section 51(b) and California Civil Code Section 54.1(b)(3)(B) for live-in aide and unit transfer
fha_claims.reasoning: Under Section 51(b) and Section 54.1(b)(3)(B), plaintiff must show failure to provide a reasonable accommodation. Defendant granted plaintiff's accommodation requests; plaintiff failed to show denial of accommodation and thus cannot demonstrate likelihood of success on the merits.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Negligence claim for failure to train, hire, supervise, and discipline employees to ensure compliance with fair housing laws; Unfair Competition Law (UCL) claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Negligence claim fails because plaintiff has not shown likelihood of success on underlying fair housing claims. UCL claim fails because plaintiff has not alleged any unfair business practices by defendant.

source_file: 9608829_2023_Rice v. City and County of San Francisco_cand
case_name: Allison Barton Rice v. City and County of San Francisco
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested permission to have a rent-paying roommate as a reasonable accommodation for his disability, recommended by his doctor.
key_holding: The court issued pretrial rulings including: (1) excluding HUD's determination as confusing and prejudicial because it was based on a different record than the CCSF's decision; (2) excluding evidence of plaintiff's HOA disputes from 2009-2012 as too attenuated from the 2016 accommodation dispute; (3) denying plaintiff's motion to exclude evidence about rent amounts as relevant to whether the accommodation was necessary and whether it would fundamentally alter the program; and (4) ruling that CCSF is not subject to punitive damages under the FHA.
brief_summary: Allison Barton Rice sued the City and County of San Francisco alleging that the city violated the Fair Housing Act by denying his request for a reasonable accommodation to have a rent-paying roommate as recommended by his doctor for his disability, and by interfering with his FHA rights. The court issued this Final Pretrial Order resolving motions in limine, ruling on the admissibility of various evidence and confirming that punitive damages are unavailable against the municipal defendant, in preparation for the scheduled jury trial.
key_cases_cited: Giebeler v. M & B Assocs., 343 F.3d 1143 (9th Cir. 2003)
Howard v. HMK Holdings, LLC, 988 F.3d 1185 (9th Cir. 2021)
Beachy v. Boise Cascade Corp., 191 F.3d 1010 (9th Cir. 1999)
City of Newport v. Fact Concerts, Inc., 453 U.S. 247 (1981)
Brooks v. Seattle Hous. Auth., 2013 WL 5493049 (W.D. Wash. 2013)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rent-paying roommate as an accommodation for plaintiff's mental health disability
fha_claims.reasoning: The case is at the pretrial order stage proceeding to jury trial on June 16, 2023. The court has not yet reached the merits of whether the City's denial of a rent-paying roommate accommodation was reasonable under the FHA's balancing test (fundamental alteration and undue financial/administrative burden). The court has ruled on evidentiary matters and motions in limine but has not decided the substantive reasonableness of the accommodation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Interference with plaintiff's exercise of rights under § 3604 in connection with the rent-paying roommate accommodation request
fha_claims.reasoning: The case is at the pretrial order stage proceeding to jury trial. The court has not yet reached the merits of the § 3617 interference/coercion claim. The claim survives to trial but has not been substantively decided.

case_name: Kevin E. Gilmore v. Wilshire Quinn Capital Inc.
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested; the case concerns allegations of predatory mortgage lending practices by defendant targeting minority borrowers, including reducing loan amounts and engaging in practices that diminished minority borrowers' home equity.
key_holding: The court granted defendant's motion to dismiss without prejudice because plaintiff's complaint failed to meet Rule 8(a)(2) pleading standards, as it lacked specific facts establishing how Wilshire Quinn Capital's predatory mortgage lending practices gave rise to plaintiff's FHA claims.
brief_summary: Kevin Gilmore, a minority senior citizen homeowner, sued Wilshire Quinn Capital Inc. under the Fair Housing Act, alleging the company engaged in predatory mortgage lending practices that targeted minority borrowers, reduced their equity, and ultimately caused him to lose two properties, over $600,000 in equity, rental income, and credit standing. The court denied dismissal on statute of limitations grounds (finding the complaint did not plead sufficient dates to evaluate that defense), but granted dismissal for failure to state a claim because the complaint contained only general allegations about industry-wide predatory lending with virtually no specific facts tying defendant's conduct to plaintiff's particular loans or injuries. Plaintiff was granted leave to file an amended complaint by July 14, 2023.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege an FHA claim under Twombly/Iqbal. The complaint lacks specific facts regarding the loans, dates, predatory practices directed at Plaintiff, or how Defendant's conduct violated the FHA. The complaint provides only conclusory allegations and general statements about predatory lending without sufficient factual detail to state a plausible claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff indicated intent to add claims for violations of ADA protected class of alcoholism and Civil Rights under Fair Housing Act, but no specific accommodation was alleged in the original complaint.
fha_claims.reasoning: The original complaint failed to allege a basis for federal subject matter jurisdiction (neither federal question nor diversity jurisdiction was properly pleaded), and was dismissed under § 1915(e)(2)(B) as lacking an arguable basis in law. The court granted leave to amend to allow plaintiff to cure jurisdictional deficiencies.

source_file: 9609460_2023_Silver v. Greystar Real Estate Partners, LLC_cand
case_name: Silver v. Greystar California, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought to voluntarily dismiss her Fair Housing Act claim; the specific accommodation at issue in the dropped FHA claim is not described in this procedural order.
key_holding: The court granted plaintiff's motion to amend complaint to remove her FHA claim, finding that voluntary removal of a claim does not prejudice the defendant and justice favors allowing plaintiffs to abandon claims they no longer wish to pursue.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Aimee Silver moved for leave to amend her complaint to voluntarily dismiss her Fair Housing Act claim against Greystar California, Inc., a property management company. The court granted the motion, finding no prejudice to defendants and that justice favors allowing plaintiffs to remove claims they no longer wish to pursue.
key_cases_cited: DCD Programs, Ltd. v. Leighton, 833 F.2d 183 (9th Cir. 1987)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not specified in opinion; claim removed by amendment
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff voluntarily moved to amend her complaint to remove her FHA claim. The court granted the motion under Rule 15(a)(2), finding that removal of a claim does not prejudice the defendant and that it would not be in the interest of justice to force plaintiff to prosecute a claim she does not wish to pursue. The FHA claim was withdrawn without substantive analysis of its merits.

source_file: 9609703_2023_Silver v. Greystar Real Estate Partners, LLC_cand
case_name: Aimee Silver v. Greystar California, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: The court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over plaintiff's state law claims after plaintiff voluntarily withdrew the sole federal Fair Housing Act claim, dismissing the complaint without prejudice.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Aimee Silver sued Greystar California, Inc. and related entities under the Fair Housing Act along with state law claims. Plaintiff subsequently moved to amend her complaint to withdraw the sole federal claim, and the court, finding no reason to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the remaining state law claims, dismissed the complaint without prejudice.
key_cases_cited: United Mine Workers of Am. v. Gibbs, 114 F.3d 999 (9th Cir. 1997)
Carnegie-Mellon Univ. v. Cohill, 484 U.S. 343 (1988)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not specified in opinion
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff voluntarily withdrew the sole federal FHA claim by motion to amend the complaint, leaving only state law claims. The court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the remaining state law claims and dismissed the complaint without prejudice.

case_name: Thomas E. Rothschild v. Stephanie Ann Gildred, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges FHA violations related to a real estate transaction involving property in Burlingame, CA, but fails to specify what accommodation was requested or denied by defendants.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA and ADA claims for failure to state a claim because they contained only conclusory statements without factual allegations explaining what discriminatory actions occurred or what reasonable accommodations were required.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Thomas Rothschild sued various defendants including Stephanie Gildred alleging ADA and FHA violations related to a real estate transaction involving property in Burlingame, California. The court dismissed the claims for failure to state a claim, finding plaintiff's allegations consisted only of conclusory statements without factual support explaining what discriminatory actions defendants took or what reasonable accommodations he required.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Duvall v. Cnty. of Kitsap, 260 F.3d 1124 (9th Cir. 2001)
Whitaker v. Tesla Motors, Inc., 985 F.3d 1173 (9th Cir. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges defendants failed to provide reasonable accommodations related to his disability (alcoholism and drug addiction) in connection with a real estate transaction involving a property in Burlingame, California.
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiff's FHA claim consisted of conclusory statements and threadbare recitals of legal elements without factual allegations plausibly supporting a claim for reasonable accommodation. Plaintiff failed to describe what specific accommodations he required or how defendants denied them, and did not connect the property sale facts to any FHA violation theory.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges defendants engaged in discriminatory actions and intentionally denied him equal access to housing opportunities and subjected him to discriminatory treatment based on his disability.
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiff's allegations of discriminatory actions and treatment were unsupported conclusory statements without factual content. Plaintiff never explained what discriminatory actions defendants took or what discriminatory treatment he suffered, providing only bare accusations of discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II ADA claim, conspiracy, civil conspiracy, unfair business practices, breach of contract, and tortious interference with business expectancy.
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the Title II ADA claim because none of the defendants are public entities as required by 42 U.S.C. § 12131(1). State law claims (conspiracy, unfair business practices, breach of contract, tortious interference) were dismissed for containing only threadbare recitals of legal elements and naked assertions with little to no factual support, failing to meet Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fraud, civil conspiracy, tortious interference with business expectancy, breach of contract, nuisance, and personal injury claims
fha_claims.reasoning: The Second Amended Complaint fails to state a claim on which relief may be granted under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) because it contains only threadbare recitals of the elements of each cause of action without sufficient factual allegations to allow the court to draw a reasonable inference of liability. The court also found the complaint lacks an adequate basis for subject matter jurisdiction due to incomplete diversity allegations.

case_name: Sarah Birdwell v. Avalonbay Communities, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested to be charged rent at the one-bedroom unit rate for a two-bedroom unit needed as a reasonable accommodation to accommodate her overnight home health aide.
key_holding: The court denied dismissal of the rent reduction claim, finding that requiring waiver of additional rent for a two-bedroom unit as an accommodation for disability does not constitute an unreasonable burden and is necessary to afford equal housing opportunity, but dismissed the power outage assistance request for failure to allege how AvalonBay could reasonably have accommodated the request.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Sarah Birdwell, a power wheelchair user with a mobility disability, sued AvalonBay Communities alleging the landlord failed to provide reasonable accommodations by charging her the two-bedroom unit rent rate when she required a two-bedroom unit to accommodate her overnight home health aide. The court denied AvalonBay's motion to dismiss the rent accommodation claim, finding the request was plausibly necessary and reasonable, but dismissed as time-barred claims regarding design and construction deficiencies and dismissed without prejudice the claim for assistance during power outages for failure to allege sufficient facts about how the accommodation could be reasonably implemented.
key_cases_cited: Howard v. HMK Holdings, LLC, 988 F.3d 1185 (9th Cir. 2021)
Giebeler v. M & B Assocs., 343 F.3d 1143 (9th Cir. 2003)
United States v. Cal. Mobile Home Park Mgmt. Co., 29 F.3d 1413 (9th Cir. 1994)
Salisbury v. City of Santa Monica, 998 F.3d 852 (9th Cir. 2021)
Garcia v. Brockway, 526 F.3d 456 (9th Cir. 2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request to be charged rent at the one-bedroom unit rate rather than the two-bedroom unit rate, despite needing a two-bedroom unit as a reasonable accommodation for an overnight home health aide
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss for denials occurring within the statute of limitations period (2018 and 2020), but granted dismissal for denials outside the two-year window. Court found plaintiff failed to allege a pattern or practice of widespread discrimination based on only three denials of the same request.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request for assistance exiting her apartment during PG&E rotating power outages when elevators were non-functional
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted motion to dismiss because plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts regarding how AvalonBay could reasonably have accommodated the request, making it impossible to analyze whether the accommodation was reasonable under the FHAA standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to construct or maintain accessible features in plaintiff's unit and common areas, including heavy entry doors, inaccessible kitchen work surfaces, bathroom maneuvering clearance deficiencies, insufficient parking spaces, non-functional pool lifts, and various code violations
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted motion to dismiss because the design-and-construction phase occurred between 2006 and 2009, well outside the two-year statute of limitations period. Plaintiff's conclusory allegation of an ongoing practice was insufficient to establish a pattern or practice of widespread discriminatory conduct.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III claim for barriers in common areas and leasing office; FEHA and Unruh Act claims based on same legal standards as federal claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted motion to dismiss ADA claims for common areas other than the leasing office because residential apartment complexes do not constitute public accommodations under the ADA unless made available to the general public. Leasing office claim survived. State law claims relying on same legal standards as dismissed federal claims were also dismissed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Private office space and flexible work schedule to manage chronic migraines and control physical work environment (light, sound, smell)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege he was denied the accommodations (he appears to concede he has a private office and flexible schedule) and failed to allege facts establishing that a reasonable accommodation is available that would not cause undue hardship given his essential job functions include public-facing duties and public presentations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a causal connection between protected activities (requesting accommodations, EEOC complaints, DFEH participation) and alleged adverse employment actions (fitness for duty exam and reprimand). The fitness for duty exam was part of the interactive process and not an adverse action; the reprimand occurred 8 months after protected activity with no temporal proximity or plausible causal link under but-for causation standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts showing coercion, intimidation, or threats related to ADA rights and failed to plead a distinct and palpable injury. Requests for medical documentation and statements about needing further documentation are part of the mandatory interactive process, not interference. Alleged office relocation and statements about documented disability do not objectively appear coercive or threatening.

case_name: Smith v. Henry
subsidy_program: HUD Model Lease for Subsidized Housing
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a squatter, alleged defendants prevented him from accessing his mail, claiming Fair Housing Act violations.
key_holding: The court dismissed the Fair Housing Act claim with prejudice because the plaintiff was a squatter rather than a tenant, and thus could not have engaged in protected activity under § 3617 or have been discriminated against in the privileges of rental under § 3604(b) since there was no rental of a dwelling.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Mark Smith sued property owners and managers claiming Fair Housing Act violations arising from denial of mailbox access; the court dismissed the case with prejudice because Smith was a squatter rather than a tenant and therefore could not establish the protected activity required for an FHA retaliation claim under § 3617 or discrimination in housing services under § 3604(b).
key_cases_cited: Walker v. City of Lakewood, 272 F.3d 1114 (9th Cir. 2001)
Edwards v. Marin Park, Inc., 356 F.3d 1058 (9th Cir. 2004)
Harris v. Itzhaki, 183 F.3d 1043 (9th Cir. 1999)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of access to mailbox
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff was a squatter, not a tenant or prospective tenant, and therefore could not have engaged in protected activity under the Fair Housing Act. The FHA protects rights in connection with the rental of a dwelling, which did not apply to plaintiff's status as a squatter.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Federal mail statutes, breach of contract, HUD Model Lease violation, breach of covenant of quiet enjoyment
fha_claims.reasoning: The HUD-lease claim was not viable because plaintiff failed to submit a lease as ordered and the only lease submitted was plaintiff's mother's, which did not give plaintiff a right to possession. Federal mail claims were not plausibly pleaded.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested a third parking sticker to park his vehicle on the apartment premises near his home, or alternatively, exemption to park in the visitor zone near his apartment without threat of tow. Plaintiff alleged he was denied this accommodation and instead was ticketed for parking in the visitor section despite displaying a disabled placard.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6), finding that defendants presented no arguments that the complaint failed to state sufficient facts to support a claim for violation of ADA Title III's reasonable modification requirement, and the claim-splitting doctrine did not bar the action because the federal and state court actions assert different claims in different forums.

case_name: Julia Hayer v. Alex Liverant
accommodation_description: Request to keep an emotional support animal in the apartment as a reasonable accommodation for disability
key_holding: Both cross-motions for summary judgment on the failure-to-accommodate claim were denied because while a reasonable jury could find the landlord's hostile letter was effectively a bad-faith summary refusal of the ESA request, genuine issues of material fact remain about whether the landlord acted in good faith when requesting additional documentation.
brief_summary: Julia Hayer sued her landlord Alex Liverant for failing to accommodate her request to keep an emotional support animal, and also alleged retaliation and disparate treatment claims. The court denied both cross-motions for summary judgment on the failure-to-accommodate claim, finding genuine disputes exist about whether the landlord's hostile response letter constituted a bad-faith refusal or a good-faith request for additional documentation, while also declining to grant summary judgment on the retaliation and disparate treatment claims due to disputed material facts.
key_cases_cited: Dubois v. Association of Apartment Owners of 2987 Kalakaua, 453 F.3d 1175 (9th Cir. 2006)
Castellano v. Access Premier Realty, Inc., 181 F. Supp. 3d 798 (E.D. Cal. 2016)
Smith v. Powdrill, 2013 WL 5786586 (C.D. Cal. Oct. 28, 2013)
Walker v. City of Lakewood, 272 F.3d 1114 (9th Cir. 2001)
Harris v. Itzhaki, 183 F.3d 1043 (9th Cir. 1999)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to keep an emotional support animal (species unspecified) in the apartment as a reasonable accommodation for mental disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Although plaintiff's request was somewhat vague, defendant's hostile and obnoxious response—questioning the therapeutic value of emotional support animals and demanding peer-reviewed citations—could constitute bad-faith summary refusal. However, because defendant's letter also included some arguably reasonable information requests about specific functional limitations and animal species, a reasonable jury could find good faith, precluding summary judgment for plaintiff.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Issuance of 10-day Warning Notice allegedly in retaliation for requesting emotional support animal accommodation
fha_claims.reasoning: Although plaintiff established a prima facie case of retaliation, defendant provided nondiscriminatory reasons for the warning notice (breach of no-pets lease provision), creating disputed issues of material fact regarding defendant's true motivation that preclude summary judgment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Differential treatment regarding pet policies compared to non-disabled tenants seeking to keep pets
fha_claims.reasoning: Although plaintiff established a prima facie case of disparate treatment, defendant provided nondiscriminatory explanations for differential treatment based on the type of animal sought by various tenants, creating disputed issues of material fact that preclude summary judgment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Intentional infliction of emotional distress and negligence claims under state law
fha_claims.reasoning: Defendant moved for summary judgment on these non-FHA claims but provided no separate argument or specific support, failing to meet the burden required to prevail on summary judgment.

case_name: Eduardo Escamilla, et al. v. Echelon Communities, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested additional time to obtain required HCD permits and decal, and rescission of the Sixty-Day Notice to vacate, as accommodations for Escamilla's disability (heart condition and renal failure requiring dialysis)
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' FHA reasonable accommodation claim for insufficiently alleging the necessity element but granted leave to amend, while rejecting defendant's arguments that plaintiffs lacked standing or failed to allege a denial of accommodation.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Eduardo Escamilla and Luisa Cordero sued Echelon Communities, LLC, operator of a mobilehome park, alleging the owner violated the Fair Housing Act by refusing to grant additional time to obtain required HCD permits and decal as a reasonable accommodation for Escamilla's disability (heart condition and renal failure requiring dialysis), and by refusing to rescind an eviction notice. The court granted defendant's motion to dismiss the FHA claim for failure to adequately allege the necessity element but granted leave to amend, while rejecting defendant's standing and denial-of-accommodation arguments.
key_cases_cited: Howard v. HMK Holdings, LLC, 988 F.3d 1185 (9th Cir. 2021)
Giebeler v. M & B Assocs., 343 F.3d 1143 (9th Cir. 2003)
Birdwell v. AvalonBay Communities, Inc., 2023 WL 6307894 (N.D. Cal. 2023)
Douglas v. Kriegsfeld Corp., 884 A.2d 1109 (D.C. 2005)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Additional time to obtain HCD permit and decal; rescission of Sixty-Day Notice to vacate mobilehome space
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege the necessity element of the reasonable accommodation claim.
