The complaint contained only vague allegations that Escamilla's disability made it 'more difficult' to obtain required documents but did not explain how, why, or the causal link between the disability and the need for additional time. The court found the allegations insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards but granted leave to amend.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) claim for failure to provide reasonable accommodation
fha_claims.reasoning: FEHA claim dismissed on the same grounds as the FHAA claim—insufficient pleading of the necessity element. The court applied the same analysis, finding that plaintiffs failed to allege sufficient facts to infer that the requested accommodations were necessary. Leave to amend was granted.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliatory eviction claim under California statutory and common law
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs abandoned the retaliatory eviction claim by failing to respond to defendant's arguments for dismissal. The court treated the lack of opposition as a concession that dismissal was warranted and granted the motion without prejudice.

case_name: Elaine Brown v. City National Bank
accommodation_description: Not applicable — this is a mortgage/lending discrimination (redlining) case; no reasonable accommodation or modification was requested.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA and Civil Rights Act claims as time-barred because the statute of limitations began running at the July 2019 loan denial—not upon her January 2023 discovery of the DOJ's redlining complaint—and dismissed the ECOA claim with leave to amend for failure to adequately connect CNB's alleged discriminatory lending policies to her specific loan denial injury.
brief_summary: Elaine Brown sued City National Bank alleging it denied her June 2019 home loan application as part of a discriminatory redlining practice targeting majority-Black and Hispanic neighborhoods in Oakland, relying heavily on a DOJ consent order against CNB for similar conduct in Los Angeles. The court dismissed her FHA and Civil Rights Act claims with prejudice as time-barred, holding that the two-year limitations period began running when CNB denied her loan in July 2019, rejecting her argument that the discovery rule tolled accrual until she learned of the DOJ complaint in January 2023. The court dismissed her ECOA claim with leave to amend because she failed to plausibly allege either discriminatory intent for a disparate treatment theory or a sufficient causal link between CNB's identified policies and her specific loan denial for a disparate impact theory.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Texas Dept. of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 135 S. Ct. 2507 (2015)
Garcia v. Brockway, 526 F.3d 456 (9th Cir. 2008)
Lukovsky v. City & Cnty. of San Francisco, 535 F.3d 1044 (9th Cir. 2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The FHA statute of limitations begins to run from the occurrence of the discriminatory act (loan denial on July 11, 2019), not from discovery. The two-year limitations period expired in July 2021, well before plaintiff filed suit in June 2023. Plaintiff's later discovery of the DOJ complaint against defendant cannot toll the claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that her specific injury (loan denial) was caused by defendant's alleged discriminatory policies. Although plaintiff alleged defendant's disparate impact on majority-Black and Hispanic neighborhoods, she did not connect these allegations to her own loan denial or show how defendant's 'policy of inaction' caused her injury.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA), 15 U.S.C. § 1691 et seq.; Civil Rights Act §§ 1981 and 1982; state law claims for fraud, intentional and negligent misrepresentation, intentional infliction of emotional distress, violation of the Unruh Act, Cal. Civ. Code § 51, and the Unfair Competition Law (UCL), California Business and Professions Code §§ 17200-17500
fha_claims.reasoning: Civil Rights Act claims under §§ 1981 and 1982 are subject to a two-year statute of limitations. Plaintiff's claims accrued when she became aware of the actual injury (loan denial on July 11, 2019), not when she discovered defendant's alleged discriminatory motive. The limitations period expired in July 2021. State law claims were dismissed without prejudice due to lack of supplemental jurisdiction after federal claims were dismissed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of hotel lodging based on presence of service animal; ADA Title III claim for discrimination in public accommodation; Unruh Act claim (dismissed without prejudice)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff survived motion to dismiss on ADA Title III claim. Court found plaintiff adequately pleaded disability under ADA (neuropathy, ADHD, PTSD, anxiety, depression, kidney issues substantially limiting major life activities) and that service dog qualifies as service animal under 28 C.F.R. § 36.104 (trained to provide counterbalance, deep tissue therapy, and covering to prevent panic attacks). Standing requirement also satisfied by adequate pleading of intent to return. Unruh Act claim dismissed without prejudice due to plaintiff's waiver of supplemental jurisdiction argument.

source_file: 9611552_2024_Coalition on Homelessness v. City and County of San Francisco_cand

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Eighth Amendment cruel and unusual punishment claim; Fourth Amendment unreasonable search and seizure claims; Fourteenth Amendment due process and state-created danger claims; ADA disability discrimination claim; California Government Code § 11135 disability discrimination claim; California Constitution cruel or unusual punishment claim; California Constitution unreasonable search and seizure claims; California Constitution due process claims; conspiracy claim
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted a partial stay of the case pending the Supreme Court's decision in City of Grants Pass v. Johnson, which directly impacts the viability of plaintiffs' Eighth Amendment claim. The court found that the third Landis factor (orderly course of justice) weighed in favor of a stay because the Supreme Court's ruling will bear directly on the scope of discovery, expert testimony, applicable legal standards, and proof at trial. However, the stay is conditioned on defendants continuing all previously ordered disclosures to allow plaintiffs to monitor compliance with the preliminary injunction.

case_name: Escamilla v. Echelon Communities, LLC
accommodation_description: Request for rescission of sixty-day notice to vacate and additional time to comply with mobilehome park permit requirements as a reasonable accommodation for Escamilla's disability-related limitations.
key_holding: The court denied defendant's motion to dismiss, finding plaintiffs sufficiently alleged requests for accommodation (Escamilla informed defendant of his disability when requesting more time in December 2022, and counsel sent multiple letters specifically requesting rescission of the notice to vacate as a disability accommodation), necessity of the accommodation (Escamilla's dialysis schedule, hospitalizations, and caregiving burdens on his wife delayed their ability to complete permit compliance), and that rescission of the notice could be a reasonable accommodation under the FHAA.
brief_summary: Eduardo Escamilla and Luisa Cordero sued Echelon Communities, LLC, the operator of their Santa Rosa mobilehome park, alleging the park failed to accommodate Escamilla's disability by seeking to terminate their tenancy for failure to obtain permit documentation when Escamilla's heart and kidney conditions and dialysis treatment delayed their compliance. The court denied Echelon's motion to dismiss, finding plaintiffs sufficiently alleged disability-related accommodation requests, necessity of the requested accommodations (additional time and rescission of the eviction notice), and that such accommodations could be reasonable under the FHAA.
key_cases_cited: Howard v. HMK Holdings, LLC, 988 F.3d 1185 (9th Cir. 2021)
McGary v. City of Portland, 386 F.3d 1259 (9th Cir. 2004)
Giebeler v. M & B Assocs., 343 F.3d 1143 (9th Cir. 2003)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Extension of time to comply with permit and registration decal requirements, and rescission of the sixty-day notice to vacate
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that plaintiffs sufficiently alleged: (1) requests for accommodation linked to disability in December 2022 conversation and May/June 2023 letters; (2) necessity because Escamilla's chronic illness and dialysis schedule impaired both his and Cordero's ability to navigate permit/decal process; and (3) reasonableness because extension of time and rescission would impose no fundamental alteration or undue burden, and no actual enforcement action was pending against defendant. Fact-specific reasonableness determination inappropriate at pleading stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) failure to accommodate disability claim; California Civil Code § 1942.5 retaliatory eviction claim (abandoned)
fha_claims.reasoning: FEHA claim rises and falls with FHAA claim and survives for same reasons. Retaliatory eviction claim was abandoned by plaintiffs' failure to address it in opposition brief to first motion to dismiss. Court exercised supplemental jurisdiction over FEHA claim because provisions involve substantially same rights as FHAA and parallel proceedings would create inefficiency and risk inconsistent outcomes.

source_file: 9611976_2024_Rice v. City and County of San Francisco_cand
case_name: Allison Barton Rice v. City and County of San Francisco
accommodation_description: Post-trial cost taxation order; underlying case involved request to lease portion of home to rent-paying roommates to ameliorate mental illness symptoms.
key_holding: The court taxes the full amount of costs ($19,469.61) against the plaintiff, rejecting arguments based on impropriety, indigence, chilling effect on civil rights plaintiffs, landmark issue status, and closeness of issues.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Allison Rice sued the City and County of San Francisco for Fair Housing Act discrimination based on a reasonable accommodation request; after a full trial resulting in a jury verdict for the defendant, the court taxed the full amount of costs ($19,469.61) against the plaintiff, rejecting his objections based on impropriety, indigence, chilling effect on civil rights plaintiffs, and the significance of the issues.
key_cases_cited: Ass'n of Mexican-Am. Educators v. California, 231 F.3d 572 (9th Cir. 2000)
Save Our Valley v. Sound Transit, 335 F.3d 932 (9th Cir. 2003)
Quan v. Comput. Scis. Corp., 623 F.3d 870 (9th Cir. 2010)
Stanley v. Univ. of S. Cal., 178 F.3d 1069 (9th Cir. 1999)
Lopez v. San Francisco Unified Sch. Dist., 385 F. Supp. 2d 981 (N.D. Cal. 2005)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to lease a portion of his home to rent-paying roommates or a rent-paying roommate to ameliorate the symptoms of his mental illness disability
fha_claims.reasoning: The case went to trial on a Fair Housing Act discrimination claim regarding the plaintiff's request for a reasonable accommodation to rent out a portion of his home. The jury returned a verdict in favor of the City and County of San Francisco, and judgment was entered accordingly.

case_name: Adams v. Community Housing Partnership
accommodation_description: Adams requested reasonable accommodations including a larger unit to accommodate her and her daughter's disabilities, but the specific accommodation requests are not detailed in this order.
key_holding: The court denied HomeRise's motion to dismiss Adams's FHA and FEHA reasonable accommodation claims, finding that Adams adequately pleaded she made reasonable accommodation requests necessary to her enjoyment of the housing, and HomeRise's factual challenges to the merits were premature at the pleading stage.
brief_summary: Amy Adams, a tenant receiving Section 8 Project-Based Voucher assistance, sued Community Housing Partnership/HomeRise for failing to reasonably accommodate her and her daughter's disabilities, and for habitability issues and harassment. The court denied HomeRise's motion to dismiss all eight claims, finding Adams's FHA reasonable accommodation claims were well-pleaded and timely, and that HomeRise's factual disputes regarding the merits could not be resolved at the pleading stage.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
McGary v. City of Portland, 386 F.3d 1259 (9th Cir. 2004)
Giebeler v. M & B Assocs., 343 F.3d 1143 (9th Cir. 2003)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request for transfer to a larger unit to accommodate plaintiff and her daughter's disabilities; plaintiff alleged HomeRise had other larger units available and could have relocated her with relative ease
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that FHA and FEHA claims are highly fact-specific and inappropriate for dismissal solely on pleadings; plaintiff adequately pleaded that she made reasonable accommodation requests necessary to her enjoyment of the unit, and that HomeRise denied them. Court rejected defendant's factual challenges as premature at the motion to dismiss stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unspecified reasonable accommodations for plaintiff's and her daughter's disabilities; plaintiff alleged she made multiple requests but HomeRise falsely told her SFHA had denied them without any denial notice being issued
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied the Ninth Circuit standard that FHA claims require case-by-case determination and are inappropriate for dismissal on pleadings alone; plaintiff's allegations that she requested accommodations, they were necessary, and HomeRise denied them are sufficient to survive motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodations for plaintiff's and her daughter's disabilities under the Unruh Civil Rights Act; plaintiff alleged she made requests on several occasions but HomeRise repeatedly failed to accommodate
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that Unruh Act claims for failure to provide reasonable accommodations are subject to a three-year statute of limitations and are timely; plaintiff's allegations of repeated requests for accommodations and HomeRise's failures are sufficient to survive motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodations for plaintiff's and her daughter's disabilities under California Government Code § 11135; plaintiff alleged HomeRise failed to provide accommodations despite requests
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that HomeRise is subject to § 11135 liability because it receives state financial assistance through the PBV program administered by SFHA, a state agency; plaintiff's allegations of failure to accommodate are sufficient to survive motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of implied warranty of habitability, breach of implied covenant of quiet enjoyment, negligence, and intentional infliction of emotional distress
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that state law claims for breach of habitability and quiet enjoyment are timely under the four-year statute of limitations because plaintiff alleged habitability issues continuing through November 2021 and the water heater explosion occurred within the limitations period; negligence and IIED claims are timely under the two-year statute of limitations based on events occurring after November 2021.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: First Amendment right to petition; Fourth Amendment search/seizure; Fourteenth Amendment equal protection; substantive and procedural due process; Monell municipal liability; 42 U.S.C. § 1985 conspiracy; 42 U.S.C. § 1981 racial discrimination; state law tort claims (defamation, intentional infliction of emotional distress, negligence, breach of contract, violation of California Consumer Legal Remedies Act, violation of California Unfair Competition Law)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly for any federal constitutional or statutory theory. First Amendment retaliation claim based on government speech requires showing of adverse action affecting rights, benefits, or status with the state, or threat of legal sanctions; plaintiff's allegations of defamatory statements in disposition report and involvement of social worker do not meet this high bar. Fourth Amendment claim fails because no search or seizure alleged. Equal protection claim fails to allege intent to discriminate based on protected class membership. Due process claims fail to identify deprivation of protected liberty or property interest or conduct shocking the conscience. Monell claim fails to adequately plead deprivation of constitutional right or municipal policy as moving force. Section 1985 claim fails to allege deprivation of legally protected right based on invidiously discriminatory class-based animus. Section 1981 claim fails to allege facts linking defendants' conduct to intent to discriminate based on race. State law claims dismissed for lack of supplemental jurisdiction.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Defendant raised Fair Housing Act discrimination as a defense to unlawful detainer action in removal notice
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that defendant's FHA defense cannot form the basis of federal question jurisdiction under the well-pleaded complaint rule; a defendant's counterclaim or defense cannot create federal jurisdiction. The case was remanded to state court for lack of subject matter jurisdiction.

source_file: 9613394_2019_White v. San Diego Sunrise Management Company_casd
case_name: White v. San Diego Sunrise Management Company
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged defendants failed to install a wheelchair ramp and handicap accessible bathroom facilities for James White, who is wheelchair bound.
key_holding: Todd White's claims under the FHA and ADA were dismissed because he failed to allege he himself suffers from a disability or that any discrimination against him was causally connected to his father's disability, and he lacks standing to bring claims on behalf of his father James White.
brief_summary: Todd White sued San Diego Sunrise Management Company and others alleging they violated the FHA and ADA by failing to make reasonable accommodations (wheelchair ramp and accessible bathroom) for his wheelchair-bound father James White, raising rent, and refusing to renew the lease unless Todd vacated. The court dismissed Todd White's claims for failure to state a claim because he failed to allege his own disability or causal connection to his father's handicap, and denied his request to proceed as guardian ad litem for his father.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 129 S.Ct. 1937 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
United States v. California Mobile Home Park Mgmt. Co., 107 F.3d 1374 (9th Cir. 1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff Todd White failed to allege a causal link between his father's wheelchair-bound disability and defendants' refusal to allow him full and equal access to the dwelling. Plaintiff instead alleged denial of access as retaliation for initiating a lawsuit, not as a result of any handicap, thus failing to state a claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(1).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Installation of a wheelchair ramp at the entry way to the apartment, a handicap accessible bathroom facility, and other necessary repairs for James White's use and enjoyment
fha_claims.reasoning: Although Todd White alleged that terms and conditions of James White's lease were modified and that reasonable accommodations were refused, Todd White failed to allege that he was a party to the lease agreement or that he himself suffered a physical or mental handicap, thus failing to state a claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(2).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) claim for denial of full and equal access to the dwelling and refusal to add plaintiff to the lease agreement
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts establishing a nexus between any disability and the alleged denial of access or refusal to add him to the lease, as he did not allege his own disability and failed to connect his father's disability to the challenged conduct.

case_name: Williams v. Camden Old Creek
accommodation_description: No accommodation request was made; this case involves alleged racial discrimination through various incidents including questioning about Williams' name, a comment about 'the ghetto' when towing her car, and a repairman's statement that the manager 'doesn't like you' because 'you are black.'
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' FHA race discrimination claim because plaintiffs failed to allege they were treated differently than any other resident of a different race, and the deterioration of the landlord-tenant relationship provided an obvious alternative legal explanation for the termination notice.
brief_summary: Shaliecia Williams, an African-American woman, and her minor daughter sued Camden USA, Inc. and Camden Old Creek apartment complex alleging racial discrimination under the Fair Housing Act based on multiple incidents including comments about her name, a 'ghetto' reference when towing her car, and a 60-day eviction notice. The court granted defendant's motion to dismiss, finding plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege discriminatory intent because they did not claim they were treated differently than similarly situated non-Black residents, and the deteriorating landlord-tenant relationship provided an obvious alternative explanation for the challenged actions.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Tex. Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Cmtys. Project, Inc., 135 S. Ct. 2507 (2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege discriminatory intent under Iqbal/Twombly. Although three incidents referenced race, they were either distasteful comments not rising to direct evidence of discrimination, stray remarks, or standing alone insufficient to infer racial motivation. Plaintiffs did not allege differential treatment compared to similarly situated residents of other races, and the deteriorating relationship between parties provided an obvious alternative legal explanation for defendant's actions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Only one incident involved enforcement of a facially neutral policy (printer use requiring residency). The court found it implausible that enforcement of this neutral residency requirement had a racially discriminatory effect, as the policy itself was not discriminatory and the enforcement was non-discriminatory.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA), California Unruh Civil Rights Act, California Unfair Competition Law (UCL), Negligence
fha_claims.reasoning: FEHA and Unruh Act claims are subject to the same analysis as FHA claims and were dismissed on the same pleading-stage grounds. UCL and negligence claims were dismissed without prejudice under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c) after dismissal of the federal FHA claim, as the court declined supplemental jurisdiction.

case_name: Christina Pierson and Brandon Bolic v. Janice E. Martinelli and Janice Martinelli as Trustee of the Janice Martinelli Trust Dated June 27, 2005
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation was requested; the case involves alleged discriminatory harassment based on disability (Lupus) including calling Pierson a 'disabled loser' and stating she should 'go live in Kimball Towers with the rest of the disabled losers.'
key_holding: The court found sufficient facts to support a disability discrimination claim under the FHA where the landlord allegedly began harassing the tenant after learning she had Lupus, including cutting off water, changing locks, and filing a meritless unlawful detainer action; however, sex discrimination claims were dismissed for failing to allege discriminatory motive beyond personal dislike.
brief_summary: Christina Pierson sued her landlord Janice Martinelli for Fair Housing Act violations, alleging disability discrimination based on Lupus and sex discrimination; the landlord allegedly made derogatory comments about disabled people after learning of Pierson's Lupus and then engaged in escalating harassment including cutting off water, changing locks, and filing a meritless eviction. The court dismissed Mr. Bolic for lack of standing, dismissed sex discrimination claims for insufficient allegations of discriminatory motive, but denied dismissal of the disability discrimination claim finding sufficient factual allegations to proceed.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Tex. Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Cmtys. Project, Inc., 135 S. Ct. 2507 (2015)
Village of Arlington Heights v. Metro. Hou. Dev. Corp., 429 U.S. 252 (1977)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Ms. Pierson alleged sufficient facts under the Arlington Heights factors to state a plausible claim of disability discrimination based on Lupus; the court accepted her allegations that Ms. Martinelli made negative comments upon learning of her disability and subsequently increased harassment, which could support an FHA violation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Ms. Pierson failed to allege sufficient facts to support gender discrimination against men; the court found that Ms. Martinelli's hiring of Mr. Bolic and subsequent dislike of him personally, rather than discriminatory animus based on gender, was insufficient to plausibly allege that harassment was motivated by gender discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: FEHA, Unruh Civil Rights Act, negligence
fha_claims.reasoning: The court did not separately analyze the FEHA, Unruh Act, or negligence claims; these claims survive the motion to dismiss to the extent they track the disability discrimination theory that survived.

case_name: Sandy A. Eulitt v. City of San Diego
accommodation_description: Request to waive San Diego's six-month maximum stay rule for automobile trailers/RV parks as a reasonable accommodation for disability
key_holding: Plaintiff failed to state a reasonable accommodation claim because she did not request an accommodation from the defendant, did not specify her disability, and did not allege how extending her stay beyond six months would address her disability needs.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Sandy Eulitt sued the City of San Diego alleging she was evicted from an RV park due to Ordinance No. 2584's six-month stay limit, claiming violations of the Equal Protection Clause, Fair Housing Act, and ADA. The court granted the motion to dismiss, finding Plaintiff failed to adequately plead a reasonable accommodation claim because she did not request an accommodation from the defendant, did not specify her disability, and did not explain how the accommodation would address her disability needs.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Ctr., Inc.
Weinreich v. L.A. County Metro. Transp. Auth.
McGary v. City of Portland

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Extended length of stay in RV park beyond the six-month limit imposed by San Diego Ordinance No. 2584
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege that she requested a reasonable accommodation from Defendant, failed to specify the length of stay requested, failed to identify her specific disability, and failed to allege how the accommodation would address her disability needs. The court found the allegations insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged interference with landlord's grant of reasonable accommodation by threatening or coercing the landlord to revoke it
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege in the SAC that the claim was based on § 3617, failed to allege that Defendant threatened the landlord because a reasonable accommodation had been granted, and failed to allege that Defendant was aware a reasonable accommodation existed. The complaint lacked sufficient factual allegations to state a plausible interference claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claim for discrimination in public services; California Civil Code § 12955 claim for source-of-income discrimination; San Diego Ordinance No. 20986 claim for source-of-income discrimination
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA claim failed because Plaintiff did not allege a qualified disability and did not allege discriminatory intent or disparate impact from the facially neutral ordinance. Civil Code § 12955 claim failed because Defendant is not an owner of a housing accommodation. Ordinance No. 20986 claim failed because Defendant does not fit the definition of 'Person' under the ordinance and the ordinance's effective date was after the complaint was filed.

case_name: Baker v. City of San Diego
race_if_mentioned: Minority/African American and other minority residents of affected San Diego communities
accommodation_description: No individual reasonable accommodation request; this is a systemic challenge to government defendants' alleged pattern of concentrating low-income housing in minority neighborhoods.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' FHA claims because they failed to establish a robust causal connection between the statistical disparity showing concentration of low-income housing in minority neighborhoods and any specific defendant policy, as required under Texas Dept. of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project.
brief_summary: Individual residents of predominantly minority San Diego neighborhoods sued the County of San Diego, City of San Diego, and San Diego Housing Commission alleging defendants concentrated low-income housing projects in their communities, perpetuating segregation and housing discrimination in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss, finding plaintiffs failed to establish a robust causal connection between the statistical disparity in housing concentration and any specific defendant policy as required for disparate impact claims.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 135 S. Ct. 2507 (2015)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Committee Concerning Cmty. Improvement v. City of Modesto, 583 F.3d 690 (9th Cir. 2009)
Ave. 6E Invs., LLC v. City of Yuma, 818 F.3d 493 (9th Cir. 2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Concentration of low-income housing projects in minority neighborhoods; construction of Southeastern Live Well Center in Affected Communities
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to identify a facially-neutral policy causing the statistical disparity and failed to establish a robust causal connection between the City's policies and the alleged disparate impact. The court found that the Southeastern Live Well Center is not a housing project and thus does not fall within FHA's scope, and that Plaintiffs' reliance on cases involving sale or rental of dwellings was inapplicable.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (Equal Protection Clause); 42 U.S.C. § 3608(e)(5); 24 C.F.R. § 903.15(d); California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA)
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 1983 claims cannot be based on state law or regulations; violations of 42 U.S.C. § 3608(e)(5) cannot form the basis of a Section 1983 claim as it governs HUD Secretary's administration; Equal Protection claim failed because Plaintiffs did not allege an invidious or discriminatory purpose underlying the County's plan to build the Southeastern Live Well Center; FEHA claim failed as derivative of the FHA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: City's zoning policies and Community Plans concentrating low-income housing in minority neighborhoods; waiver of development impact fees
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to establish a robust causal connection between the City's policies (Community Plans and waiver of development impact fees) and the statistical disparity in housing concentration. The court found no allegations showing the policy caused the disparity or that the City's housing policies lacked a legitimate basis.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (Equal Protection Clause); California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA)
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 1983 claim failed because Plaintiffs did not allege that the City acted with intent or purpose to discriminate based on protected class membership; FEHA claim failed as derivative of the FHA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: SDHC's Housing Choice Voucher program and tax credit project approvals concentrating low-income housing in minority neighborhoods
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to allege how SDHC's policies caused the statistical disparity. The court noted that CTCAC, not SDHC, has ultimate discretion over tax credit approvals, and Plaintiffs failed to allege a causal link between SDHC's requirement that buildings be tax-exempt and the alleged racial disparities.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (Equal Protection Clause); California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA)
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 1983 claim failed because Plaintiffs did not allege that SDHC acted with intent or purpose to discriminate; FEHA claim failed as derivative of the FHA claim.

case_name: Christina Pierson, et al. v. Janice E. Martinelli
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege the landlord discriminated based on disability and sex by banning male visitors to Ms. Pierson's apartment, including calling police on Mr. Bolic over 50 times.
key_holding: The court denied Defendants' motion to dismiss for lack of standing, finding that both Ms. Pierson and Mr. Bolic sufficiently alleged injury-in-fact; the court also denied the 12(b)(6) motion, finding that Plaintiffs plausibly stated a facially discriminatory policy against males under § 3604(b) based on the landlord's repeated statements that she does not want men at her property.
brief_summary: Christina Pierson and Brandon Bolic sued landlord Janice Martinelli alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act, California FEHA, and the Unruh Civil Rights Act for banning male visitors to Pierson's apartment and calling the police on Mr. Bolic over 50 times. The court denied Defendants' motion to dismiss for lack of standing, finding both plaintiffs sufficiently alleged injury-in-fact, and denied the 12(b)(6) motion, concluding that the landlord's repeated statements about not wanting men at her property plausibly stated a facially discriminatory policy based on sex.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Cmty. House, Inc. v. City of Boise, 490 F.3d 1041 (9th Cir. 2007)
Warth v. Seldin, 422 U.S. 490 (1975)
Lujan v. Defs. of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs plausibly alleged that defendant instituted a facially discriminatory policy against males by repeatedly stating she did not want men at the property and enforcing that policy through police calls and lock changes. Under the facially discriminatory policy framework, plaintiffs need only show explicitly differential treatment, not discriminatory motive or pattern, and the court found the allegations sufficient under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Disability discrimination claim based on alleged discrimination against Ms. Pierson due to her disability (Lupus)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court previously denied defendant's motion to dismiss Ms. Pierson's disability discrimination claims in its April 29, 2020 Order and found no reason to revisit the issue on the second motion to dismiss. The court did not re-analyze the merits but applied collateral estoppel to its prior ruling.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) and Unruh Civil Rights Act claims based on sex and disability discrimination
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the same legal analysis to FEHA and Unruh Act claims as to FHA claims and found that plaintiffs plausibly stated both sex and disability discrimination claims under state law, which survive the motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Access to private parking lot
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that plaintiff failed to carry his burden of proof on the ADA Title II claim because the property at issue (a private parking lot) was not a place of public accommodation, and even if it were, plaintiff had not been denied equal access. The court declined supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims.

case_name: Williams v. Camden USA Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff with PTSD and severe anxiety requested to attend her deposition via videoconference instead of in person due to disability-related panic attacks and psychological distress.
key_holding: The court denied Plaintiff's motion for protective order seeking to conduct her deposition via videoconference, finding no good cause because Plaintiff failed to demonstrate a particular and specific need for remote participation, existing safeguards were adequate, and Defendant's concerns about observing key witness credibility in person were persuasive.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Shaliecia Williams sued Camden USA Inc., the owner of an apartment complex, alleging race and disability discrimination under the Fair Housing Act, as well as state law claims. The court resolved a discovery dispute about whether Plaintiff's deposition must proceed in person, with Plaintiff seeking to participate via videoconference due to PTSD and severe anxiety causing panic attacks. The court denied Plaintiff's motion for protective order, finding she failed to demonstrate good cause for remote deposition when adequate safeguards existed and Defendant's concerns about observing key witness credibility in person were compelling.
key_cases_cited: Phillips ex rel. Estates of Byrd v. General Motors Corp., 307 F.3d 1206 (9th Cir. 2002)
WebSideStory, Inc. v. NetRatings, Inc., 2007 WL 1120567 (S.D. Cal. Mar. 22, 2007)
Gersh v. Anglin, No. CV-17-50-M-DCL-JCL, 2019 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 162473 (D. Mont. Apr. 5, 2019)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Videoconference deposition accommodation for PTSD and anxiety; also negligence and California Fair Employment and Housing Act violations; California Civil Code § 1942.5(a) retaliation claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied plaintiff's motion for protective order to conduct deposition via videoconference, finding plaintiff failed to meet her burden of showing 'particular and specific need' for the accommodation under Rule 26(c)(1). Court found existing safeguards (limited deposition hours, code of conduct, local rules, chambers procedures) were sufficient and that videoconference depositions of key witnesses present disadvantages regarding credibility assessment and witness coaching concerns.

case_name: Irvin Musgrove v. Angie Hanifin, Margery Pierce, Keysa Machado, Susana Sandoval-Soto, and Oceanside Housing Authority
accommodation_description: The order references Defendants' denial of Plaintiff’s reasonable accommodation requests but does not specify the nature of the requested accommodation.
key_holding: The court granted Plaintiff leave to file a Seventh Amended Complaint (adding FHA reasonable accommodation claims) while denying as moot Defendants' motion to dismiss the Sixth Amended Complaint, finding it would conserve judicial resources to allow Plaintiff to file and Defendants to respond to the new complaint.
brief_summary: Pro se Plaintiff Irvin Musgrove, a public housing tenant, sued Oceanside Housing Authority and individual employees alleging disability discrimination and denial of reasonable accommodation requests under the Fair Housing Act and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act. The district court granted Plaintiff leave to file a Seventh Amended Complaint adding new causes of action including FHA reasonable accommodation claims, while denying as moot Defendants' motion to dismiss the prior complaint.
key_cases_cited: Cato v. United States, 10 F.3d 1103 (9th Cir. 1995)
Noll v. Carlson, 803 F.2d 1446 (9th Cir. 1987)
Jones v. Community Redevelopment Agency, 733 F.2d 646 (9th Cir. 1984)
Wagh v. Metris Direct, Inc., 348 F.3d 1102 (9th Cir. 2003)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff's reasonable accommodation requests to Oceanside Housing Authority (specific accommodations not detailed in this order, but referenced as denied)
fha_claims.disposition: Motion to Dismiss Denied as Moot
fha_claims.reasoning: The Sixth Amended Complaint's motion to dismiss was denied as moot because the court granted plaintiff leave to file a Seventh Amended Complaint with more fully developed causes of action under the Fair Housing Act § 3604(3)(B) and implementing regulations regarding reasonable accommodations. The court found the proposed seventh amendment would cure prior pleading deficiencies and conserve judicial resources by allowing defendants to respond to the newly articulated claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act claim for denial of reasonable accommodations; Unruh Civil Rights Act (California Civil Code § 51) claim for discriminatory conduct
fha_claims.disposition: Motion to Dismiss Denied as Moot
fha_claims.reasoning: The court's prior order dismissing the Fifth Amended Complaint found that allegations were 'otherwise potentially sufficient to state a claim under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act' arising from denial of reasonable accommodation requests. The Sixth Amended Complaint's motion to dismiss was denied as moot to permit the Seventh Amended Complaint, which includes Section 504 and Unruh Act claims with more fully developed factual and legal allegations.

case_name: Nelson v. Sorrento Tower Apartments
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation was requested; this case involves alleged racial disparate treatment and application fraud in the context of a public housing transfer application, not a disability-based accommodation request.
key_holding: On sua sponte IFP screening, the court allowed the FHA disparate treatment claims (Counts I and III) and state-law defamation claim (Count IV) to proceed, but dismissed the 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 and 1985(3) claims (Counts II and V) with leave to amend because plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts showing that race was the but-for cause of his rental denial.
brief_summary: Warren Nelson, a 64-year-old African-American man, applied through HUD's portability public housing program to transfer from Minneapolis public housing to Sorrento Tower Apartments in San Diego. He alleges Defendants altered his rental application to falsely indicate he was a sex offender, used that altered document to deny his application, and reported the false accusation to the San Diego Public Housing Authority, HUD, and other agencies. The court granted IFP status, allowed the FHA disparate treatment and defamation claims to survive screening, but dismissed the §1981 and §1985(3) claims for failure to plead comparator facts establishing race as the but-for cause of the denial.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Harris v. Itzhaki, 183 F.3d 1043 (9th Cir. 1999)
Comcast Corp. v. Nat'l Ass'n of African American-Owned Media, 140 S.Ct. 1009 (2020)
Lindsey v. SLT Los Angeles, LLC, 447 F.3d 1138 (9th Cir. 2005)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found sufficient factual allegations, accepted as true, to state a plausible claim for disparate treatment under FHA § 3604(b) based on allegations that defendants passed over plaintiff's application in favor of white applicants through falsehoods and deception, and that defendants unnecessarily delayed the review process. Claim survives the low threshold of § 1915(e)(2) screening.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's allegations of interference and coercion under FHA § 3617 are encompassed within the disparate treatment claim and survive § 1915(e)(2) screening as part of the overall FHA claim alleging discriminatory conduct and unnecessary delays.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Civil Rights Act § 1981 (racial discrimination in contracts), § 1985(3) (conspiracy to deprive equal protection), California defamation per se
fha_claims.disposition: § 1915(e)(2) dismissal of § 1981 and § 1985(3) claims; defamation claim survives
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts under § 1981 to show race was the but-for cause of denial, specifically failing to allege that similarly-situated white applicants were offered housing while plaintiff was not. § 1985(3) conspiracy claim dismissed as derivative of the failed § 1981 claim. Defamation per se claim survives screening because plaintiff adequately alleged false statements (sexual offender designation) made to government entities, which defendants knew to be false given plaintiff's prior HUD-subsidized housing status.

case_name: Stephanie Johnson v. Birks Properties, LLC
accommodation_description: Request to keep an emotional support animal (dog named Benji) as a reasonable accommodation despite a no-pets policy in the lease
key_holding: Plaintiff sufficiently pled claims under § 3604(c) and § 3604(f)(2)(A) where defendant's statements about not renewing the lease because of the ESA request, without consideration of plaintiff's documented medical need, plausibly expressed a discriminatory preference against ESA users and constituted differential treatment based on disability.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Stephanie Johnson sued Birks Properties, LLC and Roger Birks alleging disability discrimination under the Fair Housing Act after the landlord threatened not to renew her lease when she requested an emotional support animal as a reasonable accommodation for her mental health disability. The court denied Defendants' motion to dismiss on the FHA claims under § 3604(c) (discriminatory statements) and § 3604(f)(2)(A) (terms and conditions of rental), finding plaintiff adequately pled a discriminatory preference against ESA users and differential treatment compared to her non-disabled roommate, while dismissing the Unruh Act and negligence claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Giebeler v. M&B Assocs., 343 F.3d 1143 (9th Cir. 2003)
United States v. Cal. Mobile Home Park Mgmt. Co., 29 F.3d 1413 (9th Cir. 1994)
Avenue 6E Investments, LLC v. City of Yuma, 818 F.3d 493 (9th Cir. 2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff plausibly alleged that Defendant's oral statements—'When your lease comes back around, I'm not going to want a dog on the property'—violated § 3604(c) by expressing a preference, limitation, or discrimination against those relying on ESAs, read in context of Plaintiff's documented medical condition and need for accommodation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Emotional support animal (ESA dog named Benji) as reasonable accommodation for mental health disability; Defendant demanded additional $700 security deposit and subsequently refused to renew lease due to presence of ESA.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff adequately pled all four elements of a reasonable accommodation claim under § 3604(f)(1)(A) and § 3604(f)(3)(B): (1) disability (mental health condition); (2) Defendants' knowledge (via doctor's paperwork); (3) necessity of accommodation (ESA needed to use and enjoy dwelling); and (4) refusal to accommodate (threatening non-renewal of lease because of the animal).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff plausibly alleged disparate treatment under § 3604(f)(2)(A): she has a handicap, was treated differently (roommate offered lease renewal while Plaintiff was not), and differential treatment was motivated at least in part by her disability (need for ESA).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (Cal. Gov't Code § 12955), California Unruh Civil Rights Act (Cal. Civ. Code § 51), Negligence, Unfair Business Practices (Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17200)
fha_claims.reasoning: FEHA claims (§§ 12955(a), (c), (d), (k)) and UCL claim survived MTD because they track the FHA claims that survived. Unruh Act claim dismissed for failure to allege intentional discrimination (disability was motivating factor but not intent to discriminate). Negligence claim dismissed as threadbare recitation of legal elements without factual support regarding hiring, training, or employment decisions. Plaintiff granted leave to amend on all dismissed state claims.

case_name: Patrice Baker, et al. v. City of San Diego, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege defendants' zoning policies created disparate impact on minority communities by concentrating low-income housing in Encanto and Southeastern San Diego
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' FHA disparate impact claim because plaintiffs failed to establish robust causality between the challenged citywide zoning policies and the alleged statistical disparity in affordable housing placement in minority communities.
brief_summary: San Diego residents sued the City of San Diego, Housing Authority, and San Diego Housing Commission alleging defendants' zoning policies and funding distribution practices concentrated low-income housing in minority communities (Encanto and Southeastern San Diego), violating the FHA. The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss, finding plaintiffs failed to establish robust causality between the challenged citywide policies and the alleged statistical disparity.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dept. of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Cmties. Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Sw. Fair Hous. Council, Inc. v. Maricopa Domestic Water Improvement Dist., 17 F.4th 950 (9th Cir. 2021)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ave. 6E Invs., LLC v. City of Yuma, 818 F.3d 493 (9th Cir. 2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to allege a robust causal connection between the City Defendants' policies (Community Plans, streamlined review process, Expedite Program, Ordinances 20916 and 20917, Resolution 313066) and the alleged statistical disparity in low-income housing concentration. Although the policies were facially neutral and statistical disparity was alleged, plaintiffs did not establish that these specific policies, rather than other factors, caused the disparate effect, and failed to allege bifurcation or targeted application of the policies.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to allege facts sufficient to establish a robust causal connection between any specific policy of the SDHC and the alleged statistical disparity. Plaintiffs made allegations based on statistical outcomes but failed to establish a nexus between any specific SDHC policy and the distribution of federal funds.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (Equal Protection Clause), California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA)
fha_claims.reasoning: The § 1983 claim failed because plaintiffs did not allege facts sufficient to show that execution of defendants' policies caused an FHA violation, and § 1983 claims cannot be based on state law violations. For the Equal Protection component, plaintiffs failed to allege an invidious or discriminatory purpose underlying the facially neutral policies, amounting only to a formulaic recitation of elements. FEHA claim was dismissed because liability under the FHA also supports liability under FEHA, and the FHA claim failed.

case_name: Tiffany Ireland et al. v. Solaris Enterprise, LLC et al.
citation: No reporter citation (S.D. Cal. docket order)
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged defendant landlord enforced rules prohibiting tenants from having emotional support animals in the apartment complex.
key_holding: The court approved the settlement as fair and reasonable for minor plaintiff G.I., finding the $10,000 settlement amount within the range of settlements approved in similar FHA discrimination cases involving minors.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Tiffany Ireland and her minor son G.I. sued Solaris Enterprises, LLC and David Zhu alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act, California Fair Employment and Housing Act, and related state laws based on the landlord's enforcement of rules prohibiting emotional support animals at their apartment complex. The parties reached a settlement at a Mandatory Settlement Conference, and the court confirmed the settlement as fair and reasonable for the minor plaintiff, approving a $10,000 payment.
key_cases_cited: Robidoux v. Rosengren, 638 F.3d 1177 (9th Cir. 2011)
Dacanay v. Mendoza, 573 F.2d 1075 (9th Cir. 1978)
Angstman v. Carlsbad Seapoint Resort IT, L.P., No. 11CV62 L(WMC), 2011 WL 13356101 (S.D. Cal. Aug. 30, 2011)
Faustino v. Cent. SDHC FHA LLC, No. 16-CV-2326-BAS-AGS, 2018 WL 1510544 (S.D. Cal. Mar. 27, 2018)
Salmeron v. United States, 724 F.2d 1357 (9th Cir. 1983)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to have emotional support animals in apartment complex where defendant enforced rules prohibiting tenants from having emotional support animals
fha_claims.reasoning: The parties settled the FHA claim regarding emotional support animals at a Mandatory Settlement Conference on April 8, 2022. The court approved the settlement as fair and reasonable, awarding the minor plaintiff $10,000 to be placed in a blocked account.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA), California Civil Code § 1942.5, negligence, and Unruh Act claims
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA claims (FEHA, § 1942.5, negligence, Unruh Act) were resolved as part of the comprehensive settlement agreement approved by the court on April 27, 2022.

case_name: Warren F. Nelson v. Sorrento Tower Apartments
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation requested; plaintiff alleges racial discrimination in denial of housing application based on falsely indicated sex offender status.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's complaint for failure to establish Article III standing (no concrete injury-in-fact) and failure to state a cognizable claim, finding plaintiff's allegations conclusory and insufficient to plead discriminatory intent or causation.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Warren Nelson, an African American applicant, sued Sorrento Tower Apartments alleging racial discrimination after his housing application was initially denied due to a falsely indicated sex offender status, later corrected. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding plaintiff lacked Article III standing (no concrete injury) and failed to state plausible claims of racial discrimination, retaliation, defamation, or conspiracy, though plaintiff was granted leave to amend.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)
Maya v. Centex Corp., 658 F.3d 1060 (9th Cir. 2011)
Lindsey v. SLT Los Angeles, LLC, 447 F.3d 1138 (9th Cir. 2006)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's allegations of racial discrimination under § 3604(b) are conclusory and lack factual support showing defendants' actions were motivated by race. Defendants' conduct in allowing plaintiff to amend his application and reinstate him on the waitlist contradicts any inference of discriminatory intent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff fails to allege facts establishing the three elements of retaliation: protected activity, adverse action, and causal nexus. Defendants' continued processing of plaintiff's application and permission to amend it negates any inference of retaliation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's § 3601-19 claim relies solely on conclusory statements without factual allegations showing discriminatory conduct or differential treatment based on a protected class.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1981 (equal contracting rights); California Civil Code §§ 44, 45a (defamation); 42 U.S.C. § 1985(3) (conspiracy); 15 U.S.C. § 1691 (credit discrimination)
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA claims fail under Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards: § 1981 claim lacks facts showing denial of contracting rights; defamation claim lacks facts showing publication, falsity, or special damages; § 1985(3) conspiracy claim is conclusory without specific factual allegations; § 1691 claim fails because defendants are not a consumer reporting agency and had no obligation to provide the requested report.

case_name: Warren F. Nelson v. Sorrento Tower Apartments
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges racial discrimination in housing application denial and that defendants falsely labeled him a sex offender.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's second amended complaint with prejudice because plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts to establish standing or state plausible claims for racial discrimination under § 3604(b), retaliation under § 3617, or defamation.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Warren Nelson sued Sorrento Tower Apartments claiming racial discrimination after his housing application was denied and later cancelled; the court dismissed the complaint with prejudice finding plaintiff failed to plead facts sufficient to establish injury-in-fact or state plausible FHA discrimination or retaliation claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Lujan v. Defs. of Wildlife

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's allegations that Defendants discriminated based on race in violation of § 3604(b) were conclusory and lacked factual content showing discriminatory motivation. The court found no facts demonstrating that Defendants' actions were motivated by Plaintiff's race, and noted that Defendants allowed Plaintiff to amend his application when he disputed the sex offender marking.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to adequately allege that Defendants subjected him to adverse action in retaliation for protected activity under § 3617. The court found that Defendants continued processing Plaintiff's application and only cancelled it when Plaintiff failed to schedule an interview, contradicting the retaliation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: California Civil Code §§ 44, 45a (defamation)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's defamation claim was conclusory and failed to allege facts showing that Defendants made false statements about Plaintiff being a sex offender, that such statements were published, or that Plaintiff suffered injury as a result. The complaint did not establish that Defendants' alleged statements actually prevented Plaintiff from obtaining housing.

case_name: Leila Cruz McCoy v. Rady Children's Hospital, San Diego Child Welfare Services, Christopher Hines, Lynette Miller, Renee Silvestri, Daniela Morales, Dr. Jenkins, Dr. Patel, Kimberly Giardina, and Nick Macchione
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, who is legally blind, repeatedly requested that hospital psychiatric unit staff provide documents in an accessible alternative audio format so she could understand her daughter's diagnosis, treatment plan, and follow-up care plan; she also attempted to use assistive technology and a screen-reader application for the blind to read paperwork but was allegedly threatened with arrest if she did not remove the assistive devices. She further alleged that San Diego Health and Human Services failed to provide accessible-format documents, publications, forms, interpreter services, and disability writing assistance.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's motion to proceed in forma pauperis due to an incomplete IFP form and sua sponte dismissed the complaint with leave to amend for failure to satisfy Rule 8 pleading standards.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Leila Cruz McCoy, a legally blind woman, filed suit against Rady Children's Hospital, San Diego Child Welfare Services, and various individual employees, alleging FHA, ADA, and other civil rights violations arising from her daughter's 5150 psychiatric hold and subsequent removal from her custody. Plaintiff alleged that hospital and CWS staff denied her requests for accessible-format documents, subjected her and her daughter to discriminatory comments based on race, religion, and disability, and retaliated against her for filing internal civil rights complaints by initiating court proceedings against her. The court denied her IFP application because she submitted an incomplete financial disclosure form, and dismissed the complaint without prejudice for failure to satisfy Rule 8's pleading requirements, granting leave to amend both.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Bautista v. Los Angeles Cnty., 216 F.3d 837 (9th Cir. 2000)
McHenry v. Renne, 84 F.3d 1172 (9th Cir. 1996)
Lopez v. Smith, 203 F.3d 1122 (9th Cir. 2000)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible formatted documents (audio format) for understanding daughter's diagnosis, treatment plan, and follow-up care plan; accessible format documents, publications, forms, and applications; interpreter and disability assistance; family accessible audio format notices
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for failure to state a claim under Rule 8 pleading standards. Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege facts supporting the elements of each cause of action, did not separate counts by claim, and did not specify which claims were made against which defendants, depriving defendants of fair notice and opportunity to defend.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for failure to state a claim under Rule 8 pleading standards. Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege facts supporting the elements of each cause of action, did not separate counts by claim, and did not specify which claims were made against which defendants, depriving defendants of fair notice and opportunity to defend.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II accessibility violations (accessible format documents, publications, forms, applications, interpreter, writing and disability assistance, family accessible audio format notices); VAWA; UCCJEA; Family Preservation Services Act; personal injury; slander/libel; harassment; discrimination based on race, religion, source of income, gender, familial status, and disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for failure to state a claim under Rule 8 pleading standards. Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege facts supporting the elements of each cause of action, did not separate counts by claim, and did not specify which claims were made against which defendants, depriving defendants of fair notice and opportunity to defend.

case_name: Edwards v. Rocky Galgano
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges race-based discriminatory eviction and disparate treatment of his African American guests, including repeated Three-Day Notices to Quit and fraudulent rental records
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claim because he failed to adequately allege a distinct and palpable injury—he did not show he was actually evicted, incurred monetary damages such as moving expenses or increased rent, or suffered compensable emotional distress as a result of defendants' alleged discriminatory conduct.
brief_summary: A veteran residing in a San Diego mobile home park sued the on-site manager and property management company under the Fair Housing Act, alleging they engaged in a fraudulent and racially discriminatory campaign to evict him and treated his African American guests disparately. The court granted leave to proceed in forma pauperis but dismissed the complaint without prejudice for failure to state a claim, finding plaintiff failed to adequately plead the distinct and palpable injury required to support an FHA discrimination claim.
key_cases_cited: Harris v. Itzhaki, 183 F.3d 1043 (9th Cir. 1999)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Ambruster v. Monument 3: Realty Fund VIII Ltd., 963 F. Supp. 862 (N.D. Cal. 1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege a distinct and palpable injury required under the FHA prima facie framework. Although the complaint alleged discriminatory conduct based on race (rude treatment of African American guests, disparate enforcement of pet policy, fraudulent eviction notices), plaintiff did not adequately allege compensable damages such as actual eviction, moving costs, increased rent, or emotional distress, and mere requests for damages without factual support are insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: State law fraud claim for creating false rental payment records to justify eviction
fha_claims.reasoning: Under California law and Federal Rule 9(b), fraud claims require pleading with particularity the who, what, when, where, and how of the misconduct. Although plaintiff alleged false statements and defendants' knowledge and intent to defraud, plaintiff failed to allege reliance on the false statements or damages resulting from them, and failed to provide the required specificity regarding dates and manner of the allegedly false statements.

source_file: 9621167_2023_Short Term Rental Alliance of San Diego v. City of San Diego_casd
case_name: Short Term Rental Alliance of San Diego v. City of San Diego
accommodation_description: Challenge to City ordinances regulating short-term rental licenses; not a disability reasonable accommodation case but a land use/regulatory challenge by short-term rental operators
key_holding: The court granted the City's motion to dismiss federal claims, finding the Alliance lacked associational standing to bring claims on behalf of guests and tenants, and failed to state viable claims under the Dormant Commerce Clause, Takings Clause, Equal Protection, or Substantive Due Process.
brief_summary: Short Term Rental Alliance of San Diego, an advocacy organization for short-term rental owners, sued the City of San Diego challenging Ordinances O-21305 and O-21464 that regulate whole-home short-term rentals in the Coastal Overlay Zone through a tiered licensing system and lottery. The court granted the City's motion to dismiss all federal claims, finding the Alliance lacked standing to assert racial disparate impact claims on behalf of guests and tenants, and failed to state constitutional claims under the Dormant Commerce Clause, Takings Clause, Equal Protection, or Substantive Due Process.
key_cases_cited: Rosenblatt v. City of Santa Monica, 940 F.3d 439 (9th Cir. 2019)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)
Colony Cove Properties, LLC v. City of Carson, 888 F.3d 445 (9th Cir. 2018)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges the Ordinance violates the Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3604, but does not articulate a specific FHA theory or claim. The complaint references FHA only in passing as one of several federal statutes allegedly violated.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed all federal claims including the FHA claim without substantive analysis of FHA elements. The opinion does not identify which FHA theory plaintiff invoked or analyze the merits of any FHA claim. The FHA claim was dismissed as part of the broader motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim under Rule 12(b)(6), applying Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards.

source_file: 9621223_2023_Moore v. Pacific View Apartments Carlsbad LLC_casd
case_name: Moore v. Pacific View Apartments Carlsbad LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges she was 'denied Reasonable Accommodation' but does not specify what accommodation was requested.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act reasonable accommodation claim because plaintiff failed to allege she is handicapped or disabled, and therefore cannot state a claim under § 3604(f)(3)(B) which requires a plaintiff to belong to the protected class of people with disabilities.
brief_summary: Brenda Moore, proceeding pro se, sued Pacific View Apartments Carlsbad LLC and property managers alleging defamation, breach of covenant of quiet enjoyment, and denial of reasonable accommodation under the Fair Housing Act. The S.D. Cal. court sua sponte dismissed the complaint without prejudice for failure to state a claim, finding Moore failed to allege she is handicapped and therefore cannot invoke the reasonable accommodation protections of § 3604(f)(3)(B), and alternatively lacked subject matter jurisdiction due to failure to establish diversity of citizenship.
key_cases_cited: Howard v. HMK Holdings, LLC, 988 F.3d 1185 (9th Cir. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges denial of reasonable accommodation but does not specify the nature of the accommodation requested or claim to have a disability.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed under § 1915(e)(2)(B) screening because plaintiff failed to allege she is handicapped or disabled, and therefore does not belong to the class of people afforded reasonable accommodation protections under the Fair Housing Act. The court found the claim frivolous as a matter of law without substantive analysis of the accommodation framework.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Defamation, libel, breach of covenant of quiet enjoyment, negligent property damage, constitutional civil rights harassment claims, and tax disclosure violations.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction. Federal-question jurisdiction was lacking because plaintiff cited inapplicable federal statutes (28 U.S.C. § 4101 on foreign defamation, 26 U.S.C. § 6103 on tax disclosure) unrelated to her claims, and failed to allege § 1983 color-of-state-law requirement for constitutional claims. Diversity jurisdiction was unavailable because plaintiff failed to allege complete diversity of citizenship and amount in controversy exceeding $75,000.

case_name: Musgrove v. Hanifin
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that the housing authority make phone calls to potential landlords on his behalf as a reasonable accommodation for his disability.
key_holding: The court recommended dismissing the case with prejudice because plaintiff knowingly, intentionally, and willfully refused to participate in discovery and comply with court orders, warranting terminating sanctions under Rules 16(f), 37, and 41(b).
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Irvin Musgrove sued Oceanside Housing Authority and its employees under the Fair Housing Act and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, alleging disability discrimination and failure to accommodate his request that defendants contact landlords on his behalf. The magistrate judge recommended granting defendants' motion to dismiss with prejudice based on terminating sanctions for plaintiff's repeated failure to comply with court orders and participate in discovery.
key_cases_cited: Ferdik v. Bonzelet, 963 F.2d 1258 (9th Cir. 1991)
Valley Engineers Inc. v. Electric Engineering Co., 158 F.3d 1051 (9th Cir. 1998)
Hernandez v. City of El Monte, 138 F.3d 393 (9th Cir. 1998)
Edwards v. Marin Park, Inc., 356 F.3d 1058 (9th Cir. 2004)
Meeks v. Nunez, 2017 WL 908733 (S.D. Cal. Mar. 8, 2017)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request for Defendants to make phone calls to potential landlords on Plaintiff's behalf to assist in locating housing units under the Section 8 HCV program
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 41(b) / Rule 37(b) — Terminating Sanctions for Failure to Comply with Court Orders and Failure to Prosecute
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the case for failure to prosecute and willful violation of court orders under Rule 41(b) and Rule 37(b), not on the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim. Plaintiff repeatedly failed to comply with discovery orders, failed to appear at the ENE conference, failed to provide initial disclosures, and failed to respond to discovery requests despite explicit warnings that dismissal could result. The court found Plaintiff's conduct was knowing, intentional, and willful, and that all five Ninth Circuit factors for dismissal were satisfied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act; Unruh Civil Rights Act; intentional infliction of emotional distress; conspiracy
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 41(b) / Rule 37(b) — Terminating Sanctions for Failure to Comply with Court Orders and Failure to Prosecute
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA claims were dismissed along with the FHA claims as a result of Plaintiff's failure to prosecute and willful violation of court orders. The court did not reach the merits of any non-FHA claims, instead imposing terminating sanctions for Plaintiff's repeated noncompliance with discovery obligations and court orders.

case_name: Erika Macias v. Myron Lange
accommodation_description: This is a post-judgment enforcement proceeding seeking an assignment order and restraining order against a judgment debtor to collect on a 2017 FHA sex discrimination judgment; no disability-related accommodation claim is at issue.
key_holding: The Court recommends granting the judgment creditor's motion for an assignment order directly assigning defendant's rental income rights and for a restraining order preventing defendant from disposing of those rights, finding the procedural requirements under California Code of Civil Procedure § 708.510 and § 708.520 are satisfied and defendant has demonstrated unwillingness to comply with prior orders.
brief_summary: Erika Macias, who obtained a 2017 jury verdict and judgment for sex discrimination under the Fair Housing Act against landlord Myron Lange, seeks post-judgment enforcement through an assignment order on rental income and a restraining order. The Court recommends granting the motion because defendant has failed to make any payments, evaded service, and demonstrated intent to evade the judgment, while plaintiff has provided sufficient evidence of defendant's rental income rights.
key_cases_cited: Credit Suisse v. U.S. Dist. Court, 130 F.3d 1342 (9th Cir. 1997)
Hilao v. Estate of Marcos, 95 F.3d 848 (9th Cir. 1996)
Gutierrez v. Vantia Properties, LLC, 2015 WL 164301 (E.D. Cal. 2015)
Innovation Ventures, LLC v. N2G Distributing, Inc., 2014 WL 10384606 (C.D. Cal. 2014)
E. Jordan Plastics, Inc. v. Suzhou Xincheng Gardening Material Co., Ltd., 2018 WL 1806699 (C.D. Cal. 2018)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff prevailed on her FHA discrimination and harassment claim based on sex in the underlying trial (October 2016 jury verdict). This opinion addresses post-judgment enforcement of the $55,320 damages award and $82,250 in attorneys' fees, not the merits of the underlying FHA claim, which was already decided in plaintiff's favor.

source_file: 9621958_2023_Grimes v. Enterprise Rent-A-Car Company of Los Angeles LLC_casd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Negligence claim regarding alleged failure to provide rental documents, wrongful vehicle return demand, and bad faith police reporting; racial discrimination claim under Title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Fair Housing Act of 1968
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the negligence claim for failure to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly, finding the complaint lacked basic factual allegations about what occurred, who was involved, and how plaintiff suffered actual loss. The racial discrimination claims under Title II and the Fair Housing Act were dismissed because a car rental company is not a place of public accommodation under Title II, and the Fair Housing Act does not apply to car rental services; additionally, the complaint was too disjointed and unintelligible to state a clear claim.

case_name: Karen Mary Asalone Iula v. James Voos
accommodation_description: N/A - case involves quid pro quo sexual harassment and hostile housing environment claims, not disability accommodation
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claims for quid pro quo harassment, hostile housing environment, and retaliatory eviction because plaintiff failed to allege sufficient factual matter to state plausible claims, and denied her TRO motion seeking to enjoin state eviction proceedings under the Anti-Injunction Act
brief_summary: Plaintiff Karen Mary Asalone Iula sued her former sublessor James Voos alleging Fair Housing Act claims for quid pro quo sexual harassment, hostile housing environment, and retaliatory eviction based on her refusal of his sexual demands. The court dismissed all FHA claims without prejudice for failure to state plausible claims, finding plaintiff provided only conclusory allegations without supporting factual details, and denied plaintiff's motion for a temporary restraining order to enjoin ongoing state eviction proceedings.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Quigley v. Winter, 598 F.3d 938 (8th Cir. 2010)
Honce v. Vigil, 1 F.3d 1085 (10th Cir. 1993)
Burlington Indus., Inc. v. Ellerth, 524 U.S. 742 (1998)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's quid pro quo sexual harassment claim under § 3604 failed to state a plausible claim because it contained only conclusory allegations that housing benefits were conditioned on sexual favors, without supporting factual allegations regarding the circumstances, timing, or specifics of the demands and refusals.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's hostile housing environment claim under § 3604 failed to state a plausible claim because she alleged only legal conclusions of sexual harassment, intimidation, and coercion without providing factual details regarding specific acts, frequency, or severity of the alleged conduct.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
