key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's § 3617 Fair Housing Act interference claim with prejudice because plaintiff failed to allege any connection between the store clerk's conduct and rights protected under the Fair Housing Act, as § 3617 only prohibits interference with rights enumerated in §§ 3603-3606 governing housing discrimination.
brief_summary: Alexander McArthur, proceeding pro se, sued Nino's Market alleging a store clerk sold him a faulty Bluetooth device, called him a homophobic slur, and attempted to assault him; he asserted claims under Title VII, § 1981, § 3617, and various state laws. The court dismissed the complaint for lack of federal question jurisdiction, including dismissing the § 3617 claim with prejudice because the plaintiff failed to allege any interference with Fair Housing rights, as that provision only covers interference with rights protected under housing discrimination statutes.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Frazier v. Rominger, 27 F.3d 828 (2d Cir. 1994)
Comcast Corp. v. Nat’l Ass’n of African Am.-Owned Media, 140 S. Ct. 1009 (2020)
Makarova v. United States, 201 F.3d 110 (2d Cir. 2000)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 3617 prohibits interference with Fair Housing Act rights only as enumerated in sections 3603-3606, which define substantive violations in housing sales, rentals, and brokerage services. Plaintiff failed to allege that the clerk interfered with rights protected by the FHA, and the claim arises from a retail store transaction unrelated to housing, placing it outside the FHA's scope.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VII employment discrimination, 42 U.S.C. § 2000a public accommodations discrimination, 42 U.S.C. § 1981 racial discrimination, Ind. Code § 35-45-2-1 intimidation, Connecticut Unfair Trade Practices Act, common law tort, Conn. Gen. Stat. § 52-571c civil harassment
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff lacks diversity jurisdiction (both parties are Connecticut citizens) and fails to state cognizable federal claims. Title VII does not apply absent an employment relationship; § 2000a claim lacks required administrative notice to CHRO; § 1981 claim fails because plaintiff alleges no facts connecting race to the alleged discrimination; remaining claims arise under state law or are not cognizable, and the court declines supplemental jurisdiction.

case_name: Karlen v. Wells Fargo Bank, N.A.
accommodation_description: No accommodation requested; case concerns race-based discrimination in mortgage servicing
key_holding: The court granted transfer to the District of Connecticut because the convenience factors weighed in favor of the forum where the property is located and where plaintiffs reside, despite plaintiffs' choice of California forum.
brief_summary: Black homeowners sued Wells Fargo alleging race-based housing discrimination including interference with property sale, surveillance, and harassment; the court granted Wells Fargo's motion to transfer venue to the District of Connecticut based on convenience factors, declining to rule on the pending motion to dismiss.
key_cases_cited: Van Dusen v. Barrack, 376 U.S. 612 (1964)
Jones v. GNC Franchising, Inc., 211 F.3d 495 (9th Cir. 2000)
Lou v. Belzberg, 834 F.2d 730 (9th Cir. 1987)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges race discrimination in mortgage servicing and property-related conduct, not failure to provide reasonable accommodation.
fha_claims.disposition: Motion to Transfer Granted; Motion to Dismiss Not Ruled Upon
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted defendant's motion to transfer the case to the District of Connecticut and declined to rule on the motion to dismiss, leaving the merits of the FHA disparate treatment claim unresolved pending transfer to the proper forum.

case_name: Alexander McArthur v. Nur Market
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; plaintiff, a store customer, alleges a clerk overcharged him for merchandise and claims discrimination as a consumer
key_holding: The complaint fails to state a federal claim because plaintiff has not alleged an employment relationship with the defendant (Title VII), has not demonstrated nexus to housing (FHA § 3617), and cannot proceed on unrelated state law or criminal statutes
brief_summary: Alexander McArthur sued Nur Market, a grocery store, alleging that a store clerk overcharged him for merchandise; the court dismissed the complaint for failure to state any cognizable federal claim, including Title VII, public accommodation discrimination under § 2000a, and Fair Housing Act claims under § 3617, declining to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Frazier v. Rominger, 27 F.3d 828 (2d Cir. 1994)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged store clerk overpriced merchandise; plaintiff attempted to invoke § 3617 (interference with Fair Housing Act rights)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed the § 3617 claim because plaintiff alleged no facts with any nexus to housing and did not allege interference with rights protected by the Fair Housing Act, which applies only to housing-related transactions enumerated in §§ 3603-3606.

case_name: McArthur v. Summit Security
accommodation_description: This case does not involve a reasonable accommodation request; it concerns an alleged racial slur uttered by a security guard at a state Department of Social Services office.
key_holding: The court dismissed McArthur's Fair Housing Act claim because he failed to allege any conduct related to a residential dwelling, which is required to state a claim under Section 3617.
brief_summary: Alexander McArthur sued Summit Security, the Connecticut Department of Social Services, and the City of New Haven alleging racial discrimination and intimidation under 42 U.S.C. § 3617 when a security guard allegedly uttered a racial slur at a DSS office. The court dismissed the case with prejudice, finding that McArthur failed to state a valid FHA claim because he made no allegations related to a residential dwelling, and alternatively that the claims against state defendants were barred by sovereign immunity.
key_cases_cited: Pennhurst State School & Hospital v. Halderman, 465 U.S. 89 (1984)
Quern v. Jordan, 440 U.S. 332 (1979)
Frazier v. Rominger, 27 F.3d 828 (2d Cir. 1994)
Benitez v. Wolff, 907 F.2d 1293 (2d Cir. 1990)
DeSouza v. Kennedy, 2017 WL 3431393 (D. Conn. 2017)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the § 3617 claim as frivolous because the alleged conduct (a racial slur uttered by a security guard on DSS premises) does not relate to the sale, rental, or enjoyment of housing rights protected by § 3617, and therefore cannot constitute the type of intimidation required to state a claim under that statute.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 due process claim for racial discrimination and intimidation
fha_claims.disposition: Sua sponte dismissal under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B); Eleventh Amendment immunity
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the § 1983 claim with prejudice because it is barred by Eleventh Amendment sovereign immunity, as § 1983 does not override state immunity as a matter of law.

case_name: Morales v. U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested to purchase a house from HACH after his mother's death, claiming discrimination and retaliation for prior complaints
key_holding: HUD's claims dismissed due to sovereign immunity and lack of waiver; HACH's claims dismissed for failure to allege sufficient facts to state plausible claims of discrimination or retaliation under Title VI and the FHA
brief_summary: Angel Morales sued HUD and Hartford Housing Authority alleging discrimination in violation of Title VI and the Fair Housing Act, claiming HACH improperly refused to let him purchase a house that his family had rented since 1999. The court granted both motions to dismiss, finding HUD immune from suit under sovereign immunity and that Morales failed to state plausible claims against HACH due to sparse factual allegations.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Lane v. Pena, 518 U.S. 187 (1996)
Godwin v. Sec'y of Hous. & Urb. Dev., 356 F.3d 310 (D.C. Cir. 2004)
Turner v. Sec'y of U.S. Dep't of Hous. & Urb. Dev., 449 F.3d 536 (3d Cir. 2006)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to sell house to plaintiff; discriminatory application of terms, conditions, and privileges of housing
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint fails to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly because it contains only threadbare allegations and does not allege facts from which the court could infer discrimination based on membership in a protected class. Plaintiff failed to identify any protected class basis for the alleged discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation for prior complaint about an employee
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint fails to allege facts suggesting coercion, intimidation, threatening, or interference with FHA rights under 42 U.S.C. § 3617. Allegations are conclusory and lack factual detail necessary to state a plausible retaliation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VI claim alleging discrimination in federal program receiving federal funding
fha_claims.reasoning: Claims against HUD dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction based on sovereign immunity. HUD, as a federal agency, is shielded by sovereign immunity, and plaintiff failed to identify an applicable waiver of sovereign immunity under the Civil Rights Acts or the APA. Dismissal without prejudice as to Title VI claim to allow plaintiff to challenge HUD's Title VI compliance determination under the APA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the § 3617 claim for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because the complaint alleges no facts relating to housing or real estate transactions; § 3617 protects rights granted under FHA §§ 3603-3606, which are housing-specific, and the underlying allegations concern only a grocery store detention.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 2000a (public accommodations discrimination); 42 U.S.C. § 1981 (racial discrimination in contract); 15 U.S.C. § 45c (unfair/deceptive practices); 28 U.S.C. § 4101 (defamation); 47 U.S.C. § 230 (internet platform immunity); 10 U.S.C. § 920 (military sexual assault); state law claims (CUTPA, common law defamation, battery, IIED, harassment, Tom Bane Act)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed all non-FHA claims for lack of subject matter jurisdiction: § 2000a claim failed because C-Town is a retail grocery store not covered by the statute and plaintiff failed to exhaust administrative remedies with CHRO; § 1981 claim failed because plaintiff did not allege race was a but-for cause; § 45c, § 4101, § 230, and § 920 claims failed because they do not provide private rights of action or are inapplicable to the facts; state law claims cannot provide federal question jurisdiction and supplemental jurisdiction was declined.

case_name: Poteat v. Hartford Housing et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges she was denied ability to port her Section 8 housing voucher due to retaliation for prior fair housing complaints and race discrimination.
key_holding: The court granted Hartford Housing Authority's motion for judgment on the pleadings on Poteat's discrimination claims for failure to allege sufficient facts, but denied the motion as to her retaliation claim under § 3617 because she plausibly alleged that defendants' refusal to port her Section 8 voucher was pretextual retaliation for her prior fair housing complaints.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Kennara Poteat sued Hartford Housing Authority, Enfield Housing Authority, CHRO, and HUD alleging fair housing violations including discrimination and retaliation related to her Section 8 voucher portability request. The court dismissed CHRO and HUD claims on sovereign immunity, dismissed discrimination and contract claims against Hartford Housing Authority, but allowed Poteat's retaliation claim to proceed based on plausible allegations that defendants refused to port her voucher in retaliation for her prior fair housing litigation.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Francis v. Kings Park Manor, Inc., 992 F.3d 67 (2d Cir. 2021)
Glover v. HPC-Eight, LLC, 2022 WL 1004572 (D. Conn. 2022)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged only conclusory facts that Hartford Housing Authority discriminated based on race without plausibly alleging membership in protected class, adverse action, and discriminatory intent. Court found allegations lacked sufficient factual support under Iqbal/Twombly standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff plausibly alleged retaliation under FHA § 3617: prior protected activity (litigation against Hartford Housing Authority), defendant awareness, adverse action (denial of Section 8 voucher portability), and causal connection (pretext that portability was impossible when it may have been administratively feasible). Claim survived motion for judgment on pleadings.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of reasonable accommodation for disability (unspecified accommodation and disability)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged CHRO denied reasonable accommodations for disability but failed to allege facts establishing what disability she has or what specific accommodation was denied. Allegations were conclusory and insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1982 (discrimination in property rights), state law breach of contract, state law fraud
fha_claims.reasoning: § 1982 discrimination claim failed for same reasons as FHA discrimination claim (conclusory allegations). Breach of contract claim failed because plaintiff did not allege formation of agreement to port voucher. Fraud claim failed for lack of particularity under Fed. R. Civ. P. 9(b).

source_file: 9632006_2023_Kalashnikov v. Myfield Lane Homeowners' Association, Inc._ctd
case_name: Kalashnikov v. Myfield Lane Homeowners' Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: This case does not involve a reasonable accommodation request under § 3604(f)(3)(B); it concerns HOA enforcement of aesthetic rules and alleged national origin/gender discrimination and retaliation.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for defendants on discrimination and harassment claims because plaintiffs failed to establish discriminatory motive, but denied summary judgment on retaliation claims, finding genuine disputes of material fact exist regarding whether defendants' enforcement actions against plaintiffs were motivated by plaintiffs' protected activity of filing a CHRO complaint.
brief_summary: Valeriy Kalashnikov and Victoria Ledeneva, Russian immigrants, sued Myfield Lane HOA and individual board members alleging discrimination on the basis of national origin, gender, and family status, as well as retaliation for filing a CHRO complaint. The court granted summary judgment for defendants on discrimination and harassment claims (finding no evidence of discriminatory motive), but denied summary judgment on retaliation claims, finding genuine disputes of material fact exist as to whether the HOA's enforcement of aesthetic rules was unlawfully retaliatory.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Glover v. HPC-Eight, LLC
Lachira v. Sutton
Moses v. St. Vincent's Special Needs Ctr., Inc.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to establish prima facie case of national origin discrimination. Stray remarks by non-decisionmaker Kimberly Lindemann were speculative and unconnected to Board's decision. Comparators cited were not similarly situated. Defendants articulated legitimate, non-discriminatory reasons (failure to obtain prior Board approval and alleged building code violations), and Plaintiffs failed to prove pretext by showing discrimination was the real reason.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs' gender discrimination claim failed because evidence of alleged conduct by Board members (refusing to discuss rule violations, excluding Ledeneva from budget discussions) does not establish gender animus. Kimberly Lindemann's comments about others' motives were speculation without personal knowledge. Ledeneva's subjective belief of bias is insufficient to support inference of discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Familial status discrimination claim failed because denial of playset while Kozo had trampoline does not establish discrimination based on family status. Both Plaintiffs and Kozo had children, so they were not treated differently because of familial status. Familial status discrimination requires showing adverse conduct based on presence of children, not differential treatment between families with children.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation for filing discrimination complaint and threatening to defend rights in court, including removal of Ledeneva from Board
fha_claims.reasoning: Defendants failed to adequately address retaliation claims in their motion, making only fleeting, conclusory reference in reply brief. Arguments not made in initial brief cannot be raised for first time in reply. Plaintiffs alleged retaliation after October 10 and October 12, 2018 protected activity (threatening court action and filing discrimination complaint), and genuine issue of material fact exists as to whether removal from Board and other conduct constituted retaliation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged quid pro quo harassment: demand that Plaintiffs pave driveways for all homeowners as condition of approval
fha_claims.reasoning: Kozo's email comment that Plaintiffs should pave everyone's driveway was not a 'demand' under quid pro quo harassment standard. No reasonable juror could find the comment was a demand or that it was based on or related to national origin, gender, or familial status. Quid pro quo harassment requires unwelcome request or demand made a condition of housing-related benefit.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged hostile housing environment based on national origin
fha_claims.reasoning: Hostile environment claim failed because evidence does not give rise to inference that Plaintiffs were harassed because of national origin or other protected status. Alleged conduct (false statements about building code violations, accusations of threats, threats of fines, statements about moving) was not sufficiently severe or pervasive to alter conditions of housing arrangement. Congress did not intend FHA to remedy every neighbor dispute.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Negligence (failure to train, monitor, supervise officers/Board members on FHA compliance); Negligent and Intentional Infliction of Emotional Distress (based on false accusations and unreasonable denial of step request); Defamation and Defamation Per Se (false statements in CHRO proceeding that Kalashnikov threatened physical violence); Perjury; Harassment; Extortion
fha_claims.reasoning: Negligence claim for failure to train/supervise on FHA compliance failed because no cognizable duty exists under FHA to train employees on fair housing laws. Negligent infliction of emotional distress failed because no evidence Defendants should have foreseen emotional distress causing illness or bodily harm. Intentional infliction failed because alleged conduct (denying request, false accusations, threats of fines) does not meet extreme and outrageous standard under Connecticut law. Defamation claims barred by absolute privilege for statements made in quasi-judicial CHRO proceedings. Perjury, harassment, and extortion are criminal offenses with no private civil causes of action.

case_name: McArthur v. Pan Del Cielo 2
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged intimidation and harassment when asked to wear a mask at a restaurant; not a housing accommodation case.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's complaint because § 3617 of the Fair Housing Act does not apply to a restaurant, and plaintiff failed to state a plausible claim for racial discrimination under § 1981.
brief_summary: Alexander McArthur sued Pan Del Cielo 2, a restaurant in New Haven, Connecticut, alleging the store manager intimidated and harassed him when he was asked to wear a mask. The court dismissed the action without prejudice, finding that § 3617 of the Fair Housing Act does not apply to a restaurant, and that plaintiff failed to state a plausible claim for racial discrimination under § 1981.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claim of intimidation by store manager regarding mask-wearing policy
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 3617 of the Fair Housing Act applies only to coercion, intimidation, threats, and interference in the context of 'the sale or rental of housing,' 'residential real estate-related transactions,' and 'the provision of brokerage services.' A restaurant mask-wearing policy falls outside the scope of FHA jurisdiction, making the claim frivolous as applied to this defendant.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Civil Rights Act of 1964 discrimination claim; § 1981 racial discrimination claim; California CCP § 527.6 civil harassment claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to state a plausible claim under § 1981, which requires allegations of (1) membership in a racial minority, (2) defendant's intent to discriminate on the basis of race, and (3) discrimination concerning an enumerated activity. Plaintiff alleged no facts of racial discrimination. State law claim under CCP § 527.6 dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction due to absence of diversity of citizenship and decline of supplemental jurisdiction.

source_file: 9632548_2023_Connecticut Fair Housing Ctr v. CoreLogic Rental Property Solutions, LLC_ctd
case_name: Connecticut Fair Housing Ctr v. CoreLogic Rental Property Solutions, LLC
accommodation_description: Mr. Arroyo, who has a traumatic brain injury, was denied housing based on a criminal background check; the accommodation claim concerns CoreLogic's CrimSAFE screening product that allegedly has discriminatory disparate impact on minorities
key_holding: The court found for CoreLogic on the FHA claims because plaintiffs failed to prove that CrimSAFE caused housing unavailability for protected groups, and found for Mr. Arroyo only on the FCRA claim regarding CoreLogic's unreasonable requirements for consumer file disclosure.
brief_summary: Connecticut Fair Housing Center and Mikhail Arroyo sued CoreLogic Rental Property Solutions, alleging that its CrimSAFE criminal background screening product has a disparate impact on Latino and African American tenants and intentionally facilitates housing discrimination. The court ruled for CoreLogic on the FHA disparate impact and intentional discrimination claims, finding plaintiffs failed to prove housing unavailability, but found for Mr. Arroyo on his FCRA claim, awarding $1,000 statutory and $3,000 punitive damages for CoreLogic's unreasonable requirements that made it impossible for a conserved person to obtain their consumer report.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dept. of Housing & Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, Inc., 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Olmstead v. L.C., 527 U.S. 581 (1999)
SafeCo Ins. Co. of America v. Burr, 551 U.S. 47 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that CoreLogic does not 'make unavailable or deny' housing under § 3604(a)-(b) because the housing provider, not CoreLogic, makes all material decisions regarding applicant qualification, configuration of criminal record filters, access to records, and final acceptance/denial. CoreLogic's role is too tenuous to establish FHA liability; it merely provides information that housing providers use according to their own policies.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that Plaintiffs failed to prove CoreLogic intentionally discriminated on the basis of race or national origin. The evidence showed CoreLogic's CrimSAFE product is a customizable tool controlled entirely by housing providers; CoreLogic does not make housing decisions and therefore cannot be liable for discriminatory intent in denying housing.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Connecticut Unfair Trade Practices Act (CUTPA); Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) §§ 1681g, 1681h
fha_claims.reasoning: Court ruled in favor of CoreLogic on CUTPA claims (which failed for the same reasons as FHA claims—CoreLogic does not make housing unavailable). Court ruled in favor of Mr. Arroyo on FCRA claims, finding CoreLogic violated 15 U.S.C. §§ 1681g and 1681h by requiring Ms. Arroyo to furnish a power of attorney (legally impossible for a conserved person) as a condition for disclosing Mr. Arroyo's consumer report from June 30, 2016 to November 14, 2016. Awarded $1,000 statutory damages, $3,000 punitive damages, and reasonable attorney's fees.

case_name: Rahul Gorawara v. John Caprio
accommodation_description: No accommodation request was at issue in this case. The claims centered on alleged racial discrimination and interference with housing rights by the plaintiff's landlords in connection with his tenancy and subsequent eviction for nonpayment of rent.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's motion for a new trial because (1) plaintiff waived the inconsistency objection by failing to raise it before the jury was discharged, and (2) even on the merits, the jury's finding of liability on slander and negligent infliction of emotional distress with a $0 damages award was not inconsistent given the jury instructions' separation of liability and damages into distinct spheres with separate burden-of-proof requirements, and the evidence of damages was too weak to constitute a seriously erroneous result or miscarriage of justice.
brief_summary: Rahul Gorawara, a tenant evicted for nonpayment of rent, sued his landlords John and Carolyn Caprio alleging racial discrimination under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1982, 1983, and 1985(3), violation of the Fair Housing Act under 42 U.S.C. § 3617, and several Connecticut state law claims. The jury found for defendants on all thirteen counts except slander and negligent infliction of emotional distress against Carolyn Caprio's estate, but awarded zero dollars on those two claims. Gorawara moved for a new trial under Fed. R. Civ. P. 59(a) arguing the liability findings with zero damages were fatally inconsistent under Connecticut law, but the court denied the motion on grounds of waiver and, alternatively, on the merits because the instructions expressly required the plaintiff to separately satisfy his burden of proof as to damages, and the evidence of damages was too limited and insufficiently linked to Carolyn Caprio's specific conduct to show a serious error.
key_cases_cited: Hall v. Bergman, 296 Conn. 169 (2010)
Malmberg v. Lopez, 208 Conn. 675 (1988)
Anderson Grp., LLC v. City of Saratoga Springs, 805 F.3d 34 (2d Cir. 2015)
ABKCO Music, Inc. v. Sagan, 50 F.4th 309 (2d Cir. 2022)
Goodyear v. Discala, 269 Conn. 507 (2004)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Violation of Fair Housing Act § 3617 (interference, coercion, or intimidation in connection with housing rights)
fha_claims.reasoning: The jury returned a verdict for the defendants on all counts except two state law claims (slander and negligent infliction of emotional distress). The FHA § 3617 claim was among the counts on which the jury found for the defendants.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1982, 1985(3) (racial discrimination); 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (conspiracy to violate equal protection); Connecticut state law claims of nuisance, breach of covenant of good faith and fair dealing, slander, negligent infliction of emotional distress, CUTPA violation, and anti-intimidation statute violation
fha_claims.reasoning: The jury returned a verdict for the defendants on all federal civil rights claims (§§ 1981, 1982, 1985(3), § 1983) and most state law claims. The jury found liability only on two state law claims (slander and negligent infliction of emotional distress) but awarded zero damages on both, which the court upheld on the motion for new trial.

case_name: Gordon Clark v. Santander Bank N.A.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged age discrimination (denial of credit increases and personal loan based on being 92 years old) and race discrimination in connection with foreclosure proceedings.
key_holding: The court granted Defendants' motions to dismiss all federal claims including FHA age and race discrimination claims for failure to state a plausible claim, and dismissed state law claims as barred or for failure to state a claim.
brief_summary: Pro se Plaintiff Gordon Clark and the Estate of Lillian Clark sued Santander Bank N.A., Wells Fargo, Bendett & McHugh P.C., and individual executives alleging fraud, Fair Housing Act violations, and various state law claims stemming from foreclosure on their home at 70 Elm Street in Enfield, Connecticut. The court granted Defendants' motions to dismiss the Amended Complaint in its entirety, finding that all federal claims (including FHA age and race discrimination claims) failed to state a plausible claim for relief, and that state law claims were barred by claim preclusion or the litigation privilege.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Gunn v. Minton, 568 U.S. 251 (2013)
Griggs v. Provident Consumer Discount Co., 459 U.S. 56 (1982)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Age discrimination claim: denial of credit increases and personal loan to 92-year-old Lillian Clark
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint lacks sufficient factual detail regarding loan applications, dates, reasons for denials, and fails to allege that Santander continued business with younger applicants. Conclusory and vague allegations do not satisfy Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Race discrimination claim: poor customer service at bank branch based on plaintiff's Asian descent
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff fails to allege he was attempting to engage in a residential real estate transaction or credit transaction. Insufficient allegations that poor customer service was based on race rather than other factors. Individual defendants not alleged to be involved in discriminatory conduct.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Redlining claim: denial of credit increases and personal loan based on property location in working-class/blue-collar town
fha_claims.reasoning: Allegations are vague and conclusory. Complaint lacks specific details about applications, dates, and reasons for denials. Cannot support plausible redlining claim under Fair Housing Act or ECOA without more concrete factual allegations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Federal criminal statutes (18 U.S.C. §§ 1005, 1341), FDCPA (15 U.S.C. § 1692e), Lanham Act (15 U.S.C. § 1125), state law claims (negligence, abuse of process, breach of contract, emotional distress, wrongful death, CUTPA)
fha_claims.reasoning: Federal criminal statutes do not provide private rights of action. Fraud claims fail Rule 9(b) heightened pleading standard—bare-bones allegations without specificity as to fraudulent statements, speakers, time/place, and reasons for fraud. FDCPA claim against Santander fails because Santander is a creditor, not a debt collector. Lanham Act claim fails because consumers lack standing under the statute. State law claims barred by res judicata, collateral estoppel, litigation privilege, or failure to state a claim.

case_name: Alexander McArthur v. Property Management, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges retaliation for filing prior civil complaints and deprivation of water/repair services, not a traditional reasonable accommodation request.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's amended complaint because he failed to state a cognizable claim, including insufficient facts to support FHA retaliation as no causal connection was alleged between protected activity and alleged adverse action.
brief_summary: Alexander McArthur, proceeding pro se, sued his property management company and landlord seeking damages for retaliation and conditions of his apartment, citing ADA retaliation and vaguely referencing the Fair Housing Act. The court dismissed the amended complaint for failure to state a claim, finding no causal connection alleged between his prior lawsuits and the alleged water deprivation, and declining supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Poteat v. Hartford Hous.
Regional Econ. Cmty. Action Program, Inc. v. City of Middletown

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts to support a prima facie retaliation claim under the FHA. Specifically, plaintiff alleged no facts establishing a causal connection between the filing of prior suits and the alleged deprivation of water, which is an essential element of FHA retaliation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA retaliation (42 U.S.C. § 12203), state law tort claims, First Amendment retaliation
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA retaliation claim dismissed for failure to allege plaintiff was an employee or establish any element beyond bare retaliation allegation. First Amendment retaliation claim improper against private defendants. State law tort claims dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction (no federal question, no diversity jurisdiction, and supplemental jurisdiction declined).

case_name: Carla Karlen et al. v. Wells Fargo Bank, N.A.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request was made; the Karlens alleged racially-motivated discriminatory conduct by Wells Fargo during foreclosure proceedings.
key_holding: The court dismissed the FHA claims because the Karlens failed to plead specific factual allegations showing discriminatory intent and because Connecticut's litigation privilege bars claims arising from conduct during legal proceedings.
brief_summary: Carla and Gerard Karlen sued Wells Fargo Bank alleging the bank violated the Fair Housing Act through racially-motivated discriminatory conduct during their home foreclosure proceedings. The court granted Wells Fargo's motion to dismiss, finding the FHA claims were conclusory, failed to plead specific facts showing discriminatory intent, and were barred by Connecticut's litigation privilege doctrine.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
MacDermid, Inc. v. Leonetti, 79 A.3d 60 (Conn. 2013)
Simms v. Seaman, 69 A.3d 880 (Conn. 2013)
Grullon v. City of New Haven, 720 F.3d 133 (2d Cir. 2013)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges racial discrimination in foreclosure conduct, not a request for reasonable accommodation.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plead FHA violations with specificity required by Twombly and Iqbal. Allegations of racial discrimination based solely on Carla Karlen's race, without disparate impact analysis, case law citations, or factual examples of discriminatory intent, are conclusory and insufficient to state a plausible claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges unlawful practices in selling, brokering, and appraising premises.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs' allegations lack legal analysis and factual basis. The claim invokes 24 C.F.R. § 135 but provides only circular logic ('as a result of such actions, Plaintiffs have been damaged by an incalculable amount') without connecting facts to any legal violation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges discriminatory conduct during foreclosure and subsequent litigation.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs tie conclusory statements to no violation of law and allege no real damage. The pleading fails to meet Twombly and Iqbal standards for plausibility.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges racial animus and malicious behavior during foreclosure action and subsequent litigation.
fha_claims.reasoning: Count Four mentions no law at all and fails to allege facts sufficient to state a plausible claim under Twombly and Iqbal. Additionally, Connecticut's litigation privilege doctrine bars claims related to conduct of legal proceedings, and plaintiffs fail to allege abuse of process required to overcome the privilege.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Effective communication accommodations including permission to pass notes during Board meetings and requirement that other members face plaintiff when speaking; auxiliary aids and services for elected Board member with autism and hearing impairment
fha_claims.reasoning: Jury found defendants violated Title II of the ADA and Section 504 by failing to provide effective communication and auxiliary aids and services to plaintiff as an elected Board member; jury rejected defendants' undue burden defense, finding that providing accommodations would not have imposed an undue burden.

case_name: Earlando Samuel v. Robert Rizzo, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a disabled individual, alleges disability discrimination including termination of his live-in aid and harassment by housing authority defendants in retaliation for complaining about conditions.
key_holding: The court dismissed most claims as time-barred but allowed Plaintiff's retaliation and interference claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3617 to proceed because he adequately alleged harassment that was sufficiently severe or pervasive to create a hostile environment.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Earlando Samuel sued New Castle County Housing Authority and related defendants alleging disability discrimination, retaliation for complaining about unsafe housing conditions, and harassment that made his living situation intolerable. The court dismissed his ADA and Fair Housing Act claims as time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations but allowed his § 3617 retaliation and interference claim to proceed, finding he adequately alleged harassment severe enough to constitute a hostile environment.
key_cases_cited: Revock v. Cowpet Bay West Condo. Ass'n, 853 F.3d 96 (3d Cir. 2017)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court liberally construed pro se allegations and found plaintiff adequately alleged harassment and retaliation under § 3617 based on complaints about unsafe conditions and alleged course of conduct that was threatening and intimidating, allowing plaintiff to proceed against specified defendants on this claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II or Title III disability discrimination claim; 18 U.S.C. § 241 conspiracy claim
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA and Fair Housing Act claims based on events prior to February 25, 2018 are barred by the applicable two-year statute of limitations period, as the complaint was filed February 25, 2020. Criminal conspiracy claim under 18 U.S.C. § 241 dismissed as frivolous because plaintiff lacks standing to prosecute criminal charges; only the United States Attorney may bring criminal prosecutions.

case_name: David Q. Webb v. State of Delaware, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a single homeless male, alleged he was denied housing at the Hope Center because he is not a family with minor children, seeking better housing placement through the DHSS-DSCC emergency hotel voucher program.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claim because plaintiff failed to state a plausible familial status discrimination claim as he is a single homeless male with no minor children, and familial status under § 3602(k) only protects families with minor children.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff David Q. Webb sued the State of Delaware and various hotel defendants alleging Fair Housing Act violations after being denied housing at the Hope Center emergency shelter because he was not a family. The court sua sponte screened the complaint and dismissed the FHA claim, finding that familial status under § 3602(k) only protects families with minor children, not single adults, and plaintiff failed to state a plausible claim for relief.
key_cases_cited: Alexander v. Sandoval, 532 U.S. 275 (2001)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of housing at New Castle County Hope Center based on familial status (plaintiff is a single male without minor children)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to state a plausible claim for FHA discrimination because he is a single male without minor children and therefore does not fall within the protected class of 'familial status' as defined by 42 U.S.C. § 3602(k). The FHA prohibits discrimination against families with minor children, and plaintiff's allegations do not speak to discrimination based on any protected characteristic under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VI Civil Rights Act claims; 42 U.S.C. § 1983 claims (Counts II-VI); Ninth Amendment claim (Count V); deliberate ignorance claim (Count VII); housing conditions claim under Section 8 of the Housing Act (Count IX); state law negligence, intentional infliction of emotional distress, and vicarious liability claims (Counts X-XIII)
fha_claims.reasoning: Title VI claims dismissed for conclusory allegations without factual basis for intentional discrimination. § 1983 claims against state and state officials in official capacities barred by Eleventh Amendment immunity; claims against county executive Meyer fail to plead Monell liability. Ninth Amendment claim not cognizable under § 1983. Deliberate ignorance claim not cognizable under federal law. Housing conditions claim under Section 8 fails because no private right of action exists. State law negligence claims barred by sovereign immunity and Delaware State Tort Claims Act. IIED claims fail to identify specific outrageous conduct with sufficient factual detail. Vicarious liability claim fails because underlying claims are not cognizable.

case_name: Earlando Samuel v. Robert Rizzo, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged that defendants harassed and retaliated against him for complaining about unsafe conditions and exposing wrongdoing, violating 42 U.S.C. § 3617.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's retaliation and interference claims under § 3617 because his factual allegations failed to meet the required standards—NCCHA's document requests were permissible regulatory actions, the inspection timing complied with biennial requirements, and the isolated instances of service providers entering his apartment did not rise to the level of actionable harassment or interference.
brief_summary: Earlando Samuel, a pro se plaintiff who rented an apartment with Section 8 assistance, sued New Castle County Housing Authority, Fairville Management Company, and Greenlawn Apartments alleging harassment and retaliation under the Fair Housing Act for complaining about unsafe housing conditions. The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss and for judgment on the pleadings, finding Samuel's factual allegations failed to state actionable retaliation or interference claims under 42 U.S.C. § 3617.
key_cases_cited: Revock v. Cowpet Bay West Condo. Ass'n, 853 F.3d 96 (3d Cir. 2017)
Lloyd v. Presby's Inspired Life, 251 F. Supp. 3d 891 (E.D. Pa. 2017)
Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009)
Henry v. City of Erie, 728 F.3d 275 (3d Cir. 2013)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's allegations against NCCHA Defendants fail to state a plausible § 3617 retaliation claim because: (1) requesting bank statements and raising rent in response to non-compliance are not retaliatory acts—they are authorized regulatory actions; (2) failure to provide documents is not a protected activity; (3) biennial inspection schedule was compliant with regulations; and (4) alleged deficiencies existed in prior inspections, breaking any causal link between complaints and adverse actions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's allegations against Greenlawn Defendants and Fairville Management Company fail to state a plausible § 3617 interference claim. Requesting renters' insurance after water damage is reasonable and not retaliatory (same request made to similarly situated neighbor). Service providers entering apartment for scheduled appointments, while potentially questionable under state law, does not rise to the level of severe or pervasive interference required under § 3617, as distinguished by case law involving sustained harassment campaigns.

source_file: 9636368_2023_Lewis v. Greenville on 141 Apartments and Townhomes - Westover Companies_ded
case_name: Racquel Lewis v. Greenville on 141 Apartments and Townhomes — Westover Companies
accommodation_description: Plaintiff's complaint does not articulate a specific disability accommodation request; the claims appear to concern source of income discrimination related to DEHAP rental assistance payments and alleged wrongful eviction attempts.
key_holding: The complaint was dismissed because plaintiff failed to state a claim under the Fair Housing Act, having alleged precious few factual allegations with specificity and relying on inapplicable Washington D.C. municipal laws.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Racquel Lewis filed suit against her apartment complex owner alleging Fair Housing Act violations related to rental assistance payments from DEHAP and an attempted eviction. The Court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim, finding plaintiff failed to plead sufficient factual allegations and relied on inapplicable Washington D.C. laws, but granted leave to amend.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Shorter v. United States, 12 F.4th 366 (3d Cir. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff references 'Source of Income Discrimination' and alleges wrongful eviction attempts, refusal to cooperate with rental assistance program (DEHAP), and unauthorized rent increases, but does not clearly identify which FHA provisions apply or what specific accommodation is sought.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for failure to state a claim under the Iqbal/Twombly standard, finding it unclear under which FHA provisions plaintiff was attempting to bring her claims and that she alleged precious few factual allegations with specificity. Plaintiff was granted leave to file an amended complaint.

case_name: Kirk Ernest Root v. Nilo Salazar
accommodation_description: Root requested to rent a unit in Salazar's duplex; Salazar refused and made statements indicating he would not rent to a person with a mobility disability.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for Root on the § 3604(c) discriminatory statements claim because Salazar's texts stating he would not rent to a 'handicap person with challenging mobility motor skills' indicated a disability-based preference, but denied summary judgment on the § 3604(f)(1) refusal-to-rent claim because genuine disputes of material fact existed regarding whether Salazar denied tenancy based on disability or financial qualifications.
brief_summary: Kirk Root, who has cerebral palsy and uses a wheelchair, sued landlord Nilo Salazar alleging disability discrimination after Salazar refused to rent a duplex unit to Root and made statements indicating he would not rent to persons with mobility disabilities. The court granted partial summary judgment for Root on his discriminatory statements claim under § 3604(c) but denied summary judgment on his refusal-to-rent claim under § 3604(f)(1), finding genuine disputes of material fact existed regarding whether Salazar denied tenancy based on disability or Root's financial qualifications.
key_cases_cited: Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condo. Ass'n, 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014)
White v. U.S. Dep't of Hous. & Urban Dev., 475 F.3d 898 (7th Cir. 2007)
Soules v. U.S. Dep't of Housing & Urban Dev., 967 F.2d 817 (2d Cir. 1992)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether disability was the but-for cause of denial versus financial unqualification (failure to meet 30% rent-to-income ratio). Salazar presented evidence of legitimate, non-discriminatory reasons for rejection, and disputes exist as to rental application requirements and Root's qualifications.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Under § 3604(c), Salazar's undisputed statements expressing preference against renting to a person with mobility impairments (e.g., 'Renting that building to a handicap person with challenging mobility motor skills will be doing a dishonesty') satisfy all three elements: statement made, with respect to rental, indicating preference/discrimination based on handicap. An ordinary listener would understand these statements as expressing a preference against renting to persons with mobility disabilities.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Orlando City Code §§ 57.48 and 57.49
fha_claims.reasoning: Orlando City Code § 57.48 is substantially identical to 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(1) and receives the same analysis; summary judgment denied on same grounds as federal disparate treatment claim. Orlando City Code § 57.49 is substantially identical to 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c) and receives the same analysis; summary judgment granted on same grounds as federal discriminatory statements claim.

case_name: Clay v. IH4 Property Florida, L.P.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested that defendants remediate toxic mold and/or provide alternative housing as a reasonable accommodation for S.C.'s severe asthma, which caused disproportionately severe reactions to mold exposure compared to non-disabled tenants.
key_holding: Mold remediation can constitute a reasonable accommodation under § 3604(f)(3)(B) when the disabled tenant suffers disproportionately severe reactions to mold compared to non-disabled tenants, even though the accommodation addresses a condition that affects all tenants, because the disability creates heightened vulnerability requiring greater remediation efforts.
brief_summary: Grace and Stephen Clay, on behalf of their minor son S.C. who suffers from severe asthma, sued IH4 Property Florida, L.P. and Invitation Homes Realty, LLC alleging the landlords failed to reasonably accommodate S.C.'s disability by refusing to remediate toxic mold that caused life-threatening asthma exacerbations after Hurricane Irma. The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss the FHA claim (Count I), holding that plaintiffs plausibly alleged mold remediation as a reasonable accommodation because S.C.'s disability creates heightened vulnerability to mold exposure beyond that of non-disabled tenants.
key_cases_cited: Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014)
Schwarz v. City of Treasure Island, 544 F.3d 1201 (11th Cir. 2008)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Mold remediation and repair of water damage to the home caused by Hurricane Irma, necessary to address the effects of S.C.'s severe asthma triggered by mold exposure
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard and found that plaintiffs plausibly alleged all four elements of a failure-to-accommodate claim: disability (severe asthma substantially limiting major life activities), request for accommodation (mold remediation), necessity (to afford equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling), and refusal. The court rejected defendants' argument that mold remediation cannot be a reasonable accommodation, finding that the consequences of mold exposure to S.C. require greater care than for an average tenant, and that mold remediation is not specifically required by Florida law for non-disabled tenants, making it a disability-specific need.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Same mold remediation and water damage repair claim brought under the Florida Fair Housing Act (FFHA), Fla. Stat. § 760.23(9)(b)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the FFHA claim for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because plaintiffs failed to allege compliance with the mandatory administrative exhaustion requirement under Fla. Stat. § 760.34, which requires filing a complaint with the Florida Commission on Human Relations and participating in the statutory conciliation process before commencing a civil action. The court followed binding intermediate Florida appellate court precedent holding that administrative exhaustion is a condition precedent to filing a judicial action.

source_file: 9637225_2019_United States v. Advocate Law Groups of Florida, P.A._flmd
case_name: United States v. Advocate Law Groups of Florida, P.A.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request — case involves predatory loan modification and foreclosure rescue services allegedly targeted at Hispanic homeowners based on national origin.
key_holding: The court dismissed claims under §§ 3604(a), 3604(b), and 3605, finding that offering loan modification assistance does not constitute 'making a dwelling unavailable' under § 3604(a), that reverse redlining theories do not extend to foreclosure rescue services, and that Defendants did not provide 'financial assistance' within the meaning of § 3605.
brief_summary: The United States and three Hispanic homeowners sued a law firm and its principals alleging national origin discrimination in connection with predatory loan modification and foreclosure rescue services targeting Hispanic homeowners. The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss, holding that offering assistance with obtaining mortgage modifications does not constitute 'making a dwelling unavailable' under § 3604(a), does not fall within § 3604(b)'s services provision, and does not constitute 'financial assistance' under § 3605.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
City of Miami v. Bank of Am. Corp., 800 F.3d 1262 (11th Cir. 2015)
People ex rel. Madigan v. Wildermuth, 91 N.E.3d 865 (Ill. 2017)
Hunt v. Aimco Props., L.P., 814 F.3d 1213 (11th Cir. 2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege that defendants made housing unavailable under § 3604(a). The court found that defendants, as a law firm offering foreclosure assistance services, lacked the power to make housing unavailable—only the lenders held that power. Reverse redlining theory did not transform an unactionable claim into an actionable one.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court rejected § 3604(b) claim for discrimination in terms, conditions, or privileges of sale/rental or in provision of services. Plaintiffs failed to allege that defendants provided services recognized as actionable under the FHA. Offering assistance in obtaining mortgage modifications from third-party lenders is not the same as providing the types of services (insurance, lending, etc.) contemplated by § 3604(b).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that plaintiffs failed to allege facts plausibly supporting that defendants' business includes engaging in residential real estate-related transactions under § 3605(a). Providing assistance with obtaining mortgage modifications does not constitute providing 'financial assistance' within the meaning of § 3605(b)(1). Defendants did not provide funds to clients; they merely assisted with paperwork.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed § 3617 claim for failure to clearly identify which FHA rights were allegedly infringed and how defendants interfered with those rights. Plaintiffs' theory was shifting and unclear, with the United States merely tracking statutory language without explanation and Intervenors changing their theory in their response brief. Dismissal without prejudice with leave to amend.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed the United States' § 3614 pattern or practice claim because it is derivative of the underlying FHA violations under §§ 3604, 3605, and 3617. Since plaintiffs failed to allege plausible violations under those provisions, they could not establish a pattern or practice of violations. Dismissal without prejudice with leave to amend.

source_file: 9639620_2020_Cobb v. Citrus Falls at Westchase Apartments, LLC_flmd
case_name: Tyrone Cobb v. Citrus Falls at Westchase Apartments, LLC
accommodation_description: Wheelchair user with end-stage renal failure, congestive heart failure, and mobility impairments seeks repair of noncompliant common areas and physical modifications to his apartment including pathways, ramps, door hardware, and bathroom fixtures.
key_holding: The court granted defendant's motion to dismiss, holding that § 3604(f)(3)(B) does not require landlords to undertake significant structural improvements, and requests for construction or repair are not actionable under subsection (B).
brief_summary: Tyrone Cobb, a wheelchair user with multiple disabilities, sued his apartment landlord seeking repairs and physical modifications to common areas and his apartment under the Fair Housing Act. The court granted defendant's motion to dismiss, holding that plaintiff's demand for structural improvements and repairs does not constitute a reasonable accommodation under § 3604(f)(3)(B), which covers accommodations in rules, policies, practices, or services—not construction or repair requests—and dismissed the complaint without prejudice with leave to amend.
key_cases_cited: Weiss v. 2100 Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 941 F. Supp. 2d 1337 (S.D. Fla. 2013)
Harding v. Orlando Apartments, LLC, 748 F.3d 1128 (11th Cir. 2014)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Correction of improper walkway/ramp grades for access to office, swimming pool, gym, and apartment; removal of obstructed paths; provision of accessible handicap parking spaces; replacement of noncompliant doorknobs and latches; correction of noncompliant sink, tub, shower, and toilet in apartment
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed under Twombly/Iqbal standard, finding that structural improvements and construction/repair are not reasonable accommodations under § 3604(f)(3)(B), which applies only to accommodations in rules, policies, practices, or services, not physical alterations to property.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Remedy of defective construction including entrance grades, doors, and locks in common areas and apartment
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for failure to state a plausible claim under §§ 3604(f)(1) and (2), which do not provide relief for failure to remedy defective construction and do not constitute independent acts of prohibited discrimination. Court noted that such claims must be brought under § 3604(f)(3) and only against the property owner involved in initial design and construction.

source_file: 9639806_2020_United States v. Advocate Law Groups of Florida, P.A._flmd
case_name: United States v. Advocate Law Groups of Florida, P.A.
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED - No reasonable accommodation request involved; case concerns alleged predatory loan modification services targeting Hispanic homeowners.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that allegations that defendants deliberately targeted Hispanic homeowners with predatory loan modification and foreclosure rescue services sufficiently stated a claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3617 for interference with housing rights, and that the § 3614 pattern-or-practice claim survived based on the § 3617 findings.
brief_summary: The United States and three Hispanic Intervenor-Plaintiffs sued a law firm and its partners alleging they deliberately targeted Hispanic homeowners with a predatory loan modification and foreclosure rescue scheme. The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss, finding the § 3617 interference claims and § 3614 pattern-or-practice claim sufficiently alleged, while noting prior dismissal of the § 3604(a), § 3604(b), and § 3605 claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Sofarelli v. Pinellas Cnty., 931 F.2d 718 (11th Cir. 1991)
Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009)
Ga. State Conf. of the NAACP v. City of LaGrange, 940 F.3d 627 (11th Cir. 2019)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed § 3604(a) claim (making unavailable or denying a dwelling based on national origin) as failing to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly standard; allegations did not plausibly connect Defendants' conduct to denial of housing based on national origin.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed § 3604(b) claim (discrimination in terms, conditions, or privileges of sale or rental based on national origin) as failing to state a plausible claim; allegations fell outside the scope of that provision.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed § 3605 claim (discrimination in residential real estate-related transactions based on national origin) because Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege that Defendants' business included engaging in residential real estate-related transactions as defined in that section.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss § 3617 claim (coercion, intimidation, threats, or interference with exercise of housing rights), finding that Plaintiffs' allegations were sufficient to state a plausible claim under the broad language and remedial purpose of the FHA, even though the facts differed from typical § 3617 cases.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss § 3614 claim (pattern or practice of resistance to full enjoyment of FHA rights), finding that because the § 3617 claims survived, the § 3614 claim alleging a pattern or practice of § 3617 violations also survives as a matter of law.

case_name: Clay v. IH4 Property Florida, L.P.
accommodation_description: Settlement of minor's personal injury claim arising from underlying Fair Housing Act complaint against property management company
key_holding: The Court denied the settlement approval petition because the parties failed to provide the actual executed settlement agreement and did not supply legal authority supporting the non-disclosure provision, requiring them to file an amended joint motion with proper documentation.
brief_summary: Grace Clay and Stephen Clay, individually and on behalf of their minor son S.C., settled their claims against IH4 Property Florida and Invitation Homes Realty (likely including Fair Housing Act claims), and the parties jointly petitioned the Court to approve the settlement of the minor's claim. The Court denied the settlement approval petition without prejudice because the parties failed to submit the actual executed settlement agreement and did not provide legal authority for the confidentiality provision, directing them to file a compliant amended motion by February 18, 2021.
key_cases_cited: In re Smith, 926 F.2d 1027 (11th Cir. 1991)
Meyers v. United States, 2014 WL 5038585 (M.D. Fla. 2014)
Burke v. Smith, 252 F.3d 1260 (11th Cir. 2001)
Erie R. Co. v. Tompkins, 304 U.S. 64 (1938)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; opinion addresses settlement approval procedure only, not substantive claims
fha_claims.disposition: Settlement approval motion denied without prejudice
fha_claims.reasoning: The court declined to approve the proposed settlement because the parties failed to submit the executed settlement agreement and did not address whether non-disclosure provisions were appropriate for filing in the public record. The court did not reach the merits of any underlying claims, including the FHA claim referenced in the Amended Complaint.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Selective enforcement of Florida Statute § 316.212 (golf cart prohibition on sidewalks) to permit use of golf cart as mobility device; Title II ADA and Section 504 Rehabilitation Act claims for denial of reasonable accommodation
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard and found plaintiffs plausibly alleged all elements of Title II ADA and Section 504 claims by asserting they are disabled and denied benefit of using sidewalks due to failure to provide reasonable accommodation of selective enforcement. Court rejected defendant's arguments that plaintiffs failed to state a claim, finding fact-specific reasonableness inquiry appropriate for summary judgment stage.

source_file: 9641354_2021_Jain v. The Towers of Channelside Condominium Association_flmd
case_name: Jain v. The Towers of Channelside Condominium Association
accommodation_description: Not a reasonable accommodation or modification request. Plaintiff sought equal treatment as afforded to other residents, specifically: repair of sliding glass doors in his unit, equal access to the BuildingLink online resident forum, and equal access to association records — all of which he alleged were denied on the basis of his national origin and/or race.
key_holding: The court granted in part and denied in part the defendants' motion to dismiss, allowing the disparate treatment FHA claims, Florida Condominium Act claims, and breach of fiduciary duty claims against individual board members to proceed, while dismissing the declaratory judgment count as improper and dismissing with leave to amend the breach of fiduciary duty count against the property manager for failure to identify a legal basis for the fiduciary duty.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Atul Jain, a condominium unit owner, sued The Towers of Channelside Condominium Association, its board members, and its property manager for a pattern of discriminatory treatment based on national origin and/or race, including denial of access to the BuildingLink online resident forum, refusal to repair the sliding glass doors in his unit, and denial of access to association records. The court denied dismissal of the disparate treatment FHA counts, the Florida Condominium Act count, and the breach of fiduciary duty count as to the board members, but dismissed the declaratory judgment count as both improper in form and duplicative, and dismissed with leave to amend the breach of fiduciary duty count against the property manager because the Florida statute creating fiduciary duties expressly excludes managers.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Housing Opportunities Project for Excellence, Inc. v. Key Colony No. 4 Condo. Assoc., Inc., 510 F. Supp. 2d 1003 (S.D. Fla. 2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to repair sliding glass doors in unit; denial of access to BuildingLink online forum; denial of access to records
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found Counts One and Two sufficiently pleaded under Twombly standard; allegations of discriminatory acts (failure to repair common elements, blocking from message board) gave defendants adequate notice of claims and survived motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Florida Condominium Act violation; Breach of Fiduciary Duty; Breach of Association Covenants
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss Count Six (Florida Condominium Act) because statutory immunity for officers/directors does not apply to willful violations of rights; Count Seven (Breach of Fiduciary Duty) survived as to Daly, Schwartz, and Petruzzella but was dismissed in part as to Walters with leave to amend for lack of clear fiduciary basis.

source_file: 9641974_2021_Williams v. Tampa Bay Extended Stay Hotel_flmd
case_name: Brittany Williams v. Tampa Bay Extended Stay Hotel
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: The court lacks subject matter jurisdiction because a plaintiff cannot remove her own action from state court; the removal statutes vest removal rights exclusively in defendants under 28 U.S.C. § 1441(a), and the case must be remanded to state court.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Brittany Williams filed a complaint in Florida state court alleging racial discrimination under Title II of the Civil Rights Act and the Federal Fair Housing Act, then improperly removed her own case to federal court. The court recommended remand because the federal removal statutes vest removal rights exclusively in defendants, and a plaintiff lacks statutory authority to remove her own action to federal court.
key_cases_cited: Shamrock Oil & Gas Corp. v. Sheets, 313 U.S. 100 (1941)
Russell Corp. v. Am. Home Assurance Co., 264 F.3d 1040 (11th Cir. 2001)
Bromwell v. Mich. Mut. Ins. Co., 115 F.3d 208 (3d Cir. 1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Racial discrimination under Title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, Federal Fair Housing Act, Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act, and premises liability
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked subject matter jurisdiction because only defendants may remove an action from state court to federal court under 28 U.S.C. § 1441(a). Plaintiff, as the party who initiated the action, lacked authority to remove it herself. The case was remanded to state court.

source_file: 9642077_2021_Williams v. Tampa Bay Extended Stay Hotel_flmd
case_name: Brittany Williams v. Tampa Bay Extended Stay Hotel
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges racial discrimination during COVID-19 pandemic at extended stay hotel, but no specific accommodation request is described.
key_holding: The case was remanded to state court because removal statutes do not allow a plaintiff to remove her own case from state court, and the court lacked subject matter jurisdiction.
brief_summary: Brittany Williams sued Tampa Bay Extended Stay Hotel alleging racial discrimination during the COVID-19 pandemic under the Civil Rights Act and Fair Housing Act. The court granted remand because Williams improperly removed her own case from state court, as removal statutes permit only defendants to remove cases, and the court lacked subject matter jurisdiction.
key_cases_cited: Cooper-Houston v. S. Ry. Co., 37 F.3d 603 (11th Cir. 1994)
Ashworth v. Glades Cnty. Bd. of Cnty. Comm'rs, 379 F. Supp. 3d 1244 (M.D. Fla. 2019)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Civil Rights Act of 1964, Federal Fair Housing Act, and Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act claims alleging racial discrimination during COVID-19 pandemic
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because the plaintiff, proceeding pro se, improperly removed the case from state court. Removal statutes contemplate removal only by state-court defendants, not by plaintiffs. The case was remanded to state court without reaching the merits of any claim.

case_name: Williams v. Aluna Largo
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges she was discriminatorily rejected as a rental applicant based on race, gender, nationality, and family status.
key_holding: The Court remanded the case to state court because removal was improper—only defendants may remove actions from state court, and plaintiff improperly removed her own case.
brief_summary: Brittany Williams sued Aluna Largo Apartments in federal court after removing her state court action, alleging she was discriminatorily rejected as a rental applicant based on race, gender, nationality, and family status in violation of federal civil rights laws. The Court remanded the case to state court for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because removal was improper—only defendants may remove an action from state court, and the plaintiff cannot remove her own case.
key_cases_cited: Cooper-Houston v. S. Ry. Co., 37 F.3d 603 (11th Cir. 1994)
Ashworth v. Glades Cnty. Bd. of Cnty. Comm'rs, 379 F. Supp. 3d 1244 (M.D. Fla. 2019)
Seminole Cnty. v. Pinter Enter., Inc., 184 F. Supp. 2d 1203 (M.D. Fla. 2000)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court remanded the action to state court for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because only defendants may remove an action from state to federal court under 28 U.S.C. § 1441(a), § 1443, and § 1446; the plaintiff's self-removal was improper.

source_file: 9642893_2022_Suntree Master Homeowners Association, Inc. v. Frison_flmd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Defendants asserted a Fair Housing Act defense regarding Plaintiff's inspection, but no specific accommodation was requested or at issue.
fha_claims.disposition: Remand for lack of subject matter jurisdiction
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that removal was improper because the FHA claim was raised only as a defense to the plaintiff's state-law claims for unpaid assessments, not as an independent federal question in the complaint. Federal defenses do not provide a basis for removal under 28 U.S.C. § 1331.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Use of golf cart as mobility device on public sidewalks in Pasco County; Title II ADA and Section 504 Rehabilitation Act claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied plaintiffs' motion to exclude expert testimony regarding whether the requested accommodation (golf cart use on sidewalks) was reasonable and safe under the ADA and Section 504. The case involves Title II ADA and Rehabilitation Act claims, not FHA claims. The motion was procedural (Daubert gatekeeping); the underlying reasonable accommodation claim on the merits remains pending for trial.

source_file: 9643667_2022_Weekley Homes, LLC v. Board of County Commissioners_flmd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exemption from School Impact Fee for age-restricted community (Communities for Older Persons) under FHA Housing for Older Persons Act exemption; plaintiff sought exemption despite Encore Declaration lacking mandatory 30-year irrevocable non-revocation clause required by County Ordinance
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that Weekley Homes failed to state a plausible 'class of one' Equal Protection claim under Iqbal/Twombly because it could not identify a similarly situated comparator—all other communities that received the exemption had the required 30-year irrevocable non-revocation clause that Encore lacked, making them dissimilar as a matter of law.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 Equal Protection claim; Florida Statutes Chapter 86 declaratory judgment claims regarding constitutionality of County School Impact Fee Ordinance
fha_claims.reasoning: The court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the state law declaratory judgment claims (Counts II and III) because they raised novel issues of Florida state law, all federal claims were dismissed, and comity, judicial economy, and fairness favored remand to state court where the case was originally filed.

case_name: Mamberto Real v. Judith Moran, Frank Diaz Gines, and Presbyterian Homes & Housing Foundation of Florida, Inc.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request — case involves alleged discriminatory refusal to rent based on national origin (Cuban) and retaliation under § 3617.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's complaint with prejudice as a shotgun pleading that failed to comply with Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, with plaintiff having had four prior opportunities to properly plead his national origin discrimination and retaliation claims.
brief_summary: Mamberto Real, a Cuban national origin individual, sued Presbyterian Homes and its employees alleging he was denied an apartment and subjected to ongoing delays as retaliation because of his national origin. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss with prejudice, finding Real's complaint was an impermissible shotgun pleading that failed to give defendants adequate notice of the claims against them despite four prior opportunities to properly plead.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Weiland v. Palm Beach Cnty. Sheriff's Office, 792 F.3d 1313 (11th Cir. 2015)
Boatman v. Town of Oakland, 76 F.3d 341 (11th Cir. 1996)
Philippeaux v. Apartment Inv. & Mgmt. Co., 598 F. App'x 640 (11th Cir. 2015)
Anderson v. District Bd. of Trustees of Cent. Fla. Cmty. Coll., 77 F.3d 364 (11th Cir. 1996)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint dismissed as a shotgun pleading for failure to provide adequate notice of claims and grounds. Plaintiff alleged national origin discrimination based on leasing agent's statement that she 'does not like Cubans,' but complaint failed to comply with Federal Rules of Civil Procedure pleading requirements through vague, conclusory allegations and improper incorporation of counts.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Retaliation claim dismissed for failure to plead the third element of prima facie retaliation—causal link between protected activity and adverse action. Plaintiff alleged defendants used 'endless delays' as retaliation but provided no factual explanation of how the delay was causally related to his verbal complaint, merely reciting legal conclusions without supporting facts.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, 42 U.S.C. § 2000d
fha_claims.reasoning: Title VI claims dismissed as shotgun pleading. Plaintiff failed to substantiate that defendants received federal financial assistance (required element of Title VI), and individual defendants (Ms. Moran and Mr. Diaz-Gines) are not proper defendants under Title VI, which applies only to 'programs or activities' receiving federal funds, not individual employees. Complaint failed to place defendants on adequate notice of which defendants were liable under which statute.

source_file: 9644128_2022_Rood v. Town of Ft. Myers Beach_flmd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Special exemption to build a dune walkover (elevated structure traversing two coastal lagoons) across environmentally critical zoning land to provide beach access from plaintiff's property
