fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to request an accommodation (vague wheelchair references in environmental proceedings did not constitute clear notice of disability or accommodation need); even if a request had been made, the Dune Walkover would fundamentally alter the Town's environmentally critical zoning scheme, was not necessary to address plaintiff's actual disability (cane use for balance, not wheelchair use), and would provide preferential treatment rather than equal access, as plaintiff had alternative public beach access options available.

case_name: James Nathaniel Douse v. Sabrina Traeger, et al.
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request was made; plaintiff made vague references to discrimination under the Fair Housing Act without identifying a protected class or discriminatory conduct covered under the statute.
key_holding: Plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claims were dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because he failed to identify his membership in any protected class (race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status, or national origin) and failed to describe any discriminatory conduct covered under the FHA.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff James Douse sued his homeowners association and an employee over a disputed pool construction deposit and assessment charges, vaguely referencing the Fair Housing Act. The court dismissed the case for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, finding the FHA claims were wholly insubstantial because plaintiff failed to identify his membership in any protected class or allege discriminatory conduct covered under the statute.
key_cases_cited: Fountain v. Metro. Atlanta Rapid Trans. Auth., 688 F.2d 1038 (11th Cir. 1982)
Bell v. Hood, 327 U.S. 678 (1946)
Steel Co. v. Citizens for a Better Env't, 523 U.S. 83 (1998)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff cites FHA §§ 3603-3606 and § 3617 alleging discrimination and harassment in connection with homeowner's association disputes over pool deposit return and assessment charges; no disability or protected class basis identified.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because plaintiff failed to identify any protected class status (race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status, or national origin) and the conduct complained of (pool deposit delay and assessment misclassification) does not fit within any prohibited discrimination enumerated in § 3604. The FHA claims are wholly insubstantial and frivolous, insufficient to confer federal question jurisdiction.

case_name: Marvin Lane and Shanita Lane v. Security National Mortgage Company, Tamara Perrin and Lisa Casanova
accommodation_description: Alleged racial discrimination during mortgage application process, including racially discriminatory remark and actions taken to delay and deter plaintiff due to race
key_holding: The complaint was dismissed for failure to state a plausible claim because plaintiffs failed to allege defendants knew of Shanita Lane's race, did not identify which FHA provisions were violated, provided no evidence of disparate treatment compared to other applicants, and failed to allege any cognizable injury.
brief_summary: Marvin and Shanita Lane sued Security National Mortgage Company and two employees alleging racial discrimination during their mortgage application process, claiming a racially discriminatory remark was made and improper actions were taken to delay and deter them due to race. The Court granted defendants' motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6), finding plaintiffs failed to state a plausible Fair Housing Act claim because they did not adequately plead disparate treatment or any cognizable injury.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to state a plausible claim of racial discrimination in mortgage lending under the Fair Housing Act because they did not allege that defendants knew of Shanita Lane's race, did not specify which FHA provisions were violated, failed to allege disparate treatment compared to similarly situated applicants, and did not allege any injury. The conclusory allegations and email correspondence provided were insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards.

source_file: 9645190_2023_Parisi v. Sabal Springs Homeowners Association Inc._flmd
case_name: Parisi v. Sabal Springs Homeowners Association Inc.
accommodation_description: Parisi requested a waiver of the Association's two-dog rule so that his emotional support dog Rokco (needed for depression and anxiety) could remain in the residence alongside co-plaintiff Clark's two pet dogs, totaling three dogs in the unit.
key_holding: The court granted in part and denied in part plaintiffs' motion to strike affirmative defenses, striking the unclean hands (Third) and reasonableness-of-accommodation (Fourth) defenses as legally insufficient, while sustaining the Second Affirmative Defense because co-plaintiff Clark never requested a reasonable accommodation as required under the FHA.
brief_summary: Joseph Parisi, who relies on an emotional support dog (Rokco) for depression and anxiety, and co-resident Terry Clark, who owns two pet dogs, sued the Sabal Springs Homeowners Association under the FHA after the Association refused to waive its two-dog-per-unit rule to allow all three dogs to remain in the residence. The Amended Complaint asserted three counts: failure to reasonably accommodate (Count I), illegal intimidation and threats (Count II), and discriminatory terms and conditions of a dwelling (Count III). The court resolved plaintiffs' motion to strike five affirmative defenses, striking the Third (unclean hands) and Fourth (accommodation not reasonable) defenses while denying the motion as to the Second Defense because Clark—unlike Parisi—never made a request for accommodation.
key_cases_cited: Hawn v. Shoreline Towers Phase 1 Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 347 F. App'x 464 (11th Cir. 2009)
Loren v. Sasser, 309 F.3d 1296 (11th Cir. 2002)
Schwarz v. City of Treasure Island, 544 F.3d 1201 (11th Cir. 2008)
Weiss v. 2100 Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 941 F. Supp. 2d 1337 (S.D. Fla. 2013)
Hunt v. Aimco Properties, L.P., 814 F.3d 1213 (11th Cir. 2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver of the two-dog rule to allow Parisi's support dog (Rokco) to remain in the residence along with Clark's two pet dogs (Soonie and Riley), for a total of three dogs.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court did not reach the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim itself. The opinion addresses only whether certain affirmative defenses should be stricken. The Second Affirmative Defense (failure to exhaust) was denied as properly asserted, and the Fourth Affirmative Defense (that the accommodation is not reasonable) was stricken as not a proper affirmative defense but rather a denial of an element plaintiffs must prove. The claim survives and proceeds to further litigation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Illegal intimidation and threats under the FHA.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court did not reach the merits of the interference/coercion claim. The opinion addresses only affirmative defenses and does not substantively analyze the elements of this claim. The claim survives the procedural ruling and remains pending.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Illegal discrimination in the terms, conditions, or privileges of the sale or rental of a dwelling based on disability.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court did not reach the merits of the disparate treatment claim. The opinion addresses only affirmative defenses and does not substantively analyze the elements of this claim. The claim survives the procedural ruling and remains pending.

source_file: 9645767_2023_Parisi v. Sabal Springs Homeowners Association Inc._flmd
case_name: Parisi v. Sabal Springs Homeowners Association Inc.
accommodation_description: Request that HOA waive its two-pet-dog rule to allow Parisi to reside with his assistance animal (Rokco) in the HOA-governed community.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiffs' motion to strike the HOA's affirmative defense because the defense was in substance a denial rather than a true affirmative defense, and thus will be treated as a denial with particularity under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 9(c).
brief_summary: Joseph Parisi and Terry Clark sued Sabal Springs Homeowners Association under the Fair Housing Act, alleging the HOA discriminated by denying their request to waive the two-pet-dog rule so Parisi could keep his assistance animal. The court issued a procedural ruling denying plaintiffs' motion to strike the HOA's First Affirmative Defense, holding that the defense was actually a denial rather than a true affirmative defense and should be treated accordingly under the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.
key_cases_cited: Hunt v. Aimco Properties, L.P., 814 F.3d 1213 (11th Cir. 2016)
Wright v. Southland Corp., 187 F.3d 1287 (11th Cir. 1999)
In re Rawson Food Serv., Inc., 846 F.2d 1343 (11th Cir. 1988)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver of HOA rule limiting residents to two pet dogs to allow Parisi to reside with his assistance animal (Rokco) in addition to Clark's two pet dogs
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the motion to strike the affirmative defense, treating it as a denial with particularity under Rule 9(c) rather than striking it as an improper affirmative defense. The reasonable accommodation claim itself survives and proceeds to further litigation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Illegal intimidation and threats of liability for Sabal Springs' attorneys' fees
fha_claims.reasoning: The court's ruling on the motion to strike does not address the merits of the interference/coercion claim. The claim survives the procedural challenge and remains pending.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Illegal discrimination in the terms, conditions, or privileges of sale of a dwelling
fha_claims.reasoning: The court's ruling on the motion to strike does not address the merits of the disparate treatment claim. The claim survives the procedural challenge and remains pending.

case_name: David Wallace v. Carefree Shadowwood LLC
accommodation_description: Request to keep an emotional support animal (ESA dog named Zena) at the manufactured home community following a dog altercation incident.
key_holding: The court denied the motion to dismiss, holding that Mr. Wallace plausibly alleged Shadowwood made housing unavailable because of his disability by forcing him to choose between his home and his assistance animal, and that Shadowwood failed to conduct an individualized assessment before requiring Zena's removal.
brief_summary: David Wallace sued Carefree Shadowwood LLC, the owner of Bahia Vista Estates manufactured home community in Sarasota, Florida, alleging the housing provider violated the FHA by forcing him to choose between his home and his emotional support animal Zena after a dog altercation, and by failing to accommodate his disability-related need for the ESA. The court denied Shadowwood's motion to dismiss both claims, finding Wallace plausibly alleged that Shadowwood made housing unavailable because of his disability and improperly refused to consider his accommodation request without an individualized assessment.
key_cases_cited: Hunt v. Aimco Props., L.P., 814 F.3d 1213 (11th Cir. 2016)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Smith v. Powdrill, No. CV 12-06388 DDP RZX, 2013 WL 5786586 (C.D. Cal. 2013)
Friedel v. Park Place Cmty. LLC, 747 F. App'x 775 (11th Cir. 2018)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Allowing plaintiff to keep emotional support animal (assistance dog) despite dog's involvement in altercation with another resident's dog
fha_claims.reasoning: At the motion to dismiss stage, plaintiff plausibly alleged that defendant made housing unavailable because of his disability by forcing him to choose between his home and his assistance animal. Although defendant claimed it terminated the lease for violation of pet removal notice, plaintiff adequately alleged the adverse action was taken because of his disability, citing defendant's knowledge of the animal's status and failure to conduct individual assessment or explore less drastic alternatives.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Allowing plaintiff to keep his emotional support dog (Zena) under mitigative measures such as keeping the dog on plaintiff's property and not allowing it off-leash
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff plausibly alleged all four elements of a failure to accommodate claim: disability (mental health impairment), request for accommodation (through brother's letter), necessity (emotional support animal needed for disability), and refusal (defendant's denial). Court rejected defendant's argument that the request was not for an accommodation to rules/policies and that it was facially unreasonable, finding that reasonableness is a question of fact and plaintiff adequately alleged mitigative measures and lack of significant threat.

case_name: Brittany Williams v. Professional Marketing Management, Inc.
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED - The complaint does not clearly articulate a specific accommodation request; the FHA claim appears to be based on race discrimination rather than disability-related accommodation denial.
key_holding: The Court dismissed plaintiff's § 1983 claims because the private landlord was not a state actor and the claims were untimely under the four-year statute of limitations, and dismissed the FHA claim as untimely under the two-year limitations period in 42 U.S.C. § 3613(a)(1)(A).
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Brittany Williams, a pretrial detainee, sued private landlord Professional Marketing Management, Inc. for evicting her in August 2018 after she fell behind on rent and allegedly attempted to pay three months late, asserting § 1983 constitutional claims and a Fair Housing Act claim. The Court dismissed all claims under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B), finding the § 1983 claims failed because the private landlord did not act under color of state law and were untimely, and the FHA claim was time-barred under the two-year limitations period.
key_cases_cited: West v. Atkins, 487 U.S. 42 (1988)
Am. Mfrs. Mut. Ins. Co. v. Sullivan, 526 U.S. 40 (1999)
Chappell v. Rich, 340 F.3d 1279 (11th Cir. 2003)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges she attempted to pay three months of rent but defendant refused to accept payments and subsequently evicted her. The specific nature of any accommodation request is not articulated.
fha_claims.reasoning: The Fair Housing Act claim is time-barred under 42 U.S.C. § 3613(a)(1)(A), which provides a two-year statute of limitations. The allegedly discriminatory acts occurred in summer 2018, over two years before the May 25, 2023 complaint was filed, and plaintiff offered no basis for tolling.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 Eighth Amendment cruel and unusual punishment claim; § 1983 Fourteenth Amendment race discrimination claim
fha_claims.reasoning: The § 1983 claims are time-barred under the four-year statute of limitations applicable in Florida. The eviction occurred in August 2018, over four years before the May 25, 2023 complaint was filed. Additionally, the § 1983 claims fail because plaintiff alleges no facts showing that PMM, a private landlord, acted under color of state law, which is required for § 1983 liability.

source_file: 9646548_2023_Parisi v. Sabal Springs Homeowners Association Inc._flmd
case_name: Parisi v. Sabal Springs Homeowners Association Inc.
accommodation_description: Request for waiver of HOA Rule #11 limiting residences to two dogs and two household pets to allow plaintiff to keep his assistance animal dog named Rokco.
key_holding: The court granted the HOA's Rule 56(d) motion and deferred ruling on plaintiffs' summary judgment motion because discovery into plaintiff's disability status is necessary since disability is an essential element of the reasonable accommodation claim.
brief_summary: Joseph Parisi and Terry Clark, homeowners in a HOA community, sued the Sabal Springs Homeowners Association alleging the HOA violated the FHA by refusing to waive Rule #11's pet restrictions to accommodate Parisi's assistance animal. The court granted the HOA's Rule 56(d) motion to defer ruling on plaintiffs' summary judgment motion because discovery into whether Parisi has a qualifying disability has not been completed, and disability is an essential element of the reasonable accommodation claim.
key_cases_cited: Hawn v. Shoreline Towers Phase 1 Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 347 F. App'x 464 (11th Cir. 2009)
Loren v. Sasser, 309 F.3d 1296 (11th Cir. 2002)
Groner v. Golden Gate Gardens Apartments, 250 F.3d 1039 (6th Cir. 2001)
Snook v. Tr. Co. of Georgia Bank of Savannah, 859 F.2d 865 (11th Cir. 1988)
Burns v. Town of Palm Beach, 999 F.3d 1317 (11th Cir. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver of HOA Rule #11 limiting residences to two dogs and two household pets to allow plaintiff Joseph Parisi to keep an assistance animal dog named 'Rokco' in addition to cohabitant Terry Clark's two pet dogs (Soonie and Riley)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court deferred plaintiffs' motion for partial summary judgment under Rule 56(d) because discovery regarding Parisi's disability status is essential to the reasonable accommodation claim and remains incomplete; the HOA is entitled to pursue discovery on this necessary element before summary judgment is decided.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged illegal interference, coercion, threats, or intimidation by the HOA
fha_claims.reasoning: The court deferred plaintiffs' motion for partial summary judgment under Rule 56(d), which encompasses all three counts; the claim remains pending pending completion of discovery.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Amended Rule #11's terms, conditions, or privileges are facially discriminatory
fha_claims.reasoning: The court deferred plaintiffs' motion for partial summary judgment under Rule 56(d), which encompasses all three counts; the claim remains pending pending completion of discovery.

source_file: 9646692_2023_E-Ventures Worldwide, LLC v. Toll Bros., Inc._flmd
case_name: E-Ventures Worldwide, LLC v. Toll Bros., Inc.
accommodation_description: Indian business owner alleges defendant homebuilder refused to sell homes because of his Indian ethnicity.
key_holding: Court granted in part defendant's motion to compel, ordering plaintiff to produce documents responsive to Request No. 7 (communications between Trika and Johnson within past five years), but denied the motion to the extent it sought documents beyond the scope of that request.
brief_summary: Plaintiff E-Ventures Worldwide, LLC sued Toll Bros., Inc. alleging the homebuilder refused to sell homes to its Indian owner (Jeev Trika) because of his ethnicity, in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The Court ruled on a discovery motion, granting in part defendant's motion to compel production of documents exchanged between Trika and sales agent Johnson, but denying relief as to documents beyond the scope of the propounded discovery request.
key_cases_cited: Grayson v. No Labels, Inc.
Douglas v. Kohl's Dept. Stores, Inc.
Henderson v. Holiday CVS, L.L.C.
Zamperla, Inc. v. I.E. Park SrL
Shanshan Zhan v. Univ. of Mississippi Med. Ctr.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: This is a discovery order, not a ruling on the merits of the FHA disparate treatment claim. The court ruled on a motion to compel production of documents between Trika and Johnson related to alleged ethnic discrimination in a real estate transaction. The underlying FHA claim remains pending.

source_file: 9646737_2023_E-Ventures Worldwide, LLC v. Toll Bros., Inc._flmd
case_name: Jeev Trika and E-Ventures Worldwide, LLC v. Toll Bros., Inc.
accommodation_description: The underlying case alleges Toll Bros. refused to sell homes to plaintiff Jeev Trika because he is Indian (national origin discrimination). This order addresses a discovery motion to compel non-party witness compliance with a subpoena.
key_holding: The court granted in part and denied in part the motion to compel, ordering non-party Johnson to comply with a second deposition (up to 3 hours) and produce documents, but denied sanctions, fees, costs, and contempt because Johnson was unrepresented, appeared under a reasonable belief about timing, and defendant had promised to accommodate her schedule.
brief_summary: Jeev Trika and E-Ventures Worldwide, LLC sued Toll Bros., Inc. alleging the homebuilder refused to sell them homes because Trika is Indian, in violation of the Fair Housing Act. This order resolves a discovery dispute, with the magistrate judge granting in part the motion to compel non-party witness Marjorie Johnson to comply with a subpoena (attending a second deposition and producing documents) but denying sanctions and fees because the circumstances did not warrant such sanctions.
key_cases_cited: Consumer Fin. Prot. Bureau v. Brown
Devaney v. Cont'l Am. Ins. Co.
Bailey Indus., Inc. v. CLJP, Inc.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: This is a discovery order enforcing a subpoena duces tecum against a non-party witness in an underlying FHA disparate treatment case alleging racial discrimination. The opinion does not address the merits of the FHA claim itself, only procedural discovery matters regarding witness testimony and document production.

case_name: City of Tampa ex rel. Bradley Toston v. D&M Assets 1 LLC
accommodation_description: Request to waive no-pets policy and pet deposit for a German Shepard service dog named Kai to assist with disabilities
key_holding: The federal FHA claims survived dismissal because it is not apparent from the face of the complaint that the statute of limitations has run, as the HUD complaint appears still pending providing tolling, while the local ordinance claims were dismissed as time-barred for lack of tolling provisions.
brief_summary: The City of Tampa sued D&M Assets 1 LLC and its owners on behalf of Bradley Toston, alleging they violated the FHA by refusing to waive their no-pets policy and pet deposit for his service dog. The court denied the motion to dismiss Counts I and II (federal FHA claims) because the statute of limitations question could not be resolved on the face of the complaint given the pending HUD proceeding, but granted dismissal of Counts III and IV (local ordinance claims) as time-barred due to the absence of tolling provisions.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Gonsalvez v. Celebrity Cruises Inc.
La Grasta v. First Union Sec.
Pielage v. McConnell

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver of no-pets policy and pet deposit requirement for service dog (German Shepherd named Kai trained to assist plaintiff with disabilities)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss Counts I and II (federal FHA claims) because it is not apparent from the face of the complaint that the statute of limitations has run. The court found that the tolling provision under 42 U.S.C. § 3613(a)(1)(B) applies to administrative proceedings, and the status of the HUD complaint is unclear from the complaint itself, so the claim survives the motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver of no-pets policy and pet deposit requirement for service dog (German Shepherd named Kai trained to assist plaintiff with disabilities) under Tampa Code of Ordinances § 12-82
fha_claims.reasoning: Counts III and IV (Tampa ordinance claims) are time-barred because the statute of limitations began to run in May 2019 when the discriminatory act occurred and expired in May 2021. The Tampa Code of Ordinances § 12-113(a)(1) provides a two-year statute of limitations with no tolling provision for administrative proceedings, unlike the federal FHA. Plaintiff did not file the complaint until August 23, 2022, more than a year after expiration.

source_file: 9647011_2023_Parisi v. Sabal Springs Homeowners Association Inc._flmd
case_name: Joseph Parisi and Terry Clark v. Sabal Springs Homeowners Association Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested that defendant accommodate their service animals, which defendant allegedly refused to do
key_holding: The court denied the motion to compel as moot (defendant had already provided discovery) but ordered defendant to pay plaintiffs' reasonable expenses incurred in bringing the motion under Rule 37(a)(5) because discovery was provided only after the motion was filed
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Joseph Parisi and Terry Clark sued their homeowners association under the Fair Housing Act, alleging the HOA refused to accommodate their service animals. The court resolved only plaintiffs' motion to compel discovery, finding that while the motion was moot because defendant had already provided the requested documents, defendant must nonetheless pay plaintiffs' reasonable expenses under Rule 37(a)(5) because the documents were produced only after the motion was filed.
key_cases_cited: Trahan v. Sandoz, Inc., No. 3:13-CV-350-J-34MCR, 2015 WL 12857088, at *1 (M.D. Fla. Sept. 24, 2015)
Devaney v. Cont’l Am. Ins. Co., 989 F.2d 1154, 1162 (11th Cir. 1993)
Bayer Healthcare Pharms., Inc. v. River’s Edge Pharms., LLC, No. 1:11-CV-1634-RLV-ECS, 2014 WL 12789352, at *6 (N.D. Ga. Mar. 21, 2014)
KePRO Acquisitions, Inc. v. Analytics Holdings, LLC, No. 3:19-CV-00842-SRW, 2021 WL 6883475, at *2 (M.D. Ala. Mar. 22, 2021)
Eichmuller v. Sarasota Cnty. Gov’t, No. 8:20-CV-47-T-33SPF, 2020 WL 10318567, at *1 (M.D. Fla. July 20, 2020)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accommodation for service animals
fha_claims.reasoning: This opinion addresses only a discovery dispute and motion to compel; it does not reach the merits of the underlying FHA reasonable accommodation claim regarding service animals. The case remains pending on the substantive FHA claim.

source_file: 9647881_2023_Jones v. Tudor Cay Condominium Association, Inc._flmd
case_name: Jones v. Tudor Cay Condominium Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges Tudor Cay failed to treat her fairly like other nonblack residents by not offering her a payment plan despite offering such plans to white and Hispanic owners who were delinquent on their dues.
key_holding: The complaint fails to state an FHA disparate treatment claim because it contains no factual allegations showing Tudor Cay had any role in offering payment plans to other residents or that any defendant acted with discriminatory intent.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Terese E. Jones sued Tudor Cay Condominium Association and related entities alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on racial discrimination, claiming she was treated differently than white and Hispanic owners regarding payment plans for delinquent dues. The Court granted the motions to dismiss, finding the complaint was a shotgun pleading that failed to state an FHA claim because it contained no factual allegations establishing discriminatory intent or connecting Tudor Cay to any allegedly disparate treatment.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Tex. Dep't of Hous. and Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Cmtys. Project, Inc.
Weiland v. Palm Beach Cnty. Sheriff's Off.
Schwarz v. City of Treasure Island

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges disparate treatment in collection practices and payment plan offers based on race, not a request for reasonable accommodation.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege disparate treatment under the FHA. The complaint alleged only that white and Hispanic owners received more favorable payment plans but provided no facts showing Tudor Cay acted with discriminatory intent or motive, nor that Plaintiff was treated differently than similarly situated residents outside the protected class.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: First Amendment, Fourteenth Amendment, Title VI of the Civil Rights Act, Equal Credit Opportunity Act, Fair Credit Reporting Act, Florida Consumer Collection Practices Act, Fair Debt Collection Practices Act
fha_claims.reasoning: Constitutional claims failed because defendants are private entities, not state actors. Title VI claim failed because no allegation that defendants received federal funding. ECOA and FCRA claims failed because plaintiff did not allege facts establishing the statutory definitions of 'creditor,' 'applicant,' or 'consumer reporting agency.' FDCPA and FCCPA claims were conclusory and failed to specify which subsections were violated by which defendants.

source_file: 9648267_2024_Frishberg v. University of South Florida Board of Trustees_flmd
case_name: Frishberg v. University of South Florida Board of Trustees
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested accommodation to keep his emotional support cat in his university dormitory room (already granted) and to take the cat outside his room into common areas of the dorm building. He also sought injunctive relief restoring access to his dorm room after defendants terminated his lease and changed his locks as a sanction for violating the policy restricting the animal to his room.
key_holding: The court granted in part and denied in part plaintiff's emergency motion for a temporary restraining order, enjoining defendants from placing holds on plaintiff's academic records or preventing class registration, but denying all other requested injunctive relief — including relief related to housing — for failure to sufficiently demonstrate irreparable harm.
brief_summary: Daniel Frishberg, a USF student, brought a federal FHA suit alleging that defendants discriminated against him and retaliated by terminating his dorm lease and locking him out after he violated a policy restricting his emotional support cat to his room. He filed an emergency motion for a TRO, primarily seeking reinstatement to housing and the ability to register for classes before a January 12, 2024 deadline. The court partially granted the TRO only to prevent academic registration holds, finding that irreparable harm from missing the registration deadline outweighed minimal burden to defendants, while denying housing-related injunctive relief for failure to demonstrate sufficient irreparable harm.
key_cases_cited: Schiavo ex rel. Schindler v. Schiavo, 403 F.3d 1223 (11th Cir. 2005)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to have emotional support animal (cat) outside of dorm room and in common areas of the dorm building
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted temporary restraining order on limited basis (preventing holds on academic records and class registration) without reaching merits of FHA claims. Court explicitly stated it has not determined whether plaintiff will succeed on claims and will subject merits to greater scrutiny at preliminary injunction hearing.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation through imposition of sanctions (fee and educational courses), termination of lease, and lockout from dorm room
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted limited temporary restraining order without reaching merits of retaliation claim. Court will subject merits to greater scrutiny at preliminary injunction hearing scheduled for January 16, 2024.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged discrimination based on disability in housing and educational access
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted limited temporary restraining order without reaching merits of discrimination claim. Court will subject merits to greater scrutiny at preliminary injunction hearing.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of contract, breach of duty under other statutes and common law principles
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted limited temporary restraining order without reaching merits of non-FHA claims. Court will subject merits to greater scrutiny at preliminary injunction hearing.

source_file: 9649187_2024_Frishberg v. University of South Florida Board of Trustees_flmd
case_name: Daniel A. Frishberg v. University of South Florida Board of Trustees
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested to keep his emotional support cat in common areas of the dorm building beyond his room.
key_holding: The court dismissed all FHA claims against USF Board of Trustees on Eleventh Amendment immunity grounds because the university is an arm of the state and neither the FHA nor FFHA contains a waiver of sovereign immunity for state entities.
brief_summary: Daniel Frishberg, a USF student, sued the University of South Florida Board of Trustees and its dormitory operator after being sanctioned, locked out, and having his lease terminated for allowing his emotional support cat outside of his dorm room. The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss, dismissing all FHA claims on Eleventh Amendment sovereign immunity grounds because USF Board is an arm of the state and Congress did not abrogate state sovereign immunity in the FHA.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
University of South Fla. Bd. of Trustees v. CoMentis, Inc.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to have emotional support animal (cat) in common areas of dorm building, not confined to plaintiff's room
fha_claims.reasoning: Eleventh Amendment immunity bars FHA claims against state university board of trustees. The FHA does not contain an explicit waiver of sovereign immunity, and Congress did not make unmistakably clear its intent to abrogate state sovereign immunity under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged discrimination based on disability in housing
fha_claims.reasoning: Eleventh Amendment immunity bars FHA disparate treatment claims against state university board of trustees and property owner acting as state agent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation for requesting accommodation (emotional support animal in common areas), including imposition of sanctions, lease termination, lock-out, and removal of personal belongings
fha_claims.reasoning: Eleventh Amendment immunity bars FHA retaliation claims under § 3617 against state university board of trustees. Ex parte Young exception does not apply because plaintiff asserted no § 1983 claims against state officers for prospective equitable relief.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claim for failure to provide reasonable accommodation for emotional support animal; breach of contract; fraudulent inducement; breach of implied covenant of good faith; unconscionability; tortious intimidation; unjust enrichment
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA Title II does not protect emotional support animals, only service animals; consequently the ADA claim fails as a matter of law. Eleventh Amendment immunity bars breach of contract, tort, and quasi-contractual claims against state university in federal court. Florida has not waived sovereign immunity for these claims.

source_file: 9649579_2024_Warner v. School Board of Hillsborough County, Florida_flmd
case_name: Warner v. School Board of Hillsborough County, Florida
accommodation_description: This is not a reasonable accommodation case; Warner alleged FHA claims related to school enrollment and housing proximity, which the court found too remote from housing to support FHA liability.
key_holding: The School Board's conduct in school enrollment and choice decisions is 'too remote' from housing to support Fair Housing Act claims, as the School Board lacks direct control over housing availability and Warner established no causal link to housing discrimination.
brief_summary: Blake Warner, proceeding pro se, sued the Hillsborough County School Board alleging Fair Housing Act claims related to his inability to enroll his child at a preferred school through school choice, along with equal protection and due process claims. The court adopted the magistrate judge's report, dismissing the FHA claims with prejudice because the School Board's decisions regarding school enrollment were too remote from housing to support FHA liability and Warner failed to establish any causal link between the Board's conduct and housing discrimination.
key_cases_cited: Bank of America Corp. v. City of Miami, Florida, 581 U.S. 189 (2017)
Stevenson v. Blytheville Sch. Dist. #5, 800 F.3d 955 (8th Cir. 2015)
Adkisson v. Blytheville Sch. Dist. No. 5, 2014 WL 6819729 (E.D. Ark. 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found the conduct too remote and lacking a direct causal link between the injury asserted and the injurious conduct alleged. The School Board lacks direct control over housing availability, and plaintiff offered no causal link evidencing racial discrimination in connection with housing services or denial of housing rights.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Same as Count I: the conduct was too remote and lacked the direct relation between injury and injurious conduct required by Bank of America Corp. v. City of Miami, Florida, 581 U.S. 189 (2017). Foreseeability alone is insufficient under the Fair Housing Act.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; complaint not filed with court
fha_claims.reasoning: The court remanded the case to state court for lack of federal subject matter jurisdiction. The defendant failed to provide a copy of the complaint to establish that FHA claims were properly pleaded in the original complaint. The court noted that the underlying state court docket indicated the matter was a straightforward eviction claim under state law, and any federal claims would be defenses or counterclaims, not the basis for removal.

case_name: George Friedel & Kathleen Friedel v. Sun Communities, Inc. & Park Place Community, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested to keep their dog Maggie as an emotional comfort assistance animal to assist George Friedel with depression, after receiving a notice of eviction for having an unauthorized animal.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' discrimination, reasonable accommodation, and retaliation claims as implausible because the most likely explanation for defendants' eviction notice was the prior jury verdict finding Maggie to be a dangerous animal, not discriminatory motive related to plaintiffs' accommodation requests.
brief_summary: George Friedel and Kathleen Friedel sued Sun Communities and Park Place for disability discrimination, failure to reasonably accommodate, and retaliation after receiving an eviction notice for their dog Maggie, who was found by a jury in prior litigation to be dangerous. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss with prejudice, finding that plaintiffs' claims were implausible because the most plausible explanation for the eviction was defendants' prior jury verdict, not discriminatory motive related to plaintiffs' accommodation requests.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Hunt v. Aimco Properties, L.P., 814 F.3d 1213 (11th Cir. 2016)
Hall v. United Ins. Co., 367 F.3d 1255 (11th Cir. 2004)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Making dwelling available to plaintiff with emotional support animal (dog)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found it implausible that Park Place's eviction notice issued the day after prevailing at trial was causally connected to plaintiff's second request for accommodation made over a month before trial, rather than to the jury verdict finding the dog dangerous. The temporal proximity and sequence of events made the discrimination allegation not plausible on its face.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Allowing plaintiff to keep emotional support animal (dog Maggie) in the community despite prior notice of violation and jury finding that the dog was dangerous
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for failure to plausibly allege that the eviction notice was issued because of the disability accommodation request rather than because of the jury verdict finding the dog dangerous. The temporal gap between the second accommodation request and the eviction notice made the causal connection implausible.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation for filing Friedel I lawsuit and submitting accommodation requests
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found it implausible that the eviction was retaliatory for filing Friedel I or submitting accommodation requests when the most plausible explanation was that Park Place prevailed at trial proving the dog was dangerous and plaintiffs refused to remove it.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of covenant of good faith and fair dealing; tortious business interference
fha_claims.reasoning: Breach of covenant claim dismissed because plaintiff failed to identify any express provision of the lease agreement that was breached, as required under Florida law. Tortious interference claim dismissed because the alleged interference (eviction) was justified by the jury verdict in Friedel I.

case_name: Deborah Engle v. Royal Bahamian Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested permission to use other areas of the condominium for her service dog, waiver of the pet fee, and access accommodations to the rear grounds due to mobility limitations from late-stage breast cancer
key_holding: The court denied RBA's motion to disqualify plaintiff's counsel because RBA failed to show that prior representation was substantially related to the current FHA case or that counsel could use confidential information to RBA's disadvantage
brief_summary: Deborah Engle, a condominium owner with mobility disabilities from late-stage breast cancer, sued Royal Bahamian Association alleging failure to accommodate her service dog and retaliation. The court denied RBA's motion to disqualify plaintiff's counsel, finding RBA failed to meet its burden to show prior representation was substantially related to the current litigation or that counsel gained confidential information that could disadvantage RBA.
key_cases_cited: Woods v. Covington Cnty. Bank, 537 F.2d 804 (5th Cir. 1976)
In re BellSouth Corp., 334 F.3d 941 (11th Cir. 2003)
Herrmann v. GutterGuard, Inc., 199 F. App'x 745 (11th Cir. 2006)
Armor Screen Corp. v. Storm Catcher, Inc., 709 F. Supp. 2d 1309 (S.D. Fla. 2010)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver of pet fee for service dog and permission to use areas other than designated dog areas due to plaintiff's difficulty accessing those areas; also requested modifications to rear grounds to allow safe entry and exit
fha_claims.reasoning: This order addresses only a motion to disqualify plaintiff's counsel and does not reach the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim. The claim survives the procedural challenge and remains pending.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges retaliation by RBA Board, including a grievance committee member following her and her dog and filming her
fha_claims.reasoning: This order addresses only a motion to disqualify plaintiff's counsel under 42 U.S.C. § 3617 and does not reach the merits of the retaliation claim. The claim survives the procedural challenge and remains pending.

source_file: 9652152_2021_Quality of Life, Corp. v. The City of Margate_flsd
case_name: Quality of Life, Corp. and MMJ Financial Services, Inc. v. The City of Margate
accommodation_description: This order concerns attorneys' fees and costs following summary judgment and appeal in an underlying case involving ADA and FHA claims; the accommodation request at issue in the underlying case is not described in this fee-motion order.
key_holding: The court denied the City of Margate's motions for attorneys' fees and appellate attorneys' fees because plaintiffs' claims were not frivolous, unreasonable, or without foundation, despite the grant of summary judgment in defendant's favor.
brief_summary: Quality of Life, Corp. and MMJ Financial Services, Inc. sued the City of Margate under the ADA and FHA; after summary judgment for the City and an unsuccessful appeal, the City moved for attorneys' fees and costs as a prevailing defendant. The court adopted the magistrate judge's recommendation to deny the fee motions but grant $23,458.04 in taxable costs, finding the plaintiffs' claims were not frivolous despite the adverse outcome.
key_cases_cited: Christiansburg Garment Co. v. Equal Emp. Opportunity Comm'n, 434 U.S. 412 (1978)
Bruce v. City of Gainesville, Ga., 177 F.3d 949 (11th Cir. 1999)
Sullivan v. Sch. Bd. of Pinellas Cnty., 773 F.2d 1182 (11th Cir. 1985)
Baker v. Alderman, 158 F.3d 516 (11th Cir. 1998)
Thomas v. Arn, 474 U.S. 140 (1985)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA and FHA claims (underlying substantive claims not detailed in this post-judgment fee opinion)
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court granted summary judgment in favor of Defendant on all ADA and FHA claims. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed in a comprehensive 22-page opinion substantively addressing all claims and arguments. The court found the claims were not frivolous despite the ultimate loss, as evidenced by extensive briefing, oral argument, and detailed judicial review.

case_name: Elgin Hilliard, Sr. v. Rene Gutierrez
accommodation_description: This is not a reasonable accommodation case; plaintiff brings false arrest and Fourth/Fourteenth Amendment civil rights claims arising from a 2016 arrest at the Hialeah Housing Authority office.
key_holding: The court granted Officer Gutierrez's motion to dismiss based on res judicata, finding that plaintiff's false arrest and constitutional violation claims were barred because they arose from the same nucleus of operative facts as claims in Hilliard I, involved parties in privity (employer-employee relationship), and could have been litigated in the prior action where final judgment on the merits was entered.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Elgin Hilliard, Sr. filed suit against Officer Rene Gutierrez asserting false arrest and § 1983 Fourth/Fourteenth Amendment claims arising from his May 17, 2016 arrest at the Hialeah Housing Authority. The court granted defendant's motion to dismiss with prejudice, finding that plaintiff's claims were barred by res judicata because they arose from the same operative facts as claims in Hilliard I, defendant was in privity with HHA (his employer), and the claims could have been raised and were actually adjudicated in the prior action where final judgment was entered on the merits.
key_cases_cited: Montana v. United States, 440 U.S. 147 (1979)
In re Piper Aircraft Corp., 244 F.3d 1289 (11th Cir. 2001)
Allen v. McCurry, 449 U.S. 90 (1980)
Citibank, N.A. v. Data Lease Fin. Corp., 904 F.2d 1498 (11th Cir. 1990)
Manning v. City of Auburn, 953 F.2d 1355 (11th Cir. 1992)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The FHA retaliation claim asserted in Hilliard II is barred by res judicata because it arises from the same nucleus of operative facts as the FHA retaliation claim (Count VII) adjudicated in Hilliard I, where a jury returned a verdict for HHA following trial. The prior judgment was final and on the merits, and Defendant is in privity with HHA as an employee whose conduct formed the basis of the claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 false arrest and Fourth Amendment violations; state tort law false arrest claim
fha_claims.reasoning: The § 1983 false arrest and Fourth Amendment claims, along with state tort false arrest claims, are barred by res judicata because they arise from the same May 17, 2016 incident and nucleus of operative facts as claims adjudicated in Hilliard I. The summary judgment order in Hilliard I granted judgment for HHA on the § 1983 false arrest claim (Count I) following substantive merits analysis, constituting a final adjudication on the merits that precludes relitigation of these claims against Defendant in privity with HHA.

source_file: 9653018_2021_LaGrasso v. Seven Bridges Homeowners Association Inc_flsd
case_name: LaGrasso v. Seven Bridges Homeowners Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege the HOA discriminated against them based on their Christian/non-Jewish religious status through disparate treatment including fines, suspensions, and selective enforcement of community rules.
key_holding: The court grants in part and denies in part the motion in limine, excluding news articles about the litigation but allowing evidence related to the tennis court incident, Facebook posts, fines, and recordings to support Plaintiffs' disparate treatment religious discrimination claim at trial.
brief_summary: Jeffrey and Deborah LaGrasso sued Seven Bridges Homeowners Association alleging religious discrimination, claiming the HOA treated them disparately due to their Christian/non-Jewish status through fines, suspensions, and selective enforcement. The court denied most of the HOA's motion in limine to exclude evidence, allowing Plaintiffs to present circumstantial evidence of discrimination at trial while excluding news articles as inadmissible hearsay.
key_cases_cited: Smith v. Lockheed-Martin Corp., 644 F.3d 1321 (11th Cir. 2011)
Luce v. United States, 469 U.S. 38 (1984)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied defendant's motion in limine to exclude evidence of the tennis court incident, Facebook posts, Pro Shop Manager termination, fining schedule, audio/video recordings, and other circumstantial evidence, finding such evidence potentially relevant to plaintiff's disparate treatment claim based on religion. The court held that plaintiffs are entitled to present a mosaic of circumstantial evidence to allow a jury to infer intentional discrimination, and that evidentiary rulings must be deferred until trial. The claim survives and proceeds to jury trial on the disparate treatment theory.

case_name: Rita Fox v. Dana James Gaines et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request at issue; case involves sexual harassment (quid pro quo and hostile housing environment) by landlord against tenant.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion for summary judgment, finding genuine issues of material fact exist on plaintiff's quid pro quo harassment, hostile housing environment, retaliation, and interference claims under the FHA.
brief_summary: Rita Fox sued her landlords Dana James Gaines and Lucille Gaines for sexual harassment and discrimination under the Fair Housing Act, alleging quid pro quo harassment and a hostile housing environment created by the landlord's sexual demands. The court denied defendants' motion for summary judgment, finding genuine disputes of material fact on all claims regarding whether sexual favors were conditioning on continued tenancy and whether defendant's post-relationship eviction proceedings constituted unlawful discrimination and retaliation.
key_cases_cited: Fox v. Gaines, 4 F.4th 1293 (11th Cir. 2021)
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Quigg v. Thomas County Sch. Dist., 814 F.3d 1227 (11th Cir. 2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine issues of material fact whether the terms and conditions of plaintiff's rental, including continued occupation, were explicitly or implicitly conditioned upon compliance with sexual demands by defendant landlord, based on deposition testimony and the temporal proximity between termination of the sexual relationship and posting of lease violation notices.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine issues of material fact whether defendant's behavior and sexual conduct was unwelcome and sufficiently pervasive as to interfere with plaintiff's use and enjoyment of the apartment, applying the totality of circumstances test and finding disputed evidence regarding whether the relationship was consensual or coerced by the power imbalance between landlord and tenant.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine issues of material fact regarding causal link between plaintiff's protected activity (terminating sexual relationship to be free from harassment) and defendant's adverse action (posting lease violation notices and filing eviction), based on close temporal proximity of only three days between the protected activity and the adverse action.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine issues of material fact regarding all three elements of a § 3617 interference claim: plaintiff exercised protected right to be free from sexual harassment, defendant's posting of lease violation notices and eviction attempt constituted interference, and close temporal proximity of a few days established causal connection between protected activity and interference.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Florida state law claims under § 760.37 and § 760.23(2), Florida Statutes
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied the same McDonnell Douglas framework and causation standards to the parallel Florida state law claims as to the FHA claims, finding genuine issues of material fact on all elements and denying summary judgment.

source_file: 9654135_2022_Gundogdu v. WDF-4 Wood Harbor Park Owner, LLC_flsd
case_name: Rengin Gundogdu v. WDF-4 Wood Harbor Park Owner, LLC
accommodation_description: The court never substantively analyzed any specific accommodation request; the complaint mentioned Fair Housing Act claims in passing but the case was dismissed for lack of jurisdiction before reaching the merits.
key_holding: The court granted the motion to dismiss and remanded the case because it lacked subject-matter jurisdiction over the removed state-court eviction case, and alternatively would have abstained under Colorado River even if original jurisdiction existed.
brief_summary: Rengin Gundogdu, a pro se tenant facing eviction from a Broward County rental property, attempted to remove the consolidated state-court eviction case to federal court, raising Fair Housing Act and CARES Act claims. The Southern District of Florida granted the Defendants' motion to dismiss, holding that it lacked subject-matter jurisdiction because Gundogdu improperly attempted to remove her own counterclaims rather than a complaint establishing federal jurisdiction, and alternatively would have abstained under Colorado River given the advanced state of the parallel state proceedings.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Caterpillar Inc. v. Williams, 482 U.S. 386 (1987)
Colorado River Water Conservation Dist. v. United States, 424 U.S. 800 (1976)
Younger v. Harris, 401 U.S. 37 (1971)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act discrimination claim; CARES Act federal eviction ban violation; Civil Rights Act violations
fha_claims.disposition: 12(b)(1) — Lack of Subject Matter Jurisdiction; Colorado River Abstention
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked subject-matter jurisdiction over the removed state-court eviction case because removal was improper (counterclaims cannot form the basis for federal question jurisdiction), diversity jurisdiction was not established (incomplete diversity and amount in controversy insufficient at $7,736.42), and removal was procedurally untimely (filed 80 days after the 30-day removal deadline). Additionally, even if the court had original jurisdiction, it would abstain under Colorado River because the federal and state proceedings involve substantially the same parties and issues, creating potential for piecemeal litigation and forum shopping.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Defendant asserted Fair Housing Act discrimination and Title VII race discrimination as a defense/counterclaim to eviction, but the complaint itself does not allege any FHA claim on its face.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court remanded the case for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because the state court complaint is a straightforward unlawful detainer action under Florida law. Federal question jurisdiction does not exist on the face of the plaintiff's well-pleaded complaint; defenses or counterclaims based on federal law (including the FHA) cannot confer federal question jurisdiction. The court never reached the merits of any FHA claim.

case_name: Eddy J. Philippeaux v. Miami Apartments Investors, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges he was retaliatorily evicted from his apartment in violation of the Fair Housing Act and Americans with Disabilities Act.
key_holding: The court dismissed Count I (ADA claim) with prejudice because the private residential apartment unit is not a place of public accommodation where Title III of the ADA applies, and dismissed Count II (FHA retaliation claim) without prejudice as the opinion contains no substantive analysis of the claim.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Eddy J. Philippeaux, proceeding pro se, sued Miami Apartment Investors LLC, Baron Residential Management, and Sharon Fothergill alleging they retaliatorily evicted him in violation of the ADA, FHA, and civil rights statutes. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss Count I with prejudice, finding that a private residential apartment is not a place of public accommodation under the ADA, and dismissed Count II (FHA retaliation) without prejudice and Count III (§ 1981 and § 1985 conspiracy claims) with leave to amend for failure to state plausible claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Griffin v. Breckenridge, 403 U.S. 88 (1971)
Bailey v. Bd. of Cnty. Com'rs of Alachua Cnty., Fla., 956 F.2d 1112 (11th Cir. 1992)
Dean v. Warren, 12 F.4th 1248 (11th Cir. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Count II (FHA retaliation claim) survived the motion to dismiss and was dismissed without prejudice, allowing plaintiff to proceed or amend. The court did not reach the merits of the retaliation claim but permitted it to continue.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III (Count I), 42 U.S.C. § 1981 (Count III), 42 U.S.C. § 1985 (Count III)
fha_claims.reasoning: Count I dismissed with prejudice because the alleged retaliatory eviction occurred in a private residential unit, not a place of public accommodation subject to ADA Title III. Count III dismissed without prejudice for failure to plead sufficient facts under § 1981 (no allegation of plaintiff's race or intent to discriminate based on race) and § 1985(3) (conclusory allegations of conspiracy without factual support or class-based animus).

case_name: Eddy J. Philippeaux v. Miami Apartments Investors, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a disabled veteran, alleges landlord retaliated against him by evicting him and refusing to renew his lease after he filed prior ADA and FHA complaints.
key_holding: The court dismissed Counts I, III, IV, and V with prejudice, finding that plaintiff failed to adequately plead claims for ADA retaliation, § 1981 race discrimination, § 1985 conspiracy, intentional infliction of emotional distress, and negligent infliction of emotional distress, leaving only the FHA retaliation claim under § 3617 to proceed.
brief_summary: Eddy J. Philippeaux, a pro se disabled veteran tenant, sued Miami Apartments Investors and related defendants alleging retaliation under the ADA and FHA, race discrimination under §§ 1981 and 1985, and state law emotional distress claims after they evicted him and declined to renew his lease following his prior fair housing lawsuit. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss with prejudice on all claims except the FHA retaliation claim under § 3617, finding plaintiff failed to adequately plead race-based but-for causation, conspiracy, or viable emotional distress claims.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Comcast Corp. v. Nat'l Ass'n of African Am.-Owned Media, 140 S. Ct. 1009 (2020)
Ziyadat v. Diamondrock Hosp. Co., 3 F.4th 1291 (11th Cir. 2021)
Dean v. Warren, 12 F.4th 1248 (11th Cir. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Count II (FHA retaliation under § 3617) survived the motion to dismiss and the case shall proceed on this claim. The court granted the motion as to Counts I, III, IV, and V but explicitly stated 'This case shall proceed as to Count II.'

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 (racial discrimination), 1985 (conspiracy), state law IIED and NIED
fha_claims.reasoning: Counts III, IV, and V dismissed for failure to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly. Count III (§ 1981 and § 1985) contained only conclusory allegations without factual support for racial animus or conspiracy elements. Counts IV and V (IIED and NIED) failed to allege facts showing conduct was outrageous or that plaintiff suffered physical injury caused by psychological trauma.

case_name: David Webb v. Miami-Dade County Government, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a homeless disabled individual, alleges discrimination by a shelter operator and county entities but does not articulate a specific accommodation request before the case was dismissed on procedural grounds.
key_holding: The court dismissed the complaint as a shotgun pleading that failed to comply with Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 8 and 10, without reaching the merits of any FHA or ADA claims.
brief_summary: David Webb, a homeless Miami-Dade County resident with a heart disability, sued Camillus House, Miami-Dade County Government, and various officials alleging they violated his ADA, FHA, and constitutional rights by discharging him to the streets. The court denied his in forma pauperis motion and dismissed the complaint as a shotgun pleading that failed to give defendants adequate notice of the claims against them or comply with Rule 10(b) requirements.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Embree v. Wyndham Worldwide Corp., 779 F. App'x 658 (11th Cir. 2019)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges denial of alternative temporary residency within an Extended Stay America Hotel and discharge from Camillus House residential facility despite disability (extreme angina) and homelessness.
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint dismissed as an impermissible shotgun pleading that fails to provide defendants adequate notice of claims and grounds, violates Rule 10(b) by combining multiple defendants, incidents, and legal theories in single paragraphs, and fails to separate distinct causes of action into different counts. Court did not reach substantive merits of FHA claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges denial of federal housing based on color, race, and national origin as a disabled senior citizen.
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint dismissed as shotgun pleading lacking minimum clarity and coherence required by Rules 8 and 10. Court did not reach substantive merits of discrimination claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges coercion, intimidation, threatening, and interference by defendants.
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint dismissed as shotgun pleading. Court did not reach substantive merits of interference/coercion claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA violations (42 U.S.C. §§ 12101, 12102, 12203), Fourth Amendment violations, Fourteenth Amendment Equal Protection violations, False Claims Act violations (31 U.S.C. §§ 3729-3733), Title VI of Civil Rights Act of 1964, § 1983 state actor liability, § 1985 conspiracy, § 1986 failure to prevent, deliberate indifference to medical needs.
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint dismissed as shotgun pleading that asserts multiple claims against multiple defendants without specifying which defendant is responsible for which act. Court did not reach substantive merits of non-FHA claims.

case_name: Chalissa Olivera Truesdale v. Venice Arms, Inc.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation request at issue; case involves allegations of racial discrimination in cooperative housing rules enforcement
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claims because the amended complaint was a shotgun pleading failing to identify specific statutory provisions, and even interpreting the claims charitably, section 3604 claims failed as they apply only to buying/selling/leasing transactions (not cooperative rule enforcement against existing owners) while section 3617 claims required allegations of conduct severe or pervasive enough to be threatening or violent.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Chalissa Olivera Truesdale, a Hispanic woman and member of a 55-and-over housing cooperative, sued Venice Arms, Inc. alleging the Swedish-dominated cooperative association engaged in racially discriminatory housing practices including enforcement of no-renter rules, guest policies, and association with a racist board motion to exclude minorities. The court granted defendant's motion to dismiss with leave to amend, finding the complaint was a shotgun pleading that failed to state viable FHA claims because section 3604 applies only to housing transactions and the section 3617 claim lacked allegations of severe or violent discriminatory conduct required to state a claim.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Lawrence v. Courtyards at Deerwood Ass'n, Inc., 318 F. Supp. 2d 1133 (S.D. Fla. 2004)
Gourlay v. Forest Lake Ests. Civic Ass'n of Port Richey, Inc., 276 F. Supp. 2d 1222 (M.D. Fla. 2003)
Sofarelli v. Pinellas County, 931 F.2d 718 (11th Cir. 1991)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges discriminatory conduct and harassment based on race, not a request for reasonable accommodation.
fha_claims.reasoning: Count I (§ 3617 retaliation/interference claim) dismissed for failure to plausibly allege that the Association endorsed or approved the racist motion or engaged in conduct severe and pervasive enough to constitute actionable interference under § 3617. Plaintiff alleged only vague, conclusory statements that hate speech was 'common and accepted' without sufficient factual support.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges discriminatory enforcement of Association rules (no-renter rule, guest policy) based on race, not a request for reasonable accommodation.
fha_claims.reasoning: Count II (§ 3604(a)-(b) disparate treatment claim) dismissed because § 3604 applies only to conduct directly impacting accessibility to housing through sale or rental. Plaintiff's allegations of discriminatory enforcement of Association rules against a unit owner who already owned the property do not implicate § 3604, which regulates the sale or rental of housing, not post-purchase enforcement of cooperative rules.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges discriminatory effect of Association rules (no-renter rule, guest policy) based on race, not a request for reasonable accommodation.
fha_claims.reasoning: Count III (§ 3604(a)-(b) disparate impact claim) dismissed on the same basis as Count II: § 3604 is limited to conduct affecting the sale or rental of housing and does not extend to post-purchase enforcement of cooperative rules. The court found no statutory basis for a disparate impact claim under § 3604 in this context.

case_name: Eli Portnoy v. MEI Condominium Association, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested accommodation to communicate with someone other than the Board President regarding residency business due to stress-related disability.
key_holding: The court denied the individual board member's motion to dismiss, finding that Florida state immunity statutes cannot bar federal FHA claims and that plaintiff adequately alleged individual liability against the board president for her personal involvement in discriminatory acts.
brief_summary: Eli Portnoy, a disabled condominium resident, sued MEI Condominium Association and its Board President Anna Strickstein-Zandman alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act, including failure to reasonably accommodate his request to communicate with someone other than the Board President due to his stress-related disability. The court denied the individual board member's motion to dismiss, rejecting her claims of immunity under Florida state statutes and finding that Portnoy adequately pleaded individual liability under the FHA for her personal involvement in discriminatory acts.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)
Housing Opportunities Project for Excellence, Inc. v. Key Colony No. 4 Condo. Assoc., 510 F. Supp. 2d 1003 (S.D. Fla. 2007)
Sabal Palm Condos. of Pine Island Ridge Ass'n, Inc. v. Fischer, 2014 WL 988767 (S.D. Fla. 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request that someone other than Anna Strickstein-Zandman interact with plaintiff regarding business matters related to his residency, due to stress-related disability and antagonistic relationship with the board president.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the motion to dismiss, finding that plaintiff adequately pleaded personal involvement by the individual defendant in the discriminatory acts and that the allegations of willful discrimination fall within the exception to state statutory immunity, allowing the claim to proceed past the motion to dismiss stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request for access to gym and recreational amenities despite medical restrictions; plaintiff's therapist cleared him to use the gym, but defendants required clearance from their own treating physician.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the motion to dismiss, finding that plaintiff adequately pleaded that the individual defendant personally determined he was not healthy enough to use the facilities and that these allegations of willful discrimination survive the motion to dismiss stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Imposition of discriminatory terms and conditions regarding use of gym and recreational facilities based on disability.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the motion to dismiss, finding that plaintiff adequately pleaded that defendants discriminated against him under different terms and conditions than non-disabled residents and that the individual defendant was personally involved in these discriminatory acts.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of lease renewal in retaliation for requesting reasonable accommodation and asserting FHA rights.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the motion to dismiss, finding that plaintiff adequately pleaded that defendants retaliated against him by refusing to renew his lease because of his disability and that the individual defendant was personally involved in this retaliatory conduct.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of housing in violation of Florida Fair Housing Act § 760.23(1); supplemental state law claims under Fla. Stat. § 760.20 et seq., specifically §§ 760.23(2), 760.23(8), 760.23(9)(b), and 760.37.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the motion to dismiss on the state law claim (Count IV), finding that plaintiff adequately pleaded personal and deliberate discrimination by the individual defendant, which survives the motion to dismiss stage under supplemental jurisdiction.

case_name: Eddy J. Philippeaux v. Miami Apartments Investors, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges retaliation through lease non-renewal after filing a prior lawsuit claiming disability discrimination, including requests for parking accommodations.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for defendants on the FHA retaliation claim because plaintiff failed to establish a causal link between filing the lawsuit and the lease non-renewal, as the approximately one-year gap between these events is insufficient under Eleventh Circuit precedent, and plaintiff failed to demonstrate that defendants' proffered legitimate reasons for non-renewal (resident complaints and disruptive behavior) were pretextual.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Eddy Philippeaux sued Miami Apartments Investors, LLC and Baron Residential Management alleging they violated the Fair Housing Act by declining to renew his lease in retaliation for filing a previous lawsuit alleging disability discrimination. The court granted defendants' motion for summary judgment, finding that the approximately one-year gap between the lawsuit and non-renewal was insufficient to establish causation under controlling precedent, and plaintiff failed to rebut defendants' legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for non-renewal based on resident complaints about his disruptive behavior.
key_cases_cited: McCall v. Owens
Higdon v. Jackson
Clark County Sch. Dist. v. Breeland
St. Mary's Honor Ctr. v. Hicks
Olmstead v. L.C.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a causal link between his protected activity (filing the prior lawsuit) and the adverse action (non-renewal of lease). The approximately one-year gap between the lawsuit and non-renewal is insufficient under Eleventh Circuit precedent, which requires temporal proximity to be 'very close' and has found three to four months insufficient. Plaintiff also failed to rebut Defendants' legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason (problematic behavior documented in warning letters) by showing it was pretextual.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA retaliation claim (Count I); Civil Rights violations under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 and 1985 (Count III); Intentional Infliction of Emotional Distress (Count IV); Negligent Infliction of Emotional Distress (Count V)
fha_claims.reasoning: Counts I, III, IV, and V were dismissed with prejudice on motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6) for failure to state a plausible claim. The ADA retaliation claim (Count I) and civil rights conspiracy claims (Count III) were dismissed as legally insufficient; emotional distress claims (Counts IV and V) were also dismissed at the pleading stage.

case_name: Hannah Gorman v. Breeze Condominium Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: Request for an emotional support dog for Mr. Tomlinson (a person with a disability) to ameliorate the effects of his disability, which was denied based on the dog's size and breed.
key_holding: Plaintiff, as a person associated with a disabled individual under § 3604(f), has standing to bring FHA claims including failure to accommodate; the complaint adequately alleges that Mr. Tomlinson is disabled, requested an ESA accommodation, and was denied, and that plaintiff suffered adverse actions causally connected to protected activity.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Hannah Gorman sued Breeze Condominium Association, its property management company Nautica Management, and property manager Richard Muller, alleging they denied her companion's request for an emotional support animal, refused to renew her lease, and denied approval of a second rental unit in retaliation for filing a HUD complaint. The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss all counts, finding that Gorman, as a person associated with a disabled individual, has standing to assert FHA claims and that she adequately pled a failure to accommodate, retaliation, and interference with housing rights.
key_cases_cited: Hawn v. Shoreline Towers Phase 1 Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 347 Fed. App'x. 464 (11th Cir. 2009)
Schwarz v. City of Treasure Island, 544 F.3d 1201 (11th Cir. 2008)
Wasserman v. Three Seasons Ass'n No. 1, Inc., 998 F. Supp. 1445 (S.D. Fla. 1998)
Moore v. Camden Prop. Tr., 816 F. App'x 324 (11th Cir. 2020)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of emotional support animal (dog) application for Mr. Tomlinson based on the dog's size and breed; plaintiff submitted application with pet form, photographs, and letter from psychiatrist on May 29, 2022; denied June 14, 2022.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that plaintiff, as a person associated with Mr. Tomlinson (who has a disability), has standing to bring a failure-to-accommodate claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f). Plaintiff adequately pleaded that Mr. Tomlinson is disabled, that she requested an accommodation (ESA), and that defendants refused it. At the motion to dismiss stage, these allegations are sufficient to survive under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiff adequately pleaded all three elements of a § 3617 retaliation claim: (1) protected activity (filing HUD complaint regarding denial of reasonable accommodation), (2) adverse action (denial of lease renewal for Unit 304 and denial of lease approval for Unit 311), and (3) causal connection (defendants' letter explicitly cited the ongoing legal matter as grounds for denial). Allegations are sufficient to survive motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Interference with plaintiff's contract to lease Unit 311 by defendants' denial of board approval based on the ongoing legal matter regarding the ESA denial in Unit 304.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that plaintiff adequately pleaded a § 3617 interference claim by alleging that defendants interfered with her contract for Unit 311 because of the disability-related denial regarding Mr. Tomlinson's ESA in Unit 304. The plain text of § 3604(f)(1)(C) covers discrimination against a renter because of a handicap of a person associated with that renter, and plaintiff's allegations fit squarely within this provision.

source_file: 9657400_2021_WODA COOPER DEVELOPMENT INC v. CITY OF WARNER ROBINS GEORGIA_gamd
case_name: Woda Cooper Development, Inc. et al. v. City of Warner Robins et al.
accommodation_description: This is not a reasonable accommodation case; plaintiffs are developers challenging the City's refusal to permit an affordable housing development, alleging discriminatory intent based on race.
key_holding: The disparate treatment claim survives because the City enthusiastically solicited the affordable housing development then abruptly reversed course when faced with political opposition, and the sequence of events plausibly alleges intentional racial discrimination; however, the disparate impact claim fails because plaintiffs only allege a one-time decision rather than a policy causing disparate impact.
brief_summary: Woda Cooper Development sued the City of Warner Robins, Mayor Randy Toms, and the Development Authority after the City reneged on agreements to allow an affordable housing development at Perkins Field, allegedly due to racial animus against the African American residents who would occupy the housing. The court dismissed the Development Authority entirely, dismissed the disparate impact and Contract Clause claims, but allowed the disparate treatment claim to proceed based on the City's unusual sequence of enthusiastically soliciting then abruptly blocking the development in response to political pressure.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Tex. Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Hallmark Devs., Inc. v. Fulton Cty., 466 F.3d 1276 (11th Cir. 2006)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Conveyance of publicly owned land (Perkins Field) for affordable housing development in downtown Warner Robins
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege a policy or practice with disparate impact.
