The complaint alleged only a one-time decision to renege on the Perkins Field development and did not establish that the City implemented a policy of confining affordable housing to less desirable areas, as the prior Pennrose developments were not alleged to have been shunted away from downtown by the City. Robust causality between any policy and harm to African Americans was not plausibly alleged.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Approval and conveyance of Perkins Field for affordable housing development; reversal of prior commitments to the development
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs plausibly alleged FHA disparate treatment claim under circumstantial evidence theory. The City initially rolled out the red carpet, enthusiastically solicited and supported the development through multiple steps, then abruptly reversed course when community opposition surfaced—opposition characterized by coded language about low-income housing and rising crime. The sequence of events, discriminatory effect on African Americans (primary consumers of affordable housing), and departure from normal criteria plausibly infer intentional discrimination based on race.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of contract (Ground Lease Agreement); specific performance to compel lease of Perkins Field; Contract Clause violation (rescission of commitment resolution and defunding of Development Authority)
fha_claims.reasoning: Breach of contract claim against Development Authority dismissed because plaintiffs failed to allege how the Authority could breach by failing to lease property it did not own when the City prevented conveyance. Specific performance claim dismissed because no valid contract existed between plaintiffs and the City. Contract Clause claim dismissed because the rescission of the commitment resolution was not a 'law' under the Contract Clause, and the defunding vote was not plausibly alleged to have caused the injuries alleged in the complaint.

case_name: Quincy Bernard Jones v. Featherstone Homeowners Association
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: The Court denied plaintiff's motion for appointment of counsel, finding no exceptional circumstances, and deferred ruling on plaintiff's renewed summary judgment motion pending completion of discovery.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Quincy Bernard Jones sued Featherstone Homeowners Association alleging Fair Housing Act failure-to-accommodate claims. The Court denied Jones's motion for appointment of counsel, finding he demonstrated sufficient ability to proceed without counsel, and deferred ruling on his renewed summary judgment motion to allow discovery to proceed.
key_cases_cited: Wahl v. McIver, 773 F.2d 1169 (11th Cir. 1985)
Reflectone, Inc. v. Farrand Optical Co., 862 F.2d 841 (11th Cir. 1989)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Specific accommodation not detailed in this order; plaintiff alleged failure to accommodate related to disability
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted plaintiff leave to proceed in forma pauperis and allowed the Fair Housing Act failure-to-accommodate claim to proceed following frivolity review under § 1915(e)(2)(B), meaning the claim survived the initial screening and was not found to be frivolous or indisputably meritless.

case_name: Adonis Berle Whitby v. Macon-Bibb County, Georgia; Mayor Lester Miller; The Board of Commissioners; Henry C. Ficklin; Doctor Keith Moffett; Director Charles Brooks; and Director Tim Wilder
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requests that the county clear, establish right of way, repair, and maintain a 500-foot portion of road in Lizella, Georgia, claiming discriminatory denial of road maintenance services based on residents' race and other protected characteristics.
key_holding: The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss based on res judicata, holding that Plaintiff's discrimination claims (including FHA, ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and Fourteenth Amendment claims) were barred because they could have been raised in a prior state court suit seeking the same relief—court-ordered road maintenance.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Adonis Berle Whitby, an African American resident, sued Macon-Bibb County, Georgia and various officials under the Fair Housing Act, Fourteenth Amendment, and other statutes, alleging that the county's failure to fully maintain a road in Lizella constitutes racial discrimination against African American homeowners. The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss on res judicata grounds, finding that Plaintiff's discrimination claims were barred because he previously sued in state court for the same relief—road maintenance—and could have raised these theories there but failed to do so.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Grappell v. Carvalho, 847 F. App'x 698 (11th Cir. 2021)
Federer v. Zurich Am. Ins. Co., 701 F. App'x 835 (11th Cir. 2017)
Bostick v. CMM Props., 772 S.E.2d 671 (Ga. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Road maintenance and repair (not an accommodation claim; plaintiff alleges discriminatory denial of road maintenance services based on race, disability, sex, and age of homeowners)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's FHA discrimination claims are barred by res judicata because he had a full and fair opportunity to litigate discrimination theories in his prior state court suit seeking the same relief (road maintenance) and failed to raise them. Claim preclusion forecloses litigation of matters that should have been advanced in the first suit.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 due process, Title VI, Title II ADA, § 504 Rehabilitation Act, age discrimination (42 U.S.C. §§ 6101–6107), Fourteenth Amendment equal protection
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA claims are barred by res judicata on the same basis as the FHA claims. Additionally, to the extent plaintiff sought to assert claims on behalf of other homeowners, he lacked standing as a pro se litigant under 28 U.S.C. § 1654.

case_name: Quincy Bernard Jones v. Featherstone Homeowners Association
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED - This order does not address the substantive accommodation request; it addresses procedural discovery matters only.
key_holding: The court denied Jones's motion to strike his deposition and motion to compel, finding no constitutional violation: Jones has no right to appointed counsel in civil cases, and his deposition was voluntary after the court properly advised him of his obligations.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Quincy Bernard Jones sued Featherstone Homeowners Association alleging Fair Housing Act failure-to-accommodate claims; this order denies Jones's motion to strike his deposition and motion to compel production of letters, finding no constitutional violation in the deposition procedures and that Jones can review his transcript under Rule 30(e).
key_cases_cited: Wahl v. McIver, 773 F.2d 1169 (11th Cir. 1985)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unspecified reasonable accommodation related to plaintiff's mental health disability; the opinion does not detail the specific accommodation requested
fha_claims.disposition: Allowed to proceed following frivolity review
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted plaintiff leave to proceed in forma pauperis and allowed the Fair Housing Act failure-to-accommodate claim to proceed following § 1915(e) frivolity review, without dismissing the claim on the merits. The opinion does not substantively analyze the elements of the reasonable accommodation claim.

case_name: Quincy Bernard Jones v. Featherstone Homeowners Association
accommodation_description: Request for installation of railings on the retaining wall in front of his duplex unit to address fear of falling while playing catch with relatives
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for defendant because plaintiff failed to establish he had a qualifying disability under the FHA, the requested retaining wall railings were neither reasonable nor necessary, and plaintiff refused to pay for the modification as required under § 3604(f)(3)(A).
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Quincy Jones sued Featherstone Homeowners Association alleging failure to accommodate or modify under the FHA by refusing to install railings on a retaining wall, claiming his paranoia and schizophrenia made him fear falling while playing catch with relatives. The court granted summary judgment for the HOA, finding that Jones failed to establish a qualifying disability, the requested modification was not reasonable or necessary, and Jones refused to pay for the modification as required under § 3604(f)(3)(A).
key_cases_cited: Johnson v. Jennings, 772 F. App'x 822 (11th Cir. 2019)
Hawn v. Shoreline Towers Phase 1 Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 347 F. App'x 464 (11th Cir. 2009)
Alonso Cano v. 245 C & C, LLC, 2019 WL 11769102 (S.D. Fla. 2019)
Peklun v. Tierra Del Mar Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 2015 WL 8029840 (S.D. Fla. 2015)
Schwarz v. City of Treasure Island, 544 F.3d 1201 (11th Cir. 2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Installation of railings on the retaining wall in front of plaintiff's duplex unit to address plaintiff's paranoia and anxiety triggered by fear of falling
fha_claims.reasoning: The court determined that plaintiff's request for retaining wall railings constitutes a request for modification under § 3604(f)(3)(A), not an accommodation under § 3604(f)(3)(B), because it involves a structural change to common use areas. The court did not apply the reasonable accommodation standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Installation of railings on the retaining wall in front of plaintiff's duplex unit
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the six-element test for FHA modifications and found that plaintiff failed to establish: (1) disability under the FHA (no documentation provided to defendant by close of discovery; diagnosis of paranoid schizophrenia came over one year after the request); (2) reasonableness and necessity (plaintiff could play catch in other areas of the property and enjoyed his unit equally to other residents); and (3) willingness to pay at plaintiff's own expense (plaintiff's post-deposition declarations contradicting his deposition testimony were treated as sham affidavits).

source_file: 9658922_2023_WODA COOPER DEVELOPMENT INC v. CITY OF WARNER ROBINS GEORGIA_gamd
case_name: Woda Cooper Development, Inc. v. City of Warner Robins
accommodation_description: Affordable housing developers allege the City rescinded support for a LIHTC-funded affordable housing development in retaliation for exercising FHA rights.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' disparate treatment claim because affordable housing developers cannot establish they were discriminated against 'because of' their race, but found genuine issues of material fact exist on the retaliation claim because defense counsel's threats of criminal prosecution and LIHTC revocation during litigation constituted adverse action taken in response to plaintiffs' pursuit of FHA claims.
brief_summary: Affordable housing developers sued the City of Warner Robins, Georgia alleging the City violated the FHA by rescinding support for a downtown affordable housing development (disparate treatment) and by making threatening statements during litigation in retaliation for pursuing FHA claims. The court granted summary judgment for the City on the disparate treatment claim, finding plaintiffs failed to establish intentional discrimination based on race, but denied summary judgment on the retaliation claim, finding genuine issues of material fact exist as to whether defense counsel's threats of criminal prosecution and LIHTC revocation constituted unlawful retaliation.
key_cases_cited: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green
Burlington N. & Santa Fe Ry. Co. v. White
Meyer v. Holley
Texas Dept. of Cmty. Affairs v. Burdine
Bone v. Vill. Club, Inc.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the Hallmark four-factor test for discriminatory intent in local governmental decisions and found that plaintiffs failed to establish that the City acted with racial discriminatory intent when rescinding the Commitment Resolution. The court found no evidence that community opposition was based on racial animus, that City officials were aware of allegedly racist social media posts, or that the City was not justified in rescinding based on the reduction in commercial retail space.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiffs established a prima facie case of retaliation under 42 U.S.C. § 3617 based on defense counsel's threats of criminal investigation and revocation of the LIHTC award made during depositions and follow-up emails in response to plaintiffs' exercise of FHA rights. The court held that the City's proffered legitimate nonretaliatory reasons were pretextual and that genuine issues of material fact remain for trial, except that plaintiffs are entitled to summary judgment that they have suffered no economic or special damages to date.

source_file: 9659108_2023_AMERICAN SOUTHERN HOMES HOLDINGS LLC v. ERICKSON_gamd
9659627_2024_MILLER v. GEORGIA DEPARTMENT OF COMMUNITY SUPERVISION_gamd
case_name: Tracy A. Miller v. Georgia Department of Community Supervision, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff challenges his assignment to Bostick Nursing Center as discriminatory, arguing the Board made housing unavailable by not placing him in his preferred location.
key_holding: The Board did not discriminate against plaintiff under the FHA because it considered his disability and assigned him to Bostick specifically to accommodate his needs as an elderly, disabled parolee; the Board could not have placed him elsewhere because his parole application lacked that information.
brief_summary: Tracy A. Miller, a paraplegic parolee, sued the Georgia Board of Pardons and Paroles and Bostick Nursing Center officials under § 1983, the ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and FHA, alleging disability discrimination in his placement at a nursing facility for parolees. The court found that because the Board assigned plaintiff to Bostick specifically to accommodate his disability-related needs rather than to exclude him from housing, and because his preferred housing information was not included in his parole application, plaintiff failed to state a viable disability discrimination or FHA claim.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Thompson v. Davis
Sailboat Bend Sober Living, LLC v. City of Fort Lauderdale
Kirby v. Siegelman

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Placement in alternative housing facility (Bostick Nursing Center) rather than plaintiff's preferred location
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege that the Board treated him less favorably than similarly situated non-disabled parolees. The Board's individualized consideration of plaintiff's disabilities in determining appropriate placement constitutes reasonable accommodation, not intentional discrimination under the ADA, Rehabilitation Act, or FHA disparate treatment theory.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request for placement in alternative housing location of plaintiff's choosing rather than Bostick Nursing Center
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts sufficient to state a reasonable accommodation claim under FHA § 3604(f)(1). Plaintiff is not a 'buyer' or 'renter' within the meaning of the statute, and the Board did not 'make unavailable' any dwelling; rather, it accommodated plaintiff's disability by releasing him to a facility designed for elderly and disabled parolees.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II, Rehabilitation Act § 504, § 1983 due process claims related to parole placement and conditions
fha_claims.disposition: § 1915(e) screening dismissal (with exception for due process and ex post facto claims against Chairman)
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA Title II and Rehabilitation Act § 504 claims fail because plaintiff did not allege disparate treatment compared to similarly situated non-disabled individuals, and individualized consideration of disability in parole placement decisions is permissible. Due process claims regarding placement location fail because parolees have no constitutional right to housing of their choice and the Board's decision was not flagrant or unauthorized. Claims against Bostick defendants are improperly joined and dismissed without prejudice.

case_name: Jean Paraison v. Nationstar Mortgage, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges race-based discrimination in a real estate transaction, claiming defendant attempted to discourage him from completing the purchase because he is African American with an accent
key_holding: The court dismissed Paraison's Fair Housing Act discrimination claim because his allegations were conclusory and speculative, failing to meet the Twombly/Iqbal pleading standard; the complaint did not allege sufficient facts to support a reasonable inference that Nationstar discriminated against him based on race.
brief_summary: Jean Paraison, an African American man, sued Nationstar Mortgage LLC alleging race-based discrimination under the Fair Housing Act after he claims the defendant's agent tried to discourage him from completing a real estate purchase by telling him to 'back out of the deal' and that he would lose money. The court granted Nationstar's motion to dismiss, finding Paraison's discrimination allegations were conclusory and failed to plausibly allege that race played a role in the defendant's conduct, as required by the pleading standards established in Twombly and Iqbal.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Hallmark Devs., Inc. v. Fulton Cnty., 466 F.3d 1276 (11th Cir. 2006)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's allegations of discrimination based on race and accent constitute naked assertions devoid of factual enhancement and fail to meet the Twombly pleading standard. The complaint does not allege facts supporting unequal treatment on the basis of race or establishing that race played a role in the challenged decision.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of contract (failure to provide title report, deliver marketable title, close transaction); specific performance under FHA
fha_claims.reasoning: The Purchase Agreement unambiguously does not obligate Nationstar to provide the title report or remove title exceptions, and expressly grants Nationstar sole discretion to terminate if unable to convey marketable title. Plaintiff failed to state a plausible breach of contract claim and waived the specific performance argument by failing to respond to defendant's contractual bar.

source_file: 9660196_2022_Fulton County, Georgia v. Wells Fargo _ Co._gand
case_name: Fulton County, Georgia v. Wells Fargo & Co.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation request - case involves claims of discriminatory predatory lending and equity stripping targeting minority borrowers
key_holding: The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss on statute of limitations grounds but permitted plaintiffs to amend, while finding that plaintiffs adequately pled proximate cause for property tax injuries and statistical disparities to survive disparate impact claims.
brief_summary: Three Georgia counties (Fulton, DeKalb, and Cobb) sued Wells Fargo alleging a predatory lending scheme that targeted minority borrowers through discriminatory mortgage origination, servicing, and foreclosure practices in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss on statute of limitations grounds but allowed plaintiffs to file an amended complaint, while denying dismissal of plaintiffs' disparate impact claims after finding adequate statistical allegations and proximate cause for certain property-related injuries.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Inclusive Communities Project v. Lincoln Prop. Co.
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman
City of Miami v. Bank of Am. Corp.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found Plaintiffs plausibly alleged disparate impact claims under FHA § 3604(a)-(b) and § 3605 based on mortgage lending, origination, and servicing practices. Plaintiffs identified specific policies (discretionary steering, compensation schemes, underwriting standards), statistical disparities (4-6x higher foreclosure rates in minority neighborhoods), and robust causal connection. Claims survive motion to dismiss but require amended complaint to address statute of limitations issue.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found Plaintiffs plausibly alleged disparate impact claims based on mortgage servicing and foreclosure practices. Plaintiffs alleged specific policies affecting loan modifications, refinancing, and foreclosure procedures that had disparate impact on minority borrowers. Claims survive motion to dismiss but require amended complaint addressing statute of limitations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found Plaintiffs plausibly alleged intentional disparate treatment through equity-stripping scheme targeting minority borrowers. Allegations included steering minority applicants into higher-cost loans despite prime qualification, inflated appraisals, and discriminatory servicing. Claims survive motion to dismiss but require amended complaint addressing statute of limitations and specificity of post-April 2019 violations.

case_name: Charles Becoat II v. PNC Bank, National Association
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested; plaintiff sought to assume his deceased mother's existing PNC mortgage loan and obtain a loan modification, temporary payment plan, or forbearance from PNC Bank after inheriting the Chicago property subject to the mortgage.
key_holding: The court granted PNC Bank's motion to dismiss plaintiff's FHA and civil rights claims with prejudice because plaintiff failed to allege any facts connecting PNC's denial of mortgage assumption to his race, and failed to identify any legal duty obligating PNC to allow him to assume his deceased mother's mortgage or provide loss mitigation options.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Charles Becoat II sued PNC Bank after it refused to allow him to assume his deceased mother's mortgage loan or provide loan modification or forbearance options following her death. Becoat alleged, among other things, that PNC violated the Fair Housing Act by engaging in practices targeting African Americans, but he offered no facts connecting PNC's denial to his race or showing PNC was even aware of his race. The court dismissed the federal civil rights claims with prejudice for failure to state a claim and declined to exercise supplemental or diversity jurisdiction over the remaining state-law claims.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Erickson v. Pardus, 551 U.S. 89 (2007)
Am. Dental Ass’n v. Cigna Corp., 605 F.3d 1283 (11th Cir. 2010)
Williams v. Best Buy Co., 269 F.3d 1316 (11th Cir. 2001)
United Mine Workers v. Gibbs, 383 U.S. 715 (1966)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Loan assumption and modification; loss mitigation options
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege any facts suggesting PNC's refusal to allow loan assumption had anything to do with plaintiff's race, and failed to allege PNC was even aware of plaintiff's race. Complaint lacks plausible factual allegations of intentional discrimination based on protected class.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of contract, wrongful foreclosure, unfair business practices, intentional infliction of emotional distress, breach of fiduciary duty, negligence, fraud, Illinois Consumer Fraud and Deceptive Practices Act, Regulation Z violations, illegal dual tracking
fha_claims.reasoning: Court lacked federal question jurisdiction because plaintiff failed to state a valid federal claim. Diversity jurisdiction was not established (citizenship not properly alleged). Court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over state-law claims under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3). State-law claims also fail on the merits under applicable substantive law (no valid contract between plaintiff and defendant, no foreclosure sale occurred, no extreme and outrageous conduct, no duty owed, insufficient particularity in fraud allegations).

case_name: Price v. Howard
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges landlord required her Black partner to undergo a background check and pay a $50 fee as a condition of leasing, based on discriminatory racial animus.
key_holding: Plaintiff failed to state a plausible claim for disparate treatment under the FHA because she did not allege any facts suggesting she was actually treated differently than similarly situated White prospective applicants, and her conclusory 'information and belief' allegations about Howard's treatment of White tenants lacked factual support.
brief_summary: Katie Price, a Black woman, sued her landlord Michael Howard alleging race discrimination under the Fair Housing Act and 42 U.S.C. § 1981, claiming Howard required her Black partner to undergo a racially-motivated background check and pay a fee as a condition of leasing. The court granted Howard's motion to dismiss, finding Price's complaint consisted entirely of conclusory allegations that failed to plausibly allege disparate treatment because she did not plead any facts showing she was treated differently than similarly situated White prospective tenants.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Jackson v. Okaloosa Cnty. Fla., 21 F.3d 1531 (11th Cir. 1994)
Bonasera v. City of Norcross, 342 F. App'x 581 (11th Cir. 2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege disparate treatment under the FHA because although she alleged pretext for the background check requirement, she did not allege sufficient facts showing that similarly situated White prospective tenants were treated differently. The conclusory 'information and belief' allegation that Howard did not require White tenants to undergo background checks lacked any factual support.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1981 race discrimination claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to state a prima facie case under Section 1981 for the same reasons she failed under the FHA: she did not allege sufficient facts showing that the defendant intended to discriminate or that she was treated differently than similarly situated non-minority applicants.

case_name: Katia Price v. Michael Howard
accommodation_description: No accommodation request — the case involves a landlord's requirement that the Black plaintiff's partner submit to a background check and pay a fee, allegedly not imposed on similarly situated White tenants.
key_holding: The court denied the defendant's motion to dismiss, finding that the plaintiff adequately alleged disparate treatment by pleading sufficient facts showing she was treated differently than a similarly situated White tenant regarding the landlord's visitor background check requirement.
brief_summary: Katia Price, a Black woman, sued landlord Michael Howard alleging race discrimination under the Fair Housing Act and 42 U.S.C. § 1981 after Howard required her partner to undergo a background check and pay a fee to lease his property. The court denied Howard's motion to dismiss, finding Price adequately alleged disparate treatment by providing sufficient facts supporting her belief that similarly situated White tenants were not subjected to the same background check requirements.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Jackson v. Okaloosa Cnty., 21 F.3d 1531 (11th Cir. 1994)
Lewis v. City of Union City, 918 F.3d 1213 (11th Cir. 2019)
Bonasera v. City of Norcross, 342 F. App'x 581 (11th Cir. 2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff adequately pleaded a prima facie disparate treatment claim under the FHA by alleging she was required to submit her partner to a background check and pay a fee while similarly situated White tenants were not subject to the same requirement, supported by investigation into comparators and the landlord's racially motivated statements.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1981 race discrimination claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff adequately pleaded a prima facie claim under Section 1981 by alleging she is a member of a racial minority, the defendant intended to discriminate on that basis, and the discrimination concerned the activity of making and enforcing a residential lease contract.

case_name: Lau v. Honolulu Park Place, AOAO
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested permission to park their wheelchair-accessible modified minivan in ground-level guest parking spaces (which have no ramps) rather than their assigned third-level parking spaces (which require using steep ramps that damage the vehicle and prevent Garrick's access).
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that plaintiffs adequately pleaded Article III standing and a valid FHA reasonable accommodation claim under § 3604(f)(3)(B), rejecting arguments that the accommodation was unreasonable, that the injury was to property rather than person, and that the AOAO lacked authority to grant the requested parking accommodation.
brief_summary: Garrick Lau (a quadriplegic), along with his parents Wilson and Mabel Lau, sued Honolulu Park Place AOAO and its board members alleging the HOA violated the FHA by refusing to allow them to park their wheelchair-accessible minivan in ground-level guest parking spaces, which are the only spaces that accommodate their modified vehicle without ramp damage. The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss, finding plaintiffs adequately pleaded standing and a facially plausible FHA reasonable accommodation claim under § 3604(f)(3)(B).
key_cases_cited: U.S. v. California Mobile Home Park Management Co., 107 F.3d 1374 (9th Cir. 1997)
Janush v. Charities Hous. Dev. Corp., 169 F. Supp. 2d 1133 (N.D. Cal. 2000)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Trafficante v. Metropolitan Life Ins. Co., 409 U.S. 205 (1972)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to park a wheelchair-accessible modified minivan in guest parking spaces on the ground level of the condominium parking structure on an as-available basis, as previously permitted prior to 2017. The minivan cannot use the ramps in the assigned resident parking spaces on the third floor due to the steep angle damaging the vehicle's lowered floor.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiffs adequately pleaded all four elements of a prima facie reasonable accommodation claim under the Iqbal/Twombly standard: (1) Garrick suffers from a handicap (quadriplegia); (2) defendants knew of the handicap; (3) accommodation may be necessary to afford equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling; and (4) defendants refused the accommodation. The court held that whether the accommodation is 'reasonable' is a fact-intensive, case-specific determination inappropriate for resolution on a motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: No non-FHA claims are alleged or addressed in this opinion.
fha_claims.reasoning: The opinion addresses only FHA claims. No non-FHA statutory claims (ADA, § 1983, § 504, state law) are alleged or discussed.

case_name: Garrick Lau, et al. v. Honolulu Park Place, et al.
accommodation_description: Request to park a wheelchair-accessible modified van in condominium guest parking (ground level) rather than assigned third-level parking space, where driving up ramps caused the van's undercarriage to strike the ground.
key_holding: The court held that the injunctive relief claim was moot because the HOA formally granted the parking accommodation during litigation, but the emotional distress damages claim survived summary judgment because plaintiffs' testimony was sufficient under Ninth Circuit law to support a jury award for emotional distress damages.
brief_summary: The Laus, whose adult son Garrick is a quadriplegic, sued their condominium association under the FHAA after it denied their request to park Garrick's wheelchair-accessible van in guest parking (ground level) rather than his assigned third-level parking space where the modified van's undercarriage scraped on ramps. The court granted summary judgment for defendants on the injunctive relief claim as moot (because defendants granted the accommodation during litigation), but denied summary judgment on the emotional distress damages claim, finding plaintiffs' testimony sufficient to support a jury award.
key_cases_cited: Giebeler v. M & B Assocs., 343 F.3d 1143 (9th Cir. 2003)
Budnick v. Town of Carefree, 518 F.3d 1109 (9th Cir. 2008)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Garcia v. Brockway, 526 F.3d 456 (9th Cir. 2008)
Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242 (1986)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Non-exclusive use of a single guest parking stall for Garrick Lau to park his modified wheelchair-accessible vehicle in the dedicated guest parking at Honolulu Park Place, subject to availability.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that Defendants met their burden on summary judgment regarding prospective injunctive relief (moot because the accommodation was granted in July 2019 and the court found it was a permanent change), but denied summary judgment on the emotional distress damages claim because the Laus' testimony alone was sufficient under Ninth Circuit law to support a jury award, making credibility determinations a jury function rather than a judicial one at the summary judgment stage.

case_name: Jason Scutt v. Maui Family Life Center, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff claims Defendant denied her rental assistance application based on her race and sexual orientation, allegedly telling her the Christian funder would not provide benefits to someone like her.
key_holding: The court dismissed Plaintiff's FHA claim because she provided only vague, conclusory allegations that failed to establish the defendant denied her rental assistance application because of her race or sexual orientation, as opposed to other eligibility grounds.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Jason Scutt sued Maui Family Life Center, alleging the organization denied her COVID-19 rental assistance application because of her race and LGBTQIA+ status, violating the Fair Housing Act and Title VI. The court dismissed the First Amended Complaint for failure to state a claim, finding the allegations were too vague and conclusory to plausibly show discriminatory motive.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Harris v. Itzhaki, 183 F.3d 1043 (9th Cir. 1999)
Fobbs v. Holy Cross Health Sys. Corp., 29 F.3d 1439 (9th Cir. 1994)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of rental assistance benefits
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged vague and conclusory facts that defendant denied her application based on race and sexual orientation, but failed to allege sufficient factual matter showing defendant denied the application because of her race or sexual orientation as opposed to other grounds for ineligibility. The complaint does not plausibly allege disparate treatment under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VI racial discrimination claim; HIPAA privacy claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Title VI claim dismissed because plaintiff's allegations of sexual orientation discrimination cannot support a Title VI claim (which covers only race, color, and national origin), and the single allegation of a racial slur was not linked to the denial of benefits. HIPAA claim dismissed with prejudice because HIPAA does not provide a private cause of action.

case_name: Jason Scutt v. Kelli Dorris, Xiayin (Gaoquiang) Lin, and Charlene Chen
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged eviction and harassment because of transgender/LGBT status and religion, rather than requesting a specific reasonable accommodation.
key_holding: The court dismissed the First Amended Complaint because Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts plausibly demonstrating discriminatory intent by landlords based on religion or transgender/LGBT status, and failed to establish agency relationship with co-tenant Dorris.
brief_summary: Jason Scutt, a pro se plaintiff, sued landlords Xiayin Lin and Charlene Chen, and co-tenant Kelli Dorris alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on religion and transgender/LGBT status, claiming they harassed and attempted to evict her because of these protected characteristics. The court dismissed the First Amended Complaint with leave to amend, finding Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts showing discriminatory intent or establishing agency relationship between the landlords and Dorris.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)
Bostock v. Clayton Cnty., 140 S. Ct. 1731 (2020)
Harris v. Itzhaki, 183 F.3d 1043 (9th Cir. 1999)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The FAC fails to allege facts plausibly demonstrating that Lin and Chen issued the Notice to Vacate or engaged in any action 'because of' Plaintiff's religion or transgender/LGBT status. The complaint contains only conclusory allegations without facts showing discriminatory intent or motive, which is a necessary element of a disparate treatment claim under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The FAC fails to allege sufficient facts to establish an agency relationship between Dorris and Lin/Chen under federal law and HUD regulations. The complaint does not allege that Dorris had the power to alter legal relations, was a fiduciary, or that Lin/Chen had the right to control Dorris's conduct with respect to matters related to rental of dwellings.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Dorris, as a co-tenant who does not own the apartment building, is not subject to liability under the FHA. Although agents or employees of property owners may be liable for their own unlawful conduct, the FAC fails to allege sufficient facts showing that Dorris was an agent of Lin and Chen under federal law.

case_name: Jason Scutt v. Kelli Dorris, Xiayin (Gaoquiang) Lin, and Charlene Chen
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; case involves claims of harassment based on transgender status and Jewish religion, and landlords' failure to prevent hostile housing environment.
key_holding: Dorris's claim dismissed because she is merely a co-tenant without agency authority over landlords; but claims against Lin and Chen may proceed for hostile housing environment under § 3617 because plaintiff adequately alleged Dorris harassed her based on sex/religion, harassment was severe or pervasive, and landlords knew of but failed to remedy the harassment.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Jason Scutt sued his former landlords and co-tenant alleging they discriminated against him based on his transgender status and Jewish religion, and that landlords failed to prevent a hostile housing environment created by co-tenant Dorris. The court dismissed the claim against Dorris because she was merely a co-tenant without agency authority over the landlords, but allowed the hostile housing environment claims against the landlords to proceed because plaintiff adequately pled Dorris harassed him because of protected characteristics, the harassment was severe or pervasive, and landlords knew of but failed to remedy it.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Hicks v. Makaha Valley Plantation Homeowners Ass'n, 2015 WL 4041531 (D. Haw. 2015)
Francis v. Kings Park Manor, Inc., 944 F.3d 370 (2d Cir. 2019)
Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts plausibly demonstrating an agency relationship between Dorris (a co-tenant) and the Landlords. Conclusory allegations that Dorris held power to alter legal relations, was a fiduciary, and had authority to impose consequences were insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly. Tenants who do not own the subject property are not liable under the FHA absent an agency relationship supported by factual allegations, not speculation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Hostile housing environment created by co-tenant harassment based on transgender status and Jewish religion; landlords' failure to take remedial action
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff plausibly alleged a hostile housing environment claim under § 3617 against Chen and Lin by showing: (1) unwelcome harassment based on transgender status and religion (timing of harassment after discovery of female clothing, use of religious slur 'kike'); (2) severity/pervasiveness sufficient to deprive enjoyment of home (regular frivolous complaints, physical obstruction preventing exit during COVID-19, blocking access to common facilities); and (3) landlords' knowledge and failure to take remedial action (ignored written complaints, served notice to vacate rather than addressing harassment). The claim survives screening and proceeds to the next stage.

case_name: Jason Scutt v. Family Life Center, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges denial of emergency housing rental funds based on race and sexual orientation discrimination, not a reasonable accommodation request
key_holding: The court found that Plaintiff sufficiently stated a claim for disparate treatment under the Fair Housing Act based on allegations that emergency housing funds were denied due to race and sexual orientation, while dismissing Plaintiff's Title VI claim to the extent it alleged sexual orientation discrimination (as Title VI only covers race, color, or national origin)
brief_summary: Pro se Plaintiff Jason Scutt sued Family Life Center, Inc. alleging the organization denied her emergency housing rental funds based on race and sexual orientation discrimination in violation of the Fair Housing Act and Title VI. The court denied Defendant's motion to dismiss the FHA claim, finding Plaintiff sufficiently alleged disparate treatment; the court dismissed Plaintiff's Title VI claim only to the extent it was based on sexual orientation, as Title VI does not cover that protected class.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Harris v. Itzhaki, 183 F.3d 1043 (9th Cir. 1999)
Holley v. Crank, 258 F.3d 1127 (9th Cir. 2001)
Fobbs v. Holy Cross Health Sys. Corp., 29 F.3d 1439 (9th Cir. 1994)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff plausibly alleged disparate treatment based on race by asserting that Defendant denied emergency housing rental funds based on her race, using racial slurs and discriminatory remarks during the application process. The court accepted her factual allegations as true and found she stated a prima facie case under FHA § 3604(b), allowing the claim to survive the motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VI racial discrimination claim; sexual orientation discrimination claim under Title VI
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the sexual orientation discrimination component of the Title VI claim with prejudice because Title VI prohibits only race, color, and national origin discrimination, not sex or sexual orientation discrimination. The racial discrimination component of the Title VI claim survived the motion to dismiss under the same plausibility standard applied to the FHA claim.

case_name: Jason Scutt v. Martin Norton, Carrie Johnson aka Norton
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges landlord harassment and use of slurs targeting her religion and gender during tenancy in an illegal structure.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claim because plaintiff's conclusory allegations failed to demonstrate that defendants caused the purported harm because of her gender or religion, and many incidents appeared to be general landlord-tenant disputes unrelated to protected grounds.
brief_summary: Jason Scutt sued landlords Martin and Carrie Norton alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on harassment and use of slurs targeting her religion and gender while she rented an illegal structure on their property. The court dismissed the complaint with leave to amend, finding the allegations were conclusory and failed to adequately demonstrate the alleged harm was caused by protected characteristics rather than general landlord-tenant disputes.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Harris v. Itzhaki

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for failure to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly standard. Plaintiff's conclusory allegations insufficiently demonstrated that defendants caused harm because of her gender or religion, and many incidents appeared to be general landlord-tenant disputes unrelated to protected grounds. Additionally, the court noted potential applicability of the single-family home exemption under 42 U.S.C. § 3603(b)(1), which would preclude FHA coverage entirely.

case_name: Jason Scutt v. Martin Norton
race_if_mentioned: Various slurs mentioned (Mexican, Hawaiian, Jewish, Black) but plaintiff did not identify as these groups; plaintiff's own race undetermined
accommodation_description: No accommodation request was made; plaintiff alleged disparate treatment harassment based on religion, sex, and LGBTQ status
key_holding: The court granted judgment for defendants because plaintiff's allegations were conclusory, internally contradictory, and unsupported by the documentary evidence, failing to establish plausible facts showing discriminatory intent as required for an FHA disparate treatment claim.
brief_summary: Jason Scutt, a pro se plaintiff, sued her former landlords Martin Norton and Carrie Johnson alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on religion, sex, and LGBTQ status discrimination during her tenancy. The court granted defendants' motion for judgment on the pleadings, finding plaintiff's allegations conclusory, internally contradictory, and implausible given her history of filing similar complaints and failure to provide evidence supporting discriminatory intent.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Harris v. Itzhaki, 183 F.3d 1043 (9th Cir. 1999)
Dahlia v. Rodriguez, 735 F.3d 1060 (9th Cir. 2013)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that Defendants discriminated against her based on religion, sex, or LGBTQ status in the terms, conditions, or privileges of the rental. The complaint contained contradictory allegations unsupported by attached exhibits, conclusory statements without factual support for discriminatory intent, and unwarranted inferences. The court found that Plaintiff's allegations were implausible given the pattern of identical slurs across multiple unrelated cases and the lack of nexus between alleged conduct and protected class status.

source_file: 9665527_2023_United States v. Albert C. Kobayashi, Inc._hid
case_name: United States of America v. Albert C. Kobayashi, Inc.
property_city: Maui and Oahu (multiple locations including Napili, Napilihau, Wailea, Kahului on Maui and Palehua on Oahu)
accommodation_description: Systemic design and construction accessibility requirements for covered multifamily dwellings (accessible routes, public use and common use areas) rather than individual tenant accommodation requests
key_holding: The court denied the defendants' motions for partial summary judgment, finding genuine disputes of material fact exist as to whether the designer, contractor, and developer defendants participated in the design and construction of multifamily housing with common and public use areas that are readily accessible to persons with disabilities.
brief_summary: The United States sued design and construction defendants alleging they violated the Fair Housing Act by failing to design and construct multifamily dwellings (Napili, Napilihau, Palehua, and Wailea) in Hawaii with public and common use areas that are readily accessible to persons with disabilities. The court denied the defendants' motions for partial summary judgment, finding genuine issues of material fact exist regarding the extent of each defendant's participation in the design and construction process that would render them liable under § 3604(f)(3)(C).
key_cases_cited: Mont. Fair Hous., Inc. v. Am. Capital Dev., Inc., 81 F. Supp. 2d 1057 (D. Mont. 1999)
Balt. Neighborhoods, Inc. v. Rommel Builders, Inc., 3 F. Supp. 2d 661 (D. Md. 1998)
Bank of Am. Corp. v. City of Miami, 581 U.S. 189 (2017)
Salisbury v. City of Santa Monica, 998 F.3d 852 (9th Cir. 2021)
Harris v. Cnty. of Orange, 17 F.4th 849 (9th Cir. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to design and construct covered multifamily dwellings with public use and common use areas that are readily accessible to and usable by persons with disabilities, including accessible routes into and through dwellings, at Napili project
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine issue of material fact regarding whether ACKI failed to design and construct common use and public use areas that are readily accessible, based on undisputed evidence that ACKI constructed sidewalks, stairs, and railings at Napili. Summary judgment denied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to design and construct accessible routes into and through dwellings at Napilihau project, including work up to five feet outside the building line
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine dispute of material fact regarding whether ACKI failed to design and construct accessible routes, based on ACKI's responsibilities for excavation, concrete laying, building construction, and work up to five feet outside building line, plus FHA project designation in meeting minutes. Summary judgment denied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to design and construct accessible routes at Palehua project, including sidewalks and walkways
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine issue of material fact regarding whether ACKI failed to design and construct accessible routes, based on evidence that ACKI designed and/or constructed sidewalks and walkways at Palehua. Summary judgment denied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to design and construct accessible routes and common use areas at Wailea project
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found ACKI's involvement in design and construction of Wailea was unclear, including as general contractor, conducting survey showing accessibility issues with roads and height differentials, and providing information to subcontractors about accessibility. Jury better equipped to resolve ACKI's involvement. Summary judgment denied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to design and construct covered multifamily dwellings with accessible site plans, floor plans, building plans, and exterior elevations at Napili project
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine dispute of material fact regarding DPI Defendants' liability under FHA based on their scope of work including site plan development, floor plans, building plans, exterior elevations, and construction administration with review of subcontractor submittals. Summary judgment denied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to design and construct covered multifamily dwellings with accessible site plans and architectural designs at Wailea project
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found DPI Defendants' participation in design and construction of Wailea was unclear at best, based on evidence of fee proposal for architectural services and site plans bearing DPI and Goshi names, despite DPI's denial of preparing 'AS BUILT' plans. Summary judgment denied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to design and construct accessible exterior components at Napilihau project, including railings, stairs, trash enclosures, barbeque areas, and ramps
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine issue of material fact regarding Cooper's involvement in designing and/or constructing Napilihau, based on evidence of site plans with Cooper's seal and signature depicting railings, stairs, trash enclosures, barbeque areas, and ramps for handicapped parking, despite Cooper's claim that exterior information was only schematic. Summary judgment denied.

case_name: Nathan Earl Aiwohi, et al. v. Bank of America, N.A., et al.
accommodation_description: Loan modification requests by mortgagors alleging denial based on race and national origin; underlying claim involves discriminatory lending and servicing practices targeting racial minorities.
key_holding: The court dismissed Plaintiffs' FHA claims because they failed to plead discriminatory intent for disparate treatment and failed to provide statistical evidence showing significantly disproportionate impact on protected classes for disparate impact.
brief_summary: Eight individual mortgagors sued Bank of America and Bank of New York Mellon under RICO and the Fair Housing Act, alleging Defendants engaged in predatory lending targeting racial minorities, falsified loan documents for fraudulent foreclosures, and denied loan modifications based on race. The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss, finding the RICO claim failed because it was based on litigation activity that cannot serve as RICO predicate acts, and the FHA claims failed because Plaintiffs alleged no discriminatory intent and provided no statistical evidence of disparate impact.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Harris v. Itzhaki, 183 F.3d 1043 (9th Cir. 1999)
Gamble v. City of Escondido, 104 F.3d 300 (9th Cir. 1997)
United Bhd. of Carpenters & Joiners v. Bldg. & Constr. Trades Dep't, AFL-CIO, 770 F.3d 834 (9th Cir. 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged they were discriminated against based on race, ethnicity, or national origin in the terms and conditions of mortgage loans and loan servicing, and were denied loan modifications based on race.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to allege discriminatory intent or motive, which is a requisite element of disparate treatment under the FHA. The complaint merely alleged 'discriminatory loan servicing practices' without explaining what those practices were or that discriminatory intent motivated the defendants' conduct.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged that defendants engaged in a pattern and practice of servicing and prosecuting predatory and discriminatory mortgage loans that disproportionately affected minority borrowers.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to establish a prima facie disparate impact case because they alleged that both minority and non-minority borrowers were affected by defendants' practices, thus failing to show a significantly disproportionate impact on protected class members. Plaintiffs provided no statistics or other proof of discriminatory impact.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: RICO claim under 18 U.S.C. §§ 1962, 1964 alleging a conspiracy to forge note endorsements, falsify MERS mortgage assignments, and use fraudulent documents in foreclosure proceedings.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to state a RICO claim because the alleged predicate acts turned on litigation activity alone, which is insufficient to state a RICO claim as a matter of law. Plaintiffs also failed to adequately plead the enterprise and failed to identify the role of each defendant in the alleged fraudulent scheme as required by Rule 9(b).

case_name: Lazarus v. Ouansafi
accommodation_description: A reasonable accommodation claim is noted as remaining against other defendants but was not analyzed in this order granting Ouansafi summary judgment.
key_holding: Plaintiff failed to establish that defendant Ouansafi knew or should have known about the alleged harassment by other tenants or that he personally participated in or ratified the alleged retaliation, and mere supervisory authority is insufficient for individual liability under the FHA.
brief_summary: Tangee Renee Lazarus, a Black woman residing in public housing administered by the Hawaii Public Housing Authority, sued Executive Director Hakim Ouansafi and other HPHA employees alleging Fair Housing Act claims for hostile housing environment based on race and retaliation. The court granted Ouansafi's motion for summary judgment, finding plaintiff failed to provide evidence that Ouansafi knew of or personally participated in the alleged harassment or retaliation, and that mere supervisory authority is insufficient for individual FHA liability.
key_cases_cited: Fielder v. Sterling Park Homeowners Ass'n, 914 F. Supp. 2d 1222 (W.D. Wash. 2012)
Hicks v. Makaha Valley Plantation Homeowners Ass'n, No. CIV. 14-00254 HG-BMK, 2015 WL 4041531 (D. Haw. 2015)
San Pedro Hotel Co. v. City of Los Angeles, 159 F.3d 470 (9th Cir. 1998)
Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)
Hansen v. United States, 7 F.3d 137 (9th Cir. 1993)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish that Defendant Ouansafi knew or should have known about the alleged harassment by other tenants. Defendant's declaration that he never received the letter and oversees 45,000 tenants without day-to-day involvement, combined with Plaintiff's failure to provide corroborating evidence of prior emails, defeated the hostile housing environment claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to provide evidence that Defendant Ouansafi was personally aware of or involved in the transfer offer alleged as retaliatory conduct. Plaintiff's uncorroborated assertion in her declaration that HPHA policy made the Executive Director responsible for all transfers, without supporting documentation, was insufficient to defeat summary judgment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation claim (specific accommodation not detailed in opinion; claim survives as to Defendants Fo and Ah Sam)
fha_claims.reasoning: Summary judgment was granted as to Defendant Ouansafi on the reasonable accommodation claim because Plaintiff failed to establish his personal involvement or knowledge of the alleged conduct. The claim survives as to Defendants Fo and Ah Sam and remains for trial.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Violation of the Hawaiʻi Fair Housing Act (Count VIII) — specific basis unclear from opinion
fha_claims.reasoning: The Officers moved for judgment on the pleadings on Count VIII (Hawaiʻi Fair Housing Act), contending they lack liability under that statute. The court held the motion in abeyance pending determination of whether a cognizable federal claim exists to support subject matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1331, as all other federal claims were dismissed and only the Monell failure to train claim (if successfully amended) would provide federal question jurisdiction.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 due process, equal protection, and First Amendment; state law tort claims (wrongful eviction, wrongful entry, breach of quiet enjoyment, invasion of privacy, unfair/deceptive trade practices, assault, defamation, civil conspiracy, negligent hiring/training/supervision, negligence, intentional and negligent infliction of emotional distress); Monell failure to train and ratification
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed all federal § 1983 claims against the Officers based on qualified immunity (unopposed by plaintiff, constituting concession). State law tort claims against the Officers and City were dismissed under the qualified/conditional privilege available to government officials acting in performance of their duties, which plaintiff failed to oppose. Monell ratification claim was conceded by plaintiff's failure to address it. Monell failure to train claim was dismissed for failure to plead specific factual allegations showing inadequate training, deliberate indifference, and causation under Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards.

case_name: Tangee Renee Lazarus v. Stephanie Fo and Ioane Ah Sam
accommodation_description: Cannot determine from this post-trial costs order; the underlying accommodation request is not described in this document.
key_holding: The Court exercised its discretion to deny Defendants' motion for costs because Plaintiff is indigent, living in public housing, unemployed, and awarding costs would chill future civil rights litigation.
brief_summary: Tangee Renee Lazarus, a disabled tenant in State of Hawaii public housing, sued employees of the State of Hawaii Public Housing Authority alleging racial discrimination, retaliation, and failure to accommodate under the Fair Housing Act; after a four-day trial, the jury returned a verdict for Defendants. This order denies Defendants' post-trial Motion for Bill of Costs, finding that awarding costs would be inappropriate because Plaintiff is indigent and doing so would chill future civil rights litigation.
key_cases_cited: Ass'n of Mexican–Am. Educators v. State of California, 231 F.3d 572 (9th Cir. 2000)
Escriba v. Foster Poultry Farms, Inc., 743 F.3d 1236 (9th Cir. 2014)
Champion Produce, Inc. v. Ruby Robinson Co., 342 F.3d 1016 (9th Cir. 2003)
Stanley v. Univ. of S. Cal., 178 F.3d 1069 (9th Cir. 1999)
Draper v. Rosario, 836 F.3d 1072 (9th Cir. 2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Jury returned verdict in favor of Defendants following four-day trial on racial discrimination claim under the Fair Housing Act.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Jury returned verdict in favor of Defendants following four-day trial on retaliation claim under the Fair Housing Act.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to accommodate plaintiff's disability in public housing
fha_claims.reasoning: Jury returned verdict in favor of Defendants following four-day trial on failure to accommodate claim under the Fair Housing Act.

case_name: Ali London v. Michael Heh, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff's FAC includes Count VIII alleging violation of the Hawai'i Fair Housing Act, but the specific accommodation request is not clearly articulated and the court did not substantively analyze this claim.
key_holding: The court dismissed London's Monell failure-to-train claim because he failed to adequately allege an inadequate training program, deliberate indifference by the City, or actual causation between the alleged training deficiency and constitutional violations.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Ali London sued the City and County of Honolulu, Honolulu Police Department officers, and his former landlords and rental agents alleging constitutional violations, including a Monell failure-to-train claim, and a claim under the Hawai'i Fair Housing Act arising from an allegedly improper eviction during the COVID-19 pandemic. The court granted the City's motion to dismiss the Monell claim with prejudice, finding London failed to adequately plead inadequate training, deliberate indifference, or causation, declined supplemental jurisdiction over remaining state claims, and denied other motions as moot.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Monell v. Dep't of Soc. Servs. of City of New York, 436 U.S. 658 (1978)
City of Canton v. Harris, 489 U.S. 378 (1989)
Connick v. Thompson, 563 U.S. 51 (2011)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Violation of Hawaiʻi Fair Housing Act (Count VIII); also includes § 1983 constitutional claims (First Amendment petition rights, Fourteenth Amendment equal protection, procedural due process, substantive due process, Monell failure to train, Monell ratification), state law claims (wrongful eviction, wrongful entry, breach of quiet enjoyment, invasion of privacy, unfair and deceptive trade practices, assault, defamation, civil conspiracy, negligent hiring/training/supervision, negligence, intentional infliction of emotional distress, negligent infliction of emotional distress)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the Hawaiʻi Fair Housing Act claim (Count VIII) as moot after dismissing all federal question jurisdiction claims. The § 1983 Monell failure to train claim failed under Iqbal/Twombly because plaintiff failed to identify an inadequate training program, show deliberate indifference, or establish actual causation—offering only conclusory allegations that implicit bias training was lacking without plausibly connecting the deficiency to the alleged constitutional violation. All other state law claims were dismissed without prejudice for lack of supplemental jurisdiction after federal claims were eliminated.

case_name: Robert LaRosa, Iva LaRosa, and Intermountain Fair Housing Council, Inc. v. River Quarry Apartments, LLC
accommodation_description: Mr. LaRosa requested a reasonable accommodation to keep his companion dog Sid without paying the pet fee as an emotional support animal for his PTSD.
key_holding: The court dismissed the reasonable accommodation denial claim because Sid was allowed to remain with the LaRosas throughout the entire tenancy even though formal approval was delayed until October 13, 2017; however, the court allowed the interference claim under § 3617 to proceed based on allegations that defendants misrepresented the outcome of Dr. Wilper's verification.
brief_summary: Robert and Iva LaRosa and Intermountain Fair Housing Council sued River Quarry Apartments and related defendants for allegedly wrongfully denying a reasonable accommodation request for an emotional support animal to assist with Mr. LaRosa's PTSD. The court dismissed the reasonable accommodation denial claim, finding no violation because the dog was allowed to remain throughout the review process even though formal approval was delayed 45 days; however, the court allowed plaintiffs' interference claim under § 3617 to proceed based on allegations that defendants misrepresented Dr. Wilper's statements during the verification process.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Dubois v. Ass'n of Apartment Owners of 2987 Kalakaua, 453 F.3d 1175 (9th Cir. 2006)
Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014)
Prindable v. Ass'n of Apt. Owners of 2987 Kalakaua, 304 F. Supp. 2d 1245 (D. Haw. 2003)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request to keep companion dog (Sid) without paying pet fees as a reasonable accommodation for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege that defendants refused the accommodation. The dog was allowed to reside in the apartment from September 19, 2017 through February 16, 2018, and the accommodation was formally granted on October 13, 2017. No fees were enforced, no removal notice was issued, and no other punitive action was taken. The court found no actual or constructive denial under Dubois and Overlook Mutual Homes precedent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged disparate treatment based on disability status, supported by fair housing tester evidence
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to clearly allege a disparate treatment theory under § 3604(f). The tester allegations were previously rejected and no new factual allegations were added to support the claim. The complaint's single FHA cause of action did not clearly delineate a disparate treatment theory separate from the failure-to-accommodate claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged interference with the LaRosas' exercise of FHA rights through misrepresentation of Dr. Wilper's October 2, 2017 conversation and attempts to dissuade the medical provider from verifying the accommodation need
fha_claims.reasoning: Under 42 U.S.C. § 3617 and the Ninth Circuit's broad interpretation of 'interference,' plaintiffs sufficiently alleged that defendants engaged in protected activity (requesting accommodation), were subjected to adverse action (misrepresentation of Dr. Wilper's statements and attempts to dissuade the medical provider), and established a causal link between the protected activity and adverse action. The claim survives the motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Negligence claim (derivative of FHA claim) and invasion of privacy claim under Idaho law
fha_claims.reasoning: The invasion of privacy claim was dismissed because the LaRosas consented to defendants' communications with Dr. Wilper through a signed release, and Mr. Cullimore's conversations related to the purpose for which consent was granted. The negligence claim is derivative of the FHA claim and may proceed only to the extent the underlying FHA claim proceeds.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discriminatory statements claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c) based on statements made by attorney Kirk Cullimore in speeches and lectures
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 3604(c) applies only to persons engaged in the sale or rental of a dwelling. Kirk Cullimore is an attorney, not a person engaged in the rental business, and therefore cannot be liable under § 3604(c) for statements made in speeches and lectures. Plaintiffs did not argue that the statements would support a § 3604(c) claim and provided minimal opposition to this claim.

case_name: Josephine Guion v. Bonner Homeless Transitions Board of Directors
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation was requested; plaintiff alleges race-based harassment and hostile housing environment discrimination rather than disability accommodation.
key_holding: Guion's Fair Housing Act race discrimination and retaliation claims are time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations and fail on the merits because no reasonable juror could conclude that any of Bonner Defendants' actions were discriminatory based on race.
brief_summary: Josephine Guion, an African American resident at a nonprofit transitional housing facility in Hope, Idaho, sued the facility operator and staff alleging race-based harassment, hostile housing environment, defamation, intentional infliction of emotional distress, retaliation under the FHA, and fraud. The court granted Bonner Defendants' motion for summary judgment on all claims, finding that the FHA claims were time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations and that, even viewing the evidence favorably to Guion, no reasonable juror could find that defendants' actions were discriminatory based on race.
key_cases_cited: Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986)
Walker v. City of Lakewood, 272 F.3d 1114 (9th Cir. 2001)
Levald, Inc. v. City of Palm Desert, 998 F.2d 680 (9th Cir. 1993)
Garcia v. Brockway, 526 F.3d 456 (9th Cir. 2008)
Orr v. Bank of Am., 285 F.3d 764 (9th Cir. 2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's FHA race discrimination claim is time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations in 42 U.S.C. § 3613(a)(1)(A). The latest alleged discriminatory act occurred on July 8, 2015, when plaintiff left the facility, but the complaint was not filed until May 22, 2018. The court also found that even on the merits, no reasonable juror could conclude that defendants' actions were discriminatory, as the evidence showed only one instance where a defendant mentioned plaintiff's race, and that instance was actually supportive rather than discriminatory.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's FHA retaliation claim under § 3617 is time-barred by the two-year statute of limitations. Additionally, on the merits, the evidence showed that defendants accommodated plaintiff throughout her stay and complied with the IHRC investigation, with no facts suggesting retaliation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Defamation, Intentional Infliction of Emotional Distress, Fraud (state law claims)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's defamation and intentional infliction of emotional distress claims are barred by Idaho's two-year statute of limitations (Idaho Code § 5-219(5) and § 5-219(4)), with the latest alleged acts occurring on July 8, 2015, and the complaint filed May 22, 2018. On the merits, the statements do not rise to the level of defamation or extreme and outrageous conduct. The fraud claim (three-year statute of limitations under Idaho Code § 5-218(4)) fails because plaintiff failed to show falsity of any representations made by defendants.

case_name: Hoffman v. Pedersen
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege defendants refused to make reasonable accommodations for Kelly Stone's disability, but the specific accommodation requested is not described in the opinion.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for defendants because plaintiffs' Fair Housing Act claim was barred by the two-year statute of limitations—no discriminatory conduct was alleged to have occurred after October 23, 2016, and plaintiffs failed to produce evidence that HUD review tolled the limitations period.
brief_summary: William Hoffman and Kelly Stone sued their former landlord Heather Pedersen and Bookpoint, LLC alleging Fair Housing Act violations, Idaho Consumer Protection Act violations, and negligence related to their eviction from a Sandpoint, Idaho apartment. The court granted summary judgment for defendants on all claims because the two-year statute of limitations had expired with no evidence of discriminatory conduct after October 23, 2016, and no evidence of HUD tolling.
key_cases_cited: Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242 (1986)
Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986)
Thomas v. Ponder, 611 F.3d 1144 (9th Cir. 2010)
Hernandez v. Spacelabs Med. Inc., 343 F.3d 1107 (9th Cir. 2003)
Devereaux v. Abbey, 263 F.3d 1070 (9th Cir. 2001)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable and necessary accommodations for Kelly Stone's handicap/disability
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that all alleged conduct occurred on or before October 23, 2016, and the complaint was filed October 24, 2018, exceeding the two-year statute of limitations under 42 U.S.C. § 3613(a)(1)(A). The court did not reach the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim because it was time-barred.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs alleged defendants coerced, intimidated, threatened, or interfered with their exercise of FHA rights in violation of 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f), but all alleged conduct occurred on or before October 23, 2016, placing the claim outside the two-year statute of limitations period.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Idaho Consumer Protection Act (I.C. § 48-603, § 48-603C, § 48-608), negligence
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA claims (ICPA violations and negligence) were time-barred under their respective two-year statutes of limitations, as no conduct was alleged to have occurred after October 23, 2016, and the complaint was filed October 24, 2018.

case_name: Josephine Guion v. Bonner Homeless Transitions Board of Directors
accommodation_description: The accommodation request at issue in the underlying case is not described in this procedural ruling on Rule 60(b) motions.
key_holding: The court denied Guion's motion to vacate summary judgment because she failed to establish fraud on the court by clear and convincing evidence, as her allegations consisted of legal challenges to the court's prior conclusions rather than actual evidence of fraud, and a mere misstatement of a date does not constitute fraud on the court.
brief_summary: Josephine Guion moved to vacate the court's prior summary judgment ruling dismissing her Fair Housing Act claims, alleging fraud on the court, and also moved to disqualify the presiding judge and for an indicative ruling under Rule 62.1. The court denied all three motions, finding that Guion failed to establish fraud on the court by clear and convincing evidence and that her allegations were merely legal challenges to the court's prior conclusions rather than evidence of an unconscionable scheme to improperly influence the court.
key_cases_cited: Estate of Stonehill v. United States, 660 F.3d 415 (9th Cir. 2011)
Alexander v. Robertson, 882 F.2d 421 (9th Cir. 1989)
Liteky v. United States, 510 U.S. 540 (1994)
Payton v. Davis, 906 F.3d 812 (9th Cir. 2018)
Chambers v. NASCO, Inc., 501 U.S. 32 (1991)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unspecified reasonable accommodation related to housing at Bonner Homeless Transitions facility
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the FHA claim on summary judgment primarily on statute of limitations grounds under 42 U.S.C. § 3613(a)(1)(A) (two-year limitations period), with the court noting that even setting aside statute of limitations issues, the claims would have been dismissed due to substantive deficiencies. The court did not reach the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim itself.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fraud claim against defendants
fha_claims.reasoning: The fraud claim was dismissed on substantive grounds (not statute of limitations). The court found no evidence of fraud on the court by clear and convincing evidence, as required under Rule 60(d)(3) and Ninth Circuit precedent.

case_name: Krahn v. Cranney
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: The court granted plaintiff's unopposed motion to amend the complaint to remove the FHA claim because defendants do not own more than three single-family homes (exempting them from FHA coverage under 42 U.S.C. § 3603), and remanded the remaining state law claims to Idaho state court for lack of federal subject matter jurisdiction.
brief_summary: Michael Krahn sued landlords John and Kathy Cranney alleging Fair Housing Act violations and Idaho Consumer Protection Act claims; plaintiff voluntarily amended his complaint to drop the FHA claim after discovering the Cranneys own fewer than three single-family homes, exempting them from FHA coverage. The federal court granted the motion to amend and remanded the case to Idaho state court for lack of subject matter jurisdiction.
key_cases_cited: Frigard v. United States, 862 F.2d 201 (9th Cir. 1988)
Carlsbad Tech., Inc. v. HIF Bio, Inc., 556 U.S. 635 (2009)
Carnegie-Mellon Univ. v. Cohill, 484 U.S. 343 (1988)
Osborn v. President, Dirs. & Co. of Bank, 22 U.S. (9 Wheat.) 738 (1824)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not specified; FHA claim removed from complaint before substantive analysis
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff discovered defendants do not own more than three single-family homes, failing to meet the FHA's exemption threshold under 42 U.S.C. § 3603. Plaintiff voluntarily removed the FHA claim via amended complaint with defendant consent, eliminating federal question jurisdiction.

case_name: James Alan Gerdon v. Reynold French
accommodation_description: This is not a housing accommodation case; plaintiff James Gerdon brings a civil rights action under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 against a probation officer for alleged criminal acts (breaking and entering, threats, taking property), requesting injunctive relief to stop alleged persecution for being an 'alternative lifestyle person'
