key_holding: The court granted defendant's motion to dismiss without prejudice because plaintiff's complaint failed to establish federal jurisdiction, did not state a cognizable Fair Housing Act claim (42 U.S.C. § 3631 was inapplicable as no housing discrimination was alleged), and failed to state a plausible § 1983 claim for violation of constitutional rights; plaintiff was given leave to amend within 30 days.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff James Gerdon sued probation officer Reynold French under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 and various criminal statutes, alleging the officer came to his home with guns, used threats and physical force, and took his property while persecuting him for being an 'alternative lifestyle person.' The court granted French's motion to dismiss without prejudice, finding Gerdon failed to establish federal jurisdiction, failed to state a viable FHA claim, and failed to allege a plausible constitutional violation under § 1983, though granting leave to amend.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Gonzaga Univ. v. Doe, 536 U.S. 273 (2002)
Will v. Michigan Dep't of State Police, 491 U.S. 58 (1989)
Ex parte Young, 209 U.S. 123 (1908)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged assault, breaking and entering, kidnapping, armed robbery, and hate crime based on sexual orientation; cited 18 U.S.C. §§ 241, 242, 245, 249; 42 U.S.C. § 3631; and state criminal law.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because criminal statutes cited do not provide private right of action, and plaintiff failed to allege facts establishing Fair Housing Act discrimination. Court also found no cognizable federal constitutional claim under § 1983 and improper service if suit was in official capacity.

source_file: 9668117_2023_Intermountain Fair Housing Council, Inc. v. Tomlinson _ Associates, Inc._idd
case_name: Intermountain Fair Housing Council, Inc. v. Tomlinson & Associates, Inc.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation request is discussed in this opinion, which addresses a motion to supplement the record on summary judgment.
key_holding: The court granted defendants' motion to supplement the record with additional documents related to the HUD complaint filing date and property ownership, denied plaintiff's sanctions request, and granted plaintiff leave to file supplemental briefing.
brief_summary: Intermountain Fair Housing Council sued Tomlinson & Associates and related entities alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on race, national origin, color, and familial status at two Boise apartment complexes. The court granted defendants' motion to supplement the record with additional documents related to the HUD complaint filing date and property ownership interests, denied plaintiff's sanctions request, and granted plaintiff leave to file supplemental briefing before ruling on the pending summary judgment motion.
key_cases_cited: Betz v. Trainer Wortham & Co., 610 F.3d 1169 (9th Cir. 2010)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claims involve discrimination based on race, national origin, color, and familial status.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court is addressing defendants' motion for summary judgment on the basis that the Council's claims are time-barred. The opinion does not reach the merits of the discrimination claims but rather addresses a procedural motion to supplement the record to establish the filing date of the administrative complaint, which is critical to the statute of limitations defense.

source_file: 9668168_2023_Intermountain Fair Housing Council, Inc. v. Tomlinson _ Associates, Inc._idd
case_name: Intermountain Fair Housing Council, Inc. v. Tomlinson & Associates, Inc.
accommodation_description: In Spring 2016, a family residing at the Greenfield Apartment complex complained to the Council that defendants would not grant a reasonable accommodation for a parking permit; this incident was ultimately found to be outside the statute of limitations.
key_holding: The court partially granted and partially denied defendants' motion for summary judgment, allowing the FHA claims to proceed only for three timely incidents — racial steering in October 2018, discriminatory parking enforcement in summer 2020, and national origin discrimination against an Iraqi American tenant in summer 2021 — while barring all earlier incidents as time-barred and rejecting application of the continuing violations doctrine.
brief_summary: Intermountain Fair Housing Council sued Tomlinson & Associates and related defendants for FHA violations at two Boise apartment complexes, alleging racial steering, discriminatory enforcement of parking rules, and various other acts of discrimination against Black/African and Iraqi American tenants spanning 2015–2021. The court held that the vast majority of alleged incidents were outside the applicable statute of limitations and that the continuing violations doctrine of Havens Realty did not save them, because the plaintiff failed to identify a single, specific discriminatory practice occurring continuously into the limitations period. The court allowed three timely claims to proceed to trial, denied summary judgment on the negligence claim, and dismissed several entity defendants and one individual defendant.
key_cases_cited: Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986)
Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242 (1986)
Lehman v. Roberts, 442 U.S. 707 (1979)
Garcia v. Brockway, 526 F.3d 456 (9th Cir. 2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Racial steering at Latah Village Apartments in October 2018; Iranian tester with obvious accent inquiring about apartments for large family was told family could not occupy three-bedroom apartment due to two-person-per-room occupancy limit and directed to larger apartments, while white/Caucasian testers with large families were not informed of occupancy limits.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that the Council timely filed its administrative complaint on June 27, 2019 (within the statute of limitations for the October 2018 incident), and viewing facts in plaintiff's favor, there is a triable issue of fact regarding discriminatory intent in the alleged steering based on national origin. The complaint survives summary judgment and proceeds to trial.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discriminatory enforcement of parking rules at Latah Village and Greenfield Apartments during summer 2020; black African tenants and their friends received car boots for parking in resident and visitor spaces even after signs indicating parking space designations were removed, while similarly situated white tenants were not subjected to the same enforcement.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework and found that when paragraphs 53-54 are viewed alongside the history of allegedly discriminatory parking enforcement, there is a triable issue of fact as to whether defendants had a discriminatory motive in renewing parking rules and booting vehicles of black tenants in summer 2020. Plaintiff need not rely on McDonnell Douglas but may produce direct or circumstantial evidence of discriminatory intent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to add roommate to lease of Iraqi American tenant (Ms. Alghizi) in summer 2021; Defendant Stewart allegedly denied the request after Ms. Alghizi informed Stewart that the would-be roommate did not yet have identification, commenting that 'illegals are not allowed.' Thereafter, Latah Village issued three lease violations to Ms. Alghizi, refused to meet with her regarding the violations, and denied her second request to add a roommate.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that reading the factual allegations of paragraph 55 together with later allegations laying out elements of FHA discrimination claims, the Council has plausibly alleged a claim for discrimination based on national origin. Defendants did not dispute the underlying factual allegations for purposes of the motion, and the Court concluded the Council may proceed to trial on this aspect of its FHA claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Negligence claim, including negligent supervision and training of employees regarding Fair Housing Act requirements; plaintiff alleges defendants failed to use reasonable care to avoid injury and prevent foreseeable risks of harm by failing to adequately train and supervise agents and employees regarding FHA requirements.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court rejected defendants' arguments that the economic loss doctrine bars the claim (finding plaintiff alleged noneconomic injury to its mission of ensuring open housing), that plaintiff failed to plead negligent supervision and training (finding paragraph 20 and 90 provided fair notice), and that no legal duty exists to train employees on FHA requirements (predicting Idaho courts would recognize such a duty as part of the broader duty to control employees to prevent harm to third parties). Negligence claim survives summary judgment.

case_name: Valencia v. City of Springfield, Illinois
accommodation_description: Request for reasonable accommodation to City's zoning ordinance and spacing rules to allow a group home for three men with intellectual and physical disabilities to remain in a single-family residential district.
key_holding: The City of Springfield's zoning ordinance that imposed a 600-foot spacing requirement between group homes for persons with disabilities violated the Fair Housing Act, ADA, and Section 504, and the Plaintiffs established they are aggrieved persons entitled to summary judgment on liability.
brief_summary: Individual Advocacy Group, individual disabled residents, and the estate of a deceased resident sued the City of Springfield, Illinois after the City denied a conditional use permit and sought to evict residents from a group home for persons with disabilities, claiming violations of the Fair Housing Act, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act. The Court granted partial summary judgment for plaintiffs on liability, finding the City's facially discriminatory zoning ordinance violated federal law and plaintiffs established standing as aggrieved persons.
key_cases_cited: Valencia v. City of Springfield, 883 F.3d 959 (7th Cir. 2018)
Oconomowoc Residential Programs v. City of Milwaukee, 300 F.3d 775 (7th Cir. 2002)
Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)
Bellwood v. Dwivedi, 895 F.2d 1521 (7th Cir. 1990)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request for reasonable accommodation to City's zoning rules, policies and practices to allow a group home for three men with intellectual and physical disabilities to remain open at 2328 S. Noble Avenue; specifically, a Conditional Permitted Use (CPU) permit or waiver of the 600-foot spacing rule that prohibited group homes for unrelated persons with disabilities from being located within 600 feet of another such home.
fha_claims.reasoning: The City admitted its zoning ordinance as applied violated the FHA by discriminating against residents based on disability. The ordinance facially discriminated by treating unrelated persons with disabilities differently from families, and the City refused to grant a reasonable accommodation (CPU or spacing rule waiver) that would have allowed the group home to operate. The court granted summary judgment on liability for the FHA violation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The City's zoning ordinance facially discriminated against persons with disabilities by prohibiting unrelated persons with disabilities from living together within 600 feet of another group home, while allowing families (defined as related persons or up to five unrelated persons) to live anywhere in residential districts. This disparate treatment violated the FHA's prohibition on discrimination in the sale or rental of housing based on disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), 42 U.S.C. § 12131 et seq.; Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, 29 U.S.C. § 794
fha_claims.reasoning: The City admitted its zoning ordinance violated Title II of the ADA and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act by discriminating against individuals with disabilities in a federally assisted housing program. The court applied the same analytical framework across all three statutes (FHA, ADA, and Section 504) and granted summary judgment on liability.

case_name: Valencia v. City of Springfield, Illinois
accommodation_description: Group home residents and operator requested a Conditional Permitted Use permit and reasonable accommodation to allow the home to remain open notwithstanding the City's 600-foot spacing rule for community residences serving persons with disabilities.
key_holding: The City violated the FHA by maintaining and enforcing a discriminatory 600-foot spacing rule that treats group homes for persons with disabilities less favorably than similarly situated non-disabled families, and by denying the reasonable accommodation request when it denied the CPU permit without properly addressing the accommodation.
brief_summary: Mary B. Valencia, Individual Advocacy Group, and the United States sued the City of Springfield after the City enforced its 600-foot spacing rule against a group home for three men with intellectual and physical disabilities at 2328 S. Noble Ave., denying their permit request and refusing a reasonable accommodation. The Court granted summary judgment for the United States, finding the City violated the Fair Housing Act by treating group homes for persons with disabilities less favorably than non-disabled families and denying the reasonable accommodation request.
key_cases_cited: Oconomowoc Residential Programs v. City of Milwaukee, 300 F.3d 775 (7th Cir. 2002)
Larkin v. Mich. Dep't of Social Servs., 89 F.3d 285 (6th Cir. 1996)
Bangerter v. Orem City Corp., 46 F.3d 1491 (10th Cir. 1995)
United States v. Balistrieri, 981 F.2d 916 (7th Cir. 1992)
Wis. Cmty. Servs., Inc. v. City of Milwaukee, 465 F.3d 737 (7th Cir. 2006)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The City's 600-foot spacing rule for group homes for persons with disabilities, applied to 2328 S. Noble Ave., violates 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(1)(B) by making housing unavailable on the basis of disability. The spacing rule treats group homes for up to five unrelated individuals with disabilities less favorably than similarly situated living arrangements of up to five unrelated non-disabled people, constituting facial discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The 600-foot spacing rule imposes discriminatory terms and conditions on housing for persons with disabilities in violation of 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(2). The rule renders certain housing unavailable to persons with disabilities that would otherwise be available to non-disabled individuals, constituting discrimination in the terms, conditions, or privileges of a dwelling.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exception to the 600-foot spacing rule to allow the three residents with disabilities to remain in their home at 2328 S. Noble Ave.; alternatively, a Conditional Permitted Use (CPU) permit to allow the group home to operate despite proximity to another group home operated by SPARC.
fha_claims.reasoning: The City refused to make a reasonable accommodation by denying the CPU permit and failing to address the reasonable accommodation request. The City had no process or policy for handling reasonable accommodation requests in zoning matters, and the City's own admission that the ordinance was discriminatory, combined with the residents' documented need for community-based housing and the home's minimal impact on the neighborhood, establishes that a reasonable accommodation should have been granted.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The City engaged in a pattern or practice of discrimination under 42 U.S.C. § 3614(a) by maintaining and enforcing a discriminatory zoning ordinance as its standard operating procedure. The City refused to grant exceptions to the spacing rule on both occasions it was asked (137 Pinehurst and 2328 S. Noble), and decision-makers expressed concern about setting a bad precedent, indicating intent to apply the same discriminatory standard to any future group homes.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The City denied fair housing rights to a group of persons (the three residents and their guardians) raising an issue of general public importance under 42 U.S.C. § 3614(a). The availability of community-based housing for persons with disabilities is an issue of general public importance, and the City's refusal to grant an exception as a reasonable accommodation violated the residents' FHA rights.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Civil penalties are available against the City under 42 U.S.C. § 3614(d)(1)(C) to vindicate the public interest. Although the City claimed lack of discriminatory intent, the evidence shows the City disregarded its FHA obligations by maintaining and enforcing a discriminatory ordinance, and by 2016 the City should have been on notice that the ordinance was potentially discriminatory based on prior Seventh Circuit case law.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Monetary damages are available to aggrieved persons under 42 U.S.C. § 3614(d)(1)(B). The record contains evidence of emotional distress suffered by the residents and their guardians regarding the possibility of losing their home due to the City's discriminatory enforcement action, which can support an award of damages even without detailed medical evidence.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible hotel reservation website with identification and description of accessible guest rooms and features
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff established Article III standing as a tester under the ADA by alleging concrete injury (inability to obtain statutorily mandated accessibility information), causation (defendant's non-compliant website), and redressability (injunctive relief). The court rejected defendant's argument that testers lack standing, citing Havens Realty and similar civil rights precedent, and found plaintiff's allegations of present deterrence and future intent to revisit the website sufficient to establish a real and immediate threat of future injury for purposes of injunctive relief.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III claim for inaccessible hotel reservation website; website does not identify accessible rooms, allow booking of accessible rooms, or provide sufficient information about accessibility features
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied defendant's motion to dismiss for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under Rule 12(b)(1), finding that plaintiff established Article III standing as a tester under the ADA by alleging concrete injury (inability to obtain statutorily mandated accessibility information) and real and immediate threat of future discrimination. The court held that testers have standing under the ADA, consistent with standing for testers under the Fair Housing Act and Title VII.

source_file: 9669841_2021_Laufer v. Lodging Enterprises of Springfield, LLC_ilcd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible hotel reservation website with identification and description of accessible guest rooms and features
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff established Article III standing as a tester under the ADA by alleging concrete injury (inability to obtain statutorily mandated accessibility information), causation (defendant's non-compliant website), and redressability (prospective injunctive relief). The court rejected defendant's mootness argument, finding websites are fluid and amenable to sudden change, and defendant failed to meet its formidable burden of showing the wrongful behavior could not reasonably recur.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Mental health treatment, access to programs and services, segregation from general population, isolation conditions, disciplinary procedures accounting for mental illness
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiffs adequately pleaded ADA and Rehabilitation Act claims by alleging qualifying disabilities and exclusion from programs/services based on disability; defendants' motion to dismiss these claims was denied and claims survive to proceed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal Protection claim alleging disparate treatment of class members of color in placement in restrictive housing, use of force, and disciplinary procedures
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted motion to dismiss Equal Protection claims because named plaintiffs failed to allege they personally suffered disparate treatment or were targeted by racially degrading language; class representatives must allege personal injury, not merely injury to other class members. Plaintiffs granted leave to amend.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Procedural due process claim regarding failure to account for mental illness in disciplinary process and segregation placement
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted motion to dismiss procedural due process claim because plaintiffs failed to identify what process is due under the circumstances and did not clearly distinguish between substantive and procedural due process; complaint did not put defendants on adequate notice. Plaintiffs granted leave to amend.

source_file: 9670630_2023_The County of Livingston v. PSA Dewberry Inc dba PSA Dewberry BCA nka Dewberry Architects Inc_ilcd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claims involve breach of contract and negligence for failure to design and construct a courthouse in compliance with Title II of the ADA, the Illinois Environmental Barriers Act, and the Illinois Accessibility Code.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the defendant's motion to dismiss on preemption grounds, holding that the plaintiff's state law claims for breach of contract and negligence constitute permissible claims for de facto contribution (not indemnification) and do not conflict with Title II of the ADA's regulatory purposes. The court adopted the Ninth Circuit's reasoning in AECOM Services, Inc., distinguishing the Fourth Circuit's holding in Niles Bolton Associates.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged discrimination based on disability in the denial of his rental application for a low-income housing unit; specifically, that defendants refused to accept disability benefits as qualifying income to meet the Minimum Income Requirement.
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 60(b)(1) Motion to Vacate Default Judgment
fha_claims.reasoning: The court did not reach the merits of the FHA claim on the default judgment itself. Instead, defendants moved to vacate the default judgment under Rule 60(b)(1), arguing good cause, quick action, and meritorious defenses. The opinion addresses defendants' arguments that they have a meritorious defense (that the Minimum Income Requirement is a legitimate business practice and that disability benefits were counted as income), but the court's ruling on the motion to vacate is not included in this opinion—only the motion itself is presented.

source_file: 9673112_2018_National Fair Housing Alliance v. Deutsche Bank National Trust_ilnd
case_name: National Fair Housing Alliance v. Deutsche Bank National Trust
accommodation_description: No individual accommodation request; fair housing organizations alleged discriminatory maintenance of REO properties based on race
key_holding: Complaint dismissed without prejudice because plaintiffs' statistical evidence was substantially time-barred under FHA's two-year statute of limitations, and plaintiffs failed to adequately plead proximate cause between defendants' alleged abdication policy and plaintiffs' claimed injuries, which were too attenuated to satisfy the direct-relation requirement.
brief_summary: Fair housing organizations sued Deutsche Bank, Ocwen, and Altisource alleging that defendants' REO property maintenance was discriminatorily disparate between white neighborhoods and communities of color, violating the Fair Housing Act. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss without prejudice, finding plaintiffs' statistical allegations substantially time-barred, proximate cause inadequately pleaded due to attenuated chain-of-injury, and discriminatory intent insufficiently alleged.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Tex. Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Cmtys. Project, Inc., 135 S. Ct. 2507 (2015)
Bank of Am. Corp. v. City of Miami, 137 S. Ct. 1296 (2017)
Cty. of Cook v. Wells Fargo & Co., 314 F. Supp. 3d 975 (N.D. Ill. 2018)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege discriminatory intent. Their statistical evidence was undermined by statute of limitations ruling, and their reliance on Deutsche Bank's alleged history of discrimination was barred by the FHA's two-year statute of limitations. Discriminatory intent cannot be inferred without plausible factual allegations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to allege all three elements of disparate impact: (1) statistical disparity was undermined by statute of limitations ruling affecting the dataset; (2) policy element was satisfied; (3) proximate causation was too attenuated under Bank of America v. City of Miami—plaintiffs' injuries resulted only after impermissible intermediate steps (delegation → poor maintenance → disparate effects → resource diversion), not at the first step of the causal chain.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to maintain REO properties in predominantly minority neighborhoods at same level as white neighborhoods
fha_claims.reasoning: Count I under § 3604(a) dismissed because plaintiffs failed to allege that properties were neglected to such an extent as to dissuade purchasers from buying them, rendering them effectively unavailable. Mere diminution in property values is insufficient under Bloch v. Frischholz.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination in terms, conditions, or privileges of sale or rental through disparate maintenance
fha_claims.reasoning: Count II under § 3604(b) dismissed on same grounds as § 3604(a)—plaintiffs failed to allege that disparate maintenance rendered properties unavailable or unfit for occupancy, which is required to state a claim under the regulation 24 C.F.R. § 100.65(b)(2).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination in residential real estate-related transactions (financing, brokering, appraising)
fha_claims.reasoning: Count III under § 3605 dismissed because plaintiffs failed to allege any specific real estate-related transaction impeded by defendants' conduct. Plaintiffs attempted to bootstrap their § 3605 claim into their § 3604 theory, but § 3605 requires allegation of a specific transaction, not merely that properties were made unavailable.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Count V under § 3617 dismissed because plaintiffs failed to allege any predicate FHA-protected activity that defendants retaliated against. The complaint alleges racial disparity in property maintenance but does not explain what FHA-protected activity by community members triggered defendants' alleged retaliation. Retaliation requires action 'on account of' protected activity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Perpetuation of segregation through disparate maintenance of REO properties
fha_claims.reasoning: Count IV for perpetuation of segregation dismissed because plaintiffs' allegations depend on statistics that have been undermined by the statute of limitations ruling. Plaintiffs must allege segregation perpetuated as a result of defendants' conduct, but cannot do so without relying on barred conduct and the reduced dataset.

source_file: 9674516_2019_Finch v. Housing Authority of Cook County_ilnd
case_name: Finch v. Housing Authority of Cook County
accommodation_description: Request for three-bedroom apartment voucher as reasonable accommodation for children Ramon's autism and Shorter's bipolar II disorder and learning disabilities, which required separate bedrooms.
key_holding: Ramon's failure to accommodate claim fails because defendant provided him a two-bedroom voucher with his own room, the precise accommodation requested; however, Shorter's failure to accommodate claim survives because she sufficiently alleged disability, defendant's knowledge, need for separate room, and denial.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Adana Finch and her children Ramon and Coya Shorter sued the Housing Authority of Cook County under the Fair Housing Act and Rehabilitation Act, alleging failure to accommodate their disabilities by refusing to approve a three-bedroom voucher so the children could have separate bedrooms due to Ramon's autism and Shorter's bipolar II disorder. The court dismissed Adana's individual claims (she conceded no disability), dismissed Ramon's failure to accommodate claim (he received a two-bedroom voucher with his own room), and dismissed all plaintiffs' disparate treatment claims as conclusory, but allowed Shorter's failure to accommodate claim to proceed.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Scheidler v. Indiana, 914 F.3d 535 (7th Cir. 2019)
Geraci v. Union Square Condo. Ass'n, 2017 WL 372303 (N.D. Ill. 2017)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Three-bedroom apartment (separate bedroom for Ramon due to autism spectrum disorder, asthma, and learning disabilities)
fha_claims.reasoning: Ramon's failure to accommodate claim was dismissed because Defendant's correspondence demonstrates that Defendant acknowledged Ramon's disability and provided him the precise accommodation requested—his own room via a two-bedroom voucher. Ramon cannot establish a failure to accommodate claim when he received the accommodation he sought.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Three-bedroom apartment (separate bedroom for Coya Shorter due to bipolar II disorder, panic disorder, claustrophobia, and learning disabilities)
fha_claims.reasoning: Shorter sufficiently alleged a failure to accommodate claim by pleading: (1) she has a disability; (2) Defendant knew of this disability; (3) she requires her own room because of her disabilities; and (4) Defendant denied her reasonable accommodation request. Whether Defendant properly relied on her certification or had prior knowledge are questions for summary judgment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Forcing Plaintiffs to move while allowing similarly situated families to remain in three-bedroom apartments; approving rent voucher increases for other similarly situated renters
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs' disparate treatment claims failed because they alleged only conclusory allegations that unidentified others were 'similarly situated' without factual enhancement regarding household composition, disability status, lease terms, or whether comparators sought or received accommodations. Such general allegations are insufficient under Iqbal and Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act claim for failure to accommodate and disparate treatment
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 504 claims were analyzed under the same standards as FHA claims and dismissed on identical grounds: Ramon's failure to accommodate claim was dismissed because he received the accommodation sought; Shorter's failure to accommodate claim survives; and the disparate treatment claims failed for lack of factual allegations regarding similarly situated comparators.

source_file: 9674906_2019_Connectors Realty Group Corporation, The v. State Farm Fire _ Casualty Company_ilnd
case_name: The Connectors Realty Group Corporation v. State Farm Fire & Casualty Company
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege State Farm discriminated in insurance claims processing based on race and neighborhood racial composition, not a disability accommodation request
key_holding: Connectors' disparate treatment claim survives dismissal based on racially discriminatory comments by State Farm adjuster, but Nash's § 1981/1982 and FHA disparate impact claims fail because he lacked sufficient factual allegations connecting his denial to racial animus and submitted industry-wide rather than State Farm-specific statistical evidence
brief_summary: The Connectors Realty Group Corporation and its African-American owner sued State Farm Fire & Casualty Company alleging the insurer racially discriminated in processing property insurance claims by redlining majority-black ZIP Codes on Chicago's South and West Sides. The court denied State Farm's motion to dismiss Connectors' disparate treatment claim based on a racially charged conversation with a claims adjuster, but dismissed Nash's claims for insufficient allegations of racial animus and dismissed Nash's disparate impact claim for reliance on industry-wide rather than State Farm-specific statistical evidence.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Ashcroft v. Iqbal

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Insurance claim processing and payment for property damage claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Connectors sufficiently pleaded discriminatory intent through allegations of racial animus in Beavers' statements ('you people,' 'homeys,' 'your area,' 'South Side of Chicago and you all's neighborhoods') and the connection between this animus and processing of claims as presumptively fraudulent. Allegations survive Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Insurance claim processing and payment for property damage claims from majority-black ZIP Codes
fha_claims.reasoning: Nash failed to adequately plead statistical disparity specific to State Farm. The Hasegawa-Wyner analysis was based on industry-wide data across all Illinois homeowners insurers, not State Farm specifically. The court found the data, nature, and methodology of the analysis unclear and insufficient to demonstrate a disparity as to State Farm alone.

case_name: Demetris Hunter v. WPD Management, LLC and 7130 S. Jeffrey, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that defendant repair the building's broken elevator to provide functional elevator service necessary for her to access her sixth-floor apartment due to mobility disability.
key_holding: The court denied WPD's motion to dismiss, holding that Hunter sufficiently alleged a reasonable accommodation claim by requesting that the elevator be repaired, and that whether the accommodation was reasonable and whether WPD provided an adequate alternative accommodation are questions of fact that cannot be resolved at the pleading stage.
brief_summary: Demetris Hunter, a tenant with a mobility disability who uses a walker and lives on the sixth floor, sued her apartment building's management company after the elevator broke and was not repaired for over ten weeks, trapping her in her apartment. The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss Hunter's reasonable accommodation claim under § 3604(f)(3)(B), holding that requesting elevator repair constitutes a request for accommodation, she need not speak magic words, and whether the accommodation was reasonable is a question of fact for trial.
key_cases_cited: Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009)
Good Shepherd Manor Found., Inc. v. City of Momence, 323 F.3d 557 (7th Cir. 2003)
Jankowski Lee & Assocs. v. Cisneros, 91 F.3d 891 (7th Cir. 1996)
Clifton Terrace Associates, Ltd. v. United Technologies Corp., 929 F.2d 714 (D.C. Cir. 1991)
Astralis Condo. Ass'n v. Sec'y, U.S. Dep't of Hous. & Urban Dev., 620 F.3d 62 (1st Cir. 2010)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Repair of broken elevator to restore access to sixth-floor apartment
fha_claims.reasoning: Court rejected defendant's habitability vs. availability distinction and found that a condition making housing uninhabitable due to disability may make it unavailable. Court left open the possibility of disparate impact liability but did not definitively decide applicability at the pleading stage, allowing the claim to survive.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Immediate repair of broken elevator to restore plaintiff's ability to access her sixth-floor apartment and leave the building; alternatively, reasonable alternative accommodation to provide equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that plaintiff need not use magic words to request accommodation and that the September 12 letter from counsel sufficiently put defendant on notice. Whether the accommodation was reasonable is a factual question that cannot be resolved against plaintiff at the motion to dismiss stage. Defendant's offer of assistance via flyer was implausibly adequate given the length of elevator outage and plaintiff's sixth-floor location.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Threat of eviction and fines for calling emergency services in response to plaintiff's request for elevator repair
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff adequately pleaded protected activity (requesting accommodation for disability) and that the flyer's threat of eviction for calling 911 was sufficient to allege coercion/intimidation. The inference that the threat was directed at disabled residents relying on emergency services to access inaccessible housing was plausible, and discrimination claims need not establish prima facie case at pleading stage under Swierkiewicz.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of Security Agreements and conversion of Reserve Fund for Replacement; claims arise under contract law and the Federal Torts Claims Act, not the Fair Housing Act
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that HUD fulfilled its obligations under the security agreements by executing UCC Termination Statements and that the reserve funds constitute project funds subject to regulatory control by HUD for continued use of the project. The court concluded that upon termination of the HAP contracts, the reserve accounts consisted of project funds that HUD properly controlled, and plaintiffs failed to maintain the property as required.

source_file: 9677610_2021_Nawrocki v. Oak Brook Towers Condominium Association_ilnd
case_name: Janet Nawrocki and H.O.P.E., INC. v. Oak Brook Towers Condominium Association
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested an assigned parking space in the row closest to the back entrance of her building as a reasonable accommodation for her mobility disability that limits her ability to walk long distances.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motions to dismiss, holding that fair housing organization HOPE had standing to sue under Havens Realty because it adequately alleged concrete injury from diverting resources to address defendants' alleged discrimination, and that the complaint stated a plausible failure-to-accommodate claim under § 3604(f)(3)(B).
brief_summary: Janet Nawrocki and HOPE Fair Housing Center sued the Oak Brook Towers Condominium Association after Nawrocki requested an assigned parking space near her unit as a reasonable accommodation for her disability that limits her ability to walk long distances, and defendants allegedly failed to respond meaningfully to the request. The district court denied both motions to dismiss, holding that HOPE had standing under Havens Realty and that plaintiffs adequately stated a failure-to-accommodate claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(B).
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Access Living of Metro. Chi. v. Uber Techs., Inc., 958 F.3d 604 (7th Cir. 2020)
Valencia v. City of Springfield, 883 F.3d 959 (7th Cir. 2018)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Assigned parking space near plaintiff's unit in the back parking lot, close to the rear entrance of the building, to accommodate plaintiff's mobility disability that makes it difficult and dangerous to walk long distances.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that the amended complaint adequately pleads a reasonable accommodation claim under § 3604(f)(3)(B) by alleging Nawrocki's disability, her request for an assigned parking space, and defendants' failure to respond or provide the accommodation. The court declined to address the merits of whether the accommodation is reasonable, noting that such determination requires fact-specific balancing and is inappropriate at the pleading stage.

source_file: 9677629_2021_County of Cook, IL v. Wells Fargo _ Co._ilnd
case_name: County of Cook v. Wells Fargo & Co.
accommodation_description: Not applicable — this is a discriminatory lending case; no reasonable accommodation or modification request is at issue.
key_holding: The court granted Cook County's motion to compel production of Wells Fargo's consulting agreements with two former County employees, holding that Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(4)(D) does not protect documents sought via request for production and does not shield the agreements themselves from disclosure, and the court also resolved several additional discovery disputes largely in the County's favor.
brief_summary: Cook County brought a Fair Housing Act suit against Wells Fargo alleging discriminatory lending practices against minority borrowers. This opinion addresses a motion to compel production of consulting agreements between Wells Fargo and two former high-level County employees (former CFO Thomas Glaser and former Comptroller John Chambers), whom Wells Fargo had retained as consulting experts. The court granted the motion to compel on two independent grounds—Rule 26(b)(4)(D) applies only to interrogatories and depositions, not requests for production, and the County sought the agreements themselves rather than facts or opinions held by the experts—and also resolved multiple additional discovery disputes concerning document production scope, privilege, and cost-of-damages materials.
key_cases_cited: United States v. Evans, 113 F.3d 1457 (7th Cir. 1997)
Barnhart v. Peabody Coal Co., 537 U.S. 149 (2003)
Upjohn Co. v. United States, 449 U.S. 383 (1981)

source_file: 9677757_2021_Trinity Sober Living, LLC v. Village of Hinsdale_ilnd
case_name: Trinity Sober Living, LLC v. Village of Hinsdale
accommodation_description: Request for waiver of zoning code family definition limiting unrelated persons to three, to allow a sober living facility for up to ten persons in recovery from addiction
key_holding: The court denied dismissal of the reasonable accommodation claim, finding that TSL adequately alleged the Village failed to engage in an interactive process by filing suit against TSL the day after receiving the accommodation request rather than assessing it or referring it to the Board of Trustees.
brief_summary: Trinity Sober Living LLC and the United States sued the Village of Hinsdale, challenging the Village's attempts to enforce its zoning code to prevent TSL from operating a sober living facility for persons in recovery from addiction in a single-family residential zone. The court denied the Village's motions to dismiss, except for TSL's retaliation claim, finding that both complaints adequately stated a claim that the Village failed to provide a reasonable accommodation by filing suit against TSL the day after receiving the accommodation request instead of engaging in the interactive process.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 554 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Valencia v. City of Springfield, Ill., 883 F.3d 959 (7th Cir. 2018)
U.S. v. Village of Palatine, Ill., 37 F.3d 1230 (7th Cir. 1994)
Bloch v. Frischolz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver of the zoning code's restriction on the number of unrelated persons that can reside together as a family, and treatment of the sober living home as a single-family use rather than a commercial use, to allow up to ten residents in recovery from alcoholism or drug addiction to reside in a single-family residential zone.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that TSL adequately alleged a request for reasonable accommodation and that the Village's immediate filing of suit rather than engaging in the interactive process or referring the request to the Board of Trustees made it reasonable for TSL to conclude the request was foredoomed, thus stating a plausible claim for failure to accommodate that survives the motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed TSL's retaliation claim under § 3617 because the Noerr-Pennington doctrine provides absolute immunity for litigation, and TSL failed to allege that the Village's state court lawsuit was a sham or that its allegations were frivolous or objectively baseless.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II discrimination claim (42 U.S.C. § 12132)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the same reasonable accommodation analysis under the ADA as under the FHA and found that TSL's ADA discrimination claim, like its FHA reasonable accommodation claim, survives the motion to dismiss because the Village failed to engage in the interactive process before filing suit.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver of the zoning code's restriction on the number of unrelated persons that can reside together as a family to allow a sober living home for persons with disabilities in recovery from alcoholism or drug addiction to operate in a single-family residential zone.
fha_claims.reasoning: The United States' complaint adequately alleges denial of a reasonable accommodation under the FHA; whether the requested accommodation was required or reasonable is a fact-specific inquiry not appropriate for resolution on motion to dismiss, and the Village's failure to assess the request or inform TSL of procedures before filing suit supports the claim's plausibility.

case_name: Trinity Sober Living, LLC v. Village of Hinsdale
accommodation_description: Request for waiver of zoning code restriction limiting unrelated persons living together to allow a sober living facility for up to ten persons in recovery from substance use disorders to operate in a single-family residential zone.
key_holding: The Village violated the FHA's reasonable accommodation requirement by failing to engage in an interactive process or give TSL's accommodation request proper consideration, instead immediately filing suit to enforce its zoning code without informing TSL of available procedures or giving it a meaningful opportunity to request a variance.
brief_summary: Trinity Sober Living LLC and the United States sued the Village of Hinsdale, Illinois, challenging the Village's enforcement of its zoning code to prevent a sober living facility from operating in a single-family residential zone. The court denied the Village's motions to dismiss the reasonable accommodation claims, finding that TSL adequately alleged the Village failed to engage in an interactive process or properly consider its accommodation request, instead immediately filing suit rather than informing TSL of available procedures or referring the request to the Board of Trustees.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 554 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
U.S. v. Village of Palatine, Ill., 37 F.3d 1230 (7th Cir. 1994)
Valencia v. City of Springfield, Ill., 883 F.3d 959 (7th Cir. 2018)
Schwarz v. City Treasure Island, 544 F.3d 1201 (11th Cir. 2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver of the zoning code's restriction on the number of unrelated persons that can reside together as a family, and treatment of the sober living home as a single-family use rather than a commercial use; specifically, allowing more than three unrelated persons in recovery from substance use disorder to reside in a single-family residential zone.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that TSL adequately alleged a request for reasonable accommodation and that the Village's immediate filing of suit rather than engaging in the interactive process or referring the request to the Board of Trustees made it reasonable to conclude the request was foredoomed, thus stating a plausible claim for failure to accommodate that survives the motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed TSL's retaliation claim under § 3617 because the Noerr-Pennington doctrine provides absolute immunity for litigation, and TSL failed to allege that the Village's state court lawsuit was a sham or that its allegations were frivolous or objectively baseless.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II discrimination claim (42 U.S.C. § 12132)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the same reasonable accommodation analysis under the ADA as under the FHA and found that TSL's ADA claim alleging failure to provide reasonable accommodation survives the motion to dismiss on the same factual basis as the FHA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver of the zoning code's restriction on the number of unrelated persons that can reside together as a family, and treatment of the sober living home as a single-family use rather than a commercial use; specifically, allowing more than three unrelated persons in recovery from substance use disorder to reside in a single-family residential zone.
fha_claims.reasoning: The United States' complaint adequately alleges that TSL sought a reasonable accommodation and that the Village filed suit rather than assessing the request or informing TSL of its procedures, stating a plausible claim for denial of reasonable accommodation; whether the accommodation was required or reasonable is a fact-specific inquiry inappropriate for resolution on motion to dismiss.

source_file: 9677892_2021_Connectors Realty Group Corporation, The v. State Farm Fire _ Casualty Company_ilnd
case_name: The Connectors Realty Group Corporation and Darryl Williams v. State Farm Fire & Casualty Company
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested in this case; the claims concern alleged racial discrimination in the handling and denial of property insurance claims, not a request for a reasonable accommodation or modification under the FHA.
key_holding: The court grants State Farm's motion to strike the plaintiffs' overbroad class allegations and grants plaintiffs' motion to dismiss State Farm's unjust enrichment/rescission counterclaim for failure to allege how plaintiffs could be restored to the status quo, while denying plaintiffs' motion to strike State Farm's affirmative defenses, with leave to amend granted to both parties.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs, a realty group corporation and its owner, allege that State Farm treated insurance claims from African-American property owners in majority-Black zip codes on Chicago's south side as presumptively fraudulent, in violation of 42 U.S.C. § 1981 and the Fair Housing Act. On cross-motions addressing pleadings, the court struck the proposed class definition as facially overbroad because it encompassed all African-American claimants in the relevant zip codes regardless of whether their claims were denied, dismissed State Farm's counterclaim for failing to adequately plead rescission (specifically the status quo ante element), and declined to strike State Farm's first three affirmative defenses as adequately pleaded. Both parties received 30 days to amend their respective deficient pleadings.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Vann v. Dolly, Inc., 2020 WL 902831 (N.D. Ill. 2020)
Buonomo v. Optimum Outcomes, Inc., 301 F.R.D. 292 (N.D. Ill. 2014)
Mussat v. IQVIA, Inc., 953 F.3d 441 (7th Cir. 2020)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act claim alleging discriminatory treatment of insurance claims from black-majority zip codes; § 1981 claim for racial discrimination in insurance claim handling
fha_claims.disposition: Not substantively addressed in this opinion
fha_claims.reasoning: The opinion addresses motions to strike class allegations, strike affirmative defenses, and dismiss the counterclaim, but does not address the merits of the underlying FHA or § 1981 claims. The FHA claim survives as the case proceeds on the merits.

source_file: 9677921_2021_City of Chicago v. Purdue Pharma L.P._ilnd

case_name: Cabrini-Green Local Advisory Council v. Chicago Housing Authority
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested in this case. The original claims concerned the unlawful displacement of public housing residents and the discriminatory impact of redevelopment initiatives on African Americans, women, and children in the Cabrini-Green area of Chicago.
key_holding: The court approved the proposed settlement between the Cabrini-Green Local Advisory Council and the Chicago Housing Authority, finding that the LAC Board validly authorized the settlement after properly recusing conflicted directors who held dual membership on both the LAC and CDC boards.
brief_summary: This case arises from a 21-year-old consent decree resolving Fair Housing Act claims brought by the Cabrini-Green Local Advisory Council against the Chicago Housing Authority, which had alleged that redevelopment of Cabrini-Green would displace residents and have a discriminatory impact on African Americans, women, and children. After an OIG investigation revealed financial mismanagement by the CDC — an affiliated development entity created under the decree — the CHA moved to enforce and modify the consent decree. Following extensive settlement negotiations supervised by a magistrate judge, the court approved the resulting settlement over the objection of non-party Carol Steele and the CDC, holding that the LAC Board had properly recused conflicted directors with dual board membership and that the remaining directors had valid authority to approve the settlement.
key_cases_cited: Rufo v. Inmates of Suffolk Co. Jail, 502 U.S. 367 (1992)
Horne v. Flores, 557 U.S. 433 (2009)
United States v. Krilich, 303 F.3d 784 (7th Cir. 2002)
Pohl v. United Airlines, Inc., 213 F.3d 336 (7th Cir. 2000)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim concerns discriminatory impact of redevelopment initiatives on housing access and displacement
fha_claims.reasoning: The original disparate impact claim under FHA § 3604 was resolved through a consent decree negotiated over two decades ago. The current opinion addresses enforcement and modification of that decree, not the underlying merits of the original claim. The settlement reflects a negotiated resolution of the motion to enforce the decree.

source_file: 9678323_2021_Illinois Conservative Union v. State of Illinois_ilnd
9678361_2021_County of Cook, IL v. Wells Fargo _ Co._ilnd
case_name: County of Cook v. Wells Fargo & Co.
accommodation_description: Not applicable — this is a municipal discriminatory lending/disparate impact case; no reasonable accommodation or modification was requested.
key_holding: The court denied Wells Fargo's Rule 12(b)(1) motion to dismiss for lack of Article III standing, holding that even if the County's financial gains from Wells Fargo-related foreclosures exceeded its losses (Y ≥ X), Cook County retains standing so long as it suffered some concrete financial injury (X > 0), because injury-in-fact and recoverable damages are legally distinct concepts.
brief_summary: Cook County sued Wells Fargo under the Fair Housing Act alleging that discriminatory lending practices caused a disproportionate number of foreclosures in the county, resulting in concrete financial harm including increased sheriff, police, judicial, and infrastructure costs. Wells Fargo moved mid-discovery to dismiss for lack of Article III standing, arguing that evidence showed the County actually netted a financial benefit from the foreclosure boom. The court denied the motion, explaining that Wells Fargo conflated the merits question of net damages (X – Y) with the threshold standing question of whether any injury occurred at all (X > 0), and that Wells Fargo made no attempt to show X equaled zero.
key_cases_cited: Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)
Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins, 136 S. Ct. 1540 (2016)
Gracia v. SigmaTron International, Inc., 986 F.3d 1058 (7th Cir. 2021)
Wigod v. Wells Fargo Bank, N.A., 673 F.3d 547 (7th Cir. 2012)
City of Miami Gardens v. Wells Fargo & Co., 931 F.3d 1274 (11th Cir. 2019)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim involves discriminatory lending practices, not accommodation
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied Wells Fargo's motion to dismiss for lack of subject matter jurisdiction on standing grounds, holding that the distinction between Article III injury (X) and damages (X – Y) means the County has standing even if net financial benefit (Y) exceeds costs (X), provided X > 0. The court found Wells Fargo failed to demonstrate X = 0 and reserved the standing question for summary judgment after discovery closes.

source_file: 9678854_2021_Connectors Realty Group Corporation, The v. State Farm Fire _ Casualty Company_ilnd
case_name: The Connectors Realty Group Corporation and Darryl Williams v. State Farm Fire & Casualty Company
accommodation_description: No disability accommodation request; case concerns alleged racial discrimination in insurance claim handling for African-American policyholders in majority Black ZIP codes.
key_holding: The court denied State Farm's motion to strike the amended class definition, finding it is not facially overbroad because it limits class members to those who had claims denied or treated as presumptively fraudulent, and also denied Plaintiffs' motion to dismiss State Farm's counterclaim for rescission as viable.
brief_summary: Connectors Realty Group Corporation and Darryl Williams sued State Farm Fire & Casualty Company alleging the insurer treated insurance claims from Black-majority ZIP codes in southern Cook County and Chicago's south side as presumptively fraudulent, violating 42 U.S.C. § 1981 and the Fair Housing Act; State Farm counterclaimed seeking rescission of the insurance policy. The court denied State Farm's motion to strike the amended class allegations (finding the proposed class definition was not facially overbroad) and denied Plaintiffs' motion to dismiss the counterclaim (finding the rescission claim viable under Illinois law).
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Buonomo v. Optimum Outcomes, Inc., 301 F.R.D. 292 (N.D. Ill. 2014)
Brunner v. Liautaud, 2015 WL 1598106 (N.D. Ill. 2015)
AnchorBank, FSB v. Hofer, 649 F.3d 610 (7th Cir. 2011)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: This case involves insurance claim discrimination based on race/zip code, not housing discrimination or reasonable accommodation. Plaintiffs allege violations of 42 U.S.C. § 1981 and the Fair Housing Act, but the FHA claim is not developed or analyzed in this opinion. The opinion addresses only class certification and counterclaim viability, not the merits of any FHA claim.
fha_claims.disposition: Motion to Strike Class Allegations Denied; Motion to Dismiss Counterclaim Denied
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied State Farm's motion to strike the amended class allegations, finding the class definition not facially overbroad at the pleading stage. The court also denied Plaintiffs' motion to dismiss State Farm's counterclaim for rescission, finding the remedy viable under Illinois law. The FHA claims themselves were not addressed on the merits in this opinion.

case_name: Richard Johnson v. Barry Flannery
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges landlord retaliated against him for reporting housing code violations to the health department by calling him racial slurs and attempting to evict him
key_holding: Plaintiff failed to state a retaliation claim under § 3617 because reporting housing code violations to a health department is not a protected activity under the Fair Housing Act; plaintiff's allegations about being called racial slurs do not save the claim because retaliation focuses on what the plaintiff did, not who he is.
brief_summary: Richard Johnson, a white tenant, sued his landlord Barry Flannery alleging retaliation under the Fair Housing Act for reporting building code and health violations to a government agency. The court dismissed the case with prejudice, finding that Johnson failed to state a viable retaliation claim because reporting housing code violations to a health department is not a protected activity under the FHA, and Johnson's allegations about being called racial slurs do not constitute protected activity under the retaliation provision.
key_cases_cited: Wetzel v. Glen St. Andrew Living Cmty., LLC, 901 F.3d 856 (7th Cir. 2018)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged retaliation under 42 U.S.C. § 3617 for reporting landlord to health department for failure to make repairs. Court held that reporting housing code violations to a government agency is not a protected activity under the Fair Housing Act (which protects only those exercising rights under §§ 3603-3606 related to discrimination based on protected class). Therefore, the alleged retaliation is not cognizable under the FHA's anti-retaliation provision, and the complaint fails to state a claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) claim for unlawful debt collection communications and false representation regarding debt collector status
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff lacked Article III standing under the FDCPA because he failed to allege a concrete injury-in-fact. Allegations of emotional distress, confusion, and frustration without detrimental action in response to the defendant's conduct are insufficient to establish standing under Seventh Circuit precedent (Pennell v. Global Trust Management, LLC, 990 F.3d 1041 (7th Cir. 2021)).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: No FHA claims alleged. Complaint alleges negligence, failure to act, publicly depicting child abuse, and publicly depicting sexual exploitation of a minor under state law and general federal law (47 U.S.C. § 230).
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint fails to state a claim under 47 U.S.C. § 230(c)(1), which provides that interactive computer service providers cannot be held liable as publishers of information provided by third parties. Plaintiff alleged only that defendant failed to remove videos posted by another user, not that defendant created or posted the content. FOSTA exception under 18 U.S.C. § 1595 does not apply because complaint does not allege facts constituting a violation of 18 U.S.C. § 1591 (sex trafficking of minors for commercial sex acts).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Removal of architectural barriers at hotel facility including: (1) designated disabled parking or passenger loading zone with access aisle and striping; (2) accessible men's restroom compliant with ADA specifications
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied defendant's motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(1) for lack of standing and Rule 12(b)(6) for failure to state a claim. Plaintiff adequately alleged concrete injury (physical harm from architectural barriers), real and immediate threat of future injury (regular travel to Chicago, prior visits, intent to return but for violations), and sufficient factual allegations of specific ADA violations under Title III. Tester status does not deprive plaintiff of standing.

case_name: Jamal A. Akbar v. Interstate Realty Management Company
accommodation_description: Akbar alleged that Interstate denied his rental application based on his disability status (receipt of disability benefits income) rather than income qualifications.
key_holding: Akbar was rejected based on his income ($731/month disability benefits vs. $746 rent requirement) not his disability, and he presented no evidence that Interstate's Admissions and Continued Occupancy Policy caused or predictably caused discrimination against applicants with disabilities.
brief_summary: Jamal Akbar, a disabled individual receiving disability benefits, sued Interstate Realty Management after being denied housing at a LIHTC property for failing to meet minimum income requirements; Akbar claimed the denial constituted disability discrimination under the FHA. The court granted summary judgment for Interstate, finding Akbar was rejected based on income alone with no evidence of intentional discrimination or discriminatory effect from the housing policy.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dept. of Hous. & Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
City of Joliet, Ill. v. New W., L.P., 825 F.3d 827 (7th Cir. 2016)
Graham v. Connor, 490 U.S. 386 (1989)
Colbert v. City of Chicago, 851 F.3d 649 (7th Cir. 2017)
Ricci v. DeStefano, 557 U.S. 557 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to present sufficient facts to plausibly suggest intentional discrimination based on disability. The undisputed evidence shows plaintiff was rejected based on failure to meet minimum income requirements ($8,772 annual income vs. $26,856 required), not disability status. Defendant presented evidence of accepting applicants with disabilities, including those receiving Section 8 assistance.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Disparate impact analysis examines the effects of policies, not one-off decisions. Plaintiff presented no evidence that defendant's Admissions and Continued Occupancy Policy (minimum income requirement) caused or predictably caused discrimination against applicants with disabilities. The same evidence defeating the disparate treatment claim also defeats the disparate impact claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (constitutional due process claim)
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 1983 requires conduct by a person acting under color of state law. Although defendant contracted with the Chicago Housing Authority, a private corporation managing LIHTC housing does not act under color of state law merely by virtue of that contract. Plaintiff presented no evidence that defendant was delegated a public function or was under state control.

case_name: Curtis K. Jackson, Sr. v. Chicago Housing Authority, et al.
subsidy_program: Housing Choice Voucher, Project Based Voucher
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a person with disabilities affecting hearing, concentrating, learning, reading, speaking, shopping, and walking, alleges he was denied access to a disabled parking space, laundry room, and other programs and services at his housing.
key_holding: The court granted CHA's motion to dismiss because plaintiff failed to allege personal involvement by CHA defendants in any constitutional violations or FHA/ADA discrimination, and his allegations showed CHA defendants actually helped him obtain housing and address problems at Lake Street Studios.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Curtis K. Jackson sued the Chicago Housing Authority and its employees alleging constitutional violations, ADA violations, and FHA violations related to his Housing Choice Voucher housing at Lake Street Studios, claiming he was denied disabled parking, laundry room access, and other services due to his disabilities. The court granted CHA's motion to dismiss, finding Jackson failed to adequately allege personal involvement by the CHA defendants in any discriminatory conduct, as his own allegations showed CHA employees assisted him with his housing transfer.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Taylor v. Hughes, 26 F.4th 419 (7th Cir. 2022)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Access to laundry room and disabled parking space; habitable unit conditions (removal of filthy conditions, repair of light fixture, remediation of flood damage)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that Jackson's ADA and FHA allegations regarding denial of services and programs due to disability were directed at Lake Street Studios, not the CHA defendants. The court dismissed the CHA defendants for lack of personal involvement in any alleged violation, applying the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard without reaching the substantive elements of the reasonable accommodation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged discrimination in provision of services, programs, and activities at Lake Street Studios apartment
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the CHA defendants from the disparate treatment claim because Jackson's allegations of discrimination were directed at Lake Street Studios and its employees, not the CHA defendants, and Jackson failed to allege personal involvement by the CHA defendants in any violation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation for informing the CHA of housing problems at Lake Street Studios
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the retaliation claim against the CHA defendants because Jackson's allegations showed that the CHA defendants actually helped him remedy the situation at Lake Street Studios, contradicting any inference of retaliatory conduct.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Constitutional violations (due process, equal protection); ADA Title II claims
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed constitutional claims against the CHA defendants under Monell, finding that Jackson failed to allege either personal involvement by the CHA defendants or a widespread custom or practice of constitutional violations by the CHA, and that the CHA defendants actually assisted Jackson rather than injured him.

case_name: Curtis K. Jackson, Sr. v. Chicago Housing Authority, et al.
accommodation_description: Pro se plaintiff with disabilities affecting hearing, concentration, learning, and walking alleges that Lake Street Studios denied him access to programs, services, and activities including the laundry room and a disabled parking space.
key_holding: The court dismissed architect Susan King because Jackson failed to adequately allege her personal involvement in any constitutional violation or that she acted under color of state law; Jackson's FHA and ADA claims against King were based on alleged misconduct of Lake Street Studios employees rather than King's architectural design work.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Curtis K. Jackson sued the Chicago Housing Authority and architect Susan F. King alleging constitutional violations and violations of the ADA and Fair Housing Act in connection with his Housing Choice Voucher at Lake Street Studios, claiming disability-based discrimination including denial of access to a disabled parking space and laundry facilities. The court granted King's motion to dismiss, finding Jackson failed to allege King's personal involvement in any constitutional violation or that she acted under color of state law, as required to hold an architect liable for private conduct.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Colbert v. City of Chicago, 851 F.3d 649 (7th Cir. 2017)
Barnes v. City of Centralia, Ill., 943 F.3d 826 (7th Cir. 2019)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Disabled parking space at Lake Street Studios
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that defendant King was personally involved in the alleged denial of accommodations. The FHA claims were based on misconduct of Lake Street Studios employees, not King, and plaintiff did not allege King was involved in or aware of the incidents underlying the disability claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Access to laundry room at Lake Street Studios
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that defendant King was personally involved in the alleged denial of accommodations. The FHA claims were based on misconduct of Lake Street Studios employees, not King, and plaintiff did not allege King was involved in or aware of the incidents underlying the disability claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Constitutional violations under § 1983 and ADA Title II
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege that defendant King acted under color of state law, which is required for constitutional claims. King was a private architect/designer with no alleged meeting of the minds with state actors, delegation of public function, or control by state actors.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Debt Collection Practices Act claims for misrepresentation of debts and attempted collection of unauthorized debts related to attorney's fees and fines imposed by condominium association
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted summary judgment against plaintiff on FDCPA claims against Lavieri based on claim preclusion (res judicata), as the claims arose from the same transaction and nucleus of operative facts as the earlier FHA lawsuit in which Lavieri was dismissed with prejudice by settlement agreement. Claims against Gardiner were barred by the doctrine of claim splitting, as both suits involved the same parties and claims but final judgment had not yet been entered in the first suit.

case_name: Sullivan v. Liberty Mutual Insurance Company
accommodation_description: No accommodation requested; case concerns alleged race and sexual orientation discrimination by insurer in processing property damage claim
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' claims for injunctive and declaratory relief for lack of standing because their cancellation of the insurance policy eliminated any real or immediate threat of future injury, but denied the motion to dismiss plaintiffs' Fair Housing Act disparate treatment claim based on race and sexual orientation, finding the allegations sufficient to survive dismissal.
brief_summary: Terrie Sullivan and Veronica Rodriguez sued Liberty Mutual Insurance Company alleging the insurer discriminated against them based on race and sexual orientation when processing their homeowner insurance claim for water damage, seeking damages and class certification under the Fair Housing Act and other statutes. The court granted the motion to dismiss in part, dismissing plaintiffs' claims for injunctive and declaratory relief for lack of Article III standing because their cancellation of the insurance policy before filing suit eliminated any possibility of future injury, but denied the motion to dismiss the underlying disparate treatment claims finding the allegations sufficient to proceed to discovery.
key_cases_cited: O'Shea v. Littleton, 414 U.S. 488 (1974)
City of Los Angeles v. Lyons, 461 U.S. 95 (1983)
Holmes v. Fisher, 854 F.2d 229 (7th Cir. 1988)
Laurens v. Volvo Cars of North America, LLC, 868 F.3d 622 (7th Cir. 2017)
Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins, 578 U.S. 330 (2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss FHA disparate treatment claim, finding that statements attributed to adjuster Sherbafi evincing animus based on race and sexual orientation, combined with pretext in the stated basis for claim denial (sump pump in home lacking basement or sump pump), raised sufficient inference of discrimination and nexus to entitle plaintiffs to discovery.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1982; Illinois Human Rights Act (IHRA) Article 3; state contract law; breach of contract; bad faith; Illinois Insurance Code § 155
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss non-FHA claims. IHRA exhaustion defense is affirmative, not jurisdictional, and plaintiffs adequately alleged Article 3 claim not subject to exhaustion. Statute of limitations defense rests on facts outside complaint and cannot be resolved at pleadings stage.

case_name: Nathaniel Satterfield, Jr. v. HSBC Bank USA, N.A., Wilmington Savings Fund Society FSB, Victor Vita, and Carrington Mortgage Services LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges Defendants violated § 3617 by using unlawful eviction proceedings aided by the state court judicial system to threaten, intimidate, and coerce him into remortgaging or leaving his property; no specific reasonable accommodation request is identified.
key_holding: The court lacks subject matter jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine because Satterfield's alleged injuries—loss of his home, failure to maintain the property, and failure to pay property taxes—were completed only when the state court ordered eviction, making his FHA claim not independent of the state court judgment; moreover, Satterfield had a reasonable opportunity to raise his FHA claims as equitable defenses in the state court eviction proceedings.
brief_summary: Nathaniel Satterfield sued HSBC Bank USA, N.A. and related defendants alleging they wrongfully obtained possession of his home through meritless state court eviction proceedings and violated the Fair Housing Act by intimidating him using the threat of unlawful eviction. The court dismissed the case for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine, holding that Satterfield's claimed injuries arose directly from the state court eviction orders and his FHA claim was therefore not independent of those judgments, and that he had a reasonable opportunity to raise his civil rights claims as defenses in the state eviction proceedings.
key_cases_cited: Hemmer v. Ind. State Bd. of Animal Health, 532 F.3d 610 (7th Cir. 2008)
Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Saudi Basic Indus. Corp., 544 U.S. 280 (2005)
Lyons v. Gene B. Glick Co., 844 F. App'x 866 (7th Cir. 2021)
Andrade v. City of Hammond, 9 F.4th 947 (7th Cir. 2021)
Holt v. Lake Cnty. Bd. of Comm'rs, 408 F.3d 335 (7th Cir. 2005)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges interference, coercion, intimidation, and threatening conduct related to eviction, not a request for reasonable accommodation.
fha_claims.reasoning: The FHA interference/coercion claim is barred by the Rooker-Feldman doctrine because plaintiff's alleged injuries (loss of house, failure to maintain property, failure to pay taxes) were complete only when the state court ordered the eviction. The claim is inextricably intertwined with the state court judgment and plaintiff had a reasonable opportunity to raise FHA defenses in the state eviction proceedings.

source_file: 9680646_2022_Williams Jr v. Heartland Realty Investors, Inc._ilnd
case_name: Andy Hope Williams, Jr., and Vonita Cruz v. Heartland Realty Investors, Inc., Heartland Willowbrook, LLC, d/b/a Willowbrook Apartment Homes, and Starr, Bejgiert, Zink, and Rowells
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs Andy Williams and Vonita Cruz, proceeding pro se, brought Fair Housing Act claims against Heartland landlords and FDCPA claims against Heartland's law firm SBZR; the FHA claims are not substantively analyzed in this ruling dismissing only the FDCPA claims against SBZR.
key_holding: The Court granted SBZR's motion to dismiss the FDCPA claims because SBZR did not make actionable misrepresentations: Heartland Realty Investors, Inc. had authority to bring the eviction as agent for Heartland Willowbrook, LLC, the lease permitted attorney's fees for the prevailing party, the federal lawsuit did not constitute a pending eviction proceeding under Illinois law, and SBZR properly attached the required demand notice to the eviction complaint.
