brief_summary: Pro se tenants Andy Williams and Vonita Cruz sued their landlord Heartland Realty Investors and its law firm SBZR, alleging Fair Housing Act violations against the landlord and FDCPA violations against the law firm for misrepresentations in a state court eviction proceeding. The Court granted SBZR's motion to dismiss the FDCPA claims because SBZR did not violate the FDCPA—Heartland Realty had authority to pursue eviction as the landlord's agent, the lease permitted attorney's fees, and SBZR attached all required documents to the eviction complaint.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Marquez v. Weinstein, Pinson & Riley, P.S., 836 F.3d 808 (7th Cir. 2016)
Harris v. United States, 13 F.4th 623 (7th Cir. 2021)
Skinner v. Switzer, 562 U.S. 521 (2011)
Doe v. Columbia Coll. Chicago, 933 F.3d 849 (7th Cir. 2019)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: FDCPA claim against law firm for alleged misrepresentations in state court eviction complaint, including: (1) misrepresenting Heartland Realty Investors, Inc. was entitled to possession; (2) misrepresenting SBZR was entitled to attorney's fees; (3) filing eviction complaint in violation of Illinois procedural rules; (4) failing to attach required notices to eviction complaint.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiffs failed to state a plausible FDCPA claim because: (1) Heartland Realty Investors, Inc. had authority as agent to bring eviction; (2) lease permitted attorney's fees to prevailing party; (3) federal lawsuit is separate from state eviction proceeding; and (4) required notices were attached to complaint. All FDCPA arguments lacked factual or legal basis.

source_file: 9680683_2022_Williams Jr v. Heartland Realty Investors, Inc._ilnd
case_name: Andy Hope Williams, Jr. v. Heartland Realty Investors, Inc.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request—case involves alleged selective enforcement of lease rules (grill prohibition) based on plaintiffs' race and national origin.
key_holding: Plaintiffs adequately stated FHA and § 1981 claims by alleging they were the only Hebrew Israelite and Puerto Rican family in the apartment complex and were selectively targeted with grill enforcement while other tenants were permitted to use grills.
brief_summary: Black and Puerto Rican tenants sued their private apartment complex alleging race and national origin discrimination when the landlord selectively enforced a grill prohibition against them while allowing other tenants to use grills, then refused to renew their lease. The court denied the motion to dismiss plaintiffs' FHA disparate treatment, interference, and § 1981 claims, finding sufficient allegations of selective enforcement based on protected characteristics.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Swanson v. Citibank, N.A.
Wigginton v. Bank of America Corp.
Griffin v. Breckenridge

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Right to have a grill on patio and continue residency
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs adequately alleged interference with protected activities under § 3617 by alleging defendants threatened non-renewal and legal action based on grill use, while treating other tenants differently. Court found allegations sufficient to survive motion to dismiss under Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to renew lease based on race and national origin
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs adequately alleged disparate treatment under § 3604(a) by alleging they were the only Hebrew Israelite and Puerto Rican family in the complex and that defendants treated other tenants differently regarding grill infractions. Allegations survive motion to dismiss despite defendants' alternative explanation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation for questioning management about grill infraction notice
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs adequately alleged retaliation under the FHA by alleging defendants non-renewed their lease after plaintiffs questioned management about the grill infraction. Court accepted allegations as true and drew inferences in plaintiffs' favor at pleading stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983, § 1985(3), § 1981 race discrimination, Illinois common law fraud, ICFA, breach of contract, Illinois Retaliatory Eviction Act, Illinois Constitution due process, Illinois Human Rights Act, intentional infliction of emotional distress
fha_claims.reasoning: § 1983 and § 1985(3) claims dismissed with prejudice because defendants are private companies and plaintiffs failed to allege state action or conspiracy with state actors. § 1981 claim survives because plaintiffs adequately alleged selective enforcement of lease terms based on race. Fraud and ICFA claims dismissed without prejudice for failure to plead with particularity under Rule 9(b). Breach of contract claim survives. Retaliatory Eviction Act claim dismissed with prejudice because plaintiffs did not allege complaints to governmental authorities about property conditions. Illinois Constitution due process claim dismissed with prejudice by agreement. IHRA claim survives because Article 3 does not require exhaustion of administrative remedies. IIED claim dismissed without prejudice for failure to allege conduct was extreme and outrageous.

source_file: 9681431_2022_Talley v. The Housing Authority of Cook County_ilnd
case_name: Charles Talley, Jr. and Christopher J. Bonds v. The Housing Authority of Cook County, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested a voucher for a two-bedroom dwelling and moving papers to transfer to accessible housing as a reasonable accommodation for their disabilities.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' failure-to-accommodate claims because plaintiffs never formally requested repairs as an accommodation, and the Housing Authority did not have authority to compel landlords to make repairs; additionally, the Housing Authority approved the voucher request and exhibits show it issued the moving papers, defeating the claim that plaintiffs were denied the requested accommodation.
brief_summary: Two Black disabled tenants using Section 8 Housing Choice Vouchers sued their landlord and the Housing Authority of Cook County for disability discrimination (failure to accommodate) and race discrimination under the Fair Housing Act. The district court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, dismissing all federal claims with prejudice, finding that plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege failure-to-accommodate claims because they never requested repairs as an accommodation and the Housing Authority approved their transfer request and issued moving papers, and also failed to adequately plead race discrimination claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Watters v. Homeowners' Ass'n at Preserve at Bridgewater, 48 F.4th 779 (7th Cir. 2022)
Khan v. Bland, 630 F.3d 519 (7th Cir. 2010)
Swanson v. Citibank, N.A., 614 F.3d 400 (7th Cir. 2010)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs sought the Housing Authority's assistance in forcing their landlords (Lee and Hart) to maintain and repair the rental property, including fixing water leaks, flooding, roof and foundation issues, heating problems, and non-functioning appliances, as an accommodation for their disabilities.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found no allegation that plaintiffs requested help maintaining their home as an accommodation, and that the Housing Authority lacked the power to compel private landlords to make repairs beyond terminating contracts. The complaint failed to plausibly allege a failure to accommodate under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested a voucher for a two-bedroom apartment and moving papers as a reasonable accommodation for their disabilities to enable them to relocate to accessible housing.
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint alleged the Housing Authority approved the request and issued the voucher and moving documents, contradicting the claim of failure to accommodate. The court found no plausible allegation that the Housing Authority failed to provide the requested accommodation, and that the Housing Authority was not responsible for finding housing for voucher participants.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged the Housing Authority discriminated based on race by refusing to actively assist them in finding accessible housing in the Village of Hoffman Estates and instead steering them toward an apartment complex in Evanston.
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint failed to identify which individual(s) allegedly discriminated or plausibly allege that discrimination occurred. Plaintiffs did not allege the Housing Authority was aware of their race or provide facts showing disparate treatment compared to white residents, and the Housing Authority was not required to actively assist in finding housing.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged Lee discriminated based on race by refusing to make timely repairs to the leased property.
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint contained no factual allegations supporting racial discrimination, such as whether Lee knew plaintiffs were Black or any facts suggesting race motivated her refusal to repair. Legal conclusions without factual support are insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of lease, breach of warranty of habitability, retaliatory eviction, negligent infliction of emotional distress, intentional infliction of emotional distress; § 1983 due process claims against Housing Authority
fha_claims.reasoning: The § 1983 due process claims against the Housing Authority failed because plaintiffs did not allege municipal action (express policy, widespread practice, or final policymaker decision) causing the constitutional deprivation. State-law claims were dismissed without prejudice when all federal claims were dismissed, and the court declined supplemental jurisdiction.

source_file: 9681456_2022_County of Cook, IL v. Wells Fargo _ Co._ilnd
case_name: County of Cook, Illinois v. Wells Fargo & Co.
accommodation_description: N/A - this is a third-party standing case where Cook County claims Wells Fargo's discriminatory mortgage lending and servicing practices caused minority borrowers to default, increasing the County's foreclosure-related expenditures
key_holding: The County's FHA claims failed because its key expert witnesses were excluded under Rule 702 for unreliable methodologies, leaving the County without evidence to establish that Wells Fargo intentionally discriminated against minority borrowers or that such discrimination proximately caused the County's claimed injuries.
brief_summary: Cook County sued Wells Fargo alleging that the bank's mortgage lending and servicing practices discriminated against minority borrowers, causing higher default and foreclosure rates that increased the County's expenditures on foreclosure-related services. The court granted Wells Fargo's summary judgment motion after excluding the County's expert witnesses under Rule 702 for unreliable statistical methodologies, finding the County lacked sufficient evidence of intentional discrimination or proximate cause.
key_cases_cited: Bank of Am. Corp. v. City of Miami, 137 S. Ct. 1296 (2017)
Tex. Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Cmtys. Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
City of Oakland v. Wells Fargo & Co., 14 F.4th 1030 (9th Cir. 2021) (en banc)
Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals, Inc., 509 U.S. 579 (1993)
Dura Auto. Sys. of Ind., Inc. v. CTS Corp., 285 F.3d 609 (7th Cir. 2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: County failed to present admissible evidence of intentional discrimination in Wells Fargo's servicing practices. Expert opinions establishing statistical disparities in loan modification denials and foreclosure rates were excluded under Rule 702 for methodological unreliability. Without such evidence, County cannot establish that Wells Fargo intentionally discriminated against minority borrowers or that any discrimination proximately caused the County's claimed injuries.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: County failed to establish robust causality between Wells Fargo's policies and disparate foreclosure outcomes for minority borrowers. The excluded expert opinions were the sole basis for demonstrating such causality. Additionally, the expert analyses improperly aggregated loans from multiple lenders and did not account for non-racial borrower characteristics relevant to lending and servicing decisions, preventing reliable attribution of disparate impact to Wells Fargo's policies.

case_name: Azroui v. Walega
accommodation_description: Not applicable - this case involves national origin discrimination in refusal to pay for property damage, not a disability accommodation request.
key_holding: The court granted the defendants' motion to stay the federal case pending resolution of the parallel state court proceedings, finding that Colorado River abstention factors weighed in favor of staying the case to avoid piecemeal litigation given the state court's significantly advanced progress.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Ghaleb Azroui (from Jordan) sued Avenue One Management Corporation and its Board directors under the Fair Housing Act alleging national origin discrimination for the Board's refusal to pay for tree damage to his car. The court granted the motion to stay the federal case pending resolution of a parallel state court case involving the same underlying property damage claim, finding that Colorado River abstention factors favored staying the case to avoid inconsistent judgments and piecemeal litigation.
key_cases_cited: Colorado River Water Conservation Dist. v. United States, 424 U.S. 800 (1976)
Clark v. Lacy, 376 F.3d 682 (7th Cir. 2004)
Loughran v. Wells Fargo Bank, N.A., 2 F.4th 640 (7th Cir. 2021)
DePuy Synthes Sales, Inc. v. OrthoLA, Inc., 953 F.3d 469 (7th Cir. 2020)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to pay for damage to plaintiff's car caused by fallen tree branch
fha_claims.reasoning: The surviving FHA claim alleging national-origin discrimination based on refusal to pay for tree damage was not decided on the merits. Instead, the federal case was stayed in favor of the parallel state court proceeding because the state law claim regarding the duty to pay is embedded in both suits, and resolution in state court would dispose of the federal claim's factual predicate. The court applied Colorado River abstention factors, finding that avoiding piecemeal litigation and the state case's advanced progress weighed heavily in favor of staying the federal action pending resolution of the state suit.

case_name: Emily Evans v. 210 East Pearson Condominium Association
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that defendants deliver packages directly to her apartment door as they do for other residents, as her disabilities prevent her from retrieving packages from the lobby.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss the reasonable accommodation claim (Count I) because plaintiff sufficiently alleged she requested package delivery accommodation before defendants initiated state court proceedings, rejecting defendants' ripeness argument; however, the court dismissed the interference claims (Counts II and IV) without prejudice for failure to allege intentional discrimination.
brief_summary: Emily Evans sued her condominium association and property management company alleging they violated the FHA by refusing to provide package delivery service to her apartment as a reasonable accommodation for her disabilities. The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss the failure to accommodate claim, finding plaintiff's claim ripe because she requested the accommodation before defendants initiated eviction proceedings, but dismissed the interference and retaliation claims without prejudice for failure to plead intentional discrimination.
key_cases_cited: Good Shepherd Manor Found., Inc. v. City of Momence, 323 F.3d 557 (7th Cir. 2003)
Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009)
Village of Palatine, Ill. v. United States, 37 F.4th 1230 (7th Cir. 1994)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Package delivery service to plaintiff's apartment door, as allegedly provided to other residents, to accommodate plaintiff's physical and mental disabilities that prevent her from retrieving packages from the lobby
fha_claims.reasoning: Court rejected defendants' ripeness argument, finding that plaintiff sufficiently alleged prior notice of disability and a request for reasonable accommodation before defendants' July 13 state court action, and that defendants had sufficient time to review the July 12 formal accommodation request. Claim survives motion to dismiss and proceeds to next stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege the essential element of intentional discrimination required under 42 U.S.C. § 3617. The record shows defendants took corrective action based on disturbances caused by plaintiff to building staff and residents, not because of her disability or protected activity. Court dismissed without prejudice, allowing amendment to specify how disturbances were disability-related or provide other evidence of intentional discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Package delivery service to plaintiff's apartment door under the Illinois Human Rights Act (IHRA), parallel to Count I FHA claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied same FHA analysis to IHRA claim and rejected ripeness argument on identical grounds as Count I. Claim survives motion to dismiss because plaintiff established sufficient prior notice and timely request for accommodation before defendants' state court action.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Parallel IHRA retaliation claim under 775 ILCS 5/3-105.1 dismissed on same grounds as Count II: plaintiff failed to plausibly allege intentional discrimination as an essential element. Court found record showed corrective action based on disturbances, not disability-based retaliation. Dismissed without prejudice with leave to amend.

case_name: Amanda Quist v. Park Tower Condominium Association and The Habitat Company
accommodation_description: Permission to keep an emotional support dog in a building with a no-dog policy, supported by documentation from her care provider including an offer of a three-way call, email/fax/phone contact information, and receipts from doctor visits demonstrating an ongoing therapeutic relationship.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss plaintiff's IIED claim (Count VII), holding that the totality of allegations—including two uses of a racial slur, denial of an emotional support animal accommodation, an escort of three security officers to retrieve packages, and refusal to return plaintiff's furniture—plausibly stated extreme and outrageous conduct under Illinois law.
brief_summary: Amanda Quist, a Black woman with documented mental health disabilities requiring an emotional support dog, applied to purchase a Chicago condominium but was denied her reasonable accommodation request by the Association and its property manager. During the process, Association employees twice referred to Quist using a racial slur, forced her to be escorted by three security officers to retrieve her packages, and refused to return her furniture, causing her to forfeit her earnest money and incur significant additional costs before purchasing a substitute unit. Defendants moved to dismiss Quist's nuisance claim (Count VI, voluntarily dismissed) and IIED claim (Count VII); the court denied dismissal of the IIED claim, finding that the combination of accommodation denial, racially derogatory treatment, and withholding of property plausibly constituted extreme and outrageous conduct.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Richards v. U.S. Steel, 869 F.3d 557 (7th Cir. 2017)
Stevens v. Hollywood Towers & Condo. Ass'n, 836 F. Supp. 2d 800 (N.D. Ill. 2011)
Van Stan v. Fancy Colours & Co., 125 F.3d 563 (7th Cir. 1997)
Bannon v. Univ. of Chicago, 503 F.3d 623 (7th Cir. 2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to keep an emotional support animal (dog) in a condominium building with a no-dog policy; plaintiff has severe PTSD, anxiety, and other mental health conditions requiring the ESA
fha_claims.reasoning: The opinion addresses only the motion to dismiss Count VII (IIED claim), not the FHA claims themselves (Counts I and II). The FHA reasonable accommodation claim survives the motion to dismiss and remains pending; the court does not reach the merits of the FHA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Intentional infliction of emotional distress (state law claim); also includes ADA and state/county/city disability discrimination claims (Counts III, IV, V)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied defendants' motion to dismiss Count VII (IIED) under Illinois law, finding that plaintiff adequately pleaded extreme and outrageous conduct (racial slurs, refusal to accept medical documentation, humiliating treatment, denial of accommodation) and the remaining elements (intent and causation of severe emotional distress). The court applied the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard and found the allegations sufficient at the pleading stage.

case_name: Williams v. Village of Hazel Crest
accommodation_description: No accommodation request - case involves alleged race discrimination in municipal sewage flooding rather than a disability accommodation request under § 3604(f)(3)(B)
key_holding: The FHA claim was dismissed because Williams's allegations that the Village jetted sewage into her property because she is Black were conclusory and unsupported by factual allegations suggesting discriminatory intent.
brief_summary: Deanna Williams, a Black property owner, sued the Village of Hazel Crest and Mayor Vernard Alsberry alleging the Village repeatedly flooded her property with sewage and discriminated against her because of her race in violation of § 3604(b). The court dismissed the FHA claim with prejudice, finding Williams failed to allege sufficient factual support for her conclusory allegation that the Village acted with discriminatory intent based on her race.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege intentional race discrimination under § 3604(b). The complaint contained only conclusory statements that the Village jetted sewage into her home because she is Black, with no factual allegations regarding the Village's discriminatory motive or any statements or actions suggesting race was a factor. Additionally, the claim failed because plaintiff did not allege constructive eviction or unavailability of the dwelling, which are required elements under Bloch v. Frischholz for post-acquisition § 3604 claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fifth Amendment unconstitutional taking claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied defendants' motion to dismiss the unconstitutional taking claim under the Fifth Amendment, finding that government-induced flooding can constitute a taking and need not be permanent to be compensable. Defendants' arguments that plaintiff failed to allege deprivation of use or permanent appropriation were rejected as unsupported by case law or contrary to Supreme Court precedent in Arkansas Game & Fish Commission v. U.S.

case_name: Belinda J. Rossetti and Ezra J. Rossetti v. Haim Saban, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege Fair Housing Act and racial discrimination claims arising from fraudulent inducement to sign a lease for student housing, but no specific disability accommodation request is made or analyzed.
key_holding: The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(2) for lack of personal jurisdiction and Rule 12(b)(3) for improper venue because Defendants lacked minimum contacts with Illinois and the lease contained a Pennsylvania forum-selection clause.
brief_summary: Illinois-resident plaintiffs sued California-domiciled defendant property owners and managers alleging fraud, consumer protection violations, and Fair Housing Act claims stemming from alleged misrepresentations about the condition of a Pennsylvania student apartment leased by their son. The court dismissed the case under Rule 12(b)(2) for lack of personal jurisdiction because Defendants had no minimum contacts with Illinois, and alternatively under Rule 12(b)(3) because the lease contained a Pennsylvania forum-selection clause and venue was improper in Illinois.
key_cases_cited: Bell v. Hood, 327 U.S. 678 (1946)
Daimler AG v. Bauman, 571 U.S. 117 (2014)
Int'l Shoe Co. v. Wash., 326 U.S. 310 (1945)
Walden v. Fiore, 571 U.S. 277 (2014)
Tamburo v. Dworkin, 601 F.3d 693 (7th Cir. 2010)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged fraud, ICFA, UDTPA, mail fraud, wire fraud, bank fraud, extortion, RICO, and discrimination under the Fair Housing Act and Civil Rights Act of 1866. The FHA and Civil Rights Act claims were alleged but not substantively analyzed by the court.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the case for lack of personal jurisdiction under Rule 12(b)(2) and improper venue under Rule 12(b)(3). The court found that none of the defendants had sufficient minimum contacts with Illinois, and the lease contained a mandatory forum-selection clause requiring litigation in Pennsylvania. The court did not reach the merits of any claim, including the FHA discrimination claim.

source_file: 9682801_2023_Huskey v. State Farm Fire _ Casualty Company_ilnd
case_name: Huskey v. State Farm Fire & Casualty Company
accommodation_description: Black homeowners allege State Farm's algorithmic claims-processing system creates racial disparities in homeowners insurance claim handling
key_holding: The court allowed Plaintiffs' disparate-impact claim under § 3604(b) to proceed, finding the complaint adequately alleged statistical disparities, a specific policy (algorithmic claims-processing), and a plausible causal connection; but dismissed § 3604(a) for failure to allege constructive eviction and § 3605 based on Seventh Circuit precedent that insurers are not in the business of covered real estate transactions.
brief_summary: Black homeowners Jacqueline Huskey and Riian Wynn sued State Farm Fire & Casualty Company alleging that its use of algorithmic decision-making tools in claims processing created statistically significant racial disparities in how it handled their homeowners insurance claims. The court granted in part and denied in part State Farm's motion to dismiss, dismissing the § 3604(a) claim for failure to allege constructive eviction and the § 3605 claim based on Seventh Circuit precedent, but allowed the § 3604(b) disparate impact claim to proceed because Plaintiffs adequately pleaded a statistical disparity, a specific policy, and a causal connection.
key_cases_cited: Tex. Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
NAACP v. Am. Fam. Mut. Ins. Co., 978 F.2d 287 (7th Cir. 1992)
Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009)
Mac's Shell Serv., Inc. v. Shell Oil Prods. Co., 559 U.S. 175 (2010)
Humana, Inc. v. Forsyth, 525 U.S. 299 (1999)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Under Seventh Circuit precedent (Bloch v. Frischholz), § 3604(a) requires that a dwelling be made 'unavailable' or that plaintiffs be 'compelled to leave,' analogous to constructive eviction. Neither plaintiff adequately alleged that State Farm's discriminatory delay rendered their homes unfit for occupancy or that they vacated within a reasonable time. Huskey alleged only 'mere diminution' in property value; Wynn's vague allegation that she 'lost use of her home' does not plausibly connect State Farm's delay to uninhabitability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Disparate-impact claim challenging State Farm's use of algorithmic decision-making tools in claims processing that allegedly result in longer processing times, additional paperwork requirements, and more interactions for Black policyholders compared to white policyholders.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs adequately pleaded a disparate-impact claim under § 3604(b) by alleging: (1) a statistical disparity (survey showing Black policyholders experienced longer wait times, more required paperwork, and more interactions with State Farm employees, with disparities statistically significant at p < 0.05 or p < 0.10); (2) a specific policy (State Farm's use of algorithmic decision-making tools since 2018 to automate claims processing); and (3) a causal connection (plausible inference that machine-learning algorithms prone to bias produced the racial disparities). At the pleading stage, plaintiffs need only allege enough facts for a plausible inference of causation, not prove every element. The survey methodology need not be airtight, and the contrast between Wynn's experience and her similarly situated white neighbor's experience bolsters plausibility.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3605 challenging discrimination in residential real estate-related transactions (specifically, homeowners insurance claims processing).
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 3605 prohibits discrimination by entities engaged in 'residential real estate-related transactions,' defined to include making or purchasing loans or providing financial assistance for purchasing, constructing, improving, repairing, or maintaining a dwelling. The Seventh Circuit held in American Family Mutual Insurance Co. v. NAACP that insurers are not entities engaged in covered transactions under § 3605 because insurance is not 'financial assistance'—payment runs from customer to insurer, not the reverse. Although plaintiffs attempted to reframe claims processing as providing 'financial assistance' analogous to a loan, the court found this effort unconvincing and binding Seventh Circuit precedent controls.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Injunctive relief claim by plaintiff Huskey seeking prospective relief from State Farm's allegedly discriminatory claims-processing practices.
fha_claims.reasoning: Huskey lacks standing to seek prospective injunctive relief because she is no longer a State Farm policyholder and therefore faces no 'real and immediate threat' of future injury from State Farm's claims-handling process. Article III requires standing for each form of relief sought. Plaintiffs did not contend otherwise.

source_file: 9682870_2023_County of Cook, IL v. Wells Fargo _ Co._ilnd
case_name: County of Cook v. Wells Fargo & Co.
accommodation_description: This is a discriminatory lending/equity stripping case, not a reasonable accommodation case under § 3604(f)(3)(B). The County alleges Wells Fargo engaged in predatory and discriminatory loan origination, servicing, and foreclosure activities targeting minority communities.
key_holding: Following Seventh Circuit precedent in County of Cook v. Bank of America Corporation, the court held that the County lacked standing to bring FHA claims because the harm to individual borrowers was too remote, and the proper plaintiffs would be the borrowers themselves; accordingly, the motion to alter or amend summary judgment was denied.
brief_summary: The County of Cook sued Wells Fargo & Co. under the Fair Housing Act alleging predatory and discriminatory lending practices ('equity stripping') targeting minority communities through loan origination, servicing, and foreclosure activities dating back to 2003. The court denied the County's motion to alter or amend summary judgment entered in Wells Fargo's favor, following Seventh Circuit precedent holding that the County lacked proximate causation because the discriminatory harm to individual borrowers was too remote to be cognizable under the FHA.
key_cases_cited: County of Cook v. Bank of America Corp., 584 F. Supp. 3d 562 (N.D. Ill. 2022)
County of Cook v. Bank of America Corp., 78 F.4th 70 (7th Cir. 2023)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equity stripping claim arising from predatory and discriminatory loan origination, servicing, and foreclosure activities
fha_claims.reasoning: The Seventh Circuit affirmed summary judgment on alternative grounds of lack of proximate causation, holding that County of Cook lacked standing as an indirect party to bring FHA claims that could only be brought by the actual borrowers. The court found the County's claims too remote to be cognizable under the FHA.

case_name: Vinzella Trimuel v. Chicago Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a domestic violence survivor with disabilities affecting her communication abilities, requested reinstatement to the public housing voucher waitlist from which she was removed for failing to complete a required survey.
key_holding: The court denied dismissal of the reasonable accommodation claim because CHA approved the accommodation request but failed to implement it, and the court rejected CHA's argument that providing the accommodation would fundamentally alter its policies as inappropriate for resolution at the motion to dismiss stage.
brief_summary: Vinzella Trimuel, a domestic violence survivor with anxiety, depression, and PTSD, sued the Chicago Housing Authority for disability discrimination after CHA removed her from its housing voucher waitlist in 2013 and then failed to reinstate her despite approving her 2020 reasonable accommodation request. The court denied CHA's motion to dismiss the reasonable accommodation claim, holding that CHA's approval of the request followed by failure to implement it stated a viable claim and that administrative burden arguments were improper at the motion to dismiss stage, while dismissing sex discrimination and promissory estoppel claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Texas Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Oconomowoc Residential Programs v. City of Milwaukee, 300 F.3d 775 (7th Cir. 2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reinstatement to prior position on Housing Choice Voucher Program waitlist; plaintiff requested return to 2008 waitlist after being removed in 2013 without notice, citing disabilities (anxiety, depression, PTSD from domestic violence) that impaired her ability to maintain communication with CHA and update her address
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff adequately pled a reasonable accommodation claim by alleging disability, CHA's awareness of disability, and CHA's failure to accommodate (despite approving the request). Court held that reasonableness is a fact-specific inquiry inappropriate at motion to dismiss stage and rejected CHA's arguments about fundamental alteration and administrative burden as premature for pleading stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: CHA's inflexible policies for Housing Choice Voucher Program waitlist alleged to have disparate impact on women as survivors of domestic violence
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed disparate impact claim for failure to plausibly allege causal connection between CHA's policies and disparate impact on domestic violence victims. Although plaintiff provided statistical evidence that women comprise majority of domestic violence victims, she failed to allege facts demonstrating that victims of domestic violence are disproportionately impacted by the specific CHA policies or connecting the disparity to those policies, as required by Inclusive Communities.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II, Rehabilitation Act § 504, Illinois Human Rights Act, promissory estoppel (state law)
fha_claims.reasoning: Promissory estoppel claim dismissed because plaintiff failed to allege facts regarding unambiguous promise (when conversations occurred, with whom), and under Illinois law, promissory estoppel cannot be applied to governmental entities absent extraordinary and compelling circumstances, which were absent here. ADA, Rehab Act, and IHRA claims survived motion to dismiss on same reasonable accommodation theory as FHA claim.

case_name: Kathleen Bankhead v. Wintrust Financial Corporation
accommodation_description: Not applicable — this case does not involve a request for a reasonable accommodation or modification; it concerns alleged racial discrimination in the origination, pricing, and terms of residential mortgage loans.
key_holding: The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss all claims without prejudice, holding that statistical data showing racial disparities in mortgage lending rates, fees, and approvals was insufficient, standing alone, to plausibly allege either disparate treatment (which requires factual allegations connecting the disparity to discriminatory intent) or disparate impact (which requires a robust causal connection between a specific identified policy and the alleged disparities) under the ECOA, 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 and 1982, or the FHA.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Kathleen Bankhead, an African American attorney, sued Wintrust Financial Corporation and Barrington Bank & Trust Co. on behalf of a putative class of Black and/or African American borrowers, alleging race discrimination in mortgage lending under the ECOA, 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 and 1982, and the FHA, based on HMDA data showing that Black borrowers received higher interest rates, paid higher fees, and were approved at lower rates than white borrowers. The court dismissed disparate treatment claims because the complaint offered no factual allegations tying the statistical disparities to discriminatory intent, and dismissed disparate impact claims because plaintiff identified only broad categories of policies without establishing the requisite robust causal link between any specific policy and the alleged racial disparities. All counts were dismissed without prejudice to allow plaintiff an opportunity to replead with additional factual support.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Texas Dept. of Housing and Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege intentional discrimination under the FHA disparate treatment theory. The complaint alleged only statistical disparities in loan approval rates and terms without any factual allegations suggesting racial animus or discriminatory intent by loan officers, falling short of the Iqbal plausibility standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to satisfy the three-element disparate impact test under the FHA. While she alleged statistical disparities, she identified only vague categories of policies and failed to allege a specific, facially neutral policy or establish a robust causal connection between any particular policy and the alleged disparities, as required by Inclusive Communities.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA), 42 U.S.C. § 1981, 42 U.S.C. § 1982, state law claims (breach of contract, promissory estoppel, fraudulent inducement)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's ECOA disparate impact claim failed for the same reasons as the FHA claim—insufficient pleading of a specific policy and causal nexus. The § 1981 claim was dismissed because it permits only disparate treatment, not disparate impact. The § 1982 claim was dismissed because that statute does not permit disparate impact theories. State law claims were dismissed for lack of supplemental jurisdiction once the federal claims failed.

source_file: 9683084_2023_Chicago Housing Initiative v. The United States Department of Housing and Urban Development_ilnd
case_name: Chicago Housing Initiative v. United States Department of Housing and Urban Development
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs did not request a specific accommodation; rather, they sought an injunction requiring HUD to conduct a full civil rights review before approving the CHA's disposition of 23 acres of vacant public housing land via a long-term lease to the Chicago Fire Football Club, arguing the lease would disproportionately harm racial minorities and people with disabilities by permanently removing land designated for future affordable public housing development.
key_holding: The court dismissed without prejudice the fair housing organizations' challenge to HUD's approval of the CHA's lease of public housing land to the Chicago Fire Football Club because plaintiffs failed to establish Article III standing under either representational or direct standing theories.
brief_summary: Three fair housing organizations — Chicago Housing Initiative, Coalition to Protect Chicago Housing Authority Land, and Lugenia Burns Hope Center — challenged HUD's approval of the Chicago Housing Authority's 60-year lease of a vacant public housing lot in the Roosevelt Square neighborhood to the Chicago Fire Football Club for a training facility, alleging violations of the Administrative Procedure Act, the Fair Housing Act, and the Rehabilitation Act. Plaintiffs sought a TRO/preliminary injunction to halt construction and challenged HUD's failure to conduct a formal civil rights review, arguing the lease would deprive racial minorities and persons with disabilities of land designated for affordable housing. The court denied the injunction and granted defendants' motions to dismiss, finding that plaintiffs lacked Article III standing because they could not demonstrate a concrete, particularized, non-speculative injury that was fairly traceable to defendants' conduct and redressable by a favorable ruling.
key_cases_cited: Warth v. Seldin, 422 U.S. 490 (1975)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)
Friends of Earth, Inc. v. Laidlaw Envtl. Servs., 528 U.S. 167 (2000)
Sierra Club v. Morton, 405 U.S. 727 (1972)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged violations of the Administrative Procedure Act, Fair Housing Act, and Rehabilitation Act based on HUD's approval of a lease of public housing land to a professional soccer team without completion of a civil rights review.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed for lack of Article III standing, finding that plaintiffs failed to establish a concrete, particularized, and actual or imminent injury fairly traceable to defendants' conduct and redressable by a favorable ruling. The court held that neither representative standing on behalf of members nor direct organizational standing was established, as the alleged injury—loss of potential future affordable housing units—was speculative and not tied to any actual displacement or thwarted development.

source_file: 9683510_2024_Haymarket DuPage, LLC v. Village of Itasca_ilnd
case_name: Haymarket DuPage, LLC v. Village of Itasca
accommodation_description: Haymarket sought municipal zoning approval (via a special use permit as a healthcare facility and/or a planned development designation) to convert a former Holiday Inn hotel in Itasca into a comprehensive substance abuse treatment and mental health facility offering inpatient treatment, outpatient treatment, detoxification services, recovery home services, GED classes, and employment placement for persons with substance use disorders and mental health disabilities.
key_holding: The court granted the Fire District's and School District defendants' motions to dismiss for lack of Article III standing because Haymarket's injury—denial of its zoning applications—was not fairly traceable to those defendants' conduct, as the Village Board held exclusive decision-making authority and the opposing defendants merely voiced concerns without a vote or determinative control over the outcome.
brief_summary: Haymarket DuPage, LLC, a nonprofit substance abuse treatment provider, purchased a former Holiday Inn in Itasca, Illinois, and spent two years seeking zoning approval from the Village of Itasca to operate a treatment center; after the Village Board unanimously denied the applications, Haymarket sued six defendants under the Fair Housing Act, ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and state law. The Fire Protection District and School District defendants (along with Superintendent Benes) moved to dismiss, arguing Haymarket lacked Article III standing to sue them. The court granted the motions, holding that while those defendants vocally opposed the project, the denial was traceable only to the Village Board—the actual decisionmaker—not to the Fire District or School District, who had no vote and no determinative or coercive control over the Board.
key_cases_cited: Warth v. Seldin, 422 U.S. 490 (1975)
Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)
Allen v. Wright, 468 U.S. 737 (1984)
Bennett v. Spear, 520 U.S. 154 (1997)
Segovia v. United States, 880 F.3d 384 (7th Cir. 2018)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Zoning approval and special use permit for a substance abuse treatment facility (inpatient, outpatient, detoxification, recovery home services, GED classes, employment placement) in a converted hotel in the B-2 District; Haymarket sought classification as a healthcare facility or planned development with zoning relief to operate the facility.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed claims against the Fire District and School District for lack of Article III standing under 12(b)(1) because the alleged injury (denial of zoning applications by the Village Board) was not fairly traceable to the conduct of those defendants. The Fire District and School District were voices in opposition but not decisionmakers; the Village Board had unfettered discretion and made the final decision. The complaint did not allege that the defendants' approval was necessary or that they had determinative or coercive control over the Board's decision.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II Americans with Disabilities Act (Count VI), Section 504 Rehabilitation Act (Count VII), Illinois state law zoning and municipal code violations (Count VIII)
fha_claims.reasoning: Claims under the ADA Title II, Section 504 Rehabilitation Act, and Illinois state law against the Fire District and School District were dismissed for lack of standing on the same traceability grounds as the FHA claims. The court did not reach the merits of these non-FHA claims because the jurisdictional defect (lack of traceability to the defendants' conduct) was fatal.

case_name: Manal Farhan v. 2715 NMA LLC and M. Fishman & Company
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that defendants' enforcement of a neutrality policy regarding the Israeli-Palestinian conflict was motivated by national origin discrimination rather than by the political nature of the flag display, as defendants would have enforced the policy regardless of the tenant's national origin.
brief_summary: Palestinian-American tenant sued her landlords for discrimination under the Fair Housing Act based on national origin, claiming they unlawfully enforced a neutrality policy by demanding she remove a Palestinian flag from her window and serving her with an eviction notice. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding the plaintiff failed to plausibly allege discriminatory intent based on national origin rather than political views, as the neutrality policy would have applied regardless of the tenant's national origin.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Texas Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 135 S. Ct. 2507 (2015)
Bloch v. Frischolz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009)
Hammad v. Dynamo Stadium, LLC, No. H-14-1938, 2015 WL 6965215 (S.D. Tex. Nov. 10, 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege discrimination based on national origin under § 3604(b). The court found that plaintiff's allegations describe enforcement of a facially neutral neutrality policy regarding the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, not discrimination based on national origin. Plaintiff did not allege that defendants knew of her Palestinian national origin when the policy was enforced, and did not allege differential treatment based on the national origin of other tenants.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege discrimination based on national origin under § 3604(b) in the second count. Same reasoning as Count I regarding the neutrality policy and lack of plausible allegation of national origin-based discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege retaliation under § 3617. The court found that plaintiff did not allege that defendants enforced the neutrality policy based on national origin or with discriminatory intent, and did not allege a pattern of harassment motivated by discriminatory intent necessary to establish interference with fair housing rights.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege retaliation under § 3617 in the second retaliation count. Same reasoning as Count III regarding lack of plausible allegation of national origin-based enforcement and discriminatory intent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Illinois Consumer Fraud and Deceptive Practices Act (ICFA), 815 ILCS 505/; Chicago Residential Landlord and Tenant Ordinance (CRLTO), 5-12-070, 5-12-110, 5-12-140; Illinois declaratory relief; eviction counterclaim under 735 ILCS 5/9-101
fha_claims.reasoning: The court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the remaining state law counts (V, VII, VIII) and defendants' counterclaim for eviction pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3) after dismissing all federal FHA claims. The claims were dismissed without prejudice.

case_name: Carl William Bass v. John Brannen and Network Property Management
accommodation_description: Bass requested that landlord control or eliminate loud noises from neighboring tenants (violin playing, TV volume, barking dog) that triggered his chronic fatigue syndrome symptoms.
key_holding: The court dismissed Bass's failure-to-accommodate claim because he failed to show his CFS was the but-for cause of his inability to enjoy his apartment, as the loud noises (screeching violin, TV at volume 70, barking dog) would be intolerable to any tenant regardless of disability; however, his disparate treatment claim survived because Brannen's statement that his building was not a 'convalescent home' and disparate treatment compared to similarly-situated tenant Berger suggested discriminatory intent.
brief_summary: Carl Bass, a tenant with chronic fatigue syndrome, sued his landlord John Brannen and property management company alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act, including failure to accommodate his disability-related noise sensitivity and discriminatory lease non-renewal. The court dismissed Bass's failure-to-accommodate claim because the complained-of noises (violin, TV at high volume, barking dog) would affect any tenant regardless of disability, but allowed his disparate treatment claim to proceed based on evidence that Brannen refused to renew his lease after making comments referencing his disability and treated him differently than a similarly-situated tenant who declined the same apartment offer.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 566 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Nikolich v. Vill. of Arlington Heights, 870 F. Supp. 2d 556 (N.D. Ill. 2012)
Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009)
Good Shepherd Manor Foundation, Inc. v. City of Momence, 323 F.3d 557 (7th Cir. 2003)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Non-renewal of lease; disparate treatment in lease renewal decision compared to similarly situated non-disabled tenant (Berger)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found Bass pleaded sufficient facts to survive motion to dismiss on disparate treatment claim. Brannen's statement that the building was not a 'convalescent home' and the disparate treatment of Bass versus Berger (who was offered apartment G but not forced to leave) support an inference of discriminatory intent based on disability at the pleading stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accommodation for chronic fatigue syndrome involving noise sensitivity; requested landlord to enforce quiet enjoyment of apartment by managing noise from neighboring tenants (violin playing, dog barking, loud TV)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed the failure-to-accommodate claim because Bass failed to establish the 'but-for' nexus between his disability and the inability to access quiet enjoyment. The court found that the loud noises (violin, TV at volume 70, barking dog) would prevent any tenant—disabled or non-disabled—from enjoying their dwelling, not just Bass due to his CFS. The disability did not cause the deprivation; the objectively excessive noise did.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged interference with fair housing rights through denial of lease renewal and discriminatory conduct
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found Bass stated a plausible § 3617 claim by alleging that Brannen denied lease renewal based on disability. The court rejected the argument that Bass must plead a pervasive pattern of harassment, noting that denying housing rights entirely (non-renewal) constitutes interference under § 3617 even without additional harassment, citing Bloch's hypothetical and the broad remedial purpose of the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title III of the American Disabilities Act (ADA), 42 U.S.C. § 12182
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed the ADA Title III claim because Bass's private apartment unit does not qualify as a 'place of public accommodation' under 42 U.S.C. § 12181(7). The statute covers only designated public accommodations (inns, motels, restaurants, museums, etc.), not private residential dwellings.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA failure to accommodate claim (window coverings, windowless workspace for administrative duties); ADA interference/coercion claim (take-it-or-leave-it ultimatum regarding PPE accommodation or job offer withdrawal)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege she could perform the essential functions of a Forensic Technician with or without reasonable accommodation, as she alleged her disability prevents exposure to natural light but did not explain how she could perform essential duties in a room with some natural light. The bare conclusory allegation that she could perform the job with or without accommodation was insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA interference/coercion claim based on employer's take-it-or-leave-it ultimatum regarding accommodation or job offer withdrawal
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege an ADA interference claim because she did not allege a pattern of harassment or invidious motivation; a single take-it-or-leave-it ultimatum regarding accommodation acceptance does not constitute the pattern of harassment required for interference under the ADA, and was merely a rehash of the failure to accommodate claim.

case_name: Bell v. Pappas
accommodation_description: No accommodation request: plaintiffs allege Cook County's property tax sale and indemnification system has disparate impact on Black and Latino homeowners and reflects discriminatory intent.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' FHA disparate impact claim because plaintiffs failed to provide statistics connecting the indemnification fund's operation to racial disparities, and dismissed the disparate treatment claim because acknowledging the existence of disparities does not establish discriminatory intent.
brief_summary: Individual homeowners and community organizations sued Cook County officials alleging the County's property tax sale system and inadequate indemnification fund have disparate impact on Black and Latino homeowners and reflect discriminatory intent. The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss, finding plaintiffs failed to allege sufficient statistics connecting the indemnification fund to racial disparities or facts showing discriminatory motive.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Tex. Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
County of Cook v. HSBC N. Am. Holdings Inc., 314 F. Supp. 3d 975 (N.D. Ill. 2018)
TBS Grp., LLC v. City of Zion, 2017 WL 5129008 (N.D. Ill. 2017)
McCauley v. City of Chicago, 671 F.3d 611 (7th Cir. 2011)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to adequately plead a prima facie disparate impact claim under Iqbal/Twombly. They did not allege sufficient statistical disparities specific to the indemnification fund's operation, did not identify a specific County policy causing any alleged disparity, and failed to plausibly connect the County's conduct to the claimed discriminatory effect.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege intentional discrimination. Knowledge of racial disparities and inaction, without more, does not support an inference of discriminatory intent. Plaintiffs did not plausibly connect Cook County's history of housing discrimination to current policies regarding compensation for homeowners subject to tax deeds.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (Fifth, Eighth, and Fourteenth Amendment claims); Illinois Civil Rights Act (ICRA)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to state a § 1983 claim against Yarbrough because her actions were mandated by state law, not County policy, and thus cannot satisfy Monell's requirement that a constitutional deprivation be caused by municipal policy or custom. Plaintiffs also failed to allege that Yarbrough's alleged inaction was the 'moving force' behind any constitutional violation or had a direct causal link to deprivation of federal rights.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged failure to accommodate disability (Leukemia and HIV), denial of long-term disability benefits, denial of rent assistance during COVID-19, wrongful termination while on medical leave, and other employment discrimination claims under Title VII, ADEA, ADA, and FHA.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the entire amended complaint for failure to comply with Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 8 and 10 due to unintelligible pleading, disjointed organization, and conclusory allegations that fail to provide fair notice of claims. The court found the complaint contained a confusing mix of narrative statements, conclusory lists, and compound paragraphs mixing factual allegations with legal conclusions, making it impossible to discern the scope and factual basis of plaintiff's claims. Although some employment discrimination claims were somewhat discernible, the overall complaint was too vague and confusing to survive Rule 12(b)(6) scrutiny under Iqbal/Twombly.

source_file: 9684517_2019_Sunnybrook LP v. City of Alton, Illinois_ilsd
case_name: Sunnybrook LP v. City of Alton, Illinois
race_if_mentioned: African-American, Hispanic or Latino, or American Indian
accommodation_description: Developer alleges city withdrew support for affordable housing development because it would serve minorities in violation of Fair Housing Act
key_holding: The court denied Defendants' motion to dismiss for lack of standing, finding that the developer sufficiently alleged injury-in-fact, causation, and redressability, and that the state and federal actions are not parallel so abstention is not required.
brief_summary: Sunnybrook LP, a developer of affordable housing, sued the City of Alton, Illinois and Mayor Brant Walker alleging they violated the Fair Housing Act, Civil Rights Acts, and Equal Protection Clause by withdrawing support for and obstructing the Sunnybrook affordable housing development because it would serve minority renters. The court denied Defendants' motion to dismiss for lack of standing, finding the developer adequately alleged Article III standing and that the parallel state court litigation did not require abstention.
key_cases_cited: Village of Arlington Heights v. Metropolitan Housing Development Corp., 429 U.S. 252 (1977)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Warth v. Seldin, 422 U.S. 490 (1975)
Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)
Colorado River Water Conservation District v. United States, 424 U.S. 800 (1976)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss for lack of subject matter jurisdiction and lack of standing. Sunnybrook, as a developer with substantial economic investment and planning expenses, satisfied Article III standing requirements under Arlington Heights. The claims alleging intentional discrimination based on race and color in making dwellings unavailable and interfering with housing rights survive the motion to dismiss and proceed to discovery.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1981 (right to make and enforce contracts); 42 U.S.C. § 1982 (right to purchase, lease, or hold property); 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (equal protection); Fourteenth Amendment Equal Protection Clause
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss on jurisdictional and standing grounds. Non-FHA civil rights claims survive because they present distinct federal questions not disposed of by parallel state court proceedings. The state court action addresses only the building permit and plat requirement; the federal claims allege violations of statutory and constitutional rights causing money damages.

case_name: Edwards v. Alexander County Housing Authority
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested in this case. Plaintiffs alleged racial discrimination, segregation, and deplorable housing conditions—including infestations, lead poisoning, and inadequate security—at public housing developments where approximately 97% of residents were Black, while white residents received better-maintained units with security cameras and guards.
key_holding: The court dismissed all claims against HUD and Ben Carson on sovereign immunity grounds and dismissed plaintiff Jamika Sueing's FHA and Illinois Civil Rights Act claims as time-barred, while denying dismissal of the remaining plaintiffs' claims against the Housing Authority defendants.
brief_summary: Six former African-American residents of the racially segregated McBride and Elmwood public housing developments in Cairo, Illinois sued the Alexander County Housing Authority, HUD, and associated officials for disparate treatment, perpetuation of racial segregation, and failure to affirmatively further fair housing, alleging that Black residents were subjected to deplorable living conditions while white residents received better-maintained units with security. The court granted HUD and Ben Carson's motion to dismiss entirely on sovereign immunity grounds, finding that neither the FHA, Title VI, nor the Illinois Civil Rights Act contained an unequivocal waiver of federal sovereign immunity. The court granted in part the Housing Authority's motion, dismissing plaintiff Sueing's FHA and Illinois Civil Rights Act claims as untimely since she moved out in 2015 and did not sue until 2019, but allowed her Title VI claim and all other plaintiffs' claims against the Housing Authority to proceed.
key_cases_cited: Tyus v. Urban Search Mgmt., 102 F.3d 256 (7th Cir. 1996)
United States v. Sherwood, 312 U.S. 584 (1941)
Alden v. Maine, 527 U.S. 706 (1999)
Lane v. Pena, 518 U.S. 187 (1996)
Beard v. Robinson, 563 F.2d 331 (7th Cir. 1977)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Count I (Disparate Treatment Based on Race) dismissed as to HUD and Ben Carson under 12(b)(1) for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction based on sovereign immunity; the Fair Housing Act does not contain an unequivocal waiver of Federal Government sovereign immunity. As to Plaintiff Jamika Sueing, dismissed under 12(b)(6) on statute-of-limitations grounds; claim accrued in 2015 and had to be filed by 2017, but was not filed until 2019.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Count II (Perpetuation of Racial Segregation) dismissed as to HUD and Ben Carson under 12(b)(1) for sovereign immunity; Fair Housing Act does not waive Federal Government immunity. As to Plaintiff Jamika Sueing, dismissed under 12(b)(6) on statute-of-limitations grounds; claim accrued in 2015 and was time-barred by 2019.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Count III (Failure to Affirmatively Further Fair Housing) dismissed as to HUD and Ben Carson under 12(b)(1) for sovereign immunity; Fair Housing Act does not contain unequivocal waiver. As to Plaintiff Jamika Sueing, dismissed under 12(b)(6) on statute-of-limitations grounds; claim accrued in 2015 and was time-barred by 2019.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964; Illinois Civil Rights Act of 2003
fha_claims.reasoning: Count IV (Title VI Racial Discrimination) dismissed as to HUD and Ben Carson under 12(b)(1) for sovereign immunity; Title VI does not abrogate Federal Government immunity. Count V (Illinois Civil Rights Act) dismissed as to HUD and Ben Carson under 12(b)(1) because the Illinois Civil Rights Act does not permit suits against the Federal Government. As to Plaintiff Jamika Sueing's Count V claim, dismissed under 12(b)(6) on statute-of-limitations grounds; claim accrued in 2015 and had to be filed by 2017 under the two-year limitations period.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Count VI (Disparate Treatment Based on Familial Status) dismissed as to HUD and Ben Carson under 12(b)(1) for sovereign immunity; Fair Housing Act does not waive Federal Government immunity. As to Plaintiff Jamika Sueing, dismissed under 12(b)(6) on statute-of-limitations grounds; claim accrued in 2015 and was time-barred by 2019.

case_name: Karnes v. Bank of Whittington/Whittington Bancorp, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff's vague complaint alleges water shutoff violates the Fair Housing Act but does not articulate a specific accommodation request; she claims the water shutoff 'feels like discrimination' due to her disability.
key_holding: The complaint was dismissed without prejudice for failing to satisfy Rule 8 pleading requirements, as plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts explaining who, what, when, where, why, and how her water was shut off and how any defendant discriminated against her because of disability.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Giasemi Karnes sued Bank of Whittington/Whittington Bancorp, Mohammad Ardehali (her former landlord), and the City of Benton, alleging her water was turned off and this violated the Fair Housing Act and ADA due to her disability. The court dismissed her complaint without prejudice for failing to satisfy Rule 8's notice-pleading requirements, finding the complaint too vague to put defendants on notice of the factual basis for her claims.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Access to running water; plaintiff alleges water was turned off by City of Benton in 2017 and again after foreclosure in 2020. Plaintiff also cites ADA, UN International Bill of Rights (right to water, sanitation, adequate housing, food).
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint fails to satisfy Rule 8 notice-pleading requirements. Plaintiff does not clearly allege the essential facts (who, what, when, where, why, how) of her claims, including the timeline of water shutoffs and the causal connection between her disability and the alleged discrimination. The court found the allegations too vague and conclusory to provide adequate notice to defendants.

case_name: Carolina Prejean v. Jen Dischbein, Kim Schaltenbrand, and Metro Landing Apartments
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges racial discrimination in refusal to lower rent or allow her fiancée to be added to the lease; disability claim regarding elevator access was not adequately pleaded.
key_holding: Plaintiff stated a colorable FHA claim against Metro Landing Apartments for racial discrimination in housing conditions, but her ADA Title II, Title VI, and Federal Tort Claims Act claims were dismissed for failure to adequately plead the essential elements of those claims.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Carolina Prejean sued Metro Landing Apartments and individual property managers alleging racial discrimination in housing after they refused to lower her rent or allow her fiancée on the lease, claiming racially motivated animus. The court granted IFP status and found plaintiff adequately stated a Fair Housing Act racial discrimination claim against the apartment complex, while dismissing ADA, Title VI, and Federal Tort Claims Act claims for failure to state viable claims.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Swanson v. Citibank, N.A., 614 F.3d 400 (7th Cir. 2010)
Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged Metro Landing refused to lower her rent or allow her fiancée to be added to the lease based on racial animus.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff sufficiently alleged racial discrimination in housing conditions by Metro Landing's refusal to lower rent or add fiancée to lease in July 2021 based on racial animus. The claim survives § 1915(e)(2) screening as a colorable Fair Housing Act violation, though individual defendants Dischbein and Schaltenbrand are dismissed for lack of individual liability under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II ADA claim regarding expired elevator certification; Title VI Civil Rights Act claim; Federal Tort Claims Act claim; state law security deposit claim.
fha_claims.reasoning: Title II ADA claims fail because plaintiff does not allege she has a disability or how her disability relates to the elevator, and individual defendants cannot be liable under the ADA. Title VI claim fails because plaintiff does not allege Metro Landing receives federal financial assistance and individual defendants are not federal grant recipients. Federal Tort Claims Act claim fails because no defendant is alleged to be a federal employee. State law security deposit claim survives under supplemental jurisdiction as arising from the same operative facts as the FHA claim.

case_name: Carl Lee Ledford v. Katrika Williams, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged denial of reasonable accommodation but failed to specify what accommodation was needed or for what reason.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for defendants on the reasonable accommodation claim because plaintiff failed to identify what accommodation he needed or for what reason, and the undisputed evidence showed the lease non-renewal was based on criminal history revealed through a background check rather than disability.
brief_summary: Carl Lee Ledford, a Section 8 tenant receiving disability income, sued Monroe Group (property manager), Community Housing Concepts East Central LLC (owner), and IHCDA, alleging race discrimination, constitutional violations, and denial of reasonable accommodation after his lease was not renewed based on criminal history and he was assessed late fees. The court granted summary judgment for defendants on all federal claims, finding no evidence of race-based discrimination and that plaintiff failed to identify any specific accommodation he needed.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Texas Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Cmtys. Project, Inc., 135 S. Ct. 2507 (2015)
Ricci v. DeStefano, 557 U.S. 557 (2009)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged denial of reasonable accommodations or alternatives but failed to identify what accommodation he needed or for what reason related to a disability.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege what accommodation he needed or for what reason, establishing no nexus between any disability and a requested accommodation. The court found the FHA claim could not apply to his situation without such allegations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged race discrimination but presented no evidence that his race played any part in defendants' decisions. The undisputed facts showed the non-renewal was based on a criminal background check, not race, and plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie case of disparate impact.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 due process claims, § 1985(3) conspiracy, state law breach of contract, intimidation, harassment, intentional infliction of emotional distress, malicious prosecution, extortion, fraud, abuse of process
fha_claims.reasoning: Defendants were not state actors; plaintiff failed to show any understanding between defendants and state officials to deprive him of constitutional rights. § 1983 conspiracy claims require evidence of state involvement and a common unconstitutional goal, neither of which was present. Malicious prosecution requires a separate constitutional deprivation not established here. State law claims were dismissed without prejudice under supplemental jurisdiction doctrine.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to train and supervise employees; Monell liability under IHCDA policies
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's allegations against IHCDA failed to state a plausible claim. Williams, Gepfert, and Cupp were not IHCDA employees, and plaintiff did not allege facts supporting deliberate indifference required for failure to train claims. Plaintiff also failed to identify any constitutional violation or denial of federal right implicated by IHCDA policies.

case_name: Mabry v. City of East Chicago
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; case concerns alleged discriminatory relocation from contaminated public housing complex based on race and national origin.
key_holding: The court dismissed the Fair Housing Act intentional discrimination and disparate impact claims because plaintiffs failed to allege that similarly situated individuals outside their protected classes (race, national origin, familial status) were treated differently, and failed to plead the statistical disparity necessary to state a disparate impact claim.
brief_summary: Hispanic and African-American residents of the East Chicago Housing Authority's West Calumet Housing Complex sued the City of East Chicago and ECHA alleging intentional racial discrimination and disparate impact under the FHA based on defendants' failure to warn of lead/arsenic contamination and subsequent relocation. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding plaintiffs failed to plead comparator allegations sufficient for intentional discrimination and failed to allege statistical disparity required for disparate impact.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dept. of Housing & Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 135 S.Ct. 2507 (2015)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Geinosky v. City of Chicago, 675 F.3d 743 (7th Cir. 2012)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to allege that non-members of the protected class (African-American and Hispanic residents) were treated differently, which is an essential element of an FHA intentional discrimination claim under Wigginton and Twombly/Iqbal pleading standards.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege a discriminatory effect on a protected class under Texas Department of Housing & Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project. Allegations that the Complex's tenants are majority-minority and that East Chicago's population is majority-minority are insufficient without comparative data showing disparate impact relative to non-protected classes or other housing complexes.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (Fourteenth Amendment Due Process), 42 U.S.C. § 1982 (Property Rights), 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (Fourteenth Amendment Equal Protection)
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 1982 claim dismissed because plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege racial animus or that deprivation of property rights was because of race; Equal Protection claim dismissed because plaintiffs failed to allege how non-members of the protected class were treated differently. Both dismissals applied Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (Fourteenth Amendment Due Process)
fha_claims.reasoning: Due Process claim survived motion to dismiss because plaintiffs adequately alleged a property interest in their leases and deprivation thereof without adequate notice and opportunity to be heard; whether relocation without pre-deprivation hearing was necessary given alleged health risks and pretext for demolition is a factual question unsuitable for resolution on a motion to dismiss.

case_name: Sandra Black v. Naomi Friedrichsen, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges she was constructively evicted through racially discriminatory harassment including false lease violation accusations and eviction proceedings.
key_holding: A plaintiff bringing Fair Housing Act claims based on discriminatory harassment under 42 U.S.C. § 3617 need not establish constructive eviction, and entering into a joint agreement to vacate does not automatically defeat such claims; the plaintiff's allegations of a pattern of racially-motivated harassment were sufficient to survive a motion to dismiss.
brief_summary: Sandra Black, an African-American tenant, sued Hunters Run Apartments and related defendants alleging they discriminated against her on the basis of race by falsely accusing her of lease violations and pursuing eviction proceedings while treating white tenants more favorably. The district court denied the defendants' motion to dismiss, holding that plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claims under 42 U.S.C. § 3617 for discriminatory harassment do not require proof of constructive eviction and that the joint agreement to vacate does not automatically defeat her claims.
key_cases_cited: Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009)
Wetzel v. Glen St. Andrew Living Cmty., LLC, 901 F.3d 856 (7th Cir. 2018)
Smith v. Hous. Auth. of S. Bend, 867 F.2d 1004 (7th Cir. 2012)
DiCenso v. Cisneros, 96 F.3d 1004 (7th Cir. 1996)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's complaint alleging racial discrimination in housing (disparate treatment based on race, African-American) survived motion to dismiss under Iqbal/Twombly standard.
