Court found allegations sufficient to state a plausible claim despite ICRC's prior finding of no probable cause, applying liberal construction to pro se pleadings and noting that statute of limitations was tolled during administrative proceedings.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged pattern of harassment, false accusations of lease violations, and interference with enjoyment of housing based on race
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's § 3617 claim for interference, coercion, intimidation, and harassment based on race survived motion to dismiss. Court rejected defendant's argument that lack of constructive eviction defeats the claim, holding that § 3617 provides an independent post-acquisition discrimination claim broader than § 3604 and does not require constructive eviction. Allegations of pattern of harassment and false lease violation accusations stated a plausible claim.

case_name: Sandra Black v. Naomi Friedrichsen, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges defendants discriminated against her on the basis of her race (African-American) by falsely accusing her of lease violations to force her to vacate.
key_holding: The court denied Plaintiff's motion to compel discovery responses, finding her requests vague and overly broad, and granted Defendants' motion to compel her deposition, finding no legal basis for her refusal to attend.
brief_summary: Sandra Black, an African-American tenant with a Section 8 voucher, sued her landlord and property management company alleging race discrimination under the Fair Housing Act, claiming defendants falsely accused her of lease violations and pursued eviction to force her out. The court denied Plaintiff's motion to compel more complete discovery responses, finding her requests vague and overly broad, and granted Defendants' motion to compel Plaintiff's deposition attendance, ruling she had no legal basis to refuse her deposition based on unresolved discovery disputes.
key_cases_cited: Krieman v. Crystal Lake Apartments Ltd. P'ship, No. 05 C 0348, 2006 WL 1519320 (N.D. Ill. May 31, 2006)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: This is a discovery dispute, not a merits ruling. The court addressed Plaintiff's FHA disparate treatment claim (alleging race-based discrimination through false lease violation accusations) only in the context of whether comparator evidence of similarly situated white tenants was discoverable. The court found Plaintiff's discovery requests regarding comparator evidence were vague and overly broad but did not dismiss the underlying FHA claim on the merits. The claim remains pending.

case_name: Kendra Mabry, et al. v. City of East Chicago, et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request - case concerns eviction from contaminated housing and alleged racial discrimination in that eviction
key_holding: The court granted leave to amend discrimination claims under the FHA and § 1982 against City and ECHA defendants because plaintiffs sufficiently alleged discriminatory intent and disparate impact at the pleading stage, but denied amendment as to previously dismissed corporate defendants and § 3617 intimidation claims.
brief_summary: Public housing residents of the West Calumet Housing Complex in East Chicago, Indiana sued the City of East Chicago, East Chicago Housing Authority, and corporate defendants for Fair Housing Act violations and constitutional claims arising from their 2016 eviction due to property contamination. The court granted leave to amend the complaint to add claims of intentional discrimination and disparate impact under the FHA based on race and familial status against the City and ECHA defendants, while denying amendment as to previously dismissed corporate defendants and § 3617 intimidation claims.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Herndon v. Hous. Auth. of S. Bend, Indiana, 670 F. App'x 417 (7th Cir. 2016)
Swanson v. Citibank, N.A., 614 F.3d 400 (7th Cir. 2010)
Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: At the pleading stage, plaintiffs need only identify the type of discrimination alleged (racial), by whom, and when. The court found plaintiffs sufficiently alleged intentional discrimination based on race against City and ECHA defendants, allowing amendment despite defendants' arguments about comparators and specific factual allegations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs plausibly alleged disparate impact on Black residents and families with children through census data showing the Complex had a higher percentage of Black residents and children than the city overall. The fact that one smaller complex had a slightly higher percentage of Black residents was not fatal at the pleading stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Official communications from government officials to tenants about a required eviction do not constitute coercion, threats, or intimidation under 42 U.S.C. § 3617. The court found that § 3617 harassment must rise to a pattern of harassment and go beyond isolated acts, and that government relocation directives do not meet this standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1982 (property rights), Fourteenth Amendment Equal Protection Clause, Fourteenth Amendment Due Process Clause
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs sufficiently alleged that City and ECHA defendants, as government entities, intentionally discriminated against members of protected classes by interfering with their rights to lease property based on race and family status, satisfying the requirements for § 1982 and Equal Protection claims against government defendants.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to allege that Corporate Defendants owned or administered the Complex or acted in any direct way to make housing unavailable. Allegations that Corporate Defendants merely coordinated with City and ECHA to conceal contamination and exerted influence to evacuate are insufficient to state a claim under FHA § 3604 without direct action by the Corporate Defendants.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1982 (property rights), Fourteenth Amendment Equal Protection Clause, Fourteenth Amendment Due Process Clause — against Corporate Defendants
fha_claims.reasoning: Constitutional claims against private Corporate Defendants require allegations of a conspiracy with state actors. Plaintiffs' bare assertions and suspicions that Corporate Defendants were 'behind' redevelopment plans, without specific factual allegations tying them to a conspiracy with state actors, are insufficient to survive a motion to dismiss under Twombly.

case_name: Norman v. Northwest Indiana CA Section 8
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation was requested in this case; the plaintiff alleged FHA violations relating to the administration of her Section 8 housing assistance payments after her rental building was sold to a new owner, arguing that payments were made to the new owner without her consent and that she was being harassed for rent she did not owe.
key_holding: The court dismissed pro se plaintiff's Fair Housing Act complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) for failure to state a claim because she did not allege membership in a protected class or that any adverse treatment occurred because of such membership, and granted leave to amend.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff LaSandra Norman, a Section 8 voucher recipient, sued her housing authority, the new owner of her rental property, and associated lenders, alleging FHA violations arising from the sale of her building and the subsequent redirection of her Housing Assistance Payments to the new owner without her consent. The court screened the complaint under the in forma pauperis statute and dismissed it for failure to state a claim, finding that the plaintiff neither identified herself as a member of a protected class nor alleged that any discrimination was based on protected-class membership. The court also found she lacked standing for her general allegations about Section 8 recipients being denied homeownership opportunities, and granted her until June 14, 2021 to file an amended complaint.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Swanson v. Citibank, N.A., 614 F.3d 400 (7th Cir. 2010)
Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009)
Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins, 136 S. Ct. 1540 (2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges discrimination in rent payment and housing terms based on alleged failure of Northwest Indiana Community Action to oppose sale of property and subsequent rent payment to new owner without consent.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege membership in a protected class under the Fair Housing Act and failed to allege facts showing discrimination based on membership in a protected class, failing to state a plausible claim for discrimination under the Iqbal/Twombly standard.

case_name: McGrath v. Dunecrest Condominium Association
accommodation_description: Family requested permission to construct a deck extension and staircase creating a second exit from their condominium to accommodate autistic twins who struggle with emergencies and unexpected circumstances.
key_holding: The McGraths stated a plausible failure to accommodate claim because the Association's two-year refusal to issue building paperwork for the requested second exit constituted constructive denial of the accommodation, and their allegations of discriminatory animus and disparate treatment of similar construction requests were sufficient to survive futility review.
brief_summary: The McGrath family sued their condominium association alleging disability discrimination under the Fair Housing Act after the association refused to issue approval paperwork for construction of a second exit to accommodate their autistic twins. The court granted leave to amend the federal FHA claims (finding them plausible) but declined jurisdiction over state condominium law claims.
key_cases_cited: Wisconsin Cmty. Servs., Inc. v. City of Milwaukee, 465 F.3d 737 (7th Cir. 2006)
Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condominium Ass'n, Inc., 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014)
Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009)
Oconomowoc Residential Programs, Inc. v. City of Milwaukee, 300 F.3d 775 (7th Cir. 2002)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Construction of a second exit from the condominium via a deck extension and staircase from the balcony to provide an alternative emergency exit for disabled family members with autism
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the five-element test for failure to accommodate (disability, request, denial, reasonableness, necessity) and found the McGraths stated a plausible claim at the pleading stage. The court rejected the Association's argument that the McGraths could not simultaneously claim victory on the vote and denial of accommodation, finding the Association's inaction constituted constructive denial. The claim survives the motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Intentional discrimination based on disability in denying approval for construction project while approving similar projects for non-disabled unit owners
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found the McGraths alleged sufficient facts to survive the motion to dismiss on an intentional discrimination theory under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(2). The court noted that discrimination claims need not establish a prima facie case at the pleading stage and cited Swierkiewicz for the proposition that such claims are not held to a higher pleading standard. The allegations of hostile comments, vote-changing efforts motivated by discriminatory animus, and disparate treatment compared to similarly situated non-disabled owners were sufficient to state a plausible claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Violations of Indiana Condominium Act regarding governance procedures and bylaw compliance
fha_claims.reasoning: The court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the state law claims under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(1) because the Indiana Condominium Act grievance provisions presented a novel issue of state law with no interpretive guidance from Indiana courts. The court found this analogous to cases where the absence of state law decisions renders a case novel for jurisdictional decline purposes.

case_name: LaSandra Norman v. Northwest Indiana CA Section 8, et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; plaintiff alleges race-based retaliation for exercising fair housing rights related to rent payment and Section 8 benefits.
key_holding: Plaintiff failed to state a claim of race-based retaliation under § 3617 because she did not allege sufficient facts to create an inference that the defendants were motivated by discriminatory intent in seeking rent payment or threatening Section 8 termination.
brief_summary: LaSandra Norman, an African American Section 8 voucher holder, sued her landlords and Northwest Indiana CA alleging race-based retaliation under the Fair Housing Act, claiming defendants harassed her about rent and threatened Section 8 termination. The court dismissed her complaint for failing to state a retaliation claim because she alleged no facts showing defendants acted with discriminatory intent.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009)
Luevano v. Wal-Mart Stores, Inc., 722 F.3d 1014 (7th Cir. 2013)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to state a claim of retaliation under § 3617 because she did not allege facts showing that defendants were motivated by discriminatory intent, did not clearly allege exercise of FHA rights, and did not connect the alleged conduct (rent collection and termination letter) to protected activity under the FHA. The court applied the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard at the screening stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VII discrimination claim (race, ethnicity, national origin); Indiana state law defamation claim; retaliatory discharge claim under Indiana law
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards and found that plaintiff adequately alleged Title VII employment discrimination based on race and national origin (adverse action and discriminatory motive), supplemental jurisdiction over the defamation claim based on common nucleus of operative fact, and vicarious liability for Dr. Badruddin's statements. The retaliatory discharge claim was voluntarily withdrawn by plaintiff.

case_name: LaSandra Norman v. Northwest Indiana CA Section 8, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff vaguely alleged discrimination based on disability but failed to state what accommodation, if any, was requested or needed.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claims for failure to state a claim because she alleged no facts connecting the collection of unpaid rent or termination of housing assistance to her race, sex, or disability, and failed to allege she was treated differently from other tenants not in her protected classes.
brief_summary: LaSandra Norman, an African American woman using Section 8 housing assistance, sued Northwest Indiana CA and her landlord alleging race, sex, and disability discrimination under the Fair Housing Act and retaliation under § 3617, claiming she was targeted for complaining about paying rent that helped her landlord cover his mortgage. The court dismissed all claims with prejudice, finding the plaintiff failed to allege any facts connecting the enforcement of standard lease obligations (rent payment, lawn care) to her protected characteristics or that she was treated differently from non-protected tenants.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009)
Wetzel v. Glen St. Andrew Living Cmty., LLC, 901 F.3d 856 (7th Cir. 2018)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege any facts connecting the collection of unpaid rent or lawn care requirements to her race or sex, and alleged no facts showing she was treated differently from other tenants not in her protected class. The complaint does not plausibly allege intentional discrimination based on race or gender under § 3604(b).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination in mortgage lending
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged she could have paid a mortgage but failed to allege that she applied for or attempted to apply for a mortgage, much less that she was discriminated against in any such effort. The claim fails under § 3605(a) for failure to state a plausible allegation of discrimination in a real estate-related transaction.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Disability discrimination in rental terms
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged defendants did not 'take into consideration' her 'disabilities' but failed to allege any information regarding what disability she has or how she was discriminated against based on disability. The complaint fails to state a plausible claim under § 3604(f).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation for complaining about landlord's mortgage
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege she complained about a discriminatory housing practice based on race, gender, or any right protected under §§ 3603–3606; she only complained about her landlord having a mortgage. Additionally, she failed to allege facts creating a reasonable inference of causal connection between any protected activity and the termination of housing assistance, which was based on failure to pay rent. The claim fails under § 3617.

case_name: Lasandra Norman v. Northwest Indiana CA Section 8, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff asserts that landlord having a mortgage on the property she rents with Section 8 assistance violates the Fair Housing Act, though no specific accommodation request is identified.
key_holding: The court denied the motion for reconsideration because the plaintiff failed to identify newly discovered evidence, an intervening change in controlling law, or a manifest legal error, and her claim—that landlord having a mortgage on a Section 8 property constitutes an FHA violation—fails to state a claim.
brief_summary: LaSandra Norman, proceeding pro se and receiving Section 8 voucher assistance, filed a motion to enforce her right to sue under Section 813(a) of the Fair Housing Act against Northwest Indiana Community Action, apparently asserting that her landlord having a mortgage on the rental property violates the FHA. The court denied the motion, finding no basis for reconsideration under Rule 59(e) as Norman failed to identify newly discovered evidence, a change in controlling law, or manifest legal error, and her claim fails to state a valid FHA claim.
key_cases_cited: Cosgrove v. Bartolotta, 150 F.3d 729 (7th Cir. 1998)
Oto v. Metro. Life Ins. Co., 224 F.3d 601 (7th Cir. 2000)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged that defendant's mortgage on the rental property constituted a Fair Housing Act violation
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a plausible claim under the Fair Housing Act. The plaintiff's allegation that a landlord's mortgage on a Section 8 rental property constitutes discrimination does not state a cognizable FHA claim and was dismissed without prejudice initially, then with prejudice after multiple amendments.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged retaliation related to her Section 8 housing
fha_claims.reasoning: The court recognized the elements of a retaliation claim under the Fair Housing Act but found that the plaintiff failed to plausibly allege facts supporting retaliation. The complaint was dismissed for failure to state a claim under Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards.

case_name: Kendra Mabry, et al. v. City of East Chicago, et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request is at issue; the case concerns eviction from contaminated housing and alleged racial discrimination in the closure of a housing complex.
key_holding: The court recommended dismissing the disparate impact claim under the FHA because the one-time decision to close the housing complex does not constitute a 'policy' as required for disparate impact analysis under Texas Dept. of Hous. & Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Communities Project.
brief_summary: Residents of the East Chicago Housing Authority's West Calumet Housing Complex sued the City of East Chicago, the Housing Authority, and individual officials alleging Fair Housing Act violations, constitutional claims, and civil rights violations arising from the 2016 closure of the contaminated complex and their subsequent eviction. The Magistrate Judge recommended granting the motion to dismiss, finding that the disparate impact claim failed because a one-time decision to close the complex does not constitute a 'policy' required for disparate impact analysis, while noting that the disparate treatment claim was adequately alleged.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Texas Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
City of Joliet, Ill. v. New W., L.P., 825 F.3d 827 (7th Cir. 2016)
Lafayette Linear v. Vill. of Univ. Park, Ill., 887 F.3d 842 (7th Cir. 2018)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Defendants conceded that Plaintiffs adequately alleged a claim for disparate treatment under the Fair Housing Act; this claim survived the motion to dismiss and was not recommended for dismissal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to allege a specific policy or policies causing the discriminatory effect; the closure of the Complex was a one-time decision, not a policy within the scope of FHA disparate impact doctrine, which targets zoning laws and housing restrictions, not individual decisions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1982 (Civil Rights Act), 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (Fourteenth Amendment due process and equal protection)
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 1982 claim fails because housing was not available to anyone after all tenants were evicted, so no comparative showing of disparate treatment can be made; due process claim fails because state law breach of contract remedies provide adequate process, and plaintiffs do not allege entitlement to a predeprivation hearing on a contested factual issue.

case_name: DeAnn Graham v. City of Elkhart
accommodation_description: Plaintiff allegedly had an emotional support animal (ESA) registered with UMH property management, and was evicted after her dog allegedly bit the property manager, with plaintiff claiming the ESA documentation was destroyed and the bite report was falsified.
key_holding: The court dismissed all federal claims against the City of Elkhart because plaintiff failed to allege a discriminatory City policy with the force of law to sustain a § 1983 claim, and plaintiff's FHA claim against the City was dismissed because she clarified she alleged UMH (not a party) violated the FHA.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff DeAnn Graham sued the City of Elkhart and Prosecutor Becker alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act, Equal Protection, and various state laws arising from her 2018 eviction related to an emotional support animal and loss of various benefits and services. The court granted the City's motion to dismiss all federal claims for failure to allege a discriminatory City policy under § 1983, granted Becker a more definite statement, and dismissed claims on behalf of plaintiff's daughters because a pro se litigant cannot represent others.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Monell v. Dep't of Social Servs. of City of N.Y., 436 U.S. 658 (1978)
Connick v. Thompson, 563 U.S. 51 (2011)
McMillian v. Monroe County, 520 U.S. 781 (1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged that her pit bull was properly registered with UMH property management as an emotional support animal and that she did not breach her lease; she claims UMH destroyed relevant documentation and that the dog bite report was false.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the Fair Housing Act claim because plaintiff clarified in her response brief that she alleged UMH, not the City of Elkhart, violated the FHA, and UMH is not a party to the case. The court did not reach the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim regarding the emotional support animal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal Protection Clause claim; negligence and defamation claims under Indiana state law; claims related to loss of unemployment benefits, child support payments, and FMLA payments; claims regarding investigation of sexual assault of daughter and arrests of other daughter.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed all federal claims against the City for failure to allege an express City policy, widespread practice with force of law, or final policymaker responsible for the injuries. Plaintiff failed to allege that the City had authority over unemployment benefits (administered by state), child support (administered by Superior Court), or FMLA (enforceable only against employers). Equal Protection claim dismissed for failure to allege widespread City practice of intentional discrimination. State law claims remain pending pending resolution of federal claims against Ms. Becker.

case_name: LaSandra Norman v. Northwest Indiana (Section 8), State of Indiana, Internal Revenue Service, and United States of America
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges Fair Housing Act violations regarding her Section 8 housing termination and eviction based on racial discrimination.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's claims with prejudice because her residence and eviction claims were barred by res judicata from a prior lawsuit, and her remaining allegations regarding being Beyoncé Knowles-Carter and conspiracy theories were facially implausible under the Twombly/Iqbal standard.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff LaSandra Norman sued Northwest Indiana Section 8 housing authority, the State of Indiana, IRS, and United States alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on racial discrimination regarding her Section 8 termination and eviction. The court dismissed the Amended Complaint with prejudice, finding that the housing-related claims were barred by res judicata from a prior lawsuit and that other claims were factually baseless and legally implausible.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 661 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Czarniecki v. City of Chicago, 633 F.3d 545 (7th Cir. 2011)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged discrimination in violation of the Fair Housing Act based on race and gender, claiming a racist coalition against African American women and children on Section 8, and that she was evicted and terminated from Section 8 because she refused to go along with intentional racial discrimination.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the FHA discrimination claim based on res judicata, finding that the same operative facts and parties were involved in a prior lawsuit (2:21-CV-158-TLS-JEM) that was dismissed with prejudice on September 24, 2021. All three elements of res judicata were satisfied: final decision, same transaction, and same litigants.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Federal conspiracy claim against the United States regarding alleged garnishment of revenue and failure to recognize plaintiff as Beyoncé Knowles-Carter; claims of mistreatment by State of Indiana regarding alleged white supremacy and abuse of power; wrongful eviction claim against State of Indiana; challenge to prior judicial decision setting aside entry of default; taxpayer standing claim.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed all non-FHA claims as frivolous and implausible under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(i) and Rule 12(b)(6). Claims based on plaintiff's assertion that she is Beyoncé Knowles-Carter were deemed 'fantastic or delusional scenarios' clearly baseless on their face. The wrongful eviction claim failed for lack of alleged landlord-tenant relationship with the State of Indiana. The challenge to the prior judicial decision was barred by res judicata and improper collateral attack. The taxpayer standing claim failed under Hein v. Freedom From Religion Foundation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA) discrimination claim based on income derived from public assistance (unemployment compensation); ECOA retaliation claim for alleged retaliation after plaintiff complained of discrimination
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient factual content to raise a plausible inference of discrimination under the ECOA. The complaint contained only conclusory allegations that the loan was denied because of unemployment income, without factual allegations showing discriminatory treatment or that plaintiff was otherwise qualified. Similarly, the retaliation claim failed because plaintiff did not allege he exercised a right under the Consumer Credit Protection Act, only that he complained to a branch manager.

case_name: Sandra Black v. Naomi Friedrichsen, et al.
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED - this opinion does not address the underlying accommodation request; it addresses defendants' motion for TRO/injunction regarding plaintiff's social media posts.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion for TRO and preliminary injunction to restrain plaintiff from social media posts because the requested injunctive relief has no relation to the merits judgment defendants seek, defendants have adequate remedies at law through protective orders and discovery sanctions, and First Amendment concerns and public interest in open litigation outweigh any reputational harm.
brief_summary: Sandra Black, a pro se litigant, sued Naomi Friedrichsen and others under the Fair Housing Act; this opinion addresses defendants' motion for a TRO/preliminary injunction to restrain Black from posting about the case on social media and for sanctions. The court denied the motion, finding the requested injunction improper because it lacks connection to the merits, adequate legal remedies exist, and First Amendment interests outweigh the defendants' reputational concerns.
key_cases_cited: USA-Halak Chamber of Com., Inc. v. Best Choice Meats, Inc., 402 F. Supp. 3d 427 (N.D. Ill. 2019)
Tully v. Okeson, 977 F.3d 608 (7th Cir. 2020)
Mazurek v. Armstrong, 520 U.S. 968 (1997)
Seattle Times Co. v. Rhinehart, 467 U.S. 20 (1984)
Union Oil Co. of Cal. v. Leavell, 220 F.3d 562 (7th Cir. 2000)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: First Amendment right to post social media comments about litigation; discovery conduct and deposition compliance
fha_claims.disposition: Motion for TRO and Preliminary Injunction Denied
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the defendants' motion for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction seeking to enjoin the plaintiff from posting social media comments, finding that such an injunction would not preserve the relative positions of the parties pending trial on the merits of the underlying Fair Housing Act claims, and that reputational harm did not outweigh the plaintiff's First Amendment interests and the public interest in open litigation. The court noted that alternative remedies under the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure (protective orders, discovery sanctions) were available.

source_file: 9695710_2022_Pinnacle Treatment Centers, Inc. v. Crown Point, Indiana City of_innd
case_name: Pinnacle Treatment Centers, Inc. v. City of Crown Point, Indiana
accommodation_description: Pinnacle sought to continue operating a group home providing temporary lodging for more than five unrelated recovering substance abuse patients in an R-1 single-family residential zone, which the City treated as a zoning violation subject to daily fines; the FHA reasonable-accommodation framework underlies Pinnacle's claim that the City must exempt the home from these restrictions.
key_holding: A group home operator for recovering substance abusers has standing under the Fair Housing Act as an 'aggrieved person' because the concrete injury of municipal fines levied against it satisfies the injury-in-fact requirement, even if Pinnacle itself is not a member of the protected class.
brief_summary: Pinnacle Treatment Centers operates a group home in Crown Point, Indiana for patients recovering from substance abuse. The City levied fines against Pinnacle for allegedly violating a zoning ordinance that limits unrelated occupants in a residential dwelling to five persons. Pinnacle sued under the Fair Housing Act, and the City moved to dismiss for lack of standing; the court denied the motion, holding that the fines constitute a sufficient concrete injury to confer Article III standing and FHA 'aggrieved person' status.
key_cases_cited: City of Edmonds v. Oxford House, Inc., 514 U.S. 725 (1995)
Gladstone, Realtors v. Village of Bellwood, 441 U.S. 91 (1979)
Gorski v. Troy, 929 F.2d 1183 (7th Cir. 1991)
Warth v. Seldin, 422 U.S. 490 (1975)
Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation to allow operation of a group home for substance abuse recovery patients in an R-1 single-family residential zone that ordinarily restricts occupancy to five unrelated individuals
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the defendant's motion to dismiss for lack of standing, finding that Pinnacle suffered concrete injury (fines levied) and has standing as an aggrieved person under the FHA to vindicate the rights of its disabled patients. The court did not reach the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim itself.

case_name: Darleana Johnson v. Housing Authority of South Bend, et al.
accommodation_description: Pro se plaintiff alleged mold and insufficient heat in public housing unit; requests repairs or, alternatively, fair and equal housing relocation assistance.
key_holding: The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because the plaintiff failed to properly invoke federal question jurisdiction (did not adequately plead Fair Housing Act claims) and failed to establish diversity jurisdiction (all parties are Indiana citizens and no amount in controversy exceeding $75,000 was alleged).
brief_summary: Darleana Johnson, a pro se plaintiff and public housing tenant in South Bend, Indiana, sued the Housing Authority of South Bend and two employees alleging substandard housing conditions including mold and insufficient heat, seeking repairs or relocation assistance. The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss, finding it lacked subject matter jurisdiction because the complaint failed to properly plead Fair Housing Act claims and failed to establish diversity jurisdiction, dismissing the case without prejudice.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Arbaugh v. Y & H Corp., 546 U.S. 500 (2006)
Long v. Shorebank Development Corp., 182 F.3d 548 (7th Cir. 1999)
Muscarello v. Ogle County Board of Commissioners, 610 F.3d 416 (7th Cir. 2010)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Repair of home with mold and insufficient heat; alternatively, fair and equal housing relocation assistance
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1331 (federal question) and § 1332 (diversity). The plaintiff failed to allege discrimination based on a protected ground under the FHA and did not invoke the FHA in her complaint; she also failed to allege citizenship of parties or amount in controversy for diversity jurisdiction. Amendment was deemed futile.

case_name: Shedrick Northern v. Pedcor Management Corp.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged water leaking into his apartment and claimed a right to a habitable home under the FHA, but did not request a specific reasonable accommodation.
key_holding: The court dismissed the Fair Housing Act claim because plaintiff did not allege membership in any protected class or that discrimination based on a protected characteristic was the basis for the defendant's conduct; the FHA is a discrimination law, not a general habitability statute.
brief_summary: Shedrick Northern sued Pedcor Management Corp., his landlord, alleging water damage to his apartment and claiming violations of the Fair Housing Act based on a right to a habitable home. The court dismissed the case without prejudice, finding that the FHA does not provide a general habitability right and that Northern failed to allege membership in any protected class or that any protected characteristic motivated the defendant's conduct.
key_cases_cited: McDaniel v. VTT Management, Inc., 2018 WL 4494985 (W.D.N.C. Sept. 18, 2018)
Valencia v. City of Springfield, Illinois, 883 F.3d 959 (7th Cir. 2018)
Walton v. Claybridge Homeowners Ass'n, Inc., 191 Fed.Appx. 446 (7th Cir. 2006)
Sanghvi v. City of Claremont, 328 F.3d 532 (9th Cir. 2003)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff cited § 3617 (interference, coercion, or intimidation) but alleged only a water leak dispute without any connection to a protected class or FHA-protected right.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed under § 1915(e)(2)(B) as frivolous because plaintiff failed to allege membership in a protected class or that discrimination based on a protected characteristic motivated the defendant's conduct. The FHA is a discrimination law that does not establish a general right to a habitable home, and plaintiff's water leak complaint does not implicate any FHA-protected right.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: State law claims: breach of implied duty of good faith and fair dealing, intentional infliction of emotional distress, and declaratory judgment relief, all arising from water leak allegations.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court declined supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims because there was no diversity of citizenship alleged and the FHA federal question claim was dismissed. The court relinquished supplemental jurisdiction and dismissed the state law claims without prejudice to allow plaintiff to pursue them in state court.

case_name: Shedrick Northern v. Pedcor Management Corp., et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged water damage and mold from toilet leak violated the Fair Housing Act, but no specific accommodation request was made.
key_holding: The court struck plaintiff's emergency amended complaint because he failed to first move to vacate the judgment under Rules 59(e) or 60(b) before seeking to amend after judgment was entered.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Shedrick Northern filed suit against Pedcor Management Corp. alleging water damage and mold from a toilet leak violated the Fair Housing Act. After the case was dismissed without prejudice for lack of federal jurisdiction, plaintiff filed an emergency amended complaint without first moving to vacate the judgment. The court struck the amended complaint as procedurally improper because plaintiff failed to comply with the requirement to first set aside the judgment under Rules 59(e) or 60(b) before seeking amendment post-judgment.
key_cases_cited: Vicom Inc. v. Harbridge Merchant Services Inc., 20 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 1994)
Amendola v. Bayer, 907 F.2d 760 (7th Cir. 1990)
Twohy v. First Nat'l Bank, 758 F.2d 1185 (7th Cir. 1985)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged failure to repair water damage in ceiling caused by toilet leak from upstairs apartment, resulting in mold development
fha_claims.disposition: Dismissed without prejudice for lack of jurisdiction
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found the claim was a typical state court landlord-tenant dispute that did not invoke federal jurisdiction or provisions of the Fair Housing Act. Judge Simon dismissed under § 1915(e)(2)(B) screening, finding the claim lacked a federal question and belonged in state court.

case_name: Black v. Friedrichsen
accommodation_description: This procedural ruling does not address any accommodation request.
key_holding: The court denied the defendants' motion for sanctions because the plaintiff completed her deposition after multiple orders to do so, and denied the plaintiff's motion to disqualify the judges as unsupported by evidence of bias.
brief_summary: Sandra Black sued Naomi Friedrichsen and others alleging racial discrimination in violation of the Fair Housing Act, claiming defendants targeted her based on race and falsely accused her of lease violations. This Opinion and Order addresses procedural matters—the court denied defendants' motion to dismiss the case as a sanction for discovery violations and denied plaintiff's motion to disqualify the judges, allowing the case to proceed.
key_cases_cited: Barnhill v. United States
Ramirez v. T&H Lemont, Inc.
Fuery v. City of Chicago
Salata v. Weyerhaeuser Co.
United States v. Barr

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.disposition: Procedural (sanctions motion; motion to dismiss previously denied)
fha_claims.reasoning: The Court denied the Defendants' motion to dismiss on the merits in an earlier ruling (ECF No. 28). This opinion addresses only discovery sanctions and procedural motions; the underlying FHA racial discrimination claim remains pending and has not been substantively resolved on the merits.

case_name: Graham v. Herron Management Property
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request — complaint alleged harassment and discrimination based on disability and race arising from delayed water heater repairs and water bill dispute.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claims because her complaint contained only conclusory allegations of discrimination based on disability and race without factual content suggesting HPM was motivated by discriminatory intent regarding the water heater repair and billing dispute.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff DeAnn Graham sued Herron Property Management alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on disability and race discrimination arising from a delayed water heater repair and disputed water bill. The district court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding the complaint contained only conclusory allegations of discriminatory intent without plausible factual content to support a FHA claim.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Watters v. Homeowners' Ass'n at Pres. at Bridgewater, No. 19-3499, 2022 WL 4128529 (7th Cir. Sept. 12, 2022)
A.B. v. Hous. Auth. of South Bend, 2012 WL 1877740 (N.D. Ind. May 18, 2012)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's allegations of discrimination based on disability and race were conclusory and lacked plausible factual content showing that defendant's conduct (delayed water heater repair, refusal to credit water bill) was motivated by discriminatory intent. The complaint failed to allege that defendant treated plaintiff differently than similarly situated tenants without disabilities or of different races.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Under § 3617, plaintiff must allege four elements including that defendant was motivated by intent to discriminate. Plaintiff's conclusory assertions of harassment and interference lacked factual allegations showing defendant coerced, threatened, intimidated, or interfered with plaintiff on account of protected FHA activity or discriminatory intent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Human Rights Act violation, falsified documents (49 C.F.R. § 1570.5), defamation (28 U.S.C. § 4101)
fha_claims.reasoning: The 'Human Rights Act' does not exist in the United States Code; 49 C.F.R. § 1570.5 addresses maritime and surface transportation security unrelated to housing; 28 U.S.C. § 4101 addresses foreign judgments and defamation definitions, not a substantive cause of action for defamation. All non-FHA claims failed to state a claim for relief.

case_name: McGrath v. Dunecrest Condominium Association
accommodation_description: Parents of autistic children requested a deck extension as a reasonable accommodation to provide a safe secondary exit from their condominium unit.
key_holding: The motion for judgment on the pleadings was denied because it is unclear when the discriminatory housing practice claims accrued—whether at the July 21, 2018 vote or as a continuing violation from ongoing withholding of building permits—and the Individual Defendants failed to adequately argue why the continuing violations doctrine would not apply.
brief_summary: The McGrath family sued the Dunecrest Condominium Association and individual unit owners for disability discrimination under the Fair Housing Act, alleging the Association improperly denied their request for a deck extension needed as a secondary emergency exit for their two autistic sons despite previously approving similar deck extensions for non-disabled residents. The court denied the Individual Defendants' motion for judgment on the pleadings on statute of limitations grounds, finding genuine disputes about when the claims accrued and whether the Association's ongoing withholding of building permits constituted a continuing violation.
key_cases_cited: Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Cada v. Baxter Healthcare Corp., 920 F.2d 446 (7th Cir. 1990)
United Here Loc. 1 v. Hyatt Corp., 862 F.3d 588 (7th Cir. 2017)
Buchanan-Moore v. Cnty. of Milwaukee, 570 F.3d 824 (7th Cir. 2009)
Luna Vanegas v. Signet Builders, Inc., 46 F.4th 636 (7th Cir. 2022)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Deck extension to provide a safe secondary exit from Unit 121 to ground level for residents with autistic children who have difficulty with emergency situations
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 12(c) Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion for judgment on the pleadings because it was unclear whether the statute of limitations accrued on the date of the vote (July 21, 2018) or on a continuing basis due to the Association's ongoing withholding of necessary paperwork, and the defendants failed to provide substantive argument regarding the continuing violations doctrine.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged discrimination in voting on deck extension request based on disability status of Tim and Martin McGrath, contrasted with approval of similar extensions for non-disabled unit owners
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 12(c) Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion for judgment on the pleadings on statute of limitations grounds because it was unclear whether the discriminatory conduct was the vote itself on July 21, 2018, or a continuing violation based on subsequent withholding of paperwork, and defendants provided insufficient argument on the continuing violations doctrine.

source_file: 9697246_2023_Johnson v. Housing Authority of South Bend_innd
case_name: Johnson v. Housing Authority of South Bend
accommodation_description: Public housing tenant sought to remain in her mold-infested unit during repairs and return afterward, rather than permanently transfer to alternative housing as HASB required.
key_holding: The federal court stayed the action under Colorado River abstention because the parallel state proceedings were substantially advanced, the state court could adequately address Johnson's federal claims, and the federal action risked duplicative and potentially inconsistent rulings.
brief_summary: Darleana Johnson, a public housing tenant, sued the Housing Authority of South Bend seeking to vacate her eviction and alleging violations of the ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and Fair Housing Act based on HASB's insistence she permanently relocate due to mold conditions rather than allow her to return after repairs. The federal court granted HASB's motion to dismiss and stayed the action under Colorado River abstention, finding the parallel state proceedings (which had been remanded to consider Johnson's federal defenses) were far advanced and warranted deference to avoid piecemeal litigation and inconsistent rulings.
key_cases_cited: Colorado River Water Conservation Dist. v. U.S., 424 U.S. 800 (1976)
Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Saudi Basic Indus. Corp., 544 U.S. 280 (2005)
DePuy Synthes Sales, Inc. v. OrthoLA, Inc., 953 F.3d 469 (7th Cir. 2020)
Freed v. J.P. Morgan Chase Bank, N.A., 756 F.3d 1013 (7th Cir. 2014)
Johnson v. Hous. Auth. of S. Bend, 204 N.E. 3d 940 (Ind. Ct. App. 2023)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested to remain in her current residence (Solomon Avenue house) during and after mold remediation rather than accept alternative housing placements offered by HASB. Plaintiff alleged she had a disability-related need to remain in the specific unit due to health difficulties related to mold.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court did not reach the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim. Instead, the court stayed the federal action under Colorado River abstention doctrine, finding that the parallel state court proceedings (which have been remanded for reconsideration of plaintiff's federal defenses) are an adequate and more efficient forum for resolving all claims, including the FHA reasonable accommodation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged HASB retaliated against her by refusing to provide a positive landlord reference to her potential new landlord upon request.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court did not reach the merits of the retaliation claim. The court stayed the federal action under Colorado River abstention, finding that the parallel state court proceedings provide an adequate forum for resolving all claims, including the supplemental retaliation claim based on the denied landlord reference.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II, Rehabilitation Act § 504, Fourteenth Amendment due process and equal protection, and Indiana state law claims related to eviction and housing discrimination.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court stayed all non-FHA claims (ADA, Rehabilitation Act, § 1983 due process and equal protection, and state law claims) under Colorado River abstention, finding that the state court proceedings are parallel and adequate to resolve all federal and state law claims, and that judicial economy and the advanced progress of the state litigation favor staying the federal action pending state court resolution.

case_name: Sandra Black v. Naomi Friedrichsen, Erika Holiday (Liddick), Hunters Run Apartments and Owners, and Interstate Realty Management Co.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges defendants targeted her based on race and falsely accused her of lease violations to force her to vacate the apartment.
key_holding: The Court denied multiple plaintiff motions (preventative injunction, motion to strike, motion to sanction, motion for appointed counsel, motion for immediate order) and took the defendants' summary judgment motion under advisement, extending plaintiff's deadline to respond.
brief_summary: Sandra Black, a pro se plaintiff, sued Naomi Friedrichsen, Erika Holiday, Hunters Run Apartments, and Interstate Realty Management Co. alleging racial discrimination in violation of the Fair Housing Act, claiming defendants targeted her based on race and falsely accused her of lease violations to force her to vacate. The Court denied the plaintiff's various procedural motions and took under advisement the defendants' pending motion for summary judgment, while extending the plaintiff's deadline to file a response brief.
key_cases_cited: In re Mann, 229 F.3d 657 (7th Cir. 2000)
United States ex rel. Fortier v. Winters, No. 00 C 7058, 2007 WL 118225 (N.D. Ill. Jan. 9, 2007)
Pruitt v. Mote, 503 F.3d 647 (7th Cir. 2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court took the defendants' motion for summary judgment under advisement pending the plaintiff's response brief. The plaintiff alleged racial discrimination and false accusations of lease violations to force her to vacate, but the motion for summary judgment has not yet been ruled upon on the merits; the court extended the plaintiff's deadline to respond to June 30, 2023.

case_name: David DeBoard v. Ventry Apartments, LLC, Domo Development Company, LLC, Sunstone Construction Company, LLC and The Ventry Apartments, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a wheelchair user, seeks injunctive relief to compel compliance with FHA design and construction accessibility requirements at newly constructed apartment complex.
key_holding: A professional tester who never intended to rent at the apartments and alleges only a statutory violation as injury lacks Article III standing to sue under TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, which requires concrete injury-in-fact beyond the mere fact of a statutory violation.
brief_summary: David DeBoard, a professional fair housing tester who uses a wheelchair, sued Ventry Apartments and related entities alleging the recently constructed apartment complex contained design and construction barriers that violated FHA accessibility requirements. The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss for lack of Article III standing, holding that under TransUnion, a professional tester who never intended to rent and alleges only a statutory violation as injury lacks the concrete and particularized injury required for standing.
key_cases_cited: TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 141 S.Ct. 2190 (2021)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Laufer v. Arpan, LLC, 29 F.4th 1268 (11th Cir. 2022)
Village of Bellwood v. Dwivedi, 895 F.2d 1521 (7th Cir. 1990)
Allen v. Wright, 468 U.S. 737 (1986)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible design and construction of apartment complex, including accessible routes to first floor units, dog park, and mailboxes; compliant slopes and cross-slopes; wheel-stops in parking areas; and doors of sufficient width to allow passage by wheelchair users
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff, a professional tester who never intended to rent at the complex and alleged only the statutory violation itself without concrete particularized injury (such as humiliation or frustration), lacks Article III standing post-TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez because he failed to allege a concrete injury in fact beyond the violation of law itself.

case_name: Sandra Black v. Naomi Friedrichsen, Erika Holiday (Liddick), Hunters Run Apartments and Owners, and Interstate Realty Management Co.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation request was made; this case involves race discrimination allegations only.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for the defendants because the plaintiff failed to produce evidence from which a reasonable jury could infer that the defendants treated her differently because of her race, as she could not identify similarly situated individuals outside her protected class who were treated more favorably.
brief_summary: Sandra Black, a Black tenant, sued Hunters Run Apartments and its management company alleging race discrimination under the Fair Housing Act, claiming the defendants targeted her based on her race and falsely accused her of lease violations to force her to vacate. The court granted summary judgment for the defendants, finding the plaintiff failed to produce evidence of discriminatory intent or identify similarly situated Caucasian tenants who were treated more favorably.
key_cases_cited: Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009)
Texas Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
East-Miller v. Lake Cnty. Highway Dep't, 421 F.3d 558 (7th Cir. 2005)
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Wetzel v. Glen St. Andrew Living Cmty., LLC, 901 F.3d 856 (7th Cir. 2018)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to produce evidence of discriminatory intent by any defendant. The tone of Ms. Friedrichsen's voice, without racial slurs or derogatory statements, is insufficient to create an inference of race discrimination. Plaintiff also failed to identify a similarly situated individual outside her protected class treated more favorably; her allegation regarding Tawnya Seacott was contradicted by Ms. Seacott's affidavit and unsupported by evidence that defendants knew of any unauthorized occupants in Seacott's apartment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish evidence of race-based discrimination necessary to support a § 3617 interference claim. Additionally, plaintiff failed to demonstrate severe or pervasive harassment; the alleged incidents (tone of voice, delayed HVAC repair, isolated police call, pet violation warning) were neither frequent nor severe and lacked evidence of race-based motivation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Constructive eviction claim based on alleged forced departure from apartment due to racial discrimination and hostile housing environment
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff voluntarily agreed to vacate under a Joint Agreement that allowed her to remain for 60 days with unauthorized occupants in exchange for departure by a specified date. At summary judgment, plaintiff failed to produce evidence of intentional discrimination or a race-based hostile housing environment that would support an inference her agreement was involuntary, despite the court having denied the motion to dismiss on this claim at an earlier stage.

case_name: Smith v. Kittle Property Group, Inc.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation was requested in this case; the dispute centers on alleged discriminatory termination of employment and eviction based on race, sex, and sexual orientation.
key_holding: The court denied Kittle's motion to dismiss the sexual orientation discrimination claim (count three), holding that because sexual orientation discrimination is a legally recognized form of sex discrimination under Title VII, Smith's EEOC charge alleging sex discrimination was sufficient to exhaust administrative remedies as to the sexual orientation claim, but merged count three into count two as a single sex discrimination count.
brief_summary: Kiontay Smith, a former maintenance technician and tenant of Kittle Property Group, was terminated and evicted after returning from sick leave, allegedly due to a confrontation with a white resident over a parking policy. She filed suit alleging wrongful termination under Title VII based on race, sex, and sexual orientation discrimination, and wrongful eviction under the FHA. Kittle moved to dismiss only the sexual orientation claim (count three) on the ground that Smith failed to exhaust administrative remedies by not checking a separate sexual orientation box on her EEOC charge. The court denied the motion, finding that sexual orientation discrimination is a form of sex discrimination under Bostock and Hively, that Smith's EEOC charge alleging sex discrimination and referencing her wife was sufficient to preserve the claim, but ordered counts two and three merged into a single count.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Bostock v. Clayton Cnty., 140 S. Ct. 1731 (2020)
Hively v. Ivy Tech Cmty. Coll. of Ind., 853 F.3d 339 (7th Cir. 2017)
Rush v. McDonald Corp., 966 F.2d 1104 (7th Cir. 1992)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VII employment discrimination (race, sex, sexual orientation); wrongful eviction under FHA
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the motion to dismiss the sexual orientation discrimination claim under Title VII, holding that sexual orientation discrimination is a form of sex discrimination under Bostock and Hively, and therefore the claim was properly exhausted in the EEOC charge where sex discrimination was alleged. The court merged counts two and three (sex and sexual orientation discrimination) into a single count but allowed the claim to proceed on the merits.

case_name: Mabry v. City of East Chicago
accommodation_description: This opinion does not analyze a reasonable accommodation claim; it addresses only a post-judgment motion to retax costs under Rule 54(d)(1).
key_holding: The court granted plaintiffs' motion to retax costs and vacated the clerk's taxation of $13,620.98 in costs, finding that plaintiffs are indigent and cannot pay, litigated in good faith, and defendants did not oppose the waiver request.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Kendra Mabry and Angela Espinoza, who lost at summary judgment on their Fair Housing Act claims regarding housing conditions at a residential complex with lead and arsenic contamination, filed a motion to retax costs seeking waiver of $13,620.98 in costs imposed against them. The court granted the motion, finding plaintiffs indigent, litigated in good faith, and unable to pay without severe impact on their families and housing stability.
key_cases_cited: Rivera v. City of Chicago, 469 F.3d 631 (7th Cir. 2006)
McGill v. Faulkner, 18 F.3d 456 (7th Cir. 1994)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act and equal protection claims related to a housing complex with lead and arsenic contamination
fha_claims.reasoning: Judgment was entered in favor of Defendants on December 28, 2023. The Fair Housing Act and equal protection claims were decided on summary judgment and resulted in a loss for Plaintiffs, though the opinion does not detail the substantive legal analysis of the FHA claims themselves—this opinion addresses only the post-judgment motion to waive costs.

source_file: 9698624_2024_Pinnacle Treatment Centers, Inc. v. Crown Point, Indiana City of_innd
case_name: Pinnacle Treatment Centers, Inc. v. City of Crown Point, Indiana
accommodation_description: Pinnacle requested a zoning variance as a reasonable accommodation to permit up to eight unrelated recovering substance abusers (disabled persons under the FHA) to reside in the group home in an R-1 single-family residential district.
key_holding: Both parties' cross-motions for summary judgment were denied because genuine disputes of material fact exist as to whether the City's denial of a zoning variance and enforcement of the five-person occupancy limit were motivated by discriminatory animus against recovering substance abusers, and whether the requested variance was reasonable and necessary to provide disabled residents an equal opportunity to live in a residential neighborhood.
brief_summary: Pinnacle Treatment Centers sued the City of Crown Point, Indiana alleging the City violated the Fair Housing Act by denying a zoning variance that would allow a group home for recovering substance abusers to house up to eight unrelated disabled residents in an R-1 single-family district. The court denied both parties' cross-motions for summary judgment, finding triable disputes exist as to whether the City's denial was motivated by discriminatory animus reflected in community opposition and whether the variance is reasonable and necessary under the FHA.
key_cases_cited: Oconomowoc Residential Programs, Inc. v. City of Oconomowoc Lake, 300 F.3d 776 (7th Cir. 2002)
Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009)
Dadian v. Village of Wilmette, 269 F.3d 831 (7th Cir. 2001)
United States v. City of Chicago Heights, 161 F. Supp. 2d 819 (N.D. Ill. 2001)
Step By Step, Inc. v. City of Ogdensburg, 176 F. Supp. 3d 112 (N.D.N.Y. 2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether City officials' enforcement of the zoning ordinance and denial of the variance were motivated by discriminatory animus against substance abuse disorder patients, based on circumstantial evidence including community opposition animated by bias, mayor's private meetings with BZA, and official questioning suggesting animus. Case inappropriate for summary judgment on intentional discrimination claims requiring credibility determinations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Zoning variance permitting up to eight unrelated individuals (residents of group home for substance abuse recovery) to live in R-1 residential district, which ordinarily limits occupancy to five unrelated persons
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied three-part FHA reasonable accommodation test (reasonableness, necessity, equal opportunity) and found genuine disputes of material fact. Delegatto's lay testimony regarding therapeutic benefits of eight-resident community-based facility was admissible and created triable issue on necessity. Evidence that group home posed no actual burden to City and that facially neutral ordinance may be applied discriminatorily supported finding that variance is reasonable and necessary to afford disabled residents equal opportunity to live in residential neighborhood.

case_name: McGrath v. Dunecrest Condominium Association
accommodation_description: Request to extend an existing second-floor balcony and add stairs leading to the ground to provide a reliable secondary exit for adult autistic children.
key_holding: The McGraths failed to establish that the balcony extension with stairs was 'necessary' under § 3604(f)(3)(B) causation standard, as they could not show Tim and Martin's autism was the but-for cause of their need for the accommodation.
brief_summary: The McGrath family sued their condominium association seeking to build a balcony extension with stairs as a reasonable accommodation for their adult autistic sons; the court granted summary judgment for the association, finding the plaintiffs failed to establish causation—that their children's autism was the but-for cause necessitating the accommodation—required under § 3604(f)(3)(B).
key_cases_cited: Oconomowoc Residential Programs v. City of Milwaukee, 300 F.3d 775 (7th Cir. 2002)
Wis. Cmty. Servs., Inc. v. City of Milwaukee, 465 F.3d 737 (7th Cir. 2006)
Texas Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Balcony extension with staircase to provide secondary exit and additional space for pacing and feeding tube administration
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the causation requirement under § 3604(f)(3)(B), holding that plaintiffs failed to establish that Tim and Martin's autism was the but-for cause of their need for the balcony extension. The problems addressed (unreliable secondary exit, wear and tear, lack of grilling space, entrapment risk) affect anyone living in the unit, not just those with autism, making them too attenuated from the disability under the Good Shepherd standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of balcony extension based on familial status (presence of disabled adult children)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that § 3604(b) familial status protection applies only to families with individuals under age 18, not families with disabled adults. Tim and Martin were 26 years old at the time of the vote. Plaintiffs failed to establish a prima facie case of familial status discrimination and did not identify similarly situated comparators with children under 18 who were treated more favorably.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Three emails from Association: lien notice for unpaid special assessment, request to remove anchors/bolts and repair garage door, and fire marshal report prohibiting grilling on decks
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that plaintiffs failed to establish an adverse outcome required for § 3617 retaliation. The three emails caused only trivial harm (inconvenience), and no further action was taken by the Association. A reasonable person would not view the emails as coercive, intimidating, threatening, or interfering with protected FHA rights under the Burlington standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Individual defendants' votes against balcony extension based on alleged discriminatory animus
fha_claims.reasoning: The court sua sponte granted summary judgment in favor of individual defendants because the discrimination claims against them were interrelated with and dependent upon the claims against the Association, which had already been dismissed. The plaintiffs had adequate opportunity to oppose the motion and the same legal deficiencies applied.

source_file: 9698899_2019_NEW HORIZONS REHABILITATION, INC. v. STATE OF INDIANA_insd
case_name: New Horizons Rehabilitation, Inc. v. State of Indiana, Executive Director, Indiana Department of Homeland Security
accommodation_description: Request to be classified as a Class 2 single-family residential structure rather than a Class 1 commercial structure, including exemption from commercial fire suppression system and architect requirements, as a reasonable accommodation for intellectually and developmentally disabled residents.
key_holding: Indiana's classification of New Horizons' supported living home as a Class 1 commercial structure, requiring commercial building codes and fire suppression systems while treating similar single-family residences differently, constitutes unlawful discrimination under the FHAA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act because the disparate treatment stems solely from the residents' disabilities.
brief_summary: New Horizons Rehabilitation, Inc., a not-for-profit operator of supported living homes for adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities, sued the State of Indiana and its Department of Homeland Security after being required to construct a new Lawrenceburg home as a Class 1 commercial structure subject to commercial building codes and fire suppression requirements, while single-family residences are classified as Class 2. The court granted New Horizons' motion for summary judgment on reasonable accommodation and disparate treatment claims under the FHAA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act, permanently enjoining DHS from enforcing Class 1 requirements on the home and awarding $30,400 in damages, but denied the Equal Protection claim.
key_cases_cited: City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Hemisphere Bldg. v. Village of Richton Park, 171 F.3d 437 (7th Cir. 1999)
Oconomowoc Residential Programs v. City of Milwaukee, 300 F.3d 775 (7th Cir. 2002)
Valencia v. City of Springfield, 883 F.3d 959 (7th Cir. 2018)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Variance from Class 1 structure requirements to allow construction of supported living home without commercial fire suppression system; treating the home as a Class 2 structure subject to residential code rather than commercial building code
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied the three-element FHAA reasonable accommodation test (reasonable, necessary, and affords equal opportunity) and found plaintiff made prima facie showing that variance was reasonable because cost DHS identified (loss of safety) is one it incurs with every single-family home. Defendants failed to rebut with evidence that the home without sprinkler system posed greater safety risk than other Class 2 structures. Accommodation is proportional to costs because DHS makes same tradeoff in all single-family homes.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that although Indiana's zoning statute is facially neutral, it is being applied as a proxy to evade prohibition of intentional discrimination. DHS treats foster children in family homes as non-tenants (Class 2) but treats intellectually/developmentally disabled adults in supported living homes as tenants (Class 1) with no systematic definition or justification for the distinction. This inconsistent application constitutes disparate treatment under the FHAA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal Protection Clause challenge to zoning scheme; Americans with Disabilities Act Title II; Rehabilitation Act Section 504
fha_claims.reasoning: Under rational-basis review for Equal Protection claim, court found the zoning statute on its face withstands scrutiny as it does not explicitly discriminate against disabled persons. Although plaintiff presented compelling argument that residents are better-prepared for safety hazards, plaintiff failed to negate the rational basis offered by defendants (safety). A reasonably conceivable set of facts (danger to residents and emergency personnel from lack of sprinkler system) could justify the law as applied, and laws have strong presumption of validity under rational-basis analysis.

source_file: 9699210_2019_WATTERS v. HOMEOWNERS ASSOCIATION AT THE PRESERVE AT BRIDGEWATER_insd
case_name: Watters v. Homeowners Association at the Preserve at Bridgewater
accommodation_description: Request for a six-foot vinyl privacy fence to enclose pool and yard area for therapeutic use due to disability (PTSD and pulmonary condition)
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for defendants on the reasonable accommodation claim because plaintiffs failed to provide sufficient admissible evidence that a privacy fence was necessary to afford equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling, and the HOA offered a reasonable alternative accommodation (wrought-iron fence with landscaping).
brief_summary: Terence and Tonca Watters sued the Homeowners Association at the Preserve at Bridgewater alleging race and disability discrimination under the Fair Housing Act, including a failure to accommodate claim for denying their request for a privacy fence. The court granted summary judgment for defendants, finding plaintiffs failed to provide sufficient admissible evidence that the privacy fence was necessary to accommodate Terence Watters's disabilities, and noting the HOA offered a reasonable alternative accommodation.
key_cases_cited: Oconomowoc Residential Programs v. City of Milwaukee, 300 F.3d 775 (7th Cir. 2002)
Howard v. City of Beavercreek, 276 F.3d 802 (6th Cir. 2002)
Stevens v. Hollywood Towers & Condominium Ass'n, 836 F. Supp. 2d 800 (N.D. Ill. 2011)
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 802 (1973)
Beck v. Univ. of Wisc. Bd. of Regents, 75 F.3d 1130 (7th Cir. 1996)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to establish a pattern of coercion, intimidation, or interference motivated by intentional race discrimination. Racial slurs by the Mamarils were isolated incidents too attenuated from challenged actions (fence denial, pool delay, pet issues, mailbox restrictions). No direct evidence of discriminatory intent; indirect burden-shifting method failed because similarly situated Caucasian homeowners were denied privacy fences and treated identically. Incidents were neighborhood quarrels, not federal discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of privacy fence request based on race
fha_claims.reasoning: Under McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting, plaintiffs failed to establish that similarly situated Caucasian neighbors were treated more favorably. The Smiths' small cedar fence and Stedrys' decorative garden fence were not similarly situated because they did not block line of sight, unlike plaintiffs' requested six-foot vinyl privacy fence. Multiple Caucasian homeowners (Dinns, Shearer, Yeary) were also denied privacy fences, demonstrating consistent neutral enforcement of covenants.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Six-foot tall vinyl privacy fence to enclose pool and portion of yard
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to establish that the privacy fence was necessary to afford Terence Watters equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling. Terence Watters lived in the home for several years without the fence, demonstrating no denial of equal opportunity. Hearsay testimony that a privacy fence would be 'beneficial' is insufficient to show necessity; 'beneficial' does not equal 'necessary.' The HOA offered reasonable alternative accommodations (wrought-iron fence with landscaping). Plaintiffs failed to disclose PTSD and dog-related trauma in their formal accommodation request, breaking the interactive process; the HOA invited alternative proposals but plaintiffs did not respond. Defendants lacked knowledge of the specific disability-related need for privacy.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1982 claim for interference with property rights based on race
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 1982 requires proof of racial animus, intent to discriminate, and deprivation of protected property rights because of race. The claim survives only if the record demonstrates triable issues of intentional discrimination, which it does not. The same analysis as the FHA claims applies: no direct evidence of discriminatory intent, and the indirect burden-shifting method fails because similarly situated Caucasian homeowners received identical treatment.

source_file: 9699611_2020_FAIR HOUSING CENTER OF CENTRAL INDIANA, INC. v. RAINBOW REALTY GROUP, INC._insd
case_name: Fair Housing Center of Central Indiana, Inc. et al v. Rainbow Realty Group, Inc. et al
race_if_mentioned: Racial minorities as a class; specific named plaintiffs are Mary Kamano, Norma Tejeda, Cordell Spencer, Maria Gaspar, and Franklin Paz
accommodation_description: No disability accommodation request; the case involves a reverse redlining challenge to a rent-to-buy program alleged to discriminate against racial minorities
key_holding: The court certified a class of all Rainbow rent-to-buy customers since 2009 and certified common questions under Rules 23(b)(2) and (c)(4), including whether Rainbow engaged in discrimination in violation of the Fair Housing Act, while denying individual damages claims that would require fact-specific inquiry.
brief_summary: Fair Housing Center of Central Indiana and five minority plaintiffs sued Rainbow Realty Group challenging its rent-to-buy program as predatory and discriminatory in violation of the Fair Housing Act (reverse redlining) and other laws. The court granted partial class certification, identifying common questions suitable for class resolution under Rules 23(b)(2) and (c)(4) while denying certification of individual damages claims requiring fact-specific inquiry.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dept. of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 135 S. Ct. 2507 (2015)
Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. v. Dukes, 564 U.S. 338 (2011)
Stevens v. Hous. Auth. of S. Bend, Indiana, 663 F.3d 300 (7th Cir. 2011)
Halprin v. Prairie Single Family Homes of Dearborn Park Ass'n, 388 F.3d 327 (7th Cir. 2004)
Estate of Davis v. Wells Fargo Bank, 633 F.3d 529 (7th Cir. 2011)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court certified the reverse redlining claim (disparate impact under FHA § 3604(b) and ECOA) as a common question suitable for class resolution. The court found that whether Rainbow's program is discriminatory or has disparate impact on racial minorities can be answered class-wide without analyzing individual home conditions. The claim survives the class certification stage and proceeds to merits.
