The court conditionally certified the 332-member settlement class and granted preliminary approval of the settlement, finding it the product of serious, non-collusive negotiations with immediate value outweighing continued litigation.
key_cases_cited: DG ex rel. Stricklin v. DeVaughn, 594 F.3d 1188 (10th Cir. 2010)
Shook v. El Paso Cnty., 386 F.3d 963 (10th Cir. 2004)
McFadden v. Sprint Commc'ns LLC, 2024 WL 1533897 (D. Kan. 2024)
In re Motor Fuel Temperature Sales Pracs. Litig., 286 F.R.D. 488 (D. Kan. 2012)
Rutter & Wilbanks Corp. v. Shell Oil Co., 314 F.3d 1180 (10th Cir. 2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to provide reasonable accommodations related to pest control, habitability, and essential services for elderly and disabled tenants suffering from bed-bug infestations, mold, flooding, and other uninhabitable conditions
fha_claims.reasoning: The parties reached a settlement agreement resolving all FHA claims without judicial determination of merits. The settlement provides class members with monetary compensation of approximately $208.04 per month of residence and injunctive relief to remedy ongoing habitability issues at the property.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Implied warranty of habitability, breach of contract and statutory duty, failure to provide essential services, negligence, and Kansas Consumer Protection Act violations
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA claims were resolved through the class settlement agreement without judicial determination of merits on the underlying legal theories.

source_file: 9711727_2024_Adam v. Andmark White Lakes Apartments, LLC_ksd
case_name: Garry Adam v. Andmark White Lakes Apartments, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, who is blind, requested that defendants put the offer to transfer units in writing, and argued that his repair requests constituted reasonable accommodation requests.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA reasonable accommodation claim because plaintiff failed to allege that defendants OPG and 37North knew or reasonably should have known of his disability, and because plaintiff's requests for repairs did not constitute requests for accommodation of an otherwise valid policy.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Garry Adam, who is legally blind due to a retinal dystrophy, sued his former landlords and property managers alleging Fair Housing Act violations including failure to accommodate, refusal to rent, and retaliation. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that plaintiff failed to state a claim because the new property managers (OPG and 37North) lacked knowledge of his disability and because plaintiff's repair requests did not constitute valid accommodation requests under the FHA.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Asbury v. Brougham, 866 F.2d 1276 (10th Cir. 1989)
Bangerter v. Orem City Corp., 46 F.3d 1491 (10th Cir. 1995)
Hatfield v. Cottages on 78th Cmty. Ass'n, No. 21-4035 (10th Cir. 2022)
Ngiendo v. Univ. Partners, LLC, No. 22-2393-HLT (D. Kan. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of opportunity to continue renting; alleged misrepresentation that unit was not available
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege that OPG and 37North had knowledge of his disability, and he was offered the opportunity to rent another unit but failed to attempt to rent it. The claim under § 3604(d) requires showing the housing opportunity remained available, which plaintiff did not establish.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request for written confirmation of offer to transfer to another unit; requests for maintenance repairs characterized as accommodation requests
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege that OPG and 37North knew or reasonably should have known of his disability, and failed to allege that he requested an accommodation necessary to afford equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling. Maintenance repair requests do not constitute reasonable accommodation requests under § 3604(f)(3)(B), which requires a change to an otherwise valid policy.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation for complaints to HUD and local housing authority regarding maintenance issues
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's protected activity (complaints to HUD and housing authority) occurred prior to OPG and 37North's ownership change, so he did not engage in protected activity regarding these defendants' actions. Additionally, plaintiff failed to allege that these defendants had knowledge of the protected activity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rehabilitation Act claim; Kansas Landlord Tenant Act claims for failure to maintain premises, unlawful entry, and retaliation
fha_claims.reasoning: Rehabilitation Act claim fails on same grounds as FHA claims (failure to allege knowledge of disability and failure to accommodate). Additionally, plaintiff failed to allege that OPG and 37North received federal financial assistance. KLTA claims fail because plaintiff failed to allege that 37North had knowledge of defects, OPG's request for vacation was reasonable given the state of disrepair, entries were made after plaintiff requested services, and retaliation claim lacks factual support.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Bivens claim for deliberate indifference to serious medical needs while incarcerated
fha_claims.disposition: Motion to Dismiss Denied Without Prejudice
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the defendant's motion to dismiss without prejudice after learning of the plaintiff's death. The case was not resolved on the merits but rather on the procedural issue of whether the plaintiff's mother would substitute as party pursuant to Rule 25 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.

source_file: 9714170_2023_Garvey Farm LP v. City of Elsmere, Kentucky_kyed
case_name: Garvey Farm LP v. City of Elsmere, Kentucky
accommodation_description: Mobile home park operator seeks to expand by rezoning adjacent vacant land for manufactured housing development, alleging discriminatory denial based on protected class composition of prospective residents
key_holding: The city council members have absolute legislative immunity for their zoning decisions regardless of alleged discriminatory motive; the vacant land satisfies the FHA definition of 'dwelling'; and plaintiffs failed to show the taking was pretextual since parks and public facilities constitute legitimate public use.
brief_summary: Garvey Farm LP, a mobile home park operator, sued the City of Elsmere, Kentucky after the city denied its zoning amendment to expand the park onto adjacent vacant land and passed an ordinance making such expansion more difficult. The court dismissed the claims against individual council members based on legislative immunity, found that vacant land qualifies as a dwelling under § 3604(b), and dismissed the takings and conspiracy claims because the city's stated public use (park and public works facility) was not pretextual.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Bogan v. Scott-Harris
Kelo v. City of New London

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that vacant land offered for sale for construction of residences qualifies as a 'dwelling' under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(b), and the plaintiffs' allegations that the city denied a zoning amendment to prevent development of affordable housing for Hispanics, Latinos, and other protected classes survived the motion to dismiss under the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Takings Clause (Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments), conspiracy to commit unlawful taking
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the takings and conspiracy claims because the plaintiffs failed to allege pretext; condemnation of land for a public park is a universally recognized public use, and the plaintiffs did not allege that the city sought the property under mere pretext of public purpose to confer private benefit, as required under Kelo v. City of New London.

case_name: Miller v. Alco Management, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges Alco Defendants discriminated against him based on gender and disabled status in the terms, conditions, and privileges of his rental and services in connection with his tenancy at Southern Oaks apartment complex.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claims as time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations, finding the alleged discriminatory housing practices occurred no later than July 24, 2020 (when plaintiff moved out) but the complaint was not filed until August 11, 2022.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Ron Miller sued Alco Management, Inc. and related entities (property management) and Georgetown Police Department, alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on gender and disability discrimination in the terms and conditions of his tenancy at Southern Oaks apartment complex. The court overruled plaintiff's objections and adopted the magistrate judge's recommendation, granting defendants' motions to dismiss because the FHA claims were time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations.
key_cases_cited: Hollis v. Chestnut Bend Homeowners Ass'n, 760 F.3d 531 (6th Cir. 2014)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's FHA disparate treatment claim based on gender and disabled status was time-barred under 42 U.S.C. § 3613(a)(1)(A), which requires civil action within 2 years of the discriminatory practice. The alleged discrimination occurred no later than July 24, 2020 (plaintiff's move-out date), but the complaint was not filed until August 11, 2022, exceeding the statute of limitations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's retaliation claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3617 against Detective Crump failed to plausibly allege discriminatory animus or disparate impact. The complaint contained only conclusory statements (e.g., alleged GPD policy of 'taking care of Georgetown's women,' alleged falsification of police report, alleged dropping of drug investigation) without supporting factual allegations sufficient to meet the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fraudulent misrepresentation, breach of contract, fraud by omission, breach of implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, tortious interference, statutory violations under U.S.C. Titles 24 and 42 (due process)
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA claims failed under Rule 12(b)(6) for failure to state a plausible claim. Fraudulent misrepresentation claims lacked sufficient factual allegations of inducement; breach of contract claims failed because the lease imposed no obligation on Southern Oaks to enforce lease terms on plaintiff's behalf; fraud by omission failed because plaintiff did not plausibly allege the principal's identity was material to his decision to lease; breach of implied covenant failed because plaintiff admitted failing to complete recertification paperwork; tortious interference failed for the same reason; and statutory due process claims lacked legal basis and were merely regurgitations of statutory code.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (deprivation of constitutional rights under color of law); 18 U.S.C. §§ 241, 242, 1621 (conspiracy, perjury, deprivation of rights); 42 U.S.C. § 3617 (cited but inapplicable)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead sufficient factual allegations showing personal involvement of Defendants Bogan and Gregory in the alleged constitutional violation. The complaint contains only conclusory allegations and broad assertions unsupported by specific facts. Respondeat superior does not apply in § 1983 actions, and Plaintiff alleged no facts showing supervisory liability, authorization, approval, or acquiescence. Criminal statutes (18 U.S.C. §§ 241, 242, 1621) cannot be enforced by private citizens. Section 3617 (Fair Housing Act) has no applicability to the facts alleged.

case_name: Alberto James Santiago, Sr. v. Elishia Chill, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that management repair a broken door that caused him physical injury and prevented him from entering and exiting his apartment due to his mobility disability and arm condition.
key_holding: The court allowed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claims alleging discrimination based on national origin and disability, retaliation, and failure to make reasonable accommodation to proceed against defendants Chill, Hext, and Key Property Management, while dismissing claims against other defendants for failure to meet pleading standards.
brief_summary: Alberto James Santiago, a 57-year-old tenant in a wheelchair with a mobility-related arm injury, sued Key Property Management and individual managers alleging discrimination, failure to accommodate (broken door not repaired for years causing physical injury and trapping him in his apartment), retaliation for filing HUD complaints, and discriminatory eviction based on his national origin (Puerto Rican) and disability. The court dismissed claims against some defendants for failing to meet pleading standards but allowed claims for discrimination, retaliation, and failure to make reasonable accommodation to proceed against the primary defendants.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Groner v. Golden Gate Gardens Apartments, 250 F.3d 1039 (6th Cir. 2001)
Larkin v. State of Mich. Dep't of Soc. Servs., 89 F.3d 285 (6th Cir. 1996)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Repair of broken apartment door that plaintiff alleged caused arm injury and mobility issues; plaintiff alleged he could not properly enter/exit apartment due to broken door requiring him to twist his arm
fha_claims.reasoning: Court allowed FHA reasonable accommodation claim to proceed against Chill, Hext, and Key Property Management without dismissing it; no substantive merits analysis was conducted at the screening stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court allowed FHA discrimination claim based on national origin and disability to proceed against Chill, Hext, and Key Property Management without substantive analysis at screening stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court allowed FHA retaliation claim under § 3617 to proceed against Chill, Hext, and Key Property Management; plaintiff alleged retaliation for filing HUD complaint and contacting Fair Housing Council.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (due process/civil rights), Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (national origin discrimination), Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act (disability discrimination)
fha_claims.disposition: § 1983 claims dismissed under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B); Title VI and § 504 claims survive
fha_claims.reasoning: § 1983 claims dismissed because defendants are private actors and § 1983 requires state action; Title VI and § 504 claims allowed to proceed against Chill, Hext, and Key Property Management as they do not require state action.

case_name: Ruth Castro Uribe v. Cynthia Ramser, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff made vague references to housing rights violations affecting minorities, elderly, and persons with disabilities but did not clearly request any specific reasonable accommodation; her filings challenged secondhand smoke exposure, rent payment practices, and sought an air purifier.
key_holding: The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss because plaintiff failed to establish federal subject matter jurisdiction by relying solely on Maine and Kentucky state law, and to the extent she attempted to raise federal claims including Fair Housing Act claims, those claims were dismissed without prejudice for failure to comply with Rule 8's pleading requirements.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Ruth Castro Uribe sued landlords Cynthia Ramser, Tom Ramser, and EER Investments, LLC alleging housing rights violations, human rights violations, and financial exploitation under Maine and Kentucky state law, complaining about secondhand smoke exposure and requiring twelve advance rent checks. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss for lack of federal subject matter jurisdiction, finding plaintiff failed to identify any viable federal cause of action despite vague references to housing discrimination affecting minorities, elderly, and disabled persons.
key_cases_cited: Twombly, 550 U.S. 544
Kensu v. Corizon, Inc., 5 F.4th 646

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged housing rights violations, discrimination based on disability, race, ethnicity, age, and economic abuse; secondhand smoke exposure; requirement to provide twelve signed checks in advance; failure to maintain hot water; and alleged retaliation for notice to vacate. Claims were brought under Maine state law (22 M.R.S. § 3472) and Kentucky state law.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because plaintiff failed to cite or allege any federal law or constitutional provision; complaint relied solely on Maine and Kentucky state law. To the extent plaintiff attempted to raise federal claims (including potential Fair Housing Act claims), they were dismissed without prejudice for failure to comply with Rule 8 because the complaint did not clearly identify any federal causes of action or develop factual allegations to support them.

case_name: Rodney L. Nance, Sr. v. Mayfield Plaza Apartments Management et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a convicted felon released from incarceration, alleges he was threatened with eviction from his fiancée's apartment based on his criminal history.
key_holding: Plaintiff lacks standing to bring FHA claims because he is not a lessee, and even construing the complaint liberally, his status as a felon is not a protected class under the FHA.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Rodney Nance sued Mayfield Plaza Apartments Management alleging he was threatened with eviction from his fiancée's apartment because he is a convicted felon. The court dismissed the case, finding plaintiff lacks standing because he is not a lessee and his status as a convicted felon is not a protected class under the Fair Housing Act.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 Fourteenth Amendment due process claim; FHA claim based on alleged felon status discrimination
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed § 1983 Fourteenth Amendment claim because defendants are private actors not acting under color of state law, and dismissed FHA claim because plaintiff is not a lessee, did not attempt to rent or buy an apartment, and felon status is not a protected class under the FHA. Court applied § 1915(e)(2)(B) screening standard and found claims frivolous or failing to state a claim.

case_name: Yusef Abdullah Bilal Ali v. Louisville Metro Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested permission to keep his 120-pound pit bull-Mastiff emotional support animal off leash during surgical recovery from knee surgery.
key_holding: The court denied Plaintiff's Emergency Motion for Injunction Pending Appeal, finding Plaintiff failed to demonstrate likelihood of success on the merits because his requested off-leash accommodation was unreasonable given the dog's documented aggressive behavior, and his transfer request was properly denied because he failed to provide required medical documentation.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Yusef Abdullah Bilal Ali, a public housing tenant with mobility impairments requiring knee surgery, sued Louisville Metro Housing Authority alleging failure to accommodate his requests to keep his emotional support animal off leash and to transfer to a two-bedroom single-family unit. The court denied Plaintiff's Emergency Motion for Injunction Pending Appeal, finding he could not demonstrate likelihood of success on the merits because the off-leash request posed unacceptable safety risks given the dog's documented aggressive history, and LMHA properly denied the transfer request after Plaintiff failed to provide required medical documentation.
key_cases_cited: Overlook Mut. Homes, Inc. v. Spencer, 415 F. App'x 617 (6th Cir. 2011)
Hollis v. Chesnut Bend Homeowner's Ass'n, 760 F.3d 531 (6th Cir. 2014)
Anderson v. City of Blue Ash, 798 F.3d 338 (6th Cir. 2015)
Howard v. HMK Holdings, LLC, 988 F.3d 1185 (9th Cir. 2021)
Kleiber v. Honda of America Mfg., Inc., 485 F.3d 862 (6th Cir. 2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to keep emotional support animal (120-pound pit bull-Mastiff mix) off leash for training purposes during surgical recovery from knee surgery
fha_claims.disposition: Emergency Motion for Injunction Pending Appeal
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied reasonableness balancing test and found the requested accommodation unreasonable because the dog had documented history of aggressive behavior toward residents, staff, and other animals, and allowing the dog off-leash would violate local ordinance and pose unacceptable risk of harm. The burden of the accommodation outweighed any benefits to plaintiff.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Transfer from current unit at 2903 Six Mile Lane to a single-family two-bedroom unit to accommodate emotional support animal safety during recovery from knee surgery
fha_claims.disposition: Emergency Motion for Injunction Pending Appeal
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff failed to satisfy the necessity element because he did not provide required physician certification that the two-bedroom unit was medically necessary, despite LMHA's repeated requests and offer to arrange transfer if documentation was provided. Court also found no refusal element because LMHA conditioned the accommodation on reasonable verification, which plaintiff failed to obtain. LMHA offered alternative one-bedroom transfer which plaintiff rejected.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged retaliation for requesting reasonable accommodation, filing HUD complaint, and filing federal action
fha_claims.disposition: Emergency Motion for Injunction Pending Appeal
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff could not establish causal connection between any protected activity and adverse action. Issues with unleashed dog and two-bedroom housing request predated HUD complaint and federal lawsuit. Eviction was based on failure to complete mandatory recertification (required of all tenants by lease and federal regulations) and alleged threats to LMHA employee, not protected activity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unlawful business practices under KRS § 367.110 and 42 U.S.C. § 3601; failure to engage in interactive process under ADA; disability discrimination under ADA, KCRA, and state law; unlawful business practices
fha_claims.disposition: Emergency Motion for Injunction Pending Appeal
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found unlawful business practices claim merely restated prior causes of action and failed for same reasons. Court rejected interactive process claim under ADA, noting FHA does not impose interactive process requirement and even if ADA requirement applied, LMHA engaged in good faith interactive process for over a year. Racial, gender, and age discrimination claims were waived as perfunctory allegations.

case_name: Watkins v. Commonwealth of Kentucky
accommodation_description: Plaintiff references Fair Housing Act violations in challenging an eviction proceeding but does not specify a particular accommodation request.
key_holding: The court dismissed Plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claim because her complaint was written solely as a legal conclusion unsupported by facts, failing to state a claim upon which relief may be granted.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Rita Watkins, proceeding pro se and in forma pauperis, sued the Commonwealth of Kentucky, her mobile home park landlord, an attorney, and two state court judges challenging an eviction proceeding for failure to pay rent and alleging Fair Housing Act and constitutional violations. The court dismissed the action for failure to state a claim, finding that while Plaintiff referenced the FHA, she provided only legal conclusions without factual support for any discrimination claim.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged violations of the Fourteenth Amendment, HUD regulations (42 CFR Title 42 Ch. 130 Sec. 231 and 212), and the Fair Housing Act in connection with eviction proceedings for non-payment of rent.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed under § 1915(e)(2)(B) as frivolous and for failure to state a claim. The FHA does not cover eviction for non-payment of rent, and plaintiff provided no factual allegations connecting her claims to any protected class or disability. The complaint was a legal conclusion unsupported by facts. Additionally, HUD regulations provide no private right of action, and § 1983 claims against the Commonwealth fail due to sovereign immunity and lack of personhood; claims against judges fail due to absolute judicial immunity; and claims against private parties fail because § 1983 requires state action.

case_name: Brenda L. Alexander v. CS/KY/LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff complained about secondhand cigarette smoke from a neighboring tenant and sought enforcement of HUD's Smoke Free Rule against that neighbor
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's claims because the HUD Smoke Free Rule does not create a private right of action for a tenant to sue the landlord for a neighbor's smoking, and the Fair Housing Act and ADA do not apply to this secondhand smoke exposure claim.
brief_summary: Brenda L. Alexander, a pro se plaintiff residing in HUD-subsidized public housing, sued her landlord and property management company seeking damages for secondhand cigarette smoke exposure from a neighboring tenant and alleging violations of the HUD Smoke Free Rule, Fair Housing Act, and ADA. The court dismissed all claims for failure to state a claim because the HUD Smoke Free Rule does not create a private right of action for tenants, and neither the FHA nor ADA apply to this type of secondhand smoke complaint.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
NYC C.L.A.S.H., Inc. v. Fudge, 47 F.4th 757 (D.C. Cir. 2022)
Hill v. Lappin, 630 F.3d 468 (6th Cir. 2010)
McGore v. Wrigglesworth, 114 F.3d 601 (6th Cir. 1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Enforcement of HUD Smoke Free Rule against neighbor's smoking; secondhand smoke exposure
fha_claims.reasoning: The court determined that the Smoke Free Rule does not create a private cause of action for a neighboring tenant to sue based on a neighbor's smoking. The rule gives PHAs discretion to enforce but does not grant individual tenants a right to sue for violations. The FHA was invoked but the court found it inapplicable without substantive analysis of any FHA theory.

case_name: Ronnie Joe Forte v. Hopkinsville Housing Authority et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested; plaintiff applied for Section 8 subsidized rental housing and sought damages and injunctive relief after his application was denied based on pending drug charges under a blanket criminal-history ban.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claim for failure to state a claim because the FHA does not prohibit discrimination based on criminal history, and federal law expressly permits public housing agencies to deny admission to federally assisted housing for drug-related criminal activity.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Ronnie Joe Forte sued the Hopkinsville Housing Authority and a Section 8 housing specialist under the FHA after his housing application was denied based on a blanket ban tied to his pending drug-related criminal charges. Conducting mandatory § 1915(e)(2) screening, the court found that the FHA does not cover discrimination based on criminal history and that 42 U.S.C. § 13661(c) expressly authorizes housing authorities to deny admission to applicants engaged in drug-related criminal activity. The lawsuit was dismissed for failure to state a claim upon which relief could be granted.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Robertson v. Olsen 2023 WL 5284480
Smith v. U.S. Dep't of Hous. & Urb. Dev. 2022 WL 18107588
Nickell v. Metro. 2018 WL 2392849

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of housing application based on pending drug-related criminal charges
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)
fha_claims.reasoning: The FHA does not prohibit discrimination based on criminal history. Plaintiff alleged denial based on pending drug-related criminal charges, which is not a protected class under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(a) (race, color, religion, sex, familial status, national origin). Additionally, 42 U.S.C. § 13661(c) explicitly permits public housing agencies to deny admission based on drug-related criminal activity.

case_name: Yusef Abdullah Bilal Ali v. Louisville Metro Housing Authority, et al.
accommodation_description: Request to keep emotional support dog off leash on LMHA property and common areas during recovery from knee surgery.
key_holding: Ali cannot show his request to keep his dog off leash was a reasonable accommodation given the dog's documented history of aggression, and his transfer request fails because he never provided the required physician's certification verifying medical necessity.
brief_summary: Ali, a public housing tenant recovering from knee surgery, sued LMHA alleging disability discrimination for denying his request to keep his emotional support dog off leash and to transfer to a single-family unit. The court granted summary judgment to defendants, finding Ali cannot show the off-leash request was reasonable given the dog's documented aggression history and that LMHA engaged in an extensive interactive process but Ali never provided required medical documentation for the transfer.
key_cases_cited: Overlook Mut. Homes, Inc. v. Spencer, 415 F. App'x 617 (6th Cir. 2011)
Hollis v. Chestnut Bend Homeowner's Ass'n, 760 F.3d 531 (6th Cir. 2014)
Howard v. HMK Holdings, LLC, 988 F.3d 1185 (9th Cir. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request to allow emotional support dog to be off-leash on LMHA property and common areas during recovery from knee surgery
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that the plaintiff could not demonstrate the requested accommodation (off-leash dog) was reasonable given the dog's documented history of aggression toward residents, staff, and other animals. The defendant fairly determined the request was unreasonable under the balancing test.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request to transfer to a single-family housing unit
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that LMHA was amenable to the transfer and agreed to it subject to plaintiff providing physician certification that the transfer was medically necessary. Because plaintiff never provided the required documentation, he could not show the defendant refused the accommodation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to engage in interactive process regarding accommodation requests
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that the FHA does not prohibit failure to engage in an interactive process. Even if analyzed under the ADA, the record demonstrated extensive interactive process engagement by defendants, including providing accommodation forms, offering transfers, explaining requirements, and continually offering assistance over more than a year.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation for requesting reasonable accommodation, failing to engage in interactive process, creating hostile living environment, filing HUD complaint, and filing this action
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiff failed to point to any evidence demonstrating a causal connection between protected activity and adverse actions by defendants. Plaintiff provided no evidence that LMHA wrongly required recertification or improperly pursued eviction following threats against staff.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unlawful business practices under KRS § 367.110 and 42 U.S.C. § 3601; disability discrimination under FHA, ADA, and KCRA; racial discrimination, gender discrimination, age discrimination under KCRA
fha_claims.reasoning: The unlawful business practices claim merely restated facts supporting other causes of action and failed for the same reasons. All non-FHA claims (KCRA discrimination claims, ADA claims, state law claims) were analyzed under the same substantive standards and failed on the merits.

source_file: 9718438_2019_Treece v. Perrier Condominium Owners Association, Inc._laed
case_name: Dwayne Treece, et al. v. Perrier Condominium Owners Association, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege discrimination based on familial status (having four children) in the rental of a condominium unit.
key_holding: The court denied summary judgment on defendants' claim of exemption under § 3603(b)(2), held they cannot claim the 'Mrs. Murphy' exemption because each unit owner owns only their individual unit and common area interest, not the entire building, and found genuine issues of material fact exist regarding whether defendants' imposition of fines, attempted eviction, occupancy rule enforcement, and storage shed lock changes constituted unlawful interference under § 3617.
brief_summary: The Treece family (with four children) sued the Perrier Condominium Owners Association and individual unit owners for Fair Housing Act violations based on familial status discrimination after the owners attempted to evict them and imposed fines on their landlord. The court granted summary judgment for defendants only on the § 3604(c) discriminatory advertising claim, but denied summary judgment on defendants' Mrs. Murphy exemption defense and on plaintiffs' § 3617 interference claims, finding disputed facts about whether the defendants' coordinated campaign to force the family out violated fair housing law.
key_cases_cited: City of Edmonds v. Oxford House, Inc., 514 U.S. 725 (1995)
Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)
Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009)
Revock v. Cowpet Bay West Condominium Association, 853 F.3d 96 (3d Cir. 2017)
Dillon v. AFBIC Dev. Corp., 597 F.2d 556 (5th Cir. 1979)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted summary judgment on the § 3603(b)(2) 'Mrs. Murphy' exemption claim, finding that defendants do not qualify for the exemption because they do not own the building as a single individual or married couple; instead, each defendant owns only an individual unit with an undivided interest in common areas, which does not satisfy the ownership requirement of the exemption.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discriminatory statement regarding familial status made in email by Haile after lease was signed
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted summary judgment on the § 3604(c) claim because Haile's email statement about the Treeces' children was made after the lease was signed and did not concern the prospective sale or rental of an available dwelling; § 3604(c) applies only to discriminatory statements made during the rental process or in connection with prospective sales, not to statements made after housing has been occupied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Imposition of daily fines, liens, attempted eviction, occupancy rule changes, lock changes on common storage shed, and installation of surveillance camera
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied summary judgment on the § 3617 interference/coercion claim because material factual disputes exist regarding whether defendants interfered with plaintiffs' fair housing rights, including disputes over whether defendants imposed fines and liens to force eviction, changed occupancy rules, locked plaintiffs out of common areas, and installed surveillance cameras—all of which could constitute unlawful interference under § 3617.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Personal liability of individual defendants (Acuff, Jablonowski, Haile) for voting to authorize discriminatory actions and making discriminatory statements
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied summary judgment on personal liability claims against individual defendants because material factual disputes exist regarding whether they personally participated in discriminatory acts through voting on discriminatory policies, making discriminatory statements to plaintiffs, and authorizing the association to take discriminatory actions such as imposing fines, pursuing eviction, and installing surveillance.

source_file: 9718630_2020_Treece v. Perrier Condominium Owners Association, Inc._laed
case_name: Dwayne Treece, et al. v. Perrier Condominium Owners Association, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: Refusal to rent a condominium unit because the applicants had three small children, allegedly misrepresenting the unit's availability to discourage their application.
key_holding: The court denied defendant's motion for partial summary judgment, finding disputed material facts exist regarding whether the defendant misrepresented unit availability and refused to negotiate with tenants because of their familial status, including direct evidence that defendant stated she did not rent to them because they had three small children.
brief_summary: Dwayne and Phallon Treece sued defendant Hannah Haile, a condominium owner, alleging she violated the Fair Housing Act by misrepresenting the availability of her rental unit and refusing to rent to them because they had three children. The court denied Haile's motion for partial summary judgment, finding disputed facts and direct evidence of discriminatory intent—specifically Haile's statement that she decided the condo was not a good fit because they have three small children—precluded summary judgment on the familial status discrimination claims under § 3604(a) and (d).
key_cases_cited: Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Darby v. Heather Ridge, 806 F. Supp. 170 (E.D. Mich. 1992)
Danenhower v. Dorsey, 1997 WL 469960 (E.D. La. 1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found disputed material facts regarding whether defendant misrepresented the availability of her condominium unit to plaintiffs based on their familial status (family of six with three small children). The defendant's statement that the current tenant's lease extended through September 28 was contradicted by the tenant's testimony that he informed defendant of his August 23 move-out date twelve days before that statement. The court held that subtle discrimination questions are best resolved by a jury, and the timeline of events (accepting other applications five days after the misrepresentation) supported a reasonable inference of intentional discrimination based on familial status.

source_file: 9718744_2020_Treece v. Perrier Condominium Owners Association, Inc._laed
case_name: Dwayne Treece, et al. v. Perrier Condominium Owners Association, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request at issue; this is a disparate impact challenge to an occupancy limit on families with children.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion for reconsideration, finding no manifest error of law in using rejection rate comparisons to analyze disparate impact, and rejecting defendants' arguments that acceptance rates should be used instead.
brief_summary: The Treece family sued the Perrier Condominium Owners Association challenging an occupancy limit as having a disparate impact on families with children in violation of the Fair Housing Act's familial status protections. The court denied defendants' motion for reconsideration of a prior order, finding no manifest error of law in its methodology comparing rejection rates to analyze disparate impact.
key_cases_cited: Inclusive Communities Project, Inc. v. Lincoln Prop. Co., 920 F.3d 890 (5th Cir. 2019)
Veasey v. Abbott, 830 F.3d 216 (5th Cir. 2016)
Langlois v. Abington Housing Authority, 234 F. Supp. 2d 33 (D. Mass. 2002)
Gashi v. Grubb & Ellis Prop. Mgmt. Servs., Inc., 801 F. Supp. 2d 12 (D. Conn. 2011)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied defendants' motion for summary judgment on the disparate impact claim under § 3604(a), finding that plaintiffs established a prima facie disparate impact by showing that renter families with children are 30.5 to 104.7 times as likely to be affected by the occupancy limit as renter households without children, and that the comparison of rejection rates (rather than acceptance rates) is the proper methodology for analyzing disparate impact under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claim that defendants attempted to evict the Treeces based on familial status and attempted to force Harlan to evict the Treeces based on familial status
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted defendants' motion for summary judgment on plaintiffs' § 3617 retaliation claim (referenced in the opinion as a separate motion), though the opinion does not provide detailed reasoning on this specific claim as it focuses primarily on the disparate impact analysis and the motion for reconsideration.

source_file: 9718781_2020_Treece v. Perrier Condominium Owners Association, Inc._laed
case_name: Dwayne Treece, et al. v. Perrier Condominium Owners Association, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: No disability accommodation requested; claim concerns alleged familial status discrimination through misrepresentations about housing availability.
key_holding: The court denied Haile's motion to reconsider because she failed to demonstrate manifest error of law, presenting instead evidence that was available during the original motion and rehashing arguments that could have been raised earlier.
brief_summary: Dwayne and Phallon Treece sued landlord Hannah Haile alleging she violated the Fair Housing Act by misrepresenting the availability of her condominium unit and making housing unavailable because of their familial status. The court denied Haile's motion to reconsider its prior order denying her motion for partial summary judgment, finding Haile failed to demonstrate manifest error of law and merely attempted to present evidence and arguments that could have been raised in the original motion.
key_cases_cited: Darby v. Heather Ridge, 806 F. Supp. 170 (E.D. Mich. 1992)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied defendant's motion for summary judgment on the disparate treatment claim alleging misrepresentation of availability and denial of housing based on familial status under § 3604(a) and (d), finding that factual disputes regarding subtle discrimination, misstatements, and discriminatory intent precluded summary judgment and that the Darby standard supported allowing the claim to proceed to trial.

case_name: Russell Andre Briley v. Ignatius Barreca Jr. et al.
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request; plaintiff generally alleges unlawful acts including discrimination related to tenants who receive government funds for disabilities.
key_holding: The court denied the motion to dismiss and granted plaintiff leave to amend because plaintiff's complaint failed to plead sufficient facts to support claims under ADA, Title VI, Title VII, or the Fair Housing Act.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Russell Andre Briley sued Barreca defendants and Josephine Broadwater alleging violations of ADA, Title VI, Title VII, and state law related to his residential tenancy and eviction in New Orleans. The court denied Broadwater's motion to dismiss and granted plaintiff leave to amend because the complaint failed to plead sufficient factual allegations to state any viable federal claim, including failing to allege a qualifying disability or discriminatory animus.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2008)
Inclusive Comtys. Project, Inc. v. Lincoln Prop. Co., 920 F.3d 890 (5th Cir. 2019)
City of Edmonds v. Oxford House, Inc., 514 U.S. 725 (1995)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title I (employment), Title II (public entity services), Title III (public accommodation); Title VI (federal financial assistance discrimination); Title VII (employment discrimination); Louisiana state law breach of contract
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to state claims under ADA (no disability alleged, no public accommodation or public entity involvement), Title VI (no race, color, or national origin discrimination alleged), Title VII (no employment relationship or protected class discrimination alleged), or state law breach of contract (no contractual relationship pled). However, motion to dismiss was DENIED and plaintiff granted leave to amend within 14 days to cure deficiencies.

case_name: Aicha Bouchgl v. Suleiman Ibrahim
accommodation_description: No disability-related accommodation requested; plaintiffs allege discrimination based on national origin, religious beliefs, and color including excessive security deposits, late fees, threats of eviction, and harassment.
key_holding: Louisiana enjoys Eleventh Amendment sovereign immunity from Fair Housing Act claims brought in federal court, and Congress did not clearly intend to abrogate state sovereign immunity under the FHA; accordingly, the state defendants (Louisiana Department of Justice and Attorney General) are dismissed without prejudice.
brief_summary: Tenants Aicha Bouchgl and Suleiman Ibrahim sued their landlord Tonti Management Co. and the Louisiana Department of Justice and Attorney General, alleging housing discrimination based on national origin, religious beliefs, and color under the Fair Housing Act and Louisiana Equal Housing Opportunity Act. The federal court granted Louisiana's motion to dismiss the state defendants without prejudice, holding that the Eleventh Amendment bars FHA claims against unconsenting states in federal court and that Congress did not abrogate state sovereign immunity under the FHA.
key_cases_cited: McCardell v. U.S. Dep't of Hous. & Urban Dev., 794 F.3d 510 (5th Cir. 2015)
Edelman v. Jordan, 415 U.S. 651 (1974)
Cozzo v. Tangipahoa Par. Council-President Gov't, 279 F.3d 273 (5th Cir. 2002)
Vogt v. Bd. of Comm'rs of Orleans Levee Dist., 294 F.3d 684 (5th Cir. 2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges discrimination based on national origin, religious beliefs, and color through extra security deposits, excessive late fees, threats of eviction, and harassment.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed claims against the Louisiana Department of Justice and Attorney General Jeff Landry under the Eleventh Amendment for lack of subject matter jurisdiction. The Fifth Circuit has held that Congress did not clearly intend to abrogate States' Eleventh Amendment sovereign immunity from suits under the Fair Housing Act, and Louisiana has not consented to suit in federal court.

case_name: Russell Andre Briley v. Ignatius Barreca, Jr. et al.
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request identified; plaintiff failed to state any coherent Fair Housing Act claim.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's federal claims with prejudice because he failed to allege any facts to state a claim under the FHA, ADA, Title VI, or Title VII, and declined supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Russell Briley sued landlords Ignatius Barreca Jr., David Barreca Sr., and Josephine Broadwater alleging violations of the ADA, Title VI, Title VII, and Fair Housing Act, though the complaint contained no factual allegations supporting any claim. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding plaintiff failed to state any claim under federal law, and declined supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff cited FHA statutory provisions (42 U.S.C. §§ 3601, 3603, 3604) but alleged no facts supporting any FHA claim; no specific accommodation or discrimination theory articulated.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff cited FHA provisions but failed to allege any facts demonstrating discrimination in rental or sale of a dwelling based on handicap, race, color, religion, sex, familial status, or national origin. The complaint contained only conclusory legal citations without factual support, failing to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA, Title VI, Title VII, and state law claims (rent overcharges, threats, unlawful acts)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege adequate facts to support claims under the ADA, Title VI, Title VII, or state law. The amended complaint contained only incomprehensible assertions, unrelated documentation (cashier's checks, utility bills), and a request for a federal gun permit unrelated to the defendants or the housing dispute. The court found no factual allegations supporting any federal or state law cause of action.

source_file: 9719738_2021_Treece v. Perrier Condominium Owners Association, Inc._laed
case_name: Dwayne Treece, et al. v. Perrier Condominium Owners Association, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs, a family of six with four children, sought to rent a condominium unit but were subject to occupancy limits (250/400 square feet per person) and attempted eviction based on familial status.
key_holding: Plaintiffs failed to establish robust causation required for a disparate impact claim under § 3604(a) because they offered no evidence that the occupancy limits caused families with children to be the dominant group of renters affected, as families with children already comprised larger households prior to the challenged policy.
brief_summary: The Treece family of six sued the Perrier Condominium Owners Association alleging that occupancy limits (250/400 square feet per person) violated the Fair Housing Act by having a disparate impact on families with children based on familial status. The court denied plaintiffs' motion for partial summary judgment and granted defendants' cross-motion, finding plaintiffs failed to establish the robust causation element of their disparate impact claim because families with children already had larger households before the challenged policy, and the 400 square foot rule was never actually enforced.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dept. of Housing & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc.
Inclusive Communities Project, Inc. v. Lincoln Property Co.
Reyes v. Azucar Bakery

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to establish the robust causation element required under ICP II and Lincoln Property. Although plaintiffs showed a substantial statistical disparity in the effect of the 250 and 400 square foot occupancy limits on families with children, they did not prove the occupancy limits caused families with children to be the dominant group affected by the policy; rather, families with children were a pre-existing condition of larger households, not created by the challenged policy.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Coercion, intimidation, and interference with exercise of FHA rights under § 3617 based on alleged violation of § 3604(a)
fha_claims.reasoning: Under Fifth Circuit precedent (Hood v. Pope and McZeal v. Ocwen Financial Corporation), a § 3617 retaliation claim requires an underlying violation of §§ 3603, 3604, 3605, or 3606. Because plaintiffs failed to establish a prima facie disparate impact claim under § 3604(a), their § 3617 claim based on that violation must also fail.

case_name: Anna Monus v. Edward Riecke
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges landlord's sexual assault and harassment during a rent payment meeting altered the conditions of her housing and created a hostile housing environment.
key_holding: The court denied defendant's motion to dismiss, holding that plaintiff's allegation of unwanted touching of intimate body parts—even a single incident—is sufficient to state a hostile housing environment claim under the FHA, and that interference with use and enjoyment of the property satisfies the alteration-of-housing-conditions requirement without requiring a change in economic benefits.
brief_summary: Anna Monus sued her landlord Edward Riecke alleging he sexually assaulted and harassed her during a rent payment meeting, creating a hostile housing environment in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The court denied Riecke's motion to dismiss under Rules 12(b)(6) and 12(b)(1), holding that a single incident of unwanted touching of intimate body parts is sufficiently severe to state a hostile housing environment claim under the FHA, and that interference with use and enjoyment of the property satisfies the required alteration of housing conditions.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Greater New Orleans Fair Hous. Action Ctr. v. Kelly, 364 F. Supp. 3d 635 (E.D. La. 2019)
Harvill v. Westward Commc'ns, L.L.C., 433 F.3d 428 (5th Cir. 2005)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard and found that plaintiff's allegations of a single incident of unwanted touching of intimate body parts, even if isolated, is sufficient at the pleading stage to state a hostile housing environment claim under FHA § 3604(b), as the Fifth Circuit has held that deliberate and unwanted touching of intimate body parts can constitute severe sexual harassment, and plaintiff alleged the conduct interfered with her use and enjoyment of the property.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: State-law tort claims for sexual assault and battery; Louisiana Equal Housing Opportunity Act (LEHOA) claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss on supplemental jurisdiction grounds; state-law claims survive as supplemental to the federal FHA claim under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(a).

source_file: 9720571_2021_Treece v. Perrier Condominium Owners Association, Inc._laed
case_name: Dwayne Treece, et al. v. Perrier Condominium Owners Association, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request was at issue; the case concerns familial status discrimination in which the condominium association and unit owners adopted and enforced occupancy limits (first a 250-sq-ft-per-person rule, then a proposed 400-sq-ft-per-person rule), threatened eviction, levied daily fines against the landlord, and otherwise pressured the Treece family—a family of six with four young children—to vacate their unit because of their familial status.
key_holding: The court granted plaintiffs' motion to modify its prior partial summary judgment order to clarify that disparate treatment claims under § 3604(a) and interference/coercion claims under § 3617 were never adjudicated and remain pending, while only disparate impact claims under § 3604(a) and discriminatory-statement claims under § 3604(c) had been dismissed, and denied defendants' motion for entry of partial final judgment.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs—a family of six (the Treeces), their landlord (Harlan), and others—sued a four-unit condominium association (PCOA) and individual unit owners alleging familial status discrimination after the Treeces moved in and faced occupancy-limit enforcement, proposed bylaw amendments, fines against Harlan, and pressure to evict the family. The court had previously granted summary judgment dismissing disparate impact claims under § 3604(a) and all § 3617 claims, but the order was later challenged as having erroneously swept in disparate treatment claims that were never briefed or decided on the merits. The court modified the prior summary judgment order to reflect that intentional disparate treatment claims under § 3604(a), Harlan's § 3604(b) claims, and all § 3617 claims remain pending, while simultaneously denying defendants' motion to enter partial final judgment on the adjudicated claims due to the risk of piecemeal appellate review.
key_cases_cited: Treece v. Perrier Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 519 F. Supp. 3d 342 (E.D. La. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted summary judgment on Dwayne and Phallon Treece's disparate treatment claim under § 3604(a) against Haile for refusing to rent her unit based on familial status. The claim was adjudicated on the merits and dismissed in favor of defendants.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted summary judgment on Dwayne and Phallon Treece's claim under § 3604(d) against Haile for representing that her unit was unavailable when it was actually available based on familial status. The claim was adjudicated on the merits.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted summary judgment on all plaintiffs' claim under § 3604(c) against all defendants for printing and publishing statements indicating occupancy limitations or discrimination based on familial status. The claim was adjudicated on the merits.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted summary judgment on all plaintiffs' disparate impact claim under § 3604(a) against all defendants for adopting occupancy limitations that have a disproportionate effect on families with children. The court found defendants entitled to summary judgment on this theory.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court modified its February 12, 2021 order to clarify that all plaintiffs' claims against all defendants for intentional disparate treatment discrimination under § 3604(a) in adopting occupancy limitations remain pending and were not addressed on the merits in the summary judgment order. These claims survive and are set for trial.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court clarified that Harlan's claims against all defendants under § 3604(a) for disparate treatment discrimination in refusing to allow him to sell his unit by discriminating against prospective buyers remain pending and were not addressed on the merits. These claims survive and are set for trial.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court clarified that Harlan's claims against all defendants under § 3604(b) for discrimination in the terms, conditions, or privileges of sale or rental based on familial status remain pending and were not addressed on the merits. These claims survive and are set for trial.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court modified its February 12, 2021 order to clarify that all plaintiffs' § 3617 claims for unlawfully coercing, intimidating, threatening, or interfering with plaintiffs in the exercise of their FHA rights remain pending because underlying violations of § 3604(a) and (b) are still pending. These claims survive and are set for trial.

source_file: 9720727_2021_Winston v. Housing Authority of Jefferson Parish_laed
case_name: Nadia Winston v. Housing Authority of Jefferson Parish
accommodation_description: Alleged discriminatory comment by housing authority employee regarding plaintiff's eight children and her children's disability status
key_holding: The court denied the motion to dismiss without prejudice and granted leave to amend because the complaint lacked sufficient factual allegations to state a claim, and individual employees cannot be held personally liable under the Fair Housing Act under vicarious liability principles.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Nadia Winston sued the Jefferson Parish Housing Authority and individual employees alleging she is owed $45,000 under the Family Self Sufficient Program and suffered discrimination based on disability and familial status, plus retaliation for reporting the housing authority to HUD. The court denied the motion to dismiss without prejudice, granting leave to amend because the complaint lacked sufficient factual allegations and individual defendants cannot be held personally liable under the FHA.
key_cases_cited: Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2008)
Bazrowx v. Scott, 136 F.3d 1053 (5th Cir. 1998)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination based on disability and familial status; alleged statement by employee regarding plaintiff's eight children
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that the complaint failed to allege sufficient facts to state a plausible claim against the individual defendants under the Fair Housing Act because it did not allege they acted outside the scope of their employment; under Meyer v. Holley, vicarious liability applies to the corporate employer, not individual employees acting within scope of employment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation for reporting JPHA to HUD; plaintiff claims she was terminated from FSSP program after threatening to report
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that the complaint failed to allege sufficient facts to state a plausible claim against the individual defendants under the Fair Housing Act because it did not allege they acted outside the scope of their employment; under Meyer v. Holley, vicarious liability applies to the corporate employer, not individual employees acting within scope of employment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of contract claim for money owed under Jefferson Parish Family Self Sufficient Program (FSSP); § 1983 or state contract law
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that the complaint failed to provide a short and plain statement of the claim and did not allege any facts regarding what actions the individual defendants took that would entitle plaintiff to relief; the complaint did not establish that the individual defendants were parties to the FSSP contract or what they specifically did to breach it.

source_file: 9720836_2022_Louisiana Fair Housing Action Center, Inc. v. Plantation Management Company, LLC_laed
case_name: Louisiana Fair Housing Action Center Inc. v. Plantation Management Co. LLC et al.
accommodation_description: Deaf prospective residents requested video remote interpreting (VRI) services as a reasonable accommodation to enable effective communication with staff at a nursing home/assisted living facility.
key_holding: The court found that the plaintiff adequately alleged ownership interest and agency relationship, sufficient to state claims for discriminatory refusal to provide interpretive services under the FHA and ADA, rejecting defendants' arguments that conclusory ownership allegations and agency relationship were insufficient at the pleading stage.
brief_summary: Louisiana Fair Housing Action Center sued nursing home owners for refusing to provide video remote interpreting services to deaf prospective residents, alleging violations of the FHA and ADA. The court denied the owners' motion to dismiss, finding the plaintiff's allegations of direct ownership and agency relationship were sufficient to put defendants on notice and survive a 12(b)(6) motion.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)
Rodriguez v. Baird's Bakery, Inc., 111 F.3d 893 (5th Cir. 1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Video remote interpreting (VRI) services and interpretive assistance for deaf residents; facility refused to provide or consider VRI despite receiving federal funds mandating non-discrimination and effective communication methods
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiff's allegations of ownership, provision of residential care, employee refusal to accommodate deaf residents, and agency relationship were sufficient to survive motion to dismiss under Twombly plausibility standard; detailed factual allegations not required at pleading stage, only enough facts to raise reasonable expectation that discovery will reveal evidence of liability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act Title III (42 U.S.C. § 12181 et seq.) - discrimination by owners/operators of places of public accommodation; Louisiana negligent hiring and supervision tort
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that under ADA Title III, defendants who own or lease public accommodations may be held liable for discrimination, including vicarious liability for agents' actions; allegations that moving defendants own the facility (a place of public accommodation) and that employees refused interpretive services based on disability were sufficient to state a claim. Louisiana negligent hiring and supervision claim survived because plaintiff alleged ownership, agency relationship, and failure to provide reasonable accommodations.

source_file: 9720937_2022_Louisiana Fair Housing Action Center, Inc. v. Plantation Management Company, LLC_laed
case_name: Louisiana Fair Housing Action Center, Inc. v. Plantation Management Company, LLC et al.
accommodation_description: Fair housing organization alleges on behalf of prospective deaf residents that nursing home staff refused to provide ASL interpretation or video remote interpreting (VRI) services.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that the fair housing organization had standing based on diverted organizational resources and adequately stated FHA reasonable accommodation claims against the facility owners/operators for refusing to provide interpretive services to deaf prospective residents.
brief_summary: Louisiana Fair Housing Action Center sued CommCare Corporation and CommCare Management Corporation (owners/operators of Greenbriar Community Care Center nursing facility in Slidell, Louisiana), alleging they violated the Fair Housing Act by refusing to provide ASL interpretation or VRI services to prospective deaf residents. The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss, finding the fair housing organization had standing to sue and adequately stated reasonable accommodation claims under the FHA.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2008)
Meyer v. Holst, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)
Gladstone Realtors v. Vill. of Bellwood, 441 U.S. 91 (1979)
Bank of Am. Corp. v. City of Miami, 137 S. Ct. 1296 (2017)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: In-person or video remote interpreting (VRI)-assisted American Sign Language (ASL) interpretation for deaf residents
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiff adequately alleged a claim under FHA § 3604(f)(3)(B) by alleging that movants, as owners/operators of a dwelling (nursing home), refused to make reasonable accommodations (ASL interpretation services) necessary to afford deaf prospective residents equal opportunity to enjoy the dwelling. The court did not apply the substantive reasonable accommodation balancing test, as the motion to dismiss was denied at the pleading stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rehabilitation Act § 504 (denial of benefits in federally-funded program based on disability); Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act § 18116 (discrimination in health programs receiving federal financial assistance); Louisiana negligent supervision and training under La. C.C. art. 2315
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiff adequately alleged claims under the Rehabilitation Act and ACA by alleging that movants denied benefits to otherwise-qualified deaf prospective residents based on disability at a federally-funded facility, and under Louisiana law by alleging movants owed a duty to provide equal opportunity and breached that duty by failing to provide interpretive services. The court applied the pleading standard (Iqbal/Twombly), not substantive merits analysis.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act Title III (denial of equal goods, services, facilities, privileges, advantages, accommodations, or other opportunities based on known disability of person with whom defendant has relationship or association)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiff adequately alleged an ADA Title II claim by alleging that movants own, operate, or manage a place of public accommodation (nursing home) and that employees engaged in discriminatory behavior by refusing to offer adequate interpretive services to prospective residents based on known disability. The court applied the pleading standard, not substantive merits analysis.

source_file: 9721018_2022_Treece v. Perrier Condominium Owners Association, Inc._laed
case_name: Dwayne Treece, et al. v. Perrier Condominium Owners Association, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; case involves familial status discrimination challenge to occupancy limits and eviction threats directed at family with four children.
key_holding: The court denied summary judgment on plaintiffs' § 3604(a) disparate treatment claim because material facts regarding defendants' intent to discriminate against families with children are in genuine dispute, but granted summary judgment on Harlan's claim that defendants blocked prospective buyers from purchasing his unit.
brief_summary: Dwayne and Phallon Treece (with their four children) and their landlord Clifford Harlan sued the Perrier Condominium Owners Association and individual unit owners for discriminatory actions including threatening eviction, changing occupancy rules from 250 to 400 square feet per occupant, and harassment based on the family's size. The court denied summary judgment for defendants on the familial status discrimination claim under § 3604(a) because disputed facts about intent preclude summary judgment, but granted summary judgment on Harlan's separate claim that the occupancy rules prevented him from selling his unit to families.
key_cases_cited: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Texas Dept. of Housing and Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Whyte v. Alston Management, Inc., 2011 WL 12450320 (S.D. Fla. 2011)
Carlson v. Sunshine Villas HOA, Inc., 2018 WL 2317820 (M.D. Fla. 2018)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework and found that plaintiffs established a prima facie case of familial status discrimination under § 3604(a) by showing: (1) membership in protected familial class; (2) qualification to rent; (3) defendants made housing unavailable through threats/acts of eviction; and (4) housing remained available to similarly situated non-protected individuals. Material factual disputes exist regarding defendants' intent and whether their non-discriminatory reasons (infrastructure/quality of life concerns) were pretextual, precluding summary judgment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Harlan failed to establish a prima facie case under §§ 3604(a) and (b) for discrimination against prospective buyers because he provided no evidence of any prospective buyer who was a member of the protected familial class. His deposition testimony only referenced prospective buyers refusing to purchase due to liens and litigation, not the occupancy limit, and was unsubstantiated speculation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Under Hood v. Pope, § 3617 claims require an underlying violation of §§ 3603-3606. The court granted partial summary judgment on Harlan's § 3617 claims to the extent they were based on his failed §§ 3604(a) and (b) claims regarding prospective buyers. However, the court denied summary judgment on the remaining § 3617 claims based on the Treeces' underlying § 3604(a) claim, which survived summary judgment due to disputed material facts regarding intent and pretext.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The time for dispositive motions on Claims 4 and 5 passed without defendants filing motions. These claims remain pending for trial, alleging that Haile refused to rent her unit to the Treeces based on familial status under § 3604(a).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The time for dispositive motions on Claims 4 and 5 passed without defendants filing motions. This claim remains pending for trial, alleging that Haile misrepresented the availability of her unit based on familial status under § 3604(d).

source_file: 9721118_2022_Louisiana Fair Housing Action Center, Inc. v. Azalea Garden Properties, LLC_laed
case_name: Louisiana Fair Housing Action Center, Inc. v. Azalea Garden Properties, LLC
accommodation_description: Blanket criminal background screening policy allegedly having disparate impact on persons with disabilities (recovering from drug addiction) by excluding them without individualized assessment
key_holding: The disability-based disparate impact claim was dismissed because LaFHAC failed to allege any statistical data showing that individuals with drug convictions are likely to be recovering from an addiction that substantially limits major life activities, failing to establish the requisite causal connection for a disparate impact claim.
brief_summary: Louisiana Fair Housing Action Center sued Azalea Garden Properties, LLC alleging that its blanket criminal background screening policy violates the FHA by having a disparate impact on African American renters and persons recovering from drug addiction. The court denied the motion to dismiss as to the race-based disparate impact claim, finding sufficient statistical allegations, but granted dismissal as to the disability claim because LaFHAC failed to allege any data connecting drug convictions to individuals with qualifying disabilities.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dept. of Housing and Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Inclusive Communities Project, Inc. v. Lincoln Property Co., 920 F.3d 890 (5th Cir. 2019)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court accepted as true that the criminal background screening policy disproportionately affects applicants based on race and that statistical data makes this plausible. Although the racial disparity is theoretical and speculative at the pleading stage, the court resolved ambiguity in the controlling law in plaintiff's favor regarding whether a disparate impact claim may be grounded on the 'predictably will cause' aspect of discriminatory effect under the 2013 HUD regulation. The motion to dismiss was denied as to the race disparate impact claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation for individuals recovering from drug addiction who are disabled under the FHA
fha_claims.reasoning: The disability claim failed to state a plausible claim because LaFHAC provided no statistical data suggesting that individuals with drug convictions are likely to be recovering from drug addiction that substantially limits major life activities, nor any data showing a causal link between the policy and disparate impact on disabled persons. The court found the claim lacked the 'robust' causal connection required by controlling law and dismissed for failure to state a claim.

source_file: 9721178_2022_Huber v. Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Florida, Inc._laed

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA wrongful termination claim based on disability (hemiplegic migraines); ADA failure to accommodate claim for use of CBD oil to manage migraines; ADA interference/coercion claim under 42 U.S.C. § 12203(b); LEDL wrongful termination and failure to accommodate claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine disputes of material fact precluding summary judgment on all claims: (1) whether passing a drug test was an essential job function for plaintiff's position; (2) whether plaintiff was actually under the influence of illegal substances or whether the positive result was a false positive from legally prescribed CBD oil; (3) whether defendant's stated reason for termination was pretextual given the high healthcare costs of plaintiff's disability and her transition to a position not requiring drug testing; and (4) whether defendant provided good faith consideration of plaintiff's explanation for the positive drug test result as required for a reasonable accommodation. The court applied the McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework and found that plaintiff's prima facie case, combined with evidence of pretext and fact issues regarding the accommodation, survived summary judgment.

source_file: 9721185_2022_Louisiana Fair Housing Action Center, Inc. v. Plantation Management Company, LLC_laed
case_name: Louisiana Fair Housing Action Center Inc. v. Plantation Management Co. LLC
accommodation_description: Prospective deaf residents requested ASL interpreter services or Video Remote Interpreting (VRI) to enable effective communication with staff at an assisted living/nursing home facility.
key_holding: The court denied the defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that the fair housing organization plaintiff had standing and adequately stated FHA and other claims based on allegations that facility employees refused to provide interpretive services (ASL/VRI) to prospective deaf residents seeking housing.
brief_summary: Louisiana Fair Housing Action Center sued St. Jude Management #2, LLC and Lawrence Stansberry (owners/operators of St. Luke's Living Center, an assisted living/nursing home), alleging they violated the Fair Housing Act and other statutes by refusing to provide ASL interpreters or VRI services to prospective deaf residents. The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss, finding the organization had standing based on resource diversion and adequately stated a reasonable accommodation claim under § 3604(f)(3)(B).
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)
OCA-Greater Houston v. Texas, 867 F.3d 604 (5th Cir. 2017)
Neff v. Am. Dairy Queen Corp., 58 F.3d 1063 (5th Cir. 1995)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Provision of qualified American Sign Language (ASL) interpreters and/or Video Remote Interpreting (VRI) services for deaf residents
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiff adequately alleged that movants own/operate the facility, that the facility is a dwelling under the FHA, that employees refused to make reasonable accommodations for prospective deaf residents, and that employees acted as movants' agents. These allegations sufficiently state a claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(B) and survive the motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rehabilitation Act § 504, ACA § 1557, ADA Title III, Louisiana negligent hiring and supervision
