fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiff adequately alleged all elements required under the Rehabilitation Act (qualifying disability, otherwise qualified, denial of benefits solely by reason of disability, federal financial assistance), ACA (same framework as Rehabilitation Act), ADA (movants own/operate public accommodation, employees discriminated based on known disability, employees acted as agents), and Louisiana negligent supervision (duty, breach, causation, legal cause). All non-FHA claims survive the motion to dismiss.

source_file: 9721277_2022_Winston v. Housing Authority of Jefferson Parish_laed
case_name: Winston v. Housing Authority of Jefferson Parish
subsidy_program: Housing Choice Voucher Program (HCVP), Family Self-Sufficiency Program (FSSP)
accommodation_description: Plaintiff asserts she was discriminated against based on disability in her termination from the Housing Choice Voucher Program and Family Self-Sufficiency Program, which resulted in forfeiture of funds owed to her.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for JPHA because the plaintiff, proceeding pro se, failed to file an opposition to the motion and therefore failed to present any evidence of discriminatory intent, discriminatory effect, or retaliation under the Fair Housing Act.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Nadia Winston, proceeding pro se, sued the Jefferson Parish Housing Authority alleging she was owed $45,000 in Family Self-Sufficiency Program funds after being terminated from the HCVP and that she was discriminated against based on disability and retaliation. The court granted JPHA's motion for summary judgment because Winston failed to file an opposition and thus presented no evidence of discriminatory intent, discriminatory effect, or retaliation under the Fair Housing Act.
key_cases_cited: Henson v. Veterans Admin., 800 F.2d 1381 (5th Cir. 1986)
Simms v. First Gibraltar Bank, 83 F.3d 1546 (5th Cir. 1996)
Scruggs v. Marshall Hous. Auth., 232 F.3d 210 (5th Cir. 2000)
Tenth Street Residential Association v. City of Dallas, 968 F.3d 492 (5th Cir. 2020)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged discrimination based on disability and familial status in connection with termination from Housing Choice Voucher Program and forfeiture of Family Self-Sufficiency Program escrow funds.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to file opposition to summary judgment motion and presented no evidence of discriminatory intent or effect. Court found JPHA entitled to judgment as a matter of law because plaintiff could not establish prima facie case of discrimination under FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged retaliation for exercising FHA rights and contacting parties about discrimination and privacy violations.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to file opposition and presented no evidence that JPHA's termination decision was causally linked to protected activity or motivated by retaliation. Court applied three-element retaliation test and found plaintiff could not satisfy burden.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of contract/unjust enrichment claim for funds allegedly owed under Jefferson Parish Family Self-Sufficiency Program escrow account.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to dispute that she was properly terminated from HCVP for failing to timely report income and failing to disclose marriage. Under program regulations, escrow funds revert to housing authority upon participant termination, and JPHA presented undisputed evidence of proper termination.

case_name: Velma Lee v. J.M. Property Holdings, LLC et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation requested; case involves refusal to rent to family with children based on policy against opposite-gender children sharing a bedroom.
key_holding: The court denied Mai's motions to dismiss and for summary judgment without prejudice under Rule 56(d), finding that genuine issues of material fact exist regarding Mai's involvement in setting and enforcing an allegedly discriminatory policy against families, and that Plaintiff needs additional discovery time to adequately oppose the motions.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Velma Lee sued J.M. Property Holdings, LLC, Thao P. Mai, and Tammy Sponberg alleging familial status discrimination after a property manager refused to rent her a unit because her two children of opposite genders were allegedly too old to share a bedroom. The court denied Mai's motions to dismiss and for summary judgment without prejudice, finding disputed facts exist regarding Mai's involvement in managing the property and setting the allegedly discriminatory policy, and that plaintiff needs additional discovery time.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied summary judgment without prejudice under Rule 56(d) because plaintiff could not adequately oppose the motion without completing discovery regarding Mai's involvement in management and the discriminatory policy. Evidence showed Mai was authorized to enter lease agreements and fired Sponberg, creating material disputes of fact requiring further discovery.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Louisiana Equal Housing Opportunity Act claims (three counts)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied summary judgment without prejudice on state law claims under the same Rule 56(d) analysis, finding material disputes of fact regarding Mai's involvement in management and the discriminatory policy that require further discovery before summary judgment can be properly decided.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: No FHA claims alleged. Plaintiff brought claims under La. Rev. Stat. § 51:2247 (Louisiana Human Rights Act), La. Rev. Stat. § 49:146 (Louisiana public accommodations statute), and Title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 for alleged discrimination based on race and sex in denial of entry to casino.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege discrimination under Iqbal/Twombly standard. Allegations that defendant's refusal to accept military ID was based on race or gender were conclusory and speculative, with no non-conclusory facts connecting defendant's statements about the ID being 'fake' to plaintiff's race or gender. Pattern-or-practice allegations based on two isolated incidents were insufficient to establish a pattern or practice of discrimination.

case_name: Victor Cagara Ortiguerra, et al. v. Grand Isle Shipyard, LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation was requested. The FHA claim alleged that defendants discriminated against Filipino workers on the basis of national origin by segregating them in substandard bunkhouse and COVID-19 quarantine accommodations, refusing to allow them to evacuate during and after Hurricane Ida while non-Filipino workers were permitted to leave, and confining them in a damaged bunkhouse without clean water or electricity for weeks.
key_holding: The court held that the narrow POEA employment contract arbitration clause—covering only disputes 'arising from' employment—required arbitration of plaintiffs' FLSA wage and overtime claims, but did not compel arbitration of plaintiffs' TVPA and FHA claims because those claims could be maintained independently of the employment relationship and did not arise from it.
brief_summary: Filipino welders and fitters employed on offshore oil rigs sued their employer, Grand Isle Shipyard, alleging violations of the Fair Labor Standards Act (unpaid wages and overtime), the Trafficking Victims Protection Act (forced labor and confinement), and the Fair Housing Act (national-origin discrimination in housing assignments and Hurricane Ida evacuation). Defendants moved to dismiss and compel arbitration of all three claims pursuant to a POEA seafarer employment contract incorporating a Philippine arbitration clause. The court granted the motion as to the FLSA claims, finding a valid arbitration agreement that covered wage disputes arising from employment, but denied it as to the TVPA and FHA claims, concluding that the arbitration clause was 'narrow' and that housing discrimination and forced labor claims could be maintained independently of the employment contract and did not arise from it.
key_cases_cited: Jones v. Haliburton, 583 F.3d 228 (5th Cir. 2009)
Maglana v. Celebrity Cruises, Inc., No. 21-14206, 2022 WL 3134373 (11th Cir. Aug. 5, 2022)
Baricuatro v. Indus. Pers. & Mgmt. Servs., Inc., 927 F. Supp. 2d 348 (E.D. La. 2013)
Lim v. Offshore Specialty Fabricators, Inc., 404 F.3d 898 (5th Cir. 2005)
Sedco, Inc. v. Petroleos Mexicanos Mexican Nat. Oil Co., 767 F.2d 1140 (5th Cir. 1985)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Housing segregation and isolation of Filipino workers in bunkhouse and COVID-19 quarantine accommodations based on national origin, while non-Filipino workers were not subjected to the same restrictions.
fha_claims.disposition: Motion to Compel Arbitration — Denied as to FHA claim
fha_claims.reasoning: The court determined that plaintiffs' FHA disparate treatment claims based on national origin discrimination in housing assignments do not fall within the scope of the narrow arbitration clause (which covers only disputes 'arising from' employment) because the claims could be maintained independently of the employment contract and are not a foreseeable result of the parties' contractual duties. The court declined to compel arbitration, allowing the FHA claim to proceed in federal court.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: TVPA forced labor claims; § 1983 due process claims (if any); state tort claims related to confinement, threats of deportation, and unsafe housing conditions
fha_claims.disposition: Motion to Compel Arbitration — Denied as to TVPA and other non-FHA claims
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that plaintiffs' TVPA forced labor claims do not arise from employment under the narrow arbitration clause because the alleged violations (confinement in bunkhouse after employment contract ended, threats of deportation, unsafe conditions) are independent of the employment relationship and not a foreseeable result of contractual duties. The claims could be maintained independently of the employment contract and thus fall outside the scope of arbitration.

case_name: Turnipseed v. APMT, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested waiver of the apartment's animal fee and 35-pound weight restriction to allow her emotional support animal dog to live in her apartment.
key_holding: The court denied dismissal with prejudice because the record did not show contumacious conduct and the arbitration order did not specify a deadline, but warned that plaintiff must initiate arbitration within 30 days or face dismissal.
brief_summary: Dory Turnipseed sued her landlord APMT LLC, alleging the property management company violated the Fair Housing Act by denying her accommodation request to waive animal fees and weight restrictions for her emotional support animal. The court previously ordered the parties to arbitrate, but four years later the plaintiff had not initiated arbitration; the court denied the defendant's motion to dismiss with prejudice for failure to prosecute, finding insufficient evidence of contumacious conduct and ordering plaintiff to initiate arbitration within 30 days.
key_cases_cited: Link v. Wabash R.R., 370 U.S. 626 (1962)
Rogers v. Kroger Co., 669 F.2d 317 (5th Cir. 1982)
Berry v. Cigna/RSI-Cigna, 975 F.2d 1188 (5th Cir. 1992)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver of apartment animal fee and weight restriction to allow plaintiff's 35-pound emotional support dog to live in the apartment
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 41(b) Motion to Dismiss for Failure to Prosecute
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied defendant's motion to dismiss for failure to prosecute under Rule 41(b), finding no clear record of contumacious conduct and noting that the prior arbitration order lacked a specific deadline. The underlying FHA reasonable accommodation claim survives and remains pending, subject to plaintiff's obligation to initiate arbitration within 30 days or face dismissal with prejudice.

source_file: 9722033_2022_Deutsche Bank National Trust Company v. Price_laed

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act claim mentioned in amended reconventional demand but not substantively addressed by the court
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked subject matter jurisdiction over the action. Bacot's federal counterclaims, including the Fair Housing Act claim, cannot serve as the basis for federal question jurisdiction under the well-pleaded complaint rule. The original complaint raised no federal questions, and Bacot as a forum defendant could not invoke diversity jurisdiction. The court therefore did not reach the merits of any federal claims.

case_name: White-Mosley v. Seasons Apartments, LLC
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED - The opinion does not describe the specific accommodation requested; it only states Plaintiff brought Fair Housing Act claims.
key_holding: The Court granted Defendant's motion to compel arbitration because the parties had a valid arbitration agreement with a delegation clause, and Plaintiff's challenges to the agreement's enforceability and constitutionality must be submitted to the arbitrator rather than the Court.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Carolyn White-Mosley, a tenant, brought Fair Housing Act claims against Seasons Apartments, LLC, and the defendant moved to compel arbitration based on an arbitration clause in the parties' lease. The Court granted the motion to compel arbitration, holding that the valid arbitration agreement contained a delegation clause that assigned questions of the agreement's scope, validity, and enforceability to the arbitrator.
key_cases_cited: Kindred Nursing Centers Ltd. P'ship v. Clark, 137 S. Ct. 1421 (2017)
Rent-A-Ctr., W., Inc. v. Jackson, 561 U.S. 63 (2010)
Moses H. Cone Memorial Hosp. v. Mercury Constr. Corp., 460 U.S. 1 (1983)
Kubala v. Supreme Prod. Servs., Inc., 830 F.3d 199 (5th Cir. 2016)

case_name: Jason Allen James, et al. v. Tangipahoa Parish
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested that Tangipahoa Parish grant a reasonable accommodation under the FHA to allow their sober home—housing up to ten persons in recovery from substance abuse—to continue operating in a single-family zoning district without being required to comply with the Parish's burdensome permit requirements for 'addictive disorder treatment facilities,' which included 24-hour on-site supervisory personnel, regular access to health care providers, significant general liability insurance, and handicap accessibility standards that plaintiffs alleged were financially impossible to satisfy.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiffs' motion for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction, holding that the Anti-Injunction Act barred injunctive relief on the FHA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act claims, and that plaintiffs failed to demonstrate a substantial likelihood of success on the merits of their Section 1983 First Amendment retaliation claim because the Parish's enforcement actions predated any reasonable accommodation request.
brief_summary: Three residents of a sober home in Hammond, Louisiana filed FHA, ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and Section 1983 claims against Tangipahoa Parish, which was seeking to shut down their sober living facility for operating without a permit as an 'addictive disorder treatment facility' under the Parish Code of Ordinances. Plaintiffs moved for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction to prevent the Parish from enforcing its ordinance and to stay a state court injunction authorizing closure. The court denied the motion, finding the Anti-Injunction Act barred injunctive relief on the federal civil rights housing claims, and independently that plaintiffs could not show a likelihood of success on the Section 1983 retaliation claim because the Parish's enforcement efforts began before plaintiffs had made any indication they would seek a reasonable accommodation.
key_cases_cited: United States v. Billingsley, 615 F.3d 404 (5th Cir. 2010)
Chezem v. Beverly Enterprises-Texas, Inc., 66 F.3d 741 (5th Cir. 1995)
Atlantic Coast Line Railroad Co. v. Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers, 398 U.S. 281 (1970)
Mitchum v. Foster, 407 U.S. 225 (1972)
Gates v. Strain, 855 F.3d 874 (5th Cir. 2018)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exemption from Parish ordinance requirements for addictive disorder treatment facilities; permission to operate sober home in single-family zoning district without obtaining permit requiring 24-hour supervisory personnel, health care access, liability insurance, and handicap accessibility
fha_claims.reasoning: The court did not reach the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim because it found the Anti-Injunction Act barred injunctive relief based on the FHA claim. The claim survives the procedural challenge to the preliminary injunction motion but has not been substantively decided on the merits.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Parish ordinance restricting number of unrelated individuals in single-family homes and requiring permits for addictive disorder treatment facilities
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs alleged the Parish's ordinances had a discriminatory impact on group homes for disabled individuals, but the court did not reach the merits because the Anti-Injunction Act barred injunctive relief based on the FHA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Parish's filing of state court injunction action after Plaintiffs requested reasonable accommodation
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs alleged retaliation under the FHA for requesting accommodation, but the court did not reach the merits because the Anti-Injunction Act barred injunctive relief based on the FHA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claim for discrimination based on disability; Rehabilitation Act § 504 claim for discrimination based on handicap; 42 U.S.C. § 1983 claim for retaliation against First Amendment right to petition government
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found the Anti-Injunction Act barred injunctive relief based on the ADA and RA claims. For the § 1983 retaliation claim, the court found Plaintiffs failed to establish a likelihood of success on the merits because the Parish's enforcement action predated any indication that Plaintiffs would request accommodation, breaking the causal chain required for retaliation.

case_name: Lisa N Carey v. St. Charles Parish
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request identifiable; plaintiff appears to allege disparate treatment discrimination based on race when parish enforcement actions intensified after learning she, a Black woman, owned the property.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claims because she failed to plead a prima facie case of disparate treatment (no facts showing she applied for housing, was rejected, or that housing remained open to similarly situated applicants), and alternatively, all claims were barred by res judicata as they arose from the same transaction as prior state court litigation.
brief_summary: Lisa N. Carey, proceeding pro se, sued St. Charles Parish in federal court alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on the Parish's enforcement of unsafe structure ordinances against her property after learning she, a Black woman, owned it. The court granted the Parish's motion to dismiss with prejudice, finding Carey failed to state a prima facie disparate treatment claim and that res judicata barred relitigating claims arising from the same transaction as prior state court proceedings.
key_cases_cited: Crain v. City of Selma, 952 F.3d 634 (5th Cir. 2020)
Stevens v. St. Tammany Parish Government, 17 F.4th 563 (5th Cir. 2021)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
England v. La. State Board of Medical Examiners, 375 U.S. 411 (1964)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts supporting elements two through four of the prima facie disparate treatment test (that she applied and was qualified, was rejected, and housing remained open to similarly situated applicants). The complaint contained only conclusory allegations and was devoid of factual support for a § 3604 claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: State law claims arising from the same transaction (unsafe structures enforcement action in state court)
fha_claims.reasoning: The action is barred by the doctrine of res judicata because all elements are satisfied: valid final judgment from state court, same parties (reversed roles), and the FHA claims arose out of the same transaction and should have been asserted as a compulsory reconventional demand in the state court proceeding. Additionally, the Rooker-Feldman doctrine precludes federal court review of state court judgments.

case_name: Victor Cagara Ortiguerra, et al. v. Grand Isle Shipyard, LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege they were segregated and isolated in housing assignments based on their Filipino national origin during COVID-19 quarantine.
key_holding: The court granted plaintiffs' motion to dismiss defendants' defamation counterclaim because the claim was not yet ripe—defamation claims arising from judicial proceedings cannot be brought until the underlying proceedings are terminated—and defendants failed to provide sufficient factual allegations to state a defamation claim.
brief_summary: Filipino welders and fitters sued their employers alleging Fair Labor Standards Act violations, Trafficking Victims Protection Act violations, and Fair Housing Act discrimination based on national origin regarding segregated housing and COVID-19 quarantine accommodations. The court granted plaintiffs' motion to dismiss defendants' defamation counterclaim, finding it was not ripe and failed to state sufficient factual allegations.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Housing and COVID-19 quarantine accommodations; segregation and isolation of Filipino workers in housing assignments
fha_claims.disposition: Not directly addressed; case involves arbitration motion and defamation counterclaim dismissal
fha_claims.reasoning: The FHA claim survived the motion to compel arbitration (court denied arbitration as to FHA claims), but this opinion addresses only the defamation counterclaim and does not reach the merits of the underlying FHA discrimination claim regarding segregated housing assignments.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: FLSA minimum wage and overtime violations; TVPA forced labor and trafficking claims; refusal to allow evacuation during Hurricane Ida
fha_claims.disposition: Motion to compel arbitration granted as to FLSA; denied as to TVPA and FHA
fha_claims.reasoning: FLSA claims were stayed pending arbitration; TVPA and FHA claims survived the arbitration motion and remain pending in federal court. This opinion does not address the merits of any non-FHA claims, only the procedural arbitration ruling and the defamation counterclaim.

case_name: Jessica Bush v. Broad Management Group, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested reasonable accommodation to keep emotional support animals in her rental apartment.
key_holding: The court granted defendants' motion to strike plaintiff's jury demand because three of five factors weighed in favor of finding the jury waiver clause in the lease to be knowing and voluntary, despite plaintiff not being represented by counsel when she signed.
brief_summary: Jessica Bush sued Broad Management Group and Cristina Perez alleging they violated the Fair Housing Act by failing to provide a reasonable accommodation for her emotional support animals. The court granted defendants' motion to strike Bush's jury demand, finding that the jury waiver clause in her lease was a knowing and voluntary waiver of her Seventh Amendment right to trial by jury.
key_cases_cited: G & C Constr., LLC v. Kiewit La. Co., No. 11-2566, 2012 WL 601887 (E.D. La. Feb. 23, 2012)
Commodity Futures Trading Comm'n v. Schor, 478 U.S. 833 (1986)
Jones v. Tubal-Cain Hydraulic Sols., Inc., 2017 WL 3887235 (S.D. Tex. Sept. 5, 2017)
Evans v. Union Bank of Switzerland, No. 01-1507, 2003 WL 21277125 (E.D. La. May 30, 2003)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation for emotional support animals
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted defendants' motion to strike plaintiff's jury demand based on a valid jury waiver clause in the lease agreement. The underlying FHA reasonable accommodation claim for emotional support animals remains pending; this order addresses only the procedural issue of jury trial waiver and does not reach the merits of the FHA claim.

case_name: Jessica Bush v. Broad Management Group, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested to keep two pit bull dogs as emotional support animals to assist with her anxiety, depression, PTSD, chemical seizures, and agoraphobia.
key_holding: The court denied summary judgment because genuine issues of material fact exist as to whether defendants had sufficient notice of plaintiff's disability and whether their April 5 denial letter, combined with the subsequent eviction notice citing unauthorized animals, constituted a refusal to provide a reasonable accommodation.
brief_summary: Jessica Bush sued Broad Management Group and property manager Cristina Perez after being denied permission to keep her two pit bull emotional support animals at Pinecrest Apartments, claiming violation of the Fair Housing Act. The court denied defendants' motion for summary judgment, finding genuine disputes of material fact as to whether defendants had adequate notice of Bush's disability and whether the denial of her accommodation request, followed by an eviction citing unauthorized animals, constituted unlawful discrimination and retaliation under the FHA.
key_cases_cited: Chavez v. Aber, 122 F. Supp. 3d 581 (W.D. Tex. 2015)
Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condo. Ass'n, 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014)
DuBois v. Ass'n of Apartment Owners of 2987 Kalakaua, 453 F.3d 1175 (9th Cir. 2006)
Elliott v. QF Circa 37, LLC, No. 16-0288, 2018 WL 2933467 (S.D. Cal. June 12, 2018)
Oxford House, Inc. v. City of Baton Rouge, 932 F. Supp. 2d 683 (M.D. La. 2013)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver of no-pet policy to allow plaintiff to keep two pit bulls as emotional support animals for anxiety, depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, chemical seizures, and agoraphobia
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine issues of material fact precluding summary judgment on whether defendants knew or should have known of plaintiff's disability (second element satisfied by plain language of accommodation request letter) and whether defendants refused the accommodation (April 5 letter constituted refusal despite 'at this time' language, and notice to vacate with eviction proceedings constituted punishment for animals' presence).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine issue of material fact on causal connection element: plaintiff engaged in protected activity (request for reasonable accommodation), suffered adverse action (eviction filing), and notice to vacate cited both non-payment of rent and 'unauthorized animals' as lease violations, creating factual dispute over whether retaliation was the motivating factor.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Louisiana Equal Housing Opportunity Act (LEHOA) violation, negligent hiring, training, and supervision under Louisiana law
fha_claims.reasoning: Court explicitly stated that defendants' motion for summary judgment addressed only FHA claims and did not address plaintiff's LEHOA or negligent training claims; court made no findings as to non-FHA claims.

case_name: Hughes v. Bouchon Properties LLC
accommodation_description: Hughes alleged in conclusory terms that Bouchon refused to permit or make reasonable modifications and failed to make reasonable accommodations necessary to afford him equal opportunity to use and enjoy his dwelling, but the complaint never identified any specific accommodation requested, any specific modification sought, or any nexus between his disability and the eviction beyond reciting statutory language under § 3604(f)(3).
key_holding: The court granted in part and denied in part defendants' Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss, allowing Hughes's § 1982 and FHA § 3604(a) racial discrimination claims to proceed while dismissing the § 3604(c) discriminatory advertising and § 3604(f) disability discrimination claims for insufficient factual allegations, with leave to amend the dismissed claims.
brief_summary: Trashawn Hughes, a disabled African-American tenant at 1602 Clearview Parkway in Metairie, Louisiana, was evicted by his new landlord Lester Bouchon in August 2023 and alleged racial remarks, racial slurs via text, and discriminatory eviction in violation of 42 U.S.C. § 1982 and the FHA. The court denied dismissal of the § 1982 and FHA § 3604(a) racial discrimination claims, finding that allegations of racial epithets and discriminatory eviction plausibly stated claims, but granted dismissal of the § 3604(c) discriminatory advertising claim (no advertising conduct alleged) and the § 3604(f) disability discrimination claims (no specific accommodation requested, no nexus between disability and eviction alleged). Hughes was granted fifteen days to move for leave to amend the dismissed claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Cox v. City of Dallas, 420 F.3d 734 (5th Cir. 2005)
Inclusive Cmty. Project, Inc. v. Lincoln Prop. Co., 920 F.3d 890 (5th Cir. 2019)
Women’s Elevated Sober Living L.L.C. v. City of Plano, Texas, 86 F.4th 1108 (5th Cir. 2023)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found Hughes plausibly alleged racial discrimination under § 3604(a) by alleging Bouchon made racial remarks, sent derogatory messages, and evicted him based on race rather than unpaid rent. All four elements of disparate treatment (protected class membership, qualification to rent, rejection, unit available to others) were sufficiently pleaded to survive 12(b)(6).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed § 3604(c) discriminatory advertising claim because the complaint alleged no facts showing Bouchon made, printed, or published any notice or advertisement indicating preference or discrimination. All allegations centered on eviction and refusal to rent, which fall outside § 3604(c)'s scope.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable modifications or accommodations related to disability; specific nature of accommodation not alleged
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed § 3604(f)(3)(B) reasonable accommodation claim because Hughes failed to allege sufficient nexus between his disability and the eviction, did not allege a specific accommodation was requested, did not allege he funded or offered to fund modifications, and did not allege any accommodation was necessary or reasonable. Conclusory allegations of refusal to accommodate were insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1982 racial discrimination claim; state law claims (eviction, breach of contract, harassment, tortious interference, etc.)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss § 1982 claim, finding Hughes plausibly alleged Bouchon's racial animus (racial remarks, derogatory text), intentional discrimination, and that eviction was motivated by race. Court retained supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims.

source_file: 9724281_2024_Military Road Revitalization Company, LLC v. St. Tammany Parish Government_laed
case_name: Military Road Revitalization Company, LLC et al. v. St. Tammany Parish Government
accommodation_description: Developers of an affordable housing project allege the parish's moratorium ordinance blocks housing for protected classes including persons with disabilities, constituting disparate impact discrimination under the FHA.
key_holding: The court granted St. Tammany's motion to dismiss BCP's claims as moot and Military Road's due process claims as unripe, but denied the motion to dismiss Military Road's Fair Housing Act claims, finding the claims are ripe and not barred by Colorado River abstention.
brief_summary: Military Road Revitalization Company and BCP (developers) sued St. Tammany Parish Government alleging that a moratorium ordinance blocking an affordable housing development violated the Fair Housing Act by having a disparate impact on African Americans, Hispanics, and persons with disabilities, and constituted intentional race-based discrimination. The court granted in part and denied in part the motions to dismiss, dismissing BCP's claims as moot and Military Road's due process claims as unripe, while allowing the FHA claims to proceed.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Tex. Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of permits for construction of affordable multifamily housing development (Covington Trace Ridge Apartments) targeting households with income at 80% or less of area median income and households with at least one member with a disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied St. Tammany's motion to dismiss Military Road's FHA claims (other than due process claims) under ripeness doctrine, finding that the moratorium ordinance itself constitutes a ripe FHA violation even though the permitting process is incomplete, and that Military Road need not exhaust a futile permitting process. Claims survive and proceed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged interference with housing opportunities through moratorium ordinance and retaliatory conduct targeting affordable housing development for low-to-moderate income residents and persons with disabilities
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied St. Tammany's motion to dismiss Military Road's FHA interference/coercion claims under § 3617, finding ripeness and denying Colorado River abstention. Claims survive and proceed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Louisiana Equal Housing Opportunity Act, Americans With Disabilities Act (Title III), Rehabilitation Act § 504, Title VI of Civil Rights Act of 1964, Fifth and Fourteenth Amendment due process claims, Louisiana Direct Action Statute claim against Safety National
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed Military Road's procedural due process claims as unripe because the permitting process has not run its course and the deprivation of property is contingent on future events. Other non-FHA claims survive. BCP's claims (all theories) dismissed as moot. Safety National's motion to dismiss denied; claims against insurer survive under Louisiana Direct Action Statute because FHA claims sound in tort.

case_name: Victor Ortiguerra, et al. v. Grand Isle Shipyard, LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs, Filipino workers, alleged housing segregation and forced bunkhouse conditions during Hurricane Ida as part of TVPA and FHA claims, but this motion addresses only T visa document discovery.
key_holding: The court granted in part defendants' motion to compel T visa documents, ordering production of limited factual portions of sworn statements with redactions under a protective order, but denied the motion as to most visa-related documents finding the Cazoria factors and T visa confidentiality policies outweigh the relevance of broader discovery.
brief_summary: Filipino welders and fitters sued their employer and related entities under the FLSA, TVPA, and FHA alleging trafficking, unpaid wages, and housing discrimination; defendants moved to compel production of T visa applications which the court granted in part, ordering limited production of sworn statements with redactions under a protective order but denying the motion as to most visa documents based on Fifth Circuit precedent counseling narrow discovery of humanitarian visa materials.
key_cases_cited: Cazoria v. Koch Foods of Mississippi, LLC, 838 F.3d 540 (5th Cir. 2016)
Ortiguerra v. Grand Isle Shipyard, LLC, 630 F. Supp. 3d 793 (E.D. La. 2022)
Samuel v. Signal Int'l LLC, No. 1:13-CV-323, 2014 WL 12597395 (E.D. Tex. Oct. 15, 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable. The opinion addresses only discovery of T visa applications and does not substantively analyze any FHA claim on the merits.
fha_claims.reasoning: This opinion is a discovery ruling on a motion to compel production of T visa applications. The court does not address the merits of any FHA claim. The opinion notes that plaintiffs alleged FHA violations (42 U.S.C. § 3613) related to segregation and isolation of Filipino workers in housing assignments and COVID-19 quarantine accommodations, and refusal to allow evacuation during Hurricane Ida, but the court's analysis is limited to the scope of discoverable documents under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 26(b)(1) and does not reach substantive FHA legal standards. The FHA claim remains pending.

case_name: Larry Jones v. Caliber Home Loans, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges he was steered into a sub-prime loan and subjected to a fraudulent mortgage document switch because he is African-American.
key_holding: The court granted defendant's motion to dismiss because plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts to support any theory of discrimination—his allegations were vague, conclusory, and devoid of factual enhancement required under Twombly and Iqbal, and plaintiff abandoned his FHA and ECOA claims by failing to substantively respond to defendant's arguments.
brief_summary: Larry Jones, an African-American homeowner, sued Caliber Home Loans alleging racial discrimination in mortgage refinancing, claiming he was steered into a sub-prime loan through a fraudulent bait-and-switch scheme. The court granted defendant's motion to dismiss, finding plaintiff's FHA and ECOA claims failed because his allegations were conclusory, lacked factual support for disparate treatment or disparate impact theories, and plaintiff abandoned his claims by failing to substantively oppose defendant's arguments.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Tex. Dept. of House & Comm. Affairs v. Inclusive Comms. Project, Inc., 135 S. Ct. 2507 (2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to identify any specific test, requirement, or practice responsible for the alleged disparity and failed to allege that defendant's policies had a disproportionately adverse effect on minorities, instead alleging impact only on all subprime borrowers generally. Plaintiff also abandoned this claim by failing to respond to defendant's arguments with any support.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff offered only vague and conclusory allegations insufficient to establish disparate treatment. Plaintiff failed to articulate facts demonstrating that actions were taken against him as a result of race and failed to allege that white or non-minority applicants received more favorable terms. Plaintiff also abandoned this claim by failing to substantively address defendant's motion in opposition.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reverse redlining—offering exorbitantly high interest rate subprime loan
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to adequately plead the fourth element of reverse redlining (that defendant intentionally targeted him for unfair loans or makes loans on more favorable terms to others). Plaintiff's allegations demonstrate he sought out the loan and defendant did not actively induce him, failing to plead the required elements for reverse redlining.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fraud, unjust enrichment, Title VII employment discrimination, UDAP, CSA, UTPCPL, § 1983
fha_claims.reasoning: Fraud claim dismissed without prejudice for failure to satisfy Rule 9(b) particularity requirement but granted leave to amend. Unjust enrichment claim dismissed with prejudice because Louisiana law precludes unjust enrichment when another remedy is available. Miscellaneous claims (Title VII, UDAP, CSA, UTPCPL) not properly pled with factual support or viable legal foundation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's original FHA claims alleging racial discrimination in making available residential real estate transactions and in terms/conditions of such transactions were dismissed with prejudice in the first motion to dismiss for failure to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly. The court did not reach the merits of these claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ECOA (Equal Credit Opportunity Act), Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, UDAP (Unfair and Deceptive Acts or Practices), CSA (Credit Services Act), UTPCPL (Unfair Trade Practices Act and Consumer Protection Law), Louisiana state law fraud, breach of contract, breach of covenant of good faith and fair dealing, TILA (Truth in Lending Act)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's breach of contract and breach of covenant of good faith and fair dealing claims were dismissed with prejudice due to waiver (failure to brief in opposition). Plaintiff's TILA claim was dismissed without prejudice for failure to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly, with leave to amend. Plaintiff's fraud claim survived the motion to dismiss and was found to state a plausible claim under Rule 9(b) particularity requirements.

source_file: 9725635_2022_Louisiana Fair Housing Action Center, Inc. v. Ollie Steele Burden Manor, Inc._lamd
case_name: Louisiana Fair Housing Action Center, Inc. v. Ollie Steele Burden Manor, Inc.
accommodation_description: Request for auxiliary aids and services for deaf residents and prospective residents at nursing homes and long-term care facilities.
key_holding: The court granted plaintiff's motion to compel discovery, finding defendants waived all objections by failing to respond to written discovery for over eight months, and awarded reasonable attorney's fees; the court also extended discovery and trial deadlines due to defendants' noncompliance.
brief_summary: Louisiana Fair Housing Action Center sued nursing home operators alleging they failed to reasonably accommodate deaf residents by not providing auxiliary aids. The court in this discovery dispute granted plaintiff's motion to compel, finding defendants waived all objections by failing to respond to discovery for eight months, and awarded reasonable attorney's fees.
key_cases_cited: In re United States, 864 F.2d 1153 (5th Cir. 1989)
B&S Equip. Co. v. Truckle Servs., Inc., 2011 WL 2637289 (E.D. La. 2011)
Marathon Fin. Ins. Inc., RRG v. Ford Motor Co., 591 F.3d 458 (5th Cir. 2009)
Leza v. City of Laredo, 496 Fed. App'x 375 (5th Cir. 2012)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation and auxiliary aids for deaf residents and prospective residents of nursing homes and long-term care facilities
fha_claims.reasoning: This is a discovery order addressing procedural compliance, not a ruling on the merits of the FHA reasonable accommodation claim. The underlying claim remains pending and has not been substantively analyzed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rehabilitation Act § 504, Section 1557 of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act, Americans with Disabilities Act Title III, and Louisiana state law claims
fha_claims.reasoning: This is a discovery order addressing procedural compliance, not a ruling on the merits of non-FHA claims. The underlying claims remain pending and have not been substantively analyzed.

source_file: 9725785_2022_Discovery Real Estate and Development, LLC v. Town of St. Francisville_lamd
case_name: Discovery Real Estate and Development, LLC v. Town of St. Francisville
accommodation_description: No accommodation or modification was requested. This case involved a real estate developer seeking to construct a 155-unit multifamily residential development (the Parker District–St. Francisville) on a 13-acre parcel, which was allegedly blocked by the Town's discriminatory amendments to its Commercial Zoning Ordinance.
key_holding: The court dismissed Discovery's FHA claim without prejudice for lack of standing and ripeness, holding that plaintiff's alleged harm was not traceable to the challenged 2022 CZO amendments because an independent, unchallenged Sewer Capacity Ordinance already prohibited the multifamily development until at least June 2023, making any injury speculative and non-redressable by the relief sought.
brief_summary: Discovery Real Estate and Development, LLC sued the Town of St. Francisville and its Mayor under the FHA, alleging that 2022 amendments to the Town's Commercial Zoning Ordinance were enacted with discriminatory intent and effect to block Discovery's planned 155-unit multifamily development. The court dismissed the FHA claim without prejudice for lack of standing and ripeness, finding that the plaintiff's injury was not traceable to the challenged CZO changes because a separate Sewer Capacity Ordinance—which imposed a moratorium on all major developments and which had not been challenged in the case—independently precluded the development from proceeding until at least June 2023. The court also denied Discovery's motion for a temporary restraining order on the alternative ground that any injury was not imminent and remained speculative given the existing development moratorium.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dept. of Housing & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 946 F.3d 649 (5th Cir. 2020)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, Inc., 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Gresham v. Windrush Partners, LTD, 730 F.2d 1417 (11th Cir. 1984)
Arizona Recovery Housing Association v. Arizona Department of Health Services, 462 F. Supp. 3d 990 (D. Ariz. 2020)
eBay Inc. v. MercExchange, L.L.C., 547 U.S. 388 (2006)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff lacked standing because its alleged injury (inability to proceed with development) was not fairly traceable to the 2022 CZO changes but rather to the Sewer Capacity Ordinance moratorium, which was not challenged. Additionally, the injury could not be redressed by enjoining the 2022 changes alone, as the moratorium would still prevent development. The claim was also unripe because it depended on contingent future events (sewer system completion, moratorium expiration) that may not occur as anticipated.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff lacked standing for the same reasons as the disparate impact claim: the injury was not traceable to the 2022 CZO changes but to the unchallenged Sewer Capacity Ordinance, and the requested relief would not redress the injury. The claim was also unripe due to dependence on future contingent events.

case_name: Wilbert Aron and Katlin Morris v. G. Lewis-Louisiana No. 2, L.L.C. and Garry Lewis d/b/a Garry Lewis Properties
accommodation_description: Request for exception to criminal background policy as reasonable accommodation for recovering drug addiction disability
key_holding: The court denied Defendants' motion, finding that Plaintiffs adequately alleged Aron has a 'handicap' under the FHA because he has 'a record of such impairment'—his addiction led to drug-related arrests and convictions, and untreated, it substantially limited major life activities including work and sleep.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Wilbert Aron and Katlin Morris sued G. Lewis-Louisiana No. 2, L.L.C. and Garry Lewis d/b/a Garry Lewis Properties, alleging Defendants violated the Fair Housing Act by refusing to make a reasonable accommodation for Aron's disability (recovering drug addiction) by waiving their criminal background policy, resulting in Morris and her children's eviction. The court denied Defendants' motion for judgment on the pleadings, finding that Plaintiffs adequately pleaded Aron has a 'handicap' under the FHA because he has a record of impairment from his addiction.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Harmony Haus Westlake, LLC v. Parkstone Prop. Owners Ass'n
Oxford House, Inc. v. City of Baton Rouge, La.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exception to criminal background policy to allow Aron to reside at the apartment complex with Morris
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the motion for judgment on the pleadings, finding that plaintiffs sufficiently alleged Aron has a 'handicap' under the FHA based on a record of impairment from substance use disorder, even though he is currently in recovery. The reasonable accommodation claim survives the pleading stage and proceeds to discovery.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The FHA disparate treatment claim based on disability survives the motion for judgment on the pleadings because plaintiffs have adequately alleged that Aron qualifies as disabled under the FHA's 'record of impairment' prong.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Louisiana Equal Housing Opportunity Act discrimination claim; negligent training and supervision under Louisiana state law; unlawful interference with FHA rights under 42 U.S.C. § 3617
fha_claims.reasoning: The state law claims and § 3617 interference claim survive the motion for judgment on the pleadings. The court noted that the negligent training and supervision claim does not necessarily depend on Aron's handicapped status, and defendants provided no legal reasoning to support dismissal of all claims based solely on the disability threshold issue.

case_name: Wilbert Aron and Kaitlin Morris v. G. Lewis-Louisiana No. 2, L.L.C., Garry Lewis d/b/a Garry Lewis Properties
accommodation_description: This case does not involve a reasonable accommodation claim; it concerns whether G. Lewis-Louisiana No. 2, LLC has standing to enforce a lease as a counterclaim plaintiff.
key_holding: The court granted Plaintiffs' motion for judgment on the pleadings and dismissed G. Lewis-Louisiana No. 2, LLC's counterclaim for breach of contract because G. Lewis-Louisiana No. 2, LLC was neither a party to the lease nor a third-party beneficiary under Louisiana law, and thus lacked standing to enforce the contract.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Wilbert Aron and Kaitlin Morris sued G. Lewis-Louisiana No. 2, LLC and Garry Lewis Properties alleging Fair Housing Act violations and seeking to dismiss the counterclaim by G. Lewis-Louisiana No. 2, LLC for breach of contract. The court granted the motion for judgment on the pleadings because G. Lewis-Louisiana No. 2, LLC lacked standing to enforce the lease—it was not a party to the contract and no facts established it was a third-party beneficiary under Louisiana law.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

source_file: 9726226_2023_Believe TGH LLC v. Pointe Coupee Parish_lamd
case_name: Believe TGH, LLC, et al. v. Pointe Coupee Parish, Louisiana
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs sought a zoning variance to expand the 'family' definition to allow ten unrelated minors with mental and emotional disabilities (PTSD, depression, developmental delays, autism) to reside together in a therapeutic group home.
key_holding: The court denied both preliminary injunction and cross-motions for summary judgment, finding genuine issues of material fact exist regarding whether the zoning accommodation is reasonable and necessary for the therapeutic group home housing minors with disabilities.
brief_summary: Believe TGH, LLC and related entities (operators of therapeutic group homes for minors with disabilities) sued Pointe Coupee Parish after the Planning and Zoning Commission denied their variance request to expand the zoning 'family' definition to permit ten unrelated disabled minors to reside together. The court denied Plaintiffs' motion for preliminary injunction and denied both parties' cross-motions for summary judgment, finding genuine disputes of material fact exist regarding whether the accommodation is reasonable and necessary.
key_cases_cited: Oxford House, Inc. v. Browning, 266 F. Supp. 3d 896 (M.D. La. 2017)
Groome Resources, Ltd., L.L.C. v. Parish of Jefferson, 52 F. Supp. 2d 721 (E.D. La. 1999)
Oxford House, Inc. v. City of Baton Rouge, 932 F. Supp. 2d 683 (M.D. La. 2013)
Elderhaven, Inc. v. City of Lubbock, 98 F.3d 175 (5th Cir. 1996)
Harmony Haus Westlake, L.L.C. v. Parkstone Prop. Owners Ass'n, 851 F. App'x 461 (5th Cir. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Variance or waiver from zoning ordinance to permit a therapeutic group home for ten minors with mental and emotional disabilities in a Rural Agricultural district that restricts congregate housing and limits unrelated occupants to four persons; alternatively, rezoning or special use permit to allow the group home use.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiffs failed to demonstrate substantial likelihood of success on the merits for preliminary injunction because evidence was insufficient on reasonableness and necessity prongs, but did not reach full merits analysis. Court found genuine disputes of material fact exist on reasonableness and necessity elements, denying both parties' summary judgment motions and allowing claims to proceed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Variance or waiver from zoning ordinance to permit a therapeutic group home for ten minors with mental and emotional disabilities in a Rural Agricultural district that restricts congregate housing and limits unrelated occupants to four persons; alternatively, rezoning or special use permit to allow the group home use.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied four-element reasonable accommodation test (disability status, request and refusal, reasonableness, necessity) and found genuine disputes of material fact on reasonableness and necessity elements. Court found prospective residents clearly disabled, accommodation was properly requested via email correspondence, but reasonableness and necessity remained genuinely disputed, precluding summary judgment for either party.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II, Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, Louisiana Equal Housing Opportunity Act, Louisiana public accommodations law
fha_claims.reasoning: Court stated that FHA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act claims are analyzed identically for reasonable accommodation purposes and applied the same four-element test. Court denied summary judgment on all claims, finding genuine disputes of material fact on reasonableness and necessity elements.

case_name: Cheryl L. Fenelon et al. v. U.S. Dept. of Housing & Urban Development et al.
accommodation_description: The complaint is too vague to identify any specific accommodation request; the court found the pleadings consisted of only four sentences with no factual allegations.
key_holding: The court declined to rule on the TRO and instead granted plaintiffs leave to amend their complaint because the complaint failed to allege sufficient facts to establish subject matter jurisdiction.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Cheryl Fenelon and Barbara Jackson filed a vague complaint against HUD, DOJ, and 19 other defendants alleging Fair Housing Act violations and seeking emergency injunctive relief, but the complaint contained only four sentences with no factual allegations and failed to establish subject matter jurisdiction. The court declined to rule on the TRO and granted plaintiffs until August 8, 2021, to amend their complaint to state a valid basis for jurisdiction.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not specified; complaint contains no factual allegations regarding any accommodation request or FHA violation
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found no factual allegations regarding FHA violations and could not determine subject matter jurisdiction. Plaintiffs granted leave to amend complaint by August 8, 2021, to state a valid basis for jurisdiction before court would rule on TRO or proceed further.

case_name: Cheryl L Fenelon et al v. U.S. Dept of Housing & Urban Development et al
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation was described; the complaint cited Fair Housing Act violations (42 U.S.C. § 3601 et seq.) in a conclusory fashion with no factual allegations identifying any particular accommodation request or discriminatory act.
key_holding: The court dismissed the case without prejudice for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because the pro se plaintiffs' complaint contained no factual allegations supporting jurisdiction under the Fair Housing Act or any other cited statute.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Cheryl Fenelon and Barbara Jackson filed a four-sentence complaint against 21 defendants—including federal agencies, federal judges, and private entities—citing Fair Housing Act violations, conspiracy to violate civil rights, and antitrust violations, but included no factual allegations describing how any statute was violated or what any defendant did. The court twice extended deadlines for plaintiffs to amend and cure the jurisdictional deficiency, but plaintiffs refused to amend and failed to comply by the final deadline. Accordingly, the court dismissed the matter without prejudice for failure to establish subject matter jurisdiction.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not specified; complaint contains no factual allegations regarding any accommodation request or FHA violation
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint asserts FHA violations but contains only four sentences with no factual allegations describing how the FHA was violated, what relief is sought, or how any defendant is connected to the alleged violations. The court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because plaintiffs failed to plead facts establishing jurisdiction despite two opportunities to amend.

case_name: Clifford Osborne et al v. Kevin Belton
accommodation_description: Request to keep an emotional support dog at the rental property as a reasonable accommodation for developmental disabilities, anxiety, and depression
key_holding: The court found that the landlord violated the FHA by refusing to accommodate Mr. Osborne's disability with an emotional support animal, establishing all five prima facie elements including that the accommodation was necessary and reasonable, and further retaliated against him by evicting him after he requested the accommodation.
brief_summary: Clifford Osborne sued his landlord Kevin Belton alleging Fair Housing Act violations after Belton refused to allow Osborne to keep an emotional support dog at the rental property and subsequently evicted him for violating the no-pets policy. The court granted Osborne's unopposed motion for summary judgment, finding Belton violated the FHA by failing to reasonably accommodate Osborne's disability and retaliated against him for requesting the accommodation.
key_cases_cited: Overlook Mut. Homes, Inc. v. Spencer, 666 F. Supp. 2d 850 (S.D. Ohio 2009)
Bryant Woods Inn, Inc. v. Howard County, Md., 124 F.3d 597 (4th Cir. 1997)
Harmony Haus Westlake, LLC v. Parkstone Prop. Owners Ass'n, Inc., 440 F. Supp. 3d 654 (W.D. Tex. 2020)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to keep an emotional support dog on the rental property to manage plaintiff's anxiety, depression, and panic attacks stemming from developmental disabilities and childhood trauma.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied the five-element prima facie test under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(B) and found: (1) plaintiff suffers from a disability (developmental disabilities, anxiety, depression); (2) defendant knew or should have known of the disability; (3) the emotional support animal was necessary to afford equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling; (4) the request was reasonable as emotional support animals are recognized accommodations under the FHA; and (5) defendant refused the accommodation by removing the dog. Defendant's failure to respond to requests for admission established admissions on all material facts.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied the three-element prima facie test under 42 U.S.C. § 3617 and found: (1) plaintiff engaged in protected activity by requesting a reasonable accommodation based on disability; (2) defendant took adverse action (eviction) against plaintiff; and (3) a causal connection existed between the protected activity and the adverse action, as the eviction occurred shortly after plaintiff complained about defendant's removal of the emotional support animal. Defendant failed to articulate a legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason for the eviction.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Louisiana Equal Housing Opportunity Act retaliation claim (La. R.S. § 51:2609)
fha_claims.reasoning: Louisiana Equal Housing Opportunity Act mirrors FHA language and retaliation standards; court applied identical prima facie framework and found plaintiff established all three elements. Defendant's failure to respond to discovery and requests for admission resulted in deemed admissions of material facts supporting the retaliation claim.

case_name: Clifford Osborne et al v. Kevin Belton
accommodation_description: Request to keep an emotional support dog as a reasonable accommodation for disability at the leased property
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment finding FHA violations, and on the damages motion awarded $29,991.80 in attorney's fees, $50,000 in compensatory damages, and $10,000 in punitive damages (reduced from the $75,000 requested), finding Belton acted recklessly but not with the requisite malice for the full punitive award.
brief_summary: Clifford Osborne and Deborah Olsen sued landlord Kevin Belton under the Fair Housing Act alleging he discriminated against Mr. Osborne by refusing to allow his emotional support dog and then retaliated by evicting them. The court previously granted summary judgment for plaintiffs on the FHA claims, and on the instant motion for damages, awarded $89,991.80 total ($29,991.80 attorney's fees, $50,000 compensatory, $10,000 punitive) while denying the full $75,000 punitive damages request.
key_cases_cited: Fender v. City of Chicago
Johnson v. Georgia Highway Express, Inc.
Hensley v. Eckerhart
Lincoln v. Case
Parris v. Pappas

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to keep an emotional support dog on the rental property; defendant initially allowed the dog, then prohibited it one month later, and ultimately forcibly removed it to a neighboring town
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted plaintiffs' unopposed motion for summary judgment on August 3, 2022, finding in favor of plaintiffs and determining that defendant violated the FHA by refusing to accommodate plaintiff's emotional support animal despite plaintiff's disability and physician's letter documenting medical necessity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Eviction in retaliation for exercising FHA rights by requesting accommodation for emotional support dog
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted summary judgment finding that defendant retaliated against plaintiffs for exercising their rights under the FHA by evicting Mr. Osborne and his dog from the property after plaintiff requested accommodation and provided physician documentation of medical necessity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought to amend complaint to include Fair Housing Act violations but provided no factual basis or specific accommodation request.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court affirmed the magistrate judge's denial of amendment as futile because plaintiff's proposed amended complaint merely concluded that she wanted to add FHA violations without pleading any factual basis or legal theory, failing to meet Rule 8's pleading requirements under Twombly.

source_file: 9730812_2019_Mannai Home LLC v. City of Fall River, Massachusetts_mad
case_name: Mannai Home, LLC v. City of Fall River
accommodation_description: Request that the City of Fall River allow conversion of a three-unit property into a sober recovery home for 20-22 individuals in recovery from substance abuse without requiring a special permit for group residences.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for defendants on the failure-to-accommodate claim because Mannai Home never requested an accommodation—it merely asserted the right to proceed as a matter of right without a special permit—and the city's failure to respond to inquiries did not constitute a denial of reasonable accommodation where no cognizable accommodation was requested.
brief_summary: Mannai Home, LLC sued the City of Fall River and its building inspector seeking to establish a sober recovery home, alleging the City violated the Fair Housing Act and Massachusetts Zoning Act by discriminatorily requiring a special permit for group residences housing disabled individuals. The court granted defendants' motion for summary judgment on the FHA reasonable accommodation claim, finding Mannai never actually requested an accommodation but instead demanded the right to proceed without permits, and denied all other motions as to intentional discrimination claims and the state zoning law claim.
key_cases_cited: Astralis Condominium Ass'n v. Secretary, U.S. Dep't of Hous. & Urban Dev., 620 F.3d 62 (1st Cir. 2010)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found Biszko's statement that the project was 'never going to happen' was too ambiguous to warrant summary judgment in either direction on the question of discriminatory intent. The evidence could plausibly reflect either discriminatory concern or legitimate concerns about property development, requiring a fact-finder to resolve the ambiguity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to develop the property as a sober recovery home without obtaining a special permit; waiver of group residence permit requirement
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that plaintiff's request to proceed as a matter of right was not a request for an 'accommodation' within the meaning of the FHA. Plaintiff never requested something out of the ordinary such as a waiver of code requirements, but merely asserted it had the right to proceed without a special permit. Therefore, defendants did not deny a request for reasonable accommodation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claim for failure to make reasonable modifications in policies and practices; Massachusetts Zoning Act § 3 claim for discrimination against disabled persons in zoning decisions
fha_claims.reasoning: On the Massachusetts Zoning Act claim, the court found the Fall River ordinance itself violated § 3 by treating families differently from group residences for the disabled, but could not resolve on summary judgment whether plaintiff was required to exhaust administrative remedies or seek building permits. On the ADA claim, the court applied the same reasonable accommodation analysis as the FHA and granted summary judgment for defendants on the failure to accommodate theory.

source_file: 9730987_2019_National Association of the Deaf v. Harvard University_mad

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Timely, accurate captioning of audio and audiovisual content made available online by Harvard to the general public for free
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 12(c) - Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied Harvard's motion for judgment on the pleadings on Title III ADA claim, finding that plaintiffs adequately pleaded a failure-to-accommodate claim under the auxiliary aids and services framework. The court held that whether captioning would result in undue burden or fundamental alteration is a question of fact unsuitable for resolution on the pleadings.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Timely, accurate captioning of audio and audiovisual content made available online by Harvard to the general public for free
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 12(c) - Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied Harvard's motion for judgment on the pleadings on Section 504 claim, finding that plaintiffs adequately pleaded discrimination under Section 504's implementing regulations. The court rejected Harvard's argument that the complaint failed to state a claim based on the 'aids, benefits, and services' language in the regulations, holding that plaintiffs alleged Harvard's administrative methods and policies resulted in lack of captioning.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Communications Decency Act § 230 immunity defense; Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act; Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 12(c) - Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted Harvard's motion in part as to embedded third-party content (holding CDA immunity applies), but denied it as to content created or produced by Harvard and content posted by students, faculty, and scholars on Harvard platforms (holding CDA immunity is premature because the record does not clearly establish Harvard is not a content provider as to such material). The court found that CDA immunity is an affirmative defense that can support dismissal only when facts establishing the defense are definitively ascertainable from the complaint.

case_name: Danyela Schonton, et al. v. MPA Granada Highlands LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; case involves Brazilian tenants alleging national origin discrimination in leasing, including allegedly discriminatory identification requirements, citizenship documentation demands, and unequal lease renewal terms.
key_holding: The court denied class certification because plaintiffs failed to establish commonality (no common discriminatory policy identified), typicality (named plaintiffs' claims varied significantly), and adequacy of representation (named plaintiffs lacked understanding of class action duties and had conflicting interests); individualized inquiries would be required for each class member's disparate treatment claim.
brief_summary: Brazilian tenants and tenant applicants sued the owner and management of Granada Highlands apartment complex alleging national origin discrimination under the Fair Housing Act, claiming defendants selectively imposed discriminatory qualification requirements including proof of citizenship, multiple forms of identification, and pet removal policies. The court denied plaintiffs' motion for class certification, finding plaintiffs failed to establish commonality, typicality, and adequacy of representation because the proposed class lacked a common discriminatory policy and individual claims required highly individualized inquiries.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Civil Rights Act § 1981, § 1982; Mass. Gen. L. c. 151B § 4(6), (10)
fha_claims.reasoning: Non-FHA claims under the Civil Rights Act and Massachusetts state law survive the motion to dismiss stage but are not addressed on the merits in this opinion, which focuses on the class certification motion for the FHA claim.

case_name: Kimlan T. Pham v. Deutsche Bank Trust Company Americas, Ocwen Loan Servicing, LLC and GMAC Mortgage, LLC
accommodation_description: Loan modification under HAMP for a homeowner whose husband receives disability benefits; plaintiff alleged discrimination because disability income rendered her ineligible for refinancing
key_holding: Plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie case of FHA discrimination because Ocwen offered two HAMP loan modifications which plaintiff rejected by not making trial payments, and there is no evidence of discriminatory intent or disparate impact from defendants' lending practices.
brief_summary: Pham sued Deutsche Bank and Ocwen alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act based on disability discrimination in loan modification, claiming she was told her husband's disability income made her ineligible for refinancing. The court granted summary judgment for defendants, finding that Ocwen never rejected Pham's modification request and instead offered two HAMP trial period plans which Pham herself rejected by failing to make required payments or submit documentation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Loan modification based on disability status; plaintiff alleged she was denied refinancing eligibility because too much of her income came from her husband's disability benefits
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie case of discrimination under the FHA. Ocwen offered two successive HAMP loan modifications, which plaintiff rejected by failing to make required trial payments or submit required documents. Ocwen had a legitimate, non-discriminatory reason for not proceeding: plaintiff's own inaction. No evidence that plaintiff was denied a housing opportunity to which she was entitled.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of contract claim alleging failure to notify of loan servicing transfer to Nationstar
fha_claims.reasoning: Record evidence establishes that Ocwen provided written notice to plaintiff on March 15, 2017, that Nationstar would assume servicing of the loan. Plaintiff's allegation that Ocwen failed to provide notice is contradicted by documentary evidence.

case_name: Danyela Schonton, et al. v. MPA Granada Highlands LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: This is not a reasonable accommodation case; it is a national origin discrimination case under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(b) involving Brazilian tenants challenging rental policy requirements for foreign citizens.
key_holding: Plaintiffs failed to establish a prima facie case of national origin discrimination because they did not demonstrate they were qualified to lease units under Granada's Rental Policy (which required a visa for foreign citizens), and they produced no evidence that similarly situated non-Brazilian tenants were subject to less stringent requirements.
brief_summary: Brazilian tenants and tenant applicants sued Granada Apartments and its owner/management, alleging national origin discrimination under the Fair Housing Act based on the property's rental policies requiring foreign citizens to provide specific identification documents including visas. The court granted summary judgment for defendants because plaintiffs failed to establish a prima facie case—they did not meet the rental policy requirements and could not identify similarly situated non-Brazilian tenants who were treated more favorably.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to establish a prima facie case of national origin discrimination under McDonnell Douglas because they did not demonstrate they were qualified to obtain or renew leases under the Rental Policy (all lacked required visa and identification documents), and they failed to identify similarly situated non-Brazilian tenants treated more favorably. The affidavits offered as direct evidence of discriminatory intent contained only conclusory statements unsupported by specific facts and did not establish a causal link between national origin and lease denials.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1981 (Civil Rights Act), Mass. Gen. L. c. 151B, § 4(6) (state fair housing law)
fha_claims.reasoning: At the motion hearing, counsel for Plaintiffs indicated they are no longer pursuing Counts II and III (§ 1981 and state law claims), which were voluntarily dismissed by the plaintiffs.

case_name: Ferahnaz Kahyaoglu v. Omar Salim Sayied and Abul Maksud Sayied
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request identified; plaintiff alleges housing discrimination based on protected characteristics (color, gender, national origin, race, ethnicity) regarding uninhabitable conditions rather than a request for reasonable accommodation.
key_holding: Plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claims were dismissed because she failed to allege sufficient facts showing discriminatory intent or that defendants' actions were motivated, at least in part, by discrimination as required to maintain FHA claims under 42 U.S.C. §§ 3604 and 3617.
