brief_summary: National Fair Housing Alliance and companion organizations sued Bank of America alleging the bank engaged in discriminatory maintenance and marketing of bank-owned properties across 37 cities, potentially on a discriminatory basis related to race or national origin. This court order resolves a discovery dispute by adopting a phased discovery approach and determining redaction requirements under state financial privacy laws.
key_cases_cited: Marks v. Glob. Mortg. Grp., Inc., 218 F.R.D. 492 (S.D.W. Va. 2003)
Williams v. Big Picture Loans, LLC, 2019 WL 1186856 (E.D. Va. 2019)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied defendants' summary judgment motions on disparate impact claim, finding that steps two and three of the Fair Housing Act's disparate impact framework had not yet been fully explored through discovery, and that subsequent motions for summary judgment on remaining issues are appropriate.

case_name: Tamara Johnson, et al. v. City of Annapolis
subsidy_program: Public Housing (Capital Fund and Operating Fund)
accommodation_description: This is not a reasonable accommodation case; it involves a class of public housing residents challenging the City of Annapolis's non-inspection policy as racially discriminatory under the Fair Housing Act.
key_holding: The court denied HACA's motion to dismiss the City's third-party indemnification and contribution claims because the City plausibly alleged that HACA's failure to maintain properties was the primary cause of plaintiffs' injuries, but granted HUD's motion to dismiss because the City lacked Article III standing—failing to show injury-in-fact separate from residents' harm, causation between HUD's actions and the City's alleged injuries, and redressability of any injury through a favorable ruling.
brief_summary: Named plaintiffs Tamara Johnson and Tyonna Holliday, representing a class of Annapolis public housing residents, sued the City of Annapolis alleging its non-inspection policy for HACA properties disproportionately impacted African American residents in violation of the Fair Housing Act; the City subsequently filed third-party complaints against HACA and HUD seeking indemnification and contribution. The court denied HACA's motion to dismiss the City's third-party claims but granted HUD's motion to dismiss, finding the City lacked Article III standing because it failed to demonstrate injury-in-fact separate from the residents' harm, causation between its alleged injuries and HUD's conduct, and redressability.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Warth v. Seldin, 422 U.S. 490 (1975)
Simon v. Eastern Ky. Welfare Rights Org., 426 U.S. 26 (1976)
Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The City, as third-party plaintiff, lacked Article III standing to assert a Fair Housing Act disparate impact claim against HUD because it failed to allege an injury separate from that of the resident-plaintiffs, could not establish a causal connection between its purported injury and HUD's conduct (the chain of causation was too attenuated and dependent on independent third-party decisions), and could not show that a favorable judgment would redress its claimed injury.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Housing Act § 1437 (failure to fund and enforce habitability requirements); Fifth Amendment equal protection claim (intentional racial discrimination)
fha_claims.reasoning: The City lacked Article III standing to assert Housing Act and Fifth Amendment equal protection claims against HUD for the same reasons it lacked standing on the FHA claim: no independent injury to the City, no fairly traceable causal connection, and no redressability. The court declined to reach the sovereign immunity question because the standing defect was dispositive.

source_file: 9741918_2023_Estate of DaMon R. Fisher v. City of Annapolis_mdd
case_name: Tamara Johnson, et al. v. The City of Annapolis, et al. / The Estate of Damon R. Fisher, et al. v. The City of Annapolis, et al.
accommodation_description: Class of Black renters allege City's non-inspection policy for rental housing produces a disparate impact based on race.
key_holding: The court granted in part the City's Rule 56(d) motion, allowing limited discovery (deposition of plaintiffs' expert Dr. Parnell and interrogatory answers from Ms. Holliday) but denied the motion as to other unspecified grounds, and extended the deadline to respond to partial summary judgment by 30 days.
brief_summary: In consolidated cases, Black renters and the Estate of Damon Fisher sued the City of Annapolis alleging the City's non-inspection policy for rental housing disproportionately impacts Black renters in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The court granted in part the City's Rule 56(d) motion for additional discovery, allowing the City to depose plaintiffs' expert Dr. Parnell and obtain Ms. Holliday's interrogatory answers, but denied the motion as to other unspecified discovery requests, and gave the City 30 additional days to respond to plaintiffs' partial summary judgment motion.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dept. of Hous. & Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Hodgin v. UTC Fire & Sec. Americas Corp., 885 F.3d 243 (4th Cir. 2018)
Pisano v. Strach, 743 F.3d 927 (4th Cir. 2014)
Nichols v. Barwick, 792 F.2d 1520 (11th Cir. 1986)
Elat v. Ngoubene, 993 F. Supp. 2d 497 (D. Md. 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted in part the City's Rule 56(d) motion for further discovery, allowing the City to depose the plaintiffs' expert Dr. Parnell and obtain interrogatory responses from class representative Ms. Holliday before ruling on the plaintiffs' partial motion for summary judgment on disparate impact liability. The merits of the disparate impact claim have not yet been decided.

case_name: Emmeleen Ulita Gilbert v. Pingtao Tang
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; plaintiff alleges sexual harassment and stalking by landlord as discrimination in housing under the FHA.
key_holding: The court denied defendant's motion to dismiss, holding that FHA exemptions under § 3603(b) are affirmative defenses that defendant bears the burden of pleading and proving, and plaintiff sufficiently alleged a quiet enjoyment claim based on sexual harassment and stalking by the landlord.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Emmeleen Gilbert sued her landlord Pingtao Tang alleging sexual harassment, stalking, and inappropriate communications following her signing of a lease for a townhome in Montgomery County, Maryland. The court denied defendant's motion to dismiss, holding that FHA exemptions under § 3603(b) are affirmative defenses that need not be negated in the complaint, and that plaintiff stated plausible claims under both the FHA and Maryland's covenant of quiet enjoyment based on allegations of repeated unwanted sexual advances and surveillance.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Goodman v. Praxair, Inc.
United States v. Space Hunters, Inc.
Baugher v. Wilkins

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that FHA exemptions under § 3603(b) are affirmative defenses that the defendant must plead and prove, not elements the plaintiff must negate in the complaint. Plaintiff's FHA claim alleging sexual harassment and stalking by her landlord survives the motion to dismiss under the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of covenant of quiet enjoyment (Maryland common law and Md. Code, Real Prop. § 2–115)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiff's allegations of repeated sexual harassment, unwanted romantic advances, and suspected stalking by her landlord, viewed in the light most favorable to plaintiff, state a plausible claim for interference with quiet enjoyment under Maryland law, which does not require the premises to be physically uninhabitable but rather an interference with use and enjoyment.

case_name: Nathan Connolly & Shani Mott v. Shane Lanham, et al.
accommodation_description: Not applicable — this case does not involve a request for a reasonable accommodation or modification; rather, it concerns allegations of intentional racial discrimination in a home appraisal conducted in connection with a mortgage refinance application.
key_holding: The court granted in part and denied in part defendants' motions to dismiss, finding that plaintiffs plausibly alleged intentional race discrimination in a home appraisal and mortgage refinancing transaction under the FHA (§ 3605), ECOA, Civil Rights Act (§§ 1981, 1982), and Maryland Fair Housing Laws, while dismissing the § 3604 FHA claim and Count V, and denying plaintiffs' motion to dismiss the appraiser's defamation counterclaims.
brief_summary: Dr. Nathan Connolly and Dr. Shani Mott, a Black married couple in Baltimore, sued appraiser Shane Lanham and lender loanDepot after their home was appraised at $472,000 during a 2021 refinance application—only to be appraised at $750,000 seven months later after plaintiffs removed markers of Black identity and had a white colleague stand in as the homeowner. The court found plaintiffs plausibly alleged intentional racial discrimination, pointing to Lanham's selection of comparable properties from majority-Black census blocks and loanDepot's failure to properly process plaintiffs' discrimination complaint, and allowed most claims to proceed. The court also denied plaintiffs' motion to dismiss Lanham's counterclaims for defamation and false light invasion of privacy arising from plaintiffs' media statements about the alleged discrimination.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Swanson v. Citibank, N.A., 614 F.3d 400 (7th Cir. 2010)
Betsey v. Turtle Creek Assocs., 736 F.2d 983 (4th Cir. 1984)
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 972 (1973)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs plausibly alleged race-based discrimination in appraisal under FHA § 3605 by alleging Lanham knew they were Black, selected comparable homes from majority-Black census blocks despite Homeland being 77.5% white, rejected a higher-priced comparable home as 'overpriced' when it later sold above asking, and the home was appraised $278,000 higher seven months later after 'whitewashing.' These allegations, construed favorably to plaintiffs, plausibly suggest intentional depression of home value based on race.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs plausibly alleged race-based discrimination by loanDepot through its employee Jorgensen's conduct: failing to inform plaintiffs of their right to formal appeal until after the deadline passed, providing a ten-day window to submit a letter but never responding, stopping communication after plaintiffs alleged discrimination, and failing to order a second appraisal. The timing of Jorgensen's change in behavior plausibly suggests a connection between plaintiffs' assertion of a right to nondiscriminatory appraisal and the adverse conduct.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Under FHA § 3617, plaintiffs plausibly alleged that loanDepot interfered with their protected right to a nondiscriminatory appraisal by failing to provide correct information about the appeal process and thereafter avoiding their calls. The statute's 'interfere' language is broadly construed, and plaintiffs need not prove a predicate violation of another FHA section to bring a § 3617 claim. The timing of Jorgensen's conduct following plaintiffs' assertion of their right to nondiscriminatory appraisal plausibly establishes the required causal connection.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Under 42 U.S.C. § 3605, plaintiffs plausibly alleged race-based discrimination in a residential real estate-related transaction (appraisal for refinancing). Section 3605(b)(2) explicitly covers 'the selling, brokering, or appraising of residential real property,' and § 3605(c) prohibits race-based discrimination during appraisals. Plaintiffs' allegations of discriminatory appraisal and loanDepot's failure to remedy it satisfy the pleading standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs' FHA claim under § 3604 was dismissed because § 3604 applies to discrimination in the sale or rental of a dwelling and services connected thereto, not to appraisals in refinancing transactions. Section 3605, the immediately following section, explicitly covers residential real estate-related transactions including appraisals, making § 3605 the appropriate vehicle for plaintiffs' appraisal discrimination claim. Allowing § 3604 to reach refinancing would render § 3605's specific prohibition superfluous.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1982 (Civil Rights Act of 1866); 15 U.S.C. §§ 1691 et seq. (Equal Credit Opportunity Act); MD. CODE ANN., State Government §§ 20-702 et seq. (Maryland Fair Housing Laws)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs' § 1981 and § 1982 claims survive because refinancing involves the right to 'hold' property, which extends to accessing equity in already-owned homes as collateral for loans. Plaintiffs' ECOA claims survive because they plausibly alleged discrimination in a credit transaction based on race. Maryland fair housing claims under §§ 20-705, 20-707 survive the motion to dismiss on the merits but are dismissed for failure to exhaust administrative remedies—plaintiffs did not file a complaint with the Maryland Commission on Human Relations before filing suit, as required by the legislative history and structure of MD. CODE ANN., SG § 20-1035.

source_file: 9742558_2023_Siguel v. King Farm Citizens Assembly, Inc._mdd
case_name: Edward Siguel v. King Farm Citizens Assembly, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested permission to construct storage sheds closer to his gardening area to reduce movement that causes him pain and bleeding due to his physical disability.
key_holding: The court dismissed most accommodation requests (balcony columns, brick patio, trellis) as not necessary because they lacked direct nexus to disability, but allowed the storage shed claims to proceed because Plaintiff adequately pled that locating sheds closer to his garden would reduce movement-related pain and bleeding.
brief_summary: Edward Siguel, a disabled individual with mobility limitations causing pain and bleeding with movement, sued King Farm Citizens Assembly, Inc. (a homeowners' association) and others, alleging the HOA violated the Fair Housing Act by denying his requests for modifications including storage sheds, a brick patio, trellis, and modifications to a balcony structure. On motion to dismiss, the court dismissed most claims finding the requests lacked direct nexus to his disability, but allowed the storage shed claims to proceed because Plaintiff adequately alleged the sheds would reduce his painful movement when accessing gardening tools.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Vorchheimer v. Philadelphi Housing Auth. Corp.
Bryant Woods Inn, Inc. v. Howard County
Gavin v. Spring Ridge Conservancy, Inc.
Anderson v. City of Blue Ash

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Removal of columns and railings from flat roof (fake balcony) on front porch; redesign of balcony; or HOA maintenance of balcony
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that the balcony removal request is not 'necessary' under the FHA because there is no direct causal nexus between the aesthetic requirement to maintain columns and the effects of plaintiff's disability (pain/bleeding with movement). Plaintiff can hire a contractor to perform the work, so he is not required to personally perform labor related to the aesthetic requirement.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Installation of brick patio on top of soil (rather than concrete or sand)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that the material upon which the patio sits bears no logical relationship to plaintiff's disabilities or the pain/bleeding he experiences with movement. The request is preferable but not necessary to ameliorate the effects of disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Installation of plant trellis
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that the trellis request bears no logical relationship to ameliorating the disabling effects of plaintiff's conditions and fails to adequately plead how a trellis will help address the disability or improve ability to use and enjoy the home.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Installation of storage sheds (horizontal shed on front porch and shed in backyard) to store gardening tools and reduce movement required to gather tools
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiff adequately pleads a direct causal connection between storage shed requests and disability (pain/bleeding with movement reduced by shorter distances to tools). Court rejected argument that FHA does not protect recreational activities (gardening), finding that accommodations enabling recreation are necessary when they provide direct amelioration of disability effects. Sheds are reasonable (no fundamental alteration, plaintiff pays costs) and necessary. Claims survive MTD against KFCA and BFMA Defendants but are dismissed against King Farm Individual Defendants and Burgess.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver or modification of HOA maintenance requirements for yard, bushes, and home exterior; or HOA performance of maintenance
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiff's Mandated Maintenance Requests are preferable but not necessary accommodations. The Charter does not require plaintiff to personally maintain the property; he can hire contractors. Plaintiff's inability to find a contractor to his liking is not a disability-based accommodation warranted under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation for requesting removal/redesign of balcony columns and railings
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that retaliation claim fails because the underlying balcony accommodation request is not necessary under the FHA, so there is no protected activity upon which to base retaliation. Additionally, plaintiff fails to plausibly allege causal nexus between accommodation request and alleged retaliatory actions due to vague and unclear factual assertions and lack of clear sequential timeline.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged disparate impact of HOA Charter on disabled individuals
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiff fails to plausibly allege that the Charter caused a significant disparate effect on a protected group (disabled individuals). Plaintiff's allegations are conclusory and limited to how the Charter negatively impacted him individually, with no broader allegations about disproportionate impact on disabled individuals as a group.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged disparate impact of HOA Charter on disabled individuals
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiff fails to plausibly allege that the Charter caused a significant disparate effect on a protected group (disabled individuals). Plaintiff's allegations are conclusory and limited to how the Charter negatively impacted him individually, with no broader allegations about disproportionate impact on disabled individuals as a group.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Forced labor claim under 15 U.S.C. §§ 1589, 1590; trafficking, involuntary servitude claims; ADA Title II claims; declaratory relief regarding HOA authority; fraud and tortious conduct claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed forced labor claim (15 U.S.C. §§ 1589, 1590) because plaintiff fails to allege facts that could plausibly establish forced labor (no allegations of force, threats, serious harm, abuse of legal process, or scheme to cause belief of serious harm). ADA claims dismissed because ADA does not apply to private residence and HOA (not public accommodation). Declaratory relief claim dismissed for failure to provide statutory or legal authority and inadequate pleading. Count IV dismissed because 24 C.F.R. § 100.7 does not contain a cause of action but merely defines scope of liability.

source_file: 9742608_2023_CASA de Maryland, Inc. v. Arbor Realty Trust, Inc._mdd
case_name: CASA de Maryland, Inc. v. Arbor Realty Trust, Inc.
accommodation_description: Class action settlement for tenants alleging Defendants failed to maintain and repair apartments, with discrimination through deficient housing conditions as the basis for FHA claim
key_holding: The court granted preliminary approval of the $3,000,000 settlement fund, finding the settlement terms fair, reasonable, and adequate in comparison to potential per-apartment damages of $18,798 per year under Maryland law, given the risks of litigation and the strength of the case.
brief_summary: CASA de Maryland and individual tenants sued Arbor Realty Trust and related entities alleging that Defendants failed to maintain and repair Bedford and Victoria Station apartment complexes, and discriminated against tenants through deficient housing conditions in violation of the Fair Housing Act, Prince George's County Code, and Maryland common law. The court granted preliminary approval of a $3,000,000 class settlement, finding the settlement terms fair and adequate given the $18,798 potential per-year recovery at trial versus the estimated average recovery of $4,750 per year under the settlement, and certified the settlement class of approximately 2,356 current and former tenants.
key_cases_cited: Amchem Prods., Inc. v. Windsor, 521 U.S. 591 (1997)
1988 Tr. for Allen Child. Dated 8/8/88 v. Banner Life Ins. Co., 28 F.4th 513 (4th Cir. 2022)
Grice v. PNC Mortg. Corp. of Am., 1998 WL 350581 (D.Md. May 21, 1998)
McDaniels v. Westlake Servs., LLC, 2014 WL 556288 (D.Md. Feb. 7, 2014)
Benway v. Res. Real Estate Servs., LLC, 2011 WL 1045597 (D.Md. Mar. 16, 2011)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs alleged Fair Housing Act violations based on discriminatory failure to maintain and repair properties. The case was resolved by settlement agreement with a $3,000,000 Settlement Fund, preliminarily approved as fair, reasonable, and adequate under Fed.R.Civ.P. 23(e). The court did not reach the merits of the FHA claims, as the parties resolved the dispute through negotiated settlement.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Prince George's County Code § 13-153; Maryland common law breach of contract and breach of implied warranty of habitability
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs alleged violations of Prince George's County Code § 13-153 and Maryland common law (breach of contract and breach of implied warranty of habitability) based on deficient maintenance and repair. These claims were resolved by the same settlement agreement, with damages measured under Maryland law as the difference between rent paid and reasonable rental value of the unit in its condition.

source_file: 9742748_2023_Group Home on Gibson Island, LLC v. Gibson Island Corporation_mdd
case_name: Group Home on Gibson Island, LLC v. Gibson Island Corporation
accommodation_description: Request to waive restrictive covenant prohibiting 'business purpose' use to permit operation of a state-licensed assisted living group home for nine seniors with disabilities on Gibson Island
key_holding: Plaintiffs failed to establish that removing the four disputed conditions in the accommodation agreement (Guarantor Provision, Dispute Resolution Provision, Septic Provision, and Arbitration Escrow Provision) was 'necessary' to provide disabled residents an equal opportunity to use and enjoy the Banbury Property under the reasonable accommodation analysis.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Group Home on Gibson Island and Assisted Living Well Compassionate Care sued Gibson Island Corporation seeking a reasonable accommodation to waive restrictive covenants prohibiting business use, so they could operate an assisted living group home for disabled seniors on the private island community. The court granted GIC's motion for summary judgment, finding plaintiffs failed to demonstrate that removing four disputed conditions from the proposed accommodation agreement was 'necessary' to provide disabled residents equal housing opportunity under the Fair Housing Act.
key_cases_cited: Bryant Woods Inn v. Howard County, 124 F.3d 597 (4th Cir. 1997)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Vorchheimer v. Penn Center North, Inc., 903 F.3d 100 (3d Cir. 2018)
Harmony Haus Westlake, LLC v. Parkstone Property Owners' Ass'n, Inc., 851 F. App'x 461 (5th Cir. 2021)
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver of restrictive covenant prohibiting single-family homes from being used for 'business purpose' to permit operation of assisted living group home for nine elderly disabled residents
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to establish that removal of the four disputed conditions in the MOU (Guarantor Provision, Dispute Resolution Provision, Septic Provision, and Arbitration Escrow Provision) was 'necessary' to afford disabled residents equal opportunity to use and enjoy housing. The court applied the Fourth Circuit's three-part test (reasonable, necessary, and affords equal opportunity) and found no direct linkage between removing these conditions and the disability-related needs of the residents. The Septic Provision, while a closer issue, addressed environmental concerns unrelated to the residents' disabilities and did not involve monitoring of residents' bodily functions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claim that GIC intentionally made unavailable or denied housing because of disability under § 3604(f)(1)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs presented no direct evidence of discriminatory intent. Under McDonnell Douglas, they failed to show that GIC's former President's statements (made before negotiations began in 2021) referenced the disabilities of potential residents or demonstrated discriminatory animus related to the accommodation request. The statements did not bear directly on the contested decision.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claim that GIC intentionally discriminated in the terms, conditions, or privileges of sale or rental of the property under § 3604(f)(2)
fha_claims.reasoning: The sale of the Banbury Property occurred on March 4, 2020, one year before the MOU was issued on March 26, 2021. The property has not been rented. The MOU does not contemplate that GIC will provide any services or facilities in connection with the property. Therefore, there is no evidence that GIC took any actions related to the sale or rental of the property or provision of services/facilities that would constitute discrimination under § 3604(f)(2).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claim that GIC's facially neutral policies had a disparate impact on individuals with disabilities
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to show that GIC had discriminatory intent or motive when responding to the reasonable accommodation request. Without evidence of discriminatory animus, disparate impact and disparate treatment claims cannot prevail.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claim that GIC retaliated against Plaintiffs for seeking to open a group home and for engaging in FHA-protected activity, including alleged defamation, anonymous harassing letters, seeking permit revocation, threatening to block views, delaying the process, and tearing up gravel access road
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to establish the required elements of an FHA retaliation claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3617. To the extent retaliation claims were based on alleged retaliation against the Lussis (not parties to the case), Plaintiffs lacked standing. Plaintiffs failed to show adverse action: alleged anonymous letters and view-blocking threats had no evidentiary support; permit questioning was legitimately aimed at covenant compliance; delay in opening was not shown to be retaliatory; road sodding did not prohibit access; and alleged defamation in November 2019 occurred months before the June 2020 accommodation request, breaking any causal connection to protected activity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Maryland Fair Housing Laws claims under Md. Code Ann., State Gov't §§ 20-706 and 20-708 (Count II)
fha_claims.reasoning: State law discrimination claims fail on the same factual and legal grounds as the FHA claims. The undisputed material facts show Plaintiffs cannot prevail on discrimination or retaliation theories under Maryland law.

source_file: 9742828_2023_Bailey v. The Queen's Landing Council of Unit Owners, Inc._mdd
case_name: Rosanna Bailey v. The Queen's Landing Council of Unit Owners, Inc.
accommodation_description: Request for installation of video cameras and motion detecting lights (not framed as disability accommodation)
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's complaint because her FHA claims are barred by claim preclusion from prior state court litigation, time-barred by the two-year statute of limitations, and fail to allege sufficient facts to state plausible claims of racial discrimination or retaliation.
brief_summary: Dr. Rosanna Bailey, a Black woman with disabilities, sued her condominium association alleging race, sex, and disability discrimination and retaliation under the FHA regarding unequal maintenance, delayed door repairs, and differential treatment compared to white neighbors. The court granted defendant's motion to dismiss, finding most claims precluded by a prior state court judgment, time-barred, or failing to state plausible claims without sufficient factual allegations of discriminatory intent.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman
Baltimore Neighborhoods, Inc. v. Rommel Builders, Inc.
Laurel Sand & Gravel, Inc. v. Wilson

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged only conclusory statements of sex discrimination without factual allegations supporting the claim. All factual assertions in the complaint relate to race discrimination, not sex, and thus fail to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged disability (mold allergy, optic neuritis, adjustment disorder, anxiety) and injury from mold infestation but did not allege she was treated differently because of her disabilities. The complaint alleged discriminatory treatment based on race with resulting harm to her disabilities, not disability-based discrimination under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(2).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act, 42 U.S.C. § 12101 et seq., 28 C.F.R. Part 36
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA Title III (28 C.F.R. Part 36) applies only to commercial facilities and public accommodations, which explicitly exclude facilities covered by the Fair Housing Act. A residential condominium is not a public accommodation or commercial facility under the ADA and thus Part 36 is inapplicable.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to maintain and replace exterior sliding doors, landscaping maintenance, storm door access, video camera and motion-detecting light installation
fha_claims.reasoning: Claims arising from sliding door disputes and related water damage are barred by claim preclusion (res judicata) based on the final judgment in the prior Queen Anne's County Circuit Court action, which involved the same parties, same transactional nucleus of facts, and final judgment on the merits. Plaintiff knew or should have known of her FHA discrimination claims during the prior action.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged disparate treatment regarding landscaping maintenance (2011, 2014), tornado debris removal (2017), sliding door replacement (2022), staff responsiveness, and video camera installation
fha_claims.reasoning: Claims arising from conduct before June 8, 2021 are barred by the FHA's two-year statute of limitations (42 U.S.C. § 3613(a)(1)(A)). Although plaintiff invoked the continuing violations doctrine, the complaint alleges isolated events by different individuals rather than a continuous unlawful practice, and thus the doctrine does not apply.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation for asserting FHA discrimination claims, including failure to maintain unit, denial of services and benefits available to other residents
fha_claims.reasoning: Retaliation claim fails to plausibly allege both protected activity of which defendant was aware and adverse action causally connected to that protected activity. The complaint does not adequately connect the alleged adverse actions to plaintiff's protected FHA activity or establish the causal nexus required under Hall v. Greystar Management Services, L.P.

source_file: 9742964_2024_Affinity Recovery Center LLC v. Town Commissioners of Sudlersville_mdd
case_name: Affinity Recovery Center LLC v. Town Commissioners of Sudlersville
accommodation_description: Affinity Recovery Center, a substance abuse treatment facility operator, requested a special exception to the Town of Sudlersville's zoning permit to operate a 16-bed residential treatment facility, which would exceed the zoning code's 8-resident limit for group homes.
key_holding: The court dismissed Affinity's FHA reasonable accommodation claim because the complaint failed to allege facts showing that a 16-bed facility was necessary to afford disabled persons equal housing opportunity—the only proffered reason was economic non-viability, not a direct linkage to disability needs.
brief_summary: Affinity Recovery Center LLC sued the Town Commissioners of Sudlersville, Maryland, alleging that the town's denial of a special exception to operate a 16-bed residential substance abuse treatment facility violated the ADA and FHA. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that the zoning code's 8-resident limitation applied equally to all group homes and did not facially discriminate against substance abuse treatment facilities, and that Affinity failed to plausibly allege a reasonable accommodation claim because economic non-viability does not establish that a 16-bed facility is necessary to afford disabled persons equal housing opportunity.
key_cases_cited: Bryant Woods Inn, Inc. v. Howard Cnty., Md., 124 F.3d 597 (4th Cir. 1997)
Scoggins v. Lee's Crossing Homeowners Ass'n, 718 F.3d 262 (4th Cir. 2013)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts showing that defendants discriminated against it or its residents on the basis of disability. The zoning code applies equally to all group homes and home day care facilities with an 8-bed limitation, and plaintiff's own admission that defendants approved an 8-bed facility undermines any claim of disability-based discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts showing that the zoning code imposes discriminatory eligibility criteria based on disability. The code does not single out substance abuse treatment facilities; it applies the same 8-bed limitation to all types of group homes serving persons with various difficulties.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Approval of a 16-bed residential substance abuse treatment facility; plaintiff sought special exception to zoning permit to operate 16-bed group home instead of 8-bed maximum allowed by code
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts showing that a 16-bed facility is necessary to afford disabled residents equal opportunity to use and enjoy housing. The complaint alleges only economic non-viability for an 8-bed operation, not that the accommodation is necessary to meet the disability-related needs of residents. The court applied the 'direct linkage' test and found no causal connection between the requested accommodation and amelioration of disability effects.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II ADA claims for discriminatory methods of administration and imposition of discriminatory eligibility criteria
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts showing that defendants discriminated against it or its residents on the basis of disability under Title II of the ADA. The zoning code applies equally to all group homes, and plaintiff's own admission that defendants approved an 8-bed facility undermines any claim of disability-based discrimination.

source_file: 9742978_2024_CMDS Residential, LLC v. Mayor and City Council Of Baltimore_mdd
case_name: CMDS Residential, LLC v. Mayor and City Council of Baltimore
accommodation_description: Permit approval to operate a residential substance-abuse treatment facility for persons with disabilities, framed as a reasonable accommodation from zoning requirements rather than an individual tenant accommodation
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for the City on the estoppel claim because CMDS failed to establish reliance on the zoning verification letter and building permit, dismissed the judicial review claim under Burford abstention, and denied both parties' motions on the discrimination claims because genuine disputes of material fact exist regarding whether the City denied the permit based on discriminatory animus toward persons with substance use disorders.
brief_summary: CMDS Residential, LLC sued Baltimore City after the City denied its permit to operate a residential substance-abuse treatment facility, claiming the denial violated the ADA, Rehabilitation Act, Fair Housing Act, and constitutional protections for persons with disabilities. The court granted summary judgment for the City on the estoppel claim (finding CMDS failed to prove reliance), dismissed the state-law judicial review claim under Burford abstention, but allowed the federal disability discrimination and equal protection claims to proceed because genuine factual disputes exist regarding whether community opposition was based on discriminatory animus toward the facility's future patients.
key_cases_cited: City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, Inc., 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Texas Dept. of Housing & Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Olmstead v. L.C., 527 U.S. 581 (1999)
New Orleans Pub. Serv., Inc. v. Council of City of New Orleans, 491 U.S. 350 (1989)
Permanent Financial Corp. v. Montgomery County, 308 Md. 239 (1986)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exemption from the discontinuation or change provision of the zoning code to permit operation of a 104-bed residential substance-abuse treatment facility without requiring City Council ordinance approval
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted summary judgment on the reasonable modification claim, finding that CMDS failed to demonstrate that the application of the discontinuation or change provision disadvantaged prospective clients because of their disabilities, and that a variance from the change provision was not necessary because CMDS could operate a 38-bed facility by right under either interpretation of the code.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether the City's denial of the U&O permit was partially motivated by discriminatory animus against individuals with substance use disorders. The court applied the Arlington Heights factors and concluded that Dorsey's acknowledgment of anticipated discriminatory community opposition as a reason for his inquiries to DHCD, combined with the City's unusual reversal of the zoning verification letter and the BMZA's consideration of community opposition, created disputed material facts precluding summary judgment on the FHA intentional discrimination claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II ADA reasonable modification claim (28 C.F.R. § 35.130(b)(7)(i)); Section 504 Rehabilitation Act claim (29 U.S.C. § 794(a)); Equal Protection Clause (Fourteenth Amendment); Substantive Due Process (Fourteenth Amendment); Equitable Estoppel (state law); Judicial Review of Administrative Action (state law)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted summary judgment on the ADA Title II reasonable modification claim on the same grounds as the FHA claim. The court granted summary judgment on the Section 504 Rehabilitation Act claim because CMDS failed to establish that discrimination was the sole motivating factor for the City's actions, as required by the 'solely by reason of' standard. The court granted summary judgment on the substantive due process claim, finding that a plausible but erroneous interpretation of a local ordinance does not constitute 'conscience shocking' state action. The court granted summary judgment on the equitable estoppel claim, finding that the zoning verification letter was not binding and that the change provision was not ambiguously applied consistently over time. The court abstained from the judicial review claim under the Burford doctrine, dismissing it without prejudice.

source_file: 9743091_2024_Estate of DaMon R. Fisher v. City of Annapolis_mdd
case_name: Estate of DaMon R. Fisher, et al. v. City of Annapolis, et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request was made; this is a disparate impact challenge to the City's policy exempting HACA properties from licensing and inspection requirements.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiffs' motions for partial summary judgment because the statistical evidence comparing HACA property populations to the general City population used an improper comparator; the proper comparison should be between HACA renters and all City renters, and additional discovery is needed to establish proximate cause for the certified class period.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs, including the Estate of DaMon R. Fisher and a certified class of HACA tenants, sued the City of Annapolis alleging that the City's policy of exempting Housing Authority properties from rental licensing and inspection requirements violated the Fair Housing Act by disproportionately affecting Black residents who comprise over 90% of HACA populations. The court denied plaintiffs' motions for partial summary judgment, finding that while statistical evidence demonstrated significant racial disparity, the expert analysis used an improper comparator population and insufficient evidence linked the non-enforcement policy to specific harms during the class period, warranting additional discovery.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dept. of Housing & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Bank of Am. Corp. v. City of Miami, 581 U.S. 189 (2017)
Reyes v. Waples Mobile Home Park Ltd. P'ship, 903 F.3d 415 (4th Cir. 2018)
Sw. Fair Hous. Council, Inc. v. Maricopa Domestic Water Improvement Dist., 17 F.4th 950 (9th Cir. 2021)
White v. City of Annapolis, 439 F. Supp. 3d 522 (D. Md. 2020)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied plaintiffs' motion for summary judgment on their disparate impact claim challenging the City's non-enforcement policy for HACA properties. The court found the statistical disparity evidence (HACA properties >90% Black vs. City 25.7% Black) facially sufficient but held that the proper comparator population should be rental households in the City, not the general population. The court also found insufficient evidence of harm during the class period (May 2019–May 2021), as the only detailed violation reports were from 2016 inspections. The court did not reach steps two and three of the disparate impact analysis and denied the motion without prejudice to renewal after additional discovery.

case_name: Tamara Johnson, et al. v. City of Annapolis
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED - The case challenges the City's non-enforcement policy of HACA property inspections as racially discriminatory under disparate impact theory; the accommodation at issue is not a traditional reasonable accommodation but rather municipal enforcement of housing code requirements.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiffs' motions for partial summary judgment because they failed to establish a prima facie disparate impact case—their statistical analysis improperly compared HACA property populations to the general City population rather than to other rental households subject to the licensing policy, and they lacked sufficient evidence of harmful conditions during the class period (May 2019 to May 2021).
brief_summary: HACA residents and class members sued the City of Annapolis alleging the City's policy of exempting HACA public housing properties from rental licensing and inspection requirements violated the Fair Housing Act on a disparate impact theory. The court denied plaintiffs' motions for partial summary judgment, finding their statistical analysis compared the wrong populations and failed to establish sufficient evidence of harm during the relevant class period.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dept. of Housing & Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Reyes v. Waples Mobile Home Park Ltd. P'ship, 903 F.3d 415 (4th Cir. 2018)
Bank of Am. Corp. v. City of Miami, 581 U.S. 189 (2017)
Sw. Fair Hous. Council, Inc. v. Maricopa Domestic Water Improvement Dist., 17 F.4th 950 (9th Cir. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exemption of HACA public housing properties from City licensing and inspection requirements applicable to all other rental properties
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied plaintiffs' motion for partial summary judgment on disparate impact claim because plaintiffs failed to establish the proper statistical comparator population (rental units in City vs. HACA rental units), failed to establish robust causal connection between non-enforcement policy and disparate impact, and failed to establish proximate causation of alleged harm with sufficient evidence for the certified class period (May 2019-May 2021). Court found deficiencies in proof at step one of the three-step disparate impact framework and determined additional discovery was necessary.

case_name: Deborah Morris, et al. v. Memorial Development Partners, LP, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged defendants failed to provide critical services to elderly and disabled residents, including failing to maintain functioning elevators, failing to install a stairway chair lift, and failing to provide support services and dispute resolution procedures for disabled tenants.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss—rejecting both the two-dismissal rule and failure-to-prosecute arguments—but granted the motion for a more definite statement, ordering plaintiffs to file a second amended complaint within 28 days that clearly identifies the jurisdictional basis, applicable statutes, and factual support for each claim.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Deborah Morris and Arnell Mason sued their Baltimore apartment complex's owner, developer, and management company alleging widespread habitability deficiencies and failure to provide critical services to elderly and disabled residents, citing the Fair Housing Act and ADA among other statutes. Defendants moved to dismiss based on the two-dismissal rule and failure to prosecute, or alternatively for a more definite statement. The court denied outright dismissal, finding the two-dismissal rule inapplicable because the Maryland case was dismissed by court order (not voluntarily) and finding no bad faith failure to prosecute, but granted the motion for a more definite statement because the amended complaint was excessively long, disorganized, and insufficiently clear as to the legal and jurisdictional basis for each claim.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
ASX Inv. Corp. v. Newton, 183 F.3d 1265 (11th Cir. 1999)
Manning v. S.C. Dep’t of Highway and Pub. Transp., 914 F.2d 44 (4th Cir. 1990)
Loper ex rel. C.D. v. Howard Cnty. Pub. Sch. Sys., 2021 WL 689963 (D. Md. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to provide critical services to elderly and disabled people, including malfunctioning elevators and no stairway chair lift or support services
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 12(e) — Motion for More Definite Statement
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found the amended complaint failed to clearly identify which statutes/legal principles underlie the claims and failed to reasonably tie factual allegations to those statutes. The complaint cited the Fair Housing Act sporadically without clearly indicating how the allegations plausibly demonstrate liability under any specific legal theory. The court granted the motion for a more definite statement and required plaintiffs to amend again, leaving the claim pending rather than dismissed on the merits.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination and unfair practices based on disability status
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 12(e) — Motion for More Definite Statement
fha_claims.reasoning: Count II asserted a claim for discrimination and unfair practices but indiscriminately cited multiple federal statutes (Fair Housing Act, ADA, Consumer Protection Procedures Act, Freedom of Information Act) without clarifying which statute provided the basis for the claim or how the allegations plausibly demonstrated intentional discrimination. The court required clarification and amendment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Elderly and Adult Disabled Exploitation and Neglect; Breach of warranty of habitability; Negligence; violations of Americans with Disabilities Act, Consumer Protection Procedures Act, Freedom of Information Act, Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, and various state and local housing regulations
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 12(e) — Motion for More Definite Statement
fha_claims.reasoning: The amended complaint cited numerous federal, state, and local statutes and regulations sporadically without clearly indicating which served as the basis for each claim or how the allegations supported liability. Count III asserted elderly and disabled exploitation without indicating the legal basis; Count V conflated breach of warranty of habitability and negligence. The court required plaintiffs to clearly identify the statutes/legal principles underlying each claim and tie factual allegations to those principles.

source_file: 9743192_2024_CASA de Maryland, Inc. v. Arbor Realty Trust, Inc._mdd
case_name: CASA de Maryland, Inc. v. Arbor Realty Trust, Inc.
accommodation_description: This is a housing conditions class action (poor maintenance and repair), not a disability accommodation case; the surviving claims were breach of contract and breach of implied warranty of habitability under state law, not reasonable accommodation claims.
key_holding: The court granted final approval of the $3 million class settlement, approved $900,000 in attorneys' fees (30% of the fund), $78,965.18 in litigation expenses, $27,701 in settlement administration costs, and $7,500 incentive payments to each of seven named plaintiffs, finding the settlement fair, reasonable, and adequate.
brief_summary: CASA de Maryland and seven named tenants sued Bedford United, LLC, Victoria United, LLC, and related parties alleging that defendants failed to maintain and repair apartments at Bedford Station and Victoria Station complexes, initially bringing Fair Housing Act and state law claims. After the court dismissed the FHA claims, the parties reached a $3 million settlement covering current and former tenants who resided at the properties between July 2018 and May 2022, and the court granted final approval of the settlement, attorneys' fees, expenses, and incentive payments.
key_cases_cited: Amchem Prod., Inc. v. Windsor, 521 U.S. 591 (1997)
Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. v. Dukes, 564 U.S. 338 (2011)
Graham v. Famous Dave's of Am., Inc., 2022 WL 17584274 (D. Md. 2022)
Singleton v. Domino's Pizza, LLC, 976 F. Supp. 2d 665 (D. Md. 2013)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act claims (dismissed on motion to dismiss); breach of contract and breach of implied warranty of habitability under Maryland law and Prince George's County Code § 13-153
fha_claims.reasoning: The parties settled all claims, including FHA claims that had been dismissed on motion to dismiss, for a $3 million settlement fund. The court approved the settlement as fair, reasonable, and adequate after a fairness hearing, finding that the settlement represented a favorable result given the genuine disputes regarding defendants' liability and the risks of continued litigation.

source_file: 9743203_2024_CMDS Residential, LLC v. Mayor and City Council Of Baltimore_mdd
case_name: CMDS Residential, LLC v. Mayor and City Council of Baltimore
accommodation_description: CMDS sought to operate a residential substance-abuse treatment facility at 6040 Harford Road, which was denied when the city required City Council approval after community opposition.
key_holding: The court denied the City's motion for reconsideration, adhering to its prior ruling that the 'motivating factor' causation standard applies to ADA Title II and FHA claims, and finding that Gentry did not abrogate Baird's controlling precedent.
brief_summary: CMDS Residential, LLC sued the City of Baltimore after the city denied its application for a use and occupancy permit to open a residential substance-abuse treatment facility, claiming the denial was motivated by discriminatory community opposition based on stereotypes about people with substance use disorders. The court denied the City's motion for reconsideration, adhering to its prior ruling that the 'motivating factor' causation standard governs ADA Title II and FHA claims and that Gentry v. E.W. Partners Club Management Co. did not abrogate Baird's controlling precedent establishing that standard.
key_cases_cited: Baird ex rel. Baird v. Rose, 192 F.3d 462 (4th Cir. 1999)
Gentry v. E.W. Partners Club Mgmt. Co., 816 F.3d 228 (4th Cir. 2016)
Wicomico Nursing Home v. Padilla, 910 F.3d 739 (4th Cir. 2018)
Thomas v. The Salvation Army, 841 F.3d 632 (4th Cir. 2016)
Neal v. East Carolina University, 53 F.4th 130 (4th Cir. 2022)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Use and occupancy permit for residential substance-abuse treatment facility
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied summary judgment on the FHA claim, finding that a jury could conclude that consideration of the community's discriminatory opposition to the substance-abuse treatment facility was a motivating factor in the City's decision to deny the U&O permit. The court applied the 'motivating factor' causation standard under Baird v. Rose, which the Fourth Circuit has consistently reaffirmed for ADA Title II and FHA claims post-Gentry.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II, Rehabilitation Act, Equal Protection Clause
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied summary judgment on the ADA Title II claim under the 'motivating factor' standard, consistent with Baird. The court granted summary judgment on the Rehabilitation Act claim because CMDS's evidence was insufficient to establish that discriminatory animus was the sole motivator as required by the RA's stricter causation standard. The court denied summary judgment on the equal protection claim because the City failed to explain why it granted the prior owner a U&O permit without strict Code compliance but denied CMDS's application.

case_name: Iguade v. First Home Mortgage Corporation
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation requested; this is a race discrimination claim in mortgage lending under ECOA and FHA § 3605.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' race discrimination claims under ECOA and FHA because plaintiffs failed to allege sufficient facts showing intentional race-based discrimination or that similarly situated non-minority applicants received more favorable treatment, and also failed to identify a neutral policy causing disparate impact.
brief_summary: Black plaintiffs Oseghae and Maurice Iguade sued First Home Mortgage Corporation alleging race discrimination under ECOA and FHA when their mortgage loan application to purchase a home in Baltimore, Maryland was denied. The court granted First Home's motion to dismiss, finding plaintiffs failed to state plausible discrimination claims because they did not allege facts showing discriminatory intent, establish they were qualified for the loan, identify similarly situated non-minority applicants treated more favorably, or identify a neutral policy causing disparate impact.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Tex. Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Cmtys. Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Reyes v. Waples Mob. Home Park Ltd. P'ship, 903 F.3d 415 (4th Cir. 2018)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to allege sufficient facts showing intentional race-based discrimination. The complaint lacks any allegation that race was raised during the mortgage application process or that First Home announced, admitted, or unmistakably indicated that race was a determining factor. The denial was based on uncontested property deficiencies and failure to meet HUD requirements, not discriminatory intent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to identify any neutral First Home policy or practice that had a disparate impact on a protected group. The complaint contained only conclusory allegations about negative impact without identifying a specific policy or demonstrating disproportionate effect on minorities, which is required to state a plausible disparate impact claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA), 15 U.S.C. § 1691 et seq. — race discrimination and source of income discrimination claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to allege sufficient facts under ECOA to show intentional race-based discrimination or to establish a prima facie case. Plaintiffs did not allege they were qualified for the loan (property had unremediable deficiencies) and did not allege similarly situated non-minority applicants received more favorable treatment. Count II (source of income) was conceded by plaintiffs to be deficient as ECOA only prohibits source of income discrimination based on public assistance, which plaintiffs did not allege.

case_name: Denise Venero, et al. v. Prince George's County Maryland
accommodation_description: Request to keep two dogs (Bella and Mimi) classified as emotional support animals without enforcement of the County's Pit Bull Ordinance
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' reasonable accommodation claim as moot because the County returned the dogs to plaintiffs and the administrative commission determined the dogs are not Pit Bull Terriers subject to the ordinance.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Denise Venero and others sued Prince George's County Maryland challenging the County's Pit Bull Ordinance and seeking to keep their dogs (Bella and Mimi), classified as emotional support animals, without enforcement of the ordinance. The court granted the County's motion to dismiss, finding plaintiffs lacked standing because their dogs were returned and the Commission determined the dogs are not Pit Bull Terriers, and further finding the reasonable accommodation claim moot.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Lujan v. Def. of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)
Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins, 578 U.S. 330 (2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged that the Pit Bull Ordinance disproportionately impacts minorities due to the population of Prince George's County by forcing owners to be without their dogs for significant periods of time.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed for lack of standing because plaintiffs failed to demonstrate an injury in fact. The dogs were returned to plaintiffs on July 24, 2022, and the County's Animal Control Commission determined the dogs were not Pit Bull Terriers, eliminating any concrete, particularized injury traceable to the defendants.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged that defendants failed to accommodate their emotional support animals (Bella and Mimi) by enforcing the Pit Bull Ordinance and seizing the dogs, forcing plaintiffs to be without their dogs for a significant period of time.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the reasonable accommodation claim for lack of standing and mootness. The dogs were returned to plaintiffs, and the Commission determined they were not subject to the Pit Bull Ordinance, eliminating the alleged injury of being forced to be without the emotional support animals.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 1983 claims (Fourteenth Amendment Procedural Due Process, Equal Protection, Fourth Amendment Unreasonable Seizure), Section 1983 Monell claims, and Maryland state law claims (Rule 7-401 through 7-403).
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA claims were dismissed for lack of standing and mootness. Plaintiffs failed to demonstrate a concrete, particularized injury in fact because the dogs were returned and the administrative process resulted in a favorable determination that the dogs were not Pit Bull Terriers subject to the ordinance.

case_name: Karen Lundregan v. Housing Opportunities Commission
accommodation_description: Request for reinstatement of Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher as reasonable accommodation for mental health disabilities (PTSD, Borderline Personality Disorder) following alleged improper termination.
key_holding: The court found genuine disputes of material fact exist as to whether HOC violated the FHA by improperly determining, without objective evidence and based only on unverified allegations from a biased former landlord, that plaintiff posed a direct threat, and by attaching unduly invasive conditions to the accommodation approval, thereby delaying restoration of her voucher for several months.
brief_summary: Karen Lundregan, a disabled tenant with PTSD and Borderline Personality Disorder, sued the Housing Opportunities Commission of Montgomery County and employee Ethan Cohen alleging they violated the Fair Housing Act by improperly delaying or denying her reasonable accommodation request to reinstate her Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher for approximately five months (April-September 2018) without sufficient evidence and without providing her a hearing. The court denied both parties' cross-motions for summary judgment, finding genuine disputes of material fact remain as to whether defendants relied improperly on unverified allegations from a biased landlord without conducting an individualized assessment before concluding plaintiff posed a direct threat, and whether the delay in reinstating her voucher constituted constructive denial of her accommodation request.
key_cases_cited: Corey v. Secretary, HUD ex rel. Walker, 719 F.3d 322 (4th Cir. 2013)
Department of Housing and Urban Development and the DOJ, Reasonable Accommodations Under the Fair Housing Act (2004)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reinstatement and extension of Housing Choice Voucher for mental and emotional disabilities (PTSD and Borderline Personality Disorder); request for accommodation to restore voucher to allow plaintiff to find new home
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether defendants properly granted the reasonable accommodation, whether the delay in reinstatement constituted denial, and whether defendants improperly imposed unduly invasive medical documentation requirements and conditions on continued treatment. Court concluded a trier of fact could reasonably find defendants violated FHA § 3604(f)(2) by denying or delaying the accommodation based on insufficient evidence and without proper interactive process.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 due process claim under Fourteenth Amendment; claim that defendants terminated housing voucher without final hearing and opportunity to confront and cross-examine witnesses
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether defendants actually terminated plaintiff's voucher, whether proper due process procedures were followed under Goldberg v. Kelly, and whether defendants violated plaintiff's Fourteenth Amendment rights by failing to provide hearing before termination became effective. Court noted defendants' inconsistent positions on whether voucher was terminated versus automatically expired.

source_file: 9743469_2024_Clark v. Council of Unit Owners of the 100 Harborview Drive Condominium_mdd
case_name: Dr. Paul C. Clark, Sr., et al. v. Council of Unit Owners of the 100 Harborview Drive Condominium Association
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege the defendant HOA took retaliatory actions (removal of possessions, imposition of unauthorized fees, publication of litigation updates) in response to plaintiffs' prior exercise of Fair Housing Act rights.
key_holding: The court granted in part and denied in part Plaintiffs' Motion for Reconsideration, ordering Defendant to search current Board Members' private email accounts for any responsive communications to John Cochran from 2019-21 regarding Plaintiffs, while also requiring production of documents the court determined were not protected by attorney-client privilege or work product.
brief_summary: Dr. Paul Clark and family sued the 100 Harborview Drive Condominium Association alleging the HOA retaliated against them for exercising Fair Housing Act rights in connection with disputes over unit conditions and remediation. This opinion addresses discovery disputes regarding search of Board Members' private email accounts and sufficiency of Defendant's privilege log. The court ordered Defendant to conduct a limited search of current Board Members' private emails for responsive communications and to produce documents the court found were not protected by attorney-client privilege or work product.
key_cases_cited: Victor Stanley, Inc. v. Creative Pipe, Inc., 250 F.R.D. 251 (D. Md. 2008)
Goodman v. Praxair Servs., Inc., 632 F. Supp. 2d 494 (D. Md. 2009)
TradeShift, Inc. v. BuyerQuest, Inc., No. 20-cv-01294-RS, 2021 WL 1586283 (N.D. Cal. Apr. 23, 2021)
Royal Park Invs. SA/NV v. Deutsche Bank Nat'l Tr. Co., No. 14-CV-4394-AJN-BCM, 2016 WL 5408171 (S.D.N.Y. Sept. 27, 2016)
Miniace v. Pac. Mar. Ass'n, No. C 04-03506 SI, 2006 WL 335389 (N.D. Cal. Feb. 13, 2006)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Removal of personal possessions from unit; charging of administrative fees not allowed under By-Laws; publication of Litigation Update stating failure to pay assessments
fha_claims.reasoning: This is a discovery dispute regarding email production and privilege log sufficiency in a retaliation case that survived a motion to dismiss. The court has not reached the merits of the retaliation claim itself; it is managing discovery to develop the factual record. The case remains pending on the underlying FHA retaliation allegations.

case_name: Morris v. Memorial Development Partners, LP
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs, elderly/disabled tenants, alleged various discriminatory housing practices but did not request a specific reasonable accommodation; court analyzed claims under discriminatory intent framework rather than accommodation analysis.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' FHA claims because they failed to plausibly allege discriminatory intent or disparate impact, instead presenting only conclusory complaints about housing conditions, differential amenities, and business practices without tying them to discrimination based on a protected class.
brief_summary: Deborah Morris and Arnell Mason, pro se elderly/disabled tenants at Linden Park Apartments in Baltimore, sued their landlord and property management company alleging Fair Housing Act violations, ADA claims, and RICO claims based on various housing conditions and business practices. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss with prejudice, finding plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege any federal cause of action because their conclusory allegations did not demonstrate discriminatory intent or disparate impact based on a protected class.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 554 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Brown v. Board of Education, 347 U.S. 483 (1954)
Jones v. Blue Ocean Realty LLC, 2023 WL 3074642 (D. Md. Apr. 25, 2023)
Hardaway v. Equity Residential Mgmt., LLC, 2016 WL 3957648 (D. Md. July 22, 2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege discriminatory intent or differential treatment based on a protected class. Allegations regarding source of income discrimination, differential treatment in lease terms, and other business practices either do not implicate protected statuses under the FHA or are too conclusory to state a plausible claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to establish that they engaged in a protected activity under the FHA. Entering another tenant's unit without permission and reporting assistance with cleaning do not constitute protected activities, and plaintiffs failed to allege discriminatory intent motivating the eviction notice.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to maintain premises; alleged mold and water damage in units
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege that defendants' alleged failure to cure mold issues was motivated by discriminatory intent or pursuant to a policy causing disparate impact on a protected group. Allegations were conclusory and framed primarily as violations of state housing codes rather than federal fair housing law.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III (elevator accessibility); Civil Rights Act §§ 1981, 1982 (racial discrimination); RICO 18 U.S.C. § 1962(c); False Claims Act 31 U.S.C. § 3729; Fair Debt Collection Practices Act
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA claims dismissed for lack of third-party standing and failure to allege facts supporting non-compliance. §§ 1981, 1982 claims dismissed for failure to allege discriminatory conduct based on race. RICO claim dismissed for failure to allege predicate criminal acts with particularity and failure to allege unlawful debt as defined by statute. FCA claim dismissed for failure to allege materiality and plead with particularity. FDCPA claim dismissed because property management company is not a debt collector under the statute.

case_name: Travis R. Jones v. Blue Ocean Realty, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff's Amended Complaint references failure to provide reasonable accommodations in violation of 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(1), but no specific accommodation request is clearly identified in the opinion; the complaint mentions Plaintiff requested a walk-through inspection given his disability.
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA housing discrimination claims were dismissed as time-barred because they were filed nearly eleven months after the two-year statute of limitations expired, and neither equitable tolling based on COVID-19 nor the continuing violation doctrine applied to excuse the late filing.
brief_summary: Travis R. Jones, a physically disabled individual, sued Blue Ocean Realty, LLC and Oaklee Village Baltimore, LLC alleging they refused to rent him an apartment and failed to provide reasonable accommodations in violation of the FHA. The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss, finding the action was time-barred because it was filed eleven months after the two-year statute of limitations expired, with no basis for equitable tolling or the continuing violation doctrine.
key_cases_cited: Rouse v. Lee, 339 F.3d 238 (4th Cir. 2003)
Cruz v. Maypa, 773 F.3d 138 (4th Cir. 2014)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Walk-through inspection of apartment unit prior to move-in, requested due to plaintiff's physical disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's FHA claims were time-barred under 42 U.S.C. § 3613(a)(1)(A), which provides a two-year statute of limitations. The alleged discriminatory conduct occurred on October 5, 2020, with final contact on November 24, 2020, making the deadline November 24, 2022. Plaintiff filed suit on October 6, 2023, nearly eleven months late. Equitable tolling was unavailable because plaintiff failed to explain how the COVID-19 pandemic prevented timely filing, and the continuing violation doctrine did not apply because plaintiff alleged no discriminatory actions after November 24, 2020.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to rent apartment based on alleged failure to meet income requirements
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's FHA refusal-to-rent claim was time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations in 42 U.S.C. § 3613(a)(1)(A). The alleged discriminatory conduct occurred on October 5, 2020, with final contact on November 24, 2020, making the deadline November 24, 2022. Plaintiff filed suit on October 6, 2023, nearly eleven months late. Equitable tolling and the continuing violation doctrine were both unavailable.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reassignment to different supervisor; leave without pay; accommodation request processing and documentation requirements
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's interference claim under the Rehabilitation Act (29 U.S.C. § 794) failed on summary judgment because: (1) the reassignment request was not a protected accommodation request as it lacked a logical bridge connecting the disability to the requested relief—it was motivated by supervisor conflict, not disability-related need; (2) even if protected, plaintiff failed to generate a genuine dispute of material fact regarding whether defendant intimidated or interfered with plaintiff's rights; and (3) plaintiff failed to establish discriminatory intent, as the delay in processing the request and other alleged actions were not motivated by disability discrimination.

case_name: Bing Chen, et al. v. Commodore Management Company, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request was made; case involves claims of racial discrimination by Chinese immigrant tenants against their landlord.
key_holding: Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege that Defendants discriminated against them on the basis of race or national origin under disparate-treatment or disparate-impact theories, and failed to state a plausible FHA retaliation claim due to insufficient allegations regarding protected activity, knowledge, and causal connection.
brief_summary: Chinese immigrant tenants sued their private landlord alleging racial discrimination in housing under the Fair Housing Act. The court granted the landlord's motion to dismiss, finding the plaintiffs failed to allege sufficient facts to support claims of disparate treatment, disparate impact, or retaliation under the FHA.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Texas Dept. of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Reyes v. Waples Mobile Home Park Ltd. P'ship, 903 F.3d 415 (4th Cir. 2018)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege that defendants treated them differently than other tenants because of their race or national origin. The complaint contains only speculative conclusions assigning racial animus without factual support showing a nexus between defendants' conduct and plaintiffs' protected status.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to allege facts supporting a disparate impact theory, including statistical or anecdotal evidence of a disproportionately adverse effect on minorities, legitimate rationale, or a robust causal connection between defendants' actions and the disparate impact.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege the required elements of FHA retaliation: no facts showing defendants knew of the 2016 complaint, and the five-year temporal gap between the protected activity and the alleged adverse actions (rent lawsuits in 2022-2023) is too remote to support a plausible causal connection.

case_name: Romane Canty-Massey v. Vantage Management, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested transfer to a different apartment unit and ultimately to a subsidized apartment due to her disabilities including cardiomyopathy, hypertension, and anxiety disorder.
key_holding: Vantage satisfied its reasonable accommodation obligation by offering comparable units at comparable prices; the FHA does not require landlords to accommodate changes in a tenant's financial status or roommate situation.
brief_summary: Romane Canty-Massey, an African American woman with disabilities, sued Vantage Management Inc. alleging race, sex, and disability discrimination under the FHA based on Vantage's failure to address neighbor harassment, denial of rental office access, and refusal to accommodate her disability-related transfer request. The court granted Vantage's motion to dismiss the disability accommodation and retaliation claims but denied it as to the race and sex discrimination claims, finding plausible allegations that Vantage treated white tenants more favorably.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Tex. Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities, 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff plausibly alleged disparate treatment based on race and sex in the provision of services and facilities (access to rental office, complaint resolution) under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(b). Court applied Iqbal/Twombly standard and found allegations sufficient to survive motion to dismiss under liberal pro se pleading standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested transfer to a subsidized apartment due to changed financial circumstances after her son moved out. Defendant offered comparable-priced units but refused subsidized transfer.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied FHA reasonable accommodation standard and found that defendant satisfied its obligation by offering units comparably priced to plaintiff's existing unit. FHA does not require accommodation for changes in financial status or roommate status; defendant's offer of comparable units more than satisfied the requirement to provide reasonable accommodation allowing equal use and enjoyment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts showing discriminatory animus based on disability status.
