fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act and Section 1983 claims alleged in the Original Action (Case 4:22-CV-00606 SEP), dismissed by Judge Pitlyk for failure to state a claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Judge Pitlyk dismissed the Original Action's federal claims (Fair Housing Act and Section 1983) for failure to state a claim upon which relief can be granted under Rule 12(b)(6). The present opinion addresses only the jurisdictional question of removal and remand, not the merits of the FHA claims themselves.

source_file: 9771854_2023_Richardson v. Cardinal Ritter Institute Residential Services Corporation_moed
case_name: Genena V. Richardson v. Cardinal Ritter Residential Services
accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought housing at defendant's Section 8 apartment complex but was denied because her mental illness did not qualify as a 'correct disability' under defendant's criteria requiring mobility, hearing, or visual impairments.
key_holding: The court found plaintiff's ADA Title II and Title III claims deficient for failing to allege sufficient facts, and noted plaintiff's complaint does not clearly articulate an FHA claim despite references to the Fair Housing Act in her attachment.
brief_summary: Self-represented plaintiff Genena V. Richardson filed suit against Cardinal Ritter Residential Services alleging she was denied housing at a Section 8 apartment complex because of her disability (mental illness) and her race. The court screened the amended complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2) and found the ADA Title II and Title III claims deficient for failure to allege sufficient facts; the court also noted the complaint did not clearly articulate an FHA claim and gave plaintiff leave to file a second amended complaint.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Koster v. Young Men's Christian Ass'n of Greater St. Louis, 855 F.3d 908 (8th Cir. 2017)
Stegar v. Franco, Inc., 228 F.3d 889 (8th Cir. 2000)
Randolph v. Rodgers, 170 F.3d 850 (8th Cir. 1999)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Housing denial based on disability; plaintiff alleged she was denied housing because she did not have the 'correct disability' (mobility, hearing, or vision impairment) and instead has a serious mental illness. Plaintiff also alleged discrimination based on race as a black American or person of color.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to state a claim under Title II or Title III of the ADA. The complaint lacked the 'who, what, when and where' of the alleged discrimination and contained only conclusory statements. The court granted plaintiff one final opportunity to amend her complaint to clarify whether she was asserting FHA claims, disability discrimination claims, race discrimination claims, or some combination thereof, and to provide non-conclusory factual support for each allegation.

source_file: 9772107_2023_Richardson v. Cardinal Ritter Institute Residential Services Corporation_moed
case_name: Richardson v. Cardinal Ritter Institute Residential Services Corporation
race_if_mentioned: Black American or person of color
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges she was denied housing at a Section 8 residential facility due to her schizophrenia (mental disability), though the complaint does not specify a requested accommodation.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA racial discrimination claim for failure to allege sufficient factual content showing discrimination based on race, but allowed plaintiff's disability discrimination claim under both the FHA and Title II of the ADA to proceed past initial review, finding she sufficiently alleged denial of housing due to her mental impairment (schizophrenia).
brief_summary: Self-represented plaintiff Gennena V. Richardson sued Cardinal Ritter Institute Residential Services Corporation, a Section 8 housing facility operator, alleging she was denied housing on May 4, 2021, because of her schizophrenia and her status as a Black American. The court dismissed her FHA racial discrimination claim for failing to allege sufficient factual content showing how she was discriminated against based on race, but allowed her disability discrimination claim under both the FHA and Title II of the ADA to proceed past initial review under 28 U.S.C. § 1915, finding she adequately alleged she was qualified for housing but denied solely due to her mental disability.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Gallagher v. Magner, 619 F.3d 823 (8th Cir. 2010)
Radecki v. Joura, 114 F.3d 115 (8th Cir. 1997)
Randolph v. Rodgers, 170 F.3d 850 (8th Cir. 1999)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Housing denial based on race (black American/person of color)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege any factual information showing she was treated differently due to her race. The complaint merely asserts a conclusory statement of discrimination without the 'who, what, when and where' of what happened, and the defendant's own stated reason for denial was disability-based, not race-based.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Housing denial based on disability (mental illness/schizophrenia); plaintiff was denied housing because she was not mobility impaired, hearing impaired, or vision impaired
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff sufficiently alleged at the pleading stage that she has schizophrenia, was qualified for housing at defendant's facility, and was denied housing because of her disability. The court allowed the disability discrimination claim to proceed under the FHA, finding the allegations plausible enough to survive § 1915 screening.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act claim for housing denial based on mental disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff sufficiently alleged the three elements of a Title II ADA prima facie claim: she is a person with a disability (schizophrenia), was otherwise qualified for housing, and was excluded due to disability discrimination. The claim survives § 1915 screening and service of process was ordered.

case_name: Catherine Christine McKee v. Busey Bank
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, an 88-year-old Black woman, alleges Busey Bank discriminated against her in mortgage lending terms and foreclosure threats based on her race and age.
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA claims fail because she has not alleged facts showing she was treated differently due to her race or age; her complaints about late fees and payment increases due to escrow shortages and nonpayment are not discriminatory conduct but rather standard loan collection practices.
brief_summary: Catherine McKee, an 88-year-old Black homeowner in Missouri, sued Busey Bank alleging race and age discrimination in mortgage lending under the Fair Housing Act. The court dismissed her complaint on initial review for failure to state a claim because she failed to allege facts causally connecting her race or age to any discriminatory conduct, as her complaints about late fees and payment increases stemmed from her own nonpayment and escrow deficiencies rather than discriminatory treatment.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts showing she was treated differently due to her race or age, and did not causally connect her protected class status to any alleged discriminatory conduct by Busey Bank. The complaint contains only conclusory allegations of discrimination without factual support.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, 42 U.S.C. § 1983 due process/equal protection, Missouri state law fraud
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege that Busey receives federal funding or that the mortgage was part of a federally-funded program (Title VI); failed to allege Busey acted under color of state law (§ 1983); and failed to plead fraud with the particularity required by Rule 9(b), including names of persons making misrepresentations, their authority, what was said, and when.

source_file: 9773027_2023_Richardson v. Cardinal Ritter Institute Residential Services Corporation_moed
case_name: Gennena V. Richardson v. Cardinal Ritter Institute Residential Services Corporation
accommodation_description: Plaintiff generally alleges she required a necessary accommodation but the complaint does not specify a particular accommodation request; the core claim is that she was denied housing at a Section 8 facility because she lacks the facility's qualifying disability categories (vision, hearing, or mobility impairment).
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claim because her allegations suggest she was denied housing because she lacked a qualifying disability (vision, hearing, or mobility impairment) rather than because she had a disability, failing to state a plausible claim that she was discriminated against 'because of' a handicap under § 3604(f).
brief_summary: Gennena Richardson, a pro se plaintiff with schizophrenia, sued Cardinal Ritter Institute Residential Services Corporation alleging she was denied Section 8 housing in May 2021 because she has a mental health disability. The court granted defendant's motion to dismiss, finding the complaint failed to state a plausible FHA claim because plaintiff was informed she did not qualify for housing as she is not vision, hearing, or mobility impaired—the very allegations suggest denial because she lacked a qualifying disability rather than because she had one.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Housing eligibility based on disability status (mental health disorder vs. mobility, hearing, or vision impairment)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that she was denied housing because of her mental health disability. The complaint allegations instead suggest she was denied housing because she lacked the specific disabilities (mobility, hearing, or vision impairment) that Defendant's facility serves, not because she had a disability. This does not raise a reasonable inference of discrimination based on disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unspecified accommodation related to mental health disability in Section 8 housing facility
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's reference to a 'necessary accommodation' that Defendant refused to provide was conclusory and not supported by specific factual allegations. The complaint does not plausibly allege what accommodation was requested or why it was necessary, failing the Iqbal/Twombly pleading standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), 42 U.S.C. § 12132
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's Title II ADA claim fails because Defendant is a private entity, not a public entity as required under Title II. Additionally, the same pleading deficiency applies: Plaintiff failed to allege facts supporting discrimination based on her disability.

case_name: Sproaps v. Brown
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged disparate treatment based on sexual orientation, including refusal to make repairs and eviction threats, rather than a request for disability accommodation.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claim because the only evidence of discrimination was a stray remark about plaintiff's 'lover boy' that was unrelated to any discriminatory conduct, and the evidence showed repairs were delayed due to a financial dispute rather than plaintiff's sexual orientation.
brief_summary: Self-represented plaintiff Marriell Sproaps sued his former property manager Kevin Brown alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on sexual orientation discrimination, claiming Brown refused to repair his vandalized apartment and threatened eviction because of plaintiff's same-sex partner. The court dismissed the complaint finding plaintiff failed to state a plausible discrimination claim because the only evidence was a stray remark unrelated to any discriminatory policy or action, and the evidence showed repairs were delayed due to a financial dispute over responsibility for damage.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Gallagher v. Magner, 619 F.3d 823 (8th Cir. 2010)
Radecki v. Joura, 114 F.3d 115 (8th Cir. 1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges discrimination in terms and conditions of rental and repair services based on sexual orientation, not a request for reasonable accommodation.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff failed to plead a plausible claim of sex/sexual orientation discrimination under the FHA. The only evidence of discriminatory animus was a stray remark about plaintiff's 'lover boy' unconnected to the actual decision to delay repairs, which was motivated by a financial dispute over who was responsible for damage costs. Plaintiff provided no comparative evidence that other tenants received faster repairs or that the defendant's stated reason (unpaid money) was pretextual.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Missouri Human Rights Act, Missouri tort law (emotional distress), breach of lease and verbal agreements
fha_claims.reasoning: Court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims after dismissing the federal FHA claim, as the federal question claims were dismissed before trial and the court exercised its discretion under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3) to decline pendent state claims.

case_name: Ernesto Varela, et al. v. William Harold Hill, et al.
accommodation_description: Hispanic/Latino family alleges neighbor engaged in years-long campaign of racial harassment including slurs, threats, and false reports to authorities, forcing them to vacate their home and asserting interference with Fair Housing Act rights.
key_holding: Hill's motion to dismiss the § 1981 claim is granted because he was not in a contractual relationship with the Varelas, but his motion to dismiss the § 1982 and § 3617 claims is denied because the complaint adequately alleges race-based harassment that interfered with their property use and right to live in the neighborhood of their choice.
brief_summary: The Varelas, a Hispanic/Latino family who moved to Wildwood, Missouri so their deaf son could attend a special education school, sued their neighbor Hill alleging years of racial harassment including slurs, threats, and false reports to authorities that ultimately forced them to move. The Court dismissed their § 1981 claim against Hill (no contractual relationship) but allowed their § 1982 and § 3617 Fair Housing Act claims to proceed, finding the complaint adequately alleges race-based interference with their housing rights.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Monell v. Dep't of Soc. Servs., 436 U.S. 658 (1978)
Domino's Pizza, Inc. v. McDonald, 546 U.S. 470 (2006)
Watters v. Homeowners' Ass'n at Pres. at Bridgewater, 48 F.4th 779 (7th Cir. 2022)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Right to equal housing and freedom from race-based harassment and intimidation that interferes with enjoyment of leased property
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiffs plausibly alleged that defendant Hill interfered with their rights under § 3617 by engaging in a years-long campaign of race-based harassment, including racial slurs, threats, false reports, and trespass that effectively made their property unavailable and compelled them to move. The court applied the four-element § 3617 test and found all elements satisfied at the pleading stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1981 (right to make and enforce contracts); 42 U.S.C. § 1982 (right to lease property); 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (equal protection); Monell claim; common law negligent supervision; prosecutorial immunity; abuse of process
fha_claims.reasoning: Count I (§ 1981) dismissed because plaintiffs failed to allege any contractual relationship with defendant Hill; they had a rental contract with a third-party landlord, not Hill. Count VI (Monell) dismissed for failure to allege facts showing a municipal policy or custom of discrimination beyond the isolated incidents in this case. Count VIII (§ 1983 equal protection against prosecutor) dismissed due to absolute prosecutorial immunity. Count IX (abuse of process) dismissed because prosecutor's discretionary decision not to prosecute and alleged failure to provide updates were not unauthorized uses of process.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1982 (right to lease and hold property free from race-based interference)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiffs stated a plausible § 1982 claim by alleging membership in a protected class (Hispanic and Latino Americans), discriminatory intent (racial slurs, epithets, threats), and interference with property rights (harassment, trespass, false reports, and intimidation that compelled them to vacate). Court applied the three-element prima facie test and found all elements satisfied at the pleading stage.

case_name: Robert Ray Young v. Liz Hagar-Mace and Amy Copeland
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges termination from SPC housing voucher program constituted discrimination based on race and disability, but no specific accommodation request is at issue.
key_holding: Plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie case of discrimination because his allegations were conclusory and failed to create a reasonable inference of discriminatory intent, and even if he had made out a prima facie case, Defendants articulated legitimate non-discriminatory reasons for terminating his housing voucher.
brief_summary: Robert Ray Young, a homeless African-American man with mental and physical disabilities, sued Liz Hagar-Mace and Amy Copeland of the Missouri Department of Mental Health alleging discrimination based on race and disability in connection with his termination from the Shelter Plus Care housing voucher program. The court granted summary judgment for Defendants, finding Plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie case of intentional discrimination because his allegations were conclusory and failed to create an inference of discriminatory intent, and Defendants had legitimate non-discriminatory reasons for terminating his benefits.
key_cases_cited: Gallagher v. Magner, 619 F.3d 823 (8th Cir. 2010)
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242 (1986)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie case of discrimination under McDonnell Douglas. He offered only conclusory allegations and a vague reference to a 'racial reply' without specific factual allegations connecting any discriminatory animus to the decision to terminate his housing voucher. Defendants articulated a non-discriminatory reason: non-compliance with program requirements and lease violations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA claim for disability discrimination
fha_claims.reasoning: The court construed the amended complaint liberally to identify an ADA claim but declined to analyze it separately, noting that the FHA provides adequate protection for disability discrimination in housing and therefore considered only the FHA claim.

case_name: Kwanza Wilson v. KLD Properties, Ken Davis, Public Administrator; and Foster House
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges she was not given the same opportunity to live at her residence, though no specific accommodation request is discernible from the complaint.
key_holding: The complaint failed to state an FHA claim because plaintiff did not allege differential treatment based on a protected characteristic under § 3604, and the court could not identify any cognizable federal claim.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Kwanza Wilson filed suit against KLD Properties and others claiming she was not given the same opportunity to live at her residence, which the court construed as a Fair Housing Act claim. The court dismissed the action for failure to state a claim because the complaint did not allege discrimination based on any protected characteristic under 42 U.S.C. § 3604, and no other cognizable federal claim was identified.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges not being given the same opportunity to live at her residence, but does not specify the nature of the requested accommodation or relief.
fha_claims.disposition: 12(h)(3) — lack of subject matter jurisdiction / failure to state a claim
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiff failed to allege facts sufficient to state a plausible claim under the Fair Housing Act. Plaintiff alleged only that she was not given the same opportunity to live at her residence but did not allege discrimination based on any protected class under 42 U.S.C. § 3604 (race, color, religion, sex, familial status, or national origin). The complaint contained no reference to disability or reasonable accommodation, and the court could identify no other cognizable federal claim.

case_name: Theresa Marie Barbero v. Wilhoit Property Management, Inc.
accommodation_description: Request to allow ESA dog to go outside off leash during brutal ice and snow storm
key_holding: The FHA reasonable accommodation claim failed because Plaintiff did not allege how Defendant's refusal to allow her ESA dog off-leash during a snowstorm affected her ability to use and enjoy her dwelling.
brief_summary: Pro se Plaintiff Theresa Marie Barbero sued Wilhoit Property Management, Inc. alleging the landlord forced her to move out two weeks after moving in and refused to allow her ESA dog off-leash during a snowstorm, violating the FHA among other statutes. The Court granted Defendant's motion to dismiss, finding the FHA reasonable accommodation claim failed because Plaintiff did not allege how the denial affected her ability to use and enjoy her dwelling, and Plaintiff failed to identify her race or disability in her other claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Count 3 alleged violation of 42 U.S.C. § 3617 (coercion, intimidation, interference) but contained only statutory recitation and case law quotations with no factual allegations of how defendant intimidated or coerced plaintiff.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Count 4 alleged retaliation under 42 U.S.C. § 2000a-2 and § 3617 but failed to allege what protected action plaintiff took that caused retaliation or that she was entitled to return of deposit and prorated rent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to allow plaintiff's emotional support animal (ESA) dog to go outside off leash during a brutal ice and snow storm
fha_claims.reasoning: Count 13 alleged discrimination under 42 U.S.C. § 3604 based on refusal to allow ESA dog off leash during snowstorm, but plaintiff failed to allege how defendant's refusal affected her ability to use and enjoy her dwelling, failing to state a plausible claim for reasonable accommodation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1981 (Equal Rights Under the Law); 42 U.S.C. § 12132 (ADA Title II discrimination); 42 U.S.C. § 12101 (ADA Title II & III); 18 U.S.C. § 2255 (sex trafficking); 42 U.S.C. § 1437z-1 (civil money penalties); 42 U.S.C. § 1437f (public housing contracts); 24 C.F.R. § 965.651 (non-smokers rights); 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (civil rights deprivation); 42 U.S.C. § 1986 (action for neglect); 42 U.S.C. § 3613 (FHA enforcement); 42 U.S.C. § 3601 (policy declaration)
fha_claims.reasoning: Counts 1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, and 14 failed for various pleading deficiencies: Count 1 failed because plaintiff did not identify her race or allege race affected interactions; Count 2 failed because plaintiff did not identify disability or allege differential treatment based on disability; Count 5 failed because plaintiff did not identify her disability or how defendant discriminated; Count 6 based on inapplicable statute (sex trafficking); Counts 7 and 8 lack private right of action; Count 9 applies only to public housing outside plaintiff's circumstances; Count 10 failed because no state actor or constitutional deprivation alleged; Counts 11 and 12 contained only statutory quotations with no facts; Count 14 is policy declaration without private right of action.

source_file: 9775286_2021_The School of the Ozarks, Inc. v. Biden_mowd
case_name: The School of the Ozarks, Inc. v. Biden
accommodation_description: The School of the Ozarks challenges HUD Memorandum on FHA enforcement as applied to its student housing policies based on biological sex and conduct codes requiring sexual relations limited to marriage between opposite-sex couples.
key_holding: Plaintiff lacks standing because the HUD Memorandum is merely policy guidance without legal force of its own, imposes no concrete restriction or penalty, and any potential FHA liability would flow directly from the statute and Bostock, not from the Memorandum itself.
brief_summary: The School of the Ozarks, Inc. sued President Biden and federal officials seeking to enjoin a HUD Memorandum on FHA enforcement, arguing it exceeds statutory authority, violates First Amendment free speech protections, and imposes burdens on religious exercise. The court denied the preliminary injunction motion and dismissed the case for lack of Article III standing, finding the Memorandum is merely non-binding policy guidance that imposes no concrete injury on Plaintiff and any potential liability would derive from the FHA itself rather than the Memorandum.
key_cases_cited: Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins, 136 S. Ct. 1540 (2016)
Clapper v. Amnesty Int'l USA, 568 U.S. 398 (2013)
DaimlerChrysler Corp. v. Cuno, 547 U.S. 332 (2006)
Philadelphia Indem. Ins. Co. v. Atl. Specialty Ins. Co., 2020 WL 4819949 (W.D. Mo. 2020)
Uzuegbunam v. Preczewski, 141 S. Ct. 792 (2021)

source_file: 9775928_2022_Doe 1 v. The Curators of the University of Missouri_mowd
9775965_2022_Kirsten v. Cape Royale at Ski Harbor Condominium Owners Association, Inc._mowd
case_name: Burton Kirsten v. Cape Royale at Ski Harbor Condominium Owners Association Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff with neurological disorder requested HOA waive policy prohibiting drop-down boat covers to allow him to independently cover his boat docked at his condominium boat well.
key_holding: The court found Plaintiff failed to demonstrate substantial likelihood of success on the merits of his reasonable accommodation claim under § 3604(f)(3)(B) and failed to show irreparable harm, as alternative means of covering the boat may be available and money damages could compensate any harm.
brief_summary: Burton Kirsten sued his condominium homeowners association seeking to prevent removal of a drop-down boat cover he installed as a reasonable accommodation for his neurological disability, claiming the HOA's policy prohibiting such covers violates the Fair Housing Act. The court denied his motion for temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction, finding he failed to show substantial likelihood of success on the merits and failed to demonstrate irreparable harm given the availability of alternative boat-covering services.
key_cases_cited: Planned Parenthood Minnesota, N. Dakota, S. Dakota v. Rounds, 530 F.3d 724 (8th Cir. 2008)
Dataphase Sys., Inc. v. C L Syst., Inc., 640 F.2d 109 (8th Cir. 1981)
Nevels v. W. World Ins. Co., 359 F. Supp. 2d 1110 (W.D. Wash. 2004)
Novus Franchising, Inc. v. Dawson, 725 F.3d 885 (8th Cir. 2013)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Modification of HOA policy to permit installation and use of a custom drop-down boat cover on plaintiff's boat well, which plaintiff claims his neurological disorder makes it physically difficult or impossible to cover manually
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied the preliminary injunction four-factor test and found plaintiff failed to demonstrate substantial likelihood of success on the merits. The court identified novel questions regarding whether the boat well constitutes a 'facility in connection with a dwelling' under § 3604(f)(2), whether § 3604(f)(3)(B) applies to such facilities, and whether the policy modification constitutes reasonable accommodation given potential safety risks and availability of alternative means of covering the boat. Court did not reach substantive merits analysis of the FHA claim itself, but applied a balancing framework to the reasonableness inquiry.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Intentional infliction of emotional distress (state tort claim)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court did not substantively address the intentional infliction of emotional distress claim in its preliminary injunction analysis, focusing instead on the FHA reasonable accommodation claim and the four-factor preliminary injunction test.

source_file: 9775966_2022_Kirsten v. Cape Royale at Ski Harbor Condominium Owners Association, Inc._mowd
case_name: Burton Kirsten v. Cape Royale at Ski Harbor Condominium Owners Association Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requests permission to keep a custom drop-down boat cover installed on the awning above his boat well, which his neurological disorder prevents him from covering manually.
key_holding: The court found Plaintiff alleged sufficient facts that the HOA's policy prohibiting drop-down boat covers may violate the FHA by preventing Plaintiff equal opportunity to use and enjoy his boat well facility, relying on Shapiro v. Cadman Towers for the proposition that policies affecting facilities in connection with dwellings require accommodation analysis.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Burton Kirsten, a Michigan resident owning a condominium in Osage Beach, Missouri governed by the defendant HOA, sued alleging the HOA's refusal to permit his drop-down boat cover violates the FHA as a reasonable accommodation/modification for his neurological disorder. The court granted in part and denied in part Defendant's motion to dismiss, dismissing Plaintiff's IIED claim with prejudice but allowing the FHA reasonable accommodation and modification claims to proceed past the pleading stage.
key_cases_cited: Shapiro v. Cadman Towers, Inc., 51 F.3d 328 (2d Cir. 1995)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Zutz v. Nelson, 601 F.3d 842 (8th Cir. 2010)
Gibson v. Brewer, 952 S.W.2d 239 (Mo. 1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exception to homeowner association policy prohibiting drop-down boat covers, or permission to modify existing premises by installing custom drop-down boat cover with tracks affixed to awning above boat well to allow plaintiff with neurological disorder to cover boat without physical maneuvering
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff alleged sufficient facts under Iqbal/Twombly to survive motion to dismiss. Plaintiff plausibly alleged the boat well is a facility in connection with the dwelling, the drop-down cover policy affects equal opportunity to use and enjoy that facility, and defendant's strict enforcement of the policy may constitute failure to make reasonable accommodation. Court did not reach substantive merits of the reasonable accommodation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Intentional infliction of emotional distress (state tort claim under Missouri law)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed IIED claim for failure to state a plausible claim under Missouri law, which requires plaintiff to allege bodily harm resulting from severe emotional distress. Plaintiff alleged only stress, anxiety, embarrassment, and loss of use and enjoyment, none of which constitute bodily harm as required by Missouri Supreme Court precedent. Plaintiff also failed to allege defendant acted solely to cause emotional distress, as defendant's stated reason was policy violation.

source_file: 9775981_2022_Auburn Hills Homeowners Association v. New Page Properties, L.L.C._mowd
case_name: Auburn Hills Homeowners Association v. New Page Properties, L.L.C.
accommodation_description: HOA seeks declaratory judgment that its property maintenance enforcement actions do not violate the Fair Housing Act
key_holding: The HOA lacks standing to bring FHA claims as it is not an 'aggrieved person' under § 3613(a)(1), and federal question jurisdiction does not exist where the FHA appears only as a potential defense to the HOA's state law breach of contract claim.
brief_summary: Auburn Hills Homeowners Association filed suit seeking a declaration that its property maintenance enforcement and fines against New Page Properties do not violate the Fair Housing Act, along with a breach of contract claim. The court dismissed the case for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, holding that the HOA lacks standing to bring FHA claims and that the FHA appears only as an anticipated defense to state law claims, not as an independent basis for federal jurisdiction.
key_cases_cited: Franchise Tax Bd. v. Construction Laborers Vacation Trust, 463 U.S. 1
Skelly Oil Co. v. Phillips Petroleum Co., 339 U.S. 667
Gully v. First Nat'l Bank, 299 U.S. 109
Aetna Health, Inc. v. Davila, 542 U.S. 200
Gaar v. Quirk, 86 F.3d 451

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of contract claim for property maintenance violations under HOA Declaration; Fair Housing Act raised only as anticipated affirmative defense by defendant
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(b)(1). The HOA's underlying cause of action is breach of contract under state law; the Fair Housing Act appears only as an anticipated affirmative defense, which does not create federal question jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1331. The Declaratory Judgment Act is procedural, not jurisdictional, and cannot be used to preemptively raise a federal defense to a state law claim.

source_file: 9776401_2024_Kirsten v. Cape Royale at Ski Harbor Condominium Owners Association, Inc._mowd
case_name: Burton Kirsten v. Cape Royale at Ski Harbor Condominium Owners Association Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff with neurological disorder requested HOA modify its policy prohibiting drop-down boat covers to allow his custom drop-down boat cover for his boat well.
key_holding: Plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie case of failure to accommodate because he did not demonstrate the policy modification was necessary to afford him equal opportunity to use and enjoy his dwelling—plaintiff never used the boat cover, used the dock only five days total in three years, and the existing awning already provides protection, making the requested modification a mere preference rather than a necessity.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Burton Kirsten sued Cape Royale at Ski Harbor Condominium Owners Association, alleging the HOA violated the Fair Housing Act by refusing to modify its policy prohibiting drop-down boat covers to accommodate his neurological disability. The court granted summary judgment for the HOA, finding Kirsten failed to establish the accommodation was necessary for equal use and enjoyment of his dwelling because he never used the cover, rarely visited the dock, and an existing awning already provided adequate protection.
key_cases_cited: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
United States v. Badgett, 976 F.2d 1176 (8th Cir. 1992)
Bronk v. Ineichen, 54 F.3d 425 (7th Cir. 1995)
Shapiro v. Cadman Towers, Inc., 51 F.3d 328 (2d Cir. 1995)
Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Modification of HOA policy to permit plaintiff's custom drop-down boat cover on his boat well, which plaintiff claims is necessary due to his neurological disorder that makes it physically difficult or impossible to manually cover his boat
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied the four-part prima facie test for failure to accommodate and found plaintiff failed to establish that the policy modification was 'necessary' to afford equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling. The court emphasized that plaintiff had never actually used the drop-down cover, used the dock only five days total since 2020, and had unencumbered access to the dock and boat independent of the HOA policy. The existing awning already provided substantial protection, and the policy did not prevent or limit plaintiff's access to the dock—it merely restricted the type of cover that could be used. The court distinguished this case from precedent where policies explicitly prevented access to facilities in connection with dwellings.

source_file: 9777537_2021_Stonewater Adolescent Recovery Center v. Lafayette County Board of Supervisors_msnd
case_name: Stonewater Adolescent Recovery Center v. Lafayette County Board of Supervisors
accommodation_description: Stonewater Adolescent Recovery Center, a residential rehabilitation facility for adolescents with substance abuse and mental health disorders, sought to expand from 16 to 80 beds, but the Lafayette County Planning Commission and Board of Supervisors denied the expansion request.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for the defendant based on res judicata because the plaintiff had already litigated the same Fair Housing Act and ADA claims in state court, where the circuit court affirmed the denial of the expansion on the merits after providing the plaintiff a full and fair opportunity to be heard.
brief_summary: Stonewater Adolescent Recovery Center, a residential rehabilitation facility for adolescent males with substance abuse and mental health disorders, sued Lafayette County Board of Supervisors alleging that the denial of its facility expansion request violated the Fair Housing Act and ADA by discriminating against its disabled residents. The court granted summary judgment for the defendant, finding that the plaintiff's claims were barred by res judicata because the same claims had been fully litigated and decided on the merits in prior state court proceedings.
key_cases_cited: Kremer v. Chemical Const. Corp., 456 U.S. 461 (1982)
Black v. N. Panola School Dist., 461 F.3d 584 (5th Cir. 2006)
EMC Mortg. Corp. v. Carmichael, 17 So.3d 1087 (Miss. 2009)
City of Jackson v. Holliday, 149 So.2d 525 (Miss. 1963)
Harrison v. Chandler-Sampson Ins., Inc., 891 So.2d 224 (Miss. 2005)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Approval of facility expansion from 16 to 80 beds for adolescent males with substance abuse and/or mental health disorders
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied res judicata doctrine to bar the FHA claim because the plaintiff had a full and fair opportunity to litigate the identical FHA claim in state court appeal, the state circuit court adjudicated the claim on the merits, and all five res judicata elements were satisfied under Mississippi law and 28 U.S.C. § 1738.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claim for denial of facility expansion; state law arbitrary and capricious challenge
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied res judicata doctrine to bar the ADA and state law claims on the same grounds as the FHA claim—the plaintiff litigated identical claims in state court, received a final judgment on the merits, and had a full and fair opportunity to present all arguments.

case_name: Martin v. RUREDY808, L.L.C.
accommodation_description: Robert Martin requested permission to keep his service dog/ESA 'Slade' in his rented condominium to assist with his mental health disabilities including anxiety, PTSD, and bipolar disorder.
key_holding: The court denied both parties' cross-motions for summary judgment on the FHA claims, finding genuine disputes of material fact exist regarding whether defendants intentionally discriminated against Martin and retaliated against him for requesting an assistance animal accommodation, precluding summary judgment for either side.
brief_summary: Robert Martin sued RUREDY808, L.L.C. and Frank Savage alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act after defendants attempted to evict him for keeping his service dog Slade despite a lease provision permitting the animal as a reasonable accommodation for his mental health disability. The court denied both parties' cross-motions for summary judgment, finding genuine disputes of material fact exist regarding whether defendants' actions constituted intentional discrimination and retaliation under the FHA, such that trial is necessary.
key_cases_cited: City of Edmonds v. Oxford House, Inc., 514 U.S. 725 (1995)
Inclusive Communities Project, Inc. v. Lincoln Prop. Co., 920 F.3d 890 (5th Cir. 2019)
Bloch v. Frischolz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009)
Texas v. Crest Asset Management, Inc., 85 F. Supp. 2d 722

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation for emotional support animal (service dog named Slade) to reside in the condominium despite no-pets lease provision. The dog was trained to alert for seizures and assist with mental health conditions including PTSD, GAD, and Bipolar Type II Disorder.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether defendants intentionally discriminated by refusing the accommodation. Evidence supported both plaintiff's account (that APM granted the accommodation and defendants wrongfully rejected it) and defendants' account (that they properly requested verification information and plaintiff failed to provide adequate documentation). Summary judgment was inappropriate because discrimination claims require determination of subjective intent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Intentional discrimination based on disability in the terms, conditions, and privileges of rental housing (§ 3604(f)(2)) and denial of housing based on disability (§ 3604(f)(1)).
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found ample evidence supporting either side. Plaintiff's evidence showed defendants demanded removal of the service dog immediately upon learning of it, terminated the management agreement when APM refused, repeatedly questioned plaintiff's disability, discounted medical information provided, and filed eviction based on no-pets clause while omitting the special lease provision for Slade. Defendants' evidence showed they consulted HUD guidelines and requested only appropriate verification information. Subjective intent determination required jury resolution.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation under § 3617 for exercising fair housing rights by requesting and obtaining a reasonable accommodation for a service animal.
fha_claims.reasoning: Summary judgment on the retaliation claim hinges on the same factual determinations as the discrimination claims. Causation is a quintessential question of fact. The court found that neither side was entitled to summary judgment because the evidence could support either plaintiff's account (defendants retaliated by demanding removal and filing eviction after plaintiff exercised his right to request accommodation) or defendants' account (they withdrew the eviction and allowed plaintiff to complete the lease term).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of contract (Count II), breach of covenant of quiet enjoyment (Count III), negligent infliction of emotional distress (Count IV), violation of Mississippi Residential Landlord Tenant Act (Count V), and personal liability of Frank Savage under veil-piercing theory.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied summary judgment on breach of contract because the record was inadequate regarding whether the Texas LLC or Frank Savage individually was the 'Lessor' under the Lease, and the Mississippi LLC (the named defendant) never owned the condominium. The court denied summary judgment on the remaining state law claims (quiet enjoyment, NIED, landlord-tenant act violation) because they involve fact-intensive inquiries and subjective determinations similar to the FHA claims. The court granted plaintiff's motion for summary judgment only to the extent that Frank Savage may bear personal liability for FHA claims if he loses on the merits.

case_name: United States of America v. SSM Properties LLC
accommodation_description: This case involves race-based steering and discrimination; no disability accommodation request is at issue.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion for summary judgment, finding genuine disputes of material fact exist regarding whether James Roe acted as an agent of SSM Properties with apparent authority to make leasing decisions and engage in discriminatory conduct, and whether the Mauldings are vicariously liable under the FHA for Roe's race-based steering and discriminatory statements to Black testers.
brief_summary: The United States and plaintiff-intervenors (Black fair housing testers from LaFHAC) sued SSM Properties LLC and its owners, alleging race discrimination and steering at their Jackson, Mississippi apartment complexes based on paired test results showing defendant James Roe made discriminatory statements to Black testers and steered them away from available units while showing units to White testers. The court denied defendants' motion for summary judgment, finding genuine disputes of material fact exist regarding whether Roe acted as the Mauldings' agent with apparent authority, making the Mauldings vicariously liable for his discriminatory conduct under the FHA.
key_cases_cited: Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Avakina v. Chandler Apartments LLC, 2015 WL 413813 (D. Or. 2015)
Garcia v. Brockway, 526 F.3d 456 (9th Cir. 2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied defendants' summary judgment motion on the race discrimination claim, finding genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether Roe acted as the Mauldings' agent or with apparent authority, and whether the Mauldings directed or controlled Roe's discriminatory conduct toward Black testers. The jury may assess credibility and determine liability under vicarious liability principles.

case_name: Resheenada Booth and Milton Jackson v. The City of Jackson; Jackson Police Department; Officer Corry Jenkins; Terramark Corporation; Terramark Holdings, LLC; Terramark Management LLC; John Does 1-5; John Doe Company 1-5
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request described; plaintiffs raised Fair Housing Act claims in connection with eviction, arrest, and alleged police misconduct, but court did not analyze any specific accommodation request.
key_holding: The court dismissed all claims against City Defendants (Officer Jenkins granted qualified immunity; Monell claims failed for lack of constitutional violation; Mississippi Tort Claims Act immunity applied); Terramark Holdings, LLC's motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim was denied but motion to dismiss for improper service was denied as to that entity.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Booth and Jackson sued the City of Jackson, Jackson Police Department, Officer Jenkins, and Terramark entities alleging wrongful eviction, arrest, police misconduct, and various federal and state claims including the Fair Housing Act. The court granted the City Defendants' motion to dismiss based on qualified immunity, failure to plead a constitutional violation for Monell liability, and Mississippi Tort Claims Act immunity; the court also declined to address the Fair Housing Act claims substantively, focusing instead on constitutional and procedural issues.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Samples v. Vadzemnieks, 900 F.3d 655 (5th Cir. 2018)
Deville v. Marcantel, 567 F.3d 156 (5th Cir. 2009)
Freeman v. Gore, 483 F.3d 404 (5th Cir. 2007)
Terry v. Ohio, 392 U.S. 1 (1968)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Second, Fourth, and Fourteenth Amendment claims; § 1983 claims; Mississippi tort law claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege specific constitutional violations under the Second, Fourth, and Fourteenth Amendments. Officer Jenkins is entitled to qualified immunity because the alleged conduct (drawing weapon in response to suspect brandishing assault rifle, handcuffing resulting in blisters, parking at convenience store) does not violate clearly established rights. Monell claims fail because no viable constitutional violation was alleged. Mississippi Tort Claims Act bars state tort claims because plaintiffs failed to allege reckless disregard meeting the statutory standard.

case_name: United States v. SSM Properties, LLC
accommodation_description: Not applicable; this case involves race-based steering and disparate treatment in rental housing, not a disability accommodation request.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for the United States and plaintiff-intervenors, holding that defendants violated the Fair Housing Act through racial steering and discriminatory treatment of prospective Black tenants, and that the Mauldings were vicariously liable as principals for the discriminatory conduct of their agent James Roe.
brief_summary: The United States and Black fair housing testers employed by the Louisiana Fair Housing Action Center brought suit against SSM Properties, LLC and its owners under FHA §§ 3604(a)-(d), alleging that agent James Roe systematically denied Black testers access to preferred properties (Pearl Manor Apartments and 468 Place Townhomes), steered them toward the less desirable Oak Manor, applied more stringent financial screening requirements to Black applicants than to white applicants, and made overtly racist statements. The court found no genuine dispute of material fact on the merits, as the Mauldings failed to adequately counter the plaintiffs' evidence, and separately held the Mauldings vicariously liable for Roe's conduct based on documentary evidence—including Roe's and Maulding's own representations in Rankin County Justice Court proceedings—establishing that Roe was their agent and employee acting within the scope of his authority.
key_cases_cited: Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Walker v. Crigler, 976 F.2d 900 (4th Cir. 1992)
Otero v. New York City Hous. Auth., 484 F.2d 1122 (2d Cir. 1973)
United States v. Real Estate Dev. Corp., 347 F. Supp. 776 (N.D. Miss. 1972)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found no genuine dispute of material fact that defendants violated 42 U.S.C. § 3604(a) by making housing unavailable or denying dwellings based on race. The test transcripts and audio recordings documented systematic differential treatment: Black testers were refused units, interrogated on finances, and steered to inferior properties, while white testers with worse qualifications were welcomed and offered units.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found no genuine dispute that defendants violated 42 U.S.C. § 3604(b) by discriminating in the terms, conditions, and privileges of rental housing based on race. The evidence showed differential application of rental standards, approval procedures, and property access based on the race of the tester.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found no genuine dispute that defendants violated 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c) through statements and conduct indicating a preference, limitation, or discrimination based on race. Roe's explicit statements comparing Black testers to zoo animals and his differential descriptions of properties to Black versus white testers constituted unlawful expressions of racial preference.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found no genuine dispute that defendants violated 42 U.S.C. § 3604(d) by representing to Black testers that dwellings were unavailable for inspection or rental when they were in fact available, while simultaneously offering the same units to white testers.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Pattern or practice of race discrimination
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that the United States established a pattern or practice of discrimination and denial of rights to a group of persons raising an issue of general public importance under 42 U.S.C. § 3614(a). The systematic steering, differential treatment across multiple properties, and explicit racial animus demonstrated by Roe constituted a pattern or practice.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Vicarious liability for agent's discriminatory conduct
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that the Mauldings are vicariously liable for Roe's discriminatory conduct under agency law and the FHA. The documentary evidence established that Roe was the Mauldings' agent and employee acting within the scope of his authority and employment. The Mauldings' own representations to Judge Shirley and to testers, combined with their provision of keys, office space, and rental authority, established the principal-agent relationship. Under respondeat superior and the non-delegable duty doctrine, the Mauldings are liable regardless of whether they knew of or authorized Roe's specific discriminatory acts.

case_name: United States v. SSM Properties, LLC
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED - This case involves civil contempt enforcement of a consent decree, not a reasonable accommodation claim
key_holding: The Court held defendant James Roe in civil contempt for failing to comply with the Consent Decree's payment obligations and for failing to appear at the show cause hearing, but deferred imposition of sanctions pending a compliance hearing.
brief_summary: The United States sued SSM Properties LLC and individual defendants alleging racial discrimination against Black rental housing applicants under the Fair Housing Act; the parties settled in 2022 via consent decree requiring defendant James Roe to pay a $3,000 civil penalty, and this order holds Roe in civil contempt for failing to make the required payments and failing to appear at the show cause hearing.
key_cases_cited: Petroleos Mexicanos v. Crawford Enterprises, Inc., 826 F.2d 392 (5th Cir. 1987)
American Airlines, Inc. v. Allied Pilots Ass'n, 228 F.3d 574 (5th Cir. 2000)
United States v. City of Jackson, Miss., 359 F.3d 727 (5th Cir. 2004)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The United States alleged racial discrimination in rental housing based on race (Black applicants denied units while white applicants were offered the same units). All parties settled via Consent Decree in 2022, with defendant Roe agreeing to cease property management work and pay a $3,000 civil penalty. This opinion addresses contempt for non-compliance with the Consent Decree, not the underlying FHA merits.

case_name: Green v. Allied First Bank SB
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested; the plaintiff sought injunctive relief to stop a foreclosure sale on her property.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's motion for a preliminary injunction to stop a foreclosure sale because the defendant had already cancelled the sale, eliminating any substantial threat of irreparable harm.
brief_summary: LaKeisha Green sued Allied First Bank (Servbank) alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act and the Equal Credit Opportunity Act in connection with a mortgage foreclosure. She sought a preliminary injunction to halt a foreclosure sale scheduled for February 23, 2024. The court denied the injunction because Servbank had already cancelled the sale due to the pending litigation and represented it had no intention of reinstating it until the case concluded, meaning Green could not demonstrate the required substantial threat of irreparable harm.
key_cases_cited: Lake Charles Diesel, Inc. v. General Motors Corp., 328 F.3d 192 (5th Cir. 2003)
Winter v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc., 555 U.S. 7 (2008)
Janvey v. Alguire, 647 F.3d 585 (5th Cir. 2011)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act and Equal Credit Opportunity Act claims related to foreclosure
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the preliminary injunction motion on the ground that plaintiff failed to demonstrate a substantial threat of irreparable harm, as the defendant had already cancelled the foreclosure sale and represented it would not reinstate it pending litigation. The court did not reach the merits of the underlying FHA or ECOA claims.

case_name: Patricia J. Reckley v. Community Nursing, Inc. d/b/a The Village Health & Rehabilitation
accommodation_description: Wheelchair-bound paraplegic resident requests to be returned to her previous room, which she alleges better accommodated her functional needs including a roll-in shower.
key_holding: The court denied preliminary injunctive relief because Plaintiff failed to establish likelihood of success on the merits, as The Village provided evidence it addressed her accommodation concerns in her new room, and she failed to demonstrate irreparable harm from remaining in her current room.
brief_summary: Patricia Reckley, a wheelchair-bound paraplegic resident of a skilled nursing facility, filed a motion for preliminary injunction seeking to be returned to her previous room after being relocated during the facility's COVID-19 unit expansion. The court denied the motion, finding Reckley failed to demonstrate likelihood of success on her failure-to-accommodate claims because The Village provided evidence it addressed her accommodation concerns in her new room, including showering assistance, and she failed to show irreparable harm.
key_cases_cited: Winter v. Natural Res. Def. Council, Inc., 555 U.S. 7 (2008)
Disney Enterprises, Inc. v. VidAngel, Inc., 869 F.3d 846 (9th Cir. 2017)
Cottonwood Envtl. Law Center v. U.S. Sheep Experiment Station, 2019 WL 3290994 (D. Mont. 2019)
Alliance of the Wild Rockies v. Cottrell, 632 F.3d 1127 (9th Cir. 2011)
Pac. Radiation Oncology, LLC v. Queen's Med. Ctr., 810 F.3d 631 (9th Cir. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Roll-in shower and other accessibility features in plaintiff's room; plaintiff was moved from her prior room on the 700-hall to a different room when the 700-hall was converted to a Covid-19 unit
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiff failed to demonstrate likelihood of success on the merits of her failure-to-accommodate claim because the Village presented evidence that it addressed plaintiff's accommodation issues in her new room, including providing shower assistance in the spa room, adjusting bed and transfer poles, and ensuring other functional needs were met. The court applied a balancing approach, weighing plaintiff's preference for her prior room against the Village's evidence of reasonable accommodations in the new room.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged retaliation for exercising ADA rights by being moved to a different room
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiff failed to demonstrate likelihood of success on a retaliation claim because the Village produced evidence that the room transfer was precipitated by its response to the Covid-19 pandemic and the need to convert the 700-hall into a Covid-19 unit, not by retaliation for exercising ADA rights.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claims under ADA Title III, ADA Title V, and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the Winter preliminary injunction standard and found that plaintiff failed to demonstrate likelihood of success on the merits of her ADA and Rehabilitation Act claims for the same reasons as the FHA reasonable accommodation and retaliation claims—the Village presented evidence of reasonable accommodations and a non-retaliatory basis for the room transfer.

case_name: Reckley v. Community Nursing, Inc.
accommodation_description: The opinion does not specify the accommodation requested; it references Title III ADA claims and mentions Fair Housing Act claims only in passing in the mootness analysis.
key_holding: Plaintiff's claims, including any Fair Housing Act claims, are moot because her death eliminates any prospect of future injury for which injunctive relief could provide a remedy.
brief_summary: Patricia J. Reckley sued Community Nursing, Inc. d/b/a The Village Health & Rehabilitation under Title III of the ADA and, to some extent, the Fair Housing Act. The court granted defendant's motion to dismiss after Reckley's death on April 13, 2022, finding all claims moot because injunctive relief—the only available remedy—is no longer meaningful when there is no prospect of future injury to the deceased plaintiff.
key_cases_cited: Pickern v. Holiday Quality Foods Inc., 293 F.3d 1133 (9th Cir. 2002)
Alvarado v. Cajun Operating Co., 588 F.3d 1261 (9th Cir. 2009)
Kalani v. Starbcuks Coffee Co., 698 Fed Appx. 883 (9th Cir. 2017)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title III ADA claims and ADA retaliation claims; to the extent FHA and Rehabilitation Act claims were also alleged, they are analyzed through the ADA framework
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's death rendered all claims moot because the only remedy available under Title III of the ADA and for ADA retaliation is injunctive relief, and there is no prospect of future injury after plaintiff's death. FHA and Rehabilitation Act claims seeking injunctive relief are analyzed through the ADA framework and are likewise moot.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Handheld shower nozzle with detachable hose in handicap-accessible shower facility
fha_claims.reasoning: Under Title II of the ADA, the facility was constructed in 2004 and therefore subject to the 1991 Standards, which permit a fixed shower head in lieu of a handheld nozzle in unmonitored facilities where vandalism is a consideration. The court found the 1991 Standards were met and that the requested accommodation (handheld nozzle with hose) was not required as a reasonable accommodation given the security concerns in a detention facility.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Eighth Amendment and Fourteenth Amendment claims regarding conditions of confinement and access to adequate medical care; ADA Title II discrimination claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Under the Fourteenth Amendment Due Process Clause for pretrial detainees, plaintiff failed to establish that the absence of a hose and nozzle placed him at substantial risk of serious harm, as the facility provided benches, handrails, and pushbutton-operated showers. The court found defendants took reasonable measures to abate any risk and plaintiff presented no evidence of injury. Under Title II ADA, the facility met the applicable 1991 Standards for accessibility.

case_name: William Harris and Phyllis Harris v. Mary Jane Vanderburg, Douglas Matthew Gurkins, Remco East, Inc., and Mary Grace Bishop
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; case involves claims of racial harassment by neighbor and retaliation via eviction filing after complaints.
key_holding: The court denied Defendant Vanderburg's motion to quash and motion for protective order, holding that Plaintiffs made a sufficient factual showing to support their FHA punitive damages claim, rendering the subpoena for Vanderburg's tax records relevant and proportional to the needs of the case.
brief_summary: African-American tenants sued their landlord, property managers, and a neighbor under the Fair Housing Act alleging racial harassment by the neighbor and retaliation through an eviction filing after they complained. This discovery ruling addressed whether to quash a subpoena for Defendant Vanderburg's tax records sought to support Plaintiffs' punitive damages claim; the court denied the motion, finding the records relevant and Plaintiffs had made sufficient factual showing to obtain pre-trial financial discovery.
key_cases_cited: In re Subpoena Duces Tecum to AOL, LLC, 2010 WL 2232261 (E.D.N.C. June 2, 2010)
In re Subpoena to Robert Kochan, 2013 WL 1704839 (S.D.W. Va. Apr. 19, 2013)
Bunch v. Robinson, 2013 WL 1833557 (M.D.N.C. Apr. 30, 2013)
In re Subpoena Duces Tecum to AOL, LLC, 2015 WL 1125108 (E.D.N.C. Mar. 12, 2015)
Muhammad v. Giant Food Inc., 2004 WL 444570 (M.D.N.C. Feb. 24, 2004)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: This opinion addresses only a discovery dispute regarding a Rule 45 subpoena for defendant's tax records in connection with a punitive damages claim under the FHA. The court did not reach the merits of the underlying retaliation claim but rather determined that financial information was discoverable to support the punitive damages aspect of the FHA claims. The retaliation claim itself remains pending.

source_file: 9785121_2021_Young v. Lake Royale Property Owners Association_nced
case_name: Eric Wayne Young and Wilma Jean Young v. Lake Royale Property Owners Association
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request at issue; plaintiffs allege race-based discriminatory treatment in building permits and inspections, and retaliation for filing HUD/NCHRC complaints
key_holding: Plaintiffs failed to state a plausible FHA retaliation claim under § 3617 because they did not allege sufficient facts showing a causal connection between their protected activity (filing HUD/NCHRC complaints) and any adverse action taken by defendants.
brief_summary: Black property owners in a private residential community sued the HOA, its private security force, and attorneys alleging race-based discrimination in building permits/inspections and retaliation under § 3617 for filing HUD and NCHRC complaints. The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss, finding plaintiffs failed to plead plausible retaliation claims because they did not allege sufficient facts showing defendants' adverse actions were caused by their protected activity rather than legitimate business reasons.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Hall v. Greystar Mgmt. Servs., L.P., 637 F. App'x 93 (4th Cir. 2016)
Burlington N. & Santa Fe Ry. Co. v. White, 548 U.S. 53 (2006)
A Soc'y Without A Name v. Virginia, 655 F.3d 342 (4th Cir. 2011)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to allege facts sufficient to show a causal connection between defendant Ragsdale's actions (filing foreclosure and sending cease-and-desist letters) and plaintiffs' protected activity of filing FHA complaints. The court found no reasonable inference of retaliatory causation beyond bare assertions, and the foreclosure was based on unpaid fines imposed by the Association, not Ragsdale's independent retaliatory intent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Posting of plaintiffs' personal checks on defendant Association's website
fha_claims.reasoning: The alleged disclosure of personal checks, while imprudent, does not constitute a materially adverse action under the Burlington standard because it would not dissuade a reasonable person from filing FHA complaints. Additionally, plaintiffs failed to allege facts supporting an inference that the posting was undertaken to retaliate for protected activity rather than merely to respond to the FHA complaint.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Assessment of attorney's fees against plaintiffs
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to allege factual basis for an inference that seeking attorney's fees constitutes unlawful retaliation. The FHA and its regulations specifically contemplate the award of attorney's fees, and plaintiffs provided only conclusory assertions of retaliatory intent without concrete factual allegations supporting an inference of impermissible motivation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Placement of plaintiffs in 'bad standing' with the Association, suspending use of community amenities
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to allege facts establishing a causal connection between the bad standing designation and protected activity. The complaint itself states that bad standing was imposed until 'unlawful attorney fees were paid,' indicating the adverse action was based on unpaid fees rather than the filing of FHA complaints.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: State law claims for malicious prosecution, punitive damages, and other state tort claims; § 1983 due process claims; False Claims Act claims (31 U.S.C. § 3729); § 1985 conspiracy claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Non-FHA claims were either not properly before the court as they were not screened for frivolity under § 1915(e)(2)(B), or were dismissed for failure to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly standards. The court declined to apply ethical codes to define standards of civil liability for lawyers in addressing fraud allegations against defendant Ragsdale.

case_name: Gary L. Swanson v. Alex King & King Management, LLC
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request described; complaint merely alleged disability-based housing discrimination.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claim for failure to state a plausible claim because plaintiff provided no factual support for his allegation that defendant discriminated against him on the basis of disability.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Gary Swanson sued landlord Alex King and King Management, LLC under the Fair Housing Act, alleging disability-based housing discrimination after being locked out of his home. The court granted the magistrate judge's recommendation and dismissed the FHA claim with prejudice for failure to state a plausible claim, finding plaintiff's complaint contained only conclusory allegations of discrimination without supporting factual details.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged discrimination based on disability but provided no factual support for the claim. The complaint contained only conclusory allegations insufficient to state a plausible claim under Ashcroft v. Iqbal and Bell Atlantic v. Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Third, Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, Seventh, Eighth, Ninth, Tenth, Eleventh, Thirteenth, and Fourteenth Amendment claims; Intentional Infliction of Emotional Distress (state law)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's proposed amendments asserting constitutional claims and state tort claims fail as a matter of law. Constitutional claims either lack factual allegations supporting the applicable constitutional standard or apply only to governmental action where plaintiff alleged only private conduct. The IIED claim fails because debt collection letters and door hangers do not constitute extreme and outrageous conduct under North Carolina law.

case_name: May v. Martin Fein Interest Ltd.
accommodation_description: Vague disability accommodation requests including being allowed to pay rent like other tenants and having defendants accept delivery of plaintiffs' medications; specific accommodation request not clearly articulated in this service-of-process ruling.
key_holding: The court granted plaintiffs' motions to extend time for service and to amend summonses based on good cause (pro se plaintiffs' diligence and COVID-19 difficulties), and denied defendants' service-of-process motions as moot; no substantive ruling on the underlying FHA claims.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Raymond and Angela May sued Creekside at Crabtree Apartments and related defendants for Fair Housing Act claims including disability discrimination and racial discrimination. The court granted plaintiffs' motions to extend the time for service, to amend summonses, and for alternative service methods based on good cause, while denying defendants' motions to dismiss for improper service as moot—this is a procedural ruling addressing service of process, not the merits of any accommodation claim.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege they were not allowed to pay rent like other tenants
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied defendants' motions to dismiss as moot after granting plaintiffs' motion to extend time for service and amend summonses. The reasonable accommodation claim regarding rent payment was not substantively analyzed on the merits but survives the procedural challenge.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege defendants refused to sign for and accept plaintiffs' medications
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied defendants' motions to dismiss as moot after granting plaintiffs' motion to extend time for service and amend summonses. The reasonable accommodation claim regarding medication acceptance was not substantively analyzed on the merits but survives the procedural challenge.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege defendants made statements and actions that are racist and discriminatory
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied defendants' motions to dismiss as moot after granting plaintiffs' motion to extend time for service and amend summonses. The racial discrimination claim was not substantively analyzed on the merits but survives the procedural challenge.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege retaliation for exercising FHA rights
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied defendants' motions to dismiss as moot after granting plaintiffs' motion to extend time for service and amend summonses. The retaliation claim was not substantively analyzed on the merits but survives the procedural challenge.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act claim, intentional infliction of emotional distress claim
fha_claims.reasoning: The Magistrate Judge's Memorandum and Recommendation recommended dismissing the ADA and intentional infliction of emotional distress claims as frivolous under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(i), which the district court adopted in full. These non-FHA claims were dismissed at the screening stage without substantive merits analysis.

case_name: Eric Wayne Young and Wilma Jean Young v. Lake Royale Association and Lake Royale Private Company Police
accommodation_description: Disputes with Lake Royale Property Owners Association regarding property access, use, and enforcement, framed as FHA retaliation claim.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' claims for retaliation in violation of the Fair Housing Act under 42 U.S.C. § 3617 for failure to state a claim, adopting the magistrate judge's recommendation.
brief_summary: Eric and Wilma Young, proceeding pro se, sued Lake Royale Association and related entities asserting Fair Housing Act retaliation claims and state law claims arising from disputes regarding property access and association enforcement. The court adopted the magistrate judge's recommendation to dismiss the FHA retaliation claims for failure to state a claim and declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims.
key_cases_cited: Diamond v. Colonial Life & Acc. Ins. Co., 416 F.3d 310 (4th Cir. 2005)
Camby v. Davis, 718 F.2d 198 (4th Cir. 1983)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; retaliation claim does not allege failure to provide accommodation
fha_claims.reasoning: The magistrate judge recommended dismissal of the retaliation claim under § 3617 for failure to state a claim under the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard. The district court adopted this recommendation without clear error, finding the magistrate judge's analysis thorough.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: State law claims (specific nature not detailed in opinion)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1367, resulting in dismissal of those claims.

case_name: William Harris and Phyllis Harris v. Douglas Matthew Gurkins, Remco East, Inc., and Mary Grace Bishop
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED - the opinion does not describe the specific accommodation request underlying the FHA retaliation claim; this is a discovery ruling on punitive damages financial discovery only.
key_holding: The court granted plaintiffs' motion to compel financial discovery from defendants because plaintiffs' FHA retaliation claim survived summary judgment and defendants' financial position is relevant to punitive damages under 42 U.S.C. § 3613(c)(1).
brief_summary: Plaintiffs William and Phyllis Harris sued defendants under the Fair Housing Act for retaliation and state law claims; defendants Remco East and Mary Grace Bishop opposed financial discovery for punitive damages. The court granted plaintiffs' motion to compel financial discovery, finding that surviving summary judgment on the FHA retaliation claim made defendants' financial position relevant and proportional to the case needs.
key_cases_cited: Robert G. Schwemm, Housing Discrimination Law and Litigation § 25:12
Hannah v. LSI Title Co., 468 F. App'x 283 (4th Cir. 2012)
Baskerville v. Blom, 208 F.3d 419 (3d Cir. 2000)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs' FHA retaliation claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3617 survived defendants' motion for summary judgment because genuine issues of material fact exist regarding the retaliation claim, creating a jury question. The court granted in part and denied in part the summary judgment motion, allowing the retaliation claim to proceed to trial.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: State law claims for trespass, assault, invasion of privacy, and unfair and deceptive trade practices
fha_claims.reasoning: State law claims for trespass, assault, invasion of privacy, and unfair and deceptive trade practices survived defendants' motion for summary judgment and were allowed to proceed to trial alongside the FHA retaliation claim.

source_file: 9786613_2024_Jett v. The Country Acres Association of Columbus County LTD_nced
case_name: Jett v. The Country Acres Association of Columbus County LTD
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs mention 'reasonable accommodations' in ADA context regarding fines/penalties on the disabled, but no specific accommodation request is analyzed as the ADA claim was dismissed for failure to state a claim.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' Fair Housing Act and ADA claims for failure to state a claim because plaintiffs did not identify which FHA provisions were violated or how the ADA was implicated, and legal conclusions of discrimination without supporting facts are insufficient.
brief_summary: Raymond and Tara Jett, an interracial couple, sued George and Michael Coleman, developer Mitchell Powell, attorney Martin Scott, and the Country Acres HOA alleging racial harassment under 42 U.S.C. § 1982 and Fair Housing Act violations. The court allowed the § 1982 and state tort claims against the Colemans to proceed but dismissed the FHA and ADA claims because plaintiffs failed to articulate which statutory provisions were violated and offered only conclusory allegations of discrimination without supporting facts.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodations related to alleged harsh and cruel fines and penalties imposed on disabled persons
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to allege which provisions of the ADA were violated or how, and even construing the complaint liberally, there are no allegations that would support an ADA claim for reasonable accommodations. The court found the allegations insufficient under the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard.
