fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 504 Rehabilitation Act, Title II ADA, Title VI Civil Rights Act, HIPAA, 41 U.S.C. § 6503, 18 U.S.C. § 1341, state law fraud
fha_claims.reasoning: Rehabilitation Act and ADA claims failed because plaintiff did not sufficiently allege that defendants' actions harmed her on the basis of her disability or that she requested a specific reasonable accommodation. Title VI claim dismissed because plaintiff alleged no racial or national origin discrimination. HIPAA, § 6503, and § 1341 claims dismissed because they do not provide private rights of action or are inapplicable. State fraud claim dismissed for failure to plead with particularity under Rule 9(b).

case_name: Livingstone v. Haddon Point Manager, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested waiver or reduction of the 10% late fee and modification of rent payment due date as an accommodation for his financial circumstances arising from delayed federal student financial aid disbursements.
key_holding: The court dismissed Plaintiff's FHA claim because the FHA is not a vehicle for general lease reformation; Plaintiff's complaint failed to allege any facts suggesting Defendants discriminated against him based on his race or that the late fee policy had a discriminatory effect on a protected class.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Michael Livingstone, a Black male graduate student, sued his private landlord Haddon Point Manager LLC and associated parties alleging violations of the FDCPA, Section 1983, and FHA related to late fees, debt collection, and eviction proceedings arising from delayed student financial aid. The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss all claims except the FDCPA claim against the debt collection attorneys, finding the FHA claim failed because Plaintiff alleged no facts showing race-based discrimination or discriminatory effect from the 10% late fee policy.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Douglass v. Convergent Outsourcing, 765 F.3d 299 (3d Cir. 2014)
St. Pierre v. Retrieval-Masters Creditors Bureau, Inc., 898 F.3d 351 (3d Cir. 2018)
Mitchell v. Walters, 2010 WL 3614210 (D.N.J. Sept. 8, 2010)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged that Defendants' 10% late fee and refusal to modify the payment date on his lease agreement violated the FHA.
fha_claims.disposition: 12(c) Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts suggesting Defendants discriminated against him on the basis of race or that Defendants' actions had a discriminatory effect on African-Americans. The complaint merely alleged the late fee was 'unreasonable' without connecting it to a protected class characteristic. The FHA is not a vehicle for general lease reformation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 due process claim, § 1983 equal protection claim, state law defamation, state law fraud, state law retaliation (Tenant Reprisal Act), state law unjust enrichment
fha_claims.disposition: 12(c) Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings
fha_claims.reasoning: All § 1983 claims failed because Plaintiff did not allege that any Defendant was acting under color of state law; Defendants are private actors. Defamation claim failed for conclusory pleading and failure to allege concrete injury from a $0.89 water bill discrepancy. Fraud claim failed for failure to plead all elements with particularity under Rule 9(b). Retaliation claim under Tenant Reprisal Act failed because Plaintiff alleged no specific injury or damages. Unjust enrichment claim failed because a valid contract governs the parties' rights and obligations.

source_file: 9802991_2020_THE HANSEN FOUNDATION, INC. v. CITY OF ATLANTIC CITY_njd
case_name: The Hansen Foundation, Inc. v. City of Atlantic City
accommodation_description: Permission for Serenity House, a recovery residence for women in addiction recovery, to operate in Atlantic City's R-2 Zoning District despite § 163-66B's restriction on group family households in that zone.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for defendant on plaintiffs' federal reasonable accommodation claims because plaintiffs failed to demonstrate that seeking a zoning variance from the City would have been demonstrably futile, a prerequisite for ripeness of FHAA reasonable accommodation claims in the Third Circuit.
brief_summary: The Hansen Foundation, Inc. and its subsidiary Hansen House, LLC sued the City of Atlantic City challenging the City's enforcement of zoning provisions against Serenity House, a recovery residence for women in substance abuse recovery, alleging violations of the FHA, ADA, RHA, and constitutional and state law provisions. The court granted summary judgment for defendant on plaintiffs' federal reasonable accommodation claims, finding plaintiffs failed to exhaust administrative remedies by not demonstrating that seeking a zoning variance would have been futile, while also granting partial injunctive relief and remanding state law claims.
key_cases_cited: Lapid-Laurel LLC v. Zoning Bd. of Adjustment of Twp. of Scotch Plains, 284 F.3d 442 (3d Cir. 2002)
Assisted Living Assocs. of Moorestown, L.L.C. v. Moorestown Twp., 996 F. Supp. 409 (D.N.J. 1998)
Village of Palatine v. United States, 37 F.3d 1230 (7th Cir. 1994)
Oxford House-A v. City of Univ. City, 87 F.3d 1022 (8th Cir. 1996)
New Jersey Chinese Community Center v. Township of Warren, 712 F. App'x. 196 (3d Cir. 2017)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: City Code § 152-1 explicitly discriminates against individuals with disabilities on its face by restricting location of housing for persons with disabilities. The provision is titled 'Housing for Persons with Disabilities' and explicitly states it regulates 'the location of housing for persons with disabilities.' Defendant failed to provide any legitimate, non-discriminatory justification for the disparate treatment, and prior courts in the district have rejected similar justifications. Plaintiff prevails on disparate treatment claim and is entitled to permanent injunctive relief enjoining enforcement of the distance requirement.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie case of disparate impact regarding City Code § 163-66B's restriction on group family households in R-1 and R-2 districts. Plaintiff provided only poverty statistics without direct evidence showing how the provision disparately impacts individuals recovering from addiction, and relied on unsupported assertions from Oxford House without statistical evidence of causation. Under Smith v. City of Jackson, plaintiff must show causation by statistical evidence sufficient to prove the policy resulted in discrimination; plaintiff failed to produce such evidence.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission for Serenity House's disabled occupants to reside in the City's R-2 Zone despite § 163-66B's restriction on group family households in that zoning district; alternatively, a waiver or modification of the City's zoning ordinances and corresponding certificate of occupancy
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's federal FHA/ADA/RHA reasonable accommodation claims are not ripe for adjudication because plaintiff failed to apply for a zoning variance from the City's Zoning Board of Adjustment. Under Lapid-Laurel, courts reviewing reasonable accommodation challenges to local land use decisions should ordinarily limit review to the administrative record, which assumes plaintiffs must first seek redress through variance applications. Plaintiff failed to demonstrate that a variance application would be demonstrably futile, as required by the Seventh and Eighth Circuit exceptions cited approvingly by the Third Circuit. The City has not yet had the opportunity to make the requested accommodation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II (42 U.S.C. § 12132), Rehabilitation Act § 504 (29 U.S.C. § 794(a)), 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (Due Process Clause of Fourteenth Amendment), New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (N.J.S.A. 10:5-1 et seq.), New Jersey Civil Rights Act (N.J.S.A. 10:6-1 et seq.)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's § 1983 and Fourteenth Amendment substantive due process claims are not ripe because the City's zoning authorities have not issued a final, definitive position on how they will apply the regulations to Serenity House. The CLUC application was denied on procedural grounds, and the Zoning Board's appeal was never reviewed on the merits due to procedural deficiencies. Plaintiff failed to demonstrate that further administrative proceedings would be demonstrably futile. The NJLAD claim is remanded for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because N.J.S.A. § 10:5-12.5 provides for exclusive jurisdiction in New Jersey Superior Court. The NJCRA claim is also not ripe under the same finality rule applicable to § 1983 claims.

source_file: 9803230_2021_FOUR S SHELL LIMITED LIABILITY COMPANY v. PMG LIMITED LIABILITY COMPANY_njd

case_name: Sharon Chavis, et al. v. State of New Jersey, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs sought transfer from Meadowview Psychiatric Hospital to Kings Adult Care Center and a court order mandating release from psychiatric facilities.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiffs' motion for a new hearing, reaffirming that psychiatric facilities (JCMC and Meadowview) are not 'dwellings' as defined under the Fair Housing Act, and therefore plaintiffs failed to state a claim under the FHA.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Sharon and Mya Chavis sued the State of New Jersey, Jersey City Medical Center, and Meadowview Psychiatric Hospital alleging Fair Housing Act violations stemming from Sharon's psychiatric hospitalization and denied transfer to another facility. The court denied plaintiffs' motion for a new hearing, reaffirming its prior dismissal because psychiatric hospitals are not 'dwellings' under the FHA, so the Act's reasonable accommodation provisions did not apply.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Transfer from Meadowview Psychiatric Hospital to Kings Adult Care Center in Brooklyn, New York
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the FHA claim for failure to state a claim because the complaint failed to demonstrate that JCMC or Meadowview constitutes a 'dwelling' as defined under the Fair Housing Act, and thus the FHA was inapplicable to the facts alleged.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA claim for denial of housing interview based on disability; New Jersey Patients' Bill of Rights claim; New Jersey involuntary commitment statute claim; New Jersey Adult Protective Services Act claim
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the ADA claim as containing only conclusory statements and labels without factual support under Twombly; the New Jersey statutory claims were dismissed because they either provided no substantive relief for the alleged conduct, lacked applicability to the facts (no involuntary commitment alleged), or vested enforcement authority exclusively in state officials rather than private parties.

case_name: Michael A. D'Antonio v. Borough of Allendale, et al.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation was requested. Plaintiff alleged that defendants discriminatorily interfered with his plans to develop the subject property for low-income and affordable housing through zoning enforcement, wetland designation, and related municipal actions, and ultimately caused his eviction from the property through foreclosure proceedings.
key_holding: The court dismissed pro se plaintiff's Third Amended Complaint with prejudice because he lacked Article III standing (having no personal legal interest in the subject property, which was owned by Calm Development, Inc.), his claims were precluded by seven prior state-court judgments under res judicata, the entire controversy doctrine, and collateral estoppel, and he failed to state any cognizable claim under the FHA, Fourteenth Amendment, Title VII, Section 1983, or fraud theories.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff D'Antonio sued the Borough of Allendale and numerous other defendants alleging they unlawfully interfered with his use and development of a property in Allendale, New Jersey—including through selective enforcement of zoning ordinances, artificial wetland designations, and ultimately foreclosure and eviction—in violation of the FHA, the Fourteenth Amendment, Title VII, Section 1983, and various state law theories. The court dismissed with prejudice on three independent grounds: plaintiff had no standing because the property was owned by corporation Calm Development throughout the relevant period and plaintiff could not demonstrate a separate personal injury; the claims were barred by res judicata, the entire controversy doctrine, and collateral estoppel based on at least seven prior state-court litigations involving the same subject property; and plaintiff failed to state any cognizable claim, including under the FHA because he never identified membership in a protected class and the claims were time-barred.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Monell v. Department of Social Services of the City of New York, 436 U.S. 658 (1974)
Bostock v. Clayton County, Georgia, 140 S. Ct. 1731 (2020)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act claim (§ 3604); Fourteenth Amendment Equal Protection and Due Process claims; Title VII employment discrimination; Section 1983 civil rights; fraud claims (fraud in concealment, fraud in inducement, theft by deception, mail fraud, wire fraud, money laundering, income tax evasion); and various state law claims listed in wherefore clause
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to identify which FHA provision he invoked and failed to allege membership in a protected class. FHA claim is also time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations. Plaintiff cannot bring third-party claims on behalf of others. Equal Protection claim fails because plaintiff is not a member of a protected class. Due Process claim fails because plaintiff never maintained a legal interest in the subject property. Title VII claim fails because this is not an employment dispute and is time-barred. Section 1983 claim fails because plaintiff did not allege violation of federal rights and is time-barred. Fraud claims fail to meet Rule 9(b) heightened pleading standard. Other claims in wherefore clause lack any supporting factual allegations.

case_name: Samantha Campaniello-Cason v. Kevin O'Reilly
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; this case concerns alleged racial and ethnic slurs, harassment, and lease non-renewal based on protected characteristics.
key_holding: The court granted plaintiffs leave to amend their FHA and NJLAD claims to add national origin and familial status discrimination because the proposed amendments would not cause undue prejudice and defendant did not demonstrate futility, but denied leave to add a claim under the New Jersey Anti-Eviction Act because the 'good cause' requirement does not apply to owner-occupied two-family homes.
brief_summary: Samantha Campaniello-Cason and her children sued landlord Kevin O'Reilly alleging racial and ethnic harassment including use of slurs, shutting off utilities, and non-renewal of lease; the magistrate judge granted plaintiffs leave to amend their complaint to add national origin and familial status discrimination claims to their existing Fair Housing Act and NJLAD claims, but denied their request to add a claim under the New Jersey Anti-Eviction Act because the statute's 'good cause' requirement does not apply to owner-occupied two-family dwellings.
key_cases_cited: Foman v. Davis, 371 U.S. 178 (1962)
Arthur v. Maersk, Inc., 434 F.3d 196 (3d Cir. 2006)
Cureton v. Nat'l Collegiate Athletic Ass'n, 252 F.3d 267 (3d Cir. 2001)
In re Burlington Coat Factory Sec. Litig., 114 F.3d 1410 (3d Cir. 1997)
Massarsky v. General Motors Corp., 706 F.2d 111 (3d Cir. 1983)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted leave to amend FHA and NJLAD claims (Counts I-IV) to expand allegations beyond racial discrimination to include national origin and familial status discrimination. The amendment was not futile and would not unduly prejudice defendant; the court applied the Rule 12(b)(6) futility standard and found the amendments viable.

source_file: 9804711_2021_THE HANSEN FOUNDATION, INC. v. CITY OF ATLANTIC CITY_njd
case_name: The Hansen Foundation, Inc. v. City of Atlantic City
accommodation_description: Hansen House requested a reasonable accommodation or waiver of City zoning requirements to operate Serenity House as a residence for women recovering from addiction.
key_holding: The Court granted Plaintiffs partial attorneys' fees following summary judgment, finding that while Plaintiffs prevailed on their disparate treatment claim invalidating the discriminatory distance requirement of City Code § 152-1, they failed on approximately 75% of their claims and goals, warranting a 70% reduction in the lodestar amount.
brief_summary: The Hansen Foundation and its subsidiary Hansen House sued Atlantic City over zoning code provisions governing community residences for persons with disabilities, seeking to operate Serenity House as a recovery residence for women in Atlantic City's R-2 Zoning District. The Court previously granted summary judgment for Plaintiffs on their disparate treatment claim finding City Code § 152-1's 660-foot distance requirement facially discriminatory, and now rules on attorneys' fees, awarding Plaintiffs $25,646.78 after a 70% reduction for limited success.
key_cases_cited: Texas State Teachers Association v. Garland Independent School District, 489 U.S. 782 (1989)
Farrar v. Hobby, 506 U.S. 103 (1992)
Hensley v. Eckerhart, 461 U.S. 424 (1983)
New Jersey Chinese Community Center v. Township of Warren, 712 F. App'x. 196 (3d Cir. 2017)
Cottrell v. Good Wheels, 2009 WL 3208299 (D.N.J. 2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Facial challenge to City Code § 152-1, which imposed a 660-foot distance requirement between community residences (housing for persons with disabilities)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found § 152-1 was explicitly discriminatory on its face because it applied only to housing for persons with disabilities and the City offered no non-discriminatory justification. The court granted summary judgment for plaintiffs on their disparate treatment claims under the FHA, ADA, and RHA, and entered a permanent injunction prohibiting enforcement of the distance requirement.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Disparate impact challenge to City Code § 163-66B regarding group family household zoning restrictions
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiffs failed to put forward sufficient measured proof to state a prima facie case that § 163-66B was discriminatory under a disparate impact theory.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request for reasonable accommodation in the form of a waiver or modification of City zoning ordinances and certificate of occupancy requirements to permit operation of Serenity House as a single-family residence or group family household
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found plaintiffs' reasonable accommodation claims under the FHA, RHA, and ADA were not yet ripe because plaintiffs had failed to seek a zoning variance through the City's prescribed administrative process prior to filing suit. The court held that plaintiffs were required to exhaust the City's administrative remedies and allow the City to reach a final decision on Serenity House's proper categorization before federal claims could be adjudicated.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claims under ADA Title II (42 U.S.C. § 12132), Rehabilitation Act of 1973 (29 U.S.C. § 791 et seq.), 42 U.S.C. § 1983, Fourteenth Amendment substantive due process, New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (N.J.S.A. 10:5-1 et seq.), and New Jersey Civil Rights Act (N.J.S.A. 10:6-1 et seq.)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted defendant's cross-motion for summary judgment on all non-FHA claims except the NJLAD claim, which was remanded to state court for lack of subject matter jurisdiction. The § 1983 and substantive due process claims were dismissed as not ripe because the City's zoning authorities had not reached a final, definitive position on how they would apply the regulations to Serenity House.

case_name: Ricky Kamdem-Ouaffo v. Plaza Square Apartments
accommodation_description: The underlying accommodation or discrimination claim is not described in the case text; the complaint is referenced only generically as alleging 'housing discrimination under the Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3601, et seq.' The current proceeding concerns only the procedural motion to vacate orders and reinstate dismissed claims.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's Rule 60(b) motion to modify or vacate prior dismissal orders because his requests were moot, he failed to demonstrate the exceptional circumstances required for Rule 60(b)(6) relief, and the court lacked subject matter jurisdiction to reinstate claims plaintiff had voluntarily dismissed.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Ricky Kamdem-Ouaffo brought a Rule 60(b) and Rule 41 motion seeking to modify or vacate the court's June 2019 and March 2020 orders—which had dismissed his FHA housing discrimination complaint with prejudice—and to reinstate claims he had voluntarily dismissed against three individual defendants. The court denied the motion on three independent grounds: (1) plaintiff's requests were moot because the Third Circuit had already resolved the relevant issues on two prior appeals; (2) plaintiff failed to identify the exceptional circumstances required for extraordinary Rule 60(b)(6) relief; and (3) the court lacked subject matter jurisdiction to reinstate the voluntarily dismissed claims.
key_cases_cited: Kamdem-Ouaffo v. Plaza Square Apartments (Plaza II), 840 F. App'x 715 (3d Cir. 2021)
In re ICL Holding Co., 802 F.3d 547 (3d Cir. 2015)
Coltec Indus., Inc. v. Hobgood, 280 F.3d 262 (3d Cir. 2002)
In re Bath & Kitchen Fixtures Antitrust Litig., 535 F.3d 161 (3d Cir. 2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not specified; original complaint alleged housing discrimination under FHA but specific claims not detailed in this opinion
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked subject matter jurisdiction to reinstate voluntarily dismissed claims against the Dismissed Defendants because a notice of voluntary dismissal extinguishes the action and deprives the court of jurisdiction over further proceedings on those claims. The original claims against Plaza were dismissed with prejudice on the merits and cannot be refiled.

source_file: 9804772_2021_LIVINGSTONE v. HUGO BOSS STORE, ATLANTIC CITY, NJ_njd
case_name: Livingstone v. Hugo Boss Store, Atlantic City, NJ
accommodation_description: No housing accommodation was requested. Plaintiff sought removal of a trespass ban from the Borgata Hotel Casino and $40 million in damages, claiming the ban was retaliation for his having previously filed FHA and other federal lawsuits against his landlord and university, respectively.
key_holding: The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss in their entirety, finding that plaintiff failed to state plausible claims under the FHA, the Civil Rights Act, or any of his numerous other federal and state law theories, because the FHA retaliation claim failed as defendants had no involvement in plaintiff's housing, and racial discrimination allegations were conclusory.
brief_summary: Michael Livingstone, a Black man of West African descent, filed suit against Hugo Boss entities, the Borgata Hotel Casino, and a Hugo Boss sales employee after being banned from the Borgata following repeated, escalating attempts to pursue a romantic relationship with the employee despite her clear rejections. Plaintiff asserted sixteen categories of claims including retaliation under the FHA, racial discrimination, ADA retaliation, and numerous state law claims, all stemming from his ban and the employee's online search of his name. The court granted all defendants' motions to dismiss, finding that the FHA retaliation claim failed because defendants were not involved in renting or selling housing to plaintiff, the racial discrimination claim lacked any factual nexus between plaintiff's ban and his race, and all remaining claims were legally deficient or implausible on their face.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that defendants interfered with his right to rent or sell housing. The FHA protects individuals in relation to the sale or rental of housing accommodations, and defendants are not involved with renting or selling housing to plaintiff. Retaliation claim under § 3617 requires interference with FHA-protected housing rights, which plaintiff did not allege.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: First Amendment retaliation for filing federal lawsuits; Title VII retaliation (employee protection); ADA retaliation (employee protection); Title VI racial discrimination; Title II public accommodations racial discrimination; federal invasion of privacy; New Jersey Personal Information Privacy and Protection Act; New Jersey invasion of privacy and intrusion upon seclusion; New Jersey stalking and cyber-stalking; identity theft; tortious interference with economic relations; negligence and gross negligence; civil harassment and intentional infliction of emotional distress; defamation and false light; breach of implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing; abuse of power and abuse of process; negligent training and supervision
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to state plausible claims under multiple non-FHA statutes and state law theories. First Amendment retaliation requires government action; Title VII and ADA retaliation require employee status; Title VI requires federal financial assistance nexus; Title II requires state notice compliance; federal privacy tort does not exist; New Jersey privacy claims fail due to lack of reasonable expectation of privacy in public information; stalking claims lack factual support; identity theft requires impersonation; tortious interference requires prospective economic relationship; negligence claims fail on duty and causation; defamation requires false factual assertions (not opinions); breach of contract requires valid contract; abuse of process applies only to court proceedings; negligent training/supervision fail on negligence elements.

case_name: Jessica Berk v. Ritz Carlton Condominium Association et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought to replace ADA claims with FHA claims, but no specific accommodation request is identified in the proposed amendment.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's motion to amend because she failed to show good cause under Rule 16(b)(4) and because amendment would cause undue delay and prejudice to defendants, as plaintiff admitted she possessed the same facts underlying her proposed amendment for over a year.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Jessica Berk, proceeding pro se, moved for leave to amend her complaint to add Fair Housing Act claims to replace her Americans with Disabilities Act claims against the Ritz Condominiums Association and other defendants; the court denied the motion, finding plaintiff failed to show good cause under Rule 16(b) and that amendment would cause undue delay and prejudice after more than a year of litigation.
key_cases_cited: Premier Comp Sols., LLC v. UPMC, 970 F.3d 316 (3d Cir. 2020)
Race Tires Am., Inc. v. Hoosier Racing Tire Corp., 614 F.3d 57 (3d Cir. 2010)
Mullin v. Balicki, 875 F.3d 140 (3d Cir. 2017)
Foman v. Davis, 371 U.S. 178 (1962)
Lorenz v. CSX Corp., 1 F.3d 1406 (3d Cir. 1993)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unspecified claims under the ADA; plaintiff alleged verbal abuse and sought relief under the Americans with Disabilities Act
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied plaintiff's motion to amend the complaint to add FHA claims based on lack of good cause under Rule 16(b)(4) (failure to show diligence—plaintiff sought to add new legal theories more than one year after the scheduling deadline based on the same facts), undue delay and prejudice under Rule 15(a)(2), and the moving-target approach to litigation. The court did not reach the merits of any proposed FHA claim because the motion to amend was procedurally barred.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA), New Jersey Truth-in-Consumer Contract Warranty and Notice Act (NJTCCWNA), right of publicity/misappropriation of likeness, and invasion of privacy through public disclosure of private facts
fha_claims.reasoning: Defendant qualifies for Section 230 immunity as an interactive computer service provider publishing information originating from third parties. Section 230 bars all four claims (FCRA, NJTCCWNA, right of publicity, and invasion of privacy) because they seek to hold Defendant liable for publishing third-party information on its website, which falls squarely within Section 230's immunity.

case_name: Michael A. D'Antonio v. Borough of Allendale, et al.
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request; case concerns land development dispute and municipal interference with property development, not disability accommodation
key_holding: Motion for reconsideration denied where plaintiff failed to identify intervening change in law, new evidence, or clear error of law, and merely attempted to relitigate previously rejected arguments regarding standing and preclusion of his FHA claims.
brief_summary: Michael D'Antonio, a developer, sued the Borough of Allendale and other defendants alleging they interfered with his attempts to build affordable housing on a property and ultimately evicted him, asserting claims including under the Fair Housing Act. The Court denied D'Antonio's motion for reconsideration of the dismissal of his Third Amended Complaint, finding he lacked standing to bring claims on behalf of a corporation, his claims were precluded, and he failed to state a viable claim.
key_cases_cited: N. River Ins. Co. v. CIGNA Reinsurance Co., 52 F.3d 1194 (3d Cir. 1995)
ABS Brokerage Servs. v. Penson Fin. Servs., Inc., 2010 WL 3257992 (D.N.J. Aug. 16, 2010)
Wayne Land & Mineral Grp., LLC v. Del. River Basin Comm'n, 959 F.3d 569 (3d Cir. 2020)
Grimm v. Borough of Norristown, 226 F. Supp. 2d 606 (E.D. Pa. 2002)
Lombreglia v. Sunbeam Prod., Inc., 2021 WL 118932 (D.N.J. Jan. 13, 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act claims (§ 3604), RICO (18 U.S.C. §§ 1961–1968), fraud statutes, and Title VII claims related to alleged interference with land development and eviction
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff lacked standing because the Subject Property was owned by Calm Corporation, not Plaintiff himself, and a corporation must bring suit on its own behalf. Additionally, Plaintiff was precluded from bringing claims already fully litigated under Rooker-Feldman, Entire Controversy, Res Judicata, and Collateral Estoppel doctrines, and failed to state a claim under Rule 8 and 9.

case_name: Selvaggi v. Point Pleasant Beach Borough
accommodation_description: Not a traditional accommodation request; plaintiffs sought to enjoin a municipal short-term rental ordinance that they alleged had a disparate impact on families with children and other FHA-protected groups by restricting rentals of less than seven days in summer and less than one month in winter, thereby reducing availability of home-like rental accommodations favored by family vacationers.
key_holding: The court granted a limited preliminary injunction enjoining the Borough's Ordinance's overbroad definition of 'Rental' as violating plaintiffs' fundamental right to privacy under the New Jersey Constitution, while denying injunctive relief on all federal claims—including substantive due process, procedural due process, equal protection, and FHA disparate impact—because plaintiffs failed to show a likelihood of success on any of those claims.
brief_summary: California-resident property owners in Point Pleasant Beach, New Jersey challenged a Borough ordinance (No. 2021-33) that regulated and restricted short-term rentals, seeking a preliminary injunction on grounds including unconstitutionality, ultra vires, and violations of the FHA. The court granted a narrow preliminary injunction solely on New Jersey constitutional privacy grounds, severing and limiting the Ordinance's definition of 'Rental' to compensated use, because the original definition—which covered non-compensated use by non-owners—overbreadly swept in normal activities like family visits. On all federal claims, including FHA disparate impact based on familial status, the court found no likelihood of success because short-term vacation rental properties do not qualify as 'dwellings' under the FHA, there is no fundamental right to rent property, and the Ordinance passes rational basis review.
key_cases_cited: Weisenberg v. Town Bd. of Shelter Island, 404 F. Supp. 3d 720 (E.D.N.Y. 2019)
Slidewaters LLC v. Washington State Dep't of Lab. & Indus., 4 F.4th 747 (9th Cir. 2021)
Village of Willowbrook v. Olech, 528 U.S. 562 (2000)
Nekrilov v. City of Jersey City, 528 F. Supp. 3d 252 (D.N.J. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged that Ordinance No. 2021-33 regulating short-term rentals has a disparate impact on families with children and groups protected by the FHA by making unavailable short-term residential rentals that uniquely accommodate family visitors and vacationers.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found no likelihood of success on the FHA claim because the complaint did not allege that plaintiffs' properties were being used by renters for long-term stays such that they could be considered the renters' residence under the FHA. The FHA defines 'dwelling' as a place 'intended to be used for living, rather than merely visiting,' and short-term vacation rentals do not meet this definition. Plaintiffs provided no case law supporting the claim that short-term rental ordinances violate the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Substantive due process (federal and state), procedural due process, equal protection, ultra vires (state law), and New Jersey Law Against Discrimination claims.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted a limited preliminary injunction on the state substantive due process claim under the New Jersey Civil Rights Act, finding that the Ordinance's overbroad definition of 'Rental' infringes on plaintiffs' fundamental right to privacy under the New Jersey Constitution by prohibiting property owners from allowing family and friends to use their homes without compensation. However, the court denied injunctive relief on the federal substantive due process claim (rational basis review), ultra vires claim (within municipal licensing authority), procedural due process claim (no protected property interest in rental certificate), and equal protection claim (no similarly situated comparators for 'class of one' theory). The court severed the offending language and limited the definition of 'Rental' to 'the use of a residence by someone other than the owner where funds are transferred for said use.'

source_file: 9806665_2022_OXFORD HOUSE, INC. v. TOWNSHIP OF NORTH BERGEN_njd
case_name: Oxford House, Inc. v. Township of North Bergen
accommodation_description: Oxford House, a recovery residence operator, sought a Certificate of Occupancy to operate a six-person group home for men recovering from substance abuse in a two-family dwelling zoned for single-family use.
key_holding: Plaintiff failed to establish likelihood of success on the merits because Defendant's denial of the Certificate of Occupancy was based on a neutral application of the Community Residence provision requiring single-family dwelling placement for persons with disabilities, and Plaintiff presented no evidence that discriminatory purpose motivated the denial.
brief_summary: Oxford House, Inc. sued Township of North Bergen seeking a preliminary injunction to compel issuance of a Certificate of Occupancy for a group home for recovering addicts in a two-family dwelling, alleging violations of the FHA, ADA, and NJLAD. The Court denied the motion because Plaintiff failed to show likelihood of success—Defendant's denial was based on neutral application of a state zoning provision requiring single-family placement for disabled residents, not discriminatory intent, and Plaintiff presented no evidence of disparate impact.
key_cases_cited: Oxford House-Evergreen v. City of Plainfield, 769 F. Supp. 1329 (D.N.J. 1991)
Oxford House, Inc. v. Twp. of Cherry Hill, 799 F. Supp. 450 (D.N.J. 1992)
United States v. Borough of Audubon, 797 F. Supp. 353 (D.N.J. 1991)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Certificate of Occupancy (COO) for operation of Oxford House in two-family dwelling
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish that Defendant's denial of the COO was motivated by discriminatory purpose or intent based on the prospective residents' status as handicapped. Defendant's denial was based on a neutral interpretation of the Community Residence provision and the Oxford House literature indicating single-family dwellings were required, not discriminatory animus toward recovering addicts.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Certificate of Occupancy (COO) for operation of Oxford House in two-family dwelling
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie disparate impact claim because Defendant acknowledged the prospective residents as the functional equivalent of a family and stated the COO would have been approved for a single-family dwelling. Plaintiff provided no statistical or other evidence showing Defendant's decision had greater adverse impact on a protected group.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claim (42 U.S.C. § 12132); NJLAD claim (N.J.S.A. § 10:5-12.5)
fha_claims.disposition: NJLAD claim dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction; ADA claim analyzed under FHA framework
fha_claims.reasoning: NJLAD § 10:5-12.5(a) claims may only be enforced in New Jersey Superior Court, not federal court, creating a bar to subject matter jurisdiction. ADA claim was analyzed under the same FHA framework and failed on the same merits (no discriminatory purpose or disparate impact shown).

case_name: Alphonse Edouard v. City of Long Branch and John Butow
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges property tax assessment discrimination based on race, ethnicity, and religion rather than requesting a reasonable accommodation
key_holding: The Tax Injunction Act bars federal jurisdiction over Plaintiff's FHA § 3605 claim because New Jersey provides adequate state remedies for challenging tax assessments, and even on the merits, Plaintiff failed to establish intentional discrimination or disparate impact as the property assessment cards contain no reference to race, ethnicity, or religion.
brief_summary: Alphonse Edouard, a Haitian American property owner, sued the City of Long Branch and its tax assessor alleging they discriminated against him by assessing his condominium at a higher value than Caucasian neighbors and denying him access to information about his assessment based on his race, ethnicity, and religion. The court granted summary judgment for defendants, holding that the Tax Injunction Act bars federal jurisdiction because adequate state remedies exist, and alternatively that Plaintiff failed to demonstrate intentional discrimination or disparate impact as the assessment records contain no reference to protected characteristics.
key_cases_cited: Fair Assessment in Real Estate Ass'n, Inc. v. McNary, 454 U.S. 100 (1981)
Mt. Holly Gardens Citizens in Action, Inc. v. Twp. of Mt. Holly, 658 F.3d 375 (3d Cir. 2011)
Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986)
Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242 (1986)
Rosewell v. LaSalle National Bank, 450 U.S. 503 (1981)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish intentional discrimination or disparate impact based on race or religion. The property assessment records contain no reference to race, ethnicity, or religion; plaintiff could not identify other similarly situated residents whose assessments were affected based on protected class status; and defendants provided legitimate, non-discriminatory explanations for the assessments. Additionally, the claim is barred by the Tax Injunction Act as a challenge to state tax procedures.

source_file: 9807546_2022_VETERAN RELOCATION PROJECT, LLC v. BOROUGH OF BRADLEY BEACH_njd
case_name: Veteran Relocation Project, LLC v. Borough of Bradley Beach
race_if_mentioned: Indian descent (intended buyer Anu Garrison); Plaintiff Marchese's race also referenced
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; plaintiff-developer claims municipality discriminated against them in property development because of intended buyer's race (Indian descent).
key_holding: The Court denied the motion to dismiss Count I (FHA discrimination) finding plaintiff-developer had standing to sue because they planned to develop housing for a protected class member (Indian national) whose sale was allegedly thwarted by discriminatory municipal conduct; Count II (NJLAD) was dismissed for lack of federal jurisdiction over municipal land use discrimination claims.
brief_summary: Veteran Relocation Project, LLC and James Marchese sued the Borough of Bradley Beach and individual officials claiming the municipality discriminated against them during a construction project because the property was being sold to Anu Garrison, a woman of Indian descent. The Court denied the motion to dismiss the FHA discrimination claim (Count I), finding plaintiffs had standing as third-party beneficiaries of FHA protections, but dismissed the NJLAD claim (Count II) for lack of federal jurisdiction over municipal land use discrimination claims under state law.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Eastampton Ctr., L.L.C. v. Township of Eastampton

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges discrimination in terms, conditions, or privileges of sale based on race, color, and national origin.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiffs pled sufficient facts to raise a plausible claim for relief under Title VIII. Plaintiffs, who are not members of a protected class, have standing to bring Title VIII claims where their plans to develop housing for a protected class member (Anu Garrison, a woman of Indian descent) are thwarted by allegedly discriminatory practices. Motion to Dismiss denied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: NJLAD discrimination claim under N.J.S.A. § 10:5-12.5 (discrimination in land use regulation by municipality); tortious interference with contract; tortious interference with prospective business advantage; defamation
fha_claims.reasoning: Federal district court lacks subject matter jurisdiction over NJLAD claims of discrimination in land use policy by a municipality arising under N.J.S.A. § 10:5-12.5. New Jersey Legislature mandated that such claims be brought in New Jersey Superior Court, and diversity and supplemental jurisdiction are improper. Count II dismissed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Tortious interference with contract; tortious interference with prospective business advantage; defamation
fha_claims.reasoning: Tortious interference with contract (Count III): Motion to Dismiss denied as to Borough of Bradley Beach and Kenneth Triano; granted as to Michael Affuso. Plaintiffs alleged sufficient facts that Triano acted outside scope of employment (harassing employees, refusing to allow storage without justification, ordering stop work beyond applicable order). Affuso's conduct was within scope of employment. Tortious interference with prospective business advantage (Count IV): Same result as Count III. Defamation (Count V): Motion to Dismiss granted. Plaintiffs failed to allege false statements of fact with sufficient specificity; vague references to Zoning Board members 'hurling abuse' and comments about 'people' do not satisfy pleading requirements.

case_name: Adams v. DMG Park, LLC
accommodation_description: No accommodation request was made; this case involves intentional race-based discrimination in housing, including being lied to about available units and subjected to a campaign of harassment because Plaintiffs are African American.
key_holding: The court dismissed claims against DMG Park and DMG Investments due to impermissible group pleading and statute of limitations, but allowed Plaintiffs leave to amend within 30 days to cure these deficiencies; the court denied the motion to compel arbitration and retained supplemental jurisdiction over parking garage claims.
brief_summary: Gerald Adams and Julia Jones, an African American couple, sued DMG Investments LLC, DMG Park LLC, DMG Property Management, and the One Park Condominium Association alleging race-based housing discrimination under the FHA and New Jersey LAD, claiming Defendants lied about available units because of their race and subjected them to ongoing harassment after purchase. The court granted in part Defendants' motions to dismiss for impermissible group pleading and time-barred claims, but denied the motion to compel arbitration and allowed Plaintiffs leave to amend.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman
Guidotti v. Legal Helpers Debt Resol., L.L.C.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs' housing discrimination claim (Count One under FHA) against DMG Investments was dismissed for impermissible group pleading under Rule 8. Plaintiffs failed to allege specific facts establishing DMG Investments' personal involvement in discriminatory conduct, relying instead on conclusory allegations that unnamed individuals were agents of all three entity defendants without setting forth specific facts supporting this belief.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs' housing discrimination claim (Count One under FHA) against DMG Park was dismissed as time-barred. The sole discriminatory event involving DMG Park occurred before Plaintiffs purchased their unit, and the complaint does not plausibly allege a continuing violation because Plaintiffs failed to adequately plead that individual wrongdoers were agents of the defendants working together in a pattern of discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs' retaliation claim (Count Three under FHA) against DMG Investments was dismissed for impermissible group pleading. Plaintiffs failed to allege specific facts establishing DMG Investments' personal involvement in any retaliatory conduct, instead relying on conclusory allegations that unnamed individuals were agents of all three entity defendants.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs' retaliation claim (Count Three under FHA) against DMG Park was dismissed as time-barred. The court did not reach the merits of the retaliation claim because the underlying discriminatory conduct occurred before the statute of limitations period and Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege a continuing violation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of contract and negligence claims relating to parking garage maintenance and operation; New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (LAD) housing discrimination and retaliation claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs' breach of contract and negligence claims (Counts Four and Five) against DMG Park were dismissed for impermissible group pleading because Plaintiffs failed to allege that DMG Park engaged in any wrongdoing related to the parking garage claims. The court noted Plaintiffs explained these claims were collectively pled 'until it is determined who is responsible' but Plaintiffs must comply with Rule 8 at the pleading stage.

source_file: 9808330_2023_THE HANSEN FOUNDATION, INC. v. CITY OF ATLANTIC CITY_njd
case_name: The Hansen Foundation, Inc. v. City of Atlantic City
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs sought to operate a group home for women recovering from drug and alcohol addiction in Atlantic City's R-2 residential zone, requesting that the City treat the facility as a permitted use or grant a reasonable accommodation under the FHA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act to exempt the facility from zoning provisions that otherwise rendered it noncompliant.
key_holding: The court granted in part and denied in part the City Defendants' motion to dismiss, dismissing the NJLAD claim for lack of jurisdiction while allowing the FHA, ADA, Rehabilitation Act, NJCRA, and MLUL claims to proceed, and converted Defendant Oliver's motion to dismiss into a motion for summary judgment with respect to the settlement and release defense.
brief_summary: The Hansen Foundation, a group home for women recovering from drug and alcohol addiction, brought suit against the City of Atlantic City challenging the city's zoning enforcement that deemed their facility noncompliant. This was a second round of litigation (Hansen II) following Hansen I, in which the court had previously resolved disparate treatment and disparate impact claims but declined to rule on other federal claims as unripe. The court in this opinion dismissed the NJLAD count for lack of jurisdiction, denied dismissal of the NJCRA and federal FHA/ADA/RHA claims, and converted the state official defendant's motion to dismiss into a motion for summary judgment to address a prior settlement and release defense.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Ashcroft v. Iqbal
The Hansen Foundation, Inc. v. City of Atlantic City, 504 F. Supp. 3d 327 (D.N.J. 2020)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Zoning accommodation to permit operation of a group home for women recovering from drug and alcohol addiction in the City's R-2 residential zone, which the City had effectively banned
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the City Defendants' motion to dismiss the FHA claim (Count One), finding that the plaintiffs had adequately pleaded a plausible claim under the Fair Housing Act. The court did not reach the substantive merits of the reasonable accommodation claim, as the motion to dismiss was denied and the claim proceeds.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II (42 U.S.C. § 12132), Rehabilitation Act § 504 (29 U.S.C. § 794(a)), NJCRA (N.J.S.A. 10:6-1, 6-2), NJLAD (N.J.S.A. 10:5-12(d) and (g)), MLUL (N.J.S.A. 40:55D-10(g)(1)–(2))
fha_claims.reasoning: Count 5 (NJLAD) was dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because the New Jersey Superior Court has exclusive jurisdiction over discrimination claims in land use policy under N.J.S.A. § 10:5-12.5. Counts 2, 3, 4, and 6 (ADA, RHA, NJCRA, and MLUL) survived the motion to dismiss and proceed.

source_file: 9808639_2015_Texas Dept. of Housing and Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc._scotus
case_name: Texas Dept. of Housing and Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc.
accommodation_description: ICP alleged the Department's allocation of low-income housing tax credits perpetuated segregated housing patterns by concentrating credits in predominantly black inner-city areas rather than predominantly white suburban areas.
key_holding: The Supreme Court held that disparate-impact claims are cognizable under the FHA, but simultaneously established strong safeguards limiting such claims—requiring plaintiffs to show causation between a specific policy and any statistical disparity, and preventing liability based on facially neutral policies that serve substantial legitimate interests, thereby rejecting the ICP's theory that mere statistical disparities in where low-income housing is built can establish liability.
brief_summary: The Inclusive Communities Project sued the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs alleging that its allocation of low-income housing tax credits perpetuated segregation by concentrating too many credits in predominantly black inner-city census tracts and too few in predominantly white suburban areas. The Supreme Court affirmed that disparate-impact claims are cognizable under the Fair Housing Act, but held that ICP's claims must be evaluated under the robust causation requirement and limited safeguards the Court announced, effectively reinstating dismissal of the case.
key_cases_cited: Griggs v. Duke Power Co., 401 U.S. 424 (1971)
Smith v. City of Jackson, 544 U.S. 228 (2005)
Ricci v. DeStefano, 557 U.S. 557 (2009)
Huntington v. Huntington Branch, 488 U.S. 15 (1988)
Wards Cove Packing Co. v. Atonio, 490 U.S. 642 (1989)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Allocation of low-income housing tax credits; plaintiff challenged the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs' disproportionate allocation of credits to predominantly black inner-city areas versus predominantly white suburban neighborhoods, seeking modification of selection criteria to encourage suburban construction.
fha_claims.reasoning: The Supreme Court held that disparate-impact claims are cognizable under the FHA based on the statute's results-oriented language ('otherwise make unavailable'), analogy to Title VII and ADEA precedent, and Congress's 1988 ratification of disparate-impact liability. The Court affirmed the Fifth Circuit's recognition of disparate-impact liability but remanded for application of proper causality and business necessity standards, cautioning that plaintiffs must establish a causal nexus between the defendant's policy and the disparate impact, and that defendants may defend by proving the policy is necessary to achieve a substantial, legitimate, nondiscriminatory interest.

source_file: 9808640_2015_Texas Dept. of Housing and Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc._scotus
case_name: Texas Dept. of Housing and Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc.
accommodation_description: This case does not involve a reasonable accommodation request; it concerns whether the Fair Housing Act authorizes disparate-impact claims challenging facially neutral state policies that result in racial segregation in affordable housing site selection.
key_holding: The Court of Appeals erred in applying heightened scrutiny to the state's asserted racial benign motives, but the FHA does authorize disparate-impact claims; the case is remanded for application of proper standards.
brief_summary: Inclusive Communities Project sued the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs claiming that its method of allocating Low-Income Housing Tax Credits perpetuated racial segregation by concentrating affordable housing in predominantly Black neighborhoods. The Supreme Court affirmed that the Fair Housing Act authorizes disparate-impact claims under § 3604(a), but remanded for the Fifth Circuit to apply proper causation standards rather than heightened scrutiny.
key_cases_cited: Griggs v. Duke Power Co., 401 U.S. 424 (1971)
Smith v. City of Jackson, 544 U.S. 228 (2005)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Ricci v. DeStefano, 557 U.S. 557 (2009)
Parents Involved in Community Schools v. Seattle School Dist. No. 1, 551 U.S. 701 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 56 / Summary Judgment affirmed on appeal
fha_claims.reasoning: The Supreme Court majority held that the Fair Housing Act encompasses disparate-impact liability under 42 U.S.C. §§ 3604(a) and 3605(a). The Court applied the disparate-impact framework to the Department's allocation of low-income housing tax credits, finding that the Department's practices had a disparate impact on minorities and that the Department failed to demonstrate that its allocation decisions served substantial, legitimate, nondiscriminatory interests that could not be achieved through less discriminatory means.

source_file: 9809373_2023_VERITAS RECOVERY CENTER, LLC v. CITY OF SOUTH AMBOY_njd
case_name: Veritas Recovery Center, LLC v. City of South Amboy
accommodation_description: Veritas Recovery Center, a for-profit substance abuse treatment facility operator, seeks to enjoin enforcement of a municipal ordinance limiting alcohol/substance abuse treatment facilities to 31,000 square feet so it can expand to serve additional disabled patients.
key_holding: The court denied the preliminary injunction because plaintiff failed to make a clear showing of immediate irreparable harm, offering only bald assertions about disabled persons needing treatment without identifying waitlist numbers, wait times, or availability of alternative facilities.
brief_summary: Veritas Recovery Center, a for-profit drug and alcohol rehabilitation facility operator, sued the City of South Amboy seeking a preliminary injunction to prevent enforcement of an ordinance limiting substance abuse treatment facilities to 31,000 square feet. The court denied the motion, finding that plaintiff failed to demonstrate irreparable harm because its assertions about disabled persons needing treatment were unsupported by evidence of waitlist size, wait times, or availability of alternative treatment options.
key_cases_cited: South Camden Citizens in Action v. N.J. Dep't of Envtl. Prot., 274 F.3d 771 (3d Cir. 2001)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Expansion of the VRC Facility footprint to accommodate additional residential patients and outpatient services; relief from the 31,000 square feet rental floor area limitation imposed by Ordinance No. 8-2013 for alcohol/substance abuse treatment facilities
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the preliminary injunction motion on the threshold ground that plaintiff failed to demonstrate irreparable harm—a prerequisite to injunctive relief—without reaching the substantive merits of the FHA reasonable accommodation claim. The court found plaintiff's assertions about disabled persons facing death without expansion were unsupported by specific evidence regarding waitlist size, wait times, or availability of alternative treatment facilities.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), Rehabilitation Act § 504, Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses (U.S. and New Jersey Constitutions), Municipal Land Use Law (N.J.S.A. 40:55D-62(a)), New Jersey Law Against Discrimination
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the preliminary injunction motion on the threshold ground of failure to demonstrate irreparable harm, without reaching the substantive merits of any non-FHA statutory or constitutional claims. The denial was based on procedural insufficiency in the preliminary injunction analysis, not on the merits of the underlying claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Ordinance 2021-33 regulating short-term rental use of residential properties; challenge to inspection and licensing requirements; challenge to definition of 'Rental' extending to non-paid use; Dormant Commerce Clause challenge to alleged discrimination against non-resident out-of-state owners
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted plaintiffs' motion to amend their complaint to add factual allegations regarding the practical application of the ordinance during the 2022 Summer Rental Season and a Dormant Commerce Clause theory. The motion to dismiss was terminated pending the amended complaint. The FHA claim (Count Three) was alleged in the original complaint but this opinion addresses only the procedural motion to amend, not the merits of any FHA theory.

source_file: 9810407_2023_QUANTUM BEHAVIORAL HEALTH, LLC v. TOWNSHIP OF BERKELEY_njd
case_name: Quantum Behavioral Health, LLC v. Township of Berkeley
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs seek to operate a residential drug and alcohol treatment facility on property located in a residential zone, requiring zoning permits and use variance approval from the municipal zoning board.
key_holding: The Court denied the motion for preliminary injunction because Plaintiffs failed to make a clear showing of immediate irreparable harm, failing to identify how many would-be patients would be denied housing, the impact of any housing shortage, or the availability of treatment at competing facilities.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Quantum Behavioral Health, LLC and Allard21, LLC sued Township of Berkeley and its Zoning Board seeking to operate a residential drug and alcohol treatment facility for recovering addicts with disabilities, alleging the denial of zoning permits and use variance was discriminatory under the FHA and ADA. The Court denied Plaintiffs' motion for a preliminary injunction because they failed to demonstrate immediate irreparable harm, providing only conclusory assertions about housing denial without evidence of patient impact or alternative treatment availability.
key_cases_cited: South Camden Citizens in Action v. N.J. Dep't of Envtl. Prot., 274 F.3d 771 (3d Cir. 2001)
Veritas Recovery Ctr. v. City of South Amboy, Civ. No. 23-2420 (D.N.J. May 4, 2023)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Zoning permit and use variance approval to operate a substance use disorder treatment and residential facility for recovering alcoholics and addicts with disabilities at the Property (formerly a nursing home)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the preliminary injunction motion on the threshold ground that plaintiffs failed to demonstrate irreparable harm, not on the merits of the FHA claim. The court found plaintiffs made only bald assertions without identifying how many patients would be denied housing or the impact on the protected group, and did not address the substantive FHA reasonable accommodation analysis.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), 42 U.S.C. § 1983, New Jersey Constitution, New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (LAD), New Jersey Municipal Land Use Law (MLUL)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the preliminary injunction motion on the threshold ground that plaintiffs failed to demonstrate irreparable harm, without reaching the merits of any non-FHA claims. The court did not substantively analyze the ADA, § 1983, LAD, or MLUL theories.

source_file: 9810891_2023_THE HANSEN FOUNDATION, INC. v. CITY OF ATLANTIC CITY_njd
case_name: The Hansen Foundation, Inc. v. City of Atlantic City
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs seek reasonable accommodation from Atlantic City's zoning requirements to permit operation of a Cooperative Sober Living Residence for women recovering from substance addiction, including a Certificate of Land Use Compliance.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for Defendant Holmes based on claim preclusion, finding that Plaintiffs' current Fair Housing Act, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act reasonable accommodation claims arose from the same transactions as prior litigation and were barred by the August 24, 2021 settlement agreement which released all claims relating to Plaintiffs' CSLRs that were or could have been asserted.
brief_summary: The Hansen Foundation and Hansen House LLC, operators of a sober living home for women in addiction recovery, sued Atlantic City, its Zoning Board, and the New Jersey Department of Community Affairs under the Fair Housing Act, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act, alleging the City refused to grant reasonable accommodations from zoning requirements. The court granted summary judgment for Defendant Holmes based on claim preclusion, finding that the reasonable accommodation claims were already resolved by a prior settlement agreement and could have been asserted in the earlier litigation.
key_cases_cited: Toscano v. Conn. Gen. Life Ins. Co., 288 F. App'x 36 (3d Cir. 2008)
Gotthelf v. Toyota Motor Sales, U.S.A., Inc., 2012 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 62045 (D.N.J. May 3, 2012)
Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986)
Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242 (1986)
Marino v. Indus. Crating Co., 358 F.3d 241 (3d Cir. 2004)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exemption from zoning ordinances and issuance of Certificate of Land Use Compliance (CLUC) to allow operation of Cooperative Sober Living Residence (CSLR) for women recovering from drug and alcohol addiction; treating CSLR residents as a 'single housekeeping unit' or functional equivalent of a family
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied claim preclusion doctrine, finding that the Fair Housing Act claim in the current litigation arises from the same transaction and occurrence as claims covered by the August 24, 2021 settlement agreement between plaintiffs and the DCA. The settlement agreement expressly released all claims 'relating to the licensing of Hansen's CSLRs, which were asserted, or could have been asserted' prior to the agreement, and plaintiffs' current FHA claim seeking a reasonable accommodation (CLUC issuance) was known to and could have been pursued by plaintiffs at the time of settlement.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) Title II claim seeking reasonable accommodation (CLUC issuance); Rehabilitation Act § 504 claim seeking reasonable accommodation (CLUC issuance)
fha_claims.reasoning: Counts Two (ADA) and Three (Rehabilitation Act) are precluded by the same settlement agreement and claim preclusion doctrine. Both claims seek the same remedy (CLUC issuance) and reasonable accommodation from the DCA that plaintiffs could have asserted prior to the August 24, 2021 settlement agreement.

case_name: Kimberley Steele v. Simone Neal, Armid Erneja, Hija Johnson, Director of Division of Family Development, Department of Human Services Division of Social Services Union County
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request can be identified; the complaint is too vague and conclusory to determine what accommodation, if any, plaintiff is seeking.
key_holding: The complaint fails to state an FHA claim because it does not allege facts suggesting plausible disparate treatment, disparate impact, or refusal to make reasonable accommodations, and the complaint is dismissed as a vague shotgun pleading that fails to comply with Rule 8.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Kimberley Steele filed a complaint against multiple defendants including Simone Neal and government agencies, selecting housing, civil rights, ADA, and constitutional claims on the civil cover sheet. The court dismissed the complaint without prejudice for failure to state a claim, finding it a vague shotgun pleading that failed to allege facts sufficient to state any plausible FHA claim, including a reasonable accommodation claim.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Hansen Found., Inc. v. City of Atl. City, 504 F. Supp. 3d 327 (D.N.J. 2020)
Schreane v. Seana, 506 F. App'x 120 (3d Cir. 2012)
Furgess v. Pennsylvania Dep't of Corr., 933 F.3d 285 (3d Cir. 2019)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges a housing claim under the FHA but does not specify the nature of the requested accommodation or relief sought.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to state a plausible FHA claim by not alleging facts supporting any of the three recognized FHA theories (disparate treatment, disparate impact, or reasonable accommodation) and did not cite to any FHA statute or provision.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Administrative Procedure Act claim, age discrimination claim under 42 U.S.C. § 12117 (ADA), constitutional claim, and civil rights prisoner petition claim.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to state plausible claims under the Administrative Procedure Act (which does not apply to state agencies), ADA Title I (no facts alleged regarding qualified individual status or disability-based discrimination), constitutional claims (no facts alleged), and civil rights prisoner petition claims (improper nature of suit code for non-prisoner).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Selective enforcement of zoning laws; defendants alleged they were singled out for enforcement of fence encroachment violation based on race/national origin while other neighbors were not cited for similar violations
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked federal question jurisdiction because the FHA claim was asserted only as a defense or counterclaim, not on the face of the plaintiff's well-pleaded complaint. Under the well-pleaded complaint rule, federal jurisdiction exists only when a federal question appears in the plaintiff's properly pleaded complaint, not in defenses or counterclaims. The court also found removal under 28 U.S.C. § 1443 failed because defendants did not demonstrate they were denied equal civil rights in terms of racial equality as required by that statute.

case_name: Jessica Berk and William Henry Kennedy v. Ritz Carlton Condominium Association, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff Berk requested to keep an emotional support cat named Gemini as a reasonable accommodation for her disabilities including mobility limitations and neurological conditions causing blackouts.
key_holding: The court dismissed most claims including the standalone FHA claims (Counts VIII and IX) for failure to state a viable claim, but permitted Plaintiff Berk's failure to accommodate claim under Count XI to proceed, along with interference claims under 42 U.S.C. § 3617.
brief_summary: Jessica Berk, a disabled Jewish woman who uses a cane or wheelchair and has an emotional support animal, sued the Ritz Carlton Condominium Association and fellow resident Stanley Maragoudakis alleging disability discrimination, harassment, and failure to accommodate. The court dismissed most claims including standalone FHA claims but allowed the failure to accommodate and interference claims under § 3617 to proceed against the Association.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Powell v. Indep. Blue Cross, Inc.
Livingstone v. Hugo Boss Store, Atl. City, NJ
Butler v. Sundo Cap., LLC

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to allow plaintiff entry to building when unable to swipe key card due to disability; charging fees for staff assistance with entry
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found allegations that Ritz staff refused entry and charged fees for assistance when plaintiff could not use key card due to disability may support § 3617 interference claim when coupled with other allegations; claim permitted to proceed against Ritz on behalf of Plaintiff Berk.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exemption from pet fees for emotional support cat (Gemini) as reasonable accommodation for disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied four-element test for failure to accommodate: (1) disability; (2) defendant's knowledge; (3) necessity of accommodation; (4) refusal. Court found allegations sufficient at pleading stage that Ritz knew of disability via social security determination, knew cat was emotional support animal, yet continued charging fees and threatened eviction; claim survives MTD for fees charged and paid.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1981 (race discrimination based on Jewish ancestry), § 1982 (property rights), § 1983 (due process), state tort claims (negligent infliction of emotional distress, intentional infliction of emotional distress, breach of contract, invasion of privacy)
fha_claims.reasoning: § 1981 claims dismissed: Plaintiff Kennedy failed to allege any protected class status; Plaintiff Berk alleged Jewish ancestry but failed to connect alleged conduct to contractual relationship or intentional discrimination by Ritz (only alleged failure to investigate another resident's conduct). § 1982 claims dismissed: no allegations of discrimination in purchasing, leasing, selling, or holding property. NIED claims dismissed: no duty of care established for Ritz to intervene in resident-to-resident conduct; allegations of emotional distress conclusory without physical or psychological symptoms. IIED claims dismissed: conduct not extreme and outrageous; failure to intervene insufficient. Invasion of privacy dismissed: photograph taken in public setting (boardwalk); no private aspect revealed. Breach of contract dismissed: governing documents do not impose duty to investigate or intervene in resident disputes.

source_file: 9811823_2024_FRANKLIN v. THE JERSEY CITY HOUSING AUTHORITY_njd
case_name: Edwina Franklin v. The Jersey City Housing Authority, Secretary, Department of Housing and Urban Development
accommodation_description: Cannot determine specific accommodation request from procedural opinion
key_holding: The court dismissed Plaintiff's motion for default judgment without prejudice because after filing the Consolidated and Amended Complaint, Plaintiff failed to obtain a new entry of default under Rule 55(a) before moving for default judgment.
brief_summary: Pro se Plaintiff Edwina Franklin filed a second motion for default judgment against the Jersey City Housing Authority and HUD, alleging Fair Housing Act and Equal Credit Opportunity Act violations in connection with her public housing. The court dismissed the motion without prejudice on procedural grounds, holding that because Plaintiff filed a Consolidated and Amended Complaint after the original default was entered, she was required to obtain a new entry of default before moving for default judgment under Rule 55.
key_cases_cited: Husain v. Casino Control Comm’n, 265 F. App’x 130 (3d Cir. 2008)
Nationwide Mut. Ins. Co. v. Starlight Ballroom Dance Club, Inc., 175 F. App’x 519 (3d Cir. 2006)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not specified in opinion
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the motion for default judgment without prejudice because plaintiff failed to obtain a new entry of default under Rule 55(a) after filing the Consolidated and Amended Complaint. The procedural defect prevented the court from reaching the merits of the underlying FHA claims.

case_name: Hilda T. Kennedy v. ESQ Capital III LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges that defendant harassed her, initiated eviction proceedings, and refused to make repairs based on her status as a disabled, elderly person.
key_holding: The court granted defendant's motion to dismiss because the claims were barred by res judicata from prior state court proceedings, and plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claims failed because she did not allege sufficient facts showing discriminatory intent, disparate impact, or a failure to reasonably accommodate her disability.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Hilda Kennedy sued her landlord ESQ Capital III LLC alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act, Americans with Disabilities Act, and Civil Rights Act based on disability discrimination, harassment, and failure to repair. The court granted defendant's motion to dismiss with prejudice, finding the claims were barred by res judicata from prior state court proceedings and that plaintiff failed to state a plausible FHA claim because she did not allege facts showing other tenants were treated differently or that defendant's actions had a discriminatory effect.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic v. Twombly

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Repair of toilet; general maintenance and habitability accommodations related to disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that the toilet repair issue or maintenance failures were connected to her disability or that she requested a reasonable accommodation. The complaint contains only conclusory allegations that Defendant's actions were based on disability without factual enhancement or nexus to the accommodation requested.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts supporting intentional discrimination based on disability or age. She did not allege that non-disabled or younger tenants received better treatment, did not allege discriminatory remarks, and did not establish a pattern of discriminatory behavior that would permit reasonable inference of discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's allegations that Defendant initiated a lawsuit and engaged in harassing behavior due to her disability status are conclusory and lack factual support. The complaint does not plausibly connect the alleged conduct to retaliation for exercising FHA rights.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) 42 U.S.C. § 12101 et seq., Civil Rights Act of 1866, state law harassment and abuse claims, landlord-tenant claims
fha_claims.reasoning: All claims are barred by res judicata as they arise from the same transaction and occurrence as prior state court cases (ATL-L-924-22 and ATL-L-3015-23) that were dismissed with prejudice on the merits. Additionally, to the extent any state law claims survive res judicata, the court would decline to exercise supplemental jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3) after dismissing all claims over which it has original jurisdiction.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation claim under New Jersey Conscientious Employee Protection Act (CEPA), N.J.S.A. 34:19-1 et seq., and breach of contract counterclaim
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie case of CEPA retaliation because she did not point to sufficient evidence of a reasonable belief that Connor's conduct violated law or public policy (fraud prong failed; Fair Housing Act discrimination claim lacked evidentiary support), did not establish protected whistleblowing activity (disputed whether she reported discrimination to HR), and failed to demonstrate that decisionmakers knew of her alleged protected activity. Additionally, Plaintiff failed to establish pretext for Defendant's stated reason (fraud investigations began five months before alleged whistleblowing). Breach of contract counterclaim succeeded on undisputed facts: Plaintiff received bonuses, failed to work 12 months as required, and did not repay them.

source_file: 9812208_2024_1940 ROUTE 9, LLC v. TOWNSHIP OF TOMS RIVER, NEW JERSEY_njd
case_name: 1940 Route 9, LLC v. Township of Toms River, New Jersey
accommodation_description: This is a discovery dispute regarding the Township's preparation of a Rule 30(b)(6) designee to testify about the Township's Fair Housing Policy and practices; no specific reasonable accommodation request is at issue.
key_holding: The court denied the motion to compel a continued deposition because the plaintiff's deposition topics were not noticed with reasonable particularity and the Township's designees were adequately prepared to answer questions within the scope of the properly noticed topics.
brief_summary: 1940 Route 9, LLC, a developer seeking to build housing for Orthodox Jewish families, sued the Township of Toms River alleging the Township improperly used eminent domain to prevent the development, in violation of the Fair Housing Act, RLUIPA, and constitutional rights. The court denied the plaintiff's motion to compel a continued Rule 30(b)(6) deposition, finding the Township's designees were adequately prepared and that many of the topics plaintiff sought to explore were not noticed with sufficient particularity.
key_cases_cited: Black Horse Lane Assoc., L.P. v. Dow Chem. Corp., 228 F.3d 275 (3d Cir. 2000)
