State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co. v. New Horizont, Inc., 250 F.R.D. 203 (E.D. Pa. 2008)
Costa v. County of Burlington, 254 F.R.D. 187 (D.N.J. 2008)
Private Solutions, Inc. v. SCMC, LLC, No. 15-3241, 2016 WL 8732078 (D.N.J. May 20, 2016)
Fifth Third Bank v. Westwood Zamias Ltd. P'ship, Civ. No. 18-143, 2019 WL 1383713 (W.D. Pa. Feb. 6, 2019)

source_file: 9812229_2024_OXFORD HOUSE, INC. v. TOWNSHIP OF NORTH BERGEN_njd
case_name: Oxford House, Inc. v. Township of North Bergen
accommodation_description: Oxford House, a substance abuse recovery residence operator, sought a Certificate of Occupancy to operate a group home for recovering addicts at 1109 8th Street, which the Township denied based on zoning ordinance interpretation.
key_holding: The court granted the motion to dismiss because Plaintiff's Amended Complaint failed to plead sufficient factual allegations from which a reasonable inference of discriminatory intent could be drawn, consisting only of conclusory allegations that the Township denied a Certificate of Occupancy for discriminatory reasons.
brief_summary: Oxford House, Inc., an operator of substance abuse recovery residences, sued Township of North Bergen after the Township denied its Certificate of Occupancy application to operate a six-person group home at 1109 8th Street, allegedly based on the Township's interpretation that the proposed use violated the New Jersey Community Residence statute. The court granted the Township's motion to dismiss, finding that the Amended Complaint failed to allege sufficient factual matter to support a plausible inference of discriminatory intent, consisting only of conclusory allegations without specific factual support.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Village of Arlington Heights v. Metropolitan Hous. Dev. Corp., 429 U.S. 252 (1977)
Cmty. Servs., Inc. v. Wind Gap Mun. Auth., 421 F.3d 170 (3d Cir. 2005)
Oxford House, Inc. v. Twp. of N. Bergen, No. 22-2336 (3d Cir. July 28, 2023)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Certificate of Occupancy for operation of Oxford House (sober living group home for individuals recovering from substance abuse)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead sufficient factual allegations supporting an inference of discriminatory intent. The complaint contained only conclusory allegations of discrimination without factual support. Defendant articulated a legitimate, non-discriminatory reason (Community Residence provision violation), and Plaintiff did not allege facts showing this was pretextual.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Certificate of Occupancy for operation of Oxford House (sober living group home for individuals recovering from substance abuse)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to adequately allege a disparate impact claim. The Amended Complaint does not contain the phrase 'disparate impact' and Plaintiff did not respond to Defendant's disparate impact arguments in its opposition brief, resulting in waiver of any such arguments.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) Title II claim; New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (NJLAD) claim
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA and NJLAD claims dismissed on the same grounds as FHA claims—failure to plead sufficient factual allegations supporting discriminatory intent or disparate impact. The court applied the same analytical framework to both FHA and ADA claims, finding them 'essentially the same.'

source_file: 9812254_2024_FRANKLIN v. THE JERSEY CITY HOUSING AUTHORITY_njd
case_name: Edwina Franklin v. The Jersey City Housing Authority, Secretary, Department of Housing and Urban Development
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested permission to use the mortgage she received under the HOPE VI program to purchase a second home; JCHA denied this request, which JCHA contends was based on the terms of the mortgage and note rather than any discriminatory motive.
key_holding: The court vacated the clerk's entry of default against JCHA upon finding good cause—no substantial prejudice to plaintiff, a meritorious defense, and non-culpable conduct—and denied plaintiff's third motion for default judgment as moot.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Edwina Franklin sued the Jersey City Housing Authority (JCHA) and HUD, alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act and the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, arising from JCHA's denial of her request to use a HOPE VI program mortgage to purchase a second home. After the Clerk entered default against JCHA for failure to respond, JCHA moved to vacate that default. The court granted JCHA's motion to vacate, finding that plaintiff would not be significantly prejudiced, JCHA articulated a meritorious defense (that the denial was based on mortgage terms rather than discriminatory animus), and JCHA's failure to respond was inadvertent rather than culpable.
key_cases_cited: Gold Kist, Inc. v. Laurinburg Oil Co., 756 F.2d 14 (3d Cir. 1985)
Mettle v. First Union Nat'l Bank, 279 F. Supp. 2d 598 (D.N.J. 2003)
Feliciano v. Reliant Tooling Co., Ltd., 691 F.2d 653 (3d Cir. 1982)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges JCHA denied her request to use a HOPE VI mortgage to purchase a second home
fha_claims.reasoning: The court vacated the entry of default against JCHA and allowed the case to proceed on the merits. JCHA articulated a viable defense that its denial was based on mortgage terms, not discriminatory animus. The complaint alleges FHA violations but the opinion does not specify which FHA theory applies or analyze the substantive legal standard.

source_file: 9816401_2022_Margaret McGuinn v. J.L Gray Company, Inc._nmd
case_name: United States of America, ex rel. Margaret McGuinn v. The J.L. Gray Company
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: The court granted plaintiff's motion to compel discovery, finding that defendants' reliance on a third-party FOIA request did not excuse their failure to respond to discovery obligations and that their general objections were impermissibly vague under Rules 33 and 34.
brief_summary: This is a qui tam False Claims Act case where relator Margaret McGuinn alleges that defendant J.L. Gray Company falsely certified compliance with the Fair Housing Act, Americans with Disabilities Act, and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act to obtain USDA Rural Development funding. The court granted plaintiff's motion to compel discovery, ordering defendants to provide complete supplemental responses to interrogatories and requests for production within 15-30 days, finding that defendants' general objections were improper and their reliance on a third-party FOIA request did not excuse their discovery failures.
key_cases_cited: Heuskin v. D&E Transp., LLC
King v. Gilbreath
Matter of Caswell Silver Family Tr.
Pulsecard, Inc. v. Discover Card Services, Inc.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: False Claims Act violations based on alleged false certifications of compliance with Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, Fair Housing Act, and Americans with Disabilities Act in connection with USDA Rural Development funding for apartment construction and rental subsidies
fha_claims.reasoning: This is a discovery order on a motion to compel, not a ruling on the merits of any FHA claim. The opinion addresses only procedural discovery disputes regarding interrogatory responses and document production in a False Claims Act case. The FHA is mentioned only as one of the statutes that Defendants allegedly falsely certified compliance with; no FHA claim is independently analyzed or adjudicated.

source_file: 9816671_2022_Margaret McGuinn v. J.L Gray Company, Inc._nmd
case_name: United States of America, ex rel. Margaret McGuinn v. The J.L. Gray Company, et al.
accommodation_description: This is a discovery sanctions motion in a qui tam False Claims Act case; while the underlying allegations involve false certifications of FHA compliance, no reasonable accommodation claim is presented.
key_holding: The court denied Plaintiff's request for entry of factual findings and daily fines as sanctions for discovery delays, finding insufficient prejudice and culpability under Ehrenhaus factors, but granted Plaintiff's request for reasonable attorney's fees and costs incurred in litigating the sanctions motion.
brief_summary: In this qui tam action, Plaintiff-Relator McGuinn moved for sanctions against Defendants for failing to produce documents in compliance with the Court's discovery order, seeking daily fines, factual findings, and attorneys' fees. The Court denied the requests for factual findings and daily fines based on insufficient prejudice and culpability under the Ehrenhaus factors, but granted Plaintiff's request for reasonable attorneys' fees and costs associated with bringing the sanctions motion.
key_cases_cited: Ehrenhaus v. Reynolds, 965 F.2d 916 (10th Cir. 1992)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: False Claims Act violation based on alleged false certifications of compliance with Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, Fair Housing Act, and Americans with Disabilities Act in connection with USDA/RD funding applications
fha_claims.reasoning: This opinion addresses only a discovery sanctions motion under Rule 37(b), not the merits of the underlying False Claims Act claim. The court denied entry of factual findings and daily fines as sanctions but awarded reasonable attorney's fees and costs. The underlying FHA/Section 504/ADA claims remain pending.

source_file: 9816777_2022_National Fair Housing Alliance v. Brookdale Santa Fe_nmd
case_name: National Fair Housing Alliance v. Brookdale Santa Fe
accommodation_description: NFHA alleged that Brookdale senior living facilities failed to provide ASL interpreters to deaf residents and prospective residents for medical visits and social activities.
key_holding: The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction, finding that NFHA failed to make a prima facie showing that the disputed Brookdale corporate entities had sufficient contacts with New Mexico to subject them to the court's jurisdiction based on an alter ego/agency theory.
brief_summary: National Fair Housing Alliance sued Brookdale senior living facilities alleging they violated the Fair Housing Act by refusing to provide ASL interpreters to deaf residents and prospective residents, requiring deaf individuals to bear the cost of interpreters for medical visits and activities. The court dismissed the case on personal jurisdiction grounds, finding NFHA failed to establish that the disputed corporate entities had sufficient contacts with New Mexico under an alter ego/agency theory to justify exercising jurisdiction over them.
key_cases_cited: Daimler AG v. Bauman, 571 U.S. 117 (2014)
International Shoe Co. v. Washington, 326 U.S. 310 (1945)
Bristol-Myers Squibb Co. v. Superior Court of Cal., 137 S. Ct. 1773 (2017)
Alto Eldorado Partnership v. Amrep, 124 P.3d 585 (N.M. Ct. App.)
Wenz v. Memery Crystal, 55 F.3d 1503 (10th Cir. 1995)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Provision of American Sign Language (ASL) interpreters for deaf residents at nursing home facilities for medical visits and social activities
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the FHA claim for lack of personal jurisdiction over most defendants. The court found that plaintiff failed to make a prima facie showing of personal jurisdiction over the disputed entities under New Mexico law's alter ego/agency theory, as plaintiff's allegations were conclusory and unsupported by competent proof of jurisdictional facts. Only two facilities (BLC-Ponce De Leon, LLC and Brookdale Place of Albuquerque, LLC) remained as defendants.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act and Section 1557 of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act
fha_claims.reasoning: Non-FHA claims under Section 504 and Section 1557 were dismissed along with the FHA claim for lack of personal jurisdiction over the disputed entities. The court did not reach the merits of these claims.

case_name: Johnny Levelt Burnside v. Monarch Real Estate Corporation
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request is described in the complaint; plaintiff alleges he was denied rental of an available property and illegally evicted.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claims without prejudice for failure to state a claim because the complaint did not identify which specific provisions of the FHA were violated, granting plaintiff leave to amend.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Johnny Levelt Burnside sued Monarch Real Estate Corporation, its property manager, and property owner alleging they denied him rental of an available property and illegally evicted him under the Fair Housing Act, ADA, and § 1983. The court granted in forma pauperis status but dismissed all claims for failure to state a claim, finding the complaint failed to identify specific statutory provisions violated, and granted plaintiff leave to amend within 21 days.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Nasious v. Two Unknown B.I.C.E. Agents, 492 F.3d 1158 (10th Cir. 2007)
Schaffer v. Salt Lake City Corp., 814 F.3d 1151 (10th Cir. 2016)
Menefee v. Werholtz, 368 Fed.Appx. 879 (10th Cir. 2010)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges denial of rental property and illegal eviction under the Fair Housing Act, but does not specify which FHA provisions were violated or what accommodation was requested.
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint fails to state a claim under the FHA because it does not identify which specific FHA provisions were violated or provide sufficient factual detail to give defendants fair notice of the claim. The court granted leave to amend rather than dismissing with prejudice, so the claim remains pending pending repleading.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 due process claim (deprivation of federally protected right); Americans with Disabilities Act claim (unspecified provisions); retaliation claim (unspecified basis).
fha_claims.reasoning: The § 1983 claim fails because defendants are private individuals, not state actors. The ADA and retaliation claims fail for lack of specificity regarding which statutory provisions were violated. The court granted leave to amend, leaving all non-FHA claims pending.

case_name: Johnny Levelt Burnside v. Monarch Real Estate Corporation, Adam Marrujo, and Bradley Berglund
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges he was denied rental of Unit #1 but does not articulate a specific accommodation request; claims mental/emotional disability was not considered
key_holding: The court dismissed the case because plaintiff's amended complaint failed to allege sufficient facts describing what each defendant did, when they did it, and what specific legal right each defendant violated, despite Judge Sweazea's explicit notice of pleading requirements.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Johnny Burnside sued Monarch Real Estate Corporation, its property manager, and owner seeking to rent Unit #1, alleging Fair Housing Act, ADA, and § 1983 claims arising from being denied the rental unit. The court dismissed the case without prejudice for failure to state a claim because plaintiff's amended complaint did not contain sufficient factual allegations to give defendants fair notice of the claims or to support a plausible inference of unlawful discrimination.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged denial of rental of Unit #1 and referenced Fair Housing Act violations, but did not specify which FHA provisions were violated or what accommodation was requested.
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint failed to state a claim under the Fair Housing Act because it did not indicate which specific FHA provisions were violated and did not contain sufficient factual allegations to give defendants fair notice of the claim and its legal basis, as required by Twombly and Iqbal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (deprivation of federally protected rights under color of state law); Americans with Disabilities Act; Title VI of the Civil Rights Act (discrimination based on race, color, or national origin); discrimination and retaliation claims.
fha_claims.reasoning: The § 1983 claim failed because defendants were private individuals, not state actors. The ADA and Title VI claims failed for lack of specificity regarding which provisions were violated. Title VI discrimination claims failed because there were no factual allegations supporting discrimination based on race, color, or national origin.

case_name: Johnny Levelt Burnside v. Monarch Real Estate Corporation
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; Plaintiff alleges race discrimination in rental housing (refusal to rent after making a bona fide offer and paying a deposit).
key_holding: The court found Plaintiff's complaint deficient for failure to state a discrimination claim because it does not contain factual allegations showing that race, color, religion, sex, familial status, or national origin were a factor in Defendants' decision to deny Plaintiff the opportunity to rent the unit.
brief_summary: Pro se Plaintiff Johnny Levelt Burnside sued Monarch Real Estate Corporation, Adam Marrujo, and Bradley Berglund alleging they discriminated against him in violation of the Fair Housing Act when he attempted to rent an apartment unit. The court found the complaint deficient because it failed to allege facts showing discriminatory intent and did not explain what each defendant did, when, how it harmed him, or what specific legal right was violated.
key_cases_cited: Asbury v. Brougham, 866 F.2d 1276 (10th Cir. 1989)
Caddy v. J.P. Morgan Chase Bank, 237 Fed. Appx. 343 (10th Cir. 2007)
Nasious v. Two Unknown B.I.C.E. Agents, 492 F.3d 1158 (10th Cir. 2007)
Yang v. Archuleta, 525 F.3d 925 (10th Cir. 2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint failed to state a plausible claim under § 3604 because it contained no factual allegations showing that race, color, religion, sex, familial status, or national origin were a factor in defendants' decision to deny plaintiff the rental opportunity. The court applied the prima facie elements from Asbury but found the complaint deficient at the pleading stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation claim under New Mexico Uniform Owner-Resident Relations Act
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint failed to state a claim under state law retaliation provisions. The court did not substantively analyze the state law claim but dismissed it along with the FHA claim for failure to plead sufficient facts.

source_file: 9817149_2022_Cruz v. Board of County Commissioners of the County of Bernalillo_nmd
case_name: Antonise Cruz v. Board of County Commissioners of the County of Bernalillo and Bernalillo County Housing Department
accommodation_description: Request for 90-day reinstatement of expired Section 8 housing voucher as reasonable accommodation for organic brain syndrome and learning disorder
key_holding: The court denied preliminary injunction because Plaintiff failed to establish likelihood of success on the merits, finding no causal connection between her disability and voucher expiration—the evidence showed expiration resulted from her delay in searching for housing, not from disability-related impairment.
brief_summary: Antonise Cruz, a disabled mother of three with organic brain syndrome and learning disorder, sued the Bernalillo County Housing Department after her Section 8 voucher expired, alleging Defendants failed to reasonably accommodate her disability by denying her requests for voucher extension or reinstatement. The court denied Plaintiff's motion for preliminary injunction, finding she failed to establish likelihood of success on the merits because the evidence showed her voucher expired due to her own delay in searching for housing, not due to her disability.
key_cases_cited: Cinnamon Hills Youth Crisis Ctr., Inc. v. St. George City, 685 F.3d 917 (10th Cir. 2012)
J.V. v. Albuquerque Pub. Sch., 813 F.3d 1289 (10th Cir. 2016)
Winter v. Nat. Res. Def. Council, Inc., 555 U.S. 7 (2008)
Denver Homeless Out Loud v. Denver, 32 F.4th 1259 (10th Cir. 2022)
McNeill v. NYC Housing Auth., 719 F. Supp. 233 (S.D.N.Y. 1989)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Extension of expired Section 8 housing voucher for 90 days as a reasonable accommodation for plaintiff's disability (organic brain syndrome and learning disorder)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found no causal nexus between plaintiff's disability and the expiration of the voucher. The evidence showed plaintiff's delay in commencing housing search was the cause, not her disability. Court also found defendants did not have notice of plaintiff's disability or need for accommodation before the voucher expired, and that a 90-day extension was not 'necessary (or indispensable or essential)' to achieving equal housing opportunities.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act Title II claim for failure to provide reasonable modification/accommodation for housing voucher extension
fha_claims.reasoning: Under ADA Title II, plaintiff failed to establish she was 'denied the benefit' of a voucher extension 'by reason of' her disability. Court found the expiration resulted from plaintiff's delay in housing search, not her disability. Additionally, defendants lacked notice of plaintiff's disability and accommodation need before voucher expiration.

case_name: Johnny Levelt Burnside v. Monarch Real Estate Corp.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged race-based discrimination in rental and eviction practices, including refusal to rent, denial of $500 payment, and retaliatory eviction.
key_holding: The court dismissed Plaintiff's FHA claims because his conclusory allegation that Defendant Monarch 'doesn't like the color of my skin' was insufficient under Bell Atlantic v. Twombly and Hall v. Bellmon standards, as the complaint lacked factual allegations showing Plaintiff's race was a motivating factor in Defendants' actions.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Johnny Levelt Burnside, a Black man proceeding pro se and in forma pauperis, sued Monarch Real Estate Corp., its owner, and agents alleging race-based housing discrimination under the FHA, Section 1983, Section 1982, and state law claims arising from an alleged refusal to rent and retaliatory eviction. The court dismissed the complaint for failure to state claims, finding Plaintiff's conclusory allegation that Defendants discriminated based on race was insufficient without supporting factual averments, and granted Plaintiff leave to amend within 21 days.
key_cases_cited: Hall v. Bellmon, 935 F.2d 1106 (10th Cir. 1991)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Woods-Drake v. Lundy, 667 F.2d 1198 (5th Cir. 1982)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff made only a conclusory allegation that Defendant Monarch 'doesn't like the color of my skin' without factual support. The statement that Plaintiff's family was the only Black family renting from Monarch for six years does not, by itself, indicate that race was a factor in Defendants' dealings with Plaintiff. Conclusory allegations without supporting factual averments are insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (civil rights deprivation under color of state law); 42 U.S.C. § 1982 (property rights); 42 U.S.C. § 804(a) (Coronavirus Relief Fund); state law regarding owner-resident relations
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii)
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 1983 claim failed because there were no factual allegations that Defendants were acting under color of state law. Section 804(a) claim failed because conclusory allegations without supporting factual averments are insufficient. Judicial immunity barred claims against Judge Madrid.

case_name: Samuel Rene Lopez v. Compa Industries Inc.
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation was requested; the ADA claim was asserted generally as disability discrimination but no particular workplace accommodation was identified in the complaint.
key_holding: The court granted plaintiff's IFP application but ordered him to show cause and file an amended complaint because his pro se complaint for employment discrimination failed to state claims under Title VII, the ADA, RICO, the Fair Housing Act, and various criminal and other federal statutes.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Samuel Rene Lopez filed a sprawling 37-page employment discrimination complaint against COMPA Industries Inc., Stratify LLC, and several individual defendants, alleging Title VII violations based on race, religion, and national origin, ADA disability discrimination, retaliation, civil RICO, and violations of numerous other federal statutes—including 42 U.S.C. § 3617 of the Fair Housing Act—arising from events spanning 1985 to 2023. The court granted IFP status but found the complaint deficient on multiple grounds: failure to allege membership in a protected class or adverse employment action under discriminatory circumstances, conclusory RICO allegations, reliance on criminal statutes that provide no private right of action, apparent statute-of-limitations bars on many state-law claims, and no factual basis for a Fair Housing Act claim. The court ordered plaintiff to show cause and file an amended complaint within 21 days or face dismissal.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Bennett v. Windstream Communications
Edmonds-Radford v. Southwest Airlines Co.
Parker Excavating, Inc. v. Lafarge West
Hall v. Bellmon

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges interference, coercion, or intimidation under 42 U.S.C. § 3617
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found the complaint failed to state a claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3617 because it contained no factual allegations showing that defendants subjected plaintiff to any discriminatory housing practice for which the Fair Housing Act provides a private cause of action. The court applied the Iqbal/Twombly pleading standard and found the allegations insufficient.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VII employment discrimination (race, religion, national origin), ADA Title I disability discrimination, retaliation, RICO, criminal statutes (18 U.S.C. §§ 241, 351, 873, 1001; 10 U.S.C. § 921.121), ERISA fiduciary duty (29 U.S.C. § 1109), federal contract breach (41 U.S.C. § 6503), and state-law tort claims
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim; statute of limitations
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed discrimination and retaliation claims for failure to plead essential elements (protected class membership, adverse employment action, causal connection). RICO claim failed for conclusory allegations without identifying specific racketeering acts or pattern. Criminal statutes do not provide private civil causes of action. Other federal statutes (ERISA, contract breach) lacked factual allegations of applicability. Many state-law claims appeared barred by statute of limitations (3-year limit under N.M. Stat. Ann. § 37-1-8 for conduct prior to April 2020). Court ordered plaintiff to show cause why claims should not be dismissed as time-barred.

case_name: Johnny Levelt Burnside v. Monarch Real Estate Corp.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged defendant refused to rent and evicted him because of his race.
key_holding: The FHA claim was dismissed for failure to state a claim because the plaintiff provided no factual, non-conclusory allegations that his race, color, religion, sex, handicap, familial status, or national origin motivated the defendants' actions.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Johnny Levelt Burnside sued Monarch Real Estate Corp., its owner, and its agent alleging they refused to rent housing to him and evicted him from another property because of his race, in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The Court dismissed the FHA claim under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) for failure to state a claim because plaintiff provided no factual, non-conclusory allegations establishing discriminatory intent.
key_cases_cited: Schaffer v. Salt Lake City Corp., 814 F.3d 1151 (10th Cir. 2016)
Webb v. Caldwell, 640 Fed.Appx. 800 (10th Cir. 2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to rent apartment and eviction allegedly based on race
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed under § 1915(e)(2) for failure to state a claim because plaintiff made no factual, non-conclusory allegations that race, color, religion, sex, handicap, familial status, or national origin were factors motivating defendants' actions. The complaint contained only conclusory allegations that defendants 'don't like the color of my skin' without supporting factual detail.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 civil rights deprivation, § 1982 property rights, Coronavirus Relief Fund Statute, New Mexico state law owner retaliation
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed § 1983 claims for failure to allege defendants acted under color of state law; dismissed § 1982 claims for failure to allege race as a motivating factor; declined supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims after dismissing all federal claims.

case_name: Ronnie J. Thomas v. Linda Bridge, Thea Guerin, and Esther Lucero
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request identified; plaintiff alleges procedural violations regarding Section 8 waiting list lottery system and failure to respond to complaints
key_holding: Complaint dismissed without prejudice for failure to state a claim, but plaintiff granted leave to amend within 21 days because it is not obvious amendment would be futile
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Ronnie Thomas sued officials of the Albuquerque Housing Authority alleging Fair Housing Act, due process, and equal protection violations related to his Section 8 voucher application and waiting list position. The Court granted in forma pauperis status but dismissed the complaint for failure to state any cognizable claim under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, finding no factual allegations establishing a protected property interest in a not-yet-awarded voucher or demonstrating how defendants treated him differently from others similarly situated.
key_cases_cited: Blessing v. Freestone, 520 U.S. 329 (1997)
Hall v. Bellmon, 935 F.2d 1106 (10th Cir. 1991)
Vill. of Willowbrook v. Olech, 528 U.S. 562 (2000)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 8 housing voucher award and processing; alleged failure to follow Section 8 policies, due process, and equal protection rights
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiff's conclusory allegations regarding Section 8 policies, due process violations, and equal protection violations failed to state a claim under § 1983 because they lacked factual allegations identifying specific policies, showing a protected property interest in an unawarded voucher, or demonstrating personal responsibility of each defendant for differential treatment. However, the court determined it was not obvious that amendment would be futile and granted leave to file an amended complaint.

case_name: Ronnie J. Thomas v. Linda Bridge, Thea Guerin, and Esther Lucero
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request identified; plaintiff alleges general violations of Section 8 policies and Fair Housing Act without requesting a particular modification or exception to a policy as a disability accommodation.
key_holding: The complaint fails to state a claim under § 1983 because plaintiff made only conclusory allegations that defendants failed to follow Section 8 policies without identifying which specific policies were violated or how they created a federal right.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Ronnie J. Thomas sued three Albuquerque Housing Authority Section 8 officials under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act, due process, and equal protection related to his Section 8 voucher application and complaints about the waiting list process. The court dismissed the case without prejudice because the complaint failed to state a claim upon which relief can be granted and plaintiff failed to file an amended complaint as ordered by the magistrate judge.
key_cases_cited: Blessing v. Freestone, 520 U.S. 329 (1997)
Hall v. Bellmon, 935 F.2d 1106 (10th Cir. 1991)
Denver Homeless Out Loud v. Denver, 32 F.4th 1259 (10th Cir. 2022)
Vill. of Willowbrook v. Olech, 528 U.S. 562 (2000)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged violations of Fair Housing Act/Albuquerque Housing Authority policies, due process rights, and equal protection rights related to Section 8 voucher application processing and failure to respond to complaints.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiff's conclusory allegations that defendants failed to follow Section 8 policies were insufficient to state a claim under § 1983 because there were no factual allegations identifying the specific policies or showing they created a federal right. The complaint also failed to allege facts showing plaintiff possessed a protected property interest in an unawarded voucher or that defendants violated procedural due process or equal protection by treating plaintiff differently from similarly situated persons.

source_file: 9820177_2019_Hillery v. Sun City Anthem Community Association Inc_nvd
case_name: Hillery v. Sun City Anthem Community Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: Mrs. Hillery, who has dementia, requested reasonable accommodation to access SCA community amenities without being required to bring her own caregiver, and the community allegedly failed to provide meaningful accommodations before banning her.
key_holding: The court struck seven of eight expert opinions as inadmissible legal conclusions or beyond the expert's qualifications, leaving only the opinion that SCA's single accommodation offer (requiring Mrs. Hillery to bring her own caregiver) was not meaningful.
brief_summary: Thomas Hillery, as Guardian Ad Litem for his mother Mary Jane Hillery who has dementia, sued Sun City Anthem Community Association alleging Fair Housing Act violations for failing to provide reasonable accommodation for her disability and subsequently banning her from community amenities. The court ruled on a motion to strike the plaintiffs' expert, striking seven of eight opinions as inadmissible legal conclusions or beyond the expert's qualifications, while admitting only the opinion that SCA's accommodation offer was not meaningful.
key_cases_cited: Barabin v. Asent Johnson, Inc., 740 F.3d 457 (9th Cir. 2014)
Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharm., Inc., 509 U.S. 579 (1993)
Hangarter v. Provident Life & Acc. Ins. Co., 373 F.3d 998 (9th Cir. 2004)
Primiano v. Cook, 598 F.3d 558 (9th Cir. 2010)
Kumho Tire Co. v. Carmichael, 526 U.S. 137 (1999)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought reasonable accommodation for Mrs. Hillery's dementia, including allowing her to bring her own caregiver, or alternatively, SCA providing monitoring, staff training, or a chaperone while she used SCA facilities.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court struck most of the expert's opinions on the reasonable accommodation claim as legal conclusions or unreliable, but allowed Opinion 4 (that SCA made no meaningful attempt to accommodate) to proceed. The underlying FHA reasonable accommodation claim survives the expert testimony challenge and remains pending on the merits.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged that SCA subjected Mrs. Hillery to a rule with special terms and conditions directed specifically at her handicap, fined her, and threatened her with arrest.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court struck the expert's opinion on this claim (Opinion 8, regarding intimidation, harassment, and coercion) as lacking foundation and expertise, but the underlying disparate treatment claim survives and remains pending.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged that SCA intimidated, harassed, and coerced the Hillerys by banning them from common areas, trespassing Mrs. Hillery, and reporting them to authorities in retaliation for requesting accommodation.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court struck the expert's Opinion 8 on interference and coercion as a legal conclusion without reliable methodology, but the underlying FHA § 3617 claim survives the expert testimony challenge.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III claims and Nevada state law claims
fha_claims.reasoning: The court struck multiple expert opinions that addressed ADA Title III and state law claims, but the underlying non-FHA claims survive the expert testimony challenge and remain pending.

case_name: Fulkerson v. The Hartford
accommodation_description: Plaintiff made vague references to Fair Housing Act violations and housing discrimination against landlord Jeff Pheasant but provided no factual allegations describing any specific accommodation request.
key_holding: The complaint was dismissed with leave to amend because Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to state any viable claim, including failing to allege factual basis for Fair Housing Act discrimination or facts supporting insurance bad faith.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Heath Fulkerson filed an in forma pauperis complaint against The Hartford (insurance company) and Jeff Pheasant (landlord) alleging insurance bad faith claims and Fair Housing Act violations. The court granted IFP status but dismissed the complaint with leave to amend for failure to state claims upon which relief may be granted, finding Plaintiff's factual allegations insufficient to support either bad faith or discrimination claims.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges housing discrimination and violations of renters' rights under the Fair Housing Act against landlord Jeff Pheasant, including claims that Pheasant demanded higher deposits and rent before and after property damage was reported.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege factual allegations as to how he was discriminated against in violation of the FHA by Pheasant; the complaint contains only conclusory assertions of discrimination without sufficient factual detail to state a plausible claim under Twombly/Iqbal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Insurance bad faith claim against The Hartford for failing to properly handle property damage and loss claims; breach of implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing under Nevada contract law.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged only that claims were made and not handled properly without factual allegations that The Hartford denied coverage with actual or implied awareness of the absence of a reasonable basis for denial, which is required to state a claim for bad faith under Nevada law.

case_name: Torres v. Rothstein
accommodation_description: N/A - case involves sexual harassment (quid pro quo and hostile environment) rather than a reasonable accommodation request
key_holding: The court denied summary judgment for plaintiff on sexual harassment claims under § 3604(b) and (c) because genuine disputes of material fact exist regarding whether the Direct Consent form was conditioned on rental, but granted summary judgment on defendants' affirmative defenses of lack of knowledge and waiver based on liability release forms.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Candy Torres sued property manager Allan Rothstein and owner Kyle Puntney alleging Rothstein sexually harassed her and required her to sign a Direct Consent for Sexual Intercourse form as a condition of renting a home subsidized by her Section 8 voucher. The court denied Torres's motion for summary judgment on her sexual harassment claims under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(b) and (c) because genuine disputes of material fact existed regarding whether the rental was conditioned on signing the form, but granted summary judgment on defendants' affirmative defenses of lack of knowledge and waiver based on liability release forms.
key_cases_cited: Burlington Indus., Inc. v. Ellerth, 524 U.S. 742 (1998)
Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)
Gamble v. City of Escondido, 104 F.3d 300 (9th Cir. 1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether Rothstein's request for the Direct Consent form constituted quid pro quo sexual harassment under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(b). Rothstein's explanation that he sought the form to protect himself from Torres's alleged sexual advances, combined with ambiguity about whether the rental was conditioned on signing, precluded summary judgment in Torres's favor.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied summary judgment on the discriminatory statements claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c) based on the same material factual disputes regarding whether the Direct Consent form was presented as a condition of the lease and whether an ordinary reader would find it discriminatory given Rothstein's disputed account.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Nevada Fair Housing Law (FHL) sexual harassment and discriminatory statements claims; vicarious liability under federal and state law
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied summary judgment on parallel FHL claims and vicarious liability claims (both federal and Nevada state law) due to material factual disputes regarding the nature of Rothstein's conduct, whether it was within the scope of his agency relationship, and whether he was aided by that relationship in committing the alleged acts.

case_name: Aimee O'Neil v. Jovi Salas, et al.
accommodation_description: No specific reasonable accommodation was described or requested; plaintiff alleged only in conclusory terms that defendants engaged in a pattern of discrimination by imposing different terms or conditions in rental dwellings and making discriminatory preferences on the basis of disability, without identifying any particular accommodation sought or denied.
key_holding: The court recommends dismissal without prejudice of plaintiff's FHA disability discrimination complaint because it contains only conclusory allegations devoid of sufficient factual matter to state a plausible claim for relief and fails to comply with Fed. R. Civ. P. 8 by not specifying the legal theory (disparate treatment, disparate impact, or reasonable accommodation) under which the claim is brought.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Aimee O'Neil filed an in forma pauperis complaint against Jovi Salas et al. alleging a pattern of disability-based discrimination in rental housing under the Fair Housing Act, claiming defendants imposed different terms or conditions and made discriminatory preferences on the basis of disability. The court screened the complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2) and found it offered only labels and conclusions without any supporting factual allegations, such as where or when the alleged discrimination occurred, and failed to specify which FHA legal theory was being pursued. The court recommends dismissal without prejudice with leave to amend, finding that amendment would not necessarily be futile.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Gamble v. City of Escondido, 104 F.3d 300 (9th Cir. 1997)
Cato v. United States, 70 F.3d 1103 (9th Cir. 1995)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged discrimination on the basis of disability in rental dwelling terms and conditions, but did not specify whether the claim was for disparate treatment, disparate impact, or failure to provide reasonable accommodation.
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint contained only conclusory allegations and naked assertions devoid of factual enhancement (where, when, specific conduct), failed to specify which FHA theory was invoked (disparate treatment, disparate impact, or reasonable accommodation), and violated Rule 8 pleading requirements. Dismissed without prejudice with leave to amend.

case_name: Victoria-Joy Godwin v. Senior Garden Apartments, et al.
accommodation_description: Cannot be determined from the case text; the complaint references Fair Housing Act violations generally but the specific accommodation or discriminatory conduct alleged is not described in this order.
key_holding: The court granted all five unopposed motions to dismiss under Local Rule 7-2(d), which treats a party's failure to file a response as consent to granting the motion, dismissing all claims against all named defendants.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Victoria-Joy Godwin filed a fourth amended complaint against Senior Garden Apartments and numerous defendants—including state court judges and court personnel—alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act, operation of a racketeering scheme, and civil conspiracy using state court personnel to intimidate her. Defendants filed five motions to dismiss, none of which plaintiff opposed. The court dismissed all claims on procedural grounds under Local Rule 7-2(d) and also granted a motion to strike plaintiff's improper request for judicial notice.
key_cases_cited: Reiger v. Nevens, Case No. 3:12-cv-00218-MMD-VPC, 2014 WL 537613 (D. Nev. Feb. 7, 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not specified; complaint alleges Fair Housing Act violations but opinion does not detail the specific claims
fha_claims.reasoning: All FHA claims against all defendants were dismissed pursuant to unopposed motions to dismiss under Local Rule 7-2(d), which treats failure to file a response as consent to granting the motion. The court did not reach the merits of any specific FHA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: RICO racketeering scheme, civil conspiracy involving state court personnel and intimidation
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA claims (RICO, civil conspiracy) were dismissed as unopposed motions to dismiss. The court did not engage substantively with the elements of these claims.

case_name: Hansen v. Delaney
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs sued state-court judges and opposing attorneys over an eviction proceeding, alleging Fair Housing Act violations among numerous federal and state claims.
key_holding: The court granted motions to dismiss on Eleventh Amendment immunity grounds, Rooker-Feldman doctrine precluding review of state-court judgments, and judicial immunity for the defendant judges and hearing master; private attorneys were not state actors under § 1983.
brief_summary: Dawn Hansen, Christopher Hansen, and Nicholas Hanson sued state-court judges, a hearing master, opposing attorneys, and the Eighth Judicial District Court for alleged constitutional and Fair Housing Act violations stemming from an eviction proceeding; the court granted all motions to dismiss on Eleventh Amendment immunity, Rooker-Feldman jurisdictional bar, judicial immunity, and state-action grounds.
key_cases_cited: Rooker v. Fidelity Trust Co., 263 U.S. 413 (1923)
D.C. Ct. App. v. Feldman, 460 U.S. 462 (1983)
Pennhurst State Sch. & Hosp. v. Halderman, 465 U.S. 89 (1984)
Schucker v. Rockwood, 846 F.2d 1202 (9th Cir. 1988)
Dennis v. Sparks, 449 U.S. 24 (1980)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act claim mentioned in complaint caption but not substantively alleged or analyzed in the opinion
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that Congress did not abrogate Eleventh Amendment sovereign immunity under the Fair Housing Act, and the FHA claim against state defendants is barred by sovereign immunity. The court also declined supplemental jurisdiction over any remaining state-law claims after dismissing all federal claims.

case_name: Victoria-Joy Godwin v. Senior Garden Apartments, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff's federal complaint raises claims of sexual harassment, emotional distress, defamation, racketeering, and civil conspiracy related to eviction proceedings; no specific reasonable accommodation request is substantively analyzed.
key_holding: The federal district court lacks subject matter jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine because the plaintiff's claims constitute a forbidden de facto appeal from state court judgments affirming her eviction, making all pending motions moot.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Victoria-Joy Godwin sued Senior Garden Apartments and related defendants alleging Fair Housing Act claims, sexual harassment, emotional distress, defamation, racketeering, and civil conspiracy arising from her 2017 eviction. The federal district court dismissed the action without prejudice under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine, finding it lacked subject matter jurisdiction because Godwin's claims constituted a forbidden de facto appeal from prior state court judgments affirming her eviction, rendering the parties' pending motions moot.
key_cases_cited: Rooker v. Fid. Tr. Co., 263 U.S. 413 (1923)
D.C. Court of Appeals v. Feldman, 460 U.S. 462 (1983)
Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Saudi Basic Indus. Corp., 544 U.S. 280 (2005)
Doe v. Mann, 415 F.3d 1038 (9th Cir. 2005)
Noel v. Hall, 341 F.3d 1148 (9th Cir. 2003)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Sexual harassment, hostile environment sexual harassment, intentional infliction of emotional distress, negligent infliction of emotional distress, defamation, racketeering, civil conspiracy
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found it lacked subject matter jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine because Godwin's claims were a de facto appeal from prior state court judgments on the same or inextricably intertwined issues, and the federal action was filed after final state court judgments were rendered.

source_file: 9827432_2021_Carpenter v. Southern Nevada Regional Housing Authority_nvd
case_name: Phyllis J. Carpenter v. Southern Nevada Regional Housing Authority
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation was requested; plaintiff's allegations included that units were not ADA compliant (referenced in the context of her employment write-ups), that her apartment was not properly repaired, and that she was paid less than a non-English-speaking coworker, but no formal accommodation request was identified.
key_holding: The court dismissed all of pro se plaintiff's claims without prejudice for failure to state a plausible claim for relief under Twombly/Iqbal, because plaintiff listed dozens of alleged legal violations without alleging supporting facts for any of them.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Phyllis Carpenter filed suit against the Southern Nevada Regional Housing Authority alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act, the ADA, the Code of Federal Regulations, HUD regulations, Title VII/EEOC, and slander, arising from her dual status as a tenant and hourly employee. The court granted her in forma pauperis application but dismissed her complaint without prejudice under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B), finding that she merely listed statutory provisions without alleging any supporting facts sufficient to cross the line from conceivable to plausible. Plaintiff was given leave to file an amended complaint by November 29, 2021.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Gamble v. City of Escondido, 104 F.3d 300 (9th Cir. 1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege any facts demonstrating a discriminatory housing practice under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(b) or other FHA provisions. The complaint merely listed legal violations without corresponding factual allegations, failing to meet the Twombly/Iqbal plausibility standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title I employment discrimination, CFR violations, EEOC/Title VII violations, state law slander
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts supporting ADA Title I employment discrimination (did not allege disability or adverse employment action), CFR violations (no factual allegations and unclear standing), EEOC/Title VII violations (failed to allege protected class status or exhaustion of administrative remedies), or slander (no factual allegations of false statements). All non-FHA claims dismissed for failure to state a plausible claim.

source_file: 9827845_2021_Seelig v. Old Vegas Manor and Estates Homeowners Association_nvd
case_name: Stephen M. Seelig and Vikki L. Seelig v. Old Vegas Manor and Estates Homeowners Association, et al.
accommodation_description: Equal access to subdivision common elements, including a pedestrian gate, public park (Satellite Park), and streets and sidewalks within the Old Vegas Manor and Estates subdivision, for a disabled resident (Mr. Seelig) and his spouse through associational discrimination principles.
key_holding: The court grants in part motions to dismiss and for judgment on the pleadings in a contentious HOA dispute, allowing ADA/FHA claims for discriminatory denial of access to subdivision common elements and a civil conspiracy claim to survive while dismissing IIED, certain contract, and state statutory claims for failure to meet pleading standards.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Stephen and Vikki Seelig sued their HOA, a landscape maintenance association, a property management company, and individual neighbors, alleging 34 claims arising from neighborhood disputes, including ADA and FHA violations based on denial of equal access to common elements such as a pedestrian gate, park, and sidewalks. The court declined to dismiss the ADA/FHA access claims, finding the plaintiffs plausibly alleged the subdivision's common elements could constitute public accommodations, and also allowed Mrs. Seelig's associational discrimination claims and the civil conspiracy claim to proceed. However, the court dismissed IIED claims for failure to allege sufficiently extreme conduct and physical impact, dismissed contract claims against individual defendants for inadequate pleading, and dismissed state statutory claims that lacked a private right of action.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal access to common elements (parks, pedestrian pathways, pedestrian gate) in the subdivision
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiffs plausibly alleged common elements could constitute public accommodations under ADA/FHA and declined to dismiss; the claim survives the motion for judgment on the pleadings.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal access to common elements (parks, pedestrian pathways, pedestrian gate) in the subdivision
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiffs plausibly alleged common elements could constitute public accommodations under ADA/FHA and declined to dismiss; the claim survives the motion for judgment on the pleadings.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal access to common elements (parks, pedestrian pathways, pedestrian gate) in the subdivision
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiffs plausibly alleged common elements could constitute public accommodations under ADA/FHA and declined to dismiss; the claim survives the motion for judgment on the pleadings.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal access to common elements (parks, pedestrian pathways, pedestrian gate) in the subdivision
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiffs plausibly alleged common elements could constitute public accommodations under ADA/FHA and declined to dismiss; the claim survives the motion for judgment on the pleadings.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal access to common elements (parks, pedestrian pathways, pedestrian gate) in the subdivision
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiffs plausibly alleged common elements could constitute public accommodations under ADA/FHA and declined to dismiss; the claim survives the motion for judgment on the pleadings.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Dwelling modifications for reason of disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs conceded to dismissal of claim 10 for failure to state a right of action under the statute cited; court dismissed with prejudice without leave to amend.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Civil conspiracy, intentional infliction of emotional distress, breach of contract, negligent supervision, respondeat superior, and other state law claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed IIED claims (27, 28, 29, 30) for failure to allege extreme and outrageous conduct and physical impact; dismissed contract claims (12, 13, 14) for failure to adequately plead capacity and contract terms; dismissed statutory claims (15, 16, 31) for failure to state a right of action; but allowed civil conspiracy (26) and respondeat superior/negligent supervision (32, 33, 34) claims to proceed.

case_name: Kenneth O'Rourke, et al. v. Kim VanHeel, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs request to retain designated service dogs without being charged fines for failure to provide proof of service dog certification.
key_holding: The court found serious questions going to the merits of plaintiffs' FHA reasonable accommodation claim regarding service dogs and granted a TRO vacating eviction orders and prohibiting reinitiating eviction during the pendency of the order.
brief_summary: Kenneth O'Rourke, Charleen Kurr-O'Rourke, and Kassidy O'Rourke sued Palm Hills HOA and related defendants alleging violation of the Fair Housing Act for refusing to accommodate their service dogs and charging fines. The court granted a temporary restraining order finding serious questions on the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim and vacated the eviction orders pending resolution.
key_cases_cited: Dubois v. Ass'n of Apartment Owners of Kalakaua, 453 F.3d 1175 (9th Cir. 2006)
Sanzaro v. Ardiente Homeowners Ass'n, LLC, 364 F. Supp. 3d 1158 (D. Nev. 2019)
Alliance For The Wild Rockies v. Cottrell, 632 F.3d 1127 (9th Cir. 2011)
Park Vill. Apt. Tenants Ass'n v. Mortimer Howard Trust, 636 F.3d 1150 (9th Cir. 2011)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retention of specifically designated service dogs to accommodate Kenneth O'Rourke's hearing disability and PTSD and Kassidy O'Rourke's Type 1 Diabetes
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found serious questions going to the merits of the FHA reasonable accommodation claim under the five-element Dubois test, determining that plaintiffs adequately alleged a handicap, defendant's knowledge, necessity of accommodation, reasonableness, and refusal. Court issued TRO to preserve status quo pending resolution of the underlying claim, finding irreparable harm from threatened eviction and balance of equities favoring plaintiffs.

case_name: Bloodgood-Loper v. Loper
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request was substantively analyzed; court dismissed conclusory FHA claims alleging familial-status and disability discrimination in eviction from rental home
key_holding: The court dismissed all FHA claims because plaintiff failed to identify any specific FHA right violated, failed to allege facts showing defendants' actions were motivated by familial status or disability, and failed to plead any causal connection between Charles's alcoholism and the eviction actions.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Katalin Bloodgood-Loper sued her husband Charles and his father Lenard Loper (a private landlord) arising from her eviction from the rental home Charles rented from Lenard, asserting federal claims under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1983, 1985, and the Fair Housing Act. The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss all federal claims without leave to amend, finding plaintiffs failed to state a plausible claim because they did not identify what specific FHA rights were violated, did not allege facts showing discrimination because of familial status or disability, and could not cure these pleading deficiencies.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Harris v. Itzhaki

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged discrimination based on familial status (as spouse of tenant) in denial of housing rights and eviction from rental property.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts showing that defendants' actions were taken because of her familial status. She acknowledged she was not named on the lease and provided no facts connecting the eviction to her status as a spouse rather than to her status as an unauthorized occupant.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged that defendants' letter threatening eviction unless Charles ceased making defamatory statements and addressed his addiction violated § 3617 interference/coercion provisions.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to identify any FHA right that defendants interfered with. The court found that because no underlying FHA right was alleged, the § 3617 interference claim could not be stated.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged discrimination based on Charles's alcoholism (identified as a handicap) and claimed defendants treated him as incompetent and denied him rights including the right to marry and to enter rehab on his own free will.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege any facts showing that defendants evicted Charles or took any action prohibited under the FHA because of his alcoholism or any other disability. The court found amendment would be futile given the robust factual record already provided.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (due process/state action); 42 U.S.C. § 1985(3) (civil conspiracy); ADA Title III (Charles's cross-claim); state law claims (breach of duty, gross negligence, intentional infliction of emotional distress).
fha_claims.reasoning: § 1983 claims failed because defendants were private actors with no state action; no facts alleged showing conspiracy with state officials. § 1985(3) failed because plaintiff alleged no class-based discriminatory animus and no constitutional right to spousal tenancy. ADA claims failed because Charles alleged no facts showing denial of rights because of disability. State law claims dismissed without supplemental jurisdiction.

case_name: Ronald Eric Kandell v. SUR 702, et al.
accommodation_description: Request to keep a service animal in the rental property without being charged a $300 pet fee after refusing to provide medical records to verify the disability-related need for the animal.
key_holding: The court recommended dismissing plaintiff's FHA disability discrimination claim because he failed to plead sufficient facts demonstrating he is disabled within the meaning of 42 U.S.C. § 3602(h) or that his use of a service animal is a necessary accommodation to afford him equal opportunity to use and enjoy his dwelling.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Ronald Eric Kandell, proceeding pro se and in forma pauperis, sued his apartment property manager and related entities alleging discrimination based on sexuality and disability under the Fair Housing Act, including claims that defendants charged him a $300 pet fee for his service animal after he refused to provide medical records. The court recommended dismissing the FHA claims because plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts establishing he is disabled or that his service animal is a necessary accommodation, despite referencing conditions including stress, seizures, epilepsy, and PTSD.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Dubois v. Ass'n of Apartment Owners of 2987 Kalakaua
Revock v. Cowpet Bay West Condominium Ass'n
Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condominium Ass'n, Inc.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts to state a claim of sexual orientation discrimination under the FHA. Although HUD has interpreted the FHA to prohibit sexual orientation discrimination since February 2021, plaintiff never explicitly stated he is a member of the LGBTQ+ community, and the alleged evidence (a derogatory comment made to a third party and a delayed maintenance request) does not rise to the level of severity required to state a discrimination claim. A single incident, especially one not made directly to the plaintiff, is insufficient.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request to allow plaintiff to keep a service animal without providing medical records to verify disability and necessity; defendants assessed a $300 pet fee after plaintiff refused to provide medical records
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts to state an FHA disability discrimination/reasonable accommodation claim. Although plaintiff made various references to stress, seizures, epilepsy, and possession of a service animal, he did not allege facts demonstrating he is disabled within the meaning of 42 U.S.C. § 3602(h), that defendants knew or should have known of his disability, or that the service animal was a necessary accommodation. The failure to allege these essential elements precludes stating a claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VII employment discrimination (sexual orientation), NRS 118A.290 (habitability), No FEAR Act, 18 U.S.C. § 249 (Hate Crime Prevention Act), 18 U.S.C. § 1621 (perjury statute), 18 U.S.C. § 650
fha_claims.reasoning: Title VII employment discrimination claim dismissed for failure to exhaust administrative remedies (no EEOC complaint or right-to-sue letter alleged). NRS 118A.290 habitability claim dismissed for failure to plead sufficient facts regarding notice to landlord and landlord's response. No FEAR Act claim dismissed because plaintiff is a private citizen, not a federal employee. Claims under 18 U.S.C. §§ 249, 1621, and 650 dismissed because these criminal statutes lack private rights of action.

case_name: Ronald A. Brown, Sr., et al. v. American Homes 4 Rent, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff Ronald Brown, who suffered a stroke leaving him disabled, requested an elongated toilet and a left-sided banister in the stairway of his rental unit as reasonable accommodations for his mobility disability.
key_holding: The court recommended dismissing the FHA reasonable accommodation claim against American Homes 4 Rent as time-barred, since the accommodation denial occurred in early 2020 but the complaint was filed in April 2023—more than two years later—without sufficient allegations of a continuing violation to reset the statute of limitations.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Ronald and Tonya Brown sued American Homes 4 Rent and related defendants alleging Fair Housing Act violations after their requests for structural accommodations—an elongated toilet and left-sided stairway banister—for Mr. Brown's stroke-related mobility disability were denied. The district court recommended dismissing the FHA claim against AHR without prejudice as time-barred because the alleged denial occurred in early 2020 but the complaint was filed in April 2023, beyond the two-year limitations period, while also dismissing individual defendant Singelyn with prejudice under principles of vicarious liability.
key_cases_cited: Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)
Dubois v. Ass'n of Apartment Owners of 2987 Kalakaua, 453 F.3d 1175 (9th Cir. 2006)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Elongated toilet and left-sided banister in stairway to address plaintiff's post-stroke mobility impairments
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs' accommodation request was made between January 3 and April 2, 2020, but the complaint was not filed until April 13, 2023—substantially more than two years after the alleged discriminatory event. The court found no continuing violation, only continuing harmful effects from the original denial, which is insufficient to reset the statute of limitations under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 18 U.S.C. § 2261A cyberstalking and harassment claims; state law lease violation claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 2261A creates a federal criminal offense with no private right of action for civil litigants. State law lease claims were dismissed for lack of supplemental jurisdiction because plaintiffs failed to state a cognizable federal claim.

case_name: Kevin Alexander & Alma Alexander v. The Croix Townhomes LLC
accommodation_description: No accommodation request at issue; plaintiffs alleged discrimination based on age and/or familial status when defendant made allegedly defamatory statements and took adverse housing actions.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' § 3604(b) housing discrimination claim with prejudice because their conclusory allegations failed to establish a prima facie case—they provided no factual allegations showing defendants' adverse housing actions were motivated by plaintiffs' protected status.
brief_summary: Kevin and Alma Alexander sued The Croix Townhomes LLC and employee Lizbeth Estrada in Nevada state court, alleging housing discrimination based on age and/or familial status under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(b) after Estrada allegedly made statements to a state services worker about the Alexanders. The federal court sua sponte dismissed the housing discrimination claim with prejudice, finding the complaint contained only conclusory allegations without factual support for a prima facie case of discrimination, then remanded the remaining state-law claims to Nevada state court.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed under Rule 12(b)(6) for failure to state a plausible claim of housing discrimination based on age and/or familial status. Plaintiffs alleged only conclusory assertions of discrimination without alleging any facts probative of causation—i.e., that defendants' non-renewal of lease and eviction were motivated by plaintiffs' protected status rather than other legitimate reasons. Under Iqbal, naked assertions devoid of factual enhancement are insufficient.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: State-law tort and contract claims (defamation, etc.)
fha_claims.reasoning: After dismissing the sole federal FHA claim, the court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over remaining state-law claims and remanded the case to Nevada state court. The balance of judicial economy, convenience, fairness, and comity favored remand, particularly because state issues substantially predominated and the case was in infancy before discovery.

case_name: Ronald Eric Kandell v. SUR 702, et al.
accommodation_description: The opinion does not specify the accommodation request; it only states the complaint alleged Fair Housing Act claims for sexual orientation and disability discrimination.
key_holding: The court accepted the Magistrate Judge's recommendation to dismiss FHA claims for disability discrimination without prejudice and with leave to amend because plaintiff failed to file objections to the report and recommendation.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Ronald Kandell filed a complaint against SUR 702 and others raising various claims including Fair Housing Act claims for sexual orientation and disability discrimination. The Magistrate Judge recommended dismissing those FHA claims without prejudice and with leave to amend, and because Kandell failed to timely object, the District Judge accepted the recommendation.
key_cases_cited: United States v. Reyna-Tapia, 328 F.3d 1114 (9th Cir. 2003)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Sexual orientation and disability discrimination
fha_claims.reasoning: The magistrate judge recommended dismissal of FHA claims for sexual orientation and disability discrimination without prejudice, with leave to amend. The district court accepted this recommendation without conducting de novo review, as plaintiff failed to timely object.

case_name: Ronald A. Brown, Sr. v. American Homes 4 Rent
accommodation_description: The opinion does not describe the specific accommodation requested; the text only states plaintiffs sued for Fair Housing Act violations without specifying the nature of the accommodation sought.
key_holding: The FHA claims were dismissed with prejudice because they were time-barred or failed to state a viable claim after multiple amendments, and supplemental jurisdiction over state-law claims was declined.
brief_summary: Pro se tenants Ronald A. Brown, Sr. and Tonya L. Brown sued their property-management company American Homes 4 Rent and its principals in Nevada federal court for Fair Housing Act violations arising from their Ohio rental housing. The district court adopted the magistrate judge's recommendation and dismissed the case with prejudice, finding the FHA claims time-barred and deficiently pled, with supplemental jurisdiction declined over state-law claims.
key_cases_cited: Concrete Pipe and Prods. of Cal., Inc. v. Constr. Laborers Pension Trust for S. Cal., 508 U.S. 602 (1993)
Grimes v. City and Cnty. of S.F., 951 F.2d 236 (9th Cir. 1991)
Palmer v. Valdez, 560 F.3d 965 (9th Cir. 2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not specified in opinion
fha_claims.reasoning: Pro se plaintiffs failed to state a viable FHA claim after multiple amendments. The magistrate judge screened the complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915 and recommended dismissal; the district court adopted that recommendation de novo, finding the FHA claims fundamentally defective and time-barred or failing to state a claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: State-law claims (unspecified)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over remaining state-law claims after dismissing all FHA claims and finding lack of personal jurisdiction over two defendants.

case_name: Christopher A. Jones v. Brenda Tierney; Larry Hastings; Robert Rosenfeld; Suzanne Doe; Sarah Doe; HOA Board
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges HOA board members created a hostile living environment, discriminated based on race by unfairly applying HOA rules, and retaliated against him for complaining about unfair treatment.
key_holding: The complaint fails to state an FHA claim because Plaintiff has not alleged facts showing disparate treatment based on race; the single comment by Defendant Tierney ('this is not the Siegle Suites where you people can just do what you want') is insufficient to demonstrate a violation of federal anti-discrimination laws.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Christopher Jones, proceeding pro se and in forma pauperis, sued HOA board members Brenda Tierney and others alleging they created a hostile living environment, discriminated based on race by unfairly applying HOA rules, and retaliated against him for complaining. The court dismissed the complaint without prejudice for failure to state a claim, finding the single offensive comment by Defendant Tierney insufficient to establish a federal anti-discrimination violation.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts showing disparate treatment based on race. A single offensive comment by one defendant, without additional facts connecting defendants' actions to plaintiff's race or showing differential treatment of similarly situated non-minority residents, is insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly to state a plausible FHA disparate treatment claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: First Amendment, Fifth Amendment, Fourteenth Amendment constitutional claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Constitutional claims against private HOA board members fail because the Constitution protects only against government action, not private action. Plaintiff did not allege facts establishing state action or a close nexus between the state and the HOA board's conduct; merely violating state law does not constitute acting under color of state law.

case_name: Fred Anthony Aragon v. Wendy Black; Coyote Corner, Inc.; Jennifer Aragon
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges defendant raised his rent because he is Hispanic, claiming racial discrimination in housing
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act racial discrimination claim as time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations since the alleged rent increase occurred in 2016 and plaintiff did not file until 2023.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Fred Aragon sued his former employer Coyote Corner, Inc., its owner Wendy Black, and his ex-wife Jennifer Aragon alleging racial discrimination in housing (raised rent because he is Hispanic) and defamation. The court granted in forma pauperis status but dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim, finding the Fair Housing Act claim time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations and the Title VII employment discrimination claim barred for failure to exhaust administrative remedies.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rent increase allegedly based on race (Hispanic)
fha_claims.reasoning: Fair Housing Act claim is time-barred because the alleged discriminatory rent increase occurred in 2016, the statute of limitations expired in 2018, and plaintiff did not file suit until 2023. The court dismissed without prejudice, allowing amendment if plaintiff can allege facts supporting tolling.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VII employment discrimination claim (termination in 2016); Nevada defamation claim (statement made in December 2016)
fha_claims.reasoning: Title VII claim dismissed for failure to exhaust administrative remedies (no EEOC charge or right-to-sue letter alleged) and statute of limitations concerns (termination in 2016, complaint filed in 2023). Defamation claim dismissed as time-barred under Nevada's two-year statute of limitations (alleged statement in December 2016, suit filed in 2023).

source_file: 9834629_2024_Perkins Jr. v. Panorama Towers Condo Unit Owners, Dennis Kariger_nvd
case_name: Preston D. Perkins, Jr. v. Panorama Towers Condominium Complex, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff's complaint references the Fair Housing Act but does not identify any specific accommodation request or discrimination claim.
key_holding: The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss because plaintiff failed to establish subject matter jurisdiction, having failed to plead facts supporting any viable federal claim including under the Fair Housing Act, which he merely cited by name without identifying any discrimination.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Preston D. Perkins, Jr. sued Panorama Towers Condominium Complex and related defendants alleging various claims including references to the Fair Housing Act. The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss without prejudice for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, finding plaintiff failed to plead facts supporting any cognizable federal claim. The court granted plaintiff leave to amend his complaint within 14 days.
key_cases_cited: Arbaugh v. Y&H Corp., 546 U.S. 500 (2006)
Kokkonen v. Guardian Life Ins. Co. of America, 511 U.S. 375 (1994)
Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Allapattah Servs., Inc., 545 U.S. 546 (2005)
Ghazali v. Moran, 46 F.3d 52 (9th Cir. 1995)
Hebbe v. Pliler, 627 F.3d 338 (9th Cir. 2010)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff cites the Fair Housing Act but fails to identify any discrimination or specific claim
