fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because plaintiff failed to allege facts supporting any claim under the Fair Housing Act. Although plaintiff cited the FHA, he did not identify any discrimination based on protected class or any cognizable claim for relief, and thus failed to establish federal question jurisdiction.

source_file: 9836005_2024_Perkins Jr. v. Panorama Towers Condo Unit Owners, Dennis Kariger_nvd
case_name: Preston D. Perkins, Jr. v. Panorama Towers Condominium Complex, et al.
accommodation_description: No specific reasonable accommodation was requested. Plaintiff cited 42 U.S.C. § 3617 of the Fair Housing Act (interference/coercion provision) in connection with general landlord-tenant grievances including alleged toxic mold, bug infestations, and malfunctioning air conditioning units, but did not articulate any discrete accommodation request or identify a protected disability basis.
key_holding: The court dismissed all federal claims with prejudice for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, finding the pro se plaintiff failed to establish either federal question or diversity jurisdiction, and denied leave to amend as futile after a prior opportunity to amend.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Preston Perkins Jr. brought a landlord-tenant action against his condominium complex and related defendants, asserting a sprawling set of federal claims including criminal statute violations, § 1983, ADA retaliation under 42 U.S.C. § 12203, FHA interference/coercion under 42 U.S.C. § 3617, § 1981, and various constitutional provisions. The court granted all five defendants' motions to dismiss, finding the plaintiff failed to establish federal question jurisdiction (because each purported federal claim was facially defective) and failed to establish diversity jurisdiction (because plaintiff and multiple defendants were all Nevada citizens). All federal claims were dismissed with prejudice, state law claims without prejudice, and leave to amend was denied as futile because the plaintiff had already been granted one amendment opportunity and still could not plead a viable federal claim.
key_cases_cited: City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Ctr., 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Harris v. Itzhaki, 183 F.3d 1043 (9th Cir. 1999)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged interference, coercion, intimidation, or retaliation under FHA § 3617 in connection with exercise of FHA rights; specific nature of alleged interference not clearly articulated in complaint.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under 12(b)(1). Plaintiff failed to establish federal question jurisdiction because the FHA claim lacked allegations that (1) plaintiff's rights were protected under the FHA, (2) plaintiff was discriminated against based on protected status, or (3) injuries resulted from discriminatory conduct. Court found no plausible federal claim even when liberally construing the complaint.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 12203 (ADA retaliation/interference); 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (First Amendment, Thirteenth Amendment, Fourteenth Amendment due process and equal protection); 42 U.S.C. § 1981 (racial discrimination in contracts); criminal statutes 18 U.S.C. §§ 241, 242, 246, 872; 29 U.S.C. § 1109(a) (ERISA); 28 U.S.C. § 1361 (mandamus); 31 U.S.C. § 6711 (local government programs).
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed all non-FHA federal claims for lack of subject matter jurisdiction. Criminal statutes do not provide private civil causes of action; § 1983 claims failed because no defendant acted under color of state law (judge entitled to absolute immunity); ADA § 12203 claim failed because no underlying ADA claim was stated; § 1981 claim failed because no allegations of racial discrimination; due process claims failed because defendants were not federal or state actors; equal protection claim failed because plaintiff did not allege membership in protected class or differential treatment.

source_file: 9836268_2019_Koso v. St. Josephs Senior Housing Village_nyed
case_name: Linda Koso v. St. Joseph's Senior Housing Village and Stanan Management
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges she was denied an apartment at a senior housing facility because of her physical disability.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claim because she failed to plausibly allege she belonged to a protected class (her unspecified physical disability was conclusory) and failed to allege facts suggesting discriminatory motivation for the denial.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Linda Koso sued St. Joseph's Senior Housing Village and Stanan Management alleging she was denied an apartment because of her physical disability in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding plaintiff failed to plausibly allege facts establishing she was a member of a protected class or that discriminatory motivation caused the denial of housing.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Boykin v. KeyCorp, 521 F.3d 202 (2d Cir. 2008)
Vega v. Hempstead Union Free Sch. Dist., 801 F.3d 72 (2d Cir. 2015)
Sybalski v. Indep. Grp. Home Living Program, Inc., 546 F.3d 255 (2d Cir. 2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of housing unit based on alleged physical disability, age, and financial status/credit score
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege membership in a protected class under the FHA (handicap) by providing only a bare statement of an unspecified physical disability, and failed to allege facts supporting a plausible inference of discriminatory motivation beyond conclusory allegations that she was denied housing because of her disability, age, and financial status.

source_file: 9836490_2019_Village Green at Sayville, LLC v. The Town of Islip_nyed
case_name: Village Green at Sayville, LLC v. The Town of Islip
accommodation_description: Developer alleges Town of Islip refused to approve rezoning and C&R amendments for a 59-unit housing development while approving a similar application for a project in a minority neighborhood, based on racial animus from residents.
key_holding: The court granted Defendants' Rule 12(b)(1) motion to dismiss Plaintiff's FHA claim for lack of standing because Plaintiff failed to establish a final decision—there was no permit denial or rezoning, only a failed motion and non-vote on Plaintiff's C&R amendment application, and a pending Article 78 proceeding in state court had not yet resolved the application.
brief_summary: Village Green at Sayville, LLC, a real estate developer, sued the Town of Islip and its officials alleging the Town discriminated against racial minorities by blocking the developer's attempts to build a 59-unit housing development in Sayville while approving a similar development in the minority neighborhood of Brentwood. The court dismissed the FHA claim for lack of standing, finding no final decision had been made on the developer's C&R amendment application since the Town Board never voted and the issue was pending in state court.
key_cases_cited: Williamson County Regional Planning Commission v. Hamilton Bank, 473 U.S. 172 (1985)
Knick v. Township of Scott, 139 S. Ct. 2162 (2019)
Mhany Mgmt., Inc. v. County of Nassau, 819 F.3d 581 (2d Cir. 2016)
Anderson v. Town of Orwell, 693 F. Supp. 2d 182 (N.D.N.Y. 2010)
Colorado River Water Conservation Dist. v. U.S., 424 U.S. 800 (1976)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Approval of application to modify covenants and restrictions to allow rental apartments instead of owner-occupied condominiums
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff lacked standing to bring FHA claim because there was no final decision on the application. The Town Board never voted on Plaintiff's application; the failed motion to approve and the Town Attorney's alleged statement were insufficient to constitute a final, definitive position from the municipal entity required for ripeness in the land-use context.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1982, 1983, Equal Protection Clause, Fourteenth Amendment substantive due process, Fifth and Fourteenth Amendment takings clause, New York State Human Rights Law § 296
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff lacked standing to bring takings, equal protection, and substantive due process claims because there was no final decision on the application, failing the ripeness requirement in the land-use context. The non-vote and alleged attorney statement did not constitute a final decision. Claims under §§ 1981, 1982, and NYSHRL survived the 12(b)(1) motion but were not addressed on the merits at this stage.

source_file: 9838610_2020_Ortega v. Samaritan Village Myrtle Ave. Men's Shelter_nyed
case_name: Ivan Fernando Ortega v. Samaritan Village Myrtle Ave. Men's Shelter
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested placement in the 'Skyway' shelter program, which he believed was better suited to manage his disabilities, rather than his current shelter placement.
key_holding: Plaintiff failed to state an FHA claim because he did not establish that he suffers from a disability as defined by the FHA, nor did he show that his current housing placement failed to accommodate his disabilities or denied him any services because of his disability.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Ivan Fernando Ortega, a homeless individual claiming to be 100% disabled, sued a NYC men's shelter, its director, and city agencies seeking placement in a different shelter program allegedly better suited to manage his disabilities. The court dismissed the amended complaint for failure to state a claim under the FHA, ADA, and Section 1983, finding that plaintiff failed to establish he suffers from a qualifying disability and failed to allege facts showing he was denied benefits or accommodations because of any disability.
key_cases_cited: Jenkins v. New York City Dep't of Homeless Servs., 643 F. Supp. 2d 507 (S.D.N.Y. 2009)
Reaves v. Dep't of Veterans Affairs, 2009 WL 35074 (E.D.N.Y. Jan. 6, 2009)
DeShaney v. Winnebago County Dep't of Social Servs., 489 U.S. 189 (1989)
Salahuddin v. Cuomo, 861 F.2d 40 (2d Cir. 1988)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Placement in the 'Skyway' shelter program, which plaintiff believed was better suited to manage his alleged disabilities
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) for failure to state a claim, finding that plaintiff alleged he is '100% disabled' and complained about housing placement but failed to show he was excluded from participation in services or that defendants failed to accommodate an alleged disability. Plaintiff did not allege that current housing failed to accommodate his disabilities or denied him services because of disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 due process claim regarding housing placement; ADA Title II claim regarding denial of services by public entity; Medicaid coverage of preferred medication; Social Security Administration benefits; civil claim for personal injury from assaults; education access claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed § 1983 claim because plaintiff did not allege a state actor violated constitutional rights and homeless persons have no liberty or property right to placement in a particular shelter type; physical injuries were inflicted by private individuals, not state actors. ADA claim dismissed for failure to show exclusion from participation in services. Social Security and Medicaid claims dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction and failure to exhaust administrative remedies. Education claim dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction.

source_file: 9838640_2020_Brown v. Fire Department of the City of New York_nyed
case_name: Brown v. Fire Department of the City of New York
accommodation_description: African American and Afro-Costa Rican tenants allege harassment and pressure to vacate rent-regulated apartments based on race.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' hostile housing environment claim because conclusory allegations of race-based harassment failed to establish discriminatory motive, and dismissed the blockbusting claim because homeless individuals are not a protected class under the FHA.
brief_summary: Five African American and Afro-Costa Rican tenants sued their landlords and the City of New York alleging Fair Housing Act claims for hostile housing environment and blockbusting based on race-based harassment to force them from rent-regulated apartments. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding plaintiffs failed to adequately plead discriminatory motive and that blockbusting claims cannot be brought against landlords inducing tenants to vacate rent-regulated apartments.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Francis v. Kings Park Manor
Cain v. Rambert
Gladstone, Realtors v. Bellwood

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege discriminatory motive for the hostile housing environment claim. While the conduct (unsafe conditions, denial of services) was sufficiently severe, plaintiffs offered only conclusory allegations of race-based discrimination and two specific allegations that were logically flawed: (1) the reference to homeless individuals is not synonymous with African Americans, and (2) a single comment about appearance does not support an inference of discriminatory motivation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Blockbusting claim under § 3604(e) fails because plaintiffs failed to allege that Building Defendants made representations regarding entry of persons in a protected class. The court declined to infer that homeless individuals or supportive housing tenants are synonymous with people of color or substance abusers, and found no authority supporting extension of § 3604(e) to landlord attempts to induce tenant vacancies.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 warrantless entry claim against Building Defendants; § 1983 warrantless entry claim against FDNY Officers; Monell failure to train/supervise claim against City of New York
fha_claims.reasoning: § 1983 claim against Building Defendants fails under joint action test because plaintiffs alleged only a contract between Building Defendants and FDNY to use building as training site, with no allegations that unconstitutional warrantless entries were required, contemplated, or a natural consequence of the contract. § 1983 claim against FDNY Officers dismissed as abandoned when plaintiffs failed to respond to statute of limitations argument. Monell claim fails because plaintiffs did not allege facts showing City Defendants had notice of training deficiency prior to the alleged violations, and two instances of warrantless entry do not establish a pattern necessary for deliberate indifference.

source_file: 9838872_2023_Reese v. Park Place Condominium Homeowners Association I_dcd
case_name: Allison Reese v. Park Place Condominium Homeowners Association I
accommodation_description: No accommodation request — case involves claim that PPCA denied Reese use of its master insurance policy for foundation repairs while allowing white unit owners to make similar repairs.
key_holding: Reese's race discrimination claim survives because she adequately alleged that PPCA treated her differently from white unit owners in allowing access to the master insurance policy for foundation repairs, while her retaliation claim fails because reporting fraud and waste of association funds is not a protected activity under the FHA.
brief_summary: Allison Reese, an African-American condominium owner, sued Park Place Condominium Homeowners Association and its property manager alleging race discrimination under 42 U.S.C. § 3605 and retaliation under 42 U.S.C. § 3617 for denying her access to the master insurance policy for foundation repairs while allowing white owners to use the same policy. The court granted MCM's motion to dismiss as time-barred, dismissed Reese's retaliation claim for failure to allege protected activity, but denied PPCA's motion to dismiss on the discrimination claim, finding Reese stated a plausible claim that PPCA treated her differently based on race.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Use of condominium association's master insurance policy to fund repairs to plaintiff's unit for foundation defects
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged sufficient facts to survive motion to dismiss under Iqbal/Twombly standard by alleging she is African-American, qualified for coverage under the master policy, and PPCA denied her coverage while allowing White residents to invoke the policy for the same or similar repairs. The fact that one other African-American resident received coverage does not negate the inference of racial discrimination at the pleading stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Use of condominium association's master insurance policy to fund repairs, allegedly denied in retaliation for plaintiff's reporting of board members' fraud and waste
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege protected activity under § 3617 because reporting fraud and waste by board members is not a protected activity under the FHA—only reporting discriminatory housing practices qualifies. Additionally, plaintiff failed to allege causation because the initial denial occurred in December 2014 before plaintiff joined the board in 2015, and the alleged retaliatory denials did not begin until 2018, creating a two-year gap insufficient to establish causal connection.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of contract and breach of fiduciary duty claims added in amended complaint
fha_claims.reasoning: Amended complaint was filed outside the 21-day window for amendment as a matter of course and without opposing party consent or court leave. Court treated the filing as a motion for leave to amend. Plaintiff failed to respond to defendants' motion to strike or dismiss the amended complaint within 14 days, resulting in concession of the motion under Local Civil Rule 7(b). Original complaint remains operative.

source_file: 9839004_2021_Village Green at Sayville, LLC v. The Town of Islip_nyed
case_name: Village Green at Sayville, LLC v. The Town of Islip
race_if_mentioned: Race mentioned - racial and ethnic discrimination
accommodation_description: Plaintiff developer sought to modify zoning covenants and restrictions to permit multi-family housing development, alleging racially discriminatory animus motivated Defendants' refusal to approve the application.
key_holding: The court dismissed all seven causes of action for lack of standing, holding that plaintiff's civil rights and Fair Housing Act claims require a final zoning decision that plaintiff has not obtained, and plaintiff failed to demonstrate that pursuing further administrative remedies would be futile.
brief_summary: Village Green at Sayville, LLC sued the Town of Islip and related defendants alleging racially discriminatory animus motivated the Town Board to stifle plaintiff's efforts to modify zoning covenants and restrictions for a multi-family housing development. The court granted defendants' renewed motion to dismiss and denied plaintiff's motion to reargue, dismissing all seven causes of action for lack of standing because plaintiff failed to obtain a final zoning decision and could not satisfy the futility exception to the finality requirement.
key_cases_cited: Williamson v. Hamilton Bank, 473 U.S. 172 (1985)
Sunrise Detox V, LLC v. City of White Plains, 769 F.3d 118 (2d Cir. 2014)
Sherman v. Town of Chester, 752 F.3d 554 (2d Cir. 2014)
Mhany Management, Inc. v. County of Nassau, 819 F.3d 581 (2d Cir. 2016)
Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff lacked standing to bring FHA claims because it failed to obtain a final decision from the municipality on its application. The court held that FHA claims in the land-use context are subject to the Williamson final-decision requirement, and Plaintiff's alleged injuries (economic losses and deprivation of right to develop) do not constitute the type of dignitary or emotional harm that would exempt the case from that requirement.

case_name: Yan Ping Xu v. Suffolk County
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested in this case. Plaintiff sought reinstatement to her residence and return of personal property following her eviction on December 14, 2018 pursuant to a state court order; the housing-related relief sought was reversal of a lawful eviction, not a disability-related accommodation.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's motion for reconsideration of the dismissal of her amended complaint under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, and further held that even if Rooker-Feldman did not apply, plaintiff's federal claims—including FHA discrimination, §1983, Fourth Amendment, and Due Process claims—were independently meritless.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Yan Ping Xu, a Chinese national, sought reconsideration of the court's July 2020 dismissal of her amended complaint after she was evicted from her home pursuant to Suffolk County Surrogate's Court orders. She alleged, among other things, national origin discrimination under the FHA and constitutional violations under §1983, arguing that Rooker-Feldman did not bar her claims because the parties and theories differed from the underlying state court proceeding. The court denied reconsideration, finding no overlooked controlling law or facts, reaffirming that her injuries were produced by the state court judgment, and holding that her discrimination claim—premised solely on her being Chinese while the opposing party was Caucasian—failed to plausibly allege discriminatory treatment or a disparate impact under the FHA.
key_cases_cited: Sung Cho v. City of New York, 910 F.3d 639 (2d Cir. 2018)
Rooker-Feldman doctrine
Monell v. Dep't of Soc. Servs. of N.Y., 436 U.S. 658 (1978)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: National origin discrimination claim based on plaintiff being Chinese and defendant being Caucasian
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege discrimination under the FHA by merely asserting that parties are of different races without factual allegations that would nudge the claim across the line from conceivable to plausible. Conclusory allegations of different races and references to 'white race friends' are insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 due process claims (procedural and substantive), Fourth Amendment seizure claim, national origin discrimination claims under federal constitutional provisions
fha_claims.reasoning: All federal claims are barred by the Rooker-Feldman doctrine because plaintiff's injuries were produced by the underlying state court judgment and her claims speak to the propriety of the state court orders. Additionally, § 1983 claims fail because individual defendants are protected by qualified and quasi-judicial immunity for executing facially valid court orders, and Monell liability is not plausibly alleged against Suffolk County. Fourth Amendment claim fails because eviction was authorized by state court order. Due process claims fail because plaintiff received a hearing in both Surrogate's Court and Appellate Division, and alleged no conduct shocking the conscience.

case_name: Birch Family Services, Inc. v. Wlody
accommodation_description: Plaintiff operates a group home for individuals with developmental disabilities; the claim concerns alleged interference through surveillance, photographing staff and residents, filing municipal complaints, and making discriminatory comments motivated by animus toward African-American staff and disabled residents.
key_holding: Plaintiff failed to establish pretext under the McDonnell Douglas framework because while discriminatory comments were made, Plaintiff did not present sufficient evidence that Defendants' proffered legitimate reasons for their conduct (documenting noise, littering, parking issues, and staff supervision failures) were false and motivated by discriminatory animus rather than genuine neighbor complaints.
brief_summary: Birch Family Services, Inc., which operates a community residence for six individuals with developmental disabilities, sued neighboring property owners Jack and Corinne Wlody under the Fair Housing Act and NYCHRL, alleging that Defendants' daily videotaping and photographing of staff and residents, filing of municipal complaints, and discriminatory comments were motivated by animus toward African-American staff and disabled residents. The court granted Defendants' motion for summary judgment, finding that while Plaintiff established a prima facie case, Defendants articulated legitimate non-discriminatory reasons for their conduct and Plaintiff failed to demonstrate pretext.
key_cases_cited: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
St. Mary's Honor Ctr. v. Hicks, 509 U.S. 502 (1993)
Texas Dept. of Cmty. Affairs v. Burdine, 450 U.S. 248 (1981)
Frazier v. Rominger, 27 F.3d 828 (2d Cir. 1994)
Ohana v. 180 Prospect Place Realty Corp., 996 F. Supp. 238 (E.D.N.Y. 1998)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Although plaintiff established a prima facie case of Section 3617 interference/coercion based on defendants' nearly five-year videotaping campaign and discriminatory statements, defendants articulated legitimate non-discriminatory reasons (documenting staff misconduct, noise, littering, parking violations, and resident supervision failures). Plaintiff failed to demonstrate by preponderance of evidence that these reasons were pretextual; plaintiff's bare assertion that defendants 'want them gone' was insufficient to overcome defendants' neutral explanations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: New York City Human Rights Law § 8-107(19) — interference/coercion/intimidation claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish that NYCHRL § 8-107 protects a right to enjoy premises free from discrimination, and plaintiff did not allege that defendants made threats to harm staff or residents, which are required to state a claim under § 8-107(19).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Remediation of mold conditions in apartment; habitability repairs
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction. Plaintiffs' allegations of negligence, harassment, and discrimination were not supported by specific factual allegations and did not raise a federal question. The vague allegations of discrimination did not suggest any form of discrimination covered by the Fair Housing Act or other federal statute, and plaintiffs failed to establish diversity jurisdiction.

source_file: 9839980_2021_Perricone-Bernovich v. Community Development Corporation of Long Island, Inc._nyed
case_name: Barbara A. Perricone-Bernovich, et al. v. Community Development Corporation of Long Island, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: Request for waiver to allow use of Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher at sister's home rather than in Perricone's own separate household
key_holding: The court did not rule on the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim; instead, it identified threshold deficiencies requiring plaintiffs to establish capacity (Perricone-Bernovich cannot represent her brother without being an attorney or obtaining a court-appointed guardian) and standing (Perricone-Bernovich and Bernovich have not established their own injury-in-fact sufficient to confer Article III standing).
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Perricone-Bernovich, Bernovich, and John Perricone (who has schizophrenia) sued the Community Development Corporation of Long Island, which administers Perricone's Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher, alleging denial of reasonable accommodation to use the voucher at Perricone-Bernovich's home. The court declined to reach the merits of the FHA claim, instead finding procedural deficiencies: Perricone-Bernovich cannot proceed pro se on her brother's behalf without being an attorney, and neither Perricone-Bernovich nor Bernovich have established Article III standing to assert claims on their own behalf, giving plaintiffs 30 days to amend.
key_cases_cited: Iannaccone v. Law, 142 F.3d 553 (2d Cir. 1998)
Berrios v. New York City Hous. Auth., 564 F.3d 130 (2d Cir. 2009)
Elk Grove Unified School Dist. v. Newdow, 542 U.S. 1 (2004)
Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver to allow Perricone to use his Housing Choice Voucher while living in the home of Perricone-Bernovich and Bernovich; transfer of Housing Choice Voucher to alternative housing arrangement
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed for lack of standing under Article III, finding that Perricone-Bernovich and Bernovich failed to allege injury in fact traceable to the challenged action and redressable by a favorable decision. The court did not reach the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim because the plaintiffs lacked capacity and standing to proceed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, right to privacy
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed for lack of standing, finding that Perricone-Bernovich and Bernovich failed to establish injury in fact or that any injury was fairly traceable to the defendants' actions and redressable by a favorable decision. The court did not reach the merits of the non-FHA claims.

source_file: 9840258_2021_Long Island Housing Services, Inc. v. NPS Holiday Square LLC_nyed
case_name: Long Island Housing Services, Inc. v. NPS Holiday Square LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs challenge NPS's income-to-rent requirement as having an unlawful disparate impact on housing voucher users with disabilities, seeking injunctive and damages relief under the FHA.
key_holding: The court admitted expert Nancy McArdle's disparate impact methodology as reliable under Daubert, finding that controlling for income level in a disparate impact analysis would improperly convert the claim into a disparate treatment analysis; the court excluded expert Michael Salve's competing methodology as unreliable, and admitted expert John Rollins's testimony regarding NPS's business necessity defense.
brief_summary: Fair housing organizations and individuals with disabilities sued NPS Property Corp. and affiliated entities alleging that NPS's income-to-rent screening policy had an unlawful disparate impact on housing voucher users, including those with disabilities, in violation of the FHA, NYSHRL, and SCHRL. The court ruled on multiple Daubert motions, admitting plaintiffs' expert McArdle's statistical analysis showing disparate impact while excluding defendants' expert Salve's methodology as improperly converting a disparate impact claim into a disparate treatment analysis, and admitting defendants' expert Rollins on business necessity.
key_cases_cited: Mhany Mgmt., Inc. v. County of Nassau, 819 F.3d 581 (2d Cir. 2016)
Texas Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Cmtys. Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharms., Inc., 509 U.S. 579 (1993)
Griggs v. Duke Power Co., 401 U.S. 424 (1971)
Dothard v. Rawlinson, 433 U.S. 321 (1977)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: NPS's income-to-rent rental application policy, which requires applicants without housing vouchers to have income double the monthly rent, and applicants with housing vouchers to have income equal to 80-100% of one month's rent.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied defendants' motion to exclude plaintiff's expert McArdle's disparate impact testimony, finding her methodology reliable and consistent with controlling precedent (Griggs, Dothard, Geller). The court held that disparate impact analysis does not require controlling for the protected characteristic itself (income level) and that McArdle's comparison of subsidized renters to all renters properly establishes a prima facie case. The claim survives expert gatekeeping and proceeds to trial on the merits.

case_name: Charles Didier Calixte v. Susan Ray Equities Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged race discrimination arising from refusal to transfer lease and lockout, with no accommodation request analyzed.
key_holding: The complaint was dismissed because plaintiff failed to allege any direct evidence of race discrimination or minimal facts to support an inference of discriminatory intent under the McDonnell Douglas framework, and plaintiff's Section 1983 claim failed for lack of state action.
brief_summary: Charles Didier Calixte sued Susan Ray Equities Inc. alleging race discrimination based on the landlord's refusal to transfer his lease and subsequent lockout. The court dismissed the complaint for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, finding that Calixte failed to state a viable Fair Housing Act claim because he offered no direct evidence of discriminatory intent and his conclusory allegations about his race and the defendant's ownership did not establish a prima facie case of discrimination.
key_cases_cited: Francis v. Kings Park Manor, Inc., 992 F.3d 67 (2d Cir. 2021)
Steel Co. v. Citizens for a Better Env't, 523 U.S. 83 (1998)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
National Collegiate Athletic Ass'n v. Tarkanian, 488 U.S. 179 (1988)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, finding that plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claim alleging race discrimination was wholly insubstantial and frivolous because he failed to allege direct evidence of discriminatory treatment or minimal support for discriminatory intent under McDonnell Douglas; mere allegation that plaintiff is Black and defendant is Jewish-owned is insufficient to raise an inference of race-based discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 due process claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed § 1983 claim for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction because plaintiff failed to allege state action; private landlord's conduct in refusing to transfer lease and locking plaintiff out does not constitute action under color of state law and lacks the requisite nexus to state action required for § 1983 liability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim involves Truth in Lending Act (TILA) disclosure requirements for a mortgage loan, not a Fair Housing Act claim.
fha_claims.disposition: Motion for Entry of Judgment Denied
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that the TIL Disclosure accurately reflected the terms of the legal obligation at the time of closing, before the borrowers' actual performance was knowable. Post-closing events (default and interest rate increases) do not render disclosures inaccurate under 12 C.F.R. § 226.17(e), which provides that inaccuracies resulting from events occurring after disclosure delivery are not violations.

case_name: Jean Robert Saint-Jean, et al. v. Emigrant Mortgage Company, et al.
accommodation_description: This opinion does not address any Fair Housing Act reasonable accommodation claim. The motion concerns a Truth in Lending Act (TILA) claim regarding alleged inaccurate loan disclosures.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's motion for entry of judgment on her TILA claim, finding that TILA's material disclosure requirements are evaluated based on the terms of the loan agreement at the time of closing, not on the borrower's subsequent actual performance; therefore, even though the loan later defaulted, the original disclosures accurately reflected the contractual payment schedule.
brief_summary: Jean Robert and Edith Saint-Jean sued Emigrant Mortgage Company alleging violations of TILA, the Fair Housing Act, ECOA, and state and city human rights laws arising from a mortgage loan. This opinion addresses only Edith Saint-Jean's motion for entry of judgment on her TILA claim, which the court denied because the TIL disclosure accurately reflected the contractual loan terms at closing, and any inaccuracies from the borrower's subsequent default did not violate TILA's disclosure requirements.
key_cases_cited: Crawford v. Franklin Credit Mgmt. Corp., 758 F.3d 473 (2d Cir. 2014)
Benion v. Bank One, Dayton, N.A., 144 F.3d 1056 (7th Cir. 1998)
Smith v. Wells Fargo Bank, N.A., 666 F. App’x 84 (2d Cir. 2016)
Nadler v. Bank of Am., N.A., 2010 WL 4922307 (S.D.N.Y. 2010)
Newa v. Castle Point Mortg., Inc., 2008 WL 3891263 (S.D.N.Y. 2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: TILA disclosure violations; ECOA; NYSHRL; NYCHRL
fha_claims.disposition: Motion for Entry of Judgment Denied
fha_claims.reasoning: The court concluded that the TIL Disclosure accurately reflected the terms of the legal obligation at the time of closing and that post-closing inaccuracies resulting from the borrowers' default do not violate TILA's material disclosure requirements under 12 C.F.R. § 226.17(e). The court rejected plaintiff's argument that Emigrant should have anticipated default and adjusted disclosures accordingly, finding that such anticipatory estimation would frustrate TILA's disclosure purposes.

source_file: 9841793_2022_Ortega v. New York State Temporary Disability Assistance_nyed

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Housing assignment and accommodation related to medical care and medication coverage
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed under § 1915(e)(2)(B) screening as frivolous, finding plaintiff has not alleged facts sufficient to state a claim under the Fair Housing Act or Americans with Disabilities Act, and does not have a constitutional right to a particular housing assignment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Constitutional due process claims regarding housing and medical care; Social Security Administration benefits review; Medicaid coverage claims
fha_claims.disposition: 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii); Eleventh Amendment; lack of subject matter jurisdiction
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed non-FHA claims as frivolous under § 1915(e)(2)(B) screening, finding no constitutional right to particular housing assignment, no final agency decision for Social Security review, and lack of federal subject matter jurisdiction over state Medicaid and housing matters.

source_file: 9841795_2022_Ortega v. Samaritan Village Myrtle Ave. Men's Shelter_nyed

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Housing assignment and accommodation related to medical care and medication coverage
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) for failure to state a claim under the Fair Housing Act. Plaintiff did not allege facts sufficient to state an FHA claim regarding housing assignment or reasonable accommodation for disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Constitutional right to housing, Medicaid coverage of medication, Social Security Administration benefits
fha_claims.disposition: 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii); Eleventh Amendment; lack of subject matter jurisdiction
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed claims related to constitutional right to housing, Medicaid coverage, and Social Security benefits as lacking federal subject matter jurisdiction. Plaintiff had not sought review of a final Social Security Administration decision, and claims regarding housing and medical care did not implicate federal law.

source_file: 9841875_2022_Fair Housing Justice Center, Inc. v. 203 Jay St. Associates, LLC_nyed
case_name: Fair Housing Justice Center, Inc. v. 203 Jay St. Associates, LLC
accommodation_description: This is a design and construction accessibility claim under § 3604(f)(3)(C), not a reasonable accommodation claim; testers and an accessibility expert observed physical inaccessibility features (heavy doors, narrow interiors, excessive slopes, beveled thresholds, inaccessible reach ranges) at a condominium building that allegedly fails to comply with FHA accessibility requirements.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motions to dismiss, holding that (1) FHJC has organizational standing based on resource diversion from testing investigations, and (2) a plaintiff need not allege an individual disabled person was denied housing to state a design and construction violation—tester observations of inaccessible architectural features suffice to establish a plausible FHA claim under § 3604(f)(3)(C).
brief_summary: Fair Housing Justice Center, Inc., a fair housing organization, sued property owners, a property management company, and an architectural firm alleging that the 203 Jay Street Condominium in Brooklyn was designed and constructed in violation of the FHA's accessibility requirements, as observed by testers and an accessibility expert who documented heavy doors, narrow interiors, excessive slopes, and other architectural barriers. The court denied defendants' motions to dismiss, holding that FHJC has organizational standing based on resource diversion and that design and construction violations can be established through tester observations without requiring an individual disabled person to have attempted to rent.
key_cases_cited: Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman
S.C. Bodner Co.
Garcia v. Brockway
Smith v. Pacific Props. and Dev. Corp.
Fair Hous. Justice Ctr., Inc. v. JDS Dev. LLC

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible design and construction of residential condominium, including accessible entrance doors, interior doors, kitchens, bathrooms, thresholds, routes, lobbies, loading zones, seating areas, and fitness equipment
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that a fair housing organization may allege a design and construction violation under § 3604(f)(3)(C) based on tester observations of inaccessible features without requiring proof of an actual attempted sale or rental to a disabled person. The complaint alleges sufficient factual detail regarding specific architectural defects observed by testers and an accessibility expert to survive the motion to dismiss under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: New York State Human Rights Law (Article 15 of N.Y. Executive Law), New York City Human Rights Law (N.Y.C. Admin. Code § 8-107 et seq.), and New York State Civil Rights Law (§ 40 et seq.)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court declined to dismiss state law claims under supplemental jurisdiction because the FHA claims survived the motion to dismiss and defendants did not proffer any independent basis for dismissal of the state law claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: NYLL wage and hour claims (unpaid overtime, wage notices, wage statements); Title VII race discrimination; NYCHRL retaliation; NYLL §§ 215 and 740 retaliation; unjust enrichment; employer liability; aiding and abetting
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss on NYLL wage and hour claims, Title VII race discrimination claim, NYCHRL retaliation claims for Murray and Welsh, NYLL § 740 claims for Welsh and Moyle, unjust enrichment claims, employer liability claims, and aiding and abetting claims for Murray and Welsh. Court granted motion to dismiss on Moyle's NYCHRL retaliation claim, NYLL § 215 claims, Murray's NYLL § 740 claim (time-barred), and Moyle's aiding and abetting claim. Claims survive MTD and proceed to next stage.

source_file: 9842313_2022_Neira Marquez v. Office of Social Security_nyed

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff references ADA, Fair Housing Act, Dodd-Frank Act, and Bank Secrecy Act in seeking relief related to alleged underpayment of SSI benefits and discrimination based on disability (legal blindness)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court construed plaintiff's references to ADA and FHA as indisputably meritless legal theories because plaintiff failed to allege that the defendant acted due to his disability or that his disability made it difficult to access benefits requiring reasonable accommodation. The court dismissed these claims as frivolous under § 1915(e)(2)(B) without substantive analysis of FHA elements.

case_name: Jane Doe v. Anthony Pistilli et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges Defendants denied lease renewal based on her sex after she rejected sexual advances from the building superintendent.
key_holding: The S.D.N.Y. transferred the case to the Eastern District of New York because the plaintiff resides there, all parties reside there, and the operative facts occurred there, making venue more appropriate in the Eastern District.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Jane Doe sued Anthony Pistilli and related entities under the Fair Housing Act, alleging sex discrimination in the denial of her lease renewal after she rejected sexual advances from the building superintendent. The S.D.N.Y. granted transfer to the Eastern District of New York for convenience of parties and witnesses and because all operative facts occurred there.
key_cases_cited: Corley v. United States, 11 F.4th 79 (2d Cir. 2021)
D.H. Blair & Co. v. Gottdiener, 462 F.3d 95 (2d Cir. 2006)
Zepherin v. Greyhound Lines, Inc., 415 F. Supp. 2d 409 (S.D.N.Y. 2006)
Bank of Am., N.A. v. Wilmington Trust FSB, 943 F. Supp. 2d 417 (S.D.N.Y. 2013)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court transferred the case to the Eastern District of New York for convenience and in the interest of justice under 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a), finding that all parties reside in the Eastern District, the locus of operative facts is there, and witnesses and documents are located there. The merits of the FHA claim alleging sex discrimination in lease renewal denial were not addressed.

case_name: Mohamed Samura v. Maria Figueroa, Castleton Park Management, and Castleton Preservation LLC
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; the case involves alleged race-based refusal to rent in housing application process
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA race discrimination claim was dismissed as time-barred because the discriminatory act (rejection of apartment application) occurred on August 22, 2017, and the complaint filed in February 2021 fell well outside the two-year statute of limitations, with neither the continuing violation doctrine nor equitable tolling applicable.
brief_summary: African American plaintiff Mohamed Samura sued property management defendants alleging they violated the Fair Housing Act by rejecting his apartment application in August 2017 based on his race, national origin, and familial status. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding the February 2021 complaint was time-barred under the FHA's two-year statute of limitations because the discriminatory act occurred in August 2017, and neither the continuing violation doctrine nor equitable tolling saved the claim.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Harper v. Ercole, 648 F.3d 132 (2d Cir. 2011)
Clement v. United Homes, LLC, 914 F. Supp. 2d 362 (E.D.N.Y. 2012)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The discriminatory conduct (rejection of application) occurred on August 22, 2017, but plaintiff did not file suit until February 24, 2021—approximately three-and-one-half years later, well beyond the FHA's two-year statute of limitations. The continuing violation doctrine does not apply because plaintiff failed to plausibly allege an ongoing policy or practice of discrimination extending into the limitations period, and equitable tolling is not warranted because the Rejection Letter expressly informed plaintiff of his right to pursue FHA claims and plaintiff failed to demonstrate fraudulent concealment or extraordinary circumstances.

source_file: 9842866_2023_Levy v. Lawrence Gardens Apartments Del, LLC_nyed
case_name: David Levy v. Lawrence Gardens Apartments Del, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought accommodations including designated handicapped parking spaces, maintenance of elevators and automatic doors, and 24-hour unlocked access to accessible lobby entrances at his apartment complex, but the court found he failed to allege that he actually requested any of these accommodations from defendants and was refused.
key_holding: The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss all federal FHA and ADA claims because: plaintiff abandoned the design-and-construction claim (building predated 1991), the reasonable accommodation claim failed for lack of any alleged specific requests and refusals, the hostile housing environment claim failed for insufficient severity/pervasiveness and timeliness, and the retaliation claim failed for lack of a cognizable adverse effect.
brief_summary: David Levy, a tenant who uses a walker at a 1961 Brooklyn apartment complex, sued his landlord under the FHA and ADA alleging failure to provide accessible facilities, a hostile housing environment based on disability and sexual orientation, and retaliation for filing a complaint with the New York State Division of Human Rights. The Eastern District of New York granted defendants' Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss all federal claims, finding that Levy never alleged he made specific accommodation requests that were refused, that the harassment allegations were untimely or insufficiently severe to constitute a hostile housing environment, and that his fear of future eviction could not alone constitute an adverse retaliatory action. The court declined supplemental jurisdiction over the remaining state and local law claims.
key_cases_cited: Reyes v. Fairfield Properties, 661 F. Supp. 2d 249 (E.D.N.Y. 2009)
Dinapoli v. DPA Wallace Ave II, LLC, 2009 WL 755354 (S.D.N.Y. Mar. 23, 2009)
Favourite v. 55 Halley St., Inc., 381 F. Supp. 3d 266 (S.D.N.Y. 2019)
Cain v. Rambert, 2014 WL 2440596 (E.D.N.Y. May 30, 2014)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Designated handicapped parking spaces; maintenance of elevators and automatic doors; 24-hour access to accessible lobby doors (currently locked at 5:00 pm)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead that he requested these accommodations from defendants and was refused. Under the reasonable accommodation framework, a plaintiff must allege that defendants 'refused to make such accommodation,' but Levy pleaded no facts showing he requested handicapped parking, elevator/door maintenance, or 24-hour lobby access and was denied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible design and construction of the Complex (built in 1961)
fha_claims.reasoning: The FHA's design and construction requirement under § 3604(f)(3)(C) applies only to buildings constructed for first occupancy after March 13, 1991. The Complex was built in 1961, so it is not subject to the design and construction standards. Plaintiff conceded this point and abandoned the claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Hostile housing environment based on sexual orientation and disability-related harassment
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's hostile housing environment claim fails on multiple grounds: (1) the 2016 harassment incident is time-barred (more than two years before March 2021 filing); (2) plaintiff failed to establish a continuing violation; (3) the 2019 physical attack by Teper without accompanying verbal abuse is not sufficiently severe; (4) the Spanish name-calling ('pendejo') does not plausibly mean what plaintiff claims and is not based on disability or sex; and (5) Rosenfield's comments about rehab/nursing home are not sufficiently serious to support a hostile environment claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliatory conduct including withholding rent bills, physical attack, threatening comments, and pressure to drop complaints
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege a cognizable adverse action. The only adverse effect alleged is a fear of future eviction, which the Second Circuit has held cannot alone support a retaliation claim without other allegations of actual adverse effects. Mere fear of future eviction is insufficient.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III claim; state and local law claims (security deposit interest, rent withholding)
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA Title III does not apply to residential facilities as a matter of law. The management office, pool, and parking garage are part of the residential Complex and therefore not public accommodations under the ADA. State and local law claims were dismissed without prejudice; the court declined supplemental jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3) because all federal claims were eliminated before trial.

case_name: Wayne J. Hall, Reina Hernandez, and Floridalma Portilla v. Nassau County, Department of Assessment of Nassau County, Assessment Review Commission of Nassau County
accommodation_description: Not applicable — this case does not involve a request for a reasonable accommodation or modification; it concerns alleged racially discriminatory property tax assessment practices by Nassau County.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' FHA and federal civil rights claims on comity grounds, finding that deference to the state adjudicative process was required because plaintiffs were challenging their own property tax assessments and New York state courts provided adequate remedies.
brief_summary: Nonwhite residential property owners in Nassau County filed a putative class action alleging that a seven-year freeze on annual property reassessments, imposed by County Executive Mangano beginning in 2010, unconstitutionally shifted the property tax burden from wealthy white communities to lower-income nonwhite communities in violation of the FHA (§§ 3604(b), 3605, 3617), 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 and 1983, and the Nassau County Charter. The district court declined to exercise jurisdiction on comity grounds, finding that the second and third comity factors—plaintiffs' direct stake in their own tax liability and the availability of adequate New York state court remedies—weighed decisively against federal adjudication. Having dismissed all federal claims, the court also declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the state law claim.
key_cases_cited: Levin v. Com. Energy, Inc., 560 U.S. 413 (2010)
Joseph v. Hyman, 659 F.3d 215 (2d Cir. 2011)
Fair Assessment in Real Estate Ass'n, Inc. v. McNary, 454 U.S. 100 (1981)
Long Island Lighting Co. v. Town of Brookhaven, 889 F.2d 428 (2d Cir. 1989)
Global Leadership Foundation v. City of New York, No. 21-CV-10942, 2022 WL 2788398 (S.D.N.Y. July 15, 2022)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Property tax assessment scheme with racially disparate impact on nonwhite property owners
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed on comity grounds, declining to adjudicate federal tax claims that are more appropriately resolved in state court where adequate remedies exist. The second and third comity factors weighed against federal adjudication: plaintiffs' own tax liability was at issue, and New York state courts provide plain, speedy, and efficient remedies for constitutional objections to real property taxes.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (Fourteenth Amendment equal protection and due process), 42 U.S.C. § 1981 (equal rights), Nassau County Charter § 603
fha_claims.reasoning: All federal claims dismissed on comity grounds. Court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims after dismissing federal claims.

case_name: Thomas v. Genova
accommodation_description: No disability accommodation requested; case involves alleged race-based selective enforcement in code prosecution for using property as two-family home.
key_holding: The court dismissed Plaintiffs' FHA claim on procedural grounds (improper amendment) and, alternatively, granted summary judgment because Plaintiffs failed to establish discriminatory motive—Plaintiffs admitted the code enforcement officer did not know Mr. Thomas's race and presented only conclusory allegations of discrimination unsupported by evidence.
brief_summary: Black and Puerto Rican homeowners sued the Town of Oyster Bay and its officials alleging race-based selective enforcement and malicious prosecution for code violations related to their two-family home use. The court dismissed the FHA claim as procedurally improper (added in violation of a prior order) and alternatively granted summary judgment for defendants because plaintiffs failed to establish discriminatory motive, admitting the code enforcement officer did not know Mr. Thomas's race and presenting only conclusory allegations without evidentiary support.
key_cases_cited: Haber v. ASN 50th St. LLC, 847 F. Supp. 2d 578 (S.D.N.Y. 2012)
273 Lee Ave. Tenants Ass'n by Sanchez v. Steinmetz, 330 F. Supp. 3d 778 (E.D.N.Y. 2018)
Mitchell v. Shane, 350 F.3d 39 (2d Cir. 2003)
Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986)
McCarthy v. Dun & Bradstreet Corp., 482 F.3d 184 (2d Cir. 2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to establish a prima facie case of FHA disparate treatment discrimination under 42 U.S.C. §§ 3604(a)-(b) and 3617. The court applied the McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework and found that plaintiffs could not prove defendants acted with discriminatory motive because: (1) Gioia did not know plaintiff's race when initiating the code enforcement action; (2) plaintiffs admitted they had no evidence of discriminatory intent; (3) plaintiffs could not identify similarly situated comparators; and (4) plaintiffs failed to depose defendants or elicit evidence of discriminatory intent during depositions. The court also noted the FHA claim was procedurally barred because it violated Judge Seybert's 2013 order limiting the scope of amendments, but ruled on the merits sua sponte under Rule 56(f).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (malicious prosecution, selective enforcement, due process); 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1982 (intentional discrimination); 42 U.S.C. §§ 1985, 1986 (conspiracy); Monell liability; state common law claims (intentional infliction of emotional distress, abuse of process, malicious prosecution)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted summary judgment on all non-FHA federal claims. Section 1983 malicious prosecution claim failed because defendants had probable cause to initiate the code enforcement action based on the totality of circumstances (property visibly operated as two-family home in single-family zone, no permit, conflicting tax records, plaintiff's admission of renting upstairs). Selective enforcement claim failed because plaintiff could not identify similarly situated comparators and presented no evidence of discriminatory motive. Due process claim was not ripe because plaintiffs never requested a variance or permit. Sections 1981/1982 claims failed due to lack of evidence of discriminatory intent and plaintiff's admission that Gioia was unaware of his race when initiating action. Sections 1985/1986 conspiracy claims failed because no underlying constitutional violation existed and plaintiffs presented only speculative allegations without factual basis for a meeting of the minds. Monell claim failed because no underlying constitutional violation and no evidence of municipal policy. The court declined supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims.

source_file: 9844374_2024_Disability Rights New York v. The State of New York_nyed

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II ADA discrimination claim; Title II reasonable modification mandate; Section 504 Rehabilitation Act claim regarding institutionalization in residential schools
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff organization (DRNY) lacked Article III standing to bring suit. Although Congress may authorize P&A systems to litigate on behalf of disabled individuals, the constitutional minimum of injury-in-fact cannot be waived. DRNY failed to establish associational standing under Hunt because it did not allege that its constituents possessed the requisite indicia of membership, and it expressly declined to pursue that theory.

source_file: 9845340_2019_UMH Properties, Inc. v. Village of Coxsackie_nynd
case_name: UMH Properties, Inc. et al. v. Village of Coxsackie et al.
accommodation_description: The accommodation request is not described in this summary order.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' third cause of action under N.Y. C.P.L.R. 3001 because that statute does not apply to federal court proceedings, dismissed the fourth cause of action under Article 78 as untimely, and dismissed all claims against the Village of Coxsackie Board of Trustees for lack of capacity to be sued.
brief_summary: UMH Properties, a manufactured housing community operator, sued the Village of Coxsackie and its officials under the Fair Housing Act and state law, challenging zoning or land-use decisions affecting its property. The court granted defendants' partial motion for judgment on the pleadings, dismissing plaintiffs' state law claims and all claims against the Board of Trustees, while declining to substantively analyze the FHA claims at this procedural stage.
key_cases_cited: Buck v. Libous, 2005 WL 1460408 (N.D.N.Y. 2005)
Riano v. Town of Schroeppel, 2013 WL 5702263 (N.D.N.Y. 2013)
Willard v. Town of Hamburg, 1996 WL 607100 (W.D.N.Y. 1996)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not specified in opinion; FHA § 3604 claim against Village of Coxsackie and Mayor Evans survives motion for judgment on the pleadings
fha_claims.disposition: Partial Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted defendants' partial motion for judgment on the pleadings only as to the third and fourth causes of action and all claims against the Board. The FHA § 3604 claim against the Village and Mayor Evans was not addressed in the motion and survives.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not specified in opinion; FHA § 3617 claim against Village of Coxsackie and Mayor Evans survives motion for judgment on the pleadings
fha_claims.disposition: Partial Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted defendants' partial motion for judgment on the pleadings only as to the third and fourth causes of action and all claims against the Board. The FHA § 3617 claim against the Village and Mayor Evans was not addressed in the motion and survives.

case_name: Doe v. YWCA of Northeastern NY
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a survivor of domestic violence with documented PTSD, sought to prevent eviction and lease non-renewal as an accommodation for her disability, claiming defendants knew of her disability but ignored her requests.
key_holding: The court granted Dozer Blaze's motion to dismiss the FHA claims because Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts creating a plausible inference that discriminatory animus based on her PTSD disability motivated her eviction and harassment.
brief_summary: Jane Doe, a Black immigrant survivor of domestic violence with PTSD, sued Dozer Blaze Properties and YWCA of Northeastern NY alleging disability discrimination after she was subjected to eviction proceedings and harassment following a death threat from her spouse. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that while Plaintiff adequately alleged membership in a protected class, she failed to plead sufficient facts creating a plausible inference that discriminatory motive based on her disability motivated her eviction.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Mitchell v. Shane, 350 F.3d 39 (2d Cir. 2003)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges hostile environment harassment and discriminatory eviction based on disability (PTSD) and/or protected class status
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff failed to allege facts sufficient to provide even a minimal inference of discriminatory motivation. While plaintiff alleged reprehensible conduct by Loeber, she alleged no facts making it plausible that discrimination because of disability motivated the defendant's action. Dismissed without prejudice to re-pleading.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Hostile housing environment claim based on harassment allegedly because of membership in protected class
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied the three-part test for post-acquisition hostile housing environment claims under § 3617 and found plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that harassment was because of PTSD or other protected class membership. Although allegations may constitute severe and pervasive conduct, plaintiff did not connect discriminatory animus to that conduct. Dismissed without prejudice.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Violence Against Women Act (VAWA) housing discrimination claim (34 U.S.C. § 12491) and VAWA confidentiality violation claim (34 U.S.C. § 12291(b)(2))
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found there is no private civil remedy under VAWA, citing United States v. Morrison, 529 U.S. 598 (2000), which found the private civil remedy under VAWA unconstitutional. All VAWA claims dismissed with prejudice.

case_name: Timmons v. Kingsley-Johnston, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested permission to continue using her motorized scooter on the lawn between her apartment patio and the parking lot as her primary means of egress.
key_holding: The court found genuine issues of material fact exist as to whether allowing scooter use on the lawn constituted a reasonable accommodation (not imposing undue hardship) and whether plaintiff provided adequate assurances for the sidewalk modification, while also finding triable issues on the retaliation claim.
brief_summary: Genevieve Timmons sued her property management company and landlords alleging they violated the FHA by refusing to accommodate her mobility disability (osteoarthritis, degenerative disc disease) that required use of a motorized scooter, and by refusing to permit installation of a sidewalk as a reasonable modification; she also alleged retaliation for requesting accommodations. The court denied defendants' motion for summary judgment, finding genuine disputes of material fact as to whether allowing scooter use on the lawn was reasonable given liability concerns, whether plaintiff's proposed sidewalk modification was adequately described, and whether the landlord's decision not to renew the lease, inspections, and code enforcement complaint were retaliatory.
key_cases_cited: Olsen v. Stark Homes, Inc., 759 F.3d 140 (2d Cir. 2014)
Austin v. Town of Farmington, 826 F.3d 622 (2d Cir. 2016)
McElwee v. Cty. of Orange, 700 F.3d 635 (2d Cir. 2012)
Warren v. Delvista Towers Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 49 F. Supp. 3d 1082 (S.D. Fla. 2014)
Tsombanidis v. City of W. Haven, 180 F. Supp. 2d 262 (D. Conn. 2001)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to continue using a motorized scooter to travel between apartment patio and parking lot across the lawn
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine issue of material fact as to whether the accommodation was reasonable. Defendants failed to demonstrate undue hardship or substantial burden; liability concerns alone without individualized assessment based on objective evidence amount to speculation. Plaintiff had used the scooter for over two years without incident.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Installation of a sidewalk from apartment patio to parking lot, funded through Onondaga County Ramp & Accessibility Modification Program
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine issue of material fact as to whether plaintiff provided adequate description of the proposed modification and reasonable assurances of workmanlike performance. The adequacy of description depends on the extent and nature of the modification; CCD's plan was sufficient to raise a triable issue, and it was unclear why defendants believed a municipality with experience in codes and ADA standards would fail to comply.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Non-renewal of lease, repeated apartment inspections, and complaint to Cicero Town Code Enforcement
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine issues of material fact on all four elements of retaliation claim: (1) protected activity established by triable issue on reasonableness of accommodation/modification; (2) defendant's awareness of March 2017 conversation about scooter need; (3) adverse actions (non-renewal, inspections, code enforcement complaint); (4) causal connection between protected activity and adverse actions, with triable issues on whether all units were inspected and the actual condition of the apartment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: New York State Human Rights Law retaliation claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Court analyzed NYSHRL retaliation claim using same prima facie framework as FHA claim (protected activity, defendant awareness, adverse action, causal connection) and found genuine issues of material fact on all elements, denying summary judgment.

source_file: 9846958_2021_George, Sr. v. Commissioner of Social Secirity_nynd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Social Security disability benefits determination under 42 U.S.C. §§ 405(g) and 1383(c)(3); plaintiff challenged ALJ's finding that he was not disabled and ineligible for SSI benefits based on arthritis, shoulder injury, and depression.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the deferential substantial evidence standard for Social Security appeals and affirmed the ALJ's five-step sequential disability analysis, finding that correct legal principles were applied and the determination was supported by substantial evidence. The court rejected plaintiff's challenges to the weight given medical opinions and the evaluation of subjective complaints.

source_file: 9847385_2021_Cedar Development East,LLC v. Town Board of Hurley_nynd
case_name: Cedar Development East, LLC v. Town Board of Hurley
accommodation_description: Developer alleges that Local Law 4, restricting multi-family housing to four units and prohibiting housing in buildings over 120 feet, violates the Fair Housing Act by effectively prohibiting its 46-unit residential conversion project.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's motion to remand, finding defendants' removal was timely, all remaining defendants properly consented, any procedural defects in removing documents were curable and non-jurisdictional, defendants did not waive removal by requesting an extension, and the court has supplemental jurisdiction over the remaining federal constitutional and statutory claims.
brief_summary: Cedar Development East, LLC sued the Town Board of Hurley and related defendants in state court challenging Local Law 4, a zoning ordinance limiting multi-family housing to four units and prohibiting housing in buildings exceeding 120 feet, alleging it violated the Fair Housing Act and Equal Protection Clause. The court denied plaintiff's motion to remand, ruling that removal was timely, defendants properly consented, any procedural defects were curable, and the court has supplemental jurisdiction over the remaining federal claims.
key_cases_cited: Murphy Bros. v. Michetti Pipe Stringing, Inc., 526 U.S. 344 (1999)

case_name: United States of America v. Douglas Waterbury, et al.
accommodation_description: Contempt proceeding to enforce a consent decree requiring defendants to relinquish property management control to an independent manager following underlying Fair Housing Act violations
key_holding: The court found clear and convincing evidence that defendants violated the consent decree by failing to relinquish control of the Morrisville property for approximately seven months and by continuing property management involvement in Oswego properties after the independent management agreement took effect, warranting $15,000 in sanctions but denying additional injunctive relief.
brief_summary: The United States moved for contempt against Douglas and Carol Waterbury for allegedly violating a 2019 consent decree requiring them to hire an independent property manager and cease property management activities at their rental properties. The court found defendants in contempt for failing to relinquish control of the Morrisville property and for continued management involvement in Oswego properties, imposing $15,000 in sanctions and requiring detailed accounting.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Contempt of Consent Decree and Order for violations of Fair Housing Act settlement agreement; alleged failures to comply with injunctions regarding property management, tenant contact, and entry restrictions
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found clear and convincing evidence that defendants violated the Consent Decree by failing to relinquish control of rental properties to the Independent Manager, continuing to engage in property management activities, and allowing Douglas Waterbury to enter properties and contact tenants in violation of explicit prohibitions. The court imposed $15,000 in total sanctions ($7,000 for Morrisville property violations, $3,000 for Oswego property violations, and $5,000 for Douglas Waterbury's personal violations) and ordered defendants to cease all property management responsibilities and provide detailed accountings.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Eighth Amendment medical indifference claim (not FHA-related)
fha_claims.reasoning: Case dismissed for failure to prosecute under Rule 41(b) due to plaintiff's failure to maintain contact with the court and comply with court orders regarding address notification. The court applied the five-factor Lucas test and found all factors weighed in favor of dismissal, though dismissal was without prejudice given plaintiff's pro se status.

source_file: 9847946_2022_CNY Fair Housing, Inc. v. Clover Group Inc._nynd
case_name: CNY Fair Housing, Inc. v. Clover Group Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested two disability-related accommodations: (1) a designated reserved parking space close to their apartment units at no charge (without the $350 fee defendants required), and (2) a waiver of the $15–$25 monthly rent surcharge imposed on first-floor apartments and units near elevators—locations that residents with mobility disabilities required in order to access their homes without significant physical difficulty.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss plaintiffs' reasonable accommodation claims based on a monthly rent surcharge for accessible apartments, holding such claims are cognizable under the FHA because the requested fee waiver directly relates to plaintiffs' mobility disabilities rather than merely remedying economic status, while granting dismissal of Welltower Inc. for lack of personal jurisdiction.
brief_summary: Five fair housing organizations and three individual tenants with mobility disabilities sued senior apartment complex operators, alleging FHA violations for (1) denying designated accessible parking spaces without a $350 fee and (2) charging a $15–$25 monthly rent surcharge for first-floor units and units near elevators that residents with disabilities required. Defendants moved to dismiss, arguing the rent-surcharge claims sought impermissible 'economic accommodations' under Salute v. Stratford Greens, that Welltower lacked contacts for personal jurisdiction in New York, and that out-of-state fair housing organizations lacked standing. The court dismissed Welltower for lack of personal jurisdiction, but denied dismissal on all other grounds, finding the rent-surcharge accommodation claim cognizable because it directly ameliorated the effects of plaintiffs' mobility disabilities, and rejecting the standing challenge because at least one plaintiff with standing existed for each claim.
key_cases_cited: Salute v. Stratford Greens Garden Apartments, 136 F.3d 293 (2d Cir. 1998)
Bentley v. Peace & Quiet Realty 2 LLC, 367 F. Supp. 2d 341 (E.D.N.Y. 2005)
Hevner v. Village East Towers, Inc., 2011 WL 666340 (S.D.N.Y. Feb. 7, 2011)
Giebeler v. M&B Associates, 343 F.3d 1143 (9th Cir. 2003)
Samuelson v. Mid-Atlantic Realty Co., 947 F. Supp. 756 (D. Del. 1996)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Designated/reserved accessible parking spaces for residents with mobility disabilities at senior living properties with first-come, first-served parking policies
fha_claims.reasoning: Court declined to dismiss the parking accommodation claim on the ground that it was not cognizable under the FHA. The court found that plaintiffs adequately alleged a failure to provide reasonable accommodations for designated parking spaces and that the claim survived the motion to dismiss, though the court did not reach the merits of the reasonableness analysis.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver of $15-$25 monthly rent surcharge for first-floor units or units near elevators that are necessary accommodations for residents with mobility disabilities
fha_claims.reasoning: Court rejected defendants' argument that the FHA does not require 'economic accommodations' and found the rent surcharge claim cognizable under the FHA because it directly relates to the disability (mobility impairment) and does not merely remedy economic status. The claim is distinguishable from Salute because plaintiffs seek an accommodation for their disability without being forced to assume additional rental expenses, analogous to Bentley v. Peace & Quiet Realty 2 LLC.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Policy of charging $15-$25 monthly surcharge for first-floor units and units near elevators, which disproportionately burdens residents with mobility disabilities
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint alleges that the rent surcharge policy is 'disproportionately born' by residents with disabilities and has been 'continuously maintained' and 'unchanged' since at least 2018. The court did not dismiss this disparate impact theory and it survives the motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claims under New York Human Rights Law and Ohio Civil Rights Law for disability discrimination in housing
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint alleges violations of New York Human Rights Law and Ohio Civil Rights Law, but the parties addressed only FHA law in their briefing. The court limited its analysis to the FHA but did not dismiss the state law claims.

source_file: 9848402_2022_Cedar Development East,LLC v. Town Board of Hurley_nynd
case_name: Cedar Development East, LLC v. Town Board of Hurley
accommodation_description: Developer alleges town discriminated through enactment of Local Law 4 and obstruction of permit approvals based on anti-Semitic and racial animus toward the developer's principals.
key_holding: The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding claims for equitable relief moot because Local Law 4 was repealed and site plan approval was granted, and rejecting the futility argument for remaining damages claims because the developer's ultimate approval demonstrates seeking a variance would not have been futile.
