brief_summary: Cedar Development East sued the Town Board of Hurley, Planning Board, and individual members alleging violations of the Equal Protection Clause and Fair Housing Act, claiming the town enacted discriminatory zoning legislation and obstructed permit approvals based on anti-Semitic and racial animus toward the developer's principals. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss on mootness and ripeness grounds, finding equitable relief claims moot since the zoning law was repealed and project approved, and rejecting the futility exception because the developer's eventual approval showed seeking variances would not have been futile.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, Inc., 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Williamson County Regional Planning Commission v. Hamilton Bank of Johnson City, 473 U.S. 172 (1985)
Murphy v. New Milford Zoning Commission, 402 F.3d 342 (2d Cir. 2005)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the Fair Housing Act claim for lack of subject matter jurisdiction on ripeness grounds. The plaintiff failed to obtain a final decision from local authorities before filing suit, and the futility exception did not apply because the Planning Board ultimately approved the project, demonstrating that denial was not inevitable. The finality requirement under Williamson County applies to FHA discrimination claims in the land use context.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal Protection Clause (Fourteenth Amendment), Substantive Due Process (Fourteenth Amendment), Procedural Due Process (Fourteenth Amendment), state law equivalent to FHA
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed all remaining constitutional claims (Equal Protection, Substantive Due Process, Procedural Due Process) and state law claims for lack of subject matter jurisdiction on ripeness grounds. The plaintiff failed to satisfy the finality requirement of Williamson County by not obtaining a final decision from local authorities before filing suit, and the futility exception did not apply because the Planning Board ultimately approved the project.

source_file: 9848408_2022_CNY Fair Housing, Inc. v. Swiss Village, LLC_nynd
case_name: CNY Fair Housing, Inc. v. Swiss Village, LLC
accommodation_description: No accommodation request - this is a disparate treatment/disparate impact challenge to defendants' English-only language policy as discriminatory based on national origin and race.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that plaintiff adequately pleaded claims for intentional discrimination, disparate impact, and discriminatory statements under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(a)-(c) based on allegations that defendants' English-language rental policy functioned as a proxy for national origin and race discrimination.
brief_summary: CNY Fair Housing, Inc., a fair housing organization, sued Swiss Village, LLC and related defendants alleging that their policy requiring prospective tenants to have an English-speaking occupant in the apartment violated the Fair Housing Act by discriminating based on national origin and race. The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss, finding the complaint plausibly alleged discriminatory treatment, discriminatory effects, and discriminatory statements under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(a)-(c), and that the 2016 HUD Guidance on limited English proficiency was entitled to Skidmore deference.
key_cases_cited: Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Reyes v. Waples Mobile Home Park LP, 903 F.3d 415 (4th Cir. 2018)
Mhany Mgt., Inc. v. County of Nassau, 819 F.3d 581 (2d Cir. 2016)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to rent based on prospective tenant's limited English proficiency (LEP) status, alleged as proxy for national origin and race discrimination under § 3604(a).
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiff plausibly alleged discrimination based on national origin and race using language-related criteria as evidence, consistent with 2016 HUD Guidance. Plaintiff need not identify specific race/national origin of testers or show defendant's awareness thereof; discriminatory intent may be inferred from totality of circumstances, including the outright refusal policy targeting LEP applicants.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination in terms, conditions, or privileges of rental based on LEP status, alleged as proxy for national origin and race discrimination under § 3604(b).
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff adequately pleaded that defendants discriminated in terms, conditions, or privileges of rental by imposing an English-language requirement that disproportionately impacts protected classes. Prima facie case requires only modest showing that member of protected class was not offered same terms/conditions under circumstances giving rise to reasonable inference of discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Statements indicating preference, limitation, or discrimination based on national origin and race through language-based rental policy under § 3604(c).
fha_claims.reasoning: Defendants' statements requiring English-speaking household members and ability to read 16-page lease constitute statements indicating discrimination. Section 3604(c) violation requires only that ordinary listener understand statements as expressing discrimination or preference against protected class; defendant need not know plaintiff's actual race/national origin.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: English-language rental policy that disproportionately impacts prospective tenants based on national origin and race, alleged under disparate impact theory.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff plausibly alleged disparate impact by providing census data showing foreign-born and Asian, Hispanic, and Black residents are significantly more likely to be excluded by defendants' language policy. Prima facie disparate impact requires identifying specific practice, demonstrating disparity, and establishing causal relationship—all adequately pleaded here.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Violations of New York State Human Rights Law (NYSHRL) § 296(5)(a)(1)-(3) and § 296(5)(c)(2) for refusal to rent, discrimination in terms/conditions/privileges, and discriminatory statements based on national origin and race.
fha_claims.reasoning: NYSHRL claims evaluated under same framework as FHA claims. Court found that language-based policy may constitute evidence of discrimination based on protected class under state law, consistent with federal FHA analysis and HUD guidance.

case_name: Weilburg v. Castellane
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: The court denied plaintiffs' motion for appointment of counsel without prejudice, finding the case was at an early stage, the defendant had not been served, and plaintiffs had demonstrated ability to file detailed pleadings and assemble documentary evidence without immediate need for counsel.
brief_summary: Daro and Maria Weilburg sued landlord Richard Castellane alleging housing discrimination under the Fair Housing Act. Magistrate Judge Baxter denied their motion for appointment of counsel without prejudice, finding the case was at an early stage with the defendant not yet served, and that plaintiffs had demonstrated capacity to proceed without immediate legal assistance.
key_cases_cited: Burgos v. Hopkins
Cooper v. A. Sargenti Co.
Hendricks v. Coughlin
Terminate Control Corp. v. Horowitz
Velasquez v. O'Keefe

fha_claims.accommodation_description: FHA claim against Richard Castellane for alleged housing discrimination; specific nature of discrimination not detailed in this opinion
fha_claims.reasoning: The magistrate judge's report-recommendation and district court's adoption allowed the FHA claim against Richard Castellane to proceed past initial screening, while dismissing claims against other defendants for failure to state a claim. The operative Third Amended Complaint survives and the case proceeds to service and answer.

case_name: Kevin V. Byng v. Bob Kelly
accommodation_description: No specific reasonable accommodation request is described in the complaint; plaintiff alleged disability-based discrimination under the FHA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act generally, but the court found the complaint devoid of any facts showing defendants' actions were taken because of plaintiff's disabilities or that they were even aware of his disabilities.
key_holding: On IFP initial review, the court recommends that plaintiff's First Amendment freedom of association claims against both defendants and his FHA racial discrimination claim against defendant Kelly survive and require a response, while recommending dismissal of his Eighth Amendment, substantive due process, § 1437d(l)(3), and disability-based ADA/RA/FHA claims.
brief_summary: Kevin Byng, a sixty-two year old pro se plaintiff with multiple disabilities, sued the Executive Director and security officer of the Utica Municipal Housing Authority under § 1983, the ADA, the Rehabilitation Act, and the FHA, alleging that defendants repeatedly threatened him with eviction, harassed him, and denied him overnight guest privileges because of his associations with African American women, while also failing to maintain building security. The court conducted an IFP initial review and found that plaintiff's First Amendment intimate association claims and FHA racial discrimination claim against defendant Kelly plausibly survived, while his disability-based discrimination claims failed for lack of factual allegations connecting the adverse actions to his disability. The court recommended dismissal with prejudice of the Eighth Amendment, § 1437d, and substantive due process claims, and dismissal without prejudice of the remaining ADA/RA/FHA disability claims and the FHA racial discrimination claim against defendant Connelly, with leave to amend.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Davis v. N.Y.C. Hous. Auth., 379 F. Supp. 3d 237 (S.D.N.Y. 2019)
McKenna v. Peekskill Hous. Auth., 647 F.2d 332 (2d Cir. 1981)
Cox v. City of Dallas, 430 F.3d 734 (5th Cir. 2005)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Disability-based housing discrimination under FHA § 3604(2)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that defendants' actions were taken because of his disability. The complaint contains no facts showing defendants knew of or discriminated against plaintiff specifically because of his disabilities.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Racial discrimination in terms, conditions, or privileges of rental under FHA § 3604(b) — threat of eviction and harassment based on plaintiff's association with African American women
fha_claims.disposition: Survives initial review as to defendant Kelly; dismissed without prejudice as to defendant Connelly
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff plausibly alleged that defendant Kelly threatened eviction, harassed plaintiff, and denied overnight guest privileges because of plaintiff's association with African American women, which could constitute discrimination in terms, conditions, or privileges of rental. Claim against Connelly dismissed without prejudice because plaintiff failed to allege Connelly's participation in the racial discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Interference, coercion, intimidation, and threats under FHA § 3617 based on racial animus
fha_claims.disposition: Subsumed within disparate treatment claim; analyzed under § 3604(b) hostile housing environment framework
fha_claims.reasoning: Court analyzed plaintiff's allegations of threats, harassment, and intimidation by defendant Kelly under the § 3617 hostile housing environment standard, finding plaintiff plausibly alleged harassment sufficiently pervasive and severe because of membership in a protected class (association with African Americans) and imputable to defendant Kelly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 First Amendment freedom of association; 42 U.S.C. § 1437d(l)(3) safe housing; 42 U.S.C. § 1983 Fourteenth Amendment due process (procedural and substantive); ADA Title III; Rehabilitation Act § 504
fha_claims.disposition: First Amendment claim survives; § 1437d(l)(3) claim dismissed with prejudice; Fourteenth Amendment claims dismissed with prejudice; ADA/RA claims dismissed without prejudice
fha_claims.reasoning: First Amendment intimate association claim survives because plaintiff plausibly alleged defendants violated his right to have overnight guests and subjected guests to harassment. § 1437d(l)(3) claim fails because the statute does not create an enforceable right to safe housing under § 1983. Substantive due process claim fails because alleged conduct (threats of eviction and broken lobby lock) does not shock the conscience and plaintiff has no special relationship with UMHA creating a duty to protect. ADA/RA claims fail at pleading stage because plaintiff did not allege defendants knew of or discriminated because of disability.

case_name: Weilburg v. Castellane
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged they were unlawfully evicted from their apartment because they are Jehovah's Witnesses, constituting religious discrimination under the FHA.
key_holding: Defendant is entitled to summary judgment because the property qualifies for the Mrs. Murphy exemption under 42 U.S.C. § 3603(b)(2), which excludes owner-occupied dwellings with four or fewer families from FHA coverage, regardless of whether plaintiffs' allegations of religious discrimination are true.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Daro and Maria Weilburg sued landlord Richard Castellane alleging they were unlawfully evicted because they are Jehovah's Witnesses, asserting religious discrimination under the Fair Housing Act. The court granted summary judgment for defendant, finding that the property qualifies for the Mrs. Murphy exemption under 42 U.S.C. § 3603(b)(2) because it is owner-occupied with four or fewer families living independently, thereby excluding it from FHA coverage.
key_cases_cited: Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242 (1986)
United States v. Space Hunters, Inc., 429 F.3d 416 (2d Cir. 2005)
Gonzalez v. Rakkas, 1995 WL 451034 (E.D.N.Y. July 25, 1995)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Defendant's property qualifies for the FHA's 'Mrs. Murphy' exemption under 42 U.S.C. § 3603(b)(2) because it is an owner-occupied dwelling with no more than four families living independently of each other. The exemption applies as an affirmative defense, and the undisputed facts establish that defendant owns the property, occupies one unit, and the property is intended for no more than four families total. Therefore, the FHA does not extend to defendant's dwelling, and defendant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.

case_name: Danielle Hendricks v. Krystal Curley, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges her Section 8 housing voucher was terminated, with FHA/ADA claims premised on disability discrimination.
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA and ADA claims were dismissed because she failed to allege sufficient facts demonstrating that her disability (schizophrenia) was the reason for termination of her Section 8 voucher, as the complaint suggested defendants learned of her mental health status only after the voucher was already terminated.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Danielle Hendricks, proceeding pro se and alleging schizophrenia, sued Section 8 employees Krystal Curley and Francis Grant claiming her housing voucher was improperly terminated without a pre-termination hearing and in violation of the FHA and ADA. The court adopted the Report-Recommendation dismissing the FHA and ADA claims without prejudice because plaintiff failed to allege facts sufficient to establish that her disability caused the termination, while allowing her Fourteenth Amendment due process claim to proceed.
key_cases_cited: Tsombanidis v. W. Haven Fire Dep't, 352 F.3d 565 (2d Cir. 2003)
Martinez by Martinez v. Lexington Gardens Assocs., 336 F. Supp. 3d 270 (S.D.N.Y. 2018)
Perricone-Bernovich v. Tohill, 843 F. App'x 419 (2d Cir. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.disposition: Dismissed without prejudice with leave to amend
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts establishing that her Section 8 voucher termination was taken because of her disability (schizophrenia). The complaint suggests defendants only learned of her mental health status after the voucher was already terminated, breaking the causal nexus required for FHA discrimination claims.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claim; § 1983 Fourteenth Amendment due process claim
fha_claims.disposition: ADA claim dismissed without prejudice with leave to amend; § 1983 due process claim survives
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA Title II claim dismissed for same nexus failure as FHA claim—no facts alleged that disability caused the adverse action. § 1983 due process claim survives because plaintiff adequately alleged deprivation of protected property interest in Section 8 assistance without pre-termination hearing.

source_file: 9849251_2023_Clover Communities Beavercreek, LLC v. Mussachio Architects P.C._nynd
case_name: Clover Communities Beavercreek, LLC v. Mussachio Architects P.C.
accommodation_description: Property owners/assignees sue architects for designing multifamily senior housing complexes that allegedly fail to comply with FHA accessibility requirements (accessible routes, bathrooms lacking required clear floor space and grab bar reinforcement, non-compliant mailboxes).
key_holding: The court dismissed the professional malpractice claim as a de facto indemnification claim preempted by the FHA, but allowed the breach of contract claim to proceed as sufficiently distinct from an indemnification claim, and denied the motion regarding assigned FHA claims without prejudice pending further briefing on assignability issues.
brief_summary: Fair housing organizations and later property owners sued architects Marc Mussachio and his firm alleging they designed senior housing complexes that fail to comply with FHA accessibility requirements under § 3604(f)(3)(C), leading to settlements with fair housing groups and subsequent claims for contribution, breach of contract, and professional malpractice. The court dismissed the professional malpractice claim as a de facto indemnification claim preempted by the FHA, but allowed breach of contract claims to proceed and reserved judgment on assigned FHA claims pending further briefing on assignability.
key_cases_cited: Equal Rights Center v. Niles Bolton Associates
Texas Dept. of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Cmtys. Project
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center
Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to design and construct multi-family rental housing complexes in compliance with FHA accessibility requirements, including defective accessible routes to interior amenities, balconies, patios, bathrooms lacking required clear floor space and reinforced walls for grab bars, and non-compliant mailboxes.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied Defendants' motion to dismiss the assigned FHA design and construction claims without prejudice, finding that the parties failed to adequately brief the assignability issue and whether the claims constitute de facto indemnification claims. The court could not adjudicate the motion on the merits and reserved the right to revisit on a renewed motion or summary judgment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of contract, professional malpractice, contribution under CPLR 1401, violation of New York State Human Rights Law, Ohio unlawful discriminatory practices statute, Indiana Fair Housing Law, and Kentucky unlawful housing practices.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted the motion to dismiss the professional malpractice claim as a de facto indemnification claim preempted by the FHA, but denied dismissal of the breach of contract claim as sufficiently distinct from indemnification because it alleged independent contractual duties to inform the owner of deviations and defects. The contribution claim under CPLR 1401 survived preemption challenge under the reasoning of City of Los Angeles v. AECOM. State law claims were not preempted. Statute of limitations defense was denied because the complaint did not clearly show when the professional relationship terminated.

case_name: Tirza F. Ming v. Julia Brouillete et al.
accommodation_description: This is not a Fair Housing Act case; it is a civil rights action under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 and the First Amendment arising from a personal living arrangement dispute and family court proceedings
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's complaint for failure to state a claim, finding defendant Land was not a state actor for § 1983 purposes and defendant Brouillete was entitled to judicial immunity for actions taken in her judicial capacity.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Tirza F. Ming sued a private individual (Mindy A. Land) and a state Family Court Judge (Julia Brouillete) alleging civil rights violations arising from a personal living arrangement dispute and family court proceedings. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding the private defendant was not a state actor for § 1983 liability and the judicial defendant was entitled to absolute judicial immunity for actions taken in her official capacity.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Mireles v. Waco, 502 U.S. 9 (1991)
Cuoco v. Moritsugu, 222 F.3d 99 (2d Cir. 2000)
Adickes v. S.H. Kress & Co., 398 U.S. 144 (1970)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Various claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, state and federal criminal provisions, 28 U.S.C. §§ 351-364, 518, 42 U.S.C. §§ 3631, 14141, and First Amendment
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed claims under 42 U.S.C. § 3631 (FHA criminal provision) and 42 U.S.C. § 14141 as frivolous under § 1915(e)(2) because neither statute provides a private right of action. The court also dismissed § 1983 claims against Defendant Land for failure to allege state actor status and against Defendant Brouillete based on judicial immunity, all without substantive merits analysis.

source_file: 9849587_2023_Chestnut Hill NY, Inc. v. City of Kingston_nynd
case_name: Chestnut Hill NY, Inc. v. City of Kingston
accommodation_description: Group home for individuals with disabilities (substance use and mental/physical disabilities) seeking to continue operating free from City of Kingston code enforcement actions
key_holding: The court denied plaintiffs' motion to proceed under pseudonyms because the public interest in disclosure outweighs the speculative privacy concerns asserted by the John Doe plaintiffs, who failed to meet their heavy burden of establishing entitlement to anonymity.
brief_summary: Chestnut Hill NY, Inc. (operator of a group home for individuals with disabilities) and three John Doe residents sued the City of Kingston, alleging Fair Housing Act, ADA, and Fourteenth Amendment violations arising from code enforcement disputes. The court denied plaintiffs' motion to proceed anonymously, finding they failed to overcome the presumption of public access to court proceedings.
key_cases_cited: Doe v. Colgate Univ., 2016 WL 1448829 (N.D.N.Y. 2016)
Sealed Plaintiff v. Sealed Defendant, 537 F.3d 185 (2d Cir. 2008)
Doe v. Black Diamond Cap. Mgmt. LLC, 2023 WL 2648017 (S.D.N.Y. 2023)
Doe v. Delta Air Lines, Inc., 2023 WL 7000939 (E.D.N.Y. 2023)
Doe #1 v. Syracuse Univ., 2018 WL 70794839 (N.D.N.Y. 2018)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the motion to proceed under pseudonym but did not address the merits of the FHA claim itself. The opinion addresses only the procedural question of whether plaintiffs may litigate anonymously, not the substantive FHA discrimination allegations. The FHA claim survives this procedural ruling and remains pending.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II, Fourteenth Amendment Due Process Clause
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the motion to proceed under pseudonym but did not address the merits of the non-FHA claims (ADA and Due Process). These claims survive the procedural ruling and remain pending.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs cited Fair Housing Act sections (42 U.S.C. §§ 3603, 3604, 3617, 3631) among dozens of other federal and state statutes in their complaint, but the court found these statutes do not apply to the facts alleged (homeschooling dispute and educational neglect reporting).
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed Plaintiffs' claims citing the Fair Housing Act and numerous other statutes because these statutes do not apply to the facts alleged in the complaint. The FHA sections were cited among inapplicable statutes in a complaint that fundamentally concerns homeschooling requirements and mandatory reporting of educational neglect, not housing discrimination or reasonable accommodations.

source_file: 9849699_2024_Clover Communities Beavercreek, LLC v. Mussachio Architects P.C._nynd
case_name: Clover Communities Beavercreek, LLC v. Mussachio Architects P.C.
accommodation_description: This is not a reasonable accommodation case; fair housing organizations assigned their design-and-construction claims under § 3604(f)(3)(C) to property owners who now sue the architects for allegedly designing senior housing complexes without required accessibility features.
key_holding: The court held that FHA claims are assignable under federal law and that the single-satisfaction rule does not bar the assigned claims at the motion to dismiss stage, as factual questions remain regarding whether the original plaintiffs were fully compensated; the court dismissed only the state fair housing claims which plaintiffs abandoned.
brief_summary: Seven fair housing organizations settled claims with property owners regarding alleged FHA design-and-construction violations at senior housing complexes; the property owners then sued the architects for those assigned claims. The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss, holding that FHA claims are assignable and the single-satisfaction rule does not bar the claims at this stage, while dismissing abandoned state fair housing claims.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dept. of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Cmtys. Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Equal Rts. Ctr. v. Niles Bolton Assocs., 602 F.3d 597 (4th Cir. 2010)
Perma Life Mufflers, Inc. v. Int'l Parts Corp., 392 U.S. 134 (1968)
In re NYSE Specialists Sec. Litig., 405 F. Supp. 2d 281 (S.D.N.Y. 2005)
Ondimar Transportes Maritimos v. Beatty Street Properties, Inc., 555 F.3d 184 (5th Cir. 2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to design and construct dwellings in compliance with 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(C) accessibility requirements
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss the assigned FHA design and construction claims, finding that FHA claims are assignable under federal law and that the single-satisfaction rule does not bar the claims at the pleading stage because a factual dispute exists regarding whether the original plaintiffs were fully compensated. The in pari delicto defense was also rejected as premature at the motion to dismiss stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: State fair housing law claims under NYSHRL, Ohio Rev. Code § 4112.02, Ind. Code § 22-9.5-5-5, and Ky. Rev. Stat. § 344.360; also breach of contract and professional malpractice
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed all state fair housing law claims with prejudice because plaintiffs explicitly abandoned these claims by failing to oppose defendants' motion to dismiss as to those counts. The court found plaintiffs had abandoned the claims by not addressing defendants' arguments for dismissal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act § 3617 cited but no housing discrimination claim alleged; plaintiff is an employee at a hospital, not a tenant or housing applicant. Claims relate to employment discrimination, retaliation, breach of union duty of fair representation, Title VII violations, HIPAA violations, state tort claims, and breach of contract.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed all federal claims for failure to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly. FHA § 3617 was cited by plaintiff but is facially inapplicable because none of the employment issues raised relate to discrimination in housing. Claims against individual defendants under Title VII were dismissed because Title VII applies only to employers, not individuals. Claims under statutes requiring state action (§ 1983, RFRA, Fifth Amendment) were dismissed because defendants are private actors. Claims under statutes with no private right of action (18 U.S.C. §§ 241, 242, 1001, 1028, 1038, 1341; 42 U.S.C. §§ 408, 1307; 28 U.S.C. § 1746; HIPAA) were dismissed with prejudice. Breach of duty of fair representation claims dismissed because plaintiff named individual union members rather than the union itself. ERISA, FLSA, and ADA claims dismissed for failure to allege facts supporting those theories. State law claims declined under supplemental jurisdiction.

case_name: Beverly Brown, et al. v. Community Preservation Partners, LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: N/A - This is a procedural ruling on party substitution after plaintiff death, not an adjudication of any accommodation request.
key_holding: The Court grants the motion to substitute Brighid McCarthy as plaintiff because Fair Housing Act claims survive the death of a party and McCarthy, as the sole beneficiary of the deceased plaintiff's estate, is a proper successor.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs' counsel moved to substitute Brighid McCarthy as plaintiff following the death of original plaintiff Mary Gladys Orlyk, who had been part of a Fair Housing Act lawsuit commenced in 2017. The Court granted the unopposed motion, holding that FHA claims do not extinguish upon death and McCarthy, as the sole beneficiary of Orlyk's estate, is the proper successor to continue the action.
key_cases_cited: Saint-Jean v. Emigrant Mortg. Co., 2022 WL 843836 (E.D.N.Y. Mar. 22, 2022)
Graham v. Henderson, 224 F.R.D. 59 (N.D.N.Y. 2004)
United States v. Walker, 2016 WL 7409688 (N.D.N.Y. Sept. 26, 2016)

source_file: 9849935_2024_CNY Fair Housing, Inc. v. Clover Group Inc._nynd
case_name: CNY Fair Housing, Inc. v. WellClover Holdings LLC
accommodation_description: Procedural ruling on admissibility of expert testimony regarding reasonable accommodation policies and organizational damages in underlying FHA case.
key_holding: The court denied as premature Defendants' motion to strike expert reports without prejudice to renewal, and denied the parties' motions to seal for failure to provide sufficient factual support and narrowly tailored redactions as required by Lugosch.
brief_summary: Fair housing organizations and individual plaintiffs sued property management companies and housing entities alleging Fair Housing Act violations, including reasonable accommodation denial claims. This opinion denies Defendants' motion to strike plaintiffs' expert reports as premature since discovery was incomplete, and denies parties' motions to seal numerous documents filed in connection with summary judgment motions for failure to provide adequate factual support for sealing requests.
key_cases_cited: Lugosch v. Pyramid Co. of Onondaga, 435 F.3d 110 (2d Cir. 2006)
Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharm., Inc., 509 U.S. 579 (1993)
United States v. Amodeo (Amodeo I), 44 F.3d 141 (2d Cir. 1995)
United States v. Amodeo (Amodeo II), 71 F.3d 1044 (2d Cir. 1995)

case_name: Smith v. Davis
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request; plaintiffs allege racially discriminatory lease non-renewal and retaliation for filing HUD complaint.
key_holding: The court accepted plaintiffs' FHA discrimination and retaliation claims for filing, finding they plausibly alleged that the Black plaintiffs received a notice to vacate while similarly situated white co-tenants were permitted to renew their leases, and that defendants took retaliatory action after plaintiffs filed a HUD complaint.
brief_summary: Bishme and Paris Smith, Black tenants with disabilities, sued their landlords alleging race-based discrimination (their lease was not renewed while a white co-tenant with multiple violations was allowed to stay) and retaliation for filing a HUD complaint. The court accepted the FHA discrimination and retaliation claims for filing while dismissing the hostile housing environment claim.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Francis v. Kings Park Manor, Inc.
City of Los Angeles v. Lyons
Treglia v. Town of Manlius

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs plausibly alleged facts suggesting Defendants acted with racially discriminatory intent by treating white tenants (Ms. Cannon) more leniently than Black plaintiff Bishme, who faced non-renewal of lease based on dropped criminal charges while white tenants with active violations and arrests had leases renewed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs met the de minimis burden at the pleading stage by alleging: (1) protected activity (filing HUD FHEO complaint regarding race and disability discrimination); (2) Defendants' knowledge of the complaint (August 23, 2022); (3) adverse action (retaliatory notice to vacate); and (4) causal connection (notice issued shortly after complaint filing).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Hostile housing environment claim based on alleged harassment due to protected status
fha_claims.reasoning: Amended complaint failed to allege facts plausibly suggesting Plaintiffs were harassed because of their race or any other protected status, as required to establish a hostile housing environment claim under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 504 Rehabilitation Act claim (29 U.S.C. § 794), Title VI Civil Rights Act claim (42 U.S.C. § 2000d), New York Executive Law §§ 296(5-7) discrimination and retaliation claims, New York Real Property Law §§ 223-b and 235-b claims, breach of contract claim, and intentional infliction of emotional distress claim
fha_claims.disposition: Mixed: Some claims accepted for filing; some dismissed
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 504 claims against individual defendants dismissed for lack of individual liability; Section 504 claims against entity defendants dismissed for lack of standing (Plaintiffs no longer reside at property and Ms. Cannon has died, eliminating immediate injury). Title VI claims against individuals dismissed for lack of individual liability; Title VI claims against entities accepted for filing. NYSHRL claims accepted for filing under same standard as FHA. NY Real Property Law claims accepted for filing. Breach of contract claim accepted for filing. IIED claim dismissed for failure to allege sufficiently egregious conduct.

case_name: Rayntha Favourite v. 55 Halley Street, Inc.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation request was made; the case involves alleged race-based hostile housing environment and retaliatory eviction.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment to defendants because plaintiff failed to proffer evidence that the cooperative board's issuance of noise complaints, a Notice to Cure, and Notice to Terminate were motivated by racial animus rather than legitimate non-discriminatory reasons.
brief_summary: Black cooperative shareholder sued the board and neighbors alleging race-based hostile housing environment and retaliation under the Fair Housing Act, claiming the board targeted her with noise complaints and eviction notices because of her race. The court granted summary judgment to defendants, finding no evidence of discriminatory animus—the complaints were supported by documented noise issues and marijuana use, and plaintiff failed to show pretext.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dept. of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 135 S. Ct. 2507 (2015)
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Reeves v. Sanderson Plumbing Products, Inc., 530 U.S. 133 (2000)
Cain v. Rambert, 2014 WL 2440596 (E.D.N.Y. 2014)
United States v. Weisz, 914 F. Supp. 1050 (S.D.N.Y. 1996)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish discriminatory animus as required under the McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework. Although defendants articulated legitimate, non-discriminatory reasons for the Notice to Cure and Notice of Terminate (documented noise complaints and lease violations), plaintiff provided no evidence that these reasons were pretextual. Stray remarks about race were too remote and oblique to support an inference of discrimination absent other indicia of discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Under 42 U.S.C. § 3617, plaintiff failed to establish that she engaged in protected activity opposing FHA-prohibited conduct or that defendants' adverse action was causally connected to any protected activity. The dispute centered on lifestyle differences and noise complaints, not on plaintiff's opposition to discriminatory housing practices. Race was never raised as a factor until plaintiff filed this action.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1982, 1983, 1985; New York Executive Law §§ 296(5), 296(6); state law claims (breach of contract, tortious interference, harassment, intentional infliction of emotional distress)
fha_claims.reasoning: Claims under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 and 1982 fail for the same reasons as FHA claims—lack of discriminatory animus. Section 1983 claim fails because defendants are private entities and no state action is present; incorporation by New York law is insufficient to establish state actor status. Section 1985 conspiracy claim fails because plaintiff did not establish that racial animus motivated defendants' conduct. New York state discrimination claims fail under the same McDonnell Douglas analysis applied to FHA claims. Remaining state law claims dismissed without prejudice for lack of supplemental jurisdiction.

source_file: 9850350_2019_Harris v. The Yonkers Department of Social Services_OTDA_OAH_nysd
case_name: Rhonda L. Harris v. The Yonkers Department of Social Services/OTDA/OAH
accommodation_description: Pro se plaintiff requested housing accommodation including hotel placement or five-bedroom apartment for herself and four children, stating they are disabled and need unrestricted, unsupervised housing.
key_holding: The court dismissed the FHA claim because plaintiff failed to allege facts suggesting any defendant discriminated against her on the basis of disability, rather than merely finding that she was entitled to reasonable accommodation under § 3604(f)(3)(B).
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Rhonda L. Harris sued the Yonkers Department of Social Services, OTDA, and OAH alleging she and her four children (identified as disabled) were illegally evicted and denied housing and public benefits, seeking emergency shelter and housing accommodations. The court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim, finding that while plaintiff identified herself and children as disabled, she did not allege facts showing defendants discriminated against them because of their disabilities, granting leave to amend within 30 days.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Goldberg v. Kelly, 397 U.S. 254 (1970)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Housing accommodation for plaintiff and four children with disabilities; plaintiff requested placement in hotel with two rooms or unrestricted unsupervised unfurnished five-bedroom apartment
fha_claims.reasoning: Although plaintiff identified herself and her children as persons with disabilities and alleged discrimination, she failed to allege facts suggesting that any defendant discriminated against her on the basis of their disabilities or that their disabilities were the basis for defendants' conduct. The complaint lacked sufficient factual allegations to state a plausible FHA claim under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Due process claim regarding denial of public benefits; Rooker-Feldman challenge to state court eviction judgment
fha_claims.reasoning: Due process claim barred because New York law provides adequate postdeprivation remedies (fair hearings under N.Y. Soc. Serv. Law § 22 and Article 78 proceedings in state court), which plaintiff failed to exhaust. Eviction-related claims barred under Rooker-Feldman doctrine because plaintiff lost in state court, complained of injuries caused by the state court judgment, invited federal court review and rejection of that judgment, and commenced federal proceedings after the state judgment was rendered.

case_name: Thompson v. NYC
accommodation_description: Disabled plaintiff Thompson requested transfer to another apartment as a reasonable accommodation for her mobility impairment.
key_holding: The court granted leave to amend because Thompson failed to plausibly allege how the requested transfer or repairs would accommodate her disability of being barely able to walk.
brief_summary: Desiree Thompson (a disabled tenant who can barely walk) and Darin Poole sued New York City, NYCHA, New York State, and Kings Towers regarding substandard housing conditions in their NYCHA apartment, asserting claims under the ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and Fair Housing Amendments Act. The court granted leave to amend, finding that while Thompson sufficiently alleged disability, she failed to plead facts connecting her mobility disability to the requested transfer accommodation or the housing repairs.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
McElwee v. Cty. of Orange

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Repairs to apartment conditions (peeling paint, lead paint, asbestos, rodents, roaches, broken countertop, leaking gas, unsecure door) and transfer to another apartment to accommodate plaintiff Thompson's mobility disability
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim / Leave to amend granted
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiff failed to connect her disability (barely able to walk) to the requested accommodations (apartment repairs and transfer), as it was unclear how addressing rodents, roaches, paint, and countertops would accommodate her mobility disability. Court granted leave to amend to allege facts suggesting defendants failed to reasonably accommodate her disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim / Leave to amend granted
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs alleged discrimination but failed to assert the basis for the discrimination claim (race, color, religion, sex, familial status, national origin, or disability). Court granted leave to amend to assert facts supporting an FHA discrimination claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II, Section 504 Rehabilitation Act claims regarding failure to accommodate disability in public housing
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim / Leave to amend granted
fha_claims.reasoning: Under ADA Title II and Section 504, plaintiff failed to allege facts suggesting defendants failed to make reasonable accommodations related to her disability. Court applied same nexus analysis as FHAA claim and granted leave to amend.

case_name: McKins v. Pye
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested an apartment equipped with railings to accommodate his disability; the court analyzed the denial as potential disparate treatment rather than as a reasonable accommodation claim.
key_holding: The court dismissed the FHA claims because plaintiff failed to plead facts showing he suffered an adverse housing action because of his race, color, religion, sex, familial status, national origin, or disability, as the denial was allegedly based on his criminal record; the court granted leave to amend.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff John McKins sued United Hebrew Soundview Senior Living and its managers alleging Fair Housing Act discrimination based on race and disability after being denied an apartment despite requesting a unit with railings to accommodate his disability; the court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim because plaintiff alleged the denial was due to his prior criminal record rather than his protected characteristics, though it granted leave to amend.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Texas Dep't of Housing and Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Cmtys. Project, Inc., 135 S. Ct. 2507 (2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Apartment with railings to accommodate plaintiff's disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that defendants denied housing because of disability; instead, plaintiff alleged denial was based on prior criminal conviction. Court granted leave to amend to allow plaintiff to allege facts showing discriminatory intent or disparate impact based on protected class.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of apartment based on race
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged he is a 60-year-old Black male but failed to plead facts showing defendants denied housing because of race; instead, alleged denial was based on prior arrests and convictions. Court found no plausible allegation of race discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Criminal conviction policy
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead facts demonstrating that Soundview has a policy or practice that has caused or predictably will cause a discriminatory effect. Court noted that at pleading stage, plaintiffs are not required to prove causation through statistical evidence, but plaintiff must allege facts showing a facially neutral policy with disproportionate impact.

source_file: 9850835_2019_De La Fuente v. The Sherry Netherland, Inc._nysd
case_name: De La Fuente v. The Sherry Netherland, Inc.
accommodation_description: Purchase application for cooperative apartment at the Sherry-Netherland, rejected based on national origin (Mexican-American)
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for defendants because plaintiff failed to establish that the Board's articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for denying his cooperative purchase application—financial concerns and litigious history—were pretext for anti-Mexican discrimination.
brief_summary: Roque De La Fuente, a Mexican-American businessman, sued The Sherry Netherland, Inc. (a cooperative housing corporation) and its Board of Directors, alleging they rejected his application to purchase a cooperative apartment because of his national origin in violation of the Fair Housing Act and related civil rights statutes. The court granted summary judgment for defendants, finding that while plaintiff established a prima facie case, he failed to demonstrate that the Board's legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for denial—financial concerns and extensive litigation history—were pretextual, and no reasonable jury could find discriminatory intent on this record.
key_cases_cited: Robinson v. 12 Lofts Realty, Inc., 610 F.2d 1032 (2d Cir. 1979)
Reeves v. Sanderson Plumbing Prods., Inc., 530 U.S. 133 (2000)
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
De La Fuente v. FDIC, 332 F.3d 1208 (9th Cir. 2003)
Haber v. ASN 50th St. LLC, 847 F. Supp. 2d 578 (S.D.N.Y. 2012)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff established prima facie case of disparate treatment based on national origin (Mexican-American), but defendants articulated three legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for denial: (1) evidence of dishonesty from FDIC litigation; (2) extensive litigation history; and (3) concerns about financial capacity. Plaintiff failed to demonstrate these reasons were pretextual for discrimination. The statement attributed to Ullman about 'your kind' could reasonably refer to plaintiff's documented problematic behavior rather than ethnicity, and the Sherry has Mexican-origin shareholders, undermining inference of anti-Mexican bias.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1982 (Civil Rights Act of 1866), New York Executive Law § 296(5)(a)(2) (NYSHRL), New York City Administrative Code § 8-107(5) (NYCHRL), New York Civil Rights Law § 19-a (NYCRL)
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 1982, NYSHRL, NYCHRL, and NYCRL housing discrimination claims are analyzed under the same McDonnell Douglas standard as FHA claims. Because plaintiff failed to establish pretext under the FHA framework, summary judgment is granted on all parallel state and federal housing discrimination claims.

source_file: 9850873_2019_Lopez v. New York City Dept. Homeless Services_nysd
case_name: Lopez v. City of New York
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a transgender woman with gender dysphoria and depression, requested transfer from a cisgender female shelter to a transgender-specific shelter as a reasonable accommodation.
key_holding: The court recommended dismissal because the WIN Defendants lacked authority over housing placement decisions—DHS retained that authority—so plaintiff's injuries lacked traceability to the WIN Defendants; additionally, plaintiff's demand for transgender-only housing was not adequately tied to her disabilities.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Mariah Lopez, a transgender homeless woman with gender dysphoria and depression, sued WIN, Inc. and Christine Quinn (WIN Defendants) for failing to accommodate her by transferring her from a cisgender female shelter to a transgender-specific shelter. The court recommended granting the motion to dismiss because the WIN Defendants lacked Article III standing—DHS, not WIN, controlled shelter placement, so plaintiff's injuries were not traceable to the WIN Defendants—and because plaintiff's accommodation demand lacked an adequate nexus to her disabilities.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Green v. City of New York
Sinisgallo v. Islip Hous. Auth.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Transfer to a transgender-specific shelter or housing facility; alternatively, assignment to a private room and removal of cisgender female occupants from shared facilities
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that the WIN Defendants, as opposed to DHS, denied her a reasonable accommodation. The complaint alleges DHS controlled shelter placement and rejected the accommodation request, not the WIN Defendants. Additionally, Plaintiff failed to allege a nexus between her alleged disabilities and the requested accommodation of living only with transgender individuals, as opposed to the medically-supported need for a private room.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III failure to accommodate (reasonable modifications); NYSHRL housing discrimination; NYCHRL housing discrimination and Local Law 3 violations; § 1983 First and Fourteenth Amendment due process; Title VI civil rights; § 504 Rehabilitation Act failure to accommodate
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA Title III claim dismissed because DHS, not WIN Defendants, controlled placement and rejected accommodation. NYSHRL and NYCHRL claims fail for same reasons as FHA claim and because Local Law 3 does not require creation of new transgender-only facilities. § 1983 claims fail because WIN Defendants are private entities not acting under color of state law; DHS retained placement authority. Title VI claim fails because no allegation that WIN Defendants received federal funds or discriminated based on race, color, or national origin. § 504 Rehabilitation Act claim fails for same reasons as ADA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Standing and Article III injury-in-fact
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff lacks Article III standing against WIN Defendants because she failed to establish a sufficient causal nexus between WIN Defendants' conduct and her alleged injuries. Although homelessness is a concrete injury, Plaintiff did not allege that WIN Defendants had authority to transfer her or that they possessed transgender-specific housing. Redressability also fails because monetary damages against WIN Defendants would not result in DHS providing the requested accommodation, and Plaintiff seeks to hold WIN responsible for DHS's independent conduct.

case_name: Vinnie Hardee v. City of New Rochelle Section 8 Housing Agency
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested an informal hearing as a reasonable accommodation for her PTSD disability under the FHA, arguing she should not be held to strict procedural requirements in requesting the hearing.
key_holding: The court granted plaintiff judgment on her procedural due process claim, ordering defendants to hold an informal hearing, but dismissed the Fair Housing Act reasonable accommodation claim as moot because plaintiff obtained the relief sought through the due process ruling.
brief_summary: Vinnie Hardee, a Section 8 voucher holder with PTSD, sued the City of New Rochelle Section 8 Housing Agency after her benefits were terminated for alleged program violations and defendants refused to provide her an informal hearing. The court granted judgment for plaintiff on her Fourteenth Amendment due process claim, finding her letters disputed the termination and constituted a timely request for a hearing under HUD regulations, and ordered defendants to provide the informal hearing; the court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act reasonable accommodation claim as moot.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Goldberg v. Kelly, 397 U.S. 254 (1970)
Ciambriello v. County of Nassau, 292 F.3d 307 (2d Cir. 2002)
Rios v. Town of Huntington Hous. Auth., 853 F. Supp. 2d 330 (E.D.N.Y. 2012)
Rivera v. Town of Huntington Hous. Auth., 2012 WL 1933767 (E.D.N.Y. 2012)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation due to disability (post-traumatic stress syndrome and other medical conditions) in connection with Section 8 program termination; plaintiff's attorney requested accommodation in September 2018 letter but specifics of requested accommodation are not detailed in the opinion
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted plaintiff's due process claim and ordered an informal hearing, which rendered all remaining claims including the Fair Housing Act reasonable accommodation claim moot because plaintiff obtained the relief she sought (the hearing itself).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 due process violation; ADA Title III; § 504 Rehabilitation Act; notice violations under 42 U.S.C. § 1437d(k) and 24 C.F.R. § 982.555; New York state law claims
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted plaintiff's § 1983 due process claim on the merits, finding that defendants violated plaintiff's procedural due process rights by failing to hold an informal hearing after plaintiff timely requested one. The court ordered defendants to conduct the hearing, which rendered all other claims moot.

source_file: 9850986_2019_A.L.M. v. Board of Managers of the Vireum Schoolhouse Condominium_nysd
case_name: A.L.M., a minor, by and through her Parent and Guardian, Scott M. Moore, and Scott M. Moore, individually v. Board of Managers of the Vireum Schoolhouse Condominium
accommodation_description: No formal reasonable accommodation request was made; the case involves claims of tenant-on-tenant harassment allegedly based on A.L.M.'s race, national origin, age, and sex, with plaintiffs complaining about noise and 'intersecting behavior' directed at the Moore family.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for the Board on plaintiffs' Fair Housing Act claims because plaintiffs failed to establish that a hostile housing environment existed, that Mulazzi or Elders acted with discriminatory animus based on A.L.M.'s protected characteristics, or that the Board could be held liable for the alleged tenant-on-tenant harassment.
brief_summary: A.L.M. (a Chinese-American minor) and her father Scott Moore sued the Board of Managers of the Vireum Schoolhouse Condominium alleging that a Board member and another resident engaged in harassment—including loud noises and physically intersecting the Moore family's movements—because of A.L.M.'s race, national origin, age, and sex, in violation of the Fair Housing Act and 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 and 1982. The court granted summary judgment for the Board, finding no evidence that the alleged harassment created a hostile housing environment or was motivated by discriminatory animus, and no basis for holding the Board liable for the conduct of its agent or other tenants.
key_cases_cited: Pierre v. Lantern Grp. Found. Inc., 2016 WL 3461309 (S.D.N.Y. June 20, 2016)
D.K. by L.K. v. Teams, 260 F. Supp. 3d 334 (S.D.N.Y. 2017)
Cain v. Rambert, 2014 WL 2440596 (E.D.N.Y. May 30, 2014)
Francis v. Kings Park Manor, Inc., 91 F. Supp. 3d 420 (E.D.N.Y. 2015)
Haber v. ASN 50th St. LLC, 847 F. Supp. 2d 578 (S.D.N.Y. 2012)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to establish a hostile housing environment under § 3617 because the conduct (noise and residents' presence in common areas) was not sufficiently severe or pervasive, the Moores remained at the property for nine years despite alleged harassment, and there was no evidence of discriminatory animus—no statements about A.L.M.'s race, no contemporaneous complaints linking harassment to protected status, and the Board took investigative and corrective steps in response to complaints.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1982 (Civil Rights Act)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to present evidence that A.L.M.'s race, national origin, sex, or age was a motivating factor in any of the actions at issue, or that the Board failed to adequately intervene in perceived discrimination, applying the same evidentiary standard as the FHA claims.

case_name: Noel v. City of New York
subsidy_program: Housing New York Plan, Mandatory Inclusionary Housing, 421-a
accommodation_description: No individual accommodation request; this is a systemic challenge to NYC's Community Preference Policy as racially discriminatory in affordable housing lotteries
key_holding: The court ruled on 350 documents in the City's privilege log, applying the Rodriguez balancing test for deliberative process privilege and finding most documents required disclosure while some remained protected under attorney-client privilege, work product doctrine, or deliberative process privilege.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs commenced this action challenging New York City's Community Preference Policy, which allocates 50% of affordable housing lottery units to community district residents, alleging it violates the Fair Housing Act by perpetuating racial segregation and disparately impacting racial minorities. This opinion resolves disputes over the City's privilege log for 350 documents, with the court ordering production of many documents after applying the Rodriguez balancing test while upholding privilege claims for others.
key_cases_cited: Winfield v. City of New York, 2017 WL 5664852 (S.D.N.Y. Nov. 27, 2017)
Rodriguez v. Pataki, 280 F. Supp. 2d 89 (S.D.N.Y.)
Noel v. City of New York, 357 F. Supp. 3d 298 (S.D.N.Y. 2019)
Grand Cent. P'ship, Inc. v. Cuomo, 166 F.3d 473 (2d Cir. 1999)
In re Cty. of Erie, 473 F.3d 413 (2d Cir. 2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: This opinion addresses a discovery dispute over privilege designations on 350 documents in an ongoing disparate impact case challenging the City's Community Preference Policy in affordable housing lotteries. The court reviewed documents for deliberative process, attorney-client, work product, and legislative privilege claims, but did not reach the merits of the underlying FHA disparate impact claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint alleges that the City's decision to establish, expand, and maintain the Community Preference Policy constitutes intentional discrimination. This opinion is a discovery ruling on privilege claims and does not address the merits of the intentional discrimination theory.

source_file: 9851239_2019_Mill Street Partners, LLC v. City of Newburgh_nysd
case_name: Mill Street Partners, LLC v. City of Newburgh
accommodation_description: This is not a reasonable accommodation case; Mill Street (a developer) alleges the City of Newburgh discriminated against its affordable housing project based on the race of intended beneficiaries.
key_holding: The FHA claim survives dismissal because Mill Street plausibly alleges the City capitulated to racially-motivated opposition and refused to support the project due to animus toward the low-income minority population the housing would serve.
brief_summary: Mill Street Partners, a private developer, sued the City of Newburgh and its city manager alleging the city discriminated against its affordable housing project based on the race of intended low-income minority beneficiaries by refusing to support removal of a deed restriction. The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss the FHA claim, finding Mill Street plausibly alleged both disparate treatment (racial animus in opposition) and disparate impact (disproportionate adverse effect on minority population).
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Mhany Mgmt., Inc. v. County of Nassau, 819 F.3d 581 (2d Cir. 2016)
Fair Hous. in Huntington Comm. Inc. v. Town of Huntington, 316 F.3d 357 (2d Cir. 2003)
LeBlanc-Sternberg v. Fletcher, 67 F.3d 412 (2d Cir. 1995)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff plausibly alleged facts suggesting racial animus played a significant factor in the opposition to the project and the City's abrupt reversal of course, including opponents' discriminatory statements, the new administration's reversal of support, and the appointment of the project's chief opponent to the NHA board. The claim survives the motion to dismiss under the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff plausibly alleged that the City maintained facially-neutral policies (delays in signing documents, failure to fill board seats, appointment of opponents) that had a significantly adverse or disproportionate impact on the low-income minority population that would have benefited from the project. The claim survives the motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Tortious interference (state law), breach of contract (state law)
fha_claims.reasoning: The tortious interference claim against Ciaravino survives because the governmental function immunity defense is premature without evidentiary support at the motion to dismiss stage. The breach of contract claim survives as a state law claim. The fraudulent misrepresentation, negligent misrepresentation, and breach of covenant of good faith and fair dealing claims are dismissed as duplicative of the breach of contract claim under New York law.

source_file: 9851565_2019_Fair Housing Justice Center, Inc. v. Cuomo_nysd
case_name: Fair Housing Justice Center, Inc. v. Cuomo
accommodation_description: Waiver of categorical 'no wheelchair' policy at assisted living facilities to permit admission of individuals who use wheelchairs for mobility
key_holding: Because ACF Defendants had categorical policies against wheelchair users and explicitly stated they would not accommodate wheelchair-bound applicants, plaintiffs adequately alleged that any accommodation request would have been futile, satisfying the reasonable accommodation claim without requiring formal request.
brief_summary: Fair Housing Justice Center and individual tenants sued assisted living facility operators and New York State Department of Health, alleging that categorical policies excluding wheelchair users from admission violated the FHA. The court denied most motions to dismiss, finding plaintiffs adequately alleged futility of requesting accommodation where facilities explicitly stated they would not admit anyone using a wheelchair under any circumstances, and that the Amended Regulations' continued exclusion of persons requiring assistance to walk did not moot the claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Olsen v. Stark Homes, Inc.
Tsombanidis v. W. Haven Fire Dep't
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of admission to assisted living facilities based on wheelchair use
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs plausibly alleged that ACF Defendants directly told testers that applicants would not be admitted because they used wheelchairs, constituting direct evidence of disability discrimination under § 3604(f)(1)-(2). The court rejected defendants' argument that testers failed to demonstrate applicants were otherwise qualified, finding that the application process ceased upon disclosure of wheelchair use.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation for wheelchair use in assisted living facilities; exception to categorical wheelchair ban policies
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs adequately alleged that ACF Defendants had categorical policies against wheelchairs and that any request for reasonable accommodation would have been futile based on defendants' explicit statements that they could not accommodate wheelchair users. The court adopted a futility exception to the requirement that plaintiffs formally request accommodation through administrative procedures.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discriminatory statements and advertisements indicating preference against wheelchair users
fha_claims.reasoning: Under § 3604(c), the court found that Plaintiffs plausibly alleged that ACF Defendants' statements about wheelchair policies indicated a preference based on disability. The court rejected defendants' argument that inquiries about wheelchair use were permitted by HUD regulations, finding that 24 C.F.R. § 100.202(c)(3) permits inquiries only to determine eligibility for priority programs, not to exclude disabled applicants. The court also rejected a First Amendment defense, noting that commercial speech related to illegal activity receives lesser constitutional protection.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Violation of § 3604(d) — alleged discriminatory statements or practices
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted ACF Defendants' motion to dismiss the § 3604(d) claim because Plaintiffs failed to address defendants' arguments regarding this claim in their opposition brief, thereby conceding that the amended complaint did not adequately allege a violation of § 3604(d).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claims under the Rehabilitation Act, the Affordable Care Act, and the Americans with Disabilities Act
fha_claims.reasoning: The court did not separately analyze the Rehabilitation Act, ACA, or ADA claims in the opinion, but noted that courts generally consider reasonable accommodation claims under the Rehab Act and FHA in tandem. The court's discussion of reasonable accommodation standards applied to all three statutes collectively, and the motion to dismiss these claims was denied as part of the overall denial of the failure-to-state-a-claim arguments.

case_name: Samuel Indig, Leah Indig, Meir Kahana, Robert Klein, and Naftali Klein v. The Village of Pomona, Brett Yagel, Louis Zummo, Leon Harris, and Doris Ulman
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs are Orthodox Jewish residents alleging discriminatory enforcement of Village building codes and municipal services based on religious affiliation, not a disability accommodation request.
key_holding: Plaintiffs adequately pleaded an Equal Protection claim and FHA discrimination claim based on intentional religious discrimination in enforcement of Village codes, surviving the motion to dismiss, but their Free Exercise claims and New York Civil Rights Law claim were dismissed.
brief_summary: Five Orthodox Jewish residents of the Village of Pomona sued the Village and its officials alleging religious discrimination in enforcement of building codes and municipal services, claiming violations of the Equal Protection Clause and Fair Housing Act. The court granted in part and denied in part defendants' motion to dismiss, allowing plaintiffs' Equal Protection and FHA claims to proceed while dismissing their Free Exercise claims and New York Civil Rights Law claim.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Village of Arlington Heights v. Metro. Hous. Dev. Corp., 429 U.S. 252 (1977)
Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye, Inc. v. City of Hialeah, 508 U.S. 520 (1993)
Congregation Rabbinical Coll. of Tartikov, Inc. v. Vill. of Pomona, NY, 280 F. Supp. 3d 426 (S.D.N.Y. 2017)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discriminatory enforcement of Village building codes and municipal services against Orthodox Jewish residents
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs adequately pleaded a disparate treatment claim under the FHA by alleging defendants enforced facially neutral Village codes discriminatorily against Orthodox Jewish residents, with evidence of discriminatory animus from the Human Rights Report and comparative treatment of non-Orthodox Jewish residents. The claim survives the motion to dismiss under the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard.

case_name: Mark Tunne v. Brenda S. Spears, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges racially discriminatory harassment during tenancy and seeks reversal of 2013 eviction order as a result of alleged race-based housing discrimination.
key_holding: The court dismissed Plaintiff's FHA claim as untimely under the two-year statute of limitations, noting that Plaintiff's tenancy ended in 2013 and the complaint was filed well after the limitations period expired.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Mark Tunne sued judges, attorneys, property managers, and private parties seeking to reverse his 2013 eviction from a rent-regulated Manhattan apartment, asserting claims including race discrimination under the Fair Housing Act. The court dismissed the action on multiple grounds, including that any FHA race discrimination claim was barred by the two-year statute of limitations, the Rooker-Feldman doctrine prohibiting federal review of state court judgments, and judicial immunity for the defendant judges.
key_cases_cited: Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Saudi Basic Indus. Corp., 544 U.S. 280 (2005)
Hoblock v. Albany Cty. Bd. of Elections, 422 F.3d 77 (2d Cir. 2005)
Mireles v. Waco, 502 U.S. 9 (1991)
Havens v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Pantoja v. Scott, No. 96-CV-8593 (AJP), 2001 WL 1313358 (S.D.N.Y. Oct. 26, 2001)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the FHA race discrimination claim as time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations in 42 U.S.C. § 3613(a). Plaintiff's tenancy ended in 2013, making any FHA claim filed in 2019 untimely, and the court found no continuing violation doctrine applied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 due process claims; state law claims for landlord harassment and retaliation
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed § 1983 claims against judges based on judicial immunity, against the City of New York for failure to allege municipal policy or custom, and against private parties for failure to allege action under color of state law. State law claims were declined under supplemental jurisdiction.

case_name: Ochei v. Lapes
accommodation_description: Pro se plaintiff alleged patterns of harassment, constructive eviction, and denial of services including utilities by landlord and homeless services, but did not articulate a specific reasonable accommodation request.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claims for failure to state a claim because even under a liberal reading, plaintiff failed to allege facts suggesting any defendant discriminated against her on the basis of a protected characteristic.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Joan Ochei sued landlord Alan Lapes, 317 Aladdin Hotel Corporation, and NYC Department of Homeless Services alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on alleged harassment, constructive eviction, and denial of services. The court dismissed the action for failure to state a claim, finding plaintiff failed to allege facts suggesting discrimination on the basis of a protected characteristic, and alternatively barred the requested injunctive relief under the Anti-Injunction Act and Younger abstention doctrine.
key_cases_cited: Younger v. Harris, 401 U.S. 37 (1971)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Sprint Communications, Inc. v. Jacobs, 571 U.S. 69 (2013)
Gladstone Realtors v. Village of Bellwood, 441 U.S. 91 (1979)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges discrimination and retaliation based on unspecified protected class; no specific accommodation requested.
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that even under liberal reading of pro se allegations, plaintiff failed to allege facts suggesting any defendant discriminated against or retaliated against her on the basis of an impermissible factor under the FHA, failing to meet the plausibility standard of Twombly/Iqbal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 claims; 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1982 claims
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii); lack of subject matter jurisdiction under Rule 12(h)(3)
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 1983 claims against private defendants (Alan Lapes and 317 Aladdin Hotel Corporation) fail because they are not state actors; claims against NYC Department of Homeless Services fail because municipal agencies cannot be sued under New York law and the agency is not a proper defendant.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges NYCHA officials discriminated against him based on race, disability, and national origin; failed to translate relevant NYCHA documents into his language; and forged documents with his signature.
fha_claims.reasoning: The amended complaint failed to allege sufficient facts to state a plausible claim of discrimination under the FHA. The court applied the Iqbal/Twombly pleading standard and found the allegations too conclusory and lacking in factual detail to support a discrimination claim based on race, disability, or national origin.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 claims alleging violations of federally protected rights; allegations regarding poor apartment conditions, attempted inspections, eviction proceedings, document forgery, and failure to translate documents.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts showing Rodriguez's personal involvement in violations of federally protected rights, and failed to allege sufficient facts showing a policy, custom, or practice of NYCHA caused such violations. The § 1983 claims against Rodriguez and NYCHA were dismissed for failure to state a plausible claim.

source_file: 9854778_2020_Fair Housing Justice Center, Inc. v. JDS Development LLC_nysd
case_name: Fair Housing Justice Center, Inc. v. JDS Development LLC
accommodation_description: Design and construction accessibility defects in multifamily housing (narrow doorways, heavy entrance doors, obstructed mailboxes, inaccessible kitchen and bathroom features) discovered by testers on behalf of a relative who uses a wheelchair
key_holding: The FHA limitations period for design-and-construction claims accrues when a protected person encounters the inaccessible design or construction elements, not when the building is completed or last unit sold; because plaintiff's testers discovered accessibility violations in August 2018 and filed suit in February 2019, the claims were timely.
brief_summary: Fair Housing Justice Center sued JDS Development LLC and related defendants alleging that a 51-unit Brooklyn apartment building failed to comply with FHA design-and-construction accessibility requirements. The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss on statute of limitations grounds, holding that the two-year limitations period begins when a protected person encounters the inaccessible design elements, not when construction is completed or units are sold, making the August 2018 filing timely.
key_cases_cited: Garcia v. Brockway, 526 F.3d 456 (9th Cir. 2008)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Eastern Paralyzed Veterans Ass'n v. Lazarus-Burman Assocs., 133 F. Supp. 2d 203 (E.D.N.Y. 2001)
Curtis v. Loether, 415 U.S. 189 (1974)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible design and construction of multifamily dwelling, including: automatic entrance door, accessible mailboxes, wider interior doorways, narrower thresholds, accessible environmental controls, adequate kitchen space, and clear floor space in bathrooms
fha_claims.reasoning: The court rejected defendant's statute of limitations defense, holding that the FHA limitations period for design-and-construction claims begins to run when a protected person encounters the unlawful building elements (August 29, 2018), not when the building was completed or sold (2013). The plaintiff's February 2019 filing was therefore timely, and the motion to dismiss was denied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: NYSHRL and NYCHRL design and construction discrimination claims
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the same accrual rule to state and local fair housing law claims (NYSHRL and NYCHRL), holding that the limitations period begins when the discriminatory act occurs—here, when testers discovered the inaccessible conditions on August 29, 2018. The three-year limitations periods for both state and local claims had not expired by February 2019, so the motion to dismiss was denied.

case_name: Stone v. 23rd Chelsea Associates, LLC
accommodation_description: No accommodation request was made; plaintiff is a disabled veteran proceeding pro se asserting racial discrimination claims (rent overcharging, disparate treatment) rather than disability accommodation claims.
key_holding: Plaintiff's Fair Housing Act and related discrimination claims were dismissed as time-barred and for failing to allege sufficient facts to raise an inference of discriminatory intent based on race; the vague allegations of discriminatory conduct did not plausibly connect any adverse treatment to plaintiff's protected class status.
brief_summary: Richard E. Stone, an African American Section 8 voucher holder and disabled veteran, sued his landlord and property management company alleging they charged him higher rent than similarly situated white tenants, sided with white tenants in disputes, monitored him, and made discriminatory comments. The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss, finding Stone's claims were time-barred and that his vague, conclusory allegations failed to raise a plausible inference of racial discrimination.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Francis v. Kings Park Manor, Inc., 944 F.3d 370 (2d Cir. 2019)
