fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts raising a plausible inference of discriminatory animus based on race. Allegations that defendants charged higher rent, sided with white tenants, and made discriminatory statements were conclusory and devoid of factual content (e.g., no information on similarly situated comparators, timing of incidents, or causal connection to protected class).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: FHA claim is time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations (42 U.S.C. § 3613(a)(1)(a)). The only conduct alleged within the limitations period (December 16, 2016 threat and March 17, 2017 eviction attempt) fails to raise an inference of discriminatory animus. The continuing violation doctrine does not apply because no unlawful act occurred during the limitations period.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, 42 U.S.C. § 2000d et seq.; Civil Rights Act of 1866, 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981–82; New York State Human Rights Law, N.Y. Exec. Law § 296; New York City Human Rights Law, N.Y.C. Admin. Code § 8–107; Federal Tort Claims Act, 28 U.S.C. §§ 1346(b), 2671-2680
fha_claims.reasoning: Title VI, § 1982, NYSHRL, and NYCHRL claims are analyzed under the same McDonnell Douglas framework as FHA claims and fail for the same reasons: conclusory allegations lacking factual specificity and failing to raise an inference of intentional discrimination. Federal Tort Claims Act claim is frivolous because it applies only to the United States, not private entities.

case_name: Bernard T. Anderson Bey v. ACS; NYCHA; DCSE; HRA (referenced as New York State and the City of New York)
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged NYCHA denied his request to transfer his daughter's daycare placement and refused to provide him with a copy of his lease, but these requests were not framed as formal disability accommodation requests.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claim because his allegations—that NYCHA denied his daycare transfer request and failed to provide a copy of his lease—do not give rise to an inference of discrimination based on any impermissible factor under the Fair Housing Act.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Bernard T. Anderson Bey, appearing against NYC child welfare and housing agencies, alleged violations of the Fair Housing Act, equal protection, and due process related to family court custody proceedings, daycare transfer, and lease documentation. The court dismissed the complaint for failure to state an FHA claim, finding the allegations that NYCHA denied his daycare transfer request and failed to provide his lease do not plausibly allege discrimination based on a protected characteristic under the FHA.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Gladstone Realtors v. Vill. of Bellwood, 441 U.S. 91 (1979)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of request to transfer daughter's daycare and failure to provide copy of lease
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that allegations of denial of daycare transfer and failure to provide lease copy do not give rise to an inference of discrimination on any impermissible FHA basis and therefore fail to state a plausible FHA claim under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 due process and equal protection claims; Eleventh Amendment immunity for state defendants; domestic relations abstention doctrine
fha_claims.disposition: 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B); Eleventh Amendment; Domestic Relations Abstention
fha_claims.reasoning: ACS and HRA are not suable entities under New York law; City of New York claims fail because plaintiff alleged no municipal policy, custom, or practice; State of New York and OCSE claims barred by Eleventh Amendment; all claims involving family court orders (custody, visitation, child support) are barred by domestic relations abstention doctrine and Rooker-Feldman doctrine.

case_name: Matthew Hannan v. Amy Rose et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges discriminatory eviction from his apartment based on his disability (HIV) and status as a gay man, claiming Fair Housing Act protections as an aggrieved person.
key_holding: The court adopted the R&R finding that plaintiff has standing under the FHA as an aggrieved person despite his unlawful occupancy arrangement with the tenant of record, rejecting defendants' argument that the FHA does not protect unauthorized occupants.
brief_summary: Matthew Hannan, a gay man with HIV, sued Rose Associates (property management) and individual employees alleging discriminatory eviction from his Henry Hall apartment after he was removed for living in a unit sublet from a friend. The court granted in part and denied in part defendants' motion to dismiss, dismissing Section 1983, state constitutional, Rehabilitation Act, NYC Admin Code Section 713, and FTCA claims but allowing the FHA claim to proceed based on finding plaintiff has standing as an aggrieved person.
key_cases_cited: Garcia v. S.U.N.Y. Health Scis. Ctr. of Brooklyn
Garcia v. S.U.N.Y. Health Scis. Ctr. of Brooklyn, 280 F.3d 98 (2d Cir. 2001)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges eviction based on disability, gender, and familial status discrimination
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found Plaintiff plausibly alleged he is an 'aggrieved person' under the FHA's broad standing provision and stated a disability discrimination claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f) by alleging eviction because of his disability. Motion to dismiss denied as to FHA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 1983 due process violation, Rehabilitation Act § 504 disability discrimination, New York State Constitution Article 1 violation, NYC Administrative Code § 26-251 unlawful eviction, NYC Administrative Code § 713 failure to provide notice to quit, Federal Trade Commission Act false advertising
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 1983 and state constitution claims dismissed for failure to plausibly allege state action; Rehabilitation Act claim dismissed because individual defendants of private property management company did not receive federal funding and § 504 does not impose liability on individual employees of private entities; FTCA claim dismissed for lack of private right of action; NYC Admin Code § 713 claim dismissed because defendants were not required to commence special proceeding. Leave to amend granted only for § 1983 and state constitution claims to extent premised on civil process and joint action with city officials.

case_name: Akasha Tania Barker v. Women In Need, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges Defendants failed to accommodate her gender identity by not placing her in appropriate housing at a homeless shelter, though the complaint lacks sufficient factual detail about the specific accommodation requested.
key_holding: The court dismissed ADA and RA claims because gender identity disorder is excluded from ADA disability classification and plaintiff alleged no other disability, but granted leave to amend FHA claims, noting that sex discrimination may include discrimination based on gender identity and that FHAA requires plaintiff to plead facts establishing a disability requiring accommodation.
brief_summary: Akasha Tania Barker, a transgender woman, sued Women in Need, Inc. (a private homeless shelter operator) and various city agencies alleging discrimination in housing based on her gender identity. The court dismissed her ADA and Rehabilitation Act claims because gender identity disorder is excluded from the ADA's definition of disability, dismissed her HIPAA and Section 1983 claims for failure to state a claim, but granted leave to amend her Fair Housing Act claims after noting that sex discrimination may include discrimination based on gender identity and that FHAA reasonable accommodation claims require pleading facts establishing a qualifying disability.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Fabian v. Hosp. of Cent. Connecticut
Logan v. Matveevskii
Kaeo-Tomaselli v. Pi'ikoi Recovery House for Women

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Housing placement that accommodates gender identity; failure to place plaintiff in appropriate housing
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed the FHA/FHAA claim for failure to state a plausible claim because plaintiff did not allege any disability and did not explain how failure to accommodate a disability (rather than gender identity discrimination) violated the FHAA. Court granted leave to amend to allow plaintiff to either allege gender identity discrimination under the FHA or allege a disability and explain the nexus between the disability and the requested accommodation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination based on gender identity in housing placement and services
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that some courts recognize sex discrimination under the FHA to include discrimination based on transgender identity, but plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts to state a plausible claim of gender identity discrimination. Court granted leave to amend to state facts supporting FHA sex discrimination claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA, Rehabilitation Act, Title VI, HIPAA, § 1983, New York State and City Human Rights Laws
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA/RA claims dismissed because plaintiff did not allege any disability (gender identity disorder is excluded from ADA protection); Title VI dismissed because plaintiff did not allege intentional discrimination based on race, color, or national origin; HIPAA dismissed because no private right of action exists; § 1983 claims against government actors dismissed because no constitutional right to adequate shelter exists and no property right to particular shelter placement; § 1983 claims against private defendants dismissed because no state action shown and housing provision is not a public function.

case_name: Williams v. Urban Pathways Inc.
accommodation_description: No accommodation requested; plaintiff alleges racial discrimination in termination from supportive housing
key_holding: The complaint failed to state a claim for racial discrimination under the FHA because plaintiff only alleged that a white female resident was not terminated while he was, without pleading sufficient facts showing the different treatment was motivated by his race.
brief_summary: Dwight Andre Williams, a Black former resident of Ivan Shapiro House operated by Urban Pathways Inc., sued alleging racial discrimination in housing, claiming staff mistreated him and terminated his residency because of his race. The court dismissed his Fair Housing Act claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(b) for failure to state a plausible claim, finding his allegations showed only that a white female resident's tenancy was not terminated while his was, without sufficient factual basis to infer the differential treatment was motivated by race.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Gladstone Realtors v. Vill. of Bellwood, 441 U.S. 91 (1979)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts to support an inference that the defendant discriminated based on race. The complaint alleged only that a white female director was not terminated while plaintiff, a black male, was terminated, but contained no factual allegations supporting the conclusion that race motivated the termination decision.

case_name: United States of America v. 111 East 88th Partners
accommodation_description: Gregory Reich sought permission to keep an emotional support dog in his rent-controlled apartment as a reasonable accommodation for his depression, personality disorders, and end-stage renal disease.
key_holding: The court granted the government's motion for summary judgment on the defendant's res judicata and collateral estoppel defenses, finding no privity between HUD and NYSDHR, and denied defendant's motion for summary judgment on the reasonable accommodation claim because genuine issues of material fact exist as to whether defendant's demands for excessive medical documentation and pursuit of eviction constituted constructive denial of Reich's accommodation requests.
brief_summary: The United States sued landlord 111 East 88th Partners for denying Gregory Reich's reasonable accommodation request to keep an emotional support dog and for interfering with his FHA rights through coercive demands for medical records while pursuing eviction. The court granted summary judgment for the government on the defendant's preclusion defenses and denied defendant's motion on the constructive denial issue, allowing the reasonable accommodation claim to proceed to trial.
key_cases_cited: Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014)
Logan v. Matveevskii, 57 F. Supp. 3d 234 (S.D.N.Y. 2014)
Revock v. Cowpet Bay W. Condo. Ass'n, 853 F.3d 96 (3d Cir. 2017)
Lance v. Dennis, 546 U.S. 459 (2006)
E. River Hous. Corp., 90 F. Supp. 3d 142 (S.D.N.Y. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to keep an emotional support animal (dog) in the apartment as a reasonable accommodation for mental health disabilities (dysthymic disorder, schizoid personality disorder, other specified personality disorder, depression) and physical disabilities (end-stage renal disease, diabetes, hypertension, coronary artery disease)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine issue of material fact as to whether Defendant constructively denied Reich's June 18, 2015 and June 7, 2017 reasonable accommodation requests through excessive demands for medical information, bad faith conduct, and simultaneous pursuit of eviction proceedings. Defendant's motion for summary judgment denied; case proceeds to trial.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Defendant's demands for extensive medical records, therapist notes, medical examinations, and testimony in response to reasonable accommodation requests, combined with simultaneous eviction proceedings, constituted interference with and intimidation regarding Reich's FHA rights
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied Defendant's motion for summary judgment on this claim, finding that Defendant's conduct in demanding excessive information while pursuing eviction created a genuine issue of material fact regarding whether Defendant interfered with Reich's FHA rights under § 3617. The claim survives and proceeds to trial.

source_file: 9856199_2020_Greens at Chester, LLC v. Town of Chester_nysd
case_name: Greens at Chester LLC v. Town of Chester
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; this is an intentional discrimination challenge under § 3604(a) alleging Town and County blocked housing development to prevent Hasidic Jewish families from moving into the community.
key_holding: The court granted the NYAG's motion to intervene, finding the NYAG has parens patriae standing to bring FHA claims under §§ 3604(a) and 3617 alleging municipal officials engaged in intentional religious discrimination by obstructing a housing development.
brief_summary: Greens at Chester LLC, a housing developer, sued the Town and County of Chester alleging municipal officials intentionally discriminated against the Hasidic Jewish community by blocking an approved housing development through denied permits, enacted restrictive laws, and costly special requests. The New York State Attorney General moved to intervene to bring claims under §§ 3604(a) and 3617 of the FHA. The court granted the motion, finding the NYAG has parens patriae standing and authority to bring FHA claims alleging religious discrimination in housing.
key_cases_cited: Bank of America Corp. v. City of Miami, Fla., 137 S. Ct. 1296 (2017)
Clearing Housing Ass'n, LLC v. Cuomo, 510 F.3d 105 (2d Cir. 2007)
Support Ministries for Persons With AIDS, Inc. v. Vill of Waterford, 799 F. Supp. 272 (N.D.N.Y. 1992)
People by Abrams v. Merlino, 694 F. Supp. 1101 (S.D.N.Y. 1988)
Trafficante v. Metro. Life Ins. Co., 409 U.S. 205 (1972)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that the NYAG's proposed complaint pleaded sufficient facts to state a disparate treatment claim under FHA § 3604(a) based on allegations that defendants' actions were motivated by discriminatory animus toward the plaintiff based on religion and familial status, including public statements about blocking the development due to the Hasidic Jewish religion and subsequent discriminatory actions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that the NYAG's proposed complaint pleaded sufficient facts to state a claim under FHA § 3617 for interference and coercion, based on allegations that defendants made multiple offers to purchase the development and efforts to rezone it for commercial use following meetings where officials expressed ways to exert pressure on the plaintiff.

case_name: Ash v. City of New York
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges landlords interfered with his religious practices and subjected him to discriminatory treatment based on race and religion during his tenancy.
key_holding: The court granted judgment on the pleadings for defendants because the FHA claim was time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations, and the § 1983 claims failed because plaintiff did not adequately allege defendants acted under color of state law.
brief_summary: Damon Ash, an African-American Jewish man proceeding pro se, sued his former landlords Betty Jacobson and Laura Porschar (employees of the United Jewish Council) for housing discrimination based on race and religion and related constitutional torts. The court granted defendants' motion for judgment on the pleadings, dismissing the FHA claim as time-barred by the two-year statute of limitations and dismissing the § 1983 claims for failure to adequately allege state action, while declining supplemental jurisdiction over state law defamation claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Francis v. Kings Park Manor, Inc., 944 F.3d 370 (2d Cir. 2019)
Stone v. 23rd Chelsea Assocs., No. 18-CV-3869 (VSB), 2020 WL 1503671 (S.D.N.Y. Mar. 30, 2020)
Vega v. Hempstead Union Free Sch. Dist., 801 F.3d 72 (2d Cir. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged discrimination in the enjoyment of residence based on religion and race; no specific accommodation requested.
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 12(c) — Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings
fha_claims.reasoning: The FHA claim is time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations. Plaintiff alleged discrimination through July 2016, but did not name defendants until December 21, 2018, well after the limitations period expired. The continuing violation doctrine does not apply, and relation back under Rule 15(c) is unavailable because defendants lacked notice of this particular action.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (religious discrimination and defamation); New York state-law defamation
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 12(c) — Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 1983 claims dismissed because plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that defendants acted under color of state law; defendants were private employees of the United Jewish Council with no alleged state affiliation. No plausible conspiracy with state actors was alleged. State-law defamation claims dismissed for lack of supplemental jurisdiction after all federal claims were dismissed.

case_name: Roslyn Alma Dames v. Bill De Blasio, Mayor, New York City; Dean Santa, Director of Asset Management, United States Department of Housing and Urban Development; St. Margaret's House; Trinity Church Wall Street; St. Paul's Church
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, who suffers from PTSD allegedly resulting from witnessing the 9-11 attacks, seeks reinstatement of her Section 8 voucher and return to her apartment at St. Margaret's House after she vacated due to her disability.
key_holding: The Court dismissed Plaintiff's FHA claim because, even liberally construing the pro se complaint, Plaintiff failed to allege facts suggesting that any Defendant discriminated against her on the basis of her disability.
brief_summary: Pro se Plaintiff Roslyn Alma Dames, who has PTSD from witnessing the 9-11 attacks, sued the City of New York, HUD officials, and St. Margaret's House seeking reinstatement of her Section 8 voucher and return to her apartment, alleging disability discrimination under the FHA. The Court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim, finding Plaintiff did not allege facts showing any Defendant discriminated against her because of her disability.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Gladstone Realtors v. Vill. of Bellwood, 441 U.S. 91 (1979)
Lindsey v. Normet, 405 U.S. 56 (1972)
Goldberg v. Kelly, 397 U.S. 254 (1970)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged disability and denial of housing but failed to allege facts suggesting that any defendant discriminated against her on the basis of disability. The complaint lacks sufficient factual allegations to state a plausible FHA claim under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts suggesting that any defendant retaliated against her for exercising FHA rights. The complaint lacks sufficient factual allegations to state a plausible FHA retaliation claim under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (due process), 42 U.S.C. § 1437f (Section 8 Housing Act)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's § 1983 claims against Mayor de Blasio failed because she did not allege facts showing his personal involvement in the alleged constitutional violation. Claims against St. Margaret's House, Trinity Church Wall Street, and St. Paul's Church failed because these entities do not constitute 'persons' under § 1983. No private cause of action exists under Section 8 of the Housing Act against private landlords.

case_name: Daryl J. Davis v. Port Jervis Community Development
accommodation_description: Plaintiff's sparse complaint alleges termination of Section 8 benefits and defamation but does not clearly articulate any specific reasonable accommodation request.
key_holding: The court granted plaintiff leave to amend his complaint, finding the original complaint failed to allege facts sufficient to state any federal claim, including any Fair Housing Act claim based on discrimination.
brief_summary: Daryl J. Davis, a pro se Section 8 tenant, sued Port Jervis Community Development alleging termination of his Section 8 benefits and defamation of character. The court found the complaint failed to state any viable federal claim and granted plaintiff sixty days to file an amended complaint with sufficient factual allegations, noting that no facts suggesting FHA-protected discrimination were alleged.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Goldberg v. Kelly, 397 U.S. 254 (1970)
Lindsey v. Normet, 405 U.S. 56 (1972)
Gladstone Realtors v. Vill. of Bellwood, 441 U.S. 91 (1979)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiff failed to allege facts suggesting discrimination or retaliation on the basis of any FHA-protected characteristic. The complaint contained only legal conclusions without factual support, failing to meet the plausibility standard under Twombly/Iqbal. Court granted leave to amend.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 8 Housing Act violation (42 U.S.C. § 1437f); defamation (state law); § 1983 due process claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found no private right of action under Section 8 of the Housing Act against a private landlord, and no constitutional right to housing benefits. Defamation is a state-law claim over which supplemental jurisdiction may be declined. Court granted leave to amend to state viable federal claims.

case_name: Tasfay v. Ramos
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation requested; complaint broadly alleges discriminatory action against family at a homeless shelter based on race, including removal without notice and alleged defamatory statements.
key_holding: Court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim, finding plaintiffs provided no factual allegations to support the inference that defendant Ramos or any other defendant acted based on racial motivation, and granted plaintiffs sixty days leave to amend.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Jama Tasfay and Desmond Rolle sued Melissa Ramos (DHS employee), Department of Homeless Services, and Acacia alleging discriminatory removal from a Bronx homeless shelter based on race, First Amendment violation when a sergeant allegedly prevented recording, and defamation. The court dismissed the complaint for failure to state claims, finding insufficient factual allegations to support an inference of racial motivation, and granted leave to amend within sixty days.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Ashcroft v. Iqbal
West v. Atkins
Monell v. Dep't of Soc. Servs. of City of New York
Connick v. Thompson

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiffs alleged only that Ramos removed them from shelter and called DHS security, and that because Ramos had not previously met them, she must have acted based on race. Without factual allegations supporting racial motivation, the complaint fails to state a plausible claim of discrimination under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 due process/First Amendment (recording police); defamation under state law
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim / § 1915(e)(2)(B); insufficient allegations
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found insufficient information to determine whether Sergeant DiSalvo qualifies as a state actor under § 1983, and even assuming a First Amendment right to record police exists, it is unclear whether that right would extend to DiSalvo in the shelter context. Plaintiffs must name DiSalvo as a defendant and provide additional facts. Defamation claim noted as state law claim, not constitutional.

case_name: Peter Thompson v. CRF-Cluster Model Program, LLC
accommodation_description: Request to transfer from fifth-floor apartment to a lower-floor apartment due to osteoarthritis of the hip
key_holding: Plaintiff stated a claim for constructive denial of reasonable accommodation where Defendant failed to address Plaintiff's transfer request for over a year, with Plaintiff asking about the request three times weekly, raising an inference of discriminatory intent rather than mere bureaucratic delay.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Peter Thompson, a Black homeless father with osteoarthritis of the hip, sued CRF-Cluster Model Program, LLC, alleging the private entity that provided temporary housing failed to accommodate his disability by refusing to transfer him from a fifth-floor apartment and discriminated against him based on race, disability, and familial status. The court denied Defendant's motion to dismiss the FHA reasonable accommodation claim, finding Plaintiff adequately alleged a constructive denial based on Defendant's year-long delay in responding to his transfer request, as well as his race-based disparate treatment claim.
key_cases_cited: Martinez ex rel. Martinez v. Lexington Gardens Assocs.
Tsombanidis v. W. Haven Fire Dep't
Austin v. Town of Farmington
Logan v. Matveevskii
Texas Dept. of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's disparate treatment claim based on familial status was dismissed for failure to state a plausible claim because Plaintiff alleged only conclusory assertions without specific factual allegations showing how treatment of his family differed from similarly situated families, and in fact alleged that two other families with children were permitted to stay longer, undermining the claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's disparate treatment claim based on race survived the motion to dismiss because he alleged facts supporting a minimal inference of discriminatory motivation: he identified three Latino individuals permitted to stay longer in temporary housing, with one stating she was never told to leave, while Plaintiff was pressured to move based on length of stay.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's disparate treatment claim based on disability survived the motion to dismiss because he adequately alleged that he was part of a protected class (disabled), that Defendant treated him and other disability-benefit recipients differently by pressuring them to move while not pressuring those who were working, and that this different treatment was based on protected status.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Transfer from fifth-floor apartment to a lower-floor apartment to accommodate osteoarthritis of the hip
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff stated a claim for constructive denial of reasonable accommodation based on a one-year delay in responding to his January 2018 request for a lower-floor apartment, coupled with his repeated inquiries three times per week and the fact that no accommodation was offered until after suit was filed, which supports an inference of discriminatory intent rather than mere bureaucratic incompetence.

case_name: Keisha A. Jones v. Steven Banks, DSS Commissioner; Nonprofit Corporation 1-5; DSS Employee 1-5
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, who is susceptible to COVID-19 due to unspecified preexisting conditions, requested transfer to an acceptable shelter location with a kitchenette closer to her primary care physician, medical lab, specialist, and other resources in Manhattan.
key_holding: The court denied Plaintiff's TRO request and dismissed the complaint without prejudice for failure to state a claim, granting sixty days' leave to amend because Plaintiff failed to identify the nature of her disability or specify the type of reasonable accommodations she requested.
brief_summary: Pro se Plaintiff Keisha A. Jones, residing in a Manhattan homeless shelter, sued DSS Commissioner Steven Banks and unnamed nonprofit shelter contractors under § 1983 and the Fair Housing Act, alleging inadequate shelter conditions and denied reasonable accommodations for her health needs. The court denied Plaintiff's motion for a temporary restraining order and dismissed the complaint without prejudice for failure to state a viable claim, finding that Plaintiff failed to identify her disability or specify what accommodations she requested, while granting sixty days' leave to amend.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Lindsey v. Normet, 405 U.S. 56 (1972)
Colon v. Coughlin, 58 F.3d 865 (2d Cir. 1995)
Monell v. Dep't of Soc. Servs. of City of New York, 436 U.S. 658 (1978)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges multiple reasonable accommodations on file at DSS, including a pending appeal for an acceptable shelter location with a kitchenette/kitchen facility closer to her primary care physician, medical lab, and specialist resources in Manhattan. Plaintiff also seeks permission to bring into the shelter a blender, juicer, and electric kettle, all necessary items for her to maintain her health given her fragile health and preexisting conditions.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiff failed to identify the nature of her disability or specify the type of reasonable accommodations she requested with sufficient factual detail to state a plausible FHA claim under Iqbal/Twombly. The court granted leave to amend to provide more facts in support of an FHA reasonable accommodation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (constitutional deprivation); state law tort claims (tortious interference, invasion of privacy, intentional infliction of emotional distress); retaliation claims under state law
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts showing personal involvement of named defendants (HRA Commissioner Banks and DSS Employees) in alleged constitutional violations. The court found no constitutional right to a well-run shelter system or to placement in a particular type of shelter. Private nonprofit defendants were not shown to be state actors under § 1983. Court granted leave to amend to cure pleading defects.

case_name: Brandon C. Jones v. Ms. Jisin H. Thomas; Mr. Jonathan Tauarez; Volunteers of America Corporation; Volunteers of America, Swartz Shelter; Volunteers of America 135 W. 50th Street, NYC, NY 10024
accommodation_description: Plaintiff made vague references to failure to provide reasonable accommodation related to medical personnel advice and medical documentation, but failed to specify the nature of the accommodation requested.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA reasonable accommodation claim because he failed to allege any facts suggesting he has a disability within the meaning of the FHA and failed to allege facts regarding the nature of any specific reasonable accommodation that defendants denied.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Brandon Jones sued Volunteers of America and its employees alleging they violated the ADA, Fair Housing Act, and his constitutional rights by failing to provide reasonable accommodation and retaliating against him at a homeless shelter. The court dismissed the § 1983 and Title VII claims, and dismissed the FHA claim with leave to amend because plaintiff failed to plead facts establishing he has a disability or identifying the specific accommodation defendants denied.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Rodriguez v. Village Green Realty, Inc., 788 F.3d 31 (2d Cir. 2015)
Fulton v. Goord, 591 F.3d 37 (2d Cir. 2009)
Roberts v. Royal Atlantic Corp., 542 F.3d 363 (2d Cir. 2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation related to medical personnel advice and medical documentation; nature of specific accommodation not clearly alleged
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts suggesting he has a disability under the FHA and did not allege the nature of the reasonable accommodation sought or that defendants discriminated in denying it. Court granted leave to amend to cure pleading defects.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts suggesting he exercised rights under the FHA or that defendants coerced, intimidated, or threatened him in connection with exercise of FHA rights. Conclusory allegations and filing of a complaint against plaintiff do not constitute intimidation or retaliation under § 3617.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (First Amendment retaliation); 42 U.S.C. § 2000e (Title VII employment discrimination); ADA Title III reasonable accommodation
fha_claims.reasoning: § 1983 claims dismissed because defendants are private parties not acting under color of state law; Title VII claims dismissed because plaintiff did not allege he was an employee; ADA Title III claims dismissed for failure to allege disability and specific accommodation sought.

source_file: 9859405_2020_Shine v. New York City Housing Authority_nysd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Remediation of mold and moisture conditions in apartment; repair of ceiling damage; abatement of mold to address respiratory and other health impacts
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that she herself had a cognizable disability under the ADA (allegations regarding her impairments lacked sufficient specificity regarding frequency, duration, and severity of limitations to major life activities). Although C.W.'s asthma was found to constitute a cognizable disability, plaintiff failed to allege that NYCHA knew or reasonably should have known of either plaintiff's or C.W.'s disabilities—she alleged only that NYCHA knew of the mold, not of any disability-related need for accommodation. Dismissal without prejudice with leave to amend.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II of the ADA, Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, New York State Human Rights Law, negligence, intentional infliction of emotional distress
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA Title II and Section 504 claims dismissed on same pleading-stage grounds as the reasonable accommodation claim (failure to allege cognizable disability and defendant's knowledge thereof). State tort claims dismissed without prejudice under supplemental jurisdiction doctrine (28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3)) after dismissal of all federal claims early in litigation.

case_name: Patricia Milhaven v. Country Village Apartment d/b/a Creekside Apartments
accommodation_description: Plaintiff with multiple sclerosis sought to keep and use her service dog Penny without restrictions, including allowing the dog to accompany her in common areas without being leashed when she uses a cane for ambulation.
key_holding: The Anti-Injunction Act bars federal court from enjoining ongoing state eviction proceedings, but the court declines to apply Younger abstention because routine landlord-tenant holdover proceedings do not fit within the narrow Sprint categories, and Plaintiff's claims for monetary damages and prospective injunctive relief unrelated to the state proceeding survive.
brief_summary: Patricia Milhaven, a disabled tenant with multiple sclerosis who uses a service dog, sued Country Village Apartments alleging the landlord violated the Fair Housing Act by refusing to renew her lease and initiating eviction proceedings based on complaints about her service dog. The court granted in part and denied in part defendant's motion to dismiss, holding that the Anti-Injunction Act bars injunctive relief directly related to the ongoing state eviction proceeding, but that Younger abstention does not apply and Plaintiff's claims for damages and prospective injunctive relief unrelated to the eviction may proceed.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Sprint Commc'ns, Inc. v. Jacobs
Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Saudi Basic Indus. Corp.
Younger v. Harris

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought to keep her service dog (Penny) in her apartment without restrictions on common area access and without being required to hold the dog's leash in her hand; instead, she attached the dog to a leash from her waist due to her disability requiring use of a cane. Defendant sent three violation notices restricting the dog from common areas and requiring hand-held leashing.
fha_claims.disposition: Anti-Injunction Act bar; Rooker-Feldman/res judicata initially applicable but cured by amendment
fha_claims.reasoning: The court did not reach the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim because it was barred by the Anti-Injunction Act and Rooker-Feldman doctrine as pleaded. However, the court granted plaintiff leave to amend her complaint to cure Rooker-Feldman defects and allowed claims for monetary damages and prospective injunctive relief unrelated to state proceedings to proceed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged that Defendant refused to renew her lease and initiated eviction proceedings based on complaints about her service dog, which she contends were frivolous complaints from a single emotionally disturbed tenant, constituting intentional discrimination based on disability.
fha_claims.disposition: Anti-Injunction Act bar; Rooker-Feldman/res judicata initially applicable but cured by amendment
fha_claims.reasoning: The court did not reach the merits of the disparate treatment claim because it was barred by the Anti-Injunction Act and Rooker-Feldman doctrine as pleaded. However, the court granted plaintiff leave to amend her complaint to cure Rooker-Feldman defects and allowed claims for monetary damages to proceed.

case_name: Danielle Hendricks v. Krystal Curley, et al.
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation was requested; plaintiff notified defendant Curley of her ninety-day mental health assessment after receiving the Section 8 termination notice, and the court analyzed potential FHA/ADA claims based on the possibility that the voucher termination was motivated by plaintiff's schizophrenia diagnosis and mental health hold.
key_holding: The court recommended that plaintiff's FHA and ADA claims be dismissed without prejudice because plaintiff failed to allege facts showing that the termination of her Section 8 voucher was taken because of her disability, while allowing her Fourteenth Amendment procedural due process claim against individual defendants to proceed.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Danielle Hendricks brought suit under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 alleging that her Section 8 housing voucher was terminated without a pre-termination hearing and that the termination was connected to her mental health disability in violation of the FHA and ADA. The court granted IFP status and recommended that the Fourteenth Amendment due process claim survive initial review against defendants Curley and Grant, while recommending dismissal of the FHA/ADA claims without prejudice because plaintiff did not allege the termination was causally connected to her disability. The court also recommended dismissal with prejudice of claims against the Urban and Economic Development department as an improper municipal defendant.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Tsombanidis v. West Haven Fire Dep't, 352 F.3d 565 (2d Cir. 2003)
Reg'l Econ. Cmty. Action Program, Inc. v. City of Middletown, 294 F.3d 35 (2d Cir. 2002)
Monell v. Dep't of Soc. Servs., 436 U.S. 658 (1978)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Continuation of Section 8 housing voucher; plaintiff alleges termination was based on mental health status (schizophrenia diagnosis and ninety-day mental health hold) rather than criminal activity
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff failed to allege facts showing defendants' actions were taken because of plaintiff's disabilities. Although plaintiff informed defendant Curley of her mental health status, plaintiff did not allege that her voucher termination was based on her mental health status, and allegations suggest termination notice preceded notification of mental health hold.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 1983 due process claim (Fourteenth Amendment procedural due process); ADA Title II claim (analyzed in tandem with FHA)
fha_claims.disposition: § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) — failure to state a claim (ADA); § 1983 due process claim survives
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA claim dismissed for failure to allege defendants' actions were taken by reason of disability. Section 1983 procedural due process claim against Curley and Grant survives § 1915 screening because plaintiff adequately alleged denial of pre-termination hearing; claim against Urban & Economic Development dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction (wrong defendant) and failure to establish Monell municipal liability.

source_file: 9861510_2020_Xia v. 65 West 87th Street Housing Development Fund Corporation_nysd
case_name: Xia v. 65 West 87th Street Housing Development Fund Corporation
accommodation_description: No accommodation request was made; the case involves a challenge to discriminatory denial of apartment purchase application based on Ms. Xia's Asian American race.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss, finding plaintiffs adequately pleaded a prima facie case of racial discrimination by alleging they were qualified applicants who were subjected to a more burdensome application process and ultimately denied purchasing an apartment, while similarly situated non-Asian applicants were approved.
brief_summary: Eva Xia, a Chinese American woman, and her husband sued the Board of Directors of 65 West 87th Street Housing Development Fund Corporation, alleging they were denied the opportunity to purchase an apartment because of Ms. Xia's race. The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss, finding plaintiffs adequately alleged facts showing they were financially qualified, that similarly situated non-Asian applicants were approved, and that plaintiffs were subjected to a more burdensome and prolonged application process after defendants learned of Ms. Xia's race.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Texas Dept. of Hous. & Comty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 517 U.S. 519 (2015)
L.C. v. LeFrak Org., Inc., 987 F. Supp. 2d 391 (S.D.N.Y. 2013)
Boykin v. KeyCorp., 521 F.3d 202 (2d Cir. 2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs plausibly alleged disparate treatment based on race (national origin) by alleging that Defendants learned of Ms. Xia's Chinese surname and race prior to or during the application process, imposed multiple burdensome application requirements and fees not required of similarly situated non-Asian applicants, made statements that Plaintiffs were 'not a good fit' after learning of Ms. Xia's race, and that the application process changes occurred soon after Defendants became aware of her protected status. At the motion to dismiss stage, Plaintiffs need only allege facts indicating the possibility of discrimination, not prove discriminatory animus or fully establish their prima facie case.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Civil Rights Act of 1866, New York State Human Rights Law, New York City Administrative Code
fha_claims.reasoning: The court's opinion addresses only the FHA disparate treatment claim and does not separately analyze or dismiss the non-FHA statutory claims. The motion to dismiss is denied as to all claims, allowing them to proceed.

case_name: Keisha Jones v. Steven Banks
accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought reasonable accommodations from HRA for shorter wait times, a private room due to health conditions, and reduced COVID-19 exposure while searching for housing.
key_holding: The amended complaint was dismissed because it failed to contain facts showing that plaintiff was discriminated against because of a disability or that she was denied reasonable accommodation for a disability, and the facts did not give rise to an inference that any named defendants violated her federally protected rights.
brief_summary: Keisha Jones, a pro se plaintiff experiencing homelessness, sued the City of New York, the Department of Social Services Commissioner, HRA officials, Urban Pathways, and Help USA alleging violations of her constitutional rights and the Fair Housing Act related to denials of reasonable accommodations in the homeless services system. The court dismissed all federal claims under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B) for failure to state a claim, finding the amended complaint lacked sufficient facts to support FHA reasonable accommodation claims or establish municipal liability.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Ashcroft v. Iqbal

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought reasonable accommodations including: (1) a private room (advocated by primary care doctor); (2) access to cooking facilities; (3) shorter wait times when visiting HRA Center #18; (4) reduced exposure to COVID-19 while searching for housing; and (5) cessation of nighttime headcount inspections in hotel room.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed under § 1915(e)(2) as frivolous, finding that plaintiff failed to allege facts showing she was discriminated against because of a disability or denied reasonable accommodation for a disability. The court did not engage substantively with the elements of a reasonable accommodation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead facts suggesting a causal link between her lodging of complaints and defendants' actions (removal from respite bed list, threats to remove her from shelter). Court found no factual allegations showing defendants' actions were motivated by or substantially caused by her exercise of First Amendment rights.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 procedural due process claims regarding delays and termination/reduction of public assistance benefits (storage payments, cash benefits); § 1983 municipal liability claim; state law claims including fraud, deliberate indifference, invasion of privacy, tortious interference, intentional infliction of emotional distress, negligent infliction of emotional distress, breach of fiduciary duty, breach of contract, misrepresentation, discrimination, and harassment.
fha_claims.reasoning: Procedural due process claims dismissed because plaintiff had access to adequate postdeprivation remedies (fair hearings under N.Y. Soc. Serv. Law § 22 and Article 78 proceedings in state court). Municipal liability claim dismissed because plaintiff failed to allege facts showing a municipal policy, custom, or practice caused violation of constitutional rights. State law claims dismissed under § 1367(c)(3) after dismissal of all federal claims.

case_name: Melvin Bell, III v. City of New York; Susan Jackson; Shatara Pell; Victor M. Hernandez
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges city employees denied him rental subsidy benefits and prevented him from obtaining affordable housing by using his disability as a basis for exclusion from housing services.
key_holding: The Court dismissed plaintiff's disability discrimination claims because he failed to allege facts showing a connection between how defendants treated him and his disability, relying only on legal conclusions that were insufficient under Rule 8.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Melvin Bell, III, proceeding pro se, sued the City of New York and three HASA/HPD employees under the Fair Housing Act and 42 U.S.C. § 1983, alleging that city caseworkers and housing officials denied him rental subsidy benefits and prevented him from obtaining an affordable apartment because of his disability. The Court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim, finding that plaintiff failed to allege facts showing that defendants' actions were connected to his disability, and granted leave to amend.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Palmer v. Fannie Mae

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges discrimination in housing application process and denial of rental subsidy benefit based on disability (HIV/AIDS status); caseworker Jackson allegedly refused to submit lease documents and denied enhanced rental subsidy benefit.
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under Iqbal/Twombly
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiff alleged only legal conclusions and unadorned accusations of discrimination without setting forth facts showing any connection between how defendants treated him and his disability. Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that defendants' conduct was motivated by his disability status.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges retaliation for complaining about housing discrimination through filing of frivolous liens for Medicaid expenses and repeated closure of public assistance and food stamps accounts.
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under Iqbal/Twombly
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed retaliation allegations as conclusory accusations without factual support showing causal connection between plaintiff's protected activity and alleged retaliatory conduct.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 procedural due process claim regarding denial/delay of public assistance benefits (rental subsidy); § 1983 municipal liability claim; HIPAA private right of action claim for disclosure of HIV status
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim; no private cause of action
fha_claims.reasoning: Due process claim failed because plaintiff did not allege facts showing denial of meaningful opportunity to be heard; New York provides adequate postdeprivation remedies (fair hearings and Article 78 proceedings). Municipal liability claim failed because plaintiff did not allege facts showing municipal policy, custom, or practice. HIPAA claim failed because HIPAA does not create a private cause of action; enforcement is reserved to the Secretary of HHS.

source_file: 9862537_2021_Mercer v. New York City Housing Authority_nysd
case_name: Robert Mercer v. New York City Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Request that NYCHA expedite or prioritize mold/plaster repairs to accommodate plaintiff's asthma
key_holding: Plaintiff's mild intermittent asthma without complication does not substantially limit a major life activity to qualify as a cognizable handicap under the FHA, and the complaint failed to allege that NYCHA knew or had reason to know of plaintiff's asthma.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Robert Mercer, a public housing tenant, sued NYCHA alleging failure to accommodate his asthma by not properly addressing mold in his apartment under the FHA's reasonable accommodation provision. The court granted NYCHA's motion to dismiss, finding the complaint failed to adequately plead a cognizable disability (mild intermittent asthma does not substantially limit a major life activity) and failed to allege NYCHA knew of his condition.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Olsen v. Stark Homes, Inc., 759 F.3d 140 (2d Cir. 2014)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to provide reasonable accommodation for asthma by completing mold repairs in a timely manner; plaintiff alleged that mold in his apartment exacerbated his asthma condition and that defendant failed to complete repair appointments.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to adequately allege the first two elements of a reasonable accommodation claim: (1) he did not allege a handicap cognizable under the FHA because his diagnosis of 'mild intermittent asthma without complication' does not substantially limit a major life activity, and (2) he did not allege that defendant knew or reasonably should have known of his asthma condition. The court declined to invent factual allegations not pleaded in the complaint.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 24 C.F.R. § 5.703(f) — regulation requiring housing to be free of health and safety hazards and mold
fha_claims.reasoning: A private citizen cannot bring a claim based solely on 24 C.F.R. § 5.703(f) because neither the United States Housing Act of 1937 nor the regulation itself creates an enforceable individual right of action; only HUD may enforce the regulation's requirements.

case_name: Myung-Ja Melton v. Malcolm Shabazz, L.P. et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges discriminatory delay in apartment repairs (cabinets, plumbing) based on race and national origin, claiming other tenants received timelier repairs.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for defendants because plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie case of disparate treatment; she presented no evidence identifying similarly situated tenants of different races who received timelier repairs and no evidence that defendants' actions were motivated by discriminatory intent.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Myung-Ja Melton, an Asian senior citizen, sued her landlord Malcolm Shabazz, L.P. and property manager Covington Realty Services alleging they delayed repairs to her apartment (plumbing issues, cabinets) because of her race and national origin. The court granted summary judgment for defendants, finding plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie case of disparate treatment because she presented no evidence identifying similarly situated tenants of different races who received faster repairs and no evidence of discriminatory intent.
key_cases_cited: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Francis v. Kings Park Manor, Inc., 944 F.3d 370 (2d Cir. 2019)
Ash v. Jacobson, No. 16-CV-09548 (GHW), 2020 WL 2848178 (S.D.N.Y. June 1, 2020)
Khodeir v. Sayyed, No. 15-CV-08763 (DAB), 2016 WL 5817003 (S.D.N.Y. Sept. 28, 2016)
Rhodes v. Advance Prop. Mgmt., Inc., No. 10-CV-00826 (JCH), 2012 WL 12904797 (D. Conn. Aug. 30, 2012)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie case of disparate treatment based on delayed repairs. Although she alleged that defendants delayed repairs to her apartment because of her race and national origin while making timely repairs to other tenants' apartments, she did not identify any specific comparator tenant or present evidence of when repairs were requested to other apartments, and thus could not show that non-Asian tenants were not subject to similar delays. The court found no evidence from which a reasonable jury could infer discriminatory motive.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's remaining claims, including allegations of hostile housing environment based on alleged harassment and gaslighting by the superintendent, failed because plaintiff presented no evidence that defendants' actions were motivated by discrimination. Her assertions that defendants believed other tenants of different races over her were based on pure speculation, and she did not cite evidence connecting the alleged harassment to her protected class status.

source_file: 9863253_2021_Commissiong v. US Dept. Housing _ Urban Development_nysd
case_name: Commissiong v. U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development
accommodation_description: Plaintiff challenges HUD's no-reasonable-cause determination regarding her underlying housing discrimination complaint alleging discrimination based on sex, race, and national origin.
key_holding: Sovereign immunity bars suit against HUD and its officials, and the Fair Housing Act does not create a private right of action against HUD for challenging its administrative no-cause determinations.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Carol Commissiong filed an Article 78 petition in state court against HUD and FHEO officials, challenging HUD's no-reasonable-cause determination regarding her housing discrimination complaint and alleging the officials were bribed by respondents. The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss, holding that sovereign immunity bars the suit against federal agencies and officials, and that the Fair Housing Act provides no private right of action to challenge HUD's administrative determinations.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Marinoff v. U.S. Dep't of Hous. & Urban Dev., 892 F. Supp. 493 (S.D.N.Y. 1995)
Weisberg v. Leon, 1999 WL 1216663 (S.D.N.Y. Dec. 20, 1999)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under the doctrine of sovereign immunity. The FHA does not waive sovereign immunity against the United States or federal agencies, and no private right of action exists under the FHA to challenge HUD's administrative determinations. The plaintiff's claims against HUD and individual FHEO employees in their official capacities are barred absent a congressional waiver of sovereign immunity.

case_name: Mohamed Samura v. Maria Figueroa; Castleton Park Management; Castleton Preservation LLC
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested; this case concerns an alleged discriminatory denial of a housing application, with defendants citing plaintiff's full-time student status as the basis for the denial.
key_holding: The Southern District of New York transferred pro se plaintiff's FHA housing application denial claim to the Eastern District of New York because all defendants and the operative events were located in Staten Island (Richmond County), which falls within the Eastern District.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Mohamed Samura filed an FHA claim alleging defendants denied his housing application on discriminatory grounds, while defendants asserted a non-discriminatory reason—his status as a full-time student at the College of Staten Island. The Southern District of New York found venue was improper because the underlying events occurred in Staten Island and defendants' addresses were in Staten Island, both of which are in Richmond County within the Eastern District of New York. The court sua sponte transferred the action to the Eastern District of New York pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a) in the interest of justice.
key_cases_cited: D.H. Blair & Co. v. Gottdiener, 462 F.3d 95 (2d Cir. 2006)
Keitt v. N.Y. City, 882 F. Supp. 2d 412 (S.D.N.Y. 2011)
N.Y. Marine and Gen. Ins. Co. v. LaFarge No. Am., Inc., 599 F.3d 102 (2d Cir. 2010)
Iragorri v. United Tech. Corp., 274 F.3d 65 (2d Cir. 2001)
Gurtu v. Northgate Tenants Corp., 2006 WL 3634839 (S.D.N.Y. 2006)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges denial of housing application; defendants offered non-discriminatory reason (plaintiff's status as full-time student)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court transferred case to Eastern District of New York for venue and convenience reasons under § 1404(a). The underlying events occurred in Staten Island (Eastern District), and the court found transfer appropriate in the interest of justice. No substantive FHA analysis was conducted; the case was transferred before any motion to dismiss or other merits determination.

case_name: Sister E. Jones Bey v. Dana La Casse, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff asserted vague housing discrimination allegations against her landlord for discrimination based on nationality, family size, religion, and source of income, but no specific accommodation request or disability-related claim was alleged or analyzed.
key_holding: The Court dismissed Plaintiff's FHA claim against her landlord because she failed to allege facts connecting Powell's conduct to any animus against a protected characteristic, relying instead on conclusory allegations insufficient to state a claim under Rule 8.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Sister E. Jones Bey, proceeding pro se, sued her landlord Vicknell Powell and numerous government defendants alleging constitutional violations under § 1983 and Fair Housing Act claims. The Court dismissed Plaintiff's FHA claim against Powell for failure to state a claim, finding she failed to allege facts showing a connection between Powell's conduct and any protected characteristic, and granted leave to replead the housing discrimination claim.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged discrimination by landlord Powell based on nationality, family size, religion, and source of income.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiff failed to allege facts showing connection between Powell's conduct and any FHA-protected characteristic, relying instead on legal conclusions and unadorned accusations of unlawful harm insufficient under Rule 8 and Iqbal/Twombly. Court granted leave to replead.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 due process claims, state law tort claims (slander, libel, fraud, mail tampering, harassment, assault and battery, identity theft, interference with business interests), federal criminal statute claim (18 U.S.C. § 1203 hostage taking)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed § 1983 claims against private defendants (Pierces and Powells) for failure to allege state action; dismissed § 1983 claims against ACS and NYPD as non-suable entities; dismissed § 1983 claims against City of New York for failure to allege municipal policy, custom, or practice; dismissed § 1983 claims against ACS employees as actions taken under valid court order; dismissed § 1983 claims against NYPD officers as lawful response to 911 call with probable cause; dismissed § 1983 claim against Officer Canales for failure to allege constitutional right to investigation; dismissed § 1983 claims against State of New York on Eleventh Amendment immunity grounds; dismissed § 1983 claims against family court judges and referee on absolute judicial immunity grounds; dismissed federal criminal statute claim for lack of private cause of action and standing.

case_name: Donald A. Lord v. City of New York et al.
accommodation_description: The case text does not specifically describe any discrete accommodation request; rather, Plaintiff asserts broadly that conditions in homeless shelters and actions of shelter staff and city agency employees violated the FHA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act, suggesting disability-related accommodation or equal-access claims arising from shelter living conditions.
key_holding: The court dismissed DHS and HRA as improper defendants because New York City agencies cannot be sued in their own name, directed identification of Doe defendants, and ordered service on newly added defendants, while denying Sera Security's earlier motion to dismiss as moot.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Donald Lord, who had been living in New York City homeless shelters since March 2017, brought claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, the ADA, the FHA, and the Rehabilitation Act against the City of New York, shelter operators (Project Renewal and CORE Services Group), a private security firm (Sera Security), and various individual employees, based on conditions in those shelters and the conduct of staff. The court dismissed DHS and HRA as improper defendants because city agencies cannot be named as defendants under New York City Charter § 396, with claims relating to those entities preserved against the City of New York itself. The court then issued procedural directives regarding identification of Doe defendants and service of process on newly added defendants.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Valentin v. Dinkins

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claims arising from shelter conditions and actions of shelter staff, DHS, HRA, and Sera Security employees; brought under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, ADA, Rehabilitation Act § 504, and FHA
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed claims against DHS and HRA because these are agencies of the City of New York that cannot be sued as separate entities under New York City Charter § 396; claims against these entities were dismissed without prejudice to litigation against the City of New York itself. The opinion does not substantively address the merits of any FHA claim.

case_name: Donald A. Lord v. City of New York et al.
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request is analyzed by the Court; the order addresses procedural matters including service, identification of Doe defendants, and dismissal of agency defendants.
key_holding: The Court dismissed claims against DHS and HRA (City agencies not subject to suit), ordered identification of unidentified defendants, directed service on newly added defendants, and denied Sera Security's motion to dismiss as moot after the Second Amended Complaint was filed.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Donald Lord, a homeless individual living in various shelters since March 2017, brings claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, the ADA, the Fair Housing Act, and the Rehabilitation Act against the City of New York, shelter operators (Project Renewal, CORE Services Group), and security personnel regarding conditions at homeless shelters. The Court issued an amended order dismissing agency defendants DHS and HRA, ordering identification of unidentified defendants, directing service on newly added defendants, and denying Sera Security's motion to dismiss as moot.
key_cases_cited: Valentin v. Dinkins, 121 F.3d 72 (2d Cir. 1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claims arising from shelter conditions and actions of shelter staff, DHS, HRA, and Sera Security employees; brought under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, ADA, FHA, and Rehabilitation Act § 504
fha_claims.reasoning: DHS and HRA are agencies of the City of New York and cannot be sued as separate entities under New York City Charter § 396; claims against these agencies are dismissed without prejudice to litigation against the City of New York itself. The court did not reach the merits of any FHA claim, focusing instead on jurisdictional defects and service of process issues.

source_file: 9864995_2021_Xia v. 65 West 87th Street Housing Development Fund Corporation_nysd
case_name: Eva Xia and Paul Privitera v. 65 West 87th Street Housing Development Fund Corporation, Christine Elbert, Samantha Pinkowitz, Anthony Sarmiento, and Angela Rojo
accommodation_description: This order does not address a reasonable accommodation request; it addresses work product privilege regarding a recorded conversation in an underlying Fair Housing Act case concerning denial of a cooperative housing purchase application.
key_holding: The court found that portions of the May 18, 2020 conversation between Pinkowitz and Pannkoke discussing the merits of the Fair Housing Act lawsuit are protected by attorney work product privilege under Rule 26(b)(3), while portions limited to insurance coverage discussions are not privileged, and the Coop did not waive the privilege through disclosure by a third-party witness.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Eva Xia and Paul Privitera sued 65 West 87th Street Housing Development Fund Corporation and its board members under the Fair Housing Act regarding denial of their application to purchase a cooperative apartment unit; this order resolves a discovery dispute over whether a recorded telephone conversation between board member Pinkowitz and an insurance claims adjuster discussing the lawsuit is protected by attorney work product privilege.
key_cases_cited: U.S. v. Adlman, 134 F.3d 1194 (2d Cir. 1998)
In re Grand Jury Proceedings, 219 F.3d 175 (2d Cir. 2000)
Parneros v. Barnes & Noble, Inc., 332 F.R.D. 482 (S.D.N.Y. 2019)
Tudor Ins. Co. v. Stay Secure Const. Corp., 290 F.R.D. 37 (S.D.N.Y. 2009)
William A. Gross Const. Assoc. Inc. v. Am. Mfrs. Mut. Ins. Co., 262 F.R.D. 354 (S.D.N.Y. 2009)

source_file: 9865041_2021_Brock v. The City of New York_nysd
case_name: Mandela Brock v. City of New York
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a homeless person, alleged discrimination because he is homeless, seeking placement in a particular type of shelter.
key_holding: Being homeless is not a protected characteristic under the Fair Housing Act, and plaintiff failed to allege facts connecting the alleged discriminatory conduct to a protected class, thus the FHA discrimination claim fails for failure to state a claim.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Mandela Brock, proceeding pro se and seeking shelter services for himself and his minor son, sued the City of New York, the Department of Homeless Services, private shelter operators, and individual employees under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 and the Fair Housing Act, alleging discrimination based on homelessness and retaliation for exercising his rights. The court dismissed the FHA claim, holding that homelessness is not a protected characteristic under the FHA, and denied the motion for a temporary restraining order because the complaint failed to state viable claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Monell v. Dep't of Soc. Servs. of City of New York, 436 U.S. 658 (1978)
Connick v. Thompson, 131 S. Ct. 1350 (2011)
Flagg v. Yonkers Sav. & Loan Ass'n, 396 F.3d 178 (2d Cir. 2005)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged discrimination based on homelessness in shelter placement and services
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B) / Iqbal-Twombly
fha_claims.reasoning: Homelessness is not a protected characteristic under the FHA or other federal antidiscrimination statute. Plaintiff relied on legal conclusions and unadorned accusations without alleging facts connecting the challenged conduct to a protected class, failing to meet Rule 8 pleading standards.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged retaliation for asserting rights regarding shelter placement and filing complaints
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B) / Iqbal-Twombly
fha_claims.reasoning: Although plaintiff may have First Amendment protection for advocacy, he failed to plead facts establishing a causal link between his exercise of rights and defendants' actions, and failed to allege that defendants' conduct effectively chilled his First Amendment rights.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 constitutional claims (First, Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, Seventh, Fourteenth Amendments); state law false misrepresentation claim; Human Rights Treaty claim
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B) and lack of state action
fha_claims.reasoning: DHS cannot be sued as an agency under New York law. City of New York lacks municipal liability because plaintiff failed to allege facts showing a municipal policy, custom, or practice caused the violation. Private defendants (Acacia, SUS, and their employees) lack state action under § 1983 because providing housing is not a public function, receipt of public funds does not convert private action to state action, and plaintiff alleged no facts showing the private defendants' conduct was fairly attributable to the state.

case_name: Daryl J. Davis v. Port Jervis Community Development; Nora Gallagher/Goetz; Valerie Maginsky
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges discrimination causing termination of Section 8 benefits but does not clearly articulate a specific reasonable accommodation request; the complaint is dismissed for failure to state a claim.
key_holding: The court dismissed the Fair Housing Act claim because Plaintiff failed to allege facts suggesting that Defendants discriminated against him on the basis of any prohibited factor under the FHA, and granted no further leave to amend.
brief_summary: Daryl J. Davis, proceeding pro se, sued Port Jervis Community Development and individual defendants alleging discrimination that resulted in termination of his Section 8 benefits. The S.D.N.Y. dismissed his Fair Housing Act claim under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B) for failure to state a plausible claim, finding the amended complaint failed to allege facts showing discrimination on the basis of any protected characteristic, and denied further leave to amend.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed plaintiff's discrimination claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B) as frivolous because plaintiff failed to allege facts suggesting defendant discriminated against him on any basis prohibited by the FHA (race, color, religion, sex, familial status, national origin, or disability). The complaint alleged only breach of contract and negligence related to Section 8 benefits termination, with no connection to a protected class.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed plaintiff's retaliation claim under § 3617 as frivolous because plaintiff failed to allege facts suggesting defendant retaliated against him for exercising or asserting FHA rights. The complaint contained only conclusory allegations of discrimination without factual support.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of contract and negligence claims related to Section 8 benefits termination
fha_claims.reasoning: Court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over state-law breach of contract and negligence claims after dismissing all federal claims. Because no federal claims remained, the court properly declined supplemental jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3).

source_file: 9865413_2021_Mercer v. New York City Housing Authority_nysd
case_name: Robert Mercer v. New York City Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Specific accommodation request not stated in this order; original complaint alleged FHA violations against NYCHA.
key_holding: Pro se plaintiff's motion for leave to amend is denied because his response failed to cure deficiencies by not identifying what major life activity is impaired by his condition or alleging defendant knew of his disability.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Robert Mercer, a Black public housing tenant, sued NYCHA alleging Fair Housing Act violations. The Court denied plaintiff's motion for leave to amend his complaint after a prior order dismissed his claims, finding he failed to adequately plead that his condition substantially limits a major life activity or that NYCHA knew of his disability.
key_cases_cited: B.C. v. Mt. Vernon Sch. Dist., 837 F.3d 152 (2d Cir. 2016)
Olsen v. Stark Homes, Inc., 759 F.3d 140 (2d Cir. 2014)
Hayden v. County of Nassau, 180 F.3d 42 (2d Cir. 1999)
Logan v. Matveevskii, 175 F. Supp. 3d 209 (S.D.N.Y. 2016)
Wood v. Mutual Redevelopment Houses, Inc., 2016 WL 11720460 (S.D.N.Y. Mar. 31, 2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unspecified reasonable accommodation related to plaintiff's alleged disability condition
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that his condition substantially limits a major life activity. The complaint listed symptoms and conditions but did not connect them to any major life activity as required under 42 U.S.C. § 3602(h)(1) and 24 C.F.R. § 100.201(b).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unspecified reasonable accommodation; plaintiff failed to allege defendant's knowledge of disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts suggesting that defendant was aware of plaintiff's alleged handicap, which is necessary to state a reasonable accommodation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Age discrimination claim
fha_claims.reasoning: The Fair Housing Act does not prohibit housing discrimination on the basis of age. 42 U.S.C. § 3604(b) and (f) protect only race, color, religion, sex, familial status, national origin, and disability.

source_file: 9865899_2021_Dodd v. City University of New York_nysd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation claim under Rehabilitation Act § 794(d), ADA, NYSHRL, and NYCHRL for retaliatory denial of tenure and reappointment application; also claims for failure to provide accommodations for muscular sclerosis-related difficulties during employment
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied defendants' motion in limine to preclude jury consideration of back pay damages. The court held that under the Rehabilitation Act § 794a(a)(2), which incorporates Title VI remedies (not Title VII), back pay is a legal remedy entitling plaintiff to jury trial. The court also held that under NYSHRL and NYCHRL, back pay is a legal remedy and individual defendants can be jointly and severally liable even though they did not directly pay plaintiff's salary. Claims survive to trial on the merits.

case_name: Joshua Kellier v. Billups
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged that defendants attempted to place him in a 'smaller facility' because of his disability, framing this as disability discrimination under the FHA and ADA; the court observed that, if anything, such conduct suggested an attempt to accommodate his disability rather than to discriminate against him.
