fha_claims.reasoning: Claims based on Accessory Apartment law dismissed for lack of standing (no injury in fact). Claims based on zoning amendments dismissed as unripe. Claims based on moratorium dismissed as moot because moratorium expired by its own terms upon adoption of CMP update and zoning amendments.

source_file: 9875229_2022_Doe v. New York City Housing Authority_nysd
case_name: Jane Doe v. New York City Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested transfer to a different building within NYCHA housing due to disability-related safety concerns following a violent assault and diagnosis of PTSD and anxiety.
key_holding: The court granted plaintiff's motion to proceed pseudonymously, finding the risk of retaliatory physical and mental harm from gang members, combined with her PTSD and anxiety vulnerability, outweighed the presumption against anonymity and the government defendants' minimal prejudice.
brief_summary: Jane Doe, a NYCHA public housing resident at Linden Houses diagnosed with PTSD and anxiety following a violent gang assault, sued NYCHA and its CEO alleging they constructively denied her request for transfer to a safer location as a reasonable accommodation under the FHA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act. The court granted her motion to proceed pseudonymously, finding the substantial risk of retaliatory harm from gang members and her psychological vulnerability outweighed the public's interest in knowing litigant identities.
key_cases_cited: Sealed Plaintiff v. Sealed Defendant, 537 F.3d 185 (2d Cir. 2008)
Rapp v. Fowler, 537 F. Supp. 3d 521 (S.D.N.Y. 2021)
Doe v. Skyline Automobiles Inc., 375 F. Supp. 3d 401 (S.D.N.Y. 2019)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Transfer to a different and more safe building within the public housing facility (Linden Houses) due to safety concerns and disability-related needs following violent assault and resulting PTSD and anxiety diagnosis
fha_claims.reasoning: This opinion addresses only the plaintiff's motion to proceed pseudonymously and does not reach the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim. The court granted the motion to seal based on risk of retaliatory harm, PTSD, anxiety, and vulnerability factors, but made no determination on the underlying FHA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (42 U.S.C. § 12131 et seq.), Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act (29 U.S.C. § 794a(a)(2)), and state and city law claims for failure to provide reasonable accommodation and ensure transfer to safe location
fha_claims.reasoning: The opinion addresses only the procedural motion to proceed pseudonymously and does not reach the merits of the non-FHA statutory claims (ADA Title II, Section 504, state/city law). These claims remain pending.

case_name: Frank Ditto; Julie Ditto v. Peterson Properties; Peterson Property Management; Ted Peterson; Steve Peterson; Does 1-10
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED - the complaint vaguely mentions 'possibly' the Fair Housing Act but does not specify the accommodation requested
key_holding: The court transferred the case to the Northern District of California because the operative events (rental of an Oakland, California apartment) occurred there, making venue more appropriate in that district under 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a).
brief_summary: Pro se tenants Frank and Julie Ditto sued their Oakland, California landlord (Peterson Properties) and associated parties in the Southern District of New York, alleging violations of the ADA and possibly the Fair Housing Act in connection with their rental apartment. The court transferred the case to the Northern District of California because the underlying events occurred in Oakland, California, and venue was therefore more appropriate in that district under 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a).
key_cases_cited: Keitt v. N.Y. City, 882 F. Supp. 2d 412 (S.D.N.Y. 2011)
N.Y. Marine and Gen. Ins. Co. v. LaFarge No. Am., Inc., 599 F.3d 102 (2d Cir. 2010)
Iragorri v. United Tech. Corp., 274 F.3d 65 (2d Cir. 2001)
D.H. Blair & Co. v. Gottdiener, 462 F.3d 95 (2d Cir. 2006)
Coppedge v. United States, 369 U.S. 438 (1962)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unspecified reasonable accommodation related to disability in rental housing
fha_claims.reasoning: The case was transferred to the Northern District of California for convenience under § 1404(a) because the operative events, defendants, documents, and witnesses are located in Oakland, California. The court did not reach the merits of any FHA claim, including the reasonable accommodation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: California state law, Oakland municipal law, Americans with Disabilities Act claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Non-FHA claims under California state law, Oakland municipal law, and the ADA were transferred along with the FHA claims to the Northern District of California without substantive review.

case_name: Belmar v. G&M Realty I LLC
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request; plaintiff makes vague allegations of race-based housing discrimination against HPD representative and landlord
key_holding: The court dismissed the complaint for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because federal courts lack jurisdiction over state landlord-tenant matters, the plaintiff failed to state a viable FHA claim (no facts plausibly suggesting discrimination on the basis of race), and diversity jurisdiction was lacking since all parties were citizens of New York.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Rene Belmar sued G&M Realty and others arising from a Bronx Housing Civil Court landlord-tenant case, alleging fair housing violations and race-based discrimination against an HPD representative. The court dismissed the complaint for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, finding that federal courts lack jurisdiction over state landlord-tenant matters, plaintiff failed to allege facts plausibly stating an FHA claim, and diversity jurisdiction was lacking, but granted plaintiff thirty days leave to amend.
key_cases_cited: Ally v. Sukkar, 128 F. App'x 194 (2d Cir. 2005)
Bay Shore Union Free Sch. Dist. v. Kain, 485 F.3d 730 (2d Cir. 2007)
West v. Atkins, 487 U.S. 42 (1988)
Rooker v. Fidelity Trust Co., 263 U.S. 413 (1923)
District of Columbia Court of Appeals v. Feldman, 460 U.S. 462 (1983)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged discrimination in housing on the basis of race by HPD Representative Silvester and G&M Realty.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege any plausible facts suggesting that any defendant subjected him to discrimination in housing on the basis of race or any other impermissible factor under the FHA. The complaint expressed dissatisfaction with state court proceedings rather than housing discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged retaliation for exercising FHA rights.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff did not allege facts suggesting he exercised rights under the FHA or that defendants coerced, intimidated, threatened, or interfered with him because of his race in violation of 42 U.S.C. § 3617.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 due process claims; constitutional right to adequate housing; Rooker-Feldman doctrine barring review of state court judgments; judicial immunity for Judge Baum.
fha_claims.disposition: Lack of subject matter jurisdiction; judicial immunity; Rooker-Feldman
fha_claims.reasoning: Private defendants (G&M Realty, landlord, Kevith, Tyger) are not state actors subject to § 1983 liability. Judge Baum is entitled to absolute judicial immunity for actions taken within the scope of judicial responsibilities. HPD Representative Silvester's alleged failure to address housing conditions does not state a constitutional claim because there is no constitutional right to adequate housing. Claims challenging state court judgments are barred by the Rooker-Feldman doctrine.

source_file: 9876248_2022_Sykes v. New York City Housing Authority_nysd
case_name: Derry Sykes v. New York City Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Pro se plaintiff requested that NYCHA prioritize apartment repairs (mold, water leaks, electrical issues, ceiling collapse) because he and his household members are disabled.
key_holding: Plaintiff failed to state a reasonable accommodation claim because he merely alleged that repairs should be given priority due to disability, without showing that but for an accommodation he was denied an equal opportunity to enjoy his housing.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Derry Sykes sued NYCHA under the FHA, ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and Section 1983, alleging that NYCHA's failure to repair dangerous conditions in his apartment (mold, water leaks, electrical hazards, collapsed ceiling) constituted disability discrimination and failure to provide reasonable accommodations. The court dismissed the action for failure to state a claim, finding that Sykes merely alleged he deserved priority repairs because he is disabled, without plausibly alleging that NYCHA's failure was motivated by disability or that he was denied equal housing opportunity.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Olsen v. Stark Homes, Inc., 759 F.3d 140 (2d Cir. 2014)
Smith v. NYCHA, 410 F. App'x 404 (2d Cir. 2011)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts showing that his disability was a motivating factor in NYCHA's failure to repair his apartment. He merely alleged that he was disabled and that repairs were not made, without any factual connection between the two.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Repairs to apartment including mold remediation, ceiling repair, water leak fixes, and electrical outlet repairs
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts showing that he was denied equal opportunity to use and enjoy his dwelling. He merely asserted that repairs should be prioritized because of his disability, but did not show that without the accommodation he would be denied equal opportunity to enjoy the housing.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act, 42 U.S.C. § 12101 et seq.; Rehabilitation Act of 1973, 29 U.S.C. § 701 et seq.; 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (safe and sanitary housing and equal protection)
fha_claims.reasoning: Under Title II/Rehabilitation Act, plaintiff failed to allege facts showing he was denied opportunity to participate in or benefit from NYCHA's services or was discriminated against by reason of disability. Under § 1983, there is no federal constitutional right to safe and sanitary housing, and plaintiff failed to allege deliberate indifference or that disability is a suspect class for equal protection purposes.

source_file: 9876695_2022_Katz v. New York City Housing Preservation _ Development_nysd
case_name: Katz v. New York City Housing Preservation & Development
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs, an Orthodox Jewish couple with many children, challenge New York City affordable housing occupancy limits (two persons per bedroom) that denied their applications twice through housing lotteries.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' FHA disparate impact claim because they failed to plausibly allege that the occupancy limits resulted in underrepresentation of Orthodox Jews or families with children in affordable housing, lacking statistical or factual comparisons to similarly situated groups.
brief_summary: Orthodox Jewish couple Chaim and Channa Katz sued New York City housing agencies and private developers after being denied affordable housing twice due to occupancy limits that capped units at two persons per bedroom, claiming the policy had a disparate impact on their religion and familial status. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding the complaint lacked sufficient factual allegations or statistics showing that the occupancy limits disproportionately affected Orthodox Jews or families with children compared to similarly situated groups.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dept. of Hous. & Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Cmtys. Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
City of Edmonds v. Oxford House, Inc., 514 U.S. 725 (1995)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Tsombanidis v. W. Haven Fire Dep't, 352 F.3d 565 (2d Cir. 2003)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege disparate impact on Orthodox Jews because they did not compare Orthodox Jews applying for NYC affordable housing to similarly situated individuals, relied on nationwide statistics rather than NYC-specific data, and failed to allege that occupancy limits resulted in or would predictably result in underrepresentation of Orthodox Jews in affordable housing units.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege disparate impact on families with children because they provided no facts or statistical evidence showing a significantly adverse or disproportionate effect on families with children, did not allege average family size for families with children, and failed to allege that the policy resulted in or would predictably result in underrepresentation of families with children.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: First Amendment Free Exercise Clause claim; New York State Human Rights Law § 296(5); New York City Administrative Code § 8-101
fha_claims.reasoning: Free Exercise Clause claim failed because plaintiffs conceded that occupancy limit policies are facially neutral and generally applicable, triggering only rational-basis review, which the occupancy limits satisfy as rationally related to the legitimate state interest in preventing overcrowding. State and city law claims were dismissed for lack of supplemental jurisdiction after federal claims were dismissed.

case_name: Chanel Moody, Ayanda Carmichael, and Ronnie Clark v. The Related Companies, L.P. and ERY South Residential Tower LLC
accommodation_description: No accommodation requested; plaintiffs allege they were denied equal access to building amenities and entrances due to their race and income status as affordable housing recipients.
key_holding: Plaintiffs failed to state a disparate treatment claim because luxury condominium owners are not similarly situated to affordable housing tenants, and failed to state a disparate impact claim because they did not adequately plead that the facially neutral policies had a disproportionate impact on Black and Hispanic persons beyond the effects of economic stratification.
brief_summary: Three Black, low-income plaintiffs sued developers of a luxury mixed-income building claiming racial segregation and discriminatory treatment based on 'poor doors' and separate amenities for affordable housing tenants. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding plaintiffs failed to adequately plead a disparate treatment claim (no proper comparator) and failed to adequately plead a disparate impact claim (no factual allegations showing facially neutral policies caused disproportionate racial impact beyond economic stratification).
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Texas Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Cmtys. Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Boykin v. KeyCorp, 521 F.3d 202 (2d Cir. 2008)
Boyd v. Lefrak Org., 509 F.2d 1110 (2d Cir. 1975)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to allege a similarly-situated comparator group (luxury condominium owners are not similarly situated to affordable housing tenants) and failed to allege facts from which the court could infer discriminatory intent based on race, color, or national origin. The differential treatment was based on economic status, not protected class membership.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to adequately plead the prima facie elements of disparate impact, specifically: (1) they failed to allege that defendants' race-neutral policies have a disproportionate impact on Black and Hispanic affordable housing residents compared to non-Black and non-Hispanic affordable housing residents, relying instead on wealth as a proxy for race; and (2) they failed to allege a causal connection between the facially neutral policies and any adverse impact on a protected class, as they did not allege that non-Black and non-Hispanic tenants disproportionately accepted apartments while Black and Hispanic tenants disproportionately rejected them.

case_name: Jama M. Tasfay et al. v. Melissa Ramos et al.
race_if_mentioned: Not specified; plaintiffs alleged removal was based on their race but no specific racial identity is named in the text
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested; this case concerns the discriminatory removal of two residents from a homeless shelter, not any request for a reasonable accommodation or modification.
key_holding: The court adopted the Magistrate Judge's Report and Recommendation in its entirety, granting Acacia's motion for judgment on the pleadings (converted to summary judgment) because plaintiffs failed to plead sufficient facts to establish Acacia Network as a state actor under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 and independently failed to plead a cognizable claim against Acacia.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Jama Tasfay and Desmond Rolle alleged that they were removed from a DHS homeless shelter operated by Acacia Network based on racial discrimination, in violation of the FHA and Section 1983. The FHA claims and all claims against Municipal Defendants had been dismissed in a prior ruling; this opinion addressed the surviving Section 1983 claims against Acacia. The court adopted the Magistrate Judge's recommendation and granted summary judgment to Acacia, finding that plaintiffs failed to plead facts establishing Acacia as a state actor under any recognized test (compulsion, joint action, or public function) and also failed to plead a cognizable Section 1983 claim against Acacia even assuming state actor status.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Sybalski v. Indep. Grp. Home Living Program, Inc., 546 F.3d 255 (2d Cir. 2008)
Hawthorne by Hawthorne v. Cnty. of Putnam, No. 19 Civ. 742 (NSR), 2020 WL 5946989 (S.D.N.Y. Oct. 6, 2020)
Cranley v. Nat'l Life Ins. Co. of Vt., 318 F.3d 105 (2d Cir. 2003)
Jackson v. Metro, Edison Co., 419 U.S. 345 (1974)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: No accommodation requested; claims involve removal from homeless shelter, seizure of property, and alleged interference with recording.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court converted the motion for judgment on the pleadings to summary judgment and granted it on two independent grounds: (1) plaintiffs failed to establish that Acacia was a state actor under Section 1983 because the complaint lacked allegations of coercive power, control, joint action, or delegation of public function; and (2) even assuming state actor status, plaintiffs failed to plead that Acacia took any role in the challenged conduct (removal, seizure, or filming interference), alleging only that Acacia owned the shelter and its employees were present.

source_file: 9877693_2017_Goncalves Ex Rel. Goncalves v. Rady Children's Hospital San Diego_ca9

case_name: Jose Antonio Ramos v. Department of Homeless Services
accommodation_description: Request for safety strips or safety bars in showers and bathrooms at a homeless shelter for seniors with handicaps
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's TRO/PI motion because plaintiff failed to demonstrate irreparable harm, noting that defendants offered plaintiff multiple housing opportunities which he refused, and that plaintiff never filed any grievances or requested reasonable accommodations for any disability.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Jose Antonio Ramos, a homeless shelter resident, moved for a preliminary injunction and TRO against the NYC Department of Homeless Services and Breaking Ground, alleging denial of safe housing and reasonable accommodations for seniors with handicaps, as well as racial discrimination in housing allocation. The court denied the motion for failure to demonstrate irreparable harm, noting defendants offered plaintiff multiple housing opportunities he refused and plaintiff never formally requested any disability accommodation.
key_cases_cited: MyWebGrocer, LLC v. Hometown Info., Inc., 375 F.3d 190 (2d Cir. 2004)
Mitchell v. Shane, 350 F.3d 39 (2d Cir. 2003)
Fair Hous. Just. Ctr., Inc. v. Cuomo, 2018 WL 4565152 (S.D.N.Y. Sept. 24, 2018)
Coscarelli v. ESquared Hosp. LLC, 364 F. Supp. 3d 207 (S.D.N.Y. 2019)
Harris v. Mills, 572 F.3d 66 (2d Cir. 2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Safety strips or safety bars in showers and bathrooms for seniors with mobility handicaps
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied preliminary injunction for failure to demonstrate irreparable harm; plaintiff provided only conclusory assertions without sufficient detail. Court noted plaintiff failed to allege any specific handicap or disability and filed no grievances or reasonable accommodation requests regarding mobility or accessibility issues.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of permanent housing based on race/national origin (Hispanic); allegation that white and Black individuals received housing after three months while Hispanic individuals were denied
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied preliminary injunction for failure to demonstrate irreparable harm and likelihood of success on merits. Under FHA § 3604(b) prima facie framework, defendants presented evidence that plaintiff was offered six separate housing opportunities (Breaking Ground) and five interviews (City), which he refused or was rejected from due to discrepancies in his application materials.

source_file: 9877800_2017_Civil Rights Education _ Enforcement Center v. Hospitality Properties Trust_ca9

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equivalent accessible transportation services (shuttle services) for individuals with mobility disabilities at hotels
fha_claims.reasoning: This is an ADA Title III case, not an FHA case. The court affirmed the district court's denial of class certification on the ground that plaintiffs failed to establish commonality under Rule 23(a)(2) because HPT, as a REIT, delegates hotel operations to independent contractors with no uniform policy regarding ADA compliance, requiring 142 separate trials to determine violations at each hotel.

case_name: Jane Doe v. Related Companies, LLP
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation or modification was requested. Plaintiff alleged racial discrimination, harassment, and condoned misconduct by building management and staff at her apartment building, asserting discriminatory treatment based on race rather than seeking any specific accommodation.
key_holding: The court denies plaintiff's motion to proceed anonymously and grants her 60 days' leave to file an amended complaint, finding the original complaint fails to state claims under Section 1983, Title VII, and the Fair Housing Act because the allegations are conclusory and lack specific factual support.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Jane Doe filed suit against the owners and managers of her Manhattan apartment building (456 Washington Street), alleging racial discrimination, harassment, and retaliation under the FHA, Section 1983, and Title VII. The court denied her motion to proceed anonymously, finding that vague allegations of potential retaliation from wealthy defendants were insufficient to overcome the presumption of public disclosure. The court found all three sets of claims deficient—Section 1983 because defendants are private parties, Title VII because no employer-employee relationship was alleged, and FHA claims because plaintiff's allegations were bare legal conclusions lacking any specific factual content—and granted leave to file an amended complaint within 60 days, warning that failure to comply would result in dismissal for failure to state a claim.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Sealed Plaintiff v. Sealed Defendant, 537 F.3d 185 (2d Cir. 2008)
Gladstone Realtors v. Vill. of Bellwood, 441 U.S. 91 (1979)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's allegations of racial discrimination are conclusory legal conclusions unsupported by factual allegations. The complaint fails to plead facts showing what occurred, which defendant did what, when, or how any particular defendant violated her rights, rendering the allegations insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's allegations fail to plead facts showing retaliation for exercising FHA rights. The complaint does not identify what any defendant did or failed to do on a particular occasion that violated her rights, and lacks sufficient factual detail to state a plausible retaliation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (Equal Protection Clause, Eighth Amendment); Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 1983 claims fail because all defendants appear to be private parties with no alleged connection to state action, and the Eighth Amendment does not apply to non-prisoners. Title VII claims fail because plaintiff does not allege an employer-employee relationship and appears to be asserting claims as a tenant seeking return of rent, not as an employee.

source_file: 9878142_2022_Mercer v. New York City Housing Authority_nysd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Safe and sanitary housing; removal of lead paint and mold from apartment
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's § 1983 claims against NYCHA for failure to provide safe and sanitary housing fail because there is no constitutional right to safe and sanitary housing under the Due Process Clause. The Court dismissed the claims as frivolous under § 1915(e)(2)(B) without reaching the underlying Monell municipal liability framework.

case_name: Gloria D. Dickerson v. BPP PCV Owners LLC
accommodation_description: No accommodation request was made; this case involves alleged racial profiling by security guards questioning plaintiff about a stolen jewelry box based on surveillance footage identification.
key_holding: The court granted defendant's motion to dismiss because plaintiff's FHA disparate treatment claim failed to allege sufficient factual support for an inference of discriminatory intent, her retaliation claim lacked causal allegations connecting prior complaints to the challenged conduct, and her ADA claim failed because residential apartment buildings are not public accommodations.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Gloria Dickerson, an African American woman, sued BPP PCV Owners LLC (owner of Peter Cooper Village in Manhattan) alleging racial profiling when a security guard questioned her about a stolen jewelry box based on surveillance footage, claiming violations of the FHA, constitutional rights, and ADA. The court granted the motion to dismiss, finding that plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to raise an inference of discriminatory intent and failed to state valid retaliation, constitutional, or ADA claims.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Francis v. Kings Park Manor, Inc., 992 F.3d 67 (2d Cir. 2021)
Flagg v. Yonkers Sav. and Loan Ass'n, FA, 396 F.3d 178 (2d Cir. 2005)
Lynn v. Vill. of Pomona, 373 F. Supp. 2d 418 (S.D.N.Y. 2005)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege discriminatory intent based on race. Although she is a member of a protected class and suffered an adverse action (being questioned and having police called), her allegations lack minimal factual support for discriminatory animus. The court found that race played only a descriptive role in identifying her from surveillance footage, and plaintiff provided no factual support for the conclusory assertion that a white counterpart would have been treated differently.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a causal connection between alleged prior complaints to Public Safety Chief Matthews about discriminatory behavior and the November 2, 2020 incident. She did not specify when prior complaints were made, preventing temporal proximity analysis, and did not allege that similarly situated neighbors who had not complained were treated more favorably.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II/III discrimination claim; § 1983 Fourth and Fourteenth Amendment claims; NYSHRL and NYCHRL housing discrimination claims (non-FHA portions)
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA claim dismissed because plaintiff did not allege defendant is a public entity or provides a public accommodation; residential apartment buildings are excluded from ADA coverage. § 1983 claims dismissed for failure to establish state action—defendant is a private business entity and the mere fact that a security guard called police does not transform private conduct into state action.

case_name: Olsen v. The Sherry Netherland, Inc.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request at issue; this is an assignee's action alleging the Board rejected De La Fuente's cooperative apartment application because he is Mexican-American.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's claims as barred by res judicata and collateral estoppel because Olsen, as assignee of De La Fuente's claims, is in privity with De La Fuente, whose prior housing discrimination claims were fully litigated and resolved against him on summary judgment.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Rey Olsen, as assignee of Mexican-American businessperson Roque De La Fuente, sued The Sherry Netherland cooperative building and its attorneys alleging racial discrimination in housing when the Board rejected De La Fuente's application to purchase an apartment. The court dismissed all claims on res judicata and collateral estoppel grounds, finding that Olsen, as an assignee of De La Fuente's legal claims, is in privity with De La Fuente, whose substantially identical housing discrimination claims were previously adjudicated against him on summary judgment.
key_cases_cited: Allen v. McCurry, 449 U.S. 90 (1980)
Cho v. Blackberry Ltd., 991 F.3d 155 (2d Cir. 2021)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Taylor v. Sturgell, 553 U.S. 880 (2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: All FHA claims against the Sherry Defendants (Counts One through Seven) are barred by res judicata because they are identical to claims previously adjudicated on the merits in De La Fuente v. Sherry Netherland, Inc., and Olsen, as assignee of De La Fuente, is in privity with De La Fuente for purposes of res judicata doctrine.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Disparate impact claim (Count Five) is barred by res judicata as it was previously dismissed in De La Fuente action and could have been raised in that prior proceeding.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Civil Rights Act of 1866 (§ 1982), Title II of Civil Rights Act of 1964 (§ 2000a), New York State Human Rights Law (§ 296), New York City Human Rights Law (§ 8-107), New York Civil Rights Law (§ 19-a), fraudulent inducement, breach of implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA claims (Counts Two, Three, Six, Seven, Eight, and Nine) against the Sherry Defendants are barred by res judicata because they involve the same cause of action and could have been raised in the prior De La Fuente litigation. Claims against Law Firm Defendants (Counts Eight and Nine) are barred by collateral estoppel as the factual issues were necessarily litigated in De La Fuente, and Count Nine fails to state a claim because Law Firm Defendants were not parties to any contract with De La Fuente or Olsen.

case_name: Eric Andrew Perez v. Andrew Carrión Jr., Commissioner HPD; Kim Truluck, Section 8; Racquel Urena, FSS
accommodation_description: Pro se disabled veteran plaintiff seeks to maintain his Section 8 rent contribution at $1372 and prevent termination or reduction of his Section 8 housing benefits
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claims because plaintiff failed to allege any facts showing the HPD officials discriminated against him based on his disability, and instead recharacterized the claims as Section 1983 procedural due process challenges to the termination or reduction of Section 8 benefits
brief_summary: Pro se disabled veteran Eric Perez sued NYC HPD officials seeking to prevent termination of his Section 8 benefits and FSS program participation, asserting claims under the FHA, ADA, and RICO. The court dismissed all federal claims, finding plaintiff failed to state a plausible FHA discrimination claim because he alleged no facts showing the officials discriminated against him based on disability, and instead construed his remaining claims as Section 1983 procedural due process challenges to benefit termination procedures.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Criminal prosecution; mandamus relief (audit of FSS escrow account, investigation); Section 1983 claims for substantive due process (failure to investigate), procedural due process (reduction/termination of Section 8 and FSS benefits)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed criminal prosecution claims for lack of subject matter jurisdiction (plaintiff lacks standing to initiate criminal prosecution); mandamus claims against NYC agency officials (not federal officers); and Section 1983 claims for failure to state a claim under Iqbal/Twombly because plaintiff failed to allege facts showing denial of procedural due process, direct personal involvement of Commissioner Carrión, or applicability of exceptions to the general rule that government has no duty to investigate. Court construed plaintiff's purported FHA, ADA, and RICO claims as Section 1983 due process claims because plaintiff did not allege discrimination or racketeering.

case_name: Frank Mazzocchi v. Windsor Owners Corp.
accommodation_description: Underlying FHA § 3604(f)(2) discrimination claim in cooperative housing; accommodation analysis not addressed in this opinion.
key_holding: The jury waiver provision in Plaintiff's proprietary lease was enforceable because Plaintiff was represented by counsel during negotiations, the waiver was sufficiently conspicuous, and Plaintiff had sufficient business acumen as a real estate developer to understand the waiver's effect.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Frank Mazzocchi, a cooperative apartment shareholder, brought this action alleging housing discrimination under § 3604(f)(2) of the Fair Housing Act. The Court granted Defendants' motion to strike Plaintiff's jury demand, finding that the jury waiver provision in Plaintiff's proprietary lease was enforceable because Plaintiff was represented by counsel during negotiations, the waiver was sufficiently conspicuous, and Plaintiff, as a real estate developer, possessed the business acumen to knowingly and voluntarily waive his jury trial right.
key_cases_cited: Price v. Cushman & Wakefield, Inc., 808 F. Supp. 2d 670 (S.D.N.Y. 2011)
Hines v. 1025 Fifth Ave., Inc., No. 14-cv-3661 (S.D.N.Y. Feb. 23, 2015)
Morgan Guar. Trust Co. v. Crane, 36 F. Supp. 2d 602 (S.D.N.Y. 1999)
Merrill Lynch & Co. Inc. v. Allegheny Energy, Inc., 500 F.3d 171 (2d Cir. 2007)
Bear, Stearns Funding, Inc. v. Interface Grp.-Nev., Inc., No. 03-cv-8259 (S.D.N.Y. Nov. 7, 2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not specified; complaint alleges discrimination under § 3604(f)(2) but the opinion does not detail the specific nature of the discrimination claim
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted defendants' motion to strike the jury demand based on enforcement of a jury trial waiver clause in the proprietary lease. The FHA discrimination claim itself was not addressed on the merits; the opinion concerns only the procedural issue of whether the jury trial right was waived by contract. The claim survives and proceeds to bench trial.

case_name: Rene Belmar v. G&M Realty, et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation was specifically requested. Plaintiff's claims centered on alleged racial discrimination and housing violations by his landlord—including apartment conditions, rent gouging, and perceived corruption in the landlord-tenant court proceedings—not a request for a reasonable accommodation or modification under the FHA.
key_holding: The court dismissed the amended complaint for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because plaintiff failed to allege any facts sufficient to state a viable FHA claim under § 3604 or § 3617, and no diversity jurisdiction existed, warranting dismissal without further leave to amend.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Rene Belmar filed suit against his landlord, management company, attorney, a fellow tenant, and others, alleging various grievances arising from a landlord-tenant proceeding in Bronx Housing Civil Court, including race and housing discrimination. The court had previously dismissed the original complaint for lack of subject matter jurisdiction and granted Plaintiff 30 days' leave to replead an FHA claim. In the amended complaint, Plaintiff reframed his grievances as criminal charges but still failed to allege any facts plausibly showing race discrimination under § 3604 or that Defendants coerced, intimidated, or interfered with his FHA rights under § 3617, and the court dismissed the action for lack of subject matter jurisdiction and declined to grant further leave to amend.
key_cases_cited: Ruotolo v. City of New York, 514 F.3d 184 (2d Cir. 2008)
Salahuddin v. Cuomo, 861 F.2d 40 (2d Cir. 1988)
Leeke v. Timmerman, 454 U.S. 83 (1981)
Conn. Action Now, Inc. v. Roberts Plating Co., 457 F.2d 81 (2d Cir. 1972)
Coppedge v. United States, 369 U.S. 438 (1962)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because plaintiff failed to allege facts suggesting he exercised FHA rights or that defendants coerced, intimidated, or threatened him because of his race in violation of 42 U.S.C. § 3617. Plaintiff's claims arose from landlord-tenant disputes and housing court proceedings, not federal fair housing violations.

case_name: Keisha A. Jones v. City of New York, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought reasonable accommodations in shelter rules and services including dietary needs, private room with bathroom, bed rest accommodations, and alternative application processes for her disability-related housing needs.
key_holding: The court dismissed Plaintiff's FHA reasonable accommodation claim because she failed to adequately plead the nature of her disability or specify what accommodations she requested and why they were necessary to afford her equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling, but granted 30 days' leave to amend.
brief_summary: Keisha Jones, proceeding pro se, sued the City of New York, multiple City agencies, and several nonprofit shelter providers alleging violations of her reasonable accommodations in the shelter system under the Fair Housing Act. Chief Judge Swain dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim, finding Jones failed to identify her disability or specify the nature of her accommodation requests, but granted her 30 days' leave to amend her FHA claim.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Olsen v. Stark Homes, Inc.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Multiple accommodations allegedly requested and approved but not provided: dietary accommodations, bed rest, private room with attached private bathroom, location-specific accommodations. Plaintiff alleges defendants failed to provide these accommodations at various shelter facilities (Help USA, Westhab, ICL).
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for failure to state a plausible FHA reasonable accommodation claim because plaintiff failed to identify the nature of her disability or specify the type of reasonable accommodation requested and how it was necessary for equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling. Court applied Iqbal/Twombly pleading standard and found allegations insufficient.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 claims (due process, equal protection); state law claims regarding shelter conditions, housing placement, investigation of complaints
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim / § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii); Claim Preclusion (Res Judicata); Lack of State Action; Jurisdictional
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed § 1983 claims against private defendants (Urban Pathways, Help USA, Westhab, ICL, Tamara Bryant) for lack of state action; dismissed claims against DSS and HPD because municipal agencies cannot be sued; dismissed claims against City of New York for failure to allege municipal policy/custom; dismissed claims against Comptroller for failure to state constitutional violation; dismissed pre-November 2020 claims against City, Urban Pathways, and Help USA under claim preclusion doctrine based on prior judgment in Banks v. Jones; dismissed shelter condition claims because no federal constitutional right to housing exists.

case_name: Dante Malik Sullivan v. City of New York, et al.
accommodation_description: Pro se plaintiff in a homeless shelter alleges shelter staff retaliated against him for advocating about living conditions and mental safety, including calling police on him and labeling him as emotionally disturbed due to his mental illness.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act retaliation claims without prejudice because plaintiff failed to allege that his complaints involved discrimination based on protected characteristics and failed to identify specific state actors responsible for the alleged retaliation, granting leave to amend.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Dante Malik Sullivan, a mentally ill resident of a New York City homeless shelter operated by Project Renewal, sued the City of New York and multiple officials alleging retaliation under the FHA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act after he complained about shelter conditions. The court dismissed the claims for failure to state a viable retaliation theory because plaintiff did not allege his complaints concerned discrimination based on a protected characteristic and failed to identify specific state actors, granting plaintiff 60 days leave to amend.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Rendell-Baker v. Kohn, 457 U.S. 830 (1982)
Spiegel v. Schulman, 604 F.3d 72 (2d Cir. 2010)
Henrietta D. v. Bloomberg, 331 F.3d 261 (2d Cir. 2003)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts showing that any named defendant retaliated against him; instead, he repeatedly alleged that unspecified Project Renewal 'staff' retaliated against him. Additionally, Plaintiff did not allege that his complaints involved discrimination based on protected characteristics such as disability or race, which is required to establish protected activity under the FHA retaliation provision.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA retaliation, Rehabilitation Act retaliation, § 1983 First Amendment retaliation, § 1983 shelter conditions, HIPAA
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA and Rehabilitation Act retaliation claims against individuals are not cognizable because these statutes do not provide for individual liability. § 1983 First Amendment retaliation claims fail because Plaintiff did not identify suable state actors—Project Renewal and its staff are private parties not acting under color of state law. § 1983 shelter conditions claims fail because there is no federal constitutional right to housing or to placement in a particular type of shelter. HIPAA claims fail because HIPAA does not provide a private right of action.

case_name: Bernadette Skorupska v. 525 West 52 Property Owner LLC
accommodation_description: Request for a two-bedroom accessible apartment under disability set-aside program for plaintiff's son with developmental disabilities.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's motion for reconsideration because she failed to demonstrate standing for her ADA accessibility claim, did not establish that she and comparator Anna Hernandez are similarly situated, and improperly raised new arguments regarding deposition discrepancies.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Bernadette Skorupska moved for reconsideration of this Court's September 2022 summary judgment order dismissing her claims that defendants discriminated against her and her son with developmental disabilities by failing to provide a two-bedroom accessible apartment. The Court denied the motion, finding plaintiff failed to demonstrate standing for her ADA claim, failed to show she and comparator Anna Hernandez were similarly situated, and improperly raised new arguments about deposition discrepancies.
key_cases_cited: TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 141 S. Ct. 2190 (2021)
Calcano v. Swarovski N. Am. Ltd., 36 F.4th 68 (2d Cir. 2022)
Kreisler v. Second Ave. Diner Corp., 731 F.3d 184 (2d Cir. 2013)
Shrader v. CSX Transp. Inc., 70 F.3d 255 (2d Cir. 1995)
DaimlerChrysler Corp. v. Cuno, 547 U.S. 332 (2006)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought a two-bedroom apartment in the Building as a reasonable accommodation for her son's developmental disability; she alleged discrimination in the allocation of disability set-aside apartments and disparate treatment in the housing assignment process.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted summary judgment on the FHA discrimination and failure to accommodate claims in the prior September 1, 2022 Opinion. The motion for reconsideration does not present new facts or law that would alter the court's conclusion; plaintiff's comparison to Anna Hernandez fails because the two residents were not similarly situated in all material respects (Hernandez did not apply for a disability set-aside apartment and was not a voucher recipient).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, Americans with Disabilities Act Title III (accessibility claim), New York State Human Rights Law, and New York City Human Rights Law claims for discrimination and failure to accommodate.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted summary judgment on all non-FHA claims in the prior September 1, 2022 Opinion. The ADA Title III accessibility claim was dismissed on standing grounds because plaintiff failed to demonstrate that she intended to return to the Building in the future, as required to establish standing for injunctive relief under the ADA.

case_name: Keisha A. Jones v. City of New York
accommodation_description: The accommodation request is not described in this procedural order granting an extension of time to amend.
key_holding: The Court granted Plaintiff's request for an extension of time to file an amended complaint by December 5, 2022, without making any substantive determination on the merits of the dismissed Fair Housing Act claims.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Keisha A. Jones, proceeding pro se, filed an action against the City of New York alleging Fair Housing Act claims that were previously dismissed for failure to state a claim. The Court now grants Plaintiff's request for an extension of time to file an amended complaint by December 5, 2022.
key_cases_cited: Coppedge v. United States, 369 U.S. 438 (1962)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not specified in opinion
fha_claims.reasoning: The Court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim under the Fair Housing Act but granted Plaintiff 30 days' leave to replead. The opinion does not specify the nature of the FHA claims or the factual allegations, only that they were found insufficient under the pleading standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 claim
fha_claims.reasoning: The Court dismissed the § 1983 claim for failure to state a claim but granted Plaintiff leave to replead. The opinion does not detail the specific allegations or legal deficiencies.

case_name: Keisha A. Jones v. City of New York, et al.
accommodation_description: Cannot be determined from this procedural order addressing only an extension of time to file an amended complaint.
key_holding: The Court granted Plaintiff's request for a 30-day extension of time to file an amended complaint, warning that failure to comply will result in entry of judgment consistent with the prior dismissal order.
brief_summary: Pro se Plaintiff Keisha A. Jones, who was previously granted leave to replead claims under the Fair Housing Act following dismissal for failure to state a claim, requested an extension of the filing deadline due to illness; the Court granted the extension allowing Plaintiff until December 15, 2022, to submit an amended complaint.
key_cases_cited: Coppedge v. United States, 369 U.S. 438 (1962)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not specified in opinion
fha_claims.reasoning: The Court dismissed the original complaint for failure to state a claim under the Fair Housing Act but granted Plaintiff 30 days' leave to replead. The opinion does not specify the nature of the FHA claims or the factual allegations, as it addresses only a procedural extension request following the initial dismissal order.

case_name: Stone v. City of New York
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, who has unspecified mental illness and chronic asthma, alleged retaliation for complaining about shelter conditions that exacerbated his disabilities; the court found the complaints did not constitute protected activity under the FHA because they concerned general conditions rather than disability discrimination.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA retaliation claim with leave to amend because plaintiff failed to allege facts showing his complaints involved disability-based discrimination, as required to establish protected activity under the FHA.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff John Stone, a homeless individual with mental illness and asthma residing in New York City shelters, sued the City of New York and various officials and shelter operators alleging retaliation under the FHA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act for complaining about shelter conditions. The court dismissed the claims with leave to amend, finding plaintiff failed to allege protected activity because his complaints concerned general shelter conditions rather than disability-based discrimination, and failed to establish personal involvement of individual defendants or state action by private shelter operators.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Weixel v. Bd. of Educ. of City of N.Y.
Lindsey v. Normet
Spiegel v. Schulman

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; retaliation claim, not reasonable accommodation claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts showing that any named defendant retaliated against him; instead alleged only that unspecified Project Renewal 'staff' retaliated. Additionally, plaintiff's complaints about general shelter conditions do not constitute protected activity under the FHA because they do not involve discrimination based on disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA retaliation claim, Rehabilitation Act retaliation claim, § 1983 First Amendment retaliation claim, HIPAA claim, state law claims
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA and Rehabilitation Act retaliation claims fail because individuals cannot be held liable under those statutes. § 1983 First Amendment retaliation claim fails because Project Renewal staff are private actors not acting under color of state law, and plaintiff failed to allege personal involvement by named state actors. HIPAA claim fails because HIPAA provides no private right of action. Shelter conditions claims fail because there is no federal constitutional right to housing or to placement in a particular type of shelter.

case_name: Housing Rights Initiative v. Compass, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff challenges landlords' policy of refusing to rent to Housing Choice Voucher holders as having a disparate impact on disabled, Black, and Hispanic individuals.
key_holding: Although the court denied defendants' motions to dismiss, finding HRI had organizational standing and adequately pleaded disparate impact claims, this is a procedural ruling denying dismissal—the case proceeds to discovery rather than ruling on the merits of the FHA claims.
brief_summary: Housing Rights Initiative, a fair housing nonprofit, sued landlords and brokers for refusing to rent to Housing Choice Voucher holders, alleging disparate impact on disabled, Black, and Hispanic individuals under the FHA and state/local source-of-income discrimination laws. The court denied all defendants' motions to dismiss and for judgment on the pleadings, finding HRI had organizational standing based on diversion of resources and adequately pleaded disparate impact claims against each defendant.
key_cases_cited: Mhany Mgmt., Inc. v. County of Nassau, 819 F.3d 581 (2d Cir. 2016)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Connecticut Parents Union v. Russell-Tucker, 8 F.4th 157 (2d Cir. 2021)
Olsen v. Stark Homes, Inc., 759 F.3d 140 (2d Cir. 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to rent to Housing Choice Voucher (HCV) holders; policy of denying housing to individuals using HCV subsidies
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found HRI adequately pleaded a disparate impact claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(1) based on disability. HRI alleged defendants' facially neutral policy of refusing HCV holders has a disparate impact on disabled individuals (28% of HCV holders are disabled vs. 9.8% of non-HCV holders; disabled residents 3.3 times more likely to be adversely affected). At pleading stage, HRI need only plausibly allege disparate impact, not prove it; statistical allegations suffice to survive motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to rent to Housing Choice Voucher (HCV) holders; policy of denying housing to individuals using HCV subsidies
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found HRI adequately pleaded a disparate impact claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(a) based on race and national origin. HRI alleged defendants' policy of refusing HCV holders has disparate impact on Black and Hispanic individuals (82% of HCV holders are Black or Hispanic vs. 50% of general population; Black and Hispanic residents 3.2 times more likely to be adversely affected). At pleading stage, statistical allegations and plausible inference of disparate impact suffice to survive motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: New York State Human Rights Law § 296 et seq. (NYSHRL) and New York City Human Rights Law § 8-502(a) et seq. (NYCHRL) claims for source-of-income discrimination
fha_claims.reasoning: Court exercised supplemental jurisdiction over state and local law claims under 28 U.S.C. § 1367 because federal FHA claims survived motion to dismiss. Court did not reach merits of non-FHA claims but allowed them to proceed.

case_name: Michael Reeves v. CMP Consultants, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges racial discrimination in housing and retaliation for filing a NYSDHR complaint; no reasonable accommodation request is at issue.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's request for preliminary injunctive relief because plaintiff failed to allege facts sufficient to state a plausible FHA discrimination claim—specifically, plaintiff did not identify his own race or allege facts showing discriminatory animus caused the leasing delays.
brief_summary: Michael Reeves, proceeding pro se, sued CMP Consultants, Inc. and other defendants alleging they discriminated against him on the basis of race by obstructing his access to a NYC Housing Lottery apartment and retaliating against him for filing a NYSDHR complaint. The court denied plaintiff's motion for preliminary injunction and temporary restraining order, finding the complaint failed to state a plausible FHA claim because plaintiff did not identify his own race or allege facts demonstrating discriminatory animus caused the leasing delays, and granted plaintiff 60 days leave to amend.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Gladstone Realtors v. Vill. of Bellwood
Mazzocchi v. Windsor Owners Corp.
Premium Mortg. Corp. v. Equifax

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged only legal conclusions of racial discrimination without pleading sufficient facts showing that defendants subjected him to an adverse housing action because of his race. Plaintiff did not identify his own race, did not allege facts connecting the delays to discriminatory animus, and made only speculative assertions. The court found these allegations insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Although plaintiff alleged that defendants retaliated by repeatedly requesting documents after he filed a complaint with NYSDHR, the court did not separately analyze this retaliation claim. The dismissal was based on the overarching failure to plead sufficient facts under Iqbal/Twombly standards to support any FHA claim, including retaliation under § 3617.

case_name: Jimmy Avila v. Acacia Network, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested transfer from BASICS to a one-bedroom apartment at an alternate site as a reasonable accommodation for his medical condition (infection/osteomyelitis requiring bed rest).
key_holding: The court found plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts showing the accommodation was necessary to afford equal opportunity to use the dwelling, was reasonable, and was refused by defendant, but granted plaintiff 60 days' leave to amend.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Jimmy Avila, proceeding pro se, sued Acacia Network, Inc., Lorraine Coleman, and Bronx Addiction Services Integrated Concepts System, Inc. (BASICS), alleging disability discrimination under the FHA, including failure to accommodate his request to transfer to a different apartment as recommended by his physician. The Southern District of New York found the complaint failed to adequately plead the elements of a reasonable accommodation claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(B) but granted plaintiff 60 days' leave to amend his complaint.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Olsen v. Stark Homes, Inc.
Rodriguez v. Village Green Realty, Inc.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Transfer from BASICS to a one-bedroom apartment at an alternate site, as recommended by plaintiff's physician for medical treatment of chronic infection and osteomyelitis
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to state a reasonable accommodation claim under the FHA. Specifically, plaintiff did not allege that the requested accommodation was likely necessary to afford equal opportunity to enjoy the dwelling, that the accommodation was reasonable, or that the defendant refused the accommodation. The court applied the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard at the pleading stage without reaching the substantive reasonable accommodation balancing test.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts showing that his disability was a motivating factor in any adverse action by defendants. The court found no plausible allegation of discriminatory animus or intent based on disability, applying the Iqbal/Twombly standard without substantive merits analysis.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claim for failure to provide reasonable accommodations in services, programs, or activities of a public entity
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts showing he was denied opportunity to participate in or benefit from defendants' services, programs, or activities because of his disability under ADA Title II. The court applied the Iqbal/Twombly pleading standard without substantive analysis of the ADA claim.

case_name: Baltazar v. Goldfarb Properties Management, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested an emergency transfer from his current apartment in Far Rockaway to Manhattan or the Bronx, claiming isolation at his current location was exacerbating his disability.
key_holding: The court found plaintiff's complaint failed to allege sufficient facts to state a claim for reasonable accommodation under the FHA because he did not allege facts showing the accommodation was necessary to afford him an equal opportunity to enjoy the dwelling, that the accommodation was reasonable, or that defendants refused to make the requested accommodation.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Mynor Federico Nunez Baltazar sued Goldfarb Properties Management and related defendants under the FHA and ADA, alleging disability discrimination and failure to accommodate his request for emergency transfer from Far Rockaway to Manhattan or the Bronx to address isolation exacerbating his medical condition. The court denied the preliminary injunction request and dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim, finding plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts showing the accommodation was necessary, reasonable, or denied, but granted leave to amend within 60 days.
key_cases_cited: Olsen v. Stark Homes, Inc., 759 F.3d 140 (2d Cir. 2014)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Transfer to Manhattan or the Bronx on emergency basis via Section 8 Move Voucher to alleviate isolation and segregation exacerbating plaintiff's mental health condition; second accommodation request for transfer due to isolation causing suicidal ideation and attempted suicide
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to state a reasonable accommodation claim under the FHA. Even assuming disability, plaintiff did not allege that the requested accommodation was likely necessary to afford equal opportunity to enjoy the dwelling, that the accommodation was reasonable, that defendants refused the accommodation, or that but for the accommodation he would be denied equal opportunity to enjoy his apartment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts showing that his disability was a motivating factor in any adverse action taken by defendants. The complaint lacks factual allegations of intentional discrimination based on disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claim for failure to provide reasonable accommodation and denial of services, programs, or activities; ADA Title III claim for discrimination in access to public accommodations
fha_claims.reasoning: Even assuming plaintiff is a qualified individual with a disability under the ADA, plaintiff alleged no facts showing he was denied opportunity to participate in or benefit from defendants' services, programs, or activities, or was otherwise discriminated against by reason of his disability.

case_name: Jane Doe v. Anthony Pistilli et al.
accommodation_description: No disability accommodation requested; claim concerns denial of lease renewal after plaintiff rebuffed sexual advances from building superintendent.
key_holding: The S.D.N.Y. transferred the case to the Eastern District of New York because all parties reside in the EDNY and the operative facts occurred there, making transfer appropriate under 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a).
brief_summary: Jane Doe sued Anthony Pistilli and related defendants alleging sex discrimination in violation of the Fair Housing Act, claiming her lease was not renewed after she rejected sexual advances from her building superintendent. The S.D.N.Y. granted transfer to the Eastern District of New York, finding that all parties reside there and the operative facts occurred there, making transfer appropriate for convenience of parties and witnesses and in the interests of justice.
key_cases_cited: Corley v. United States, 11 F.4th 79 (2d Cir. 2021)
D.H. Blair & Co. v. Gottdiener, 462 F.3d 95 (2d Cir. 2006)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court transferred the case to the Eastern District of New York for convenience and in the interest of justice under 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a), finding that all parties reside in the Eastern District, the locus of operative facts is there, and witnesses and documents are located there. The merits of the FHA claim alleging sex discrimination in lease renewal denial were not addressed.

case_name: Elaine Williams Bethea v. NYCHA Law Department
accommodation_description: Plaintiff's complaint concerns denial of a two-bedroom apartment assignment in 2001 and substandard housing conditions, which she characterizes as race-based discrimination under the FHA.
key_holding: The complaint fails to state a claim under the FHA because Plaintiff does not allege facts plausibly suggesting that Defendant discriminated against her based on race, exercised FHA rights, or was subjected to retaliation under § 3617.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Elaine Williams Bethea sued NYCHA Law Department alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on race discrimination and intimidation. The court dismissed her complaint for failure to state a claim, finding she failed to allege facts plausibly suggesting discrimination based on race or retaliation under the FHA. The court granted Plaintiff 30 days' leave to file an amended complaint to cure the deficiencies, including addressing timeliness concerns under the FHA's two-year statute of limitations.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Havens v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Lindsay v. Normet, 405 U.S. 56 (1972)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges she was approved and selected for a two-bedroom apartment in 2001 but was instead assigned a one-bedroom apartment; she also alleges discrimination and racism in the tenant selection and assignment process.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts plausibly suggesting that defendant subjected her to discrimination or retaliation in housing on the basis of any impermissible factor. She did not allege her race, did not allege defendant discriminated based on race, and did not connect any alleged harm to a protected class characteristic.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 1983 due process claim based on alleged inadequate housing conditions (mold, mildew, odor, water leaks, brown water from faucets); state law claims for breach of warranty of habitability or negligence.
fha_claims.reasoning: There is no constitutional right to adequate or safe housing under the Due Process Clause. The court declined supplemental jurisdiction over any state law claims after dismissing all federal question claims.

case_name: Jimmy Avila v. Sun River Health, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested a safety transfer from his current housing unit to a one-bedroom apartment at an alternate location based on medical documentation.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's ADA and Rehabilitation Act claims without prejudice for failure to state a plausible claim, granting plaintiff sixty days leave to amend his complaint to allege sufficient facts.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Jimmy Avila sued Sun River Health, Inc. and individual defendants alleging they failed to provide required medical accommodations, specifically a safety transfer to a different apartment unit. The Southern District of New York dismissed the ADA Title II and Rehabilitation Act claims without prejudice for failure to state a plausible claim, granted plaintiff leave to amend within sixty days, and denied his preliminary injunction request without prejudice.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Safety transfer from BASIC to a one-bedroom apartment at an alternate scatter site, as recommended by Dr. Martynowicz in a March 22, 2020 letter
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts showing he was denied the opportunity to participate in or benefit from defendants' services, programs, or activities because of his disability. The complaint lacked factual detail regarding what defendants did or failed to do and how this violated the FHA, failing to meet the plausibility standard under Twombly/Iqbal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation for reporting illegal acts by Melissa Shoupe and Lester to colleagues, agencies, and local authorities
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint failed to allege sufficient facts to state a plausible retaliation claim under the FHA. The court found the allegations too conclusory and lacking in factual detail regarding the causal connection between the protected activity and the alleged retaliation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claims under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1346 and 2671 (Federal Tort Claims Act), Title II of the ADA, the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, the New York City Human Rights Law, and the New York State Human Rights Law
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that even assuming plaintiff has a disability, he failed to allege facts showing he was denied the opportunity to participate in or benefit from defendants' services, programs, or activities, or was otherwise discriminated against because of his disability under Title II of the ADA and the Rehabilitation Act. The complaint lacked sufficient factual allegations to state a plausible claim.

case_name: Joaquin Dean v. Jeremy Doberman and Marc Wohlgemuth
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation requested; plaintiff primarily seeks to enjoin foreclosure sale and eviction, with claims of discriminatory statements by attorneys during litigation.
key_holding: The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss because plaintiff's claims to enjoin the sale and eviction are barred by Rooker-Feldman and Younger abstention doctrines, and plaintiff's FHA discrimination claim fails because he did not plausibly allege defendants acted with discriminatory intent in connection with the sale or rental of a dwelling.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Joaquin Dean sued attorneys Jeremy Doberman and Marc Wohlgemuth, alleging they made discriminatory statements during quiet title and holdover proceedings in state court in violation of the Fair Housing Act, and sought to stop the sale of his foreclosed property and his eviction. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that plaintiff's claims to reverse the sale and eviction are barred by the Rooker-Feldman doctrine and Younger abstention, and that his FHA discrimination claim fails because he did not plausibly allege defendants acted with discriminatory intent regarding housing.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Francis v. Kings Park Manor, Inc., 992 F.3d 67 (2d Cir. 2021)
Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Saudi Basic Industr. Corp., 544 U.S. 280 (2005)
Hoblock v. Albany Cnty. Bd. of Elections, 422 F.3d 77 (2d Cir. 2005)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege defendants discriminated against him based on race or that their alleged conduct occurred in connection with the sale or rental of a dwelling. Defendants' statements about plaintiff's bankruptcies and litigation tactics during the Quiet Title Action do not evince racial discriminatory intent and are insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 1982 (Civil Rights Act of 1866), FDCPA (Fair Debt Collection Practices Act), First Amendment, Fifth Amendment, Fourteenth Amendment, emotional distress claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff raised these non-FHA claims for the first time in his opposition and they cannot be construed from the amended complaint. The Court declined to consider them as new causes of action improperly raised in briefing. Additionally, even if considered, Section 1982 claims would fail for the same reasons as the FHA claim—failure to allege discriminatory intent or that the alleged conduct concerned property transactions.

case_name: Katz, et al. v. New York City Housing Preservation & Development, et al.
accommodation_description: This case does not involve a disability accommodation request; it challenges occupancy limits applied to a large family based on family size (number of occupants) rather than familial status (presence of children under 18).
key_holding: The court granted defendants' motion for an extension of time to file a motion to dismiss and stayed discovery pending resolution of the anticipated motion, finding that the dispositive motion may eliminate all claims and that plaintiffs have not been prejudiced given delays caused by plaintiffs.
brief_summary: The Katz family sued NYC HPD and HDC alleging the occupancy limits in affordable housing lotteries discriminated against them based on familial status; defendants moved to dismiss and stay discovery, arguing the amended complaint conflated family size (not protected) with familial status (protected). 30 Clinton Place Owners Inc. v. City of New Rochelle, 2014 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 31839 (S.D.N.Y. Feb. 27, 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Defendants argue that plaintiffs' original disparate impact claim based on occupancy standards is inadequately pleaded. case_name: McKins v. Pye
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: This procedural order vacates the Order to Show Cause and directs the Clerk to issue summonses and complete service through the U.S. Marshals Service; the substantive FHA claims have not been analyzed.

The Court vacated the Order to Show Cause and directed service of process through the U.S. Marshals Service; the substantive merits of the FHA claims remain unadjudicated.
key_cases_cited: Walker v. Schult, 717 F.3d 119 (2d Cir. 2013)
Meilleur v. Strong, 682 F.3d 56 (2d Cir. 2012)

source_file: 9883432_2023_Xia v. 65 West 87th Street Housing Development Fund Corporation_nysd
case_name: Xia v. 65 West 87th Street Housing Development Fund Corporation
accommodation_description: Not applicable — this case does not involve a reasonable accommodation or modification request; it involves a discriminatory denial of a cooperative apartment purchase application.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion for summary judgment, finding genuine disputes of material fact as to whether the HDFC cooperative board's repeated rejection of plaintiffs' purchase applications was motivated by racial animus against Eva Xia as a Chinese American woman.
brief_summary: Eva Xia, a Chinese American woman, and her husband Paul Privitera attempted to purchase a cooperative apartment at 65 West 87th Street in Manhattan, an HDFC building, but were rejected by the board's special committee on multiple occasions. Plaintiffs brought claims under the Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 1981/1982, and state and city human rights laws, alleging the rejections were motivated by racial discrimination. The court denied defendants' motion for summary judgment, finding sufficient evidence of pretextual reasons for rejection and potential racial animus—including board member Rojo's contemporaneous comments, disparate treatment compared to prior applicants, and evidence of prior hostility toward Asian tenants—to require resolution by a jury.
key_cases_cited: Village of Arlington Heights v. Metropolitan Housing Development Corp., 429 U.S. 252 (1977)
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Quad Enters. Co., LLC v. Town of Southold, 369 F. App'x 202 (2d Cir. 2010)
Sassower v. Field, 752 F. Supp. 1182 (S.D.N.Y. 1990)
Reeves v. Sanderson Plumbing Products, Inc., 530 U.S. 133 (2000)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied summary judgment on disparate treatment claim under FHA, finding genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether defendants' stated nondiscriminatory reasons (incomplete applications, financial concerns) were pretextual for discrimination based on Xia's race/national origin. Evidence of procedural irregularities, differential treatment compared to similarly situated applicants, and board members' comments regarding Asian applicants created sufficient circumstantial evidence for jury determination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Civil Rights Act of 1866 (§§ 1981, 1982), New York State Human Rights Law, New York City Human Rights Law
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework to non-FHA discrimination claims under the same legal standard as FHA disparate treatment claim. Summary judgment denied on all non-FHA claims for the same reasons as FHA claim: genuine disputes of material fact regarding pretext and discriminatory intent.

case_name: Chanel Moody, Ayanda Carmichael, and Ronnie Clark v. The Related Companies, L.P., and Ery South Residential Tower LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs, Black low-income individuals selected for affordable housing units, alleged they were treated less favorably than market-rate tenants, raising disparate treatment and disparate impact claims under § 3604(a) based on race.
key_holding: The court declined to impose Rule 11 sanctions against plaintiffs' counsel because, despite finding the underlying racial discrimination claims had no chance of success under Second Circuit precedent, counsel's good faith belief in extending civil rights law to address the intersection of race and economic status warranted protection from sanctions in light of the potential chilling effect on civil rights litigation.
brief_summary: Black low-income plaintiffs sued private developers of a mixed-use building in Hudson Yards alleging they were treated less favorably than market-rate tenants based on race in violation of § 3604(a). The court denied defendants' motion for Rule 11 sanctions against plaintiffs' counsel, finding that while the racial discrimination claims had no chance of success under Second Circuit precedent, counsel's good faith effort to extend civil rights law merited protection from sanctions given the importance of avoiding chilling effects on civil rights advocacy.
key_cases_cited: Boyd v. Lefrak Org., 509 F.2d 1110 (2d Cir. 1975)
Salute v. Stratford Greens Garden Apts., 136 F.3d 293 (2d Cir. 1998)
Fed. R. Civ. P. 11(b)
Morley v. Ciba-Geigy Corp., 66 F.3d 21 (2d Cir. 1995)
Ipcon Collections LLC v. Costco Wholesale Corp., 698 F.3d 58 (2d Cir. 2012)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to allege a similarly-situated comparator group; luxury condominium owners are not similarly situated to affordable housing tenants. Additionally, Plaintiffs failed to allege facts tending to show discriminatory intent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
