The court dismissed the complaint under § 1915(e)(2)(B) for failure to state a claim because plaintiffs failed to provide sufficient factual allegations giving defendants fair notice of their claims, and dismissed claims on behalf of minor children because parents cannot represent minors pro se.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents of Federal Bureau of Narcotics, 403 U.S. 388 (1971)
Coleman v. Indymac Venture, LLC, 966 F. Supp. 2d 759 (W.D. Tenn. 2013)
Shepherd v. Wellman, 313 F.3d 963 (6th Cir. 2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act claim (among others: § 1983, ADA, VAWA, HUD regulations)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed under § 1915(e)(2)(B) as frivolous/failing to state a claim because the complaint was written jointly by two plaintiffs and failed to give fair notice of what claims Mr. McCoy individually asserted or the factual basis for those claims. The court applied Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards but did not engage substantively with any FHA elements.

case_name: Ameer Alghusain v. Jason L. Nemeth, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges wrongful eviction based on race, national origin, religion, and disability, but does not request a specific accommodation.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claim because his allegations were entirely conclusory and failed to provide facts plausibly suggesting his eviction was motivated by race, national origin, religion, or disability.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Ameer Alghusain sued his landlord Jason Nemeth, his brother Joseph Nemeth, and numerous other defendants alleging wrongful eviction from rental property in violation of the Fair Housing Act and various state law claims. The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss, finding that plaintiff's FHA claim was entirely conclusory and failed to allege sufficient facts to state a plausible claim that his eviction was motivated by his race, national origin, religion, or disability.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Wrongful eviction allegedly motivated by race, national origin, religion, and/or disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's FHA claim is entirely conclusory with no factual allegations plausibly suggesting the eviction was motivated by race, national origin, religion, or disability. The complaint fails to meet the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard and provides defendants no fair notice of the claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Ohio Revised Code § 4112.02 discrimination claim; negligence and wrongful eviction under Ohio Revised Code §§ 1923 and 5321; legal malpractice
fha_claims.reasoning: State discrimination claims under Ohio Revised Code § 4112.02 are entirely conclusory and fail to allege facts plausibly suggesting denial of benefits or eviction was motivated by protected characteristics. Legal malpractice claim is time-barred under Ohio's one-year statute of limitations, accruing in 2016 when Buckingham filed suit against plaintiff.

case_name: Donald Davis v. Mary Z. Cornely, et al.
accommodation_description: No disability accommodation was requested; this case involves allegations of racial discrimination in housing conditions, a racially derogatory verbal attack, retaliation for complaining about property conditions and filing a civil stalking protection order, and interference with plaintiff's foster-care arrangements.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's motion to dismiss defendants' amended state law counterclaims, holding that 28 U.S.C. § 1367 confers supplemental jurisdiction over those counterclaims because they arise from the same landlord-tenant relationship and share a common nucleus of operative facts with plaintiff's federal FHA and civil rights claims.
brief_summary: Donald Davis, an African American tenant, sued his landlord Mary Cornely and property manager Carl Wood alleging race-based discrimination and retaliatory conduct in violation of the Fair Housing Act (§§ 3604(a), 3604(b), 3604(c), 3617) and the Civil Rights Acts of 1866 and 1870, stemming from an incident in which Wood allegedly used a racial slur and threatened him, as well as Defendants' failure to make repairs and interference with his foster-care placements. Defendants filed amended state law counterclaims for bad-faith rent deposit, tortious interference, civil liability for false alarms, abuse of process, defamation, and assault. The court denied Davis's Rule 12(b)(1) motion to dismiss the counterclaims, concluding that all counterclaims derive from the same disputed landlord-tenant relationship and conduct underlying the federal claims, satisfying the 'common nucleus of operative facts' standard for supplemental jurisdiction.
key_cases_cited: Harper v. AutoAlliance Int'l, Inc., 392 F.3d 195 (6th Cir. 2004)
Gentek Bidg. Prods., Inc. v. Sherwin-Williams Co., 491 F.3d 320 (6th Cir. 2007)
Frisby v. Keith D. Weiner & Associates Co., LPA, 669 F. Supp.2d 863 (N.D. Ohio 2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Bad-faith rent deposit (Ohio Rev. Code § 5321.09(D)); tortious interference with contract or business relationship; civil liability for criminal acts (false alarm under Ohio Rev. Code § 2917.32(A)(3)); abuse of process; defamation; assault; civil liability for criminal acts (assault and attempted assault under Ohio Rev. Code § 2923.02(A))
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied plaintiff's motion to dismiss defendants' counterclaims for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(b)(1), finding that 28 U.S.C. § 1367 confers supplemental jurisdiction over state law counterclaims that derive from a common nucleus of operative facts with plaintiff's federal FHA claims arising from the same landlord-tenant relationship and disputed conduct.

case_name: Albert Pickett, Jr. v. City of Cleveland
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; this is a disparate impact challenge to the City of Cleveland's water lien policy allegedly placing liens disproportionately on Black homeowners' properties.
key_holding: The court found that Plaintiffs satisfied Rule 23(a) numerosity, commonality, typicality, and adequacy requirements, and that predominance and superiority were established for the Water Lien Class under Rule 23(b)(3), warranting class certification because the city’s facially neutral water lien policy disproportionately impacted Black homeowners in violation of the FHA.
brief_summary: African-American customers of Cleveland Water sued the City of Cleveland alleging that the city's water lien policy, which converts overdue water bills into tax liens on properties, disproportionately impacts Black homeowners and violates the Fair Housing Act. The court granted class certification for the Water Lien, Shutoff, and Overbilling Classes, finding that plaintiffs established Rule 23(a) requirements and that common questions predominate over individual issues regarding whether the city's facially neutral policy created a disparate impact on the basis of race.
key_cases_cited: Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. v. Dukes, 564 U.S. 338 (2011)
Texas Dept. of Housing & Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Tyson Foods, Inc. v. Bouaphakeo, 136 S.Ct. 1036 (2016)
In re Whirlpool Corp. Front-Loading Washer Prod. Liab. Litig., 722 F.3d 838 (6th Cir. 2013)
Powers v. Hamilton Cnty. Public Defender Comm'n, 501 F.3d 592 (6th Cir. 2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted class certification for the Water Lien Class under Rule 23(b)(2) and (b)(3) on a disparate-impact theory under the FHA, finding that Defendant's facially neutral water lien policy disproportionately impacts African-American homeowners. The court did not reach the merits of the FHA claim itself but rather certified the class to proceed to litigation on the disparate-impact theory.

case_name: United States of America v. Joseph Pedaline, et al.
accommodation_description: Sexual harassment by property manager/owner including making housing benefits contingent on sexual acts, unwanted touching, and eviction threats against female tenants who rejected advances.
key_holding: The court denied Defendants' motions to dismiss, finding the complaint plausibly alleges YLP's vicarious and direct liability for Pedaline's sexual harassment, direct § 3617 interference claims against Pedaline personally, and a timely-filed pattern-or-practice claim.
brief_summary: The United States sued property owner/manager Joseph Pedaline and YLP LLC under the FHA's pattern-or-practice provision, alleging that from 2009-2020 Pedaline sexually harassed female tenants by conditioning housing benefits on sexual acts, making unwanted advances, and evicting those who rejected him. The court denied both defendants' motions to dismiss, finding the complaint sufficiently pleaded vicarious liability against YLP, direct liability for YLP's failure to respond to complaints, personal liability against Pedaline under § 3617, and that the complaint was timely filed.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Quaker Oats Co. v. Universal Food Corp., 392 U.S. 409 (1968)
United States v. City of Chicago, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that the government plausibly alleged a pattern or practice of sexual discrimination and harassment against female tenants based on sex under 42 U.S.C. § 3604, satisfying the Iqbal/Twombly pleading standard. The complaint sufficiently alleged facts supporting vicarious liability of YLP and direct liability for failure to correct discriminatory conduct by its agent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that the government sufficiently alleged that Pedaline's coercive and intimidating behavior (sexual harassment, conditioning housing benefits on sexual acts, unwanted touching, and adverse housing actions) directly interfered with tenants' right to discrimination-free housing under 42 U.S.C. § 3617, establishing the required elements of coercion, intimidation, and causal connection at the pleading stage.

source_file: 9906570_2024_Mindale Farms Co. v. City of Tallmadge, Ohio_ohnd
case_name: Mindale Farms Co. v. City of Tallmadge, Ohio
accommodation_description: N/A - This case involves a developer's challenge to a rezoning denial framed as a disparate impact claim, not a traditional reasonable accommodation request by a tenant or person with a disability.
key_holding: Mindale Farms failed to state an FHA or ADA claim because it attempted to use age as a proxy for disability without establishing a sufficient nexus, and the court refused to effectively rewrite the FHA and ADA to include age as a protected class.
brief_summary: Mindale Farms Co., a land developer, sued the City of Tallmadge, Ohio alleging the city's denial of its rezoning application and subsequent repeal of the R-6 District violated the Fair Housing Act and ADA by reducing housing available to disabled individuals. The court granted the city's motion for judgment on the pleadings, finding that Mindale Farms failed to state a valid FHA or ADA claim because it improperly attempted to use age (55 and older housing) as a proxy for disability without establishing a sufficient causal nexus between age and disability.
key_cases_cited: Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
MX Grp., Inc. v. City of Covington, 293 F.3d 326 (6th Cir. 2002)
Budnick v. Town of Carefree, 518 F.3d 1109 (9th Cir. 2008)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of rezoning application to allow development of senior housing (55+) that would allegedly provide housing for disabled individuals; City's subsequent repeal of R-6 zoning district
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege a nexus between disability and the challenged zoning action. Plaintiff attempted to use age (55+) as a proxy for disability based on a CDC statistic that 40% of those 65+ have disabilities, but this inferential chain is too attenuated and would improperly rewrite the FHA to include age as a protected class. The connection between disability and the age-based development plan is too loose to state a plausible claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal protection (class-of-one theory), regulatory taking (partial taking under Penn Central), First Amendment retaliation, ADA Title II disparate impact
fha_claims.reasoning: Equal protection claim failed because plaintiff did not plausibly allege similarly situated comparator (Ripley Farm) and did not negate rational basis for denial (aesthetic concerns). Regulatory taking claim failed because plaintiff lacked investment-backed expectations and the government action had legitimate public purpose. First Amendment retaliation claim failed because temporal proximity alone (5 months between application and repeal) is insufficient to establish causal connection without additional allegations of hostility. ADA claim failed on same nexus-to-disability grounds as FHA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges discriminatory and selective enforcement of occupancy and use codes; claims racial discrimination in application of A-3 Use Occupancy requirement to his church compared to similarly situated white pastor's church
fha_claims.reasoning: Court abstained under Younger v. Harris because state criminal proceeding is pending, involves important state interest (building code enforcement), and plaintiff failed to demonstrate state procedural law bars presentation of federal claims. Court did not reach merits of any claim.

case_name: Chelsea Culver, et al. v. Melissa Churchill, et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request was made; plaintiffs merely invoke the FHA in connection with state law eviction and defamation claims without alleging denial of any accommodation.
key_holding: The court dismissed the complaint for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because plaintiffs failed to establish federal question jurisdiction (the FHA is irrelevant to state law eviction and defamation claims) and no diversity of citizenship exists between the Ohio parties.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Chelsea Culver and Ben Smith sued their former landlords Melissa Churchill and Donald Zeiters in federal court, attempting to bring state law eviction and defamation claims under the Fair Housing Act. The court dismissed the complaint for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, finding no federal question (the FHA is irrelevant to the alleged claims) and no diversity of citizenship since all parties are Ohio residents.
key_cases_cited: Spotts v. United States, 429 F.3d 248 (6th Cir. 2005)
Neitzke v. Williams, 490 U.S. 319 (1989)
Sistrunk v. City of Strongsville, 99 F.3d 194 (6th Cir. 1996)
Ohio ex rel. Skaggs v. Brunner, 549 F.3d 468 (6th Cir. 2008)
Caterpillar Inc. v. Williams, 482 U.S. 386 (1987)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege defendants violated the Fair Housing Act by refusing further rent payments and initiating a second eviction action after the first was dismissed, but fail to allege discrimination based on any protected class or disability.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because plaintiffs failed to allege discrimination based on any protected class under the FHA and the case involves only state law eviction and defamation claims. Neither diversity nor federal question jurisdiction exists.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Defamation claim under 28 U.S.C. § 410
fha_claims.reasoning: 28 U.S.C. § 410 provides a definition of defamation only in the context of collection of foreign defamation judgments and does not create a federal cause of action for state law defamation torts. Claim lacks federal question jurisdiction.

source_file: 9909319_2020_Cooper v. PJ Apartments, LLC, dba Village Square Apartments_ohsd
case_name: Lisa Renee Cooper v. PJ Apartments, LLC, dba Village Square Apartments
accommodation_description: Plaintiff with asthma, osteoarthritis, and torticollis requested transfer to a first-floor apartment as a reasonable accommodation for her mobility limitations.
key_holding: The court found genuine disputes of material fact exist as to whether plaintiff is disabled within the meaning of the FHA, whether a first-floor unit was necessary as an accommodation to afford her equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling, and whether defendants' non-renewal of her lease was retaliatory, warranting denial of both parties' cross-motions for summary judgment.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Lisa Cooper, a Section 8 voucher holder with asthma, osteoarthritis, and torticollis limiting her mobility, sued her apartment complex for failing to accommodate her request to transfer to a first-floor unit and for retaliating against her by issuing a lease non-renewal notice after she requested the accommodation. The court denied both parties' cross-motions for summary judgment, finding genuine issues of material fact exist regarding whether Cooper is disabled, whether the first-floor unit was necessary as a reasonable accommodation, and whether defendants' conduct constituted unlawful retaliation.
key_cases_cited: Hollis v. Chestnut Bend Homeowners Ass'n, 760 F.3d 531 (6th Cir. 2014)
Groner v. Golden Gate Gardens Apartments, 250 F.3d 1039 (6th Cir. 2001)
Overlook Mut. Homes, Inc. v. Spencer, 415 F. App'x 617 (6th Cir. 2011)
Logan v. Matveevskii, 57 F. Supp. 3d 234 (S.D.N.Y. 2014)
Powers v. Kalamazoo Breakthrough Consumer Hous. Co-op, 2009 WL 2922309 (W.D. Mich. Sept. 9, 2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Transfer from third-floor apartment to first-floor apartment to accommodate plaintiff's asthma, osteoarthritis, and torticollis, which make walking and climbing stairs difficult.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine issues of material fact as to whether plaintiff is disabled (substantial limitation in walking/climbing stairs despite mitigating measures), whether defendants rescinded their March 2018 offer of a first-floor unit, and whether the accommodation was necessary for equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling. Both parties' summary judgment motions denied; case proceeds to trial.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Lease non-renewal notice issued August 1, 2018, allegedly in retaliation for plaintiff's written requests for accommodation (April, May, June 2018) and assertion of FHA rights.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that exercise of a contractually specified right (non-renewal) can constitute retaliation under § 3617 if done to interfere with FHA rights. Genuine issues of material fact exist as to defendants' intent and causal connection between plaintiff's accommodation requests and the non-renewal notice. Defendants' motion for summary judgment denied because they failed to provide developed argument and genuine factual disputes remain.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claims under Ohio Revised Code § 4112.02 and § 5321.02 (state fair housing and landlord-tenant statutes)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court noted that state FHA-parallel claims are analyzed under the same standards as federal FHA claims and are considered together. Both parties' summary judgment motions denied on state law claims as well, with same genuine issues of material fact regarding disability status, necessity of accommodation, and retaliation.

source_file: 9910433_2021_Freedom's Path at Dayton v. Dayton Metropolitan Housing Authority_ohsd
case_name: Freedom's Path at Dayton v. Dayton Metropolitan Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought that defendant housing authority apply for 60 VASH project-based vouchers on behalf of the veterans housing project and/or amend its Administrative Plan to permit award of vouchers based on prior third-party competition without competitive RFP process.
key_holding: The requested accommodation lacked sufficient nexus to disability because defendant would have denied the voucher application request regardless of the disabled status of prospective tenants—disabled and non-disabled veterans were equally affected by defendant's RFP policy requirements.
brief_summary: Freedom's Path, a developer of supportive housing for homeless veterans, sued Dayton Metropolitan Housing Authority alleging violations of the ADA and FHA for refusing to apply for VASH project-based vouchers on its behalf and refusing to amend its Administrative Plan to permit voucher awards based on prior third-party competition. The court granted summary judgment to defendant, finding no genuine issue of material fact because plaintiff failed to establish the required nexus between the accommodation request and any disability, as defendant's policy denial would have applied equally to disabled and non-disabled housing projects.
key_cases_cited: Smith & Lee Assocs., Inc. v. City of Taylor, Mich., 102 F.3d 781 (6th Cir. 1996)
City of Edmonds v. Washington State Bldg. Code Council, 18 F.3d 802 (9th Cir. 1994)
Bronk v. Ineichen, 54 F.3d 425 (7th Cir. 1995)
Bryant Woods Inn, Inc. v. Howard County, Md., 911 F. Supp. 918 (D. Md. 1996)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Amendment of defendant's administrative plan to permit award of project-based VASH vouchers based on prior competitive selection (LIHTC award) without requiring a separate RFP process; alternatively, honoring prior commitment of 33 project-based vouchers and applying for additional 35 vouchers on behalf of Freedom's Path
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the FHA reasonable accommodation framework and found that plaintiff failed to establish the 'necessary' element because there was no nexus between the disability status of prospective tenants and the requested accommodation. The accommodation (amending the administrative plan) would have benefited both disabled and non-disabled tenants equally, and non-disabled developers would have faced the same regulatory barriers. Therefore, plaintiff could not show that but for the accommodation they would be denied equal opportunity to enjoy housing of their choice.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court previously ruled (in the March 25, 2019 order) that defendant was entitled to summary judgment on plaintiff's claims of intentional discrimination. The court affirmed that ruling in this reconsideration opinion.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court previously ruled (in the March 25, 2019 order) that defendant was entitled to summary judgment on plaintiff's disparate impact claim. The court affirmed that ruling in this reconsideration opinion.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), 42 U.S.C. § 12132 - denial of reasonable accommodation
fha_claims.reasoning: The ADA Title II reasonable accommodation claim was analyzed under the same framework as the FHA claim and failed on the same basis: lack of nexus between the disability status of prospective tenants and the requested accommodation, and failure to establish necessity because non-disabled developers would face identical regulatory barriers.

case_name: UFM Realty Corporation v. Matthews
accommodation_description: No formal reasonable accommodation request is central to this case; Matthews invoked a CDC Declaration order to seek a stay of the eviction proceedings based on her alleged status as an individual at risk for COVID-19, and she had separately filed HUD administrative complaints alleging discriminatory housing practices by the property owner.
key_holding: The court recommended remanding the improperly removed state eviction case to Middletown Municipal Court for lack of federal subject matter jurisdiction, because the plaintiff's complaint relied exclusively on state law and a defendant's assertion of federal defenses or counterclaims—including FHA, HUD complaints, and the CDC order—is legally insufficient to confer removal jurisdiction.
brief_summary: UFM Realty Corporation filed a state court eviction action against pro se defendant Rashawnda Matthews for failure to comply with her month-to-month lease. Matthews removed the case to federal court, alleging the eviction constituted racial and civil-rights discrimination and retaliation for HUD complaints she had filed regarding discriminatory housing practices. The magistrate judge recommended dismissal for lack of subject matter jurisdiction and remand to state court, finding that the well-pleaded complaint rule bars removal based solely on a defendant's federal defenses or counterclaims when the plaintiff's own complaint invokes only state law.
key_cases_cited: Caterpillar Inc. v. Williams, 482 U.S. 386 (1987)
Caterpillar Inc. v. Lewis, 519 U.S. 61 (1987)
Arbaugh v. Y&H Corp., 546 U.S. 500 (2006)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Defendant alleged Fair Housing Act violations and retaliation in counterclaim; also alleged CDC order protection and civil rights violations related to eviction
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked subject matter jurisdiction because the original state court complaint relied exclusively on state law (eviction under lease agreement) and did not arise under federal law. Defendant's assertion of federal defenses and counterclaims, including Fair Housing Act claims, cannot support removal jurisdiction under the well-pleaded complaint rule. The case was remanded to state court.

case_name: Vanessa McQueen v. City of Cincinnati
accommodation_description: Not described in the case text; the specific nature of the alleged Fair Housing Act violation or any accommodation requested is not identified in the order.
key_holding: The court adopted the Magistrate Judge's Report and Recommendation and dismissed the pro se plaintiff's Fair Housing Act complaint with prejudice under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B) because plaintiff failed to include sufficient factual context from which the court could reasonably infer that any defendant discriminated against her.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Vanessa McQueen filed a Fair Housing Act complaint against the City of Cincinnati and other defendants, alleging unspecified FHA violations. The Magistrate Judge recommended dismissal with prejudice for failure to state a claim, finding the complaint lacked the factual context necessary to support any inference of discrimination. After a de novo review of plaintiff's timely objections and applying a liberal construction to her filings, the district court agreed with the Magistrate Judge and dismissed the action with prejudice, also denying plaintiff leave to appeal in forma pauperis.
key_cases_cited: United States v. Walters, 638 F.2d 947 (6th Cir. 1981)
Erickson v. Pardus, 551 U.S. 89 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not specified; plaintiff alleged Fair Housing Act violations but failed to provide factual context
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed under § 1915(e)(2)(B) for failure to state a claim because plaintiff failed to include factual context from which the court could reasonably infer that any named defendant discriminated against her in violation of the Fair Housing Act or otherwise violated her federal or constitutional rights. The complaint was deemed frivolous and clearly baseless.

source_file: 9911698_2021_Seattle House LLC v. City of Delaware, Ohio_ohsd
case_name: Seattle House, LLC v. City of Delaware, Ohio
accommodation_description: This is not a reasonable accommodation case; it concerns whether municipal water and sewage capacity fees that allegedly prevent affordable housing development constitute a disparate impact under the FHA.
key_holding: The developer plausibly alleged standing by claiming financial injury from allegedly discriminatory fees and stated a cognizable disparate impact claim by alleging the City's fee policy causes an affordable housing crisis disproportionately impacting racial minorities, surviving dismissal on the FHA claim while constitutional claims were dismissed.
brief_summary: Seattle House LLC, an apartment developer, sued the City of Delaware, Ohio alleging the City's water and sewage capacity fees create an affordable housing crisis that disproportionately impacts racial minorities in violation of the Fair Housing Act. On the City's motion for judgment on the pleadings, the court dismissed the Equal Protection and Substantive Due Process claims but allowed the FHA disparate impact claim to proceed, finding the developer adequately pleaded standing and sufficient facts showing the City's fee policy causes a disparate impact.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Tex. Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Cmtys. Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that Seattle House sufficiently pleaded a disparate impact claim under the FHA by alleging that the City's water and sewage capacity fee policy creates a barrier to affordable housing and disproportionately impacts racial minorities. The court rejected the City's argument that ICP imposes a heightened pleading requirement, holding that the prima facie causality standard applies at summary judgment, not at the pleading stage. At the pleading stage, plaintiff need only allege facts plausibly giving rise to an inference that the challenged policy causes disparate impact.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal Protection Clause violation (42 U.S.C. § 1983); Substantive Due Process violation (42 U.S.C. § 1983); Ohio state law claims (unjust enrichment, Ohio Constitution Article XVIII § 4, City code violation)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted motion to dismiss on Equal Protection Clause claim (Count II) because the City has a rational basis for treating residential and non-residential properties differently in fee calculations based on administrative efficiency considerations. Court granted motion to dismiss on Substantive Due Process claim (Count III) because Seattle House failed to allege violation of a fundamental right; a state-law right to fair and reasonable fees does not constitute a fundamental right under the U.S. Constitution.

case_name: Deborah Jetter, et al. v. City of Cincinnati
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; plaintiffs are African-American homeowners alleging the City's Property Tax Abatement Program causes racial segregation in violation of the FHA.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' intentional discrimination claims but allowed their disparate impact claims to proceed, finding plaintiffs adequately pleaded that the City's tax abatement program causes racially segregative effects; the court also denied class certification for failure to establish commonality and typicality.
brief_summary: African-American homeowners in Cincinnati sued the City of Cincinnati alleging its Residential Tax Abatement Program violates the Fair Housing Act by disproportionately directing tax benefits to Caucasian neighborhoods, causing racial segregation and economic harm to African-American communities. The court dismissed the intentional discrimination claims but allowed the disparate impact claims to proceed, and denied class certification finding the proposed class lacked commonality and typicality.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dept. of Hous. & Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Gladstone Realtors v. Bellwood, 441 U.S. 91 (1979)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs invoked the word 'intentional' but pleaded no non-conclusory facts suggesting race-based animus played any role in the development of the RTA policy. Under Iqbal/Twombly, conclusory allegations of intentional discrimination without factual support fail to state a plausible claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs adequately pleaded a disparate-impact claim by alleging facts showing the RTA policy, while facially available to all homeowners, has gone disproportionately to predominantly Caucasian neighborhoods, creating a plausible inference of robust causal connection between the policy and segregative harms. The court applied the plausibility standard at the pleading stage, not the prima facie evidentiary standard, and found Plaintiffs need not prove the RTA is the exclusive cause of segregation.

source_file: 9912452_2021_Price v. Country Brook Homeowners' Association, Inc._ohsd
case_name: Katherine Bebe Price, et al. v. Country Brook Homeowners' Association, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged national origin discrimination based on HOA enforcement of pet restrictions against their Vietnamese pot belly pig, framed as a cultural/traditional pet issue rather than a disability accommodation request.
key_holding: Plaintiffs failed to state plausible claims for intentional discrimination, disparate impact, or hostile environment harassment because they offered no factual allegations that defendants treated them differently from any other homeowner with a pot belly pig, and Mr. Price himself suggested the enforcement was motivated by retaliation for an unrelated neighbor dispute rather than national origin.
brief_summary: Richard and Katherine Price sued Country Brook Homeowners' Association after it sought to enforce its pet restrictions against their Vietnamese pot belly pig, alleging national origin discrimination under the Fair Housing Act. The court granted judgment on the pleadings for defendants, finding plaintiffs failed to allege sufficient facts to support claims of intentional discrimination, disparate impact, or hostile environment harassment.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Texas Dept. of Housing & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
HDC, LLC v. City of Ann Arbor, 675 F.3d 608 (6th Cir. 2012)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plead factual allegations of intentional discrimination based on race or national origin; the complaint contained only conclusory allegations that defendants interpreted the CCR pet restriction to exclude pot belly pigs, with no factual basis connecting enforcement to discriminatory animus.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to satisfy the 'robust causality requirement' for disparate impact; they alleged Mrs. Price is a Vietnamese immigrant and that pot belly pigs are culturally significant in Vietnam, but provided no factual allegations showing they were treated differently from other homeowners with non-permitted animals.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Hostile environment harassment based on national origin
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to plead facts sufficient to infer hostile environment harassment based on national origin; the allegations show only a legal dispute over a pet restriction with no factual connection to discriminatory animus, and plaintiff's own admission in state court suggested the dispute was motivated by retaliation for an unrelated neighbor dispute.

case_name: Katherine Bebe Price, et al. v. Scott G. Oxley, et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; plaintiffs allege defendants interfered with their FHA lawsuit by threatening sanctions if they did not dismiss related fair housing claims.
key_holding: The amended complaint failed to state an interference claim under § 3617 because plaintiffs failed to allege any facts showing they were discriminated against on the basis of a protected characteristic, and plaintiffs' conclusory allegations of coercion and intimidation were not supported by factual content allowing the court to infer discriminatory animus.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Katherine and Richard Price sued attorneys Scott G. Oxley and Gregory S. Page (and their law firms), alleging the attorneys violated the FHA by sending a letter threatening sanctions if plaintiffs did not dismiss their related FHA lawsuit. The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss, finding plaintiffs failed to allege facts showing discriminatory animus or that defendants engaged in conduct constituting unlawful interference with FHA rights.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Wells v. Rhodes, 928 F. Supp. 2d 920 (S.D. Ohio 2013)
HDC, LLC v. City of Ann Arbor, 675 F.3d 608 (6th Cir. 2012)
Givens v. Wenker, 2012 WL 1680099 (S.D. Ohio 2012)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to allege facts showing defendants exercised or enjoyed a right guaranteed by §§ 3603-3606 (no discrimination based on protected class alleged), failed to allege intentional conduct constituting coercion/intimidation/threat under § 3617, and failed to allege facts showing discriminatory animus. The allegation that defendants 'enlisted' Page to interfere amounts to a legal conclusion unsupported by factual content. Attorneys prosecuting or defending client interests in FHA-related litigation cannot be held liable under the FHA for the client's alleged violations.

case_name: United States v. Klosterman
accommodation_description: N/A - this case involves enforcement of a consent decree regarding sexual harassment of female tenants, not a reasonable accommodation request
key_holding: The court found clear and convincing evidence that defendant John Klosterman violated multiple provisions of the Consent Decree including making false affirmations about property holdings, personally interacting with tenants in violation of injunctive provisions, failing to complete required Fair Housing Act training, and failing to establish a required interest-bearing escrow account for monetary damages; the court recommended finding civil contempt and imposing prospective sanctions.
brief_summary: The United States and intervenor HOME sought to enforce a Consent Decree against landlord John Klosterman for violations of the Fair Housing Act's prohibition on sex discrimination through sexual harassment of female tenants, alleging defendant made false affirmations about property holdings, continued prohibited contact with tenants, failed to complete required FHA training, and failed to establish required escrow accounts for monetary damages. The Magistrate Judge recommended granting the motion to enforce and finding defendant in civil contempt, recommending prospective monetary sanctions, extended decree term, and additional injunctive relief to ensure compliance.
key_cases_cited: McGoldrick v. Bradstreet, 397 F.3d 1029 (6th Cir. 2005)
McGoldrick v. Bradstreet, 397 F.3d 1029 (6th Cir. 2005)
Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians v. Engler, 146 F.3d 367 (6th Cir. 1998)
United States v. Bayshore Assocs., Inc., 934 F.2d 1391 (6th Cir. 1991)
Gascho v. Global Fitness Holdings, LLC, 875 F.3d 795 (6th Cir. 2017)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Sexual harassment and discrimination against female tenants, including unwelcome sexual comments, advances, text messages, photographs, non-consensual touching, offers of housing benefits in exchange for sex, adverse housing actions (refusal to make repairs, eviction threats), preference for renting to single females, and unauthorized entry/monitoring of homes.
fha_claims.reasoning: The parties entered into a Consent Decree on October 1, 2020, resolving the United States' allegations of sex discrimination and sexual harassment under the Fair Housing Act. The Decree included injunctive relief prohibiting Defendant John Klosterman from property management activities and contact with tenants, and required monetary damages of $177,500.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: State criminal charges for Menacing by Stalking and violation of protective order; state civil litigation by City of Cincinnati for code enforcement violations and receivership proceedings.
fha_claims.reasoning: The Consent Decree resolved the federal FHA claims. Related state court proceedings (criminal charges, code enforcement, receivership) are referenced as context for the federal enforcement action but are not independently adjudicated in this opinion.

source_file: 9913261_2022_TD Investments LLC v. National City Bank_ohsd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: This case involves declaratory judgment claims regarding alleged loans and loan guaranties between PNC Bank and CBST. The plaintiff seeks declarations that certain loans are fraudulent and do not exist. This is a commercial/banking dispute with no housing, disability, or Fair Housing Act component.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court adopted the Magistrate Judge's recommendation to grant PNC's Motion to Dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6), finding that TD Investments failed to allege an injury in fact or standing under Article III. The court applied the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard and found the complaint's allegations insufficient to state a plausible claim for relief.

source_file: 9913564_2022_Freedom's Path at Dayton v. Dayton Metropolitan Housing Authority_ohsd
case_name: Dayton Veterans Residences Limited Partnership v. Dayton Metropolitan Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Request for project-based housing vouchers as a reasonable accommodation for homeless disabled veterans seeking housing at a VA Medical Campus development.
key_holding: The court denied DMHA's motion to withdraw its jury demand, finding that Freedom's Path is entitled to a jury trial because it seeks monetary damages under the FHA, which constitutes a legal remedy triggering Seventh Amendment rights.
brief_summary: Freedom's Path, a developer seeking to create housing for homeless veterans on a VA campus, sued DMHA for allegedly reneging on a commitment for project-based housing vouchers and denying reasonable accommodation requests for disabled veterans. The court denied DMHA's motion to withdraw its jury demand, holding that Freedom's Path has a Seventh Amendment right to a jury trial because it seeks monetary damages under the FHA, which constitutes a legal rather than equitable remedy.
key_cases_cited: Chauffeurs, Teamsters and Helpers, Local No. 391 v. Terry, 494 U.S. 558 (1990)
City of Monterey v. Del Monte Dunes at Monterey, Ltd., 526 U.S. 687 (1999)
Curtis v. Loether, 415 U.S. 189 (1974)
Tull v. United States, 481 U.S. 412 (1987)
LeBlanc-Sternberg v. Fletcher, 67 F.3d 412 (2d Cir. 1995)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Commitment of 33 housing vouchers (later 60 vouchers) for a housing project for homeless veterans with disabilities; plaintiff sought reasonable accommodation regarding the voucher commitment
fha_claims.reasoning: The court did not address the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim. The opinion addresses only the procedural question of whether plaintiff is entitled to a jury trial on its FHA claims, finding that plaintiff has a Seventh Amendment right to a jury trial on legal claims seeking monetary damages under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act, 42 U.S.C. § 12132
fha_claims.reasoning: The court did not address the merits of the ADA claim. The opinion addresses only the procedural question of whether plaintiff is entitled to a jury trial, finding that claims under the ADA seeking monetary damages also entitle plaintiff to a jury trial under the Seventh Amendment.

source_file: 9913567_2022_Freedom's Path at Dayton v. Dayton Metropolitan Housing Authority_ohsd
case_name: Freedom's Path at Dayton v. Dayton Metropolitan Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Request by housing developer for DMHA to provide project-based vouchers and modify its administrative plan to accommodate homeless veterans with disabilities
key_holding: The court granted DMHA's motion to limit damages, finding that Freedom's Path's $21 million damage claim was speculative and remote because the proposed project was abandoned, and the claimed tax credits, VA grants, and increased construction costs would not have been retained by Freedom's Path but spent on project costs.
brief_summary: Freedom's Path at Dayton sued DMHA, alleging the housing authority discriminatorily blocked funding for 60 units of project-based housing for homeless veterans with disabilities, violating the ADA and FHA. After partial summary judgment narrowed liability to a December 2015 reasonable accommodation request, the court granted DMHA's motion in limine to exclude $21 million in claimed damages as too speculative and remote, allowing only the developer's fee to potentially be recovered.
key_cases_cited: Curtis v. Loether, 415 U.S. 189 (1974)
Anderson Grp., LLC v. City of Saratoga Springs, 805 F.3d 34 (2d Cir. 2014)
Grantham and Mann, Inc. v. American Safety Prods., 831 F.2d 596 (6th Cir. 1987)
Silver Sage Partners v. City of Desert Hot Springs, 251 F.3d 814 (9th Cir. 2001)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request for DMHA to provide project-based housing vouchers and amend its administrative plan to accommodate homeless veterans with disabilities; specifically, a December 2015 request for reasonable accommodation and a September 2, 2016 request to amend the administrative plan
fha_claims.disposition: Motion in Limine to Limit Damages
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that the September 2, 2016 accommodation request was unreasonable as a matter of law because the time required to amend DMHA's administrative plan rendered it impossible, and therefore no reasonable jury could find that accommodation reasonable. The December 2015 request survived summary judgment as the sole remaining liability theory, but the court limited damages to direct consequences of proven discrimination, excluding speculative and remote damages.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), 42 U.S.C. § 12132
fha_claims.disposition: Motion in Limine to Limit Damages
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied ADA damages standards, which are narrower than FHA damages, and limited plaintiff's damages presentation to direct consequences of any proven discrimination. The court noted that damages available under the ADA are narrower than those under the FHA, and the FHA represents the outside limit of recoverable damages in this action.

source_file: 9913576_2022_Freedom's Path at Dayton v. Dayton Metropolitan Housing Authority_ohsd
case_name: Freedom's Path at Dayton v. Dayton Metropolitan Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Request that DMHA amend its Administrative Plan to allocate project-based housing vouchers and apply for VASH vouchers to support Freedom's Path's veterans housing project
key_holding: The court denied DMHA's motion to limit trial testimony to events before September 2, 2016, finding that the law of the case doctrine does not mandate such a temporal limitation and that the court should defer evidentiary rulings until trial context is available.
brief_summary: Freedom's Path at Dayton, a housing developer for homeless veterans, sued Dayton Metropolitan Housing Authority alleging it failed to provide reasonable accommodation under the FHA and ADA by refusing to amend its Administrative Plan to allocate housing vouchers and apply for VASH vouchers. The court denied DMHA's motion in limine to limit trial testimony to events before September 2, 2016, finding the law of the case doctrine does not require such a temporal cutoff and that evidentiary rulings should be deferred to the trial context.
key_cases_cited: Sperberg v. Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co., 519 F.2d 708 (6th Cir. 1975)
GMAC Mortg., LLC v. McKeever, 651 F. App'x 332 (6th Cir. 2016)
Arizona v. California, 460 U.S. 605 (1983)
Scott v. Churchill, 377 F.3d 565 (6th Cir. 2004)
United States v. Love, 254 F. App'x 511 (6th Cir. 2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request for DMHA to grant 33 project-based housing vouchers and apply for Veterans Affairs Supportive Housing (VASH) vouchers on behalf of Freedom's Path, requiring exception to DMHA's Administrative Plan which limited project-based voucher awards to RFP-initiated proposals
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied DMHA's motion in limine to exclude post-September 2, 2016 testimony and evidence, finding that the law of the case doctrine did not bar such evidence and that the relevance of post-request communications and the timing of DMHA's amendment to its Administrative Plan (April 2017) remained material to whether DMHA's delay in providing the accommodation constituted a denial. The court previously found that DMHA's failure to timely amend its plan had the same effect as an outright denial, making delay-as-denial analysis central to the claim.

source_file: 9913601_2022_Freedom's Path at Dayton v. Dayton Metropolitan Housing Authority_ohsd
case_name: Freedom's Path at Dayton v. Dayton Metropolitan Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Request that DMHA amend its Administrative Plan to allocate project-based vouchers to the Freedom's Path veteran housing project without competitive RFP process as a reasonable accommodation for disabled veterans.
key_holding: The court largely denied Plaintiff's motions in limine, allowing Defendant to present evidence on whether the proposed accommodation (amending the Administrative Plan to award project-based vouchers without competitive RFP) was reasonable, with the court noting a jury could find either way on this central dispute.
brief_summary: Freedom's Path at Dayton, a developer of supportive housing for disabled veterans, sued Dayton Metropolitan Housing Authority for denying its reasonable accommodation request to receive project-based vouchers without competitive bidding. The court issued pretrial rulings on evidentiary matters, largely denying Plaintiff's motions to exclude Defendant's evidence and arguments regarding whether the accommodation was necessary and reasonable, finding these were questions for the jury.
key_cases_cited: Dayton Veterans Residences Ltd. P'ship v. Dayton Metro. Hous. Auth., 2021 WL 5411220 (6th Cir. Nov. 19, 2021)
Overlook Mut. Homes, Inc. v. Spencer, 415 F. App'x 617 (6th Cir. 2011)
Sutton v. United Airlines, 527 U.S. 471 (1999)
MX Group, Inc. v. City of Covington, 293 F.3d 326 (6th Cir. 2002)
DiCarlo v. Potter, 358 F.3d 408 (6th Cir. 2004)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Amendment of DMHA's Administrative Plan to allow award of project-based VASH vouchers to Freedom's Path project without competitive request for proposals; alternatively, award of project-based vouchers to enable disabled veterans to live near VA campus
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied plaintiff's motion in limine to preclude defendant from arguing the accommodation was unreasonable because it would violate DMHA's administrative plan and federal law. The Sixth Circuit had previously held that a jury could find amending the plan was necessary to advance equality of opportunity for disabled veterans, and the court allowed the reasonableness question to proceed to trial as a central dispute.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Oral accommodation requests beginning December 15, 2015, regarding project-based VASH vouchers and amendment of Administrative Plan timeline
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied plaintiff's motion to preclude defendant from arguing the accommodation was unreasonable based on administrative plan violations. The court clarified that denial of summary judgment on this issue means it must be addressed at trial, and a jury may determine whether amending the plan was a reasonable accommodation.

case_name: Tasha Chapman v. Franklin County Sheriff
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: The court adopted in part the magistrate judge's report and dismissed claims against the correctional center and Doe defendants, but recommitted the case for further review of whether plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claims are plausibly alleged.
brief_summary: Tasha Chapman, a recently released inmate, sued the Franklin County Sheriff asserting multiple constitutional and statutory claims including two Fair Housing Act claims. The court adopted the magistrate judge's report dismissing claims against the correctional center and Doe defendants, but recommitted the case for specific review of whether the remaining claims—including the FHA claims—state a plausible cause of action under § 1915A screening.
key_cases_cited: Pleasant-Bey v. Shelby Cty., No. 18-6063, 2019 WL 11769343 (6th Cir. Nov. 7, 2019)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unspecified reasonable accommodation related to disability in jail/correctional facility setting
fha_claims.reasoning: The court remitted the case to the magistrate judge for specific consideration of whether Plaintiff plausibly alleged the Fair Housing Act claims under § 1915A screening, without conducting substantive merits analysis. The opinion does not indicate whether the FHA claims were ultimately dismissed or survived screening.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: First Amendment, Fourteenth Amendment, Eighth Amendment, Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA), state-law intentional infliction of emotional distress, Americans with Disabilities Act
fha_claims.reasoning: The court remitted non-FHA claims to the magistrate judge for § 1915A screening to determine whether Plaintiff stated a plausible claim or sought money damages from an immune defendant. No substantive merits analysis was conducted at this stage.

case_name: Dennis Howell, et al. v. City of Cincinnati
accommodation_description: This is a systemic challenge to the City of Cincinnati's Residential Tax Abatement program, not a reasonable accommodation request; plaintiffs allege the program has discriminatory effects on Black communities.
key_holding: The City's motion for reconsideration of the Court's Notation Order requiring the City Manager to submit a proposed nonbinding calendar for RTA program reform is denied because the order did not violate separation of powers—it merely requested a proposed timeline, not mandatory legislative action.
brief_summary: Black residents of Cincinnati sued the City of Cincinnati alleging that the Residential Tax Abatement program, which provides property tax benefits for home renovations, has deepened racial segregation and disproportionately benefits white neighborhoods in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The Court denied the City's motion to reconsider a Notation Order requiring the City Manager to submit a proposed timeline for presenting RTA reform legislation to City Council, finding no separation of powers violation because the order merely requested a nonbinding proposed schedule for legislative consideration.
key_cases_cited: Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co. v. Haeger, 137 S. Ct. 1178 (2017)
Al-Sadoon v. FISA Madison Financial Corp., 188 F. Supp. 2d 899 (M.D. Tenn. 2002)
Rodriguez v. Tennessee Laborers Health & Welfare Fund, 89 F. App'x 949 (6th Cir. 2004)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Modification of the City's Residential Tax Abatement (RTA) program to eliminate or reduce disparate impact on Black communities and non-white neighborhoods
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the City's motion for reconsideration of an interlocutory order requiring the City Manager to submit a proposed nonbinding calendar with milestones for presenting a draft ordinance to City Council. The court did not reach the merits of the underlying FHA disparate impact claim; this opinion addresses only the procedural motion to reconsider a settlement-facilitation order.

case_name: Chapman v. Franklin County Sheriff
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a pretrial detainee, requested to wear a hijab as part of her Muslim religious practice while incarcerated at the county correctional center.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claim because she failed to allege facts plausibly showing she qualifies for FHA protection in the jail context; her primary surviving claim is a First Amendment free exercise claim, not an FHA reasonable accommodation claim.
brief_summary: Tasha Chapman, a Muslim pretrial detainee with Bipolar Disorder II, sued the Franklin County Sheriff alleging violations including First Amendment free exercise, Fair Housing Act, ADA, and state law claims arising from being forced to remove her hijab at the county jail. The court dismissed most claims but permitted the First Amendment claim to proceed, finding plaintiff stated a plausible claim that jail policy prohibiting hijabs violated her sincerely held religious beliefs.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Ctr.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation for mental health care and treatment for Bipolar Disorder II while incarcerated; plaintiff alleges she was denied medical and mental health treatment for seven days of incarceration and was given a form to request medical attention but no pen to complete it.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the ADA Title II claim for failure to allege discrimination on the basis of disability rather than religion, and found that denial of medical treatment does not state a cognizable ADA claim where the underlying allegation is merely an Eighth Amendment deliberate indifference claim in statutory disguise.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: First Amendment free exercise of religion (hijab wearing); Equal Protection Clause (Fourteenth Amendment); Eighth Amendment/Due Process Clause (Fourteenth Amendment) conditions of confinement and denial of medical care; RLUIPA religious freedom; state law intentional infliction of emotional distress; ADA Title II disability discrimination
fha_claims.reasoning: The court allowed the First Amendment free exercise claim to proceed as plausibly alleging a policy or practice of denying Muslim inmates the right to wear hijabs, finding the complaint alleged facts showing sincerely held religious belief and responsibility of the Sheriff under Ohio law. However, the court dismissed the Equal Protection claim for failure to allege differential treatment of similarly situated inmates; the Eighth Amendment/Due Process claim for temporary exposure to unsanitary conditions and failure to allege personal involvement of the Sheriff in denial of medical care; the RLUIPA claim because no private cause of action for monetary damages exists; the intentional infliction of emotional distress claim because political subdivisions are immune from intentional tort liability under Ohio law; and the ADA Title II claim for failure to allege discrimination based on disability rather than religion.

case_name: Robert McComb v. Dominium Property Management, et al.
accommodation_description: The complaint references a request for reasonable accommodation regarding a trash dumpster, but the incoherent pleading prevents clear identification of the accommodation's nature.
key_holding: The magistrate judge recommended dismissal with prejudice because plaintiff's third complaint was so verbose, confused, and redundant it disguised the true substance of his claims, and despite multiple opportunities to amend and specific guidance from the court, plaintiff persisted in noncompliance with Rule 8 pleading standards.
brief_summary: Robert McComb, proceeding pro se, sued Dominium Property Management and individual defendants alleging Fair Housing Act, ADA, and other discrimination claims related to his housing at Voyageur Apartment. The magistrate judge recommended granting defendants' motion to dismiss with prejudice because plaintiff's third amended complaint was a 72-page, single-spaced, confusing document that failed to comply with Rule 8 despite multiple court orders and opportunities to amend, and the court never reached the merits of any accommodation or discrimination claim.
key_cases_cited: Kensu v. Corizon, Inc., 5 F.4th 646 (6th Cir. 2021)
Plymale v. Freeman, 1991 WL 54882 (6th Cir. 1991)
Robinson v. Overseas Military Sales Corp., 21 F.3d 502 (2d Cir. 1994)
Asbury v. Bisig, 70 F. App'x 247 (6th Cir. 2003)
Heyerman v. County of Calhoun, 680 F.3d 642 (6th Cir. 2012)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation for trash dumpster access
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 8 / Failure to Comply with Court Orders
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint was dismissed for failure to comply with Rule 8 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and prior court orders. The complaint was so verbose, confused, and redundant that its true substance was disguised, preventing the court from identifying the specific claims asserted. The plaintiff was afforded multiple opportunities to amend and was warned that noncompliance could result in dismissal.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged discrimination under the Americans with Disabilities Act and Fair Housing Act
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 8 / Failure to Comply with Court Orders
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint was dismissed for failure to comply with Rule 8 and prior court orders. The court could not discern the specific factual allegations supporting discrimination claims due to the complaint's prolix and confusing presentation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (constitutional rights), 18 U.S.C. § 241 and § 242 (conspiracy and criminal interference), Title VI of Civil Rights Act, Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, 5th and 14th Amendment claims
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 8 / Failure to Comply with Court Orders
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint was dismissed for failure to comply with Rule 8 and prior court orders. Additionally, the court noted that 18 U.S.C. § 241 and § 242 are criminal statutes that do not provide a private cause of action, and the § 1983 claims lacked sufficiently specific factual allegations and improperly referenced generic 'Defendants and their Agents' without specifying which defendants were at fault.

source_file: 9914456_2022_Freedom's Path at Dayton v. Dayton Metropolitan Housing Authority_ohsd
case_name: Freedom's Path at Dayton v. Dayton Metropolitan Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Developer requested that Dayton Metropolitan Housing Authority amend its administrative plan to award project-based vouchers to support a housing development for disabled homeless veterans.
key_holding: The jury's verdict for the defendant was supported by sufficient evidence, and the district court did not abuse its discretion in its rulings on the motions in limine and jury instructions regarding the reasonable accommodation claim.
brief_summary: Dayton Veterans Residences Limited Partnership, a housing developer, sued Dayton Metropolitan Housing Authority alleging the housing authority's refusal to award project-based vouchers to support a veterans housing project constituted a failure to accommodate disabled veterans under the Fair Housing Act. Following a jury verdict for the defendant, the court denied the plaintiff's motion for a new trial, finding the verdict was supported by the evidence and the challenged jury instructions and evidentiary rulings did not warrant disturbing the judgment.
key_cases_cited: Anderson v. City of Blue Ash, 798 F.3d 338 (6th Cir. 2015)
Howard v. City of Beavercreek, 276 F.3d 802 (6th Cir. 2002)
Overlook Mutual Homes v. Spencer, 666 F. Supp. 2d 850 (S.D. Ohio 2009)
Schaw v. Habitat for Humanity of Citrus County, Inc., 938 F.3d 1259 (11th Cir. 2019)
Hollis v. Chestnut Bend Homeowners Ass'n, 760 F.3d 531 (6th Cir. 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Allocation of project-based vouchers (VASH vouchers) based on previous competition rather than requiring a Request for Proposals (RFP) process; amendment of Defendant's administrative plan to allow this alternative allocation method
fha_claims.reasoning: The jury, after full trial on the merits, rendered a verdict in favor of Defendant. The court applied the four-element reasonable accommodation framework (disability, request, necessity, refusal) and the jury found that Plaintiff failed to prove the accommodation was necessary or that Defendant knew or should have known the prospective tenants were disabled. The court rejected Plaintiff's argument that VASH vouchers are restricted to disabled veterans, finding Plaintiff's own witness testified they are not so restricted.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title I and Title III claims; § 504 Rehabilitation Act claims; state law claims (if any)
fha_claims.reasoning: The opinion references ADA and § 504 claims in the context of Plaintiff's standing argument and the court's discussion of whether Plaintiff had standing as an entity serving disabled individuals. The jury verdict was rendered in favor of Defendant on all claims, including non-FHA statutory claims.

source_file: 9914459_2022_Freedom's Path at Dayton v. Dayton Metropolitan Housing Authority_ohsd
case_name: Dayton Veterans Residences Limited Partnership, d/b/a Freedom's Path at Dayton v. Dayton Metropolitan Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Freedom's Path requested that DMHA provide 33 project-based housing vouchers (later revised to 60) as a reasonable accommodation to allow disabled homeless veterans to obtain housing in the Dayton community on equal footing with non-disabled persons, in connection with a housing development on the VA Medical Campus.
key_holding: The court denied DMHA's motion for $250,000 in attorney's fees because Freedom's Path's FHA and ADA claims were not frivolous, as demonstrated by the Sixth Circuit's reversal allowing the reasonable accommodation theory to proceed to trial.
brief_summary: Freedom's Path, a developer of affordable housing for disabled homeless veterans on the Dayton VA Medical Campus, sued DMHA under the FHA and ADA, alleging DMHA reneged on a commitment of 33 project-based housing vouchers and denied reasonable accommodation requests. After the Sixth Circuit reversed dismissal of the reasonable accommodation claim, a six-day jury trial resulted in a verdict for DMHA. This opinion resolves DMHA's post-trial motion for attorney's fees, denying it on the grounds that Freedom's Path's claims were not frivolous, its settlement demand was not unreasonable, and its alleged improper motivations were unproven.
key_cases_cited: Christiansburg Garment Co. v. EEOC, 434 U.S. 412 (1978)
E.E.O.C. v. Peoplemark, Inc., 732 F.3d 584 (6th Cir. 2013)
Dayton Veterans Residences Ltd. P'Ship v. Dayton Metro. Hous. Auth., 2021 U.S. App. LEXIS 34511 (6th Cir. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Commitment of 33 housing vouchers (later 60 vouchers) for affordable housing project for homeless veterans with disabilities on the VAMC campus in Dayton, Ohio
fha_claims.reasoning: After the Sixth Circuit reversed the district court's summary judgment dismissal and held that a reasonable jury could find DMHA should have provided the accommodation, the case proceeded to a six-day jury trial. The jury returned a verdict for DMHA on June 21, 2022, finding that DMHA was not required to provide the requested voucher commitment as a reasonable accommodation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Intentional discrimination based on disability status of veterans
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court dismissed Freedom's Path's intentional discrimination theory at the summary judgment phase prior to trial, finding insufficient evidence to establish a prima facie case of intentional discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Facially neutral policy regarding housing voucher allocation disproportionately burdening disabled veterans
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court dismissed Freedom's Path's disparate impact theory at the summary judgment phase prior to trial, finding the theory insufficient to proceed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act claim
fha_claims.reasoning: The amended complaint alleged one claim under the Americans with Disabilities Act alongside the Fair Housing Act claim. The case proceeded to trial on the ADA claim as well, and the jury returned a verdict for DMHA on June 21, 2022.

source_file: 9914849_2022_A. R. v. Wyndham Hotels and Resorts, Inc._ohsd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Civil liability under the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act (TVPRA), 18 U.S.C. § 1595(a), for benefiting financially from sex trafficking venture; direct liability, vicarious liability, and joint employer liability theories
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss, finding plaintiff sufficiently pleaded all three elements of the TVPRA beneficiary theory under Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard: (1) knowing financial benefit from room rentals; (2) constructive knowledge of trafficking based on red flags and franchisor's notice of prevalence of trafficking; and (3) participation in commercial venture through franchise relationship, control of operations, and profit-sharing. Court also found sufficient allegations of agency, vicarious liability, and joint employer status to survive MTD.

case_name: Alicia A. Epps v. Carl Linder, III, et al.
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation was requested; plaintiff's claims concerned the alleged failure by city officials and FC Cincinnati to replace public housing that was demolished in Cincinnati's West End neighborhood to construct a Major League Soccer stadium, framed as a pattern and practice of discrimination denying low-income families the benefits of federal housing programs.
key_holding: The court recommends dismissal of plaintiff's second Fair Housing Act complaint as duplicative and malicious under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(i), and separately dismisses all claims against the United States on sovereign immunity grounds.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Alicia Epps filed her second lawsuit in the Southern District of Ohio challenging the demolition of public housing in Cincinnati's West End neighborhood to construct a professional soccer stadium for FC Cincinnati, again alleging Fair Housing Act and constitutional violations based on defendants' alleged failure to replace the demolished public housing. The court conducted a sua sponte screening under the in forma pauperis statute and found the complaint essentially duplicative of plaintiff's previously dismissed 2019 action involving the same facts, parties, and claims. The court recommended dismissal as frivolous or malicious, and additionally recommended dismissal of claims against the newly added defendant, the United States of America, because plaintiff failed to identify any statutory waiver of sovereign immunity.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Neitzke v. Williams, 490 U.S. 319 (1989)
Denton v. Hernandez, 504 U.S. 25 (1992)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges violations of Fair Housing Act and United States Constitution related to failure to replace public housing demolished for stadium construction; also names United States of America as defendant.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed complaint as frivolous and malicious under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(i) because it is duplicative of plaintiff's previously litigated claims against the same defendants arising from the same factual allegations regarding demolition of public housing for stadium construction. The complaint merely realleges claims already dismissed in the prior action without significant substantive differences.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Civil liability under the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act (TVPRA), 18 U.S.C. § 1595(a), for beneficiary liability in a sex trafficking venture; also vicarious liability under agency and joint employer theories.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied the motion to dismiss, finding that plaintiff sufficiently pleaded direct civil liability under the TVPRA beneficiary theory by alleging: (1) knowing financial benefit from room rentals; (2) constructive knowledge of trafficking through general awareness, failure to train staff, and red flags; and (3) participation in a commercial venture with traffickers. The court also found sufficient allegations of vicarious liability under a joint employer theory based on defendant's control over employment policies, training standards, and hotel operations.

case_name: Ronald D. Leonard v. Amy Montgomery
accommodation_description: No accommodation request was made; plaintiff brought First Amendment retaliation and other claims unrelated to disability accommodation.
key_holding: The Magistrate Judge recommends dismissal because Younger abstention applies to ongoing state eviction proceedings, and even if the court could hear the case, plaintiff failed to state a valid § 3604 claim since he made no allegations of housing discrimination based on a protected class.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Ronald Leonard, a tenant of the Hocking Metropolitan Housing Authority, brought suit against Office Manager Amy Montgomery alleging First Amendment retaliation and claims under 42 U.S.C. § 3604 and state law after receiving a Notice to Leave the Premises following his refusal to permit a unit inspection and his photographing of staff. The Magistrate Judge recommends dismissal under Younger abstention doctrine since state eviction proceedings are ongoing, and alternatively because plaintiff failed to state a viable claim under § 3604 as he made no allegations of discrimination based on a protected class.
key_cases_cited: Younger v. Harris, 401 U.S. 37 (1971)
Pennzoil Co. v. Texaco, Inc., 481 U.S. 1 (1987)
Holmes v. Lakefront at Westchester, LLC, 2022 U.S. App. LEXIS 17060 (6th Cir. 2022)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (First Amendment retaliation); 42 U.S.C. § 3604 (housing discrimination); state law claims (breach of lease, slander, false light/invasion of privacy)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court recommended dismissal under § 1915(e)(2) as frivolous and failing to state a claim. The § 1983 retaliation claim failed because plaintiff's own allegations showed the eviction was based on refusal of entry and disrespectful conduct, not protected speech. The § 3604 claim failed because plaintiff alleged no discrimination based on protected classes. State law claims were insufficiently pleaded and supplemental jurisdiction was declined.

case_name: Jeanette Brown v. Dominion Management Services LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges housing discrimination based on race, age, and disability when she was repeatedly turned away from a senior housing complex and removed from an application list.
key_holding: Plaintiff's complaint failed to state a plausible Fair Housing Act claim because it contained only vague and conclusory allegations of discrimination without sufficient factual detail from which the Court could infer that Defendants acted with discriminatory intent.
brief_summary: Jeanette Brown, a Black woman over age 55 with a disability, filed a pro se complaint alleging that Dominion Management Services LLC and a property manager discriminated against her by repeatedly denying her housing application at a senior apartment complex. The Magistrate Judge recommended dismissal because the complaint contained only vague and conclusory allegations without sufficient factual detail to state a plausible discrimination claim under the Fair Housing Act.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
HDC, LLC v. City of Ann Arbor, 675 F.3d 608 (6th Cir. 2012)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's complaint contains only vague, conclusory allegations of discrimination based on race, age, and disability without sufficient factual detail to state a plausible claim. The allegations lack specificity regarding dates, actions, and causal connection to any discriminatory intent, failing to meet the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard.

Plaintiff's allegations lack sufficient factual content to state any plausible claim under 42 U.S.C. § 1982 or § 1983. The complaint contains no factual allegations against Dominion Management Services LLC and only conclusory allegations against the individual defendant without supporting factual detail.

case_name: Dawn Chappel v. Adams County Children's Services
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged a conspiracy to interfere with her housing rights under § 3617 of the Fair Housing Act in connection with child removal proceedings and an eviction.
key_holding: The proposed Fair Housing Act claim would not survive a Rule 12(b)(6) motion because plaintiff failed to allege any discriminatory animus, and her conspiracy allegations were too vague and conclusory to state a claim.
brief_summary: Dawn Chappel, a pro se plaintiff and public housing resident in Winchester, Ohio, filed a motion for leave to amend her civil rights complaint against Adams County Children's Services and several individual defendants to add claims including a Fair Housing Act interference claim under § 3617. The court recommended denying the motion to amend because the proposed FHA claim was futile—it failed to allege discriminatory animus—and because plaintiff's constitutional claims (Fourth Amendment, Fourteenth Amendment due process, First Amendment retaliation, and § 1985 conspiracy) also failed to state viable claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Wells v. Rhodes, 928 F. Supp. 2d 920 (S.D. Ohio 2013)
Hood v. Midwest Sav. Bank, 95 F. App'x 768 (6th Cir. 2004)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged a conspiracy to interfere with her housing rights under 42 U.S.C. § 3617, claiming defendants Moore, Meyer, Anderson, and Edgington interfered with her exercise of FHA-protected rights.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege discriminatory animus required to state an FHA § 3617 interference claim. The complaint contained only vague and conclusory allegations that defendants 'tried to interfere' with housing rights without factual specificity or evidence of discriminatory intent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1985(3) civil rights conspiracy claim; Fourth Amendment unlawful search claim; Fourteenth Amendment substantive and procedural due process claims; First Amendment retaliation claim.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's § 1985(3) conspiracy claim failed because it lacked factual specificity regarding the alleged agreement and contained no allegation of racial or class-based discriminatory animus. Substantive due process claim failed because caseworkers have no independent ability to deprive parental rights—that authority rests with the juvenile court. Procedural due process claim failed because caseworkers are shielded by quasi-prosecutorial immunity when acting as legal advocates in custody proceedings, and voluntary consent to a safety plan requires no hearing. Fourth Amendment search claim failed because the search was pursuant to a court order. First Amendment retaliation claim failed because the removal order was equivalent to a judicially authorized warrant supported by probable cause, which defeats retaliation claims as a matter of law.

case_name: Alicia A. Epps v. Carl Linder, III, et al.
