fha_claims.reasoning: Section 1983 claims against HUD failed because federal agencies are not 'persons' under § 1983; claims against Borough of Pottstown and Housing Authority failed for lack of alleged municipal policy or custom; claims against private defendants (McCright, Hussein, H&H Estates) failed for lack of state action; state law claims dismissed for lack of supplemental jurisdiction and failure to establish complete diversity under 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a).

source_file: 9932182_2020_HORIZON HOUSE, INC. v. EAST NORRITON TOWNSHIP_paed
case_name: Horizon House, Inc. v. East Norriton Township
accommodation_description: Request that defendant waive the conditions for obtaining a Special Exception for a Group Home (fire sprinkler system, fire alarm, parking, staffing, and disability disclosure requirements) so that plaintiff can establish a Community Home for up to three intellectually and developmentally disabled individuals
key_holding: The reasonable accommodation claim was dismissed because plaintiff alleged only that the requested waiver of zoning conditions would cause additional costs and delays, but failed to plausibly allege that the accommodation was essential or required to make the Community Home financially viable rather than merely preferable.
brief_summary: Horizon House, Inc., a non-profit operator of Community Homes for individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities, sued East Norriton Township after being denied a Use and Occupancy permit and required to obtain a special exception as a "Group Home" subject to additional conditions including sprinkler systems and staffing requirements. The court granted defendant's motion to dismiss the reasonable accommodation claim because plaintiff failed to plausibly allege the requested waiver of conditions was essential rather than merely causing additional costs and delays, while denying dismissal of the disparate treatment and disparate impact claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Larkin v. State of Mich. Dep't of Soc. Servs., 89 F.3d 285 (6th Cir. 1996)
Bangerter v. Orem City Corp., 46 F.3d 1491 (10th Cir. 1995)
Sharpvisions, Inc. v. Borough of Plum, 475 F. Supp. 2d 514 (W.D. Pa. 2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff plausibly alleged that the Zoning Ordinance's definition of 'Group Homes' singles out for regulation facilities 'specifically designed to create a residential setting for the mentally and physically handicapped,' making the regulation facially discriminatory under the FHAA. The court held that at the pleading stage, plaintiff need only allege that a protected characteristic played a role in defendant's decision, not apply the McDonnell Douglas framework.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff plausibly alleged that the Zoning Ordinance, as applied, has a disparate impact on individuals with disabilities because unrelated disabled residents are more likely to reside together and require care, allowing the municipality to classify nearly every living arrangement for disabled individuals as a 'Group Home' subject to additional conditions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver of conditions required for Group Home special exception (fire sprinkler system, fire alarm system, four off-street parking spaces, staff person on-site at all times, disclosure of resident disabilities)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege the 'necessity' element under § 3604(f)(3)(B). Plaintiff alleged only that the requested waiver would avoid 'additional costs and delays' of approximately $40,000, but courts require that an accommodation be 'essential' to make the proposed use 'financially viable or medically effective,' not merely preferable. The dismissal was without prejudice to amendment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), 42 U.S.C. § 12101 et seq.; Rehabilitation Act (RA), 29 U.S.C. § 701 et seq.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the same legal analysis to ADA and RA claims as to FHAA claims and did not separately analyze or dismiss the non-FHA statutory claims. The disparate treatment and disparate impact claims under ADA and RA survive the motion to dismiss on the same basis as the FHAA claims; the reasonable accommodation claim under ADA is dismissed on the same basis as the FHAA claim.

source_file: 9932222_2020_GLYNN v. ELLSWORTH CONGREGATION OF LEHOVAH'S WITNESSES_paed
case_name: Glynn v. Ellsworth Congregation of Jehovah's Witnesses
accommodation_description: The incomprehensible complaint contains no discernible accommodation request, consisting primarily of biblical scripture and demands that defendants 'do according to all that the Levitical Priest will instruct.'
key_holding: The complaint was dismissed without prejudice for failure to state a claim because it provided no factual allegations whatsoever—only biblical verses and incomprehensible demands—failing to put defendants on notice or establish any basis for federal jurisdiction.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Jermaine Glynn filed an in forma pauperis complaint against the Ellsworth Congregation of Jehovah's Witnesses alleging housing discrimination under 42 U.S.C. § 3604, but the complaint contained only biblical scripture and incomprehensible demands without any factual allegations. The E.D. Pa. court dismissed the complaint without prejudice for failure to state a claim under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) and Rule 8, granting Glynn leave to file an amended complaint.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Tourscher v. McCullough, 184 F.3d 236 (3d Cir. 1999)
Grayson v. Mayview State Hosp., 293 F.3d 103 (3d Cir. 2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: No specific accommodation identified; complaint references 42 U.S.C. § 3604 but provides no factual allegations regarding housing discrimination or any requested accommodation.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the complaint as frivolous under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) because it failed to provide any factual allegations, failed to comply with Rule 8's pleading requirements, and was so confused and unintelligible that its true substance could not be discerned. The complaint cited § 3604 but contained no facts establishing jurisdiction, putting defendants on notice, or describing any conduct related to housing discrimination.

case_name: Catherine Coyne v. Holy Family Apartments, Allentown Archdiocese, Randy Wadsworth, Karen Ohm, Sarosky Heating & Air Conditioning, and HUD
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested transfer to a first-floor accessible unit after being reassigned to a second-floor senior unit following an assault and subsequent injury (broken foot, rotator cuff injury, PTSD).
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHAA claims because she failed to plead sufficient facts showing that a first-floor unit was necessary to afford her equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling, as required by 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(B), and because she could not establish a nexus between her alleged disabilities and her accommodation requests.
brief_summary: Catherine Coyne, a disabled resident of Holy Family Apartments in Bethlehem, PA, sued the property management company and individual defendants alleging Fair Housing Amendments Act violations after they failed to move her to a first-floor accessible unit and make repairs to her unit. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts demonstrating that her requested accommodations were necessary to afford her equal housing opportunity under § 3604(f)(3)(B).
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Cmty. Servs., Inc. v. Wind Gap Mun. Auth., 421 F.3d 170 (3d Cir. 2005)
Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)
Vorchheimer v. Phila. Hous. Auth., 903 F.3d 100 (3d Cir. 2018)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Age discrimination claim based on refusal to move plaintiff to first-floor unit until age 62
fha_claims.reasoning: Age is not a protected class under the FHAA and therefore age discrimination claims are not actionable under the statute.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Replacement of polished floors in second-floor unit to prevent slipping and falling
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead facts showing that her specific disabilities (cancer and Von Willebrand Disease) required replacement of polished floors to afford equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling; the complaint contained only conclusory statements without factual nexus between disability and accommodation necessity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Transfer to first-floor accessible unit when available, rather than remaining in second-floor senior unit
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead facts demonstrating how her disabilities (cancer and Von Willebrand Disease) made it difficult to climb stairs or required first-floor living; she provided only conclusory statements that she 'must' live on the first floor without explaining the disability-related necessity under the FHAA standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Repair or replacement of furnace producing excessive carbon monoxide
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found no nexus between plaintiff's alleged disabilities and the request for furnace repair; carbon monoxide exposure is a risk to all people regardless of disability status, and plaintiff failed to allege how her specific disabilities made furnace repair necessary for equal housing opportunity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible parking spot in front of building rather than regular spot at end of building
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead facts showing she required a parking spot near her building because of a specific handicap; she also failed to allege she possessed a handicap placard entitling her to accessible parking.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Repair or modification of doorbell to accommodate hearing impairment
fha_claims.reasoning: Residential facilities are not covered by Title III of the ADA; the doorbell claim was analyzed under ADA rather than FHAA and dismissed as legally frivolous because apartments are not public accommodations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III discrimination claims (parking and doorbell); negligence claims against Holy Family Apartments, Karen Ohm, Randy Wadsworth, and Sarosky Heating & Air Conditioning; defamation claims; civil rights claims under unspecified Civil Rights Act
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA parking claim dismissed for failure to establish parking lot is covered by Title III and failure to allege facts showing disability-related necessity; ADA doorbell claim dismissed because residential facilities are not covered by ADA Title III; negligence claims dismissed for failure to plead duty, breach, proximate cause, and damages; defamation claim dismissed for failure to identify which defendants are responsible and failure to plead elements of defamation; civil rights claims dismissed for failure to identify which Civil Rights Act and failure to allege facts supporting any recognized civil rights theory.

source_file: 9932569_2020_WOMACK v. HOUSING AUTHORITY OF CHESTER COUNTY_paed
case_name: Womack v. Housing Authority of Chester County
accommodation_description: Requests for voucher term extensions, increased payment standards, and exception rents under HUD regulations as reasonable accommodations for family members' disabilities
key_holding: The court denied dismissal of plaintiffs' FHA reasonable accommodation claim because plaintiffs plausibly alleged HACC denied requests for voucher extensions, payment standard increases, and exception rents under HUD regulations as disability accommodations, and whether these denials were reasonable cannot be determined at the pleadings stage.
brief_summary: Mellissa Womack and her two disabled children sued the Housing Authority of Chester County under the Fair Housing Act, alleging HACC failed to make reasonable accommodations by denying requests for voucher term extensions, increased payment standards, and exception rents under HUD regulations. The court denied HACC's motion to dismiss the FHA reasonable accommodation claim, finding plaintiffs plausibly alleged HACC denied disability-related accommodation requests.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Vorchheimer v. Philadelphian Owners Ass'n, 903 F.3d 100 (3d Cir. 2018)
Cmty. Servs., Inc. v. Wind Gap Mun. Auth., 421 F.3d 170 (3d Cir. 2005)
Growth Horizons, Inc. v. Delaware County, 983 F.2d 1277 (3d Cir. 1993)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Installation of special sanitizing washer and dryer, second refrigerator, grab bars in shower, and second handrail on stairs to accommodate family members' disabilities (emotional and developmental disorders, hypersensitivity to chemicals, asthma, allergies, and anxiety)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege that HACC itself refused the modifications; rather, the requests were made to the townhouse community (TC), not HACC. The FHA requires a refusal by the defendant, and HACC cannot be held liable for enforcing the FHA against third parties absent a statutory duty to do so. Additionally, § 3604(f)(3)(B) accommodations are limited to 'rules, policies, practices, or services,' not serious physical changes to premises.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exception to rent payment standard under 24 C.F.R. § 982.503(b)(1)(v) to accommodate family members' disabilities
fha_claims.reasoning: Whether denying the request for an exception payment standard amounted to a denial of reasonable accommodation is a fact-based inquiry unfit for resolution at the pleadings stage. The complaint plausibly alleges that HACC denied a request for an exception that may have been necessary as a reasonable accommodation, sufficient to survive motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Extension of Section 8 voucher term beyond the initial and two granted extensions, as necessary to accommodate family members' disabilities and provide reasonable time to locate accessible housing
fha_claims.reasoning: Under 24 C.F.R. § 982.303(b)(2), a PHA must extend the voucher term up to the term reasonably required as a reasonable accommodation for a person with disabilities. Although HACC granted two extensions, whether an additional extension was reasonably required is a fact-based inquiry unsuitable for resolution at the pleadings stage. The complaint plausibly alleges that further extension may have been necessary.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (procedural due process); Pennsylvania Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Law (UTPCPL)
fha_claims.reasoning: § 1983 claim for procedural due process survives motion to dismiss as to allegations that HACC failed to schedule a hearing in expeditious manner and failed to provide access to file, but fails to the extent it relies on alleged failures to accommodate disabilities (which relate to HUD regulations not privately enforceable under § 1983) and allegations regarding use of withheld funds (no underlying federal constitutional right identified). UTPCPL claim dismissed for failure to allege a deceptive act or intentional misleading falsehood with justifiable reliance; boilerplate allegations insufficient.

case_name: Davis v. Rubin
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request; complaint challenges eviction and alleged harassment based on disability.
key_holding: The court dismissed Davis's FHA claims for failure to state a plausible claim, finding her allegations of disability discrimination, harassment, and retaliation were conclusory and failed to allege sufficient factual matter from which discriminatory motive or causal connection could be inferred.
brief_summary: Krystal Davis, a Black woman with a chronic illness, sued her landlords Daniel Rubin and Shannon McGroarty alleging Fair Housing Act violations including disability discrimination, harassment, and retaliation following her eviction from a Section 8 property. The court dismissed her complaint without prejudice for failure to state plausible claims, finding her allegations were conclusory and failed to adequately allege that disability was a motivating factor in her eviction or that retaliation was causally connected to her protected activity of filing a HUD complaint.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Revock v. Cowpet Bay W. Condo. Ass'n, 853 F.3d 96 (3d Cir. 2017)
Cmty. Servs., Inc. v. Wind Gap Mun. Auth., 421 F.3d 170 (3d Cir. 2005)
White v. Barbe, 767 F. App'x 332 (3d Cir. 2019)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient factual matter to support a plausible disparate treatment claim under § 3604(f)(2)(A). Although plaintiff alleged eviction based on disability and that defendants mocked her disability, she did not describe the specific disability, the mocking conduct, or facts from which one could infer disability was a motivating factor in the eviction decision. Vague allegations without factual elaboration are insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged harassment by defendants and neighbors
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's § 3617 interference claim based on harassment failed to state a plausible claim because she did not describe the alleged harassment with particularity or link it to her exercise or enjoyment of FHA rights. Conclusory allegations of harassment without factual elaboration are insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation for filing fair housing complaint with HUD
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's § 3617 retaliation claim failed to state a plausible claim because she did not establish that defendants were aware of her HUD complaint before initiating eviction, did not describe the underlying harassment with particularity, and did not sufficiently link the adverse action (eviction) to protected activity and retaliatory motive. The temporal proximity alone was insufficient to plausibly allege retaliation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 due process claim; Supremacy Clause claim based on CDC eviction moratorium; no FHA claim alleged
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's claims are barred by the Anti-Injunction Act, 28 U.S.C. § 2283, which prohibits federal courts from enjoining state court proceedings except in narrow circumstances. None of the statutory exceptions apply to plaintiff's request to stay an eviction hearing in state court. The court lacks jurisdiction to grant the requested relief.

case_name: Thermuthis Lee v. HUD, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, proceeding pro se, generally alleges discrimination and retaliation related to her medical conditions (hypertension, heart issues, pending organ transplant) due to HUD's failure to intervene with the Philadelphia Housing Authority regarding her neighbors.
key_holding: The court dismissed Lee's FHA claim because she failed to allege an unlawful discriminatory housing practice by HUD or its employees as a result of her disability; her generalized, conclusory allegations of discrimination and retaliation did not state a plausible FHA claim.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Thermuthis Lee sued HUD and three HUD employees alleging they failed to intervene with the Philadelphia Housing Authority regarding her neighbors' alleged harassment and the PHA's failure to evict them, causing aggravation of her health conditions. The court granted leave to proceed in forma pauperis but dismissed the complaint with prejudice for failure to state a plausible Fair Housing Act claim, concluding that Lee's conclusory allegations of disability-based discrimination and retaliation did not plead an unlawful discriminatory housing practice.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Revock v. Cowpet Bay W. Condo. Ass'n, 853 F.3d 96 (3d Cir. 2017)
Sharpvisions, Inc. v. Borough of Plum, 475 F. Supp. 2d 514 (W.D. Pa. 2007)
Lee v. Petrolichio, 697 F. App'x 112 (3d Cir. 2017)
Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents of Federal Bureau of Narcotics, 403 U.S. 388 (1971)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's conclusory allegations of discrimination or retaliation related to disability fail to state a plausible claim under FHA § 3604(f) because the complaint focuses on HUD's alleged failure to intervene with the PHA and negligent investigation, not on unlawful discriminatory housing practices by HUD based on disability. The complaint alleges only that HUD's inaction aggravated plaintiff's existing medical conditions, which does not constitute a basis for discrimination or retaliation under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 due process claim; Bivens claim for constitutional violation by federal officers
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's § 1983 claims against HUD fail because HUD is a federal agency and not a 'person' under § 1983, and federal agencies are exempt from § 1983 liability as they act pursuant to federal law. Any potential Bivens claim is barred because the Supreme Court has consistently refused to extend Bivens to new contexts, and plaintiff has not plausibly alleged a due process violation.

case_name: Alexy Dejesus v. Vicky; Arbor Village & Old Forge Apartments
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested to use his Section 8 housing voucher to rent a one-bedroom apartment at defendants' property.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claim because private landlords are not required to participate in the Section 8 voucher program, and discrimination based on voucher status alone does not state a cognizable FHA claim.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Alexy Dejesus sued private landlords Vicky and Arbor Village & Old Forge Apartments, alleging Fair Housing Act discrimination after they refused to rent him a one-bedroom apartment because they do not accept Section 8 housing vouchers. The court dismissed the complaint, holding that source-of-income discrimination based on Section 8 voucher status is not prohibited under the FHA since participation in the voucher program is voluntary for private landlords.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Inclusive Communities Project, Inc. v. Lincoln Prop. Co.
Graoch Assocs. #33, L.P. v. Louisville/Jefferson Cnty. Metro Human Relations Comm'n

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Acceptance of Section 8 housing voucher
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege discrimination based on a statutorily protected class under the FHA. Discrimination based solely on status as a Section 8 voucher holder does not state a claim under the FHA, which prohibits discrimination only on the basis of race, color, religion, sex, familial status, national origin, or disability. Landlord participation in the Section 8 voucher program is voluntary.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 — deprivation of constitutional rights
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege that defendants were acting under color of state law, which is a threshold requirement for § 1983 liability. Private landlords and their employees are not state actors merely by virtue of participating in or refusing to participate in the Section 8 housing program.

case_name: Magistrate Mahdi Sufi El v. People's Emergency Center, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff previously alleged in El I that PEC denied him use of a community room and discriminated against him by treating him differently from other tenants.
key_holding: Plaintiff's retaliation claims were dismissed because claims related to the 4050 Haverford eviction were barred by the settlement agreement in El I, and Plaintiff failed to adequately plead any conspiracy or nexus between the alleged retaliatory actions and protected activity.
brief_summary: Plaintiff, proceeding pro se, filed this action alleging retaliation under § 3617 of the Fair Housing Act against his former landlord (PEC), a housing development corporation (PHADC), and a community radio association (WPEB) for filing a previous Fair Housing Act lawsuit (El I) that was settled. The Court granted defendants' motions to dismiss because the claims regarding the eviction were barred by the settlement agreement's release, and Plaintiff failed to adequately plead any conspiracy or connection between the alleged retaliatory conduct and protected activity.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's retaliation claim under FHA § 3617 regarding eviction from 4050 Haverford apartment was dismissed because all claims against PEC related to the eviction were waived by the settlement agreement in the prior case (El I). Claims against PHADC were dismissed for failure to plead facts showing PHADC's connection to the apartment or relationship to PEC, relying only on conclusory allegations of concerted action.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's retaliation claim regarding eviction from LAVA space was dismissed because Plaintiff alleged only conclusory allegations of conspiracy between PEC and Winter without factual allegations showing their relationship, and failed to allege facts connecting the LAVA eviction to the protected activity in El I.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's retaliation claim against WPEB for denial of access to radio station was dismissed because Plaintiff alleged no cause of action against WPEB in the Second Amended Complaint and offered no facts showing WPEB's relationship to any other defendant or connection to protected activity.

source_file: 9934801_2021_FAIR HOUSING RIGHTS CENTER IN SOUTHEASTERN PENNSYLVANIA v. SJ LOFTS, LLC_paed
case_name: Fair Housing Rights Center in Southeastern Pennsylvania v. SJ Lofts, LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Tester-identified design and construction deficiencies at Michener Lofts including thermostat height, balcony door width, bathroom clearance, and electrical outlet height that allegedly render the building inaccessible to wheelchair users.
key_holding: The court denied the motion to dismiss as to the Streamline Entities because FHRC alleged sufficient facts showing their involvement in construction and identified specific design violations, but granted dismissal without prejudice as to Michael Stillwell individually because the complaint contained only conclusory alter-ego allegations lacking sufficient factual detail.
brief_summary: Fair Housing Rights Center in Southeastern Pennsylvania sued SJ Lofts, Lion Construction LLC, Streamline Entities, and Michael Stillwell alleging that Michener Lofts, a 44-unit apartment building constructed in Philadelphia in 2018, contained design and construction violations that discriminated against people with disabilities. The court denied the motion to dismiss as to the Streamline Entities, finding FHRC alleged sufficient facts to proceed, but dismissed individual defendant Stillwell without prejudice for failing to allege sufficient facts to support alter-ego liability.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)
Fair Housing Rights Center in Southeastern Pennsylvania v. Post Goldtex GP, LLC, 823 F.3d 209 (3d Cir. 2016)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible design and construction compliance: (1) thermostat located 55 inches above floor instead of maximum 48 inches; (2) balcony door 23 inches wide, too narrow for wheelchair access; (3) bathroom clear floor space inadequate for wheelchair access; (4) electrical outlets in common area below minimum 15-inch height requirement.
fha_claims.reasoning: FHRC pleaded sufficient factual allegations to show that the Streamline Entities were involved in construction of the multifamily dwelling and identified four specific FHA design and construction violations; the level of involvement and responsibility cannot be determined without a developed factual record, so motion to dismiss as to Streamline Entities was denied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible design and construction compliance: (1) thermostat located 55 inches above floor instead of maximum 48 inches; (2) balcony door 23 inches wide, too narrow for wheelchair access; (3) bathroom clear floor space inadequate for wheelchair access; (4) electrical outlets in common area below minimum 15-inch height requirement.
fha_claims.reasoning: Under FHA agency principles, vicarious liability does not extend to individual officers or owners absent some showing of individual action giving rise to liability; FHRC alleged only that Stillwell was an owner and director of the contracting entities, which is insufficient to state a plausible claim against him individually. Dismissal was without prejudice to allow amendment if discovery reveals facts supporting individual involvement or alter-ego liability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged deprivation of due process rights in connection with eviction proceedings; also alleged RICO conspiracy, extortion, and fraud under Pennsylvania law
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 1983 claim dismissed because no defendant was alleged to be a state actor, making the due process claim implausible. RICO claim dismissed for failure to allege injury to business or property (only emotional and physical damages alleged), failure to allege pattern of racketeering activity (only one predicate act alleged), and failure to allege a RICO enterprise. State law claims (extortion, fraud) dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a) due to failure to establish complete diversity of citizenship.

case_name: Reginald Carter v. Donna M. Murray
accommodation_description: Plaintiff with lung disease/COPD requested permanent relocation and implementation of a smoke-free policy as accommodation for disability-related environmental sensitivities.
key_holding: The complaint failed to state a plausible FHA reasonable accommodation claim because defendants addressed plaintiff's requests by offering alternative housing, hotel relocation during repairs, and proposing a smoke-free policy, and plaintiff rejected these accommodations.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Reginald Carter sued property management officials at Venango House in Philadelphia alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on race and disability, claiming defendants failed to accommodate his lung disease by refusing to relocate him or implement a smoke-free policy. The court granted leave to proceed in forma pauperis and dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim, finding Carter's race discrimination allegations were conclusory and his reasonable accommodation claim implausible because defendants had offered and implemented accommodations.
key_cases_cited: Vorchheimer v. Philadelphian Owners Ass'n, 903 F.3d 100 (3d Cir. 2018)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
White v. Barber, 767 F. App'x 332 (3d Cir. 2019)
Wilson v. Hillsborough Twp. Constr. Dep't, 779 F. App'x 969 (3d Cir. 2019)
Lapid-Laurel, L.L.C. v. Zoning Bd. of Adjustment, 284 F.3d 442 (3d Cir. 2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's allegations of race discrimination were conclusory and generalized, merely stating his race and that other tenants were African-American without plausibly alleging that defendants' failure to timely address repair requests was motivated by race. The court found such vague speculation insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Smoke-free policy or exemption from smoking in the building; relocation to a different apartment; temporary relocation to a hotel during repairs; exemption from door painting due to lung disease exacerbation from paint fumes
fha_claims.reasoning: Although plaintiff alleged lung disease (COPD) and breathing difficulties exacerbated by smoke and fumes, the complaint failed to plausibly allege the statutory elements of a failure to accommodate claim. The record showed defendants offered alternative apartments without carpeting, temporary hotel relocation, and indicated willingness to implement a smoke-free policy, demonstrating they addressed his requests rather than refusing accommodation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 First and Fourteenth Amendment constitutional claims; state law tort claims (defamation, slander)
fha_claims.reasoning: § 1983 claims failed because none of the defendants acted under color of state law; they were private citizens. State law tort claims lacked subject matter jurisdiction because complete diversity did not exist under § 1332(a)—plaintiff and defendants Moragne and Clay were all Pennsylvania citizens residing in the same building.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Work from home accommodation for insulin-dependent Type-1 diabetic employee during COVID-19 pandemic
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that plaintiff stated a plausible claim for ADA interference under 42 U.S.C. § 12203(b) by alleging that defendant repeatedly moved the goalposts and asked for additional information each time plaintiff provided a doctor's note, thereby meddling in or hampering plaintiff's ability to invoke ADA rights. Claim survived motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: EPSLA paid sick leave, ADA reasonable accommodation
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that plaintiff stated a plausible claim for violation of the Emergency Paid Sick Leave Act (EPSLA) by alleging that defendant failed to provide sick leave after plaintiff's doctor advised work-from-home accommodation. Although defendant argued the EPSLA was not yet in effect when plaintiff was terminated, the court found the statute's effective date ambiguous and held that defendant bore the burden of persuasion on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion, which it failed to satisfy. Claim survived motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: EPSLA retaliation claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed plaintiff's EPSLA retaliation claim under 29 U.S.C. § 5104 because the statute requires both that an employee (1) take leave in accordance with the EPSLA AND (2) file a complaint or institute a proceeding. Plaintiff neither took leave under the EPSLA nor filed a complaint prior to this lawsuit. Court applied plain language interpretation and rejected plaintiff's argument for a remedial construction, holding that Congress used the conjunctive 'and' and the Court must enforce the statute as written.

case_name: Justin C. Heimbach v. Ronald Hill
accommodation_description: Plaintiff did not request a reasonable accommodation; he seeks federal court review of an adverse state court eviction judgment as a FHA violation.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claims because his complaint contained no factual allegations suggesting discrimination on any impermissible basis including race, color, religion, sex, familial status, national origin, or disability.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Heimbach sued landlord Hill seeking federal court review of an adverse state court eviction judgment and claiming violations of the Fair Housing Act. The court dismissed claims seeking review of state court judgments under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine and dismissed FHA claims for failure to state a claim because the complaint contained no factual allegations of discrimination on any protected basis.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Great W. Mining & Mineral Co. v. Fox Rothschild LLP, 615 F.3d 159 (3d Cir. 2010)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; no specific accommodation requested or alleged.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the FHA claim for failure to state a plausible claim because the complaint contained no allegations of discrimination based on any protected class (race, color, religion, sex, familial status, national origin, or disability) and consisted only of vague allegations of wrongdoing without factual elaboration. Dismissal was without prejudice to allow amendment.

source_file: 9935747_2021_United States v. THE DORCHESTER OWNERS ASSOCIATION_paed
case_name: United States of America v. The Dorchester Owners Association
accommodation_description: Residents requested permission to keep emotional support animals in their apartments despite the building's no-pets policy.
key_holding: The court denied the United States' motion for partial summary judgment because genuine issues of material fact exist regarding whether the residents were disabled within the meaning of the FHA, whether the requested ESA accommodations were necessary, and whether the animal ban interfered with residents' housing rights.
brief_summary: The United States sued The Dorchester Owners Association for disability discrimination based on the Association's ban on emotional support animals. The court denied the government's motion for partial summary judgment because genuine issues of material fact remain for trial regarding whether the residents are disabled, whether the ESA accommodations are necessary, and whether the ban interfered with their housing rights.
key_cases_cited: Vorchheimer v. Philadelphian Owners Ass'n, 903 F.3d 100 (3d Cir. 2018)
Cmty. Servs., Inc. v. Wind Gap Mun. Auth., 421 F.3d 170 (3d Cir. 2005)
Lapid-Laurel, L.L.C. v. Zoning Bd. of Adjustment of Twp. of Scotch Plains, 284 F.3d 442 (3d Cir. 2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to keep emotional support animals in the condominium building; the defendant had allegedly implemented a discriminatory ban on emotional support animals
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found genuine issues of material fact regarding whether residents were disabled within the meaning of the FHA, whether their requested accommodations were necessary in light of their disabilities, and whether the alleged ban on emotional support animals actually interfered with residents' opportunity to use and enjoy their dwellings. The court determined these fact-intensive inquiries were inappropriate for summary judgment and more suitable for jury determination with witness testimony and credibility assessments.

case_name: DeJesus v. Lucey
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges defendants rented him an illegal apartment lacking heat and seeks compensation for paid rent; no disability or accommodation request is alleged.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claim because he failed to allege discrimination based on any protected characteristic, instead merely complaining that defendants rented him an illegal apartment lacking heat.
brief_summary: Alex DeJesus, proceeding pro se, sued private landlords Bill Lucey and Martin Garcia under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 and the Fair Housing Act, alleging they rented him an illegal apartment lacking heat and sought to evict him. The court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim, finding no plausible FHA claim because plaintiff did not allege discrimination based on any protected characteristic.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged defendants rented him an illegal apartment lacking heat and sought to evict him; no accommodation was requested or at issue.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege discrimination based on any protected characteristic under the FHA. The complaint alleged only that defendants rented an illegal apartment lacking heat, which does not constitute discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, familial status, national origin, or disability. The court applied the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard and found the allegations insufficient to state a plausible FHA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (First and Fourteenth Amendment claims); Pennsylvania landlord-tenant law claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Section 1983 claims dismissed because plaintiff failed to allege that defendants acted under color of state law; defendants were private individuals (landlord and agent). State law claims dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction: no complete diversity (all parties citizens of Pennsylvania) and amount in controversy ($500 rent) falls below the $75,000 threshold. Court declined supplemental jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3).

case_name: Alex DeJesus v. Bill Lucey and Martin Garcia
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: The court dismissed the Fair Housing Act claims without prejudice, allowing the pro se plaintiff leave to amend the complaint.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Alex DeJesus filed a complaint against Bill Lucey and Martin Garcia alleging Fair Housing Act claims, seeking to proceed in forma pauperis. The court granted in forma pauperis status but dismissed the FHA claims without prejudice, providing plaintiff an opportunity to file an amended complaint.
key_cases_cited: Weber v. McGrogan, 939 F.3d 232 (3d Cir. 2019)
Borelli v. City of Reading, 532 F.2d 950 (3d Cir. 1976)
In re Westinghouse Sec. Litig., 90 F.3d 696 (3d Cir. 1995)
Poulis v. State Farm Fire & Casualty Co., 747 F.2d 863 (3d Cir. 1984)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not specified in opinion
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed all FHA claims without prejudice under § 1915(e) screening as the complaint was deficient and did not adequately plead facts supporting any FHA theory. The plaintiff was given opportunity to amend.

case_name: Eldon Chick, et al. v. Serrano Acquisitions, et al.
accommodation_description: Homeless plaintiffs who occupied an abandoned property without permission seek declaratory relief and injunction against eviction under the Fair Housing Act, but no formal reasonable accommodation request was made to a housing provider.
key_holding: Plaintiffs fail to state a claim under the FHA because they are neither buyers nor renters within the meaning of the Act, and they have not alleged any facts suggesting HSBC Bank made the property unavailable because of a protected characteristic under § 3604(a).
brief_summary: Homeless plaintiffs Eldon Chick and others, represented by the Poor People's Economic Human Rights Campaign, sued private property owners and government entities seeking to remain in an abandoned property they occupied without permission, asserting Fair Housing Act and constitutional claims. The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss, holding that plaintiffs failed to state a claim because they were neither buyers nor renters under the FHA and had not adequately alleged discrimination based on race or other protected characteristics.
key_cases_cited: Fowler v. UPMC Shadyside, 578 F.3d 203 (3d Cir. 2009)
Bright v. Westmoreland Cnty., 443 F.3d 276 (3d Cir. 2006)
In re Burlington Coat Factory Sec. Litig., 114 F.3d 1410 (3d Cir. 1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to state a claim under the FHA because they were neither buyers nor renters within the meaning of the statute. They did not allege a bona fide offer to purchase or rent the property, nor did they allege that the property was made unavailable because of a protected class characteristic (race, color, religion, sex, familial status, or national origin).

source_file: 9936025_2022_HONKALA v. U.S. DEPARTMENT OF HOUSING _ URBAN DEVELOPMENT_paed
case_name: Cheri Honkala et al v. U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development et al
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs are homeless individuals who occupied a vacant property owned by the Philadelphia Housing Authority without permission and sought declaratory relief to remain in the property.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' Fair Housing Act claims because plaintiffs are not 'buyers or renters' under the FHA—they occupied the property without permission from the owner, and their unilateral decision to rehabilitate the property does not constitute consideration creating a legally enforceable rental relationship.
brief_summary: Homeless individuals and the Poor People's Economic Human Rights Campaign sued the Philadelphia Housing Authority, HUD, and other defendants after occupying a vacant PHA-owned property without permission, claiming Fair Housing Act discrimination, constitutional violations, and seeking declaratory relief to remain in the property. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, holding that plaintiffs lack standing under the FHA because they are not 'buyers or renters'—they occupied the property without any agreement with the owner—and that their constitutional claims also fail for lack of a protected property interest.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Growth Horizons, Inc. v. Delaware Cty., 983 F.2d 1277 (3d Cir. 1993)
Wartluft v. Milton Hershey Sch. and Sch. Trust, 400 F. Supp. 3d 91 (M.D. Pa. 2019)
Pocono Springs Civic. Assoc., Inc. v. MacKenzie, 667 A.2d 233 (Pa. 1995)
City of Boerne v. Flores, 521 U.S. 507 (1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to establish they are 'renters' under the FHA because they did not supply consideration in exchange for an interest in the property; they occupied the property without permission and without any mutual agreement with the owner. The court applied the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard and found the complaint failed to allege facts sufficient to state a plausible FHA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Religious Freedom Restoration Act (RFRA), Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act, McKinney-Vento Act, 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (Due Process Clause, Equal Protection Clause, state-created danger), Declaratory Judgment Act, Monell claim
fha_claims.reasoning: RFRA claims against state actors (PHA and City of Philadelphia) fail as a matter of law because RFRA does not apply to states or state agencies following City of Boerne v. Flores. Religious Land Use Act claim fails because plaintiffs have no property interest in the property. McKinney-Vento Act claim fails because plaintiffs did not allege they applied to HUD for use of surplus property as required by the statute. Due process claims fail because plaintiffs lack a lawful property interest in the property. Equal protection claim fails because plaintiffs failed to plead facts showing individuals in encampments were similarly situated. State-created danger claim fails because the City's eviction action is a response to illegal occupation, not an affirmative creation of danger rising to the level of shocking the conscience. Monell claim fails because no underlying federal law violation was established.

source_file: 9936028_2022_HONKALA v. U.S. DEPARTMENT OF HOUSING _ URBAN DEVELOPMENT_paed
case_name: Honkala et al v. U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs, unhoused individuals and a housing advocate organization, seek declaratory and injunctive relief to occupy a HUD-owned vacant property, asserting general housing rights under the FHA.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' FHA claim because plaintiffs are neither buyers nor renters within the meaning of the FHA and therefore lack standing to bring a fair housing claim.
brief_summary: Unhoused plaintiffs Cheri Honkala, PPEHRC, and individual families occupied a HUD-owned vacant property in Philadelphia without authorization; HUD filed an ejectment action and plaintiffs responded with claims including FHA violations. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, holding plaintiffs lacked standing because they were neither buyers nor renters under the FHA, and dismissed the entire action with prejudice as further amendment would be futile.
key_cases_cited: Fowler v. UPMC Shadyside, 578 F.3d 203 (3d Cir. 2009)
In re Burlington Coat Factory Sec. Litig., 114 F.3d 1410 (3d Cir. 1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege they should be permitted to occupy abandoned federal property (2009 E. Tioga Street) without permission from HUD as a housing solution during the COVID-19 pandemic and homelessness crisis.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed FHA claims because plaintiffs failed to allege they were 'buyers or renters within the meaning of the FHA.' The property was not alleged to be available for rent or purchase, and plaintiffs occupied it without permission, placing them outside the FHA's protected class of housing consumers.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claims under Religious Freedom Restoration Act (RFRA), Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLIUPA), McKinney-Vento Act, § 1983 due process and equal protection, state-created danger, Monell liability, and Declaratory Judgment Act.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed all non-FHA claims for failure to state a plausible claim. RFRA claims failed because federal defendants' ejectment action was brought under state common law and Pennsylvania civil procedure, not federal law. Due process claims failed because plaintiffs received due process through state court proceedings with counsel. All other claims failed for reasons set forth in the companion case (21-0684), which the court incorporated by reference.

case_name: Heimbach v. Hill
accommodation_description: No specific reasonable accommodation request was identified in the complaint; plaintiff alleged general FHA violations regarding landlord-tenant eviction proceedings.
key_holding: The Amended Complaint was dismissed with prejudice for failure to state an FHA claim because plaintiff failed to allege facts suggesting discrimination on an impermissible basis, and state law claims were dismissed for lack of diversity jurisdiction.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Justin Heimbach sued his private landlord Ronald Hill seeking review of state court eviction proceedings and alleging Fair Housing Act violations, FDCPA claims, and state law torts. The federal court dismissed the Amended Complaint with prejudice for failure to state an FHA claim because plaintiff failed to allege facts suggesting discrimination on an impermissible basis, and dismissed state law claims for lack of diversity jurisdiction since both parties are Pennsylvania citizens.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Great W. Mining & Mineral Co. v. Fox Rothschild LLP, 615 F.3d 159 (3d Cir. 2010)
Piper v. Portnoff Law Assocs., Ltd., 396 F.3d 227 (3d Cir. 2005)
West v. Atkins, 487 U.S. 42 (1988)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: FDCPA debt collection claim, § 1983 civil rights claim, state law claims (malicious abuse of process, wrongful use of civil proceedings, civil fraud, intentional infliction of emotional distress, conspiracy to violate civil rights)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed FDCPA claim as conclusory and unsupported; § 1983 claims failed because defendants were not state actors; state law claims dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under § 1332(a) due to lack of complete diversity (both parties Pennsylvania citizens).

source_file: 9936337_2022_United States v. THE DORCHESTER OWNERS ASSOCIATION_paed
case_name: United States v. The Dorchester Owners Association
accommodation_description: Ms. Hamburg requested an accommodation to keep an emotional support animal (dog) in her condominium unit despite the Dorchester Owners Association's no-pet policy.
key_holding: The court denied DOA's motion for summary judgment, finding genuine disputes of material fact exist as to whether Ms. Hamburg is a person with a disability, whether she has a disability-related need for an ESA, and whether DOA engaged in the interactive process in good faith or constructively refused the accommodation through delay.
brief_summary: The United States and plaintiff-intervenor Louise Hamburg sued the Dorchester Owners Association, alleging it violated the Fair Housing Act by refusing to grant Ms. Hamburg a reasonable accommodation for an emotional support animal under its no-pet policy. The court denied DOA's motion for summary judgment, finding genuine factual disputes exist as to Ms. Hamburg's disability status, the legitimacy of her ESA need, and whether DOA's handling of the request constituted a constructive refusal to accommodate.
key_cases_cited: Community Services, Inc. v. Wind Gap Mun. Auth., 421 F.3d 170 (3d Cir. 2005)
Lapid-Laurel, LLC v. Zoning Bd. of Adjustment, 284 F.3d 442 (3d Cir. 2002)
Vorchheimer v. Pennrose Properties, 903 F.3d 100 (3d Cir. 2018)
Revock v. Cowpet Bay W. Condo. Ass'n, 853 F.3d 96 (3d Cir. 2017)
Castillo Condo. Ass'n v. U.S. Dep't of Hous. & Urban Dev., 821 F.3d 92 (1st Cir. 2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exception to no-pet policy to allow an emotional support animal (dog) for Ms. Hamburg's Generalized Anxiety Disorder with Panic Attacks
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine disputes of material fact precluding summary judgment: (1) whether Ms. Hamburg is a person with a disability (supported by treating physician declaration); (2) whether the ESA accommodation is necessary to afford equal opportunity to use and enjoy her dwelling; and (3) whether DOA refused or constructively refused the accommodation through undue delay. A reasonable jury could find the accommodation necessary and DOA's refusal unlawful.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination in terms, conditions, or privileges of dwelling based on disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied summary judgment on § 3604(f)(2) disparate treatment claim because genuine disputes of material fact exist regarding whether Ms. Hamburg has a disability and whether DOA discriminated against her based on that disability. The case involves factual disputes best resolved by jury.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Making dwelling unavailable or denying dwelling because of disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied summary judgment on § 3604(f)(1) claim because material factual disputes exist regarding whether Ms. Hamburg was denied the dwelling or its use based on her disability. The case involves complex factual issues requiring jury determination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Pattern or practice of resistance to full enjoyment of FHA rights through no-pet policy applied to ESA requests
fha_claims.reasoning: DOA's motion for summary judgment did not address the United States' pattern or practice claim under § 3614(a). The claim remains pending and was not substantively analyzed in this opinion.

case_name: Aimee Moran and Jessica Mazzeo v. Rockwell Development Group, LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs are single mothers alleging sex discrimination and harassment in the sale of new construction homes; no disability accommodation requested.
key_holding: The court held that single mothers constitute a protected class under the FHA through a sex-plus-marital-status discrimination theory, and plaintiffs adequately alleged harassment sufficient to survive dismissal, while dismissing fraud and negligent misrepresentation claims under the gist-of-the-action doctrine.
brief_summary: Two single mothers sued a housing developer alleging sex discrimination and harassment during home construction and purchase, claiming they received inferior service and were sexually harassed by employees compared to other homebuyers. The court denied the motion to dismiss on the FHA claims, finding plaintiffs adequately alleged protected-class discrimination and hostile-environment harassment, but granted dismissal on fraud and negligent misrepresentation claims as barred by the gist-of-the-action doctrine.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Revock v. Cowpet Bay W. Condo. Ass'n
Rosencrans v. Quixote Enters.
Curto v. A Country Place Condo. Assoc.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges sex and marital status discrimination in terms and conditions of home sale and construction services, not a request for reasonable accommodation.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that plaintiffs stated a plausible FHA claim under sex-plus discrimination theory (gender plus marital status as single mothers). Plaintiffs adequately alleged specific instances of harassment and discriminatory treatment in the provision of services and conditions of the home sale. Defendants' motion to dismiss the FHA claim was denied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Not applicable; claim alleges harassment and interference with plaintiffs' exercise of FHA rights through unwanted sexual advances, touching, and intimidation by defendants' employees.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiffs' allegations of harassment by defendants' employees—including unwanted advances, comments on appearance, unwanted touching, and invitations into homes—were sufficiently specific and plausibly constituted interference under § 3617 when harassment intruded on the well-being and tranquility of the home. Defendants' motion to dismiss was denied.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Pennsylvania Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Law (73 P.S. § 201-1); breach of contract; fraudulent misrepresentation and/or concealment; negligent misrepresentation and/or concealment.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted defendants' motion to dismiss fraudulent misrepresentation and negligent misrepresentation claims (Counts IV and V) under the gist-of-the-action doctrine, finding that all alleged fraudulent and negligent misrepresentation claims were centered around defendants' breach of contractual duties and thus duplicated breach of contract claims. Court retained supplemental jurisdiction over remaining state law claims (breach of contract and UTPCPL) because plaintiffs adequately pled an FHA violation and no other basis for dismissal was argued.

case_name: Edward Haywood Payne, Jr. v. The Galman Group and Sedgwick Station Apartments
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges the landlord selectively enforced its no-dog policy against white tenants, constituting racial discrimination in provision of housing services.
key_holding: The complaint fails to state a plausible race discrimination claim because plaintiff admits he never requested permission to keep a dog, does not know whether the white tenant paid a pet deposit, and provides only vague, conclusory allegations of racial motive rather than factual allegations sufficient to establish a prima facie case.
brief_summary: Black tenant Edward Haywood Payne sued his landlords alleging they discriminated against him by race in enforcing the building's no-dog policy, allowing a white tenant to keep a dog while he would not be permitted to do so. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding the complaint deficient because Payne never requested a dog accommodation, admitted he had no knowledge about whether the white tenant paid a pet deposit, and provided only speculative, conclusory allegations about racial discrimination insufficient to establish a plausible claim.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Community Services, Inc. v. Wind Gap Mun. Authority, 421 F.3d 170 (3d Cir. 2005)
Fowler v. UPMC Shadyside, 578 F.3d 203 (3d Cir. 2009)
Curto v. A Country Place Condominium Assoc., Inc., 921 F.3d 405 (3d Cir. 2019)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege racial discrimination in disparate enforcement of pet policy. He never requested a dog and was denied one, nor did he allege he owned a dog and faced repercussions. His allegations that a white tenant was allowed a dog while he was not are conclusory and insufficient to establish a prima facie case of race discrimination under the FHA.

source_file: 9936771_2022_United States v. ONE BOYERTOWN PROPERTIES LP_paed
case_name: United States of America v. J. Randolph Parry Architects, P.C., et al.
accommodation_description: The United States alleges that fifteen senior living facilities across Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Virginia, and Connecticut violate design and construction accessibility requirements under the FHA and ADA.
key_holding: The court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the architect's state law indemnification and contribution crossclaims and third-party complaints, finding they would substantially predominate over the federal civil rights claims and that judicial economy, convenience, and fairness did not support accepting jurisdiction.
brief_summary: The United States brought this enforcement action under the Fair Housing Act and ADA against facility owners and an architect, alleging that fifteen senior living facilities across four states fail to meet disability accessibility requirements. The court granted motions to dismiss the architect's crossclaims and third-party complaint, declining supplemental jurisdiction over the architect's state law indemnification and contribution claims because they would substantially predominate over the federal civil rights claims and the principles of judicial economy, convenience, and fairness did not support accepting jurisdiction.
key_cases_cited: City of Chicago v. Int'l Coll. of Surgeons, 522 U.S. 156 (1997)
United Mine Workers of Am. v. Gibbs, 383 U.S. 715 (1966)
Growth Horizons, Inc. v. Delaware Cnty., Pa., 983 F.2d 1277 (3d Cir. 1993)
Borough of W. Mifflin v. Lancaster, 45 F.3d 780 (3d Cir. 1995)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible design and construction of senior living facilities to comply with FHA and ADA accessibility requirements across fifteen facilities in Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Virginia, and Connecticut
fha_claims.reasoning: The court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the architect's state law crossclaims and third-party complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(2) because the state law claims would substantially predominate over the federal FHA/ADA claims and judicial economy, convenience, and fairness would not be served. The underlying federal FHA/ADA design and construction claims remain pending against the defendants.

source_file: 9937109_2022_HORIZON HOUSE, INC. v. EAST NORRITON TOWNSHIP_paed
case_name: Horizon House, Inc. v. East Norriton Township
accommodation_description: Horizon House sought a certificate of use and occupancy to operate a single-family dwelling housing up to three individuals with intellectual disabilities in a BR-1 zoning district as a matter of right—i.e., without being classified as a 'group home' and without having to obtain a special exception requiring fire sprinkler systems, floor plan disclosures, disability disclosures, 24/7 on-site staffing, and enhanced parking, among other requirements.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for plaintiff Horizon House, holding that East Norriton Township's zoning ordinance was facially discriminatory under the FHAA because it singled out housing for individuals with disabilities ('group homes') for substantial additional burdens not imposed on comparable non-disabled households, and the Township failed to justify that differential treatment.
brief_summary: Horizon House, a nonprofit providing supportive housing to individuals with intellectual disabilities, contracted to purchase a single-family house in East Norriton Township's BR-1 residential zoning district to house up to three disabled individuals. The Township denied Horizon House's applications for a certificate of use and occupancy, classifying the proposed use as a 'group home' under its zoning ordinance and requiring a special exception with onerous conditions—including fire sprinkler installation, public disclosure of residents' disabilities, and 24/7 on-site staffing. On cross-motions for summary judgment on liability, the court found the Township's zoning ordinance facially discriminatory under the FHAA because it imposed significant burdens exclusively on housing for individuals with disabilities and the Township offered no justification that no less restrictive course of action was available, resulting in summary judgment for Horizon House.
key_cases_cited: Hovsons, Inc. v. Twp. of Brick, 89 F.3d 1096 (3d Cir. 1996)
Cmty. Servs., Inc. v. Wind Gap Mun. Auth., 421 F.3d 170 (3d Cir. 2005)
Larkin v. State of Mich. Dep't of Soc. Servs., 89 F.3d 285 (6th Cir. 1996)
Sharpvisions, Inc. v. Borough of Plum, 475 F. Supp. 2d 514 (W.D. Pa. 2007)
Barnabei v. Chadds Ford Twp., 125 F. Supp. 3d 515 (E.D. Pa. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The Township's zoning ordinance is facially discriminatory because it singles out group homes for individuals with disabilities for special exception requirements while allowing three unrelated non-disabled individuals to occupy a single-family dwelling by right. The Township failed to rebut Horizon House's prima facie case by demonstrating that no less restrictive course of action could be adopted, thereby establishing a violation of 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(1).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court declined to address the disparate impact claim because it had already found the Township liable for disparate treatment under the FHAA, making the disparate impact analysis unnecessary.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (42 U.S.C. §§ 12132), Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act (29 U.S.C. §§ 794 et seq.)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the same analysis to the ADA and Section 504 claims as it did to the FHAA disparate treatment claim, finding the Township liable under all three statutes for the facially discriminatory zoning ordinance.

source_file: 9937341_2022_ALLENTOWN VICTORY CHURCH v. CITY OF ALLENTOWN, PENNSYLVANIA_paed
case_name: Allentown Victory Church v. City of Allentown, Pennsylvania
accommodation_description: AVC requested a zoning variance to operate its drug and alcohol recovery facility with 15-18 residents instead of the maximum 12 residents permitted under Allentown's zoning ordinance for group homes.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for the city because AVC failed to produce sufficient evidence that a 15-18 resident facility was necessary to make the recovery home financially viable, presenting only conclusory statements rather than specific financial data showing why 12 residents would be inadequate.
brief_summary: Allentown Victory Church, operator of a Christian drug and alcohol recovery home for men, sued the City of Allentown after its Zoning Hearing Board denied requests to house 15-18 residents despite the zoning ordinance capping group homes at 12 residents. The court granted summary judgment for the city on all FHA claims, finding the church failed to demonstrate that operating with more than 12 residents was necessary for financial viability.
key_cases_cited: 431 E. Palisade Ave. Real Estate, LLC v. City of Englewood, 977 F.3d 277 (3d Cir. 2020)
Lapid-Laurel, L.L.C. v. Zoning Bd. of Adjustment of Twp. of Scotch Plains, 284 F.3d 442 (3d Cir. 2002)
New Directions Treatment Servs. v. City of Reading, 490 F.3d 293 (3d Cir. 2007)
Dr. Gertrude A. Barber Ctr., Inc. v. Peters Twp., 273 F. Supp. 2d 643 (W.D. Pa. 2003)
Get Back Up, Inc. v. City of Detroit, 606 F. App'x 792 (6th Cir. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Facial discrimination claim challenging the zoning ordinance definition of 'Institutions or Residences for Children, the Aged, or the Handicapped' which requires a variance (rather than special exception) to operate in residential districts
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the facial discrimination standard and found that Allentown's zoning ordinance does not facially discriminate because it does not single out disabled individuals for uniquely different treatment; other uses (boarding houses, dormitories, veterans treatment centers) also require variances in the same residential districts, and plaintiff failed to show that RVH is similarly situated to uses permitted by right or special exception.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: As-applied disparate treatment claim alleging that the disability of RVH residents was a motivating factor in the Board's denial of the variance application
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff presented only conclusory allegations and unsupported assertions of discriminatory animus by Board members, without citation to relevant case law or direct evidence of discriminatory intent such as statements of generalized prejudice; the 'deliberate indifference' argument was made without legal support.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claim that the zoning ordinance's cap of twelve residents for 'Institutions or Residences for Children, the Aged, or the Handicapped' (while allowing up to 30 persons in other classifications) has a disparate impact on disabled persons by making housing unavailable
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to provide any evidence—statistical or otherwise—to support the notion that the zoning ordinance had a greater adverse impact on the protected group; the claim rested on mere speculation and unsupported assertions without citation to the record.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request for a zoning variance to waive the maximum number of residents for a group home above 12 residents, allowing RVH to house 15 residents to make the facility financially viable
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to meet its initial burden of showing that the requested accommodation (housing 15 residents instead of 12) was necessary to afford handicapped persons equal opportunity to use and enjoy housing; the only evidence was conclusory testimony that 15 residents would be the 'lowest common denominator' for economic viability, without affidavits, financial data, licensing requirements, or evidence that a 12-person home would not be financially viable. The shifting nature of the request (from 18 to 15 residents) and the fact that RVH continued to operate after denial further undermined necessity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) Title II claim and Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) claim
fha_claims.reasoning: For the ADA claim, the court applied the same FHA analysis and granted summary judgment on all three theories (disparate treatment, disparate impact, and reasonable accommodation). For the RLUIPA claim, plaintiff failed to cite any facts suggesting the Board's decision forced it to choose between following religious precepts and forfeiting benefits, or that substantial pressure was applied to modify religious behavior; the claim was threadbare and dismissed.

case_name: White v. Pagotto
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges discriminatory eviction and differential treatment based on perceived disability and race, but does not articulate a specific accommodation request.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's complaint for failure to comply with Rule 8 and failure to state plausible claims under § 1983, § 1981, and the Rehabilitation Act, noting that conclusory allegations of discrimination based on race and perceived disability were insufficient to survive Iqbal/Twombly scrutiny.
brief_summary: Tyrone K. White, a Black tenant evicted from subsidized housing managed by Bethesda Project and subsidized through PHA's Housing Choice Voucher Program, filed a pro se complaint alleging discrimination, retaliation, and constitutional violations. The court dismissed the complaint under Rule 8 and for failure to state plausible claims, finding White's allegations too conclusory and disjointed to establish discrimination based on race or perceived disability.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Ctr., 473 U.S. 432 (1985)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 equal protection claim; § 1981 race discrimination claim; § 504 Rehabilitation Act disability discrimination claim; Pennsylvania Human Relations Act claims; defamation, retaliation, failure to stop harassment, physical abuse, assault, self-neglect, financial exploitation, senior abuse, fraudulent admission
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint fails to comply with Rule 8 because factual allegations are unclear, disjointed, and contradictory, preventing fair notice of the grounds for claims. Additionally, plaintiff failed to plausibly allege purposeful discrimination based on race or disability, or that he was treated differently from similarly situated individuals. Conclusory allegations unsupported by clear facts are insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly.

source_file: 9937562_2022_EQUAL EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITY COMMISSION v. GEISINGER HEALTH_paed

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title I ADA employment discrimination claims, including failure to provide reasonable accommodations (medical leave, reassignment to vacant position), retaliation, and interference with ADA rights. Non-FHA claims under Title I and Title V of the Americans with Disabilities Act.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed failure to accommodate and discrimination claims because EEOC failed to plead that Casterline was disabled under the ADA (failed to allege substantial limitation in major life activities or record of impairment). Court also dismissed retaliation claim for failure to plead causation between protected activity and adverse action. Interference claim survived MTD.

case_name: King Anthony Alvarez v. HUD, et al.
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation requested; plaintiff alleged retaliation for filing complaints and lawsuits against TURN regarding housing conditions and funding mismanagement.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claims because he failed to allege membership in a protected class, which is fatal to any FHA claim regardless of whether the claims are framed as discrimination, interference, or retaliation.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff King Anthony Alvarez, proceeding in forma pauperis, filed a Second Amended Complaint against HUD, the City of Philadelphia, DHCD, TURN (a nonprofit housing organization), and various individuals alleging that his subsidized housing benefits were terminated in retaliation for criticizing TURN and filing this lawsuit. The court dismissed the Second Amended Complaint, finding that plaintiff's FHA claims failed because he did not allege membership in a protected class, and dismissed state law claims for lack of diversity jurisdiction.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Mt. Holly Gardens Citizens in Action, Inc. v. Twp. of Mount Holly, 658 F.3d 375 (3d Cir. 2011)
Dew v. S. Columbia Terrace, LLC, 854 F. App'x 460 (3d Cir. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege membership in a protected class or that alleged retaliation was based on exercise of FHA rights. The FHA is an anti-discrimination statute targeting protected classes, and plaintiff's allegations of termination for abusive behavior and complaints about funding mismanagement do not connect to protected activity under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege that alleged interference was directed at him because of membership in a protected class or in connection with exercise of FHA rights. Section 3617 requires that interference be 'because of' protected class status or reported discriminatory housing practice.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II Civil Rights Act of 1964, Title VI Civil Rights Act of 1964, state law claims for libel, gross negligence, negligent infliction of emotional distress, dereliction of duty, and 18 U.S.C. § 1512 (witness tampering)
fha_claims.reasoning: Title II and Title VI claims fail for same reason as FHA claims—no allegation of discrimination based on protected class. State law claims dismissed for lack of diversity jurisdiction; plaintiff and at least some defendants are Pennsylvania citizens. Section 1512 does not provide a private cause of action.

source_file: 9938100_2023_United States v. THE DORCHESTER OWNERS ASSOCIATION_paed
case_name: United States v. The Dorchester Owners Association
accommodation_description: Request by residents with mental health disabilities to keep emotional support animals in a no-pet high-rise condominium, including waiver of no-pet policies, insurance requirements, common area restrictions, and breed/weight restrictions.
key_holding: The jury found the DOA engaged in a pattern or practice of disability discrimination through unreasonable delays and conditions on ESA applications, but the court denied punitive damages finding insufficient evidence of reckless indifference to federally protected rights, awarded the Halperns $37,431 in damages, and required the DOA to maintain its revised ESA policy with prompt review requirements.
brief_summary: The United States sued the Dorchester Owners Association (a high-rise condominium association in Philadelphia) alleging that its policies and practices regarding emotional support animals—including excessive documentation requirements, insurance mandates, common area prohibitions, and unreasonable delays—constituted a pattern or practice of disability discrimination under the Fair Housing Act. After a jury trial returned a split verdict finding the DOA not liable to Ms. Hamburg individually but liable on the pattern-or-practice claim, the court awarded the Halperns $37,431 in damages, declined to impose civil penalties or punitive damages, and ordered the DOA to maintain its revised ESA policy with prompt review requirements.
key_cases_cited: Alexander v. Riga, 208 F.3d 419 (3d Cir. 2000)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
431 East Palisade Avenue Real Estate, LLC v. City of Englewood, 977 F.3d 277 (3d Cir. 2020)
Olmstead v. L.C., 527 U.S. 581 (1999)
Sierra Pacific Industries, Inc., 862 F.3d 1157 (9th Cir. 2017)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission for Louise Hamburg to live with an emotional support animal (ESA) at The Dorchester condominium
fha_claims.reasoning: Jury found that while Hamburg had a mental impairment, the DOA did not know, was informed of, or reasonably should have known of her disability and need for an ESA because Hamburg's initial documentation from Carla Black was obtained through a website without a treating relationship, and Hamburg failed to correct false statements in the letter claiming Black was her treating mental health professional.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission for Bernard and Cynthia Halpern to live with an emotional support animal (ESA) at The Dorchester condominium without unreasonable delay and without restrictive conditions (freight elevator and rear door requirements)
fha_claims.reasoning: Jury found that the Halperns had a mental impairment substantially limiting major life activities, the DOA made their dwelling unavailable because of disability, imposed different terms and conditions on them than non-disabled residents, and unreasonably delayed responding to their ESA request.
