fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege intentional discrimination required for compensatory damages under ADA Title II. Additionally, declaratory relief is unwarranted because the Zoning Hearing Board's decision was reversed in state court and Plaintiff's permit was granted, eliminating the actual controversy required under the Declaratory Judgment Act. ADA Title V interference claim fails for the same reasons as the FHA § 3617 claim.

source_file: 9947666_2024_Ewideh v. Homesite Insurance Company of the Midwest_pamd
case_name: Ewideh v. Homesite Insurance Company of the Midwest
accommodation_description: Insurance claim dispute involving property damage losses; plaintiffs alleged Fair Housing Act violations related to insurer's handling of their property insurance claim
key_holding: The court transferred the case to the Middle District of Pennsylvania because a virtually identical action involving the same parties and claims was already pending there, making transfer the most efficient resolution to avoid duplicative litigation.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Omar Ewideh and Nivertiti Geaith sued their insurer Homesite Insurance Company and its attorneys for mishandling insurance claims related to property damage at their York, Pennsylvania residence, asserting claims including breach of contract, bad faith, and Fair Housing Act violations. The court granted defendants' motion to transfer venue to the Middle District of Pennsylvania, finding that a virtually identical action between the same parties was already pending there, and the transfer would serve judicial economy by avoiding duplicative litigation.
key_cases_cited: Jumara v. State Farm Ins. Co., 55 F.3d 873 (3d Cir. 1995)
Continental Grain Co. v. The Barge FBL-585, 364 U.S. 19 (1960)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act claim mentioned in complaint but not substantively analyzed; case involves insurance coverage dispute, breach of contract, bad faith, tortious interference, civil conspiracy, civil racketeering, libel, and slander.
fha_claims.disposition: Transfer to Middle District of Pennsylvania pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court transferred the case to the Middle District of Pennsylvania based on Jumara factors, finding that a related pending action with nearly identical claims and parties was already filed in the Middle District, and that the plaintiffs' residence and the subject property were located in York, Pennsylvania (Middle District). The court did not reach the merits of any claim, including the FHA claim, as the case was transferred before substantive analysis.

case_name: Lynne Thompson v. George C. Bromall, George C. Miller, Hon. Judge Chris Sherer, Leslie J. Schupp, Anthony Cimino
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested injunctive relief rescinding a state court eviction order and preventing eviction as a defense to residential eviction proceedings, invoking Fair Housing Act protections.
key_holding: The Anti-Injunction Act precludes a federal court from enjoining state court eviction proceedings absent express congressional authorization, necessary aid of jurisdiction, or need to protect federal court judgments, and because none of these exceptions apply, the court denied Thompson's motions for injunctive relief without reaching the merits of her Fair Housing Act claims.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Lynne Thompson filed an emergency motion seeking to enjoin state court eviction proceedings, naming her landlord, his attorney, real estate agents, and the state court judge as defendants, and raising Fair Housing Act claims in addition to challenges based on the CDC COVID-19 eviction moratorium. The court denied the motions for injunctive relief, holding that the Anti-Injunction Act prohibits federal courts from enjoining state court proceedings absent applicable exceptions that do not apply in this case.
key_cases_cited: Frankel v. Guzman, No. 20-5208, 2020 WL 6161512 (E.D. Pa. Oct. 21, 2020)
Oliver v. Ricci, No. 17-cv-40, 2017 WL 255623 (E.D. Pa. June 13, 2017)
Scott v. Fam. Dollar Stores, No. 2:20-CV-00773, 2020 WL 7296780 (W.D. Pa. Dec. 11, 2020)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act claim; CDC eviction moratorium defense; § 1983 due process claim
fha_claims.reasoning: The Anti-Injunction Act, 28 U.S.C. § 2283, prohibits federal court from enjoining pending state court eviction proceedings. None of the three statutory exceptions apply: (1) no clear Congressional authorization for FHA to override state court proceedings; (2) state court proceedings do not interfere with federal court jurisdiction; (3) no prior federal court judgment exists. The court did not reach the merits of the FHA or CDC moratorium claims because the Anti-Injunction Act bars the requested relief.

case_name: Gregory Louis Funyak and Sharon Lynn Funyak v. Pennrose Management Company and Monroe Meadows Housing Partnership, LP
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested that Defendants disregard their prior negative rental history when processing their rental application, arguing the negative history resulted from Mr. Funyak's disability-related job loss.
key_holding: The court dismissed the failure to accommodate claim because Plaintiffs failed to establish a nexus between Mr. Funyak's disabilities and the requested accommodation—the denial was based on poor rental history, not on disability, and the mere correlation between disability-related job loss and financial hardship does not establish that overlooking the screening criterion was necessary to afford equal housing opportunity.
brief_summary: Gregory and Sharon Funyak, Section 8 beneficiaries, sued Pennrose Management Company and Monroe Meadows Housing Partnership, alleging disability discrimination under the Fair Housing Act for denying their rental application based on poor rental history. The court granted Defendants' Motion to Dismiss, finding that Plaintiffs failed to establish the required nexus between Mr. Funyak's disabilities and the requested accommodation—waiving the rental history screening—because the connection between disability-related job loss and financial difficulties affecting rental history is insufficient to show the accommodation would directly ameliorate a disability's effect.
key_cases_cited: Lapid-Laurel v. Zoning Bd. of Adjustment, 284 F.3d 442 (3d Cir. 2002)
Bell v. Tower Mgmt. Serv., L.P., 2008 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 53514 (D.N.J. July 15, 2008)
Dr. Gertrude A. Barber Ctr., Inc. v. Peters Twp., 273 F. Supp. 2d 643 (W.D. Pa. 2003)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Disregarding or overlooking prior negative rental history (specifically a rental judgment from 2014) to approve the rental application; alternatively, continuing to process the rental application despite the negative rental history.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the reasonable accommodation claim because plaintiffs failed to establish a nexus between Mr. Funyak's unspecified disabilities and the requested accommodation. The court found that the impediment to renting was the poor rental history (a financial problem affecting people of limited means generally), not a disability-related barrier, and that overlooking rental history does not directly ameliorate any effect of the disabilities on the plaintiff's use and enjoyment of the dwelling.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of contract claim alleging defendants breached an agreement to rent by: (1) indicating plaintiffs passed credit/criminal check; (2) faxing Section 8 voucher to housing authority; and (3) providing expected move-in date conditioned on inspection. Also includes ADA Title II, Rehabilitation Act § 504, and state law breach of contract claims.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the breach of contract claim under Pennsylvania law because the complaint failed to allege the existence of a contract, its essential terms, or any breach thereof. The alleged conduct (passing a check, faxing a voucher, mentioning a conditional move-in date) fell short of manifesting mutual intent to be bound with sufficiently definite terms.

case_name: Butler v. Sundo Capital, LLC
accommodation_description: Ms. Butler requested early lease termination as a domestic violence victim facing stalking by her ex-husband; the court analyzed this as a disparate impact claim rather than a reasonable accommodation request.
key_holding: Domestic violence victims can bring disparate impact claims under a sex discrimination theory because the early termination clause's application to domestic violence victims disproportionately impacts women, who comprise 85% of intimate partner violence victims.
brief_summary: Ashley Butler and Fair Housing Partnership of Greater Pittsburgh sued Sundo Capital and related parties after Defendants refused to release Butler from her lease early when she faced domestic violence and stalking by her ex-husband, then sought accelerated rent payments. The court denied Defendants' motion to dismiss, holding that Butler adequately pled a disparate impact claim based on sex discrimination because the early termination/rent acceleration policy disproportionately impacts women who are domestic violence victims, and also adequately pled a retaliation claim under § 3617.
key_cases_cited: Tex. Dep't of Housing & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Reyes v. Waples Mobile Home Park Ltd. P'Ship, 903 F.3d 415 (4th Cir. 2018)
Wilson v. Guardian Mgmt., LLC, 383 F. Supp. 3d 1105 (D. Or. 2019)
Dickinson v. Zanesville Metro. Hous. Auth., 975 F. Supp. 2d 863 (S.D. Ohio 2013)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that domestic violence victims can bring disparate impact claims under the FHA as a form of sex discrimination, and that plaintiffs adequately pled causation through statistics showing that domestic violence victims are overwhelmingly women, are more likely to be forced to leave homes, and are often in precarious economic situations, creating a plausible causal chain linking the early termination/rent acceleration policy to disparate impact on women.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiffs adequately pled all three elements of a § 3617 retaliation claim: (1) protected activity (filing PHRC complaint), (2) adverse action (filing new legal claims), and (3) causal link (one-month temporal proximity coupled with the fact that defendants could have asserted the claims in the original complaint but only did so after the PHRC filing, supporting a plausible inference of retaliation).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Pennsylvania state law claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Court retained supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims because the FHA claims survived the motion to dismiss and defendants asserted no independent reason to dismiss the state law claims.

case_name: James Mims v. City of New Castle
accommodation_description: Landlord plaintiff alleges city discriminated against him through selective enforcement of rental inspections because he rents to racial minorities and people with disabilities
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claim because his amended complaint failed to allege sufficient facts to raise a reasonable expectation that discriminatory purpose was a motivating factor in the city's enforcement actions against him as a landlord.
brief_summary: James Mims, a landlord who rents to racial minorities and disabled tenants, sued the City of New Castle alleging the city violated the Fair Housing Act by selectively enforcing rental inspections and denying occupancy permits because of the protected characteristics of his tenants. The court granted the city's motion to dismiss, finding that while plaintiff alleged discriminatory intent by city officials, he failed to plead sufficient facts showing a causal connection between his tenant demographics and the adverse city actions.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
City of Englewood v. 431 E. Palisade Ave. Real Estate, LLC, 977 F.3d 277 (3d Cir. 2020)
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Village of Willowbrook v. Olech, 528 U.S. 562 (2000)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to raise a reasonable expectation that discovery would reveal evidence of disparate treatment or discriminatory purpose as a motivating factor. Plaintiff did not show he rents to minorities at a rate greater than the city's population, provided no specific examples of citations tied to tenant characteristics, and made only conclusory allegations about a custom and policy without factual support.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1982 retaliation claim; 42 U.S.C. § 1983 Equal Protection, Due Process, Fourth Amendment, and Eighth Amendment claims; state law tortious interference and abuse of process claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's non-FHA claims failed under Twombly/Iqbal pleading standards. Equal Protection claim lacked identification of similarly situated individuals treated differently; Due Process claim failed to allege facts showing deficient process despite available remedies; Fourth Amendment claim lacked standing as mere property ownership is insufficient to establish privacy interest; Eighth Amendment claim inapplicable to non-criminal context; § 1982 retaliation claim lacked causal connection between protected activity and adverse action; remaining claims were conclusory without specific factual allegations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: No FHA claims alleged. Plaintiff references Fair Housing Act in context of alleged murder by police officer but does not assert any FHA-based claim for relief.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed complaint under § 1915(e)(2)(B) for failure to state a claim under Iqbal/Twombly standard. Plaintiff's complaint was incoherent and failed to identify any constitutional or federal statutory right allegedly violated by defendants acting under color of state law. The complaint referenced 18 U.S.C. § 1091 (federal genocide statute), which creates no private right of action and cannot support a § 1983 claim.

case_name: James Mims v. City of New Castle
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested; this case concerns alleged discriminatory enforcement of municipal building and rental inspection codes against the plaintiff's rental properties, and the City's refusal to consider the plaintiff's bid to purchase a tax repository property.
key_holding: The court granted the City of New Castle's motion to dismiss with prejudice, finding that all claims based on code enforcement were barred by the applicable two-year statutes of limitations and that claims based on the attempted repository property purchase failed to state a claim due to lack of a protected property interest and failure to identify similarly situated individuals.
brief_summary: James Mims, a landlord who owned rental properties in New Castle, Pennsylvania, sued the City alleging discriminatory enforcement of the building and rental inspection code against his properties from 2006 through 2019, and interference with his March 2020 attempt to purchase a repository property when the City Council tabled his purchase request. The court dismissed all counts, holding that the code enforcement claims under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1983, 1982, and the FHA were time-barred because all identified enforcement events predated November 18, 2018—two years before the initial complaint was filed—and Mims failed to identify any timely triggering event. The claims arising from the 2020 property purchase attempt were dismissed for failure to state a claim, as Mims had no protected property interest in the repository property and failed to allege the existence of any similarly situated individual for his equal protection claim.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Braun v. Gonzales, 557 F. App'x 176 (3d Cir. 2014)
Hill v. Borough of Kutztown, 455 F.3d 225 (3d Cir. 2006)
Board of Regents v. Roth, 408 U.S. 564 (1972)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (due process and equal protection); 42 U.S.C. § 1982 (property rights); state law abuse of process claim (voluntarily withdrawn)
fha_claims.reasoning: All § 1983 and § 1982 claims based on code enforcement citations, inspections, and occupancy permit denials occurring between 2004-2017 are time-barred under Pennsylvania's two-year statute of limitations, as the complaint was filed November 18, 2020, and no triggering events occurred after November 18, 2018. Claims based on the Repository Property purchase attempt in March 2020 fail because plaintiff lacks a protected property interest and fails to identify similarly situated individuals for equal protection analysis.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged discriminatory enforcement of rental inspection program and refusal to approve purchase of Repository Property
fha_claims.reasoning: Count V Fair Housing Act claim based on code enforcement actions is time-barred under 42 U.S.C. § 3613(a)(1)(A)'s two-year statute of limitations, as all alleged discriminatory acts occurred prior to November 18, 2018. The complaint does not identify any code enforcement citations, failed inspection reports, or occupancy permit denials occurring after the limitations period.

case_name: United States of America v. Perry Homes, Inc., Allyson Whittington, and Robert Whittington
accommodation_description: Request to keep emotional support animals in rental housing, which defendants allegedly refused.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss the 3604(f)(3)(B) failure to accommodate claim, finding that fair housing organizations can use fictional testers to advance FHA purposes, but also rejected the magistrate's recommendation to dismiss 3604(f)(1) and (f)(2) claims, effectively allowing most claims to proceed.
brief_summary: The United States brought suit on behalf of Southwestern Pennsylvania Legal Services against Perry Homes and individual defendants alleging they refused to allow emotional support animals in violation of the FHA. The court adopted the magistrate's recommendation to deny defendants' motion to dismiss the 3604(c) and 3604(f)(3)(B) claims, but rejected the recommendation to dismiss 3604(f)(1) and (f)(2) claims, allowing those claims to proceed.
key_cases_cited: Reyes v. Waples Mobile Home Park Ltd. P'ship, 903 F.3d 415 (4th Cir. 2018)
Swierkiewicz v. Sorema N.A., 534 U.S. 506 (2002)
Connelly v. Lane Constr. Corp., 809 F.3d 780 (3d Cir. 2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to allow emotional support animals
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiff sufficiently pleaded a § 3604(c) discrimination claim based on defendants' refusal to allow emotional support animals, which constitutes a preference, limitation, or discrimination based on handicap. Claim survives motion to dismiss at the pleading stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to accommodate test callers' reported disabilities by refusing to allow emotional support animals
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that fair housing organizations may use fictional testers to advance FHA purposes, and plaintiff adequately pleaded a § 3604(f)(3)(B) failure to accommodate claim. Claim survives motion to dismiss despite defendants' argument that no actual disabled person was injured.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to accommodate under § 3604(f)(1) and (f)(2) (specific accommodations not detailed in opinion)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that plaintiff need not specify whether claims proceed under disparate treatment or disparate impact theory at the pleading stage; Twombly standard requires only enough facts to raise reasonable expectation that discovery will reveal evidence of necessary elements. Allegations in amended complaint are sufficient to survive motion to dismiss.

case_name: United States of America v. LRG Corporation, Lewis R. Gainfort
accommodation_description: Request for an emotional support animal (dog named Onyx) for Monica Samulski's son Sabastian to accommodate his disability-related needs
key_holding: The court resolved evidentiary disputes before trial, granting the United States' motions to exclude evidence regarding school accommodation requests, the defendant's updated policies, HUD investigation challenges, other tenants' accommodation requests, and evidence of a prior civil suit, while limiting evidence of the ESA's barking to impeachment purposes.
brief_summary: The United States sued LRG Corporation and its owner alleging they violated the Fair Housing Act by refusing to approve tenant Monica Samulski's request for an emotional support animal for her son Sabastian and then evicting her for having the ESA in February 2019. The court resolved pre-trial motions in limine, granting most of the United States' requests to exclude irrelevant or prejudicial evidence while denying LRG's motion to preclude emotional distress damages as premature.
key_cases_cited: Revock v. Cowpet Bay W. Condo. Ass'n, 853 F.3d 96 (3d Cir. 2017)
Anderson v. City of Blue Ash, 798 F.3d 338 (6th Cir. 2015)
United States v. Greenidge, 495 F.3d 85 (3d Cir. 2007)
Regents of Mercersburg Coll. v. Republic Franklin Ins. Co., 458 F.3d 159 (3d Cir. 2006)
Bolden v. Se. Pa. Transp. Auth., 21 F.3d 29 (3d Cir. 1994)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Emotional support animal (ESA)—a dog named Onyx—for plaintiff's son's mental health disability
fha_claims.reasoning: This opinion addresses only evidentiary motions in limine prior to trial. The underlying reasonable accommodation claim for the ESA has not been decided on the merits; the court is managing trial evidence and procedure. The claim survives and proceeds to trial.

case_name: Glagola v. MacFann
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; case involves quid pro quo sexual harassment (conditioning housing on sex) and hostile housing environment sexual harassment.
key_holding: The Court denied Defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that Plaintiff adequately stated claims for quid pro quo sexual harassment, hostile housing environment sexual harassment, discriminatory statements under § 3604(c), and claims under the Trafficking Victims Protection Act.
brief_summary: Alyssia Glagola sued Walter MacFann, Tri-County Realty Associates, L.P., and AMW Consulting, LLC alleging that Mr. MacFann conditioned free rent on sex and created a hostile housing environment through sexual harassment, stalking, and physical abuse. The Court denied Defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that Plaintiff adequately stated quid pro quo harassment, hostile environment claims, discriminatory statements under § 3604(c), and Trafficking Victims Protection Act claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Krueger v. Cuomo, 115 F.3d 487 (7th Cir. 1997)
Noah v. Assor, 379 F. Supp. 3d 1284 (S.D. Fla. 2019)
Richardson v. Nw. Univ., No. 21-522, 2023 WL 6197447 (N.D. Ill. 2023)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiff adequately pleaded quid pro quo sexual harassment under the FHA by alleging that landlord conditioned rent waiver/payment on submission to sexual demands, satisfying the plausibility standard under Iqbal/Twombly. The court rejected the magistrate judge's semantic distinction between 'waiving' and 'paying' rent and found that MacFann's authority to unilaterally change lease terms in exchange for sex stated a claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiff adequately pleaded hostile housing environment sexual harassment by alleging unwelcome conduct (sexual propositions, unwanted sexual messages, stalking behavior, physical trespasses, threats) that was sufficiently severe or pervasive to interfere with use and enjoyment of the dwelling. The totality of circumstances test was satisfied under the pleading standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiff adequately pleaded a claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c) for discriminatory statements by alleging that MacFann made sexually harassing statements in connection with the lease that an ordinary listener could find discriminatory based on sex. Sexual harassment statements can constitute discriminatory statements under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Trafficking Victims Protection Act (18 U.S.C. § 1589 forced labor; 18 U.S.C. § 1591 sex trafficking)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that plaintiff adequately pleaded forced labor and sex trafficking claims under the TVPA by alleging threats of serious harm (homelessness), actual and threatened force (grabbing, screwdriver threat), and a scheme or pattern of coercion to compel sexual services. The court rejected the narrow reading that the statute does not extend to rent-payment-for-sex arrangements.

case_name: Euripides Del Villar-Rosario v. Victor Roberto Fernandez-Ramos, et al.
accommodation_description: The complaint is too vague to identify a specific accommodation request; it broadly alleges housing violations including unauthorized entry, property destruction, and an eviction process in violation of § 3604 and other statutes.
key_holding: The complaint was dismissed sua sponte because it failed to state a plausible claim, as it contained only scant factual allegations without sufficient detail to give defendants fair notice of the claims against them.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Euripides Del Villar-Rosario filed a vague complaint against multiple defendants alleging housing violations including unauthorized apartment entry, property destruction with a machete, and an unauthorized eviction process in violation of § 3604 and numerous other statutes and constitutional provisions. The court dismissed the complaint sua sponte under § 1915(e)(2) and Rule 12(b)(6) because the allegations were wholly insufficient to establish a plausible claim or provide fair notice to defendants.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Gonzalez-Gonzalez v. United States

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged unlawful entry into apartment and destruction of property
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint alleged violations of § 3604 and multiple constitutional provisions but failed to plead sufficient factual matter to state a plausible claim. The allegations were too scant and conclusory to give defendants fair notice of the claim or allow the court to draw a reasonable inference of liability under the Iqbal/Twombly standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 due process, § 1981, § 1985, § 1986, ADA, Title VII, constitutional claims (First, Fourth, Fifth, Eighth, Thirteenth, Fourteenth Amendments), negligence, breach of contract
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA claims were dismissed for failure to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly. The complaint's allegations regarding alleged unlawful entry, destruction of property, and eviction proceedings were too vague and conclusory to satisfy Rule 8(a) pleading requirements or provide fair notice to defendants.

case_name: Carlos Erazo-Santana v. Constructora Del Río, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff's complaint references the Fair Housing Act among approximately a dozen federal statutes but does not articulate a specific reasonable accommodation request; the core dispute concerns whether an agreement constitutes a mortgage or sale at deferred price.
key_holding: The court granted Colorado River abstention, dismissing the federal case without prejudice because a parallel state court proceeding in Aibonito, Puerto Rico (Civil Case No. BCD 2018-0018) involves the same parties and substantially the same claims regarding the nature of the mortgage agreement.
brief_summary: Carlos Erazo-Santana filed this federal action against Constructora Del Río, Inc. and related defendants alleging violations of multiple federal statutes including the Fair Housing Act, Truth in Lending Act, and state law claims stemming from a mortgage loan transaction. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss based on Colorado River abstention, finding that a parallel state court proceeding in Aibonito, Puerto Rico (Constructora del Río Inc. v. Erazo Santana, Civ. No. BCD 2018-0018) involves the same parties and nearly identical claims regarding whether the agreement constitutes a mortgage or an agreement of sale at deferred price, and is further advanced in litigation.
key_cases_cited: Colorado River Water Conservation District v. United States, 424 U.S. 800 (1976)
Jiménez v. Rodríguez-Pagán, 597 F.3d 18 (1st Cir. 2010)
Moses H. Cone Mem. Hosp. v. Mercury Constr. Corp., 460 U.S. 1 (1983)
Kokkonen v. Guardian Life Ins. Co. of Am., 511 U.S. 375 (1994)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Truth in Lending Act, Equal Credit Opportunity Act, Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act, New Homeowners Protection Act, Nationwide Licensing System and Standards, Home Mortgage Disclosure Act, Community Reinvestment Act, Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, and other federal statutes related to mortgage lending and disclosure
fha_claims.disposition: Colorado River Abstention / Dismissal without Prejudice
fha_claims.reasoning: The court exercised Colorado River abstention based on a parallel state court proceeding (Aibonito case) involving substantially identical claims and remedies. The court found that factors favoring abstention—avoiding piecemeal litigation, relative progress of concurrent proceedings, state law control over contract interpretation, and the vexatious nature of duplicative filings—outweighed the federal court's obligation to exercise jurisdiction. The case was dismissed without prejudice.

source_file: 9953766_2021_Rodriguez-Luna v. Finance of America Mortgage LLC_prd
case_name: Francisco A. Rodriguez-Luna v. Finance of America Reverse, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that the mortgage servicer advance funds to pay property taxes and provide Spanish-speaking representative availability, framing these as FHA violations.
key_holding: The Fair Housing Act does not impose an obligation on mortgage servicers to retain Spanish-speaking representatives, and the servicer had no legal duty to advance funds for plaintiff's property taxes under the HECM agreement.
brief_summary: Francisco Rodriguez-Luna sued Finance of America Reverse, Compu-Link/Celink, and HUD alleging that the mortgage servicer violated the Fair Housing Act and other federal laws by failing to provide Spanish-speaking representatives and by not advancing funds to pay post-closing property taxes on his reverse mortgage. The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss, finding no legal basis for the claimed obligations and that the FHA does not require servicers to provide language accommodations where no discriminatory intent was alleged.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dept. of Housing v. Inclusive Communities Project, 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic v. Twombly

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Availability of Spanish-speaking representative to discuss mortgage servicing matters
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege a plausible FHA violation. The Fair Housing Act does not impose an obligation on mortgage servicers to retain Spanish-speaking representatives. Plaintiff did not allege that anyone refused his calls because of his national origin or Puerto Rico origin, only that calls were transferred between departments. Lack of Spanish-language service is a business practice issue, not an FHA violation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Advancement of funds for post-closing property taxes; face-to-face meeting within 200-mile radius; loss mitigation services; compliance with National Housing Act 24 C.F.R. § 203.604 and § 203.605; TILA and RESPA violations
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to state plausible claims under the National Housing Act, TILA, RESPA, and state tort law. The mortgage agreement clearly imposed the obligation to pay property taxes solely on plaintiff, not the servicer. Section 203.604(d) explicitly exempts servicers from face-to-face meeting requirements when the property is more than 200 miles away. Section 203.605 loss mitigation duties do not apply to reverse mortgages with no monthly installments. Plaintiff did not explain how TILA or RESPA were violated.

case_name: Gloria Rivera de Dávila v. Mora Development Corporation
accommodation_description: Rivera requested assignment of a handicap parking space near the second-floor elevator entrance to Tower I as a reasonable accommodation for her mobility disabilities including cardiac arrhythmia, limited mobility due to leg surgery, neuropathy, herniated discs, and osteoarthritis.
key_holding: A failure to respond to a reasonable accommodation request can constitute a constructive denial for purposes of stating a prima facie case, and the plaintiff adequately pled all four elements of a failure-to-accommodate claim under the FHA.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Gloria Rivera de Dávila sued Mora Development Corporation, the Condominium Torre Cibeles Board of Directors, and the Condominium Torre Cibeles Association alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on the defendants' failure to provide her a reasonable accommodation in the form of handicap parking near her Tower I residence. The court granted the Association's motion to dismiss the ADA claim (residential condominiums are not public accommodations) but denied the motion to dismiss the FHA reasonable accommodation claim, finding the plaintiff adequately alleged all elements of a prima facie case and that failure to respond to her accommodation requests constituted constructive denial.
key_cases_cited: Astralis Condo. Ass'n v. Sec'y, U.S. Dep't of Hous. & Urban Dev., 620 F.3d 62 (1st Cir. 2010)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ocasio-Hernández v. Fortuño-Burset, 640 F.3d 1 (1st Cir. 2011)
Salisbury v. Caritas Acquisitions V, LLC, 2018 WL 10483437 (C.D. Cal. 2018)
Salehi v. Lakeview Terrace Homeowners Assn., 2022 WL 3018063 (N.D. Cal. 2022)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Handicap parking space at the second-floor elevator entrance to Tower I of the condominium
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found Rivera pled sufficient facts to state a prima facie case for FHA reasonable accommodation claim under the four-element test (disability, defendant's knowledge, reasonable and necessary accommodation, refusal). Failure to respond to accommodation request can constitute constructive refusal; interactive process required. Claim survives motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Handicap parking space near Tower I entrance for Dávila (deceased husband); defendant offered space at Tower II entrance instead
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found allegations state prima facie case for Dávila's reasonable accommodation claim but expressed concern about statute of limitations timing. Dismissal inappropriate without clear allegation of when denial occurred; claim survives motion to dismiss pending clarification of temporal facts.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Policy or practice resulting in no designated handicap parking spaces at Tower I
fha_claims.reasoning: Court declined to analyze disparate impact theory at motion to dismiss stage because neither party briefed the issue. Court directed plaintiff to clearly spell out theories in future filings but did not dismiss the theory; claim remains pending clarification.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title III ADA claim for discrimination in public accommodations (parking area)
fha_claims.reasoning: Residential condominiums are not covered by Title III ADA as public accommodations. No commercial space alleged within the condominium. Dismissed without prejudice; plaintiff may amend if additional facts show ADA applicability.

case_name: Gloria Rivera De Davila v. Mora Development Corporation
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested accessible handicap parking at the second-floor door entrance to the elevator in Tower 1 of Torre Cibeles, and restoration of designated handicap parking spaces 172, 173, and 178.
key_holding: Mora Development Corporation could not have violated the FHAA because it ceased administering the property in 2014 and thus had no knowledge of plaintiff's disability status, no ability to receive or respond to accommodation requests, and no authority to provide any accommodation.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Gloria Rivera De Davila sued Mora Development Corporation, the developer of Torre Cibeles condominium, alleging Fair Housing Act violations for the sale of designated handicap parking spaces and failure to provide reasonable accommodations for her disability. On reconsideration, the Court granted Mora's motion to dismiss with prejudice because Mora ceased administering the property in 2014, making it impossible for Mora to have knowledge of plaintiff's disability, receive her accommodation requests, or provide any accommodation.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Astralis Condominium Ass'n v. Secretary, U.S. Dept. of Housing & Urban Development, 620 F.3d 62 (1st Cir. 2010)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible handicap parking spaces (172, 173, and 178) at the second-floor door entrance to the elevator in Tower 1 of Torre Cibeles condominium
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead a prima facie case of reasonable accommodation discrimination under the FHAA because: (1) Mora ceased administration of the building in 2014 and could not have known of plaintiff's disabled status when she requested accommodation in 2021; (2) plaintiff never requested accommodation from Mora after the parking space sales; and (3) Mora could not refuse an accommodation it had no ability to provide. The complaint contains only conclusory allegations without factual support for how the sale of designated handicap spaces violates the FHAA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III claims regarding accessible parking and reasonable accommodations
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's ADA Title III claims were dismissed in a prior order (Docket No. 101) for failure to state a claim. The court noted that plaintiff largely relied on ADA allegations to frame her claims but those claims were not viable.

case_name: United States of America v. Maria Trini Menendez, et al.
accommodation_description: Request to rent an apartment with a service dog despite the property's no-pet policy, by a legally blind tenant
key_holding: The court denied the De La Fuente defendants' motion for summary judgment because genuine disputes of material fact exist as to whether defendants actually refused the accommodation request and whether their subsequent offer to rent the apartment came only after HUD conciliation proceedings rather than promptly upon learning of the service dog.
brief_summary: The United States sued property owners and their real estate agent on behalf of a legally blind woman who was denied the ability to rent an apartment because of her service dog, alleging violation of the Fair Housing Act's reasonable accommodation provision. The court denied the defendants' motion for summary judgment, finding genuine factual disputes about whether they refused the accommodation and whether their later offer to rent came only after HUD proceedings rather than promptly upon learning of the service dog.
key_cases_cited: Bryant Woods Inn, Inc. v. Howard Cnty., Md., 124 F.3d 597 (4th Cir. 1997)
Castillo Condo. Ass'n v. U.S. Dep't of Housing & Urban Dev., 821 F.3d 92 (1st Cir. 2016)
Rivera v. Mora Development Corporation, 624 F. Supp.3d 80 (D.P.R. 2022)
Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986)
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation to allow complainant Fernández-Montero, who is legally blind, to keep a service dog in a rental apartment despite the landlord's no-pet policy
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether defendants actually denied the accommodation and the timing of any subsequent offer. The court held that under FHA, a violation occurs when a disabled resident is first denied reasonable accommodation, irrespective of remedies granted later, and that failure to accommodate can be inferred even without explicit denial. The defendants' initial refusal to rent due to the no-pet policy, followed by a delayed offer only after HUD complaint and conciliation, presents factual disputes precluding summary judgment for defendants.

case_name: Stack v. Kuligowski
accommodation_description: Request for transfer to a larger unit to accommodate disabled son who came to live with plaintiff
key_holding: Court granted limited-purpose appointment of counsel to assess whether plaintiff or his disabled son has a viable fair housing claim arising from LHA's refusal to transfer to a larger unit, finding the complaint too vague to assess merits but sufficient circumstances warranting limited counsel.
brief_summary: Kurt Z. Stack sued the Town of Lincoln Housing Authority alleging violations of the FHA, ADA, and IDEA based on LHA's refusal to transfer him to a larger unit after his disabled son came to live with him; the court granted limited appointment of counsel for the narrow purpose of assessing claim viability and drafting an amended complaint, finding the current complaint too vague to survive a motion to dismiss.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
DesRosiers v. Moran, 949 F.2d 15 (1st Cir. 1991)
R.I. Comm'n for Human Rights v. Graul, 120 F. Supp. 3d 110 (D.R.I. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Transfer to a larger unit to accommodate plaintiff's disabled son who came to live with him
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint is utterly lacking in plausible factual allegations required under Twombly and is at serious risk of dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6). The court found the complaint so vague that it is impossible to ascertain what plaintiff is alleging, though based on hearing representations, plaintiff may potentially have a viable disparate impact claim under Graul.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II and IDEA claims related to failure to accommodate disabled son
fha_claims.reasoning: The complaint fails to state plausible claims under the ADA and IDEA due to lack of factual allegations. The court found the complaint conclusory and at serious risk of dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6) for failure to meet Twombly pleading standards.

case_name: Clinton-Brown v. Hardick
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged defendant refused to sell real property because one buyer was African American, constituting racial discrimination in housing.
key_holding: The court lacks personal jurisdiction over Florida-resident defendants who owned Rhode Island property in Massachusetts, and venue was improper, so the case was transferred to the District of Rhode Island pursuant to 28 U.S.C. §§ 1631 and 1406(a).
brief_summary: Ebony Clinton-Brown and Todd Brown sued Helene and John Hardick alleging the Hardicks refused to sell them a Rhode Island property because Ms. Clinton-Brown is African American, in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The Hardicks moved to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction and improper venue. The court granted the motion in part, finding it lacked personal jurisdiction over the Florida-resident defendants and that venue was improper in Massachusetts, but transferred the case to the District of Rhode Island rather than dismissing it.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Burger King Corp. v. Rudzewicz
Atlantic Marine Const. Co. v. U.S. Dist. Ct. for W. Dist. of Texas
Leroy v. Great Western United Corp.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked personal jurisdiction over the defendants under the Massachusetts long-arm statute and Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 4(f) because the defendants' contacts with Massachusetts were insufficient and the alleged discriminatory conduct (refusal to sell based on race) occurred in Rhode Island. The case was transferred to the District of Rhode Island rather than dismissed.

case_name: Trenda Taylor and Rhode Island Commission for Human Rights v. National Investments, Ltd., et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; case involves claims of racial discrimination in housing recertification and retaliation for complaints about racial discrimination.
key_holding: The court found genuine disputes of material fact exist as to whether defendant landlord's refusal to process plaintiff's Section 8 recertification and subsequent adverse actions were motivated by race rather than legitimate non-discriminatory reasons, and whether retaliation for complaints of racial discrimination played a but-for causal role.
brief_summary: Trenda Taylor, an African American tenant with Section 8 project-based housing assistance, sued her landlord alleging racial discrimination in refusing to process her income recertification paperwork and retaliation for complaining about that discrimination. The court denied both parties' cross-motions for summary judgment on the discrimination and retaliation claims, finding genuine disputes of material fact exist regarding whether the landlord's stated race-neutral reasons were pretextual, but granted summary judgment for the landlord on Taylor's claim that HUD regulations created an implied private right of action.
key_cases_cited: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Reg'l Econ. Cmty. Action Program, Inc. v. City of Middletown, 294 F.3d 35 (2d Cir. 2002)
Wetzel v. Glen St. Andrew Living Cmty., LLC, 901 F.3d 856 (7th Cir. 2018)
University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center v. Nassar, 570 U.S. 338 (2013)
Gross v. FBL Fin. Servs., Inc., 557 U.S. 167 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rent reduction during interim and annual recertifications based on job loss and income decrease
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff established prima facie disparate treatment by showing she was denied rent recertification while similarly situated white women received recertifications despite incomplete forms; genuine dispute of material fact exists as to whether defendants' proffered race-neutral reasons (income verification requirements) are pretextual.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rent reduction during interim and annual recertifications based on job loss and income decrease under RIFHPA
fha_claims.reasoning: Under Rhode Island Fair Housing Practices Act, plaintiff established prima facie disparate treatment; genuine dispute of material fact exists as to pretext, applying same McDonnell Douglas framework as FHA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to process recertification paperwork, calling police and seeking temporary restraining order, issuing non-compliance notice and pursuing eviction
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff established prima facie retaliation under FHA § 3617 by showing protected activity (complaints of racial discrimination), adverse actions (refusal to process paperwork, police call, eviction), and causal connection; defendants' proffered non-retaliatory reasons contradicted by their own documentation showing complaints of discrimination were the driving cause.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to process recertification paperwork, calling police and seeking temporary restraining order, issuing non-compliance notice and pursuing eviction under RIFHPA
fha_claims.reasoning: Under RIFHPA anti-retaliation provisions, plaintiff established prima facie case with same three elements as FHA claim; genuine dispute of material fact exists as to whether defendants acted in retaliation for discrimination complaints.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VI of Civil Rights Act of 1964, Rhode Island Civil Rights Act of 1990, Rhode Island Fair Housing Practices Act (disparate treatment claims)
fha_claims.reasoning: Title VI and RICRA disparate treatment claims analyzed under same McDonnell Douglas framework as FHA; genuine dispute of material fact exists as to pretext for defendants' actions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1437f (Section 8 Housing Program) - alleged violation of rent recertification and hardship exemption regulations
fha_claims.reasoning: No implied private right of action exists under 42 U.S.C. § 1437f or its implementing regulations; applying Cort v. Ash four-factor test, statute focuses on obligations of entities receiving federal funds rather than rights of beneficiaries, and Supreme Court disfavors implying private remedies in regulatory statutes.

case_name: Madeliene Y. Jeffreys v. Marcia L. Fudge, Secretary of U.S. Housing & Urban Development, et al.
accommodation_description: Request for renewal of live-in aide certification to assist disabled daughter and grandson in Section 8 housing program, which was denied after the WHA allegedly failed to provide a replacement medical form despite multiple requests.
key_holding: The court dismissed HUD from the case, declined to dismiss the Woonsocket Housing Authority and Ms. Ferri despite caption deficiencies, dismissed the Fair Housing Act claim for lack of private right of action, but allowed the § 1983 due process claim to proceed based on allegations that the WHA obstructed the live-in aide recertification process.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Madeliene Jeffreys, who served as a live-in aide for her disabled daughter and grandson in Section 8 housing, sued HUD, the Woonsocket Housing Authority, and a WHA employee after her recertification was denied when the WHA allegedly withheld a medical form and refused alternative documentation. The court granted HUD's motion to dismiss for failure to allege facts connecting HUD to the claimed wrongdoing, declined to dismiss the WHA and Ms. Ferri despite caption deficiencies, dismissed the FHA claim for lack of private right of action, but allowed the § 1983 procedural due process claim to proceed.
key_cases_cited: UNDETERMINED

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Certification and recertification as a live-in aide for plaintiff's disabled daughter and grandson in Section 8 housing
fha_claims.disposition: Dismissed for lack of private right of action under FHA
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968 (FHA) does not establish a private right of action for money damages, and therefore dismissed plaintiff's direct FHA claim. The court noted that while the FHA regulations require PHAs to approve live-in aides as reasonable accommodations, the FHA itself provides no private remedy.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 due process claim; deprivation of property interest in continued Section 8 housing assistance and live-in-aide status through obstruction of recertification process
fha_claims.disposition: Survives motion to dismiss; case proceeds against properly named defendants
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that plaintiff stated a plausible § 1983 due process claim by alleging that the WHA obstructed the recertification process by refusing to provide a duplicate form while insisting documentation be submitted on that withheld form, combined with allegations of false evidence and an arbitrary deadline. The court found a sufficient property interest in continued Section 8 assistance to warrant due process protection.

case_name: Scott Ellis, Jr. v. Jackie Alvarez
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a transgender woman, allegedly requested that defendant refer to her by her preferred name 'Hope' rather than her legal name 'Scott'; no specific disability-related accommodation request was clearly articulated in the complaint.
key_holding: The court recommended dismissal because plaintiff's complaint failed to comply with Rule 8 pleading standards, did not allege sufficient facts to support any Fair Housing Act theory (disparate treatment, disparate impact, or reasonable accommodation), and failed to establish a basis for the claimed $50,000 in damages.
brief_summary: Scott Ellis, Jr. sued Jackie Alvarez and JJ Property Management alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on defendant's alleged discriminatory behavior regarding her preferred name and a text message about parking. The court recommended summary dismissal under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2), finding the complaint failed to state a cognizable FHA claim because plaintiff failed to allege sufficient factual matter to support any recognized theory of housing discrimination.
key_cases_cited: Batista v. Cooperativa De Vivienda Jardines De San Ignacio, 776 F.3d 38 (1st Cir. 2015)
Neitzke v. Williams, 490 U.S. 319 (1989)
Estelle v. Gamble, 429 U.S. 97 (1976)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged discrimination based on failure to use preferred name (Hope instead of Scott) and alleged passive-aggressive behavior by defendant.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the complaint as frivolous and failing to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B) because plaintiff failed to allege facts that might reasonably support a housing discrimination claim based on defendant's failure to use plaintiff's preferred name. The court found that while such behavior was insensitive and disrespectful, it did not constitute actionable housing discrimination under the Fair Housing Act.

case_name: Little Tom Childress, Jr. v. Rebecca Roberts, Babbie M. Jaco, and Boyd Management LTD
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation requested; case involves claims of racial harassment and hostile housing environment based on race under § 3604(a)
key_holding: The court denied Defendants' motion for summary judgment because a reasonable jury could find that Plaintiff, an African American tenant, was subjected to racially hostile housing environment conduct that was sufficiently severe or pervasive to alter his housing conditions under § 3604(a).
brief_summary: Little Tom Childress, Jr., an African American tenant at West End Manor apartment complex in Union, South Carolina, sued property manager Rebecca Roberts and Boyd Management LTD alleging racial harassment and a hostile housing environment in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The court denied Defendants' motion for summary judgment, finding genuine issues of material fact exist as to whether Roberts' alleged racially discriminatory statements and differential treatment were sufficiently severe or pervasive to create an abusive housing environment.
key_cases_cited: Smith v. Town of Clarkton, N.C., 682 F.2d 1055 (4th Cir. 1982)
Williams v. Poretsky Memt., Inc., 955 F. Supp. 490 (D. Md. 1996)
DiCenso v. Cisneros, 96 F.3d 1004 (7th Cir. 1996)
Honce v. Vigil, 1 F.3d 1085 (10th Cir. 1993)
Boyer-Liberto v. Fontainebleau Corp., 786 F.3d 264 (4th Cir. 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that a reasonable jury could conclude that Childress was subjected to racial harassment that was sufficiently severe and pervasive to alter his housing conditions and create an abusive environment, satisfying all four elements of a hostile housing environment claim under the FHA: unwelcome conduct, based on race, severe or pervasive, and imputable to defendants. The cumulative effect of multiple race-based incidents in 2015, including racial slurs and discriminatory statements, created a genuine issue of material fact precluding summary judgment.

source_file: 9956870_2020_United States v. Irmo South Carolina, Town of_scd
case_name: United States of America v. Town of Irmo, South Carolina
accommodation_description: Patricia Witt requested a zoning variance to build a carport on her property to accommodate her physical disability.
key_holding: The court granted in part Plaintiff's Motion to Compel, ordering Defendant Town of Irmo to produce documents in native electronic format, provide discovery spanning five years, and supply an adequate privilege log conforming to Rule 26(b)(5).
brief_summary: The United States sued the Town of Irmo, South Carolina on behalf of homeowner Patricia Witt, alleging the municipality violated the Fair Housing Act by improperly refusing to provide a reasonable accommodation or modification when denying her petition for a zoning variance to build a carport to accommodate her physical disability. This order addresses Plaintiff's Motion to Compel discovery, with the court granting most of the relief sought regarding ESI format, scope of production, and privilege log deficiencies, while denying the motion only as to Interrogatory No. 13.
key_cases_cited: Nat’l Union Fire Ins. Co. v. Murray Sheet Metal Co., Inc., 967 F.2d 980 (4th Cir. 1992)
Hagenbuch v. 3B6 Sistemi Elettronici Industriali S.R.L., 2006 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 10838 (N.D. Ill. Mar. 8, 2006)
AVX Corp. v. Horry Land Co., Inc., 2010 WL 4884903 (D.S.C. Nov. 24, 2010)
Victor Stanley, Inc. v. Creative Pipe, Inc., 250 F.R.D. 251 (D. Md. 2008)
Nationwide Mut. Fire Ins. Co. v. Kelt, Inc., 2015 WL 1470971 (M.D. Fla. Mar. 31, 2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Zoning variance to build a carport on residential property to accommodate plaintiff Patricia Witt's physical disability
fha_claims.reasoning: This opinion addresses only discovery disputes (motion to compel) regarding the underlying FHA reasonable accommodation claim. The court did not reach the merits of whether the Town of Irmo unlawfully refused to provide a reasonable accommodation for the zoning variance. The case remains pending on the substantive FHA claim.

source_file: 9957341_2020_United States v. Irmo South Carolina, Town of_scd
case_name: United States of America v. Town of Irmo, South Carolina
accommodation_description: Patricia Witt, a homeowner with mobility disabilities including four hip surgeries in one year, sought a zoning variance to build a carport covering her mobility ramp and a portion of her driveway for safety and accessibility.
key_holding: Both parties' cross-motions for summary judgment were denied because genuine disputes of material fact exist regarding whether the carport modification is necessary to afford Ms. Witt equal opportunity to use and enjoy her dwelling, and the court rejected Irmo's mootness argument because a violation occurred at the time of the initial denial.
brief_summary: The United States sued the Town of Irmo, South Carolina, alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act when the municipality denied homeowner Patricia Witt's zoning variance request to build a carport covering her disability-related mobility ramp. The court denied both parties' cross-motions for summary judgment, finding genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether the carport was necessary and reasonable to afford Ms. Witt equal opportunity to use and enjoy her home, and that Irmo's subsequent ordinance change did not moot the claim because a violation occurred at the time of denial.
key_cases_cited: Bryant Woods Inn, Inc. v. Howard Cty., Md., 124 F.3d 597 (4th Cir. 1997)
Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986)
Anderson v. Liberty Lobby Inc., 477 U.S. 242 (1986)
Scoggins v. Lee's Crossing Homeowners Ass'n, 718 F.3d 262 (4th Cir. 2013)
Oxford House, Inc. v. City of Raleigh, 1999 WL 1940013 (E.D.N.C. 1999)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Zoning variance to permit construction of a 24-foot by 11-foot carport with attached ramp to cover mobility ramp and driveway, to protect Ms. Witt from slippery surfaces due to her mobility disability (four hip surgeries, knee replacement needed, use of walker and cane, history of falls).
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the three-pronged Bryant Woods Inn test (reasonable, necessary, equal opportunity) and found genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether the carport as designed would have an ameliorative effect on Ms. Witt's disability and the degree of benefit it would provide. The court found the reasonableness element satisfied (no undue financial/administrative burden, no fundamental alteration), but could not resolve the necessity and equal opportunity elements without speculation, requiring denial of both parties' summary judgment motions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable modification under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(A) to permit Ms. Witt to make modifications to her existing premises (carport construction) at her own expense.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court noted that the elements for establishing a prima facie case of discrimination for failure to permit a reasonable modification under § 3604(f)(3)(A) are the same as for failure to grant a reasonable accommodation under § 3604(f)(3)(B), and therefore did not provide separate analysis. The claim survives summary judgment on the same basis as the reasonable accommodation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination because of disability in violation of 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(2).
fha_claims.reasoning: The court did not separately analyze the disparate treatment claim; the opinion focuses on the reasonable accommodation and reasonable modification theories under § 3604(f)(3)(A) and (B). The claim survives summary judgment as part of the overall denial of both parties' motions.

case_name: Flordeliza A. Hawkins v. Court of Common Pleas of Anderson South Carolina
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation was requested; Plaintiff made vague Fair Housing Act allegations (insufficient to identify a discrete accommodation request) in connection with a state court foreclosure and eviction proceeding.
key_holding: The court dismissed the case without service of process because the Rooker-Feldman doctrine barred federal review of the state foreclosure judgment, § 1983 claims failed for lack of proper defendants, and the Fair Housing Act allegations (§ 3617) were insufficient to state a plausible claim.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Flordeliza Hawkins filed a civil rights complaint arising from a state court foreclosure action, naming the Anderson County Court of Common Pleas, Suntrust Bank, and Joseph Partain as defendants. The court adopted the Magistrate Judge's recommendation and dismissed the action, finding that the Rooker-Feldman doctrine precluded federal review of the state court foreclosure judgment, that no named defendant was amenable to suit under § 1983, and that any Fair Housing Act allegations under § 3617 were insufficient to state a plausible claim. The court also denied Plaintiff's request for appointment of counsel and found that amendment would be futile.
key_cases_cited: Lance v. Dennis, 546 U.S. 459
Smalley v. Shapiro & Burson, LLP, 526 F. Appx. 231
Parker v. Spencer, No. 4:13-cv-00430-RBH
Will v. Mich. Dep't of State Police, 491 U.S. 58

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged Fair Housing Act § 3617 retaliation claim; specific accommodation not identified
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiff's Fair Housing Act § 3617 retaliation assertions insufficient to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly, noting that although plaintiff alleged her adult son is disabled, she failed to assert that any defendant acted adversely due to protected activity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 civil rights claims arising from state court foreclosure action
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied Rooker-Feldman doctrine to preclude federal review of state court foreclosure judgment; additionally, § 1983 claims failed because the Court of Common Pleas is not a 'person' subject to suit, judges are entitled to judicial immunity, and neither Suntrust Bank nor Joseph Partain are state actors as required by § 1983.

case_name: Reaves v. Evans
accommodation_description: No disability-related accommodation request; complaint alleges racial discrimination in enforcement of a trash policy and wrongful eviction.
key_holding: Plaintiffs' discrimination claims were summarily dismissed because their conclusory allegations lacked sufficient factual matter to state a plausible claim, and the private landlord defendants could not be held liable under § 1983 as they did not act under color of state law.
brief_summary: Pro se tenants sued their private landlord, property management company, and other defendants alleging racial discrimination in enforcement of a trash policy and wrongful eviction. The court recommended dismissal of claims against Clemson University and the Florence County Sheriff's Office based on insufficient allegations and sovereign immunity, dismissed § 1983 claims against private landlords for failure to state state action, and found plaintiffs' conclusory discrimination allegations insufficient to survive dismissal.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Rooker v. Fidelity Trust Co.
District of Columbia Court of Appeals v. Feldman
Monell v. Dep't of Soc. Servs.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged various constitutional violations (Thirteenth and Fourth Amendment), Civil Rights Act of 1964, Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act 1968, § 1983 due process claims, § 1988 attorneys' fees, 18 U.S.C. § 873 (blackmail/extortion), and state law claims including discrimination, conspiracy, breach of contract, and property damage.
fha_claims.disposition: Recommended for summary dismissal under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed all claims as frivolous or lacking arguable basis in law or fact. Constitutional claims against private defendants failed because they are not state actors under § 1983. § 873 claims failed because no private right of action exists. Discrimination claims were conclusory without factual support. Conspiracy claims lacked concrete facts of mutual understanding. § 1988 claim failed because pro se litigants cannot recover attorneys' fees. State law claims were dismissed for lack of supplemental jurisdiction after federal claims failed.

case_name: Stewart R. Buchanan a/k/a Daphne Renee' Stewart v. JumpStart South Carolina; Michael Scharff; Daniel Sulton; Bob Caldwell; Sharon McDowell; Chris Phillips; Chuck Fields; Tommy Holt; Mike Kiriakides; Chris Urban; Tommy Moore; Casey Sanders; David Johnson; NFN Beard; Bryan Stirling; Larry Epps; Charles Williams; Willie Davis
accommodation_description: Inmate discharged from prison re-entry program employment and denied state-assisted housing opportunities allegedly due to his transgender status
key_holding: The court adopted the R&R denying JumpStart defendants' motion to dismiss (claims against defendants in official capacities survive) and denying Buchanan's motion for default judgment, dismissing claims against JumpStart Board defendants in their individual capacities for failure to allege personal participation in constitutional violations.
brief_summary: An inmate at Perry Correctional Institution sued JumpStart South Carolina (a private nonprofit operating a Christian religious re-entry program in prison) and various officials, alleging violations of civil rights, constitutional rights, Title VII, and the Fair Housing Act after he was discharged from program employment and denied housing opportunities due to his transgender status. The court adopted the magistrate's recommendation to deny JumpStart's motion to dismiss (allowing official-capacity claims to proceed) and deny Buchanan's motion for default judgment (dismissing individual-capacity claims against board defendants for insufficient personal participation).
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Baynard v. Malone, 268 F.3d 228 (4th Cir. 2001)
Shaw v. Stroud, 13 F.3d 791 (4th Cir. 1994)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged violations under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1985, 1986 (conspiracy to violate civil rights); 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (First and Fourteenth Amendment violations); Title VII of the Civil Rights Act; Fair Housing Act; and South Carolina statutory and constitutional law. The opinion does not substantively analyze the FHA claim or any specific accommodation request.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court adopted the Magistrate Judge's recommendation to deny the JumpStart defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that Buchanan plausibly alleged the defendants were state actors or had been delegated statutory government authority. The FHA claim was not separately analyzed on the merits; it survives the motion to dismiss along with the other claims.

source_file: 9962351_2023_South Carolina State Conference of NAACP v. South Carolina Department of Juvenile Justice_scd

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Various accommodations and services for juveniles with disabilities in state custody, including accessible conditions and disability-related services
fha_claims.reasoning: The court reversed the magistrate judge's recommendation to dismiss for lack of standing, finding that organizational plaintiffs (NAACP, DRSC, Justice 360) had alleged concrete and particularized injuries—diversion of resources and impairment of advocacy activities—caused by alleged violations of the ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and IDEA, and that such injuries were redressable by favorable judicial decision. The court rejected the magistrate's requirement that organizational injuries must align with interests protected by the underlying statutes.

source_file: 9963465_2023_South Carolina State Conference of the NAACP v. Georgetown County_scd
case_name: South Carolina State Conference of the NAACP v. Georgetown County
accommodation_description: This is a zoning denial case, not a reasonable accommodation case—the NAACP and developers allege Georgetown County denied rezoning for an affordable housing development (Porter's Landing) based on racial discrimination.
key_holding: The court denied the motion to dismiss, finding that Plaintiffs sufficiently alleged standing, plausibly stated disparate treatment and disparate impact claims under the FHA, and adequately pled that Defendants' denial of the zoning application was motivated by discriminatory intent with substantial disparate impact on Black households.
brief_summary: NAACP organizations and developers FourSix Development and We Do Good Work sued Georgetown County, alleging the County's denial of a zoning application for Porter's Landing, an affordable housing development, violated the Fair Housing Act and constitutional guarantees by perpetuating racial segregation. The court denied Defendants' motion to dismiss, finding Plaintiffs adequately alleged standing and stated plausible claims for disparate treatment, disparate impact, and perpetuation of segregation.
key_cases_cited: Arlington Heights v. Metro. Hous. Dev. Corp., 429 U.S. 252 (1977)
Tex. Dept. of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Cmtys. Project, 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Warth v. Seldin, 422 U.S. 490 (1975)
Monell v. Dep't of Soc. Svcs., 436 U.S. 658 (1978)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs plausibly alleged discriminatory intent under the Iqbal/Twombly standard by alleging racially coded language by Council members, intense public opposition characterized by racist euphemism, and departures from the County's regular zoning practices. The Court found sufficient circumstantial evidence of discriminatory purpose to survive the motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: At the motion to dismiss stage, Plaintiffs satisfied step one of the disparate impact burden-shifting framework by demonstrating a robust causal connection between the County's denial of the zoning application and disparate impact on Black residents through statistical evidence showing Black residents are nearly eight times as likely as White renters to receive subsidized housing support.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs' perpetuation of segregation claim, characterized as an alternate avenue of pleading disparate impact, survived the motion to dismiss. Plaintiffs plausibly alleged using statistical evidence that the County's denial prevented racial integration that Porter's Landing would have provided and that the policy perpetuates segregated housing patterns.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment), 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 and 1982
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs' § 1983 Equal Protection claim survived because they plausibly alleged discriminatory intent and a causal connection between the County's zoning decision and the alleged injury, satisfying Monell's requirement of an official policy or custom. Plaintiffs' §§ 1981 and 1982 claims survived because they satisfied the § 1983 requirement of an official policy or custom of discrimination, as required by the Fourth Circuit in Dennis v. County of Fairfax.

case_name: Powers Properties v. Partee
accommodation_description: The specific accommodation is not described in detail in this order; Partee raised disability discrimination counterclaims referencing her son's disabilities (as evidenced by her 'Evidence of Support' filing) and asserted claims under the Fair Housing Act, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act in the context of a landlord-initiated eviction proceeding.
key_holding: A tenant-defendant's federal counterclaims for disability discrimination under the Fair Housing Act, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act cannot serve as the basis for removal jurisdiction under the well-pleaded complaint rule, and the case must be remanded to state court for lack of subject matter jurisdiction.
brief_summary: Powers Properties filed a rent/eviction action against tenant Shasta Partee in Richland County Magistrate Court. Partee, proceeding pro se, removed the case to federal court, asserting federal counterclaims for disability discrimination (based on her son's disabilities) under the Fair Housing Act, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act, as well as retaliation. The district court adopted the Magistrate Judge's Report and Recommendation, overruled Partee's objections, and remanded the matter to state court, holding that under the well-pleaded complaint rule a defendant's federal counterclaims cannot confer federal question jurisdiction, and that Partee failed to establish diversity jurisdiction.
key_cases_cited: Holmes Group, Inc. v. Vornado Air Circulation Sys., Inc., 535 U.S. 826 (2002)
Mathews v. Weber, 423 U.S. 261 (1976)
In re Shell Oil Co., 932 F.2d 1518 (5th Cir. 1991)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Disability discrimination claims under Fair Housing Act, ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and retaliation
fha_claims.disposition: Remand for lack of subject matter jurisdiction
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked federal question jurisdiction because the FHA and other federal claims were raised as counterclaims in a state eviction action, which cannot serve as a basis for removal under the well-pleaded complaint rule. The court also lacked diversity jurisdiction because the defendant was a South Carolina citizen and failed to allege damages exceeding $75,000 or establish complete diversity.

case_name: Shasta Partee v. Power Properties
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested additional time (30-60 days) to vacate her apartment so her son could receive medical treatment for his mental health conditions.
key_holding: The court dismissed the FHA failure to accommodate claim because Partee failed to allege that the requested delay would directly ameliorate her son's mental impairments or ensure the safety of other residents, as required under the Bryant Woods Inn standard.
brief_summary: Shasta Partee, proceeding pro se, sued Power Properties alleging the landlord failed to provide reasonable accommodation for her son's mental health disability by refusing to delay her eviction, and engaged in retaliation and discriminatory terms and conditions. The court dismissed the failure to accommodate claim because Partee failed to allege the accommodation would directly ameliorate her son's disability effects, but allowed her retaliation and discriminatory terms and conditions claims to proceed.
key_cases_cited: Bryant Woods Inn, Inc. v. Howard County, 124 F.3d 597 (4th Cir. 1997)
Lapid-Laurel, L.L.C. v. Zoning Bd. of Adjustment of Twp. of Scotch Plains, 284 F.3d 442 (3d Cir. 2002)
Winter v. Nat. Res. Def. Council, Inc., 555 U.S. 7 (2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Delay in removal/eviction to allow plaintiff's son to obtain mental health treatment and medication adjustment from his medical provider
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege that the requested accommodation (delay in eviction) would directly ameliorate the effect of her son's mental impairments or ensure the safety of other residents. Under Bryant Woods Inn, an accommodation that provides no direct amelioration of the disability's effect cannot be 'necessary' under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court determined that plaintiff's retaliation claim, including allegations that filing a fair housing complaint was followed by forced early rent payment, removal of online payment ability, and delayed maintenance, is best adjudicated at the summary judgment stage and survives the motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discriminatory terms and conditions of rental, including forced early rent payment and removal of online payment ability
fha_claims.reasoning: The court deferred substantive discussion of the discriminatory terms and conditions claim to the summary judgment stage because the retaliation claim will move forward and the claims are interrelated. The claim survives the motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Intentional infliction of emotional distress (state tort); breach of contract; perjury; civil conspiracy to commit perjury and perjury by omission; civil conspiracy to commit infliction of emotional distress; ADA Title II, 42 U.S.C. § 12101 et seq.; Rehabilitation Act, 29 U.S.C. § 701 et seq.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's allegations of intentional infliction of emotional distress, even when considered together, do not rise to the level of conduct 'utterly intolerable in a civilized community' as required under South Carolina law. The court found that inconsiderate and insulting behavior is insufficient to state an IIED claim.

source_file: 9964824_2018_Noble v. American National Property _ Casualty Insurance Co._sdd
case_name: Marty Noble and Holli Telford v. American National Property & Casualty Insurance Co.; Boardwalk Property Management Co.; Kevin West; Lehi Oasis, LLC; David L. Parker; Austin B. Cales; Jared Eldridge; Larry Deiter; Robert J. Poulsen and Poulsen & Skousen
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request was analyzed; the court examined whether defendants discriminated against plaintiffs based on disabilities (brain injury, seizures, mobility challenges) including refusing to accommodate disability needs related to the tenancy.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' FHA disability discrimination claim for failure to adequately plead the elements of a prima facie case, finding plaintiffs failed to establish protected class membership, defendant's knowledge, qualification to rent, or refusal to accommodate.
