case_name: Gerald Bollfrass v. City of Phoenix
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; claim involves alleged discrimination based on sexual orientation in federally funded public housing
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed the district court's rejection of plaintiffs' Fair Housing Act claim because plaintiffs failed to plead sufficient facts to raise a plausible inference that any adverse action was motivated by discriminatory animus based on sexual orientation rather than legitimate non-discriminatory reasons.
brief_summary: Gerald Bollfrass and Frank Czyzewski, a married same-sex couple residing in federally funded public housing managed by the City of Phoenix, appealed the district court's dismissal of their claims including First Amendment retaliation under § 1983 and Fair Housing Act discrimination based on sexual orientation. The Ninth Circuit affirmed the dismissal of the FHA claim, holding that plaintiffs failed to plead sufficient factual allegations to support a plausible inference that adverse actions (employment termination, eviction notice, financial audit) were motivated by sexual orientation discrimination rather than legitimate non-discriminatory reasons.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Sampson v. County of Los Angeles, 974 F.3d 1012 (9th Cir. 2020)
Hoefler v. Babbitt, 139 F.3d 726 (9th Cir. 1998)
Brown v. City of Los Angeles, 521 F.3d 1238 (9th Cir. 2008)
Crosby-Garbotz v. Fell ex rel. Cnty. of Pima, 434 P.3d 143 (Ariz. 2019)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination based on sexual orientation in housing decisions and treatment
fha_claims.reasoning: Court held that plaintiffs failed to plead sufficient facts to raise a plausible inference that any adverse action was motivated by sexual orientation discrimination. Purely conclusory allegations of discriminatory intent are insufficient under Iqbal, and the complaint failed to connect specific adverse actions (firing, eviction) to discriminatory animus rather than legitimate reasons.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 First Amendment retaliation, Equal Protection Clause discrimination, Arizona Revised Statutes § 33-1381 retaliatory threats of eviction
fha_claims.disposition: Affirmed in part, reversed in part
fha_claims.reasoning: Court affirmed summary judgment on § 1983 First Amendment retaliation claims, finding insufficient evidence of retaliatory intent for firing, eviction notice, and audit. Court reversed dismissal of § 33-1381 retaliatory threats claim, holding that district court erred in concluding no remedy was available under Arizona law; remanded for further proceedings on that claim.

case_name: Sandpiper Residents Association v. United States Department of Housing & Urban Development
accommodation_description: Residents of a Section 8 project-based assistance property sought Tenant Protection Vouchers from HUD to relocate from uninhabitable housing conditions.
key_holding: The court affirmed dismissal on the merits because the statutory condition for issuing vouchers—'the owner' receiving a Notice of Default—was not met when the current owner Winnie Street had not received a Notice of Default, even though the prior owner Compass Pointe had.
brief_summary: Sandpiper Cove residents and their association sued HUD seeking an order compelling the agency to issue Tenant Protection Vouchers so they could relocate from uninhabitable housing conditions, alleging discrimination on the basis of race and ethnicity. The D.C. Circuit held that the district court erred in dismissing the case as moot but affirmed on the merits, concluding that HUD lacked statutory authority to issue vouchers because the current property owner had not received a Notice of Default as required by the Consolidated Appropriations Act.
key_cases_cited: Chafin v. Chafin, 568 U.S. 165 (2013)
Marino v. Nat'l Oceanic & Atmospheric Admin., 33 F.4th 593 (D.C. Cir. 2022)
Steel Co. v. Citizens for a Better Env't, 523 U.S. 83 (1998)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Cisneros v. Alpine Ridge Grp., 508 U.S. 10 (1993)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Issuance of Tenant Protection Vouchers to allow relocation from uninhabitable Section 8 project-based assistance property
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to state a plausible claim for intentional discrimination under the Fair Housing Act because they did not allege facts showing that the current owner (Winnie Street) had received a Notice of Default, which is a statutory prerequisite for HUD to issue vouchers under the Consolidated Appropriations Act. The complaint's allegations regarding a prior owner's Notice of Default do not satisfy the statutory requirement that 'the owner' (present tense) has received such notice.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Administrative Procedure Act claim for arbitrary and capricious agency action; Fifth Amendment equal protection claim for intentional discrimination on basis of race and ethnicity; statutory claim for violation of HUD's obligations under Consolidated Appropriations Act § 219
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to state a plausible claim under the Administrative Procedure Act and Fifth Amendment because they did not allege facts demonstrating that the current owner had received a Notice of Default, which is the statutory prerequisite for HUD to issue vouchers. The complaint is devoid of facts meeting this condition, and the court applied the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard at the motion to dismiss stage.

source_file: 9999651_2024_Emory Christian v. Rancho Grande Manufactured Home Community_ca9
case_name: Emory D. Christian v. Rancho Grande Manufactured Home Community
accommodation_description: No disability accommodation request; Christian alleged racial discrimination in housing based on her being Black, differential treatment compared to white residents, and a reference in an email to her race.
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed dismissal of Christian's racial discrimination claims under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 and 1982 because she failed to plead sufficient facts to raise a plausible inference that racial animus was a but-for cause of any defendant's actions, and properly denied leave to add FHA race discrimination and retaliation claims that were inadequately pled.
brief_summary: Emory Christian, a Black woman residing in the Rancho Grande Manufactured Home Community in Rohnert Park, California, sued the mobile home park, its managers, and a neighbor alleging racial discrimination and constitutional violations arising from a property dispute. The Ninth Circuit affirmed dismissal of her federal claims, finding that she failed to plead sufficient facts to support a plausible inference that racial animus motivated any defendant's conduct, and properly denied leave to add Fair Housing Act claims for race discrimination and retaliation.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Comcast Corp. v. Nat'l Ass'n of Afr. Am.-Owned Media, 589 U.S. 327 (2020)
General Bldg. Contractors Ass'n, Inc. v. Pennsylvania, 458 U.S. 375 (1982)
Griffin v. Breckenridge, 403 U.S. 88 (1971)
Southwest Fair Hous. Council, Inc. v. Maricopa Domestic Water Improvement Dist., 17 F.4th 950 (9th Cir. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Proposed FHA § 804(b) claim for intentional race-based discrimination in terms, conditions, or privileges of rental housing
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts to raise a plausible inference of race-based discrimination. The complaint alleged only a property dispute with a neighbor and subjective impressions of facial expressions, which do not support a plausible inference that race was a but-for cause of the alleged discriminatory treatment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Proposed FHA § 804(b) disparate-impact claim based on alleged application of one-of-a-kind policies to plaintiff
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to explain how a singular impact on one person satisfies the legal requirements for a disparate-impact claim under the FHA, which requires showing that a facially neutral policy disproportionately burdens a protected class.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1982 (racial discrimination), 42 U.S.C. § 1981 (racial discrimination), 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (due process and equal protection), 42 U.S.C. § 1985(3) (conspiracy to interfere with constitutional rights)
fha_claims.reasoning: All non-FHA federal claims failed under Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards. Plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts to support a plausible inference of intentional racial discrimination or racial animus on the part of any defendant. The alleged facts—a property dispute, subjective impressions of facial expressions, and a disputed email reference—do not support a plausible inference that race was a but-for cause of defendants' actions.

source_file: ABDELRASOUL v. Trustees of Boston University
case_name: Abdelrasoul v. Trustees of Boston University
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested to transfer from a studio apartment to a one-bedroom apartment as a reasonable accommodation for his mental health disability
key_holding: Counts 11-13 alleging disability discrimination under the FHA are dismissed because plaintiff failed to adequately plead a qualifying disability or explain why the one-bedroom accommodation was necessary for equal opportunity to use and enjoy his dwelling, while Count 14 alleging retaliation survives because plaintiff adequately pleaded a causal connection between his accommodation requests and BU's decision to decline his housing renewal.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Islam Abdelrasoul, a Ph.D. student at Boston University, sued BU alleging disability discrimination under the Fair Housing Act for denying his request to transfer from a studio to a one-bedroom apartment and refusing to renew his housing agreement. The Court granted BU's motion to dismiss Counts 11-13 for failure to adequately plead a qualifying disability and explain why the accommodation was necessary, but denied the motion as to Count 14 (retaliation), finding plaintiff adequately pleaded that BU's decision to block his housing renewal was motivated by his accommodation requests.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Astralis Condo. Ass'n v. Sec'y, U.S. Dep't of Hous. & Urban Dev., 620 F.3d 62 (1st Cir. 2010)
Dixon v. Hallmark Cos., 627 F.3d 849 (11th Cir. 2010)
Valle-Arce v. P.R. Ports Auth., 651 F.3d 190 (1st Cir. 2011)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request to move from studio apartment to one-bedroom apartment for mental health reasons
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead disability with specificity regarding the nature of the mental health condition and how it substantially limits major life activities. The psychologist's letter contained only formulaic legal conclusions without factual detail, and plaintiff did not allege facts showing the accommodation was both reasonable and necessary for equal opportunity to use and enjoy housing.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of housing renewal based on disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish the first element of a discrimination claim under § 3604(f)(1)(A) and (f)(2)(A) by failing to allege facts demonstrating a qualifying handicap with sufficient specificity regarding the nature and limitations of the alleged mental impairment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation for requesting accommodation and threatening to report BU to City of Boston
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff adequately alleged all three elements of a retaliation claim under § 3617: (1) protected activity (self-advocacy requesting accommodation), (2) adverse action (interference with housing portal access and denial of renewal), and (3) causal link (complaint alleges accommodation requests motivated the decision, with the missing consent form offered as a pretext). At the motion to dismiss stage, construing facts in plaintiff's favor, the complaint states a plausible claim for relief.

case_name: King Anthony Alvarez v. City of Philadelphia, et al.
accommodation_description: Pro se plaintiff alleges retaliation for filing fair housing complaints; no reasonable accommodation request is at issue.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA retaliation claim as barred by res judicata because the same claim was raised and dismissed with prejudice in a prior lawsuit, and alternatively because plaintiff failed to allege membership in a protected class as required to state an FHA retaliation claim.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff King Anthony Alvarez sued the City of Philadelphia, HUD, and nonprofit organizations, alleging that his termination from a subsidized housing program in November 2022 constituted FHA retaliation for filing fair housing complaints. The court dismissed the complaint as barred by res judicata because the same retaliation claim had been litigated and dismissed with prejudice in a prior case, and alternatively because plaintiff failed to adequately allege membership in a protected class required for an FHA retaliation claim.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Beasley v. Howard, 14 F.4th 226 (3d Cir. 2021)
Gimenez v. Morgan Stanley DW, Inc., 202 F. App'x 583 (3d Cir. 2006)
Haefner v. N. Cornwall Twp., 40 F. App'x 656 (3d Cir. 2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the FHA retaliation claim under the doctrine of claim preclusion (res judicata) because Alvarez's 2022 lawsuit (Case No. 22-3631) resulted in a final judgment on the merits of his FHA retaliation claims based on the same November 2022 termination from subsidized housing, and the new evidence (Zoom video) does not overcome the preclusive effect. Alternatively, the claim fails on the merits because Alvarez did not allege that he was a member of a protected class or that he was discriminated against based on a protected characteristic, which is fatal to any FHA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claims against HUD for breach of duty to maintain fair housing rights; claims against CLS for alleged conflict of interest in representation
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed claims against CLS as specious because there were no allegations that CLS was responsible for the termination of subsidized housing or any plausible basis for any claim against CLS. Claims against HUD based on alleged breach of duty to maintain fair housing rights were conclusory and failed to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly.

source_file: Amber Reineck House v City of Howell Michigan

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiffs established a prima facie case of discriminatory intent in enacting the Moratorium under the Arlington Heights factors, creating a genuine dispute of material fact for jury determination. However, the court granted summary judgment against plaintiffs on their disparate treatment claim regarding Ordinance 929, finding no reasonable jury could conclude it was enacted with discriminatory intent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied plaintiffs' motion for summary judgment on their § 3617 interference claim, holding that discriminatory effect alone does not establish the required discriminatory animus element. The court found a genuine dispute whether the Moratorium was enacted with discriminatory intent versus legitimate regulatory purposes.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exception to the moratorium on special land use applications to allow immediate consideration of plaintiff's application for a sober living home for six women in recovery from substance use disorders
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found plaintiffs established that the first accommodation (moratorium exemption) was necessary to provide equal housing opportunity for women in recovery, as no sober living homes for women existed in the city and the moratorium prevented approval. However, whether the accommodation was reasonable presented a genuine factual dispute regarding the balance of benefits to disabled residents against administrative burdens to the city.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exception to nine procedural and substantive zoning requirements including public hearing requirements, public notice requirements, site plan review, planning commission review, and one-year expiration of permission
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted summary judgment for defendants on the second accommodation request, finding that while waiver of public hearing and notice requirements might have been necessary, plaintiffs failed to establish that exemption from all nine requirements was necessary. The court found that requirements like the one-year expiration of permission were not essential to afford equal housing opportunity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claims under Michigan Persons with Disabilities Civil Rights Act (MPDCRA) §§ 37.1501-07 (real estate transaction provisions); ADA Title II discrimination and reasonable accommodation claims; ADA Title V retaliation claims
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed MPDCRA §§ 37.1501-07 claims as outside the court's jurisdiction because those provisions govern only real estate transactions and broker actions, not municipal zoning decisions. The court treated FHA and ADA claims as interchangeable with MPDCRA § 37.1302 claims and proceeded on the FHA/ADA framework.

source_file: Avenue 6E Investments LLC v City of Yuma Arizona

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rezoning of 42-acre parcel from R-1-8 (8,000+ sq ft lots) to R-1-6 (6,000 sq ft lots) to permit development of affordable/moderately priced homes ($125,200-$159,800) rather than large-lot, higher-priced homes ($258,000-$386,000)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found plaintiffs established prima facie disparate impact using HMDA data showing Hispanics disproportionately priced out of market by rezoning denial (45% Hispanic in proposed price range vs. 30% in higher price range); genuine issues of material fact remain as to whether city's stated justifications (neighborhood character, preliminary plat reliance, buffer compromise) were necessary to achieve legitimate zoning goals and whether less discriminatory alternatives existed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Rezoning denial based on discriminatory intent/animus against Hispanic homebuyers
fha_claims.reasoning: Ninth Circuit reversed district court's dismissal of disparate treatment claim, finding plausible allegations that city council's denial was motivated by racially charged code words in neighbor opposition (e.g., 'group of people' with incomes under $75k 'statistically account for 91% of rape, murder, assault'), unanimous planning commission approval, and city's three-year history of approving rezoning requests. Case remanded for further proceedings.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal protection and substantive due process claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1983; violations of Arizona constitutional and statutory law
fha_claims.reasoning: District court granted motion to dismiss all non-FHA claims under Rule 12(b)(6) for failure to state a plausible claim; only FHA disparate impact claim survived initial motion to dismiss.

source_file: BOARD OF COUNTY COMMISSIONERS OF JOHNSON COUNTY v. Jorgensen
case_name: BOARD OF COUNTY COMMISSIONERS OF JOHNSON COUNTY v. Jorgensen
accommodation_description: Johnson County requested that group homes for developmentally impaired adults be exempted from state fire code requirements as a reasonable accommodation under the FHA.
key_holding: A blanket exclusion from an exhaustive regulatory scheme does not constitute a reasonable accommodation under the FHA; an appropriate accommodation requires a more tailored modification of specific requirements rather than a wholesale exemption that amounts to a fundamental alteration of the regulatory scheme.
brief_summary: Johnson County appealed a district court decision upholding the State Fire Marshal's denial of an exemption from state fire code requirements for group homes housing developmentally impaired adults, arguing the exemption constituted a reasonable accommodation under the FHA. The Kansas Court of Appeals affirmed, holding that a blanket exclusion from an exhaustive regulatory scheme does not constitute a reasonable accommodation under the FHA because it amounts to a fundamental alteration of the regulatory framework rather than a tailored modification of specific requirements.
key_cases_cited: Summers v. City of Fitchburg, 940 F.3d 133 (1st Cir. 2019)
Davis v. Echo Valley Condominium Association, 945 F.3d 483 (6th Cir. 2019)
Giebler v. M & B Associates, 343 F.3d 1143 (9th Cir. 2003)
Alexander v. Choate, 469 U.S. 287 (1985)
Texas Dept. of Housing and Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Exemption from state fire code (K.S.A. 31-132 et seq.) for group homes housing four or five developmentally impaired adults; categorical exclusion from fire prevention and safety requirements such as panic bars, fire retardant doors, interconnected smoke alarms, and sprinkler systems
fha_claims.disposition: Affirmed on appeal from district court denial of relief
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that a blanket categorical exemption from an exhaustive regulatory scheme does not constitute a reasonable accommodation under the FHA because it amounts to a fundamental alteration of the regulatory scheme rather than a tailored modification of specific requirements. The court applied the Rehabilitation Act framework prohibiting accommodations that work a fundamental alteration in a program, and found that Johnson County's request failed because it sought to exclude all group homes from fire code coverage entirely, posed threats to public safety of vulnerable residents, and was not a mere moderate adjustment to policy.

source_file: Bailey v. THE QUEEN'S LANDING COUNCIL OF UNIT OWNERS, INC.
case_name: Bailey v. The Queen's Landing Council of Unit Owners, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a disabled unit owner with severe allergies triggered by mold, alleges the Council failed to remediate mold in her condominium unit, rendering it uninhabitable, which the court treats as disparate treatment discrimination rather than analyzing as a standalone reasonable accommodation request.
key_holding: The Court dismissed plaintiff's sex discrimination claim for failure to state facts supporting disparate treatment because of sex, but denied motion to dismiss as to race and disability discrimination claims (finding sufficient allegations of differential treatment in repair services based on plaintiff's race and disability) and retaliation claim (finding sufficient causal connection between protected activity and adverse action).
brief_summary: Dr. Rosanna Bailey, a Black disabled condominium owner, sued the Queen's Landing Council of Unit Owners (her HOA) alleging race discrimination, disability discrimination, and retaliation under the Fair Housing Act, claiming the Council treated her inequitably regarding facility repairs and maintenance compared to white and non-disabled neighbors. The Court dismissed her sex discrimination claim for failure to state a claim but allowed her race and disability discrimination and retaliation claims to proceed past the motion to dismiss stage.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Reyes v. Waples Mobile Home Park Ltd. P'ship, 903 F.3d 415 (4th Cir. 2018)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's allegations of sex discrimination were conclusory and devoid of specific factual averments suggesting disparate treatment because of sex, failing to meet the Iqbal/Twombly pleading standard.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff plausibly alleged disparate treatment based on race within the limitations period, including delayed repairs, differential treatment regarding security devices, and differential insurance coverage, sufficient to survive motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Although disability discrimination allegations were aggregated with race discrimination claims, Plaintiff alleged sufficient disability-related facts (mold remediation failures, denial of security devices to disabled owner) to state a plausible claim of discrimination because of disability under § 3604(f)(2)(A).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Remediation and removal of mold from unit; repair of leaking exterior sliding doors; provision of remediation services covered by community master insurance policy
fha_claims.reasoning: Court noted in footnote 2 that Plaintiff may be alleging failure to accommodate her disabilities (severe allergies triggered by mold), and although many allegations appear barred by claim preclusion, the amended complaint sufficiently states a failure-to-accommodate claim to proceed past the pleadings stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged all four elements of retaliation under § 3617: protected activity (complaints to Association, HUD, MCCR, and courts), Defendant's awareness, adverse action (delayed repairs, refusal to communicate), and causal connection (repairs scheduled differently and later due to protected activity).

case_name: Banks v. Ross
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a wheelchair user with arthritis and anxiety, alleges he was denied receipt of a donated vehicle and transportation services from a transitional housing program as an accommodation for his disability.
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA and ADA claims fail because he has not alleged sufficient facts showing a nexus between his alleged disabilities and the defendants' actions; additionally, his Title III ADA claim fails because he seeks monetary damages rather than injunctive relief.
brief_summary: Rickey Banks, a veteran in transitional housing who uses a wheelchair and has anxiety, sued program directors and staff at Open Door Ministries alleging they denied him transportation services and a donated vehicle in violation of the ADA and FHA, and discriminated against him based on race and disability. The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss, finding the complaint failed to state plausible federal claims because plaintiff did not adequately allege how his disabilities connected to the alleged discriminatory conduct, and his ADA Title III damages claim was improper.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Thomas v. The Salvation Army S. Territory, 841 F.3d 632 (4th Cir. 2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination on the basis of race in denial of donated vehicle from donation program
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff alleged race discrimination in denial of vehicle from donation program but failed to allege supporting facts or draw a nexus between race and the alleged denial. Conclusory allegations of discrimination without factual support are insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of transportation services, including denial of ability to purchase a vehicle and denial of receipt of donated vehicle; alleged denial of access to Cassell House based on disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a nexus between his alleged handicaps (arthritis, use of wheelchair/cane/walker, anxiety, possible diabetes and high blood pressure) and the defendants' actions. Plaintiff did not explain how he was precluded from housing because of his handicap or how the complained-of actions constituted discrimination based on handicap.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Constitutional claims under First, Fourth, Fifth, and Eighth Amendments; ADA Title III claims for discrimination and failure to provide reasonable modifications; assault and related state law claims against co-resident Michael Huggins
fha_claims.reasoning: Constitutional claims dismissed because defendants are private actors not acting under color of state law. ADA Title III claims for monetary damages dismissed because Title III provides only injunctive relief. ADA claims also fail on merits because plaintiff failed to allege he was qualified for any program or excluded because of disability. State law assault claims against co-resident remanded to state court.

case_name: Rickey Banks v. Ryan Ross et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff allegedly requested accommodations including transportation services, a donated vehicle, and continued housing at a transitional shelter, but the accommodation requests are vaguely pleaded.
key_holding: Plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claims were dismissed because his complaint failed to allege sufficient facts connecting his alleged disabilities (arthritis, wheelchair/cane/walker use, anxiety) to Defendants' actions, and his Title III ADA claims fail because Title III does not provide for monetary damages.
brief_summary: Rickey Banks, a pro se plaintiff who uses a wheelchair and alleges various disabilities, sued Ryan Ross (Executive Director of Open Door Ministries) and other employees of the Arthur Cassell Memorial Transitional House, a VA-funded transitional housing program, alleging discrimination and failure to accommodate under the ADA and FHA. The court recommended dismissing the federal claims without prejudice because the complaint failed to state plausible claims—Plaintiff's ADA Title III claims cannot seek monetary damages, his FHA claims lack sufficient factual nexus between his disabilities and Defendants' actions, and his constitutional § 1983 claims fail because Defendants are private actors not acting under color of state law.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Thomas v. The Salvation Army S. Territory, 841 F.3d 632 (4th Cir. 2016)
PGA Tour, Inc. v. Martin, 532 U.S. 661 (2001)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination based on race in denial of vehicle from donation program
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to support a claim of race discrimination under the FHA. The complaint contains only conclusory allegations of discrimination without factual support regarding the vehicle donation program or defendants' involvement in excluding plaintiff based on race.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of transportation services and vehicle; denial of receipt of donated vehicle; denial of ability to purchase vehicle without repercussions
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a nexus between his alleged disability and the denial of transportation services or vehicle receipt. The complaint does not explain how he was discriminated against based on his handicap or how defendants' actions constituted disability-based discrimination in violation of the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination based on disability in denial of vehicle from donation program and other services
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to support a claim of disability discrimination under FHA § 3604(f). The complaint does not establish which alleged medical condition constitutes the handicap at issue, does not explain how plaintiff was precluded from housing because of that handicap, and fails to draw a sufficient nexus between the alleged disability and defendants' challenged actions.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III discrimination; constitutional claims (First, Fourth, Fifth, Eighth, Fourteenth Amendments); state law claims (elder abuse, assault by fellow resident)
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA Title III claims seeking monetary damages fail as a matter of law; constitutional claims fail because defendants are private actors not subject to § 1983 and constitutional protections do not apply to private conduct; state law claims lack federal jurisdiction and should be dismissed without prejudice to re-filing in state court.

case_name: Latonia Black v. Royal American Management, et al.
accommodation_description: Procedural order granting leave to amend complaint; underlying complaint alleged reasonable accommodation denial and race discrimination in rental housing.
key_holding: The court granted Black leave to file an amended complaint under Rule 15(a)(2)'s liberal standard, finding no undue prejudice to defendants despite Black's delay and carelessness in the amendment process, as the amendment was filed before the scheduling order deadline.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Latonia Black sued Royal American Management and others alleging Fair Housing Act violations including reasonable accommodation denial and race discrimination in connection with her rental property. After the Magistrate Judge recommended dismissing two retaliation claims and Black missed the deadline to amend as a matter of course, the court granted Black leave to file an amended complaint under Rule 15(a)(2)'s liberal standard because no undue prejudice would result and the amendment was filed before the scheduling order deadline.
key_cases_cited: In re Engle Cases, 767 F.3d 1082 (11th Cir. 2014)
Foman v. Davis, 371 U.S. 178 (1962)
Bryant v. Dupree, 252 F.3d 1161 (11th Cir. 2001)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denying or making a dwelling unavailable
fha_claims.reasoning: Claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(1) alleged in original complaint; motion to dismiss Counts Five and Six was granted, but plaintiff granted leave to file amended complaint addressing deficiencies, making the Report and Recommendation moot.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination in terms and conditions of housing
fha_claims.reasoning: Claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(2) alleged in original complaint; survives as plaintiff granted leave to amend and cure pleading deficiencies.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to reasonably accommodate (specific accommodation not detailed in opinion)
fha_claims.reasoning: Claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3) alleged in original complaint; survives as plaintiff granted leave to amend and cure pleading deficiencies.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation for filing complaint with HUD and exercising FHA rights
fha_claims.reasoning: Retaliation claim alleged in original complaint; survives as plaintiff granted leave to amend and cure pleading deficiencies.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 and 1983 retaliation claims; Alabama Code 1975 § 35-9A-501 state law retaliation claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Non-FHA claims (federal civil rights and state law retaliation) alleged in original complaint and proposed amendment; Report and Recommendation recommending dismissal of Counts Five and Six becomes moot upon filing of amended complaint.

case_name: Sonja Marie Boyce v. St. Vincent DePaul (Lane County), GBM Garder Beckley Meadows
accommodation_description: Plaintiff filed a vague complaint alleging housing discrimination under the FHA but failed to articulate a specific accommodation request; court analyzed disparate treatment and disparate impact theories rather than reasonable accommodation denial.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's complaint because she failed to allege sufficient facts to establish federal jurisdiction, constitutional violations, or viable FHA claims under either disparate treatment or disparate impact theories.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Sonja Marie Boyce sued St. Vincent DePaul and GBM alleging Fair Housing Act violations related to an eviction and back rent dispute in Eugene, Oregon. The court dismissed the complaint without service of process for failure to state claims, finding plaintiff's allegations too vague to establish federal jurisdiction, constitutional violations, or viable disparate treatment or disparate impact claims under the FHA.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 554 (2007)
Gamble v. City of Escondido, 104 F.3d 300 (9th Cir. 1997)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege facts from which the court could infer that the rental relationship or housing-related term, condition, or privilege remained available to other similarly situated individuals not in plaintiff's protected class, which is required to establish a prima facie disparate treatment claim under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege any outwardly neutral practices of defendants or any significantly adverse impacts of those policies on individuals in a protected class, which are required elements of a prima facie disparate impact claim under the FHA.

source_file: Brandt v Village of Chebanse Ill

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The magistrate judge found no discrimination based on handicap under § 3604(f)(1)(B) because the Village had previously denied Brandt's request to build a four-unit building at the same site without handicap modifications, demonstrating the denial was based on multi-family zoning concerns, not the tenants' disability status. The court credited the Village Trustees' testimony regarding congestion and water runoff concerns.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Variance to allow demolition of single-family house and construction of four-unit, two-story apartment building with first-floor units accessible to wheelchair users
fha_claims.reasoning: The Court of Appeals held that the variance was not a necessary accommodation under § 3604(f)(3)(B) because handicapped persons capable of independent living could live equally well in renovated or new single-family houses. The court applied a balancing test and found the costs to the Village (flooding risk, loss of single-family zoning tranquility) outweighed the benefit, especially since the building could be constructed elsewhere in areas already zoned for multi-family use. The court rejected the argument that the Fair Housing Act requires municipalities to waive single-family zoning whenever a developer makes first-floor units accessible.

source_file: CORI'S PLACE v. THE ZONING HEARING BOARD OF THE CITY OF NANTICOKE
case_name: Cori's Place v. The Zoning Hearing Board of the City of Nanticoke
accommodation_description: Zoning permit to allow four adults with intellectual disabilities to reside in a single-family residential zone with staff supervision, including the ability to have separate leases.
key_holding: The court found Plaintiff adequately pleaded a reasonable accommodation claim under § 3604(f)(3)(B) because allowing four individuals with intellectual disabilities to live together in an R-2 residential zone with separate leases is a plausibly reasonable accommodation necessary to afford them equal opportunity to housing.
brief_summary: Cori's Place, an operator providing residential services for adults with intellectual disabilities, sued the City of Nanticoke and its Zoning Hearing Board after being denied a zoning permit to operate a group residence for four disabled individuals in an R-2 residential zone. The court granted in part and denied in part Defendants' motion to dismiss, dismissing intentional discrimination, disparate impact, interference, and ADA claims but allowing the reasonable accommodation claim under § 3604(f)(3)(B) to proceed because Plaintiff adequately pleaded that separate leases for four disabled residents constitute a plausibly reasonable accommodation necessary to afford them equal housing opportunity.
key_cases_cited: Vorchheimer v. Philadelphian Owners Assoc., 903 F.3d 100 (3d Cir. 2018)
Hovsons, Inc. v. Twp. of Brick, 89 F.3d 1096 (3d Cir. 1996)
Lapid-Laurel, L.L.C. v. Zoning Bd. of Adjustment, 284 F.3d 442 (3d Cir. 2002)
Cmty. Servs., Inc. v. Wind Gap Mun. Auth., 421 F.3d 170 (3d Cir. 2005)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Zoning permit allowing four individuals with intellectual disabilities to reside in a residential home in an R-2 (Two-Family Residential) Zoning District, with staff supervision present; alternatively, allowing separate leases for the four residents contrary to the Zoning Ordinance's restrictions.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard and found that Plaintiff adequately pleaded all three elements of a §3604(f)(3)(B) reasonable accommodation claim: (1) refusal (denial of permit), (2) reasonableness (no undue burden or fundamental alteration shown; similar to existing zoning exceptions for day-care centers and group residences), and (3) necessity (equal opportunity for individuals with disabilities to live in residential zones as non-disabled persons do). The claim survives the motion to dismiss.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Discrimination in denial of zoning permit based on disability status of intended residents.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court treated Plaintiff's §3604(f)(1) and (f)(2) claims (disparate treatment and disparate impact) as abandoned because Plaintiff did not allege discriminatory intent and did not plead disparate impact. The court noted these claims were subsumed by the reasonable accommodation theory, which does not require proof of intent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged interference with Plaintiff's exercise of FHA rights by requiring submission to zoning permit approval process and denying the permit application.
fha_claims.reasoning: Under §3617, interference requires conduct akin to harassment or persistent and intentional efforts to undermine statutory rights, not merely the application of ordinary bureaucratic procedures. The court held that requiring submission to a standard zoning permit process, even if the Board reached an erroneous legal conclusion, does not constitute unlawful interference.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claim for discrimination and failure to accommodate; ADA Title V interference claim.
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA Title II claims for compensatory damages require allegations of intentional discrimination, which Plaintiff failed to plead. Declaratory relief is moot because the Zoning Hearing Board's decision was reversed in state court and Plaintiff's permit was granted, eliminating the actual controversy required under the Declaratory Judgment Act. The ADA Title V interference claim fails for the same reasons as the §3617 claim.

source_file: CYMBALSKY v. 522 SHORE ROAD OWNERS, INC.
case_name: Gerald Cymbalsky v. 522 Shore Road Owners, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged he was subjected to adverse housing actions due to his disabilities (osteoarthritis, anxiety, morbid obesity) but did not request any specific accommodation.
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA claim fails because he continues to reside in his apartment, prevailed in the underlying state court action, and critically, he never requested any accommodation for his disabilities; the court dismissed the FHA claim finding no adverse action and no causal connection to disability.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Gerald Cymbalsky, a disabled tenant with osteoarthritis and anxiety disorders, sued his cooperative apartment building, property management companies, and attorneys for alleged Fair Housing Act violations, civil RICO violations, constitutional rights violations, and FDCPA violations stemming from a state court 'furniture eviction' proceeding. The court granted all motions to dismiss, finding that Cymbalsky's FHA claim failed because he continues to reside in his apartment, he 'won' the state court action, and he never requested any accommodation for his disabilities.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Francis v. Kings Park Manor, Inc., 992 F.3d 67 (2d Cir. 2021)
Logan v. Matveevskii, 175 F. Supp. 3d 209 (S.D.N.Y. 2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged discrimination based on disability (severe osteoarthritis requiring walker, persistent open leg wound, anxiety disorder, morbid obesity) in connection with co-op's commencement of state court action seeking to clean his apartment.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege discriminatory intent or causal nexus to disability. Plaintiff alleged he continues to reside in his apartment and 'won' the state court action, demonstrating no adverse action. The commencement of the state court action was alleged to be motivated by profit, not discriminatory animus based on disability. Additionally, Finkelstein Defendants lacked standing as they neither owned, managed, nor were affiliated with the property beyond providing legal representation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: RICO (18 U.S.C. § 1961 et seq.), Constitutional rights to privacy/property, FDCPA (15 U.S.C. § 1692 et seq.)
fha_claims.reasoning: RICO claim failed because plaintiff alleged insufficient predicate acts (only disappearance of cash/silver and state court action), which were not related and did not demonstrate a pattern of racketeering activity or affect interstate commerce. Constitutional claims failed because defendants were private parties, not state actors. FDCPA claim failed because co-op defendants were creditors, not debt collectors, and Finkelstein Defendants were not alleged to regularly collect debts.

source_file: Candlehouse Inc v Town of Vestal NY

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Waiver of the zoning ordinance's 'functional equivalent of a family' requirement to permit Candlehouse to operate a residential facility for 12 students (exceeding the 5-person limit for unrelated persons) in an RA-1 residential district, or amendment of the zoning ordinance to permit the desired use.
fha_claims.reasoning: Material disputes of fact exist regarding whether the Town Board's denial of the reasonable accommodation request was based on the students' disabilities and whether the accommodation was necessary to serve the students' impairments. The court found conflicting evidence as to the Town Board's motivation and denied summary judgment for both parties.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Material disputes of fact exist regarding whether the Town's Code Enforcement Officer and Zoning Board of Appeals were motivated by discriminatory animus against disabled persons. Evidence was conflicting on whether community opposition influenced the decision-makers, and the court found sufficient factual disputes to preclude summary judgment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie disparate impact claim. Although the zoning ordinance is facially neutral, plaintiff provided no statistical evidence or qualitative comparison demonstrating that the ordinance actually or predictably created a shortage of housing for disabled persons. Plaintiff serves a mixed population with varying impairments, and the court found no reliable analytical mechanism to show disproportionate impact on this heterogeneous group.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: RLUIPA substantial burden on religious exercise claim; also voluntarily dismissed First Amendment free exercise claim (Count V), Fourteenth Amendment equal protection claim (Count VI), and RLUIPA equal terms provision claim (Count IV)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish a substantial burden on religious exercise under RLUIPA. Although a nexus exists between the Town's denial and Candlehouse's religious exercise, the Town's ordinance permits residential use for up to five unrelated persons, and plaintiff failed to show how precluding an additional seven students coerces the organization to change its religious behavior. The burden is merely inconvenient, not substantial.

source_file: Caron Foundation of Florida Inc v City of Delray Beach

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request to allow seven unrelated individuals recovering from alcoholism and substance abuse to reside together in a single-family residence (Second Ocean Drive House) in violation of the city's occupancy ordinance limiting unrelated residents to three persons.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found the reasonable accommodation claim unripe because the city had requested additional information (evidence of medical necessity for seven residents) that Caron failed to provide, despite the city's letter stating it would reconsider if additional information was submitted. The court also found that even if ripe, Caron failed to demonstrate a substantial likelihood of success on the merits because it did not establish the direct linkage between the accommodation and equal opportunity to use the dwelling—the necessity element required showing that housing seven individuals actually alleviates the effects of the disability, not merely that it would be beneficial.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: City's amendment to the transient use ordinance on February 21, 2012, which reduced the number of times a dwelling could be rented per year from six times to three times in single-family zoning districts, applied to the entire dwelling or any part thereof.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the Arlington Heights burden-shifting framework and found that Caron established a substantial likelihood of success on its disparate treatment claim. The court identified discriminatory intent through: (1) historical background—the city's 2002 attempt to restrict substance abuse treatment centers after DOJ warning, and adoption of the transient use ordinance after Schwarz upheld such ordinances; (2) specific sequence of events—the ordinance was amended immediately after Caron's application and community outcry, with the city's counsel website stating the ordinance was being tightened in response to Caron's plans; (3) administrative history—planning board members made blatantly discriminatory statements calling sober homes a 'cancer,' and at least one city commissioner adopted the public's discriminatory comments. The city provided legitimate nondiscriminatory reasons (infrastructure strain, neighborhood disruption, property stewardship), but Caron showed these were pretextual given the suspicious timing and discriminatory animus. The court granted a preliminary injunction preventing enforcement of the amended ordinance against Caron.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: City's transient use ordinance as applied to sober living facilities.
fha_claims.reasoning: Caron briefly asserted a disparate impact claim but offered no statistical evidence or substantive argument in support. The court found that Caron failed to show a substantial likelihood of success on a disparate impact claim, citing Schwarz for the requirement of statistical showing.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) claims parallel to the FHA claims.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court analyzed ADA claims alongside FHA claims, noting the similarity of protections and that both statutes apply to municipal zoning decisions. The court's analysis of the reasonable accommodation claim and disparate treatment claim under the ADA paralleled the FHA analysis. The court granted preliminary injunctive relief on the disparate treatment claim under both statutes.

case_name: Chapman v. Davis
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested to keep her dog Nemo as an emotional support animal as a reasonable accommodation for her disability.
key_holding: The housing provider's request for the ESA's vaccination records was not a refusal to make a reasonable accommodation but merely a request for information, and plaintiff failed to allege defendants refused to make the accommodation after learning of her disability and ESA status.
brief_summary: Tasha Chapman, an African American woman with minor children participating in the Section 8 HCV program, sued her private landlords and property managers alleging they discriminated against her based on race, familial status, and disability by refusing to allow her emotional support animal and initiating eviction proceedings. The court dismissed all claims on initial screen, finding the ESA accommodation request failed because requesting vaccination records was not a refusal to accommodate, and plaintiff failed to allege any discriminatory statements supporting her race and familial status claims.
key_cases_cited: Overlook Mut. Homes, Inc. v. Spencer, 415 F. App'x 617 (6th Cir. 2011)
Miami Valley Fair Hous. Ctr., Inc. v. Connor Grp., 805 F. Supp. 2d 396 (S.D. Ohio 2011)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege any discriminatory statement or action by CMHA and CGI based on family status. The demand for an updated lease and notice of program termination for failure to provide requested information do not indicate a preference, limitation, or discrimination based on family status.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege any racially discriminatory action or statement by CMHA and CGI. Merely alleging that plaintiff and her children are African American and defendants are white, without more, is insufficient to state a claim for racial discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Permission to keep an emotional support animal (ESA dog named Nemo) in violation of the lease's no-pets policy
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege that Heels Homes and 4 Real Estate refused to make the accommodation. The defendants' request for vaccination records does not constitute a refusal to allow the ESA as a reasonable accommodation; requesting information about the animal is not a denial of the accommodation itself.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged retaliation through initiation of eviction proceedings
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to state a retaliation claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3617 because she failed to allege facts showing that the eviction was initiated in retaliation for exercising FHA rights. The mere fact of eviction initiation, without more, does not support a retaliation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Human trafficking claim under the Trafficking Victims Protection Act, 18 U.S.C. § 1595
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege any facts supporting a human trafficking claim. The complaint cited only a definitions section and failed to allege facts showing that the eviction proceedings constituted an abuse of legal process or human trafficking.

source_file: City of Grants Pass Oregon v Johnson

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of housing voucher application based on alleged disability; refusal to accept resubmitted application and police escort from premises
fha_claims.reasoning: This is an appeal of the trial court's grant of summary judgment in favor of the State Attorney General. The underlying disability discrimination complaint filed by Ron Bircher against the City of Tempe was not adjudicated on the merits in this opinion; rather, the court affirmed that the Arizona Attorney General had authority to investigate the complaint and that the City of Tempe, as a municipal corporation, is a 'person' subject to the Arizona Fair Housing Act. The merits of Bircher's discrimination claim were never reached because the City's challenge was to the Attorney General's authority to investigate, not to the substance of the discrimination allegation.

source_file: DELAWARE HUMAN AND CIVIL RIGHTS COMMISSION EX REL. MILLAR v. GREENBRIER CONDOS, LLC
case_name: Delaware Human and Civil Rights Commission ex rel. Millar v. Greenbrier Condos, L.L.C.
accommodation_description: Ms. Millar preferred to lease a first-floor apartment because she has difficulty walking.
key_holding: The court denied Defendants' motion to dismiss Counts I and III, holding that the Commission could pursue claims beyond those specifically found to have reasonable cause in the Division's Written Findings, as long as the claims arise from the same operative facts in the Charge.
brief_summary: The Delaware Human and Civil Rights Commission (on behalf of Relator Gabrielle Millar, a disabled person with an emotional support animal) sued Greenbrier Condos and its property manager alleging they refused to rent to Ms. Millar and failed to accommodate her ESA request in violation of the Delaware Fair Housing Act. The court denied Defendants' motion to dismiss Counts I and III, holding that under Delaware law, the Commission could pursue additional claims arising from the same operative facts as the Division's Charge, even though the Division did not find reasonable cause on all claims.
key_cases_cited: Central Mortg. Co. v. Morgan Stanley Mortg. Capital Holdings LLC, 227 A.3d 531 (Del. 2011)
Doe v. Cedars Academy, 2010 WL 5825353 (Del. Super. Oct. 27, 2010)
Ramunno v. Crawley, 705 A.2d 1029 (Del. 1998)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to rent apartment to plaintiff based on disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss Count I (DFHA § 4603(b)(1)) on standing grounds, finding that the Commission had authority to pursue claims arising from the operative facts in the charge even if not all claims were supported by reasonable cause in the Division's written findings.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to rent apartment to plaintiff based on disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss Count II (DFHA § 4603(b)(2)), which was included in the Division's charge and is proceeding on the merits.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation for disability (emotional support animal and first-floor apartment preference due to difficulty walking)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss Count III (DFHA § 4603A(a)(2)) on standing grounds, finding that the Commission had authority to pursue the reasonable accommodation claim arising from the operative facts in the charge even though the Division found no reasonable cause on this specific claim.

source_file: Dews v Town of Sunnyvale Tex

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Challenge to town zoning ordinances banning apartments and imposing one-acre minimum lot size requirement for residential development
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that Sunnyvale's one-acre zoning and apartment ban had a significant discriminatory effect on African Americans by disproportionately burdening minority users of apartments and subsidized housing, and perpetuating racial segregation. Town failed to prove a compelling governmental interest, and less discriminatory alternatives existed.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Challenge to town's maintenance of one-acre zoning ordinance and apartment ban with discriminatory intent; challenge to town's denial/tabling of Hammer-Smith's rezoning application for multifamily and affordable housing development
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied Arlington Heights discriminatory intent test and found: (1) discriminatory impact; (2) historical background of discouraging African American housing since 1953 incorporation; (3) specific sequence of events showing town ignored planners' advice; (4) procedural departures in Hammer-Smith application review; (5) substantive departures showing town's stated justifications were pretextual. Town failed to prove same decision would have resulted absent discriminatory purpose.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claims under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1982, 1983 (racial discrimination in contracts, property rights, and equal protection); 42 U.S.C. § 2000d (Title VI discrimination in federally funded programs)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found liability under §§ 1981, 1982, and 1983 by proving discriminatory intent using the same Arlington Heights analysis applied to FHA claims. Court did not reach § 2000d liability question. Town's zoning policies and practices were maintained with discriminatory intent to exclude African Americans and affordable housing.

case_name: Dunn v. Manuel
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested a temporary substitute apartment to live in while her apartment was being repaired and she dealt with personal items related to her hoarding disorder.
key_holding: The court dismissed all FHA claims because plaintiff failed to establish that hoarding disorder qualifies as a 'handicap' under the FHA, as she did not plead facts showing it substantially limits major life activities, and separately failed to state a plausible failure-to-accommodate claim.
brief_summary: Nora Dunn sued her landlord Sharon Hydinger alleging the landlord discriminated against her based on her hoarding disorder by refusing to repair her apartment, refusing to provide a substitute apartment as an accommodation, and attempting to evict her. The court granted the motion to dismiss, finding that hoarding disorder is not a protected disability under the FHA and that even if it were, Dunn failed to plead sufficient facts to support her claims for intentional discrimination, failure to accommodate, retaliation, or hostile environment.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014)
Sailboat Bend Sober Living, LLC v. City of Fort Lauderdale, 46 F.4th 1268 (11th Cir. 2022)
Bonasera v. City of Norcross, 342 F. App'x 581 (11th Cir. 2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead a disability under the FHA (hoarding disorder does not substantially limit major life activities as required by 42 U.S.C. § 3602(h)(1)). Additionally, even assuming a disability, plaintiff failed to allege that she was treated differently than similarly situated non-disabled persons, which is required to state a disparate treatment claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead a disability under the FHA. Additionally, plaintiff failed to allege that she engaged in a protected activity, as she did not demonstrate a good faith, reasonable belief that the defendant's conduct was unlawful under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Hostile environment claim; unclear whether brought under FHA or Alabama Fair Housing Law
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead a disability under the FHA. Additionally, plaintiff's allegations of harassment (blaming, victimizing, calling apartment 'dirty and trashy,' characterizing tenant as poor credit risk) do not rise to the level of 'severe' conduct, and plaintiff failed to allege that such conduct was pervasive or occurred more than once.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Temporary substitute apartment to allow plaintiff time to deal with personal items while repairs were made
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead a disability under the FHA. Additionally, plaintiff failed to plead that the requested accommodation was reasonable and proportional to costs, or that it was necessary to ameliorate the effects of her disability, as required by the reasonable accommodation framework.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alabama Landlord Tenant Act violation, Breach of Duty of Reasonable Care/Affirmative Negligence, Wanton/Recklessness, Breach of Contract, Wrongful Eviction/Abuse of Process
fha_claims.reasoning: All federal FHA claims were dismissed, eliminating the court's original jurisdiction. Under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3), the court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims where all federal claims have been dismissed prior to trial. Additionally, state law claims are barred by res judicata because defendant Hydinger was in privity with the state court defendants (Carter Manuel and RMI Realty Group) whose claims were dismissed with prejudice.

source_file: EIGHT IS ENOUGH, LLC v. OHLIG
case_name: Eight Is Enough, LLC v. Ohlig
accommodation_description: Tenant requested permission to keep an emotional support dog, have a live-in caretaker (her adult grandson), and receive help with cleaning and maintenance as reasonable accommodations for anxiety, depression, and PTSD.
key_holding: The appellate court held that the trial court erred by failing to consider Ohlig's disability discrimination defense (including retaliation for requesting reasonable accommodations) at the show cause hearing, and remanded for the court to expressly consider the defense and determine if genuine issues of material fact require trial; the court otherwise affirmed the judgment for unpaid rent and rejected the notice-of-proposed-judgment argument.
brief_summary: Tenant Cynthia Ohlig appealed an unlawful detainer judgment seeking possession of her rental home, arguing the trial court erred by failing to consider her disability discrimination defense (that the eviction was retaliatory for her reasonable accommodation request for an emotional support dog and live-in caretaker) at the show cause hearing. The Washington Court of Appeals held that under Josephinium and the Washington Law Against Discrimination, discrimination defenses that affect the right to possession must be considered at show cause hearings, and remanded for the trial court to expressly evaluate Ohlig's discrimination defense and determine whether genuine issues of material fact require trial.
key_cases_cited: Josephinium Assocs. v. Kahli, 111 Wn. App. 617
Faciszewski v. Brown, 187 Wn.2d 308
Hansen v. Boeing Co., 903 F. Supp. 2d 1215

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Emotional support dog (ESA) and live-in caretaker (adult grandson); tenant also requested help with cleaning and maintaining the apartment. Tenant submitted medical documentation from Dr. Gerald Lee diagnosing anxiety, depression, and post-traumatic stress disorder, with recommendation that tenant have 'a pet or emotional support animal/person' as necessary for mental health.
fha_claims.reasoning: The trial court failed to expressly consider the tenant's disability discrimination defense at the show cause hearing, despite the tenant presenting competent evidence of a prima facie case. The appellate court held that under Washington law (WLAD and Josephinium precedent), a discrimination defense affecting the right of possession must be considered at a show cause hearing, and remanded for the trial court to hold another hearing to expressly consider whether genuine issues of material fact exist requiring trial.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliatory eviction claim based on tenant's request for reasonable accommodation (ESA and live-in caretaker). Tenant alleged that landlord issued 90-day termination notice five days after tenant submitted written accommodation request on May 20, 2022, and that landlord had previously shown animus toward the service animal and caregiver in January 2022.
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court held that requesting a reasonable accommodation is a protected activity under RCW 49.60.210 (WLAD anti-retaliation provision), and that temporal proximity between the accommodation request and the termination notice (five days) supports a prima facie retaliation claim. The trial court erred by failing to consider this defense at the show cause hearing. The court noted that circumstantial evidence, including proximity in time, may be sufficient to establish causal connection for retaliation claims.

source_file: EWIDEH v. HOMESITE INS. CO. OF THE MIDWEST
case_name: EWIDEH v. HOMESITE INS. CO. OF THE MIDWEST
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs vaguely alleged discrimination based on unidentified health conditions and sexuality by an insurance claims adjuster, but this claim was not a reasonable accommodation request and was dismissed for failure to state a claim.
key_holding: The plaintiffs' FHA claim was dismissed without prejudice because the complaint failed to adequately plead any cognizable federal claim, failing to identify what disability was at issue or articulate a viable theory of housing discrimination.
brief_summary: Omar Ewideh and Nivertiti Geaith, proceeding pro se, sued Homesite Insurance Company and other defendants asserting breach of contract, bad faith insurance denial, and a cursory Fair Housing Act claim alleging discrimination based on unspecified health conditions and sexuality. The court recommended granting the motion to dismiss because the plaintiffs failed to oppose the motion, violated numerous court orders demonstrating failure to prosecute, and failed to adequately plead any cognizable federal claim, dismissing the FHA claim without prejudice.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Ashcroft v. Iqbal

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged discrimination based on unidentified 'health conditions' and complained that a claims adjuster used a slur regarding plaintiff's sexuality. The specific nature of the alleged FHA violation (intentional discrimination, disparate impact, or disability-based discrimination) was not clearly articulated.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found the FHA claim was advanced in an 'enigmatic fashion' and failed to adequately plead the claim under Iqbal/Twombly standards. The plaintiffs failed to clearly identify whether they were pursuing intentional discrimination or disparate impact, whether the claim rested on disability or sexuality discrimination, and what disability was allegedly at issue. Dismissal was without prejudice to allow amendment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Breach of contract (insurance policy), tortious interference with contract, civil RICO conspiracy, libel, and slander claims.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court lacked subject matter jurisdiction over state law claims because complete diversity of citizenship was lacking—both plaintiffs and many named defendants were Pennsylvania residents. Federal diversity jurisdiction requires complete diversity among all parties. The court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Zoning variances to permit transitional housing for homeless mentally ill persons on property zoned for semi-industrial use, including: (1) allowing residential use within 200 feet of general industrial district; (2) waiver of 8-foot sideyard requirement; (3) waiver of 20-foot rear yard requirement; (4) waiver of landscaping provisions; and (5) waiver of 8-foot landscaped barrier requirement.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish both elements of reasonable accommodation claim: (1) variances were not reasonable because they would constitute a fundamental alteration of the city's zoning policy of maintaining a 200-foot buffer between industrial and residential uses, which the city had consistently enforced; and (2) variances were not necessary to provide equal housing opportunity because the city would have denied the same variances to anyone regardless of disability, so mentally ill persons did not lose an equal opportunity available to others.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish discriminatory intent or animus. Although neighborhood residents opposed the facility, the board's questioning during the hearing focused on whether the building was suitable for residential use, not on the disability of the residents. Plaintiff could not show a causal link between community opposition and the board's decision, and the board articulated nondiscriminatory reasons (unsuitability of a windowless, jail-like facility for residential purposes) even if some animus could be inferred.

source_file: FAIR HOUS. JUST. CTR., INC. v. PELICAN MGMT., INC.
case_name: Fair Housing Justice Center, Inc. v. Pelican Management, Inc.
accommodation_description: Facially neutral minimum income policy (40x rent requirement for partially subsidized applicants) challenged as having disparate impact on renters with disabilities who receive rental subsidies.
key_holding: The Second Circuit affirmed that the district court properly credited FHJC's expert methodology in finding that Goldfarb's 2019 Policy—requiring partially subsidized applicants to earn 40 times their share of monthly rent while fully subsidized applicants faced no income requirements—had a disparate impact on applicants with disabilities who receive rental subsidies, in violation of the NYCHRL.
brief_summary: Fair Housing Justice Center sued Goldfarb Properties (a large New York managing agent) alleging that Goldfarb's minimum income policies violated the Fair Housing Act and New York City Human Rights Law by disparately impacting applicants with disabilities who receive rental subsidies. The Second Circuit affirmed the district court's judgment, holding that the 2019 Policy's requirement that partially subsidized applicants earn 40 times their share of monthly rent had a statistically significant disparate impact on protected applicants.
key_cases_cited: Tsombanidis v. W. Haven Fire Dep't, 352 F.3d 565 (2d Cir. 2003)
Levin v. Yeshiva Univ., 96 N.Y.2d 484 (2001)
Mihalik v. Credit Agricole Cheuvreux N. Am., Inc., 715 F.3d 102 (2d Cir. 2013)
Clerveaux v. E. Ramapo Cent. Sch. Dist., 984 F.3d 213 (2d Cir. 2021)
Sacerdote v. N.Y. Univ., 9 F.4th 95 (2d Cir. 2021)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court found that Goldfarb's 2015 minimum income policy (requiring gross annual income of at least 43 times total monthly rent) had a disparate impact on renters with disabilities because a large percentage of renters receiving rental subsidies—a disproportionate share of whom have disabilities—were excluded by the policy. The appellate court affirmed this finding on the merits after a bench trial with expert testimony.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The district court found that Goldfarb's 2019 policy, which required partially subsidized applicants to earn 40 times their share of monthly rent (versus 43 times full rent for unsubsidized applicants), continued to have a disparate impact on the basis of source of income under the NYCHRL. The court credited the plaintiff's expert methodology including 'insufficient voucher' denials and properly compared partially subsidized to unsubsidized applicants, excluding fully subsidized applicants who were not subject to the challenged income requirement. The appellate court affirmed.

source_file: FAIR HOUSING JUSTICE CENTER, INC. v. BRUCKNER TOWER LLC
case_name: Fair Housing Justice Center, Inc. v. Bruckner Tower LLC
accommodation_description: Fair housing organization alleges design and construction accessibility violations in a residential complex, seeking to present evidence of statutory violations at trial.
key_holding: A certificate of occupancy does not constitute conclusive evidence of compliance with design and construction requirements under § 3604(f)(3)(C), and § 3604(f)(6)(B) expressly provides that state/local government determinations shall not be conclusive in enforcement proceedings.
brief_summary: Fair Housing Justice Center sued Bruckner Tower LLC and related entities alleging Federal Fair Housing Amendments Act violations regarding design and construction accessibility requirements for a residential complex in the Bronx. The court denied the defendants' motion in limine to preclude evidence of statutory violations, holding that a certificate of occupancy does not provide conclusive evidence of substantial compliance with § 3604(f)(3)(C) design and construction requirements.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Compliance with accessible design and construction requirements for covered multifamily dwellings under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(C)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied defendants' motion in limine to preclude evidence of statutory violations based on Certificate of Occupancy compliance. The court held that a Certificate of Occupancy does not conclusively establish compliance with § 3604(f)(3)(C) design and construction requirements, and determinations by state or local government are not conclusive in FHA enforcement proceedings under § 3604(f)(6)(B).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: New York State Executive Law § 296 et seq., New York State Civil Rights Law § 4, Administrative Code of the City of New York § 8-107 et seq.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court's ruling on motion in limine applies equally to state and local fair housing law claims; no separate analysis of non-FHA claims was conducted in this opinion.

source_file: FAIR HOUSING JUSTICE CENTER, INC. v. BRUCKNER TOWER, LLC
case_name: Fair Housing Justice Center, Inc. v. Bruckner Tower, LLC
accommodation_description: Fair housing organization alleged that the 130-unit multi-family building known as the Crescendo was designed and constructed with accessibility violations requiring physical modifications to common areas and individual dwelling units to comply with FHAA design and construction requirements.
key_holding: The parties settled via consent judgment requiring the owner defendants to perform remediation items to address alleged design and construction accessibility violations and pay $200,000 in damages, fees, and costs, while defendants denied any admission of liability.
brief_summary: Fair Housing Justice Center sued Bruckner Tower LLC, Carnegie Management, and related architect entities alleging that the 130-unit multi-family residential building at 25 Bruckner Boulevard in the Bronx was designed and constructed in violation of the Fair Housing Act's accessibility requirements under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(C). The parties settled via consent judgment requiring owner defendants to perform physical remediation modifications to the building's common areas and individual units within specified deadlines, hire a neutral inspector to verify compliance, adopt fair housing policies and training programs, and pay $200,000 in damages, attorneys' fees, and costs.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Alleged failures in design and construction of a 130-unit multi-family residential building (Crescendo) to comply with accessibility requirements of the Fair Housing Act, including modifications to common use areas and individual dwelling units
fha_claims.reasoning: Parties resolved all claims without trial or adjudication of fact or law. Defendants agreed to pay $200,000 in damages and perform comprehensive remediation of design and construction deficiencies identified in the complaint, including retrofits to common areas and individual units, subject to neutral inspector oversight and compliance deadlines.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claims under New York State Executive Law § 290 et seq., New York State Civil Rights Law § 40, and New York City Administrative Code § 8-101 et seq.
fha_claims.reasoning: Parties resolved all state and local human rights law claims without trial or adjudication. Defendants agreed to the same remediation and compliance obligations applicable to federal FHA claims.

source_file: George v. OVERALL CREEK APARTMENTS, LLC
case_name: Cynthia George v. Overall Creek Apartments, LLC et al.
accommodation_description: Design and construction accessibility claim under § 3604(f)(3)(C) — plaintiff, a wheelchair user, alleged the defendant failed to design and construct the property in compliance with Fair Housing Act accessibility guidelines
