key_holding: The plaintiff's design and construction claim under § 3604(f)(3)(C) is time-barred because the statute of limitations begins running when the last available unit is initially rented, and here the final unit was rented on March 19, 2021, more than two years before the lawsuit was filed on March 31, 2023; the model unit (No. 1107) did not toll the limitations period because it was never intended to be made available for rent.
brief_summary: Cynthia George sued Overall Creek Apartments, LLC and related defendants alleging the multifamily housing development in Murfreesboro, Tennessee was designed and constructed in violation of the Fair Housing Act's accessibility requirements for persons with disabilities. The court granted summary judgment for defendants, holding that George's FHA design-and-construction claim was time-barred because the two-year statute of limitations began running when the last available rental unit was initially occupied on March 19, 2021, more than two years before she filed suit, and the model unit she identified did not toll the limitations period since it was never offered for rent.
key_cases_cited: Fair Hous. Council, Inc. v. Vill. of Olde St. Andrews, Inc., 210 F. App'x 469 (6th Cir. 2006)
Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242 (1986)
Miami Valley Fair Hous. Ctr., Inc. v. Preferred Living Real Est. Invs., LLC, 2018 WL 4690790 (S.D. Ohio 2018)
Hous. Rsch. & Advoc. Ctr. v. WXZ Residential Grp./Circle Lofts 118 LLC, 2017 WL 1078956 (N.D. Ohio 2017)
Hous. Advocs., Inc. v. Berardi & Partners, Inc., 2010 WL 4905547 (N.D. Ohio 2010)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible and adaptable design features for persons with disabilities in multifamily housing development; plaintiff alleged accessibility barriers in common areas and units that would interfere with wheelchair access and use of facilities
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that under 42 U.S.C. § 3613(a)(1)(A), the two-year statute of limitations for FHA design and construction claims begins to run upon the initial rental of the final unit available for rent. The last unit was rented on March 19, 2021, and plaintiff filed suit on March 31, 2023—more than two years later—making the claim time-barred. The court rejected plaintiff's argument that Unit 1107, used as a model unit for marketing, should toll the limitations period, finding that treating model units as available units would defeat Congress's intent in enacting the limitations period.

source_file: George v. OVERALL CREEK APARTMENTS, LLC (1)
case_name: George v. Overall Creek Apartments, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff who uses a wheelchair encountered physical accessibility barriers at the apartment complex that would interfere with her ability to access and use the facilities.
key_holding: The FHA preempts state law claims for equitable indemnification (which shift the entire loss to another party) as an obstacle to the FHA's remedial purposes, but does not preempt state law claims for equitable contribution (which apportion only a proportionate share of liability) because such claims do not frustrate congressional objectives.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Cynthia George sued property owners and developers alleging Fair Housing Act violations for failing to design and construct accessible apartment units; the property owners filed a third-party complaint against the architect seeking indemnification, contribution, and breach of contract damages. The court granted the architect's motion to dismiss the indemnification claim as preempted by the FHA but denied dismissal of the contribution claim, holding that proportional fault-sharing claims do not obstruct FHA enforcement objectives.
key_cases_cited: Equal Rights Ctr. v. Niles Bolton Assocs., 602 F.3d 597 (4th Cir. 2010)
City of L.A. v. AECOM Servs., Inc., 854 F.3d 1149 (9th Cir. 2017)
United States v. Murphy Dev., LLC, No. 3:08-0960, 2009 WL 3614829 (M.D. Tenn. Oct. 27, 2009)
Miami Valley Fair Hous. Ctr., Inc. v. Campus Vill. Wright State, LLC, 2012 WL 4473236 (S.D. Ohio Sept. 26, 2012)
County of Livingston v. PSA-Dewberry, Inc., No. 19-CV-01334, 2023 WL 5962079 (C.D. Ill. Sept. 13, 2023)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equitable indemnification, equitable contribution, and breach of contract claims asserted by third-party plaintiffs (Overall Creek and Chandler Properties) against third-party defendant (NBA, the architect). These are state law claims arising from alleged FHA violations by the original defendants.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted the motion to dismiss the equitable indemnification claim as preempted under the FHA under obstacle preemption doctrine, finding that allowing indemnification would allow wrongdoers to escape liability and frustrate the FHA's purpose. The court denied the motion as to the equitable contribution claim, finding it not preempted because contribution requires only proportionate share liability and does not frustrate the FHA's objectives. The breach-of-contract claim was granted in part (to the extent it seeks full indemnification) and denied in part (to the extent it seeks contribution).

source_file: Greater New Orleans Fair Housing Action Center v St Bernard Parish

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Moratorium on construction of multi-family housing with more than five units
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found the moratorium had a disparate racial impact on African-Americans, with statistical evidence showing African-Americans were 85% more likely to live in multi-family structures and twice as likely to live in rental housing. The moratorium reduced supply of rental properties disproportionately affecting African-American households across multiple income ranges.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Moratorium on construction of multi-family housing with more than five units
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found discriminatory intent based on: (1) historical background of similar ordinances targeting multi-family housing; (2) sequence of events showing positive reception until racially-coded editorial, followed by swift introduction of moratorium three days later; (3) departures from normal zoning procedure (parish-wide blanket moratorium rather than geographically limited); (4) substantive departures from normal decision-making (parish officials initially supported development for $60M investment and $40K annual tax revenue); and (5) admission by Councilman Lauga that public outcry was a factor in introduction of moratorium.

case_name: Michael S. Hartley v. United Student Rentals, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges disability-based discrimination arising from landlord's failure to repair apartment front door over approximately one year period.
key_holding: The complaint fails to state an FHA claim because plaintiff does not describe how his mental impairments limit major life activities, nor does he allege facts connecting defendants' failure to repair the door to his disability.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Michael Hartley sued private landlords and their attorney alleging the defendants violated the Fair Housing Act by failing to repair his apartment's front door over approximately one year despite his disability-related mental health conditions. The N.D.N.Y. recommended dismissing the complaint because plaintiff failed to allege facts connecting any failure to repair the door to his disability or showing defendants were responsible for the repair.
key_cases_cited: Francis v. Kings Park Manor, Inc., 992 F.3d 67 (2d Cir. 2021)
Ingraham v. Red Carpet Hous. Corp., 2017 WL 5152343 (N.D.N.Y. 2017)
Robinson v. Soc. Serv., 2013 WL 1122450 (N.D.N.Y. 2013)
Fabrikant v. French, 691 F.3d 193 (2d Cir. 2012)
Triestman v. Fed. Bureau of Prisons, 470 F.3d 471 (2d Cir. 2006)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Repair of broken front door with defective lock
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts connecting his mental health impairments to the requested accommodation (door repair) or demonstrating that defendants were responsible for the failure to repair. The complaint did not describe how impairments limit major life activities or establish nexus between disability and the accommodation need.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: § 1983 claims for constitutional violations (First, Sixth, Eighth, Fourteenth Amendments); state law breach of warranty of habitability
fha_claims.disposition: 12(b)(1) and failure to state a claim
fha_claims.reasoning: § 1983 claims dismissed because defendants are private parties, not state actors, and complaint alleges no facts supporting state action. State law habitability claim dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because all parties are New York residents (no diversity) and claim does not arise under federal law.

source_file: Hispanics United of DuPage County v Village of Addison Ill

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied defendant's motion for summary judgment on FHA disparate treatment claims brought by absentee landlords (Contis and Husbys), Hispanic resident (Rivera), white residents (Cagles), and organizational plaintiffs. Court found standing under FHA exists for all plaintiffs based on Article III injury-in-fact, causation, and redressability; FHA standing is as broad as Article III permits with no prudential barriers. Merits of discrimination claim not reached at this stage.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1982, 1983 claims for discrimination and equal protection violations
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted summary judgment dismissing Rivera's §§ 1981, 1982, and 1983 claims and Cagles' §§ 1981 and 1982 claims for lack of standing under prudential doctrine. Rivera lacked contractual or social relationship with Hispanic TIF residents; Cagles lacked contractual relationship required by §§ 1981 and 1982. Cagles retained standing under § 1983 for Equal Protection claim based on alleged denial of their own constitutional rights to associate with minorities.

source_file: Humphries v. US DEPARTMENT OF HOUSING & URBAN DEVELOPMENT
case_name: Humphries v. U.S. Department of Housing & Urban Development
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested to respond in writing or by electronic communication instead of telephone conversations during HUD's investigation of her housing discrimination complaints, as an accommodation for her disabilities (anxiety, depression, memory loss, brain injuries).
key_holding: The court dismissed all claims because HUD is immune from suit under the ADA and Rehabilitation Act due to sovereign immunity, the FHA provides no private right of action against HUD, and the individual HUD employees cannot be held liable under the ADA, RA, or Bivens.
brief_summary: Jacqueline Humphries, proceeding pro se, sued HUD and HUD employees alleging they denied her reasonable accommodations (requesting written/electronic communication instead of phone calls) during HUD's investigation of her housing discrimination complaints against housing authorities. The court dismissed all claims, finding HUD immune from ADA and Rehabilitation Act claims, no private right of action under the FHA against HUD, and no individual liability under any asserted theory.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2009)
Biven v. Six Unknown Named Agents of Fed. Bureau of Narcotics, 403 U.S. 388 (1971)
Turner v. Sec'y of U.S. Dep't of Hous. & Urban Dev., 449 F.3d 536 (3d Cir. 2006)
Venter v. Potter, 435 F. App'x 92 (3d Cir. 2011)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested to respond to HUD FHEO investigation in writing or by electronic communication rather than by telephone, citing disabilities including memory loss, confusion, brain injuries, and anxiety/depression.
fha_claims.reasoning: The FHA provides no express or implied right of action against HUD or its employees for failure to investigate discrimination complaints or provide accommodations during the investigation process. Federal courts lack subject matter jurisdiction over such claims against federal agencies.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II claims for denial of reasonable accommodations during HUD investigation; Section 504 Rehabilitation Act claims for denial of accommodations; 42 U.S.C. § 1983 constitutional claims; 18 U.S.C. §§ 241 and 242 criminal deprivation claims; Bivens claims for discrimination by federal officials.
fha_claims.reasoning: The ADA does not apply to the federal government or its agencies; Title II provides no individual liability. The Rehabilitation Act does not waive sovereign immunity for federal agencies. Section 1983 applies only to state actors, not federal agencies. Sections 241 and 242 are criminal statutes with no private civil cause of action. Bivens claims against federal officials are barred by sovereign immunity and lack non-conclusory allegations of discriminatory motivation or personal involvement.

source_file: Huntington Branch NAACP v Town of Huntington

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Refusal to amend zoning ordinance to permit private construction of multi-family housing outside urban renewal area; refusal to rezone Elwood-Pulaski parcel to R-3M status to allow construction of integrated subsidized housing project (Matinecock Court) in white neighborhood
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied disparate impact analysis without requiring proof of discriminatory intent. Town's zoning ordinance restricting multi-family housing to 52% minority urban renewal area had substantial adverse impact on minorities seeking affordable housing and perpetuated racial segregation. Town's proffered justifications (traffic, parking, fire protection, proximity to utilities, inadequate recreation, undersized units) were insubstantial and could be addressed through design modifications or less discriminatory alternatives (tax incentives). Court ordered site-specific relief requiring rezoning of Matinecock Court site and amendment of ordinance.

source_file: Jackson v City of Auburn Ala

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to establish a prima facie case of intentional racial discrimination under the Fair Housing Act disparate treatment theory. The court applied the McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework and found that plaintiffs could not identify similarly situated white developers who received conditional-use permits for comparable projects, nor could they prove the City's stated reason (incompatibility with surrounding neighborhood) was pretextual for racial discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal Protection Clause violation under 42 U.S.C.A. § 1983
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to establish either element of their equal protection claim: (1) they did not identify similarly situated white developers treated differently, as prior projects either predated the conditional-use requirement or involved different site conditions and deficiency levels; and (2) they did not prove intentional racial discrimination, as the City's stated reason (neighborhood incompatibility) was supported by the property's location at the end of a cul-de-sac surrounded by single-family subdivisions, and there was no evidence the City knew of any racial animus motivating public opposition.

case_name: Anthony Alexander James v. Metzger Management Company
accommodation_description: No disability accommodation request was made; plaintiff alleged race-based housing discrimination under § 3604(b).
key_holding: The complaint failed to allege sufficient facts showing plaintiff was subjected to different terms, conditions, or privileges because of his race or any other protected characteristic, warranting dismissal for failure to state an FHA claim.
brief_summary: African-American tenant sued property management company alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on race discrimination after the defendant required him to vacate his apartment following a fire and sought back rent. The court granted defendant's motion to dismiss, finding the complaint failed to allege facts sufficient to show plaintiff was subjected to different terms or conditions because of his protected status.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Cabrera v. Alvarez, 977 F.Supp.2d 969 (N.D. Cal. 2013)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint alleges discrimination based on race but fails to allege any facts showing plaintiff was subjected to different terms, conditions, or privileges because of race or any other protected status. The complaint contains only conclusory allegations unsupported by factual content sufficient to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Landlord negligence, defamation, emotional distress
fha_claims.reasoning: State law claims for landlord negligence, defamation, and emotional distress are vague and conclusory, lacking factual allegations regarding defendant's conduct. The complaint attributes fire reports to the fire department and PG&E rather than the defendant, failing to allege overt acts by the defendant supporting the claims.

source_file: Jones v. BLUE OCEAN REALTY, LLC
case_name: Travis R. Jones v. Blue Ocean Realty, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a physically disabled person injured in a bus crash, alleges Defendants refused to rent him an apartment and failed to provide reasonable accommodations.
key_holding: Plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claims were dismissed as time-barred because the complaint was filed nearly eleven months after the two-year statute of limitations had expired, and neither equitable tolling based on COVID-19 nor the continuing violation doctrine applied to excuse the late filing.
brief_summary: Travis R. Jones, a physically disabled plaintiff, sued Blue Ocean Realty, LLC and Oaklee Village Baltimore, LLC alleging they violated the Fair Housing Act by refusing to rent him an apartment and failing to provide reasonable accommodations. The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss, finding the action was barred by the two-year statute of limitations because Plaintiff filed his complaint nearly eleven months after the limitations period expired, and neither equitable tolling nor the continuing violation doctrine applied.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Cruz v. Maypa, 773 F.3d 138 (4th Cir. 2014)
Rouse v. Lee, 339 F.3d 238 (4th Cir. 2003)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The alleged discriminatory conduct occurred on October 5, 2020, with final contact on November 24, 2020. The two-year FHA statute of limitations expired on November 24, 2022, but Plaintiff did not file suit until October 6, 2023—nearly eleven months late. Equitable tolling was not available because Plaintiff failed to explain how COVID-19 prevented timely filing, and the continuing violation doctrine did not apply because Plaintiff alleged no discriminatory acts after November 24, 2020, only continued effects of prior violations.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Walk-through inspection of apartment unit prior to move-in, requested due to Plaintiff's physical disability
fha_claims.reasoning: The failure to provide a reasonable accommodation claim is barred by the same statute of limitations analysis. The alleged refusal to accommodate Plaintiff's request for a walk-through inspection occurred in September 2020, well outside the two-year filing window. The court did not reach the merits of whether the accommodation was reasonable or necessary because the claim was time-barred.

source_file: KRASZYNSKI v. ROB ROY COUNTRY CLUB VILLAGE ASSOCIATION

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Cessation or cessation of pesticide and herbicide spraying on and around plaintiff's condominium unit to accommodate claimed chemical sensitivity and autoimmune disorder (Crohn's disease, asthma, COPD)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted judgment as a matter of law on Count I because: (1) plaintiff failed to establish she had a qualifying disability with sufficient notice to defendants prior to filing suit (no specific diagnosis communicated until January 2019 letter, after complaint filed); (2) plaintiff failed to prove defendants actually applied glyphosate or other chemicals at or near her property (no evidence of exposure, frequency, or route of entry); (3) plaintiff failed to establish the requested accommodation was necessary to alleviate effects of her handicap (only subjective belief offered, no causal link between cessation of spraying and amelioration of disability); and (4) § 3604 does not apply to post-acquisition conduct under Halprin precedent, and plaintiff failed to show constructive eviction.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted judgment as a matter of law on Count III (retaliation under § 3617) because plaintiff failed to introduce evidence of: (1) protected activity (no clear notice of qualifying disability); (2) adverse action (alleged fines, plant removal, continued spraying, verbal harassment were not supported by evidence); and (3) causal connection between protected activity and adverse action. Court found no evidence defendants acted with knowledge plaintiff was member of protected class or that they coerced, intimidated, threatened, or interfered with her rights. Plant removal was by third-party contractor without evidence of defendant direction; spraying was pursuant to legitimate policy applied to all units; and alleged verbal abuse was entirely unsupported.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Intentional infliction of emotional distress (Illinois state tort law)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court granted judgment as a matter of law on Count IV (IIED under Illinois law) because plaintiff failed to prove: (1) conduct was extreme and outrageous (applying pesticides to common areas for legitimate property maintenance purpose does not meet threshold; plant removal by third-party contractor was not shown to be directed by defendants; alleged unjust fines were unsupported by evidence); (2) defendants intended to inflict severe emotional distress or knew of high probability thereof; and (3) plaintiff suffered severe emotional distress (only evidence was fear/phobia of pesticides, which does not rise to requisite level). Court applied McGrath factors and found defendants pursued legitimate objective of property maintenance without extreme or outrageous conduct.

source_file: LABOR COMMISSION v. FCS COMMUNITY MGMT.
case_name: Labor Commission v. FCS Community Management
accommodation_description: Request to keep eight chickens as emotional support animals for the daughter with PTSD, anxiety, and sensory processing disorder, and for Natalie's reactive hypoglycemia.
key_holding: The Court of Appeals reversed the district court's determination of constructive denial, holding that no constructive denial occurred because the HOA allowed the Sackses to keep all eight chickens during the investigation period, did not punish them during that time, and ultimately granted a reasonable partial accommodation (two chickens) that UALD found reasonable.
brief_summary: The Sackses, whose daughter has PTSD and sensory processing disorder, requested that their HOA allow them to keep eight chickens as emotional support animals despite CC&Rs prohibiting poultry. The HOA initially denied a variance request, then conducted an investigation after the UFHA was invoked, ultimately offering to allow two chickens. The district court found constructive denial based on delay, but the Court of Appeals reversed, holding no constructive denial occurred because the HOA allowed all chickens during review, did not punish the Sackses during investigation, and granted a reasonable partial accommodation.
key_cases_cited: LaRosa v. River Quarry Apartments, LLC, 2019 WL 3538951 (D. Idaho 2019)
Dubois v. Association of Apartment Owners of 2987 Kalakaua, 453 F.3d 1175 (9th Cir. 2006)
Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condo. Ass'n, 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014)
Astralis Condo. Ass'n v. Secretary, U.S. Dep't of Housing & Urban Dev., 620 F.3d 62 (1st Cir. 2010)
Haws v. Norman, 2017 WL 4221064 (D. Utah 2017)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request to keep eight chickens as assistance animals/emotional support animals for Natalie's reactive hypoglycemia and her daughter's sensory processing disorder and PTSD/anxiety
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court reversed the district court's finding of constructive denial, holding that the HOA did not refuse to make a reasonable accommodation because: (1) the Sackses were allowed to keep all eight chickens during the HOA's evaluation period; (2) the HOA never punished or threatened to punish them during the interim; (3) the HOA ultimately granted a partial accommodation (two chickens) that UALD found reasonable; and (4) the 58-day review period was not unreasonably long given the novel nature of comfort chickens and the need to investigate health and safety concerns. The court applied a direct balancing approach, examining whether the delay and lack of interactive process constituted a constructive denial, and concluded it did not.

case_name: Lax v. Adobe Services
accommodation_description: Plaintiff Crystal Lax, who uses a wheelchair, alleges housing agencies refused to find her permanent housing because of her disability and race while she held an emergency housing voucher.
key_holding: The complaint fails to state an FHA claim because it contains no specific factual allegations that defendants subjected plaintiffs to different terms, conditions, or privileges because of disability or race—the complaint only states plaintiffs 'suspect' discrimination without supporting facts.
brief_summary: Crystal and Dominique Lax sued housing agencies alleging they were denied access to low-income housing because of Crystal's race and disabilities while she held an emergency housing voucher. The court dismissed the complaint with leave to amend, finding the allegations too conclusory to state a Fair Housing Act claim because there were no specific facts showing defendants discriminated based on disability or race rather than simply failing to locate suitable housing.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Harris v. Itzhaki, 183 F.3d 1043 (9th Cir. 1999)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Accessible housing without stairs; plaintiff in wheelchair required accessible apartment but defendants only offered housing accessible by stairs
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint fails to allege that defendants refused to provide accessible housing because of plaintiff's disability; merely states defendants could only find housing accessible by stairs, which does not support an inference of discriminatory refusal based on disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of housing placement based on race
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint contains no allegations that defendants knew of plaintiff's race or discriminated because of it; plaintiff merely 'suspects' discrimination without specific factual allegations supporting racial discrimination claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983, Fourteenth Amendment, Eighth Amendment, Thirteenth Amendment claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Complaint asserts constitutional violations under § 1983, but none of the defendants are alleged to be state actors, which is a required element for § 1983 liability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The jury found the Village violated the Fair Housing Act by adopting a zoning code designed to restrict home synagogues and make dwellings unavailable to Orthodox and Hasidic Jews based on their religion. The appellate court reversed the district court's judgment as a matter of law, finding the jury verdict was fully supported by evidence of discriminatory animus and intent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (First Amendment free exercise of religion and free speech); 42 U.S.C. § 1985(3) (conspiracy to deprive equal protection and equal privileges and immunities)
fha_claims.reasoning: The jury found the Village conspired to violate plaintiffs' First Amendment rights to free exercise of religion and free speech. The appellate court reversed the district court's judgment as a matter of law, finding the jury verdict was supported by evidence that the Village and the Airmont Civic Association shared a conspiratorial objective to restrict Orthodox Jewish worship in homes.

source_file: MALAVE-SYKES v. GEODIS SCO USA LLC

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title VII employment discrimination claim based on race, disability, and gender; ADA retaliation claim; ADA disability discrimination claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to state a plausible claim for wrongful termination under Title VII, retaliation under the ADA, or disability discrimination under the ADA. Conclusory allegations of discrimination without specific facts linking the adverse action to protected status are insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly.

source_file: MHANY Management Inc v Incorporated Village of Garden City

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that Garden City Defendants acted with discriminatory intent when they eliminated R-M zoning (permitting 311 multi-family units) and endorsed R-T zoning (severely restricting multi-family housing) after receiving public opposition to affordable housing. The sequence of events, statistical evidence of disproportionate impact on minorities, and race-based animus in community opposition supported a finding that discrimination played a determinative role in the zoning decision, even though defendants offered some legitimate justifications (traffic, townhomes).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found that R-T zoning had a disparate impact on minorities by significantly decreasing the potential pool of minority residents able to afford housing at the Social Services Site compared to the rejected R-M zoning. The zoning also perpetuated segregation in a community that was only 2.6-4.1% minority. Although defendants offered legitimate governmental interests (traffic reduction, townhome provision), they failed to prove the absence of less discriminatory alternatives, as R-M zoning could have achieved similar goals with less discriminatory effect.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1983, Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found liability under §§ 1981 and 1983 and the Equal Protection Clause by proving Garden City acted with discriminatory intent in the zoning decision. The court rejected the defendants' argument that a zoning ordinance does not constitute a 'policy or custom' under § 1983, holding that municipalities may be sued for constitutional deprivations pursuant to a governmental ordinance, regulation, or decision.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. § 1982 (property rights claim)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court dismissed the § 1982 claim as a matter of law, finding that plaintiffs failed to identify a cognizable property interest in as-yet-built or planned affordable housing. The court noted that § 1982 protects the property rights of 'citizens of the United States' and that plaintiffs lacked a property interest in hypothetical future housing development.

source_file: May v. MARTIN FEIN INTEREST LTD.
case_name: May v. Martin Fein Interest Ltd.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege defendant discriminated against their adult daughter Alexis (who has multiple sclerosis and uses a wheelchair) by misrepresenting Unit 237 as handicap-accessible and refusing to accept deliveries of her medical supplies.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment to defendant because plaintiffs failed to establish prima facie cases of disability or race discrimination—the Mays cannot assert claims on behalf of their adult daughter Alexis, and the evidence failed to show defendant's actions were motivated by discriminatory intent or had a discriminatory impact based on either Alexis's mobility disability or plaintiffs' race.
brief_summary: Raymond and Angela May, proceeding pro se, sued Martin Fein Interest Ltd. (the former property manager of Creekside at Crabtree Apartments) alleging disability discrimination regarding their adult daughter Alexis who has multiple sclerosis and uses a wheelchair, and race discrimination. The court granted summary judgment for defendant, finding that plaintiffs cannot assert claims on behalf of their non-party daughter, and failed to produce evidence that defendant's employees discriminated against them based on Alexis's disability (by allegedly misrepresenting unit accessibility and refusing to sign for medical deliveries) or based on race (through various alleged mistreatment).
key_cases_cited: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)
Martin v. Brondum, 535 F. App'x 242 (4th Cir. 2013)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Reeves v. Hampton Forest Apts, 689 F. App'x 768 (4th Cir. 2017)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged that Defendant's employee misrepresented that Unit 237 was handicapped accessible when it was not, preventing Alexis (their disabled adult daughter with multiple sclerosis) from accessing various rooms and areas in her wheelchair.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that Plaintiffs' own allegation that they were shown Unit 237 prior to leasing it fatally undermined their claim of deception, as the alleged deficiencies (bathtub vs. shower, counter heights, door peephole, door openings) would have been readily apparent upon viewing. No reasonable jury could find for Plaintiffs on this claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged that Defendant's employees refused to accept deliveries of Alexis's medical supplies and medications, claiming it was an administrative burden.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework and found that Plaintiffs failed to demonstrate disability discrimination. The statement about administrative burden was made by William Hubbard, who was employed by Bell Partners, Inc. (not Defendant) after Defendant's management agreement terminated on November 1, 2019. For other alleged package mishandling incidents, Defendant provided legitimate non-discriminatory reasons (e.g., package addressed to Alexis Lucas, not immediately associated with Plaintiffs), and Plaintiffs provided no evidence that the reasons were pretextual or disability-motivated.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged that Defendant's employee placed an insufficient funds notice on Plaintiffs' door knowing that Raymond May had a heart condition.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs asserted no evidence from which a reasonable jury could find that the placement of the notice was motivated by or had a discriminatory impact related to May's heart condition. The court found no prima facie case of disability discrimination under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged that Defendant's employees engaged in a pattern of racially discriminatory conduct, including placing late rent notices, refusing to sign for deliveries, increasing rent, requiring certified funds payment, failing to honor rent concessions, and calling police on Raymond May.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework. For direct evidence, the court found that photographs allegedly showing racist behavior were either innocuous or attributable to Bell Partners employees (Pridemore, Hubbard, Dawes), not Defendant. For circumstantial evidence, Plaintiffs failed to show they were treated differently than other tenants because of race. Defendant provided legitimate non-discriminatory reasons for each alleged action: certified funds requirement due to credit history (authorized by lease); late notices authorized by lease terms; rent concessions granted as courtesy; rent changes occurred after Defendant's management ended; and police called as precaution due to threat to kick down door to retrieve gun. Plaintiffs provided no evidence that these reasons were false or pretextual.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged that after filing a HUD complaint on June 20, 2019, Defendant retaliated by advising them they had not been paying correct rent amounts, not honoring promised rent concessions, and filing summary ejectment actions.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that Plaintiffs engaged in protected activity (filing HUD complaint) and Defendant was aware of it, but Plaintiffs failed to establish adverse action causally connected to the protected activity. Evidence did not support that rental rates were changed or concessions were not honored. Uncontroverted evidence established that Defendant did not file any summary ejectment or other action against Plaintiffs; those actions were filed by Creekside Crabtree Apartments, Inc. Plaintiffs' allegation regarding denial of financial assistance documents lacked supporting evidence and could not rely on alleged retaliation against non-party Alexis.

source_file: McFARLAND FARM PROPERTY OWNERS'ASSOCIATION v. Ryan

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation for traumatic brain injury in enforcement of protective covenants regarding roof replacement and property maintenance; extension of time to comply with covenant requirements due to disability
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court declined to reach Ryan's Fair Housing Act claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(B) because Ryan failed to provide meaningful analysis on appeal, did not identify the specific accommodation needed, did not explain why it was reasonable, and did not adequately explain how the Association refused it. The claim was not properly raised below with argument from both sides or a trial court ruling.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Procedural accommodation as pro se litigant with traumatic brain injury; GR 33 accommodation request; claims regarding trial court's failure to accommodate disability in litigation
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court held that the trial court did not fail to accommodate Ryan as a pro se litigant with traumatic brain injury because Ryan did not make a formal request for specific accommodation under GR 33, and the trial court took reasonable steps to ensure Ryan was heard, including providing a hearing device, explaining trial procedures, clarifying testimony, allowing breaks, and assisting with witness examination and testimony.

case_name: McGinn v. Broadmead, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested gluten-free food preparation and dining services to accommodate her celiac disease at a continuing care retirement community.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment to Broadmead on the FHA reasonable accommodation claim because many claims were time-barred, discrete incidents of alleged gluten exposure did not establish a continuing violation, and plaintiff failed to demonstrate that Broadmead denied her a 'like experience' or failed to accommodate her disability under federal law.
brief_summary: Eleanor McGinn, an 83-year-old resident with celiac disease at Broadmead, a continuing care retirement community in Hunt Valley, Maryland, sued Broadmead under the Fair Housing Act alleging the community failed to accommodate her disability by not providing adequate gluten-free food options. The court granted summary judgment to Broadmead, finding most claims time-barred, the continuing violation doctrine inapplicable to discrete accommodation failures, and insufficient evidence that Broadmead denied McGinn a like experience or failed to accommodate her celiac disease.
key_cases_cited: Ott v. Maryland Dep't of Pub. Safety and Corr. Servs., 909 F.3d 655 (4th Cir. 2018)
A Soc'y Without A Name v. Virginia, 655 F.3d 342 (4th Cir. 2011)
Semenova v. Maryland Transit Admin., 845 F.3d 564 (4th Cir. 2017)
Thomas v. The Salvation Army S. Territory, 841 F.3d 632 (4th Cir. 2016)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Safe, gluten-free dining options and preparation in a certified gluten-free kitchen with adequately trained staff; alternatively, return of entrance fee and payments for services not rendered
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that plaintiff's FHA claim accrued in January 2019 when she first complained about insufficient variety and quality of gluten-free options, which is beyond the two-year FHA statute of limitations (claim filed September 26, 2023). The continuing violation doctrine does not apply to failure-to-accommodate claims under the FHA. The court also found that plaintiff failed to establish standing for injunctive relief because she refused to eat at Broadmead despite improvements being made, and her fear of future harm was too speculative and conjectural.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act (29 U.S.C. § 794); Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act (42 U.S.C. § 12181 et seq.); state law claims for breach of contract, negligence, negligent misrepresentation, breach of express warranty, breach of implied warranty of merchantability, and breach of implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose
fha_claims.reasoning: For the ADA Title III claim, plaintiff lacked Article III standing to seek injunctive relief because she failed to demonstrate a concrete and imminent injury; her past injuries and speculative fear of future harm were insufficient. For the Rehabilitation Act claim, it was time-barred under the three-year Maryland statute of limitations, with the continuing violation doctrine inapplicable to failure-to-accommodate claims. For breach of contract, plaintiff failed to show Broadmead breached its obligation to provide gluten-free meals; the three alleged gluten exposures were either time-barred or unsupported by evidence. For negligence, plaintiff failed to establish that Broadmead breached a duty of care or caused her injury regarding the chicken marsala incident; her evidence was speculative and did not create a genuine issue of material fact. For negligent misrepresentation, plaintiff failed to identify specific false statements made by Broadmead at the time of contracting. For warranty claims, the UCC does not apply because the R&C Agreement is primarily a services contract, and Maryland law does not recognize implied warranty claims against food-service establishments.

source_file: Miller v. GEORGIA DEPARTMENT OF COMMUNITY SUPERVISION
case_name: Tracy A. Miller v. Georgia Department of Community Supervision, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a paraplegic parolee, alleges the Board discriminated against him by placing him at a nursing facility (Bostick) for elderly and disabled parolees rather than allowing him to reside elsewhere.
key_holding: The court found that Bostick was designed to accommodate elderly and disabled parolees and represents a legitimate effort to accommodate plaintiff's paraplegia, not discrimination; plaintiff failed to state an FHA claim because he was not a buyer or renter and the Board did not 'make unavailable' any dwelling.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Tracy A. Miller, a paraplegic parolee, sued the Georgia State Board of Pardons and Paroles and others, claiming disability discrimination under the ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and Fair Housing Act for being paroled to a nursing facility (Bostick) designed for elderly and disabled parolees rather than being allowed to reside elsewhere. The court recommended dismissing the FHA claim because plaintiff failed to show he was a buyer or renter and the Board did not make housing unavailable but rather attempted to accommodate his disability.
key_cases_cited: Kirby v. Siegelman
Thompson v. Davis
Jenkins v. N.Y. City Dep't of Homeless Svcs.
Abdus-Sabur v. Hope Village, Inc.
Sailboat Bend Sober Living, LLC v. City of Fort Lauderdale

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Placement at Bostick Nursing Center rather than plaintiff's preferred housing location
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege that the Board treated him less favorably than a similarly situated non-disabled parolee. The Board's individualized consideration of plaintiff's disabilities in determining appropriate placement constitutes lawful accommodation, not discrimination. Plaintiff did not allege categorical exclusion based on disability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II, Section 504 Rehabilitation Act, and FHA § 3604(f)(1) claims regarding placement at Bostick Nursing Center
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege he was a 'buyer' or 'renter' under FHA § 3604(f)(1) and did not demonstrate that defendants denied or made a dwelling unavailable to him. The Board's placement decision accommodated rather than denied housing. Plaintiff's parole application did not include a preferred residence address, so the Board could not have considered alternative placement.

case_name: Deborah Morris v. City of Baltimore
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, an elderly/disabled resident, allegedly requested that the City transform her private apartment building into accessible housing through elevator repairs, ventilation improvements, and installation of chair lifts for emergency evacuation.
key_holding: The Court dismissed Plaintiff's claims because she sued the wrong party (City instead of her private landlord), lacked Article III standing as any alleged harm was not traceable to City actions, and failed to allege sufficient facts that the City took any discriminatory action against her because of disability.
brief_summary: Deborah Morris, a disabled/elderly resident of a privately-owned apartment building in Baltimore, sued the City of Baltimore alleging the City violated the ADA, Section 504, and Fair Housing Act by failing to ensure her building provided accessible housing. The Court granted the City's motion to dismiss without prejudice, finding Morris sued the wrong party (the City rather than her private landlord), lacked Article III standing because her alleged harms were not traceable to City actions, and failed to allege facts plausibly showing the City took discriminatory action against her because of her disability.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Woods v. City of Greensboro, 855 F.3d 639 (4th Cir. 2017)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Elevator repairs and maintenance, ventilation in elevators, installation of chair lifts for emergency evacuation in a 12-floor, 266-apartment building housing elderly and disabled residents
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to support a plausible claim that the City of Baltimore took any action against her because of her disability. The complaint does not allege that any Baltimore City official was aware of plaintiff's disability or acted in any discriminatory manner toward her, and plaintiff's alleged harm stems from her private landlord, not the City.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II, Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to support a plausible claim under the ADA and Section 504 that the City took any action against her because of her disability. The complaint does not allege that any Baltimore City official was aware of plaintiff's disability or acted in any discriminatory manner toward her.

source_file: Nelson v. HOUSING AUTHORITY OF SOUTH BEND
case_name: Nelson v. Housing Authority of South Bend
accommodation_description: Tenant facing eviction for being over-housed requested to add an adult family member to her lease or be permitted to remain in a two-bedroom unit as an accommodation for disability.
key_holding: Nelson waived arguments about HASB's Occupancy Plan by not raising them below, explicitly disavowed a failure-to-accommodate claim at trial, and the trial court's factual findings that she violated her lease by failing to transfer or add an adult were not clearly erroneous; HASB provided due process.
brief_summary: Nelson, a public housing tenant, appealed an eviction order after refusing HASB's transfer demand from a two-bedroom to a one-bedroom unit, arguing she was entitled to reasonable accommodation for disability. The Indiana Court of Appeals affirmed, finding Nelson explicitly disavowed the failure-to-accommodate claim at trial, her other arguments were waived for not being raised below, and the trial court's factual findings were not clearly erroneous.
key_cases_cited: Trinity Homes, LLC v. Fang, 848 N.E.2d 1065 (Ind. 2006)
Berg v. Berg, 170 N.E.3d 224 (Ind. 2021)
Horner v. Carter, 981 N.E.2d 1210 (Ind. 2013)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Nelson requested to add an adult (her son or another person) to her lease as a live-in aide or additional household member to avoid transfer from her two-bedroom unit after HASB determined she was over-housed as a single resident.
fha_claims.disposition: Judgment for defendant on lease violation
fha_claims.reasoning: The trial court found Nelson did not establish she had a disability within the meaning of the Fair Housing Act, did not credit her testimony or medical documentation, and Nelson herself stated at trial she was 'not making a claim of failure to accommodate.' The court found Nelson failed to follow through on HASB's offer to add an adult to her lease and did not timely invoke the grievance procedure. On appeal, Nelson waived the reasonable accommodation argument by not raising it to the trial court.

case_name: Matter of Oceanview Home for Adults, Inc. v. Zucker
accommodation_description: Adult home challenged state regulations capping admissions of persons with serious mental illness at facilities with 80+ beds if the SMI population exceeds 25%, arguing the restriction violates the FHA
key_holding: The Court of Appeals held that the challenged regulations do not facially discriminate against persons with disabilities because the admissions cap reflects a professional clinical judgment about appropriate therapeutic settings for persons with serious mental illness, furthers the integration mandate of Olmstead, and gives SMI residents greater ability to interact with non-disabled persons.
brief_summary: Oceanview Home for Adults, an adult home licensed by the New York Department of Health, brought a facial challenge to state regulations restricting facilities with 80+ beds from admitting additional residents with serious mental illness if their SMI population exceeds 25%, claiming the admission cap violates the Fair Housing Act. The Court of Appeals affirmed that the regulations do not make housing unavailable on the basis of disability because they reflect professional clinical judgment about therapeutically appropriate settings and further the integration mandate by giving SMI residents greater opportunity to interact with non-disabled persons.
key_cases_cited: Olmstead v. L.C., 527 U.S. 581 (1999)
Community House, Inc. v. City of Boise, 490 F.3d 1041 (9th Cir. 2007)
Larkin v. State of Mich. Dept. of Social Servs., 89 F.3d 285 (6th Cir. 1996)
Bangerter v. Orem City Corp., 46 F.3d 1491 (10th Cir. 1995)
Disability Advocates, Inc. v. Paterson, 653 F. Supp. 2d 184 (E.D.N.Y. 2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Facial challenge to DOH regulations prohibiting adult homes with 80+ beds and 25%+ residents with serious mental illness from admitting additional persons with serious mental illness
fha_claims.reasoning: The Court of Appeals held that the challenged regulations do not 'deny' or 'make unavailable' housing on the basis of disability because they concern the type of institutional setting in which services may be provided, reflect professional clinical judgment about therapeutic effectiveness, and further the integration mandate by giving persons with serious mental illness greater ability to interact with non-disabled individuals. The regulations do not rest on stereotypes, prejudice, or fear.

source_file: Oakwood at Madison Inc v Madison Tp
Oconomowoc Residential Programs Inc v City of Greenfield

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Facial challenge to Wisconsin's 2,500-foot spacing requirement for community living arrangements serving developmentally disabled persons
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found the spacing statute was not facially neutral because it explicitly classified persons on the basis of disability and thus could not support a disparate impact claim, which requires facial neutrality. The court declined to address the disparate impact theory because it had already ruled the statute was preempted on other grounds.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Facial challenge to Wisconsin's 2,500-foot spacing requirement for community living arrangements (Wis.Stat. § 62.23(7)(i)1 & 2r) as facially discriminatory
fha_claims.reasoning: The court held that the facial challenge failed because the spacing requirement does not impact disabled persons in every instance of its application—it also applies to foster homes and group homes for children. A facial challenge requires showing the law is invalid under all circumstances.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Preemption claim: Wisconsin's 2,500-foot spacing requirement for community living arrangements preempted by the Fair Housing Amendment Act and Americans with Disabilities Act
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that Wis.Stat. § 62.23(7)(i)1 & 2r classify persons on the basis of disability and substantially limit meaningful access to housing for developmentally disabled persons, thereby conflicting with and preempted by the FHAA and ADA. Congress intended these remedial laws to preempt state laws that burden disabled persons' access to housing, and benign legislative intent cannot justify discriminatory laws.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Grant of special zoning permission/variance to allow operation of community-based residential facilities (CBRFs) for developmentally disabled adults within 2,500 feet of existing group homes, in violation of Wisconsin spacing requirement
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the three-part reasonable accommodation test (reasonable, necessary, and affording equal opportunity) and found plaintiff met all three elements. The special zoning permissions were reasonable because the benefit to disabled residents (less restrictive environment, residential living) outweighed speculative community concerns that were largely licensing rather than zoning matters. The accommodations were necessary because developmentally disabled persons cannot live independently and CBRFs provide essential congregate living. Without the accommodation, disabled persons lacked equal opportunity to live in residential neighborhoods. The municipalities failed to grant reasonable accommodations as required by the FHAA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Equal Protection Clause challenge (Fourteenth Amendment); Americans with Disabilities Act Title II claim
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff waived its Equal Protection theory and ADA Title II claim by failing to brief them adequately at summary judgment. The court noted plaintiff omitted arguments in support of its equal protection theory and failed to brief its ADA theory, giving it only passing mention. Because parties agreed to resolve all issues via cross-motions for summary judgment, failure to brief constituted waiver.

source_file: Open Homes Fellowship Inc v Orange County Fla

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Special exception or zoning variance to permit operation of a faith-based substance abuse recovery residential program (Regeneration Program) for 16-20 men in an R-3 (Multiple Family Dwelling District) zone without requiring a special exception permit, or alternatively, approval of the special exception application that was denied.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court did not reach the merits of the FHA reasonable accommodation claim because it resolved the case on equal protection grounds, finding the County violated plaintiff's equal protection rights by requiring a special exception for Open Homes while permitting similarly situated uses (community residential homes, dormitories, fraternities, sororities, daycare centers) as of right. The court granted summary judgment for plaintiff on constitutional grounds and did not substantively analyze the FHA claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II, Rehabilitation Act § 504, Equal Protection Clause, RLUIPA, First Amendment, Florida RFRA, equitable estoppel
fha_claims.reasoning: The court granted summary judgment for plaintiff on equal protection grounds (as-applied violation under the Fourteenth Amendment), finding that the County failed to proffer any rational basis for requiring Open Homes to obtain a special exception when similarly situated uses were permitted as of right, and that the County's denial was based on irrational prejudice and unfounded fears rather than legitimate government interests in safety, traffic, or neighborhood disruption. The court did not reach the statutory claims (ADA, Rehabilitation Act, RLUIPA, RFRA) because the constitutional violation was dispositive.

case_name: Henry Ortiz v. Doug V. Mull, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff allegedly requested ground-floor unit, garage storage, and Jacuzzi access for therapy due to mobility limitations, but these requests were denied without stated reason.
key_holding: The second amended complaint was dismissed without leave to amend because plaintiff failed to allege specific facts showing defendants knew of his disability or that any discriminatory conduct was undertaken 'because of' his handicap, and failed to plausibly allege causation between protected activity and alleged retaliatory conduct.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Henry Ortiz sued property manager Karissa Hailer, regional manager Doug Mull, and Lewis Management Corporation alleging disability discrimination under § 3604(f)(2), FHA retaliation under § 3617, and First Amendment retaliation under § 1983 based on denied accommodation requests for a ground-floor unit and therapy amenities, surveillance, and alleged retaliatory eviction. The magistrate judge recommended dismissal without leave to amend, finding the complaint lacked specific factual allegations showing defendants' knowledge of plaintiff's disability or that any adverse actions were motivated by his handicap or protected complaints.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
United States v. Cal. Mobile Home Park Mgmt., 107 F.3d 1374 (9th Cir. 1997)
Harris v. Itzhaki, 183 F.3d 1043 (9th Cir. 1999)
Walker v. City of Lakewood, 272 F.3d 1114 (9th Cir. 2001)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Ground-floor unit, garage for mobility storage, and Jacuzzi access for therapy
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)
fha_claims.reasoning: The SAC contains only conclusory allegations that defendants were aware of plaintiff's conditions through 'medical documentation and oral requests' but lacks specific facts about what documentation defendants saw, when, or to whom specific oral requests were made. The court found these threadbare recitals insufficient under Iqbal/Twombly to plausibly infer the challenged conduct was undertaken 'because of' plaintiff's handicap.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)
fha_claims.reasoning: Although plaintiff alleged protected conduct (complaints to HUD and housing advocacy organizations) and temporal proximity to adverse consequences (surveillance, false notices, parking citations within weeks), the SAC lacked sufficient factual allegations about the conduct or knowledge of individual defendants Mull and Hailer, or how knowledge of protected conduct could be attributed to Lewis Management Corporation. The court rejected reliance on post hoc ergo propter hoc reasoning and found the allegations too conclusory to nudge the claim across the line from conceivable to plausible.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: First Amendment Retaliation under 42 U.S.C. § 1983
fha_claims.disposition: Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to adequately allege state action required for § 1983 liability. The bare allegation that private defendants acted jointly with state officers when engaging law enforcement was conclusory and insufficient to establish that private conduct may be fairly treated as state action. The SAC lacked specific factual allegations supporting a nexus between the State and the challenged action.

case_name: Henry Ortiz v. Doug V. Mull, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges generally that defendants denied housing-related services routinely granted to other tenants without disabilities and failed to accommodate his PTSD, though no specific accommodation request is clearly identified in the complaint.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claims because his conclusory allegations failed to plausibly allege that defendants knew of his PTSD, that a specific accommodation was requested and necessary, or that defendants refused to make such accommodation.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Henry Ortiz, proceeding pro se, sued individuals associated with Homecoming at Creekside Apartments and Evergreen Park Apartments alleging Fair Housing Act, ADA, § 1983, and state law claims stemming from disability discrimination related to his PTSD and alleged retaliation for protected activity. The court dismissed the first amended complaint with leave to amend, finding that plaintiff's FHA claims were conclusory and failed to plausibly allege defendants knew of his disability, that a reasonable accommodation was requested and necessary, or that defendants refused to provide such accommodation.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
San Pedro Hotel Co., Inc. v. City of Los Angeles, 159 F.3d 470 (9th Cir. 1998)
United States v. Cal. Mobile Home Park Mgmt., 107 F.3d 1374 (9th Cir. 1997)
Budnick v. Town of Carefree, 518 F.3d 1109 (9th Cir. 2008)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Unit repairs, accommodations, and garage parking access promised by leasing agents but not fulfilled; accommodations necessary to afford plaintiff equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's conclusory allegations fail to demonstrate that defendants knew or reasonably should have known of plaintiff's handicap, that plaintiff communicated his disability to defendants, or that defendants refused to make necessary accommodations. The complaint lacks sufficient factual specificity to plead a failure to accommodate claim under the FHA.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's conclusory allegations that defendants denied housing-related services to plaintiff but granted them to other tenants without disabilities, and selectively enforced policies, lack factual specificity demonstrating discriminatory intent or identifying similarly situated comparators treated better than plaintiff. Bare conclusions without factual enhancement do not satisfy Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff's allegations of retaliation under the FHA are wholly conclusory and do not adequately identify specific misconduct or allege facts suggesting a causal link between plaintiff's protected activities (filing administrative complaints, consulting counsel) and defendants' adverse actions (notices to cure or quit, vehicle towing, deposit withholding). Plaintiff must plead facts that nudge the claim from conceivable to plausible.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title (unspecified), 42 U.S.C. § 1983 due process and equal protection, state law breach of contract and intentional infliction of emotional distress
fha_claims.reasoning: ADA claim fails because defendants are not public entities and apartment residences do not constitute public accommodations. § 1983 claims fail because plaintiff has not adequately alleged state action (bare conspiracy allegations are conclusory) or violation of federal constitutional rights (due process does not require pre-towing hearing; equal protection requires discriminatory intent not adequately pleaded). State law claims dismissed without prejudice to supplemental jurisdiction under § 1367(c)(3).

case_name: Ortiz v. Valasek
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested installation of a handicap ramp for her mother who could not use stairs due to disability.
key_holding: The federal district court lacked subject matter jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine because plaintiff's claims arose from and sought to reverse the state court eviction judgment, and alternatively abstained under Younger doctrine since ongoing state eviction proceedings afforded adequate opportunity to raise federal claims.
brief_summary: Andrea Ortiz, proceeding pro se, sued Douglas County Housing Authority and related defendants alleging disability discrimination and retaliation under the Fair Housing Act arising from her eviction from public housing for unpaid rent. The court dismissed the complaint without prejudice, finding it lacked subject matter jurisdiction under Rooker-Feldman because the claims sought to reverse the state court eviction judgment, and alternatively abstained under Younger since the state eviction proceedings remained ongoing and provided adequate opportunity to raise federal claims.
key_cases_cited: Mosby v. Ligon, 418 F.3d 927 (8th Cir. 2005)
D.C. Court of Appeals v. Feldman, 460 U.S. 462 (1983)
Rooker v. Fid. Trust Co., 263 U.S. 413 (1923)
Younger v. Harris, 401 U.S. 37 (1971)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Installation of a handicap ramp to allow plaintiff's mother (who could not use stairs) to access the rental property
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine because plaintiff's claims arise solely from and seek relief from the state court eviction judgment. The court did not reach the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Change of rent due date to align with when plaintiff and her mother received their disability checks; request for payment plan and supportive services to address financial hardship caused by mother's health issues
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine because plaintiff's claims arise solely from and seek relief from the state court eviction judgment. The court did not reach the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges that after she complained to Fair Housing, HUD, and NEOC, Valasek filed for eviction, constituting retaliation under § 3617
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine because plaintiff's claims arise solely from and seek relief from the state court eviction judgment. The court did not reach the merits of the retaliation claim.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Due process claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1983
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine because plaintiff's claims arise solely from and seek relief from the state court eviction judgment. The Rooker-Feldman doctrine bars federal courts from hearing cases brought by losing parties in state court proceedings alleging injury caused by the state-court judgment.

source_file: Oxford House, Inc. v. TP. OF NORTH BERGEN
case_name: Oxford House, Inc. v. Township of North Bergen
accommodation_description: Oxford House sought to operate a recovery home for individuals with substance use disorders, and the Township denied a Certificate of Continuing Occupancy based on zoning classification.
key_holding: The Third Circuit affirmed dismissal of the First Amended Complaint for failure to adequately plead discriminatory intent but vacated the denial of leave to amend, holding the District Court incorrectly concluded amendment would be futile because the prior preliminary injunction rulings addressed evidentiary sufficiency, not pleading standards.
brief_summary: Oxford House, Inc., a recovery housing operator, sued North Bergen Township after the municipality denied a Certificate of Continuing Occupancy for a two-family dwelling based on zoning classification, alleging discrimination under the FHA, ADA, and NJLAD. The Third Circuit affirmed dismissal of the First Amended Complaint for failure to plead discriminatory intent but vacated the denial of leave to amend and remanded, finding the District Court incorrectly used prior preliminary injunction rulings—which addressed evidentiary sufficiency—to preclude amendment when the plaintiff had never been given proper notice of the pleading deficiencies.
key_cases_cited: Village of Arlington Heights v. Metropolitan Hous. Dev. Corp., 429 U.S. 252 (1977)
Cmty. Servs., Inc. v. Wind Gap Mun. Auth., 421 F.3d 170 (3d Cir. 2005)
Tex. Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Cmtys. Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Fowler v. UPMC Shadyside, 578 F.3d 203 (3d Cir. 2009)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The First Amended Complaint failed to allege sufficient facts to support a plausible inference of discriminatory intent. The complaint alleged only misapplication of zoning law, absence of similar housing, procedural deviation, and conflicting explanations from officials—none of which, individually or collectively, support a reasonable expectation that discovery will reveal evidence of discriminatory animus based on disability status.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Oxford House forfeited its disparate impact arguments by failing to respond to the Township's arguments on this theory in the District Court. The appellate court did not reach the merits of the disparate impact claim because the arguments were not properly preserved.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title II, NJLAD (removed from First Amended Complaint)
fha_claims.reasoning: The ADA and NJLAD claims were analyzed under the same discriminatory intent framework as the FHA claims and failed for the same reasons—insufficient factual allegations to support a plausible inference of discrimination based on disability.

source_file: Oxford House, Inc. v. Township of North Bergen
case_name: Oxford House, Inc. v. Township of North Bergen
accommodation_description: Oxford House, a substance abuse recovery residence operator, requested a Certificate of Occupancy to operate a group home for six men recovering from alcoholism/substance abuse in a two-family dwelling, which the Township denied based on the Community Residence provision.
key_holding: The court granted the motion to dismiss because Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient factual matter from which the court could reasonably infer discriminatory intent—the Amended Complaint contained only conclusory allegations of discrimination without factual support for the Township's denial of the Certificate of Occupancy.
brief_summary: Oxford House, Inc. sued the Township of North Bergen alleging the Township violated the Fair Housing Act and ADA by denying a Certificate of Occupancy for a substance abuse recovery residence, arguing the denial was motivated by discriminatory intent toward disabled prospective residents. The court granted the motion to dismiss, finding the Amended Complaint failed to plead sufficient factual allegations supporting an inference of discriminatory intent, containing only conclusory allegations that the Township's application of the Community Residence zoning provision was discriminatory.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Cmty. Servs., Inc. v. Wind Gap Mun. Auth., 421 F.3d 170 (3d Cir. 2005)
Village of Arlington Heights v. Metro. Hous. Dev. Corp., 429 U.S. 252 (1977)
Oxford House, Inc. v. Twp. of N. Bergen, No. 22-2336, 2023 WL 4837835 (3d Cir. July 28, 2023)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Certificate of Occupancy for operation of Oxford House (group home for individuals recovering from substance abuse/alcoholism)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead sufficient factual allegations supporting an inference of discriminatory intent. The complaint contained only conclusory allegations of discrimination without factual support; the mere fact that no Oxford Houses exist in the Township, without more, is insufficient to support discriminatory intent; and the possibility that Defendant misapplied zoning laws does not evidence intentional discrimination.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Certificate of Occupancy for operation of Oxford House (group home for individuals recovering from substance abuse/alcoholism)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to respond to Defendant's disparate impact arguments in its opposition brief, resulting in waiver of any arguments in opposition to the disparate impact claim. The Amended Complaint does not contain the phrase 'disparate impact' and does not allege facts supporting such a theory.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) Title II claim; New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (NJLAD) claim
fha_claims.reasoning: The ADA claim was analyzed under the same framework as the FHA disparate treatment claim and failed for the same reasons (insufficient factual allegations of discriminatory intent). The NJLAD claim was not cognizable in federal court.

source_file: PLAYERS PLACE II CONDO. v. KP
case_name: Players Place II Condominium Association, Inc. v. K.P. and B.F.
accommodation_description: Request to keep an emotional support dog (Luna, weighing approximately 63 pounds) in the condominium unit despite a 30-pound pet weight restriction
key_holding: B.F. has a disability under the LAD and presented sufficient evidence that her emotional support animal may be necessary to afford her equal opportunity to use and enjoy her dwelling; the burden therefore shifts to the Association to prove the requested accommodation is unreasonable, and the dismissal of defendants' counterclaims under the LAD and FHA was improperly granted.
brief_summary: The Players Place II Condominium Association sued K.P. and B.F. to enforce its 30-pound pet weight limit after they obtained an emotional support dog (Luna, 63 pounds) as an accommodation for B.F.'s mental health conditions including bipolar II disorder, PTSD, and anxiety. The Supreme Court of New Jersey reversed the lower courts' dismissal of defendants' counterclaims under the New Jersey Law Against Discrimination and the Fair Housing Act, held that B.F. established she has a disability and presented sufficient evidence that her ESA may be necessary to afford her equal opportunity to use and enjoy her dwelling, and remanded for further proceedings on whether the accommodation was unreasonable.
key_cases_cited: Oras v. Hous. Auth. of Bayonne, 373 N.J. Super. 302, 861 A.2d 194 (App. Div. 2004)
Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014)
Revock v. Cowpet Bay W. Condo. Ass'n, 853 F.3d 96 (3d Cir. 2017)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request to keep an emotional support animal (dog named Luna weighing 63 pounds) in violation of condominium pet policy limiting pets to 30 pounds or less
fha_claims.reasoning: The New Jersey Supreme Court held that the trial and appellate courts erred in dismissing defendants' LAD and FHA reasonable accommodation claims. The court established a framework requiring: (1) plaintiff to show disability and that accommodation may be necessary for equal opportunity to use and enjoy dwelling; (2) housing provider to prove accommodation is unreasonable through fact-specific balancing of costs/benefits and whether it would fundamentally alter operations or impose undue burden. The court found B.F. established disability (bipolar II disorder, depression, anxiety, PTSD, ADD) and that Luna ameliorated symptoms, but remanded to Law Division for jury determination on whether the Association proved the accommodation unreasonable, as no interactive process occurred and Luna caused no documented problems.

source_file: PLAYERS PLACE II CONDOMINIUM ASSOCIATION, INC. v. KP
case_name: Players Place II Condominium Association, Inc. v. K.P.
accommodation_description: B.F., a person with mental health disabilities, requested an accommodation to keep a 63-pound emotional support dog (Luna) despite the condominium association's 30-pound pet weight limit.
key_holding: The New Jersey Supreme Court held that B.F. established she has a disability under the LAD, presented sufficient evidence that the ESA accommodation may be necessary to afford her equal opportunity to use and enjoy her dwelling, and that the burden shifts to the housing provider to prove the accommodation is unreasonable; because the trial court and Appellate Division failed to apply this framework, the dismissal of defendants' discrimination claims was vacated and remanded.
brief_summary: Players Place II Condominium Association sued unit owner K.P. for violating the Association's pet weight limit by keeping a 63-pound emotional support dog for his spouse B.F., who has mental health disabilities; defendants counterclaimed under the New Jersey LAD and federal FHA, alleging disability discrimination. The New Jersey Supreme Court reversed the dismissal of defendants' discrimination claims, holding that B.F. established a disability and presented sufficient evidence that the ESA accommodation may be necessary for her equal use and enjoyment of the dwelling, and that the matter must be remanded for the housing provider to prove the accommodation is unreasonable after engaging in a good-faith interactive process.
key_cases_cited: Oras v. Bayonne Housing Authority, 373 N.J. Super. 306 (App. Div. 2006)
Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014)
Castillo Condo. Ass'n v. U.S. Dep't of Hous. & Urb. Dev., 821 F.3d 92 (1st Cir. 2016)
Revock v. Cowpet Bay W. Condo. Ass'n, 853 F.3d 96 (3d Cir. 2017)
Lapid-Laurel, L.L.C. v. Zoning Bd. of Adjustment of Scotch Plains, 284 F.3d 442 (3d Cir. 2002)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request to keep a 63-pound emotional support dog (Luna) in violation of condominium pet policy limiting pets to 30 pounds or less
fha_claims.reasoning: The New Jersey Supreme Court held that the trial and appellate courts improperly dismissed the reasonable accommodation claim.
