The court established a burden-shifting framework: plaintiff must show disability and necessity of accommodation; housing provider must then prove unreasonableness through fact-specific balancing of costs/benefits and whether accommodation would fundamentally alter operations or impose undue burden. The court found B.F. established disability and presented evidence of necessity (Luna ameliorates symptoms), and the Association failed to engage in interactive process or prove unreasonableness. The case was remanded to the Law Division for jury determination on the merits.

case_name: PRJ Capital, LLC v. Moran
accommodation_description: Defendant requested that plaintiff provide documentation to support her application for rent assistance from the Salvation Army, which she claimed was necessary due to a disability that diminished her earning capacity.
key_holding: The trial court properly dismissed defendant's disability discrimination claims because she failed to plead sufficient facts establishing she had a disability within the meaning of the PWDCRA or FHAA, and she did not inform the landlords of any disability until after they decided to terminate her tenancy.
brief_summary: Valerie Moran sued PRJ Capital and David James, her former landlords, claiming disability discrimination and retaliation under the PWDCRA and FHAA after they terminated her month-to-month tenancy while she sought rent assistance. The Michigan Court of Appeals affirmed the dismissal of her counterclaims, holding that Moran failed to plead sufficient facts to establish she had a disability within the meaning of the statutes, and she did not inform the landlords of any disability until after they had already decided to terminate her tenancy.
key_cases_cited: Riverbrook v. Fabode, 333 Mich App 645 (2020)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Bachman v. Swan Harbour Ass'n, 252 Mich App 400 (2002)
Jankowski Lee & Assoc. v. Cisneros, 91 F.3d 891 (7th Cir. 1996)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Cooperation with and provision of documentation to support defendant's application for rent assistance from the Salvation Army, allegedly necessary due to disability-related financial hardship
fha_claims.reasoning: Defendant failed to plead sufficient facts establishing that she had a disability within the meaning of the FHAA (i.e., a condition substantially limiting a major life activity). She alleged only that she had health issues that were being managed or had resolved, and provided a generic description of relapsing polychondritis without specifying how it substantially limited any major life activity. Additionally, she failed to inform defendants that her request for assistance was related to a disability until after they terminated the tenancy, so defendants could not have known of any disability when they denied the accommodation request.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Under the FHAA, defendant failed to plead that she engaged in protected activity (requesting an accommodation for a disability) because she did not sufficiently allege that she informed defendants her request was related to a disability. Additionally, defendants terminated the tenancy before defendant framed her request as a possible accommodation request, so there was no causal connection between any protected activity and the adverse action.

source_file: Pinnacle Treatment Centers Inc v City of Crown Point Indiana

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether the City's enforcement of the zoning ordinance was motivated by discriminatory animus against substance abuse disorder patients. Circumstantial evidence of community opposition animated by bias, combined with evidence of mayoral involvement in closed-door sessions and official questioning suggesting animus, precluded summary judgment for either party. The court held that credibility determinations and weighing of competing evidence required jury resolution.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Zoning variance to permit up to eight unrelated individuals to reside in the group home in an R-1 residential district, notwithstanding the city's five-person family definition restriction
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the Seventh Circuit's burden-shifting framework for reasonable accommodations in zoning cases, requiring plaintiff to show the accommodation is (1) reasonable, (2) necessary, and (3) affords equal opportunity to use and enjoy housing. The court found genuine disputes of material fact: (1) whether the variance is reasonable given the therapeutic benefits of peer support in a larger group home and the absence of demonstrated harm to the neighborhood; (2) whether the accommodation is necessary because disabled residents require community-based residential facilities to have equal opportunity to live in residential neighborhoods; and (3) whether the City's denial was pretextual discrimination rather than legitimate zoning enforcement. Delegatto's lay testimony regarding therapeutic benefits was admissible, and the absence of complaints post-opening supported Pinnacle's position.

source_file: Portnoy v. MEI CONDOMINIUM ASSOCIATION, INC.
case_name: Eli Portnoy v. MEI Condominium Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: Portnoy requested accommodation that someone other than Anna Strickstein-Zandman interact with him about any business regarding his residency, due to disability-related stress from their antagonistic relationship.
key_holding: The court denied the individual board director's motion to dismiss, holding that Florida state immunity statutes cannot shield individuals from Fair Housing Act liability and that Portnoy sufficiently alleged willful discrimination to overcome statutory immunity.
brief_summary: Eli Portnoy sued MEI Condominium Association and its Board President Anna Strickstein-Zandman under the Fair Housing Act, alleging they denied his reasonable accommodation request to communicate with someone other than the Board President due to disability-related stress, and then discriminated against him by restricting gym access and refusing to renew his lease. The court denied Strickstein-Zandman's motion to dismiss, rejecting her immunity defense under Florida state statutes and finding that Portnoy adequately alleged willful individual discrimination to survive dismissal.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)
Housing Opportunities Project for Excellence, Inc. v. Key Colony No. 4 Condo. Assoc., 510 F. Supp. 2d 1003 (S.D. Fla. 2007)
Sabal Palm Condos. of Pine Island Ridge Ass'n, Inc. v. Fischer, 2014 WL 988767 (S.D. Fla. 2014)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request that someone other than Anna Strickstein-Zandman interact with plaintiff regarding business matters related to his residency, based on medical advice to reduce stress and stressful communications due to disability.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss, finding that plaintiff adequately pleaded individual liability of board member under FHA and that state law immunity does not bar federal FHA claims. Allegations of willful discrimination fall within exception to state immunity. Claim survives at pleading stage but merits not yet reached.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of access to gym and recreational facilities based on disability; discriminatory terms and conditions of provision of services and facilities.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss under § 3604(f)(2), finding plaintiff adequately pleaded that defendant personally involved in denying gym access based on disability and that individual board member can be held liable under FHA despite state law immunity arguments.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of lease renewal in retaliation for requesting reasonable accommodation and asserting FHA rights.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss retaliation claim under § 3617, finding plaintiff adequately pleaded that defendant refused to renew lease because of plaintiff's disability and in retaliation for requesting accommodation, with allegations of willful discrimination sufficient to overcome state immunity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of housing (non-renewal of lease) based on disability.
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied motion to dismiss Count IV (state law claim under Florida Fair Housing Act § 760.23(1)), finding plaintiff adequately pleaded personal and deliberate discrimination by individual defendant, sufficient to survive pleading stage and overcome state immunity.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Federal Equal Protection Clause (§ 1983), Michigan state equal protection claim, Title VII employment discrimination
fha_claims.reasoning: State of Michigan is not a 'person' subject to § 1983 liability; state equal protection claim barred by Eleventh Amendment sovereign immunity; Title VII claim fails because plaintiff did not plausibly allege state employment and Title VII was not designed to protect convicted felons.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Fair Housing Act claim regarding public housing eligibility based on criminal history
fha_claims.reasoning: FHA does not mandate housing availability to individuals whose tenancy would constitute a direct threat to health or safety; public housing authorities retain discretion to deny applications based on history of convictions for property and assaultive crimes; plaintiff did not name Detroit Housing Commission as defendant.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Aggregate dataset containing 802 classified FHA cases with mixed accommodation types including policy exceptions (21.8%), structural modifications (3.7%), assistance animals (4.7%), parking (2.4%), transfers (1.7%), live-in aides (0.9%), and sober living/group home zoning (7.0%)
fha_claims.reasoning: This is a research summary/statistical compilation of 802 FHA cases classified across multiple procedural stages (motion to dismiss, summary judgment, trial, appeal) and outcomes (defendant win 57.9%, plaintiff win 8.5%, mixed 9.2%). No individual case opinion is provided for substantive legal analysis.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: This is a research summary/statistical compilation of 1,029 FHA cases, not a single case opinion. No individual claim can be extracted.
fha_claims.reasoning: This document is a subscription-database research summary aggregating data from 1,029 federal court FHA opinions. It contains statistical distributions of accommodation types, disability categories, outcomes, procedural postures, parties, and courts, but does not present a single case opinion with extractable claims, holdings, or reasoning.

source_file: Rehabilitation Support Services Inc v City of Albany New York

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Zoning ordinance requiring use variance for community residences (group homes for people with disabilities recovering from substance abuse) in R-2A residential zone, while single/two-family dwellings and houses of worship are permitted as of right
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the Johnson Controls framework for facial discrimination and held that RSS failed to establish a prima facie case of intentional discrimination because community residences are not singled out or treated differently from similarly situated uses (apartment buildings and rooming houses also require use variances), and RSS presented no evidence that community residences are materially similar to uses permitted as of right or by special permit.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Zoning ordinance requiring use variance for community residences in R-2A residential zone
fha_claims.reasoning: Because the court found the ordinance is not facially discriminatory and RSS failed to establish a prima facie case of intentional discrimination, the court did not need to reach or analyze any disparate impact theory; the grant of summary judgment on the disparate treatment claim was dispositive.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), 42 U.S.C. § 12131 et seq.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court treated FHA and ADA claims as interchangeable in the zoning discrimination context and applied the same Johnson Controls framework, holding that the ordinance is not facially discriminatory under either statute because community residences are not singled out or treated differently from similarly situated non-disabled uses.

source_file: Roberts v. SACRAMENTO HOUSING AND REDEVELOPMENT AGENCY
case_name: Sydney Brooke Roberts and David Tyrone Samuel v. Sacramento Housing and Redevelopment Agency
accommodation_description: Request for an additional bedroom on their Housing Choice Voucher to accommodate David Samuel's and minor daughter AIMS's disabilities (Autism, ADHD, PTSD, depression) so each can have a separate bedroom.
key_holding: The motion for summary judgment was denied because plaintiffs failed to meet their burden: the housing authority granted the extra bedroom accommodation in March 2023, making it unclear whether a benefit was denied, and plaintiffs' motion was vague about what accommodations remained at issue.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs David Samuel (disabled adult with ADHD, Autism, PTSD, and depression) and Sydney Roberts, holders of a HUD Housing Choice Voucher, sued the Sacramento Housing and Redevelopment Agency alleging disability discrimination for denying their reasonable accommodation request for an additional bedroom to accommodate disability-related needs. The court denied plaintiffs' motion for summary judgment because the housing authority had granted the extra bedroom accommodation in March 2023, and plaintiffs failed to demonstrate they were entitled to additional benefits or to identify what accommodations remained in dispute.
key_cases_cited: Giebeler v. M & B Associates, 343 F.3d 1143 (9th Cir. 2003)
Duvall v. County of Kitsap, 260 F.3d 1124 (9th Cir. 2001)
Weinreich v. Los Angeles County Metro. Transp. Auth., 114 F.3d 976 (9th Cir. 1997)
Zukle v. Regents of Univ. of Cal., 166 F.3d 1041 (9th Cir. 1999)
Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Extra bedroom to allow David Samuel and minor child AIMS to each have their own bedroom; later requests for five bedrooms total, housekeeping services, soundproofing, and blackout curtains
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied plaintiff's motion for summary judgment because the record showed defendants granted the three-bedroom accommodation in March 2023, making it unclear whether plaintiffs were actually denied a benefit, and plaintiffs failed to present evidence that they were entitled to additional accommodations (five bedrooms, housekeeping services, etc.). The motion was vague as to which accommodations remained at issue and did not address the March 2023 grant letter.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II ADA, Section 504 Rehabilitation Act, Fourteenth Amendment due process, and ineffective communication claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Court applied the Title II ADA prima facie test (qualified individual with disability, exclusion/denial of benefits, discrimination by reason of disability) and Section 504 Rehabilitation Act test (disability, otherwise qualified, denied benefits solely because of disability, program receives federal assistance), finding the evidence insufficient to warrant summary judgment because the March 2023 grant of the three-bedroom accommodation created a factual dispute as to whether plaintiffs were denied benefits.

case_name: Rodriguez v. City of Chicago
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that the City preserve an existing driveway apron she used as a safe location to access medical transportation, which was necessary due to her mobility disability preventing her from being picked up on busy streets.
key_holding: The FHA reasonable modification claim fails because the driveway apron was not within the property line of Rodriguez's residence but rather on an adjacent commercial lot, so it did not fall within the 'premises' of her dwelling that she is entitled to modify under § 3604(f)(3)(A).
brief_summary: Mari Rodriguez, a tenant with mobility disabilities, sued the City of Chicago after the city planned to remove a driveway apron on an adjacent commercial lot that she used to safely access medical transportation. The court granted the City's motion to dismiss, holding that the FHA reasonable modification claim failed because the driveway was not part of Rodriguez's premises but rather on an adjacent property, and the ADA claim failed because the driveway was not a City service.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Moore v. W. Illinois Corr. Ctr., 89 F.4th 582 (7th Cir. 2023)
Barden v. City of Sacramento, 292 F.3d 1073 (9th Cir. 2002)
Wetzel v. Glen St. Andrew Living Cmty., LLC, 901 F.3d 856 (7th Cir. 2018)

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retention or restoration of a driveway apron adjacent to plaintiff's residential building to permit safe pick-up and drop-off by medical transportation providers due to plaintiff's mobility disability and dangerous traffic conditions in the alley and street.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the FHA claim because the driveway apron was not part of the 'premises' of plaintiff's dwelling under the FHA—it was located on an adjacent property outside plaintiff's property line. The court held that while exterior accessible routes may be required, plaintiff sought to alter a public way outside a neighboring property, not to modify the premises she occupied. Amendment would be futile.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the retaliation claim because plaintiff failed to allege a causal connection between exercise of FHA rights and adverse action by the City. Plaintiff did not allege that aldermanic staff were aware of her disability or her June 2024 communications with CDOT regarding her need for the apron when they initiated action in February 2024, breaking the temporal nexus required for retaliation.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act Title II claim for failure to provide reasonable modification to public entity services, programs, or activities; claim that City failed to engage in interactive process to identify reasonable accommodations.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court dismissed the ADA Title II claim because the driveway apron was not a 'service, program, or activity' provided by the City—it was a privately permitted driveway created for a neighboring commercial property. Plaintiff did not allege that any actual City service (such as sidewalks or curb ramps) was inaccessible to her because of her disability. The court also noted that Title II does not require public entities to engage in an interactive process.

case_name: Sproaps v. Brown
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; plaintiff alleges intentional discrimination based on sexual orientation through hostile treatment and failure to make repairs.
key_holding: The court found that plaintiff's allegation of a stray discriminatory remark about his 'lover boy' and delayed repairs did not state a plausible claim of sex discrimination under the FHA because there was no evidence linking Brown's discriminatory remark to any discriminatory conduct, repairs were delayed due to financial disputes rather than sexual orientation, and plaintiff provided no examples of other tenants treated more favorably.
brief_summary: Marriell Sproaps, proceeding in forma pauperis, sued his former property manager Kevin Brown alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on sexual orientation discrimination, claiming Brown treated him with hostility and refused to make repairs because of his same-sex partner. The court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a plausible claim, finding that Brown's single discriminatory remark about plaintiff's 'lover boy' was an isolated stray comment unconnected to any discriminatory policy, and the delayed repairs were motivated by a financial dispute over responsibility for vandalism damage rather than sexual orientation bias.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Gallagher v. Magner
Ellis v. City of Minneapolis
Tex. Dep't of Hous. Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to plead a plausible claim of sex/sexual orientation discrimination under § 3604(b). The only evidence of discriminatory animus was a stray remark about plaintiff's 'lover boy' unconnected to the refusal to make repairs, which was motivated by a financial dispute over past-due rent and responsibility for damage. Isolated remarks unrelated to management policy or discriminatory impact do not support a prima facie case under Iqbal/Twombly.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Missouri Human Rights Act, Missouri tort law (emotional distress), breach of lease and verbal agreements
fha_claims.reasoning: Court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over pendent state law claims after dismissing the federal FHA claim, as the federal claims were dismissed before trial and discretionary dismissal of state claims was appropriate.

source_file: South-Suburban Housing Center v Greater South Suburban Bd of Realtors

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 52 (findings of fact and conclusions of law)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that SSHC and Park Forest's affirmative marketing plan directing special outreach to white home buyers did not violate 42 U.S.C. § 3604(a) because the plan did not deter black home buyers from pursuing their interests in the Apache Street homes; it merely created additional competition in the housing market. The plan furthered both integration and equal housing opportunity without lessening efforts to attract black buyers.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 52 (findings of fact and conclusions of law)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that SSHC and Park Forest's affirmative marketing plan did not violate 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c) because the plan merely directed additional promotional advertising toward a racial group that would normally have little interest in the homes; it contained no racial quota or provision making race a factor in who could see or purchase the homes.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 52 (findings of fact and conclusions of law)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that the Realtors' exclusion of the Apache Street homes from the MLS and conditioning of listing on indemnification did not violate 42 U.S.C. § 3606 because the Fair Housing Act permits but does not require affirmative marketing plans; the Realtors' color-blind marketing policy does not constitute discrimination on account of race.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 52 (findings of fact and conclusions of law)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that the Realtors' exclusion of listings from the MLS and disciplinary proceedings against Motluck did not violate 42 U.S.C. § 3617 because the Realtors never interfered with white persons learning about, seeing, or purchasing the Apache Street homes on an equal basis with black persons; they merely disagreed with special outreach efforts to whites.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 52 (findings of fact and conclusions of law)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that the municipalities' anti-solicitation ordinances did not violate the Fair Housing Act under a disparate impact theory because the record was devoid of substantial evidence showing the ordinances were intended to discriminate against blacks or had a racially discriminatory effect; the ordinances only barred solicitation of those who requested it, and such persons were least likely to offer homes for sale anyway.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.disposition: Rule 52 (findings of fact and conclusions of law)
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that the municipalities' restrictions on the size, placement, and number of 'for sale' signs did not violate the Fair Housing Act because there was little evidence the regulations had a discriminatory impact on black home seekers or denied access to housing to anyone; the regulations were modest and reasonable aesthetic measures.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Glenwood's enforcement and cessation of enforcement of a ban on 'for sale' signs
fha_claims.reasoning: The trial court failed to make specific findings of fact or conclusions of law regarding whether Glenwood's enforcement and pre-trial cessation of enforcement of its 'for sale' sign ban violated 42 U.S.C. § 3604(a) and warranted punitive damages. The appellate court remanded for the trial judge to provide adequate findings to permit meaningful appellate review.

source_file: Southern Burlington County NAACP v Mount Laurel Tp
Southwest Fair Housing Council Inc v Maricopa Domestic Water Improvement District

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Although the court held that plaintiffs established a prima facie disparate-impact claim (significant adverse disproportionate effect on Black, Native American, and unmarried women customers; robust causation demonstrated), the defendant established a legitimate business justification (preventing unrecovered delinquencies from public housing tenants whose landlord was immune to liens) served in a significant way, and plaintiffs failed to identify equally effective, less discriminatory alternatives. Summary judgment affirmed for defendant.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs failed to produce direct or circumstantial evidence demonstrating that discriminatory intent more likely than not motivated the defendant's decision to implement the security deposit policy. The statement about 'influx of people and tenants' was not code for protected class membership, and knowledge of disparate impact alone is insufficient to establish discriminatory motive absent evidence of pretext.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: 42 U.S.C. §§ 1983, 1986 (civil rights claims against Pinal County)
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiffs and Pinal County (named as defendant for § 1983 and § 1986 claims) reached a settlement, resolving those non-FHA claims.

source_file: State Financial Bank National Association v City of South Milwaukee

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of housing availability through efforts to prevent construction and raze Lake Bluff Apartments; alleged steering of tenants to segregated public housing (Parkcrest)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine issues of material fact on disparate impact claim. Evidence showed Lake Bluff tenants were disproportionately African American (16% vs. 1.39% of city population), City's zoning and moratorium decisions had greater adverse impact on African Americans, and City's subsequent steering of tenants to segregated Parkcrest housing perpetuated segregation. Court applied Arlington Heights II four-factor test and found sufficient evidence of discriminatory effect, intent, and City's interest to preclude summary judgment.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation for disabled tenants at Lake Bluff: whether granting housing preference at Parkcrest public housing is adequate; whether City should consider alternative accommodations rather than razing apartments; accessibility of Parkcrest units for mobility-impaired tenants
fha_claims.reasoning: Court found genuine issues of material fact regarding whether Parkcrest housing preference constitutes reasonable accommodation for disabled Lake Bluff tenants. Evidence showed 11 of 56 Lake Bluff households had mobility-impaired members, scarcity of affordable accessible family housing, and Parkcrest's accessibility limitations (only 3 accessible units, two-story townhouses precluding wheelchair access, centralized heat system). Court could not resolve as matter of law whether preference at Parkcrest is reasonable accommodation without further factual development.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Title II Americans with Disabilities Act claim; § 1983 due process claim (dismissed by separate order)
fha_claims.reasoning: Court denied summary judgment on ADA Title II claim, finding genuine issues of material fact regarding whether City engaged in unlawful practice continuing into limitations period through moratorium, rezone ordinance, and subsequent steering practices. Court rejected City's argument that these were discrete acts outside statute of limitations. § 1983 due process claim was dismissed by separate order (not addressed in this opinion).

source_file: Sunlight of Spirit House Inc v Borough of North Wales Pennsylvania

fha_claims.accommodation_description: N/A
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found genuine issues of material fact regarding whether disability was a motivating factor in the ZHB's denial decision. The record contained evidence of discriminatory neighbor opposition based on residents' substance use disabilities and evidence that ZHB members relied on neighbor comments in their decision, creating a factual question about discriminatory intent that precludes summary judgment for either party.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Request for special exception to zoning ordinance to permit ten unrelated residents (persons in recovery from alcoholism and drug addiction) to occupy a single-family dwelling as a 'functional family equivalent,' rather than the standard three-unrelated-person limit
fha_claims.reasoning: Under the Third Circuit's burden-shifting framework, the court found genuine disputes of material fact on both prongs: (1) whether plaintiffs established necessity for ten residents (conflicting expert testimony on optimal occupancy levels), and (2) whether defendants demonstrated unreasonableness (undefined zoning terms 'nonprofit' and 'transient,' plaintiffs' offer to limit parking, and factual questions about whether accommodation would fundamentally alter the zoning program). Summary judgment was inappropriate on either side.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act, Title II, 42 U.S.C. § 12132
fha_claims.reasoning: The court analyzed the ADA Title II claim using the same reasonable accommodation framework as the FHA claim, finding that the legal standards are essentially identical. The court denied summary judgment on the ADA claim for the same reasons as the FHA reasonable accommodation claim—genuine disputes of material fact regarding necessity and reasonableness of the requested accommodation.

source_file: Support Ministries for Persons With AIDS Inc v Village of Waterford NY

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of zoning approval to establish a residential facility for HIV-positive homeless persons through enactment and application of Local Law No. 2 of 1990, which amended the definition of 'boarding house' to exclude facilities for persons with illnesses requiring medical care
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that Local Law No. 2 of 1990 was enacted with discriminatory intent to prevent Support Ministries from establishing a residence for HIV-positive persons, based on the timing of the amendment, the legislative history showing the board's intent to block the specific project, community opposition rooted in fear and prejudice against PWAs, and the board members' own statements opposing the facility. The HIV-positive status of the proposed residents was at least one factor, and probably the primary factor, motivating the discriminatory ordinance.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Enactment and application of Local Law No. 2 of 1990, which banned occupancy by persons suffering from or recovering from any illness or disease requiring medical or nursing care, thereby excluding virtually all handicapped persons from boarding or rooming houses in Waterford
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied the four-pronged Arlington Heights disparate impact test and found: (1) strong showing of discriminatory effect on handicapped persons; (2) evidence of discriminatory intent; (3) defendants failed to establish a legitimate, bona fide governmental interest—their actions were based on unfounded fear of AIDS and prejudice, not legitimate zoning concerns; and (4) plaintiffs sought only to restrain defendants from interfering with private property use, not to compel affirmative provision of housing.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Coercion, intimidation, threats, and interference with Support Ministries' attempts to establish a residence for PWAs, including the mayor's call for all opponents to stand at a public meeting, appointment of known opponents to zoning positions, unprecedented call for a referendum on zoning matters, and communication of anonymous threats to burn the building
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found that defendants violated 42 U.S.C. § 3617 by coercing, intimidating, threatening, and interfering with Support Ministries' exercise of FHA rights through multiple actions: the mayor's orchestration of public opposition, appointment of petition signers to zoning positions, unprecedented referendum proposal, and communication of threats to burn the facility, all contributing to a threatening and coercive environment designed to dissuade the project.

case_name: Walter Tanner v. Rochdale Village, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges a management staff member directed personnel not to repair his unit because of a false perception that plaintiff was a sexual offender and HIV positive.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA disparate treatment claim because his allegations were too vague and speculative to support an inference of discriminatory animus, and the claim based on retaliation for litigation against the MTA failed because litigants are not a protected class under the FHA.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Walter Tanner sued Rochdale Village Inc., a housing cooperative in Jamaica, Queens, alleging disability discrimination under the Fair Housing Act and Americans with Disabilities Act, claiming management refused to repair his unit based on a perceived disability. The court granted defendant's motion to dismiss, finding plaintiff failed to state a plausible discrimination claim because his allegations were speculative and unsupported by factual details, and because being a litigant is not a protected class under the FHA.

fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to state a plausible disparate treatment claim under the FHA. The allegation that management desired to evict plaintiff because he was suing the MTA cannot support a discrimination claim because litigants are not a protected class. The allegation regarding perceived disability (sexual offender/HIV status) lacks sufficient factual support beyond vague speculation based on a confidential source, with no explanation of why management perceived plaintiff as disabled or how other residents were treated differently.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: ADA Title III discrimination claim; also includes NYSHRL § 296, NYCHRL, and New York Not-for-Profit Corporation Law claims
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to state a claim under ADA Title III because Rochdale is a private housing cooperative, not a place of public accommodation. Residential facilities and apartment buildings are excluded from the definition of public accommodation under Title III. State-law claims were dismissed without reaching the merits as supplemental jurisdiction was declined after federal claims were dismissed.

brief_summary: The United States sued Rutherford Tenants Corp. and its Board President James Ramadei for discriminating against a disabled tenant (Meril Lesser) by refusing to allow her to keep emotional support animals and attempting to evict her, in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The parties resolved through a consent decree requiring Rutherford to pay $165,000 in damages, offer to purchase the complainant's cooperative shares for $585,000, adopt a reasonable accommodation policy, and provide staff training.

fha_claims.reasoning: The United States and Defendants resolved the claim through a consent decree in which Defendants agreed to adopt a reasonable accommodation policy, pay $165,000 in damages to Complainant, and offer to purchase Complainant's shares for $585,000, without admission of liability.

fha_claims.reasoning: The Secretary of HUD determined reasonable cause to believe Defendants discriminated against Complainant on the basis of disability. The parties resolved this claim through a consent decree with injunctive relief prohibiting discrimination under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(1)(A) and § 3604(f)(2).

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Retaliation through eviction proceedings and other adverse actions for exercising FHA rights
fha_claims.reasoning: The Secretary of HUD determined reasonable cause to believe Defendants engaged in retaliation against Complainant. The parties resolved this claim through a consent decree with injunctive relief prohibiting coercion, intimidation, threats, or interference under 42 U.S.C. § 3617.

source_file: United States v. TOLL BROTHERS, INC.
case_name: United States of America v. Toll Brothers, Inc.
accommodation_description: Design and construction accessibility requirements for covered multifamily dwellings including accessible common areas, door widths, accessible routes, environmental controls, grab bar reinforcements, and usable kitchens and bathrooms
key_holding: GreenbergFarrow Architecture consents to a three-year consent decree requiring FHA compliance training, record-keeping, and a $30,000 civil penalty for failing to design and construct accessible covered multifamily dwellings as required by 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(C)
brief_summary: The United States sued Toll Brothers and its affiliates, including architecture firm GreenbergFarrow, alleging that the North 8th Street condominium in Brooklyn was not designed and constructed with required accessible features as mandated by 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(C). The court approved a consent decree resolving the claims against GreenbergFarrow, requiring the firm to pay a $30,000 civil penalty, implement FHA compliance training programs, and maintain compliance records for three years.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to design and construct North 8th Street condominium building with accessible and adaptive design features required by FHA, including: (i) public use and common use portions readily accessible to and usable by persons with disabilities; (ii) doors sufficiently wide for wheelchair passage; (iii) accessible routes into and through dwellings; (iv) accessible light switches, electrical outlets, thermostats, and environmental controls; (v) bathroom wall reinforcements for grab bars; and (vi) usable kitchens and bathrooms for wheelchair maneuverability.
fha_claims.reasoning: The United States and GreenbergFarrow Architecture, Inc. resolved the design and construction discrimination claim through a consent decree without admission of liability. The decree imposes injunctive relief requiring FHA compliance in future projects, mandatory training, record preservation, and a $30,000 civil penalty. The complaint was dismissed as to GreenbergFarrow without prejudice, subject to reinstatement if GreenbergFarrow breaches the decree.

source_file: United States v. TOLL BROTHERS, INC. (1)

key_holding: Lendlease LMB agreed to a Consent Decree requiring FHA compliance training, retention of an FHA compliance adviser for future projects, and payment of a $10,000 civil penalty, without admitting liability, to resolve claims that North 8th Condominium was not designed and constructed in compliance with the FHA's accessible design requirements.
brief_summary: The United States brought this action against Toll Brothers, Inc. and related entities including Lendlease LMB alleging that North 8th Condominium in Brooklyn was designed and constructed in violation of the FHA's accessibility requirements under § 3604(f)(3)(C). Lendlease LMB, the construction manager, entered into a Consent Decree requiring compliance training, an FHA compliance adviser for future projects, record-keeping, and a $10,000 civil penalty to resolve the claims without admission of liability.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Failure to design and construct North 8th Street property in compliance with FHA Accessible Design Requirements, including: (i) public use and common use portions not readily accessible to and usable by persons with disabilities; (ii) doors not sufficiently wide for wheelchair passage; (iii) lack of accessible routes, inaccessible environmental controls, missing bathroom grab bar reinforcements, and unusable kitchens and bathrooms for wheelchair users.
fha_claims.reasoning: The United States and Lendlease LMB resolved the design and construction violation claim through a consent decree without admission of liability. The decree imposes prospective compliance obligations, civil penalty, training, and monitoring requirements on Lendlease LMB for future covered multifamily dwellings, and dismisses the complaint as to Lendlease LMB without prejudice to reinstatement for breach.

source_file: WILLOW HAVEN ON 106th STREET, LLC v. NAGIREDDY

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Zoning variance or reasonable accommodation to permit operation of an unlicensed housing with services establishment for elderly individuals with Alzheimer's disease or dementia in a single-family residential (S1) zoning district without obtaining a variance from the Board of Zoning Appeals
fha_claims.reasoning: The trial court found that Willow Haven's unlicensed housing with services establishment does not fall within the UDO's express definition of 'group home' (which requires licensing), and thus a variance was required. The court held that whether federal and state law mandate a variance be granted or a reasonable accommodation be made is a matter for the Board of Zoning Appeals to decide, not the City Director. The preliminary injunction was upheld because the Nagireddys established a prima facie case that the Home violates the UDO as written, and the Director lacked authority to unilaterally grant a variance determination.

source_file: Woodfield Equities LLC v Incorporated Village of Patchogue

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Use variance or special permit to operate a residential recovery center for recovering alcohol and drug addicts in a single-family residential zoning district; rental permit for expanded occupancy
fha_claims.reasoning: The court found the claim was not ripe for adjudication because plaintiffs never applied for the required use variance or special permit before or after purchasing the property, failing to exhaust administrative remedies. The court held that ripeness requires either a final determination by a decision maker (a denied application) or a showing that further administrative efforts would be futile, neither of which plaintiffs demonstrated.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Claim that condemnation of property was pretext for discrimination against use as residential recovery center for individuals with substance use disability
fha_claims.reasoning: Applying the Arlington Heights intentional discrimination framework, the court found no evidence of discriminatory intent. The Village had legitimate, documented reasons for condemnation predating plaintiffs' purchase (relocation of community services), minimal community opposition compared to similar cases, no departures from normal condemnation procedures, and plaintiffs' own failure to apply for required zoning relief undermined any inference of pretext. The timing of condemnation was based on property vacancy, not the identity of occupants.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) Title II and Rehabilitation Act § 504 claims alleging failure to provide reasonable accommodation and discrimination in municipal zoning decisions
fha_claims.reasoning: The court denied preliminary injunction relief on ripeness grounds applicable to all three statutes (FHA, ADA, Rehabilitation Act). Plaintiffs failed to exhaust administrative remedies by never applying for required zoning variance or special permit, and the condemnation proceeding was not yet final under New York EDPL § 207, which requires appellate review. The court declined to act as a substitute zoning board.

source_file: Yates Real Estate Inc v Plainfield Zoning Board of Adjustment

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Zoning variances and waivers (38 variances and 33 waivers) to permit construction of a 25-unit apartment building in a historic district zoned for single/two-family residential use, including use variance, density variance (36.2 units per acre vs. 2 permitted), height variance, bulk variances, and waivers from minimum unit size requirements (500 sq ft minimum; proposed units ranged from 256-595 sq ft), parking requirements (11 spaces vs. 45 required), and storage space requirements.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish the initial burden on necessity and equal opportunity elements. The court found: (1) plaintiff failed to establish a protected class because it did not commit to limiting residency to veterans with PTSD, only to veterans generally; (2) plaintiff failed to show the specific size of the facility (25 units) was necessary for therapeutic benefit, as general testimony about group living benefits did not establish that 25 units or 36 residents were required; (3) plaintiff failed to show financial necessity because the expert's pro forma was based on unverified figures from the developer, including a purchase price inflated from $100,000 to $300,000, and comparable facilities (All Saints Apartments, Basking Ridge veterans housing) operated viably without such accommodations; and (4) even if plaintiff met its burden, the municipality demonstrated the accommodation was unreasonable because it would fundamentally alter the city's zoning scheme by requiring 38 variances and 33 waivers that would undermine historic preservation goals, violate minimum unit size protections, create severe parking deficiencies, and increase density 18 times the permitted maximum.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Denial of zoning variances and waivers based on alleged discriminatory animus toward veterans with PTSD.
fha_claims.reasoning: Plaintiff failed to establish discriminatory purpose. Although plaintiff pointed to certain board member comments during testimony about veterans with PTSD and trust issues, the court found these comments, when read in context, did not evince discriminatory animus or NIMBY concerns. The board presented legitimate, neutral, and persuasive reasons for denial based on zoning compliance, historic preservation, parking, unit size standards, and density restrictions. There was no indication the denial was guided by negative attitudes toward the disabled or discriminatory intent.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), Rehabilitation Act, and New Jersey Municipal Land Use Law (MLUL) claims.
fha_claims.reasoning: The court applied FHAA analysis to the ADA and Rehabilitation Act claims, finding the same deficiencies in establishing necessity and equal opportunity, and the same reasonableness of the municipality's denial. The MLUL claim was not briefed by plaintiff on the preliminary injunction motion and was therefore not addressed. The court noted that even under the MLUL's rational basis standard of review, the zoning board's decision was supported by the record and not arbitrary or capricious.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Construction of a five-foot-wide elevator shaft on the side elevation of a four-story oceanfront townhouse to accommodate the property owner's mobility disability (inability to safely navigate stairs). The accommodation required variances from zoning regulations requiring a ten-foot side yard setback and a two-foot, six-inch landscape area.
fha_claims.reasoning: The appellate court affirmed the Board's determination that the requested variances constituted a reasonable and necessary accommodation under Title II of the ADA. The court applied a balancing test considering: (1) whether the accommodation undermined legitimate zoning purposes (it did not, as the Town Code expressly permits variances and recognizes ADA accessibility needs); (2) whether less intrusive alternatives existed (substantial evidence showed the side yard was the only practical location given the building's floor plan, parking requirements, and structural constraints); and (3) the costs to surrounding property owners (the Board properly discounted the real estate broker's opinion regarding property value loss, as credibility assessment is entrusted to the administrative agency). The court found substantial evidence that Mr. Peroutka's disability prevented safe stair use and that the elevator was necessary to allow him continued use of his property.

case_name: Jennifer L. Hernandez v. Alex DiBiaso and Michael Kusper
key_holding: Section 3604(c) encompasses post-acquisition statements that condition continued tenancy on submission to sexual harassment, and Hernandez adequately stated a claim by alleging Kusper implied she must acquiesce to his advances to prevent her eviction.
brief_summary: Tenant Jennifer Hernandez sued her building manager and landlord under FHA § 3604(c) and 24 C.F.R. § 100.600(a) after the manager made repeated unwelcome sexual advances, conditioned her continued tenancy on submission to those advances, and ultimately caused her eviction. key_holding: The court granted the City's motion to compel because Oxford House failed to establish an attorney-client relationship between its general counsel and the landlords, and therefore the common-interest doctrine could not preserve privilege over communications between landlords and non-lawyer Oxford House employees.

case_name: Dana Bowman v. 1933 Argo Rd, LLC, et al.
key_holding: The court found that Bowman has standing to sue under the FHA because he personally visited the property, encountered accessibility barriers, and suffered concrete injury, distinguishing his situation from a mere 'tester' who never visited the property.
brief_summary: A disabled veteran who uses prosthetic legs and wheelchairs sued the owner, manager, and developer of an apartment complex under the Fair Housing Act, alleging that design and construction defects created accessibility barriers that he encountered during a property visit. The court recommended denying the defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that the plaintiff had standing to sue because he suffered a concrete injury by personally encountering the barriers.
accommodation_description: The case involves design and construction accessibility requirements for multifamily dwellings under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(C), including accessible routes, door widths, environmental controls, grab bar reinforcements, and usable kitchens and bathrooms. The plaintiff alleges the property lacks these mandatory accessibility elements.

fha_claims.accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges disability discrimination based on schizophrenia and sex discrimination under the Fair Housing Act
42 U.S.C. § 1983 civil rights claims, due process violations, state law claims, and allegations of fraudulent fees and harassment

case_name: Martino O'Bryant v. Nico Terrace, et al.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA and Civil Rights Act claims as frivolous under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e) because the factual allegations were 'clearly baseless,' 'fanciful,' 'fantastic,' and 'delusional,' and any legal theories were indisputably meritless.
brief_summary: Self-represented plaintiff Martino O'Bryant alleged his landlord orchestrated a campaign of harassment—including use of sound devices, orchestrating a shooting, sabotaging his car, and blocking his medical devices—to exacerbate his schizophrenia and force him to vacate his apartment, seeking $400 million in damages. The court dismissed all claims on initial § 1915(e) review as frivolous, finding the allegations delusional and lacking any arguable basis in law or fact.
accommodation_description: No discrete reasonable accommodation request is identifiable; plaintiff alleged disability (schizophrenia) and sex discrimination under the FHA in the context of a landlord harassment and wrongful eviction narrative, but did not articulate a specific accommodation that was requested and denied.
key_cases_cited: Neitzke v. Williams, 490 U.S. 319 (1989)
Denton v. Hernandez, 504 U.S. 25 (1992)

case_name: Ronald Satish Emrit v. Senator John Thune, et al.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's complaint with prejudice as frivolous because no law mandates individual members of Congress assist citizens in obtaining a Section 8 housing voucher, making members of Congress improper defendants under the FHA or ADA, and the complaint was also barred by the Speech or Debate Clause and improper venue.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Ronald Satish Emrit sued five members of Congress alleging, among other claims, that their failure to help him obtain a Section 8 housing voucher violated the Fair Housing Act and the Americans with Disabilities Act based on his bipolar/schizoaffective disorder diagnosis. The court dismissed the complaint with prejudice on § 1915 screening as frivolous, finding members of Congress are not proper defendants under the FHA or ADA, the Speech or Debate Clause immunized legislative conduct, venue was improper, and the suit was duplicative of identical complaints filed in other districts.

key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claims because she failed to allege facts plausibly suggesting that defendant's alleged interference, failure to respond to neighbor harassment, or actions related to her lease occurred because of her protected status, and failed to plausibly allege that harassment by her neighbor was because of her protected status or imputable to defendant.

case_name: Valerie Sayles v. Ashtabula Metropolitan Housing Authority
key_holding: AMHA did not violate the FHA because it granted a reasonable accommodation in January 2024 by withdrawing the eviction and giving plaintiff additional time to comply with housekeeping standards, and plaintiff's failure to bring the property into compliance during the accommodation period did not entitle her to a second indefinite extension; AMHA was also entitled to summary judgment on breach of contract, wrongful eviction, and constructive eviction claims.
brief_summary: Public housing tenant Valerie Sayles sued AMHA alleging it denied her reasonable accommodation requests for additional time to comply with housekeeping standards due to her mental health disabilities, and also asserted breach of contract and constructive eviction claims. The court granted AMHA's motion for summary judgment, finding that AMHA made a good-faith effort at accommodation by withdrawing the first eviction and granting additional time, and that plaintiff failed to show a further extension was reasonable or necessary given her repeated non-compliance over several years.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested (1) additional time to bring her unit into compliance with AMHA's housekeeping standards, (2) permission to sign a 'last chance' agreement with bi-weekly case manager meetings and a commitment to speak respectfully to staff, (3) at least 48-hour written notice before scheduled inspections, and (4) at the March 2024 hearing, an additional 90 days to achieve compliance — all requested as accommodations for her major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, somatic symptom disorder, and adjustment disorder.

case_name: Cynthia Bittenbender v. Family Services Association of Bucks County, et al.
subsidy_program: County-funded emergency medical housing administered by FSABC; Housing Choice Voucher (pending issuance)
key_holding: The court dismissed all FHA claims because Bittenbender failed to plausibly allege that Extended Stay America constituted a 'dwelling' under the FHA, that FSABC was a proper defendant under § 3604(f), or that her conditions substantially limited a major life activity, and dismissed her ADA claims because emotional support animals are explicitly excluded from ADA service-animal protections.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Cynthia Bittenbender was ejected from an Extended Stay America hotel room where she had been placed by a nonprofit social services agency (FSABC) for emergency medical housing, after a dispute over her emotional support animals including a bearded dragon. The court dismissed all federal claims at screening, holding that the hotel did not qualify as a 'dwelling' under the FHA, FSABC was not a proper FHA defendant as a housing-placement intermediary rather than a property owner, and emotional support animals are not cognizable as service animals under the ADA.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that defendants allow her to keep her emotional support animals—a cat and a bearded dragon—in her extended-stay hotel room as a reasonable accommodation for her disabilities (autism, ADHD, PTSD, COPD, and neuropathy), and alleged she was threatened with and ultimately subjected to removal from the hotel when she refused to surrender her bearded dragon.

brief_summary: Plaintiffs, operators of sober living homes for individuals in recovery from substance use disorders, challenged the City of Springfield's denial of their reasonable accommodation request to waive spacing requirements and treat their homes as the functional equivalent of a single family for zoning purposes.
